questions.question: Which hot drink, made from roasted beans, makes Colombia famous around the world?

questions.question: How much of Colombia's flag does the yellow stripe take up?
hints: The flag's three stripes are not all the same size.

questions.question: What are arepas traditionally made from?
hints: It's a yellow or white grain.

questions.question: What is Colombia's national bird?

questions.question: Which Colombian writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982?

questions.question: What is Colombia's national flower?

questions.question: What is the capital of France?

Its name comes from “fraile,” the Spanish word for a friar… a big one.
questions.description: A fuzzy plant that put on a sweater because the páramo is freezing.
questions.fun_fact: Frailejones grow very slowly, about one centimeter (less than half an inch) a year, so a tall one can be very, very old.

questions.question: Which national park near Santa Marta is home to the famous Cabo San Juan beach?
hints: It's on the Caribbean coast, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
Its name comes from an ancient Indigenous people of that region.
It sounds just like “Tairona”, the name of that Indigenous people.
questions.description: White sand, blue sea and a hammock: the perfect plan while your parents complain about the heat.
questions.fun_fact: Inside the park are the ruins of Pueblito, an old village built by the Tairona people.

questions.question: What is the largest national natural park in Colombia?
hints: It's deep in the Amazon rainforest.
It has flat-topped mountains called tepuis and thousands of rock paintings.
Its name starts with “Chiri…”.
questions.description: A park so big that if you play hide-and-seek there, nobody ever finds you.
questions.fun_fact: Chiribiquete was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018 and holds thousands of ancient paintings on its rocks, many of them of jaguars.

questions.question: He's a rat with an amazing sense of smell who dreams of being a chef in Paris, and he cooks hidden under a young man's hat. Which Pixar character is he?
hints: His movie is named after a French vegetable dish.
His hero is the chef Gusteau, who said “Anyone can cook!”.
His movie is “Ratatouille”, and his name starts with R.
questions.description: If you find one of these in a restaurant kitchen, you usually call pest control, not a food critic.
questions.fun_fact: Real ratatouille is a vegetable stew from the south of France, made with eggplant, zucchini, tomato and bell pepper.

questions.question: In a Pixar movie, what is the name of the robot left alone on Earth, squashing garbage into cubes?
hints: His only friend is a cockroach.
He falls in love with a shiny white robot who arrives from space.
His name is also the movie's title, and it sounds like a part of a house.
questions.description: He's been cleaning up other people's mess for centuries, like your mom with your bedroom, but without complaining.
questions.fun_fact: In the first minutes of “WALL·E” almost nobody speaks: the story is told with robot sounds and looks.

questions.question: He wears a green tunic and a pointed cap, carries a sword and shield, and travels the kingdom of Hyrule to save a princess. Who is he?
hints: He is the hero of a Nintendo adventure series.
Many people think he has the same name as the princess in the game's title.
His name is also the word for one ring in a chain.
questions.description: He has spent years saving a whole kingdom, and people still call him by the wrong name.
questions.fun_fact: Lots of people think the hero is called Zelda, but Zelda is the princess: the hero is Link.

questions.question: According to its creator, what food inspired Pac-Man's round shape with an open mouth?
questions.answer: A pizza with a slice missing
wrong_answers: A cookie with a bite missing
An orange with a segment missing
A cake with a slice missing
hints: It's a round food that people often share, cut into triangles.
It has melted cheese on top.
It comes from Italy and is a favorite for home delivery.
questions.description: A hungry friend's lunch inspired one of the most famous characters in video games.
questions.fun_fact: Pac-Man's Japanese creator, Toru Iwatani, said the idea came to him when he saw a pizza with one slice taken out.

questions.question: Look at the picture: what is this famous pirate flag called?
hints: Its name sounds like a nickname for a person.
The other options are nicknames for national flags or for flags on ordinary ships.
The first word of its name means “cheerful”.
questions.description: A flag that stands for no country, yet scares people more than all of them put together.
questions.fun_fact: Many pirates sailed under other countries' flags to get close without scaring anyone, and only raised the skull at the last moment.

questions.question: Which Colombian city built great stone walls to protect itself from pirate attacks?
hints: It’s on the Caribbean coast.
Today tourists walk on top of its walls to watch the sunset.
It’s nicknamed “La Heroica”, and its historic center is called the Walled City.
questions.description: A city so tired of unwanted visitors that it turned itself into one giant gated community.
questions.fun_fact: The English privateer Francis Drake captured Cartagena in 1586 and only left once he was paid a huge ransom.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this typical Colombian dish called?
hints: It’s so big that many people can’t finish it.
Its name refers to what it’s served on.
It’s the most famous dish of Antioquia and the Medellín region.
questions.description: A lunch so big that a nap afterwards is mandatory.
questions.fun_fact: Bandeja paisa has so many things on it that it doesn’t fit on a normal plate, which is why it’s served on a bandeja (platter).

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which Colombian food is it?
hints: It is fried in oil until it turns golden and crispy.
Inside, it almost always has potato and meat.
It is shaped like a half moon and eaten with ají, a spicy sauce.
questions.description: An envelope that brings no letters, just something much tastier inside.
questions.fun_fact: The word “empanada” comes from the Spanish “empanar”, which means to wrap something in dough or bread.

review.feedback: this doesn't belong in the base question bundle

questions.question: Which bird reaches the highest speed in the world when it dives?
hints: It's a hunting bird that catches other birds in midair.
It sets its record by folding its wings and dropping from very high up.
Its name means it wanders all over the world, like a pilgrim.
questions.description: This question is so fast that if you blink, you'll miss it.
questions.fun_fact: In a dive it can go faster than 300 km/h (186 mph), more than three times the speed of a car on the highway!

questions.question: How tall can an adult male giraffe be, from its feet to the top of its head?
hints: It's the tallest animal in the world, much taller than any person.
It could peek into a second-floor window.
It's about as tall as three grown-ups standing on top of each other.
questions.description: An animal that never has to ask anyone to reach the top shelf for it.
questions.fun_fact: Even though its neck is super long, a giraffe has only 7 bones in it, the same number as you!

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this lizard called, the largest in the world?
hints: It lives only on a few islands in Indonesia.
It can grow to about 3 meters (10 feet) long.
Its name is the same as a fire-breathing creature from fairy tales.
questions.description: If dragons were real, they would look something like this… and it turns out one is.
questions.fun_fact: Some female Komodo dragons in zoos have had babies without any male at all.

questions.question: What decides whether a sea turtle hatches male or female?
wrong_answers: The order the eggs were laid
hints: Mom turtle has nothing to do with it: she's already back in the sea when it's decided.
It has to do with where the eggs are buried.
When it's warmer, more females hatch.
questions.description: A very important decision, made without asking anyone in the family.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists remember it with a short saying: warm sand makes female turtles, cool sand makes male turtles.

questions.question: Look closely: which reptile does this eye belong to?
hints: The eye sits inside a kind of cone covered in scales.
Each eye can look in a different direction.
It's famous for changing color.
questions.description: This animal can look at you and your brother at the same time, and it's not your mom.
questions.fun_fact: A chameleon catches insects by shooting out its tongue, which can be longer than its own body.

questions.question: Which region of Colombia is currulao from, the rhythm played with marimba and drums?
hints: It's a region with lots of rain and lots of jungle.
There they play the chonta marimba and drums called cununos.
Cities like Buenaventura and Tumaco, beside the largest ocean in the world, are its home.
questions.description: A rhythm with a tongue-twister name that makes even the floorboards want to dance.
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO lists the marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia's southern Pacific as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: The word “robot” was made up in 1920 from a Czech word. What did that Czech word mean?
hints: It first appeared in a stage play.
It has to do with what people expected robots to do for them.
It's the opposite of a vacation: being made to work.
questions.description: If your robot could complain, this question would explain why.
questions.fun_fact: Czech writer Karel Čapek used the word first, but he said the idea came from his brother Josef.

questions.question: Unimate, the first industrial robot, worked in a car factory. What shape was it?
hints: It didn't walk: it stayed fixed in one spot.
Its job was to grab and move very hot pieces of metal.
It had an elbow, a wrist and a kind of hand or gripper.
questions.description: Before robots danced on the internet, there was one that could do only one thing, with endless patience.
questions.fun_fact: Today, thousands of arm-shaped robots work in car factories, welding and painting.

questions.question: What is pumice made of, the stone so light that it floats on water?
hints: It is born when a volcano erupts.
It is full of tiny holes where there used to be gas.
It is melted rock that cooled so fast it trapped the bubbles inside.
questions.description: A stone that never got the memo that stones are supposed to sink.
questions.fun_fact: After some eruptions at sea, giant “rafts” of pumice form and drift across the ocean for months.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this giant fish from the rivers of the Amazon called?
hints: It is one of the biggest freshwater fish in the world: it can grow over 2 m (6.5 ft) long.
It has to come up to the surface to breathe air, like a swimmer.
In Brazil it is called pirarucu, which means “red fish”, after its reddish tail.
questions.description: A fish so big that the frying pan fits inside it, not the other way around.
questions.fun_fact: The arapaima's tongue is so hard and bony that people in the Amazon have used it as a grater.

questions.question: Listen: which Amazon rainforest animal makes this sound?
hints: It lives high up in the trees, not on the ground.
It hangs from branches by its tail and often “sings” in a group at dawn.
Its name describes exactly what it is doing in the recording.
questions.description: The jungle's alarm clock has no snooze button.
questions.fun_fact: The howler monkey is one of the loudest land animals: its howls can be heard several kilometers (a few miles) away.

questions.question: In “Dragon Ball”, how many Dragon Balls must you gather to call the dragon Shenron and make a wish?
hints: It's an odd number.
It's more than the fingers on one hand.
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.description: Collecting them all is harder than filling a World Cup sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: Goku is based on Sun Wukong, the Monkey King from an old Chinese novel called “Journey to the West”.

questions.question: What are the Japanese comics that many anime are based on called?
hints: It's a Japanese word.
They are almost always printed in black and white.
“One Piece” and “Naruto” are famous examples.
questions.description: Books full of drawings that you read backwards, and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, manga are read from right to left, starting from what would be the last page of a Western book.

questions.question: What kind of tree is the tallest in the world?
hints: It grows in forests near the coast of California, in the United States.
The tallest one is taller than a 30-story building.
Its name tells you the color of its bark and wood.
questions.description: A question you'll need to tilt your head way, way back for.
questions.fun_fact: The tallest known redwood is called Hyperion, it is about 116 m (381 ft) tall, and its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: what is it?
hints: It grows on a tree, not in a vegetable garden.
Inside, it keeps seeds between its woody scales.
It comes from a tree that many people use as a real Christmas tree.
questions.description: It looks like a suit of armor made of scales, but nobody's inside.
questions.fun_fact: Pine cones open when the air is dry and close when it's damp, as if they could check the weather forecast.

questions.question: What were the names of the brothers who made the first flight in a powered airplane, in 1903?
hints: They were American, and their first names were Orville and Wilbur.
Before building airplanes, they had a shop where they fixed and sold bicycles.
Their last name sounds just like a word that means “correct”.
questions.description: Two brothers who, instead of fighting over the TV remote, started inventing things that fly.
questions.fun_fact: The Wright brothers’ first flight lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 m (120 ft), shorter than a modern passenger jet!

questions.question: What is the largest passenger airplane in the world?
hints: It is built by a European company.
It has two full decks of passengers, from nose to tail.
Its name starts with “Airbus” and its number ends in 80.
questions.description: A plane so big that if it were a bus, it wouldn't fit on any street in your neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: The Airbus A380 is allowed to carry up to 853 passengers, which is more people than many schools have!

questions.question: In the NBA, a game is split into four quarters. How many minutes long is each quarter?
hints: It's longer than a quarter at the Olympics.
All four quarters together add up to almost an hour: 48 minutes.
It's the same number as the months in a year.
questions.description: The basketball clock is so stingy it stops every few seconds so it never gives away a single one.
questions.fun_fact: Because the clock stops for every foul and every time the ball goes out, an NBA game can really last more than two hours.

questions.question: In basketball, what do you call the play where a player jumps and pushes the ball down through the hoop from above?
hints: There are whole contests just for this play, full of amazing jumps.
Sometimes the player hangs from the rim for a moment afterward.
It's also what you do when you dip a cookie into a glass of milk.
questions.description: A play that leaves the hoop shaking and the other team looking up.
questions.fun_fact: Some dunks have been so hard that they shattered the glass backboard in the middle of a game.

questions.question: Look at this badge: which car brand is it?
hints: It's a brand of very red, very fast sports cars.
It comes from Italy and races in Formula 1.
Its founder was named Enzo, and its badge has a little black horse on it.
questions.description: A horse that has never eaten grass but runs at more than 300 km/h (186 mph).
questions.fun_fact: The little horse was painted on the plane of an Italian pilot, and the pilot's mother suggested Enzo Ferrari use it for good luck.

questions.question: Which country does the sports car brand Lamborghini come from?
hints: It's a country in Europe.
Pizza was invented there too.
The country is shaped like a boot.
questions.description: A car so low that you almost have to lie down to get in.
questions.fun_fact: Before he made sports cars, Ferruccio Lamborghini built tractors for farms.

questions.question: Which brand made the famous Model T, one of the first cars built on a factory assembly line?
hints: It's an American brand.
It was made more than 100 years ago, in a factory where each worker built just one part of the car.
Its founder's first name was Henry, and the brand carries his last name.
questions.description: The grandfather of every car honking on your street today.
questions.fun_fact: More than 15 million Model T cars were built between 1908 and 1927.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this famous castle?
hints: It sits high on a mountain in Europe, surrounded by forests.
A king of Bavaria, in Germany, who loved fairy tales and operas had it built.
Its long German name talks about a “new swan stone”, and it inspired Disney.
questions.description: A castle so fairy-tale that it looks like someone drew it before they built it.
questions.fun_fact: King Ludwig II never saw his castle finished, and many of its rooms are still unfinished today.

questions.question: What are the tooth-shaped stone blocks along the top of a castle wall called?
hints: You see them in almost every drawing of a castle, along the tops of the towers.
The gaps between the blocks were used for shooting arrows.
Their name starts with a word for a big fight between two armies.
questions.description: Castles had smiles too, but their teeth were always ready for a fight.
questions.fun_fact: Many modern buildings have battlements just for decoration, even though nobody hides behind them from arrows anymore.

questions.question: The black sheet wrapped around many sushi rolls is called nori. What is it made of?
hints: It comes from a place full of water.
Before it was dried, it grew stuck to rocks.
If you see it at the beach, it sways with the waves.
questions.description: It looks like black paper and crunches like paper, but don't even think about writing on it.
questions.fun_fact: Nori sheets are made almost like paper: the seaweed is chopped, spread in thin layers and left to dry.

questions.question: Tempura came to Japan about 450 years ago from a European country. Which one?
hints: It is a country on the Iberian Peninsula.
It is the same country that colonized Brazil.
Its capital is Lisbon.
questions.description: A dish so Japanese that, surprise, it came over on a ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: The word “tempura” is thought to come from the Latin “tempora”, the fasting days when the Portuguese ate no meat and fried fish and vegetables instead.

questions.question: In the photo, pork turns on a vertical spit with a pineapple on top. What are these tacos called?
hints: Immigrants from Lebanon brought the idea of cooking meat on a turning spit to Mexico.
The taco maker slices thin pieces of meat and of the pineapple on top, straight onto the tortilla.
In Spanish, its name means “shepherd style”.
questions.description: It spins like a top, but nobody's playing with it: it's just spinning to make you hungry.
questions.fun_fact: Tacos al pastor grew out of the shawarma that Lebanese immigrants brought to Mexico, but made with pork instead of lamb.

questions.question: Roughly how much blood is in an adult's body?
hints: It's a lot less than a big bucket holds.
When someone gives blood, they take about half a liter, and the person is fine.
It's about as much as two and a half big soda bottles hold.
questions.description: If you squeezed a person like an orange, how much red juice would come out? Better not find out.
questions.fun_fact: If you laid all of an adult's blood vessels end to end, they would wrap around the Earth more than twice.

questions.question: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
hints: It's in Africa.
It covers a large part of the north of that continent.
Its name comes from an Arabic word that simply means “desert.”
questions.description: A sandbox so big that all the cats in the world couldn't fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The Sahara is almost as big as the whole United States, and if you count cold deserts too, the largest desert of all is Antarctica.

questions.question: The Taroa dunes, where desert sand falls straight into the Caribbean Sea, are in which department of Colombia?
hints: It's on the Caribbean coast.
Punta Gallinas, the northernmost point of South America, is nearby.
It's the land of the Wayuu people and their woven mochila bags.
questions.description: A place where the sand gets to the beach without paying the bus fare.
questions.fun_fact: Punta Gallinas, near the Taroa dunes, is the northernmost point of all of South America.

questions.question: What happens to a camel's hump when it goes many days without eating?
questions.answer: It shrinks and flops over to one side
wrong_answers: It swells up and gets harder
It fills with water to store it
It changes color and turns white
hints: The hump doesn't store water, even though many people think so.
Inside, it's full of fat, which the camel uses as an energy reserve.
If the camel uses up that reserve, the hump ends up almost empty.
questions.description: The only animal that carries its lunchbox stuck to its back.
questions.fun_fact: A very thirsty camel can drink about 100 liters (26 gallons) of water in just about 10 minutes.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this Colombian street treat called?
hints: It's made of two round, thin, crispy wafers.
The middle is almost always filled with arequipe, sometimes with cheese or jam too.
Its name starts with the letter O.
questions.description: Two wafers so thin they need sweet glue to keep from flying away.
questions.fun_fact: Floridablanca, in Santander, is famous all over Colombia for its obleas.

questions.question: What fruit is bocadillo veleño made from?
hints: It is a round fruit with lots of hard little seeds inside.
Inside it can be pink or red, and it is also used to make juice.
Its name starts with “gua”.
questions.description: It comes wrapped in a leaf like a present, and inside is a fruit dressed up as a tiny brick.
questions.fun_fact: Bocadillo veleño is wrapped in bijao leaves, from a plant that helps it keep longer.

questions.question: Which Colombian department is famous for manjar blanco served in a mate (totuma)?
hints: It's a department with a coastline on the Pacific Ocean.
Huge fields of sugarcane grow there.
Its capital is Cali, the capital of salsa.
questions.description: A sweet so sticky the spoon stands up on its own, as if waiting its turn.
questions.fun_fact: Manjar blanco is made by stirring milk, sugar and rice for hours in a copper paila.

questions.question: What do Colombians call the sweet that Argentinians call “dulce de leche”?
hints: It's made by cooking milk with sugar for a long time.
It's light brown, creamy and sticky.
It's what goes inside the famous “brevas con …”.
questions.description: Argentina and Colombia fight over soccer, but they share this sweet under another name.
questions.fun_fact: The name “arequipe” is thought to come from Arequipa, a city in Peru.

questions.question: What did the ancient Egyptians do to a pharaoh's body after death, to preserve it for thousands of years?
hints: They used salts, oils and resins to dry it out.
At the end, they wrapped it in lots and lots of cloth bandages.
In horror movies, this bandaged body climbs out of its stone coffin.
questions.description: Pharaohs wanted to look good for thousands of years, and anti-wrinkle cream hadn't been invented yet.
questions.fun_fact: Preparing a pharaoh's body could take about 70 days.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this ring of light that sometimes appears around the Sun called?
hints: It shows up on days with very high, thin clouds.
It is made by millions of tiny ice crystals that bend the sunlight.
It has the same name as the ring drawn above angels' heads.
questions.description: Looks like the Sun put on a giant hoop to go out partying.
questions.fun_fact: The ice crystals that make a halo have six sides, like a tiny pencil, which is why the ring is almost always the same size.

questions.question: In which Colombian city is the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos held?
hints: It takes place in early January, right after New Year's.
The city is in the south of the country, not far from Ecuador.
It is the capital of Nariño, at the foot of the Galeras volcano.
questions.description: A party where ending up covered in talcum powder and paint means you had a great time.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, UNESCO named the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos a Masterpiece of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: In a right triangle, what is the longest side called, the one opposite the right angle?
hints: The other two sides, the ones that form the right angle, have a different name.
It appears in the famous Pythagorean theorem.
Its long name starts with a sound like “hippo”.
questions.description: The longest side in the family, and it loves to show off about it.
questions.fun_fact: By the Pythagorean theorem, if a right triangle has legs of 3 and 4 centimeters, its hypotenuse is exactly 5.

questions.question: A cube, like a die, has 6 faces. How many edges (the lines where two faces meet) does it have?
hints: There are more of them than the cube has faces.
Think of a square on top, another on the bottom and the edges that join them.
4 edges on top, 4 on the bottom and 4 standing up.
questions.description: A question with lots of corners and edges, like the brick that just landed on your foot.
questions.fun_fact: Add a cube's faces and corners (6 + 8), subtract its edges (12), and you get 2, and that works for every solid with flat faces and no holes!

questions.question: The cells of a honeycomb, most nuts for bolts and many pencils seen from the end: what shape do they share?
hints: It is a shape with all its sides equal.
It has one side more than a pentagon.
It has as many sides as an insect has legs.
questions.description: Bees are engineers, and they never even went to college.
questions.fun_fact: Hexagons fit together with no gaps, so bees can store lots of honey using very little wax.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what breed is this cat?
hints: Its skin feels soft and warm, like a peach.
Its name sounds Egyptian, but the breed started in Canada.
It's named after the giant statue with a lion's body that sits next to the pyramids.
questions.description: A cat that left the house and forgot to put on its coat.
questions.fun_fact: The Sphynx breed started in Canada in the 1960s, with a kitten that just happened to be born without fur.

questions.question: What does a cat use its whiskers for?
questions.answer: To sense the space and tell if it fits through a gap
wrong_answers: To wipe its face clean after eating
To smell food from very far away
To keep its nose warm in winter
hints: Whiskers are connected to lots and lots of nerves, almost like fingers.
They help it move around in the dark without bumping into things.
Before squeezing into a box or a narrow gap, the cat “measures” with them.
questions.description: A cat doesn't wear them to look fancy, even though it looks fancy anyway.
questions.fun_fact: A cat's whiskers are so sensitive that they can feel tiny changes in the air around it.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this ancient board game called?
hints: It is one of the oldest board games in the world, and it is very popular in Africa.
You play it by moving seeds or small stones from hole to hole, with no dice.
Its name comes from an Arabic word that means “to move,” and it starts with “Man...”.
questions.description: A game where sowing seeds has nothing to do with gardening.
questions.fun_fact: Mancala boards carved into stone have been found that are more than a thousand years old.

questions.question: In chess, which piece moves in an “L” shape and can jump over other pieces?
hints: It's the only piece that can jump over others.
On the board, it's shaped like an animal's head.
It's the animal that neighs.
questions.description: One piece can't walk in a straight line, and it jumps over everyone too.
questions.fun_fact: A chess knight can visit all 64 squares of the board without landing on any square twice, a puzzle called the “knight's tour”.

questions.question: In the story of Pinocchio, what happens to him every time he tells a lie?
hints: It happens on his face.
You can see it from far away, and it gets longer.
It's the part of the body we smell with.
questions.description: A wooden puppet with a lie detector built right into his face.
questions.fun_fact: Pinocchio was written by the Italian author Carlo Collodi and first came out in chapters in a children's newspaper in 1881.

questions.question: If you add up all the dots on all the faces of a standard die, how many dots are there in total?
hints: The faces of a die have 1 to 6 dots.
The total is between 20 and 22, and it's odd.
questions.description: A little cube that decides your fate in board games, yet nobody has ever counted it all.
questions.fun_fact: On a standard die, opposite faces always add up to 7: 1 is opposite 6, 2 is opposite 5, and 3 is opposite 4.

questions.question: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the giant tree that connects the nine worlds?
hints: It is an ash tree so big that its branches reach the sky.
An eagle lives at its top, and a dragon gnaws at its roots.
Its name starts with “Y” and has two “g”s in a row.
questions.description: The Vikings had no GPS, so they connected the whole universe with gardening.
questions.fun_fact: According to the myth, a squirrel called Ratatoskr runs up and down the tree carrying gossip and insults between the eagle at the top and the dragon at the bottom.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the Americas?
hints: It is in the Andes mountains.
It is in Argentina, close to the border with Chile.
Its name starts with “Acon…” and it is almost 7,000 m (23,000 ft) high.
questions.description: From Alaska down to the tip of Chile, only one peak gets to wear the crown.
questions.fun_fact: Aconcagua is the highest, but the top of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth farthest from the planet's center, because Earth bulges out a little at the equator.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this plant that decorates so many homes in December?
hints: It comes from Mexico, where the Aztecs already knew it.
The red parts you see aren't petals: they're leaves that change color.
Its English name honors Joel Poinsett, a US diplomat who brought it home from Mexico in the 1820s.
questions.description: This plant dresses up in red every December, as if it were off to a New Year's party.
questions.fun_fact: The real flowers of a poinsettia are the little yellow buds in the center; the red parts are leaves called bracts.

questions.question: Which country does the custom of decorating a tree at home for Christmas come from?
hints: It's a European country with cold winters and lots of pine trees.
It's famous for its Christmas markets and for brands like Volkswagen.
Its capital is Berlin.
questions.description: Bringing a tree into the living room and covering it in shiny balls: someone had to think of it first.
questions.fun_fact: The custom became famous in England around 1840 thanks to Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's German husband.

questions.question: Complete the chorus of the gozos of the novena: “Dulce Jesús mío, mi niño adorado, ¡ven a nuestras almas! ¡Ven, no tardes…!”
hints: It's sung between each verse of the gozos, nine nights in a row.
It's a word about how much, not about when.
In English, the line asks the Child Jesus: “Come, don't take so long!”
questions.description: The part of the novena everyone sings at the top of their lungs, with or without a tambourine.
questions.fun_fact: The gozos of the novena were written by a nun from Bogotá, Mother María Ignacia, in the late 19th century.

questions.question: In Colombia, when someone says a person is very “lagarta,” what do they mean?
questions.answer: They flatter others to get favors
wrong_answers: They are very lazy and sleep all day
They always show up late everywhere
They talk so much nobody else gets a word in
hints: It has nothing to do with skin or the color green.
It's the kid who brings the teacher an apple right before report cards.
It's almost the same as being “lambón.”
questions.description: A reptile that in Colombia doesn't live in the wild, but in offices and classrooms.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia even has the verb “lagartear”: going around paying compliments to land a job or a favor.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do you call the little extra a seller gives you for free when you buy something?
hints: It happens a lot at the market, when you buy fruit.
It's free, a gift for buying.
The word has a letter that doesn't exist in English.
questions.description: The best part of going to the corner store: when the man gives you something without charging.
questions.fun_fact: “Ñapa” comes from “yapa,” a word from Quechua, the language of the Incas, meaning “to add.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this called in Colombia?
hints: It's the classic snack for watching a movie at the theater.
It's made from corn that pops in a hot pot.
Its name sounds like something crisp and crunchy.
questions.description: The only food that explodes before you even eat it.
questions.fun_fact: Every kernel of popcorn corn (maíz pira) holds a tiny bit of water: when heated it turns to steam and, pop, the kernel bursts.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what breed is this very wrinkly dog?
hints: It is a very old breed from China.
Its tongue is usually dark blue, almost purple.
Its name has two short parts, and the first one starts with “Sh”.
questions.description: A dog born with skin two sizes too big.
questions.fun_fact: The Shar Pei has a dark blue tongue, just like the Chow Chow.

questions.question: The Bronze Age is named after bronze, which is made by mixing copper with another metal. Which one?
hints: It's not a precious metal: nobody made expensive jewelry from it.
It can't be iron, because iron got its own age later.
It's a soft, gray metal used to solder electronic wires.
questions.description: The secret recipe of prehistory: take one metal, add another, and name a whole era after it.
questions.fun_fact: The Iron Age came next, because working iron needed much hotter furnaces than bronze did.

questions.question: In Colombia, what color is the caneca (bin) for recyclables, like clean plastic and paper?
hints: It's the bin for things that can be used again or recycled.
The green one is for food scraps, and the black one is for things nobody can use anymore.
It's the same color as a new sheet of paper.
questions.description: Even taking out the trash has a dress code, and you have to guess the color of the uniform.
questions.fun_fact: Recicladores de oficio (informal waste pickers) collect much of what gets recycled in Colombia, and for years the law has recognized them as part of the public cleaning service.

questions.question: What is the fertilizer called that you make by letting peels, dry leaves and food scraps break down?
hints: You can make it at home, in a box or a hole in the yard.
Worms and fungi help make it.
Its name sounds a lot like the word “compose”.
questions.description: Banana peels dream of a second life in the garden too.
questions.fun_fact: About half of a home's trash can be food scraps and other organic waste that could be turned into fertilizer.

questions.question: Which anime character is this? He ate a strange fruit, and ever since, his body stretches like rubber.
hints: He sails the sea with his crew, searching for a legendary treasure.
He always wears a straw hat and dreams of becoming King of the Pirates.
His anime is called “One Piece.”
questions.description: A boy who never needs to stretch before exercise, because he is the stretch.
questions.fun_fact: “One Piece” is the best-selling manga in history, with more than 500 million copies sold around the world.

questions.question: What does the Japanese word “kawaii” mean?
hints: It became famous around the world thanks to Japanese fashion and cartoons.
It's what people say when they see a baby kitten.
Hello Kitty is the perfect example of this word.
questions.description: Japan sent us cars, video games and words that stick like chewing gum.
questions.fun_fact: Hello Kitty is drawn without a mouth, and she is still one of the most famous characters in the world.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this palm called?
hints: It grows in the cold mountains of the Andes, not on the beach.
It is Colombia’s national tree.
Its trunk is covered in a substance that people once used to make candles.
questions.description: It’s so tall and skinny it seems to have forgotten to stop growing.
questions.fun_fact: The wax palm can grow taller than 50 m (164 ft), making it the tallest palm in the world.

questions.question: When basketball was invented in 1891, what was hung on the gym walls for players to throw the ball into?
hints: They were containers used on farms and at markets.
They were used to carry fruit.
That fruit is round, fuzzy on the outside, and has a big pit inside.
questions.description: Before modern hoops, basketball had to make do with whatever was lying around in the storeroom.
questions.fun_fact: The first baskets still had their bottoms, so every time someone scored, the ball had to be fetched out with a ladder or a stick.

Because Peach baskets is now the only fruit container among the options, hint 2 ("They were used to carry fruit") gives the answer away. Make one wrong answer another fruit container, e.g. "Apple baskets", or keep the source's "Apple crates". Alternatively, rewrite hint 2 so it doesn't single out fruit.

questions.question: In which country was basketball invented, in 1891?
hints: People there speak English.
The city where it was invented is called Springfield, just like the town in The Simpsons.
Its flag has 50 stars.
questions.description: A teacher needed a game to keep his students from getting bored in winter, and he ended up with a sport the whole world plays.
questions.fun_fact: Basketball's inventor, James Naismith, was Canadian, but he came up with the game while working at a school in the United States.

questions.question: Listen: what is making this sound?
hints: You hear it on the street almost every day.
You make it by pressing a button on the steering wheel.
Drivers use it to warn: “Watch out, here I come!”
questions.description: A sound that yells “Move it!” without saying a single word.
questions.fun_fact: The first cars had no electric horn: they had a rubber bulb horn that the driver squeezed by hand.

questions.question: Which Colombian soccer club plays in green and white and has its home games at the Atanasio Girardot stadium?
hints: Its big rival shares the same stadium but plays in red and blue.
Its name sounds like it belongs to the whole country, not one city.
Its fans are called “verdolagas”.
questions.description: A team so green that if it stands still on the field, people mistake it for the grass.
questions.fun_fact: In 1989 Atlético Nacional became the first Colombian club to win the Copa Libertadores, and it won it again in 2016.

questions.question: Mole poblano, a thick, dark sauce from Mexico, has chilies, spices and one ingredient that surprises many people. Which one?
hints: The Aztecs had this ingredient too, but bitter and as a drink.
It comes from seeds that grow in a pod on a tropical tree.
Easter eggs and many candy bars are made from it.
questions.description: A sauce so fancy it has more ingredients than your monthly shopping list.
questions.fun_fact: Mole poblano can have more than 20 ingredients, and it is often served over chicken or turkey.

questions.question: What is it called when your body jumps by itself again and again, and people say a scare or a drink of water makes it stop?
hints: Sometimes it starts after eating too fast or laughing a lot.
It comes in little jumps, one after another.
Its name sounds almost like the noise it makes.
questions.description: A little noise that shows up uninvited and won't leave no matter how nicely you ask.
questions.fun_fact: An American man named Charles Osborne had the hiccups for about 68 years in a row.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this Colombian desert of reddish earth and dry canyons?
hints: It's in the south of the country, near the Magdalena River.
It's famous for its night sky: lots of people go there to stargaze.
It's in Huila, near Villavieja, and its name starts with “Ta”.
questions.description: A desert that sneaked into Colombia without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it's called a desert, the Tatacoa is actually a tropical dry forest.

questions.question: What is the writing system of the ancient Egyptians called?
hints: They carved it into temples and tombs, and also painted it on papyrus.
For centuries nobody could read it, until the Rosetta Stone was found.
When someone's handwriting is impossible to read, people say it looks like… this.
questions.description: Long before emojis, the Egyptians were already sending messages full of little faces, birds and eyes.
questions.fun_fact: In 1822, the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion cracked the code of hieroglyphs with the help of the Rosetta Stone.

questions.question: In “Alice in Wonderland”, which cat slowly disappears until only its grin is left?
hints: It gives Alice very strange advice when she is lost in the woods.
Its name comes from a region of England.
Its name starts with “Che…”.
questions.description: A cat that leaves the room but forgets to take its smile along.
questions.fun_fact: In England, people said “grinning like a Cheshire cat” even before Lewis Carroll wrote the book.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which Winter Olympic sport are they playing?
hints: This sport was born in Scotland centuries ago.
Players slide a heavy stone across the ice toward a target made of circles.
Teammates scrub the ice with brooms in front of the stone to guide it.
questions.description: A sport so calm your grandpa could play it in his slippers, and they still hand out Olympic medals for it.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all Olympic curling stones are made of granite from one small Scottish island called Ailsa Craig.

questions.question: Which Winter Olympic sport combines cross-country skiing with shooting at targets with a rifle?
hints: Its name tells you how many events are joined into one.
The athletes ski with the rifle on their back and stop to shoot.
Its name starts the same way as “bicycle”, because it joins two events.
questions.description: For when your gym teacher and the shooting club coach finally agree on something.
questions.fun_fact: If an athlete misses a shot, they usually have to ski a 150 m (about 490 ft) penalty loop before going on with the race.

questions.question: Which character is this? He lives alone on a tiny asteroid and travels to other planets, where he meets a king, a vain man and a drunkard.
hints: On his planet he looks after a very proud rose.
On Earth he meets a pilot stranded in the Sahara Desert.
His title says he's a king's son, only a small one.
questions.description: The only resident of a planet so small you can sweep it in one morning.
questions.fun_fact: His author, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, really did crash his plane in the Sahara Desert in 1935.

questions.question: “Second star to the right, and straight on till morning” is the way to Neverland. Who says it?
hints: It's someone who can fly without a plane.
At the start of the story, he comes in through the window of Wendy's house in London, looking for his shadow.
He's the boy who never wanted to grow up.
questions.description: Directions so vague that no GPS would ever accept them.
questions.fun_fact: The writer J. M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to a children's hospital in London, which still receives money from them.

questions.question: At a store, you buy 3 empanadas at 2,500 pesos each and a soft drink for 3,000 pesos. You pay with a 20,000-peso bill. How much change do you get?
hints: First work out how much the three empanadas cost.
The three empanadas cost 7,500 pesos; now add the drink.
You spend 10,500 pesos in total: subtract that from 20,000.
questions.description: A question to find out if you can afford your snack or need to borrow money from your brother.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's old 20,000-peso bill showed Julio Garavito, an astronomer from Bogotá who has a crater on the Moon named after him.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this famous mountain?
hints: It stands on the border between Switzerland and Italy.
Its shape, like a crooked pyramid, makes it one of the most photographed mountains in the world.
For years it was drawn on the box of a famous Swiss chocolate made of triangles.
questions.description: A mountain so pointy it looks like a first grader drew it.
questions.fun_fact: The Matterhorn, called Cervino in Italian, was on the Toblerone chocolate logo until 2023, and that logo had a bear hidden in it!

questions.question: How many mountains in the world are taller than 8,000 m (26,247 ft)?
hints: There are so few that mountain climbers know the list by heart.
All of them are in Asia, in the Himalayas and the Karakoram.
There are more than 10 but fewer than 20.
questions.description: A club so exclusive that you need your head above the clouds to get in.
questions.fun_fact: These peaks are called “eight-thousanders,” and the first climber to reach the top of all 14 was Reinhold Messner from Italy, in 1986.

questions.question: On which continent is Mount Kilimanjaro?
hints: It sits very close to the equator.
It is the highest mountain on its continent, and lots of wild animals live around it.
It's the continent of safaris and “The Lion King”.
questions.description: A mountain so tall you need a jacket at the top, even when it's boiling hot at the bottom.
questions.fun_fact: Kilimanjaro is a sleeping volcano, and you can walk all the way up without ropes or climbing gear.

questions.question: What day does the Novena de Aguinaldos start?
hints: It starts a few days after the Día de las Velitas.
It ends on December 24, Christmas Eve.
Count nine days back from Christmas Eve, counting Christmas Eve itself.
questions.description: A party so good it won't fit in one night, so you have to repeat it with natilla and buñuelos.
questions.fun_fact: The Novena de Aguinaldos was written by a friar about 240 years ago, and it's prayed mostly in Colombia and Ecuador.

questions.question: What is the smallest dog breed in the world?
hints: Its name comes from a place, not a person.
It has huge ears for its tiny head and often shivers a lot.
It comes from Mexico and shares its name with a state in the north of that country.
questions.description: A tiny dog that still thinks it's the boss of the house.
questions.fun_fact: Miracle Milly, named the world's smallest dog by Guinness World Records, was a Chihuahua less than 10 cm (4 in) tall.

questions.question: What do you call a group of dogs that roam or hunt together?
hints: The same word is used for a group of wolves.
It was often used for the dogs that went hunting with their owners.
It rhymes with “snack” and “track”.
questions.description: For when one dog alone isn't enough to make a real mess.
questions.fun_fact: African wild dogs hunt as a group and then bring food back to the puppies that stayed at the den.

questions.question: Look at this museum skeleton: which prehistoric animal is it?
hints: It lived during the Ice Age, and early humans hunted it.
Look at those huge, curved tusks.
Manny from the movie “Ice Age” is one of them.
questions.description: This museum gentleman doesn't have an ounce of meat left, but he still poses for photos.
questions.fun_fact: The last mammoths lived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt had already been built.

questions.question: Many modern soccer jerseys are made from thread spun out of recycled trash. What trash is recycled to make that fabric?
hints: Almost every home throws this kind of trash out every week.
They are shredded, melted and stretched into thin threads.
Before becoming a jersey, it may have held water or juice.
questions.description: Your favorite jersey may have a secret past it would rather not talk about.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2010 World Cup, several national teams played in jerseys made from up to eight recycled plastic bottles each.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this waterfall, the tallest in the world?
hints: It is in South America, in a land of jungles and grasslands.
It drops from a flat-topped mountain called a tepui, in southeastern Venezuela.
It inspired Paradise Falls in the film “Up”, and its name is a heavenly being with wings.
questions.description: A shower so tall that the water turns to mist before it reaches the floor.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the pilot Jimmie Angel, who landed his small plane on top of the tepui in 1937, and the plane got stuck up there.

questions.question: What happens to anyone caught in Wonder Woman's golden lasso?
hints: The lasso doesn't hurt anyone.
It's very handy for questioning villains.
Nobody caught in that lasso can tell a lie.
questions.description: No cape, no laser eyes: this hero's favorite weapon is a rope that glows.
questions.fun_fact: Wonder Woman's creator, William Moulton Marston, worked on one of the first tests for finding out whether someone was lying.

questions.question: The Flash, Aquaman and Cyborg: what do they have in common?
hints: All three fight together in a famous superhero team.
Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman are on that team too.
The team's name sounds like a group that stands up for what is fair.
questions.description: One runs, one swims and one is half robot: the strangest group chat in the universe.
questions.fun_fact: A movie about this team came out in 2017, and in 2021 the same director released another version that ran about 4 hours!

questions.question: He's a millionaire with no superpowers, goes out at night to watch over his city and has a secret hideout in a cave. Which superhero is he?

questions.question: What planet does Superman come from?
hints: It's a made-up planet that exploded when Superman was a baby.

questions.description: An alien who works at a newspaper, and nobody recognizes him because he puts on glasses.
questions.fun_fact: There is a real gas called krypton, discovered in 1898; its name comes from a Greek word meaning “hidden.”

questions.question: In which city did the world's first underground railway open?
hints: It opened in 1863, before there were any cars.
It is a European capital.
People there call their metro “the Tube”.
questions.description: A city that got tired of traffic and decided to go underground.
questions.fun_fact: The first trains on the London Underground ran on steam, and they puffed smoke right inside the tunnels!

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this piece of a knight's armor called?
hints: It protected the knight's most important part: the one that does the thinking.

It's a short word that starts with H.
questions.description: Medieval safety gear from the year 1200: no plastic, no padding to speak of, and a terrible view.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer (Helm) and the wrong answers (Breastplate, Gauntlet, Greave) are right. The hints are fine: the helm protects the head, it has narrow eye slits, and "Helm" is four letters starting with H. The fun fact is shaky. The sources I found put great helms at about 1.5–3 kg, with a 1375 Pembridge-type helm at 2.4–2.6 kg. They don't support 3–4 kg (7–9 lb) as typical. Only a different helm type, a c. 1460 kettle hat, weighed more (5.66 kg).

Fact check: wrong. The answer (Helm) and the wrong answers (breastplate, gauntlet, greave) are right, and the hints are fine. The fun fact overstates the weight. Surviving 13th-century great helms weigh about 1.5–3 kg: examples are 2.26 kg, 2.7 kg and a Templar-style helm at 3.0 kg. 4 kg (9 lb) is above that range.

questions.question: What was the name for the young man who helped a knight with his weapons and his horse?
hints: He was like an apprentice: if he did well, one day he could become a knight himself.

questions.question: What is the name of King Arthur's legendary sword?
hints: According to the legend, a mysterious lady who lived in a lake gave it to him.

Its name starts with “Ex” and ends with “bur”.

questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the legend, the sword Arthur pulled from the stone and Excalibur are two different swords: Excalibur was a gift from the Lady of the Lake.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this kind of weather called?
hints: It spins super fast, like a giant spinning top.
It is shaped like a funnel that reaches down from a cloud to the ground.
In “The Wizard of Oz”, one of these lifts Dorothy's house and carries it away.
questions.description: The wind tried spinning like a top and got a little carried away.
questions.fun_fact: The United States gets more tornadoes than any other country in the world: more than 1,000 every year.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this Italian dish called?
hints: It is baked in a rectangular dish and served in square pieces.
It has layer after layer of flat pasta, ground meat, tomato sauce and cheese.
It is the favorite food of Garfield the cat.
questions.description: The dish an Italian grandma makes when she wants nobody to leave the table for three hours.
questions.fun_fact: In Bologna, traditional lasagna is made with green pasta sheets, colored with spinach.

questions.question: Which Italian coffee dessert has a name that means “pick me up” or “cheer me up”?
hints: It is served cold, with cocoa powder dusted on top.
It is built in layers in a dish, using long sponge cookies called ladyfingers.
Its name starts with “tira”...
questions.description: A dessert with caffeine: finally, something parents and kids both want to share.
questions.fun_fact: Two Italian regions, Veneto and Friuli, have been arguing for years over which one invented tiramisu.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which adventure sport is this?
hints: There's no engine: it flies using the wind and rising warm air.
You usually take off by running down a hill until the fabric fills with air.
Its soft wing looks like a parachute, but you can steer it and stay up for hours.

questions.question: In Colombia, what are you being told when someone says “no dé papaya”?

Hurry up and finish your homework

questions.question: In which month is Medellín’s Feria de las Flores held?
hints: It’s in the second half of the year.
The Battle of Boyacá is remembered in the same month.
It comes right after July.
questions.description: The month when Medellín smells better than any perfume counter at the mall.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the wooden horse called from the Greek legend where soldiers hid inside it?
hints: The horse is named after the city that received it as a gift, not after the Greeks who built it.
The war against that city lasted ten years and is told in the “Iliad.”
Some computer viruses that disguise themselves as harmless programs are named after this city.

questions.question: According to legend, the Greek hero Achilles was almost invincible. What was the only part of his body that could be wounded?
hints: It's where his mother held him when she dipped him in a magic river as a baby.
It's very close to the ground.

questions.description: An almost invincible warrior, and that “almost” cost him dearly.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this legend, the tendon that joins the calf to the heel is called the “Achilles tendon.”

questions.question: Which language has the most native speakers (people who learn it as babies) in the world?
hints: It is spoken mostly in one country in Asia.

questions.question: Many English words that start with “al-”, like “algebra”, “alcohol” and “alchemy”, come from the same language. Which one?

questions.question: What do you call a program that chats with you in writing as if it were a person?
hints: Its name is made of two short words stuck together.

questions.question: Which inflatable Disney robot takes care of people's health and is Hiro's best friend?
hints: The movie is set in a city that mixes San Francisco with Tokyo.
In the end, he becomes a superhero with red armor in “Big Hero 6”.
His name starts with “Bay” and ends like the start of “maximum”.

questions.question: In 1997, IBM's supercomputer Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a famous match. In which game?

questions.description: The day a machine with no hands beat a human at a game where you move pieces by hand.

questions.question: What do you call the junk emails that pile up in your inbox without anyone asking for them, like ads and strange offers?
hints: Almost every email program has a special folder for them.

It's a four-letter word that starts with “S”.
questions.description: A letter nobody asked for, from someone nobody knows, offering something nobody wants.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “spam” because of a British Monty Python comedy sketch in which characters keep repeating the name of a canned meat called Spam.

questions.question: What do the letters “www” stand for at the start of many website addresses?
hints: It's three English words, and the first one means the whole planet.
It's a huge network linking pages from all over the planet.
The last word is what a spider spins.
questions.description: Three letters you type without thinking, like saying “hello” without knowing where the word comes from.
questions.fun_fact: British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, a lab in Switzerland.

questions.question: In which country was the Rubik's Cube invented?
hints: It's a country in Europe.
Its inventor, Ernő Rubik, was an architecture teacher in that country.
Its capital is Budapest.
questions.description: A puzzle that has made more people cry than an onion.
questions.fun_fact: Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, and at first even he didn't know how to solve it: it took him about a month!

questions.question: Before it made its famous plastic bricks, what material did the LEGO company use to make its toys?
hints: The company's founder was a carpenter.
It made ducks, trains and yo-yos from the same material as tables and chairs.
This material comes from trees.
questions.description: Long before stepping on one of these became the world's worst ouch, there was a different kind of ouch.
questions.fun_fact: The name LEGO comes from “leg godt”, which means “play well” in Danish.

questions.question: Which magician, famous about 100 years ago, escaped from chains, handcuffs, straitjackets and tanks full of water?
hints: He lived in the early 1900s, long before television.
People called him “the Handcuff King”, and his name became another word for an escape artist.
His first name is the same as a certain young wizard from Hogwarts.
questions.description: If you locked him up with a padlock, all you got for your trouble was a lost padlock.
questions.fun_fact: Houdini’s real name was Erik Weisz, and he was born in Hungary.

questions.question: What is the art of making coins or cards vanish with quick, secret moves, without the audience noticing?
hints: It's one of the oldest branches of magic.
Magicians who do it train their fingers a lot.
Its name tells you which body part does all the tricky work.
questions.description: Now you see it, now you don't, and now you're checking your own pockets.
questions.fun_fact: Some sleight-of-hand tricks with cups and little balls were already being done in ancient Rome.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this animal that some people keep in an aquarium?
hints: It is an amphibian that spends its whole life in water.
It comes from lakes in Mexico, and it is also in Minecraft.
Its name comes from Nahuatl, the Aztec language, and starts with “A”.
questions.description: It never stops smiling, not even on Mondays.
questions.fun_fact: An axolotl can regrow a whole leg, and even parts of its heart and brain.

questions.question: How many tentacles does a garden snail have on its head?
hints: Not all of its tentacles are the same size.
It has long ones on top, with eyes at the tips, and shorter ones below.
It has two pairs.
questions.description: It carries its house on its back and its eyes on the tips of little sticks.
questions.fun_fact: If a snail loses one of its eye tentacles, it can grow back.

questions.question: What do you call the loss of forests when people cut down or burn so many trees that the forest disappears?
hints: It is one of the biggest problems in the Amazon rainforest.
Its opposite is planting trees to bring the forest back.
The word starts with “de-”, as if you were undoing a forest.
questions.description: When a forest goes bald and no shampoo can fix it.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon rainforest is so big that it makes much of its own rain from the water its leaves release.

questions.question: You fill a glass to the brim with water and a floating ice cube. What happens to the water level when the ice melts?
hints: Floating ice is already “taking up its space” in the water.
As it melts, the ice shrinks and fits exactly into the space its underwater part filled.
Not a single drop spills, and no water goes missing either.
questions.description: A science experiment you can do with the drink in your lunchbox.
questions.fun_fact: That's why melting sea ice at the North Pole barely raises sea levels, but ice sitting on land, like in Greenland and Antarctica, does raise them when it melts.

questions.question: What was the name of the Roman god of fire and blacksmiths, who made weapons in a forge hidden under a mountain?
hints: He was married to Venus, the goddess of love.
The Greeks called him Hephaestus.
His name sounds a lot like the mountains that spit out lava.
questions.description: The only god on Mount Olympus who went to work in overalls and smelled of coal.
questions.fun_fact: The word “volcano” comes from Vulcan, because the Romans believed the smoke from volcanoes came from his forge.

questions.question: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods. When the Romans adopted him, what name did they give him?
hints: He stayed king of the gods and kept throwing lightning bolts.
A planet has the same name.
It's also the name of the largest planet in the solar system.
questions.description: Same boss, same lightning bolt, brand-new passport.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans called Jupiter “the best and the greatest” and built his most important temple on a hill in Rome.

questions.question: Which Roman god gave his name to the month of March?
hints: He was the god of war.
A red planet is named after him.
His name sounds almost the same as the month's, just a few letters shorter.
questions.description: A calendar month that, deep down, is itching for a fight.
questions.fun_fact: For the ancient Romans, the year began in March; that's why “September” (from the Latin for seven) was the seventh month.

questions.question: What is the name of the big stone box that held a mummy's coffin?
hints: The word comes from ancient Greek.
Archaeologists find it inside tombs, sometimes with the dead person's face carved on the lid.
It starts with “sar-” and ends with “-ophagus”.
questions.description: A box so fancy that nobody is in a hurry to try it out.
questions.fun_fact: The word “sarcophagus” comes from Greek and means something like “flesh-eater”.

questions.question: Look at this famous painting, “Las Meninas,” which hangs in the Prado Museum in Madrid. Who painted it?
hints: He was a 17th-century Spanish painter who worked for King Philip IV.
The painter put himself in the picture, on the left, holding his brush and palette.
His last name starts with “Vel…”.
questions.description: A painting where the artist sneaks into the royal family photo, like that uncle who shows up in every picture.
questions.fun_fact: Pablo Picasso liked “Las Meninas” so much that in 1957 he painted 58 versions of his own.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this swimming stroke called?
hints: Both arms come out of the water and go back in at the same time.
The legs move together, like a dolphin's tail.
It has the same name as an insect with big, colorful wings.
questions.description: A swimming style so tiring that even Olympic swimmers finish asking for a coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Butterfly grew out of breaststroke: some swimmers began bringing both arms out of the water at once, and in 1952 it became a stroke of its own.

questions.question: What do you call a whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and by itself?
hints: The number 1 isn't allowed in this club, but 2 is.
7, 13 and 17 are all this kind of number.
Its name also means “the very best”, like a ___ seat at the front of the show.
questions.description: Some numbers love company, but these ones are famously hard to split up.
questions.fun_fact: Computers use giant prime numbers to protect passwords and secret messages.

questions.question: What number comes next in this series: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25...?
hints: Look at how much it grows each time: 3, 5, 7, 9...
Each number is another number multiplied by itself.
questions.description: A series that grows like the pile of homework you leave for Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: They're called “square numbers” because 36 tiles can make a perfect 6-by-6 square.

questions.question: If you write the number one billion in digits, how many zeros does it have?
hints: One million already has 6 zeros.
A thousand has 3 zeros: add those to the zeros of a million.
Write it with commas: 1,000,000,000.
questions.description: How many times your mom has told you “clean your room”, according to you.
questions.fun_fact: If you counted one number per second without stopping, it would take you more than 31 years to reach one billion.

questions.question: In Roman numerals, what number does the letter D stand for?
hints: It's a three-digit number.
It's bigger than C, which stands for 100.
It's exactly half of M, which stands for 1,000.
questions.description: The Romans conquered half the world without a calculator, and this is how they wrote their sums.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans had no symbol at all for zero.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this water plant from the rivers and lakes of the Amazon called?
hints: Its round leaves have edges that turn up, like a baking tray.
Underneath, the leaves are covered in spines so fish don't eat them.
Its scientific name honors a British queen of the 19th century.
questions.description: The Amazon's favorite floating dance floor, and the frogs never pay to get in.
questions.fun_fact: Its flower opens at night as white, and by the next night it has turned pink.

questions.question: What is the white sap of the rubber tree, the one used to make rubber, called?
hints: It comes out white like milk and gets sticky in the air.
Balloons and doctors' gloves are made from it.
A common type of wall paint is named after it.
questions.description: Trees cry too, but their tears end up as car tires.
questions.fun_fact: Long before Europeans arrived, Indigenous peoples of the Americas were already making bouncing balls from this tree's sap.

questions.question: What is meringue, the base of Bogotá's merengón dessert, made of?
hints: It's whipped and whipped until it's white and stiff, then baked.
It comes from something that hens lay.
It's the clear part of the egg, not the yellow part.
questions.description: A dessert so fluffy it looks like a cloud that let itself get caught.
questions.fun_fact: If the whites are whipped well enough, you can turn the bowl upside down over your head and they won't fall out.

questions.question: In the Colombian dessert of brevas with dulce de leche, the breva is the fruit of which tree?
hints: It is a tree with big, wide leaves that comes from the Mediterranean region.
In old paintings, Adam and Eve cover themselves with a leaf from this tree.
Its best-known fruit has purple or green skin, is soft and pink inside, full of tiny seeds, and is often eaten dried.
questions.description: A fruit so fancy it never goes anywhere without its dulce de leche.
questions.fun_fact: The breva is the fig tree's first crop of the year; the second crop, which comes later, gives the ordinary figs.

questions.question: What is the long, hollow tube that some Amazon peoples use to shoot small darts when hunting?
hints: It needs no string and no rubber band, only air.
It's used to hunt birds and monkeys high up in the trees, without making a sound.
Its name starts with what you do to the candles on a birthday cake.
questions.description: A hunting tool for people who like to keep things very quiet in the treetops.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon hunters coat their dart tips with curare, a plant poison that paralyzes the prey.

questions.question: Casabe is the flat, round bread of the Amazon's Indigenous peoples. What is it made from?
hints: It's a plant whose edible part grows underground.
Across Latin America and Africa people eat it boiled or fried, a lot like potatoes.
It's white inside, has a thick brown skin, and tapioca is made from it.
questions.description: A bread so flat and crunchy it looks like a jungle frisbee.
questions.fun_fact: One kind, bitter yuca (also called cassava), is poisonous raw, so Indigenous cooks grate it and squeeze it in a woven tube called a sebucán before making casabe.

questions.question: What is the largest single flower in the world?
hints: It grows in the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia.
It has no leaves, no stem and no roots: it lives as a parasite on a vine.
It can be nearly a meter (about 3 ft) across and smells like rotting meat to attract flies.
questions.description: A flower so big it fits in no vase, and it smells awful too.
questions.fun_fact: Rafflesia smells like rotting meat on purpose: that's how it attracts the flies that help pollinate it.

questions.question: Guinness World Records began in 1951 with an argument that nobody could settle. What was the argument about?
questions.answer: The fastest game bird in all of Europe
wrong_answers: The tallest man in all of Europe
The highest mountain in all of Europe
The longest river in all of Europe
hints: The argument happened during a day out in the countryside.
That day, the men had gone out hunting.
It was about some feathered animals and how fast they are.
questions.description: It all started like one of those dinner-table arguments nobody can settle without checking a phone.
questions.fun_fact: The first Guinness book came out in 1955, written by twin brothers Norris and Ross McWhirter.

questions.question: Robert Wadlow is the tallest man in history. About how tall was he?
hints: He was much taller than any basketball player.
A normal door is about 2 meters (6.5 ft) tall, and he had to duck low to get through.
He was almost three meters tall, but not quite.
questions.description: This man never had to ask for help reaching the top shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Wadlow kept growing his whole life because his body made too much growth hormone.

questions.question: Which country does the Rubik's Cube, the best-selling puzzle of all time, come from?
hints: It was invented in 1974 by an architecture professor who wanted to explain movement to his students.
It's a landlocked country in Central Europe.
Its capital is Budapest.
questions.description: A toy that has made millions of people say “almost done” for three hours straight.
questions.fun_fact: A Rubik's Cube can be scrambled in more than 43 quintillion different ways.

questions.question: What do you call the label with the # symbol that groups posts about the same topic?
hints: The word is made of two shorter words joined together.
Its second half is another word for a label.
The # symbol is also called the “hash” sign.
questions.description: A symbol that used to be just a button on landline phones and now thinks it's a big deal.
questions.fun_fact: A Twitter user named Chris Messina came up with the first hashtag in 2007, and at first the company thought the idea was too strange.

questions.question: The company that created TikTok is from which country?
hints: It's a country in Asia.
Paper and gunpowder were invented there.
The Great Wall is there.
questions.description: An app that turns five quick minutes into three hours, and nobody knows how.
questions.fun_fact: TikTok isn't used inside that country, which has its own version called Douyin.

questions.question: What is the name of the festival in India where people throw colored powder at each other in the streets?
hints: It celebrates the arrival of spring.
Besides the powder, many people soak each other with water guns and water balloons.
Its name sounds just like an English word that means “sacred”.
questions.description: The only party where getting your clothes dirty isn't just allowed, it's the whole point.
questions.fun_fact: Holi is also known as “the festival of colors” and celebrates the victory of good over evil.

questions.question: You're watching a downpour in the distance while the sun warms the back of your neck. Looking toward the rain, what are you most likely to see in the sky?
hints: It always appears on the side opposite the sun.
Each tiny raindrop works like a prism that splits the light.
It is shaped like an arch and has seven colors, from red to violet.
questions.description: The weather can't decide between rain and sunshine, so the sky solves the problem in style.
questions.fun_fact: From an airplane you can sometimes see a complete rainbow shaped like a circle, because there is no ground to cut it off.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Canadian dish is fries topped with bits of cheese and hot gravy. What is it called?
hints: Canada speaks English and French, and this dish's name comes from the French-speaking part, the province of Quebec.
It's so popular in Canada that even burger chains sell it as a side.
Its name starts with the letter P and rhymes with “routine”.
questions.description: French fries that bundled up warmly to survive the winter.
questions.fun_fact: The cheese in real poutine is so fresh that it squeaks against your teeth when you chew it.

questions.question: The word “ketchup” comes from a sauce from southern China. What was that original sauce made of?
hints: The original sauce didn't have a single bit of tomato in it.
It was a salty sauce with a very strong smell, not sweet at all.
It smelled more like the sea than like a garden.
questions.description: Long before it painted fries red, this sauce had a very strange past.
questions.fun_fact: Tomato came to ketchup much later: in England, people used to make it with mushrooms or even walnuts.

questions.question: Which Colombian town is famous as the capital of adventure sports?
hints: It's in Santander.
The Chicamocha Canyon is close by, and the Fonce River runs through the town.
Its name starts like a saint's name.
questions.description: A town where moms live with their hearts in their mouths.
questions.fun_fact: In San Gil's El Gallineral park, the trees are covered in gray “barba de viejo” (old man's beard), a plant that hangs down like curtains.

questions.question: If someone in Germany says “Danke” to you, what are they saying?
hints: Your parents taught you to say it when you were little.
It's one of the “magic words” of good manners.
It sounds a lot like its English meaning.
questions.description: Germany has some super long words, but this one is so tiny it fits on a stick of gum.

questions.question: What is the official language of Brazil?

questions.description: A country so huge that even its parrots dance samba and its soccer players do magic tricks.
questions.fun_fact: Brazil has far more Portuguese speakers than Portugal itself: over 200 million against about 10 million.

questions.question: When someone says they saved their photos “in the cloud,” what do they mean?
questions.answer: They saved them on faraway computers reached over the internet
wrong_answers: They sent them over the internet to a satellite circling Earth
They turned them into Wi-Fi signals floating in the air at home
They saved them only in their own phone's memory
hints: It has nothing to do with the sky or the weather.

The photos sit on a company's machines, somewhere else, connected to the network.
questions.description: A cloud where it never rains, but your vacation photos keep pouring in.
questions.fun_fact: “The cloud” is really giant buildings called data centers, full of thousands of computers working day and night.

questions.question: The guinea pig is a popular pet. Which continent does it originally come from?
hints: Indigenous peoples tamed it thousands of years ago.

In Peru and Ecuador it's a traditional dish.
questions.description: Its name says pig, but it never oinks or rolls around in the mud.
questions.fun_fact: When a guinea pig is very happy, it jumps into the air; this is called “popcorning,” like a kernel of popping corn.

questions.question: What does a hedgehog do when it gets scared?
questions.answer: It rolls up into a ball
wrong_answers: It shoots its spines like arrows
hints: It uses its spines to defend itself, but without losing them.
This way it hides its soft belly, which has no spines.
Sonic does something similar when he attacks by spinning.
questions.description: An animal with a punk hairdo that needs no gel to keep it standing up.
questions.fun_fact: A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines, and they are really very stiff hairs.

questions.question: Look at this famous bronze statue of a she-wolf feeding two babies. According to legend, what were the twins' names?
hints: They were left in a river as babies, and a she-wolf looked after them.
One of them gave his name to a city.
One name starts almost like “Rome”.
questions.description: Twins who skipped the baby bottle and got a very furry babysitter instead.

questions.question: What fabric were the bandages made of that the ancient Egyptians used to wrap their mummies?
hints: It's a fabric made from a plant, not from animal hair or from worm cocoons.
That plant grew on the banks of the Nile River, and the fabric feels cool and wrinkles a lot.
Today it's used for cool summer shirts, and its name is also used for bed sheets and tablecloths.
questions.description: Wrapping holiday gifts is easy; try wrapping a pharaoh without running out of fabric.
