questions.question: Look at the photo: which famous museum in Paris has this glass pyramid at its entrance?
hints: Before it was a museum, this building was a palace of the kings of France.
The most famous painting in the world is kept here: the Mona Lisa.
Its name starts with the letter L.
questions.description: A royal palace that now gets more visitors than any king ever did in a lifetime.
questions.fun_fact: The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world, and it has so many works that seeing them all, one minute each, would take weeks.

questions.question: Which museum in Bogotá keeps the famous Muisca Raft, a small figure of a chief and his companions on a raft?
hints: It was created by the Banco de la República and stands next to Parque Santander, in downtown Bogotá.

questions.description: A museum so valuable that even the security guards need security guards.
questions.fun_fact: The Gold Museum holds more than 30,000 objects of gold and other metals made by Indigenous peoples of Colombia.

questions.question: How many meters long is an Olympic swimming pool?

In the 100-meter race, swimmers go to the far end and come back just once.
questions.description: A pool so big that your mom yells “Don't go too far!” and you're already halfway across.
questions.fun_fact: An Olympic pool holds at least 2.5 million liters (about 660,000 gallons) of water, enough to fill more than 10,000 bathtubs!

questions.question: Where does açaí, the purple fruit eaten in bowls with banana and granola, come from?
questions.answer: From a palm in the Amazon rainforest
wrong_answers: From a shrub in the high Andes grasslands
From a palm on Caribbean beaches
From a tree on Colombian coffee farms
hints: It grows somewhere very hot and humid, where it rains almost every day.
People there have eaten it for a very long time, long before it became trendy in cities.
It comes from the same rainforest as the river that carries the most water in the world.
questions.description: It's purple, comes with granola and costs more than a full lunch.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brazilian Amazon, many people eat açaí without sugar as part of lunch, with fish and cassava flour.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this typical sweet from the Colombian coast called?
hints: They're sold all over the beaches of Cartagena and Santa Marta, on trays carried on the head.
They're sticky and sweet, with little white shreds inside.
Their main ingredient is the hairy fruit that falls from palm trees.
questions.description: A sweet so sticky it keeps your teeth glued together until the next day.
questions.fun_fact: In Cartagena, the palenqueras, women street sellers in colorful dresses, sell cocadas in many flavors, like guava, pineapple and even milk.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which dessert is it?
hints: It's a creamy dessert that lots of grandmas make in a pot.

questions.fun_fact: Rice pudding is made in almost every Spanish-speaking country, and there's even a children's song about it: “Arroz con leche, me quiero casar” (“Rice pudding, I want to get married”).

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this big shared house with a palm roof, typical of the Amazon's Indigenous peoples, called?
hints: It isn't built over water or on tall posts: its huge roof reaches almost down to the ground.

questions.question: April O'Neil, Shredder and Splinter: what do they have in common?
questions.answer: They're Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles characters
hints: The heroes of this show live hidden beneath a big US city.

questions.description: A group of friends so odd it includes a reporter, a villain covered in blades and a wise rat.
questions.fun_fact: The four turtles are named Leonardo, Raphael, Donatello and Michelangelo, after four famous Italian Renaissance artists.

questions.question: In tennis, what do you call a serve so good that the other player can't even touch the ball?
hints: Every player dreams of hitting one when stepping up to serve.

It shares its name with a playing card: the one with a single symbol in the middle.
questions.description: A serve so fast that the other player is still looking for the ball in the parking lot.
questions.fun_fact: The world's best servers hit over 220 km/h (137 mph), and the official record is around 250 km/h (155 mph).

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this type of tennis court surface called?

At the French Open (Roland Garros) in Paris, players slide on it and kick up red dust.

questions.fun_fact: Rafael Nadal won the French Open, which is played on this surface, 14 times.

questions.question: On which night does Colombia celebrate Día de las Velitas, when families light candles and lanterns in windows and on sidewalks?
hints: It's one of the first celebrations of the Christmas season.
The next day is a public holiday in Colombia.
It's the eve of the Feast of the Immaculate Conception.
questions.description: The one night a year nobody gets scolded for playing with fire on the sidewalk.
questions.fun_fact: In Quimbaya, Quindío, neighborhoods compete every year in a festival of candles and lanterns that fills the whole town with light.

questions.question: The sombrero vueltiao, a cultural symbol of Colombia, is woven from braids of a plant fiber. Which one?
hints: Zenú artisans weave it in Córdoba and Sucre, above all in Tuchín.

questions.description: A hat with so many turns you get dizzy just looking at it.

questions.question: What is a “vlog”?
questions.answer: A diary-style video where someone shows their everyday life
wrong_answers: A video where someone plays video games live
A short video where someone dances to a trending song
A video where someone teaches how to cook a recipe
hints: The word mixes “video” with another internet word.

It's like writing a diary, but with a camera in your hand.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a swamp creature, but actually lives on YouTube.
questions.fun_fact: “Vlog” comes from joining “video” and “blog”, and “blog” itself comes from “web log”, something like a logbook of the web.

questions.question: Finish the SpongeBob SquarePants theme song: “Absorbent and yellow and ___ is he!”
hints: Like “absorbent” and “yellow”, it describes a real sponge.

questions.description: A song your parents know by heart too, even if they say they don't.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this object, once used to store computer files, called?

questions.description: Your parents saved their school homework on this and prayed it wouldn't break.

questions.question: What do you call the physical parts of a computer, the ones you can touch, like the keyboard, the screen and the mouse?
hints: Like the other options, it ends in “-ware”.

questions.description: The thing you might want to kick when the computer freezes (please don't).

questions.question: The social network now called X changed its name in 2023. What was it called before?
hints: Posts were short: at first, 140 characters at most.
Its logo was a little blue bird.
The posts people shared there were called “tweets.”
questions.description: A social network that changed its name as casually as you change a profile picture.
questions.fun_fact: The little blue bird in the logo had a name: Larry, after the basketball player Larry Bird.

questions.question: At the Wimbledon tennis tournament in London, what color must almost all of the players' clothing be?
hints: It's a very old and very strict rule: they even check socks and caps.
People say it was once meant to hide sweat stains.
It's the color of milk and snow.
questions.description: A tournament so fancy it has a dress code, like your rich aunt's wedding.
questions.fun_fact: About 2 million strawberries with cream are eaten at Wimbledon during the tournament.

questions.question: In tennis, the points in a game go like this: 0, 15, 30… What number comes next?
hints: Careful: tennis doesn't follow the rules of math.
It's not the number you'd get by adding 15.
It's a big birthday that many parents celebrate with a party: turning ...
questions.description: Where the umpire counts out loud and everyone pretends it makes perfect sense.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody knows for sure why tennis counts this way; one theory says a clock face was once used (15, 30, 45), and 45 was shortened to 40.

questions.question: An earthquake starts at a point deep underground. What is the point on the surface right above it called?
hints: This word comes up a lot in the news every time the ground shakes.
It starts with a Greek prefix that means “on” or “above.”
It literally means “the center on top.”
questions.description: When the Earth starts dancing without asking, this is where the party begins… at least when you look from above.
questions.fun_fact: The underground point where an earthquake really starts is called the hypocenter, and it can be more than 600 km (370 miles) deep.

questions.question: In which country did the strongest earthquake ever recorded happen?
hints: It happened in 1960 and measured 9.5 in magnitude.
It is a country in South America.
The city hit hardest was Valdivia, in a very long and very thin country.
questions.description: The day the planet decided to turn the shaking all the way up.
questions.fun_fact: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake caused a tsunami that crossed the whole Pacific Ocean and reached Hawaii and Japan.

questions.question: What device records the movements of the ground during an earthquake?
hints: It draws zigzag lines: the stronger the shaking, the bigger the peaks.
Its name ends in “-graph”, from a Greek word meaning “to write”.
Its name starts like “seismic”, a word for anything to do with earthquakes.
questions.description: A gadget so nosy it knows every time the Earth moves, even when nobody else feels a thing.
questions.fun_fact: Around the year 132, Zhang Heng in China invented an earthquake detector: a bronze vessel with dragons that dropped little balls into the mouths of bronze toads.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what are these farmers called who parade through Medellín carrying huge flower displays on their backs?
hints: They parade every August at the Feria de las Flores.
They come from Santa Elena, a rural district in the mountains above Medellín.
Their name comes from the wooden frame they carry, which looks like a chair.
questions.description: Men who throw a whole garden on their backs like it's a school backpack.
questions.fun_fact: The Desfile de Silleteros has been held since 1957, and some silletas are so big they weigh more than 60 kg (130 lb).

questions.question: What happens if you put a raw egg in a glass of water with lots and lots of salt stirred in?
hints: The salt doesn't disappear: it makes the water “heavier” (denser).
In a glass of plain water with no salt, a fresh egg goes to the bottom… but salt changes things.
It's the same thing that happens to swimmers in the Dead Sea, where almost nobody sinks.
questions.description: A kitchen experiment that, for once, doesn't end in scrambled eggs.
questions.fun_fact: The Dead Sea is so salty that people float without any effort and can even lie back and read on the water.

questions.question: Think of a number. Multiply it by 2, add 10, divide the result by 2, and subtract the number you first thought of. What do you get?
hints: Try it with an easy number, like 1.
When you divide by 2, your number goes back to what it was… and the 10 gets cut in half too.
You end up with half of the number you added at the start.
questions.description: A magic trick where the magician is secretly a calculator in disguise.
questions.fun_fact: The trick works with any number: with 7, with 1,000, and even with your phone number.

questions.question: In skateboarding, what is the basic jump called where the board rises stuck to your feet, without using your hands?
hints: It's the first trick almost every skater learns, and the base of many others.
In this trick the board doesn't spin or slide along a rail: it just goes up with you and comes back down.
Its name sounds like a nickname and starts with the letter O.
questions.description: Flying with no wings, four wheels and zero hands.
questions.fun_fact: It's named after Alan “Ollie” Gelfand, the American skater who invented it in the late 1970s.

questions.question: Look at this close-up of a vegetable cut in half: which vegetable is it?
hints: The wavy white lines are really leaves packed tightly against each other.
Whole, it's a heavy round ball, and people eat a lot of it in salads.
It's a purple cousin of the green leafy ball used to make sauerkraut.
questions.description: A purple maze that someone sliced in half with a knife.
questions.fun_fact: Red cabbage juice changes color: it turns pink with lemon and green or blue with baking soda.

questions.question: The first carrots people grew, more than a thousand years ago in Asia, were not orange. What color were they usually?
hints: Some markets still sell carrots in this color today as something special.
It's a dark color, like the skin of an eggplant.
Mix red and blue paint and you get this color.
questions.description: A vegetable that changed its outfit a few centuries ago and never changed back.
questions.fun_fact: Orange carrots became popular thanks to farmers in the Netherlands about 400 years ago.

questions.question: Which company bought YouTube in 2006, just one year after it started?
hints: This company's name comes from a math word for a gigantic number.
This company also makes Android, the system on lots and lots of phones.
When you don't know something, you look it up on its famous search engine.
questions.description: YouTube has a dad too, and it's a very, very rich dad.
questions.fun_fact: The first YouTube video, uploaded in 2005, is only 19 seconds long and shows one of its creators in front of some elephants at a zoo.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call a very stingy person, someone who won't even lend you a pencil?
hints: The word is also the name of something we all have on our body.
People say this person's arm is so stiff it won't bend to reach for the money in their pocket.
It's the part of the arm between the hand and the shoulder, right where it bends.
questions.description: This person gives you hugs on every birthday, and nothing else.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico a stingy person is called the same thing, and to say it without words, people tap that part of their arm.

questions.question: Listen: which farm animal makes this sound?
hints: It's a working animal that carries loads on many farms.
It has very long ears.
Its sound is called braying: “hee-haw, hee-haw”.
questions.description: This farm neighbor sings at five in the morning, and nobody asked for a serenade.
questions.fun_fact: A donkey's bray can be heard more than 3 km (about 2 miles) away.

questions.question: Who holds the world record in the 100 meters?
hints: He's from a Caribbean country famous for its sprinters.
He's Jamaican and celebrated his wins by pointing at the sky as if throwing lightning.
His last name is also a word for a flash of lightning.
questions.description: If this man is late for school, it's because he never even left the house.
questions.fun_fact: Usain Bolt ran the 100 meters in 9.58 seconds in 2009, reaching almost 45 km/h (28 mph) at his fastest.

questions.question: What do you call the front part of a ship, the part that cuts through the water?
hints: It's a short word that sailors use.
The back of the ship, at the opposite end, is called the stern.
It's spelled just like what performers do at the end of a show.
questions.description: If ships had noses, this question would be about them.
questions.fun_fact: Old ships often had a carved wooden figure on the front, often a mermaid, called a “figurehead”.

questions.question: What unit is normally used to measure the speed of ships?
hints: It's a word you also use in everyday life, but for something else.
Sailors long ago measured it by throwing a rope into the sea and counting.
It's what you tie in your shoelaces.
questions.description: There are no speed cameras at sea, but someone is still keeping count.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from sailors dropping a rope with knots tied along it into the sea and counting how many knots ran out in a set time.

questions.question: Coffee is one of Colombia's most famous drinks, but the plant isn't from there. Which country does it originally come from?
hints: An old legend says a goat herder discovered coffee when his goats got very restless after eating some red berries.
It's a country in Africa.
Its capital is Addis Ababa.
questions.description: Colombian parents can't get going without their cup of coffee, but this plant came from very far away.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the goats of a herder named Kaldi started jumping around like crazy after eating coffee berries.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this scale-covered animal called?
hints: It lives in Africa and Asia, not in the Americas.
Its scales are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails, and when it gets scared it rolls up into a ball.
Its name comes from the Malay language and starts with “pan”.
questions.description: A pine cone that woke up one day and decided to go for a walk.
questions.fun_fact: The pangolin has no teeth: it swallows small stones that help grind up the ants inside its stomach.

questions.question: In 2007, which tiny animal, less than a millimeter long, survived the vacuum of outer space outside the spacecraft?
hints: It lives in damp moss, maybe even in your backyard.
It has eight chubby little legs with claws and can dry up like a raisin for years without dying.
Its nickname is “water bear”.
questions.description: An astronaut with no suit, no helmet and no fear.
questions.fun_fact: When it dries out, a tardigrade shrinks into a little ball called a “tun” and can last for years without water.

questions.question: In the cartoons, what does Popeye the Sailor eat to become super strong?
hints: Lots of kids push it to the side of their plate.
It's a green, leafy vegetable.
He eats it straight from a can that he squeezes open.
questions.description: The sailor who got half the world eating vegetables without anyone forcing them.
questions.fun_fact: Popeye first appeared in 1929 in a newspaper comic strip, before he ever made it into cartoons.

questions.question: Who was the first Colombian to win the Tour de France?
hints: He won it in 2019 and was one of the youngest champions ever.
He was born in Bogotá and grew up in Zipaquirá, the town with the Salt Cathedral.
His first name starts with E and his last name rhymes with “canal”.
questions.description: Three weeks of pedaling around France, and at the end they give you a yellow shirt: the deal of the century.
questions.fun_fact: Egan Bernal won the Tour de France at just 22, and before racing on the road he was a mountain biker.

questions.question: Which Colombian climb, about 80 km (50 miles) long, is considered by many cyclists the longest paved climb in the world?
hints: It climbs from Tolima toward the department of Caldas.
It starts in Mariquita, in the hot lowlands, and reaches more than 3,600 m (11,800 ft).
Its name in Spanish means what the alphabet is made of.
questions.description: A climb so long you start in the lowland heat and finish begging for a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Riding up Alto de Letras, you go from the heat of the lowlands to the cold of the páramo: several climates in a single day of pedaling!

questions.question: On a painter's color wheel, red sits directly opposite green. By the same rule, what color sits directly opposite blue?
hints: Look closely: green is made by mixing the two primary colors that aren't red.
The color opposite a primary color is made by mixing the other two primary colors.
Mix red with yellow and you get the color of a fruit that has the same name.
questions.description: Some colors get along so badly that they stand face to face, just glaring at each other.
questions.fun_fact: Opposite colors are called complementary colors, and side by side they look brighter, which is why so many movie posters use blue and orange.

questions.question: Tejo used to be called “turmequé” too, after the name of a town. Which department is that town in?
hints: It's a department of cold mountains, on the high plateau where the Muisca lived.
Its capital is Tunja.
In 1819 it was the site of the battle that sealed Colombia's independence.
questions.description: A sport named after a town, as if soccer were called “Fusagasugá”.
questions.fun_fact: The Muisca played something like tejo centuries ago, and the story goes that they threw discs of stone or gold.

questions.question: Who patented the telephone in 1876?
hints: He was born in Scotland but made his invention in the United States.
He also spent much of his life teaching deaf people to speak.
His last name is also the word for the thing that rings at a door or in a church tower.
questions.description: Before this invention, gossiping with Grandma meant walking all the way to her house.
questions.fun_fact: Bell's first words on the telephone were to his assistant: “Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.”

questions.question: A long-lasting light bulb, the phonograph and one of the first movie cameras: which inventor developed them?
hints: He was from the United States and worked with a big team in his lab.
This inventor was called “the Wizard of Menlo Park” and held more than a thousand patents.
His last name starts with E.
questions.description: Three inventions, one proud dad, and not one of them ever helped him with his homework.
questions.fun_fact: Edison registered more than 1,000 patents, and as a boy he went to school for only a few months: his mom taught him the rest.

questions.question: What invention did the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta present in 1800?
hints: His last name is hidden in a word used to measure electricity.
He stacked metal discs separated by cardboard soaked in salt water.
Today you put one in the TV remote when it stops working.
questions.description: An Italian with so much energy that they even named a unit of measurement after him.
questions.fun_fact: The unit “volt”, which you see printed on chargers and batteries, is named in honor of Volta.

questions.question: Papyrus, the sheet the ancient Egyptians wrote on, was made from a plant that grew along a river. Which river?
hints: It is a river in Africa.
It is one of the longest rivers in the world.
It flows very close to the pyramids and into the Mediterranean Sea.
questions.description: Long before notebooks, the Egyptians had their own stationery store… right by the water.
questions.fun_fact: The word “paper” comes from “papyrus”, even though today's paper is made from wood, not from that plant.

questions.question: How many national teams played at the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada?
hints: More than at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, which had 32.
They were split into 12 groups of 4 teams.
There were 16 more teams than at the previous World Cup.
questions.description: A World Cup so big that the sticker album could barely fit everyone.
questions.fun_fact: The 2026 World Cup was the first one hosted by three countries at once, and it had 104 matches.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this instrument of Aboriginal Australians called?
hints: It is made from a eucalyptus trunk that termites have hollowed out.
You play it by blowing with buzzing lips, and it makes a deep, nonstop drone.
Its name sounds almost like a tongue twister: it starts with “didge”.
questions.description: A very long stick that sounds like a giant bumblebee with a cold.
questions.fun_fact: Skilled didgeridoo players breathe in through the nose while still blowing out through the mouth, so they can play for minutes without stopping.

questions.question: Which country does the tango come from, the partner dance with elegant steps and very serious looks?
hints: It's a country in South America, but people there don't speak Portuguese.
Its star instrument is the bandoneon, which looks a bit like an accordion.
It's Messi's home country, and its capital is Buenos Aires.
questions.description: A dance so dramatic it's like a soap opera, but with better shoes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, UNESCO added the tango to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, after Argentina and Uruguay applied together.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this famous site with its Maya pyramid?
hints: It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
It is on the Yucatán Peninsula, in Mexico.
Its name has two words, and the second one starts with “I”.
questions.description: A pyramid with stairs on all four sides, in case the god couldn't be bothered to walk around.
questions.fun_fact: At the equinoxes, the shadows on the stairs form a serpent of light that seems to slide down the pyramid.

questions.question: Roughly how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
hints: Think of a globe: which color do you see the most?
There's more water than land, but the continents aren't that tiny either.
It's roughly three quarters of the planet.
questions.description: They named the planet “Earth,” but from space anyone would say they picked the wrong name.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all that water is salty: only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and at the poles.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which flower has this center packed with seeds in spirals?
hints: This flower can grow taller than a grown-up.
Its seeds give a very common cooking oil, and people also eat them roasted as a snack.
When it is young, it turns during the day to follow the sun.
questions.description: Somebody out in nature clearly did their math homework and drew it in spirals.
questions.fun_fact: Young sunflowers follow the sun, but grown-up ones mostly stay facing east, where the sun rises.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It's in the far south of Colombia.
A little tip of it reaches a giant river, on the border with Brazil and Peru.
Its capital is Leticia.
questions.description: A piece of Colombia highlighted, like when you underline the important part before a test.
questions.fun_fact: Amazonas is Colombia's largest department, but one of the least populated.

questions.question: What is the only department of Colombia with a coast on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean?
hints: It's in the west of the country, and almost all of it is rainforest.
It's one of the rainiest places on the planet.
It's the only department that borders Panama.
questions.description: A department so indecisive it couldn't pick just one ocean.
questions.fun_fact: It rains so much in Chocó that it ranks among the rainiest places in the whole world.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this little frog from Colombia's rainforests called?
hints: Its name has to do with a material you find in the kitchen.
Look closely at its belly: what can you see through it?
The skin on its belly is see-through, like a window pane.
questions.description: A frog from Colombia's forests so tiny it fits on a bottle cap.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the countries with the most glass frog species in the world.

questions.question: Listen: which animal makes this deep sound?
hints: It's an animal that lives between water and land.
When it was little, it swam with a tail.
Its name combines an amphibian with a big animal that charges at a red cape.
questions.description: This noisy neighbor keeps the whole street awake all night.
questions.fun_fact: The bullfrog gets its name because its call sounds like a bull's moo, and it can be heard up to 1 km (more than half a mile) away.

questions.question: The word “amphibian” comes from Greek. What does it mean?
hints: It has to do with the places where these animals live.
“Bio” is the same root as in “biology,” the study of living things.
First they live in water, and later on land too: they have two lives.
questions.description: The ancient Greeks had a word for everything, even for creatures that hang out in puddles.
questions.fun_fact: Besides using their lungs, many amphibians breathe through their skin, which is why they need to keep it moist.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this bird that many farmers raise?
hints: It loves eating bugs and ticks in the grass.
It is dark gray, covered in little white dots, and has a bald head.
Its name joins an African country and an old word for farm birds like chickens.
questions.description: It wore a polka-dot dress to the party and forgot to comb its hair.
questions.fun_fact: Many farms keep them as an “alarm”: they screech loudly when a stranger arrives or they spot a snake.

questions.question: How many toes does a horse have on each leg?
hints: Fewer than the fingers on one of your hands.
A horse's hoof is made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
A cow's hoof is split in two, but a horse's hoof is one single piece.
questions.description: This animal has spent its whole life walking on tiptoe, like a ballet dancer.
questions.fun_fact: Millions of years ago, the horse's ancestors were the size of a dog and had several toes on each foot.

questions.question: What is a baby sheep called?
hints: It's not the baby of a cow or a horse.
Its mom's wool is used to make scarves.
Nativity scenes often have a small, white, woolly one next to the shepherds.
questions.description: So fluffy you'd love to use it as a pillow, but it would rather you didn't.
questions.fun_fact: A sheep can recognize the faces of about 50 other sheep and remember them for years.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which track and field event is this?
hints: The athlete doesn't jump with just their legs: they carry some help.
They use a long, bendy rod to push themselves very high.
Its name joins a word for a long stick with another word for jumping.
questions.description: An event for people who dream of flying but were born without wings.
questions.fun_fact: Modern vaulting poles are made of fiberglass or carbon fiber and bend so much that they launch the athlete like a catapult.

questions.question: In a relay race, what is the small tube that each runner passes to the next one called?
hints: If it falls to the ground, the team can be disqualified.
It is a light, hollow tube, about 30 cm (1 ft) long, that runners grip tightly in one hand.
Its name starts with “ba…”.
questions.description: A little stick so important that if it falls, the whole team cries.
questions.fun_fact: The baton must be passed inside a marked zone on the track; if it is handed over outside it, the team is disqualified.

questions.question: In the shot put, roughly how much does the shot thrown by men weigh?
hints: It is thrown with one hand, pushed off from the neck.
It weighs about as much as a well-fed six-month-old baby.
It weighs more than 5 kg, but less than 10 kg.
questions.description: It's not a bowling ball, but you still don't want to drop it on your foot.
questions.fun_fact: The men's shot weighs exactly 7.26 kg (16 lb), and the women's weighs 4 kg (about 8.8 lb).

questions.question: Look at this picture, taken very, very close up: what is it?
hints: These little tiles are so tiny that, all together, they look like dust.
Its owner flies, but it isn't a bird.
If you touch it with your fingers, you're left with a colorful powder.
questions.description: Colorful tiles for a roof the size of a fingernail.
questions.fun_fact: The “dust” left on your fingers after touching a butterfly is thousands of tiny scales from its wings.

questions.question: What nickname have Colombian cyclists, famous for how well they climb mountains, had for decades?
hints: The nickname is the name of an animal.
It's an animal much smaller than a bicycle.
It's an insect with a hard shell; some roll little balls of dung.
questions.description: They ride up mountains faster than your dad climbs the stairs after lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Herrera, one of the most famous escarabajos, won the Alpe d'Huez stage in 1984 and became the first Colombian to win a stage of the Tour de France.

questions.question: Traditionally, how many colors is a rainbow said to have?
hints: It starts with red and ends with violet.
One of its colors has an unusual name that hardly anyone uses: indigo.
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.description: After the rain, the sky puts on its best striped pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: The scientist Isaac Newton decided the rainbow had seven colors to match the seven musical notes; in reality, the colors blend into each other with no clear edges.

questions.question: Red, blue and yellow can't be made by mixing other paints, but they can make lots of other colors. What are they called?
hints: By chance, they're the same three colors as the flag of Colombia.
The colors you get by mixing them are called “secondary.”
They share their name with the kind of school where many kids learn to read.
questions.description: They're the parents of all the other colors, and nobody knows who their parents are.
questions.fun_fact: On phone and TV screens, the basic colors of light are different: red, green and blue.

questions.question: Crimson, scarlet and vermilion: what do they have in common?
hints: Painters use these names for colors.
Their color is one of the three primary colors in painting.
It's the color of a ripe strawberry.
questions.description: Three fancy names for something the rest of us call with just one word.
questions.fun_fact: Centuries ago, carmine, a very fine red, was made from tiny insects called cochineal that live on cactus plants in the Americas.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“what do they have in common?”). That format is retired (reason 7), in the translation just as in the source, so this question should be dropped or recast as a new question.

questions.question: According to the title of the famous book, for how many nights does Scheherazade tell the king stories?
hints: The stories are full of palaces, sultans and magic lamps from the East.
Each night she left the story unfinished so the king would want to hear the ending the next day.
The answer is hidden in the book's title.
questions.description: The greatest procrastinator in history, and it actually worked out for her.
questions.fun_fact: The stories of Aladdin and Ali Baba weren't in the old Arabic manuscripts: a French translator added them about 300 years ago.

questions.question: What is the corner-store game where you toss metal disks into the holes of a wooden table?
hints: It's played a lot in small-town stores and courts, often right next to tejo.
The hole worth the most points is in the mouth of a little metal figure.
The figure is a green animal that hops and goes “ribbit.”
questions.description: An aiming game so corner-store that it practically comes with a soda.
questions.fun_fact: In Peru it's played almost the same way, but there they call it “el sapo” (the toad).

questions.question: In tejo, little “mechas” are placed around the bocín. What are the mechas made of?
hints: They sit on the edge of the bocín, in the clay pit.
When the tejo hits one, the whole place knows it from the noise.
They hold the same stuff as the totes and voladores of December.
questions.description: Colombia's national sport: throwing a metal disc into a pit of clay and celebrating like it's a goal.
questions.fun_fact: Mechas are small triangles, and setting one off scores more points than just landing near the bocín.

questions.question: In which month is the Feria de Cali held, with its famous parade of salsa dancers?
hints: It's a time of year when many Colombians are on vacation.
In this month, many homes fill up with lights and nativity scenes.
It starts on the 25th and ends before the year is over.
questions.description: In Cali, people dance salsa so fast that their shoes ask for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Cali began in 1957 and today opens with the Salsódromo, a parade with hundreds of salsa dancers.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this old invention called?
hints: Over 100 years ago, families had one at home for entertainment.
Many worked without electricity: you wound them up with a crank.
You set a black disc spinning and the music came out of that big horn.
questions.description: Your great-grandparents kept it in the living room and treated it better than the cat.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, gramophone records weren't made of vinyl but of shellac, a material that comes from an insect.

questions.question: Before the electric light bulb, what wax object with a wick did people use to light their homes at night?
hints: People still use it at home when the power goes out.
It slowly melts, little by little, while it gives light.
Your birthday cake has one for every year you turn.
questions.description: A dark time in history… and we mean really, truly dark.
questions.fun_fact: Thomas Edison ran thousands of tests with different materials before he made a light bulb that could stay lit for many hours.

questions.question: Which ghost of the Llanos legends is very tall and skinny, roams the plains at night, and carries his own father's bones in a sack?
hints: It's a legend from the Llanos Orientales, which Colombia shares with Venezuela.
They say that if you hear him close by, he's actually far away.
His name comes from a sound he makes with his lips.
questions.description: A traveler of the plains who never goes empty-handed, though you'd better hope he doesn't show you what he's carrying.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says El Silbón whistles the notes do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, which is why hearing someone whistle the scale on the plains at night is so frightening.

questions.question: In which track and field event did Caterine Ibargüen win gold at the Rio 2016 Olympics?
hints: It's a jumping event where you land in a sand pit.
Before landing in the sand, you make several bounds in a row: hop, step and jump.
The event's name tells you how many jumps you make: three.
questions.description: Jumping on the bed doesn't count as Olympic training, no matter how hard you try.
questions.fun_fact: Four years earlier, at London 2012, Caterine had already won silver in the same event.

questions.question: Who was the first Colombian woman to win an Olympic gold medal?
hints: She did it at the Sydney Olympics in 2000.
Her sport is all about lifting very, very heavy bars.
She's a weightlifter from Valle del Cauca who later became a member of Congress.
questions.description: Before her, Colombia kept its gold medals in the same place as the unicorns.
questions.fun_fact: That gold at Sydney 2000 was also Colombia's first Olympic gold ever, counting both men and women.

questions.question: What is the largest pyramid in the world by volume (all the space it takes up)?
hints: It's not the tallest, but it's the “chubbiest”: its base is huge.
It's not in Egypt, but in the Americas.
It's in the state of Puebla, Mexico, and today it looks like a hill with a church on top.
questions.description: This time the prize doesn't go to the tallest kid in class, but to the one who takes up the most room on the bus.
questions.fun_fact: The Pyramid of Cholula is covered in earth and grass and has a church built on top, so for centuries many people thought it was just an ordinary hill.

questions.question: What is the longest mountain range on land in the world (not counting those under the sea)?
hints: It runs along one whole side of a continent, from north to south.
The Inca lived there, and llamas and alpacas still graze there today.
In Colombia, it splits into three ranges: the Western, the Central and the Eastern.
questions.description: A line of mountains so long that, if it were the line at the bank, nobody would ever reach the teller.
questions.fun_fact: The Andes are about 7,000 km (4,300 miles) long, and they are still slowly growing because two of Earth's plates push against each other beneath them.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this meat-eating plant called?
hints: In the wild, it grows only in a few swamps in the United States.
Its leaves look like a mouth with teeth and snap shut when an insect touches them.
Its name includes a planet and tells you what it catches.
questions.description: A plant that ordered food delivery, and lunch flew right in.
questions.fun_fact: So it doesn't waste energy on false alarms, the trap only closes if an insect touches its tiny trigger hairs twice within a few seconds.

questions.question: Which river plunges over the famous Tequendama Falls, in Cundinamarca?
hints: It starts in a páramo in Cundinamarca, in the town of Villapinzón.
Before reaching the falls, it flows past the country's biggest city.
It has the same name as Colombia's capital.
questions.description: A river that dives headfirst from over 100 meters up and doesn't even scream.
questions.fun_fact: Tequendama Falls is about 157 m (515 ft) high, and the old mansion next to it is now a museum.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of the river that flows under this famous bridge?
hints: This river ends in the North Sea.
It's the river of London, the capital of England.
Its name starts with “Th…”.
questions.description: A bridge that throws its arms in the air like someone just scored a goal.
questions.fun_fact: Tower Bridge opens in the middle to let tall ships through, and it still does so hundreds of times a year.

questions.question: In which year did Colombia's senior national team win its first Copa América, playing at home?
hints: That year, Colombia hosted the tournament.
The final was in Bogotá against Mexico, and Colombia won 1–0.
It was the first year of the 21st century.
questions.description: A year when the whole country shouted so loud that the neighbors in Panama asked for some quiet.
questions.fun_fact: In that Copa América, Colombia won all six of its matches without letting in a single goal.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this stadium, the usual home of Colombia's national team in World Cup qualifiers?
hints: Visiting teams don't like playing there because of the heat and humidity.
It's on the Caribbean coast, near where the Magdalena River meets the sea.
It's in Barranquilla and is named after a Barranquilla-born soccer player, Roberto Meléndez.
questions.description: Thousands of fans shouting at once: here even your eardrums break a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: Many visiting teams complain about Barranquilla's heat and humidity, which is why the national team prefers to play its most important games there.

questions.question: Which player is this? A Colombian midfielder with a huge curly blond mane, famous for his magical passes and for barely running.
hints: He was the national team's great idol in the 1990s.
He wore the number 10 shirt and played at the 1990, 1994 and 1998 World Cups.
He is from Santa Marta, and everyone knows him as “el Pibe.”
questions.description: No barber ever dared to touch this hairdo.
questions.fun_fact: In Santa Marta, his hometown, there is a giant bronze statue of el Pibe, mane and all.

questions.question: In Colombia, on which day is the Day of the Holy Innocents, when people play pranks on each other?
hints: It is not the same day as April Fools' Day in the United States.
It falls in the middle of the end-of-year holidays.
It comes a few days after Christmas and before New Year's Day.
questions.description: If someone tells you today that school has been canceled forever, check the calendar first.
questions.fun_fact: The pranks played on that day are called “inocentadas”, and in some countries even newspapers print fake joke news stories.

questions.question: Lechona, the famous stuffed pig, is a typical dish of which Colombian department?
hints: It's a department in the center of the country, with no coastline.
The Magdalena River crosses its hot, flat lowlands, and its mountains have a snow-capped volcano.
Its capital is Ibagué, the “Musical Capital of Colombia.”
questions.description: A pig that showed up to the party full of itself. Literally.
questions.fun_fact: A big lechona can feed more than 50 people, which is why it rules at family parties.

questions.question: In which present-day country was Tetris, the game where you fit falling blocks together, invented in 1984?
hints: It wasn't invented at a video game company, but at a computer research center.
The first Tetris ran on a computer so simple it had no graphics: the blocks were drawn with letters and symbols.
The inventor worked in Moscow, in what was then the Soviet Union.
questions.description: The one game where tidying up is fun, something your mom never managed with your bedroom.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Tetris tune on the Game Boy is an old Russian folk song called “Korobeiniki.”

questions.question: Which video game character is this? A round pink ball from Nintendo that sucks in enemies, swallows them and copies their powers.
hints: Its first game came out in 1992 on the Game Boy.
Besides swallowing enemies, it can puff up like a balloon to fly.
Its name starts with K.
questions.description: A piece of pink bubble gum with endless hunger and zero table manners.
questions.fun_fact: On the box of Kirby's first game in the United States, he was drawn white, because the Game Boy couldn't show colors.

questions.question: What is the largest tributary of the Magdalena River, the one that gives it the most water?
hints: It rises in the Colombian Massif, very close to where the Magdalena itself begins.
It runs from south to north through the valley where Cali lies.
It has the same name as the department whose capital is Popayán.
questions.description: Even Colombia's biggest river needs a friend to help carry the water.
questions.fun_fact: The Cauca and the Magdalena run almost parallel for more than 1,000 km (620 miles), separated by the Cordillera Central, and only meet near Mompox.

questions.question: What is the longest river in Africa?
hints: It crosses a huge desert before it reaches the Mediterranean Sea.
The ancient Egyptians lived along its banks.
The pyramids and the pharaohs depended on it for water and crops.
questions.description: A river so long that if you paddle it in a canoe, you'll grow a beard on the way, even if you can't grow one.
questions.fun_fact: The Nile runs about 6,650 km (4,130 miles) through 11 countries, and for thousands of years its floods made Egypt's fields fertile.

questions.question: Which European river flows through more countries than any other river in the world, ten in total?
hints: It starts in Germany and flows into the Black Sea.
It passes through Vienna, the capital of Austria, and Budapest, the capital of Hungary.
A very famous waltz is named after it, with the word “blue” in its title.
questions.description: This river has more passport stamps than an airline pilot.
questions.fun_fact: The Danube flows through four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, more than any other river in the world.

questions.question: Which Marvel character is this? He's a scientist who turns into a super-strong green giant when he gets angry.
hints: He's one of the Avengers.
When he changes, his shirt rips to pieces, but his pants almost always survive.
When he's calm, his name is Bruce Banner.
questions.description: This guy has a serious temper problem, and it costs him a fortune in clothes.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comic, in 1962, Hulk was gray, but he was made green because the printer had trouble printing that color well.

questions.question: In the Marvel movies, what metal is Captain America's round shield made of?
hints: It's a made-up metal that doesn't exist in real life.
It can soak up hits and vibrations with almost no damage.
Black Panther's suit is made of this same metal.
questions.description: If this shield were made of cardboard, Captain America's career would have been very short.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comic, from 1941, Captain America's shield wasn't round: it was shaped like a knight's shield, pointed at the bottom.

questions.question: Thor, Iron Man and Black Widow: what do they have in common?
wrong_answers: They are in the Fantastic Four
They are in the Justice League
hints: All three are from Marvel and work on the same team.
Hulk and Captain America are on that team too.
Their battle cry is “___ Assemble!”
questions.description: Three people who are never on time for lunch because the world always needs saving.
questions.fun_fact: Captain America wasn't in this team's first comic in 1963: he only joined in issue 4.

questions.question: In the Marvel movies, what is the name of Black Panther's hidden, high-tech African kingdom?
hints: From the outside it looks like a poor farming country, but inside it is pure technology.
Its people say goodbye by crossing their arms over their chest.
Its famous cry is “___ forever!”
questions.description: A country so well hidden that not even Google Maps knows where it is.
questions.fun_fact: This kingdom first appeared in 1966 in a Fantastic Four comic, the same one where Black Panther made his debut.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this colorful painted wooden vehicle, typical of Colombian towns, called?
hints: It has ladders on the outside to climb up to the roof, where bags and sacks are loaded.
In many cities you can rent one for parties, with music and people dancing inside.
Its name is also the Spanish word for a goat.
questions.description: A bus that went out partying and never got serious again.
questions.fun_fact: In small towns, the chiva carries all sorts of things on its roof: sacks of coffee, bunches of plantains, and sometimes even chickens.

questions.question: What is Colombian Christmas natilla made from?
hints: It's almost always eaten next to buñuelos.
It's cooked in a pot and stirred nonstop until it gets thick.
It has a dark brown sugarcane sweet and a white powder that comes from corn.
questions.description: The dessert that shakes with fear every December because it knows it's about to be eaten.
questions.fun_fact: In many homes, natilla is stirred for a long time in a big paila, and you can't stop stirring or it sticks to the pan.

questions.question: Which video game character is this? A blue robot boy built by the kind Dr. Light, with a cannon arm that copies each defeated boss's weapon.
hints: His first game came out in 1987 for the Nintendo NES console.
He was created by the Japanese company Capcom, and his great enemy is the evil Dr. Wily.
His name puts a word for “huge” in front of a word for “guy”.
questions.description: A robot with a simple shopping plan: beat the villain, then take his weapon home for free.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan he is called Rockman, and his robot sister is called Roll: together they make “Rock and Roll”.

questions.question: In the Pokémon video games, what does Pikachu evolve into when you give it a Thunder Stone?
hints: It is bigger than Pikachu and orange.
It can't be Pichu: that's the form before Pikachu, not after.
Its name starts with “Rai”, which has to do with thunder in Japanese.
questions.description: What happens when an electric mouse decides it's time to start going to the gym.
questions.fun_fact: In the cartoon series, Ash's Pikachu refuses to use a Thunder Stone because it wants to stay a Pikachu.

questions.question: In the Super Mario games, which princess does Bowser kidnap again and again for Mario to rescue?
hints: She is the princess of the Mushroom Kingdom.
She wears a pink dress and a golden crown.
She shares her name with a soft, fuzzy fruit.
questions.description: The princess with the worst security system in the whole kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: In the game “Super Princess Peach,” the roles are reversed: she is the hero and has to rescue Mario.

questions.question: In the original 1980 Pac-Man, how many ghosts chase Pac-Man around the maze?
hints: They come out of a little house in the middle of the maze.
Each one is a different color.
They are red, pink, light blue and orange.
questions.description: Eating dots in a maze would be a very relaxing job if it weren't for these neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The ghosts are called Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde, and each one chases you in its own way: the red one comes straight at you.

questions.question: In the rainforests of Colombia, this animal is called a saíno. It looks like a wild pig, but it isn't one. What group does it really belong to?
hints: This group lives only in the Americas, from the southern United States down to Argentina.
They look like pigs, but their family split off from pigs millions of years ago.
Scientists also call this group tayassuids.
questions.description: It has the face of a pig, the smell of cheap perfume and zero interest in being mistaken for one.
questions.fun_fact: The saíno has a gland on its back that gives off a strong smell, and the herd uses it to recognize each other.

questions.question: What does Nuuk, the name of Greenland's capital, mean in Greenlandic?
hints: The name has to do with the shape of the land where the city stands.
The city sits at the tip of a peninsula, between fjords that reach into the sea.
It's the same kind of place as Good Hope at the tip of Africa or Horn at the tip of South America.
questions.description: A capital with a name so short it fits inside an igloo.
questions.fun_fact: Nuuk used to be called Godthåb, a Danish name meaning “Good Hope.”

questions.question: In Colombia, what are people called who talk with “ajá”, “eche” and “¡qué nota!”?
hints: They're named after the region of Colombia they come from.
They live near the Caribbean Sea, where it's hot all year.
The word comes from “costa”.
questions.description: In this region “ajá” works as a greeting, a question, a complaint and a yes, all at once.
questions.fun_fact: Costeños often “swallow” the s at the end of words, so “los cocos” can sound like “lo' coco'”.

questions.question: Which of these words is NOT another name for the person who directs the players from the sideline?
hints: Three of the words name the same person on the bench.
The odd word out names someone who also runs around the field but plays for neither team.
This person carries a whistle and yellow and red cards.
questions.description: The only person in the stadium who gets paid to yell at people without being sent off.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, soccer coaches are also called “profe” (short for teacher), even though they don't teach at any school.

questions.question: I'm a university in Bogotá named after the first president of the State of Cundinamarca, in 1811. Which one am I?
hints: My name is a person's full name.
That founding father was the son of the Marquis of San Jorge.
Many people just call me “la Tadeo”.
questions.description: A founding father who, instead of a statue, got thousands of students with ID cards.
questions.fun_fact: The university bearing his name was founded in Bogotá in 1954, almost 140 years after his presidency.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says the university was founded in 1954, "almost 140 years" after the 1811 presidency, but that gap is 143 years, so it should say "more than 140 years". The translation copies this faithfully, so the source needs correcting. Also from the source: the question says the university is named after a person, and only the answer is a person's full name, so the options give it away (hint 1 says so outright). Consider replacing a wrong answer with a university named after a person (e.g. Universidad Sergio Arboleda).

Source: the fun fact says the university was founded "almost 140 years" after Lozano's 1811 presidency, but 1954 − 1811 = 143 years, so it should say "more than 140 years". The error is in the Spanish source ("casi 140 años"), so the source needs the fix first. The translation itself is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: They built the great pyramid of Chichén Itzá, and their languages are still spoken in Mexico and Guatemala. Who are they?
hints: They wrote with glyphs, little pictures that stood for words and sounds.
They used zero long before the Europeans did.
Their name is also the name of a famous cartoon bee.
questions.description: Neighbors who kept track of the days better than the calendar on your fridge.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya were using zero in their math more than 1,500 years ago, long before it was known in Europe.

questions.question: Scandinavia, in northern Europe, is the land of Vikings, fjords and northern lights. Which three countries make it up?
hints: All three are kingdoms that still have kings and queens.
Their languages are so alike that people there can almost understand each other.
One inspired the landscapes of “Frozen”, and another is the home of LEGO.
questions.description: A region so serious about the cold that even the furniture comes flat-packed in a box.
questions.fun_fact: Norwegians, Swedes and Danes can understand each other quite well while each speaks their own language.

questions.question: This huge palace in Beijing, the Forbidden City, was built in the early 15th century. Which emperor ordered it built?
hints: He belonged to the Ming dynasty.
He was the one who moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing.
His reign name means “perpetual happiness.”
questions.description: A palace with so many rooms that getting lost in it was almost an imperial tradition.
questions.fun_fact: The Forbidden City was home to 24 emperors of China for almost 500 years.

questions.question: “The Sabana is to Bogotá as the Valle de Aburrá is to…”. Which city completes the sentence?
hints: It's a city in Antioquia.
A river with the same name as the city runs along the bottom of that valley.
It's the city of the Metrocable and the Feria de las Flores.
questions.description: A city tucked into a giant cooking pot, but a pretty one, with mountains for a lid.
questions.fun_fact: The Valle de Aburrá isn't home to just one city: ten municipalities share it, joined in one metropolitan area.

questions.question: It's called the “lily of the Incas,” and its petals have little stripes that look hand-painted. What is this flower called in Colombia?
hints: It's native to South America and grown in huge numbers on the Sabana de Bogotá and in Antioquia.
It's very common in the bouquets sold in supermarkets and flower shops.
Its name sounds a bit like “astro,” as in the stars.
questions.description: A flower named after a Swedish baron and an Andean empire, both at once.
questions.fun_fact: Cut astromelias can last about two weeks in a vase, which is why florists love them.

questions.question: In Colombia, what one word covers voladores, totes and luces de bengala?
hints: It makes a lot of noise and fills the sky with lights.
Kids should never handle it, because it can burn.
It's also the Spanish word for gunpowder.
questions.description: The reason every dog in the neighborhood hides under the bed in December.
questions.fun_fact: Gunpowder was invented in China more than a thousand years ago.

questions.question: You're reading the menu at a juice stand on Colombia's coast. Which of these names is NOT a fruit?
hints: Three grow on a tree or plant; the other comes out of the blender.
The odd one out is served cold and has milk in it.
It's made by blending guanábana (soursop) with milk and sugar.
questions.description: One of these names snuck into the fruit bowl, but it really came in a glass.
questions.fun_fact: Guanábana champola is typical of Colombia's Caribbean coast, and Cuba has a drink with the same name.

questions.question: In which decade did George Eastman launch the first Kodak camera, with the slogan “You press the button, we do the rest”?
hints: It was in the same century that photography was invented.
Around those years, the telephone and Edison's light bulb also appeared.
The 20th century was only a little more than ten years away.
questions.description: Before phone cameras, taking a photo was an act of faith: you waited days to find out if your eyes were closed.
questions.fun_fact: The 1888 Kodak camera came loaded with film for 100 photos, and you had to mail the whole camera back to the factory to get them developed.

questions.question: Look at this old light bulb: which part gets so hot that it glows and gives off light?
hints: It sits in the middle, inside the glass ball.
It is a very thin metal thread.
When a bulb burns out, it's usually because this part broke.
questions.description: A gadget that spends its whole life shining, until one day it goes “tink” and falls asleep forever.
questions.fun_fact: The filaments in today's incandescent bulbs are made of tungsten, a metal that can take more than 3,000 °C (5,400 °F) without melting.

questions.question: I'm “en passant”, a special chess move that many people don't know. Which pieces take part in me?
hints: It's the only capture in chess where the capturing piece doesn't land on the square of the piece it takes.
It can only happen right after an enemy piece moves two squares on its first move.
They are the same pieces that can be promoted when they reach the far end of the board.
questions.description: A move so rare that many players think their opponent is cheating.
questions.fun_fact: “En passant” is French for “in passing”, and the chance lasts only one turn: if you don't take it right away, it's gone for good.

questions.question: In Monopoly, you run out of cash and mortgage a property that cost you $200. Under the classic rules, how much does the bank give you?
hints: The bank doesn't give back everything you paid.
The mortgage value is printed on the back of the title deed card.
It's exactly half the price.
questions.description: For when you run out of cash and pawn your streets to the bank like an old phone.
questions.fun_fact: While a property is mortgaged you can't collect rent on it, and to get it back you must pay the bank the mortgage plus 10% interest.

questions.question: Each player hides their dice under a cup and bets how many dice on the table show the same number. What is the game called?
hints: Pirates play it in “Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest”.
When you don't believe someone's bet, you call out “Dudo!”, Spanish for “I doubt it”.
Its name sounds like a South American country famous for Machu Picchu.
questions.description: A game where lying with a straight face is part of the rules, not a problem.
questions.fun_fact: It is also known as “Liar's Dice”, and it is said to come from the Inca Empire.

questions.question: In ancient Greece, one athlete ran, jumped, threw the discus and javelin, and wrestled. What was this contest called?
hints: Count on your fingers how many events the athlete had to do.
The Greek prefix in the name means the same number as the sides of a pentagon.
Penta- = five.
questions.description: When one sport wasn't enough to show off, the Greeks invented the full combo.
questions.fun_fact: In the long jump of the ancient pentathlon, athletes jumped holding stone or metal weights in their hands to push themselves farther.

questions.question: Walking under a ladder, a black cat crossing your path and opening an umbrella indoors: what do they have in common?
questions.answer: Superstitions say they bring bad luck
wrong_answers: Superstitions say they bring good luck
hints: People who avoid them don't do it for safety, but out of belief.
People say the same thing about Friday the 13th.
The opposite of a lucky charm.
questions.description: Your aunt has more rules for leaving the house than the school has for recess.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody knows for sure where the superstition about not walking under a ladder came from, though there are many theories about its origin.

questions.question: People hang me on their keychains for good luck, and I come from an animal that hops instead of walking. What am I?
hints: I'm not made of metal, and I'm not a plant.
The animal I come from has long ears.
Bugs Bunny would never carry me around.
questions.description: Everyone's favorite lucky charm, except for its original owner.
questions.fun_fact: In folk tradition, the luckiest foot of all was the rabbit's left hind foot.

questions.question: “Half man, half horse” is to centaur as “half woman, half fish” is to…
hints: She lives in the sea, but she is a creature from legends.
In the stories, she sings beautifully to lure sailors.
Ariel, from the Disney movie, is one of them.
questions.description: A singer who never goes on tour because she has no feet.
questions.fun_fact: When Christopher Columbus saw manatees in the Caribbean, he wrote that he had seen mermaids, but that they were not as pretty as people painted them!

questions.question: Coral reefs are built by millions of tiny polyps like the ones in the photo. Which group of animals do they belong to?
hints: They are not plants or rocks: they are real animals.
They have tentacles with stinging cells to catch their food.
They are close relatives of jellyfish and sea anemones.
questions.description: Animals so small that, to get anyone to notice them, they had to build something you can see from space.
questions.fun_fact: Australia's Great Barrier Reef, built by polyps, is the largest structure made by living things in the world and can be seen from space.

questions.question: In what year did James score his famous chest-and-volley goal against Uruguay that sent Colombia to the World Cup quarterfinals?
hints: It was at a World Cup where James finished as the top scorer.
That World Cup was played in South America, in Colombia's biggest neighbor.
It was the same World Cup where Germany beat Brazil 7–1.
questions.description: Some goals get celebrated once, and some your dad keeps celebrating at every family lunch.
questions.fun_fact: That goal won FIFA's Puskás Award for the best goal of 2014.

questions.question: How old was Linda Caicedo when she scored a stunning goal against Germany at the 2023 Women's World Cup?
hints: She was one of the youngest players on the team.
The year before, she also played in both the U-17 and U-20 World Cups.
She had only just reached voting age in Colombia.
questions.description: At that age, some people are just learning to brew a tinto, and others are already scoring at World Cups.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia beat Germany 2–1 in that match, with a header by Manuela Vanegas in the final seconds.

questions.question: Listen: Clara Schumann, a German child prodigy, became famous all over Europe playing this instrument. What is it?
hints: You play it sitting down, using both hands at once.
It has lots of keys.
Its keys are black and white.
questions.description: She was giving concerts at nine; at that age you were still losing your gloves.
questions.fun_fact: Clara Schumann's face appeared on Germany's 100 Deutsche Mark banknote.

questions.question: In the classic cartoon “The Rabbit of Seville,” Bugs Bunny is to the barber as who is to the customer who gets shaved and styled against his will?
hints: He’s a Looney Tunes character.
He’s a hunter who is always chasing the rabbit.
He’s bald and can’t say his R’s, so “rabbit” comes out as “wabbit.”
questions.description: A cartoon where a trip to the barber turns into an opera, and the opera turns into a disaster.
questions.fun_fact: The cartoon uses the music from Rossini’s opera “The Barber of Seville,” which he is said to have written in less than three weeks.

questions.question: During a “red tide”, the sea looks reddish. Where does that color come from?
hints: The color comes from something alive.
They are too small to see with the naked eye, but millions of them together paint the water.
It's a kind of microscopic sea plant that multiplies like crazy.
questions.description: The sea blushes too, but not because it's embarrassed.
questions.fun_fact: Some of these microscopic algae make toxic substances, so during a red tide eating shellfish from the area is sometimes banned.

questions.question: If you tie a polystyrene foam cup to an underwater robot and send it down more than 6,000 m (19,700 ft), what happens to it?
questions.answer: It shrinks into a tiny cup
wrong_answers: It bursts into a thousand bits
It puffs up like a balloon
hints: Think about all the weight of the water above the cup.
The pressure down there is hundreds of times greater than at the surface.
Polystyrene foam is full of tiny air bubbles, and the pressure squashes them.
questions.description: Down there, the water squeezes harder than a hug from Grandma.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists on deep-sea trips often decorate foam cups and send them to the bottom, and they come back as souvenirs the size of a thimble.

questions.question: In deep-sea anglerfish like Ceratias holboelli, the male lives attached to the female. Up to how many times longer than him can she be?
hints: The difference is huge, much bigger than between a big dog and a small one.
The male is so tiny that he stays stuck to the female for the rest of his life.
If the female were the size of a car, the male would be the size of a finger.
questions.description: A marriage where one partner takes “clingy” to a whole new level.
questions.fun_fact: In some deep-sea anglerfish the male fuses with the female until they share blood, and one female can carry several males attached to her.

questions.question: In the morning you build a sandcastle at low tide, when the water is farthest out. About how many hours until the next low tide?
hints: The tide goes up and down more than once in the same day.
Most beaches have two low tides a day.
It's roughly half a day.
questions.description: The sea keeps office hours: it leaves, comes back, and leaves again.
questions.fun_fact: Tides come about 50 minutes later each day because they follow the rhythm of the Moon, not the Sun.

questions.question: Which country has this long, narrow shape, stretching more than 4,000 km (2,500 miles) from north to south?
hints: It is in South America, along the Pacific Ocean.
The Andes mountains separate it from its neighbor to the east.
Its capital is Santiago.
questions.description: If this country were a spaghetti noodle, it would be the longest one on the plate.
questions.fun_fact: Chile has one of the driest deserts in the world, the Atacama, and also glaciers in the south.

questions.question: In which century did the Roman general Pompey clear the pirates out of the Mediterranean Sea?
hints: It was during the Roman Republic, before Rome had emperors.
Pompey was a rival of Julius Caesar.
It was just a few decades before the birth of Christ.
questions.description: Before streaming, Romans kept busy chasing pirates all over the Mediterranean.
questions.fun_fact: A few years earlier, a young Julius Caesar was kidnapped by pirates and, offended, told them to ask for a bigger ransom for him.

questions.question: Which of these people is not from Colombia's Andean region?
hints: The odd one out lives near the sea, not in the mountains.
Their department is one of the rainiest places in the world.
Its capital is Quibdó.
questions.description: A family photo where somebody clearly wandered into the wrong picture.
questions.fun_fact: Chocó is one of the rainiest places on Earth: in some areas it rains almost every day of the year.

questions.question: Listen: which bird makes this sound?
hints: It is a completely black bird.
Its call sounds like a deep “kraa, kraa!”.
In Norse myths, the god Odin had two of these birds, called Huginn and Muninn, that flew around the world and brought him news.
questions.description: A bird that's a genius in science and a villain in fairy tales.
questions.fun_fact: Ravens are so clever that they can remember a person's face for years.

questions.question: What is the flesh of the zapote like?
questions.answer: Orange and fibrous, with large seeds
wrong_answers: White and creamy, with black seeds
Yellow and jelly-like, with small seeds
Red and watery, with small black seeds
hints: It grows on a tree in hot climates.
On the outside it has a rough, greenish-brown skin.
Its flesh is about the color of a tangerine.
questions.description: It looks like a rough brown rock on the outside, but it's one of the sweetest things at the market.
questions.fun_fact: Zapote flesh is so fibrous that eating it leaves little threads stuck between your teeth.

questions.question: Taken literally, what is a «tusa»?
questions.answer: The empty core of an ear of corn
wrong_answers: The peel of a green plantain
The large seed of an avocado
The hard stone of a mango
hints: Karol G and Nicki Minaj used it in a song about heartbreak, but here we mean the literal thing.
You throw it away after eating, and it comes from a plant whose food grows wrapped in leaves.
It's what's left in your hand when you finish a grilled ear from a street cart in the park.
questions.description: A word that works just as well for a broken heart as for Grandma's kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: That's why Colombians say someone «está con la tusa»: they're left empty, like the cob after all the kernels have been eaten.

questions.question: Complete: Grupo Niche is to “Cali pachanguero” as Fruko y sus Tesos is to…
hints: The song was recorded by the Discos Fuentes label from Medellín.
It was sung by Wilson “Saoko” Manyoma, in a mournful voice.
It tells the story of someone locked up in a jail.
questions.description: A classic danced so often in December that it should have its own ID card and a pension by now.
questions.fun_fact: The great Joe Arroyo began his career singing with Fruko y sus Tesos before starting his own orchestra.

questions.question: In which city, near where the Magdalena River reaches the sea, is the Estadio Romelio Martínez?
hints: Every year the queen of a very famous festival is crowned there.
It was home to the team nicknamed “el Tiburón” (the Shark) until 1986.
It's the city of the Batalla de Flores and the Marimonda.
questions.description: A veteran stadium that has seen more goals and more queens than any other in the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Junior left the Romelio Martínez when the Estadio Metropolitano, one of Colombia's biggest stadiums, opened.

questions.question: Near Lake Maracaibo, the Catatumbo lightning flashes almost every night in the same spot. What did sailors use it for?
questions.answer: As a lighthouse to find their way
wrong_answers: As a clock to tell the time
As a warning of a hurricane
As a sign that pirates were near
hints: Think about what a ship needs when everything is dark.
What makes it useful is that the flashes always appear in the same spot and can be seen from very far away.
Sailors named it after the towers with lights that stand on coasts.
questions.description: A storm that works overtime almost every night of the year and never asks for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The Catatumbo lightning can produce thousands of flashes in a single night, and from far away you can hardly hear the thunder.

questions.question: I'm a saying grandmas repeat when troubles are finally over. I start like this: “After the storm comes the…”. What word do I end with?
hints: Think about how everything feels when the storm finally goes away.
It also describes a sea with no waves and no wind.
It rhymes with “palm” and means peace and quiet.
questions.description: A saying for days when everything goes wrong… until it stops going wrong.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages share this saying, and Spanish has an equally famous version: “After the storm, the sun comes out.”

questions.question: What is the outermost layer of the atmosphere called, where the air fades into space and some atoms escape?
hints: It is much higher up than where airplanes fly.
It begins above the height where the International Space Station circles Earth.
Its name starts with a Greek prefix that means “outside.”
questions.description: The top floor of Earth's air: no railings, but a great view of space.
questions.fun_fact: By some definitions, the exosphere reaches up to about 10,000 km (6,200 mi), only about 3% of the way to the Moon.

questions.question: What do you call a river mouth that splits into many branches and forms a triangle, like the Nile's?
hints: The same word is also used in math and physics.
It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.
It is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet: alpha, beta, gamma…
questions.description: A river so long that by the end it gets tired and spreads out like a fan.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek historian Herodotus called the mouth of the Nile a “delta” because it looked like the Greek letter Δ.

questions.question: At a Colombian quinceañera, costumed characters suddenly burst in with whistles, foam, lights and giant hats. What has just started?
hints: It usually comes late at night, when the party is already heating up.
There are stilts, masks, glow necklaces and music at full blast.
Its name says that for a while everyone goes a little crazy.
questions.description: The moment of the party when even Grandpa puts on a colorful hat.
questions.fun_fact: The hora loca is so popular at Colombian parties that some companies do nothing but run it.

questions.question: In a mango, mesocarp is to flesh as… what is to skin?
hints: It is a layer of the fruit, not of the seed.
The prefix means “on” or “over”, as in “epidermis”.
It is the outermost layer of the fruit: epi-…
questions.description: Peeling a fruit is easy; giving a scientific name to the part you throw away is another story.
questions.fun_fact: All three layers together (epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp) make up the pericarp, the whole wall of the fruit.

questions.question: A mule is to a mare and a donkey as the atemoya is to the cherimoya and… which other fruit?
hints: The two fruits in the mix are cousins: same family, white flesh and black seeds.
The other mom is small and green, with skin covered in little scales.
Elsewhere it's called saramuyo or sugar apple; in Colombia its name has just four letters and sounds like “anona”.
questions.description: A fruit with two moms and zero family drama.
questions.fun_fact: The atemoya was first bred on purpose in Florida in the early 1900s (around 1907), and its name blends “ate” (another name for the anón) with “cherimoya”.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a tower with a metal ring on top, and Nikola Tesla invented me. What am I for?
wrong_answers: Cooling the air in a room
hints: My inventor worked with electricity his whole life.
When I'm switched on, I give off sparks that look like lightning.
My bolts jump through the air because the electricity I make pushes with enormous force.
questions.description: An invention that makes even the most bored parents at a museum pull out their phones to film it.
questions.fun_fact: Some Tesla coils can “sing”: by changing the rhythm of their sparks, they play tunes you can hear in the air.

questions.question: Mario is Nintendo’s mascot, just as the man with a white mustache, a top hat and a cane is the mascot of…
hints: It’s a game where you can win lots of money… but only pretend money.
In it, you buy streets, build little houses and hotels, and collect rent.
Land on the wrong square and you go straight to jail.
questions.description: A man so rich he never takes off his top hat, not even to sleep.
questions.fun_fact: The Monopoly man first went by the name “Rich Uncle Pennybags” and only became officially known as “Mr. Monopoly” in 1999.

questions.question: Take a close look at this ball: which Olympic sport is it used in?
hints: In this sport you can't catch the ball, only hit it.
