The teams are split by a high net.
It's also played on the sand at the beach.
questions.description: A ball with more stitches than your school uniform after recess.
questions.fun_fact: Volleyball was invented in 1895 in the United States and was first called “mintonette”.

questions.question: At the ancient Greek Olympic Games, winners got a crown of branches instead of medals. Which tree were the branches from?
hints: It was a tree sacred to the goddess Athena.
It's a typical Mediterranean tree with silvery leaves.
Its fruit gives an oil that is very famous in cooking.
questions.description: A prize you couldn't keep in a display case, because it dried up in a few weeks.
questions.fun_fact: At the Athens 2004 Olympics, winners also received olive crowns, as a tribute to the ancient Games.

questions.question: The ancient Olympic Games had races with two-wheeled chariots. Which animals pulled them?
hints: They had to be very fast animals.
People still race them today at racetracks.
They neigh.
questions.description: The Formula 1 of the ancient world, but with no fuel and no pit stops.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient chariot races the prize went to the owner of the horses, not the driver, which is how a Spartan princess, Cynisca, became the first woman to win at Olympia.

questions.question: Every year, more than a million wildebeest, zebras and gazelles travel in a big loop through the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara. Why?
questions.answer: To follow the rains and fresh grass
wrong_answers: To escape fires on the savanna
To look for salt in the mountains
To find shade in the rainforest
hints: The African savanna has dry seasons and rainy seasons.
Wildebeest are plant-eaters and eat a huge amount every day.
Where it rains, the food they need starts to grow.
questions.description: More than a million travelers with no suitcases, no GPS and no stops for gas.
questions.fun_fact: During the migration, hundreds of thousands of wildebeest calves are born within a few weeks, and they can walk just minutes after birth.

questions.question: Its name comes from a Russian word meaning “white.” What is this Arctic whale called?
hints: It lives in icy waters near the North Pole.
Sailors called it the “canary of the sea” because of its whistles and squeaks.
Its name starts with “Be…” and has three syllables.
questions.description: A Russian name for an animal that has never set foot in Moscow.
questions.fun_fact: Belugas are born gray and slowly turn white as they grow up.

questions.question: Pegasus is to “wings” as Sleipnir, the god Odin's horse, is to…
hints: Sleipnir was the fastest horse in the Norse myths.
It has twice the usual number.
It has as many as a spider.
questions.description: There's no traffic in Asgard, but this taxi still gets you to any of the nine worlds in no time.
questions.fun_fact: According to the myths, Sleipnir's parent was Loki, who had turned himself into a mare.

questions.question: In which city was Antonio Vivaldi, the composer of “The Four Seasons”, born?
hints: It is in northern Italy, on the Adriatic Sea.
It is famous for its carnival of masks.
Instead of streets it has canals, and people get around by gondola.
questions.description: Spring, summer, fall and winter: a musician who never had to go shopping for inspiration.
questions.fun_fact: Vivaldi was called “il Prete Rosso”, the Red Priest, because he was a priest with red hair.

questions.question: Riddle: “In me the story is told through singing, and Mozart used me for The Magic Flute.” What am I?
hints: It mixes music with theater.
Its singers often have very powerful voices, like sopranos and tenors.
La Scala in Milan is world-famous for staging this kind of work.
questions.description: Nobody talks here: if you want someone to pass the salt, you have to sing it.
questions.fun_fact: The Queen of the Night’s aria climbs to a note so high that it’s a challenge even for professional sopranos.

questions.question: Which country is highlighted on this map?
hints: It sits in the southwest corner of Europe, facing the Atlantic Ocean.
People there speak a language very much like the one spoken in Brazil.
Cristiano Ronaldo was born on one of its islands, and its capital is Lisbon.
questions.description: A country that sat down in the corner of Europe, like the student who always asks for the window seat.
questions.fun_fact: The border between Portugal and Spain is one of the oldest in Europe: it has barely changed in more than 700 years.

questions.question: Which of these Spanish forts, built against pirates, is NOT on Colombia's Caribbean coast?
questions.answer: Castillo de San Lorenzo del Chagres
wrong_answers: Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas
Fuerte de San Fernando de Bocachica
Fuerte de San Sebastián del Pastelillo
hints: Three of them are in the same walled Colombian city.
The odd one out guarded the mouth of a river that gold and silver passed through.
That country split from Colombia in 1903.
questions.description: A perfect vacation plan until someone asks: “Wait, did you bring your passport?”
questions.fun_fact: In 1671, the pirate Henry Morgan took the castle of San Lorenzo before crossing the isthmus and sacking Panama City.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: “In Colombia, when someone says they're rolo, it means they're…”
hints: It's an inland city, far from the sea.
Monserrate hill is there.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: A nickname you get for being born in a certain city, no exam required.
questions.fun_fact: On the Caribbean coast, people from the Andean interior, Bogotanos included, are called “cachacos”.

questions.question: On the island of San Andrés, the Raizal people speak Creole. Which language do most of its words come from?
hints: The island is in the Caribbean, very close to Central America.
For centuries the island had more contact with Jamaica than with Bogotá.
It's the language of the songs played most on radio in the United States.
questions.description: An island where even the black land crabs seem bilingual.
questions.fun_fact: On San Andrés you can hear three languages: Creole, Spanish and English.

questions.question: Riddle: “I'm a giant snake sleeping under a school of magic, in the Chamber of Secrets. Anyone who sees my eyes in a reflection is petrified.” What am I?
hints: I appear in the second Harry Potter movie.
Harry defeats me with the sword of Gryffindor.
A real lizard that runs on water shares my name.
questions.description: A reptile with a serious eye-contact problem.
questions.fun_fact: A real lizard called the basilisk runs across water on its back legs, which is why some people call it the “Jesus Christ lizard.”

questions.question: What do Colombians call the small, all-black cousin of the condor that circles over garbage dumps and eats dead animals?
hints: It's not very pretty, but it does a very important cleanup job.
It's black, with a bare gray head, and clears the countryside of dead animals.
Its name starts with “galli…”.
questions.description: Dressed in black, always hanging around the dump, and still nobody tells it to clean up its act.
questions.fun_fact: Gallinazos can eat rotten meat without getting sick thanks to their very acidic stomach juices.

questions.question: What is this building in downtown Bogotá used for?
questions.answer: It's the president's official office and residence
wrong_answers: It's the seat of the Congress of the Republic
It's the seat of Bogotá's city government
It's the seat of the Supreme Court of Justice
hints: The person who runs the country works here, surrounded by their team.
The changing of the presidential guard takes place in front of it.
Whoever wins the election every four years moves in here.
questions.description: A house so well guarded that not even the pizza delivery guy makes it to the door.
questions.fun_fact: The Casa de Nariño stands where Antonio Nariño was born, the independence hero who translated the Rights of Man into Spanish.

questions.question: Which Colombian department has a flag with just two horizontal stripes, white on top and green below?
hints: It's a department in the Andes.
Its capital is famous for the Feria de las Flores and its metro.
It's the land of the paisas and the bandeja paisa.
questions.description: A painting exercise where you only need two colors and a lot of regional pride.
questions.fun_fact: On the Antioquia flag, white stands for purity and green for hope and abundance.

questions.question: In Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, what does the name of the volcano Popocatépetl mean?
hints: The name describes something the volcano does almost all the time.
From Mexico City, you can sometimes see a gray column above it.
Think of what comes out of a chimney.
questions.description: A giant neighbor of Mexico City whose name is a real tongue twister.
questions.fun_fact: Mexicans lovingly call it “Don Goyo,” and it is one of the most active volcanoes in Mexico.

questions.question: What is the name of the camera that shows how hot everything is, with cold things in blue and hot things in yellow?
hints: Firefighters also use it to see through smoke.
It can also find animals hiding in the middle of the night.
Its name shares a root with “thermometer” and with the “thermos” that keeps your coffee hot.
questions.description: A photo where nobody shows up in their real colors, not even the volcano.
questions.fun_fact: With thermal cameras, volcanologists can notice a crater heating up before the volcano erupts.

questions.question: I'm Ryan, from the channel “Ryan's World”. I started on YouTube at age 3 and became the world's top-earning YouTuber. What kind of videos made me famous?
hints: What he did is what any kid does on Christmas morning.
Companies sent him boxes and boxes of stuff to show off.
He opened boxes, took out what was inside, played with it and said if he liked it.
questions.description: A kid who made more money before learning to tie his shoes than your dad will in his whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Forbes magazine named Ryan the world's highest-paid YouTuber in 2018 and 2019, when he was only about 7 or 8 years old.

questions.question: This volcano is Anak Krakatau, the “child of Krakatoa.” In which country is it?
hints: It is in Asia, in a country made up of thousands of islands.
It lies between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The country's capital is Jakarta.
questions.description: Like father, like son: just as explosive.
questions.fun_fact: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard almost 4,800 km (3,000 miles) away, on islands in the Indian Ocean.

questions.question: In 1816, it snowed in June in Europe because of ash from Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia. Roughly how far is it from Europe?
hints: Indonesia is on the other side of the world, in Asia.
No two places on Earth are more than about 20,000 km (12,400 miles) apart.
It's roughly the distance of a flight from New York to Tokyo.
questions.description: You asked for a summer vacation and got a winter, gift-wrapped with a bow.
questions.fun_fact: People called 1816 “the year without a summer”, and the bad weather kept Mary Shelley indoors, where she wrote “Frankenstein”.

questions.question: It's the tiny picture you see before you open a video. YouTubers design it with wild faces and big letters so you click. What is it called?
hints: It's not the channel's profile picture.
Its name is about how small it is.
Its name says it's about as small as a fingernail on your hand.
questions.description: The reason every YouTuber poses with their mouth wide open, as if they'd just seen a ghost.
questions.fun_fact: Long before the internet, artists made quick little drawings called “thumbnail sketches”, because they were barely bigger than a thumbnail.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a huge frog from North America. I was raised on farms in other countries, escaped, and now I eat the frogs there. What kind of species am I?
hints: It's a problem for the wildlife of the place where it arrived.
It's the opposite of a species native to that place.
It's like someone who walks into a stranger's house and takes over everything.
questions.description: A frog with the appetite of a bull and the manners of a guest nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: A bullfrog will eat almost anything that fits in its mouth: insects, fish, other frogs, and even small birds!

questions.question: Fill in the blank: “Heal” is to your scraped knee as ______ is to an axolotl's lost leg.
hints: The word means forming again something that was lost.
Lizards do something similar with their tails.
It starts with “re-” and means growing a body part all over again.
questions.description: A superpower that superheroes with scraped knees can only dream of.
questions.fun_fact: An axolotl can grow back its legs, its tail and even parts of its heart and spinal cord.

questions.question: Which animal's name completes both? “___man” (a military diver) and “___ kick” (the leg kick of breaststroke).
hints: It swims by pushing with its back legs.
It lives between water and land.
It croaks in puddles.
questions.description: A question best answered with fins on and a mask pushed up on your forehead.
questions.fun_fact: Modern diving fins were inspired by the webbed feet of frogs and other swimming animals.

questions.question: Many male frogs have it: it puffs up like a balloon on the throat or the sides of the head and makes their call much louder. What is it called?
hints: It has to do with the frog's voice.
It works like a sound box, just like the body of a guitar.
Its name says it is a little bag for the voice.
questions.description: A balloon you won't find at any kids' birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to their vocal sacs, some tiny frogs call so loudly that you can hear them more than a kilometer (over half a mile) away.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in the wild, this black salamander with yellow spots lives in the damp forests of which continent?
hints: It lives on a continent with oak and beech forests.
You can see it in Spain, France and Germany.
It's the continent of medieval castles.
questions.description: An animal dressed up as a bee that never buzzes and never stings.
questions.fun_fact: People once believed this salamander was born from fire, because it came running out of logs thrown onto the fire.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many vertebrae does this rainforest animal usually have in its neck?
hints: It is one of the few exceptions among mammals.
Almost all mammals, even the giraffe, have 7 neck vertebrae.
It has more than a giraffe, which helps it turn its head a very long way.
questions.description: An animal so laid-back that even its neck came with spare parts.
questions.fun_fact: The three-toed sloth can turn its head about 270 degrees without moving its body.

questions.question: A harmless butterfly copies the colors of a bad-tasting one, so birds don't eat it. The trick is named after an English naturalist. What is it called?
hints: The naturalist spent eleven years collecting insects in the Amazon rainforest.
He traveled to the Amazon with Alfred Russel Wallace, but the trick isn't named after Wallace.
His first names were Henry Walter.
questions.description: Nature's most successful Halloween costume is worn all year round.
questions.fun_fact: In the Amazon, Henry Walter Bates collected about 14,700 species, and about 8,000 of them were new to science.

questions.question: I have little horns above my eyes and I live in the Amazon. I bury myself in leaves and wait for something to pass by. What is my favorite food?
hints: I'm not picky at all: I swallow whatever fits in my mouth.
My mouth is so big that I'm nicknamed after a round, yellow video game character who gobbles everything.
My prey is often almost as big as I am.
questions.description: This frog is hungrier than an uncle at a family lunch.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazonian horned frog is nicknamed the “Pac-Man frog” because of its huge, round mouth.

questions.question: A “prehensile tail” can grab things like a hand. Which of these animals does NOT have a prehensile tail?
hints: Three of them can hang from a branch by their tail alone.
The one we're looking for uses its tail for balance, not for grabbing.
It is the biggest wild cat in the Americas.
questions.description: Some animals have an extra hand right where you have your back pocket.
questions.fun_fact: The tip of a spider monkey's tail is hairless underneath and has ridges like the prints on our fingertips.

questions.question: In a documentary, a mother pipa toad from the Amazon has dozens of eggs sunk into the skin of her back. What comes out of those holes months later?
wrong_answers: Eggs that drop into the water
hints: They skip a stage that almost all frogs spend swimming freely.
The whole transformation happens inside the mother's skin.
They come out ready to live like tiny adults.
questions.description: A mom who literally carries her kids on her back… on the inside.
questions.fun_fact: The pipa toad is so flat that it looks like a dead leaf floating in the water.

questions.question: Roughly how wide is a great egret from wingtip to wingtip with its wings spread?
hints: It's a big bird, but it's no condor.
With its wings open, it would be almost as wide as an adult is tall.
A little less than the length of a bed.
questions.description: A bird so elegant it always looks dressed for a wedding.
questions.fun_fact: In the early 1900s, so many egrets were hunted for hat feathers that they almost disappeared, which led to new laws to protect them.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: a white liquid comes out of this tree's bark. What material is made from it?
hints: That white liquid is called latex.
It's stretchy: it stretches and goes back to its shape.
It's used to make car tires and pencil erasers.
questions.description: Give this tree a tiny cut and it answers with something useful.
questions.fun_fact: The Olmecs of Mexico were already making rubber balls to play with more than 3,000 years ago.

questions.question: Ana checks every comma in her report but forgets the conclusion; Luis compares 30 paint colors and misses the leaking roof. Which saying fits them?
questions.answer: Can't see the forest for the trees
wrong_answers: As the twig is bent, so grows the tree
The apple doesn't fall far from the tree
Great oaks from little acorns grow
hints: They focus so hard on the details that they miss something important.
They need to step back and look at the whole picture.
The saying talks about lots of trees together.
questions.description: For people who grab a magnifying glass when they really need binoculars.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish has almost the same saying: “los árboles no dejan ver el bosque”, meaning “the trees don't let you see the forest”.

questions.question: In a carpentry workshop, someone spills oil on the floor, and the carpenter throws a handful of sawdust on it. Why?
wrong_answers: To make it smell like wood
hints: Afterward, he sweeps it up with a broom.
That's also why people put it in hamster cages.
It works like a sponge in powder form.
questions.description: What's left of wood once it gets tired of being a board.
questions.fun_fact: Sawdust and wood shavings pressed together with glue make particleboard, which is used to build furniture.

questions.question: A coast redwood's bark can be 30 cm (1 ft) thick, fibrous and spongy, with almost no resin. What is bark like that good for?
wrong_answers: Floating if it falls in a river
hints: Think of the worst enemy of a dry forest in summer.
Resin catches fire very easily.
Many redwoods are black on the outside of the trunk and are still alive.
questions.description: A tree wearing a coat thicker than a mattress.
questions.fun_fact: Coast redwoods can take in water from fog directly through their leaves.

questions.question: Winning Roman generals wore a crown that the god Apollo always wore; its dried leaves go into soups and stews. What was it made of?
hints: It's a fragrant plant with tough, shiny leaves.
In cooking, the leaf goes in whole and is taken out before serving.
The word “laureate”, as in Nobel laureate, comes from this plant.
questions.description: Before gold medals, champions wore a salad on their heads.
questions.fun_fact: In Greek myth, the nymph Daphne turned into this tree to escape Apollo, and “daphne” is the Greek word for laurel.

questions.question: What material are almost all of these giant statues on Easter Island made of?
hints: The island was formed by volcanoes.
They were carved on the slope of a crater.
It is a stone that came out of the Earth's fire long ago.
questions.description: Giant heads that have been staring without blinking for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all the moai were carved in the quarry of the Rano Raraku volcano, where hundreds of unfinished ones still lie.

questions.question: A star-shaped cutter makes cookies that all look the same. A cookie cutter is to a cookie as a ___ is to graffiti repeated on many walls.
hints: It's a sheet with a shape cut out of it.
You hold it against the wall and spray paint over it.
The street artist Banksy made this method world-famous.
questions.description: Street art for people who don't dare to draw freehand.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago, in caves in Argentina and elsewhere, people already made “stencils” by blowing paint around their own hands.

questions.question: This building is in the neoclassical style, which means “new classical.” The temples of which place and time does it copy?
hints: Look at the big columns and the triangle-shaped roof.
According to their myths, gods like Zeus and Jupiter lived there.
Think of the Parthenon and the Colosseum.

questions.question: Bushido, “the way of the warrior”, was a code of honor that also valued the tea ceremony. Which country does it come from?

questions.question: What is the final step of 3D animation, where the computer works out light, shadows and textures to make the finished image?

questions.question: Which of these groups of characters is NOT from Warner Bros.?

questions.question: Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote the songs for Encanto, was born in New York, but his parents come from a Caribbean island. Which one?

questions.question: What do the zoetrope, the thaumatrope and the praxinoscope, all 19th-century inventions, have in common?

questions.question: In “Jurassic Park,” the mosquito with dinosaur blood was trapped in…

questions.question: A princess is playing by a well when her ball falls into the water, and a frog offers to fetch it if she'll be his friend. What is the ball made of?

questions.question: Who wrote the original stories of Mowgli, the boy raised by wolves in India?

questions.question: In a tandem skydive, roughly how high up do you jump out of the plane?

review.feedback: source: Hint 3 says 4,000 m is "about the height of a very tall mountain in the Andes". That is misleading, because the very tall Andean peaks are 6,000–7,000 m (Aconcagua is about 6,960 m), and many Andean cities sit near 4,000 m. The translation copies this faithfully, so the source hint needs correcting first, for example: "It's about the height of the highest cities in the Andes" or "a bit lower than Mont Blanc". Everything else in the translation is faithful and reads naturally. Fact check: wrong. Hint 3 is misleading. 4,000 m is not 'a very tall mountain in the Andes'. Many Andean peaks and cities are at or above that height (Aconcagua is about 6,960 m). The answer itself is fine: tandem jumps go from about 3,000 to 4,200 m (10,000 to 14,000 ft), and freefall lasts about 50 to 60 seconds. This is from memory; I ran no searches.

questions.description: A job where the office is on the roof of the world.
questions.fun_fact: On the summit of Everest, Tenzing Norgay left some candy and cookies as an offering, following his Buddhist tradition.

questions.question: It's a made-up planet covered in sand, with giant worms under its dunes, where people mine the spice, the most valuable substance in the universe. Which planet is it?
hints: It appears in a 1965 science fiction novel that has been made into films more than once.
Its people, the Fremen, even collect the water from their sweat.
It's the world of the “Dune” saga.
questions.description: A place where even the worm from your garden wouldn't dare go for a walk.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Herbert got the idea for “Dune” from sand dunes creeping over towns on the coast of Oregon, in the United States.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Mongolian nomads in the Gobi Desert live in this round home they can take apart and carry along. What is it called?
hints: It has a wooden frame covered with wool felt.
It isn't the cone-shaped tent of the North American plains peoples.
In Mongolian, it's called a “ger.”
questions.description: A house you can put up, take down and load onto a camel: perfect for escaping unwanted visitors.
questions.fun_fact: A Mongolian family can take down its yurt in one or two hours and load it onto just a few animals.

questions.question: Many African countries are planting a long green wall of trees along the southern edge of the Sahara. What is it for?
questions.answer: To stop the desert from spreading
hints: Its enemy has no weapons: it's the sand.
Plant roots hold the soil so the wind can't blow it away.
Without it, the fertile land would slowly turn into sand.
questions.description: A wall built not with bricks, but with seeds and patience.
questions.fun_fact: The plan for the Great Green Wall is to cross Africa from side to side, from Senegal to Djibouti.

questions.question: It's a natural freshwater pool that forms when the roof of a cave falls in, and Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has thousands. What is it called?
hints: The Maya used them to get water.
Many people travel to Mexico to swim in them.
The word comes from the Maya word “ts'ono'ot”.
questions.description: A natural swimming pool that made itself when the ground got tired of holding up.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya believed cenotes were doorways to Xibalba, the underworld.

questions.question: Roughly how hot is lava when it comes out of a volcano?
hints: It's much hotter than boiling water.
It melts almost any rock, but it's not as hot as the Sun.
It's a one followed by three zeros.
questions.description: If Earth had pimples, this would be the most explosive one.
questions.fun_fact: Lava glows red when it's very hot (about 1,000 °C, or 1,800 °F); as it cools, it turns black and hard as rock.

questions.question: Complete: “Argentina is to the 2022 men's World Cup as Spain is to the…”
hints: It's a championship that Spain's women's team won.
It was the biggest title in women's national-team play.
It was played in Australia and New Zealand.
questions.description: An analogy question, so even your English teacher gets to cheer at a match.
questions.fun_fact: The first FIFA Women's World Cup was played in China in 1991, and the United States won it.

questions.question: The whole stadium does it together: people stand up and sit back down in turn. It became world famous at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. What is it?
hints: You don't need to bring anything to the stadium to do it.
It travels around the stands like a movement going all the way around.
It has the same name as something that forms in the sea.
questions.description: The only thing in a stadium that moves faster than the popcorn seller.
questions.fun_fact: In many countries it's called the “Mexican wave”, precisely because of that 1986 World Cup.

questions.question: Look at the rectangular area marked in front of the goal. If a defender fouls an opponent inside it, what does the referee award?
hints: It's what defenders fear most.
It's taken one-on-one against the goalkeeper.
It's kicked from a white spot 11 meters (12 yards) from the goal.
questions.description: A rectangle painted on the grass that makes defenders very nervous.
questions.fun_fact: The penalty spot is 11 meters (12 yards) from the goal line.

questions.question: What do Barcelona's Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets have in common?
hints: All three played in the middle of the field.
They were famous for short passes and almost never losing the ball.
The style's name sounds like the ball going from foot to foot.
questions.description: Three men more in sync than a family group chat planning a birthday surprise.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish TV commentator Andrés Montes made the word “tiki-taka” popular during the 2006 World Cup.

questions.question: Look at this plant: it makes many cats wild with joy. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Look at the shape of its leaves, with edges like a saw.
Its cousins are used a lot in cooking and in herbal teas.
If you crush it, it smells a bit like a plant used in chewing gum and mojitos.
questions.description: The only plant that turns a serious cat into a 1970s hippie.
questions.fun_fact: About one in three cats feels nothing at all from catnip: whether a cat reacts to it is inherited.

questions.question: Kittens are born with their eyes closed. About how long does it take them to open them?
hints: It's not a matter of minutes: kittens are born very helpless.
By the time they're running all over the house, they've been able to see for a while.
It's less than a month; a week and a bit.
questions.description: Babies who arrive in the world without reading the instructions on how to open their eyes.
questions.fun_fact: All kittens are born with blue eyes; their final eye color shows up weeks later.

questions.question: People born in this city are nicknamed “gatos” (cats). Look at this detail from one of its most famous statues: which city is it?
hints: It's the capital of a country.
The statue appears on the city's coat of arms.
It stands in the Puerta del Sol, in the capital of Spain.
questions.description: A city where calling someone a “cat” is almost like checking their ID.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says they're called “cats” after a soldier who climbed Madrid's city wall like a cat in the Middle Ages.

questions.question: Look at this cat with its back arched and its fur puffed up. What is it feeling?
hints: It's not an invitation to pet it.
It wants to look bigger than it really is.
This is how it looks when it comes face to face with an angry dog.
questions.description: A cat that turns itself into a footbridge whenever something bothers it.
questions.fun_fact: By puffing up its fur and arching its back, a cat can look almost twice as big to an enemy.

questions.question: What breed are Meredith and Olivia, Taylor Swift's famous cats?
hints: They're famous for sitting in odd poses, almost like people.
The most striking thing about them is their ears.
Their ears fold forward, and the breed's name also tells you where it first came from.
questions.description: Cats so famous they have more fans than your favorite sports team.
questions.fun_fact: Every cat of this breed descends from Susie, a farm cat found in Scotland in 1961.

questions.question: My name is Muezza. Legend says I fell asleep on my owner's sleeve, and he cut it off rather than wake me. Who was my owner?
hints: My owner lived on the Arabian Peninsula about 1,400 years ago.
He is a very important religious figure.
He is the prophet of Islam.
questions.description: A cat who napped so sweetly that someone gave up part of his clothes for her.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to stories like this one, cats are much loved in many Muslim countries and are even allowed inside mosques.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The question says "The story goes", so the answer Muhammad matches the popular legend, and the wrong answers are wrong. But the story is not in any verified hadith. Scholars say it probably comes from a tale about the saint Ahmad al-Rifa'i (d. 578 AH), and the cat is not named Muezza there. The fun fact about cats being loved and allowed in mosques is broadly true. The hint "He is a very important religious figure" is vague but fine.

questions.question: In Greek mythology, how many eyes do three cyclopes have in total?
hints: Cyclopes don't have faces like yours.
Their name comes from Greek and describes their face.
One eye for each cyclops.
questions.description: Giants who worked as blacksmiths for the gods, with no vacation and no fixed hours.
questions.fun_fact: Zeus got his thunderbolt as a gift from the cyclopes for freeing them from a prison.

questions.question: Who led the roughly fifty Greek heroes who sailed on the ship Argo in search of the Golden Fleece?
hints: He had to bring back the fleece to win back the throne that had been taken from him.
The sorceress Medea helped him.
His sailors are called the Argonauts, “the sailors of the Argo.”
questions.description: A luxury cruise where every passenger is a hero and nobody packed sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the story, Hercules also sailed on the Argo but was left behind on land halfway through the trip.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Greek hero, dressed in a lion's skin, had to complete twelve almost impossible labors. Who is he?
hints: He was a son of Zeus.
He was the strongest man in the world.
Disney made a movie about him in 1997.
questions.description: The man with the longest to-do list in all of Greece.
questions.fun_fact: His first labor was to defeat the Nemean lion, and from then on he wore its skin.

questions.question: In Roman mythology: Zeus is to Jupiter as Hades is to…
hints: The Romans' name for him was later given to a planet… or almost a planet.
That world is so small and far away that today it counts as a dwarf planet.
Mickey Mouse's dog has exactly the same name.
questions.description: A villain with flaming hair who also has a spare name.
questions.fun_fact: The name of the dwarf planet Pluto was suggested in 1930 by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old English girl.

questions.question: Listen: this insect sings by stridulation, rubbing one wing against the other. Which insect is it?
hints: You hear it mostly at night, in the grass or in the yard.
It has long back legs for jumping.
In Pinocchio, one of them acts as his conscience.
questions.description: A night-time concert with no tickets, no stage and no permission from the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: Crickets chirp faster when it's warmer: by counting their chirps, you can estimate the temperature.

questions.question: Wasps build gray nests like this one. What are they made of?
wrong_answers: Wax that comes from their bodies
hints: They get the material by scraping things in the yard.
It looks a lot like paper.
They scrape tree trunks and old fences and chew it up.
questions.description: Builders with no license, no bricks and no cement, and still nobody dares to knock their house down.
questions.fun_fact: In the 18th century, the French scientist Réaumur suggested making paper from wood after watching wasps build their nests.

questions.question: In 1947, fruit flies like this one became the first animals sent into space. Which country launched them?
hints: It wasn't the country of Laika the dog.
They used a V-2 rocket captured after the Second World War.
The launch took place in the New Mexico desert.
questions.description: Before dogs, monkeys and astronauts, space was reached by the little pest that keeps landing on your bananas.
questions.fun_fact: The flies came back alive in a capsule with a parachute, which showed that living things could survive that high up.

questions.question: In which decade did the British series “Black Mirror” first come out?
hints: It arrived when smartphones were already in everyone's pocket.
Netflix bought it after its first two seasons on British TV.
It premiered in December 2011.
questions.description: You switch off your phone and there it is: your own tired face staring back at you from the screen.
questions.fun_fact: Its interactive episode “Bandersnatch” (2018) let viewers use the remote to choose what the main character did.

questions.question: The Ten Commandments are to believers as ___ are to the robots in “I, Robot”. What is missing?
hints: They are rules built into the robots in that story, and the robots cannot disobey them.
The first one says a robot may not harm a human being.
They were invented by the writer Isaac Asimov, who wrote the book behind the Will Smith movie.
questions.description: Rules so serious that even the most rebellious robot can't break them… in theory.
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Asimov wrote or edited more than 500 books, and he made the word “robotics” popular.

questions.question: Riddle: “I was an 18th-century automaton in a turban; I beat Napoleon at chess, but a human player hid inside me.” What was I called?
hints: Wolfgang von Kempelen built me to impress Empress Maria Theresa of Austria.
My name comes from my Ottoman-style clothes.
Amazon has a service called “Mechanical ___” named after me.
questions.description: The first famous “artificial intelligence” had a trick: it was more human than it looked.
questions.fun_fact: Amazon named its “Mechanical Turk” service after it: real people do tasks that look like they were done by machines, just like the original trick.

questions.question: The AI AlphaFold predicts the 3D shape of hemoglobin, insulin and collagen. What do these three have in common?
hints: They are made of chains of smaller pieces that fold up like origami.
Those pieces are called amino acids.
It's the same nutrient found in large amounts in meat, eggs and beans.
questions.description: Folding a bedsheet is hard enough; now try folding a molecule.
questions.fun_fact: AlphaFold has predicted the structure of more than 200 million proteins, almost every one known to science.

questions.question: The phrase “Internet of Things” was first used in a presentation for Procter & Gamble. In what year?
hints: It was before smartphones like the iPhone existed.
Many homes already had the internet, but almost everyone went online through the phone line.
It was very shortly before the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: Your fridge has Wi-Fi now, and soon it will have more followers than you.
questions.fun_fact: Kevin Ashton, from Britain, came up with the phrase to talk about tags that let stores track products on their shelves.

questions.question: You're in a park with no Wi-Fi and want to watch a video on your phone. What do you need to turn on?
hints: You need to get online without a router nearby.
The signal comes from your phone company's antennas.
Your phone plan comes with a few gigabytes for this.
questions.description: A park with no Wi-Fi: this generation's idea of an extreme adventure.
questions.fun_fact: Airplane mode does the exact opposite: it switches off all the phone's signals, data included.

questions.question: A phone network splits the map into areas, each served by one antenna. What are these areas called?
hints: Each antenna serves only a small piece of the map, and your phone jumps from one to the next.
In technical drawings they are often shown as hexagons, like a honeycomb.
It's also the name of the little boxes in a spreadsheet.
questions.description: Giant antennas passing your call around like a ball.
questions.fun_fact: These areas gave the “cell phone” its name, and engineers draw them as hexagons because they fit together without leaving gaps.

questions.question: I'm two letters you see when you write an email, and my name comes from the carbon paper of typewriters. If you put someone in me, what do you do?
questions.answer: Send them a copy everyone can see
hints: My letters are “CC.”
I have a brother, BCC, who does the same thing but in secret.
The two letters stand for “carbon copy.”
questions.description: An invention from the typewriter age that survived into the email era.
questions.fun_fact: With carbon paper, you typed once and got two identical sheets: the original and the copy.

questions.question: I'm the “s” added to the end of “http” in some web addresses. What am I for?
questions.answer: To encrypt data between your browser and the website
wrong_answers: To make the page load faster
To show that the page is a store
To show that the page is from the government
hints: I matter most when you pay by card or type your password.
A little padlock often shows up next to me in the browser.
I turn what you send into a code that nobody can read along the way.
questions.description: One letter worth more than the rest of the alphabet when you pay online.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2018, the Chrome browser has labeled websites that don't use HTTPS as “Not secure”.

questions.question: Roughly how far would you have to swim from the prison island of Alcatraz to the San Francisco shore?
hints: From the island, you can clearly see the city's buildings.
The hard part wasn't the distance, but the icy water and the currents.
It's about the same as five laps around a running track.
questions.description: The prison with the best view of the city and the worst beach service.
questions.fun_fact: Today there are swim races from Alcatraz to San Francisco, and even kids take part.

questions.question: It may not seem like it, but the coconut, the peach and the olive belong to the same group of fruits. Which one?
hints: The coconut's name is misleading: botanically, it isn't what many people think.
They are fruits with a single seed protected by a hard stone.
The mango and the cherry are also in this group.
questions.description: A question with a hard shell on the outside and something juicy on the inside.
questions.fun_fact: Coconuts can float at sea for months and sprout when they wash up on another beach, which is why coconut palms grow on islands all across the tropics.

questions.question: This word comes from a made-up island in “Gulliver's Travels” whose people are about 15 cm (6 in) tall. Today it means “tiny”. What is it?
hints: When Gulliver reaches the island, he wakes up tied to the ground by a crowd of little people.
The island is at war with its neighbor over which end of an egg you should break.
It describes something very small, like a toy train or a miniature dog.
questions.description: A word so small it fits in a giant's pocket.
questions.fun_fact: In Lilliput, a whole war broke out over whether boiled eggs should be cracked at the big end or the small end.

questions.question: In January 2022, an undersea volcano erupted with a boom heard as far away as Alaska. Which Pacific kingdom is it in?
hints: It is an island country in Polynesia.
It is the only kingdom in the South Pacific that was never a colony.
The volcano is called Hunga ___-Hunga Ha'apai.
questions.description: A volcano with so much energy that the whole world heard it slam the door.
questions.fun_fact: The blast threw water vapor more than 50 km (31 miles) high, up into the mesosphere.

questions.question: A tiger, an orangutan and a rhinoceros all carry the name of the same island. Which one?
hints: It is an island in Indonesia, crossed by the equator.
It is the sixth-largest island in the world.
Its name also shows up on bags of coffee.
questions.description: Three endangered animals sharing a last name, like cousins in one big jungle family.
questions.fun_fact: This island's tiger is the smallest of all the tigers still alive today.

questions.question: What do a swing, an old wall clock and the gadget that keeps the beat in piano lessons have in common?
hints: All three make the same movement over and over, always at the same pace.
All three go from side to side, like the watch a hypnotist uses in the movies to put someone to sleep.
Their name starts with “pen” and comes from the Latin word for “to hang.”
questions.description: Back and forth, back and forth: the only trip where you never get anywhere and still love it.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that Galileo watched a lamp swaying in Pisa Cathedral and found that every swing took the same time, whether it was big or small.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many pieces does this cube-shaped puzzle have?
hints: Count slowly, one at a time.
It's more than the fingers on one hand.
It's the same number as the days of the week.
questions.description: A cube that fell to pieces and is waiting for you to put it back together without glue.
questions.fun_fact: Danish inventor Piet Hein created the Soma cube in 1933, and its seven pieces can be put together into a cube in 240 different ways.

questions.question: You push your toy car hard along the floor a few times, then let go and it zooms off by itself. What's hidden inside that stores that push?
questions.answer: A heavy wheel that keeps spinning
hints: You don't need to charge it or change anything: just use your hand.
While you rub it, something inside spins faster and faster.
It's like a hidden spinning top that keeps turning for quite a while.
questions.description: A race car whose only pit crew is your own hand.
questions.fun_fact: That heavy wheel is called a flywheel, and some buses and trains use the same idea to store energy when they brake.

questions.question: The Super Soaker is the famous water gun you pump by hand. In which decade did it go on sale?
hints: It came out around the time The Simpsons first appeared on TV.
Its inventor was an engineer who worked with NASA.
It was the same decade the World Wide Web was born.
questions.description: A toy that turns any hot afternoon into a war with no wounded, only the soaked.
questions.fun_fact: The Super Soaker was invented by Lonnie Johnson, a NASA engineer, while he was testing a cooling system in his bathroom at home.

questions.question: Which of these characters is NOT a toy from Toy Story?
hints: Three of them live in Andy's room.
The odd one out is from a different Pixar movie.
The odd one out is a red race car.
questions.description: Toys that come to life when nobody's looking… and one party crasher who shouldn't be here.
questions.fun_fact: Rex is a toy T. rex who dreams of being scary, but he's the most nervous of all of Andy's toys.

questions.question: What is the name of the shape with 20 faces, all of them triangles?
hints: It's a special die, very popular in role-playing games.
Its name comes from Greek and means “twenty faces.”
It starts with “ico.”
questions.description: A shape with so many faces that even the most two-faced person can't compete.
questions.fun_fact: Many viruses, like the adenovirus, have an outer shell shaped like an icosahedron.

questions.question: You open a book and a paper castle rises up by itself as you turn the page; pull a tab and a dragon flaps its wings. What do these surprises have in common?
hints: Everything is made of folded and cut paper.
The figures seem to jump out of the page.
Its name is what toast does when it's ready in the toaster.
questions.description: A book that won't sit still, no matter how nicely you ask.
questions.fun_fact: Books with moving paper parts have existed for centuries: they were used to teach astronomy and anatomy long before children's stories.

questions.question: A hen raises chicks. In “The Wild Robot”, the robot Roz is shipwrecked on an island and raises a baby…
hints: It's a bird that swims in lakes.
It has to learn to fly so it can migrate with its flock.
It's related to the duck, but has a longer neck.
questions.description: The most metal mom in the whole forest.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Brown wrote and illustrated the book, and in 2024 it became an animated DreamWorks movie.

questions.question: Which of these words is NOT a name for the text that introduces a book before Chapter 1?
hints: Three of the words are about the beginning of a book.
Look at the start of each word: “pro-”, “pre-” and “fore-” all mean “before”.
The odd one out comes at the end, after the story is over.
questions.description: The part of a book nobody reads, because everyone wants to get to the action.
questions.fun_fact: “Prologue” comes from Greek and means something like “words that come before”.

questions.question: Content, cheerful, joyful, sad, furious: how many of these words are synonyms of “happy”?
hints: A synonym means the same thing, or almost the same.
“Sad” is the exact opposite of happy.
“Furious” doesn't fit either: count only the good-mood words.
questions.description: Twin words that look nothing alike but mean the same thing.
questions.fun_fact: English has plenty of synonyms for “car”: auto, automobile, motorcar and more.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. Content, cheerful and joyful are all synonyms of happy, so 3 is right. But the description says 'Twin words that look nothing alike but mean the same thing', which is off for this question. The fun fact (car/auto/automobile/motorcar) is true but only loosely related. The third hint, 'Furious doesn't work either', is fine. The main problem is the description, which doesn't match the question. 'Content' is also a slightly weaker synonym (it means satisfied), so the answer is arguable.

questions.question: What is the great prize for Spanish-language literature, given every year at the University of Alcalá de Henares in Spain?
hints: It's often called the “Nobel Prize of Spanish-language literature”.
It is given around April 23, World Book Day.
It is named after the author of “Don Quixote”.
questions.description: The fanciest trophy for anyone who writes in the language of the ñ.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian writer Álvaro Mutis won the Cervantes Prize in 2001.

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what does the spell “Wingardium Leviosa!” do?
hints: It's one of the first spells Harry learns in his first year.
In class, they practice it with a feather.
Look at “Leviosa”: it sounds like “levitate”.
questions.description: A spell you have to say just right, or you end up like Ron.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Hermione corrects Ron: it's “Levi-O-sa”, not “Levio-SA”.

questions.question: I'm the king of the Greek gods, I live on Mount Olympus, and I throw lightning bolts when I'm angry, like a video game wizard. Who am I?
hints: I'm the dad of many gods and heroes, like Hercules.
My brothers rule the sea and the underworld.
The Romans called me Jupiter.
questions.description: Long before video games, someone was already casting lightning spells without using up any mana.
questions.fun_fact: According to myth, the Cyclopes made Zeus's lightning bolts as a gift for setting them free.

questions.question: I'm a legendary stone that alchemists hunted for centuries, said to turn metals into gold and make the elixir of eternal life. What am I?
hints: Alchemists were a mix of chemists and magicians in the Middle Ages.
In most of the world, it's in the title of the first Harry Potter book.
In that book, it was made by Nicolas Flamel.
questions.description: Something everyone has searched for over centuries and nobody has ever found, just like the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: Nicolas Flamel from Harry Potter was a real person: a 14th-century scribe in Paris, and the legend of his stone only began after he died.

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what are the Elder Wand, the Resurrection Stone and the Cloak of Invisibility called together?
hints: In a wizard fairy tale, the three Peverell brothers were given these objects.
Their symbol is a triangle with a circle and a line inside it.
The seventh book in the series is named after them.
questions.description: Three gifts so powerful that nobody should ever own all of them, not even your little brother.
questions.fun_fact: Most invisibility cloaks in the wizarding world wear out over time, but Harry's never loses its power.

questions.question: Like corals, some sea animals can bleach because they carry tiny algae inside them. Which of these can NOT bleach?
hints: When they bleach, these animals push out their partner algae, called zooxanthellae.
The ones with these algae often sit in the sun, almost like plants.
It's the only one of the four that spends its day scraping algae off rocks and eating them, instead of carrying them inside.
questions.description: When the reef goes from full rainbow to “blank page” overnight.
questions.fun_fact: A bleached coral isn't dead yet: if the water cools down in time, it can get its algae and its color back.

questions.question: Riddle: “My name is El Niño, but I'm no baby. When I arrive, Colombia gets drought, heat and even power rationing.” What am I?
questions.answer: A warming of the Pacific Ocean's water
wrong_answers: A hurricane that forms in the Caribbean Sea
An underwater volcano off the coast
An icy current coming from Antarctica
hints: The fishermen on the coast of Peru see me first.
I got my name because I used to show up around Christmas.
The sea gets warmer than usual in the Pacific.
questions.description: It doesn't wear diapers, but all of Colombia still worries about its tantrums.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the baby Jesus (“El Niño” in Spanish): Peruvian fishermen noticed the warm water arrived around December.

questions.question: A giant worm with a red plume has no mouth or stomach and lives off the bacteria inside it. Where does it live?
questions.answer: At hydrothermal vents on the seafloor
hints: It lives where sunlight never reaches.
Its bacteria use chemicals instead of light.
It lives next to chimneys that blast very hot water from deep inside the Earth.
questions.description: A worm with no mouth and no stomach that still never orders takeout.
questions.fun_fact: These worms were discovered in 1977 and surprised scientists, who never expected to find so much life without sunlight.

questions.question: Waves wear away the base of a coastal rock until the top collapses, leaving a vertical wall above the sea. What is formed?
hints: It isn't made by a river or a glacier.
From the top, there's a very long drop to the water.
It's the rock wall the famous Acapulco divers jump from.
questions.description: Waves have endless patience and a very bad temper with rocks.
questions.fun_fact: The famous White Cliffs of Dover in England are made of chalk: the remains of tiny sea algae from millions of years ago.

questions.question: What is the abbreviation for an underwater robot steered from afar through a cable, like the one exploring the shipwreck at the start of “Titanic”?
hints: Nobody rides inside it.
Scientists and oil companies send it down to check the deep seafloor and underwater pipes.
The first letter stands for “remotely.”
questions.description: An explorer that goes where no one else can… as long as its extension cord doesn't get tangled.
questions.fun_fact: In 1986, a small robot named Jason Jr. went inside the wreck of the Titanic, guided by a cable from the submarine Alvin.

questions.question: What do substitution, elimination and the comparison method have in common?
questions.answer: They are methods for solving systems of equations
wrong_answers: They are types of triangles by their angles
They are properties of addition and multiplication
They are ways to calculate the area of a circle
hints: It's a topic from early high school algebra.
You can check the result by drawing two lines that cross.
They help you find several unknowns that must fit several equations at once.
questions.description: The night before the test, YouTube becomes your favorite private tutor.
questions.fun_fact: About 2,000 years ago, the Chinese book “The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art” already solved systems of equations with a method much like elimination.

questions.question: This 17th-century French philosopher made it popular to use the last letters of the alphabet, like x, y, z, for unknowns. Who is he?

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer and wrong answers are fine: a ship's course is its heading, not speed, cargo or depth. The fun fact is shaky. "Course" comes from Latin cursus ('a running, path') through Old French cours, so the word was not born at sea. Only the phrase "off course" is plausibly nautical in origin. Some tiny critters that eat clothes really hate it.
They are small insects that flutter around light bulbs.
questions.description: A tree that makes the house smell better than the air freshener in the bathroom.
questions.fun_fact: Cedar balls for the closet lose their smell over the years, but a light sanding makes them smell fresh again.

questions.question: Riddle: I live inside a frozen mountain on a Norwegian island near the North Pole, and people call me the “Doomsday Vault”. What do I keep?
questions.answer: Crop seeds from around the world
wrong_answers: Gold bars for the world's reserves
hints: What I keep could help the world start over after a huge disaster.
Almost every country in the world has sent me something to keep safe.
If you opened me, you would find beans, rice, corn and wheat… uncooked and ready to plant.
questions.description: A place so cold and so hidden that not even the bravest delivery driver dares to go there.
questions.fun_fact: The vault is in Svalbard because the cold of the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even if the power went out.

questions.question: The real flowers of the bougainvillea are tiny and white. So what makes it look so colorful?
wrong_answers: A fungus that dyes its branches
hints: It isn't part of the flower, even though it's attached to it.
Botanists call them “bracts.”
It's the same plant part that does photosynthesis, just in a different color.
questions.description: A plant that dresses up for a party but hides its real face.
questions.fun_fact: The poinsettia, the famous Christmas flower, pulls the same trick: its red “flower” is also made of modified leaves.

questions.question: Riddle: I live on tree branches without touching the ground, and I keep a little pool of rainwater in the center of my leaves. Who uses my pool as a nursery?
hints: My guests start their lives in water.
Their parents carry them on their backs up into the tree.
When they grow up, they will be brightly colored amphibians.
questions.description: A plant with its own swimming pool that it lends to the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The pineapple is a bromeliad, a relative of these plants that live high up in the trees.

questions.question: In biology class, you take apart a lily flower and separate the stigma, the style and the ovary. Which part of the flower are all three pieces of?
hints: It is the female part of the flower.
It usually sits right in the center of the flower.
Pollen lands there, and that is where the seeds form.
questions.description: The part of the flower where everything starts turning into fruit.
questions.fun_fact: The red threads of saffron, one of the most expensive spices in the world, are the stigmas of a flower.

questions.question: It appears when a seed sprouts, before the true leaves, and often stores food for the tiny plant. A bean has two, corn has one. What is it called?
hints: It is a very special leaf of the plant embryo.
Its name comes from Greek and has to do with a cup.
How many a plant has gives monocots and dicots their names.
questions.description: The lunch box a seed packs for its first day of life.
questions.fun_fact: When you sprout a bean on cotton, the two “halves” that open up are its cotyledons.

questions.question: Riddle: “I am the manguaré, the great drum of the Bora people; when struck, my voice carries messages for kilometers through the jungle.” What am I made of?
hints: My material comes straight from the jungle, and it's very heavy.
I have no animal skin that vibrates.
A whole tree, emptied out on the inside.
questions.description: The jungle's group chat: no Wi-Fi, but plenty of rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: Manguarés are played in pairs: a “male” one and a “female” one, each with its own sound.

questions.question: According to a famous legend of the South American rainforest, what is Paititi?
questions.answer: A lost city of the Incas
wrong_answers: A sunken galleon full of treasure
hints: It is said to be hidden in the jungle where Peru, Bolivia and Brazil meet.
People say it had streets, palaces and lots of people living there.
It's a “cousin” of the legend of El Dorado.
questions.description: A name that sounds like baby talk, but hides a giant legend.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, the Incas hid their treasures there so the Spanish conquerors couldn't find them.

questions.question: What does the Greek root “glyph” mean, as in “petroglyph” and “hieroglyph”?
hints: Think about how you make shapes on very hard rock.
“Petro” is the part that means something else.
It’s what a sculptor does with a chisel.
questions.description: Some pictures have been on the rocks for thousands of years… and in the dictionary too.
questions.fun_fact: In the Colombian Amazon there are rocks covered in thousands of ancient pictures, like those in the Serranía de Chiribiquete.

questions.question: What is the main component of the gas that is collected from landfills and burned to make electricity?
hints: Microbes make it when they break down garbage without air.
Cows also let it out when they burp.
It is the main component of the natural gas used in kitchen stoves.
questions.description: Garbage passes gas too, and someone had the bright idea to put it to work.
questions.fun_fact: Landfill biogas is roughly half methane and half carbon dioxide.

questions.question: You want to buy cheap used clothes. Which of these places is NOT a typical place to find them?
hints: Think carefully about what each word means.
One of these places sells new things for sewing.
It's where you buy buttons, thread and zippers.
questions.description: Your favorite jacket had a whole other life before it met you.
questions.fun_fact: The name “flea market” comes from the French “marché aux puces”, because the old clothes sold in Paris markets were said to have fleas.

questions.question: Your bathroom mirror falls and shatters. According to the famous superstition, how many years of bad luck are coming your way?
hints: Many people think of it as a lucky number.
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
It's also the number of dwarfs in Snow White.
questions.description: A piece of glass that copies everything you do, and then gets grumpy if you break it.
questions.fun_fact: Mirrors aren't recycled with glass bottles, because the metal coating on the back spoils the new glass.

questions.question: What do you call this way of selling without packaging, where you bring your own jar and pay by weight for what you scoop from big containers?
hints: You can buy a little or a lot, as you like.
Ships that carry loose grain or sand are called carriers of this kind.
Think of the big bins of rice, nuts and oats that you fill your own bag from.
questions.description: A store where you bring the packaging and the scale does the rest.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “bulk” comes from the Old Norse “búlki”, meaning a ship's cargo.

questions.question: Each green dot in this photo is a complete living thing, smaller than a grain of rice. Which group does it belong to?
hints: They make food from sunlight, like the grass in the park.
Hard to believe, but they are distant relatives of roses and sunflowers.
It's the smallest in the world of all those that can bloom.
questions.description: Blink and you'll miss a whole garden.
questions.fun_fact: Wolffia is the smallest flowering plant in the world: its flowers are so tiny you can barely see them with the naked eye.

questions.question: Roughly how long can a Greenland shark live?
hints: It outlives any person… by a long way.
Some swimming today may already have been alive when Mozart was writing his music.
It's several centuries, but not thousands of years.
questions.description: A shark so slow it makes a sloth look like it's in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The Greenland shark is the longest-living vertebrate known, and it grows only about 1 cm (0.4 in) a year.

questions.question: What do Mount Everest, Aconcagua and Mount Vinson have in common?
questions.answer: Each is its continent's highest peak
wrong_answers: Each is in the Andes mountains
Each is in the Himalaya mountains
hints: They are on different continents.
Mount Vinson is in Antarctica.
Aconcagua holds that same title in the Americas.
questions.description: A to-do list for climbers with way too much vacation time.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Vinson, about 4,892 m (16,050 ft) tall, is so remote in Antarctica that nobody climbed it until 1966.

questions.question: I'm the largest tree in the world by volume, a California sequoia named after a US Civil War general. What's my name?
hints: That general fought for the North.
His first names were William Tecumseh.
My surname rhymes with “Herman”.
questions.description: A tree with a military rank, even though it has never given a single order.
questions.fun_fact: General Sherman holds about 1,500 cubic meters (53,000 cubic feet) of wood in its trunk, and it is thought to be about 2,200 years old.

questions.question: I'm a pine tree in the mountains of California, over 4,800 years old. I'm named after a Bible figure famous for living 969 years. Who is he?
hints: He was the grandfather of someone famous for building an ark.
People say someone is “as old as…” him when they mean very, very old.
His name starts with M.
questions.description: A tree so old its birthday cake would need a whole forest of candles.
questions.fun_fact: The exact location of the Methuselah tree is kept secret to protect it from visitors who might want to take home a souvenir.

questions.question: Bagger 288, a German excavator, is taller than a 30-story building. About how much does it weigh?
hints: It is one of the heaviest land machines ever built.
It weighs far more than a jumbo jet, which weighs about 400 metric tons even with all its passengers.
It weighs about as much as 90 blue whales put together.
questions.description: The neighborhood backhoe, after a very serious growth spurt.
questions.fun_fact: In 2001, Bagger 288 moved under its own power about 22 km (14 miles) to another mine, crossing a river and a highway on the way.

questions.question: How many chambers (atria and ventricles) does a frog's heart have in total?
hints: It has fewer chambers than a human heart.
In this, amphibians are halfway between fish and mammals.
It's an odd number: two atria and just one ventricle.
questions.description: An organ that works day and night without a vacation, even if its owner lives in a puddle.
questions.fun_fact: Because its heart mixes the blood a little, a frog gets extra help by also breathing through its moist skin.

questions.question: Complete: the elephant is to its trunk as the giant anteater is to its…
hints: It pokes its snout into ant and termite nests.
It doesn't have a single tooth.
It's long and sticky, and it flicks in and out super fast.
questions.description: An animal whose whole menu is right there in its name.
questions.fun_fact: A giant anteater's tongue is about 60 cm (2 ft) long and can flick in and out about 150 times a minute.

questions.question: While it sleeps, the glass frog stores almost all its blood in its liver and turns transparent. What does this help it do?
hints: It has to do with its enemies, like birds and snakes.
Red blood would make it much easier to spot.
Light passes right through it, so it blends into the green of the leaf.
questions.description: A frog so see-through it could get a job as a window.
questions.fun_fact: A 2022 study found that the glass frog hides about 90% of its red blood cells in its liver while it sleeps.

questions.question: Look at this cross section of a tree trunk: what is the dark wood in the center called?
hints: It's wood that no longer carries sap.
It's the strongest part of the trunk.
Its name compares it to the organ at the center of your chest.
questions.description: Dark, old and already retired: the wise elder of the tree trunk.
questions.fun_fact: Heartwood turns dark because the tree fills it with substances that protect it from fungi and insects, which is why it is often the most valuable wood.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a mangrove root, but I don't dig down. I poke up out of the mud like a pencil, and the tide covers and uncovers me. What am I for?
questions.answer: Taking in oxygen from the air
hints: I do most of my work when the tide goes out.
There's almost no oxygen in mangrove mud.
I work like a diver's snorkel.
questions.description: A tree standing with its feet in salty mud came up with a clever trick.
questions.fun_fact: These roots are called pneumatophores, from Greek words meaning “air carriers”.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a famous painting: the face has no outlines, its edges fade softly into light and shadow. What is this technique called?
hints: It's a technique from the Italian Renaissance.
Its great master was Leonardo da Vinci.
Its name comes from the Italian word “fumo”, which means smoke.
questions.description: A painter who was allergic to sharp lines.
questions.fun_fact: Leonardo painted layers so thin that some are only a few thousandths of a millimeter thick.

questions.question: In Collodi's book “Pinocchio”, a coachman sells donkeys at the market. What were those donkeys before?
questions.answer: Boys who didn't want to study
hints: The same thing happens to Pinocchio himself.
Before they had long ears, they spent all day playing.
The coachman took them to a place with no school and no teachers.
questions.description: A trip that's pure fun from start to finish, until it ends in a hee-haw.
questions.fun_fact: In the Disney film that place became an island, but in the book it's a land the children reach in a cart pulled by little donkeys.

questions.question: J. M. Barrie is to “Peter Pan” as Lewis Carroll is to…
hints: It's a book full of characters who don't make much sense.
It has a grinning cat and a queen who plays croquet with flamingos.
The heroine chases a white rabbit.
questions.description: A math teacher who got bored with numbers and started making up stories.
questions.fun_fact: “Lewis Carroll” was a pen name: his real name was Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, and he taught math at Oxford.

questions.question: What do Grave Digger, El Toro Loco and Bigfoot have in common?
hints: They make a lot of noise and jump in stadiums.
They have engines and lots of power.
They have giant wheels.
questions.description: Three names that start more fights in your house than the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: Bigfoot, built by Bob Chandler in the mid-1970s, is considered the very first monster truck.

questions.question: In 1875, who did the explorer name the Great Victoria Desert after? It's the largest desert in Australia.
hints: Australia was a British colony at the time.
This person ruled for much of the 19th century.
She was such a famous queen that a whole era is named after her: the Victorian era.
questions.description: Crossing this desert on foot would be quite a victory, but nobody wants to try.
questions.fun_fact: Queen Victoria also gave her name to an Australian state, a huge waterfall in Africa and an enormous lake, but she never visited any of them!

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the ice sheet that covers almost all of Antarctica. What treasure of the planet do I keep frozen?
hints: When I melt, rivers are born from me.
What I keep is something you could drink if you melted it.
It's not seawater, but the other kind.
questions.description: The biggest freezer in the world, and nobody ever unplugs it to defrost it.
questions.fun_fact: Antarctica is the largest desert in the world: it hardly ever rains or snows there, even though it is covered in ice.

questions.question: In the hills of Chile's Atacama Desert, big nets hang up to collect water for some villages. What do the nets catch to get the water?
hints: The water arrives floating in from the sea, not falling from the sky.
Its tiny droplets hit the net and drip down into a tank.
People there call it “camanchaca”.
questions.description: Yes, you can go fishing in the desert, but the only catch is water.
questions.fun_fact: On a good day, a single square meter of these nets can collect several liters of water.

questions.question: What is special about the sky of Tatooine, the desert planet where Luke Skywalker grew up?
hints: It's one of the most famous scenes in “Star Wars”.
It looks best at sunset.
If you counted the stars that warm it, you would get to two.
questions.description: A planet so dry that even the robots complain about the sand.
questions.fun_fact: Many Tatooine scenes were filmed in the desert of Tunisia, and the town of Matmata still keeps a set from the movie.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the largest continuous sea of sand in the world, I cover the south of the Arabian Peninsula, and my name means “the empty quarter.” Who am I?
hints: Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates share my land.
My dunes can be more than 200 m (650 ft) tall.
My name is in Arabic and starts with “Rub.”
questions.description: A desert named after a room nobody ever wants to clean.
questions.fun_fact: Beneath its sands lies Shaybah, one of Saudi Arabia's great oil fields.

questions.question: The oilbird nests in pitch-dark caves and flies between the rocks without crashing. How does it find its way?
questions.answer: With the echo of its own sounds
wrong_answers: With the heat of the rocks
hints: It's about how they find their way without seeing anything.
They make sounds and listen to what comes back.
It's called echolocation.
questions.description: A place so dark that not even a lamp would help you find the way out.
questions.fun_fact: The oilbird is the only flying bird that feeds on fruit at night, and Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1799 in the Cueva del Guácharo in Venezuela.

questions.question: I glow inside every lightning bolt and every star, and I'm the most common state of matter in the visible universe. What am I?
hints: It appears when something gets extremely hot.
It's a gas so hot that its atoms lose electrons.
It shares its name with a kind of old flat-screen TV.
questions.description: Up there it's everywhere, but you'll almost never see it in your kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Lightning heats the air to about 30,000 °C (54,000 °F), roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

questions.question: It happens at night, the Moon turns reddish for a while, and you don't need special glasses to watch it. What is a “blood moon”?
wrong_answers: The second full moon of a month
hints: It doesn't happen every month: certain objects in the sky have to line up.
The Moon ends up in Earth's shadow.
Earth moves exactly between the Sun and the Moon.
questions.description: It sounds like a horror movie, but it's one of the prettiest things you can see at night.
questions.fun_fact: The Moon looks red because Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it: it's as if every sunset on the planet reached it at once.

questions.question: It cools the Pacific Ocean, brings more rain and floods to Colombia, and its name is the opposite of another famous one. What is it?
hints: It shows up every few years, just like its partner.
Its “opposite” brings drought and heat to Colombia.
Take the name of the drought-bringing phenomenon and swap the boy for a girl.
questions.description: When it's on the news in Colombia, out come the umbrellas and rain boots.
questions.fun_fact: El Niño got its name from Peruvian fishermen, who noticed the warm water around Christmas, the feast of the Christ Child (“el Niño”).

questions.question: In a cave, a stalactite grows down from the ceiling and a stalagmite grows up from the floor. When they finally meet, what do they form?
hints: It joins top to bottom.
It looks like something holding up the ceiling.
Greek temples have lots of them.
questions.description: A love story so slow it takes thousands of years to reach the first kiss.
questions.fun_fact: Stalactites grow so slowly that sometimes they gain only about one centimeter (less than half an inch) in a hundred years.

questions.question: What do planting trees on a bare mountain, building farming terraces and planting rows of vetiver grass have in common?
hints: All three help stop the rain from carrying something away.
Roots hold on to the soil.
It's the wearing away of the ground by water and wind.
questions.description: When a mountain starts going bald, it needs a really good hair transplant.
questions.fun_fact: The roots of vetiver grass can grow more than 3 meters (10 ft) deep into the ground.

questions.question: Benjamin Franklin, the man with the famous kite in the storm, invented three of these things. Which one did he NOT invent?
hints: One of his inventions came straight from his kite experiment.
The one that isn't his came more than a hundred years later.
That one is mostly credited to Thomas Edison.
questions.description: A man who flew kites in the middle of a storm… and no, don't try this at home.
questions.fun_fact: Franklin never patented his inventions: he wanted everyone to be able to use them for free.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a very famous trophy. Who competes to win it every year?
wrong_answers: National teams from around the world
hints: It isn't played by countries, but by teams.
Its name honors the heroes of the wars of independence.
It's the Copa Libertadores.
questions.description: A trophy so coveted that some fans get its outline tattooed on their skin.
questions.fun_fact: The first Copa Libertadores was played in 1960, and it was won by Peñarol of Uruguay.

questions.question: The referee sprays a line that vanishes on its own, so the wall can't creep forward. At which World Cup was it first used?
hints: It's more recent than you might think.
It was at a World Cup in the 2010s.
Germany won that World Cup.
questions.description: The only graffiti a referee can paint on the field without getting sent off.
questions.fun_fact: One of its inventors is Argentina's Pablo Silva, and the foam disappears by itself in a minute or two.

questions.question: What do a cat, an owl and a crocodile have in common?
wrong_answers: They see in black and white
hints: It has to do with how they protect their eyes.
It's a thin film that slides sideways across the eye.
On top of the usual two, they have one more.
questions.description: A cat, an owl and a crocodile walk into a doctor's office… and no, this isn't the start of a joke.
questions.fun_fact: You can sometimes see a cat's third eyelid when it's half asleep or sick: it's a thin white film in the corner of the eye.

questions.question: Daedalus designed it, it was on Crete, and Theseus got out of it by following Ariadne's thread. What was it?
hints: A monster was locked up inside it.
That monster was half man, half bull.
It is full of corridors and dead ends.
questions.description: A job for a king with more secrets than Grandma's junk room.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew,” an old word for a ball of thread, like the one Ariadne gave Theseus.

questions.question: Guess who: “A goddess cursed me to repeat only the last words others say, and I fell for a young man who only looked at himself in the water.” Who am I?
hints: The young man I fell in love with was called Narcissus.
The goddess Hera punished me because my chatter kept distracting her.
Shout your name into a canyon and I’ll answer… with your name.
questions.description: A girl who always gets the last word… but never the first.
questions.fun_fact: The word “echo” comes from this nymph, and the word “narcissist” comes from the young Narcissus.

questions.question: Guess who: “I married Eros, the god of love, but I wasn’t allowed to see his face. My name means ‘soul’ in Greek.” Who am I?
hints: In the end, Zeus made me a goddess.
Artists sometimes paint me with butterfly wings.
Words like “psychology” come from my name.
