questions.description: A love story where one of them couldn’t even see the other’s profile picture.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Greek, “psyche” meant both “soul” and “butterfly”.

questions.question: A kitchen knife is to a Swiss Army knife as an AI that can only play chess is to…
hints: The Swiss Army knife isn't bigger: it can do more things.
Scientists haven't managed to actually build it yet.
Its short name is AGI, and it's the opposite of a “narrow” or specialized AI.
questions.description: Machines have their own “when I grow up, I want to be…” too.
questions.fun_fact: Several AI labs, such as OpenAI, openly say that building artificial general intelligence is their main goal.

questions.question: Copilot is made by Microsoft and shows up in Windows, Word and Excel with a colorful icon. Its name comes from the person who sits next to the pilot. What is Copilot?
questions.answer: An assistant that answers your questions
wrong_answers: A checker that underlines your mistakes
A guard that blocks computer viruses
A search tool that finds your files
hints: It has nothing to do with planes, even if the name sounds like it.
You can ask it to sum up a document or help you write an email.
It's a chatbot, from the same family as ChatGPT.
questions.description: Someone has to sit next to the pilot, and it isn't always a person.
questions.fun_fact: Before it came to Windows, the name was used for GitHub Copilot, launched in 2021 to help programmers write code.

questions.question: It started in 2013 as a joke, its symbol is the Shiba Inu dog from the Doge meme, and Elon Musk has posted about it many times. What is it?
hints: Some people buy and sell it.
It doesn't exist as paper bills or metal coins.
It's a relative of Bitcoin.
questions.description: Such doggo. Very internet. Wow.
questions.fun_fact: The dog in the meme was named Kabosu and lived in Japan with her owner, a teacher.

questions.question: Samoa and American Samoa are less than 200 km (125 miles) apart. How many hours apart are their clocks?
hints: A very special imaginary line runs between the two islands.
That line marks where each new day begins on the planet.
The clocks show the same time, but on one island it's already tomorrow.
questions.description: Neighbors so close they could borrow sugar from each other, yet they never agree on the clock.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, Samoa skipped December 30 entirely so it would end up on the other side of the International Date Line.

questions.question: The city of Bombay (now Mumbai), in India, was made by joining several islands with landfill. How many islands were there?
hints: The English took more than a century to join them all with landfill.
There were few enough to count on your fingers.
It is the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.description: A giant city that is really a jigsaw puzzle put together with dirt and patience.
questions.fun_fact: The English got Bombay as part of the dowry of a Portuguese princess who married King Charles II.

questions.question: The name of the Canary Islands comes from Latin and hides an animal. Which one?
hints: The Romans already knew about these islands in the Atlantic.
In Latin, this animal was called “canis.”
It's the animal that wags its tail when you come home.
questions.description: A name that looks obvious, but has hidden a surprise since Roman times.
questions.fun_fact: It's the other way around from what most people think: the canary bird is named after the islands, not the islands after the bird.

questions.question: What do Hong Kong, Singapore and Jamaica have in common in their history?
hints: That European empire left all three its language as an official language.
That empire had the most powerful navy in the world in the 19th century.
In all three places, people still drive on the left.
questions.description: Three places with beaches, lots of heat and a past that arrived by ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997, after more than 150 years under British rule.

questions.question: In the film “My Neighbor Totoro,” how many Totoros appear?
hints: He is not alone in the forest.
They are not all the same size: the biggest one is the one waiting for the bus in the rain.
It's the same number as the little pigs in the story with the big bad wolf.
questions.description: The giant cuddly toy everyone would love as a pillow on a rainy day.
questions.fun_fact: Totoro appears in the logo of Studio Ghibli, the Japanese studio that made the film in 1988.

questions.question: In a famous picture book, a turtle, an elephant, a giraffe, a zebra and even a mouse climb on top of each other. What did they all want to taste?
hints: What they want is very, very high up.
You can only see it well at night.
The book's title is about getting a taste of it.
questions.description: A tower of animals that no architect would ever approve.
questions.fun_fact: The book was written and illustrated by Polish-born Michael Grejniec, and at the end a fish can't see why they tried so hard, because it has another moon right beside it, reflected in the water.

questions.question: In a Roald Dahl book, three men named Boggis, Bunce and Bean spend days chasing a very clever fox. What are the three men?
hints: The three are neighbors, very rich and very stingy.
One is fat, one is short and one is thin, and none of them can stand the fox.
One keeps chickens, one keeps ducks and geese, and one keeps turkeys and apples.
questions.description: Three neighbors with very bad luck and one furry neighbor with very good luck.
questions.fun_fact: Wes Anderson turned “Fantastic Mr. Fox” into a 2009 movie, using puppets animated one frame at a time.

questions.question: García Márquez is to “One Hundred Years of Solitude” as Isabel Allende is to…
hints: It is Isabel Allende's first novel, from 1982.
It tells the story of several generations of the Trueba family.
Its title is about a home full of ghosts.
questions.description: A question for people who read long novels with even longer family trees.
questions.fun_fact: “The House of the Spirits” began as a letter Isabel Allende started writing to her grandfather in 1981.

questions.question: In “Love in the Time of Cholera”, Florentino Ariza waits and waits for his love, Fermina Daza. How many years does he wait, according to the novel?
hints: It's a very long time: when they finally get together, they are both old.
The novel says: “… years, nine months and four days.”
It's a number just over 50.
questions.description: The longest wait in literature, worse than the line at the bank on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez based this novel partly on the love story of his own parents.

questions.question: In many video games, characters drink little red bottles in the middle of a battle. What does one of those bottles almost always do?
hints: Think about what happens when an enemy hits you.
When you drink it, a bar that was running low goes back up.
It's the same color as the little hearts many games show in a corner.
questions.description: A colorful little drink that's worth more than gold in video games.
questions.fun_fact: In many games, health potions are red and magic potions are blue, a color code players understand without reading a word.

questions.question: Which legendary magician from Madrid does impossible card tricks and sings “¡Tararí, que te vi!”?
hints: He is seen as one of the best card magicians in the world.
He is a master of card magic who spent decades on Spanish TV.
His surname starts with “Tam”.
questions.description: A magician who laughs more than his audience, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: Many professional magicians around the world study this Spanish magician's books on how to fool the audience's memory.

questions.question: I'm the Minecraft enchanting table: I have a book that floats and opens when you come close. What happens if you surround me with bookshelves?
wrong_answers: You can enchant several items at once
You no longer need lapis lazuli
hints: The bookshelves must be nearby, but with one free block between them and the table.
Look at the numbers next to each enchantment option.
More books around it, more magical wisdom for the table.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that reads more than you do, and it doesn't even have eyes.
questions.fun_fact: With enough bookshelves around it, the Minecraft enchanting table can offer level 30 enchantments.

questions.question: On a day trip, you drink tap water, swim in a river and later row on a mountain lake. What do those three waters have in common?
hints: None of them tastes like the sea.
It's the kind people and animals can drink.
Its name uses the same word as bread just out of the oven.
questions.description: A day out in the country with three different dips and not a single wave.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all the water on Earth is salty: fresh water is only about 3%, and most of it is frozen.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“What do those three waters have in common?”). That style is retired (reason 7), and it applies to the source too. The translation itself is faithful, and the new hint 3 (fresh bread) works well in English.

questions.question: A shark has several rows of teeth and loses them easily. What happens when one falls out?
questions.answer: A tooth from the row behind moves forward
wrong_answers: The gap stays there for the rest of its life
The whole row of teeth falls out with it
It stops eating until the gum heals
hints: It never runs out of teeth.
Its teeth work like a conveyor belt.
Spare teeth are already waiting behind.
questions.description: If the Tooth Fairy paid for every shark tooth, she would go broke.
questions.fun_fact: Fossil shark teeth are so common on some beaches that you can find them just by walking along the shore.

questions.question: Take a close look at this water animal. Which group of animals does it belong to?
hints: It has whiskers on its snout.
It comes up to the surface to breathe air.
The mothers feed their babies with milk.
questions.description: A calm, chubby fellow who spends all day eating grass… underwater.
questions.fun_fact: The manatee's closest living relatives are dugongs, and outside their own group, its closest relatives are elephants and hyraxes.

questions.question: He's called the father of geometry, wrote a book called “Elements” and lived about 2,300 years ago. Which civilization was Euclid from?
hints: His civilization was famous for its philosophers.
He came from the same culture as Pythagoras and Archimedes.
His civilization also invented the Olympic Games.
questions.description: The man who turned triangles into a bestseller for more than 2,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Euclid's “Elements” is one of the most-printed books in history and was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.

questions.question: Complete: “equilateral” is to three equal sides as “scalene” is to…
hints: Its name comes from a Greek word.
The one with two equal sides is called isosceles.
You measure its three sides and get three different numbers.
questions.description: Triangles have some really strange names too.
questions.fun_fact: “Scalene” comes from the Greek word “skalenos,” which means limping or uneven.

questions.question: This lump of corroded bronze was pulled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901. What was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
questions.answer: Predicting eclipses and movements in the sky
wrong_answers: Measuring how deep the sea is
hints: It had dozens of gear wheels, like a clock.
It showed the Sun, the Moon and maybe some planets.
It is seen as the oldest known astronomical calculator.
questions.description: Divers looking for sea sponges found a 2,000-year-old bronze puzzle on the seabed.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody built a device with such complex gears again until the astronomical clocks of the Middle Ages, more than a thousand years later.

questions.question: At the beach you see a starfish, in the water a jellyfish, and in the kitchen you cut an orange in half. What do they have in common?
hints: It has to do with how their parts repeat.
Their parts spread out from a center, like the spokes of a wheel.
Its name comes from “radius,” like the radius of a circle.
questions.description: Nature is the best artist in geometry class.
questions.fun_fact: Baby starfish have bilateral symmetry, like us, and only become radial as they grow up.

questions.question: Which of these energy sources is NOT renewable?
hints: Renewable sources never run out: they come back on their own.
The one you want is dug out of a mine, like a rock.
It's used in nuclear power plants, like the one where Homer Simpson works.
questions.description: Some energy comes back by itself every day, and some is gone for good once it runs out.
questions.fun_fact: One uranium fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, gives as much energy as a ton of coal.

questions.question: Hyenas, vultures and condors have something in common in what they eat. What are they?
hints: None of them eats grass or flowers.
They love finding food that's already… not moving.
They eat the remains of animals that were already dead.
questions.description: Three animals that look nothing alike, but would happily order from the same dinner menu.
questions.fun_fact: An Andean condor's open wings can measure more than 3 m (10 ft), almost the length of a small car.

questions.question: Hoover in the United States, Itaipu between Brazil and Paraguay, and Three Gorges in China. What are all three?
hints: All three sit on huge rivers.
They hold back water with a giant wall.
They make electricity from the force of falling water.
questions.description: Three concrete giants so famous they have more fans than most movie stars.
questions.fun_fact: Brazil and Paraguay share Itaipu and split the electricity it makes.

questions.question: Which of these four people never won the Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: The other three won the prize between 2004 and 2014.
One of them planted millions of trees in Kenya, and she did win it.
The person you're looking for is famous for studying chimpanzees.
questions.description: An inconvenient truth: not every hero of the planet has the same medal.
questions.fun_fact: Wangari Maathai was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, in 2004, for a movement that planted millions of trees.

questions.question: This radioactive chemical element was discovered by a Swedish chemist in the 19th century and named after the Norse god of thunder. What is it?
hints: Several elements are named after gods or planets.
The chemist was Jöns Jacob Berzelius.
Take the thunder god's name and add “-ium”.
questions.description: The thunder god sneaked onto the periodic table too, and he didn't even need his hammer.
questions.fun_fact: Years earlier, Berzelius had already used the name “thorium” for a supposed new element that turned out to be a mistake.

questions.question: Riddle: I am Brísingamen, the golden necklace of the goddess Freya. Four brothers in Norse myth forged me. What kind of beings were they?
hints: In Norse myths, these beings also made famous weapons for the gods.
They live underground and are the best blacksmiths.
They are small, bearded and work in mines.
questions.description: The shiniest jewel in Asgard, and nobody bought it at the mall.
questions.fun_fact: In the myths, dwarves also forged Mjölnir, Thor's hammer.

questions.question: Bollo preñao is from Asturias, a must at every romería, and is baked with something tucked inside the dough. What?
hints: It's a cured sausage.
It lets out a red fat that soaks into the bread.
It's made from pork and seasoned with paprika.
questions.description: A bun that comes out of the oven with a surprise already inside.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “preñao” (pregnant) because the bread looks as if it's expecting the chorizo inside it.

questions.question: I have one name in Spanish and another in Basque, and the Basque Parliament and Government meet in me. Which city am I?
hints: I am not the biggest city in my region.
I am the capital of the province of Álava.
In 1813, a battle where Wellington beat Napoleon's troops was named after me.
questions.description: A city with two names on every sign and a free txirimiri drizzle on top.
questions.fun_fact: Vitoria-Gasteiz was European Green Capital in 2012 thanks to the ring of parks around the city.

questions.question: Guadalajara, the Guadalquivir and the Guadiana all start the same way, because that part of their names comes from Arabic. What does it mean?
hints: Think about what the Guadalquivir and the Guadiana have in common.
Guadalajara stands on the banks of the Henares.
Guadalquivir means “the great …”.
questions.description: More than a thousand years ago, someone named half of Spain and everything came out starting the same way.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has another Guadalajara, founded by Spaniards and now much bigger than the original.

questions.question: The highest mountain in Spain is on the island of Tenerife. What is it called?
hints: It's a volcano.
It's more than 3,700 m (12,000 ft) high.
Its name starts with “T,” like the island.
questions.description: An island that keeps a record at home too big to fit on any shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Measured from the ocean floor, Teide is more than 7,000 m (23,000 ft) tall.

questions.question: Which province is marked on this map?
hints: It has a coastline on the Mediterranean.
It is the northernmost province of the Valencian Community.
Its capital's full name ends in “de la Plana”.
questions.description: A colored patch of map waiting for someone to recognize it without GPS.
questions.fun_fact: Castellón is home to Peñíscola, a town on a rock in the sea, with the castle where Pope Luna lived.

questions.question: They separate Spain from France, Andorra sits in the middle and their highest peak is Aneto. Which mountain range is it?
hints: It is in the north of the peninsula.
It runs from the Bay of Biscay to the Mediterranean.
The Way of St. James pilgrimage route enters Spain over it at Roncesvalles.
questions.description: Mountains so tall that in winter they put on a snow hat and fill up with skiers.
questions.fun_fact: This range is home to the bearded vulture, a bird that lives mostly on bones.

questions.question: Don Pelayo won the Battle of Covadonga, in Asturias. About how many years ago was that?
hints: It was in the Middle Ages.
It was long before Columbus reached America.
It was a few years after the Muslims arrived in the Iberian Peninsula, in the year 711.
questions.description: A fight so old that not even your great-great-grandparents' great-great-grandparents saw it.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, Don Pelayo is buried in the Holy Cave of Covadonga.

questions.question: What is the capital of the autonomous community marked on the map?
hints: This community has only one province.
The capital isn't the community's biggest city.
Its people are nicknamed “carbayones.”
questions.description: A land of green mountains, fine drizzle and cider poured from way up high.
questions.fun_fact: Oviedo has a statue of Woody Allen, who shot part of one of his films in the city.

questions.question: Look at the flag of Aragon. How many red stripes does it have on its yellow background?
hints: More than three.
It's an even number.
As many as a dog has legs.
questions.description: A striped flag that is neither a zebra nor a pair of pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: The red stripes on yellow come from the old Crown of Aragon and also appear on the flags of Catalonia, the Valencian Community and the Balearic Islands.

questions.question: You're in the province that produces more olive oil than any other in the world. What are the people from there called?
hints: This province is in Andalusia.
Its capital has a Renaissance cathedral and the Castle of Santa Catalina.
Its capital starts with “J”.
questions.description: A province so full of oil that even the toast gets nervous.
questions.fun_fact: The province of Jaén has more than 60 million olive trees.

questions.question: Cider is the most famous drink of Asturias, and it's poured from very high up. What fruit is it made from?
hints: It's a fruit that grows on trees.
It can be red, green or yellow.
It's the fruit that, as the story goes, fell on Newton's head.
questions.description: A drink poured from so high up that it looks like a circus act.
questions.fun_fact: Pouring cider from high up is called “escanciar,” and it puts bubbles into the cider as it splashes into the glass.

questions.question: You drive along Spain's north coast from west to east: Galicia, Asturias… which region comes next?
hints: It is a region with only one province.
Its capital is Santander.
The Altamira caves are there.
questions.description: A road trip where the green never ends and the sea is always on your left.
questions.fun_fact: The Altamira caves have bison painted more than 15,000 years ago.

questions.question: Margarita Salas, a student of Severo Ochoa, found a protein that earned Spain's CSIC its most profitable patent. What is it used for?
hints: She studied it in her Madrid lab in the 1980s.
She found it in phi29, a virus that infects bacteria.
It is a DNA polymerase that multiplies tiny samples of genetic material.
questions.description: A Spanish scientist whose discovery paid out more than a whole stack of Christmas lottery tickets.
questions.fun_fact: Margarita Salas was the first Spanish woman to join the US National Academy of Sciences.

questions.question: Musa ibn Nusayr, governor of North Africa, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar with his army and then took Mérida. In which year did he cross?
hints: It was during the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.
He came to join an invasion that had started shortly before.
It was exactly one year after the Battle of Guadalete.
questions.description: A leader who showed up late to the party but still grabbed the best dishes.
questions.fun_fact: Soon after conquering half the peninsula, Musa was called back to Damascus by the caliph, and he never returned to Hispania.

questions.question: Babieca was El Cid's faithful companion in all his battles. What animal was Babieca?
hints: El Cid never went into battle without him.
He had four legs and was very fast.
He neighed.
questions.description: Every great hero needs a good travel buddy.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says El Cid picked Babieca as a foal, and his godfather shouted “¡babieca!” (“fool!”) at him for choosing such a weak-looking horse.

questions.question: Look at this detail of an Andalusi machine beside the Guadalquivir river in Córdoba. What is it?
hints: Its job had to do with the river.
It turns thanks to the river's current.
It's a giant wheel that lifted river water up to the palace gardens.
questions.description: A medieval machine that worked day and night with no plug and no vacation days.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word for it, “noria,” comes from the Arabic “na'ura,” which imitates the groaning sound the wheel made as it turned.

questions.question: A very Spanish dish owes its name to the Arabic word for this nut. Which dish is it?
hints: It's a meat dish.
It's often served in tomato sauce.
They're little balls of ground meat.
questions.description: A dish named after what a squirrel keeps in its pantry.
questions.fun_fact: “Albóndiga” comes from Andalusi Arabic “al-búnduqa,” “the little ball,” and “búnduq” meant hazelnut.

questions.question: Ildefons Cerdà, who planned Barcelona's Eixample, published his great work in 1867. Complete the title: “General Theory of…”
hints: The book explains how cities should grow and be organized.
With his plan, Cerdà wanted streets with more light, more air and more green space.
In Spain, the same word also names a housing estate with a shared pool.
questions.description: An engineer who drew a grid over Barcelona like a page from a math notebook.
questions.fun_fact: Cerdà cut off the corners of the Eixample's blocks, the chaflanes, so vehicles could see better when turning.

questions.question: Many telescopes at the Teide Observatory, like this one, study just one object in the sky. Which one?
hints: These telescopes need very strong filters.
Looking straight at it without protection harms your eyes.
It is the closest star to Earth.
questions.description: Telescopes with a luxury view, more than 2,000 meters (6,600 ft) above the sea.
questions.fun_fact: The sky over Tenerife is so steady that several European countries have built their solar telescopes there.

questions.question: Newspapers and school projects often use posters that explain facts with icons, charts and very little text. What are they called?
hints: It helps you understand something complicated at a glance.
It mixes numbers and pictures.
Its name joins “information” and “graphic.”
questions.description: For people who read the news but only look at the pictures.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1800s, the nurse Florence Nightingale used colorful charts to convince the British government to improve hospitals.

questions.question: It's clear, fizzy and a little sweet. Mixed with red wine, it makes tinto de verano. What is it?
hints: In many homes it was mixed with the wine at lunch.
It used to be sold in returnable glass bottles.
La Casera is its best-known brand.
questions.description: The shyest drink in the fridge: it doesn't even dare to have a color.
questions.fun_fact: Gaseosa is also used in cooking: a few drops in batter make it lighter and fluffier.

questions.question: In Spain, what do you call a block of ice cream squeezed between two wafers?
hints: You eat it with your hands, biting around the edges.
The ice cream man used to make it on the spot in the street.
Its name comes from the way each portion was taken from the big block.
questions.description: The sandwich no mom ever packs as an afternoon snack in January.
questions.fun_fact: It gets its name because the ice cream man would cut (cortar) each portion from a big block of ice cream.

questions.question: Cava from Sant Sadurní d'Anoia gets its bubbles the same way as French champagne. Where do the bubbles come from?
questions.answer: A second fermentation inside the bottle
wrong_answers: Carbon dioxide pumped in by a machine
Sparkling water mixed into the wine
hints: The bubbles are made by tiny living things, not a machine.
Yeasts eat the sugar and give off gas, just like in bread.
The wine ferments again, but this time sealed in its own bottle.
questions.description: A wine with so much energy its cork needs a muzzle.
questions.fun_fact: Cava bottles are slowly turned upside down so the yeast sediment collects in the neck and can be removed.

questions.question: Since 2016 it has been held every third Thursday of June, promoted by Saborea España, a network of food destinations. What day is it?
hints: It doesn't celebrate a specific drink.
It celebrates a bar habit, not one particular dish.
Its star is a small bite that was once placed on top of the glass.
questions.description: A day on the calendar that's celebrated standing up, with an elbow on the bar.
questions.fun_fact: According to legend, the tapa was born when people covered their glass of wine with a slice of ham or bread to keep flies out.

questions.question: A Spanish mesón has hams hanging up, wooden beams and home cooking. Where does the word “mesón” come from?
questions.answer: From Latin “mansio”, a stop to spend the night
wrong_answers: From Latin “mensa”, the table people ate at
hints: It comes from the language of the Romans.
The Romans had official stopping places along their roads.
It's related to the word “mansion”.
questions.description: A restaurant with more wooden beams than a cowboy movie.
questions.fun_fact: Even though they look alike, “mesón” and “mesa” (table) aren't related: “mesón” is a cousin of “mansion”.

questions.question: In summer, bars in Andalusia serve them in a broth with mint and cumin. What are they?
hints: In France people eat them too, but with butter and garlic.
In Lleida they love them, but there they're cooked on the grill.
They don't come from the sea: they carry their house on their back.
questions.description: A summer tapa served in a bowl and slurped down to the last drop.
questions.fun_fact: In Seville, when the heat arrives, many bars put up a sign saying “Hay caracoles” (“We have snails”) to announce the season.

questions.question: You open a can of stuffed olives to snack on before lunch. What fish is the classic filling?
hints: It's a small, very salty fish.
Its little fillets also go on top of pizza.
On the Cantabrian coast, the town of Santoña is famous for them.
questions.description: An olive that swallowed a fish without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: Stuffed olives are pitted and filled by machines that can handle hundreds of olives a minute.

questions.question: I'm a daughter of the King of Spain, but not the heir to the throne, so I'm not called Princess of Asturias. What is my title?
hints: It's a title used in the royal houses of Spain and Portugal.
Unlike noble titles, it isn't tied to lands: you get it by being born a child of the king.
It's the title of Sofía, Leonor's younger sister.
questions.description: Being second in line has a name too, and it isn't “substitute”.
questions.fun_fact: “Infante” comes from the Latin “infans”, meaning “one who doesn't speak”, that is, a small child.

questions.question: How many daughters do King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia have?
hints: One of them will be queen one day.
The older one is called Leonor.
The younger one is called Sofía, and there are no more.
questions.description: At Zarzuela Palace, they also argue about who picks the Saturday night movie.
questions.fun_fact: Before she became queen, Letizia was a journalist who presented the news on Spanish TV channel TVE.

questions.question: This four-masted sailing ship of the Spanish Navy has been at sea for almost a century. What is it used for?
wrong_answers: Patrolling fishing in the Cantabrian Sea
hints: Young students board it every year.
Princess Leonor sailed on it in 2025.
Think of it as a school that floats.
questions.description: If sails could tell stories, this ship would have enough for an encyclopedia.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the sailor who completed the first voyage around the world, and the ship itself has now sailed around it about ten times.

questions.question: The brown tone of old photos is called sepia. Where did that pigment originally come from?
hints: It comes from an animal.
That animal lives in the sea and is a relative of the squid.
The animal lets out a dark cloud when it gets scared.
questions.description: Your great-great-grandparents' photos hide a rather strange secret.
questions.fun_fact: The cuttlefish, whose scientific name is Sepia, can change color in less than a second to hide.

questions.question: I'm an economist and moved into the Moncloa in 2018. A year later, my government moved Franco's remains out of the Valley of the Fallen. Who am I?
hints: I became prime minister through a vote of no confidence.
I belong to the PSOE.
My initials are P. S.
questions.description: The Moncloa got a new tenant in 2018, and it wasn't thanks to a rental ad.
questions.fun_fact: The remains were flown by helicopter to the Mingorrubio cemetery in El Pardo on October 24, 2019.

questions.question: The Egyptian vulture is the smallest vulture in Spain. What is its wingspan?
hints: It's bigger than a seagull.
Roughly the length of a person lying down.
More than one and a half meters, but less than two.
questions.description: In the vulture family, someone had to be the baby.
questions.fun_fact: It is one of the few birds that use tools: it throws stones at ostrich eggs to crack them open.

questions.question: Carp now live in many rivers and reservoirs in Spain, but their ancestors came from Asia. Why are they here?
wrong_answers: Because they swam across the Mediterranean
Because they swam down rivers from France
Because they survived here since the Ice Age
hints: It's a freshwater fish: it can't cross the sea.
River fish can't cross the Pyrenees, and there were no carp here in the Ice Age.
For centuries it was raised in ponds, then released into rivers and reservoirs.
questions.description: A fish with a mustache and plenty of patience at the bottom of the reservoir.
questions.fun_fact: A carp can live for more than 40 years.

questions.question: Which leader of the Lusitanians stood up to Rome in the 2nd century BC?
hints: He has a famous statue in Zamora.
According to tradition, he had once been a shepherd.
His name sounds a bit like the word “virile”.
questions.description: A man who gave Rome more headaches than a Latin exam.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the Spanish saying “Rome does not pay traitors” comes from his story.

questions.question: In the prehistory of Spain, which period came right before the Metal Ages?
hints: It was the age of polished stone.
Farming and herding began in this period.
Its name means “new stone”.
questions.description: The last stage before humans found out that tools could shine too.
questions.fun_fact: At La Draga (Banyoles, Girona) there's a Neolithic village about 7,000 years old where the lake water has preserved wooden tools.

questions.question: You're watching TV on New Year's Eve, and before the twelve chimes, the cuartos ring. How many are there?
hints: Many people get confused and start eating their grapes with them.
There are fewer than five.
Their name comes from the quarter hours.
questions.description: The “here they come, here they come!” warning that sends half of Spain reaching for the grapes too soon.
questions.fun_fact: The cuartos ring every 15 minutes all year round on the Puerta del Sol clock, not just on New Year's Eve.

questions.question: It's December 28 and you cut out a little paper doll. What are you going to do with it?
wrong_answers: Hang it on the Christmas tree
Put it in your shoe for the Three Kings
hints: It's a prank for that day.
It's the Día de los Santos Inocentes, the day of “inocentadas” (pranks).
The victim can't see it, but everyone else can.
questions.description: Arts and crafts with very bad intentions.
questions.fun_fact: In France and Italy the prank happens on April 1, and what they stick on people is a paper fish.

questions.question: At Easter, many godparents give a mona (an Easter cake) topped with eggs. What are those eggs usually made of today?
hints: You can eat them.
They're sweet and melt in the heat.
They're made from cocoa.
questions.description: Eggs that no hen would ever recognize as her own.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, the mona de Pascua was topped with hard-boiled eggs instead of chocolate ones.

questions.question: It's fried squid rings in a bread roll, ordered in the bars around the city's Plaza Mayor, and the city is far from the sea. Which city is it?
hints: It's inland, right in the middle of the meseta.
In the middle of its Plaza Mayor stands a statue of a king on horseback.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.description: A sandwich that tastes of the sea, in a city that can't even see it from far away.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid is about 300 km (190 miles) from the sea, and still this seafood sandwich is one of its great symbols.

questions.question: I'm a goddess riding a chariot pulled by two lions, and Real Madrid fans climb my fountain to celebrate titles. Who am I?
hints: I was the goddess of the earth and nature.
The Romans brought me from Asia Minor and called me “the Great Mother.”
My name starts with “C.”
questions.description: Madrid has plenty of statues, but only one gets visitors every time a cup is won.
questions.fun_fact: The fountain was built under King Carlos III in the 18th century, and it gave water to water carriers and horses.

questions.question: What is an oath, like the one some people make to their flag?
hints: It is said out loud and with great respect.
Whoever makes it commits to doing something.
It's like saying “I promise”, but in a very serious way.
questions.description: When school asks you to be really serious, at least for a little while.
questions.fun_fact: In many Latin American countries, children make their oath to the flag at a special school ceremony.

questions.question: Seville's Triana district, across the Guadalquivir, is the birthplace of flamenco singers and bullfighters. What have its workshops made for centuries?
hints: They're made from clay and fired in a kiln.
You see them on building fronts, fountains and benches all over Seville.
They're pieces of painted ceramic for covering walls.
questions.description: A neighborhood with more art per square meter than a museum on free-entry day.
questions.fun_fact: One of Triana's streets is called Calle Alfarería (Pottery Street) after the ceramic workshops that once lined it.

questions.question: Which city holds the Fallas, where huge figures are burned every March?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean coast.
Paella was born there.
Its autonomous community has the same name as the city.
questions.description: A city that spends a whole year building things just to burn them in one night.
questions.fun_fact: Every year two “pardoned” ninots are saved from the flames, one from the big fallas and one from the children's, and they end up in the Fallas Museum.

questions.question: Benidorm is to the Costa Blanca as Marbella is to the…
hints: Marbella is in the province of Málaga.
This coast is famous for good weather all year round.
Its name comes from the star that keeps us warm.
questions.description: Yachts, marinas and celebrities posing on the seafront promenade.
questions.fun_fact: Marbella's old town has the Plaza de los Naranjos, named after the orange trees that surround it.

questions.question: It's a damp forest of shiny evergreen trees, wrapped in fog, that survives in Garajonay park on La Gomera. What is it called?
hints: Millions of years ago it covered much of southern Europe.
Today it survives only on Atlantic islands like the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores.
Its name joins “laurel” with the Latin word for “forest”.
questions.description: A forest so old it was vintage before humans even existed.
questions.fun_fact: Garajonay National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.

questions.question: I'm a crustacean that's red even before I'm cooked. I'm caught in deep water off the Costa Brava, and a quality label carries my port's name. Who am I?
hints: My port is in the north of Spain's Mediterranean coast, not far from France.
My town has a fishing museum.
My town's name starts with “Pala…”.
questions.description: A seafood so famous it uses its hometown as a last name.
questions.fun_fact: The red shrimp lives several hundred meters (over 1,000 ft) deep, where almost no light reaches.

questions.question: It's the most common gull on Spain's coast, has yellow legs and its call rings out in every port. Where does it nest more and more often?
wrong_answers: In the tops of pine trees
hints: It nests close to easy food, like garbage.
It used to nest mostly on cliffs and small islands, but its habits have changed.
It looks for high, flat, quiet places, like rooftop terraces.
questions.description: A seabird with plenty of nerve and not a shred of shame.
questions.fun_fact: Gull chicks peck at the red spot on their parents' beak to ask them for food.

questions.question: Which gulf is formed by the coast between Cape St. Vincent, in Portugal, and the Strait of Gibraltar?
hints: It's a gulf of the Atlantic Ocean.
The Guadalquivir flows into it, next to Doñana.
It's named after a city said to be the oldest in Western Europe.
questions.description: A stretch of sea where the waves reach the beach already knowing the way.
questions.fun_fact: The Guadalquivir, the Guadiana and the Tinto, a river with reddish water, all flow into the Gulf of Cádiz.

questions.question: Which of these beings does NOT belong to Basque mythology, the world of the goddess Mari?
hints: Three of them live in the mountains and rivers of the Basque Country and Navarre.
Sugaar is Mari's partner, shaped like a serpent.
The odd one out is a one-eyed giant from Cantabria.
questions.description: A goddess who lives in a cave and still has a packed calendar.
questions.fun_fact: Mari was said to have her main cave on Mount Anboto and to travel across the sky from one mountain to another as a ball of fire.

questions.question: The Tragantía, half woman and half serpent, sings in a castle on Saint John's Eve and swallows anyone who hears her. Which town is the legend from?
hints: It's in Andalusia.
It's in the province of Jaén.
It's the gateway to the mountains where the Guadalquivir River begins.
questions.description: A singer with a very loyal audience, mostly because she never lets them leave.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, the Tragantía was a Moorish princess left under a spell in the castle when the Christians conquered the town.

questions.question: In Hundir la flota, Spain's Battleship, you say “agua” for a miss and “hundido” when a ship sinks. What do you say for a hit that doesn't sink it?
hints: The ship is still afloat, but damaged.
It means you hit one part of the ship, but not all of it.
Spaniards also say it about someone shaken by a piece of news.
questions.description: A pen-and-paper naval war where nobody gets wet.
questions.fun_fact: Before it was sold in a box, people played it on grids drawn on paper, like in school.

questions.question: When you jump rope with a long rope, how many people usually turn it?
hints: It's a schoolyard game played in a group.
Whoever turns the rope stands still, facing the jumper.
The rope is held at both ends.
questions.description: A schoolyard sport where the hard part is knowing when to jump in.
questions.fun_fact: Many jump-rope songs, like “Al pasar la barca”, help keep the rhythm of the jumps.

questions.question: Sargadelos pottery, famous for its blue designs, comes from which autonomous community?
hints: It's in the north of Spain.
This region has its own co-official language.
It's the land of pulpo a feira and the Camino de Santiago.
questions.description: Dishes so elegant it feels wrong to wash them.
questions.fun_fact: Antonio Raimundo Ibáñez founded the first Sargadelos factory in 1806, and in the 20th century Isaac Díaz Pardo brought the brand back to life.

questions.question: You draw it on the ground in chalk, throw a stone onto a square and hop on one foot. What game is it?
hints: The squares are numbered.
You can't step on the square where the stone is.
In some parts of Spain it's called “el tejo”.
questions.description: Recess: the place where knees find out what bandages are for.
questions.fun_fact: Julio Cortázar named one of his most famous novels “Rayuela”, published in English as “Hopscotch”.

questions.question: He rides through the streets on a bike, plays a panpipe to say he's coming and carries a spinning stone wheel. What does he do?
hints: You can hear his tune from your window.
What he works on cuts better afterwards.
Sparks fly when he rubs metal against the stone.
questions.description: The only street musician people run out to meet with something in their hand.
questions.fun_fact: Many traveling knife grinders came from Ourense, in Galicia, and they even had their own secret slang.

questions.question: It's made with silk thread, it trims mantillas and it gives its name to the cut-out paper bakeries put under cakes. What is blonda?
hints: It's very fine needlework, full of holes.
Holy Week mantillas are often made of it.
It's like what bobbin workers make on their cushions.
questions.description: A fancy word that ends up under your birthday cake.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the French “blonde”, because of the natural golden color of the silk it was made from.

questions.question: In pilla-pilla (tag), whoever chases the others “se la queda” (is “it”). If you get tagged, what happens?
wrong_answers: You go back to the start
hints: You're not out.
You switch roles.
Now you're the one running after everyone else.
questions.description: The national sport of every school recess, with no ball and no referee.
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the part of Spain, the chaser is said to “quedársela” or to “ligarla”.

questions.question: Vichy Catalán is a water that comes out hot from a spring in Girona. What kind of water is it?
hints: Many people order it at the bar after a meal.
It tickles your tongue.
When you open the bottle, it goes “pssst”.
questions.description: Water, yes, but with a bit more personality.
questions.fun_fact: Vichy Catalán comes from Caldes de Malavella (Girona), where the water rises from the ground at about 60 °C (140 °F).

questions.question: I'm a triangle of vineyards on white albariza soil in Cádiz, and my wines age in casks using criaderas and soleras. What am I called?
hints: My wines have been sailing to England for centuries.
One of my corners sits by the mouth of the Guadalquivir river.
My name holds the name of the city behind fino and oloroso.
questions.description: A triangle you never studied in geometry class, but it smells like a wine cellar.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “sherry” comes from how the English pronounced the name Jerez.

questions.question: This portrait shows the heir of Philip II whose own father had him arrested in 1568. Who is he?
hints: He was Philip II's first son, by his first wife, Maria Manuela of Portugal.
Schiller wrote a play about him, and Verdi wrote an opera about him.
He shares his name with his grandfather, Emperor Charles V.
questions.description: Being the son of the most powerful king in the world didn't guarantee nice family dinners.
questions.fun_fact: His death in prison, a few months after his arrest, gave rise to a “black legend” that inspired novels, plays and operas all over Europe.

questions.question: The potato reached Europe on Spanish ships in the 16th century. Where does it come from?
hints: It arrived in Spain after Columbus's voyages.
The Incas had been growing it for a very long time.
It comes from the Andes mountains, in Peru and Bolivia.
questions.description: As Spanish as the tortilla… or so we thought.
questions.fun_fact: Peru grows more than 3,000 kinds of potato, in colors like purple and bright yellow.

questions.question: The ancient Egyptians painted this eye on their boats and wore it around their necks. What did they use it for?
questions.answer: To protect themselves and stay healthy
wrong_answers: To guide their boats along the Nile
To show that they were nobles
To measure the passing of time
hints: Both rich and poor people used it.
The living wore it, and it was also placed on mummies.
According to the myth, the falcon god's eye was healed after a fight.
questions.description: An eye that has been watching for thousands of years and still doesn't need glasses.
questions.fun_fact: The Eye of Horus is still worn today as a pendant on necklaces and shows up in many video games.

questions.question: The Royal Monastery of Guadalupe, in Cáceres, was founded by King Alfonso XI after the Battle of Río Salado. In which century?
hints: It is older than the Catholic Monarchs, who visited it many times.
Alfonso XI is a distant ancestor of Isabella the Catholic.
It is the same century as the Black Death in Europe.
questions.description: A monastery so old its stones could teach history classes.
questions.fun_fact: In 1493, Columbus named a Caribbean island Guadeloupe in honor of this monastery's Virgin.

questions.question: This detail is from a famous Velázquez painting in the Prado. Which painting is it?
hints: It shows an episode from the wars in Flanders.
A defeated general hands something small to the winner, who receives it with respect.
It's also called “The Lances”.
questions.description: Velázquez painted so well that some Prado visitors are still waiting for his figures to move.
questions.fun_fact: Velázquez painted the scene about ten years after the surrender, without ever having been to Breda.

questions.question: Quevedo and Gracián were great writers of conceptismo, a style of the Spanish Baroque. What was it based on?
questions.answer: On wit and double meanings in few words
wrong_answers: On learned words and very twisted sentences
On showing life as it is, without ornament
On singing of ideal love in a country setting
hints: The idea mattered more to it than the rare word.
Its writers often wrote satires and moral maxims.
Gracián summed it up: “Good things, if brief, are twice as good.”
questions.description: In the Golden Age, even poets had to pick a team.
questions.fun_fact: Quevedo and Góngora, the great writer of the rival style, culteranismo, wrote each other mocking sonnets for years.

questions.question: The phrase “dark night of the soul”, used for a deep inner crisis, comes from a poem by a Spanish mystic. Who?
hints: He was a Carmelite friar in the 16th century.
He reformed the Carmelite order together with a saint from Ávila.
He wrote several poems while locked up in a convent in Toledo.
questions.description: A phrase used today even by people who have never set foot in a convent.
questions.fun_fact: He escaped his prison in Toledo by climbing down from a window on a rope made of blankets.

questions.question: Which of these businesses is the Spanish company Repsol NOT in?
hints: Repsol is mainly an energy and fuel company.
The business you're looking for is in a very different sector, with no tanks or pumps.
In Spain, this business is run mainly by Renfe.
questions.description: A company with more businesses than fit in a full tank.
questions.fun_fact: For almost 30 years, Honda's official MotoGP bikes raced in Repsol's orange colors.

questions.question: At the Fallas Ofrenda, the falleras' bouquets cover a huge figure of the Virgin. What flowers are they mostly?
hints: They are small, very cheap flowers with frilly petals.
The most common colors are red and white.
It's the flower many people picture in a flamenco dancer's hair.
questions.description: The best-smelling dress in all of Valencia, and no shop sells it.
questions.fun_fact: The wooden frame of the Virgin that gets covered in flowers is about 15 m (50 ft) tall.

questions.question: In which decade did Los Chunguitos release their rumba “Me quedo contigo”?
hints: Spain already had its Constitution when it came out.
It came out in the early years of democracy.
It was used in Carlos Saura's film “Deprisa, deprisa” (1981).
questions.description: Some songs turn up at every wedding, like the cousin nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: Rosalía sang it at the 2019 Goya Awards gala, and the song became popular all over again.

questions.question: My wooden floor shakes with zapateados, and every night there's flamenco singing, guitar and dance for an audience. What am I?
hints: Seville and Madrid have lots of us, full of tourists.
My stage is a slightly raised wooden platform.
My name comes from “tablado” (stage), said the Andalusian way.
questions.description: Here, if the floor isn't making noise, something has gone wrong.
questions.fun_fact: Corral de la Morería in Madrid opened in 1956 and is one of the most famous tablaos in the world.

questions.question: You're in a Spanish village in September and everyone is talking about the vendimia. What is the vendimia?
hints: It has to do with the countryside and the end of summer.
It's the first step in making wine.
Bunches are cut in the vineyards.
questions.description: The time of year when nobody in the village is home, not even to open the door.
questions.fun_fact: Long ago, grapes were crushed with bare feet, and many vendimia festivals still hold a grape-stomping to celebrate.

questions.question: Spain's rules for Iberian ham give every ham a colored tag. What color is the tag on 100% ibérico de bellota ham?
hints: White is for the lowest grade of ham.
It marks the most prized and expensive ham, from purebred pigs fed on acorns in the dehesa.
It's the color of these pigs' famous “pata” (hoof).
questions.description: A color code for hams that is stricter than a traffic light.
questions.fun_fact: The 2014 rules set the colors: black for 100% ibérico de bellota, red for crossbred bellota, green for cebo de campo and white for cebo.

questions.question: Look at this photo: who works behind a counter like this one?
hints: They use big knives.
They cut steaks and chops.
In Spain, their shop is called a carnicería.
questions.description: A job with an apron, a scale and lots of neighborhood chatter.
questions.fun_fact: In many Spanish markets, butchers grind the meat fresh right in front of the customer.

questions.question: In Spain, if you got up “con el pie izquierdo” (on your left foot), how long will everything go wrong, according to the saying?
hints: It starts the moment you get out of bed.
The bad luck doesn't last forever, but it's not a short while either.
It lasts until you go back to bed.
questions.description: The alarm went off, but something went crooked from the very first step.
questions.fun_fact: Since ancient Rome, the left side has been linked to bad luck: in Latin, “left” was “sinister”.

questions.question: It's the night of San Juan and you're on the beach. Which of these is NOT a tradition of that night?
hints: Think about what time of year each thing is done.
The odd one out belongs to another celebration.
That other celebration comes with the chimes of a clock.
questions.description: The shortest night of the year, with more fire than a village barbecue.
questions.fun_fact: In Alicante, the Hogueras de San Juan end with the “cremà”: huge cardboard monuments are burned on the night of June 24.

questions.question: “We're picked on the day of the shortest night of the year, we sleep in water out in the open, and in the morning you wash your face with us.” What are we?
hints: We're plants like rosemary, fennel or mallow.
The custom is very strong in Galicia and Asturias, where we're left outside all night in a basin.
We're picked on June 23.
questions.description: A bunch of flowers that spends the night outdoors to give you a face fit for a commercial.
questions.fun_fact: One of these plants, St. John's wort, takes its name from the saint because it blooms right at the end of June.

questions.question: The story goes that in 1909, farmers in Alicante turned a problem into a tradition and made New Year's Eve grapes popular. What problem?
questions.answer: They had far too many grapes
hints: It had to do with the harvest.
They were table grapes from the Vinalopó valley in Alicante.
They had more grapes than they could sell.
questions.description: Twelve quick bites so the new year doesn't catch you with your mouth full.
questions.fun_fact: Even earlier, around 1880, some people in Madrid ate grapes on New Year's Eve as a joke, copying the champagne drunk by the rich.

questions.question: Cuenca's San Pablo Bridge, opened in 1902, crosses the Huécar gorge to the old San Pablo convent. What is it made of?
hints: It replaced an old bridge that had fallen down.
It is from the same era as many train stations and covered markets.
It's a metal, like the one in the Eiffel Tower.
questions.description: A bridge you can see from the Hanging Houses, for anyone who finds hanging not thrilling enough.
questions.fun_fact: The first San Pablo Bridge, from the 16th century, was made of stone and paid for by a canon so he could reach his convent.

questions.question: In Madrid's Cibeles Fountain, the goddess sits in a chariot. Which animals pull it?
hints: They are wild animals.
They are felines.
They have a big mane.
questions.description: A goddess who rides around central Madrid in a chariot without a driver's license.
questions.fun_fact: Real Madrid fans celebrate their titles at the Cibeles Fountain.

questions.question: I'm a red flower with a black center and petals as thin as paper. In spring I grow among the wheat and along roadsides. What am I?
hints: If you pick me, I wilt almost right away.
I pop up by the hundreds in grain fields.
My name starts with “p”.
questions.description: Spring fields put on their party clothes, and this flower never misses the party.
questions.fun_fact: Poppy seeds can wait for years underground until someone turns over the soil.

questions.question: What international title do places like the Alhambra get for their outstanding value to the whole planet?
hints: It is given by a UN body based in Paris.
Spain is one of the countries with the most places that have it.
Think of it as an inheritance left to every person on the planet.
questions.description: A seal of quality that never goes on a jar, only on cathedrals and mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Teide National Park was named a World Heritage Site in 2007.

questions.question: This shrub grows in many forests in northern Spain, and in some areas it’s illegal to cut it. What is it called?
hints: Its shiny leaves have prickly edges.
Its little red berries appear in winter and are poisonous to people.
It’s the plant on many Christmas wreaths and cards.
questions.description: A plant that’s more famous in December than in the whole rest of the year.
questions.fun_fact: In Soria you’ll find the Acebal de Garagüeta, one of the largest holly forests in southern Europe.

questions.question: This mountain on Lanzarote has a big round hole at the top. What is it?
hints: A long time ago, smoke came out of that hole.
The rocks around it are black and reddish.
Burning-hot lava came out of it.
questions.description: A mountain with its mouth wide open, as if it had been yawning for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Lanzarote had eruptions for six years in a row, from 1730 to 1736, and they created the landscape of Timanfaya.

questions.question: This cave in Lanzarote is a very long, almost flat tunnel. What kind of cave is it?
hints: It formed very quickly, not over millions of years.
Something very hot once flowed through it.
A river of molten rock drained away and left a hollow channel, like a pipe.
questions.description: A tunnel nobody ever dug, and yet it's kilometers long.
questions.fun_fact: The lava tube of the Corona volcano in Lanzarote is more than 6 km (3.7 miles) long, and part of it continues under the sea.

questions.question: Under Spain's law on protected areas, what does a «monumento natural» (natural monument) protect?
wrong_answers: A rural landscape with villages and crops
hints: It usually covers a very small area.
It is protected for being rare, beautiful or of scientific interest.
Roque Nublo, on Gran Canaria, is one of them.
questions.description: A monument that nobody sculpted and that needs no pedestal.
questions.fun_fact: In Malpartida de Cáceres, Los Barruecos are a natural monument thanks to their huge granite boulders, with stork nests on top.

questions.question: The Segura River waters the farmland of Murcia and Orihuela before reaching the Mediterranean at Guardamar. In which province does it begin?
hints: It starts far from the sea, among mountains covered in pine trees.
Its spring is in a mountain range that shares its name.
It begins in Andalusia, in the province famous for its olive groves.
questions.description: A river that works full-time watering crops and never charges overtime.
questions.fun_fact: The Segura starts at a spring in the town of Santiago-Pontones, deep in the mountains.

questions.question: Look at this clay dish, a classic in bars on the Galician coast. Which shellfish is in it?
hints: Huge amounts of them are farmed in the Galician rías.
Their shells are long and bluish black.
They're grown hanging from bateas, floating platforms in the rías.
questions.description: A Galician bar classic you eat with your fingers and plenty of bread for dipping.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to the bateas in its rías, Galicia is one of the biggest mussel producers in the world.

questions.question: They're eaten mostly around All Saints' Day and fried in oil. Why are buñuelos “de viento” (“of wind”) called that?
wrong_answers: Because they were made on windy days
Because they're dried in the open air
Because they're sold in the street
hints: They're so light they hardly weigh anything in your hand.
When fried, the dough puffs up like a balloon.
That's why they can be filled with custard, cream or chocolate.
questions.description: An autumn treat with a name straight out of the weather forecast.
questions.fun_fact: In Madrid, buñuelos de viento share the bakery window with huesos de santo (marzipan “saints' bones”) every November 1.

questions.question: Finish the name of this tapa of battered, fried squid rings: calamares a la…
hints: The rings are coated in flour and egg before frying.
The missing word makes you think of an ancient empire.
It's the word for something from the city of the Colosseum.
questions.description: Rings nobody wears on a finger, but everyone eats with a squeeze of lemon.
questions.fun_fact: In Madrid, the bocadillo de calamares (squid sandwich) is a classic, especially in the bars near the Plaza Mayor.

questions.question: In Spain, what is the top-quality olive oil, made only by pressing olives, called?
hints: Its name has two words.
It is the highest grade you see on the labels.
One of its words means “more than usual.”
questions.description: Liquid gold that isn't kept in a bank, but next to the stove.
questions.fun_fact: The province of Jaén produces more olive oil than many whole countries.

questions.question: Menestra is a classic in Navarra and La Rioja. What is a menestra?
hints: It's a savory dish eaten hot.
It's usually served as a first course.
It often has artichokes, peas and asparagus.
questions.description: A dish they take very, very seriously in Tudela.
questions.fun_fact: The word “menestra” comes from the Italian “minestra”, which means soup.

questions.question: You're visiting the City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia. Which of these buildings is NOT part of it?
hints: One of the four is in another autonomous community.
It stands beside the Nervión estuary.
It is covered in titanium and is the great symbol of Bilbao.
questions.description: A whole neighborhood that looks like it landed straight out of a spaceship movie.
questions.fun_fact: Its main architect, Santiago Calatrava, was born in Valencia itself.

questions.question: Which autonomous community is marked on this map?
hints: It wraps around the Community of Madrid to the south and east.
It has five provinces, including Toledo and Cuenca.
It is the land of Don Quixote and his windmills.
questions.description: A piece of the map any geography teacher would tap with a pointer.
questions.fun_fact: Toledo, its capital, is known as the “city of three cultures” because Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side there.

questions.question: If you paddle a canoe down the Duero from its source in Soria to the sea at Porto, about how many kilometers do you travel?
hints: It's one of the longest rivers on the Iberian Peninsula.
It crosses all of Castilla y León and then Portugal.
It's farther than the drive from Madrid to Barcelona, but shorter than the drive from Madrid to Paris.
questions.description: A river so long it starts out speaking Spanish and ends up speaking Portuguese.
questions.fun_fact: In Portugal the Duero is called the Douro, and the grapes for the famous port wine grow on its hillsides.

questions.question: Every August since 1930, thousands of canoeists have raced from Arriondas down to the coast of Asturias. Which river do they paddle down?
hints: It's an Asturian river that rises in the Picos de Europa.
The race is called the “Descenso Internacional del …”.
The finish is in a coastal town that has the river's name inside its own.
questions.description: A party where getting soaked is normal, and so are paddling and singing.
questions.fun_fact: The Descenso del Sella is a serious race and a huge party at the same time, with thousands of people following it from the riverbank and from a train.

questions.question: Explorer Ramón Larramendi invented it, it has no engine or dogs, and it has crossed Antarctica. What pulls his “wind sled”?
hints: Larramendi has used it in Greenland and Antarctica.
It's tied to the sled with long lines and flies out in front.
Kids fly one at the beach on a string.
questions.description: To reach the Pole, some bring dogs, some bring snowmobiles, and this man brings ideas.
questions.fun_fact: With his wind sled, Larramendi has traveled thousands of kilometers across Greenland and Antarctica without burning a single drop of fuel.

questions.question: It's in the Pyrenees, in the Val d'Aran, and the Spanish royal family often skis there. In which autonomous community is Baqueira Beret?
hints: This region shares a border with France.
In the Val d'Aran, people speak Aranese as well as Spanish.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.description: A place where going down is the easy part; the pricey bit is the lift pass to get back up.
questions.fun_fact: The Garonne River starts in the Val d'Aran, but instead of flowing into Spain it crosses France and reaches the Atlantic near Bordeaux.

questions.question: Legend says the last Nasrid king of Granada sighed at the Suspiro del Moro pass as he looked back one last time at his city. Who was he?
hints: He lived in the late 15th century.
He handed the keys of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.
His name starts with B.
questions.description: A mountain pass named like a Spanish meringue, with a goodbye story behind it.
questions.fun_fact: The Suspiro del Moro pass is on the road from Granada to the coast, and you can still see the city in the distance from there.

questions.question: It flows under the Roman bridge of Ourense, next to the As Burgas hot springs, and further down forms the border with Portugal. Which river is it?
hints: It's the most important river in Galicia.
It starts in the province of Lugo.
It flows into the Atlantic next to A Guarda.
questions.description: A bridge with almost two thousand years of experience getting its feet wet.
questions.fun_fact: The big central arch of the Ourense bridge isn't Roman: it was rebuilt in the Middle Ages after the original collapsed.

questions.question: For millions of years, the Júcar River has carved the limestone next to Cuenca. What is the narrow, deep valley it has formed called in Spain?
hints: It has very high rock walls on both sides of the river.
Cuenca has two famous ones: the Júcar's and the Huécar's.
In Spanish, it has the same name as the curved tool used to cut wheat.
questions.description: A very patient river with all the time in the world to carve stone.
questions.fun_fact: Cuenca's famous Hanging Houses don't look out over the Júcar, but over the gorge of its neighbor, the Huécar River.

questions.question: Peñalara, in the Sierra de Guadarrama, is the highest peak in the Community of Madrid. About how high is it?
hints: In winter it is usually covered in snow.
It is lower than Teide and Mulhacén.
It is well over 2,000 meters.
questions.description: Madrid has no beach, but it does have a penthouse with a great view.
questions.fun_fact: Peñalara has lakes dug out by glaciers in the last Ice Age, when the mountains near Madrid had permanent ice.

questions.question: Brazil will host the first Women's World Cup ever played in South America. In which year?
hints: Brazil had already hosted the men's World Cup in 2014.
The Women's World Cup is played every four years, like the men's.
The previous one was held in Australia and New Zealand in 2023.
questions.description: A party so long awaited that the samba is already rehearsing.
questions.fun_fact: The first Women's World Cup was played in 1991, in China.

questions.question: The Jarama river collects the water of the Manzanares, Madrid's river. Near Aranjuez, which river does it flow into?
hints: It's the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula.
It flows past Toledo.
It reaches the Atlantic at Lisbon.
questions.description: A river that spends its life collecting water from others just to hand it over to a bigger one.
questions.fun_fact: The Jarama gives its name to a famous racetrack near Madrid that hosted the Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix.

questions.question: The Fuente de Piedra lagoon in Málaga hosts the largest breeding colony on the Iberian Peninsula of which bird?
hints: It likes salty, shallow water.
It often rests on one leg.
It is pink.
questions.description: A salty lagoon in Málaga with very elegant guests who arrive every spring.
questions.fun_fact: A flamingo's pink color comes from what it eats: tiny shellfish and algae full of pigments.

questions.question: In 2021, the Tajogaite volcano erupted on the island of La Palma. How long did the eruption last?
hints: It started in September.
It ended in December of the same year.
It was the longest eruption ever recorded on La Palma.
questions.description: A volcano that showed up without warning and stayed much longer than anyone wanted.
questions.fun_fact: The lava reached the sea and made new land: La Palma grew by several dozen hectares (over 100 acres).

questions.question: Around 2002, fewer than 100 were left in the wild. It lives in Doñana and Sierra Morena and eats mostly rabbits. Which wild cat became the most endangered in the world?
hints: It lives in Mediterranean scrub and woodland.
It has tufts of black hair on the tips of its ears.
Its name comes from the peninsula where it lives.
questions.description: A wild cat that never shows up in savanna documentaries, but deserves to.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to breeding programs, there are now more than 2,000 Iberian lynxes, and in 2024 it moved from “endangered” to “vulnerable”.

questions.question: The Tormes flows through Salamanca and gives its name to a famous rogue of Spanish literature. Why is Lázaro called “de Tormes”?
questions.answer: Because he was born in a mill on the river
wrong_answers: Because he was a boatman on the river
Because his master, the blind man, came from there
Because he was rescued from the river as a baby
hints: He explains it himself at the start of the book.
The nickname doesn't come from his job or from any of his masters.
He says he was born “inside the Tormes River”.
questions.description: A river in Salamanca that earned itself a surname in literature.
questions.fun_fact: “Lazarillo de Tormes” was published in 1554 with no author's name, and even today nobody knows for sure who wrote it.

questions.question: This is the Gran Telescopio Canarias, run by the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias. Which island is it on?
hints: It's one of the western islands of the archipelago.
It's known as “la isla bonita” (the beautiful island).
In 2021 it had a volcanic eruption that was all over the news.
questions.description: A giant eye that spends the night staring at the sky and the day taking a siesta.
questions.fun_fact: Since 1988, a “sky law” has required the island's streetlights not to shine upward, so they don't spoil the telescopes' view.

questions.question: “Al filo de lo imposible” aired on TVE starting in 1982. What was the show about?
hints: It was almost always filmed outdoors, in remote places.
It followed athletes like Juanito Oiarzabal and Edurne Pasaban.
They climbed Himalayan eight-thousanders carrying the camera on their backs.
questions.description: A TV show to watch from the couch under a blanket, without your feet touching the floor.
questions.fun_fact: The show won a huge number of awards at international mountain and adventure film festivals.

questions.question: In 1565 Urdaneta found the “tornaviaje”, the way back across the Pacific: sail north to Japan's latitude, catch westerly winds, reach Acapulco. Where did it start?
hints: Spain had just set up a base on those islands.
The galleons that used this route were named after its capital.
Its capital is Manila.
questions.description: Getting there was easy; the hard part was finding the way home without GPS.
questions.fun_fact: The Manila Galleon used Urdaneta's route for about 250 years, until 1815.

questions.question: Which Basque conquistador from Gipuzkoa founded Spanish Manila in 1571 and became the first governor of the Philippines?
hints: Before he set sail, he was a notary and a mayor in Mexico City.
He was born in Zumárraga.
His surname is the name of a Madrid neighborhood and a metro station.
questions.description: Founding a capital on the other side of the world: the longest office move in history.
questions.fun_fact: Manila has a monument that shows him next to Andrés de Urdaneta, the sailor friar of his expedition.

questions.question: He was doctor to Pope Julius III and in 1555 published Dioscorides' great book of medicinal plants in Spanish. Where was Andrés Laguna born?
hints: It's a city in Castile and León.
It's a provincial capital with fewer people than Valladolid.
It has a Roman aqueduct right in the city center.
questions.description: A Renaissance doctor with more herbs in his head than an herbal shop.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes mentions his book in Don Quixote as “the Dioscorides, illustrated by Doctor Laguna.”

questions.question: The “Mona Lisa” is to the Louvre as which painting is to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam?
hints: It was painted by the same artist the museum is named after.
It shows yellow flowers in a vase.
These flowers turn their heads to follow the sun.
questions.description: A museum for a painter who sold almost nothing while he was alive and is now too famous to fit through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted several versions of “Sunflowers” to decorate the bedroom of his friend, the painter Paul Gauguin.

questions.question: “I'm an 18th-century botanist from Valencia, I ran the Royal Botanical Garden of Madrid and I named the dahlia, a flower from Mexico.” Who am I?
hints: Besides being a botanist, I was a priest.
I lived in Paris for several years before returning to Spain.
A biodiversity institute at the University of Valencia bears my surname.
questions.description: Someone who named flowers the way you'd name a litter of newborn kittens.
questions.fun_fact: He named the flower “Dahlia” in honor of the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl.

questions.question: Take a close look: what is this little breakfast cake called?
hints: Every supermarket sells it in bags of twelve.
It sits in a crinkly paper cup and has a puffed-up top.
It shares its name with many grandmothers and with a great river in Colombia.
questions.description: The only thing that dives into breakfast milk more happily than you do on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says its name comes from a young French woman named Madeleine who baked them in the 18th century.

questions.question: Take a close look: these tiny black licorice pastilles, Juanola, carry their creator's surname. Who was he?
hints: They were created in the early 20th century.
People took them to soothe a sore throat.
Their creator worked behind a counter with a green cross on the door.
questions.description: Tiny, black and older than your great-grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: Manuel Juanola created them in 1906, and they are still made in Catalonia today with licorice extract.

questions.question: Dipped in milk and layered with chocolate and custard, galletas María make a homemade cake. Which one?
hints: It's a classic at birthday parties at home.
You build it on a tray and leave it to set in the fridge.
Its name recalls the person in the family who made it best.
questions.description: A cookie that got famous for letting itself be dunked without complaining.
questions.fun_fact: María cookies were created in London in 1874 to celebrate the wedding of the Russian Grand Duchess Maria Alexandrovna to the Duke of Edinburgh.

questions.question: They're white, hard and oval, people eat them at Christmas, and the town of Alcoy is famous for them. What is a peladilla?
wrong_answers: A pine nut coated in honey
hints: They make a loud crunch when you bite them.
Inside, they hide a whole nut.
It's the same nut you find in hard turrón.
questions.description: A sweet so hard that dentists look forward to it every December.
questions.fun_fact: At many Spanish weddings, guests get peladillas wrapped in tulle as a keepsake.

questions.question: Flan is yellow, wobbles on the plate and is made with eggs and milk. What is the dark caramel on top made from?
hints: It's made in a small pan on the stove.
Before you heat it, it's white and comes in tiny grains.
It's what you stir into milk to make it sweet.
questions.description: A dessert that shakes more than you do in the dentist's waiting room.
questions.fun_fact: If you leave sugar on the heat too long, the caramel burns and turns bitter.

questions.question: Take a close look: in the fall, street stalls sell these piping hot. What are they?
hints: They grow on a tree that protects them in prickly spiky husks.
Peeling them, you often burn your fingers a little.
In Galicia they are celebrated with the magosto festival.
questions.description: The only street snack that doubles as a hand warmer.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalonia they are eaten at the Castanyada, on the night of October 31 to November 1, along with panellets and sweet potatoes.

questions.question: Take a close look: in Spain, what is this crunchy thing your scoops of ice cream are served in called?
hints: When you're done, you can eat it too.
It's wide at the top and pointy at the bottom.
Its name starts with “cu”.
questions.description: A question to answer fast, before everything melts.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the cucurucho (ice cream cone) became famous at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis, when an ice cream seller ran out of dishes.

questions.question: Toledo's little marzipan figures, shaped like animals and stars, are made mainly from two ingredients. Which ones?
hints: They contain no flour at all.
One of the two ingredients is a ground nut.
It's the same nut used in turrón.
questions.description: A whole zoo that fits on one tray and vanishes on Christmas Eve.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the nuns of the San Clemente convent in Toledo invented marzipan during a famine, using the only things they had: almonds and sugar.

questions.question: I'm yellow, you eat me with a spoon, and I often have a cookie floating on top with cinnamon. Which dessert am I?
hints: I'm made with milk, eggs and sugar.
I'm served in bowls or little cups.
My name comes from “nata” (cream).
questions.description: The dessert staring at you from the fridge, waiting for you to finish dinner.
questions.fun_fact: The name “natillas” comes from “nata” (cream), because they turn out so creamy.

questions.question: You've been in the pool for ages and suddenly start shivering and your teeth chatter. Why does your body do that?
wrong_answers: To get water out of your ears
hints: Your muscles do it without you deciding to.
It happens most when the water or the air is cold.
It's a bit like rubbing your hands together on a freezing day.
questions.description: Your body has a secret trick it switches on without asking you first.
questions.fun_fact: When you shiver, your muscles move very fast without you deciding to, just to make heat.

questions.question: In Spain, the perfect finishing touch is called “la … del pastel”, after the little red fruit in this photo. Which word is missing?
hints: It's small and round, with a little stem.
It's a cousin of the cherry, just a bit more sour.
It goes on top of the whipped cream as the very last touch.
questions.description: The last thing to go on, and the first thing someone steals.
