questions.fun_fact: The guinda is a sour kind of cherry, often used in Spanish baking and liqueurs.

questions.question: It's made in a pitcher with red wine, chunks of fruit like orange and peach, and lots of ice. What is this drink called?
hints: It's a summer drink for grown-ups.
It has wine in it, so kids can't drink it.
Its name comes from the Spanish word for blood, because of its red color.
questions.description: The pitcher that pops up on every terrace as soon as the thermometer climbs.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2014, an EU law says that only sangría made in Spain or Portugal may be called just “sangría”.

questions.question: When you're done at a bar, you ask the waiter for it: it shows the price of everything you had, and then you pay. What is it?
hints: It comes at the end, not the beginning.
It has numbers and a total on it.
You can ask for it with a gesture, as if writing in the air.
questions.description: The little slip of paper that makes everyone suddenly stare at the ceiling.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, people often ask for it from across the room by pretending to sign in the air with their hand.

questions.question: A tortilla sandwich is a school-break classic. What is a tortilla española made with?
hints: It's cooked in a frying pan and flipped over with a plate.
It usually comes out round and thick, the size of the pan.
One of the ingredients is usually fried in thin slices.
questions.description: The sandwich that hides a whole other dish inside it.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain there is an endless debate over whether a tortilla should have onion in it or not.

questions.question: For jamón de bellota, Iberian pigs spend the fall roaming free, eating acorns under holm and cork oaks. In what landscape?
hints: It's a very open woodland, with trees spaced far apart and grass between them.
It's typical of Extremadura and western Andalusia.
In Portugal, the same landscape is called the montado.
questions.description: A ham that owes its flavor to a very exclusive fall menu.
questions.fun_fact: During the montanera, the acorn-feeding season, an Iberian pig can eat about 10 kg (22 lb) of acorns a day.

questions.question: Old Spanish grocery stores called “ultramarinos”, with wooden counters, coffee, cocoa and sugar, got that name because they sold goods…
wrong_answers: meant to be carried on ships
hints: Look at the two parts of the word.
The same first part appears in “ultraviolet” and “ultrasound”.
Many of those goods came from the Americas and the colonies.
questions.description: Here the shopkeeper kept a pencil behind his ear and wrapped your lentils in a paper cone.
questions.fun_fact: Several Spanish cities still have ultramarinos over a hundred years old that keep their original counters.

questions.question: These battered strips of squid are called “rabas”, and they're the star snack of one Spanish region. Which one?
hints: It's a region in northern Spain, with a coastline and very green mountains.
Its capital has a famous beach called El Sardinero.
Its capital is Santander.
questions.description: Golden strips that vanish from the plate before the second beer arrives.
questions.fun_fact: Unlike “calamares a la romana”, which are cut into rings, rabas are cut into strips.

questions.question: In what year did Princess Leonor swear allegiance to the Constitution before the Cortes Generales?
hints: She did it on the very day she came of age.
It happened in the fall, during the reign of her father, Felipe VI.
It was the same year Spain won the Women's World Cup in soccer.
questions.description: Some birthdays come with cake and candles, others with a speech in front of parliament.
questions.fun_fact: Her father, Felipe, also swore allegiance to the Constitution on his 18th birthday: January 30, 1986.

questions.question: It has your photo, you show it to vote, and its number has eight digits and a letter. Which Spanish document is it?
hints: You show it when someone asks you to prove who you are.
In Spain you must have one from age 14.
Its three initials start with D, for “Documento”.
questions.description: The card that proves you're you… even when the photo says otherwise.
questions.fun_fact: The final letter isn't random: it's calculated from the number to catch copying mistakes.

questions.question: “El Reina Sofía” is in Madrid, next to Atocha station, and is named after King Felipe VI's mother. What is it?
hints: Millions of people visit it every year.
It's a short walk from the Prado Museum.
Picasso's “Guernica” hangs there.
questions.description: Putting your name on something in Madrid is classier than carving it into a park bench.
questions.fun_fact: Its main building used to be a hospital: Madrid's old General Hospital.

questions.question: The walls of the “Water Cube,” Beijing's Olympic swimming pool, are covered in irregular cells. What inspired its architects?
hints: It lasts only a very short time before it disappears.
You see it in the bathtub or when you wash the dishes.
Kids make them by blowing through a little ring.
questions.description: Architects who went looking for ideas somewhere not serious at all.
questions.fun_fact: For the 2022 Winter Olympics, the Water Cube became the “Ice Cube” and hosted the curling games.

questions.question: Which autonomous community of Spain has this flag?
hints: It's in the south of the peninsula.
It's the autonomous community with the most people in Spain.
Seville, Granada and Málaga are there.
questions.description: Seventeen communities, seventeen flags flying: let's see if you know this one.
questions.fun_fact: February 28 is Andalusia Day, marking the 1980 referendum on its self-government.

questions.question: Five seats are shared out with the D'Hondt method. Party A gets 100 votes, B gets 60 and C gets 25. How many seats does A win?
hints: Each party's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3…
The five highest results win the seats.
A gets 100, 50 and 33 from its first three divisions.
questions.description: Elementary school math used to decide who gets a seat in Congress.
questions.fun_fact: The method is named after Victor D'Hondt, a 19th-century Belgian lawyer.

questions.question: In Spain's Congress, the chamber where the deputies sit is called the «hemiciclo», a word from Greek. What does it mean?
hints: The word is made of two Greek parts.
Look at how the seats are arranged.
“Hemi” means the same as “semi”, and “ciclo” comes from the Greek “kyklos”, circle.
questions.description: Journalists say it so often that nobody wonders where it comes from anymore.
questions.fun_fact: The ceiling of the hemiciclo still has bullet holes from the attempted coup of February 23, 1981.

questions.question: It's Christmas Eve, and almost every TV channel shows the same speech as every year. Who gives it?
hints: It's recorded in a palace.
This person is the head of state.
Felipe VI has given it since 2014.
questions.description: Turrón, carols and a speech: the full Christmas Eve menu.
questions.fun_fact: The first royal Christmas message aired in 1975, just one month after Juan Carlos I came to the throne.

questions.question: The phrase “café para todos” (coffee for everyone) was born in the Transition and is credited to minister Manuel Clavero Arévalo. What was given to everyone?
hints: It was decided in the years when the 1978 Constitution was being written.
Clavero was a minister under Adolfo Suárez in the first governments of the democracy.
That's why Spain has 17 regions today, each with its own parliament.
questions.description: A phrase you'd hear at a bar counter that ended up in the history books.
questions.fun_fact: The idea was not to limit self-rule to Catalonia, the Basque Country and Galicia, which had already voted on a statute of their own under the Second Republic.

questions.question: We are life, freedom of speech and education. If we're trampled on, you can turn to the Constitutional Court. What are we?
hints: Every person has us, simply for being a person.
We're in Section 1 of Chapter II of Title I of the Constitution.
Our name says we are the base, the “foundation.”
questions.description: What nobody can take away from you, not even your big brother.
questions.fun_fact: The Constitution was approved in a referendum on December 6, 1978, and that day is now a public holiday in Spain.

questions.question: Spanish laws are published in this official gazette to come into force. Who must sign them into law first?
wrong_answers: The President of the Supreme Court
hints: He has 15 days to do it.
He is the head of state.
He signs with his name followed by an “R”.
questions.description: The newspaper with the fewest readers by choice and the most by obligation.
questions.fun_fact: The BOE stopped being printed on paper in 2009 and is now published only online.

questions.question: I'm in Madrid, and inside me 350 elected people debate and vote on laws. Two bronze lions guard my door. What am I?
hints: This is where the vote on who becomes Prime Minister takes place.
I'm on Carrera de San Jerónimo, near Puerta del Sol.
Together with the Senate, I make up the Cortes Generales.
questions.description: A building where people talk and talk and, in the end, decide everything by pressing a button.
questions.fun_fact: The lions were cast from the bronze of cannons captured in the Hispano-Moroccan War of 1859–60, and people call them Daoíz and Velarde.

questions.question: At Spain's national team games, fans wear red and paint their faces red and yellow. Why those colors?
questions.answer: They're the colors of Spain's flag
wrong_answers: They're colors that bring good luck
They're the colors the coach picked
hints: The same colors fly over town halls.
It's the country's most visible symbol.
It has a yellow stripe between two red ones.
questions.description: Red and yellow: not ketchup and mustard, but something far more serious.
questions.fun_fact: The red and yellow flag was created in 1785 so that Spanish ships could be easily recognized at sea.

questions.question: The common toad lays its eggs in ponds, in long strings of jelly. How many can it lay at once?
hints: It lays a huge number, because almost none grow up into adult toads.
The strings of eggs can be several meters long.
It's several thousand.
questions.description: If you think your family is big, wait until you meet this pond mom.
questions.fun_fact: Many toads return every spring to the same pond where they hatched, even if they have to cross roads to get there.

questions.question: It's added to swimming pools to kill germs and, together with sodium, makes table salt. Which element is it?
hints: Its name comes from the Greek word for “pale green.”
It's also in the bleach people use to clean at home.
Its chemical symbol is Cl.
questions.description: The secret ingredient of the swimming pool, though your nose always finds it out.
questions.fun_fact: The famous “pool smell” doesn't come from chlorine alone, but from what forms when chlorine mixes with sweat and other things swimmers leave behind.

questions.question: Listen: which bird of Spain's squares and rooftops chirps like this?
hints: It's small and brown.
It hops up to café tables looking for bread crumbs.
Its name rhymes with “arrow”.
questions.description: The neighbor who never pays rent but is always up on the roof.
questions.fun_fact: The house sparrow almost always lives near people: in forests with no houses you hardly ever find one.

questions.question: This night bird of prey, about the size of a thrush, has yellow eyes, is seen by day on posts and olive trees, and appears in a Spanish saying about going home. What is it?
hints: It fits in the palms of two hands.
Its scientific name, Athene noctua, recalls the goddess Athena.
The saying goes: “Each … to its own olive tree.”
questions.description: It always looks grumpy, like someone woken up at seven on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: It was the bird of the goddess Athena: it appears on ancient coins of Athens and today on the Greek 1-euro coin.

questions.question: Listen: which bird sings like this in Spain's forests in spring?
hints: Its song has only two notes.
Some wall clocks copy it.
Its name sounds just like its call.
questions.description: A spring singer who never bothers learning a new song.
questions.fun_fact: The cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests, and they raise its chick as if it were their own.

questions.question: The Spanish galgo is very thin, runs over 60 km/h (37 mph) and was bred to hunt hares. What does «¡échale un galgo!» mean?
wrong_answers: That it must be kicked out
hints: Think about what such a fast dog is for.
It's said of something that has gone very far or very fast.
Not even the fastest dog would catch it.
questions.description: The dog that doesn't chase the ball: it leaves the ball behind.
questions.fun_fact: Galgos have almost no body fat, so they get cold easily, and many wear coats in winter.

questions.question: This Iberian reptile looks like a snake, but it has four tiny legs with three toes each and gives birth to live young. What is it?
hints: It moves through the grass wriggling like a snake.
It belongs to a family of smooth, shiny lizards.
In Spain it's called the «eslizón».
questions.description: A reptile that can't decide between being a lizard or a snake, so it does a bit of both.
questions.fun_fact: Its legs are so small that when it flees in a hurry, it presses them to its body and slithers like a snake.

questions.question: Adult eels from Spain's rivers swim down to the sea and travel thousands of kilometers across the Atlantic. Why?
questions.answer: To spawn in the Sargasso Sea
wrong_answers: To spend the winter in African waters
To look for food in the North Sea
To escape the heat of the Spanish summer
hints: It's the last great journey of their lives.
Their young make the trip in reverse and reach Spain as angulas.
They go back to where they were born, near the Caribbean.
questions.description: It looks like a snake, but its passport is full of stamps.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody has ever seen a European eel spawn in the wild: we know about it from the tiny larvae found in the Sargasso Sea.

questions.question: It's the smallest deer in the Iberian Peninsula: the male has short three-pointed antlers and, when scared, it barks like a dog. What animal is it?
hints: It lives mostly in forests in the north and center.
It weighs about 25 kg (55 lb), like a big dog.
The first word of its name is also a word for fish eggs.
questions.description: A forest animal whose dream of being a guard dog never came true.
questions.fun_fact: Roe deer fawns are born with white spots and stay still in the grass; if you find one, don't touch it: its mother is nearby.

questions.question: Which bird of the Spanish countryside is this?
hints: It lives in open fields and olive groves and nests on the ground.
It is the queen of small-game hunting in Spain.
Spanish fairy tales end with the couple living happily ever after and eating a few of these.
questions.description: A countryside neighbor who prefers to walk everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the world's red-legged partridges live in Spain.

questions.question: Look at this insect. What sweet food does it make?
hints: It lives in a hive with thousands of companions.
It makes it from the nectar of flowers.
You spread it on toast, and it's golden and sticky.
questions.description: Works all day, buzzes nonstop and never earns a single cent.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the biggest honey producers in Europe.

questions.question: You find a bill in a drawer that says “N$10 nuevos pesos.” In which year did the new pesos start circulating?
hints: It was during Carlos Salinas de Gortari's six-year term.
It was one year before NAFTA came into force.
It happened in the early 1990s.
questions.description: A currency so new they put “new” right in its name, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: The new peso dropped three zeros: 1,000 old pesos were worth 1 new peso.

questions.question: In what year did Michael Phelps win 8 gold medals at the Beijing Olympics?
hints: It was in the first decade of this century.
That same year, Barack Obama was elected president of the United States.
The year ends in the same number as Phelps's gold medals.
questions.description: Eight gold medals: even a pirate's treasure chest doesn't shine that bright.
questions.fun_fact: With those 8 golds, Phelps beat Mark Spitz, who had won 7 at Munich 1972.

questions.question: Roberto Gómez Bolaños was known as “Chespirito.” Finish what his nickname means: “little…”
hints: A film director gave it to him for his talent at writing scripts.
It comes from the name of a very famous writer who wasn't Mexican.
That English writer wrote “Romeo and Juliet.”
questions.description: A nickname with a lot of culture hiding inside a barrel.
questions.fun_fact: “Chespirito” comes from saying “Shakespeare” the Spanish way, as “Chéspir,” and adding the diminutive “-ito.”

questions.question: Consuelo Velázquez, who wrote “Bésame mucho,” was born in Ciudad Guzmán, hometown of the muralist Orozco. Which state is it in?
hints: It's a state in western Mexico.
It lies on the Pacific and has a huge mariachi tradition.
Its capital is Guadalajara.
questions.description: A song sung by the Beatles, Andrea Bocelli and half the planet, and a Mexican woman wrote it.
questions.fun_fact: “Bésame mucho” is one of the most recorded Spanish-language songs in history, with versions by the Beatles and Andrea Bocelli.

questions.question: I was the first civilian president after the Revolution, I had Ciudad Universitaria built, and I boosted tourism in Acapulco. Who am I?
hints: He governed from 1946 to 1952.
He was a lawyer from Veracruz, not a soldier.
His son, with almost the same name, became governor of Veracruz.
questions.description: A president who left his stamp on schools, airports and even beaches.
questions.fun_fact: Miguel Alemán was the first Mexican president to speak before the US Congress.

questions.question: At school you dress up for the November 20 parade. Who called all of Mexico to take up arms on that day in 1910?
hints: He wasn't a general: he was a rich man from the north who wanted to be president.
His slogan was “Sufragio efectivo, no reelección” (“Effective suffrage, no re-election”).
He wrote the Plan of San Luis.
questions.description: The day half the school shows up with a painted-on mustache and a sombrero.
questions.fun_fact: Madero even set the time of the uprising: November 20 at 6 in the evening.

questions.question: Alfonso Cuarón's “Roma” follows a family in Colonia Roma and their live-in housekeeper, Cleo. In what decade is it set?
hints: It's based on Cuarón's own childhood; he was born in 1961.
The film shows the Halconazo, which came after the 1968 student movement.
Luis Echeverría was president in those years.
questions.description: A black-and-white film that makes you miss a house you never lived in.
questions.fun_fact: Cuarón didn't just direct “Roma”: he was also its cinematographer and won the Oscar in that category.

questions.question: Every September 19, Mexico holds a nationwide drill in memory of a big 20th-century earthquake. What year was it?
hints: It struck on a Thursday morning, just after seven o'clock.
It happened a year before Mexico hosted its second World Cup.
It was during Miguel de la Madrid's presidency.
questions.description: A September 19 that nobody in Mexico City wants to live through again.
questions.fun_fact: After the quake, the famous “Topos” (Moles) were born: rescue volunteers who now help in disasters all over the world.

questions.question: Which of these songs did Pedro Infante NEVER sing?
hints: One of them came out many years after Pedro Infante died.
It's from the 1970s.
Vicente Fernández made it famous.
questions.description: The Idol of Guamúchil had lots of songs, but not every song in the songbook.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Infante's version of “Las mañanitas” still plays at thousands of Mexican birthday parties.

questions.question: This mural is made of colored stones and covers all four walls of a famous building. Which building is it?
hints: It's in Ciudad Universitaria.
It opened in the early 1950s, along with the rest of the campus.
Juan O'Gorman decorated it.
questions.description: A building that dressed itself in a mosaic of stones from all over Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: Juan O'Gorman used naturally colored stones from different parts of Mexico so the mosaic would never fade.

review.feedback: source: Hint 2 says the library opened in the early 1950s "along with the rest of the campus", but the UNAM Central Library opened on April 5, 1956. It was built from 1950 to 1952, and the campus was inaugurated in 1952. The translation copies this error from the source. Fix the source hint first, for example to "It was built in the early 1950s, along with the rest of the campus.", and then translate it again. Fact check: wrong. Hint 2 is inaccurate: the Central Library opened on April 5, 1956 (construction began 1950). The main campus was inaugurated in 1952, but the library wasn't open then.

questions.question: He wore a wrestler's mask and cape, appeared after the 1985 earthquake and was called Superbarrio Gómez. Who did he defend?
wrong_answers: Sellers of bootleg lucha libre gear
hints: He came out of a Mexico City neighborhood movement: the Asamblea de Barrios.
Instead of climbing into the ring, he showed up at marches and in front of officials.
He took on landlords who wanted to throw families out.
questions.description: A superhero with no superpowers, but plenty of patience for neighborhood meetings.
questions.fun_fact: In 1996, Superbarrio even “ran” as a symbolic candidate for president of the United States.

questions.question: I'm named after a wild cat, I play at the Estadio Olímpico Universitario and I represent Mexico's largest university. Who am I?
hints: My colors are blue and gold.
My home is Ciudad Universitaria, in the south of Mexico City.
My cat is also known as the mountain lion.
questions.description: A team with a student ID and real claws.
questions.fun_fact: UNAM's most famous cheer is the “¡Goya!”, shouted both in the stadium and in the classrooms.

questions.question: It came out in 2021, celebrates Mexico's rivers and lakes and shows a corn plant. Which animal is on the 50-peso bill?
hints: It's an animal that lives in fresh water or close to it.
It lives in the canals of Xochimilco.
It always seems to be smiling and breathes through pink, feathery gills.
questions.description: A bill that doesn't burn a hole in your pocket, it just leaves it soaking wet.
questions.fun_fact: The 50-peso bill with the axolotl was named the world's best banknote of 2021 by the International Bank Note Society.

questions.question: Which of these snakes that live in Mexico has NO venom?
hints: It's very good at climbing trees and at swimming too.
It's one of the biggest snakes in Mexico.
It wraps itself around its prey like a hug that's way too tight.
questions.description: Four snakes in a row, and only one without dangerous fangs… or so it says.
questions.fun_fact: The boa doesn't bite to poison its prey: it squeezes so hard that the blood stops flowing.

questions.question: It lives in the deserts of Sonora and Baja California, has huge ears and escapes by jumping with all four legs at once. What animal is it?
hints: It's a deer, and the males have antlers.
Its tail is white with a black tip.
In Mexico it's called «venado bura».
questions.description: The Sonoran Desert is so hot that even the cacti look for shade.
questions.fun_fact: The mule deer's antlers fall off every year and grow back again.

questions.question: In the Revillagigedo Islands it swims next to divers, filters plankton with its mouth open, and its “wings” span up to 7 m (23 ft). What animal is it?
hints: It's related to sharks, but it has no teeth for biting.
Its body is flat like a rug.
It's the biggest ray in the world.
questions.description: A fish that flies underwater without ever taking a single flying lesson.
questions.fun_fact: The giant manta ray has one of the biggest brains of any fish and seems to recognize itself in a mirror.

questions.question: In Mexico it's called the camaleón cornudo; it lives in the desert and eats ants. Why does it squirt blood from its eyes?
questions.answer: To scare off coyotes and foxes
wrong_answers: To cool off in the sun
hints: It raises the blood pressure in its head so much that tiny vessels near its eyes burst.
The blood tastes awful to certain animals.
It works best on the dog's wild relatives.
questions.description: A lizard that looks like a mini dinosaur and eats ants for breakfast, lunch and dinner.
questions.fun_fact: The camaleón cornudo isn't a chameleon at all: it's a horned lizard, and its squirt of blood can reach more than 1 m (3 ft).

questions.question: At a get-together, out come little plates of peanuts, chips and chicharrones to nibble while everyone chats. What is that called in Mexico?
hints: It's something you eat bit by bit, before the meal or with drinks.
The supermarket has a whole aisle of bags of it.
It starts with “bo” and has three syllables.
questions.description: The real reason everyone comes to the party, though they say it's for the guests.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican cantinas the botana is free: they keep bringing it as long as you keep ordering drinks.

questions.question: At the stand, you're craving tacos al pastor freshly sliced from the trompo. Who makes them for you?
hints: He works with nice warm tortillas.
He asks if you want them “con todo”: onion and cilantro.
His name comes from what he sells.
questions.description: At midnight, when the craving hits, this street hero always has the light on.
questions.fun_fact: Tacos al pastor were born from the shawarma that Lebanese immigrants brought to Mexico.

questions.question: It's nighttime, and a bit of the famous recording plays down the street: “¡Ricos… oaxaqueños, calientitos!” Who is passing by?
hints: What he sells is a favorite for dinner or breakfast.
He often brings atole or champurrado too.
He sells something wrapped in banana leaf or corn husk and steamed.
questions.description: The tastiest nighttime alarm clock in Mexico's neighborhoods.
questions.fun_fact: On February 2, Candelaria Day, whoever found the little figurine in the rosca has to treat everyone to tamales.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico, at which shop do you buy this?
hints: It's very cold inside its freezers.
It tastes best on a hot day.
Many of these shops are called “La Michoacana.”
questions.description: The only place where you're allowed to melt with happiness.
questions.fun_fact: Many paleterías are called “La Michoacana” because the business spread from Tocumbo, a small town in Michoacán.

questions.question: It's sold on Mexico City street corners in the morning, comes with atole, and its name recalls the female guajolote (turkey). What is it made of?
hints: It's a torta.
It combines two very filling things.
The filling comes wrapped in a corn husk before it goes into the bread.
questions.description: A breakfast for anyone who thinks one antojito just isn't enough.
questions.fun_fact: It's also called “torta de tamal”, and one of the favorite fillings is green chicken tamal.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a Mexican antojito?
hints: You can find the other three at any fonda in Mexico.
It looks a bit like a gordita, but it isn't from Mexico.
It's very famous in Colombia and Venezuela.
questions.description: When a craving hits, it doesn't ask what country you're from.
questions.fun_fact: They're called «antojitos» because they're foods you get a craving (antojo) for at any time of day, not just at mealtimes.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which antojito is this?
hints: It's made of corn masa and cooked on the comal.
It's topped with beans, cheese and salsa.
Its edge is pinched up so the toppings don't fall off.
questions.description: Fresh off the comal and ready for salsa: an antojito that waits for no one.
questions.fun_fact: The edge of a sope is pinched with the fingers while the masa is still warm on the comal.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico, what's the friendly street name for this drink?
hints: You order it with your torta or your tacos.
It has bubbles and comes in a bottle or a can.
It's a short way of saying “refresco.”
questions.description: No street-corner taco is complete without its ice-cold sidekick.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries where people drink the most soda per person in the world.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which agua fresca is it?
hints: It's white like milk.
It has cinnamon on top.
It's made with rice.
questions.description: At the corner stand, a glass barrel holds the best cure for the afternoon heat.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican horchata is made with rice, but in Valencia, Spain, it's made with tiger nuts, a tiny tuber.

questions.question: The cuerno from Mexican bakeries is crescent-shaped, flaky and crackles when you bite it. It's a version of which famous bread from another country?
hints: It's a very typical breakfast pastry in France.
It has lots and lots of butter between its layers.
Its French name means “crescent”, like the moon.
questions.description: A moon-shaped bread that traveled a long way to reach the bakery.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, cuernos are also filled with ham and cheese and sold as a torta.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which botana is this?
hints: They're sold in little bags outside schools.
They're shaped like little wheels and super crunchy.
You eat them with lime and hot sauce.
questions.description: Little wheels that won't fit a car, but work great with salsa.
questions.fun_fact: Duritos are made from wheat flour and puff up when they're fried in hot oil.

questions.question: They cook for hours in a big copper pot, in their own lard, until golden and tender. Which animal do carnitas come from?
hints: It's a farm animal.
Chicharrón and cueritos come from the same animal.
It goes “oink, oink.”
questions.description: A meat that takes a long, hot bath before it lands in your taco.
questions.fun_fact: The most famous carnitas in Mexico come from Michoacán, especially from the town of Quiroga.

questions.question: In December you set it up at home with moss, hay and little figures of Joseph, Mary and the shepherds, and on the 24th the Baby Jesus is laid in it. What is it?
wrong_answers: The Day of the Dead altar
hints: It stays up until Día de la Candelaria (Candlemas).
It has a little stable, animals and even the Three Kings.
Its name comes from a word that means being born.
questions.description: The only spot in the house where a cow, three kings and an angel live together without fighting.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican nativity scenes have figures that aren't in the Bible, like a little devil, a rooster or even a woman making tortillas.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which Mexican plant is the queen of the December holidays?
hints: Markets sell tons of it in December.
The red parts aren't petals but colored leaves.
Its Spanish name is the same as the night of December 24.
questions.description: A plant that dresses up just as everyone pulls on their ugly Christmas sweater.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica called it cuetlaxóchitl, and the world knows it as the poinsettia after Joel Poinsett, a US ambassador who took it back home.

previous.feedback: This duplicates q-0254, which is already approved: both ask the player to name the poinsettia from a photo of the December plant, and in English both have the answer "poinsettia". The rater flagged this too. Rewording can't fix it, so drop this question or replace it with a different poinsettia fact (for example its Nahuatl name cuetlaxóchitl).

questions.question: You got the little figurine in the rosca, so you're the godparent of the Niño Dios. Besides giving tamales on February 2, what else do you have to do?
questions.answer: Dress him and take him to be blessed
wrong_answers: Hide him in the next rosca
Hang him on the Christmas tree
Carry him in the last posada
hints: It happens on Día de la Candelaria.
Some stores sell special little outfits for him.
He's taken to Mass in new clothes.
questions.description: Biting into the rosca can cost you: in February you get the tamale bill, plus one more job.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico City, some stores dress the Niño Dios as a doctor, a soccer player and even a firefighter.

questions.question: Turkey is to Christmas dinner in the US as ________ is to Christmas dinner for millions of families in Japan.
hints: You buy it from a famous fast-food chain.
The custom started with an ad campaign in the 1970s.
It comes in buckets, and the brand's founder was a colonel with a white beard.
questions.description: A Christmas tradition that was born in an advertising office.
questions.fun_fact: So many families in Japan order it that they have to reserve their Christmas bucket weeks in advance.

questions.question: In Mexican nacimientos, among the hay and the moss, there is always a “portal de Belén”. What is that portal?
questions.answer: The stable where the Baby Jesus is born
wrong_answers: The road the Three Kings travel on
The hill where the shepherds sleep
The star that shines above it all
hints: It's usually the center of the nativity scene, and the other figures face it.
It's often made of wood or cork, with a little roof.
The mule and the ox are there too.
questions.description: Not a door, not a video game, not a website: this portal is a lot more rustic.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican nacimientos, the Baby Jesus figure is only placed in the portal at midnight on December 24, when he is “born”.

questions.question: In Mexico, many people call the Christmas tree by the name of an evergreen tree with needle-like leaves. Which one?
hints: It smells great when it's a real one.
Its leaves look like tiny needles.
Its fruits are scaly cones.
questions.description: The only tree that gets covered in ornaments, lights and even the decorations your cousin made in kindergarten every December.
questions.fun_fact: In Amecameca, in the State of Mexico, there are forests where families can go to pick and cut their own Christmas tree.

questions.question: I arrive on the night of January 5. In Mexico they say I come on horseback, I'm the one with the white beard, and I brought gold to Baby Jesus. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the Three Kings.
They say I'm the oldest of the three.
My name starts with M.
questions.description: A gift deliverer who shows up without GPS and still finds your shoe.
questions.fun_fact: In the Mexican version, Gaspar arrives on a camel and Baltasar on an elephant, which is why many nativity scenes include a little elephant.

questions.question: According to tradition, who saw the Virgin who is venerated in this church?
hints: It happened on Tepeyac Hill in 1531.
He was an Indigenous man who carried roses in his tilma (cloak) to the bishop.
Today he is a saint, and his name holds the names of two apostles.
questions.description: A place where every December “Las Mañanitas” is sung on a grand scale.
questions.fun_fact: Every December 12, millions of pilgrims come to the Basilica, one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world.

questions.question: The National Silver Fair awards prizes to jewelry like this. Who revived silversmithing in its host city in the 1930s?
hints: He wasn't born in Mexico.
He was an architect and a teacher in New Orleans.
He opened a workshop in 1931 and trained hundreds of silversmiths.
questions.description: A fair where all that glitters really is silver… and finely crafted, too.
questions.fun_fact: Before coming to Mexico, Spratling shared an apartment in New Orleans with the writer William Faulkner.

questions.question: This jericalla, a dessert of milk, egg and cinnamon with a toasted top, is typical of one city. Which one?
hints: It's a city in western Mexico.
It's said to have been born at the Hospicio Cabañas, to feed the children there.
It's the home of mariachi and the torta ahogada.
questions.description: A cousin of flan that stayed in the oven a little too long.
questions.fun_fact: One legend says its name comes from Jérica, the town in Spain where its inventor came from.

questions.question: I own the Media Luna ranch and rule over Comala. My son comes looking for me and finds only whispers. Who am I?
hints: I'm a character in a 1955 novel.
Juan Rulfo wrote me.
My name is also the title of the book.
questions.description: A town so quiet that even the whispers have an echo.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriel García Márquez said he had read “Pedro Páramo” so many times he could recite it from memory.

questions.question: It comes rolled into a ball, you pull it apart into strings, and in many places it's called quesillo. Which cheese is it?
hints: It's the favorite for quesadillas because it melts and gets stringy.
It's named after a state in the south of Mexico.
That state is also famous for tlayudas and black mole.
questions.description: The never-ending debate: does a quesadilla come with cheese or not? Here, the cheese is a must.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, this cheese was born in the late 19th century in Reyes Etla, Oaxaca.

questions.question: Taxco, in Guerrero, has steep streets, the Santa Prisca church and lots of workshops. Which craftspeople made it famous?
hints: Centuries ago, it had very rich mines.
Their jewelry shines brightly.
They work a shiny white metal.
questions.description: A town so steep that even the vochos huff and puff on the way up.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa Prisca church was paid for in the 18th century by José de la Borda, a miner who got rich in Taxco.

questions.question: In the film about a man who swears he's the real Santa Claus at a New York department store, what street number is in the title?
hints: The original film is from 1947, and it was remade in 1994.
Macy's, the store famous for its Thanksgiving parade, is on that street.
It's double 17.
questions.description: In New York, even the street addresses have the holiday spirit.
questions.fun_fact: Edmund Gwenn won an Oscar for playing Santa Claus in the 1947 version.

questions.question: It's in Chiapas, it's a Pueblo Mágico, and in colonial times it was called Ciudad Real. What does “de las Casas” in its name mean?
questions.answer: It honors a friar who defended Indigenous people
wrong_answers: It recalls its brightly painted houses
It honors a general of the Independence war
It recalls the adobe houses of the Maya
hints: It has nothing to do with houses.
“De las Casas” was added to the city's name in the 19th century.
He was the bishop of Chiapas, and his first name was Bartolomé.
questions.description: A name so long it needs its own jacket for the cold of the Chiapas Highlands.
questions.fun_fact: People born in San Cristóbal de las Casas are called “coletos”.

questions.question: Since when has Mexico City held its big Day of the Dead parade?
hints: It's much newer than it looks.
It was inspired by a movie.
That movie is a James Bond film released in 2015.
questions.description: A parade where the skeletons dance better than your uncles at a wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The James Bond movie “Spectre” opens with a Day of the Dead parade that didn't exist yet; after seeing it, Mexico City created a real one.

questions.question: The Niños Héroes fought at this castle in 1847. In which park in Mexico City is it?
hints: Emperor Maximilian and Carlota lived there.
It's the city's most famous park, and it has a zoo.
Its name in Nahuatl means “grasshopper hill.”
questions.description: The only castle in the Americas with an emperor, cadets and a line for the museum.
questions.fun_fact: It's the only castle in the Americas where an emperor lived, and today it's the National Museum of History.

questions.question: You buy camotes (sweet potato candies) on Puebla's Calle de los Dulces. Before there were candy shops, who made them, according to tradition?
questions.answer: The nuns of the Santa Clara convent
wrong_answers: The soldiers of Cinco de Mayo
The miners of Real del Monte
The sailors of the Manila galleon
hints: It was in colonial times.
According to Puebla legend, cooks like them also invented mole poblano.
That's why they are still called “camotes de Santa Clara”.
questions.description: A candy wrapped in paper as if it were a present for grandma.
questions.fun_fact: Today Puebla's camotes come in many flavors, such as pineapple, strawberry, lime and orange.

questions.question: I'm made of colored tissue paper, with flowers and skulls cut out of me, and I hang on strings at parties. What am I?
hints: I decorate Day of the Dead altars and Independence Day celebrations.
I'm made with scissors, or with a chisel and hammer.
My Spanish name says I'm full of tiny cuts and holes.
questions.description: A craft project that turned out way better than the one from your art class.
questions.fun_fact: San Salvador Huixcolotla, in Puebla, is famous for its papel picado artisans.

questions.question: I was an Archduke of Austria. The French army brought me to rule Mexico in 1864, and my empire ended in Querétaro in 1867. Who am I?
hints: I wasn't born in the Americas.
My wife's name was Carlota.
I was the emperor of the Second Mexican Empire.
questions.description: He came from Europe with a crown, a cape and big plans to rule… and things didn't go as planned.
questions.fun_fact: Maximilian had the Paseo de la Emperatriz laid out, and today it is Mexico City's Paseo de la Reforma.

questions.question: At a noche mexicana you order gorditas, made with corn masa. Which of these antojitos is NOT made with that masa?
hints: Three of them are cooked on the comal like a thick tortilla.
The odd one out is built on something you buy at the bakery.
It's made with a bolillo or a telera.
questions.description: A DNA test for antojitos: who's a true child of corn, and who's adopted?
questions.fun_fact: Gorditas puff up on the comal, so they can be opened like a little pocket and stuffed.

questions.question: Complete: the euro is to Spain as the… is to Mexico.
hints: You pay with it at any little corner store in Mexico.
It comes in bills and coins, like the 10 coin.
In Spanish, its name also means what the scale shows when you step on it.
questions.description: What flies out of your wallet every time you walk past the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before the US dollar ever used it.

questions.question: Who were the first to come and worship baby Jesus, on the very night he was born?
hints: They were working at night in the fields near Bethlehem.
An angel brought them the news while they watched over their animals.
Their job was looking after sheep.
questions.description: The most exclusive guest list in history, and not a single celebrity on it.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, the Wise Men didn't arrive that night: the Gospel says they found the child in a house.

questions.question: In September you paint the Mexican flag on your cheek, starting with green. Which color comes after white?
hints: It's a color on the flag.
You already used green at the start.
It's the color of a ripe tomato.
questions.description: Your face turned into a patriotic canvas, glitter included.
questions.fun_fact: The green, white and red come from the flag of the Army of the Three Guarantees in 1821.

questions.question: When saluting the flag at the honores a la bandera, how do you place your hand on your chest?
hints: The hand is open, not closed.
It goes at the height of the heart.
It's the hand most people write with.
questions.description: A gesture made from the heart… literally right on top of it.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican law calls this gesture the “saludo civil” (civil salute).

questions.question: Lots of students do gymnastics moves at the same time to music, and show it off in the November 20 parade. What is it called?
hints: The students don't play any instruments.
Sometimes they use hoops, balls or ribbons.
Its name has a word that has to do with the beat of the music.
questions.description: A hundred students moving in perfect sync: the teacher calls it art, they call it rehearsal number 47.
questions.fun_fact: The November 20 parade is also called the sports parade because of all the athletes and gymnasts who march in it.

questions.question: “Cielito lindo” is sung at patriotic fiestas and in stadiums, and its chorus starts “Ay, ay, ay, ay…”. What comes next?
questions.answer: Canta y no llores (sing and don't cry)
wrong_answers: Baila y no pares (dance and don't stop)
Ríe y no grites (laugh and don't shout)
Vuelve y no te vayas (come back and don't go)
hints: It's advice to stay cheerful.
It has to do with using your voice.
Doing the opposite of what it says would mean bursting into tears.
questions.description: The song that even the most off-key singer belts out at full volume.
questions.fun_fact: “Cielito lindo” was written by Quirino Mendoza y Cortés around 1882.

questions.question: The Purépecha people called him “Tata Vasco.” Before becoming bishop of Michoacán, what was Vasco de Quiroga?
questions.answer: A judge of the Real Audiencia
hints: He didn't come to New Spain as a churchman.
He studied law in Spain.
He was sent to Mexico to fix the abuses of an earlier court.
questions.description: Before he put on the bishop's hat, this man already wore another very fancy uniform.
questions.fun_fact: Vasco de Quiroga took ideas from Thomas More's book “Utopia” to organize his hospital-towns.

questions.question: You're in Guelatao, Oaxaca, where a Zapotec boy was born who went on to become president of Mexico. Who is he?
hints: He only learned Spanish as a boy.
He governed in the 19th century and defended the country against the French invasion.
He is remembered for the phrase “respect for the rights of others is peace”.
questions.description: From shepherd boy to the face of a banknote: not even a telenovela would dare.
questions.fun_fact: As a child, Benito Juárez spoke only Zapotec and learned Spanish at age 12 in the city of Oaxaca.

questions.question: It's inside the Church of Santo Domingo in Puebla, it's covered in gold leaf, and in the 1600s it was called the “eighth wonder of the world.” What is it?
hints: It's a jewel of New Spain's Baroque style.
It was finished and consecrated in the late 17th century.
It's dedicated to a title of the Virgin Mary linked to a string of prayer beads.
questions.description: If you like things plain and minimalist, better not even walk in here.
questions.fun_fact: The Capilla del Rosario was consecrated in 1690, and its walls are covered in gilded plasterwork of angels, flowers and fruit.

questions.question: I'm a pedestrian street in Mexico City's Historic Center. In colonial times I was called “Plateros” because the silversmiths' guild worked there. Who am I?
hints: I run from the Zócalo toward the Torre Latinoamericana.
My name was changed in 1914.
Today I carry the surname of the president who started the Revolution.
questions.description: Before shopping malls, neighbors grouped together by trade.
questions.fun_fact: In 1914, Pancho Villa himself put up the plaque with the street's new name.

questions.question: The name “New Spain” comes up a lot in Mexican history books. What was it?
questions.answer: Mexico's name when Spain ruled it
wrong_answers: A ship in Christopher Columbus's fleet
A city the Aztecs founded in Europe
A peace treaty between Aztecs and Spaniards
hints: It lasted about 300 years.
A viceroy governed it in the name of the king.
It ended when Mexico won its independence.
questions.description: Everything called “new” gets old sooner or later, just like last year's sneakers.
questions.fun_fact: New Spain once included lands as far away as the Philippine Islands, in Asia.

questions.question: You're in Villahermosa, by the river named after a Spanish explorer who sailed it in 1518, a year before Cortés. Who was he?
hints: He was sent from Cuba to explore the Gulf coast.
He was a relative of the governor of Cuba.
His river forms a large basin together with the Usumacinta.
questions.description: Some get there first and others get the fame; this one got a consolation river.
questions.fun_fact: When Grijalva's expedition returned to Cuba with gold, it encouraged the planning of Hernán Cortés's expedition.

questions.question: At the festival in this photo, each year is named after an animal. How many different animals are in the cycle before it starts over?
hints: It is the biggest festival in China, with red lanterns and dragons.
The cycle includes the rat, the ox, the tiger, the dragon and the pig, among others.
There are as many as there are months in a year.
questions.description: A party where the year gets a mascot instead of a number.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the order of the animals was decided by a race, and the rat won by riding on the ox's back.

questions.question: New Spain had obrajes (workshops) in Puebla, Querétaro and Texcoco, where workers sometimes lived locked in. What did they make?
hints: What they made was sold across the viceroyalty, and people used it every day.
Centuries later, Puebla and Querétaro were still famous for factories in that same industry.
Its raw material came from sheep.
questions.description: A colonial factory where nobody was eager to clock in for the day.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its obrajes, Querétaro became one of the great textile centers of New Spain.

questions.question: My ancestors lived in the Americas but vanished thousands of years ago. I came back with Hernán Cortés in 1519, and the Mexica called me “deer.” What am I?
hints: Cortés brought only about sixteen of us.
In battle, I gave the Spanish a big advantage.
I have a mane and horseshoes.
questions.description: A homecoming after thousands of years: not even the cousin who moved up north takes that long to visit.
questions.fun_fact: Horses evolved in North America and crossed into Asia before dying out in the Americas.

questions.question: After meeting Cortés in 1519, Moctezuma ended up a prisoner of the Spanish. Who ruled the Mexica right after him?
hints: He was Moctezuma's brother.
He ruled for a very short time, just a few months.
He led the Mexica on the Noche Triste.
questions.description: The Mexica throne was fought over harder than the last pan dulce in the basket.
questions.fun_fact: Cuitláhuac ruled for about 80 days before dying of smallpox, a disease brought by the Europeans.

questions.question: Which of these words for places does NOT come from Nahuatl?
hints: Three of them were used in the Valley of Mexico.
The odd one out comes from another Indigenous language, spoken far from the Valley of Mexico.
It comes from a language of the Yucatán Peninsula.
questions.description: Words that arrived before Cortés and decided to stay for good.
questions.fun_fact: “Tianguis” comes from the Nahuatl “tianquiztli”, which means market.

questions.question: Fray Junípero Serra built this mission in the Sierra Gorda before leaving for California. In which Mexican state is it?
hints: It is one of five Franciscan missions that are World Heritage Sites.
The town where it stands bears the friar's surname.
The capital of that state has a famous aqueduct.
questions.description: Before leaving for California, this friar left behind facades more decorated than a wedding cake.
questions.fun_fact: The mission's town is called Jalpan de Serra in honor of the friar, who was born on the island of Mallorca.

questions.question: Martín Cortés, son of Hernán Cortés, is called one of the first mestizos of Mexico. Who was his mother?
wrong_answers: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
hints: She was an Indigenous woman.
She spoke Nahuatl and Maya.
She was Cortés's interpreter.
questions.description: A boy with a very famous dad and a mom people talk about even more.
questions.fun_fact: La Malinche was also known as Malintzin or Doña Marina.

questions.question: At a market in Oaxaca, you try on an embroidered blouse made of manta. What fiber is manta made of?
hints: It's a plant fiber that doesn't come from any animal.
The plant grows fluffy white puffs.
Most T-shirts are made of the same fiber.
questions.description: A top so pretty you'd feel bad wearing it to eat pozole.
questions.fun_fact: Manta is unbleached cotton cloth, which is why it has that typical off-white color.

questions.question: It's made of clay, goes straight on the fire and mole is cooked in it. In which part of the house is it used?
hints: From there, the good smell reaches the whole house.
The pot gets washed right there, in the sink.
That's also where the plates and spoons are kept.
questions.description: A pot that smells like Sunday at Grandma's house.
questions.fun_fact: Many grandmas say beans taste better when they're cooked in a clay pot.

questions.question: This cloth is woven from ixtle, the fiber of the maguey. It was used to carry things, and the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared on Juan Diego's. What is it called?
hints: It's a rough, scratchy cloth, nothing like silk.
Juan Diego's is also called a “tilma”.
Its name starts with “aya…”.
questions.description: A cloth so humble it ended up as one of the most famous in Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: The original image of the Virgin of Guadalupe is kept in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

questions.question: Which animal has these two humps?
hints: It lives in cold deserts of Asia, like the Gobi in Mongolia.
Its one-humped cousin lives in Arabia and North Africa.
Its name starts with “C”.
questions.description: An animal that carries its packed lunch on its back, sometimes in a double portion.
questions.fun_fact: A camel's humps don't store water but fat, which the animal uses as an energy reserve.

questions.question: The front of the Casa de los Azulejos in Mexico City is covered with pieces like these. What are they made of?
hints: It's the same material as many pots and jugs.
It's shaped while wet and then baked in a kiln.
It's what potters work with.
questions.description: A house that dresses up in blue and white to look good in photos.
questions.fun_fact: The Casa de los Azulejos dates from the 18th century, and today there's a restaurant inside.

questions.question: It's made of painted clay, has a slot in its back and gets broken once it's full. What animal is the classic coin bank shaped like?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It's pink and loves mud.
It says “oink.”
questions.description: The smallest bank in the world, and the only one you break to get your money out.
questions.fun_fact: In many languages a coin bank is called a “little pig,” even though the Spanish word “alcancía” comes from Arabic.

questions.question: Chignahuapan, Puebla, makes millions of Christmas ornament balls by hand and holds a fair just for them. What are they made of?
hints: You have to handle them very carefully.
They shine brightly and light passes through them.
They're shaped by blowing, and if they fall on the floor they shatter.
questions.description: A town in Puebla where December starts halfway through the year.
questions.fun_fact: In Chignahuapan the ornaments are painted by hand, and many carry whatever name the customer asks for.

questions.question: You spin it on the table. It has six sides that say things like “toma todo” (take all) or “todos ponen” (everyone pays). What is it called?
hints: It's played in a group, betting candy or beans.
You spin it with two fingers, with no string.
Its name starts with “piri…”.
questions.description: A toy that decides whether today you're a candy millionaire or left with nothing.
questions.fun_fact: Similar toys exist in other parts of the world, like the dreidel played at Hanukkah.

questions.question: The Jalisco dress has a wide skirt and colorful ribbons, and it's worn to dance the jarabe tapatío. What does “tapatío” mean?
hints: It's a word for where someone comes from.
It refers to a city.
It's the capital of Jalisco.
questions.description: A skirt that spins so much it makes the charro dizzy.
questions.fun_fact: The jarabe tapatío is so famous that outside Mexico many people know it as the “Mexican hat dance.”

questions.question: The Vochol is a vocho (VW Beetle) covered in glass beads by artisans of a people who call themselves Wixárika. What is their other name?
hints: They live in the mountains where Jalisco, Nayarit, Zacatecas and Durango meet.
They are famous for their yarn art and beadwork.
They hold peyote and the deer sacred.
questions.description: A vocho that dressed up for a gala and never drove again.
questions.fun_fact: The Vochol, from 2010, has more than 2 million beads glued on by hand.

questions.question: On ranches, the morral isn't only carried on the shoulder: it also goes over the horse's head. What for?
wrong_answers: To shade it from the sun
hints: The horse loves this moment.
There's something inside it.
It holds oats or corn.
questions.description: A bag that the rancher and his horse share without a fight.
questions.fun_fact: The first meaning of “morral” in the Spanish dictionary is exactly that bag of food hung from an animal's head.

questions.question: It's a cotton bandana, usually red or blue with little teardrop patterns, and charros and farmers wear it around the neck. What's it called?
hints: It's much smaller than a blanket.
Folded up, it fits in a pants pocket.
Its name starts with “pa…”.
questions.description: A little cloth that does it all: wipes off sweat, ties back your hair or shows off at the jaripeo.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Pulicat, a town in India that these bandanas used to come from.

questions.question: Every Saturday, Mexico City hosts the Bazar Sábado, famous for its crafts and painters. In which neighborhood?
hints: It's in the south of the city, with cobblestone streets.
It's held on Plaza San Jacinto.
It's home to the house-studio of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo.
questions.description: A market so punctual it only shows up for work one day a week.
questions.fun_fact: While the bazaar fills an old mansion, painters show their canvases outside on the plaza.

questions.question: Which of these Mexican crafts is NOT made of clay?
hints: One of them comes from Guerrero.
That one never goes into the potter's kiln.
It is made on wood or gourds.
questions.description: Three cousins who came out of the kiln, and one who crashed the family reunion.
questions.fun_fact: Olinalá lacquerware is traditionally made on linaloe wood, from a very fragrant tree.

questions.question: Which ancient people gave Mexico its name and founded their capital where Mexico City stands today?
hints: They ruled central Mexico when the Spanish arrived.
Their capital was called Tenochtitlan and was built on a lake.
They called themselves the “Mexica.”
questions.description: A city so important that it lent its name to the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City was built on a lake, so some of its buildings are slowly sinking.

questions.question: Many ofrendas include the departed person's favorite drink, such as pulque. Which plant does pulque come from?
hints: It's a big plant with thick leaves and spines along the edges.
Its sweet sap, before it ferments, is called aguamiel.
It's a close relative of the agave used for tequila.
questions.description: Because even in the afterlife you crave something cool to drink after such a long trip.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Spanish arrived, pulque was a sacred drink that almost only elders, priests and people at ceremonies were allowed to drink.

questions.question: For the Mexica, people who died a natural death traveled for four years through nine levels, guided by a dog. Where did they end up?
hints: It was a dark, cold place under the earth.
Warriors and people who drowned didn't go there, only those who died of old age or illness.
Its lord was Mictlantecuhtli, the god of death.
questions.description: A four-year trip with no layovers, no luggage and no Wi-Fi.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the xoloitzcuintle dog helped the soul cross a raging river on one of the levels of the journey.

questions.question: Every October, the Monumental Alebrijes Parade moves through Mexico City. Which cartonero invented alebrijes after dreaming of them?
hints: He was a Mexico City craftsman who made papier-mâché Judas figures and piñatas.
He had that dream in 1936, while he was very sick.
His first name was Pedro.
questions.description: Some dreams are forgotten when you wake up, and others end up parading down Reforma.
questions.fun_fact: As he told it himself, in his dream some fantastic creatures shouted a single word: “Alebrijes!”

questions.question: Every year, Aguascalientes holds the Festival de Calaveras to honor the creator of this engraving, who was born in that city. Who was he?
hints: He was an engraver who worked for Mexico City newspapers in the late 19th century.
He didn't call her Catrina, but “La Calavera Garbancera.”
His initials are J. G. P.
questions.description: A very elegant lady who hasn't eaten in over a century.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Catrina” came from Diego Rivera, who painted her in his mural “Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central.”

questions.question: In Mexico, when someone says “el 2 de noviembre vamos al panteón,” where are they going?
hints: On that day, many families spend hours there with food and music.
Families bring cempasúchil flowers.
It's where the dead are buried.
questions.description: On November 2, the whole family packs up flowers, food and even the guitar, and nobody stays home.
questions.fun_fact: The word “panteón” comes from Greek and means “of all the gods”: it was the name of a temple in ancient Rome.

questions.question: In Mexico, what is this candle in a glass jar called, the kind placed on ofrendas and altars?
hints: You can buy it at the corner store or at the market.
It can stay lit for several days in a row.
Its name comes from the Spanish «velar», to keep watch over someone at night.
questions.description: Works the night shift, never complains and brings its own glass.
questions.fun_fact: The glass shields the flame from the wind, which is why veladoras stay lit all night in the cemetery.

questions.question: In the movie Coco, which of these characters is NOT related to Mamá Coco?
hints: He is a very famous singer in the movie.
For most of the movie, Miguel thinks he is his great-great-grandfather.
He stole his friend's songs.
questions.description: A family tree with more branches than a bunch of cempasúchil marigolds.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Mamá Coco's real name is Socorro.

questions.question: On the ofrenda, a cloth covers the table. It is often embroidered and almost always white. What does that color stand for?
hints: It has to do with the color, not the fabric.
It's the same thing many people link to a bride's white dress.
It means clean, without a stain.
questions.description: They tell the family not to spill the atole, and for good reason.
questions.fun_fact: Papel picado, candles, water, salt and pan de muerto usually go on top of the white cloth.

questions.question: At the agua fresca stand there's a dark purple one made with zarzamora. Which group of fruits does zarzamora belong to?
hints: It isn't sour like a lime or hard like a walnut.
It grows on thorny bushes.
Each fruit is a cluster of tiny juicy beads, and the plant is related to the rose.
questions.description: A drink that leaves your tongue purple, as if you'd been snacking on crayons.
questions.fun_fact: Michoacán grows the vast majority of Mexico's zarzamoras, and many of them are sold abroad.

questions.question: It's sold in rolled-up sticks, smells sweet, and is always in café de olla and arroz con leche. What is it?
hints: It's a brown spice.
It comes from the bark of a tree.
It's also sprinkled on churros with sugar.
questions.description: It makes abuelita's kitchen smell wonderful before you're even awake.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries that imports the most cinnamon in the world.

questions.question: Which believers mainly celebrate the festival of lights in this photo, with little clay lamps and colorful patterns on the ground?
hints: It is the most famous festival in India.
It is called Diwali and celebrates the victory of light over darkness.
Their religion has gods like Ganesha, the one with an elephant's head.
questions.description: A festival where nobody fears the electricity bill, because it all runs on tiny candles.
questions.fun_fact: The word Diwali comes from the Sanskrit “Deepavali,” which means “row of lamps.”

questions.question: I'm a grain sold in flakes. Cooked with milk I become porridge, and at the market they blend me with banana. What am I?
hints: Horses eat a lot of me too.
My flakes are flat and cream-colored.
My name starts with O and has just four letters.
questions.description: Breakfast for people running late, gulped down standing up at the market.
questions.fun_fact: An oat and banana licuado is one of the quickest and cheapest breakfasts at Mexican markets.

questions.question: It's clear, tied with a rubber band around the straw, and the tiendita hands you your soda to go in it. What is it made of?
hints: The soda doesn't make it soggy or tear it.
That's why it causes so much pollution when it's thrown in the street.
It's the same material as lots of water bottles.
questions.description: The most Mexican way to drink a soda with no cup and no bottle.
questions.fun_fact: You get your soda in a bag so the tiendita can keep the returnable bottle.

questions.question: In October 1810, the insurgents beat the royalists at Monte de las Cruces, but their leader refused to enter Mexico City. Who was he?
hints: It was just a few weeks after the War of Independence began.
This leader had started the rebellion in a town in Guanajuato.
He is the priest who gave the Grito de Dolores.
questions.description: A mountain forest, a crowd of insurgents and a decision people still argue about.
questions.fun_fact: The battle took place in a mountain forest between Toluca and Mexico City, at about 3,000 m (9,800 ft) above sea level.

questions.question: In 1861, Spain, France and Britain signed the Convention of London and sent ships to Veracruz. Which decision by Juárez caused it?
questions.answer: Suspending payments on the foreign debt
wrong_answers: Closing the port of Veracruz to trade
hints: Juárez had just won the Reform War, and the government had no money.
The three countries said a Mexican law from July 1861 was costing them money.
Juárez decreed that they would not be paid for two years.
questions.description: Three European powers agreed on a group trip to Veracruz, and it wasn't exactly a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Spain and Britain pulled out in 1862 after the Treaties of La Soledad; only France stayed and invaded the country.

questions.question: It's named after a priest who was a hero of Independence, its capital is Cuernavaca and it borders Mexico City. Which state is it?
hints: Cuernavaca is called “the city of eternal spring.”
The hero it's named after held out in the famous Siege of Cuautla, in this same state.
That priest wore a bandana tied around his head.
questions.description: A state that took a hero's name and ordered spring weather all year round.
questions.fun_fact: Morelos is Mexico's second-smallest state; only Tlaxcala is smaller.

questions.question: Every September 13, Mexico remembers the Niños Héroes, who defended Chapultepec Castle in 1847. They were cadets: what is a cadet?
questions.answer: A student at a military school
wrong_answers: A drummer in the military band
hints: They defended the castle during the war against the United States.
They were teenagers; the youngest was only 13.
A cadet is still studying to become an officer.
questions.description: A pressed uniform, shiny boots and a castle for an address: that's how fancy this word sounds.
questions.fun_fact: The Niños Héroes monument in Chapultepec has six columns, one for each cadet.

questions.question: In what year was Agustín de Iturbide crowned Agustín I, Mexico's first emperor, in the Metropolitan Cathedral?
hints: It was shortly after independence was won.
Before becoming emperor, Iturbide had been a royalist officer who switched sides.
It was the year after independence was completed.
questions.description: Crown, cape and cathedral: the fanciest ceremony in the capital, no red carpet needed.
questions.fun_fact: The First Mexican Empire lasted less than a year: Iturbide gave up the throne in March 1823.

questions.question: Complete Vicente Guerrero's famous phrase from when he refused to give up the insurgent fight: “La patria es…”
hints: He said it when he was asked to surrender in exchange for a pardon from the viceroy.
He said it to his own father, who had brought him the offer.
It means the opposite of “last.”
questions.description: A short phrase that fits on a coat of arms, on a wall, and in many hearts.
questions.fun_fact: As president, Vicente Guerrero decreed the abolition of slavery in Mexico in 1829.

questions.question: In the 1906 Cananea strike, Mexican miners at a copper mine demanded the same pay as American workers. In which state was it?
hints: The mine was very close to the US border.
It's a northwestern state, famous for its desert and its carne asada.
Its capital is Hermosillo.
questions.description: Miners in helmets, lots of copper, and zero interest in earning less than the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The miners also demanded an 8-hour workday, a right that was later written into the 1917 Constitution.

questions.question: Who was the first Indigenous Mexican woman nominated for the Oscar for Best Actress, for the film “Roma”?
hints: She is from Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca.
Before acting, she trained to be a preschool teacher.
In “Roma” she played Cleo, a live-in housekeeper.
questions.description: Gown, high heels and nerves of steel: welcome to Hollywood's fanciest night.
questions.fun_fact: Yalitza had never acted before “Roma” and ended up at the casting almost by chance, thanks to her sister.

questions.question: Guess who I am: I'm the Gym Leader of Pewter City, I use Rock-type Pokémon, and I travel with Ash, cooking for everyone. Who am I?
hints: I was one of Ash's very first travel companions.
I always fall in love with every Nurse Joy and Officer Jenny.
My first Pokémon is Onix, a giant stone snake.
questions.description: A boy who has been traveling for years and still hasn't finished school.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, Brock is called Takeshi, and Ash is called Satoshi, after Pokémon creator Satoshi Tajiri.

questions.question: The Indigenous faja (sash) wraps several times around the waist, holds up a skirt or trousers, and is woven on a backstrap loom. What fibers is it traditionally made of?
hints: One fiber comes from a plant, the other from an animal.
They're the same fibers as in many sarapes and huipiles.
One grows in a fluffy white boll; the other is sheared from sheep.
questions.description: The original belt: no buckle, no holes, and more colors than a market.
questions.fun_fact: On a backstrap loom, the weaver keeps the threads tight with her own body by leaning back.

questions.question: If you run the Caballo Blanco Ultramarathon in Urique, in the Sierra Tarahumara, about how far do you run?
hints: It's much longer than a 42 km marathon.
It's finished in a single day.
That's about 50 miles.
questions.description: A race where the best runners don't need designer sneakers.
questions.fun_fact: The race became famous worldwide thanks to the book “Born to Run”, about the Rarámuri runners.

questions.question: I'm spoken in Hidalgo, Querétaro and the State of Mexico; in the Mezquital Valley I'm called Hñähñu, and Tenango embroidery comes from my people. Which language am I?
hints: I'm one of the most widely spoken languages of central Mexico.
My embroidery is full of colorful animals and plants.
Many tourists buy the “Lele” dolls of Querétaro, made by my people.
questions.description: A language with more embroidery than a Sunday tablecloth.
questions.fun_fact: The Lele doll from Amealco, Querétaro, is made by Otomí women artisans and has become a symbol of the state.

questions.question: In most municipalities of Oaxaca, people choose their leaders in a community assembly, with no political parties. What is this system called?
hints: It rests on traditions passed down from generation to generation.
Today the law also calls it “indigenous normative systems.”
Its name refers to the practices and habits of each community.
questions.description: Democracy with no ballots, no billboards and no catchy campaign jingles.
questions.fun_fact: More than 400 of Oaxaca’s 570 municipalities choose their leaders this way.

questions.question: It's a wool blanket with stripes of many colors, worn over the shoulders, and the most famous one comes from Saltillo. What is it called?
hints: It's worn mostly by men against the cold.
Mariachis and charros sometimes carry it on their shoulder.
Saltillo, Coahuila, is its world capital.
questions.description: The blanket that refused to stay in bed.
questions.fun_fact: A sarape with an opening in the middle for your head is usually called a jorongo.

questions.question: You see a woman dressed as a tehuana at a vela (festival) on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. Which item is NOT part of her outfit?
hints: The tehuana outfit is famous for its colorful embroidered flowers.
The odd one out comes from the tradition of another region of Mexico.
That item is typical of the men in a mariachi band.
questions.description: Isthmus fashion: so elegant that Frida Kahlo made it her uniform.
questions.fun_fact: The resplandor is a lace headdress that frames the face; at some festivals it is worn to go to Mass.

questions.question: For curanderos, “susto” comes after a big fright, takes away sleep and appetite, and is cured with a limpia. What is believed to happen to the person?
questions.answer: Part of their soul leaves them
wrong_answers: Food gets stuck in their stomach
hints: It isn't a stomach or tooth problem.
The curandero “calls” the person by name so that something comes back.
Something invisible stays behind where the fright happened.
questions.description: When a big jump leaves you with more than a racing heart.
questions.fun_fact: In some communities, to cure susto, people go back to the place of the fright to call the person's spirit home.

questions.question: In Guerrero, many wooden masks are carved for the tlacololeros dance. By tradition, what is this dance for?
questions.answer: To protect the milpa and ask for a good harvest
wrong_answers: To celebrate a victory in battle
To ask for good fishing at sea
hints: The dancers play farmers.
A “tlacolol” is a plot of land cleared for planting.
They chase a “tiger” that damages the crops.
questions.description: A wooden face, a whip in hand, and a big cat nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: The tlacololeros crack huge whips, and the snap sounds like gunshots in the middle of the fiesta.

questions.question: Kiliwa, from northern Mexico, has only a handful of speakers left. Which language family does it belong to?
hints: It is not related to Nahuatl.
It is spoken in Baja California.
It shares a family with Paipai, Cucapá and Kumiai.
questions.description: A language so rare that all its speakers could fit around one family dinner table.
questions.fun_fact: The Yuman family also reaches across the border into Arizona and California.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this big, fleshy pepper that isn't spicy at all called?
hints: They come in red, yellow, orange and green.
It's almost square, with three or four bumps on the bottom.
It's often used on pizzas and in salads.
questions.description: A relative of the chiles that came out with no personality at all.
questions.fun_fact: The bell pepper is the same species as the jalapeño and the serrano, but it has almost no capsaicin.

questions.question: Charmander is to Fire type as Lucario is to…
hints: Lucario can sense other creatures' aura, but that's not what decides its type.
Machop and Hitmonchan are this type too.
It's the type of Pokémon that throw punches and kicks.
questions.description: A dog that never barks, but can read everyone's energy.
questions.fun_fact: Lucario actually has two types at once: Fighting and Steel.

questions.question: Salsa de cacahuate is ground from roasted peanuts, garlic and a thin, dried, bright red, very hot chile. Which one?
hints: It is not a wide or dark chile.
It is small and long, and it's pretty hot.
Its Spanish name sounds like something that grows in a forest.
questions.description: A salsa that starts out crunchy and ends in a house fire.
questions.fun_fact: The word “cacahuate” comes from the Nahuatl “tlalcacahuatl,” meaning “earth cacao.”

questions.question: The Mexica called it xitomatl, and the Spanish took it to Europe. In which century was that?
hints: It reached Europe long before it became a common ingredient in Italian cooking.
It happened at the time of the Spanish conquest of the Mexica.
It's the same century Shakespeare was born in.
questions.description: A red fruit crossed the ocean, and then Europe showed it off as its own.
questions.fun_fact: At first, many Europeans thought the tomato was poisonous and grew it only as a decorative plant.

questions.question: You ask for “una rebajita” and haggle over the price. Where is haggling NOT usually done?
hints: In one place, the price is printed on labels.
There you pay at a cash register.
There you push a cart down the aisles.
questions.description: The art of saying “Can you do it for less?” with a face like you're about to leave.
questions.fun_fact: “Tianguis” comes from the Nahuatl word “tianquiztli”, which means market.

questions.question: They're squash seeds: toasted with salt and lime, sold in little bags, and ground for pipián. What are they called?
hints: They're green inside and flat.
You eat them one by one, as a snack.
Their name means “little seeds” in Spanish.
questions.description: What the squash hides inside and you snack on in the park.
questions.fun_fact: Pipián is a mole thickened with ground squash seeds.

questions.question: It's a long brown seed with a strong smell, used in adobos and birria, and people say “me importa un…”. Which spice is it?
hints: It's used whole or ground.
It smells strong and a bit earthy.
It's part of a Spanish saying for not caring about something at all.
questions.description: A tiny seed that matters a lot, whatever the saying claims.
questions.fun_fact: Cumin came to Mexico with the Spanish: it's from the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

questions.question: These giant warrior statues stand in Tula, Hidalgo. Which people carved them?
hints: They lived before the Aztecs.
Tula was the capital of their kingdom.
The Aztecs admired them so much that they used their name to mean “great artist.”
questions.description: They've been standing guard for more than a thousand years and haven't asked for a bathroom break once.
questions.fun_fact: The Atlantes are about 4.6 m (15 ft) tall and once held up the roof of a temple.

questions.question: It's in central Mexico City, people call it “el barrio bravo,” and boxing champions came from there. What is Tepito most famous for?
hints: It's a very old, traditional neighborhood that gets busy very early.
People from all over the city go there on weekdays and weekends looking for good prices.
They say you can find everything there, from clothes to gadgets.
