questions.question: Finish Benito Juárez's saying: “Among individuals, as among nations, respect for the rights of others is…”
hints: Juárez said it after defeating Maximilian's empire.
It is shown as a white dove.
It is the opposite of war.
questions.description: The most famous line of a president who fits on a banknote and on a chalkboard.
questions.fun_fact: Juárez said those words in a statement on July 15, 1867, when he returned to Mexico City.

questions.question: It's the night of September 15 and you're in the Zócalo. Who steps out onto the central balcony of the National Palace to give the Grito?
wrong_answers: The Head of Government of Mexico City
hints: Only one person does it, and it is shown on TV across the whole country.
After shouting “¡Viva México!”, this person rings a bell and waves the flag.
In the states the governors do it; in the Zócalo, someone even more important.
questions.description: A balcony overlooking thousands of people shouting… and nobody complains about the noise.
questions.fun_fact: The bell that is rung is the original one from Dolores, brought to the National Palace in 1896.

questions.question: In 1908, Porfirio Díaz told a US magazine that Mexico was ready for democracy. Which journalist interviewed him?
hints: He was Canadian and wrote for US newspapers.
His last name was joined to Díaz's in the name of the famous interview.
His first name was James.
questions.description: Don Porfirio said something meant for American readers, and Mexico never forgot it.
questions.fun_fact: Those statements encouraged Francisco I. Madero to write his book “La sucesión presidencial en 1910” (The Presidential Succession in 1910).

questions.question: In Aztec dance it is blown through the tip like a trumpet, and the Mexica played it to call people to ceremonies. What is this instrument made of?
hints: The Mexica had no cows or bulls.
It comes from an animal that lived in water.
It was brought from the coast, and it once had a resident who carried its house on its back.
questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the Mexica already had their own megaphone.
questions.fun_fact: When the caracol (conch) is blown, players often greet the four directions: north, south, east and west.

questions.question: Rarámuri runner Lorena Ramírez won ultramarathons in traditional huaraches. What are their soles made of?
hints: The Rarámuri make these huaraches themselves, from cheap materials they have at hand.
It is a recycled material that once had another use.
It comes from a car or a truck.
questions.description: Running shoes with zero cushioning and zero sports stores involved.
questions.fun_fact: In 2017, Lorena Ramírez won the Cerro Rojo ultramarathon, 50 km (31 miles) in Puebla, running in a skirt and huaraches.

questions.question: Making rajas de poblano takes several kitchen steps. Which of these is NOT one of them?
hints: Think about the dish's name.
Rajas come to the plate in a shape you can see at a glance.
If you do this step, you don't get strips anymore, you get a sauce.
questions.description: A chile that got so fancy it only goes out with crema and elote.
questions.fun_fact: Roasted poblanos go into a bag or under a cloth for a few minutes so they “sweat” and the skin peels off easily.

questions.question: Take a close look: what snack is this?
hints: They're made from something found on almost every table in Mexico.
They're cut into triangles before frying.
They're served with beans or salsa, or in chilaquiles.
questions.description: The snack that always shows up when someone says “Want to come over and watch the game?”
questions.fun_fact: Chilaquiles are made with totopos covered in green or red salsa.

questions.question: If you eat this salsa and your mouth is on fire, which ingredient is to blame?
hints: It's the bravest ingredient in the salsa.
There are many kinds: habanero, serrano, jalapeño…
In Mexico, burning your mouth this way is called “enchilarse”, and the word hides its name.
questions.description: A salsa with an innocent face that can make you cry.
questions.fun_fact: The heat in a chile comes from capsaicin, and most of it sits in the white veins inside.

questions.question: What do water lettuce, water hyacinth and the giant water lily have in common?
wrong_answers: They only grow in salt water
They are algae that live underwater
hints: All three live in rivers and lakes.
Sometimes they cover whole ponds like a green carpet.
Their leaves stay on top of the water without sinking.
questions.description: A garden where watering the plants is completely pointless.
questions.fun_fact: Water lettuce has tiny hairs on its leaves that trap air, so even if you push it under, it pops right back up.

questions.question: Refried beans are mashed and fried in a pan. How many times are they usually fried?
hints: Before they reach the pan, the beans are already cooked in a pot.
In Mexican Spanish, the “re” in words like “rebueno” or “rebonito” means “really.”
The Spanish name “frijoles refritos” means “well-fried beans.”
questions.description: Mashed beans that land on the plate ready to go with a good plate of chilaquiles.
questions.fun_fact: The English name “refried beans” came from translating the Spanish “re” too literally, as if they were fried twice.

questions.question: It's beige with brown spots, and in northern Mexico it's the top pick for frijoles charros. Which bean is it?
hints: Its spots almost disappear when it's cooked.
It isn't just one color.
It shares its name with a spotted horse.
questions.description: A northern bean that's always there when there's carne asada on Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: The pinto bean is one of the most widely grown beans in northern Mexico.

questions.question: They're small, shiny beans, their broth turns almost purple, and in southern Mexico they're cooked with epazote. Which beans are they?
hints: They're often served refried next to breakfast eggs.
They're the favorite in Veracruz, Oaxaca and Yucatán.
They're the color of the night.
questions.description: Beans that people in the southeast wouldn't trade for anything, not even at breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: Epazote goes into beans for its flavor, and many people say it also makes them easier to digest.

questions.question: At Chichén Itzá, the great pyramid of El Castillo has staircases leading up to its temple. How many staircases does it have?
hints: It's an even number.
The Maya built it as a giant stone calendar.
Its base is a square, and each side has its own staircase.
questions.description: A pyramid made for people who never get tired of climbing steps.
questions.fun_fact: Each staircase has 91 steps; add the platform at the top and you get 365, like the days of the year.

questions.question: It sits next to La Merced in Mexico City. What is mostly sold at the Mercado de Sonora?
hints: It's right downtown, and its aisles are always packed.
There they can give you a “limpia” with branches and an egg.
People call it “the witches' market.”
questions.description: A market with so many aisles that even the GPS asks for help getting out.
questions.fun_fact: Besides its mystical aisles, it is famous for its toys, piñatas and pottery.

questions.question: Diego Rivera designed it, it's made of volcanic stone and it looks like a pyramid. What did he create the Anahuacalli for?
wrong_answers: To live there with Frida Kahlo
To use it as an observatory
To open a school of painting
hints: Rivera was a passionate collector.
He gathered thousands of pieces made long before the Spanish arrived.
It displays clay and stone figures from ancient cultures of Mexico.
questions.description: A painter who got tired of painting walls and decided to build some very, very dark ones of his own.
questions.fun_fact: Rivera gathered more than 50,000 pre-Hispanic pieces for his collection.

questions.question: Carlos Slim founded it in Polanco, thousands of hexagonal aluminum tiles cover it, and it holds many Rodin sculptures. Which museum is it?
hints: Admission is free.
Its shape looks like a twisted hourglass.
It's named after its founder's wife.
questions.description: A building so shiny that on a sunny day you should visit it wearing sunglasses.
questions.fun_fact: Its building is covered with about 16,000 hexagonal aluminum tiles.

questions.question: This snowy volcano next to Popocatépetl is famous for the shape of its outline. What does it look like?
wrong_answers: An old man with a cane
hints: Its name in Nahuatl describes exactly that shape.
It has a “head”, a “chest” and “feet”.
According to legend, it's a princess waiting for her warrior.
questions.description: A volcano that's more famous as a model than as a mountain.
questions.fun_fact: The parts of Iztaccíhuatl are named after body parts: climbers head for “the chest”, its highest summit.

previous.feedback: source: hint 1 says the Nahuatl name "describes exactly that figure". That is false: Iztaccíhuatl means "white woman", not "sleeping woman", so the source hint needs correcting first, e.g. "Its Nahuatl name means “white woman.”". On the translation side, "the Popocatépetl's neighbor" is awkward English and should be "Popocatépetl's neighbor", with no article. Fact check: wrong. Hint 1 is false. The Nahuatl name Iztaccíhuatl means 'white woman', not 'sleeping woman'. The sleeping-woman figure comes from the outline and the legend. The answer and the fun fact are correct: El Pecho is the highest summit, at about 5,230 m.

questions.question: This is Lake Catemaco, in Veracruz. What kind of people is it famous for all over Mexico?
hints: It has to do with mystery.
Every March, a big gathering of them takes place there.
They do “limpias” (cleansings) with herbs and eggs.
questions.description: A lake in Veracruz that is more famous than a lot of TV stars.
questions.fun_fact: On an island in Lake Catemaco lives a colony of monkeys that were brought there for a scientific study.

questions.question: In Yucatán, hundreds of cenotes form a huge ring that marks the edge of the buried Chicxulub crater. Roughly how wide is it?
hints: The asteroid that made it helped wipe out the dinosaurs.
The ring is too big to see from the ground.
Driving across it by road would take about two hours.
questions.description: A necklace of natural swimming pools that a space rock left behind as a souvenir.
questions.fun_fact: The crater was found in the 1970s thanks to measurements taken while searching for oil; the ring of cenotes was linked to it later.

questions.question: In the Celestún estuary in Yucatán, fresh water from springs mixes with seawater. What is this kind of water called?
hints: It's not good to drink.
It has some salt, but less than the sea.
The word also describes a slightly salty, unpleasant taste.
questions.description: Not river, not sea: water that just can't make up its mind.
questions.fun_fact: The flamingos of Celestún are pink because of the tiny crustaceans they eat.

questions.question: In this 2011 Mexican animated film, the second in the Leo San Juan saga, children go missing in a town by the water. Which film is it?
hints: It's part of Mexico's “Leyendas” film saga.
The villain is a spirit that roams near rivers and canals at night.
Her best-known cry is “¡Ay, mis hijos!”
questions.description: Second film, second scare: Leo San Juan never gets a single day of vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The saga began in 2007 with La Leyenda de la Nahuala, set in Puebla.

questions.question: In a Maya myth, the earth formed on the back of a huge animal floating in the water. What animal is it?
hints: It's a reptile.
It can stay still for hours with only its eyes above the water.
Its long mouth is full of teeth, and it lives in the mangroves of Yucatán.
questions.description: According to the Maya, the whole planet began as a very uncomfortable boat ride.
questions.fun_fact: In Chiapas, the Sumidero Canyon is famous because from the boat you can see crocodiles sunbathing.

questions.question: Xiuhtecuhtli, the lord of fire, presided over the New Fire ceremony. How often did the Mexica hold it?
hints: It was when their two calendars lined up again: the 365-day one and the 260-day one.
This period was called the “binding of the years.”
It's a number between 50 and 55.
questions.description: A god so old the candles wouldn't fit on his birthday cake… so he lit a bonfire instead.
questions.fun_fact: Before the New Fire, every fire was put out, and people waited in the dark for the new flame to be lit on the Cerro de la Estrella.

questions.question: This Mexica piece from about 500 years ago is made of green quetzal feathers. What kind of object is it?
hints: Rulers and high nobles showed their rank with pieces like this.
It has hundreds of long feathers spread in a half circle and small gold plates.
The most famous one is credited to the ruler Moctezuma II.
questions.description: A piece so elegant it left many quetzal birds without their best outfit.
questions.fun_fact: Moctezuma's headdress has been in Austria for centuries (today in a museum in Vienna), and Mexico still asks for it to come back.

questions.question: After defeating Azcapotzalco, the tlatoani Itzcóatl ordered something burned that didn't suit the Mexica. What?
hints: He wanted the past told his way.
They were painted on amate paper or deerskin.
They were the painted books of Mesoamerica.
questions.description: A tlatoani who wasn't afraid of some serious spring cleaning.
questions.fun_fact: Itzcóatl also formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, the base of Mexica power.

questions.question: In the ball game the Mexica called tlachtli, the courts had stone rings like this one. What were they for?
questions.answer: To send the ball through them
wrong_answers: To tell the time by their shadow
hints: They were set high up on the walls of the court.
Players hit the rubber ball with their hips, not their hands.
Doing it was so hard that a player who managed it usually won the game on the spot.
questions.description: A game so old the referee probably wore feathers.
questions.fun_fact: The ball was solid rubber and could weigh up to about 4 kg (9 lb), so players wore leather padding.

questions.question: This codex page shows blankets, shields and warrior suits delivered to Tenochtitlan. Who delivered them?
hints: They did it at regular times, because they had to.
It was called tribute.
They were cities defeated in war.
questions.description: Mexico's oldest to-do list, with little drawings instead of letters.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to tribute, cacao, feathers, cotton and even jade reached Tenochtitlan from faraway places.

questions.question: The traje de tehuana, like the ones worn in Juchitán, Oaxaca, became world-famous thanks to a painter who wore it every day. Who?
hints: She was Mexican and lived in Coyoacán.
She painted herself in this dress in several self-portraits.
She was married to Diego Rivera.
questions.description: Long skirts, ruffles and flowers in the hair: on the Isthmus, getting dressed is a full production.
questions.fun_fact: In Juchitán, women are famous for running the markets and the fiestas called velas.

questions.question: Curicaueri was the main god of the Purépecha, patron of their kings and worshipped in Tzintzuntzan. What does his name mean?
hints: He was linked to the Sun.
The Purépecha saw him as a god of the sky and of war.
His followers offered him firewood.
questions.description: The Purépecha gave their main god a real tongue-twister of a name; now it's your turn to translate it.
questions.fun_fact: The yácatas of Tzintzuntzan, next to Lake Pátzcuaro, were temples with a very unusual shape that mixes rectangles and semicircles.

questions.question: In 1939, Matthew Stirling found Stela C at Tres Zapotes, with a very early date in the system that counts days from a starting day. What is that system called?
hints: The Maya used it most of all, on their stelae.
It counts days in a row and doesn't start over every 52 years.
Its name tells you how far it stretches.
questions.description: The ancients kept their calendars up to date, and without a single phone app.
questions.fun_fact: The date on Stela C helped prove that the Olmecs were older than the Classic Maya.

questions.question: Aridoamerica was the great dry region of the north, with deserts, little rain and peoples like the Chichimecas. What kind of peoples mostly lived there?
hints: There was hardly any place to grow corn.
They didn't always live in the same place.
They moved around following wild animals and plants.
questions.description: A region where water was so scarce that owning a puddle made you a millionaire.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica liked to boast of having Chichimeca roots, meaning they came from the peoples of the north.

questions.question: My temple in Teotihuacan's Ciudadela is covered in carved heads of me, and in 2003 a tunnel full of offerings was found under it. Who am I?
hints: I was also worshipped as a god of the wind.
Legend says I brought corn to humans.
My name joins a bird with green feathers and a serpent.
questions.description: A temple with so many carved faces it looks like an end-of-year class photo.
questions.fun_fact: The tunnel under the temple is more than 100 m (330 ft) long and held thousands of objects, even balls covered in pyrite that shone like stars.

questions.question: Look at this mural from Cacaxtla, in Tlaxcala. Which two sides are fighting in the battle?
hints: It was painted long before the Spanish arrived.
Look closely at the warriors' skins and headdresses.
Some wear big-cat spots; others wear feathers.
questions.description: More than a thousand years later, the colors are still as lively as a family argument at Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: The Cacaxtla murals survived so well because the people who lived there covered them with earth when they rebuilt their buildings.

questions.question: When Monte Albán declined, Zapotec power moved to a city in the Valley of Oaxaca, seat of King Cosijoeza, whose tombs full of offerings were found in 1962. Which city?
hints: Today it's a town in the Valley of Oaxaca with a very busy market.
It was the political capital of the Zapotecs, not their great religious center.
Its name starts with Z, like “Zapotec.”
questions.description: When the capital empties out, someone has to take charge of the move.
questions.fun_fact: Tombs 1 and 2 at Zaachila were excavated in 1962 and held rich offerings of gold, turquoise and pottery.

questions.question: In “El compadre Mendoza” (1934), a hacienda owner swaps the portrait in his living room to suit each visitor and ends up betraying his compadre, General Felipe Nieto. Which side was Nieto on?
hints: The film was directed by Fernando de Fuentes and is part of his trilogy about the Revolution.
Mendoza hung Huerta's or Carranza's portrait depending on who arrived; for Nieto he put up a third one.
Nieto's side fought under the cry “Land and liberty!”
questions.description: A host so polite he changes the decor depending on who knocks at the door.
questions.fun_fact: “El compadre Mendoza” is considered one of the best Mexican films of all time.

questions.question: Which famous Mexican revolutionary led the División del Norte?
hints: He was one of the most famous leaders of the Mexican Revolution.
He was from Durango, and his riders were called “los Dorados”.
His real name was Doroteo Arango.
questions.description: If you see him on horseback looking grumpy, don’t even think about borrowing his sombrero.
questions.fun_fact: Pancho Villa signed a contract with a US film company so it could film his battles.

questions.question: I was born in Guanajuato, I painted Mexico’s history on the walls of the Palacio Nacional, and I married the same painter twice. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the great Mexican muralists.
I also painted murals in Detroit and San Francisco.
My wife was Frida Kahlo.
questions.description: An artist who never minded drawing all over the walls.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo divorced in 1939 and married each other again in 1940.

questions.question: I was a soldadera in the Revolution, a song bears my name, and today all the women who fought are called after me. Who am I?
hints: I followed the troops, cooked, treated the wounded, and sometimes fought too.
My song says a sergeant was in love with me.
My name starts with A, and in the plural it's used for all soldaderas.
questions.description: She marched on foot behind the troops with a cooking pot in one hand and plenty of courage in the other.
questions.fun_fact: Many soldaderas rode on the roofs of trains with their families, pots and comales.

questions.question: At the Battles of Celaya in 1915, trenches and machine guns stopped the cavalry charges of a revolutionary leader. Whose?
hints: Until then, his cavalry had seemed unstoppable.
He was the head of the División del Norte.
Later he attacked a town in the United States.
questions.description: When horses run into technology, the horses almost never win.
questions.fun_fact: The Battles of Celaya were fought with trenches and barbed wire, just like World War I, which was going on in Europe at the same time.

questions.question: With the 1911 Plan de Ayala, the Liberation Army of the South refused to recognize which man as president?
hints: This army had supported him not long before.
They accused him of not giving the land back to the farmers.
He wrote the Plan de San Luis.
questions.description: A time when every rebel leader had his own plan, his own sombrero and his own bandolier.
questions.fun_fact: The motto of the Plan de Ayala was “Reform, Liberty, Justice and Law.”

questions.question: Some of the first shots of the Revolution were fired at the Serdán family's house in Puebla. How many days before November 20, 1910?
hints: It was in the same month of November.
Police came to search the house because they suspected an uprising.
It happened on November 18.
questions.description: Some families just can't wait for the party to start.
questions.fun_fact: Today the house is a museum, and its walls still show the bullet marks.

questions.question: I was president, I took over the oil industry in 1938, and a port in Michoacán and Mexico City’s Eje Central bear my name. Who am I?
hints: I governed from 1934 to 1940.
I was born in Jiquilpan, Michoacán.
My son Cuauhtémoc also became a well-known politician.
questions.description: So many streets carry his name that it’s hard not to drive down one.
questions.fun_fact: After the oil expropriation, many people donated chickens, jewelry and even their wedding rings to help pay for it.

questions.question: Which leader of the Mexican Revolution was nicknamed “el Manco de Celaya”?
hints: He was from Sonora.
He defeated Pancho Villa in 1915.
He was president from 1920 to 1924.
questions.description: A nickname earned in battle that he could never shake off.
questions.fun_fact: He liked to joke that his lost arm was found by tossing a gold coin into the air, because the hand reached up to catch it.

questions.question: The National Museum of the Revolution lies under a Mexico City monument that began as a big project of Porfirio Díaz. What was it meant to be?
hints: Construction stopped when the Revolution broke out.
Only the frame of the dome was left standing.
Deputies and senators were supposed to meet there.
questions.description: A building that changed plans more times than a family on vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The remains of Madero, Carranza, Villa, Calles and Cárdenas rest inside the monument's pillars.

questions.question: Emiliano Zapata was called “el Caudillo del Sur.” In which state was he born?
hints: It is a small state next to Mexico City.
Its sugarcane fields were owned by large haciendas.
Its capital is Cuernavaca.
questions.description: A nickname that comes with a built-in compass.
questions.fun_fact: Zapata was born in Anenecuilco and was famous as a great rider and an expert on horses.

questions.question: In 1915, Francisco Lagos Cházaro was the last president named by the Convention of Aguascalientes. Whom did he succeed?
hints: The Convention had three presidents in all.
His predecessor was from Coahuila and close to Villa.
He was the second president the Convention named.
questions.description: In 1915, the presidential chair came with a revolving door.
questions.fun_fact: The Convention met at the Teatro Morelos in Aguascalientes, where the delegates signed their names on a Mexican flag.

questions.question: In 1961, María Félix played a fierce soldadera from Zacatecas on the big screen. Complete her nickname: Juana…
hints: There's also a corrido with that name.
It's a farm animal.
That animal crows at sunrise.
questions.description: A woman so tough that even the camera asked her permission.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the real Juana Gallo was named Ángela Ramos and fought against Huerta's troops.

questions.question: The Los Manantiales restaurant in Xochimilco has a wavy concrete roof just 4 cm (1.5 in) thick. Which Spanish exile architect designed it?
hints: He did most of his work in Mexico in the 1950s and 1960s.
He became famous for his concrete shells shaped like hyperbolic paraboloids.
He also designed the roof of the Palacio de los Deportes for the 1968 Olympic Games.
questions.description: A roof so thin it looks like paper, yet it holds up better than your patience in traffic.
questions.fun_fact: His shells were so thin and efficient that they used far less concrete than a normal roof of the same size.

questions.question: Nachos carry the nickname of the person who improvised them in 1943 in Piedras Negras, Coahuila. Who was he?
hints: Piedras Negras sits right on the border, across from Eagle Pass, Texas, and his customers came from the other side of the river.
He used what he had on hand: totopos, cheese and jalapeño peppers.
His name was Ignacio Anaya, and his job was looking after the diners.
questions.description: A snack so good it carries someone's nickname, like a pet would.
questions.fun_fact: Piedras Negras holds a nacho festival every year in honor of the dish's origin.

questions.question: In which season do people in Japan have picnics under the blooming cherry trees?
hints: It comes right after the cold.
It is when the school year starts in Japan.
It is the season that brings the flowers back.
questions.description: A tree that puts on its best outfit for just a couple of weeks a year.
questions.fun_fact: The Japanese custom of gathering to admire the cherry blossoms is called “hanami”.

questions.question: I’m a Mexican soda in a glass bottle, with flavors like tamarind, mandarin and tutifruti, and my name recalls little clay jugs. What am I?
hints: You can find me in almost any taquería.
My bottles have little ridges in the glass.
People used to drink agua fresca from small clay jarros.
questions.description: Colorful bubbles that taste like a birthday party at the fonda.
questions.fun_fact: This soda is now sold in many countries and is one of the most popular drinks in taquerías across the United States.

questions.question: In November 1985 I flew aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis and became the first Mexican to travel to space. Who am I?
hints: I’m an engineer, born in Guerrero.
My mission helped put a Mexican communications satellite into orbit.
One of my last names is also the Spanish word for a ship’s sail.
questions.description: A Mexican who went so far away that nobody could reach him on his cell phone.
questions.fun_fact: He asked to take tortillas into space, because they don’t leave crumbs floating around the spacecraft.

questions.question: You walk into an OXXO to buy something. What WON'T you find there?
hints: It's a small store.
People go there for something quick to eat or drink.
A couch wouldn't even fit through its door.
questions.description: There's one on every corner, and sometimes two facing each other.
questions.fun_fact: OXXO has more than 20,000 stores, almost all of them in Mexico.

questions.question: What is the Mexican park where children play firefighter, doctor and pilot in a city built to their size?
hints: There, children “work” and earn play money.
It was born in Santa Fe, in Mexico City.
Its name begins with a short English word for a child.
questions.description: The only place where kids are the boss and parents wait outside.
questions.fun_fact: This Mexican park now has locations in many countries around the world, from Japan to Brazil.

questions.question: Which region of Mexico does the Tren Maya run through?
hints: It's a region with a hot climate and jungle.
Cancún and Chichén Itzá are there.
It's named after an ancient culture that lived right there.
questions.description: A train that gets closer to the pyramids than your school bus ever will.
questions.fun_fact: Its route is about 1,500 km (930 miles) long and passes through five states: Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

questions.question: A farmer watched a volcano rise out of his milpa (cornfield) in Michoacán: today it's Paricutín. In what year did it happen?
hints: It's one of the youngest volcanoes in the world.
It happened in the 20th century, when there were already cameras.
It was during the years of World War II.
questions.description: A farmer went to check on his cornfield, and the cornfield had a surprise for him.
questions.fun_fact: Lava buried the town of San Juan Parangaricutiro, but its church tower still sticks out above the rocks.

questions.question: It makes Gansitos, Pingüinos, and Submarinos, and it belongs to Grupo Bimbo. Which brand is it?
hints: It makes snack cakes, not chips.
Its name sounds like something from the sea.
It starts with “Mari…”.
questions.description: The brand that makes your lunch box the most envied one at recess.
questions.fun_fact: The Gansito is filled with strawberry jam and cream, and it's one of the best-selling snack cakes in Mexico.

questions.question: I founded the Tonantzintla Observatory in Puebla, and today the planetarium of the Instituto Politécnico Nacional bears my name. Who am I?
hints: I was an astronomer and also a politician in the 20th century.
My observatory opened in 1942.
My last name has only four letters, and two of them are “r”.
questions.description: A man who gazed at the sky so much that they named a pretend one after him.
questions.fun_fact: A crater on the Moon is named Erro in his honor.

questions.question: Which doctor to Philip II traveled across New Spain from 1571 to 1577 to make the first great study of its medicinal plants?
hints: He lived in the same century that Tenochtitlan fell.
He recorded thousands of plants with their names in Nahuatl.
He was born in the province of Toledo, Spain.
questions.description: The very first herb expert, but with the king's permission.
questions.fun_fact: Many of his original manuscripts burned in the El Escorial fire of 1671.

questions.question: These enchiladas have dough dyed with red chile and are filled with cheese. Which state are they typical of?
hints: It's a state in north-central Mexico.
Its name recalls a famous silver mine in Bolivia.
Its people are called “potosinos.”
questions.description: Enchiladas that blush before you even add the salsa.
questions.fun_fact: They're folded like little quesadillas and usually served with potatoes, carrots, lettuce and crumbled cheese.

questions.question: Nepenthes is a plant from Asia's rainforests with pitcher-shaped leaves. Complete: “The stomach is to food as the Nepenthes pitcher is to…”
hints: What goes into the pitcher never comes out.
It lures its visitors with sweet nectar and a very slippery rim.
It is a meat-eating plant.
questions.description: A pitcher you really shouldn't pour the juice into.
questions.fun_fact: Some Nepenthes plants in Borneo have a deal with tree shrews: they give them nectar, and the shrews leave their poop behind as fertilizer.

questions.question: Roughly how long is the Río Bravo from end to end?
hints: It starts in the mountains of Colorado, in the United States, and flows into the Gulf of Mexico
It forms much of the border between Mexico and the United States
It's a four-digit number
questions.description: A river so long that one side calls it “Bravo” and the other side gives it a whole new nickname.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States it isn't called the Río Bravo but the Rio Grande.

questions.question: This hill is the symbol of Monterrey. Going by its name, what object does it look like?
hints: Look at the dip between its peaks
That object is used with horses
It goes on a horse's back so the rider can sit
questions.description: The most famous neighbor the regios have, and it has never once moved out.
questions.fun_fact: The Cerro de la Silla is about 1,800 m (5,900 ft) high and has been a protected Natural Monument since 1991.

questions.question: This glazed pottery, hand-painted in blue on white, is typical of Puebla and Tlaxcala. What is it called?
hints: Its name comes from a town in Spain.
It decorates building fronts, kitchens and the Casa de los Muñecos in Puebla.
It gets the nickname “poblana” from its state.
questions.description: Plates so pretty it feels wrong to pour mole on them.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, together with the pottery of Talavera de la Reina in Spain.

questions.question: This cathedral is in the state capital nicknamed “la Ciudad de la Cantera Rosa” (the City of Pink Stone). Which city is it?
hints: It's in western Mexico, home of the Purépecha people
It used to be called Valladolid
Its name honors José María Morelos
questions.description: A city that sees everything through rose-colored glasses, and not because it's an optimist.
questions.fun_fact: Morelia also boasts a colonial aqueduct with more than 250 arches.

questions.question: This headdress is worn in the Deer Dance of the Yaqui people. Which state does this dance come from?
hints: It's a northern state with lots of desert
It borders Arizona, in the United States
Its capital is Hermosillo
questions.description: A dance where the star takes his animal costume very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: The dancer copies the movements of a deer to the beat of rattles, a water drum and a reed flute.

questions.question: What is this crunchy snack called, a classic from Oaxaca?
hints: They're insects
They're eaten with lime, salt and chili
They're toasted grasshoppers
questions.description: A snack for the brave ones who dare to try something new.
questions.fun_fact: Gram for gram, dried chapulines have more protein than beef.

questions.question: The Mexican part of this peninsula is split between three states. Which are they?
hints: One of them has the same name as the peninsula.
Another has the Caribbean coast.
Their capitals are Mérida, San Francisco de Campeche and Chetumal.
questions.description: A piece of Mexico sticking out into the sea like a thumbs-up.
questions.fun_fact: It has almost no rivers on the surface: the water flows underground and comes up in the cenotes.

questions.question: The Spanish named it Antequera, after a town in Andalusia, and its green stone earned it the nickname “la Verde Antequera.” Which capital is it?
hints: It's in southern Mexico
It's famous for its moles and the Guelaguetza
Its official name honors Benito Juárez
questions.description: A city with green in its nickname, and it's not because of the nopales.
questions.fun_fact: The name Oaxaca comes from the Nahuatl “Huaxyácac,” meaning “at the tip of the guaje trees.”

questions.question: Look at this slice of panqué marmoleado (marble cake). What flavor are the dark swirls?
hints: It's the flavor many kids pick for their birthday cake.
It comes from cacao
It's dark brown, like the outside of a Gansito
questions.description: A cake that couldn't make up its mind, so it kept everything.
questions.fun_fact: Marble cake gets its name because its swirls look like the veins in a slab of marble.

questions.question: Borrachitos are soft sweets from Puebla, coated in sugar and wrapped in paper. Which of these gives them their classic flavor?
hints: Take a close look at their name
It's a yellow drink made with milk and eggs
It has a splash of liquor and was born in Puebla's convents
questions.description: The only candy that's already giggling before anyone tells the joke.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, rompope was born in the nuns' convents of Puebla.

questions.question: A woman cooks cassava bread on a budare griddle and keeps waving a palm-leaf fan. What is she using it for?
hints: It has to do with cooking, not with resting.
What she cares about is under the griddle.
Embers need air to glow red and give off more heat.
questions.description: Air conditioning in the rainforest longhouse runs on pure arm power.
questions.fun_fact: Many Amazon peoples weave their fans from palm leaves and use them almost like a kitchen bellows.

questions.question: I'm long and thin like spaghetti, a fruit-flavored gummy covered in chili, and my name sounds English. What am I?
hints: You can wrap me around your finger
I also come in a filled version
I'm made by the brand behind the Lucas chili powders
questions.description: A candy that's spicy, gets tangled up, and nobody can say its name right.
questions.fun_fact: Skwinkles are made by Lucas, the same brand as the famous chili powder candies.

questions.question: This fonda dessert is served with cream and condensed milk. Which fruit was fried to make it?
hints: It's a long fruit
Its peel turns black when it's ripe
It's the big cousin of the plátano Tabasco
questions.description: A fruit that took “jumping into the frying pan” very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Plantains are almost never eaten raw: they're firmer and starchier than the plátano Tabasco.

questions.question: This pan de muerto is made from egg-yolk bread, has a little painted face stuck on, and gets dunked in hot chocolate. Which state is it typical of?
hints: It's in southern Mexico
It's famous for its seven moles
Its capital has the same name as the state
questions.description: A bread so yellow it looks like it ate nothing but eggs for breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The little face on Oaxacan pan de muerto is made from flour paste and painted by hand.

questions.question: You're at the store and ask for a Bubulubu. What do you get?
questions.answer: A chocolate with marshmallow and strawberry
wrong_answers: A vanilla cookie with chocolate chips
hints: It comes wrapped in shiny paper
It's brown on the outside
Inside, it's soft, white and red
questions.description: Its name sounds like bubbles, but you can't drink it.
questions.fun_fact: Bubulubu is made by Ricolino, the same brand that makes Panditas.

questions.question: A chamoyada has shaved ice, chamoy and chili powder, and comes with a straw coated in a spicy candy. Which fruit is that candy made from?
hints: It's a brown fruit
It grows in pods
It's sweet, sour and sticky, like a Pulparindo
questions.description: Ice that went partying with the whole spicy-candy aisle.
questions.fun_fact: Chamoy comes from a salted plum that Asian immigrants brought to Mexico.

questions.question: In gallinita ciega, you're blindfolded, catch someone and guess who it is by touching their face. If you guess right, who is the new gallinita?
hints: The role of gallinita doesn't stay with you: it passes to another player.
It goes to someone who was running around the gallinita.
It goes to the one who couldn't get away from you.
questions.description: A game where nobody can see a thing and everyone laughs anyway.
questions.fun_fact: In the 18th century, the painter Francisco de Goya painted young people playing gallina ciega.

questions.question: In the game Snakes and Ladders, what happens when you land on a square with a ladder?
questions.answer: You climb to a square further ahead
wrong_answers: You slide back to an earlier square
hints: It's good news.
The snakes do the exact opposite.
Think about what a ladder is for at home.
questions.description: A board where one roll of the die can ruin your afternoon or save it.
questions.fun_fact: The game was born in India centuries ago and was used to teach that good deeds lift you up and bad ones bring you down.

questions.question: La Sirena has her own card in Mexican Lotería. Which of these characters does NOT have a Lotería card?
hints: The other three show up in any Lotería game at the fairs.
One of the others is a very elegant gentleman with a cane.
The missing one breathes fire.
questions.description: A game where little beans are worth gold and someone always shouts “¡Lotería!” before you do.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional Mexican Lotería has 54 cards.

questions.question: It's played with paper and pencil: a random letter is picked, and there are columns like name, animal and fruit. What does shouting “¡Basta!” mean?
hints: The fastest player at the table shouts it.
After it's shouted, the points are counted.
“Basta” means “that's enough.”
questions.description: A game where knowing a fruit that starts with “Ñ” makes you a legend.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries, the same game is called “Stop” or “Tutti frutti.”

questions.question: In Chinese checkers, each player sets up their marbles in a triangle on one point of the star. How many marbles does each player have?
hints: The triangle has four rows.
The row at the tip has just one marble.
questions.description: A marble game that travels more than a tourist.
questions.fun_fact: Chinese checkers isn't from China: it was invented in Germany in 1892 under the name “Stern-Halma”.

questions.question: Lope de Aguirre sailed the Amazon River in 1561, rebelled against his own king and wrote that king a very rude letter. What country was he from?
hints: He was a European conquistador.
His king also ruled cities like Bogotá and Lima.
He came from the same kingdom that paid for Christopher Columbus's voyage.
questions.description: A tourist who went for a nice boat ride down the river and ended up in a fight with the king.
questions.fun_fact: Lope de Aguirre called himself “the Pilgrim,” and history remembers him as “Aguirre the Madman.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: these painted cardboard dolls are a tradition from a city in Guanajuato. Which one?
hints: It's a city in the Bajío region.
It's said to be the birthplace of the Mexican cardboard doll.
The city is also famous for its cajeta.
questions.description: A doll that's afraid of nothing, except the rain.
questions.fun_fact: Cardboard dolls are made from paper and flour paste over a mold, just like many piñatas.

questions.question: Riddle: “They call me guayuco. I'm tied around the waist, and in the hot jungle I was almost all many people wore for centuries.” What am I?
hints: It's a piece of clothing.
It's worn from the waist down.
It covers just enough and nothing more.
questions.description: The coolest outfit in the jungle, with no buttons and no zipper.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional guayucos were sometimes made from tree bark, pounded until it was as soft as cloth.

questions.question: A giant tree trunk is hollowed out with fire and an ax, and left long and pointed at both ends. What is it used for?
hints: The pointed ends help it cut through something that moves.
In the rainforest, rivers are like roads.
It's going to need some paddles.
questions.description: A tree that got hollowed out and found itself a whole new career.
questions.fun_fact: Some canoes carved from a single tree trunk can carry more than ten people.

questions.question: At a school fair, one ticket buys one cupcake. In the carbon credit market, one credit stands for… what?
questions.answer: One metric ton of CO₂ kept out of the air
wrong_answers: One kilogram of CO₂ kept out of the air
One liter of CO₂ kept out of the air
100 metric tons of CO₂ kept out of the air
hints: It's an amount of greenhouse gas.
It's a fairly big unit, not one you'd use on a kitchen scale.
It's a thousand kilograms of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: Polluting with permission: the grown-up version of “I'll trade you my dessert for your homework.”
questions.fun_fact: Carbon credits became famous with the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in Japan in 1997.

questions.question: Tiny plastic beads, smaller than a grain of sand, were banned because they went down the drain into the sea. What products were they in?
hints: People bought them at the pharmacy or the supermarket.
They were used to gently scrape something.
People rubbed them on their face to remove dead skin.
questions.description: Beads so small they ended up being a giant problem.
questions.fun_fact: The United States banned plastic microbeads in rinse-off cosmetics with a law passed in 2015.

questions.question: What is the model called where products are used, repaired, recycled and used again and again, instead of being bought, used and thrown away?
hints: Many governments and companies in Europe promote it.
Its name describes a path that comes back to where it started.
Its name is the shape of a wheel or a ring.
questions.description: An economy where “throw it away” is almost a forbidden phrase.
questions.fun_fact: In a circular economy, even a fruit peel can go back to the soil as fertilizer.

questions.question: What do you call the local business that buys old metal things by the kilo, like pots, car rims and cables?
hints: Its name comes from another word for old, leftover metal.
Old cars that no longer run often end up there, crushed into cubes.
Its name starts with a word for leftover bits, like the pieces of paper you throw away.
questions.description: A place where your trash is someone else's treasure… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: Steel can be melted down and recycled again and again without losing its strength.

questions.question: If Europe's border runs along the Caucasus Mountains, as most geographers say, what is the highest mountain in Europe?
hints: It is a sleeping volcano.
It is in Russia and has two snowy summits.
Both of its summits are over 5,600 meters (18,370 ft) high.
questions.description: Europe has a rooftop too, but hardly anyone remembers where it put it.
questions.fun_fact: Elbrus is about 5,642 m (18,510 ft) tall, more than 800 m higher than Mont Blanc (4,806 m / 15,770 ft), which many people think is Europe's highest.

questions.question: Monarch butterflies fly from Canada and the United States to spend the winter in mountain forests. In which country are they?
hints: Spanish is spoken in this country.
The butterflies never cross the equator.
It's the country of mariachis and tacos.
questions.description: Travelers who need no passport, just a pair of colorful wings.
questions.fun_fact: No single monarch butterfly makes the whole round trip: its great-grandchildren finish the journey back north.

questions.question: What is the name of the old man in the Pixar movie who ties thousands of balloons to his house?
hints: He travels with a young explorer scout and a talking dog.
The movie is called “Up”.
His first name starts with C, like “cloud”.
questions.description: A mountain so strange it looks like it came from another planet… or from a movie.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Roraima is a tepui with rocks about 2 billion years old, some of the oldest on the planet.

questions.question: Off California there are underwater “forests” over 40 m (130 ft) tall that grow more than half a meter a day. What are these “trees”?
hints: They use sunlight to make food, through photosynthesis.
Sea otters wrap themselves in them to sleep without drifting away on the current.
The green film that grows in a neglected fish tank belongs to the same group.
questions.description: A forest where nobody ever has to water the trees.
questions.fun_fact: Giant kelp is the largest alga in the world, and its underwater forests are home to hundreds of species.

questions.question: On which day is the crown-shaped sweet bread with candied fruit and a hidden surprise inside traditionally eaten?
hints: By that day, Christmas and New Year's are already over.
Its crown shape is a clue about who is celebrated that day.
It's the day of Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
questions.description: A bread with a prize inside, like cereal boxes used to have.
questions.fun_fact: A tiny baby Jesus figure is hidden inside the bread, and in Mexico whoever finds it must treat everyone to tamales on February 2.

questions.question: What is the best-selling album of all time?
wrong_answers: The Dark Side of the Moon
hints: It came out in the early 1980s.
Its singer was famous for a dance move that made him look like he was walking backward on stage.
It's by the King of Pop.
questions.description: Music from the days when people still bought their albums in a store.
questions.fun_fact: The music video for “Thriller” is almost 14 minutes long, longer than many short films.

questions.question: How high did Cuba's Javier Sotomayor jump in 1993 to set the high jump world record?
hints: He jumped well over the height of a normal door.
He didn't reach three meters.
It's almost exactly the height of the crossbar on a full-size soccer goal.
questions.description: A man who could get over your front door without bothering to open it.
questions.fun_fact: Sotomayor is the only human ever to clear 8 feet (2.44 meters).

questions.question: Methuselah, a pine in California’s White Mountains, is one of the oldest trees in the world. About how old is it?
hints: It is far older than any person or tortoise.
It was already growing while the pyramids of Egypt were being built.
Its age has four digits.
questions.description: A grandpa with more birthdays than candles could ever fit on a cake.
questions.fun_fact: Methuselah’s exact location is kept secret to protect it from visitors and souvenir hunters.

questions.question: “Horseshoe Falls is to Niagara Falls as ___ is to Iguazu Falls.” What fills the blank?
hints: You're looking for the most famous and spectacular part of a group of waterfalls.
It sits on the border between Argentina and Brazil, and it is shaped like a U.
Its name points to a body part of someone with horns and a tail.
questions.description: A challenge for travelers who aren't afraid of getting soaked right down to their socks.
questions.fun_fact: Iguazu Falls is made up of about 275 separate waterfalls, and Devil's Throat is the tallest and most powerful of them all.

questions.question: What is the longest river in France?
hints: It doesn't flow through Paris.
Its valley is full of castles built for kings and nobles.
Its name starts with L.
questions.description: A river so French it surely has a croissant for breakfast every day.
questions.fun_fact: The Loire is just over 1,000 km (about 625 miles) long, and its valley, with dozens of castles, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: iCub is a robot the size of a small child, built at an institute in Genoa. Which Italian scientist co-led its development?
hints: He has worked in Genoa for most of his career.
He became scientific director of the Italian Institute of Technology.
His first name is the Italian form of “George”.
questions.description: A baby that never cries, never sleeps and comes with an instruction manual anyone can read.
questions.fun_fact: Dozens of iCub copies are spread across labs around the world, and they all share their design freely.

questions.question: In which year did “The Wild Robot” come out, the animated film where the robot Roz raises an orphaned gosling?
hints: It's a fairly recent film.
It was made by DreamWorks, the studio behind “Shrek” and “Kung Fu Panda”.
It came out the same year as the Paris Olympic Games.
questions.description: A robot who showed up to work and ended up as a mother goose, without even asking for parental leave.
questions.fun_fact: The film is based on an illustrated book by Peter Brown, published in 2016.

questions.question: This is Robby the Robot from the film “Forbidden Planet” (1956). Its story was inspired by a play by which writer?
hints: The original play doesn't have a single robot in it.
The original play takes place on an island, with a magician and a storm.
He also wrote “Romeo and Juliet”.
questions.description: A robot from the 1950s that already had more style than most of today's kitchen appliances.
questions.fun_fact: Robby cost a fortune for his time, so the studio got its money's worth by putting him in many other films and TV shows.

questions.question: This robot is Maria, from the silent film “Metropolis” (1927). Her design inspired a very famous robot from another film series. Which one?
hints: That robot is shaped like a human, just like her.
It appears in “Star Wars”.
It speaks a huge number of languages and is always with a short friend who beeps.
questions.description: A robot so stylish that almost 100 years later, people are still copying her look.
questions.fun_fact: “Metropolis” was the first film ever added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

questions.question: Which of these places will you NOT find in Patrick Star's neighborhood at the bottom of the sea?
hints: Patrick lives in Bikini Bottom, next door to SpongeBob.
One of these places is from a Disney movie, not from SpongeBob.
The father of a red-haired mermaid lives there.
questions.description: He lives under a rock and still has a better social life than you.
questions.fun_fact: Real sea stars can grow back an arm they have lost.

questions.question: How many wheels does Curiosity have, the robot NASA sent to explore Mars?
hints: It has more wheels than a normal car.
Each wheel has its own motor and a special suspension for climbing over rocks.
It's the same as the number of legs an ant has.
questions.description: A toy car that cost more than every car on your street put together.
questions.fun_fact: Curiosity's wheels have holes that spell “JPL” in Morse code, so it leaves that message in the Martian sand as it drives.

questions.question: You walk through a museum room of German Romantic paintings. Which work does NOT belong there?
wrong_answers: “The Monk by the Sea” by Caspar David Friedrich
“The Hülsenbeck Children” by Philipp Otto Runge
“Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” by Caspar David Friedrich
hints: Romanticism flourished from about 1800 to 1840.
One painting was made about 100 years later.
Its painter belonged to the New Objectivity and showed the nightlife of the Weimar Republic.
questions.description: Fog, moonlight, longing – and somebody got the wrong century.
questions.fun_fact: The “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle – just like Runge's “Hülsenbeck Children”.

questions.question: In 1937, the Nazis showed works by Kirchner, Nolde and Dix in Munich, and over 2 million people came. What was the show for?
hints: The pictures had just been taken from German museums.
The rulers called the artists “sick”.
The show was called “Degenerate Art”.
questions.description: An exhibition with more visitors than many a theme park.
questions.fun_fact: Today, many of the works mocked back then are among the most valuable treasures in German museums.

questions.question: Ceiling decorations like the one in the photo are typical of German Altbau apartments. What are they usually made of?
hints: The material is white and is mixed with water.
It is worked while soft and then hardens.
Doctors use it for hard casts on broken bones.
questions.description: High ceilings, creaky floorboards and a landlord who calls it “charm”.
questions.fun_fact: Many old buildings in German cities date from the Gründerzeit boom around 1900, and their ceilings are often over 3 m (10 ft) high.

questions.question: This pink building with golden balls and trees on the roof stands in Magdeburg. Which artist designed it?
hints: He was mainly a painter and disliked straight lines.
He came from Vienna.
A colorful apartment building in Vienna is named after him.
questions.description: A house that looks like a child drew the building plans, and that was the whole idea.
questions.fun_fact: The Green Citadel opened in 2005, five years after its creator died; it was his last project.

questions.question: Since 1955, documenta has been held in Kassel for 100 days, about every five years. What is it?
hints: You walk through halls, parks and museums there.
Joseph Beuys had 7,000 oak trees planted for it.
It is also called the “museum of 100 days.”
questions.description: Every five years, a town in northern Hesse becomes the center of the world.
questions.fun_fact: For Beuys's work “7000 Oaks,” trees were planted across Kassel from 1982, each next to a basalt column, and the last one went into the ground in 1987.

questions.question: Prints of Albrecht Dürer's “Praying Hands” hang in many living rooms. In what year was the drawing made?
hints: Dürer lived in Nuremberg during the Renaissance.
A few years earlier, Columbus had reached America.
In the same year, Michelangelo began painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
questions.description: Probably the most-framed pair of hands in Germany.
questions.fun_fact: The hands were a study for an altarpiece whose central panel was lost in a fire in 1729, but the drawing survived.

questions.question: This 1912 almanac bears the name of a Munich artists' group. Who founded it in 1911 together with Franz Marc?
hints: He came from Moscow.
He is seen as one of the inventors of abstract painting.
He wrote the book “Concerning the Spiritual in Art”.
questions.description: One color, one rider, and suddenly painting looks completely different.
questions.fun_fact: According to Kandinsky, the name came up over coffee: both loved blue, Marc loved horses, and Kandinsky loved riders.

questions.question: Grand buildings in Hameln, Lemgo and Hämelschenburg Castle, built around 1520 to 1620: what is this architectural style called?
hints: The style was influenced by Italy and the Netherlands.
Typical features are decorated gables and bay windows, locally called “Utluchten”.
It is named after the river that Hameln lies on.
questions.description: Here the gables have more swirls than a wedding cake.
questions.fun_fact: A famous example is the Rat Catcher's House in Hameln, where an old inscription recalls the legend of the Pied Piper.

questions.question: The Bismarck was a famous German ship of World War II. What type of ship was it?
hints: It was a warship that sailed on the surface.
Its strength was in its giant guns, not in planes.
Its type is named after the “line of battle” that the biggest gun ships once formed.
questions.description: A ship named after a man with a big mustache and a temper to match.
questions.fun_fact: The wreck of the Bismarck was found in 1989 by Robert Ballard, the same explorer who found the Titanic.

questions.question: “I sprint for Germany, threw myself across the finish line in Munich in 2022 and became European 100-meter champion.” Who am I?
hints: I come from Westphalia.
At the 2024 Olympics, I won bronze with the relay team.
My last name starts with “Lücken…”.
questions.description: A hundred meters, a blink of an eye, and in the end a belly flop trimmed in gold.
questions.fun_fact: Lückenkemper fell as she dived across the finish line, but she still got there first.

questions.question: Patrick Lange won the Ironman World Championship in 2017, 2018 and 2024, and in 2018 was the first to finish it in under eight hours. On which island?
hints: The island is volcanic.
The swim is in the Pacific Ocean.
The race starts in Kona.
questions.description: Swim, bike, run – and then a week on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: After his 2018 win, Lange proposed to his girlfriend right at the finish line.

questions.question: Claudia Pechstein competed at her eighth Olympic Games in Beijing in 2022. In what year were her first?
hints: Back then, the Summer and Winter Games were still held in the same year.
The Games took place in Albertville, France.
They were the first Winter Games of reunified Germany.
questions.description: Others retire; she'd rather do one more lap on the ice.
questions.fun_fact: At Beijing 2022, Pechstein, at nearly 50, carried the German flag at the opening ceremony.

questions.question: Kristin Otto, later a presenter on German TV channel ZDF, swam for East Germany at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. How many gold medals did she win there?
hints: No other woman won more at those Games.
At the time, it was a record for a woman at a single Olympics.
It was half a dozen.
questions.description: A whole swimming pool full of gold, and nobody had to dive for it.
questions.fun_fact: Otto won her gold medals in three different strokes: freestyle, backstroke and butterfly.

questions.question: Which left winger from Mannheim was captain of Germany's national handball team for years and played for Paris Saint-Germain?
hints: He played almost his whole career in his home region.
His club was the Rhein-Neckar Löwen.
His first name has only three letters.
questions.description: He stood way out on the edge, and yet everything revolved around him.
questions.fun_fact: Gensheimer won his first German championship with the Rhein-Neckar Löwen in 2016.

questions.question: This racetrack in Baden-Württemberg, near Mannheim, is named after its town and has often hosted Formula 1. Which one?
hints: The town is close to Heidelberg.
Part of its grandstands is called the “Motodrom”.
The name starts with “Hocken…”.
questions.description: It roars louder here than at a lawnmower race.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2001, the track ran deep into the forest; in 2002 it was made much shorter.

questions.question: Newton's apple is to gravity as Archimedes' bathtub is to…
hints: Archimedes noticed that the water rose when he got in.
His famous principle is taught in physics class with water and objects of different weights.
It has to do with water pushing things upward.
questions.description: The only time in history that taking a bath led to a scientific discovery.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Archimedes jumped out of the bath and ran off shouting “Eureka!”, which is Greek for “I found it!”.

questions.question: Sebastian Brendel won three Olympic golds kneeling in his boat, using a paddle with only one blade. In which type of boat?
hints: He always paddles on just one side of the boat.
He won two golds at once in Rio in 2016.
Indigenous peoples of North America built this kind of boat from birch bark.
questions.description: One man, one boat, one paddle, and surprisingly little splashing.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2016 Rio Olympics, Brendel won gold in both the singles and the doubles.

questions.question: I'm small, I stick to scraped knees, and I have a soft pad in the middle. Which brand name do many people know me by?
hints: I belong in every first aid kit.
My name starts like the old trading league of Hamburg and Lübeck.
Hanse + Pflaster (German for “bandage”) almost makes my name.
questions.description: The thing that helps more than any excuse after you fall off your bike.
questions.fun_fact: Hansaplast, Nivea and Tesa all come from the same Hamburg company: Beiersdorf.

questions.question: An electronics store ad on TV uses the slogan “Geiz ist geil!”. Which decade are you most likely in?
hints: The Deutsche Mark was already gone by then.
The campaign ran while the euro was still brand new.
It started in 2002.
questions.description: A slogan that makes every piggy bank squeal with joy.
questions.fun_fact: The Jung von Matt agency came up with the slogan for the Saturn chain, and it ran until about 2007.

questions.question: It has two ends: one makes blue fountain pen ink disappear, the other writes over it. What is this pen called in Germany?
hints: It's in almost every pencil case in German primary school.
It goes with the fountain pen the way an eraser goes with a pencil.
Its name sounds like it finishes off the ink.
questions.description: A lifesaver for anyone who misspells a word in the middle of a school dictation.
questions.fun_fact: The erasing end bleaches the blue dye chemically, which is why it usually doesn't work on black ink.

questions.question: Which of these candies is NOT made by Maoam?
hints: Three of them are chewy candies.
The odd one out comes from the big company that owns Maoam today.
It's an animal, and its name has the color of treasure in it.
questions.description: Chew on one of these and a classroom goes quiet for a moment… almost.
questions.fun_fact: Maoam has belonged to Haribo since 1986, so the Goldbären and Maoam are siblings.

questions.question: In Ravensburger's “Labyrinth” you hunt for treasures, and when you set up, one path tile is always left over. What is it used for?
hints: It looks just like the other path tiles and passes from player to player.
You use it on every turn, before you move your piece.
Afterwards, a whole row slides along by one space.
questions.description: Even people with GPS get lost in here.
questions.fun_fact: The game was invented by Max Kobbert and came out from Ravensburger in 1986.

questions.question: When the An der Alten Försterei stadium was rebuilt in 2008/09, Union Berlin fans helped for free. About how many were there?
hints: More than would fit in a school gym.
Together they put in about 140,000 hours of work.
The number is between 2,000 and 2,500.
questions.description: A club where the fans don't just sing, they also swing a shovel.
questions.fun_fact: Union fans are called “die Eisernen” (the Iron Ones), and at Christmas tens of thousands of them sing carols together in the stadium.

questions.question: The linesman's flag goes up, the whistle blows, and the goal doesn't count: “Offside!” What did the attacker do wrong?
questions.answer: At the pass, he was too far forward behind the defense
wrong_answers: He touched the ball with his hand
He knocked an opponent over from behind
He played the ball over the sideline
hints: The rule was already part of the early rules of the game in the 1800s.
The rule stops strikers from simply waiting next to the other team's goal.
He was closer to the goal than the second-to-last defender.
questions.description: The rule that gets argued about at every Stammtisch in the country.
questions.fun_fact: You can never be offside in your own half.

questions.question: On the road to the German championship: how many points does a team get for a win in the Bundesliga?
hints: A draw gets you less.
A draw is worth exactly one point.
It's the number of sides of a triangle.
questions.description: If you want to become German champion, you have to keep collecting, just like with a sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1995, a win in the Bundesliga was worth only two points.

questions.question: A Bundesliga season ticket covers every home game of the season. How many Bundesliga home games is that?
hints: There are 18 teams in the Bundesliga.
Each team plays every opponent once at home and once away.
It is exactly half of 34.
questions.description: The most expensive piece of paper in many fans' wallets.
questions.fun_fact: At some clubs, fans spend many years on a waiting list for a season ticket.

questions.question: German youth soccer runs from the G-Jugend up to the A-Jugend. The E-Jugend is for children aged…
hints: The G-Jugend is for the very youngest.
The E-Jugend is also called U11.
They are kids in third and fourth grade.
questions.description: Where the shin guards are almost as big as the players.
questions.fun_fact: In the E-Jugend, teams usually play with seven players on a smaller field.

questions.question: A defender touches the ball last, and it rolls over the goal line next to their own goal. What does the other team get?
hints: The ball is played from the edge of the field.
A small flag stands there.
It is taken from one of the four corners of the field.
questions.description: One little slip by the defender, and the away fans are already cheering.
questions.fun_fact: You're allowed to score straight from a corner kick, and it's called an “Olimpico” or “Olympic goal”.

questions.question: In the circle game „Taler, Taler, du musst wandern“, an old silver coin travels around. Which modern currency is named after it?
hints: This currency is known all over the world today.
In Dutch, “Taler” became “daalder”.
It's what people pay with in the USA.
questions.description: A coin that gets around more than any backpacker.
questions.fun_fact: The name Taler comes from the “Joachimsthaler”, a silver coin from the town of Joachimsthal in Bohemia.

questions.question: In the children's song “Wer hat die Kokosnuss geklaut?” (“Who stole the coconut?”), which animals shout it together as a whole gang?
hints: These animals love to climb.
At the zoo, their house often has lots of climbing ropes.
They swing from branch to branch and like bananas.
questions.description: A crime under the palm trees, and the loot is rock hard.
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, a coconut isn't a nut at all but a drupe, a fruit with a stone inside.

questions.question: In the song “Sankt Martin ritt durch Schnee und Wind”, Martin cuts his cloak with his sword. Into how many pieces?
hints: The song is sung at the lantern parades in November.
A freezing beggar sits in the snow, and Martin gives him some of his cloak.
One piece for Martin, one piece for the beggar.
questions.description: If you have no scissors on you, just grab a sword.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chapel” (German “Kapelle”) comes from Martin's cloak (Latin “cappa”), later kept as a relic in a small prayer room.

questions.question: They wiggle back and forth, crawl up and down, and hide at the end. What are the “Zehn kleine Zappelmänner” (ten little wiggle men)?
hints: You play it with small children, without any toys.
You always have them with you.
You have five of them on each hand.
questions.description: Ten little fellows who can never sit still. Sound familiar?
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the game, the wiggle men usually hide behind your back or inside your fist.

questions.question: In “Ringel, Ringel, Reihe”, the children sit “unterm Hollerbusch”. What bush is that?
hints: People make syrup from its white flowers.
Its berries are small and almost black.
Its usual German name sounds almost like “Holler”.
questions.description: A bush you sit under, shout at, and then run away from in a flash.
questions.fun_fact: “Holler” is an old southern German name for the Holunder; in the north it is also called “Flieder”.

questions.question: In the lullaby “Schlaf, Kindlein, schlaf”, the mother shakes the little tree. What falls down from it?
hints: Meanwhile, the father is looking after the sheep.
It goes very well with falling asleep.
You have it at night with your eyes closed.
questions.description: A tree that delivers more at bedtime than any fruit stand.
questions.fun_fact: In another verse, sheep wander across the sky: the little stars are the lambs, and the moon is the shepherd.

questions.question: In the circle game song “Dornröschen war ein schönes Kind”, the wicked fairy casts a curse. How many years must Dornröschen sleep?
hints: It's a very round number.
It's longer than most people live.
This stretch of time is also called a century.
questions.description: The longest nap in fairy-tale history, and no alarm clock allowed.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brothers Grimm tale, not only Dornröschen falls asleep but the whole castle, even the flies on the wall.

questions.question: I'm the name of the horsemen of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, and I come from a Turkic word. What did my name, “Cossack”, first mean?
hints: The same word gave its name to a country in Central Asia.
The name tells how they lived, not where they lived.
The opposite of a serf or a slave.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a Russian dance, but has more galloping in it than squatting.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Cossack” has the same origin as the name of the Kazakhs, the people of Kazakhstan.

questions.question: Finish the German finger rhyme: “Das ist der Daumen, der schüttelt die …” What does the thumb shake?
hints: It's a fruit.
It's usually purple or blue.
In German, the word rhymes with “Daumen”.
questions.description: Five fingers, one fruit harvest and one very greedy little guy.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the rhyme, the little finger eats up all the plums by himself.

questions.question: A little mole asks lots of animals who pooped on his head. Two flies solve the case. Which animal was it?
hints: The culprit doesn’t live in a pasture or a barn.
It belongs to a butcher.
Its name is Hans-Heinerich and it barks.
questions.description: A crime case where the evidence literally falls from the sky.
questions.fun_fact: In the end the mole gets his revenge and drops a little “sausage” of his own on the culprit’s head.

questions.question: I'm a little toy rabbit. My friend Sophie lost me, and now I send her letters from all over the world. Who am I?
hints: My books have real letters inside that you can take out.
In Latin, my name means “the lucky one”.
My name sounds like a famous cartoon cat.
questions.description: The busiest letter writer in the world has two long ears and no stamp collection.
questions.fun_fact: The Felix books have real envelopes glued inside, and you can pull out the rabbit's letters.

questions.question: In Kästner’s “Das doppelte Lottchen” (Lisa and Lottie), Luise lives with her father in Vienna. In which city does Lotte live with her mother?
hints: The city is in Germany.
It’s in the south, not far from the Alps.
Oktoberfest is celebrated there every year.
questions.description: Two girls, one face, and a summer camp where suddenly everyone is seeing double.
questions.fun_fact: Kästner first wrote the story as an idea for a film; the book didn’t come out until 1949.

questions.question: I'm a chubby, shy boy. I took a book from Mr. Koreander's secondhand bookshop and read it in my school's attic. Who am I?
hints: The book I'm reading never ends.
Later I end up in Phantásien myself.
My last name is Bux.
questions.description: A boy who sinks so deep into reading that he never surfaces for dinner.
questions.fun_fact: “Die unendliche Geschichte” (The Neverending Story) is printed in two colors: red for the real world, green for Phantásien.

questions.question: You're reading about Carag, a boy who can turn into a puma. Which author wrote this “Woodwalkers” series?
hints: The author also wrote about shapeshifters in the sea.
Her other series is called “Seawalkers.”
Her first name is Katja.
questions.description: A school with side effects: stay after class and you might suddenly grow fur.
questions.fun_fact: In the follow-up series “Seawalkers,” the students turn into sharks, dolphins and other sea animals.

questions.question: In which decade did the first audio drama cassettes of “Benjamin Blümchen” and “Die drei ???” come out?
hints: The cassette itself was introduced in 1963.
It was the decade of bell-bottoms and disco.
Die drei ??? started in 1979.
questions.description: Back then, you rewound the tape with a pencil whenever it got tangled.
questions.fun_fact: Benjamin Blümchen and Bibi Blocksberg were both created by the same author: Elfie Donnelly.

questions.question: I belong to the Greenskins, my horse is called Artax, and I must save the sick Childlike Empress. Who am I?
hints: I come from a book by Michael Ende.
My horse sinks in the Swamps of Sadness.
Later I ride a white luckdragon.
questions.description: A hero with green skin who is never green with envy.
questions.fun_fact: In the book, the name Atreyu means “Son of All”, because he was an orphan raised by his whole people.

questions.question: I fell from the sky and broke off one of my points. A girl fixed me up with a bandage. Who am I?
hints: I shine at night.
Now I live with a girl in her bedroom.
My story was written and drawn by Klaus Baumgart.
questions.description: An emergency where no doctor is needed, just a bandage and lots of love.
questions.fun_fact: In 2004, the story came to movie theaters as an animated film.

questions.question: The locomotive Emma runs on the tiny island of Lummerland. Who drives her?
hints: He is Jim Knopf's best friend.
He smokes a pipe and is very strong.
His name starts with L.
questions.description: She's chubby, loves to puff, and everyone adores her anyway.
questions.fun_fact: “Jim Knopf und Lukas der Lokomotivführer” (Jim Button and Luke the Engine Driver) was Michael Ende's first book, and it won the German Youth Literature Prize in 1961.

questions.question: I wrote the “Lola” books. In my thriller “Isola,” twelve teenagers shoot a film on an island off Rio. Who am I?
hints: I live in Hamburg.
Another of my books is called “Whisper.”
My first name is Isabel.
questions.description: An author who likes to leave her characters on islands, no return ticket included.
questions.fun_fact: Before she wrote books, Isabel Abedi worked as an advertising copywriter.

questions.question: A girl called George who'd rather be a boy, her dog Timmy and rocky Kirrin Island: which gang do they belong to?
hints: The books are by an English author.
The kids usually have their adventures during the summer vacation.
Just count all the members, the dog included.
questions.description: A gang that empties more picnic baskets than it solves cases.
questions.fun_fact: Enid Blyton wrote 21 books about the gang in total.

questions.question: In which year did Guido Hammesfahr, as Fritz Fuchs, take over the show “Löwenzahn” from Peter Lustig?
hints: By then Peter Lustig had been hosting the show for over 20 years.
It was a few years after euro cash was introduced.
The year is in the second half of the 2000s.
questions.description: A fox takes over the territory of a man in overalls.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Lustig hosted “Löwenzahn” for almost 25 years.

questions.question: Which presenter of the Sachgeschichten (explainer films) in “Die Sendung mit der Maus” almost always wears a green sweater?
hints: He has been explaining things on the show since the 1970s.
He wears glasses and has a mustache.
His first name starts with “Ch.”
questions.description: How do the stripes get into the toothpaste? This man gets to the bottom of it.
questions.fun_fact: October 3 is Maus Door-Opener Day, when companies, labs and workshops open their doors to children.

questions.question: Samson, the big bear, lived on the German “Sesamstraße”. Who was NOT one of his neighbors there?
hints: Three of the four were created just for the German Sesame Street.
The one we're looking for comes from a different German kids' show.
He's a bear too, but a seafaring one.
questions.description: A bear so big there's hardly any room left on his street for neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: “Sesamstraße” has been on German TV since 1973.

questions.question: Listen closely to the word “Fliewatüüt” and it tells you how the vehicle gets around. In how many ways?
hints: Robbi the robot and the boy Tobbi travel the world in it.
Part of the name is hidden in the German word “fliegen” (to fly).
“Flie” stands for the air, “wa” for “Wasser” (water) and “tüüt” for the horn on the road.
questions.description: A vehicle that just couldn't decide what it wanted to be when it grew up.
questions.fun_fact: Boy Lornsen wrote the book “Robbi, Tobbi und das Fliewatüüt” in 1967.

questions.question: In which decade did “Löwenzahn” start, the show with Peter Lustig in his blue trailer?
hints: Today's grandparents didn't know it as children.
Many of today's parents grew up with it.
The Berlin Wall fell in the same decade.
questions.description: Living with no foundation, but with a whole lot of knowledge.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of every episode, Peter Lustig told the kids: “Abschalten!” (“Switch off!”)
