questions.question: How many hairs does the Little Mole (der kleine Maulwurf) have on top of his head?
hints: There are only very few.
There are more than two.
Count as far as a triangle has corners.
questions.description: A gardener's nightmare with the happiest laugh in the world.
questions.fun_fact: The Little Mole comes from Czechia; the artist who drew him was Zdeněk Miler.

questions.question: “I wrote “Little Muck”, which DEFA filmed in 1953, and also “Dwarf Nose”. I died aged just 24. Who am I?”
hints: He lived in Württemberg in the early 19th century.
He also wrote “The Cold Heart” (“Das kalte Herz”).
His surname has just five letters and starts with “H”.
questions.description: With magic slippers like these, any mail carrier would finish the route in record time.
questions.fun_fact: The 1953 film is one of the most successful children's films ever made in East Germany.

questions.question: Which color is NONE of the three characters Mouse, Elephant and Duck from “Die Sendung mit der Maus”?
hints: Each of the three characters has its own main color.
The little elephant is the color of the sky.
The duck looks like a rubber duck.
questions.description: Three friends who never argue, because none of them ever says a word.
questions.fun_fact: The Mouse was drawn by the artist Isolde Schmitt-Menzel.

questions.question: I'm a warrior of the First Crusade, and people call me a “crusader”. Where does my name come from?
questions.answer: From the cross sewn on their clothes
wrong_answers: From crossing the sea by ship
hints: Before setting out, they made a vow in a religious ceremony.
They wore it on them, where everyone could see it.
It is a Christian symbol.
questions.description: A warrior name so tangled it could have come straight out of a crossword.
questions.fun_fact: The First Crusade set out in 1096, and many of its warriors walked thousands of kilometers to reach Jerusalem.

questions.question: What is the grasshopper called in the cartoon series “Die Biene Maja”?
hints: He is a good friend of Maja.
He is green and can jump very far.
His name has only four letters and sounds like a jump.
questions.description: The poppy meadow has more musicians than some orchestras.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Biene Maja” is based on a 1912 book by Waldemar Bonsels.

questions.question: Who is NOT one of the classic characters of the Kasperletheater puppet show?
hints: The one you're looking for has his own series.
He lives with a master carpenter.
He has red hair and is a kobold.
questions.description: A theater where the audience is louder than the actors.
questions.fun_fact: “Der Räuber Hotzenplotz” by Otfried Preußler is really a Kasperle story.

questions.question: “I'm young, I can do magic and I live in Neustadt. I fly on Kartoffelbrei, and my spells end with “Hex-hex!”. Who am I?”
hints: There are lots of audio plays and movies about her.
Kartoffelbrei is the name of her broom.
Her friend Tina has a riding stable.
questions.description: Who needs a driver's license when you have a broom?
questions.fun_fact: The first Bibi Blocksberg cassette came out in 1980.

questions.question: How far into the future can Cassiopeia, Momo's tortoise, see?
hints: It's less than a day.
It's just enough to escape the Men in Gray in time.
It's less than an hour, but more than a few minutes.
questions.description: If you never have any time, ask this tortoise for directions.
questions.fun_fact: Michael Ende wrote “Momo” in Italy, where he lived near Rome from 1971.

questions.question: Hans im Glück (Hans in Luck) keeps trading away his lump of gold. Which animal did he NEVER own along the way?
hints: Hans usually trades for something smaller.
In the end he only has stones, and then nothing at all.
The animal you're looking for bleats.
questions.description: The worst businessman in all of fairy-tale land, and somehow the happiest.
questions.fun_fact: Hans got the lump of gold, as big as his head, as pay for seven years of work.

questions.question: In the novel “The German Lesson” (“Deutschstunde”), a village policeman in the Nazi era makes sure his old friend no longer works. What is the friend's job?
hints: The friend is called Max Ludwig Nansen.
The ban comes from Berlin, but the friend secretly keeps working.
The character is based on Emil Nolde.
questions.description: A school subject that, in this book, gets you a punishment essay.
questions.fun_fact: Nansen is modeled on Emil Nolde, who, as we know today, was himself a member of the Nazi Party.

questions.question: Christoph Martin Wieland was the first to translate some 20 of Shakespeare's plays into German. In which decade were they published?
hints: Goethe was still a teenager in Frankfurt at the time.
Wieland worked on them as a town clerk in Biberach, where he grew up, years before he moved to Weimar.
The Seven Years' War was just coming to an end.
questions.description: To be or not to be: in German, that was at first just a question of time.
questions.fun_fact: Wieland translated almost everything into prose; Shakespeare's verse was only recreated in German later, by Schlegel and Tieck.

questions.question: Herr von Ribbeck auf Ribbeck im Havelland took me with him to the grave, and I grew into a tree for the children. What am I?
hints: Theodor Fontane wrote a poem about me.
I am a fruit with a core of seeds in the middle.
My shape looks like a light bulb.
questions.description: A nobleman who keeps handing out sweets even after he's dead.
questions.fun_fact: The real tree in Ribbeck was knocked down by a storm in 1911; its stump now stands in the village church.

questions.question: In the fairy tale “Brüderchen und Schwesterchen” (Brother and Sister), what does the brother turn into after drinking from an enchanted spring?
hints: The animal lives in the forest.
His sister ties her golden garter around his neck.
It's a relative of the stag.
questions.description: Why you'd better pack a water bottle for the fairy-tale forest.
questions.fun_fact: Two other springs would have turned the brother into a tiger and a wolf, and those times he managed to resist.

questions.question: We're a gang of kids in the Ruhr area. To join, you climb onto a high roof, and we take in a boy in a wheelchair. Who are we?
hints: We're pretty brave, but we're not a soccer team.
Our book was written by Max von der Grün.
Our name is a reptile from the edge of town.
questions.description: A gang whose entry test is harder than any school exam.
questions.fun_fact: The 1976 book was made into a film twice: in 1977 and again in 2009.

questions.question: Aschenputtel picks lentils out of the ashes, doves help her, and she runs away from the prince's ball. Where does her shoe get stuck?
hints: The prince had set a trap.
He had something coated with sticky pitch.
You climb it one step at a time.
questions.description: A party that comes to a very sticky end at midnight.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brothers Grimm version the shoe is golden; the glass slipper comes from the French version.

questions.question: In the concert hall, the romances from Ludwig Tieck's “Magelone” are sung. Who composed this song cycle?
hints: The composer was from Hamburg.
He also wrote a world-famous lullaby.
His last name starts with the same letter as Bach and Beethoven.
questions.description: A knight's love story so beautiful that someone turned it into a whole concert.
questions.fun_fact: Brahms set 15 of the poems from Tieck's story to music as his Opus 33.

questions.question: I went to prison for fraud, made up heroes of the Wild West and the Orient, and Bad Segeberg stages my stories every summer. Who am I?
hints: I came from Saxony.
I only visited America very late in life.
My most famous hero is an Apache chief.
questions.description: A man who knew the prairie better than anyone else who had never been there.
questions.fun_fact: Karl May only traveled to America in 1908, 15 years after the first three Winnetou books came out.

questions.question: A communist kangaroo moves in with a small-stage comedian in Berlin-Kreuzberg. Who wrote “The Kangaroo Chronicles”?
hints: The author is also the narrator in the book.
He comes from Berlin's scene of live reading shows.
He also wrote the novel “QualityLand.”
questions.description: A roommate who never pays rent but always has an opinion.
questions.fun_fact: The kangaroo stories ran on the radio first, before they became a best-selling book.

questions.question: In Janosch's stories, Little Tiger pulls it behind him on a string. What is the yellow-and-black striped wooden animal on wheels called?
hints: It is made of wood.
It has a beak.
Its name joins a big cat with a water bird.
questions.description: A pet that never barks and never needs feeding.
questions.fun_fact: Janosch's real name is Horst Eckert.

questions.question: In a poem by Christian Morgenstern, “Ein Wiesel saß auf einem Kiesel inmitten Bachgeriesel.” Why did the weasel sit there?
questions.answer: For the sake of the rhyme
hints: A moon calf gave away the reason.
The poem calls the weasel a “raffiniertes Tier”, a crafty creature.
Wiesel, Kiesel, Bachgeriesel: listen closely.
questions.description: An animal with very serious reasons, or maybe not.
questions.fun_fact: The poem comes from Morgenstern's “Galgenlieder” (Gallows Songs), first published in 1905.

questions.question: A child has secretly swiped some cookies, and Grandma smiles and says: “Du Schlawiner!” What does she mean?
hints: Grandma isn't really angry. If anything, she's a little impressed.
You hear the word most often in southern Germany and Austria.
It's a word for someone sly and cheeky who gets away with things.
questions.description: Grandma's vocabulary: as old as the cookie jar and just as well stocked.
questions.fun_fact: “Schlawiner” probably comes from “Slowene” (Slovene), an old name for traveling traders that people didn't quite trust.

questions.question: This was once the name for Slavic fishing villages near castles. Today Berliners use it for their neighborhood, and in Hamburg it means St. Pauli. What's the word?
hints: The word has only four letters.
People in Cologne say “Veedel” for the same thing.
It sounds almost like the German word “Kies” (gravel), just with a z at the end.
questions.description: Here everyone knows the baker, the late-night shop and the neighbor's dog.
questions.fun_fact: Berlin and Brandenburg still have places and streets called “Kietz” that recall the old fishing villages.

questions.question: Baden-Württemberg used a famous slogan for years. How does it end: “Wir können alles. Außer …” (“We can do everything. Except …”)?
hints: The slogan pokes a little fun at the people there.
You notice this “weakness” right away when people from there visit other parts of Germany.
It means the language of the news and of schoolbooks.
questions.description: A German state that is quite honest about its own weakness.
questions.fun_fact: The ad campaign started in 1999 and became so famous that it won awards and was copied many times.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this shiny round part with a small arm on top sits inside a device. What device is it?
hints: It's hidden inside many computers.
It keeps your photos and files even when you turn the computer off.
The first word of its name is the opposite of “soft”.
questions.description: Something that spins faster than you do when you hunt for the remote under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The arm of a hard drive floats above the spinning disk at a gap far smaller than the width of a hair.

questions.question: At a bakery in Bavaria, people say “Pfiat di” when they leave. What do they say instead at a bakery in Cologne?
hints: The word is even shorter than the goodbye people say in northern Germany.
The word belongs to Kölsch, the dialect of Cologne.
There's a saying that goes “… mit ö”.
questions.description: Every region has its very own way of saying goodbye.
questions.fun_fact: “Tschüss” comes from the Low German “adjüs” and goes back to Romance goodbyes like “adieu” or “adiós”, meaning “to God”.

questions.question: It has only two letters, you hear it all the time in Saxony, and Standard German speakers mix it up with “nun” (now). What does “nu” mean?
hints: It's an answer to a question.
It's one of the most common words in Saxon dialect.
It's the opposite of “nee”.
questions.description: The shortest conversation in Saxony fits on a beer coaster.
questions.fun_fact: It's not just Saxony: people in Upper Lusatia and Silesia also say “nu” when they mean “yes”.

questions.question: Germans say it to people they love, it often ends in “-i”, and “Mausi” is one. What kind of word is it?
hints: You wouldn't use a word like this to annoy anyone.
“Hasi” and “Schatzi” belong to this group too.
In English, “honey” and “sweetie” are examples.
questions.description: Small animals, big feelings.
questions.fun_fact: “Schatz” (treasure) is one of the most popular pet names in Germany.

questions.question: You're thirsty and order a Schorle. What do you get?
hints: Lots of people order it in a beer garden or after sports.
It's especially popular in southern Germany.
The best-known kind is made with apples.
questions.description: After a long bike ride, people order this before they've even sat down.
questions.fun_fact: In the Palatinate, wine Schorle is traditionally served in a half-liter glass covered in dimples, the “Dubbeglas”.

questions.question: What is the “Rheinisches Grundgesetz” (Rhineland Basic Law)?
questions.answer: A collection of Cologne life wisdom
wrong_answers: A set of traffic rules for Rhine ships
The rulebook of the Cologne Carnival
hints: No court in the world has ever passed it.
It's written in Kölsch and has eleven articles.
One article says: “Et hätt noch immer jot jejange.”
questions.description: A law book best read with a glass of Kölsch in your hand.
questions.fun_fact: Article 1 says “Et es wie et es”, which means “It is what it is.”

questions.question: This man directed “(T)Raumschiff Surprise – Periode 1” and also acted in it. Who is he?
hints: He comes from Munich.
Everyone just calls him “Bully”.
He also made “Der Schuh des Manitu”.
questions.description: Endless space, pink uniforms and a spaceship full of glitter.
questions.fun_fact: The film grew out of the “Unser (T)Raumschiff” space sketches on the TV show “Bullyparade”.

questions.question: Which future star played one of the three friends in “Die Drei von der Tankstelle” (1930), the film with “Ein Freund, ein guter Freund”?
hints: He later became one of the most popular German actors of all time.
He played Father Brown and the Captain of Köpenick.
He is also famous for “Die Feuerzangenbowle.”
questions.description: Fill it up, please, and add a little song you'll never forget.
questions.fun_fact: The Comedian Harmonists turned “Ein Freund, ein guter Freund” into an evergreen.

questions.question: I'm a Bavarian cabaret artist who has mocked narrow-minded petty bourgeois types for decades, and my film's title “Man spricht deutsh” is misspelled on purpose. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Munich in 1942.
I often performed with the musicians of Biermösl Blosn.
My TV series was called “Fast wia im richtigen Leben”.
questions.description: A man who watches stuffy small-minded folks so closely that they recognize themselves.
questions.fun_fact: “Man spricht deutsh” takes place almost entirely on a beach in Italy, where a Bavarian family is on vacation.

questions.question: I was a voice actor in Munich and for over 20 years gave the German voice to a yellow, donut-loving family man. Who am I?
hints: I voiced the role from 1991.
My character works at the Springfield nuclear power plant.
My first name starts with N.
questions.description: A voice you've heard more often than your own uncle's.
questions.fun_fact: Norbert Gastell voiced Homer Simpson until his death in 2015.

questions.question: What technology does the super-fast train between Shanghai and its airport use?
hints: It floats a tiny bit above the track.
It works with the same force that sticks things to the fridge door.
It uses very powerful magnets.
questions.description: A train that gets you to the airport before you've finished looking for your passport.
questions.fun_fact: Shanghai's maglev train covers about 30 km (19 miles) in under 8 minutes.

questions.question: Who plays the vain forensic pathologist Professor Karl-Friedrich Boerne in the Münster “Tatort”?
hints: He was born in Dresden in 1964.
He also makes music, including with the band Radio Doria.
His partner in the crime show is Detective Thiel.
questions.description: In Münster, murders are apparently best solved with a pinch of arrogance.
questions.fun_fact: The Münster “Tatort” regularly ranks among the episodes with the most viewers.

questions.question: I go to the Goethe-Gesamtschule, my teacher is Zeki Müller, and he tells me to cry quietly. Who am I?
hints: I'm a character in “Fack ju Göhte”.
I'm played by Jella Haase.
My name sounds French.
questions.description: A class so wild that even the school bell asks for some quiet.
questions.fun_fact: “Chantal, heul leise!” (“Chantal, cry quietly!”) became one of the best-known lines in German cinema after the film came out.

questions.question: Who directed “Rosenstraße” (2003), about the protest of Berlin women in 1943?
hints: She is one of the best-known female directors of New German Cinema.
She also made “Marianne and Juliane” and “Hannah Arendt.”
She was married to Volker Schlöndorff.
questions.description: A street name with brave women hiding behind it.
questions.fun_fact: Katja Riemann won the best actress award in Venice for her role in “Rosenstraße.”

questions.question: In which decade did Uwe Ochsenknecht become famous alongside Heiner Lauterbach in the comedy “Männer”?
hints: Shortly before, he had already appeared in “Das Boot”.
It was directed by Doris Dörrie.
Back then, Germany was still two separate countries.
questions.description: An actor whose last name sounds more like a farmhand who looks after oxen than a movie star.
questions.fun_fact: Ochsenknecht's sons Wilson Gonzalez and Jimi Blue became movie stars themselves with “Die Wilden Kerle” (“The Wild Soccer Bunch”).

questions.question: In East Germany, the Leipzig Trade Fair was held every spring and every fall. What does its logo of two stacked M’s stand for?
hints: The logo is older than East Germany and describes a certain kind of trade fair.
Leipzig is said to have invented this kind of fair.
Traders brought just one sample of each product, not their whole stock.
questions.description: Twice a year Leipzig was so packed that even the hotel beds worked overtime.
questions.fun_fact: In 1895 Leipzig became the world’s first sample fair; before that, traders hauled all their goods to market.

questions.question: In East Germany, every June 1 brought school parties, games and small presents for all pupils. What day was it?
hints: It is still celebrated in eastern Germany today.
Adults were not the center of attention on this day.
Everyone who still went to school or kindergarten was celebrated.
questions.description: The one day adults openly admit who really runs the house.
questions.fun_fact: International Children's Day on June 1 has been celebrated since 1950, while western Germany mostly marks World Children's Day in September instead.

questions.question: “I took old paper, bottles and jars, Young Pioneers brought me whole handcarts full, and paid pfennigs for it.” Who am I?
hints: My collection points were in almost every town and neighborhood in East Germany.
School classes competed in collection drives to see who could bring me the most.
Spelled out, my name is Sekundärrohstofferfassung.
questions.description: Lugging clinking bags through the whole neighborhood, and in the end your pocket money jingles too.
questions.fun_fact: The state paid so well for recyclables that many kids topped up their pocket money by collecting bottles.

questions.question: At the campsite on the Baltic coast, the family next door is setting up their “Klappfix”. What is it?
hints: It was made in East Germany and in great demand.
It had wheels.
You hitched it to the back of your Trabi and unfolded it into a sleeping cabin when you arrived.
questions.description: A Baltic vacation: three weeks of neighbors you didn't choose.
questions.fun_fact: Spots at popular Baltic campsites were assigned in East Germany, and some families came back to the same place for decades.

questions.question: From 1964, the prefab city of Halle-Neustadt was built next to Halle an der Saale. Who was it mainly built for?
hints: The jobs were at big plants close by.
Many residents took factory trains every day to their plants south of the city.
The plants were called Leuna and Buna and made plastics and gasoline.
questions.description: A city planned on the drawing board that for a long time didn't even need street names.
questions.fun_fact: In Halle-Neustadt, apartment blocks at first had numbers instead of street addresses, so you might live in “Block 314.”

questions.question: In East Germany, many people simply joined a line as soon as they saw one. Why?
questions.answer: Something rare was probably on sale.
wrong_answers: Standing in line was required by law.
Lottery tickets were being handed out.
hints: This is about shopping.
Many didn't even know what they were waiting for.
Bananas or jeans were reasons to stand in line for a long time.
questions.description: East Germany's favorite sport: all you needed was patience and good shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Many East Germans always carried a string shopping bag, in case something rare suddenly turned up on the way.

questions.question: In October 1989, I attended East Germany's 40th anniversary celebration. The line “Life punishes those who come too late” is credited to me. Who am I?
hints: At the time, I was the leader of a communist party.
I stood for “glasnost” and “perestroika”.
I was the last leader of the Soviet Union.
questions.description: A state guest who came to the birthday party and brought a warning as a gift.
questions.fun_fact: Gorbachev never said the line in exactly those words: the short version probably came from his spokesman, Gennady Gerasimov.

questions.question: I was a 1952 offer from Moscow to the Western powers: a united but neutral Germany. Adenauer turned me down. What am I called?
hints: I was a diplomatic letter.
The man I'm named after died a year after me, in 1953.
I'm named after the Soviet Union's ruler at the time.
questions.description: Mail from Moscow: sender known, hidden motives unknown.
questions.fun_fact: Historians still argue whether the offer was serious or only meant to disrupt West Germany's ties to the West.

questions.question: It was required at flag roll call, had a rising sun on the sleeve and belonged to the FDJ. What was this piece of clothing called?
hints: It was a top with a collar.
It was also worn at big parades like the May Day demonstration.
The FDJ flag was this color too.
questions.description: A dress code where nobody ever asked what to wear today.
questions.fun_fact: The sun on the sleeve was the emblem of the FDJ, the Free German Youth.

questions.question: In which year was a state of emergency declared after a popular uprising in East Berlin and across much of the GDR?
hints: It was a few months after Stalin's death.
The uprising began on a day in June.
A big street in Berlin bears the date: “Straße des 17. Juni”.
questions.description: A summer when suddenly nobody in East Berlin was allowed out for a stroll after 9 p.m.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1990, June 17 was a public holiday in West Germany, called the “Day of German Unity”.

questions.question: An old radio in the attic is labeled “VEB Stern-Radio Berlin”. What does “VEB” tell you about the maker?
questions.answer: The factory was owned by the people
wrong_answers: The set was made for export
The factory was a family business
The set was tested by the state
hints: It's about who owned the factory.
In the GDR there were hardly any private factories left.
The abbreviation stands for “Volkseigener Betrieb”.
questions.description: Three letters stuck on every other East German product like a family name.
questions.fun_fact: After 1990 the Treuhand agency took over about 8,500 people-owned enterprises to privatize them.

questions.question: The GDR's largest mass organization was called the FDGB. How does its name continue: “Freier Deutscher …”?
hints: It was about the interests of workers.
This organization was meant to represent employees in the workplace.
In West Germany its counterpart is called the DGB.
questions.description: Almost every worker was a member, and the reward was a vacation on the Baltic Sea.
questions.fun_fact: The FDGB's holiday service was the GDR's biggest travel agency, arranging millions of vacation trips every year.

questions.question: After President Wilhelm Pieck died in 1960, East Germany got a Council of State. Who was its first chairman?
hints: He was already head of the SED party at the time.
He came from Leipzig and had trained as a carpenter.
He is the man who said “No one has the intention of building a wall.”
questions.description: A brand-new boss’s chair, freshly set up in 1960.
questions.fun_fact: The former Council of State building in Berlin now houses a private business school.

questions.question: I was founded on October 7, 1949, a few months after my western neighbor. My holiday was called “Day of the Republic”. Who am I?
hints: I was in Central Europe.
I was a member of the Warsaw Pact.
My capital was East Berlin.
questions.description: A birthday celebrated every October with flags and parades, and the guest of honor wasn't a person.
questions.fun_fact: Just six days before the GDR, on October 1, 1949, the People's Republic of China was proclaimed.

questions.question: I'm hidden at the end of level 1-2 in Super Mario Bros.: run across the ceiling and you'll find me, with three pipes waiting. What am I?
hints: I let you skip whole levels.
My name uses a word that science fiction uses for super-fast space travel.
A sign inside me says “WELCOME TO ... ZONE!”.
questions.description: A secret so famous it's not a secret anymore, yet everyone still goes looking for it.
questions.fun_fact: Using the warp zones, you can finish Super Mario Bros. by playing only 8 of its 32 levels.

questions.question: Empty yogurt cups, food cans and chip bags go into this bin. Which bin is it?
hints: This is where packaging ends up.
Instead of the bin, there's often a bag of the same color.
Its color is that of a ripe banana.
questions.description: Home to everything you never want to see again once you've unpacked it.
questions.fun_fact: From 1991 on, the “Grüner Punkt” (Green Dot) on packaging showed that it belonged in the Gelber Sack, the yellow bag.

questions.question: You drive out of a 30 km/h zone onto a normal city street with no sign. What is the speed limit there?
hints: It's more than 30.
Outside towns, on country roads, it's usually 100.
It's exactly half the country-road limit.
questions.description: Here cars cruise as calmly as Grandpa on a Sunday drive.
questions.fun_fact: One of Germany's first 30 km/h zones was tested in the town of Buxtehude in 1983.

questions.question: Here you buy stamps at a counter and send packages, often inside a supermarket or stationery store. What is it called?
hints: A person stands behind the counter there.
A yellow sign with a post horn shows the way.
The word combines “Post” with the German word for a branch office.
questions.description: A place where people line up of their own free will just to get rid of packages.
questions.fun_fact: Most Postfilialen in Germany aren't run by Deutsche Post itself, but by partners such as kiosks and supermarkets.

questions.question: In many German villages, the siren suddenly wails during the day, even though nobody there is in danger. Who is it calling together?
hints: These helpers actually have perfectly normal jobs.
They drop everything and rush to the equipment shed.
Their vehicles are red and carry a ladder.
questions.description: It never sings nicely, yet the whole village still listens.
questions.fun_fact: On the nationwide Warning Day in September, sirens wail all across Germany at the same time as a test.

questions.question: You've just changed the full vacuum cleaner bag. Which German trash does it go in?
hints: It's neither packaging nor food scraps.
Its bin is usually gray or black.
Everything that doesn't fit in any other bin ends up here.
questions.description: It spent years eating crumbs, and now it gets thrown out itself.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, diapers, ashes and old toothbrushes also go in the Restmüll.

questions.question: You have your Gesundheitskarte (health insurance card) with you. Where do you usually NOT need it?
hints: The card comes from your Krankenkasse.
Since the e-prescription, you even put it in the reader when picking up medicine.
It won't help you get a new Personalausweis.
questions.description: A little plastic card that has been to the doctor more often than you.
questions.fun_fact: From age 15, your Gesundheitskarte must show a photo of you.

questions.question: In German stores, you often can't exchange something without this slip of paper. What is it?
hints: You get it when you pay.
It shows what you bought and how much it cost.
It comes out of the cash register.
questions.description: The sweater itches and the color is wrong. Luckily, there's this piece of paper.
questions.fun_fact: If the item isn't faulty, a German store doesn't have to exchange it at all, but many do anyway as a goodwill gesture.

questions.question: Its tower is 259 m (850 ft) tall and stands in the city of the European Central Bank. Where does Commerzbank have its headquarters?
hints: The city has more skyscrapers than anywhere else in Germany.
Germany's most important stock exchange is there too.
Because of its skyline, people call it “Mainhattan”.
questions.description: Here money lives way up high, with a view.
questions.fun_fact: When it opened in 1997, the Commerzbank Tower was the tallest skyscraper in Europe.

questions.question: How many 5-euro bills do you need to make 50 euros?
hints: Count in fives: 5, 10, 15 …
Two fives already make 10 euros.
That's how many fingers you have on both hands.
questions.description: The smallest bill in the wallet wants its big moment too.
questions.fun_fact: The 5-euro bill is the smallest euro bill, and it shows buildings from ancient times.

questions.question: The flea market is named after an animal. How many legs does this animal have?
hints: The animal is tiny and jumps very high.
It's an insect.
Beetles and ants have the same number of legs.
questions.description: This is where you buy Grandpa's old record player, no itching included.
questions.fun_fact: The name probably comes from Paris: the “Marché aux puces” sold old clothes that sometimes had fleas in them.

questions.question: In German, what does it mean if someone “jede Mark zweimal umdreht” (turns every Mark over twice)?
hints: The Mark was Germany's money before the euro.
Someone like this thinks long and hard before spending anything.
It's the opposite of throwing money around.
questions.description: A saying older than any euro in your wallet.
questions.fun_fact: When Germany switched to the euro, one euro was worth exactly 1.95583 Deutsche Mark.

questions.question: What is the shop called where you can buy fresh Brötchen, pretzels and cake?
hints: There's a big, hot oven there.
You need flour for what they make.
The person working there often starts at 3 in the morning so the rolls are ready for breakfast.
questions.description: It smells so good here in the morning that even late sleepers get up.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2014, German bread culture has been on Germany's national list of intangible cultural heritage.

questions.question: What's inside a “gemischte Tüte” from the kiosk?
hints: Kids love it the most.
It's colorful and usually tastes sweet.
Inside you'll find gummy bears, licorice and sour strings.
questions.description: For a few coins, the kiosk hands you a big surprise.
questions.fun_fact: For a gemischte Tüte, you often pick the treats yourself, one piece at a time.

questions.question: It's small, often red and white, and says “No thanks” to flyers and free papers. Where does the “Bitte keine Werbung” (no ads, please) sticker go?
hints: The ads would get put in there.
The mail carrier stops at it nearly every day.
Otherwise it is where letters and postcards end up.
questions.description: A tiny sticker with great power over flyers.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, anyone who puts ads in despite the sticker can be given a legal warning; the Federal Court of Justice ruled this back in 1988.

questions.question: The Winterschlussverkauf, Germany's big winter sale full of bargains, traditionally began in which month?
hints: It cleared out winter stock before the new spring fashion arrived.
The Christmas shopping rush was already over.
It's the first month of the year.
questions.description: When the coats suddenly cost less than the snow outside.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2004, German law set the dates of the winter and summer sales; today stores can offer discounts whenever they like.

questions.question: At German glass recycling containers, used glass is sorted by color. How many colors are there?
hints: Clear glass has its own bin.
Green bottles go into another one.
Clear, green and one more color.
questions.description: Here things clink and clatter, and nobody gets scolded for it.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, blue glass goes into the container for green glass.

questions.question: Who became the first chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949?
hints: He came from Cologne.
He was already over 70 when he became chancellor.
His nickname was “der Alte” (the Old Man).
questions.description: Somebody had to go first, and luckily he'd already had some practice at being the boss.
questions.fun_fact: Adenauer was 73 when he took office, and he stayed chancellor until 1963.

questions.question: After Angela Merkel's grand coalition, an alliance of the SPD, the Greens and the FDP took over in 2021. What was it called?
hints: The Bundestag has had nicknames like this for alliances for decades.
The name comes from the party colors.
Red, green and yellow, just like at every intersection.
questions.description: When three parties share power, the team needs a colorful nickname.
questions.fun_fact: The coalition fell apart in November 2024, and an early federal election followed in February 2025.

questions.question: At this ceremony to bid farewell to Angela Merkel in 2021, “Du hast den Farbfilm vergessen” was played. Who sang the original?
hints: The song came out in East Germany in 1974.
The singer later became known as the “Godmother of Punk.”
Her daughter is called Cosma Shiva.
questions.description: Torches, marching music and a song about forgotten vacation photos.
questions.fun_fact: Merkel also asked for Hildegard Knef's “Für mich soll's rote Rosen regnen” and the hymn “Großer Gott, wir loben dich.”

questions.question: You go in alone, a screen hides where you mark your cross, and nobody may watch. Which voting principle does this protect?
hints: It's about the voting booth.
Nobody should find out where you put your cross.
Like a diary with a lock.
questions.description: A tiny booth where a whole country speaks its mind.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2017, it has been illegal in Germany to take photos or videos in the voting booth.

questions.question: The word is Greek for “rule by the people”. Germany's Basic Law says: “All state authority is derived from the people.” Which form of government is meant?
hints: Germany is one.
You're allowed to vote freely.
The word starts like “demo”.
questions.description: Even the ancient Greeks argued loudly in the marketplace about who was in charge here.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Athens, only adult male citizens could vote, not women, enslaved people or newcomers.

questions.question: How many crosses may you mark on the ballot paper in a German federal election (Bundestagswahl)?
hints: The ballot paper has a black column and a blue column.
One vote goes to someone running in your own constituency.
Erststimme and Zweitstimme (first and second vote).
questions.description: A sheet of paper as long as the poll workers' patience.
questions.fun_fact: For how seats in the Bundestag are shared out, the second vote is the more important of the two.

questions.question: What do German adults mean when they say “Am Sonntag gehen wir zur Urne” (on Sunday we're going to the urn)?
hints: It usually happens on a Sunday.
You need a pen and a slip of paper.
You mark a cross.
questions.description: A sentence that makes kids think of Grandma's flower vase for a second.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Urne” comes from the Latin “urna”, a water jug.

questions.question: On TV you see soccer players with an eagle and four stars on their jerseys. Who do they play for?
hints: They play at World Cups and European Championships.
Each star stands for one World Cup title.
They play for the whole country.
questions.description: A bird on the chest that has never scored a single goal.
questions.fun_fact: The fourth star was added after Germany won the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

questions.question: The Basic Law learned from the Weimar Republic and created the “wehrhafte Demokratie” (militant democracy). What does that mean?
questions.answer: It may defend itself against enemies of the constitution
wrong_answers: All citizens must do military service
The army guards the polling stations
Every citizen may carry a weapon
hints: Weimar was also brought down from the inside.
The Office for the Protection of the Constitution is part of it.
Tolerance ends where someone wants to abolish freedom itself.
questions.description: A term from the Basic Law that sounds like a knight with a shield.
questions.fun_fact: Because of the “eternity clause,” human dignity and the principles of Article 20 can't be abolished, not even by a large majority.

questions.question: Haydn wrote the tune of the Deutschlandlied in 1797 as an imperial anthem for Francis II. Which anthem he heard in London was his model?
hints: Haydn visited England twice.
The anthem was sung for a monarch.
It's still the British national anthem today.
questions.description: A tune that moved countries and swapped an emperor for a whole nation.
questions.fun_fact: Haydn reused the tune in his String Quartet Op. 76 No. 3, which is why it's called the “Emperor Quartet.”

questions.question: When voting by mail in Germany, you send back a signed document along with your ballot. Which one?
hints: You get it with your mail-in voting papers.
On it, you declare that you marked the ballot yourself.
Without it, you can't vote anywhere other than your own polling station.
questions.description: Voting in your pajamas at the kitchen table, but not entirely without paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2021 federal election, almost half of all voters voted by mail, a record.

questions.question: How often is the Bundestag normally elected?
hints: It's a shorter term than the European Parliament's.
The Federal President is elected for a longer term.
The men's World Cup comes around just as often.
questions.description: An appointment you don't need an alarm clock for, just a very long calendar.
questions.fun_fact: Early federal elections have only happened four times so far: in 1972, 1983, 2005 and 2025.

questions.question: It's named after a Greek philosopher, fools your touch rather than your eyes, and you can test it on your nose. What is “Aristotle's illusion”?
questions.answer: Feeling two objects where there is only one
wrong_answers: Feeling warm water as cold after touching hot water
Feeling your phone buzz in your pocket when it doesn't
Feeling itchy when you see someone else scratch
hints: You need two fingers of the same hand.
The fingers must be in a position that isn't their normal one.
Cross your index and middle fingers and touch a marble with the tips.
questions.description: A Greek philosopher who also ran experiments you can repeat from your couch.
questions.fun_fact: Aristotle described this illusion more than 2,300 years ago, and brain scientists still study it today.

questions.question: The SRP was banned in 1952 and the KPD in 1956; two attempts against the NPD failed. Which court decides whether to ban a party?
hints: It is based in Karlsruhe.
The Bundestag, the Bundesrat or the federal government must file the request.
It is known as the “guardian of the Basic Law.”
questions.description: Democracy's sharpest sword, and only one place is allowed to draw it.
questions.fun_fact: In 2017 the NPD wasn't banned because it was too insignificant to actually achieve its goals.

questions.question: Johannes R. Becher wrote the words of the East German anthem in 1949. Which line meant it was no longer sung from the 1970s on?
wrong_answers: “Von der Maas bis an die Memel”
hints: At the time, East Germany wanted to clearly set itself apart from West Germany.
The line no longer fit two separate states.
In 1989, protesters chanted exactly these words.
questions.description: An anthem that, at some point, you were only allowed to hum.
questions.fun_fact: Becher's lyrics “Auferstanden aus Ruinen” also fit Haydn's tune for the West German anthem, and the other way around.

questions.question: Which German national team player is shown in this photo?
hints: He has played for FC Bayern Munich since 2015.
He can play at right back and in midfield.
In 2024 he was named captain of the national team.
questions.description: A man who probably pulls up his socks even in his sleep.
questions.fun_fact: Kimmich was born in Rottweil, the town the Rottweiler dog breed is named after.

questions.question: Berlin, July 2014: at the World Cup party, players crossed the stage first bent over, then upright, singing about their final opponents. What is this act called?
hints: The final opponents came from South America.
The song said this is how the opponents “walk”: bent over.
It refers to the horsemen and cattle herders of the Argentine pampas.
questions.description: When soccer players play dance teacher, someone should check the routine first.
questions.fun_fact: The act at the Brandenburg Gate was later strongly criticized as disrespectful, in Germany too.

questions.question: You're watching a replay: Germany beats host Brazil 7–1 in a World Cup semifinal. What year was that?
hints: The World Cup was held in South America.
Germany won the World Cup at this tournament.
It was four years after the World Cup in South Africa.
questions.description: A score that looks more like handball than soccer.
questions.fun_fact: After 29 minutes it was already 5–0, and four of those goals came in only about six minutes.

questions.question: You walk through a German city, and posters with the World Cup motto “Die Welt zu Gast bei Freunden” hang everywhere. What year is it?
hints: The mascot was a lion named Goleo.
Germany finished third at this tournament.
Today this time is called the “Sommermärchen” (summer fairy tale).
questions.description: A summer when suddenly every rearview mirror wore a tiny flag.
questions.fun_fact: Italy won the 2006 World Cup, beating France on penalties in the final in Berlin.

questions.question: In old footage you see a striker doing somersaults after his goals. With 71 goals, he is Germany's all-time top scorer. Who is it?
hints: He was born in Poland.
With 16 goals, he is also the all-time top scorer at World Cups.
His first name is often shortened to “Miro”.
questions.description: Gymnastics and goals: some strikers can just do both.
questions.fun_fact: Gerd Müller scored 68 goals for Germany in only 62 games.

questions.question: Lothar Matthäus holds Germany's record for international caps. About how many games did he play for Germany?
hints: His national team career lasted from 1980 to 2000.
He played at five World Cups.
It's well over 100, but under 200.
questions.description: So many games that his jersey has surely earned a pension by now.
questions.fun_fact: Matthäus was captain in 1990 when Germany became world champions in Rome.

questions.question: In their World Cup opener, Germany led Japan 1–0 and then lost 2–1. In which year was that?
hints: For once, the World Cup was played in winter.
The host country was Qatar.
The tournament ended just before Christmas, with Argentina as world champions.
questions.description: A World Cup opener after which many fans would rather have gone out for sushi.
questions.fun_fact: İlkay Gündoğan scored Germany's goal from a penalty, and both of Japan's scorers played in the Bundesliga.

questions.question: I was born in Berlin, have sung with my guitar since the 1960s, and in 1974 sang that above the clouds, freedom must be boundless. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of Germany's best-known singer-songwriters (Liedermacher).
For decades I've worn a mop-top haircut, and I fly planes as a hobby.
My first name is Reinhard.
questions.description: One man, one guitar and plenty of room to climb.
questions.fun_fact: Reinhard Mey has a pilot's license and flies himself, so his song about flying comes from experience.

questions.question: In 1983, at the height of the Cold War, a song told of balloons that start a war by mistake. Who sang “99 Luftballons”?
hints: The singer gave her band her own stage name.
She also sang “Irgendwie, irgendwo, irgendwann”.
Her stage name has only four letters.
questions.description: A kid’s birthday party that got a little out of hand.
questions.fun_fact: Sung in German, “99 Luftballons” climbed to number 2 on the US charts in 1984.

questions.question: I came to Germany from Romania at 14, sang “Über sieben Brücken musst du gehn” and co-created Tabaluga, the little green dragon. Who am I?
hints: I’ve been making German rock since the 1970s.
I was born in Brașov, in Transylvania.
My first name is Peter.
questions.description: A rocker in a leather jacket who raised a dragon on the side.
questions.fun_fact: “Über sieben Brücken musst du gehn” was first recorded by the East German band Karat; Maffay’s version made it famous in the West.

questions.question: I write my own lyrics, mostly sing them with a guitar, often with a political message, and East Germany expelled one of us in 1976. What am I?
hints: For me, the words matter more than the show.
Reinhard Mey and Wolf Biermann are among us.
My German name sounds like a trade that makes songs.
questions.description: Songs you don't clap along to, but think about first.
questions.fun_fact: After a concert in Cologne in 1976, the Liedermacher Wolf Biermann was not allowed back into East Germany.

questions.question: It takes place on a former Soviet military airfield in Mecklenburg, with stages in aircraft hangars and no ads or sponsors at all. Which festival?
hints: The airfield is in Lärz, in the Mecklenburg Lake District.
Many people call it, half jokingly, “Ferienkommunismus” (holiday communism).
The name means merging together.
questions.description: A weekend when Mecklenburg briefly becomes the loudest village in the world.
questions.fun_fact: At Fusion, taking photos and filming on the grounds is frowned upon: you're meant to live the moment.

questions.question: I acted in the film “Das Boot”, lived in London for a long time, and my song “Mensch” hit No. 1 in Germany in 2002. Who am I?
hints: I once sang a song asking when a man is a man.
I wrote a song about my hometown, Bochum.
My last name has an “ö” in it.
questions.description: He mumbles, he dances like his knees are plugged into a socket, and everyone loves him anyway.
questions.fun_fact: The album “Mensch” is one of the best-selling albums ever released in Germany.

questions.question: In the 1980s, Tamara Danz was East Germany's best-known female rock singer. Which band did she sing in?
hints: The band had a hit called “Bataillon d'Amour”.
The band's name is an English word.
The word means about the same as “goofy” or “foolish”.
questions.description: East German rock with a voice that could fill a stadium: nobody whispered here.
questions.fun_fact: Later, the actress Anna Loos took over as the band's singer.

questions.question: I’m from Augsburg, and my song “Auf uns” was playing everywhere in 2014 when Germany won the soccer World Cup. Who am I?
hints: My first hit was called “Nur in meinem Kopf”.
German TV channel ARD used my song for its World Cup coverage.
My first name is Andreas.
questions.description: A song for raising a toast, ideally with a trophy.
questions.fun_fact: “Auf uns” became the unofficial anthem of Germany’s World Cup win in Brazil.

questions.question: I came fourth in the first season of “The Voice of Germany” in 2012, and my song “80 Millionen” was everywhere during Euro 2016. Who am I?
hints: I’m from Baden-Württemberg.
Another hit of mine is called “Wenn sie tanzt”.
My first name is short for Maximilian.
questions.description: He doesn’t have 80 million friends, but at least he sang about them.
questions.fun_fact: The “80 million” in the title means the number of people living in Germany.

questions.question: After the Berlin Wall fell, Berlin's Tresor club brought in DJs from the city in the photo, seen as the birthplace of techno. Which city is it?
hints: The city is in the northern US, on the border with Canada.
Most American cars used to be built here.
Its nickname is “Motor City.”
questions.description: Berlin's Tresor always had friends with very heavy bass on the other side of the Atlantic.
questions.fun_fact: The techno pioneers from this city were huge fans of Kraftwerk from Düsseldorf, so the music later found its way back to Germany.

questions.question: In German youth slang, someone who embarrasses themselves badly gets “minus 1000…” what? It was the German youth word of 2024.
hints: The word existed long before the internet, for example among fortune tellers.
It describes a kind of glow or presence around a person.
The word has only four letters and starts and ends with A.
questions.description: An invisible score you lose faster than your phone charger.
questions.fun_fact: The German youth word of the year is chosen by the publisher Langenscheidt, and mostly teenagers themselves vote on it.

questions.question: Sido's real name is Paul Würdig, and Apache 207's is Volkan Yazıcı. What do you call a name like this that someone performs under?
hints: Actors and magicians often have one too.
It's on posters and album covers, not necessarily on your ID.
Its first word is the place where performers stand during a show.
questions.description: Paul and Volkan just didn't sound tough enough to them.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, you can even have your stage name added to your official ID card.

questions.question: This DJ from Osnabrück became famous worldwide in 2014 with remixes of “Waves” and “Prayer in C”. Who is in the photo?
hints: He is known for relaxed deep house with a summer feeling.
His last name is one of the most common in Germany.
His first name also belongs to Batman's sidekick.
questions.description: From Osnabrück straight onto playlists around the world, no change of trains needed.
questions.fun_fact: His remix of “Prayer in C” went to No. 1 in many countries, including the UK.

questions.question: Which composer created “Gesang der Jünglinge” (Song of the Youths) in 1956 at the WDR studio for electronic music in Cologne?
hints: He is seen as one of the most important pioneers of electronic music.
The Beatles put him on the cover of “Sgt. Pepper's”.
His last name begins with “Stock”.
questions.description: Long before laptops existed, people in Cologne built music out of vacuum tubes and cables.
questions.fun_fact: Stockhausen appears on the famous cover of the Beatles' “Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band”.

questions.question: Which rapper from near Stuttgart almost always performs wearing a panda mask?
hints: He became famous in 2012 with the song “Easy”.
He calls his music “Raop”, a mix of rap and pop.
His name has only three letters.
questions.description: Eating bamboo is optional, but the mask has to stay on.
questions.fun_fact: The mask is meant to let him go shopping or ride the train in daily life without being recognized.

questions.question: With which 1974 album did Kraftwerk make their breakthrough in the US?
hints: Its title track lasts over 20 minutes.
It was the band's fourth studio album and came out before the other three named here.
It's about a road that often has no speed limit.
questions.description: Four gentlemen from Düsseldorf who'd rather play with knobs than guitars.
questions.fun_fact: For radio, the title track of over 22 minutes was cut to about three, and that's how it got into the US charts.

questions.question: This word comes from German rap, became Jugendwort des Jahres in 2018 and has a female counterpart. What is an “Ehrenmann”?
wrong_answers: A person who likes to show off
A person who is never on time
A person with lots of money
hints: It's a compliment.
You say it when someone helps you without being asked.
Someone who gives you their last piece of gum is one.
questions.description: When parents use this word, all they usually get is an eye roll.
questions.fun_fact: The Jugendwort des Jahres (youth word of the year) was first chosen in 2008 by the publisher Langenscheidt.

questions.question: During big soccer tournaments, the Munich crew Blumentopf rapped match reports in rhyme. What were these called?
hints: The group was founded in Freising in the early ’90s.
The name is a pun on a type of journalistic piece.
Take the German word “Reportagen” (reports) and swap one part for “Rap”.
questions.description: When the commentator suddenly has a rhyme for every pass.
questions.fun_fact: In the ’90s, Blumentopf was one of the bands that made German rap from Munich known all over Germany.

questions.question: Which key nutrient found in meat can you also get from beans, lentils and chickpeas?
hints: Meat and eggs have this nutrient too.
Your body uses it to build and repair itself.
Athletes drink shakes full of it.
questions.description: Never eaten a burger in its life, and still nobody beats it in a race.
questions.fun_fact: Rice and beans eaten together give a more complete protein than either one eaten alone.

questions.question: Which artist made a famous rhinoceros woodcut in 1515 without ever having seen a rhino?
hints: He lived in Nuremberg.
He painted a famous self-portrait in a fur-trimmed coat.
His monogram is made of the letters A and D.
questions.description: An animal in a knight's armor, drawn from hearsay.
questions.fun_fact: The real rhino was on its way as a gift to the Pope, but in early 1516 its ship sank off the Italian coast.

questions.question: Sprinter Marcel Kittel won more Tour de France stages than any other German. How many stage wins was that?
hints: It's more than a handful.
In 2017 alone, he won five stages.
The number is between 12 and 16.
questions.description: A man who pedals faster in the final sprint than some mopeds can drive.
questions.fun_fact: Kittel won the first Tour stage in both 2013 and 2014, earning the right to wear the yellow jersey.

questions.question: “I come from the Ammersee and was a motorcycle world champion five times in the 1980s.” Who am I?
hints: I won titles in the 250 cc and 350 cc classes.
Most of the time I rode a green Kawasaki.
My nickname is the short form of Anton.
questions.description: Two wheels, one Bavarian lake and quite a lot of noise in the eighties.
questions.fun_fact: Mang won his first titles on a Kawasaki, but his last one, in 1987, on a Honda.

questions.question: Rudolf Caracciola drove Silver Arrows for Mercedes in the 1930s. What nickname did he get for being almost unbeatable in certain weather?
hints: He was European Grand Prix champion three times.
When others drove carefully, he stepped on the gas.
On a wet track, he was the best.
questions.description: A Silver Arrow driver whom the weather could never rattle.
questions.fun_fact: In 1938, Caracciola raced at over 430 km/h (267 mph) on the autobahn near Frankfurt, a record on a public road for decades.

questions.question: “In 1991, I beat Boris Becker in the Wimbledon final.” Who am I?
hints: I come from northern Germany.
In 1993, I won the ATP World Championship in Frankfurt.
My last name is the German word for what a bee does to you.
questions.description: A tennis final that Germany was guaranteed to win.
questions.fun_fact: A year after that final, Stich and Becker won Olympic doubles gold together in Barcelona.

questions.question: Pattex has been around for decades, belongs to Henkel and sits as a tube in many toolboxes. What do you use it for?
hints: You often need it when something has broken.
Hobbyists use it on wood, leather or rubber.
It's a relative of the Pritt stick, only much stronger.
questions.description: A toolbox classic, right next to the long-lost Allen wrench.
questions.fun_fact: The Pritt stick and the laundry detergent Persil also belong to Henkel.

questions.question: What does the store chain Deichmann mainly sell?
hints: It has things for kids, women and men in lots of sizes.
When trying things on there, you often sit on small stools.
You can also get sneakers, boots and sandals there.
questions.description: A store whose sign hangs in almost every German pedestrian zone.
questions.fun_fact: Heinrich Deichmann opened a small shoemaker's workshop in Essen in 1913, and it grew into Europe's biggest shoe retailer.

questions.question: On many German autobahns, a “Richtgeschwindigkeit” applies. What does that mean?
wrong_answers: A top speed for trucks only
hints: It applies wherever there is no speed limit sign.
If there's an accident, driving too fast can still count against you.
It's only advice, not a law with a fine.
questions.description: The German autobahn: where your speed easily becomes a question of character.
questions.fun_fact: Courts have ruled that drivers going faster than 130 km/h (about 80 mph) can share the blame for an accident.

questions.question: What is this kind of bike called, often used in German cities to carry kids or groceries?
hints: It has lots of room at the front or back.
Many cities pay part of the price when you buy one.
Its name tells you it carries loads.
questions.description: The SUV of bicycles, minus the hunt for a parking spot.
questions.fun_fact: In the Netherlands this kind of cargo bike is called a “bakfiets”, which means roughly “box bike”.

questions.question: What kind of train is in this photo?
hints: Nobody rides on this train except the driver.
Its cars have no windows.
It carries containers, cars or wood.
questions.description: Deutsche Bahn offers more than just delays.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, a freight train can be up to 740 m (about 2,430 ft) long.

questions.question: In many sushi restaurants, the “wasabi” is really a different spicy root dyed green. Which one?
hints: It grows underground and gets really hot when you grate it.
In Europe it goes into sauces served with meat.
Its name puts a small red salad vegetable together with a farm animal.
questions.description: An impostor hiding out in sushi restaurants.
questions.fun_fact: Real wasabi is so expensive and rare that even in Japan many restaurants serve the imitation.

questions.question: Victoria Carl and Katharina Hennig won Olympic gold together in cross-country skiing at Beijing 2022. In which event?
hints: The event is fairly short and fast.
Each skier goes out on the course several times, taking turns.
It is the team version of a short-distance race.
questions.description: Cross-country skiing: the sport where walking uphill counts as a top performance.
questions.fun_fact: Back in 2010 in Vancouver, Claudia Nystad and Evi Sachenbacher-Stehle had already won this event for Germany.

questions.question: I come from a musical. Before every Dortmund home game, tens of thousands sing me, holding up their scarves. Which song am I?
hints: The band Gerry and the Pacemakers made me famous in the 1960s.
I'm also the fans' anthem in Liverpool.
I begin with “When you walk through a storm …”.
questions.description: Goosebumps guaranteed, tissues recommended.
questions.fun_fact: The song comes from the 1945 Broadway musical “Carousel”.

questions.question: He surprisingly won the German title with VfL Wolfsburg in 2009 and was known for brutal medicine ball workouts. Who is he?
hints: As a player, he was a star at Hamburger SV.
In 1983, his goal won the European Cup for Hamburg.
His players called him “Quälix” (from “quälen”, to torment).
questions.description: A coach whose contracts came with free sore muscles.
questions.fun_fact: As Bayern Munich coach, Magath won both the league and the German Cup in 2005 and again in 2006.

questions.question: Manuel Neuer became a world champion in 2014 and is seen as one of the best ever in his position. Which position made him famous?
hints: He usually stands far back.
He is very tall, almost 1.93 m (6 ft 4 in).
His spot is right in front of the net.
questions.description: A world champion whose job puts him in the spotlight for 22 people at once.
questions.fun_fact: Manuel Neuer often came far out of his goal and played almost like an extra outfield player.

questions.question: Dortmund vs. Schalke: two neighboring cities, yellow fans against blue fans, and the match is called the “Revierderby”. Where does the “Revier” come from?
questions.answer: From the Ruhr area and its coal mines
hints: It has to do with the region both clubs come from.
Lots of miners used to work there.
People also call the region “Kohlenpott”.
questions.description: A neighborhood feud with 80,000 people watching.
questions.fun_fact: Schalke's nickname “Knappen” is an old word for miners.

questions.question: In this song the thrush and the blackbird play the lead roles, everyone sings “Fidiralala” and the eagle owl shuts the shutters. What is it called?
wrong_answers: Kuckuck, Kuckuck, ruft’s aus dem Wald
hints: It is an old folk song often sung in kindergarten.
The party takes place “in dem grünen Walde” (in the green forest).
The thrush is the groom and the blackbird is the bride.
questions.description: A song with more birds in it than a bird feeder in winter.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Vogelhochzeit” has lots of verses, and in almost every one a different bird brings something to the party.

questions.question: In the lap-bouncing rhyme “Ri-ra-rutsch”, you ride “mit der Kutsch”. What is a Kutsche?
hints: Long ago, kings and princesses rode in one.
People used it to travel overland from town to town.
The animals up front neigh.
questions.description: A ride that never needs a gas station, and still gets you there.
questions.fun_fact: In the rhyme you also ride the “Schneckenpost” (a coach as slow as a snail), where it “keinen Pfennig kost’”: slow, but it doesn't cost a penny.

questions.question: This short German song is sung to honor someone, and it ends with a triple cheer. What is it called?
wrong_answers: Wie schön, dass du geboren bist
hints: It's sung not only on birthdays but also at anniversaries.
While it's sung, the guests often clink their glasses.
The title wishes the person a long life.
questions.description: A song that makes the birthday child forget for a moment that they're getting older.
questions.fun_fact: The song is also popular at weddings, anniversaries and award ceremonies: all that matters is that someone is being celebrated.

questions.question: Kasperl and Seppel are the heroes of a children's book series by Otfried Preußler. Which robber do they chase?
hints: The robber stole Grandmother's coffee grinder.
He carries a pepper pistol and seven knives.
His name ends in “plotz”.
questions.description: Two boys against one villain: sounds unfair, and it is – for the villain.
questions.fun_fact: When you turn the stolen coffee grinder, it plays the song “Alles neu macht der Mai” (“May Makes Everything New”).

questions.question: In “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban,” how many years did Peter Pettigrew hide as Scabbers, the Weasleys' pet rat?
hints: A normal rat lives about 3 years, and Scabbers lived much longer.
It's the same amount of time Sirius Black spent in Azkaban.
It's more than ten years, but less than 15.
questions.description: The oldest pet in the wizarding world, and not because of a healthy diet.
questions.fun_fact: Lupin learned that Pettigrew was still alive when he saw his name moving on the Marauder's Map.

questions.question: “I have long ears, I'm all blue, and I sing and dance with the littlest viewers on kids' TV. Who am I?”
hints: We're looking for a cartoon character for preschool kids.
This animal hops and likes carrots.
The name contains the name of the TV channel.
questions.description: Long ears, a big head and a good mood even before breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The children's channel KiKA has been on the air since January 1, 1997.

questions.question: I was born in Masuria in 1926, wrote “So zärtlich war Suleyken” and became an honorary citizen of Hamburg. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the most widely read storytellers of the postwar years.
In 1988 I received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade.
In my best-known novel, Siggi has to write an essay on “The Joys of Duty.”
questions.description: A Hamburger with an East Prussian filling.
questions.fun_fact: After Lenz died in 2014, his early novel “Der Überläufer” (The Turncoat), which he had held back for decades, was published in 2016.

questions.question: I stitched “Seven at one blow” on my belt, but I had only swatted flies. Who am I?
hints: I'm small, but very sure of myself.
I trick two giants.
My tools are a needle and thread.
questions.description: Bragging at the highest level, and all because of a sweet breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The hero beats one giant by squeezing cheese instead of a stone and letting a bird fly off as his “throwing stone.”

questions.question: The youngest little goat hid inside me, and it was the only one the wolf didn't find. What am I?
hints: I stand in the mother goat's living room.
I'm hollow inside and just big enough for a small goat.
I tick and strike every hour.
questions.description: The best hiding place in the whole house, even better than under the bed.
questions.fun_fact: In the end, the wolf falls into the well with his belly full of heavy stones.

questions.question: What does the Cologne saying “Et kütt wie et kütt” mean?
questions.answer: It comes the way it comes
wrong_answers: It cools the way it cools
It works the way it works
It cooks the way it cooks
hints: The saying is an attitude to life: stay relaxed.
It's part of the so-called “Kölsches Grundgesetz” (Cologne's basic law).
The idea: there's no point worrying about what the future brings.
questions.description: A saying from the city where even the cathedral secretly sways along at Carnival.
questions.fun_fact: In Kölsch, a “g” often turns into a “j”: “gut” (good) becomes “jot”.

questions.question: The word comes from Low German (Plattdeutsch). What is a “Klönschnack”?
hints: You can't eat it or drink it.
All you need for it is time and an open mouth.
It's a relaxed talk about anything and everything.
questions.description: Up north the wind blows so hard that even a “Moin” arrives sideways.
questions.fun_fact: Up north, “klönen” means to chat cozily and “schnacken” just means to talk, so a Klönschnack is talking twice over.

questions.question: Which of these baked goods does NOT taste sweet?
hints: People like to eat three of them as a dessert or treat.
In Bavaria, people like to eat the one you're looking for with Weißwurst.
It's twisted into a knot and sprinkled with coarse salt.
questions.description: The bakery smells of breakfast, school break and afternoon coffee.
questions.fun_fact: A Laugenbrezel gets its brown crust from a quick dip in lye before baking.

questions.question: In the Bavarian Forest, someone says: “I geh in d'Schwammerl.” Who is talking?
hints: This person needs no rifle and no saw.
They're looking for something that loves to pop out of the ground after rain.
Chanterelles and porcini end up in their basket.
questions.description: Someone is out in the woods, and looking pretty far down.
questions.fun_fact: “Schwammerl” is the Bavarian diminutive of “Schwamm”, an old German word for mushroom.

questions.question: German Film Award – cinema. Grimme Award – …?
hints: The award has nothing to do with the Brothers Grimm.
It is presented every year in Marl.
Winners include series and documentaries, for example.
questions.description: An award whose name sounds like fairy tales, but it doesn't tell any.
questions.fun_fact: The award is named after Adolf Grimme, the first director general of the broadcaster NWDR (Northwest German Broadcasting).

questions.question: I'm Sinestro, Green Lantern's great enemy, and I wear a yellow ring. What emotion gives my ring its power?
hints: The green ring runs on willpower.
Scarecrow, one of Batman's enemies, also uses this emotion as a weapon.
My followers scare people to grow stronger.
questions.description: A villain so vain he grew a movie-star mustache and put on a ring the color of a baby chick.
questions.fun_fact: Before he turned villain, Sinestro was a Green Lantern himself and even trained Hal Jordan.

questions.question: What was the name of the comedy show that made Kaya Yanar famous in the early 2000s?
hints: The show aired on Sat.1.
Its characters included Hakan the bouncer and Ranjid from India.
The title asks a question about looking at someone.
questions.description: A comedian who played more roles in a single show than a whole city theater.
questions.fun_fact: Kaya Yanar was born in Frankfurt am Main in 1973.

questions.question: “From 1948 I was East Germany's state retail chain. I owned supermarkets, department stores and even restaurants. You paid in East marks.” Who am I?
hints: My name sounds more like a government office than a store.
I wasn't a cooperative; I belonged directly to the state.
My abbreviation has exactly two letters.
questions.description: A store where the state didn't just govern, it also sat at the checkout.
questions.fun_fact: At first, the HO sold goods without ration cards, at much higher prices, to pull money away from the black market.

questions.question: Singer and actor Dean Reed lived in East Germany from the 1970s. Which of these is NOT true about him?
questions.answer: He won the Eurovision Song Contest.
wrong_answers: He came from the United States.
hints: He was a star in Eastern Europe but barely known in the West.
Among other films, he made “Blutsbrüder” with Gojko Mitić.
East Germany never took part in the contest mentioned in one of the options.
questions.description: A star who crossed the Wall from the wrong side, at least in most people's eyes.
questions.fun_fact: Dean Reed was born in Denver and was so famous in the Soviet Union that he played to huge stadium crowds there.

questions.question: The abbreviation “USSR” stood for the country whose soldiers were stationed in East Germany. What did it stand for?
wrong_answers: Union of Socialist States of Russia
hints: It was the largest country on Earth and broke apart in 1991.
The Russian word “soviet” means “council.”
The state ideology sits right before “Republics” in the name.
questions.description: The big brother who didn’t just come to visit, but stayed for decades.
questions.fun_fact: The last Russian soldiers did not leave Germany until 1994.

questions.question: In East Germany, each neighborhood had its own Volkspolizei officer who knew the residents well. What was his German title?
hints: The title was so long that almost everyone just used three letters.
He walked his area, knew the people in each building and checked residents' registrations.
For short, people called him “ABV”.
questions.description: A police officer who knew your stairwell better than the building's caretaker.
questions.fun_fact: The ABV also checked the Hausbuch, a building's guest book where visitors staying more than three days had to sign in.

questions.question: There's a notification card from Deutsche Post in your mailbox. What is it telling you?
questions.answer: A package is waiting for you
hints: The slip is usually yellow.
The carrier rang your bell earlier, but no one answered.
You have to take your ID to the post office or a Packstation.
questions.description: Mail about mail: practically a poem.
questions.fun_fact: At DHL, a package that couldn't be delivered usually waits seven working days to be picked up.

questions.question: Jafar's parrot in “Aladdin” has the same name as the traitor in Shakespeare's “Othello”. What is that name?
hints: He is a red parrot who never stops talking.
The name is an old form of James.
It has four letters, starting with “I” and ending with “O”.
questions.description: A name so sneaky that Shakespeare used it first, and then someone gave it to a parrot.
questions.fun_fact: Comedian Gilbert Gottfried voiced Iago in the 1992 film, and Alan Tudyk voiced him in the 2019 remake.

questions.question: In 1883, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck pushed through a law for workers. What did it give them for the first time?
hints: Workers and employers paid into it together.
To this day, nearly every employee has a contribution taken from their pay for it.
Anyone who fell ill now had the doctor, medicine and sick pay covered.
questions.description: A chancellor with a mustache who handed out a surprisingly modern gift.
questions.fun_fact: Accident insurance (1884) and pension insurance (1889) soon followed, which is why Germany is seen as the birthplace of social insurance.

questions.question: Every yellow Deutsche Post mailbox shows a horn. What was this horn blown for in the past?
hints: This was common long before cars and railways.
Anyone who heard the horn knew something important was about to happen in town.
People were meant to know that letters and passengers were about to arrive.
questions.description: A musical instrument that made a career as a company logo.
questions.fun_fact: Austria's postal service still has a post horn in its logo, too.

questions.question: Out in the countryside, it sells its own eggs and potatoes, and you often pay into an honesty box. What is this shop called?
hints: Here the farmer does the selling.
The goods often come from the field next door.
The first part of its name is the German word for a farmyard.
questions.description: The trip from hen to breakfast egg can hardly get any shorter.
questions.fun_fact: Some farms have vending machines where you can buy fresh milk or eggs around the clock.

questions.question: In a German supermarket, a sign says “SB-Kasse”. What does the “SB” stand for?
hints: There are SB gas stations and SB car washes too.
Nobody helps you; you do it all yourself.
The word starts with “Selbst”.
questions.description: A checkout where the line somehow never gets any shorter.
questions.fun_fact: Many self-checkouts use a scale to check that what you put down really is the product you scanned.

questions.question: German license plates have a “D” in a blue strip on the left. How many stars form a circle above it?
hints: They are the stars of the European flag.
The number has nothing to do with how many countries there are.
That's how many months a year has.
questions.description: A starry sky that races down the Autobahn every day.
questions.fun_fact: The twelve stars of the European flag stand for perfection, and their number doesn't change when new countries join.

questions.question: Complete the famous saying of Germany coach Sepp Herberger: “After the game is …”
hints: Herberger coached the 1954 world champions.
It means you shouldn't rest on a win.
The idea: as soon as one game ends, preparing for the next one begins.
questions.description: Soccer wisdom is like bratwurst: simple, but everyone has an opinion on it.
questions.fun_fact: Herberger is also behind “The ball is round” and “A game lasts 90 minutes.”

questions.question: Hamburg band Helloween's album “Keeper of the Seven Keys” is seen as a pioneer of power metal. When did Part 1 come out?
hints: It was the age of perms and cassette players.
The Neue Deutsche Welle peaked in the same decade.
The Berlin Wall fell two years later.
questions.description: Pumpkins on the cover, screaming vocals in your ears and Hamburg in its heart.
questions.fun_fact: The band's name is a pun mixing “Halloween” and “hell.”

questions.question: Which Berlin rapper is known for martial arts and lyrics about discipline and never giving up?
hints: His songs are often played at the gym.
One of his albums is called “Erfolg ist kein Glück” (Success Isn't Luck).
His name sounds like he's up against something.
questions.description: He trains his muscles as hard as his rhymes.
questions.fun_fact: Kontra K's real name is Maximilian Diehn.

questions.question: Loud techno, dancing until morning, often in old warehouses or power plants in Berlin: what is this kind of party called?
hints: Parties like this first boomed in Britain in the late 1980s.
The Love Parade was basically a giant one out on the streets.
The word has only four letters and rhymes with “wave”.
questions.description: Sleep can wait until Monday.
questions.fun_fact: In English, “to rave” first meant to rant wildly, long before anyone used it for dancing all night.

questions.question: “Läuft bei dir!” was Germany's youth word of the year in 2014 and is often said sarcastically too. What does it mean?
hints: It's actually meant as praise.
You say it when someone is doing great.
Said sarcastically, it's what you say when someone has just dropped their ice cream.
questions.description: A phrase said so often that it ended up winning a title.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has picked a youth word of the year since 2008, and these days young people vote online for the winner.

questions.question: For long stretches of the Middle Rhine there are no bridges. How do cars and bikes get to the other bank there?
hints: Between Wiesbaden and Koblenz, not a single bridge crosses the Rhine.
You drive your car onto it and drive off again on the other bank.
Its name rhymes with “merry”.
questions.description: The Rhine is too wide to jump and too cold to swim, so luckily there's a plan C.
questions.fun_fact: In Basel, some Rhine ferries cross with no motor at all: they hang from a cable, and the current alone pushes them to the other bank.

questions.question: You're standing in the woods and a voice calls: “Nibble, nibble, little mouse, who is nibbling at my house?” Which fairy tale are you in?
hints: The fairy tale comes from the Brothers Grimm.
Two siblings are the main characters.
The two of them drop breadcrumbs to find their way back home.
questions.description: When you live alone in the woods, you rarely get such hungry visitors.
questions.fun_fact: In the fairy tale, the children answer: “The wind, the wind, the heavenly child.”

questions.question: The German saying “alles über einen Kamm scheren” (to shear everything over one comb) most likely comes from which trade?
hints: Every medieval town had people doing this job.
These craftsmen often ran a bathhouse on the side.
Today we would mostly call this job a hairdresser.
questions.description: Treating every customer exactly the same doesn't always earn you bigger tips.
questions.fun_fact: In the Middle Ages, bathhouse keepers and barbers ran public baths and even treated wounds.
