questions.question: A school fair classic: you run lap after lap, and for each one, Grandma or the neighbors give money to a good cause. What is it called?
hints: Beforehand, you collect names and amounts on a list.
The people giving the money back you without running themselves.
Soccer clubs have backers like these on the front of their shirts.
questions.description: Lap after lap, until the sneakers are smoking and the teachers are clapping.
questions.fun_fact: A single sponsored run often raises several thousand euros for one school.

questions.question: First graders get a giant cone, the second graders put on a play, and all the parents film it. Which celebration is this?
hints: It usually takes place in August or September.
For the kids, it's a brand-new start.
Afterwards, you're officially a schoolkid.
questions.description: A party where grandmas need more tissues than at a wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The Schultüte has been around for about 200 years and first became popular in Saxony and Thuringia.

questions.question: At the ping-pong table, each kid hits the ball once, then runs to the other side. Miss, and you're out. What is the game called?
hints: At the end, two players are left for the final.
Everyone is on the move the whole time.
You keep running in a circle around the table.
questions.description: A game where you cover more miles than you score points.
questions.fun_fact: In some regions, the game is also called “Chinesisch” (Chinese).

questions.question: At a German university, what do you call the newcomers who have just started their studies?
hints: A German academic year has two halves: winter and summer.
They get their own orientation week.
For short, they're also called “Erstis”.
questions.description: Between the lecture hall, the Mensa and the shared-apartment party, there's one word you learn by October at the latest.
questions.fun_fact: At most German universities, the winter semester starts on October 1, and at many Fachhochschulen (universities of applied sciences) as early as September.

questions.question: What does NOT appear in the story “Jim Knopf und Lukas der Lokomotivführer” (Jim Button and Luke the Engine Driver)?
hints: Michael Ende also wrote “The Neverending Story”.
Lukas is an engine driver, and his locomotive is called Emma.
Frau Mahlzahn is a dragon, and Lummerland is a tiny island.
questions.description: Michael Ende sent two friends on a trip you can't book at any travel agency.
questions.fun_fact: The Augsburger Puppenkiste puppet theater brought Jim Knopf to TV with marionettes as early as 1961.

questions.question: A hospital is to a medical drama as a … is to “Schloss Einstein”?
hints: The series is about teenagers.
The characters study there, and they live there too.
It's a school with bedrooms.
questions.description: Fights, flirting and making up again, all with a view of the castle.
questions.fun_fact: “Schloss Einstein” has been running since 1998 and now has more than 1,000 episodes.

questions.question: The Sandmännchen comes on TV every evening. What comes next for many children?
hints: It's usually already dark outside.
Before it, you brush your teeth.
His sand is meant to make you sleepy.
questions.description: A little man with a pointy beard who has been more punctual than any train for decades.
questions.fun_fact: “Unser Sandmännchen” started on East German TV in 1959 and is still on the air today.

questions.question: Since 1998, I have been the main character of the hospital series “In aller Freundschaft” and work at the Sachsenklinik. Who am I?
hints: I am a surgeon.
I am played by Thomas Rühmann.
My last name suits my job: “heilen” is German for “to heal.”
questions.description: A man in a white coat who has worked his shifts in Leipzig longer than any real doctor.
questions.fun_fact: “In aller Freundschaft” has been on the air since 1998 and even has spin-offs such as “Die jungen Ärzte” and “Die Krankenschwestern.”

questions.question: I'm square, I have short arms and legs, and I'm almost always in a bad mood. On KiKA I often shout “Mist!” Who am I?
hints: I'd just like to be left alone.
I have two friends: Chili the sheep and Briegel the bush.
You can buy me at the bakery, luckily not quite as grumpy.
questions.description: Celebrities who never sign autographs, and yet every child knows them.
questions.fun_fact: Bernd das Brot even won the Grimme Prize in 2004, though he surely wasn't happy about it.

questions.question: Since 1999, I've asked questions on RTL that can win you a million. Lifelines like 50:50 help out. Who am I?
hints: I live in Potsdam.
I also hosted “stern TV” for many years.
My last name rhymes with the German word “Bauch” (belly).
questions.description: A man who has spent decades asking questions as if he had no clue himself.
questions.fun_fact: The first million winner, in 2000, was history professor Eckhard Freise.

questions.question: After soccer practice, you've got real “Kohldampf”. What does that mean?
hints: Kohldampf has nothing to do with coal (Kohle) or steam (Dampf).
It describes how your body feels, not your mood.
When you have Kohldampf, your stomach growls.
questions.description: Sounds like a steam train in a coal cellar, but it's something else entirely.
questions.fun_fact: “Kohldampf” comes from Rotwelsch, an old secret language of travelers on the road, where “Kohler” and “Dampf” both already meant hunger.

questions.question: Researchers found the short word “Hä?” in similar forms in languages all over the world. What does it mean?
hints: People often say it when it's very loud.
Afterwards, the other person usually repeats what they said.
A more polite way would be “Pardon?”
questions.description: Maybe the most international word that isn't in any schoolbook.
questions.fun_fact: In 2015, language researchers won an Ig Nobel Prize for finding that “Huh?” exists almost everywhere. It's a prize for research that first makes people laugh, then makes them think.

questions.question: It's black, red and gold, has the federal eagle on a shield in the middle, and only federal authorities may fly it. What is it called?
hints: It doesn't belong to one single person or army unit.
The plain version without the eagle may be flown by anyone.
Its name says it is there for the work of the federal government.
questions.description: Black, red and gold for advanced players: not everyone may run this one up the flagpole.
questions.fun_fact: Using the federal service flag without permission counts as an administrative offense in Germany.

questions.question: At a knights' tournament, who called out the knights and had to recognize all their coats of arms?
hints: He needed a loud voice.
He also announced the king's messages.
The study of coats of arms is named after him.
questions.description: Medieval contest of strength: whoever is still on the horse at the end wins.
questions.fun_fact: Heralds often wore a tunic with their lord's coat of arms, so everyone could see who they spoke for.

questions.question: I stand at the very top of a donkey, a dog and a cat and make noise until the robbers run away. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the Town Musicians of Bremen.
I have a red comb on my head.
In the morning I call “cock-a-doodle-doo”.
questions.description: Sitting at the very top of the most animal-packed tower in German fairy tales.
questions.fun_fact: In Bremen, people say touching the front legs of the bronze Town Musicians donkey brings you good luck.

questions.question: North Sea tides reach far inland through the mouth of the Elbe. In which big city does the Elbe rise and fall twice a day because of this?
hints: The city is only a little over 100 km (60 miles) from the North Sea.
Huge container ships sail up the Elbe all the way to this city.
This is home to the Fischmarkt and the Elbphilharmonie.
questions.description: A river that forgets which way it's supposed to flow twice a day.
questions.fun_fact: Because the Elbe has been dredged deeper again and again, the gap between low and high tide is now even bigger in Hamburg than in Cuxhaven at the river's mouth.

questions.question: It is Germany's largest predator, has white pups in winter and loves lying on the Düne island off Helgoland. Which animal is it?
hints: This animal lives in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
It is a close relative of the harbor seal, but much bigger.
Its English name is also a color.
questions.description: It lies around lazily on the beach all day and still holds an impressive title.
questions.fun_fact: A male gray seal can weigh over 300 kilograms (660 lb), as much as four adults.

questions.question: Complete this: “Bowser is to Super Mario Bros. as M. Bison is to…”
hints: It's a one-on-one fighting video game.
Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li are characters in this game.
One of its fighters shouts “Hadouken!”
questions.description: A final boss in a red cape and military cap who won't even let you win at rock, paper, scissors.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, M. Bison is called Vega, and the name M. Bison belongs to the boxer there.

questions.question: I'm made of concrete or stone, I stand across a valley and hold back a whole lake. The Sauerland has lots of me. What am I?
hints: Behind me there is often drinking water for whole cities.
Hydropower can be made inside me.
Beavers build a small version of me out of sticks.
questions.description: A structure whose life motto is: “Nobody gets through here!”
questions.fun_fact: The Ruhr region gets a large share of its drinking water from reservoirs in the Sauerland.

questions.question: Which of these East Frisian Islands is NOT car-free?
hints: Of the four, this island has the most residents.
It is considered Germany's oldest North Sea resort.
Its name starts with the compass direction where it lies.
questions.description: On some islands, the fastest way to get around is a horse in a bad mood.
questions.fun_fact: The singer Lale Andersen, famous for “Lili Marleen”, lived on Langeoog and is buried there.

questions.question: On the North Sea coast, the babies of one animal are called “Heuler” (howlers). What does a Heuler grow up to be?
hints: This animal lives in the Wadden Sea.
It swims and dives well and hunts fish.
Its German name means “sea dog”.
questions.description: A baby that calls for its mom so loudly that it got named after it.
questions.fun_fact: At the seal station in Friedrichskoog, abandoned Heuler pups are nursed back to health and later released into the sea.

questions.question: In the 19th century, the Baden engineer Johann Gottfried Tulla had the Upper Rhine straightened. What was one result?
questions.answer: Swamp fever disappeared from the Rhine valley
wrong_answers: Salmon became more common in the Rhine
hints: Many side channels and islands of the old river landscape disappeared.
Wet floodplains and marshes turned into dry farmland.
Mosquitoes had few places left to breed, and a disease known today from the tropics went away.
questions.description: An engineer who wanted to cure a river of its wiggling habit.
questions.fun_fact: Tulla's straightening made the Rhine about 80 km (50 miles) shorter between Basel and Worms.

questions.question: The Wupper river flows through Wuppertal, right under the suspension railway. What does the German saying „über die Wupper gehen“ mean?
questions.answer: To break down or go bust
hints: It's nothing you'd wish for.
People say it about a company or an old cell phone, for example.
It's a bit like “going down the drain.”
questions.description: A small river with a big career in the German language.
questions.fun_fact: The Wuppertal suspension railway has been running since 1901 and hangs right above the river for long stretches.

questions.question: This lake lay on the inner-German border, is now a UNESCO biosphere reserve and, at just over 70 m (230 ft), is northern Germany's deepest lake. Which one?
hints: It lies between Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Because of the border, its nature stayed almost untouched for decades.
Its name sounds like the German word for the peel of a fruit.
questions.description: A lake that used to be watched by two countries at the same time.
questions.fun_fact: Because the border zone was off-limits in GDR times, rare animals like white-tailed eagles and cranes could settle there undisturbed.

questions.question: The dam wall of the Rappbode Dam in the Harz mountains is the tallest in Germany. About how tall is it?
hints: It is much taller than an ordinary house.
Cologne Cathedral, at 157 meters (515 ft), is taller still.
It is about as tall as a 30-story high-rise.
questions.description: A wall that even the biggest bathtub in the Harz can't push over.
questions.fun_fact: One of the world's longest pedestrian suspension bridges, the “Titan-RT”, spans the Rappbode Dam.

questions.question: You take a boat on the Oder and keep going downstream. Which sea do you reach at the end?
hints: The Oder forms part of the border between Germany and Poland.
Just before the end, it flows through the Szczecin Lagoon.
The islands of Usedom and Rügen also lie on this sea.
questions.description: A border river that knows exactly where it's going.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has two cities called Frankfurt, which is why one of them is called “Frankfurt (Oder)”.

questions.question: When Lake Edersee in northern Hesse runs low, old walls and a stone bridge appear. What was there before the reservoir?
hints: The reservoir was built in the early 20th century.
The dam was meant to slow floods and supply water for shipping on the Weser.
Some people call the remains “Edersee Atlantis.”
questions.description: A lake that can't keep its secrets to itself by late summer.
questions.fun_fact: When the water is low, you can walk across the Asel Bridge without getting your feet wet, even though it usually lies deep underwater.

questions.question: Which of these German states does NOT have its own Wadden Sea National Park?
hints: The mudflats dry out twice a day at low tide.
Even a city-state has a Wadden Sea national park around the island of Neuwerk.
The state you're looking for lies only on the Baltic Sea.
questions.description: Three states share the mud, and one just watches with envy.
questions.fun_fact: The Wadden Sea, from Denmark to the Netherlands, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, just like the Grand Canyon.

questions.question: We are the Borg from “Star Trek”: we travel in a cube-shaped ship and always say “Resistance is futile.” What do we want to do to you?
hints: We are half living beings, half machines.
For us, the word “I” doesn't exist: there is only “we.”
We would give you implants so you think exactly like us.
questions.description: Space neighbors who aren't here to borrow sugar, or to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: The Borg Queen first appeared in the 1996 movie “Star Trek: First Contact.”

questions.question: Why were lakes like the Brombachsee built in Middle Franconia from the 1970s on?
questions.answer: To move water from the Danube basin to northern Bavaria
wrong_answers: To store drinking water for Munich
For the sailing events of the 1972 Olympics
To flood old brown coal pits
hints: The north of Bavaria is much drier than the south.
Rivers like the Regnitz and the Main often ran low in summer.
The water is moved across the European watershed.
questions.description: Swimming lakes with a side job the vacationers know nothing about.
questions.fun_fact: Danube water is also pumped north through the Main-Danube Canal, uphill over the watershed.

questions.question: In the photo, boats are sitting high and dry on the mud. What will bring the water back in a few hours?
hints: This happens every day on the North Sea coast.
It comes about twice a day.
It is the opposite of low tide.
questions.description: Boats taking an unplanned lunch break.
questions.fun_fact: About 12 and a half hours pass between two high tides, so high tide comes a little later each day.

questions.question: When something is utterly silly, Germans say „Da lachen ja die …“ (“That makes the … laugh”). Which animals are missing?
hints: These animals live on a farm.
They have feathers.
They cluck and lay eggs.
questions.description: Some animals have a better sense of humor than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: Chickens can make about two dozen different sounds.

questions.question: This phrase came out of German youth slang around 1980, means “can't be bothered,” and gave a whole generation its name. Which is it?
hints: It is made of two words.
Newspapers and magazines in the early 1980s used it to describe a whole frustrated youth.
The first word is German for zero; the second is also the word for a male goat.
questions.description: The favorite phrase of everyone who doesn't feel like mowing the lawn on Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: Germans still say “Bock haben” when they're in the mood for something.

questions.question: Germans say it about someone who doesn't seem very bright, and it has a small number in it. Which saying is it?
hints: It's about counting.
Even kindergarten kids can do it.
The number is between two and four.
questions.description: Sadly, no amount of math tutoring will help here.
questions.fun_fact: In experiments, crows can tell small amounts apart, so in a way they really can count to three.

questions.question: Which German exclamation means roughly the same as „Ich glaub, mich tritt ein Pferd!“?
hints: You shout both of them with wide eyes.
It's all about pure amazement.
The animal in the answer makes a sound it can't really make.
questions.description: Horses rarely kick anyone in real life, but in German they do it all the time.
questions.fun_fact: German has lots of ways to say you're amazed, such as „Ich glaub, ich steh im Wald!“ (“I think I'm standing in the forest!”).

questions.question: People often say “Abwarten und Tee trinken” when someone is getting worked up. What does the saying really advise?
questions.answer: Stay patient until things clear up
wrong_answers: Drink plenty when you have a cold
hints: Rushing is out of place here.
It isn't about the drink at all.
What's needed is the opposite of impatience.
questions.description: Advice that only needs you to boil some water.
questions.fun_fact: The East Frisians are among the biggest tea drinkers in the world.

questions.question: Many German fairy tales end with „Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind …“ (“And if they haven't died …”). How does the line go on?
wrong_answers: “… then they still live in the castle.”
hints: It's about the present.
The fairy tale is meant to reach all the way to our time.
The opposite of “died” is hidden in it.
questions.description: The happy ending with a built-in back door.
questions.fun_fact: The line leaves it open whether the fairy-tale characters might still be living somewhere in the world.

questions.question: If you practice something again and again, you get really good at it. How does the German saying “Übung macht den …” end?
hints: It's a title for people who know their trade inside out.
In the skilled trades, you have to pass an exam to earn it.
In the Bundesliga, every club wants to finish the season as one.
questions.description: Piano practice drives the neighbors crazy, but this saying is on your side.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, craftsmen had to make a “Meisterstück” (masterpiece) before they could call themselves a Meister.

questions.question: What does the German saying “Kommt Zeit, kommt Rat” mean?
questions.answer: Given time, a solution will turn up.
wrong_answers: Whoever comes late gets no advice.
Time is worth more than any advice.
Good advice always takes a long time.
hints: The saying is meant to cheer you up.
It tells you not to panic.
Some problems solve themselves if you just wait a little.
questions.description: The saying for everyone who puts off their homework until tomorrow.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Rat” once also meant “supplies” or “means”: the things you need to live.

questions.question: In a German saying, someone who won't get to the point creeps like which animal around the hot porridge?
hints: This animal often lives in people's homes.
It likes to wash itself, and takes its time doing it.
It purrs.
questions.description: The porridge is hot, patience is short, and nobody dares to go near it.
questions.fun_fact: In English, people don't creep around porridge, they “beat around the bush” instead.

questions.question: With a Ferienpass, kids get cheap entry to outdoor pools, the zoo or craft classes over summer vacation. Who usually issues it?
hints: A Ferienpass from Cologne isn't valid in Munich.
All the activities are close to where you live.
You can often pick it up at the town hall or citizens' office.
questions.description: Six weeks of boredom? There's actually a special ID card for that.
questions.fun_fact: Many Ferienpass activities are run by local clubs and volunteers who set up classes just for it.

questions.question: You get your class test back, and under it is the worst grade there is up to 10th grade. Which number is it?
hints: In Germany, 1 is the best grade.
A 5 means “mangelhaft” (poor), but it gets even worse.
This grade is called “ungenügend” (unsatisfactory).
questions.description: Nobody wants to see this number under their work, no matter what color the ink is.
questions.fun_fact: In the last years of high school, grades become points from 0 to 15, and there 15 is the best.

questions.question: You go to a Realschule, finish 10th grade and pass the final exam. Which qualification do you get?
hints: It isn't enough yet to go to university.
Afterwards you can start an apprenticeship or the upper school years.
Its name says it sits between two other qualifications.
questions.description: Ten years of school, and at the end a sheet of paper with a big effect.
questions.fun_fact: In many German states, its official name is “Mittlerer Schulabschluss” or “Realschulabschluss”.

questions.question: I'm a schoolyard game: one player is “it” and runs off, and whoever they touch is “it” next. What am I?
hints: All you need is quick legs.
If you run fast, you don't get caught.
The shout “Du bist!” is part of it.
questions.description: The school bell always rings right when things are getting good.
questions.fun_fact: In some parts of Germany, the game is also called “Kriegen” or “Ticken”.

questions.question: Your class sits in a circle of chairs: 24 children and the teacher, each on one chair. How many chairs are in the circle?
hints: Count everyone who is sitting.
The children plus one grown-up.
It is one more than 24.
questions.description: Here, nobody gets a seat in the back row.
questions.fun_fact: In a circle of chairs everyone can see everyone, which is why German elementary schools like to use it for morning circle and storytelling time.

questions.question: In German primary school, one subject teaches you about plants, animals, the weather and road safety. What is it called?
hints: In this subject you do small experiments and sometimes go on field trips.
It mixes a little bit of lots of things.
In Bavaria it's called “Heimat- und …”.
questions.description: A subject where you might grow cress on cotton wool.
questions.fun_fact: At secondary school, Sachunterricht is split into subjects like Biologie, Erdkunde and Physik.

questions.question: During the long break I stand in the schoolyard, often in a safety vest, making sure nobody falls off the jungle gym. Who am I?
hints: Most of the time I am a teacher.
My colleagues and I take turns according to a schedule.
My job is named after the place I keep an eye on.
questions.description: The schoolyard has no security cameras, but it has something much better.
questions.fun_fact: For teachers, break duty counts as working time, so their own break is often shorter.

questions.question: On your way to school you have to cross a big street. Who helps you across with a stop paddle and a safety vest?
hints: Often they are older students or parents.
They stand at the crosswalk in the morning.
Their German name compares them to the pilots who guide ships into port.
questions.description: At 7:30 in the morning, this job matters more than any boss's.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has had student crossing guards, called “Schülerlotsen”, since the 1950s.

questions.question: I'm a skinny old horse. My owner took four days to pick my name, because he wanted one worthy of a great knight-errant's horse. What's my name?
hints: My owner read far too many books about knights.
I live in La Mancha.
My rider is Don Quixote.
questions.description: A horse showing more bones than any desire to gallop.
questions.fun_fact: Sancho Panza's donkey has a name too: Dapple (el Rucio in Spanish).

questions.question: The children's news show “logo!” has been made by ZDF since 1989 and airs daily on KiKA. In which city is it produced?
hints: The city lies on the Rhine.
It is the capital of Rhineland-Palatinate.
ZDF's famous cartoon mascots are named after this city: the …zelmännchen.
questions.description: News that even grown-ups secretly watch, because they can finally understand it.
questions.fun_fact: In 1989, “logo!” was one of the first news shows made just for children on German TV.

questions.question: Thomas Gottschalk is to “Wetten, dass..?” as Eduard Zimmermann is to …?
hints: Zimmermann hosted the show for about 30 years.
The show started in 1967, two years before “Der Kommissar.”
On the show, viewers help hunt for real criminals.
questions.description: Some men are so tied to one TV show that you could match them up in your sleep.
questions.fun_fact: Eduard Zimmermann hosted “Aktenzeichen XY … ungelöst” from 1967 to 1997, and many cases were solved thanks to tips from viewers.

questions.question: In which year did the RTL II series “Berlin – Tag & Nacht” start?
hints: Smartphones already existed back then.
It was in the same decade that Instagram launched.
The show began shortly after 2010.
questions.description: A shared apartment with more drama than your whole life, every single weekday.
questions.fun_fact: “Berlin – Tag & Nacht” uses amateur actors who improvise a lot instead of following a script word for word.

questions.question: Who played the junior doctor Gretchen Haase in the RTL series “Doctor's Diary”?
hints: The series ran from 2008 to 2011.
The actress first became known through the “Mädchen, Mädchen” movies.
Her first name sounds like that of a British princess.
questions.description: A doctor whose diary is more embarrassing than any medical file.
questions.fun_fact: “Doctor's Diary” won awards including the Grimme Prize and was sold to many countries.

questions.question: “Sturm der Liebe” has aired on ARD almost every weekday since 2005. About how many episodes are there by now?
hints: A year has about 250 weekdays.
The series has been running for about 20 years.
Work out roughly 20 times 220.
questions.description: Love, scheming and weddings in a hotel where nobody ever just goes on vacation.
questions.fun_fact: “Sturm der Liebe” is filmed at Bavaria Studios near Munich, and the outdoor shots of the Hotel Fürstenhof are taken at a real castle in Bavaria.

questions.question: Starting in 1960, I hosted “Der schwarze Kanal” on East German TV, commenting on clips from West German TV. Who am I?
hints: The show ran for almost 30 years, until 1989.
After the war, I first worked as a radio journalist at the NWDR in Cologne.
My nickname was “Sudel-Ede”.
questions.description: A man who showed West German TV so that people would stop wanting to watch it.
questions.fun_fact: When “Der schwarze Kanal” came on, many East Germans switched channels right away, often straight to West German TV.

questions.question: In what year did ZDF's Christmas series “Timm Thaler” start, with Tommi Ohrner as the boy who sells his laugh?
hints: The series aired before private TV channels came to Germany.
By then, many German living rooms already had a color TV.
The series ran over New Year's into the 1980s.
questions.description: A boy sells something you can't buy, and the whole country watches at Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: James Krüss wrote the book it was based on back in 1962: the novel “Timm Thaler oder Das verkaufte Lachen” (“Timm Thaler, or The Sold Laugh”).

questions.question: “Club der roten Bänder” ran on VOX from 2015 and follows teenagers on a children's ward. What was it based on?
hints: The original is based on its author's real experiences.
The original was remade in several countries, in the US as “Red Band Society”.
The author comes from Barcelona.
questions.description: A series that proves you can laugh more in a hospital than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: In the original, Albert Espinosa drew on his own cancer, which he survived as a teenager.

previous.feedback: Source: the fun fact says Espinosa beat cancer “as a teenager” („als Jugendlicher überstand“). He was ill from about 14 to 24 and spent roughly ten years in hospitals, so he wasn't cured until his early twenties. The source fun fact should say something like “which he fought for ten years from the age of 14”, and then the translation should follow it. The rest of the translation is faithful and natural.

questions.question: Which police officer has been in “Alarm für Cobra 11” since the first season in 1996?
hints: He works for the Autobahn police.
His partners have changed many times over the years, but he stayed.
He is played by Erdoğan Atalay.
questions.description: On this Autobahn, more cars fly through the air than at any airport.
questions.fun_fact: Over the years, several thousand cars have been wrecked for “Alarm für Cobra 11.”

questions.question: Which character is NOT from the RTL series “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten”?
hints: Three of these characters live in the show's version of Berlin.
The one you're looking for comes from another, older series.
She was the “mother” of “Lindenstraße”.
questions.description: In this Berlin neighborhood, everyone has already married, left or sued everyone else.
questions.fun_fact: GZSZ has been on the air since 1992, and its first episodes were adapted from an Australian series.

questions.question: The rose is to the kings of England as the fleur-de-lis is to the kings of…
hints: Many of these kings were crowned in Reims Cathedral.
Their royal banners were blue with golden flowers.
Its capital is Paris.
questions.description: A flower that has spent centuries on flags, coats of arms and even American football helmets.
questions.fun_fact: The fleur-de-lis is also the symbol of the Scouts all over the world.

questions.question: Police work is to “Alarm für Cobra 11” as … is to “Alles was zählt”?
hints: The RTL series is set at a sports center in Essen.
In this sport, judges give points for the artistic performance.
Spins and jumps are part of it.
questions.description: Love, scheming and big feelings, served fresh every evening.
questions.fun_fact: “Alles was zählt” has been on RTL since 2006, right before “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten”.

questions.question: You switch on RTL in the evening and the main edition of “RTL Aktuell” is on. What time is it?
hints: It's still before the “Tagesschau”.
It's even before the “heute” news on ZDF.
It's a quarter of an hour before 7 o'clock.
questions.description: The moment dinner officially turns into a news break.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Kloeppel hosted “RTL Aktuell” for more than 30 years.

questions.question: You're watching the quiz show „Wer weiß denn sowas?“ on Das Erste. Who is NOT a regular on it?
hints: The show has one host and two team captains.
Both team captains come from comedy, and one worked with Stefan Raab for years.
The one you're looking for hosted other quiz shows himself, such as „Das Quiz“.
questions.description: A show where knowing a little about everything finally becomes a superpower.
questions.fun_fact: „Wer weiß denn sowas?“ has been on since 2015 and is one of the most successful early-evening shows on Das Erste.

questions.question: Who won “Deutschland sucht den Superstar” in 2011 and later married his fellow finalist Sarah Engels?
hints: He comes from Karlsruhe.
His winning song was called “Call My Name”.
His last name sounds Italian.
questions.description: A final that ended with a trophy, and a few years later with wedding rings.
questions.fun_fact: Pietro Lombardi later sat on the DSDS jury himself, next to Dieter Bohlen.

questions.question: Whoever wins RTL's Dschungelcamp gets a title. What is it?
hints: The title comes from the world of fairy tales and castles.
It makes you think of a crown.
In the animal world, the lion holds this title.
questions.description: Two weeks of hammocks, beans and cockroaches, and a title of honor at the end.
questions.fun_fact: The first winner, in 2004, was the Schlager singer Costa Cordalis.

questions.question: On Das Erste, contestants run from a quiz pro who tries to catch them on a ladder. Which show is it?
hints: The show is hosted by Alexander Bommes.
On the show, the quiz pros are called “Jäger” (hunters).
Both words of the title begin with “Ge-”.
questions.description: Couch, chips and shouting answers at the TV: the perfect evening in.
questions.fun_fact: The show is the German version of the British quiz show “The Chase”.

questions.question: Which German YouTuber, real name Erik Range, is seen as a pioneer of Let's Play videos?
hints: For many years he has shown video games while commenting on them.
His Minecraft series has well over a thousand episodes.
His screen name sounds like a grunt.
questions.description: A man who got famous for playing video games, and parents still find that suspicious.
questions.fun_fact: Gronkh's Minecraft Let's Play is one of the longest German YouTube series ever.

questions.question: I was on camera back on East German TV, and I've read the “Tagesschau” news since 1999. In 2021, the youth word “cringe” made me go viral. Who am I?
hints: I am a woman from eastern Germany.
I announced the youth word of the year on the news with a completely straight face.
I was born in Halle an der Saale.
questions.description: It doesn't get more serious than this, and yet it ended up in the meme hall of fame.
questions.fun_fact: The “cringe” clip was shared millions of times, especially by teenagers.

questions.question: Inka Bause is to “Bauer sucht Frau” as Kai Pflaume is to …?
hints: It's a big Saturday night family show.
The stars there often lose to much younger challengers.
The title names two opposite sizes.
questions.description: A host whose last name could go straight into a fruit cake.
questions.fun_fact: Before this, Kai Pflaume hosted the Sat.1 show “Nur die Liebe zählt” for many years.

questions.question: In the cult Hessischer Rundfunk show with Heinz Schenk, guests drank apple wine. What was it called: “Zum Blauen …”?
hints: Like the other options, it's a typical German inn name.
It's an animal with horns.
It's also the name of a strong type of beer.
questions.description: Coziness, swaying to the music, and a jug that was never allowed to run dry.
questions.fun_fact: Famous guests on the show got a Bembel, the typical apple wine jug, as a souvenir.

questions.question: Which TV host launched a magazine named after her first name in 2015 and has hosted Germany's Eurovision selection show several times?
hints: She was born in Munich.
She appears on every cover of her magazine.
Her last name contains the German word “schön” (beautiful).
questions.description: A woman who talks so much that a single TV show isn't enough for her.
questions.fun_fact: Barbara Schöneberger also sings and has released several albums of her own.

questions.question: People used to wear it on their heads at night to keep warm. Today it means someone who dawdles or sleeps through everything. Which German word is it?
hints: It started out as a piece of clothing.
People used to wear it in bed.
The word is made of “Schlaf” (sleep) and a word for something you wear on your head.
questions.description: A word for everyone you can't talk to before their third hot chocolate of the morning.
questions.fun_fact: The “deutscher Michel”, a figure who pokes fun at Germans, still wears a pointed nightcap to show that he supposedly sleeps through everything.

questions.question: A “Spickzettel” is small, fits up any sleeve and usually turns up at school. What is it used for?
questions.answer: For secretly copying answers during a test
wrong_answers: For passing love notes during class
As a written excuse note from parents
hints: Teachers really don't like seeing it.
“Spicken” roughly means to take a secret peek.
If you get caught with one, you often get a “Sechs”, the worst grade.
questions.description: Paper that lives a very exciting life inside a pencil case.
questions.fun_fact: Writing a Spickzettel in tiny letters means going over the whole topic, so some people don't even need it afterwards.

questions.question: A child holds their nose, pulls a face and shouts “Igitt!” What are they showing?
hints: It's not a nice feeling.
You might feel it with spoiled food, for example.
With this feeling, your stomach almost turns over.
questions.description: A tiny word that comes with a big face.
questions.fun_fact: Disgust is a protective feeling: it stops us from tasting spoiled food, for example.

questions.question: I spot every comma mistake, insist on every rule and make a big deal out of tiny things. Which German word describes me?
hints: I'm terribly fussy, but not necessarily stingy.
I count and double-check even the tiniest detail.
Supposedly I count tiny green balls one by one.
questions.description: For people who laminated the Monopoly rules.
questions.fun_fact: German has even more teasing words for such people, like “Haarspalter” (hair splitter) or “Paragraphenreiter” (rule rider).

questions.question: German teens borrowed this word from English, where it originally means “to kill,” and social media made it famous. What does “Du slayst!” mean?
hints: It's a compliment.
People often say it about a great outfit or performance.
It means you're totally owning the moment.
questions.description: A word that sounds a lot more dangerous than it is meant to be.
questions.fun_fact: “Slay” became big in New York's ballroom scene, where dancers competed against each other on the runway.

questions.question: German teens call someone who acts like a background extra with no opinions an “NPC.” What comes after “Non-Player …”?
hints: The abbreviation comes from games.
In games, they're shopkeepers or villagers who always say the same line.
It's the word for a figure in a story, like Mario or Pikachu.
questions.description: For everyone who only ever says “Nice weather today” in real life.
questions.fun_fact: The term NPC was used in tabletop role-playing games like “Dungeons & Dragons” before it showed up in video games.

questions.question: Half German, half English, with no “ist”: “Das crazy” became Germany’s Youth Word of the Year 2025. What is it mostly used for?
wrong_answers: To invite people to a party
hints: People often say it when someone is telling a story.
It fits good news as well as bad news.
It replaces a real answer.
questions.description: Two words that leave parents waiting for the rest of the sentence.
questions.fun_fact: The Youth Word of the Year is chosen by the publisher Langenscheidt, and young people help pick it by voting online.

questions.question: What does the German abbreviation “z. B.” mean?
hints: You often find it in school textbooks.
It's usually followed by a short list.
In English, the Latin abbreviation “e.g.” does the same job.
questions.description: Two letters and two dots that live in every German schoolbook.
questions.fun_fact: By the official German spelling rules, there should be a small space between “z.” and “B.”.

questions.question: In what year was the Obelisk of Buenos Aires unveiled, as a kind of birthday present for the city?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was in the first half of that century.
It marked 400 years since Buenos Aires was first founded, in 1536.
questions.description: A giant pencil that nobody has ever managed to sharpen.
questions.fun_fact: The Obelisk is about 67 m (220 ft) tall and was built in just over a month.

questions.question: In German schoolyards you hear many words from other languages. Which of these does NOT come from Arabic?
hints: Three of the words share the same origin.
“Inshallah” means “God willing”.
The word you’re looking for comes from the German “Dicker” (“fatty”).
questions.description: Sometimes the schoolyard is a language course with a recess bell.
questions.fun_fact: “Inshallah” also lives on in the Spanish word “ojalá”, which came from Arabic to Spain more than 500 years ago.

questions.question: The city's coat of arms shines above the entrance of Hamburg City Hall. Bear is to Berlin as … is to Hamburg?
hints: The answer is the picture on Hamburg's coat of arms.
It is white on a red background.
It has three towers and a gate.
questions.description: Behind this grand front the city is governed, and above the door hangs the city's family photo.
questions.fun_fact: Hamburg City Hall stands on about 4,000 oak piles driven into the wet ground.

questions.question: I look like a white horse, I have a pointed horn on my forehead, and I leap on the coat of arms of Schwäbisch Gmünd. Who am I?
hints: I appear in lots of fairy tales.
I don't have wings.
My name means “one horn”.
questions.description: A horse that got extra dressed up for the coat of arms.
questions.fun_fact: The unicorn is also the national animal of Scotland.

questions.question: Which city does this coat of arms belong to, with a green cloverleaf above the gate?
hints: The city is a state capital.
It lies on the Leine river.
The state parliament of Lower Saxony meets here.
questions.description: Here they built luck right into the city gate, just one leaf short.
questions.fun_fact: The cloverleaf is so well known in Hanover that it also shows up on the city's artworks and logos.

questions.question: On Baden-Württemberg's large coat of arms, a golden animal holds the shield next to a griffin. Which animal?
hints: It lives in the forest.
In fairy tales it often roams the forest with roe deer and wild boar.
In autumn the male roars loudly through the forest.
questions.description: Apparently one German state needs bodyguards to hold up its coat of arms.
questions.fun_fact: A stag sheds its antlers every year and grows a new set.

questions.question: What is the yellow sign with the town's name, after which cars usually must keep to 50 km/h (31 mph)?
hints: It stands at the edge of a village or town.
The town's coat of arms often hangs next to it.
Once you drive past it, you have arrived in town.
questions.description: The yellow bouncer at every village gate: from here on, slow down.
questions.fun_fact: In the German road traffic rules, the sign is officially called the “Ortstafel”, sign number 310.

questions.question: The Franconian Rake stands for Franconia in the Bavarian coat of arms. How many silver points stick up from it?
hints: There are fewer than five.
On the Franconian flag, the white points reach up into the red.
It is also the number of the Musketeers.
questions.description: A garden tool that made it onto a state coat of arms without ever raking a single leaf.
questions.fun_fact: The rake was first the coat of arms of the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg.

questions.question: I have wings, you never see me, and I watch over you when you ride your bike. Who am I?
hints: People say I live in heaven.
Many people keep a little figure of me in their car.
My name says that I keep you safe.
questions.description: Some beings no one has ever seen, and still half of Germany believes in them.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, small guardian angel charms for the car or the school backpack are a popular gift.

questions.question: In Germany, every bicycle must have one. It sits on the handlebar and by law must have a “bright” sound. What is it?
hints: You use it with your thumb.
People walking hear it when you come from behind.
It goes “Ring, ring!”
questions.description: The quietest instrument in the street orchestra, yet it has quite a lot to say.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, a horn isn't even allowed on a bicycle, only a bright-sounding bell.

questions.question: In this aerial photo, two autobahns meet and both keep going. What is a junction like this called in Germany?
hints: Neither of the two autobahns ends here.
The name fits a shape with four arms.
The classic design looks like a cloverleaf.
questions.description: From above it looks like a lucky charm, from below like a GPS nightmare.
questions.fun_fact: An Autobahndreieck (“triangle”) gets its name because one autobahn runs into another and ends there.

questions.question: What nickname is given to the city where this monument stands?
hints: The nickname comes from poets of ancient times.
A famous saying claims that all roads lead to this city.
It is the opposite of “temporary.”
questions.description: A city with so much history that even its ruins have ruins.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman poet Tibullus was already calling it that in the 1st century BC.

questions.question: In Germany, 110 is the number for the police. When do you NOT call it?
wrong_answers: A burglar is in the house
Someone is stealing a car right now
There's a fistfight on the street
hints: Three of these are emergencies with criminals.
In one of them, nobody is in danger.
A locksmith would help more here.
questions.description: A short number for big problems, but not for every problem.
questions.fun_fact: For the fire department and ambulance in Germany you dial 112, which works all over Europe.

questions.question: Emma from “Jim Knopf” is a steam locomotive. What does she NOT need to run?
hints: Steam comes out of her chimney.
Lukas shovels something black into her belly.
Emma is not an electric locomotive.
questions.description: Emma is chubby, round and puffs a lot, and still everyone loves her.
questions.fun_fact: The Augsburger Puppenkiste puppet theater made Emma famous in Germany with its Jim Knopf films.

questions.question: During German rail strikes you often hear “GDL”. Complete its name: “Union of German …”
hints: Its members work for the railroad.
They sit right at the front of the train.
In German they're called “Lokführer”.
questions.description: Three letters that make commuters all over Germany flinch.
questions.fun_fact: The GDL was founded back in 1867, which makes it the oldest union in Germany.

questions.question: I'm a train in Berlin, Hamburg or Munich. I bring people from the suburbs into the city, often above ground. My sign is green. What am I?
hints: I don't run on the street between cars.
My sister with the blue sign mostly runs underground.
My letter is also the first letter of “Stadt”, the German word for city.
questions.description: I'm as punctual as clockwork, except when I'm not.
questions.fun_fact: In Berlin, S-Bahn trains have run on electricity since 1924.

questions.question: What do you call the small, flat plastic disc you sit on to slide down a snowy hill?
hints: It is much lighter than any sled.
It has no runners underneath.
Its name comes from something you put under a teacup.
questions.description: To slide in winter, you don't need an excuse, just a hill and the right gear.
questions.fun_fact: Many snow saucers have handles to hold on to, but you can hardly steer them.

questions.question: In German, the heavy tracked vehicle that smooths the ski slopes at night is named after which animal?
hints: The vehicle runs on wide tracks instead of wheels.
The animal is small and you can find it in the garden.
This crawling creature later turns into a butterfly.
questions.description: This vehicle works the night shift so everyone gets a smooth run in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Many of these vehicles are called “PistenBully,” after a brand made by the company Kässbohrer from Laupheim in Baden-Württemberg.

questions.question: I'm from Bavaria, I ski and I shoot. In the 2024/25 winter, I won the biathlon overall World Cup. Who am I?
hints: The overall World Cup winner gets the big Crystal Globe.
Magdalena Neuner and Denise Herrmann-Wick had already retired by that winter.
My nickname is “Franzi.”
questions.description: Heart rate at 180, and yet the hand must stay perfectly still.
questions.fun_fact: In prone shooting, the target is 50 m (164 ft) away and only about 4.5 cm (1.8 in) wide.

questions.question: Kitzbühel, January 2018: for the first time since 1979, a German wins the downhill on the Streif. Who?
hints: We're looking for a downhill specialist, not a slalom skier.
He comes from the Werdenfels region in Upper Bavaria.
His first name is Thomas.
questions.description: The Streif is so steep that just watching it makes your legs sore.
questions.fun_fact: Every winner on the Streif gets a cable car gondola of the Hahnenkamm lift with their name on it.

questions.question: I was born in Spain in 1959 and today I'm sold all over the world. My name means “wonderful” in Esperanto. What am I?
hints: I'm a soft drink, and my most famous flavor is orange.
Since 1970 I've belonged to the same company as Pepsi.
My name sounds almost like the girl's name Miranda.
questions.description: A fizzy drink with bubbles and, apparently, a degree in languages.
questions.fun_fact: Mirinda was born in Spain and PepsiCo bought it in 1970; today it sells mostly in Asia, the Middle East and Latin America.

questions.question: What has been special about public transportation in Luxembourg since 2020?
wrong_answers: It runs only on solar power
hints: Tourists and the people who live there enjoy it just the same.
No other country had done this before across its whole territory.
You can leave your wallet in your pocket.
questions.description: A tiny country with a very big idea for getting around town.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, Luxembourg became the first country in the world with free public transportation across its whole territory.

questions.question: They sell everything from batteries to pool floats, stay open long hours, and their name comes from a Persian word for “market.” What shop is it?
hints: They usually have products piled on shelves up to the ceiling.
In many Spanish neighborhoods, there's one on every corner.
In cities like Istanbul, one of these huge covered markets is world-famous.
questions.description: You leave home “to get just one thing” and your family reports you missing.
questions.fun_fact: The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul has more than 4,000 shops and is one of the oldest covered markets in the world.

questions.question: A Catalan brand founded in 1958, with a thumbs-up logo and famous for its Sherpa T trials motorcycle. Which is it?
hints: Its founder had left another Catalan motorcycle brand.
It won five trials world championships in a row in the 1970s.
Its name comes from its founder's surname, Francesc Xavier Bultó.
questions.description: A brand so upbeat that even its logo gives you the OK.
questions.fun_fact: The factory closed in the early 1980s, but its old motorcycles are still highly sought after by collectors.

questions.question: Look at this photo of a neighborhood shop. What do you buy here?
hints: It's usually bought by the handful, in a little bag.
It's sweet and comes in lots of colors.
Gummy bears, licorice and marshmallows.
questions.description: Paradise for any kid with a coin in their pocket.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, candy is lovingly called «chuches», short for «chucherías», a word grandparents already used.

questions.question: Which of these dolls is NOT made by the Spanish toy company Famosa?
hints: Famosa was born in Onil, Alicante.
The odd one out comes from a US company.
She's the blonde doll whose boyfriend is Ken.
questions.description: A parade of dolls heading for the Nativity scene… and one that snuck into the line.
questions.fun_fact: Famosa stands for “Fábricas Agrupadas de Muñecas de Onil” (Grouped Doll Factories of Onil).

questions.question: I'm a construction worker, but I dream of being an archaeologist. I travel with my dog Jeff and a parrot that can't talk. Who am I?
hints: My movies are made in Spain.
In my first movie, I travel to Peru in search of a lost city.
My last name is the same as a famous movie archaeologist with a whip and a hat.
questions.description: A man with his hard hat on his head and his head in the ancient ruins.
questions.fun_fact: Before he had any movies, this character was born in a 2004 short film that won the Goya for best animated short.

questions.question: He was a hedgehog, he was pink and he never wore clothes… except for one item. What did Espinete wear in Barrio Sésamo?
hints: The other neighbors never thought it was strange that he went around without clothes.
This item usually comes as a set: a top and a bottom.
He wore it to get into bed.
questions.description: The prickliest neighbor on TV had a very particular dress code.
questions.fun_fact: Espinete was created for the Spanish version: he never existed on the US Sesame Street.

questions.question: This song is sung again and again, swapping words for gestures: “My beard has three hairs, three hairs has my beard; if it didn't have three hairs…”. How does it go on?
hints: The last word has already come up in the song.
It's about what the beard would be, or wouldn't be.
Without those three hairs, the beard would stop being one.
questions.description: A beard so thin you can count its hairs on one hand.
questions.fun_fact: In the gesture version, the last round is almost silent: you just point to your chin and hold up three fingers.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The song is a Spanish clowns' game, and the usual lyric ends "no sería mi barba" (my beard), not "una barba". The answer "it wouldn't be a beard" is close, and the wrong answers are clearly wrong. The fun fact is unsupported. The source describes the rounds as banning "barba", then "barba" and "pelos", and ending with a faster full sing-through. It does not describe a nearly silent last round with a chin point and three fingers. I could not find the lyric text itself.

previous.feedback: Source: the fun fact ("almost nothing is sung on the last round: you just point to your chin and hold up three fingers") can't be confirmed and seems overstated. In the usual game, only "barba", "pelos" and "tres" turn into gestures, so words like "tiene", "si no tuviera" and "pues no sería" are still sung. The fact check also found a source saying the last round is sung in full, just faster. Fix the source's fun fact, for example: "In the gesture game, a word is swapped for a gesture each round (beard, hairs, three) until the song is half mime." Then carry the change into the translation. The rest of the translation is faithful and natural. Fact check: uncertain. The song's ending is right: sin los tres pelos, it would no longer be a beard. The wrong answers (mustache, shave it off, four hairs) are clearly wrong. Two things are shaky. (1) Versions differ on the wording: "no sería mi barba" vs "no sería una barba". (2) The fun fact is not supported. The only source I could open (Guiainfantil) says the last round is sung in full, just faster, and does not describe pointing to the chin with three fingers. In the usual game, words are replaced by gestures round by round. It is not verified that nothing is sung at the end.

Fact check: uncertain. The answer fits the song: without the three hairs, it wouldn't be a beard. The usual line is "no sería mi barba" ("wouldn't be my beard"), a minor difference. The wrong answers are wrong. The fun fact is shaky. In the standard game, each word (barba, pelos, tres, tiene and so on) is replaced by its own gesture, not just a chin point and three fingers. One source summary said the final round is the full song sung fast, which conflicts with the fun fact. I couldn't see the exact lyrics or the last-round rules.

Fact check: uncertain. The usual lyric ends "no sería mi barba" (it wouldn't be my beard), and some versions say "una barba". The answer fits only loosely. The fun fact is also doubtful: in the last round every word (my, beard, three, hairs) is replaced by its own gesture, so nothing is sung. It isn't just pointing to the chin and holding up three fingers. I checked this from memory, not from a source.

questions.question: I'm bald, I wear a scarf, I tried to steal the Moon and I ended up adopting three girls. Who am I?
hints: In Spain, the title of my film starts with my name.
My daughters are Margo, Edith and Agnes.
My helpers are the Minions.
questions.description: A super-duper bad guy with a heart softer than a stuffed unicorn.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, Gru is voiced by the comedian Florentino Fernández.

questions.question: I'm at the bottom of the sea, my owner is Mr. Krabs, and SpongeBob works in my kitchen. What am I?
hints: I'm a restaurant.
Plankton is always trying to steal my secret recipe.
My name puts a kind of shellfish together with a word for something crunchy on the outside.
questions.description: The only place where the boss counts coins faster than you can count your fries.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the restaurant is called “Crustáceo Crujiente”, while in the Latin American dub it's “Crustáceo Cascarudo”.

questions.question: In Barrio Sésamo, Epi shares an apartment with his inseparable friend. What is his name?
hints: He's much more serious than Epi.
He loves pigeons and has a unibrow.
In the original US show, his name is Bert.
questions.description: The roommate who never lets you read in peace.
questions.fun_fact: In English they're called Bert and Ernie: Epi is Ernie and his friend is Bert.

questions.question: Complete: “Buster the dog is to Andy as Scud the dog is to…”
hints: Scud is a fierce dog who chases toys.
His owner lives in the house next door to Andy.
His owner wears a skull T-shirt and takes toys apart.
questions.description: A question for people who even know the names of the characters' pets.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of Toy Story 3, a grown-up Sid shows up working as a garbage collector.

questions.question: It was founded in 1991, has centers in dozens of countries and runs the DELE Spanish exams for foreigners. What institution is it?
hints: It doesn't make the dictionary; it teaches the language outside Spain.
Its head office is in Madrid, on Calle de Alcalá.
It is named after the most famous author in Spanish literature.
questions.description: A language school with more passport stamps than an airline pilot.
questions.fun_fact: In the old bank vault of its head office, the “Caja de las Letras”, writers and artists leave objects in safe-deposit boxes.

questions.question: I mock ladies and don't fear the dead. I was born in Seville in a play by Tirso de Molina, and every November I return to the stage. Who am I?
hints: My fame as a seducer has given a name to a type of man.
José Zorrilla made me even more famous in the 19th century.
My beloved is called Doña Inés.
questions.description: Curtain up, curtain down: some characters simply refuse to retire from the stage.
questions.fun_fact: Zorrilla wrote “Don Juan Tenorio” in just a few weeks and sold the rights for very little money, which he regretted all his life.

questions.question: Villancico is to Christmas as saeta is to…
hints: The saeta is a deeply moving Andalusian song, sung without any accompaniment.
It is usually sung from a balcony as something passes in the street.
It is sung to the religious statues carried in processions.
questions.description: Every season of the year has its own soundtrack, and it isn't always the radio.
questions.fun_fact: The word “saeta” means “arrow”: the song is shot like a dart toward the statue passing by.

questions.question: A squire in Toledo goes out with a toothpick between his teeth to pretend he has eaten. In what year was his novel published?
hints: It’s an anonymous novel from the 16th century.
The narrator is a boy who serves several masters, among them a blind man.
It’s the first great picaresque novel: the Lazarillo de Tormes.
questions.description: A master with plenty of poise, plenty of cape and hardly any stew in the pot.
questions.fun_fact: The squire is so poor that Lázaro himself ends up begging to feed his master.

questions.question: Garcilaso brought it from Italy, and Quevedo used it to make fun of a huge nose. What is a sonnet?
hints: Its fixed form is the one Lope de Vega followed in “Un soneto me manda hacer Violante”.
Shakespeare and Petrarch also wrote some very famous ones.
It's split into two groups of four lines and two groups of three.
questions.description: Quevedo and Góngora got along so badly that even their insults ended up in schoolbooks.
questions.fun_fact: “Sonnet” comes from the Italian “sonetto”, which means something like “little sound”.

questions.question: Manuel Machado was a modernist poet, the author of “Cante hondo” and the older brother of Antonio Machado. In which city was he born?
hints: It is a city in Andalusia.
He was born in a palace owned by the House of Alba.
His brother wrote: “My childhood is memories of a patio in…”
questions.description: The brother who didn't make it into the textbooks, but did make it into the same family photo.
questions.fun_fact: Manuel and Antonio Machado were born in the Palacio de las Dueñas, where their family rented a home.

questions.question: Rinconete and Cortadillo, two young rascals who end up in Monipodio’s courtyard in Seville, star in a story published in which century?
hints: It’s part of a book of twelve short novels.
Its author also wrote Don Quixote.
It came out in the “Exemplary Novels”, in 1613.
questions.description: Two kids with more tricks than coins, and they still made it into the books.
questions.fun_fact: Rinconete and Cortadillo are nicknames: their real names are Pedro del Rincón and Diego Cortado.

questions.question: In the schoolyard, children hold hands in a circle and go round while they sing. What kind of song is it?
hints: Children have passed it on to each other in schoolyards for generations.
A famous example is about a potato.
The circle of children gives this kind of song its name.
questions.description: A song that goes round and round and ends with everyone on the floor.
questions.fun_fact: In “Al corro de la patata”, when the children reach “sentadita me quedé” (“and down I sat”), everyone drops to the floor.

questions.question: Which of these movies did NOT win the Oscar for Best Animated Feature?
hints: The odd one out was nominated, but it lost.
It lost to a movie about dancing penguins.
Its hero is a red race car.
questions.description: A golden statuette that lots of cartoon characters dream of hugging.
questions.fun_fact: The first Oscar for Best Animated Feature went to Shrek, in 2002.

questions.question: We are short poems of love and mystery, written by a poet from Seville in the 19th century. In one of us, “volverán las oscuras golondrinas.” What are we?
hints: Our author is Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer.
His other famous work is written in prose, not verse.
One of us says: “¿Qué es poesía? Poesía eres tú.”
questions.description: Poems so short they fit in one romantic sigh.
questions.fun_fact: The first manuscript was lost in the revolution of 1868, and Bécquer had to rewrite the poems from memory in the “Libro de los gorriones” (Book of the Sparrows).

questions.question: How many official languages does Andorra, the little country in the Pyrenees, have?
hints: You hear lots of Spanish and French in its streets, but that doesn't make them official.
Its 1993 Constitution makes it very clear.
It's the same language spoken in Barcelona, and it doesn't share the job with any other.
questions.description: A country so small you can see all of it in one ski weekend.
questions.fun_fact: Andorra is the only country in the world where Catalan is the only official language.

questions.question: You're in the Barcelona metro. If the way in says “Entrada”, which sign do you look for to get out to the street?
hints: The signs are in Catalan.
It comes from the Catalan verb that means “to go out”.
It's very close to the French word for exit, “sortie”.
questions.description: Any door will get you in; the hard part is seeing the sun again.
questions.fun_fact: In Valencian, the word “eixida” is also used for exit.

questions.question: It's on the coast of Alicante, at the foot of the Montgó, and its Valencian name is Xàbia. What is its name in Spanish?
hints: The Valencian “X” turns into a “J” in Spanish.
It has beaches: the other three towns are far from the sea.
Its Spanish name has an accent on the first “a”.
questions.description: One town, two names and just one Sunday paella.
questions.fun_fact: On clear days, you can see Ibiza from Cape La Nao in Xàbia.

questions.question: What is the Galician word for “beach”?
hints: It's almost the same as in Portuguese.
Change a couple of letters in the Spanish word “playa”.
It's in the name of a famous beach in Ribadeo: “… das Catedrais”.
questions.description: The perfect place to lose your flip-flops and find seashells.
questions.fun_fact: The Praia das Catedrais has giant rock arches that you can only walk through at low tide.

questions.question: The official language of all Spain has two names: “Spanish” and… what else?
hints: It's a very old name, from more than a thousand years ago.
The name comes from an old kingdom in the middle of the peninsula.
It was born in the old kingdom of Castile.
questions.description: A language with two names, like someone with a real name and a nickname.
questions.fun_fact: It's called Castilian because it was born in the old kingdom of Castile, more than a thousand years ago.

questions.question: “Txiki” means “small”, is spelled with “tx” and is a very common nickname. Which region's language is this word from?
hints: The “tx” sounds like the “ch” in “church”.
The language has no known link to any other language in Europe.
People there speak Euskera.
questions.description: A teeny-tiny word for teeny-tiny things.
questions.fun_fact: Euskera was already spoken before Latin arrived, and nobody knows for sure where it came from.

questions.question: Complete the official Valencian name of this provincial capital: “Castelló de la …”.
hints: Its Spanish name has the same ending too.
The same word names two districts of the province, one “Alta” and one “Baixa”.
Its full Spanish name is “Castellón de la …”, with a word close to the English “plain”.
questions.description: A city with two ID cards, one for each language.
questions.fun_fact: The Magdalena festival remembers how, in 1251, the townspeople came down from the hill to found the city on the flat land below.

questions.question: In this autonomous community of Spain, people say «grazas» to say thank you. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the northwest corner of Spain.
It borders Portugal.
Santiago de Compostela is there.
questions.description: A land where it rains so much that even the umbrellas say thank you.
questions.fun_fact: Galician and Portuguese grew from the same medieval language, Galician-Portuguese.

questions.question: I dress in black, carry an umbrella and love playing mean tricks on everyone. Jorge drew me in Pulgarcito in the 1940s. Who am I?
hints: I’m a character from the Bruguera school, but I’m neither a mother-in-law nor a maid.
I’m an old lady famous for my bad temper, not for my job.
My name is the Spanish word for a black-and-white bird said to steal shiny things.
questions.description: If your neighbor hides your ball and laughs about it, she may have stepped out of a comic.
questions.fun_fact: Her creator signed as “Jorge”, but his real name was Miguel Bernet Toledano, and he was the father of the artist Jordi Bernet.

questions.question: Who created “Arrugas” (“Wrinkles”), the graphic novel about Alzheimer’s that won Spain’s National Comic Award in 2008?
hints: He is from Valencia.
He also wrote “La casa” and “Los surcos del azar”.
His first name is Francisco, and his surname is the Spanish word for “rock”.
questions.description: A story that leaves your heart as wrinkled as its title.
questions.fun_fact: The animated film based on “Arrugas” won two Goya Awards in 2012.

questions.question: I'm a bald scientist with a huge beard and I work at a spy agency. My inventions always go wrong for Mortadelo y Filemón. Who am I?
hints: I always wear a white lab coat.
Mortadelo y Filemón are forced to test my inventions.
My name sounds like a germ.
questions.description: At this agency, the danger doesn't come from the enemy, but from inside.
questions.fun_fact: Mortadelo y Filemón often end up chasing their own scientist because of one of his inventions.

questions.question: I was born in Salamanca in 1925, won the Nadal Prize for “Entre visillos”, and wrote “Caperucita en Manhattan” and a novel called “Retahílas”. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the generation of Spanish writers of the 1950s.
I won the Prince of Asturias Award for Literature in 1988.
My first name is Carmen.
questions.description: A writer who could talk and talk and talk… and turn it all into literature.
questions.fun_fact: “Retahílas” (1974) is written almost entirely as one very long night-time conversation between an aunt and her nephew.

questions.question: Who collected the “Cuentos al amor de la lumbre”, a large collection of Spanish folk tales?
hints: He also studied how fairy tales are built.
He is a writer from Andalusia.
He shares a surname with a famous film director from La Mancha.
questions.description: The man who sat down by the fire and didn’t get up until he’d heard every tale in Spain.
questions.fun_fact: He won Spain’s National Award for Children’s and Young Adult Literature in 2005 with “El bosque de los sueños”.

questions.question: Which cartoonist filled his comic strips with big-nosed office workers and made-up words like «gensanta»?
hints: He published in the newspaper El País for many years.
One of his characters was Blasillo, a little bald man.
His real name was Antonio Fraguas.
questions.description: A cartoonist who made Spain laugh every morning, one big nose at a time.
questions.fun_fact: After the 2010 earthquake, Forges added the line «No os olvidéis de Haití» (“Don't forget Haiti”) to his cartoons for years.

questions.question: I'm a secret agent with only two hairs on my head, and I'm in charge of my partner, though he always gets me into trouble. Who am I?
hints: My partner is very tall and dresses up as anything.
I wear a white shirt and red pants.
My surname is Pi.
questions.description: Being the boss doesn't always mean coming out on top.
questions.fun_fact: Ibáñez created Mortadelo and Filemón in 1958, and at first they were private detectives, not spies.

questions.question: I'm a spy agency full of disasters. My boss is the Súper and my most famous agents are Mortadelo and Filemón. Who am I?
hints: I appear in Francisco Ibáñez's comics.
My name is written with dots between the letters.
In Spanish, my name is the word for your mom's sister.
questions.description: Spies so secret that the whole neighborhood knows about them.
questions.fun_fact: Its name is a parody of the American C.I.A.

questions.question: Zipi y Zape were born in 1948 in Pulgarcito magazine, from the publisher Bruguera, drawn by Josep Escobar. In which city was that publisher?
hints: It's a city by the sea.
Mortadelo y Filemón were published there too.
The Sagrada Família is there.
questions.description: Two twins who couldn't sit still, not even on paper.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word «zipizape» really exists and means a noisy scuffle, just like the twins' pranks.

questions.question: When he takes off his cape, he's an office worker in Barcelona. Superman is to Clark Kent as Superlópez is to…
hints: It's a very common name in Spain.
His surname is already in his superhero name.
He has the same name as his creator, Jan.
questions.description: A superhero who has to clock in at nine.
questions.fun_fact: His creator, Jan, is really named Juan López Fernández, just like his character.

questions.question: Which singer was a coach on the first season of “La Voz” on Telecinco, in 2012?
hints: He became famous on the first season of Operación Triunfo.
He’s from Andalusia and has a famous mane of curly hair.
He’s from Almería and sang “Ave María”.
questions.description: Four chairs that spin more than a Ferris wheel at the town fair.
questions.fun_fact: “The Voice” format was born in the Netherlands in 2010, and the first Spanish coaches were Bisbal, Malú, Melendi and Rosario Flores.

questions.question: Until 2016, the music radio station LOS40 had a longer name. What was it?
hints: The missing word is about the most important songs on the chart.
In Spanish, it's the word for a town's main square: the “plaza …”.
In Spanish, the lead actor in a film is the “actor …”.
questions.description: A radio station that went on a diet and lost almost all its letters.
questions.fun_fact: LOS40 started in 1966 as a show on Cadena SER before it became a whole station of its own.

questions.question: Antena 3’s impersonation show is called “Tu cara me suena”. What does it mean when a face “te suena”?
wrong_answers: It makes you laugh a lot
hints: It has nothing to do with hearing sounds.
You say it when you pass someone in the street and keep thinking about it for a while.
It’s the opposite of someone being a complete stranger.
questions.description: A show where celebrities dress up as other celebrities and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: “Tu cara me suena” is a Spanish-made format that has been sold to many countries as “Your Face Sounds Familiar”.

questions.question: In what year did Rosalía release her album “Motomami”?
hints: It came out after the 2020s had already begun.
“El mal querer” had come out four years earlier.
It was the same year as the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: An album that showed up wearing a helmet and revving like a motorbike.
questions.fun_fact: “Motomami” won the Grammy for Best Latin Rock or Alternative Album.

questions.question: This Madrid indie band hit it big with “Copacabana” and released the album “Agujeros de gusano”. Where does the name Izal come from?
hints: The band started playing in Madrid around 2010.
Many famous bands got their names the same way.
Its lead singer's first name is Mikel.
questions.description: In indie music, picking the band's name is harder than writing the first album.
questions.fun_fact: Izal is also the name of a small village in Navarre.

questions.question: I'm held every winter on the Costa Blanca, I was born in 2022, and I sent Chanel with “SloMo” to Eurovision. What am I?
hints: I'm organized by RTVE.
I choose the song that represents Spain at Eurovision.
I take place in the city of skyscrapers by the beach.
questions.description: A festival that hands out tickets to Europe's biggest stage.
questions.fun_fact: Chanel's third place in 2022 was Spain's best Eurovision result since 1995.

questions.question: Before she was Lola Índigo, Miriam Doblas was a contestant on Operación Triunfo. In what year did her season start?
hints: It was the season that brought OT back to TV after years off the air.
Amaia won it.
That season sent Amaia and Alfred to Eurovision 2018.
questions.description: An artist who swapped her name for a color.
questions.fun_fact: Lola Índigo was the first contestant voted out of her OT season, and she still became a star.

questions.question: In what year did Quevedo release his “Quédate” session with Bizarrap, which became a worldwide hit?
hints: It was after the pandemic.
It was the summer after the Tokyo Olympics.
It was the year of the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: A song that begged you to stay, and nobody left.
questions.fun_fact: The song reached number 1 on Spotify's global chart.

questions.question: Barcelona's Primavera Sound festival held its first edition at the Poble Espanyol. In which year?
hints: It's already more than two decades old.
It was born the same year as Wikipedia.
It was the first year of the 21st century.
questions.description: A festival named after a season with the sound of a city.
questions.fun_fact: Today Primavera Sound takes place by the sea, at Barcelona's Parc del Fòrum.

questions.question: I’m from San Fernando, Cádiz; as a kid I sang on Canal Sur’s “Menuda noche”, then hit it big with “Loco enamorado”. Who am I?
hints: I was born in 1998.
I started singing on TV when I was about seven or eight.
My first name is that of a Bible patriarch.
questions.description: A child star who grew up in front of the cameras.
questions.fun_fact: Abraham Mateo recorded his first album while he was still a child.

questions.question: Since 2022, Spotify has put its name on the shirt and the stadium of a Spanish club. Which one?
hints: The deal also covers its women’s team.
In some Clásicos, its shirt has carried the logo of Drake or the Rolling Stones.
Its stadium is called Spotify Camp Nou.
questions.description: A music app that can also score goals.
questions.fun_fact: In the March 2023 Clásico, Barça’s shirt carried the “Motomami” logo of Rosalía.

questions.question: In a village near Burgos, Spain, at Corpus Christi, a man dressed as a devil jumps over people lying on mattresses in the street. Who are they?
hints: The festival is called El Colacho and is several centuries old.
Their families dress them in their best clothes before laying them on the mattresses.
All of them were born during the past year.
questions.description: A festival where the one who jumps highest is also the ugliest guy in town.
questions.fun_fact: By tradition, the devil's leap “cleanses” the children of original sin and protects them from illness.

questions.question: There are three of us: two write the lyrics and one the music. We wrote «Y sin embargo te quiero» and «Ay pena, penita, pena». Who are we?
hints: We were hits in the 1940s and 1950s, with singers like Juanita Reina and Lola Flores.
One of us was a poet from Seville named Rafael.
The one who wrote the music was called Manuel, and he was from Seville too.
questions.description: Three men, one copla-making machine, and not a single tonadillera out of work.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael de León, the trio's lyricist, was the son of a count and a friend of Federico García Lorca.

questions.question: The famous song says this city “tiene un color especial” (has a special color). Which city is it?
hints: It's the city of the April Fair.
The Guadalquivir River runs through it.
Its most famous tower is the Giralda.
questions.description: A city so vain it has its own color palette.
questions.fun_fact: The Giralda was the minaret of a mosque before it became the cathedral's bell tower.

questions.question: Who traditionally wears a big flower in her hair and a ruffled polka-dot dress?
hints: You see it a lot at the Seville April Fair.
She dances to hand-clapping and guitar.
She stamps her feet hard on the floor of a tablao.
questions.description: A whole garden won't fit on your head, but one flower does the job.
questions.fun_fact: Where the flower goes changes with each year's fashion: on top, at the side or at the back of the head.

questions.question: Look at this polka-dot dress with ruffles. Why do people in Andalusia wear it?
hints: It's worn in spring, for a party.
People dance in it in the casetas.
In Seville, the most famous one is held in April.
questions.description: A dress with so many dots it looks like a domino with ruffles.
questions.fun_fact: The flamenca dress is one of the few traditional costumes that changes with fashion every year.
