questions.question: The lullaby «Duérmete, niño» warns that if you don't fall asleep, someone will come and eat you. Who?
hints: Nobody really knows what it looks like.
It's a figure from Spanish and Portuguese folklore, used to scare children who won't go to sleep.
Its name is the Spanish word for a hairy tropical fruit with water inside.
questions.description: The oldest threat Spanish parents use to get you to turn the light off at last.
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese sailors named the palm fruit “coco” because its three holes reminded them of a face, like the monster in the lullabies.

questions.question: Gustavo Pascual Falcó wrote it in 1937. It plays at weddings and street fiestas and is danced crouching, hands on hips. What is “Paquito el chocolatero”?
hints: It's the classic music of village brass bands.
You also hear it in bullrings.
Its name means “double step”.
questions.description: The song that turns your uncle into a squat champion at every wedding.
questions.fun_fact: Its composer was from Cocentaina (Alicante) and dedicated it to his brother-in-law, who was nicknamed Paquito el chocolatero.

questions.question: Look: what accessory is this, which flamenco dancers open and close as they dance?
hints: People use it a lot in summer.
It's made of fabric or paper folded over thin sticks.
It opens like a peacock's tail.
questions.description: The basic kit for any bailaora who wants to shine at the feria.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century there was a “language of the fan”: how you moved it sent secret messages.

questions.question: Look at this band: what is the cheerful piece called that it plays while marching through town during the fiestas?
hints: It is played while walking, not sitting down.
It opens many fiestas in the morning.
Its name says what it does: “pasar las calles,” passing through the streets.
questions.description: Music with legs: it won't even stay still on the stage.
questions.fun_fact: The “passacaglia” of Baroque music, which Bach used, comes from the Spanish pasacalle.

questions.question: I'm a famous saint of Ireland. Legend says I taught with a three-leaf clover, and on my day, March 17, half the world wears green. Who am I?
hints: I lived more than a thousand years ago.
A huge cathedral in New York is named after me.
In Irish, my name is Pádraig.
questions.description: A saint so green that even his symbol is a plant.
questions.fun_fact: In Chicago, the city's river is dyed green to celebrate Saint Patrick's Day.

questions.question: In the Spanish children's song “Cinco lobitos”, where does the mother wolf keep her five little wolves?
hints: It's something you have at home.
It often stands in a corner of the kitchen.
It sweeps the floor.
questions.description: The busiest mother wolf in the world: five cubs and not one day off.
questions.fun_fact: You sing it while turning your open hand, and each finger is one of the little wolves.

questions.question: The song says Mambrú went off to war and nobody knows when he'll come back. When does it say he might return?
hints: It's a spring holiday.
If not then, the song says “por la Trinidad”.
It's when Spanish families eat monas and torrijas.
questions.description: A general who left home and kept everyone waiting, just like the delivery driver.
questions.fun_fact: Mambrú is the Duke of Marlborough, an ancestor of Winston Churchill.

questions.question: It's danced with jumps and castanets, sung in coplas (short verses), and the most famous one is from Aragón. Which dance is it?
hints: It's danced in almost every part of Spain.
In Zaragoza it's danced a lot during the Fiestas del Pilar.
Its name is also what Spaniards call one letter of the alphabet.
questions.description: A dance for people with springs in their legs.
questions.fun_fact: Almost every region of Spain has its own jota: there's a Navarrese, Castilian, Valencian and Riojan jota, and more.

questions.question: In a famous Christmas carol, a poor boy comes to Bethlehem with no gift and offers to play an instrument for Baby Jesus. Which one?
hints: It's a percussion instrument.
Soldiers used to march to its beat.
It goes “pa rum pum pum pum”.
questions.description: An unwrapped present that makes quite a lot of noise.
questions.fun_fact: The original song is American, from 1941, and in Spain it was made famous by Raphael.

questions.question: In the song “Debajo un botón”, “botón” goes with “ton, ton” as “Martín” goes with…
hints: The end of the word gets repeated.
Look at the last syllable of “Martín”.
It ends just like “chiquitín”.
questions.description: A song with a built-in echo, so nobody misses the end of a word.
questions.fun_fact: Under the button that Martín found was a mouse: “¡ay, qué chiquitín!” (oh, how tiny!).

questions.question: It's sweet, made from egg whites and sugar, and gives Real Madrid fans their nickname. What's the word?
hints: You can find it in a bakery.
You whip it for a long time until it turns foamy.
It's as white as the team's shirt.
questions.description: Some teams earn their nickname on the field, and others at the bakery.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that Real Madrid chose white to copy Corinthian, a very stylish English club from the early 1900s.

questions.question: You're watching the final in Rome where Barça won the first treble by a Spanish club: La Liga, Copa del Rey and Champions League. What year is it?
hints: It was Guardiola's first season as coach.
In the final, Barça beat Manchester United.
It was the year after Spain won the Euros in Vienna.
questions.description: Three trophies in one season: the trophy cabinet asked for an urgent extension.
questions.fun_fact: That same year Barça won six titles, every one it played for: the famous “sextete”.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who is this young Barça player?
hints: He made his first-team debut at just 15.
He won the European Championship with Spain in 2024.
He celebrates goals by making “304” with his fingers, for his neighborhood in Mataró.
questions.description: At his age, some kids are still hunting for their lost phone; he's hunting for the top corner.
questions.fun_fact: The “304” sign comes from the postal code of Rocafonda, the Mataró neighborhood where he grew up.

questions.question: In 2005, the whole Bernabéu applauded a Brazilian Barça player after he scored two amazing goals. Who was he?
hints: He won the Ballon d'Or in 2005.
He was famous for his smile and his long hair.
His name is a cute “little” form of another name.
questions.description: When the rival stadium stands up to cheer you, you've done something really big.
questions.fun_fact: Before him, Maradona also got a standing ovation at the Bernabéu in a Barça shirt, in 1983.

questions.question: Fernando Hierro captained Real Madrid, scored 29 goals for Spain and coached Spain at the 2018 World Cup. What position made him famous?
hints: Many of his goals were headers and set pieces.
He spent almost the whole game near his own goal.
His main job was to stop the strikers.
questions.description: A surname made of metal, and a captain's armband that weighed even more.
questions.fun_fact: Before making it big at Real Madrid, Hierro played for Real Valladolid.

questions.question: At the harvest festival called Pongal, people boil rice and milk in a pot until it spills over, for good luck. In which country is it celebrated?
hints: It's a country in Asia.
The Ganges River is sacred there.
Diwali, the festival of lights, is also celebrated there.
questions.description: A festival where letting the pot boil over isn't a kitchen disaster, it's good luck.
questions.fun_fact: “Pongal” comes from a Tamil word meaning “to boil” or “to overflow”, which is exactly what the pot does.

questions.question: In each La Liga season, how many times do Real Madrid and Barça play each other?
hints: In La Liga, every team plays every other team the same number of times.
La Liga has 20 teams and 38 matchdays.
Once at the Bernabéu and once at Barça's stadium.
questions.description: The match where half of Spain is too nervous to touch the popcorn.
questions.fun_fact: Their first match was in 1902, in the Coronation Cup, and Barça won 3–1.

questions.question: I was born in Pamplona, came up through Athletic Club with my older brother and scored Spain's first goal in the Euro 2024 final. Who am I?
hints: I play on the wing and I'm very fast.
My older brother plays for Ghana's national team.
I share a last name with my brother Iñaki.
questions.description: A winger so fast that his shadow is still back at midfield.
questions.fun_fact: Spain won that final 2–1 against England in Berlin.

questions.question: Spain has won the men's World Cup. In which year did it win?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
That World Cup was played in Africa.
It was the year the vuvuzelas never stopped buzzing.
questions.description: A golden cup that's useless for orange juice, but gets a whole country jumping.
questions.fun_fact: Spain won that World Cup even though it lost its first match, against Switzerland.

questions.question: Spain beat Germany in the Euro 2008 final and knocked them out again at the Euro hosted by Germany. How many years apart were they?
hints: The Euros are played every four years.
The Euro in Germany is the one Spain won with Lamine Yamal and Nico Williams.
That Euro was in 2024.
questions.description: A rivalry so long it deserves its own soap opera, starring sausages and tortilla.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024 Spain knocked Germany out in the quarterfinals with a Mikel Merino header near the very end of extra time.

questions.question: Fabián Ruiz came up through Betis, played for Napoli and won the 2025 Champions League with a foreign club. Which city is that club from?
hints: It's a European capital.
His club had lost a Champions League final before, but had never won one.
It's the city of the Eiffel Tower.
questions.description: A left-footed Andalusian who has caught more planes than a flight attendant.
questions.fun_fact: In that 2025 final, Fabián's club beat Inter Milan 5-0, the biggest win ever in a Champions League final.

questions.question: By winning the 2024 final in Berlin, Spain became the team with the most European Championships. How many did it have with that one?
hints: It won its first one in the 1960s.
Its golden tiki-taka era was the time of the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.
It overtook Germany, which has three.
questions.description: A July night in Berlin when Spain went home with more luggage than it came with.
questions.fun_fact: At Euro 2024 Spain won all seven of its matches, something no team had ever done before at a European Championship.

questions.question: Basque goalkeeper of the Barcelona Dream Team that won the 1992 European Cup at Wembley, who played in four World Cups for Spain. Who was he?
hints: Before joining Barça, he played for Athletic Bilbao.
He was Spain's most-capped player until Casillas passed him.
Many people called him “Zubi”.
questions.description: Being the last line of defense of Cruyff's Dream Team: a job with lots of applause and no breaks.
questions.fun_fact: Years after retiring, Zubizarreta went back to Barça as sporting director.

questions.question: I was Casillas's backup for the Spain team that won in 2008, 2010 and 2012, a Liverpool hero and the showman at team parties. Who am I?
hints: I came up through Barça's youth academy.
My father, Miguel, was also a goalkeeper for Barça and Atlético de Madrid.
At the title parties, I introduced my teammates one by one with funny lines.
questions.description: A goalkeeper who stopped shots and, at the celebrations, kept the microphone.
questions.fun_fact: In 2008, Reina introduced his teammates over the loudspeakers at the Madrid celebration, and it became a tradition after every title.

questions.question: Fernando Fernán Gómez’s “Las bicicletas son para el verano” follows a Madrid family. In what period is it set?
hints: The father promises his son a bike, but summer brings something much worse.
In the play, Madrid is under siege for almost three years.
It begins in July 1936.
questions.description: A play that proves asking for a bike for your birthday can turn into a very long wait.
questions.fun_fact: The play opened in 1982, and in 1984 Jaime Chávarri turned it into a film.

questions.question: José Agustín Goytisolo wrote “Palabras para Julia,” which Paco Ibáñez turned into a song. Which group of poets did Goytisolo belong to?
hints: It's a group of poets from the years after the Spanish Civil War.
His fellow members included Jaime Gil de Biedma and Ángel González.
Its name holds the decade when they started publishing.
questions.description: A poem strummed on more guitars than “Happy Birthday” in a student dorm.
questions.fun_fact: His brothers Juan and Luis Goytisolo were also famous writers.

questions.question: Every February 2 in the US, Phil the groundhog comes out of his burrow. Depending on whether he sees his shadow, what does he “predict”?
wrong_answers: Whether the corn harvest will be good
Whether the year will bring good luck
How many hurricanes there will be
hints: Phil lives in a town in Pennsylvania called Punxsutawney.
It has to do with the weather in the coming weeks.
If he sees his shadow, he hides back in his burrow… and the cold sticks around.
questions.description: The only celebrity in the world whose job is to climb out of a hole once a year.
questions.fun_fact: The tradition inspired the movie “Groundhog Day” (1993), in which Bill Murray lives the same February 2 over and over again.

questions.question: His name is Manolito García Moreno, he lives in Carabanchel and calls his little brother “el Imbécil”. What is his nickname?
hints: His nickname is also the title of the book series.
Elvira Lindo first gave him a voice on the radio.
He got it for something he wears on his nose to see the blackboard.
questions.description: The most famous kid in Carabanchel, and no, it’s not because he’s a soccer star.
questions.fun_fact: In 1999, a movie about Manolito directed by Miguel Albaladejo came out.

questions.question: From Barcelona, literary agent Carmen Balcells, nicknamed “la Mamá Grande” (Big Mama), launched the authors of a 1960s phenomenon. Which one?
hints: Its authors wrote in Spanish, but on the other side of the Atlantic.
They included Gabriel García Márquez and Mario Vargas Llosa.
Its name sounds like an explosion.
questions.description: A woman with more novelists in her address book than you have contacts on your phone.
questions.fun_fact: Balcells is said to have paid García Márquez's bills so he could devote himself entirely to writing.

questions.question: “Finis Mundi”, Laura Gallego’s first published novel, follows a monk trying to stop the end of the world. Which year was everyone afraid of?
hints: “Finis Mundi” means “end of the world” in Latin.
The story is set in the Middle Ages.
People feared the world would end when the first millennium arrived.
questions.description: A novel with a Latin title, to make it sound even more apocalyptic.
questions.fun_fact: Laura Gallego won the El Barco de Vapor prize with “Finis Mundi” when she was only 21.

questions.question: The poet Carolina Coronado, from Almendralejo, published her “Poesías” with a foreword by Hartzenbusch. In which decade?
hints: She was one of the great female voices of Spanish Romanticism.
Hartzenbusch premiered “Los amantes de Teruel” in 1837.
It was a few years after that premiere.
questions.description: A poet from Extremadura who wrote verses back when young ladies were only expected to embroider.
questions.fun_fact: Carolina Coronado lived until 1911 and spent her last years in Lisbon.

questions.question: Which of these novels did Fernando Aramburu NOT write?
hints: Aramburu is from San Sebastián and writes about the Basque Country.
One of them became an HBO series about the years of ETA.
The odd one out was written by María Dueñas.
questions.description: An intruder has sneaked into a stall at the Madrid Book Fair and nobody has noticed.
questions.fun_fact: Aramburu has lived in Germany since the 1980s.

questions.question: What is the name of the boy who narrates “Los Futbolísimos” and plays for Soto Alto?
hints: He tells the team’s adventures himself, though he isn’t its star.
He often starts the matches on the bench.
It’s the Spanish word for the parcel you get when you shop online, but with a k.
questions.description: A kids’ soccer team that solves more mysteries than it scores goals.
questions.fun_fact: Its author, Roberto Santiago, also directed the film “El penalti más largo del mundo”.

questions.question: A boy, a Cemetery of Forgotten Books and a mysterious author named Julián Carax: in which city is “The Shadow of the Wind” set?
hints: Its author, Carlos Ruiz Zafón, was born in that city.
It takes place after the Civil War, among Gothic streets and the harbor.
The Sagrada Família is there.
questions.description: A novel where forgotten books even get their own cemetery.
questions.fun_fact: “The Shadow of the Wind” has been translated into more than 30 languages.

questions.question: I'm a girl from Madrid who tells grown-ups what I think. I was in a magazine before I was in books, and in 1993 TVE made me a TV series. Who am I?
hints: My stories began before the Spanish Civil War.
My author wrote under a pen name.
My little brother is called Cuchifritín.
questions.description: A girl with so many questions that the adults ran out of answers.
questions.fun_fact: The 1993 series was directed by José Luis Borau.

questions.question: Which poet, winner of the 2019 Cervantes Prize, worked as an architect on the structures of this church?
hints: He wrote in Catalan and in Spanish.
He was a professor of structural engineering.
He was born in Sanaüja (Lleida) in 1938 and died in 2021.
questions.description: A poet who knew all about verses, and also about how much weight a column can hold.
questions.fun_fact: Margarit usually wrote his poems in Catalan and then rewrote them himself in Spanish.

questions.question: “Lo que escondían sus ojos” tells of the romance between the Marquise Sonsoles de Icaza and Ramón Serrano Suñer, Franco's brother-in-law. In which decade?
hints: The novel is by Nieves Herrero, and Blanca Suárez starred in the TV series.
Serrano Suñer was a government minister in the years after the Civil War.
It takes place while Europe is living through a world war.
questions.description: A high-society romance with more glances than dialogue.
questions.fun_fact: Its author, Nieves Herrero, is a radio and TV journalist.

questions.question: In which decade did Elena Fortún start publishing the stories of her famous girl heroine in the magazine “Gente Menuda”?
hints: It was before the Spanish Civil War.
After the war, the author went into exile in Argentina.
The first book, “Celia, lo que dice,” came out shortly before 1930.
questions.description: The storybook grandmother of a whole generation of Spanish grandmothers.
questions.fun_fact: Elena Fortún was the pen name of Encarnación Aragoneses.

questions.question: I happen in cafés like the Café Gijón in Madrid: writers and artists meet in me every week to talk about books. What am I?
hints: There's no dancing and no procession.
What matters is talking in a group, always with the same regulars.
Radio and TV have them too, with a panel of regular guests debating.
questions.description: Coffee, ideas flying around and someone who always starts with “Well, I think…”.
questions.fun_fact: The Café Gijón opened in 1888 and is still on the Paseo de Recoletos.

questions.question: It's an orange light you put on the car roof; it alerts the DGT (Spain's traffic authority) and since 2026 replaces warning triangles. What is it called?
hints: It is used when the car breaks down on the road.
This way you don't have to walk along the shoulder to warn others.
Its name contains a letter and a number.
questions.description: The two triangles in the trunk have just lost their jobs.
questions.fun_fact: Since January 1, 2026, the beacon in Spain must be “connected”: it sends its location so it shows up on road signs and navigation apps.

questions.question: In Spain, CCOO and UGT are the two biggest: they defend workers, negotiate collective agreements and call strikes. What are they?
hints: They are all over the news on May 1.
They represent employees, not companies.
Their members are workers who join together to be stronger.
questions.description: If you and your boss can't agree, this is when they show up with banners.
questions.fun_fact: UGT was founded in Barcelona in 1888 and is one of the oldest labor unions in Spain.

questions.question: In Spain, if a company fires you without a justified reason, what is that dismissal called?
hints: It's the best result for the worker when a judge rules on the case.
It forces the company to pay higher compensation or take you back.
It's the exact opposite of “procedente”.
questions.description: A word you hear a lot in courtrooms, and in football news when a coach gets sacked.
questions.fun_fact: When a dismissal is ruled improcedente, the company can choose between hiring you back or paying you compensation.

questions.question: “I'm your name written your own way, with lines only you can make. I'm on your DNI (ID card) and important papers.” What am I?
hints: You make it with a pen.
Grown-ups put it at the end of documents.
Famous people give it to their fans as an autograph.
questions.description: A drawing you make in a hurry that's still worth a lot.
questions.fun_fact: On the Spanish DNI, your signature is scanned and printed on the card, next to your photo.

questions.question: The great blackout of April 28, 2025 cut the power across mainland Spain and Portugal. At what time did it start?
hints: That day was a Monday.
Lots of people were at work or at school.
It happened a while after mid-morning, getting close to lunchtime.
questions.description: The day half the peninsula found out the battery radio still worked.
questions.fun_fact: The blackout began at 12:33, and in many areas the power didn't come back until that night or the early hours of the next day.

questions.question: In Spain many people take out a hipoteca to buy a home. What is a hipoteca?
questions.answer: A bank loan with the home as security
wrong_answers: A tax paid every year for owning a home
An insurance policy against fire and flooding
A contract to rent an apartment to someone
hints: Many people sign one when they become homeowners.
It is usually paid every month for many years.
If you don't pay it, the bank can take the home.
questions.description: A word that makes anyone hunting for an apartment tremble.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain it is common to sign a hipoteca for 25 or 30 years.

questions.question: Complete the name: on January 6, children in Spain open the presents brought by the Reyes…
hints: They come from the East.
Their names are Melchor, Gaspar and Baltasar.
Their name sounds a lot like the English word “magic.”
questions.description: The one night of the year when leaving your shoes in the living room is a good idea.
questions.fun_fact: A roscón de Reyes usually hides a small figure and a dried bean: whoever finds the bean has to pay for the roscón.

questions.question: When Spain's national anthem plays in a stadium, people sing “lo, lo, lo”. Why?
questions.answer: Because it has no official lyrics
wrong_answers: Because its lyrics are in Latin
Because singing the lyrics is banned
Because the lyrics are too long
hints: It's not a memory problem.
People have tried to put words to it, but none have caught on.
The Marcha Real is music only.
questions.description: Eighty thousand people in a stadium singing exactly the same thing: a national mystery.
questions.fun_fact: The Marcha Real is one of the oldest national anthems in the world: it already appears in a book of military fife and drum calls from 1761.

questions.question: The first gold star above the crest of Spain's men's national soccer team marks a World Cup. Where was it played?
hints: It was the first World Cup Spain won.
Iniesta scored the goal in the final.
It was the first time this big tournament was played in Africa.
questions.description: A golden star sewn onto the shirt that won't come off, not even in the washing machine.
questions.fun_fact: Iniesta scored the winning goal in the final against the Netherlands in the 116th minute, in extra time.

questions.question: Which Mediterranean region of Spain, next to the Valencian Community, does not have Aragon's red and yellow stripes on its flag?
hints: Its flag is almost all one color.
It has castles and crowns on it.
It is a land of huerta (market gardens) and pimentón.
questions.description: Four red stripes that have traveled more than a Mediterranean cruise.
questions.fun_fact: The same stripes also appear in one of the quarters of Spain's coat of arms.

questions.question: Tradition says the golden chains on Navarre's coat of arms were won in a battle in 1212. Which battle?
hints: It was a battle of the Reconquista against the Almohads.
The kings of Castile, Aragon and Navarre fought side by side.
It was fought in the Sierra Morena, in the province of Jaén.
questions.description: A flag wearing more jewelry than a summer street market.
questions.fun_fact: Navarre's king in that battle was Sancho VII, nicknamed “the Strong” because he was so very tall.

questions.question: Goya's etching “The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters” is part of a series of prints published in 1799. Which one?
hints: The series came before the war against Napoleon.
In it, Goya makes fun of the superstitions, vices and customs of his time.
Its name means whims or fancies.
questions.description: The perfect print for explaining why you shouldn't nap on top of your homework.
questions.fun_fact: Goya put Los Caprichos on sale in 1799 but took them off the market after a few days, perhaps out of fear of the Inquisition.

questions.question: This building in Barcelona houses the MACBA, the Museum of Contemporary Art. Which architect designed it?
hints: The architect isn't Spanish.
He's American and famous for buildings that are almost always white.
He also designed the Getty Center in Los Angeles.
questions.description: A building so white that nobody in El Raval can keep the skateboards away from its front door.
questions.fun_fact: The open square in front of the MACBA is one of the most famous skateboarding spots in Europe.

questions.question: It's a bronze statue by Ricardo Bellver that shows Lucifer falling from heaven, and it sits on top of a fountain. Which park is it in?
hints: It's in the capital of Spain.
The park has a large pond where you can go rowing.
The Palacio de Cristal is right next to it.
questions.description: There are statues of kings, generals and poets, but this one chose a different kind of star.
questions.fun_fact: Bellver took inspiration from “Paradise Lost”, the poem by the English writer John Milton.

review.feedback: source: hint 3 is wrong. The Fuente del Ángel Caído stands in the southern part of the Retiro, a few hundred meters from the Palacio de Cristal, so the Palacio is not "right next to it" ("junto a él"). The source hint needs rewording (for example "The Palacio de Cristal is in the same park"), and the translation should then follow it. Otherwise the English is faithful and natural.

questions.question: I'm almost 8 m (26 ft) long, painted only in grays, black and white, and since 1992 I've lived in the Museo Reina Sofía. Which painting am I?
hints: I was painted in 1937.
My painter was born in Málaga.
I'm named after a Basque town that was bombed.
questions.description: A whole museum wall for a single painting: some people don't have that much space at home.
questions.fun_fact: Guernica spent more than 40 years in New York and didn't arrive in Spain until 1981.

questions.question: At Els Quatre Gats in Barcelona, a copy of a painting of two men riding a tandem bicycle hangs on the wall. Who painted it?
hints: He is one of the great painters of Catalan modernisme.
One of the two cyclists is the painter himself; the other is the owner of the café.
He also made the famous Anís del Mono poster.
questions.description: Two gentlemen with mustaches, a ride built for two and no helmets: Barcelona in 1900.
questions.fun_fact: In 1901 the painter swapped the tandem painting for a new one showing the two friends in a car, to keep up with the times.

questions.question: I was a painter in Toledo, became a Carthusian monk in 1603, and painted quinces, cardoons and cabbages hanging on strings against a black background. Who am I?
hints: I am one of Spain’s first great still-life painters.
I spent my last years in the Charterhouse of Granada.
My “Still Life with Cardoon” is kept in Granada’s Museum of Fine Arts.
questions.description: A painter who turned the shopping list into a masterpiece.
questions.fun_fact: One of his most famous still lifes, with a hanging quince and cabbage, is now in San Diego, in the United States.

questions.question: This portrait of Goya at 80, painted in Madrid in 1826, now hangs in the Prado Museum. Who painted it?
hints: He was from Valencia.
He was First Court Painter to King Ferdinand VII.
His first surname is one of the most common in Spain.
questions.description: Painting the greatest painter of his time: no pressure at all.
questions.fun_fact: Goya sat for this portrait during a trip to Madrid from his exile in Bordeaux.

questions.question: This ceiling of colorful stalactites covers the Human Rights Room at the UN in Geneva. Which Spanish artist created it?
hints: The artist also works with ceramics.
He was born in Majorca.
He also decorated a chapel in Palma Cathedral.
questions.description: A ceiling that looks like a colorful cave: perfect for staying awake in long meetings.
questions.fun_fact: About 35,000 kg (77,000 lb) of paint were used for that ceiling.

questions.question: Dalí bought Púbol Castle for Gala in 1969. Which animals with extremely long legs decorate its garden?
hints: Dalí had already painted them in his pictures.
In his paintings they seem to walk on spider legs.
They are the largest land animals in the world.
questions.description: An anniversary present that no wrapping paper could ever cover.
questions.fun_fact: Gala only let Dalí into the castle if she had invited him in writing.

questions.question: Complete: Málaga is to Picasso as Figueres is to…
hints: Figueres is in the province of Girona.
A Surrealist painter was born there, and his theater-museum is there too.
The museum has giant eggs on its roof.
questions.description: A trip around Spain where every town introduces you to its favorite painter.
questions.fun_fact: Dalí is buried in a crypt beneath the stage of his own Theater-Museum in Figueres.

questions.question: The painter Salvador Dalí was famous for something very long and thin, with the tips twisted upward. What was it?
hints: It was on his face.
It sat right above his mouth.
The Dalí masks in “Money Heist” have it too.
questions.description: A painter who always wore his most famous work, from ear to ear.
questions.fun_fact: In 1954 Dalí and the photographer Philippe Halsman published a whole book of photos of his mustache.

questions.question: Since 1966, these Hanging Houses of Cuenca have held the Museum of Spanish Abstract Art. Which painter founded it?
hints: The founder gave his collection to the Juan March Foundation in 1980.
He was born outside Spain, in Asia.
He was from Manila, in the Philippines.
questions.description: Abstract art inside houses that were already defying gravity all by themselves.
questions.fun_fact: Fernando Zóbel was born in Manila in 1924 and studied at Harvard University.

questions.question: This 1909 painting of two women in white strolling by the sea is by a painter from Valencia. Who?
hints: He is called the painter of light.
He painted a huge number of Mediterranean beach scenes.
His house in Madrid is now a museum named after him.
questions.description: So much sunshine in one painting that you almost need sunscreen to look at it.
questions.fun_fact: The woman in the white dress is Clotilde, Sorolla’s wife, and the young woman is their daughter María.

questions.question: The Seven Dwarfs are to Snow White as the ___ are to Gru.
hints: They are small and very mischievous.
They are yellow, and many of them wear goggles.
They love bananas.
questions.description: A villain so bad that everyone ends up loving him, especially his little helpers.
questions.fun_fact: The Minions speak a made-up language that mixes words from many languages, including Spanish.

questions.question: Which singer from Barcelona released his first solo album, “Arena en los bolsillos”, in 1998, with the hit “Pájaros de barro”?
hints: He was born in Barcelona in 1955.
Besides singing, he paints and shows his work in exhibitions.
Before going solo, he was the voice of a famous '80s duo with Quimi Portet.
questions.description: A Barcelona man who has spent half his life emptying sand out of his pockets before laundry day.
questions.fun_fact: Manolo García is also a painter, and many of his album covers and artwork come from his own paintings.

questions.question: In what year did Jarabe de Palo, Pau Donés's band, release its first album, “La flaca”?
hints: It was in the 1990s.
Soon after, the song “La flaca” became hugely famous thanks to a TV ad.
It was a few years before the Sydney Olympics, held in 2000.
questions.description: A syrup you can't buy at the pharmacy, and yet it still makes you feel great.
questions.fun_fact: Pau Donés was inspired to write “La flaca” by a Cuban woman he met on a trip to Havana.

questions.question: In the song “Hijo de la Luna”, who begs the Moon until dawn for a man to marry?
hints: The song begins by saying “a legend tells”.
The man she gets later distrusts her because the baby is born white with gray eyes.
She belongs to a people known for flamenco and a wandering life.
questions.description: A home-delivery order, arriving at dawn, with fine print included.
questions.fun_fact: José María Cano wrote it for Mecano in 1986, and even Montserrat Caballé recorded her own version.

questions.question: In which decade did Mecano release their song “Hoy no me puedo levantar”?
hints: It was the time of the Movida madrileña.
It was on the band's first album.
It came out early in the decade when the CD was born.
questions.description: The official anthem of Monday mornings.
questions.fun_fact: In 2005 the song gave its name to a musical full of Mecano hits that ran for years in Madrid.

questions.question: Who first sang “Resistiré”, the 1988 song that goes “Cuando pierda todas las partidas…”?
hints: They were two singers who were already hits in the 1960s.
They also sang “Quisiera ser” and “Perdóname”.
Their name sounds like a superhero pair.
questions.description: Tougher than a loaf of bread left out since the day before yesterday.
questions.fun_fact: In spring 2020, “Resistiré” was sung from balconies all over Spain and returned to the charts more than 30 years later.

questions.question: In which decade was Camilo Sesto's “Vivir así es morir de amor” a big hit?
hints: It was the decade when Spain approved its Constitution.
It was the age of bell-bottoms and disco music.
It came out at the end of that decade, just before the '80s.
questions.description: A song so intense you should listen to it with a tissue in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo Sesto also starred in the Spanish version of the musical “Jesus Christ Superstar” in 1975.

questions.question: At a wedding, “Corazón partío” comes on and everyone sings “¿Quién me va a entregar sus emociones?”. Who sings it?
hints: He's a singer from Madrid with a raspy voice.
The song is from 1997, from the album “Más”.
He has won loads of Latin Grammys, and his surname is very short.
questions.description: When the most serious uncle in the family starts singing with his tie around his forehead.
questions.fun_fact: The album “Más”, which has “Corazón partío” on it, is one of the best-selling albums in the history of Spanish music.

questions.question: In which decade did Robe Iniesta found the band Extremoduro in Plasencia?
hints: It was before the band recorded “Agila” and “So payaso”.
It was in the same era as the Movida madrileña.
It was at the end of that decade, in 1987.
questions.description: Rock so hard you could use it to break stones in Extremadura.
questions.fun_fact: The name Extremoduro blends “Extremadura”, the band's home region, with “duro” (hard), for their hard rock.

questions.question: In my song they tell me to give my body joy, and in my dance you put your hands on your head and hips. What's my name?
hints: My song is by two singers from Seville.
People dance it at every party and wedding.
My name starts with “Maca…”.
questions.description: A girl who loved dancing so much that half the world copied her moves.
questions.fun_fact: Los del Río's “Macarena” spent 14 weeks at number 1 on the US charts in 1996.

questions.question: It was born in 1966 on Cadena SER as a chart of hit songs, and today it hands out music awards with its name every year. Which station is it?
hints: It's a station for pop music and the latest hits.
Its name includes a number.
For decades its name ended in “Principales”.
questions.description: The station that has spent decades deciding which song will be stuck in your head this summer.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, “Los 40 Principales” shortened its name and became simply LOS40.

questions.question: A streamer says: “I'm going live today!”. What does that mean?
questions.answer: That you watch it as it happens
wrong_answers: That the video is already recorded
That the video has no sound
That it's only shown on TV
hints: You can write to them in the chat and they answer.
There's no way to cut out the mistakes.
It's the opposite of a recorded, edited video.
questions.description: Gaming chair, giant headphones and a family-size bag of snacks: the official uniform of any streamer.
questions.fun_fact: Twitch, one of the most famous live streaming platforms in the world, was born in 2011.

questions.question: On channels like Vegetta777's or Willyrex's, a “gameplay” can last for hours and be split into episodes. What is it?
wrong_answers: A review with a final score
hints: You see the game screen the whole time.
The YouTuber talks while playing.
English-speaking YouTubers often call this kind of video a “Let's Play”.
questions.description: YouTuber slang: the language your parents swear is not real Spanish.
questions.fun_fact: In English, “gameplay” mostly means the way a game plays, but in Spain the word is used for a video of someone playing.

questions.question: I'm a station of Radio Nacional de España, I have a number in my name and my last name is “Todo Noticias”. Who am I?
hints: My programming is news bulletins and information around the clock.
Radio 3 is the alternative music one; that's not me.
My number comes right after 4.
questions.description: If you wake up at 4 in the morning craving current affairs, they're waiting for you here.
questions.fun_fact: RNE has several stations: Radio Clásica for classical music, Radio 3 for alternative music and Radio 4 in Catalan.

questions.question: A Seville studio made it in 2019, its hero is the Penitent One, and it draws on Andalusian religious art. Which video game is it?
hints: It is a dark, tough 2D action game.
The hero wears a tall, pointed hood.
Its title is a word for showing disrespect to something sacred.
questions.description: A video game with more incense than a procession in the small hours of Holy Week.
questions.fun_fact: Blasphemous, by the studio The Game Kitchen, was partly funded through a Kickstarter campaign.

questions.question: Which former Spanish soccer player created the Queens League, the women's 7-a-side league followed on Twitch?
hints: He had already created a similar league for men, the Kings League.
He played as a defender for FC Barcelona.
He won the 2010 World Cup with Spain, partnering Puyol in central defense.
questions.description: Soccer with dice, secret cards and team presidents who livestream.
questions.fun_fact: The Queens League kicked off in 2023, and its teams are run by streamers and content creators.

questions.question: Which Andalusian cry of surprise came from saying «¡Jesús!» very fast?
hints: People let it out when something amazes or overwhelms them.
Say «Jesús» fast with an Andalusian accent and the J almost disappears.
It starts with an O and ends in «zú».
questions.description: An exclamation in such a hurry that it ate half a word on the way.
questions.fun_fact: The same «¡Jesús!» also gave the variant «¡Ojú!», heard a lot in Cádiz and Seville.

questions.question: “Bon dia” is to “good morning” as “bon profit” is to…
hints: Both phrases are in Catalan.
It's a polite phrase you hear many times a day in Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands.
In Spanish, people say “¡Que aproveche!” for the same thing.
questions.description: Half of Spain says “bon dia” and the other half looks like it's sitting a language exam.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, many people say “bon profit” even when they're speaking Spanish.

questions.question: In Spain, what do you call the Y-shaped toy with a rubber band for shooting small stones?
hints: You pull the rubber band back and let go.
It's a classic toy of village streets, and grown-ups always told you to be careful with it.
“Chinas” are small stones.
questions.description: For those summers of scraped knees, bandages and whole afternoons out in the street.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico a tirachinas is called a “resortera”, and in Argentina a “gomera”.

questions.question: Which of these words is NOT a name used in Spain for the judía (bean)?
hints: Three of them can go into a fabada or a potaje.
One is a different legume, fatter and flatter, from another plant.
It's the one eaten in Granada with jamón, taken from a very thick pod.
questions.description: A legume with more nicknames than a soccer player.
questions.fun_fact: The fabes in Asturian fabada are actually beans, even though their name sounds like habas (fava beans).

questions.question: In Andalusia you often hear “¡Quillo, ven!” (Quillo, come here!). Which word is “quillo” a short form of?
hints: It's used to call out to a friend or a young guy.
The full word can also mean a small child.
It's missing the “chi” at the start.
questions.description: An Andalusian greeting so fast it left half the word at the door.
questions.fun_fact: “Quillo” gets even shorter as “illo”, which you hear a lot in Seville.

questions.question: Olive oil is made from olives, and balsamic vinegar of Modena is made from…
hints: It's a fruit that grows in bunches.
It's a small, round fruit, green or purple.
The same fruit is used to make wine.
questions.description: A dark dressing that makes any salad feel important.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena is aged in wooden barrels for at least 12 years.

questions.question: You're at a playground in Spain. Which of these words would you NOT use for any of the things to play on?
hints: Any Spanish child uses three of them.
The odd one out is what Mexicans call something you slide down.
In Spain, that thing is called a tobogán.
questions.description: A playground where one of the words snuck in from across the ocean.
questions.fun_fact: In Chile a slide is called a “resbalín”, and in Colombia a “rodadero”.

questions.question: The music of the Galician anthem, “Os Pinos”, was written by a composer born in Mondoñedo. Who?
hints: He died in 1906, before his work was played as an anthem.
The anthem premiered in Havana in 1907; the words are by someone else.
His first name comes from the Spanish word for Easter.
questions.description: An anthem so Galician that it premiered across the ocean, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: The Galician anthem premiered at the Great Theater of Havana in 1907, in front of Galician emigrants living in Cuba.

questions.question: This region celebrates its day every May 2, in memory of the 1808 uprising against French troops. Which one is it?
hints: Goya painted that day, and the executions the day after.
Its flag is red with seven white stars.
The capital of Spain is in it.
questions.description: A region that celebrates its birthday by remembering the day its people got really, really angry.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid has a Plaza del Dos de Mayo in the Malasaña district, where the Monteleón barracks defended by Daoíz and Velarde once stood.

questions.question: It's September 11, a public holiday, with flowers laid as tributes and flags on balconies for the region's official day. Where are you?
hints: It remembers the end of a siege in 1714.
The flowers are taken to the statue of Rafael Casanova.
That siege was the siege of Barcelona.
questions.description: A holiday that takes its flowers and its balconies very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: The Diada remembers the fall of Barcelona on September 11, 1714, during the War of the Spanish Succession.

questions.question: The Basque Country's 1979 Statute of Autonomy is named after the town where this tree stands. Which town?
hints: It's an oak tree under which the laws of Biscay used to be sworn.
The Basque assembly house stands right next to it.
Picasso painted a famous picture named after this town.
questions.description: Some laws get signed in an office, and others take the surname of an entire town.
questions.fun_fact: The oak standing in Guernica today descends from the original tree: new saplings from it keep being replanted.

questions.question: It's made of gold and gems, an alpha and an omega hang from it, and it appears in yellow on the blue flag of Asturias. What is it called?
hints: It's kept in Oviedo Cathedral.
Tradition links it to Don Pelayo.
Its name recalls the triumph at Covadonga.
questions.description: A cross with two letters dangling from it, like key chains from another alphabet.
questions.fun_fact: The original cross was made in the year 908 for King Alfonso III and is kept in the Cámara Santa of Oviedo.

questions.question: I'm a green holm oak with a red cross above me, in the first quarter of Aragon's coat of arms, and I recall an old Pyrenean territory. What am I?
hints: Legend says the cross appeared above me before a battle against the Muslims.
The territory I recall is in northern Huesca, with Aínsa as its capital.
My name is the name of a district in the Aragonese Pyrenees.
questions.description: A tree that gives nobody shade, but has a permanent spot on a coat of arms.
questions.fun_fact: Aragon's coat of arms has four quarters: the tree of Sobrarbe, the cross of Íñigo Arista, the cross of Alcoraz with four heads, and the red and yellow stripes.

questions.question: What fruit is this?
hints: It ripens in autumn.
Inside it has hundreds of juicy red seeds.
In Spanish, it has the same name as a city in Andalusia.
questions.description: An autumn fruit that takes more patience to eat than a 1,000-piece puzzle.
questions.fun_fact: At the bottom of Spain's coat of arms there is an open pomegranate.

questions.question: I'm sold in packs at the supermarket and end up in lots of paellas. My name is the three letters a ship in trouble sends. What am I?
hints: You can also hear my name out at sea, though not in the kitchen.
In Morse code it would be three dots, three dashes and three dots.
It's the most famous distress signal in the world.
questions.description: For people who measure rice by the handful and patience by the spoonful.
questions.fun_fact: The Morse distress signal was picked because it is very easy to send and recognize, not because the letters stand for anything.

questions.question: Raffaele Esposito, Naples in 1889 and the colors of the Italian flag. According to the most famous story, which dish links all three?
hints: The flag's colors were red, white and green, just like its ingredients.
It is baked in a wood-fired oven.
It was named after the queen of Italy at the time.
questions.description: A tale of royalty, patriotism and a lot of hunger in the 19th century.
questions.fun_fact: The pizzeria where Esposito worked still exists in Naples and is now called Pizzeria Brandi.

questions.question: It was born in 1987, was founded by a Cuban-American businessman and brought pizza delivery to half of Spain. Which chain is it?
hints: It is the youngest of these four chains.
Its first restaurant opened in the Barrio del Pilar, in Madrid.
Its name recalls the days when dinner was ordered by phone.
questions.description: For the nights when nobody at home feels like turning on the oven.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, its founder, Leopoldo Fernández Pujals, also created the phone company Jazztel.

questions.question: In Spain, the January sales traditionally start the day after a long-awaited visit. Whose visit?
hints: That visit is the last big moment of the Christmas season.
That visit comes in January, not December.
They come from the East, and there are three of them.
questions.description: First they bring you presents, then they sell you what they didn't bring, only cheaper.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2012, each shop in Spain can choose when its sales start, and many now begin them before January 6.

questions.question: I'm made of wood and steered by a peg in my forehead; a duke and duchess use me to make a knight and his squire believe they're flying. Who am I?
hints: I appear in the second part of a very famous novel.
The duke and duchess blindfold the riders and blow air at them with bellows.
My name joins “clavija” (peg) and “leño” (log).
questions.description: A budget flight with guaranteed turbulence that never leaves the garden.
questions.fun_fact: The duke and duchess end the Clavileño prank by blowing it up with gunpowder rockets.

questions.question: In Galician, what is a “rúa”?
hints: Every town and city has lots of them.
Its name goes on envelopes, next to the house number.
In Catalan it's called “carrer”.
questions.description: In Galicia even everyday words sound a little bit homesick.
questions.fun_fact: In Salamanca, a Castilian city, one of the most famous streets is called Rúa Mayor.

questions.question: In a shop in Bilbao you hear “eskerrik asko”. What does it mean?
hints: It's one of the first polite words tourists learn.
They say it to you in the shop right after you pay.
It's what you say when someone does you a favor.
questions.description: In Basque, even good manners sound like a championship tongue twister.
questions.fun_fact: Basque has no known relationship to any other living language in the world.

questions.question: In many Spanish cities, which other vehicles may use the bus lane besides buses?
hints: They usually have a color that's very easy to spot.
Their passengers pay for the ride.
You stop one by raising your hand in the street.
questions.description: A private highway for the city's biggest vehicles.
questions.fun_fact: In many cities, cameras catch and fine cars that sneak into the bus lane.

questions.question: What is a cruise ship mainly used for, like the ones that arrive every day in the ports of Barcelona or Palma?
wrong_answers: To fish on the high seas
hints: Its passengers aren't going to work.
On board there are pools, restaurants and shows.
People stop at different ports to go sightseeing.
questions.description: Ships with more floors than your apartment building.
questions.fun_fact: Barcelona is one of the busiest cruise ports in Europe for passengers.

questions.question: BiciMAD belongs to Madrid City Council and has been running since 2014. What is it?
hints: You don't need your own bike to use it.
You pay with your phone or a card.
You pick up a bike at one station and drop it off at another.
questions.description: A Madrid invention with two wheels and thousands of users.
questions.fun_fact: BiciMAD was one of the first public bike services in Europe where every single bike was electric.

questions.question: Every night on TVE, what did the Lunnis announce with their famous song?
hints: The song played at night on TVs in many homes.
Parents used it as a signal for their kids.
After hearing it, it was time to put on your pajamas.
questions.description: Some neighbors who came from very far away and became famous on Spanish TV.
questions.fun_fact: The song «Los Lunnis y los niños nos vamos a la cama» (“The Lunnis and the kids are off to bed”) became the signal for many Spanish children to go to sleep.

questions.question: I'm a police inspector in a TVE series, a mother of twins, and I solve crimes without losing my smile. Who am I?
hints: My series is Spanish and aired from 2009 to 2014.
My name is in the title of my mystery series.
My surname is the Spanish word for a very fast hunting dog.
questions.description: She solves mysteries somewhere between school drop-off and the washing machine.
questions.fun_fact: The series got an American version, “The Mysteries of Laura”, starring Debra Messing.

questions.question: At the store you see butterfly-shaped pasta called “farfalle”. If “farfalle” is to “butterflies”, “orecchiette” is to…
hints: It's a part of the body.
You have two of them, one on each side of your head.
You use them to listen to music.
questions.description: A pasta so tiny it fits on the tip of your finger.
questions.fun_fact: In Bari, in southern Italy, women make orecchiette by hand right in the street, pressing each piece of dough with their thumb.

questions.question: When is TVE's daily soap opera “Acacias 38” set at the start of the series?
hints: The gentlemen wear top hats and the maids wear caps.
There are far more horse-drawn carriages than cars in the streets.
The story begins in 1899.
questions.description: An apartment building where the masters give the orders and the maids know everything.
questions.fun_fact: The title is the address of the building where the rich families and their maids live: number 38, Acacias Street.

questions.question: You walk into the Alcántara family's living room in the first episode of «Cuéntame cómo pasó». Which device didn't exist yet?
hints: The series starts shortly before the first Moon landing.
The Alcántaras are thrilled with their first TV.
What you're looking for reached homes about thirty years later.
questions.description: A family that has been on TV for longer than many of its viewers have been alive.
questions.fun_fact: The story of «Cuéntame cómo pasó» begins in 1968, and the series was on the air from 2001 to 2023, more than twenty years.

questions.question: In Catalan, at what time of day do you say “bon dia”?
hints: “Bon” means “good”.
It sounds a lot like a greeting in Spanish.
It's what you say when you get to school.
questions.description: Two Catalan words that will make you the favorite of your neighbor in the elevator.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalan, “bona tarda” means “good afternoon” and “bona nit” means “good night”.

questions.question: It's the invention in Mortadelo y Filemón's first long adventure, from 1969. It turns bugs into giants, and spies from Tirania want to steal it. What is it called?
hints: At first it was meant to wipe out pests on farms.
Professor Bacterio invents it in the T.I.A. labs.
Its name ends with the Spanish word for “atomic”.
questions.description: A garden fertilizer that went just a little too far.
questions.fun_fact: “El sulfato atómico” was the series' first long story and ran in Gran Pulgarcito from January to June 1969.

questions.question: In which decade were Pepe Gotera y Otilio, Ibáñez's “chapuzas a domicilio” (home-repair botchers), born?
hints: They came after Mortadelo y Filemón.
They appeared in Tío Vivo, a magazine from the publisher Bruguera.
It was the same decade humans first landed on the Moon.
questions.description: If your faucet drips, better not call them: you'll end up with a flooded kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Otilio is famous for being the laziest of the pair and for wrecking everything he touches.

questions.question: It's given by the Spanish government, and musicians like Paco de Lucía have received it, and so have bullfighters. What is this honor called?
questions.answer: Gold Medal of Merit in the Fine Arts
wrong_answers: Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts
hints: It's awarded on the proposal of the Ministry of Culture.
It goes to several people from the world of culture at once, every year.
It's a golden medal that honors the arts.
questions.description: An honor you can't win by singing in the shower, no matter how good it sounds.
questions.fun_fact: Besides musicians and painters, its winners include bullfighters, flamenco dancers and actors.

questions.question: I was born in Barcelona, spent part of my teens in Tokyo and became a star in Italy and Germany with “El mismo sol” and “Sofia”. Who am I?
hints: My father is German.
I was a judge on the talent show X Factor in Italy.
I share my first name with the soccer player Morata.
questions.description: A guy from Barcelona who sings in Spanish and provides the soundtrack to half of Europe's summers.
questions.fun_fact: “El mismo sol” got a version with Jennifer Lopez in 2015.

questions.question: Which of these famous people has NEVER been a judge on “Got Talent España”?
hints: The other three have all pressed the golden buzzer.
He hosts a different show on Antena 3.
He’s the host of “El Hormiguero”.
questions.description: A show where anything goes: singing, dancing or juggling potatoes.
questions.fun_fact: The “Got Talent” format was created by Britain’s Simon Cowell, but the first version to air was the American one, in 2006.

questions.question: Andalusia has hundreds of peñas flamencas. What is a peña flamenca?
wrong_answers: A rock where Roma people sang
A style of singing without guitar
hints: Many Andalusian towns and neighborhoods have had peñas for decades.
In Spanish football the word “peña” is used too, and not to talk about rocks.
It's where people who love flamenco singing, guitar and dance get together.
questions.description: Here, a good quejío at midnight is worth more than all the applause on TV.
questions.fun_fact: In the peñas people listen in silence, and many great flamenco singers started out singing in them.

questions.question: Flamenco shoes make a loud sound when the dancer stamps. What do they have in the toe and heel to sound like that?
hints: It's something made of metal.
They go in with a hammer.
It's the same thing you use to hang a picture on the wall.
questions.description: Shoes that never learned how to tiptoe.
questions.fun_fact: A good flamenco shoe can have dozens of nails in the toe and heel.

questions.question: You just picked olives in an olive grove in Italy, as people have done since ancient Rome. Where do you take them to make oil?
hints: That's where they get crushed with stones or machines.
The old ones had big stone wheels that turned round and round.
The same kind of place is used to grind wheat.
questions.description: A fruit so oily that people squeeze the oil right out of it.
questions.fun_fact: Some olive trees in Italy are more than a thousand years old and still grow olives.

questions.question: Look: this percussion instrument came from Peru, and Paco de Lucía brought it into flamenco. What is it?
hints: It is played with the hands, without drumsticks.
The player sits on top of it.
It is a wooden box with a hole in the back.
questions.description: It crossed the ocean without a passport and reached Andalusia without losing the beat.
questions.fun_fact: Paco de Lucía got his first cajón in Lima in 1977, and within a few years it became a must in flamenco.

questions.question: A man in traditional costume with a scarf tied on his head is called a “baturro”. What is a baturro?
hints: Its most famous fiestas are held in October.
The Ebro River flows through it.
Its biggest city is Zaragoza.
questions.description: A man who wears his handkerchief on his head instead of in his pocket.
questions.fun_fact: The checked scarf that baturros wear on their heads is called a cachirulo.

questions.question: David Villa was born in a mining village, and his nickname “el Guaje” means “kid”. What language does it come from?
hints: It's a language from northern Spain.
Its homeland is famous for cider and fabada.
It's the traditional language of the region around Oviedo and Gijón.
questions.description: Some nicknames are earned by scoring goals, others come from home, accent included.
questions.fun_fact: David Villa is the all-time top scorer for Spain's national team, with 59 goals.

questions.question: You're at La Romareda watching a 17-year-old named Raúl make his Real Madrid debut. What year is it?
hints: Back then, people in Spain still paid in pesetas.
It was the year of the World Cup in the United States.
It was in the mid-nineties.
questions.description: A 17-year-old, a shirt number and a huge stadium: nerves guaranteed.
questions.fun_fact: Raúl started in Atlético Madrid's youth academy and moved to Real Madrid when Atlético shut down its youth teams.

questions.question: Messi is to Barça as Cristiano Ronaldo is to…
hints: It is Barça's great rival.
It plays in Spain's capital.
Its stadium is the Santiago Bernabéu.
questions.description: Two stars, two jerseys and a rivalry that lasted for years.
questions.fun_fact: Cristiano Ronaldo is Real Madrid's all-time top scorer, with 450 goals.

questions.question: In 2025, Lamine Yamal took over Messi's old number 10 shirt at Barça. What number did he wear just before?
hints: It's an odd number.
It's the same number he wore for Spain at Euro 2024.
It's the number that comes right before 20.
questions.description: Some jerseys weigh more than a backpack full of schoolbooks.
questions.fun_fact: Lamine Yamal won Euro 2024 the day after he turned 17.

questions.question: In extra time, Iniesta scored the goal that gave Spain its first World Cup. In which minute?
hints: It came in the second half of extra time, which starts at minute 105.
There were less than five minutes left before a penalty shootout.
There were exactly four minutes left until minute 120.
questions.description: The moment half of Spain hugged the other half without ever having met.
questions.fun_fact: Celebrating the goal, Iniesta showed a shirt dedicated to his friend Dani Jarque, an Espanyol player.

questions.question: The Pichichi Trophy goes to the top scorer in the Spanish league. Where does its name come from?
wrong_answers: From a journalist at the newspaper Marca
hints: The nickname belonged to a real person from more than a hundred years ago.
He died very young, aged just 29, in 1922.
At San Mamés there is a bust of him, and teams visiting the stadium for the first time bring it flowers.
questions.description: An award with a cute nickname that every striker wants to take home.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Moreno, known as “Pichichi,” scored the very first goal at the old San Mamés stadium, in 1913.

questions.question: Dani Olmo finished Euro 2024 as one of the tournament's top scorers. How many goals did he score?
hints: Five other players finished level with him, Harry Kane among them.
He scored in the quarterfinal against Germany and in the semifinal against France.
Before that, he scored against Georgia in the round of 16: one goal in each of those games.
questions.description: A player who comes off the bench and doesn't ask permission to score.
questions.fun_fact: Olmo left Barça's youth academy at 16 for Dinamo Zagreb and came back to the club in 2024.

questions.question: At Euro 2024, Spain won every game it played, from the group stage to the final. How many games was that?
hints: Spain played three games in the group stage.
After the groups, every game was a knockout game, all the way to the final.
After the groups came the round of 16, the quarterfinal, the semifinal and the final.
questions.description: A summer in Germany when Spain won so much that the calculators got tired.
questions.fun_fact: No team had ever won all seven games at a Euro before.

questions.question: On August 20, 2023, in Sydney, Spain became women's world champions. Which team did they play in the final?
hints: They were the reigning European champions.
A year later, Spain's men's team also beat them in a final.
Their players are known as the “Lionesses”.
questions.description: On the other side of the world, while Spain was getting Sunday lunch ready, history was being written.
questions.fun_fact: The only goal of that final was scored by left back Olga Carmona.

questions.question: I was born in Cádiz in 1962 and worked in radio, where I first gave a voice to a boy from Carabanchel. I also wrote the Olivia stories. Who am I?
hints: I also write columns for the newspaper El País.
My most famous character has a grandfather called Nicolás.
That boy wears glasses and is called Manolito.
questions.description: A writer who made people laugh on the radio first, and on paper later.
questions.fun_fact: Before he was in a book, the character was a radio monologue that she performed herself.

questions.question: Fray Perico arrives at a convent in Salamanca with twenty friars and his faithful donkey. What is the donkey's name?
hints: At the convent, the donkey ends up almost like one more friar.
The book came out in 1980 and many children in Spain read it at school.
Its name is the Spanish word for something you wear on your feet, inside your shoe.
questions.description: A scatterbrained friar and his four-legged sidekick, the most famous duo in any convent.
questions.fun_fact: “Fray Perico y su borrico” by Juan Muñoz Martín is one of the bestselling children's books in Spain.

questions.question: Álvaro Cunqueiro, author of “Merlín e familia,” was born in a small Galician town with a cathedral. Which one?
hints: It was one of the seven capitals of the old Kingdom of Galicia.
It's in the north of Galicia.
It's famous for its almond tart and its As San Lucas fair.
questions.description: A Galician who mixed Merlin the wizard with empanada without breaking a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: Cunqueiro was also a great food writer and wrote about Galician cooking.

questions.question: Since 2021, Spanish electricity bills have three periods called punta, llano and valle. What do they show?
questions.answer: The times of day when electricity costs more or less
wrong_answers: The parts of the home that use the most power
The three types of outlets in a home
The usage levels of each household appliance
hints: It has to do with the clock, not with the appliances.
That's why some people run the washing machine or dishwasher at night.
The “valle” period is the cheapest and the “punta” period the most expensive.
questions.description: The one piece of paper that arrives every month and is scarier than a horror movie.
questions.fun_fact: Saturdays, Sundays and national holidays count as valle period for all 24 hours.

questions.question: Almost every shop receipt in Spain shows the letters IVA. What are they?
questions.answer: A tax added to the price
wrong_answers: A fee charged by the bank
A discount for paying by card
A warranty insurance for the product
hints: The shop collects it, but the money ends up with the tax office.
You pay it almost every time you buy something.
In English it is known as VAT: “value-added …”.
questions.description: Three tiny letters at the bottom of the receipt that hardly anyone stops to read.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the standard IVA rate is 21%, but bread, milk and fruit carry a much lower rate.

questions.question: Many Spaniards study a set syllabus for years and sit exams against thousands of rivals to win a permanent post. What are they doing?
hints: The prize is a job working for the state.
People talk about “sacarse la plaza” (landing the post).
It comes from “oposiciones”.
questions.description: An activity with more library hours than a whole season of a TV series.
questions.fun_fact: There are oposiciones for almost everything: teachers, firefighters, judges, police officers and even jobs at Correos, the Spanish post office.

questions.question: At the swearing-in at a Spanish town hall, the vara de mando (a ceremonial staff) is handed over. What does it stand for?
wrong_answers: The authority of the justice of the peace
The authority of the town clerk
The authority of the festivities councilor
hints: It is handed over at the council meeting, right after a vote.
The staff usually bears the town's coat of arms and some tassels.
It is carried by whoever holds the most important seat on the town council.
questions.description: A cane that isn't for walking, yet the whole town respects it.
questions.fun_fact: Many mayors only bring out the vara de mando for solemn occasions, such as the processions of the town's patron saint festivities.

questions.question: Every year at the Princess of Asturias Awards ceremony in Oviedo, the heir to the throne gives a speech. Who is she?
hints: She was born in Madrid in 2005.
She studied in Wales and then at military academies.
She is the older sister of Infanta Sofía.
questions.description: Some jobs get passed down like grandma's sofa, but this one comes with a throne.
questions.fun_fact: Leonor swore to uphold the Constitution before the Spanish parliament on October 31, 2023, her 18th birthday.

questions.question: The Spanish Constitution sets me at 18. What am I?
wrong_answers: The age you finish the ESO
The age a DNI becomes required
hints: I appear in Article 12 of the Constitution.
From that day on, you can vote in elections.
I make you an adult in the eyes of the law.
questions.description: The birthday when the cake comes with paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1978, you didn't come of age in Spain until you turned 21.

questions.question: Minestrone, ribollita and pasta e fagioli: what do they have in common?
hints: They are served hot in a deep bowl.
They contain vegetables, beans and sometimes pasta.
Minestrone is the one with lots of chopped vegetables.
questions.description: Three names that sound like opera singers, but you eat them.
questions.fun_fact: “Ribollita” means “reboiled”: it was made by heating up the previous day's soup with stale bread.

questions.question: It's golden, it sits at the top of Spain's coat of arms, and the Second Republic swapped it for a city wall. What is it?
hints: It has to do with who the head of state is.
It stands for the monarchy.
The king in the Spanish deck of cards wears it on his head.
questions.description: A golden detail that has gone on and off the coat of arms, depending on who was in charge.
questions.fun_fact: On top of the crown on the coat of arms sits a small globe with a cross, a symbol of the king's power.

questions.question: Marta Sánchez sang her own lyrics to Spain's national anthem at a concert in Madrid. In what year?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
The video spread like wildfire on WhatsApp and Instagram.
It was the year Pedro Sánchez became Prime Minister of Spain.
questions.description: A singer, an anthem with no words and a pen: what could go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: In 2008 the Spanish Olympic Committee tried to give the anthem official lyrics, but withdrew them a few days later.

questions.question: This is Spain's coat of arms. Which old kingdom does the golden castle on a red background stand for?
hints: Its historic capital was Burgos.
Isabella I, the Catholic Queen, was its queen.
Its name sounds almost the same as the picture.
questions.description: A coat of arms with more tenants than a Madrid apartment block.
questions.fun_fact: At the bottom of the coat of arms there is a pomegranate (granada in Spanish), standing for the Kingdom of Granada, conquered in 1492.

questions.question: On the carvings in Valladolid's National Museum of Sculpture, the skin was painted in oils with its natural color and shine. What is this technique called?
hints: It is a technique for painting wooden religious statues.
It is different from the one used to paint the robes with gold.
Its name comes from the Spanish word “carne,” meaning flesh.
questions.description: Carvings painted so well you feel like asking them if they're cold.
questions.fun_fact: Some image-carvers gave their statues glass eyes, ivory teeth and even tears made of resin.

questions.question: This painting, “The Milkmaid of Bordeaux”, was painted around 1827 by a Spanish painter living in exile in that French city. Who?
hints: He was from Aragon.
He died in Bordeaux in 1828, aged over 80.
Earlier he had painted the Black Paintings at the Quinta del Sordo.
questions.description: A girl who brings the milk and, while she's at it, wraps up a sixty-year career.
questions.fun_fact: Goya died in Bordeaux in 1828, and his remains did not return to Spain until 1899.

questions.question: It plays nonstop at chiringuitos (beach bars) and parties, has an easy dance, and by September everyone forgets it. What is it called in Spain?
hints: It has to do with a season of the year.
Every year, journalists try to guess which one it will be.
It's the one for vacation, sunshine and the beach.
questions.description: Everyone says they hate it, and everyone knows the chorus by heart.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has been picking one of these songs every year for decades, since the days of Georgie Dann and “La barbacoa”.

questions.question: I was the voice of Danza Invisible, the band from Torremolinos that hit it big with “Sabor de amor”. Who am I?
hints: I'm Andalusian, from the Costa del Sol.
My band was a hit in the 1980s with very danceable songs.
My surname starts with O.
questions.description: A voice from the Costa del Sol with more tan than a lifeguard in August.
questions.fun_fact: Danza Invisible started out in Torremolinos in the early 1980s with a darker sound, before switching to the Latin rhythms of “Sabor de amor”.

questions.question: Which Barcelona duo, with Quimi Portet as one half, sang “Insurrección” and split up in 1998?
hints: Before that, they had played together in the band Los Rápidos.
They also sang “Como un burro amarrado en la puerta del baile”.
The other member of the duo was Manolo García.
questions.description: Two friends from Barcelona more popular than sandwiches on a school trip.
questions.fun_fact: They said goodbye in 1998, but in 2026 El Último de la Fila got back together for a tour with stadium concerts.

questions.question: Which singer represented Spain at Eurovision 1997 with the song “Sin rencor”?
hints: He's a Catalan singer.
He came sixth, one of Spain's best results in the 1990s.
His father is also a singer, famous for his boleros.
questions.description: Twelve points to anyone who gets this one without cheating.
questions.fun_fact: Marcos Llunas is the son of Dyango, the bolero singer famous for “Corazón mágico”.

questions.question: In me, Eva and Juan teamed up in 1992 to form Amaral, and before them Héroes del Silencio came from my streets. What city am I?
hints: I'm in northern Spain, but not by the sea.
The Ebro River flows through me.
I'm the capital of Aragon.
questions.description: A city with so much rock that even the pigeons wear earplugs.
questions.fun_fact: Amaral is named after its singer, Eva Amaral; the other half of the duo is guitarist Juan Aguirre.

questions.question: It has sushi rice tucked inside a sweet fried tofu pouch, and legend says it's the favorite food of a Japanese god's fox messengers. What is it called?
hints: It has no raw fish and no seaweed on the outside.
Its pouch is golden or brown and tastes sweet.
Its name comes from the Japanese god of rice, guarded by foxes.
questions.description: A sushi that climbed into a little bag and refuses to come out.
questions.fun_fact: Inari shrines in Japan have fox statues, and people leave fried tofu for them as an offering.

questions.question: Which singer, son of the bullfighter Luis Miguel Dominguín, was a hit in the 1980s with “Amante bandido”?
hints: His mother was an Italian actress.
He also sang “Bambú” and “Te amaré”.
His mother, Miss Italy 1947, starred in films by Antonioni.
questions.description: A bandit who stole hearts instead of stagecoaches.
questions.fun_fact: His godfather at his baptism was the Italian film director Luchino Visconti.

questions.question: This Spanish YouTuber got famous playing games and goofing around in the videos of his close friend El Rubius. Who is he?
hints: He has his own channel, but many people know him mostly from his friend's videos.
His nickname is a short form of his real name.
His real name is Miguel Ángel.
questions.description: The friend who always ends up as the victim of the latest prank.
questions.fun_fact: Mangel has appeared in so many of El Rubius's videos that many fans see them as an inseparable duo.

questions.question: TheGrefg unveiled his own Fortnite skin to almost 2.5 million people at once, a Twitch record at the time. In what year?
hints: It happened in January.
It was right in the middle of the pandemic.
It was just after the lockdown year.
questions.description: More people staring at one screen than live in many Spanish cities put together.
questions.fun_fact: The next year, Ibai beat that number with “La Velada del Año”, a boxing event between streamers.

questions.question: Radio Barcelona, call sign EAJ-1, was Spain's first licensed radio station. In what year did it start broadcasting?
hints: It was in the “Roaring Twenties”.
It was during the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera.
It was one year before the middle of that decade.
questions.description: Back when radio was so new that people listened with headphones and a look of pure amazement.
questions.fun_fact: Radio Barcelona is still on the air and today is part of Cadena SER.

questions.question: It's a Canary Islands word that recalls an ancient Germanic people and is said half-jokingly. Where is someone called a “godo” in the Canaries from?
hints: The Goths were a people who came to Hispania from northern Europe.
To a Canary Islander, this person comes from outside the islands.
They arrive by plane or boat from Madrid, Seville or Valladolid.
questions.description: A word with more centuries behind it than the tortilla de patatas, and more trips than a suitcase at an airport.
questions.fun_fact: The Visigoths ruled Hispania until the year 711, with their capital in Toledo.

questions.question: You hear it all over Spain, and it's named after a holiday. What does “hacerle la pascua” to someone mean?
hints: It has nothing to do with bunnies or chocolate eggs.
It's an old expression that grandparents still use a lot.
It means the same as “chincharle” or “jorobarle”.
questions.description: Some holidays on the calendar are good for much more than a long weekend.
questions.fun_fact: There's also “y santas pascuas”, which means “and that's the end of it”.

questions.question: It's a thin little tube for sipping juice or a milkshake, and these days it's often made of paper. What is it called in Spain?
hints: It usually sits in the glass of a soft drink.
Other Spanish-speaking countries have very different names for it.
Long ago it was made from dry cereal stalks.
questions.description: A little tube that turns any milkshake into a lung workout.
questions.fun_fact: Before plastic, these tubes were made from dry rye stalks, which is how both “pajita” (from “paja”) and the English “straw” got their names.

questions.question: If someone calls you «guapín» quite naturally, where are they most likely from?
hints: Look at the diminutive ending.
People there say «pequeñín» and «poquitín» all the time.
It's the land of fabada and the Picos de Europa.
questions.description: A compliment so teeny-tiny it fits in your jacket pocket.
