questions.fun_fact: The -ín diminutive is so Asturian that even names get shortened that way: «Xuanín», «Pepín».

questions.question: Complete the sentence: shōjin ryōri, the traditional cooking of the monks in Japan's temples, is completely…
hints: It has to do with what the monks choose not to eat.
It uses tofu, vegetables, seaweed and mushrooms.
It has no meat and no fish.
questions.description: A menu so calm it meditates before it's served.
questions.fun_fact: Many Japanese temples still serve shōjin ryōri to visitors, on lacquered trays.

questions.question: It lives under damp stones, it's grayish, has fourteen tiny legs and a body made of plates. What is it called in many parts of Spain?
hints: It often turns up when you lift a flowerpot or a log.
If you touch it, it rolls itself up.
Its name says what it turns into when it gets scared.
questions.description: A garden tenant who never pays the rent.
questions.fun_fact: The bicho bola isn't an insect: it's a crustacean, like crabs, even though it lives on dry land.

questions.question: This diminutive ending is heard a lot in Aragon and Murcia, and also in Granada and Almería. Which one is it?
hints: You hear it in Aragonese jota songs.
In Zaragoza, people add it when they ask for «un poco».
«Momentico», «pequeñico», «majico».
questions.description: An ending that isn't big, but has plenty of character.
questions.fun_fact: Costa Ricans are called «ticos» because they use this diminutive all the time: «chiquitico», «momentico».

questions.question: In the Spanish of one Mediterranean region with three provinces and its own language, you often hear «poquete» and «chiquete». Which one?
hints: In the region's other language, the diminutive ends in «-et».
Its capital is the third-largest city in Spain.
Its capital is famous for paella.
questions.description: A diminutive with a poquete of sparkle and plenty of party spirit.
questions.fun_fact: In Valencian, «xiquet» means “kid”, and Valencian human towers are called «muixeranga».

questions.question: You're doing the laundry: a hanger is to the closet as a clothespin is to the…
hints: Think about where each object is used.
The clothespin holds wet clothes so they can dry.
It's stretched between two posts, and you hang wet laundry on it to dry outside.
questions.description: A question to keep your T-shirt from flying away.
questions.fun_fact: In Argentina a clothespin is called a «broche», and in Colombia a «gancho».

questions.question: Its flag has four horizontal stripes, red, white, green and yellow, adopted with its 1982 Statute. Which region is it?
hints: It's a single-province region in northern Spain.
The Ebro River runs through it.
Its capital is Logroño.
questions.description: Four stripes in perfect order, better behaved than a line of schoolkids.
questions.fun_fact: La Rioja is the smallest autonomous community on the Spanish mainland.

questions.question: The red and yellow stripes on the Balearic flag recall the Crown of Aragon. Which king conquered Majorca in 1229?
hints: He was born in Montpellier in 1208.
Years later he also conquered Valencia.
His nickname describes exactly what he did to Majorca.
questions.description: A flag with more history than a whole textbook.
questions.fun_fact: The white castle on a purple background on the Balearic flag comes from the flag of the city of Palma.

questions.question: In Spain, if someone says a concert “ha sido la leche”, what do they mean it was?
hints: It's a very casual expression you hear a lot from young people.
It's like saying it was “una pasada”.
It's the opposite of saying it was “un rollo”.
questions.description: It doesn't come in a carton, but it's served at concerts, matches and birthday parties.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Eres la leche!” can be said both to someone who leaves you speechless and to someone who drives you crazy.

questions.question: It closes with a zipper, goes in your backpack and you open it in class. What's usually inside a pencil case?
hints: You need it to write and draw.
If you make a mistake, you take something out of here to fix it.
What's inside writes, rubs out and sharpens.
questions.description: A little zippered house where nobody pays rent.
questions.fun_fact: Before erasers existed, people rubbed out pencil marks with soft bread.

questions.question: In Spain, when do people usually say “¡Jesús!” to someone?
wrong_answers: Right after they blow out candles
hints: It's a very old custom of good manners.
It happens a lot when someone has a cold.
Just before it, you hear an “aaachoo!”.
questions.description: A tiny word that people in Spain throw out like a protective shield.
questions.fun_fact: Some people keep count: “Jesús” for the first sneeze, “María” for the second, and “y José” for the third.

questions.question: You hear some unbelievable gossip and, jaw on the floor, blurt out a Spanish phrase you could also say about a bodybuilder. Which one?
hints: It shows surprise or outrage.
It has nothing to do with being bored or having a nerve.
A bodybuilder lifts lots of heavy weights.
questions.description: Some news leaves you speechless, and then you have to find a word anyway.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Qué fuerte!” works for amazing news and for terrible news alike: it all depends on your tone of voice.

questions.question: In Spanish slang, this person always gets the job nobody wants and falls for every prank. Literally, the word means “smeared with grease.” What is it?
hints: It's the opposite of someone clever who always gets out of things.
It comes from a verb used for dipping bread in sauce.
If you get oil all over your clothes in Spain, you say «me he…»
questions.description: Every group of friends has one, and almost nobody volunteers for the role.
questions.fun_fact: «Pringar» first meant dipping bread in grease; later it came to mean getting stuck with the dirty work or getting into a mess.

questions.question: I was born in Vitoria, played Miguel de Unamuno in “Mientras dure la guerra” and was Koldo, Amaia's father, in “Ocho apellidos vascos”. Who am I?
hints: I'm Basque, from Álava.
I won the Goya for Best Supporting Actor for “Ocho apellidos vascos”, and before that for “También la lluvia”.
My first name starts with K.
questions.description: An actor who can go from grumpy father-in-law to philosopher in a single career.
questions.fun_fact: Karra Elejalde was nominated for the Goya for Best Actor for playing Unamuno in “Mientras dure la guerra”.

questions.question: Motorcycle racer Maverick Viñales is named after a fighter pilot from a movie. Which one?
hints: It's a movie from the 1980s.
Its star was Tom Cruise.
In 2022 it got a sequel named after the same pilot.
questions.description: A racer with a pilot's name: not quite the same job, but pretty close.
questions.fun_fact: Maverick Viñales was the Moto3 world champion in 2013.

questions.question: Àlex Márquez won Moto3 in 2014 and Moto2 in 2019, and his older brother is a MotoGP champion. In which Spanish region was he born?
hints: The region has a Mediterranean coastline.
The region borders France.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.description: The upside of being the little brother: there's always someone to chase around the track.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019 both Márquez brothers became world champions in the same year: Marc in MotoGP and Àlex in Moto2.

questions.question: I'm a Formula 1 driver born in Madrid, named after my father, who won the Dakar several times and two World Rally titles. Who am I?
hints: People call me “Smooth Operator.”
I drove for Ferrari from 2021 to 2024.
My father is nicknamed “El Matador.”
questions.description: In this family you don't just inherit the name, you inherit a right foot glued to the accelerator.
questions.fun_fact: His first Formula 1 win came at the 2022 British Grand Prix at Silverstone.

questions.question: Its basketball team won the EuroLeague in 2003 and 2010, and Pau Gasol and Juan Carlos Navarro played there. Which city is it from?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean Sea.
Its soccer club shares its name and colors with the basketball team.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: A city where the ball gets bounced, not just kicked.
questions.fun_fact: Barça won the 2003 EuroLeague at home, in the Final Four played at the Palau Sant Jordi.

questions.question: I was born in 1969 at a house in Acapulco, Mexico, and a prince brought me to Marbella in the 1970s. Which sport am I?
hints: I'm almost always played in pairs.
My court is surrounded by walls, and the ball can bounce off them.
I'm played with a pala, not a strung racket.
questions.description: The sport that has turned Sunday mornings into a sacred date.
questions.fun_fact: Padel was invented by Enrique Corcuera at his home in Acapulco, and Alfonso de Hohenlohe brought it to the Marbella Club.

questions.question: It's April and you're heading out. According to the saying “En abril, aguas mil”, which of these will you NOT need?
hints: The saying is about the weather.
“Aguas mil” means a whole lot of rain.
Three of these things keep you from getting wet.
questions.description: Spain's big book of sayings has a very clear opinion about spring.
questions.fun_fact: Some people make it longer: “En abril, aguas mil, y todas caben en un barril” (and they all fit in a barrel), because some years it hardly rains.

questions.question: In a Spanish apartment building, what is the “portero automático”?
questions.answer: The device to open the street door from home
wrong_answers: A guard who watches the entrance at night
A door that opens by itself as you approach
A mailbox that tells you when a letter arrives
hints: Almost every apartment building has one next to the entrance.
It rings when someone presses a button down on the street.
You pick up, ask “¿quién es?” and press the button with the key on it.
questions.description: The neighbors on the fifth floor know it better than they know the people on the fourth.
questions.fun_fact: In many new buildings the portero automático now has a camera, so you can see who's calling before you open.

questions.question: I have plots, shared showers, camper vans and tents, and in summer I fill up with families. What am I?
hints: At night you hear crickets and zippers.
You sleep there almost in the open air.
In Spain, people call me by an English word for an outdoor activity.
questions.description: Summer vacation officially starts when the trunk won't close anymore.
questions.fun_fact: In English “camping” is the activity and the place is a “campsite”, but in Spain people say «un camping» for the place itself.

previous.feedback: The translation adds the answer's root word to the question. “Camping spots” and “campers” both echo “campground”, which makes it the only option that matches by sound. The source's “parcelas” and “caravanas” don't contain “camping”. Reword these as “sites” (or “plots”) and “RVs” (or “trailers”), so no word in the question shares “camp” with the answer.

questions.question: At a Japanese restaurant, the menu lists “nigiri” and “onigiri.” Besides rice, what do they have in common?
questions.answer: They are shaped by squeezing by hand
wrong_answers: They are fried in hot oil
They are served in a broth
They are eaten with a spoon
hints: The clue is in the part of the name they share.
“Nigiru” is a Japanese verb that has to do with your fingers.
It means something like “to grip” or “to squeeze.”
questions.description: Two dishes with almost twin names, like cousins who dress alike.
questions.fun_fact: A good nigiri chef presses the rice just enough to hold together, but still melt in your mouth.

questions.question: I glow green on the front of a building, I have four equal arms, and sometimes I tell you the time and temperature. What am I?
hints: You see me in almost every neighborhood in Spain.
Under me, they sell cough syrup and bandages.
The people who work under my light wear white coats and hand out medicine.
questions.description: It has more lights than a Christmas tree, and it isn't even Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: Many pharmacy crosses in Spain are LED screens that show pictures, the time and the temperature.

questions.question: Today you go to school in a chándal (tracksuit) instead of your usual clothes. What day is it most likely?
wrong_answers: The day of the class photo
The day of the Christmas show
hints: You're going to sweat a bit that day.
That day you need comfy sneakers and maybe a water bottle.
That day there are races, balls and jumping.
questions.description: The comfiest clothes in your closet, after your pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: “Chándal” comes from the French “marchand d'ail”, “garlic seller”, after the warm clothes those sellers wore.

questions.question: In Spain, what kind of doctor is the “médico de cabecera”?
questions.answer: The family doctor at your health center
wrong_answers: The surgeon in the operating room
hints: You're assigned one, and they often know your whole family.
If you feel unwell, they're the first one you book to see.
They send you to a specialist if needed.
questions.description: A doctor named after a piece of bedroom furniture.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “de cabecera” (of the headboard) because doctors once visited the sick at home and treated them at the head of the bed.

questions.question: You're 5 and in the last year of Educación Infantil. Which school stage do you move up to next year?
hints: It's the stage where you fully learn to read and write.
It lasts six school years.
Its first year is called “primero de …”.
questions.description: Goodbye playdough on the table, hello graph-paper notebooks.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, Educación Infantil isn't compulsory, but almost all children aged 3 to 6 go to school anyway.

questions.question: By Spanish custom, how many ear tugs do you get on your birthday?
questions.answer: One for each year you turn
wrong_answers: One for each guest at the party
hints: It happens once a year, and the birthday kid doesn't get to choose.
The number changes from one birthday to the next.
You count them just like the candles on the cake.
questions.description: A tradition that leaves birthday kids with ears as red as tomatoes.
questions.fun_fact: Many people finish with one extra tug “so you'll grow”.

questions.question: You use tempera paints, scissors, glue and card stock to make murals and drawings. Which school subject is it?
hints: You do a lot of it with brushes.
When you're done, you wash the brushes in the sink.
It's the class for crafts and painting.
questions.description: The school subject where getting your hands dirty isn't a problem, it's the plan.
questions.fun_fact: Painters long ago made tempera paint by mixing their colors with egg yolk.

questions.question: Which free phone number do you call in Spain for any emergency: fire, ambulance or police?
hints: It works the same across the whole European Union.
It's free, and you can call it even when your phone has no credit left.
Add up its three digits and you get 4.
questions.description: Three digits you'd better know and hope you never need.
questions.fun_fact: In 1991 the European Union decided that 112 would be the shared emergency number for all its countries.

previous.feedback: Source: the fun fact says the European Union chose 112 in 1991, but the EU didn't exist until 1993 (Maastricht). The 1991 decision (91/396/EEC) came from the Council of the European Communities. The Spanish source has the same error, so it should say "la Comunidad Europea" (or drop the year), and the English then follow it as "the European Community". The rest of the translation is faithful and natural.

questions.question: It's stuck into the sand, opens like a giant umbrella and stands next to your towel. What is a sombrilla for?
wrong_answers: To keep you dry if it rains
To stop your towel blowing away
hints: You use it on very sunny days.
It's cooler underneath it.
Its Spanish name grows out of the word for what it gives you.
questions.description: An umbrella that went on vacation to the beach.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain people keep the two apart: a paraguas is for rain, and a sombrilla is for sun.

questions.question: When the teacher says “para mañana hay deberes”, what does it mean?
questions.answer: That you have schoolwork to do at home
wrong_answers: That you have to tidy your room
That there's a field trip tomorrow
hints: You'll have to open your notebook in the afternoon.
The next day, the teacher checks it in class.
It's exercises for school, but you do them outside school.
questions.description: Teachers' favorite line, said right before the last bell rings.
questions.fun_fact: In Latin America, deberes are usually called “tareas”.

questions.question: You finish 4.º de la ESO and want to learn a trade right away, like electrician or hairdresser. What do you study next?
questions.answer: A ciclo de FP de Grado Medio
hints: You learn a lot in workshops, with your hands.
It includes an internship at a real company.
Its initials are two letters: F and P.
questions.description: To become an electrician, first you need a bit of spark.
questions.fun_fact: Many FP programs are “dual”: part of the learning happens while working at a company.

questions.question: Finish the translation: “okonomiyaki,” the grilled Japanese pancake with cabbage, means roughly “grilled the way you…”
hints: The missing word is about the person who is going to eat it.
Everyone adds whatever they enjoy most.
“Okonomi” means “to your taste.”
questions.description: A Japanese pancake that took the whole cabbage thing very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: In many okonomiyaki restaurants, the table has a hot griddle and each customer cooks their own.

questions.question: In Spain, “ESO” is to “instituto” as “Primaria” is to…
hints: You go there before moving up to the instituto.
You go there from first to sixth grade, from age 6 to 12.
Every morning, kids cut its name down to a short word when they say they're off to school.
questions.description: Analogies are like school years: you take them one step at a time and don't skip any.
questions.fun_fact: Primary school (Primaria) in Spain lasts six years, usually from age 6 to 12.

questions.question: In Spain, what do you call a student who failed too many subjects and is now doing the same school year again with younger classmates?
hints: You hear this word a lot in Spanish secondary schools.
It has to do with what happens when end-of-year grades go badly.
It's also the name of the antenna that sends a TV signal on again.
questions.description: A face so familiar in that classroom they know every stain on the ceiling by heart.
questions.fun_fact: «Repetidor» is also the device that picks up a radio, TV or phone signal and sends it out again so it reaches farther.

questions.question: In class, at the office and in shared apartments, people in Spain say «es mi compi». What is a «compi»?
hints: It's someone you share something with every day.
They sit next to you in class or at work.
It's the short form of a word that starts with «compa…».
questions.description: A word so lazy it got tired halfway through.
questions.fun_fact: «Compañero» comes from Latin and literally means “the one who shares bread” with someone else.

questions.question: «Finde» is to «fin de semana» as «depre» is to…
hints: It's one of those words you use with friends, very casual.
Like «finde», it's made by cutting off the end of a longer word.
It's the opposite of feeling happy and full of energy.
questions.description: A chopped-off word for when you can't even be bothered to finish your words.
questions.fun_fact: In everyday speech, «estar depre» usually just means feeling a bit down, like on a Sunday afternoon.

questions.question: It comes from «señorita» and you hear it in elementary school classrooms, with a hand in the air: «¡Seño, seño!». Who are they calling?
hints: She's inside the classroom.
She gives homework and corrects notebooks.
She's the one teaching the class.
questions.description: A word that always comes with an arm stretched up toward the ceiling.
questions.fun_fact: Many children keep calling their teacher «seño» even if she's married or sixty years old.

questions.question: They live stuck to rocks in the sea, sometimes hide a pearl, and in Spain people shout their name when surprised. What are they?
hints: They are shellfish with two shells.
They are famous for making pearls.
Their Spanish name starts the same way as «ostentoso».
questions.description: Some animals get eaten and some get shouted; this one does both.
questions.fun_fact: A pearl forms when the oyster coats something that slipped inside its shell with layer after layer of mother-of-pearl.

questions.question: In Spain, one short word names both the appliance that heats your milk and the thing you hold to sing karaoke. Which word?
hints: The two long words start the same way.
One ends in «-ondas» and the other in «-fono».
It means “small” in Greek.
questions.description: A word with a double life: in the kitchen by day, at karaoke by night.
questions.fun_fact: In countries like Chile and Argentina, a «micro» is also a bus, so there you can actually ride the micro.

questions.question: The bell rings and you head out for recess. Which of these do you NOT usually do at recess?
hints: Recess is for taking a break from class.
Three of these happen in the playground.
The odd one out is done sitting at your desk, in silence.
questions.description: The fastest thirty minutes of the whole day.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word «recreo» comes from «recrear», which means to have fun and rest so you come back refreshed.

questions.question: Which of these things would a «gamberro» NOT do?
questions.answer: Help a neighbor carry her groceries
wrong_answers: Kick the trash cans on the street
hints: A «gamberro» does things to annoy people.
Three of these actions make the neighbors angry.
The odd one out is a good deed.
questions.description: The terror of the neighborhood has a very impressive résumé.
questions.fun_fact: Ringing doorbells and running away is a prank known all over the world: in English it's called “ding dong ditch” in the US and “knock down ginger” in the UK.

questions.question: A basketball coach sentenced to community service trains a team of players with intellectual disabilities. It won the Goya for Best Film. What is it called?
wrong_answers: Padre no hay más que uno
hints: Javier Fesser directed it, and it came out in 2018.
The team in the movie is called Los Amigos.
The title is the Spanish word for what every team wants to be at the end of the season.
questions.description: A movie that proves height is the least important thing in basketball.
questions.fun_fact: The actors who play the team had never acted before, and Jesús Vidal won the Goya for Best New Actor.

questions.question: Gazpacho spiked with sleeping pills is the famous scene in an Oscar-nominated Almodóvar film. In which year did it come out?
hints: The film is “Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown”.
It was the time of the Movida, before the Barcelona Olympics.
It came out in the late 1980s.
questions.description: A cold soup that knocks you out harder than a siesta in August.
questions.fun_fact: Pepa, who makes the gazpacho, is played by Carmen Maura, who won the Goya for Best Actress for the role.

questions.question: “Landismo”, the comedies about the short, flustered average Spanish guy, is named after Alfredo Landa. In which decade was it at its peak?
hints: It was in the last years of the Franco regime.
One of its best-known movies is “No desearás al vecino del quinto”.
It's the decade of bell-bottom pants.
questions.description: A genre of socks, berets and a big hurry to get to the beach.
questions.fun_fact: Alfredo Landa went on to win two Goya Awards for Best Actor in dramatic roles, such as in “El bosque animado”.

questions.question: In the comedy “Toc Toc”, which actor from Seville plays Federico, the patient with Tourette syndrome?
hints: He became famous with the TV series “Aída”.
He has directed movies such as “Carmina or Blow Up”.
In “Aída” he was Luisma, the main character's brother.
questions.description: A waiting room where nobody gets bored, even though everyone keeps repeating themselves.
questions.fun_fact: “Toc Toc” is based on a French stage play by comedian Laurent Baffie.

questions.question: In “Money Heist”, Úrsula Corberó plays the show's narrator. Which city gives her character its name?
hints: All the robbers use the names of cities.
Her boyfriend in the gang is called Rio.
It's the capital of Japan.
questions.description: An actress so well traveled that her character carries a map in her name.
questions.fun_fact: Before “Money Heist”, Úrsula Corberó became famous as Ruth in the TV series “Física o química”.

questions.question: Fernando Tejero for “Días de fútbol”, Alberto Ammann for “Cell 211” and Miguel Herrán for “Nothing in Return” all won this Goya. Which one?
hints: All three were little known when they won it.
For “Cell 211”, the Goya for Best Lead Actor went to Luis Tosar.
It's the award for someone who has only just broken through.
questions.description: An award handed out in the hope that it won't be the last one.
questions.fun_fact: Miguel Herrán won the Goya for his very first film and later played Río in “Money Heist”.

questions.question: In Icíar Bollaín's “Even the Rain”, a crew shooting a film about Columbus runs into the “Water War.” In which country?
hints: It is an Andean country with a large Indigenous population.
The Water War took place in the city of Cochabamba in 2000.
Its constitutional capital is Sucre, and the government sits in La Paz.
questions.description: A film about making a film, so nobody can say cinema is running out of ideas.
questions.fun_fact: The script of “Even the Rain” was written by Paul Laverty, Ken Loach's regular screenwriter and Bollaín's partner.

questions.question: In the animated film about Buñuel, he can shoot “Las Hurdes” because a friend of his won the lottery. Who?
hints: He was an artist and teacher from Huesca.
He was an anarchist and had promised to pay for the film if he won.
He was from Aragon like Buñuel, a painter and sculptor, and his surname has four letters.
questions.description: A friend who pays for your shoot with a lottery ticket: now that's independent film.
questions.fun_fact: Salvador Simó's film adapts a comic by Fermín Solís and won the Goya for Best Animated Film.

questions.question: Which Catalan director won the Golden Bear in Berlin in 2022 with “Alcarràs”?
hints: Her first film was “Summer 1993.”
“Alcarràs” is about a family of farmers from Lleida.
Her surname is almost the same as Paul's, the singer who formed a duo with Art Garfunkel.
questions.description: A director who turned a peach harvest into German gold.
questions.fun_fact: “Alcarràs” was shot in Catalan with non-professional actors from the area.

questions.question: If you count the green jackets José María Olazábal won as Masters champion at Augusta, how many do you get?
hints: It's more than one.
He matched Seve Ballesteros's total at this tournament.
He won in 1994 and again in 1999.
questions.description: At Augusta, green isn't just on the grass: you wear it too.
questions.fun_fact: Olazábal was Europe's captain at the 2012 Ryder Cup, the comeback known as the “Miracle at Medinah”.

questions.question: It's a Japanese lunch box with food decorated to look like characters such as Pikachu or Totoro, and its name blends “character” and “bento.” What is it called?
hints: Many parents in Japan make it for their kids to take to school.
They use rice, seaweed and vegetables as if they were modeling clay.
“Kyara” comes from the English word “character.”
questions.description: A lunch so cute it feels mean to eat it.
questions.fun_fact: Japan holds contests for decorated lunch boxes, and some look like real works of art.

questions.question: Jorge Martín, nicknamed “Martinator”, won Moto3 in 2018 and MotoGP in 2024 with a private team. In which city was he born?
hints: It's a city with no sea.
He grew up in San Sebastián de los Reyes, just outside his home city.
Real and Atlético play there.
questions.description: They call him “Martinator”, but he didn't come from the future: he came from much closer by.
questions.fun_fact: Martín was the first champion of the MotoGP era to win with a private team, Pramac.

questions.question: I'm a motorcycle racer, born in Cervera, nicknamed “la Hormiga” (the Ant). I lean so far in corners that my elbow touches the track. Who am I?
hints: My race number is 93.
I'm Catalan, from the province of Lleida.
My younger brother Àlex also races in MotoGP.
questions.description: A tiny insect that lifts far more than its own weight… in trophies.
questions.fun_fact: In 2025, after years of serious arm injuries, Marc Márquez became MotoGP world champion again.

questions.question: I was born in Barcelona in 2002 and grew up in Jávea. At just 19 I made the Vuelta a España podium, and in 2025 I won Tirreno–Adriatico. Who am I?
hints: I'm a good climber and a good time trialist.
I was Tadej Pogačar's teammate at UAE Team Emirates.
My first name has only four letters.
questions.description: Some people get their driver's license at 19; others climb onto the podium of a three-week race.
questions.fun_fact: Ayuso finished third in the 2022 Vuelta while he was still 19.

questions.question: Three of these Spanish cyclists have won the Tour de France. Which one has NOT?
hints: The one you're looking for is the youngest of the four.
He's from Mallorca.
He has finished second in the Vuelta a España several times.
questions.description: In Paris they hand out a yellow jersey, and not everyone has taken one home.
questions.fun_fact: Enric Mas finished second in the Vuelta a España three times: in 2018, 2021 and 2022.

questions.question: At Rio 2016, Carolina Marín became the first non-Asian woman to win Olympic gold in her sport. Which sport?
hints: It's played with a racket.
It's hugely popular in Asia, especially in China, Indonesia and Malaysia.
It's played with a feathered shuttlecock.
questions.description: A woman from Huelva who turned a schoolyard game into an Olympic final.
questions.fun_fact: Carolina Marín is from Huelva and has also been world champion three times.

questions.question: Which left-handed tennis player from Mallorca liked to bite his trophies in photos?
hints: He won 22 Grand Slam titles.
He's from Manacor.
His uncle Toni was his coach for many years.
questions.description: For some people, lifting a cup is the best moment of the season… and the best photo of the year.
questions.fun_fact: Nadal writes with his right hand but plays tennis with his left.

questions.question: Who won Spain's first-ever Winter Olympic gold medal?
hints: It happened in Sapporo, Japan, in 1972.
The gold came in the slalom, in alpine skiing.
He was from Cercedilla, near Madrid.
questions.description: Before this, snow in Spain was mostly for building snowmen.
questions.fun_fact: His sister Blanca won bronze at Albertville 1992, the first Olympic medal ever won by a Spanish woman.

questions.question: In 2022, at 19, Carlos Alcaraz became the youngest world No. 1 in men's tennis history. Which Spanish region is he from?
hints: It's in the southeast of the Spanish mainland.
It has an almost closed-off lagoon by the sea called the Mar Menor.
His hometown is El Palmar.
questions.description: A kid who reached the top of tennis before he was old enough to rent a car.
questions.fun_fact: Alcaraz won Wimbledon in 2023 and 2024, both times beating Novak Djokovic in the final.

questions.question: In what year did Queralt Castellet win her first Olympic medal, a silver in snowboard halfpipe?
hints: It was at her fifth Olympic Games.
Those Games were held in Asia.
They were the Beijing Games.
questions.description: An athlete who makes a living flying around inside a giant tube of frozen snow.
questions.fun_fact: Queralt Castellet made her Olympic debut at Turin 2006, when she was only 16.

questions.question: You're watching Rafa Nadal lie down on the clay after winning the Grand Slam he won 14 times. Which tournament is it?
hints: It's the only one of the four majors played on clay.
It's played every spring in France.
It's held in Paris and named after a French aviator.
questions.description: The only place where ending up covered in orange dust means you've won.
questions.fun_fact: Nadal won Roland Garros 14 times, more than anyone has won any single Grand Slam tournament.

questions.question: Caesar salad, with romaine lettuce, croutons and Parmesan cheese, is famous all over the world. In which country was it invented?
hints: It's not the country the name makes you think of.
It was born in a border city, very close to California.
It was invented in Tijuana.
questions.description: A salad with an emperor's name and a passport full of surprises.
questions.fun_fact: Italian chef Caesar Cardini invented it at his restaurant in Tijuana in the 1920s, which is why it's called “Caesar”.

questions.question: You're in Tarragona in 2018, watching the Mediterranean Games. Counting these, how many times has Spain hosted them?
hints: It wasn't the first time Spain had hosted them.
One of the earlier hosts was a city in Andalusia, in 2005.
Before Tarragona came Barcelona in 1955 and Almería in 2005.
questions.description: Games with a sea view and some Roman ruins thrown in for free.
questions.fun_fact: The Tarragona Games were planned for 2017 but were pushed back a year, to 2018.

questions.question: You're at a game in the Palau Blaugrana, Barça's indoor arena that opened in 1971. About how many fans fit inside?
hints: It's an indoor arena, not a huge open-air stadium.
It holds far more people than a local sports hall.
It's somewhere between 5,000 and 10,000.
questions.description: An arena where the shouting bounces around more than the ball does.
questions.fun_fact: Basketball isn't the only Barça sport played at the Palau Blaugrana: the club's handball, futsal and roller hockey teams play there too.

questions.question: In which year did Spain win its first Olympic gold in men's soccer, with a last-minute goal by Kiko against Poland?
hints: That summer, all of Spain was hooked on the Games.
The Games were held at home.
It was the year of the mascot Cobi.
questions.description: A gold that got more screaming than any other medal that summer.
questions.fun_fact: The final was played at the Camp Nou in front of more than 90,000 people, and Spain came back from 0–1 to win 3–2.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this point guard was named MVP of the 2019 Basketball World Cup in China, which Spain won. Who is he?
hints: He made his ACB debut at just 14.
He was born in El Masnou and played for Joventut.
His last name means “blond” in Spanish.
questions.description: A point guard who handed out so many assists he nearly ran out of balls.
questions.fun_fact: Spain beat Argentina 95–75 in the 2019 final in Beijing.

questions.question: I'm the top men's basketball league in Spain. The ACB runs me, and I'm named after an electricity company. What's my name?
hints: Real Madrid, Barça and Valencia Basket play in me.
The women's basketball league has the same sponsor.
My sponsor's name starts with “E”.
questions.description: A league with so much energy that someone else pays the bill.
questions.fun_fact: The ACB league has carried the Endesa name since 2011.

questions.question: In what year did Spain start its points-based driver's license?
hints: Cell phones with cameras were already around.
It arrived after euro coins came into use.
It was the same year Germany hosted the World Cup.
questions.description: A video game where you lose lives if you goof around behind the wheel.
questions.fun_fact: A regular driver starts with 12 points and a new driver with 8, and good driving can take you up to 15.

questions.question: In Spain, it has a little green light on the roof when it's free and a device that shows how much you'll have to pay. What is it?
hints: It takes you exactly where you ask.
A driver takes you, and you pay at the end of the ride.
In Madrid it's white with a red stripe.
questions.description: Getting around the city comes with more choices than a restaurant menu.
questions.fun_fact: In Barcelona, taxis are black and yellow, and in Madrid they're white with a red stripe on the door.

questions.question: In Spain, which part of the street are you not allowed to ride an electric scooter on?
hints: It's where the most people are walking.
People on foot need to feel safe there.
It's the raised part of the street, right next to the front doors.
questions.description: Two wheels, a battery and a strong wish not to walk.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2021, electric scooters in Spain can't go faster than 25 km/h (about 15 mph).

questions.question: I walk through the train car by car and ask every passenger to show me their ticket. Who am I?
hints: I don't drive the train.
I walk up and down the aisles while the train is moving.
My job title includes the thing I ask you to show me.
questions.description: If you have no ticket, this is the moment you try to look invisible.
questions.fun_fact: Ticket inspectors used to punch holes in cardboard tickets with special pliers to show they had been used.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: “To get into the metro, you tap your card on the reader and go through the…”
hints: It's a barrier.
Its arms rotate when you push it.
The first part of its name means “to spin around.”
questions.description: Metal arms that only hug you once you've paid.
questions.fun_fact: In Argentina, this same gadget is called a “molinete” (little windmill).

questions.question: I'm a Mexican breakfast: fried eggs on a tortilla, covered in tomato and chili sauce. I'm called huevos rancheros. What does “rancheros” mean?
hints: Think of Mexican ranchera music.
It comes from the Spanish word “rancho”.
Farm workers used to eat it.
questions.description: A breakfast with so much personality it even has a last name.
questions.fun_fact: It was the hearty breakfast of farm workers, to keep them going through a long day in the fields.

questions.question: How many radial national roads, numbered in Roman numerals, ran out of Madrid across Spain?
hints: Today almost all of them have become highways.
One goes to Andalusia and another to Galicia.
The last one reaches A Coruña.
questions.description: Madrid in the middle and roads sticking out like the spokes of a bike wheel.
questions.fun_fact: They are all measured from Kilómetro Cero, a plaque set in the ground at Madrid's Puerta del Sol.

questions.question: In Mexico the red octagonal sign says “ALTO”, and in Argentina “PARE”. What word is on the ones in Spain?
hints: Spain uses the same word as most of its European neighbors.
It is the same word you would see on signs in France or Portugal.
It is a four-letter word borrowed from English.
questions.description: An eight-sided sign that doesn't take no for an answer.
questions.fun_fact: The stop sign has eight sides so people can recognize it even from behind or when it's covered in snow.

questions.question: For decades it had a tropical garden under its old iron train shed, and it is Spain's busiest train station. Which is it?
hints: It's in the capital.
The first AVE high-speed train left from here for Seville in 1992.
It's next to the Reina Sofía Museum.
questions.description: A station where for years there were more turtles than late trains.
questions.fun_fact: In 2022 the station was officially renamed Madrid Puerta de Atocha-Almudena Grandes, after the Madrid-born writer.

questions.question: This gray metro Line 6 has no start and no end, and it stops at Argüelles and Cuatro Caminos. Which city is it in?
hints: This city has the largest metro network in Spain.
There, people simply call it “la circular”.
It is the capital.
questions.description: A metro line that takes you right back where you started if you fall asleep.
questions.fun_fact: One full loop of Line 6 takes almost an hour and passes through 28 stations.

questions.question: In 1988 it became the third city in Spain to get a metro, and its tram takes you to Malvarrosa beach. Which city is it?
hints: It lies on the Mediterranean coast.
It is famous for its City of Arts and Sciences.
It is the home of paella.
questions.description: A city that waited for its metro more patiently than a passenger on the platform.
questions.fun_fact: Before it, only Madrid (since 1919) and Barcelona (since 1924) had a metro.

questions.question: It leaves Madrid, passes Benavente, Ponferrada and Lugo, and ends in A Coruña. What is this highway called?
hints: It is one of the highways that start at Kilómetro Cero in Madrid.
It takes you to Galicia.
Its name is a compass direction… halfway between two of them.
questions.description: A road that starts out smelling of cocido and ends up smelling of octopus.
questions.fun_fact: To get into Galicia, the A-6 climbs the Piedrafita pass on some very tall viaducts.

questions.question: In Spain, what do the letters DGT stand for?
hints: It's an agency of the Spanish government.
It handles driver's licenses and traffic fines.
It warns drivers about traffic jams on the roads.
questions.description: Three letters that make the news every time Spain packs the car for the big vacation getaway.
questions.fun_fact: The DGT was created in 1959, when there were still very few cars in Spain.

questions.question: Its city buses are blue, at night it runs the “búhos”, and it belongs to Madrid City Council. Which company is it?
hints: It is a city-owned company.
It only runs buses inside the city.
Its initials stand for “Empresa Municipal de Transportes”.
questions.description: The company that turns Madrid locals into experts at waiting at the bus stop.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's night buses are called “búhos” (owls) because they run while everyone else is asleep.

questions.question: Which actor played Pepe, owner of the beach bar in Peñíscola, in «Chiringuito de Pepe»?
hints: Before running a beach bar, he played the main character's brother in a very famous family series.
In «Los Serrano» he was Santi, Diego's brother.
He also directed and starred in the film «El oro de Moscú» (2003).
questions.description: A Mediterranean beach bar owner with more bad temper than beach umbrellas in August.
questions.fun_fact: In the series, Santi Millán played Sergi, a top chef who ends up working at his father's beach bar.

questions.question: If you sat in front of the TV to watch the bandit Curro Jiménez ride the Serranía de Ronda for the first time, what decade was it?
hints: Spain was going through big political changes at the time.
It premiered in the middle of the Transition.
It was the same decade in which Franco died.
questions.description: Blunderbuss, sideburns and a horse: the full kit of the TV bandit.
questions.fun_fact: Sancho Gracia, TV's Curro Jiménez, became so popular that many people kept calling him by that name for the rest of his life.

questions.question: I'm fried dough eaten at Christmas. In Mexico I'm flat and crunchy with honey; in Colombia I'm a little cheese ball. What am I?
hints: I'm fried in very hot oil.
In Spain I'm sometimes filled with cream.
My name starts with “Bu”.
questions.description: Dough, hot oil and a little patience: the recipe for happiness in December.
questions.fun_fact: Buñuelos came to the Americas with the Spanish, and each country changed them in its own way.

questions.question: I live in Mirador de Montepinar, I sell seafood wholesale and I always insist: “Soy mayorista, no limpio pescado.” Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the neighbors in «La que se avecina».
My wife is Berta and my mother is Gregoria.
I'm played by Jordi Sánchez.
questions.description: A neighbors' association where the meeting never ends peacefully.
questions.fun_fact: Jordi Sánchez, who plays Antonio Recio, is also a playwright: he wrote the play «Krámpack», which Cesc Gay turned into the 2000 film “Nico and Dani”.

questions.question: In what year did Telecinco air the finale of “Los Serrano”, where Diego wakes up and it all seems to have been a dream?
hints: The show had premiered in 2003.
The last episode aired in the middle of summer.
It was the same year Spain won the European Championship in Austria and Switzerland.
questions.description: The most controversial alarm clock in the history of Spanish TV.
questions.fun_fact: When Diego wakes up, he is next to Lucía, his wife from the start of the show, played by Belén Rueda.

questions.question: In “Money Heist”, the robbers raid the Fábrica Nacional de Moneda y Timbre. Which of these does the real one NOT make?
hints: “Timbre” is an old Spanish word for official stamps.
It also makes identity documents.
What you're looking for is made by licensed private companies, and it gets screwed on.
questions.description: The favorite building of robbers in red jumpsuits.
questions.fun_fact: The outside shots in the series weren't filmed at the real mint, but at the headquarters of the CSIC, Spain's national research council, in Madrid.

questions.question: What is the name of the schoolteacher hiding behind the mask of Águila Roja in the TVE series?
hints: The series is set in 17th-century Madrid.
He was played by David Janer.
His surname sounds like the Spanish words for a mountain and a pale white color.
questions.description: By day he grades homework; by night, he sets wrongs right.
questions.fun_fact: The series was such a hit that a movie, «Águila Roja», came out in theaters in 2011.

questions.question: If you were one of the “Cable Girls”, connecting calls by hand in Madrid when the series begins, which decade would you live in?
hints: Women still couldn't vote in Spain.
The Second Republic was only a few years away.
The series begins in 1928.
questions.description: A job where you were meant to connect calls, not listen in on them.
questions.fun_fact: «Las chicas del cable» (“Cable Girls”) was the first Netflix original series made in Spain.

questions.question: I'm Basque. In 2023 I started hosting a chain-word game show on Telecinco, where Los Mozos de Arousa triumphed. Who am I?
hints: I had already hosted other shows for the channel, like the «Supervivientes» debates.
I'm from San Sebastián and my surname sounds very Basque.
My first name has only three letters and starts with I.
questions.description: One word leads to another, and that one leads to all of Spain's afternoon snack time.
questions.fun_fact: Los Mozos de Arousa, three friends from Galicia, became TV stars thanks to their incredibly long winning streak on the show.

questions.question: In which year did Telecinco launch “Esta noche cruzamos el Mississippi”, Pepe Navarro's late-night show?
hints: It was in the decade when private TV channels were born in Spain.
It was a couple of years before “Crónicas marcianas” started.
It was in the mid-1990s.
questions.description: An American river you could cross every night without leaving a studio in Madrid.
questions.fun_fact: After the success of “Mississippi”, Pepe Navarro moved to Antena 3 with “La sonrisa del pelícano”, which was off the air very quickly.

questions.question: Celebrities face extreme challenges every week on Antena 3: who has hosted “El Desafío” since 2021?
hints: He's a much-loved TV host from Seville.
He hosted “Operación Triunfo” when it returned to TV.
In the afternoons he also hosts “Pasapalabra”.
questions.description: Celebrities hanging from a helicopter or underwater: all for a round of applause.
questions.fun_fact: On “El Desafío” the celebrities train for weeks for each challenge, and the prize money goes to charity.

questions.question: In “La ruleta de la suerte”, right after spinning the wheel, what must the contestant say?
hints: It has to be on the board to win the money on that space.
The more times it appears on the board, the more money they win.
It's not A, E, I, O or U.
questions.description: Spin, spin, spin… and please don't land on Bankrupt.
questions.fun_fact: On the show you don't win vowels by spinning: you have to buy them with the money you've collected.

questions.question: Which comedian from Málaga became famous in 1994 on “Genio y figura” with expressions like “¡Jarl!” and “condemor”?
hints: He told his jokes while hopping around the stage.
He also said “¡fistro!” and “pecador de la pradera”.
His stage name seems to say he was small.
questions.description: A man who spoke a language only he understood, and still we all laughed.
questions.fun_fact: Chiquito was already over 60 when TV made him famous; before that he had been a flamenco singer.

questions.question: I'm the pib, the traditional Maya oven of Yucatán, and cochinita pibil comes out of me. What am I made of?
wrong_answers: An adobe dome with a chimney
hints: The Maya used me long before modern kitchens existed.
The food is covered and cooks slowly for hours.
People dig me and fill me with stones and embers.
questions.description: A kitchen so old it isn't in any appliance catalog.
questions.fun_fact: “Pibil” means “cooked in the pib”, in other words, buried underground.

questions.question: I was born in 2005 in the slot left by Canal+, “El hormiguero” started on me before moving to Antena 3, and my name is a number. Which channel am I?
hints: Today I belong to the same group as Telecinco.
“Cuarto milenio” is on my schedule.
My number comes right before Telecinco's.
questions.description: A channel that comes right after another channel with a number.
questions.fun_fact: “El hormiguero” started on Cuatro in 2006 and moved to Antena 3 in 2011.

questions.question: Every year TVE airs José Mota's comedy special. On which night does it usually air?
hints: It's a winter holiday night.
Shortly after the special, half of Spain watches a much-awaited live broadcast on La 1.
It's the last night of the year.
questions.description: A comedian from La Mancha with more characters than Campo de Criptana has windmills.
questions.fun_fact: Before going solo, José Mota was half of the comedy duo Cruz y Raya with Juan Muñoz.

questions.question: Which of these channels is NOT part of RTVE, Spain's public broadcaster?
hints: It's a cartoon channel.
It belongs to the same group as Telecinco.
Its name sounds like a spring bouncing.
questions.description: Everyone's TV has lots of children, but one of these belongs to another family.
questions.fun_fact: Clan, RTVE's channel for children, started broadcasting in 2005.

questions.question: In which year did “Crónicas marcianas”, Javier Sardá's late-night show, start on Telecinco?
hints: It ran until the mid-2000s.
It started in the 1990s.
It was in the second half of that decade.
questions.description: A late-night show so out of this world it kept us up until all hours.
questions.fun_fact: Boris Izaguirre and Carlos Latre both became famous on “Crónicas marcianas”.

questions.question: On laSexta, El Gran Wyoming opens “El intermedio” with: “You already know the news; now we'll tell you…”. How does it end?
hints: It's a joke about serious news shows.
The line suggests other newscasts keep something quiet.
What witnesses swear to tell in court.
questions.description: A newscast that puts on a tie just so it can take nothing seriously.
questions.fun_fact: “El intermedio” has been on laSexta since 2006, the same year the channel was born.

questions.question: In what year did “First Dates”, Carlos Sobera's blind-date show, start on Cuatro?
hints: It started in the 2010s.
It was in the second half of that decade.
It was the same year as the Rio Olympics.
questions.description: A restaurant where the food is the least important thing.
questions.fun_fact: “First Dates” is based on a British format, and in Spain it has already hosted thousands of dates.

questions.question: In how many different weight divisions did Julio César Chávez, “El Gran Campeón Mexicano”, become world champion?
hints: More than one, but not as many as Manny Pacquiao.
He started at super featherweight and moved up.
Super featherweight, lightweight and light welterweight.
questions.description: They call him that for a reason, and it's not because he likes to show off.
questions.fun_fact: In 1993, Chávez fought in front of more than 130,000 people at Estadio Azteca, one of the biggest crowds in boxing history.

questions.question: Which Mexican boxer, nicknamed “Dinamita,” knocked out Manny Pacquiao in December 2012?
hints: He's from Mexico City and fought Pacquiao four times.
The punch landed in the sixth round of their fourth fight.
He has a brother who is also a boxer, named Rafael.
questions.description: A nickname you won't find for sale at the hardware store.
questions.fun_fact: Márquez and Pacquiao fought four times between 2004 and 2012, and only the last fight ended in a knockout.

questions.question: I'm the lightest division in men's pro boxing, with a limit of about 47.6 kg (105 lb), and Ricardo “Finito” López ruled me unbeaten. What am I?
hints: I'm even below flyweight.
I'm also called “minimumweight.”
My name is what country hats are woven from.
questions.description: Blow hard enough and the wind might carry it away.
questions.fun_fact: Finito López retired undefeated, with 51 wins and just one draw.

questions.question: Complete the boxing phrase we use when someone gives up: “I can't take it anymore, I'm going to throw in the…”
hints: It's something the corner keeps close at hand.
The corner throws it into the ring to stop the fight.
You also use it when you get out of the shower.
questions.description: A phrase born in the corner of the ring that ended up in your living room.
questions.fun_fact: In boxing, when the corner throws this into the ring, the fight is stopped to protect their boxer.

questions.question: Boxer Alfonso Zamora won an Olympic silver medal for Mexico at bantamweight. In which city were those Games held?
hints: They were the first Games after the ones in Mexico.
They were in a European city.
The city is famous for its Oktoberfest.
questions.description: A piece of silver that never made it to Taxco.
questions.fun_fact: After the Games, Zamora turned pro and became WBA world bantamweight champion.

questions.question: Which Mexican boxer from Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, had a trilogy of fights with Nicaragua's Román “Chocolatito” González?
hints: He fought in the small weight classes, like flyweight and super flyweight.
He beat Chocolatito in 2021, in their second fight.
His nickname is a farmyard animal.
questions.description: A guy from Sonora who gets up early, not to sing, but to fight.
questions.fun_fact: The second fight between Estrada and Chocolatito, in 2021, was seen as one of the best fights of that year.

questions.question: In what year did Andy Ruiz knock out Anthony Joshua to become the first heavyweight world champion of Mexican descent?
hints: It was in the late 2010s.
It happened in June, at Madison Square Garden in New York.
It was one year before the pandemic.
questions.description: The night a Mexican wrecked everyone's predictions.
questions.fun_fact: Andy Ruiz took that fight as a late replacement, with only a few weeks' notice.

questions.question: In boxing, if a fighter goes down and doesn't get up before the referee finishes counting, it's a knockout. What number does the referee count to?
hints: It's more than the fingers on one hand.
The referee counts out loud, one number per second, and it takes more than a few seconds.
It's the number a rocket launch countdown starts from.
questions.description: A countdown, but the other way around.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican Spanish, the English word “knockout” is written “nocaut.”

questions.question: In Mexico, a rooster is the mascot on the box of a Kellogg's cereal. Which cereal is it?
hints: It's a cereal of plain flakes, with no chocolate and no colors.
It's one of Kellogg's oldest cereals.
His Mexican name is Cornelio, which makes him sound like he's made of the cereal's own grain.
questions.description: An alarm clock with feathers that moved from the farmyard to the breakfast table.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico the rooster is called Cornelio, and in English he's Cornelius: both names sound like “corn.”

questions.question: What is the name of the Sabritas bag that mixes several of its snacks together in one bag?
hints: It's a mix, not just one kind of chip.
Its name sounds like something really big.
It sounds like “paquetazo”, but spelled with a k and an x.
questions.description: For people who can't make up their minds at the corner store: why pick one when you can take them all?
questions.fun_fact: The name plays on the Spanish word “paquetazo”, meaning a huge package of snacks.

questions.question: Lucas Gusano is a candy in a little bottle you squeeze to get it out. What's inside?
hints: It's a flavor you also find in lots of other Mexican snacks and candies.
It's made with fruit, like apricot or plum.
It's sweet and sour, and people put it on fruit and raspados.
questions.description: A bug nobody wants in their apple, but everybody wants in their backpack.
questions.fun_fact: Lucas candies were born in Mexico and today belong to Mars, the company behind M&M's.

questions.question: It's made of plastic, the delivery man carries it on his shoulder, and it goes upside down on the dispenser. What's in the garrafón?
hints: It has no color.
You pour it for someone who's thirsty.
It has no flavor and no sugar.
questions.description: The only houseguest that always ends up standing on its head.
questions.fun_fact: A full 20-liter (5-gallon) garrafón weighs about 20 kg (44 lb): like carrying a five-year-old!

questions.question: Chokis are round cookies made by Gamesa. What do they have on top and inside?
hints: They're sweet and brown.
Their name already gives you a clue.
They're little bits of something made from cacao.
questions.description: Cookies so good they vanish before they ever reach the glass of milk.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate chip cookies were invented in the United States in the 1930s.

questions.question: Danonino comes in small fruit-flavored cups. What is it mainly made of?
hints: You keep it in the fridge.
Lots of kids eat it at breakfast or at recess.
It comes from cows.
questions.description: A cup so tiny it fits in the lunchbox with room left over for the torta.
questions.fun_fact: Danonino started in France as a fresh petit-suisse cheese, a name that means “little Swiss” in French.

questions.question: Pickled chiles, like the ones that come in a can, go with lots of tacos. Which chile is most often used to make them?
hints: It's green and medium-sized.
They often come sliced, with carrots and onions.
Its name comes from Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz.
questions.description: Some chiles took a sour bath and came out more famous than ever.
questions.fun_fact: When a jalapeño is dried and smoked, it becomes a chipotle.

questions.question: Which actor played el Chómpiras, the clumsy thief from “Los Caquitos”?
hints: He also played many of the lead characters in his own shows.
He wrote the scripts for his shows, too.
People called him “Chespirito.”
questions.description: A thief so clumsy the only thing he ever steals is a laugh.
questions.fun_fact: El Chómpiras’s wife, la Chimoltrufia, was played by Florinda Meza, who was also Doña Florinda in the vecindad.

questions.question: I’m a teacher, I’m super tall, and I always bring flowers to a neighbor who offers me “una tacita de café.” Who am I?
hints: I teach the kids of the vecindad.
My favorite neighbor is Quico’s mom.
My last name sounds like an animal with a very long neck.
questions.description: In the vecindad, whoever shows up with a bouquet becomes the gossip of the whole courtyard.
questions.fun_fact: Rubén Aguirre, the actor who played Profesor Jirafales, was about 1.96 m (6 ft 5 in) tall.

questions.question: In “El Chavo del Ocho”, the word “chavo” means…
hints: It's a very common word in everyday Mexican Spanish.
For a girl, you say “chava”.
It's used to talk about a child or a young guy.
questions.description: A word so Mexican it comes with its own barrel.
questions.fun_fact: Roberto Gómez Bolaños, who created the show, was already in his forties when he started playing the eight-year-old El Chavo.

questions.question: Doña Clotilde lives in the vecindad, is in love with Don Ramón, and the kids call her “la Bruja del 71.” Where does the 71 come from?
hints: It has nothing to do with how old she is.
El Chavo has a similar number in his name.
It's the number on the door of her home.
questions.description: A neighbor with a flying-broomstick reputation who only wanted Don Ramón to notice her.
questions.fun_fact: Actress Angelines Fernández, who played Doña Clotilde, was born in Spain and came to Mexico as a refugee.

questions.question: Profesor Jirafales shouts it louder and louder up to the final “taaa!” How does he feel when he says “Ta ta ta ta!”?
hints: It's almost always El Chavo's fault.
It usually happens in the classroom, after a student plays a prank.
It's the opposite of feeling happy and calm.
questions.description: The vecindad's classroom has a teacher who doesn't need a ladder to erase the top of the chalkboard.
questions.fun_fact: Profesor Jirafales was played by Rubén Aguirre, an actor so tall that his name on the show comes from “jirafa” (giraffe).

questions.question: It shows up after a hit, swells up on your head, and El Chapulín Colorado named his hammer after it. What is a “chipote”?
hints: It hurts, but it almost never bleeds.
You can feel it like a little ball.
It goes down if you put ice on it.
questions.description: A souvenir the kitchen door gives you when you open it too fast.
questions.fun_fact: The chipote chillón (squeaky mallet) goes “squeak!” with every hit, but it never really hurts anyone.

questions.question: In the Christmas carol “Los peces en el río”, which object does NOT appear in the lyrics?
hints: Think about what the Virgin Mary does in each verse.
In the song, she combs her hair and washes baby clothes.
This object rings in church towers to call people to Mass.
questions.description: The fish keep drinking and drinking, but the thinking is up to you.
questions.fun_fact: The song says the Virgin's comb is made of “plata fina” (fine silver) and her hair is made of gold.

questions.question: The polka, still alive in norteño music, reached northern Mexico in the 19th century. Who brought it?
hints: They settled in northern Mexico and in Texas.
They also brought the accordion, which every norteño band has today.
They came from the land of Oktoberfest and from Bohemia.
questions.description: A rhythm that came from very far away and moved in for good with an accordion and a cowboy hat.
questions.fun_fact: The polka was born around 1830 in Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic.

questions.question: In the famous Mexican song “La cucaracha,” what kind of animal is the cucaracha?
hints: Lots of people scream when they find one in the kitchen.
It has antennae and six little legs.
It's a distant relative of the cricket, just like Cri-Cri.
questions.description: It can't walk anymore, but it can still make you scream in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: “La cucaracha” became famous during the Mexican Revolution and is now known all over the world.

questions.question: According to the most common story, the first cheeseburger was made in Pasadena, California. In which decade?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was the age of jazz and silent films.
It was the same decade that radio became popular.
questions.description: Someone looked at a burger and thought: “It needs a little yellow blanket.”
questions.fun_fact: The cheeseburger is usually credited to Lionel Sternberger, who, the story goes, was only 16 or 17 years old when he made it.

questions.question: In the Christmas carol “Campana sobre campana”, why do you look out of the window?
questions.answer: To see the Christ Child in his cradle
wrong_answers: To see the Three Wise Men arrive
To see the snow falling outside
To see the Star of Bethlehem
hints: The song is about what happened in Bethlehem.
Angels ring the bells to share some big news.
There's a newborn baby.
questions.description: A tower of bells so tall that nobody dares to ring the one at the bottom.
questions.fun_fact: It's a traditional carol from Andalusia, in Spain, that Mexicans sing at the posadas.

questions.question: It's sung softly and slowly, and it compares a star to a diamond. Why do people sing “Estrellita, ¿dónde estás?”?
questions.answer: To lull a baby to sleep
hints: It's sung at night.
Moms sing it next to the crib.
It helps someone close their little eyes.
questions.description: A star that everyone asks for its address, but it never answers.
questions.fun_fact: Its tune is the same as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”, and Mozart wrote variations on it.

questions.question: Genaro Codina wrote it in the 19th century, and people call it “the second national anthem.” Where do you hear the Marcha de Zacatecas?
hints: It's a military march.
Drum and bugle bands play it.
Think of September 16 and the flag ceremony at school.
questions.description: A march so famous that even people who can't march stand up a little straighter.
questions.fun_fact: Its composer, Genaro Codina, was born in the city of Zacatecas itself.

questions.question: Your grandparents' record player is spinning a record with “La patita” and “El ratón vaquero.” Who sings them?
hints: He started out on the radio in the 1930s.
His creator was born in Orizaba, Veracruz.
He's known as “el Grillito Cantor” (the Little Singing Cricket).
questions.description: Before streaming, music went round and round… literally.
questions.fun_fact: Behind Cri-Cri was Francisco Gabilondo Soler, who wrote more than 200 children's songs.

questions.question: Which singer is known in Mexico as “la Reina de los Niños” (the Queen of Kids)?
hints: She has been singing for children for more than 30 years.
At her concerts, kids and their parents jump around together.
Her name is a Russian woman’s name, like Olga or Natasha.
questions.description: A crown you win with jumping, clapping and balloons.
questions.fun_fact: Tatiana started out as a teen pop singer in the 1980s before she turned to children’s music.

questions.question: In “Juguemos en el bosque”, the wolf answers: “I'm putting on my shirt,” then “my pants,” then “my shoes.” What is he doing?
hints: Think of what you do every morning before school.
Shirts, pants and shoes are all clothes.
When he's done, he'll be ready to go out.
questions.description: The least punctual wolf in the forest: the kids are tired of waiting for him.
questions.fun_fact: When the wolf is finally ready, he comes out to chase the kids, and everyone runs so he won't catch them.

questions.question: You sing “Witsi witsi araña” while moving your fingers. After the rain washes the spider out, when does it climb up again?
hints: First the rain has to dry up.
It happens when the sky clears.
It's when it gets warm and everything shines.
questions.description: A spider more stubborn than you when you're told it's time for bed.
questions.fun_fact: The English version, “Itsy Bitsy Spider,” is sung with the very same finger movements.

questions.question: I was born as a movie character in 1952, and later a real wrestler brought me to life in the ring. A flying move bears my name worldwide. Who am I?
hints: In my first movie, the actor David Silva played me.
The wrestler Daniel García was the one who took me into the ring.
The move is called the “hurricanrana”.
questions.description: Shiny capes, colorful masks and a whole arena screaming: welcome to the ring.
questions.fun_fact: The “hurricanrana” is used today in wrestling all over the world, from Japan to the United States.

questions.question: Cartoonists Jis and Trino started out together with the magazine “La Mamá del Abulón” and created “El Santos”. What city are they from?
hints: It's one of the biggest cities in Mexico.
It's in the west of the country.
Its people are called tapatíos.
questions.description: Two moneros who have spent decades making people laugh without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: Trino is also famous for his “Crónicas marcianas”, strips about aliens watching humans.

questions.question: Next to the newsstand, the voceador (newspaper seller) shouts “¡Extra, extra!”. What does he mean?
questions.answer: A special edition is out with big news
wrong_answers: He's giving away a free magazine
The newsstand is about to close
hints: It's about what's inside the paper, not its price.
Something happened that everyone will want to know about.
It's a special newspaper printed because of one huge story.
questions.description: Before phone notifications, the news arrived at the top of someone's lungs.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, newspaper sellers are called “voceadores” because they shout out the headlines as loud as they can.

questions.question: The most common story says mayonnaise got its name from the French capture of Mahón, Menorca, in 1756. Which noble led those troops?
hints: It happened during the reign of King Louis XV.
He was a Marshal of France, and one of his relatives had been a very powerful cardinal.
That cardinal relative is the villain in “The Three Musketeers”.
questions.description: A sauce with more military history than many generals.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this story, many people in Spain still call it “mahonesa”.

questions.question: I'm a little mouse with a huge sombrero, the fastest in all of Mexico, and I shout “¡Ándale, ándale, arriba, arriba!” Who am I?
hints: I appear in the Looney Tunes cartoons.
I always beat Sylvester the cat in a race.
My cousin is Slowpoke Rodriguez, the slowest mouse in Mexico.
questions.description: He gets here before you finish reading this sentence.
questions.fun_fact: The 1955 short “Speedy Gonzales” won the Oscar for best animated short film.

questions.question: You're watching an old movie where El Santo teams up with his most famous rival, born in Nuevo León. Who is he?
hints: Together they fought monsters and vampires on screen.
He never took off his mask in public.
His mask is the color of the sky, with silver trim.
questions.description: Every great friendship starts with a good fight in the ring.
questions.fun_fact: Blue Demon, whose real name was Alejandro Muñoz, also starred in his own comic book.

questions.question: I was born in Zamora, Michoacán, in 1934, spent time in a seminary, then explained history, politics and healthy food with cartoons in cheap books. Who am I?
hints: My real name was Eduardo del Río.
I drew “Los Supermachos” and “Los Agachados.”
I signed my work with a single four-letter word.
questions.description: With pencil, paper and plenty of stubbornness, he taught more than a few textbooks did.
questions.fun_fact: Rius published more than a hundred books, including “Marx for Beginners,” which was translated into many languages.

questions.question: In Mexico, on Saturday mornings many kids watch “caricaturas” on TV. What are they?
hints: They're what kids love to watch most.
Their characters do impossible things, like falling off a cliff and getting up as if nothing happened.
Bugs Bunny and SpongeBob are in them.
questions.description: The best Saturday plan starts in pajamas in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico cartoons are called “caricaturas,” but in other countries they're called “comiquitas” or “dibujitos.”

questions.question: Many Mexican luchadores, like El Santo, spent almost their whole careers without taking off their masks. Why did they wear them?
questions.answer: To keep who they were a secret
hints: Comic book heroes sometimes live two lives.
Outside the ring, they could walk down the street like any neighbor.
Like superheroes, nobody was supposed to see their real face or know their name.
questions.description: Shiny capes, tall boots and masks in every color: that's how a ring idol gets dressed.
questions.fun_fact: El Santo was buried wearing his mask, just as he had asked.

questions.question: Its owner fought mummies and vampires in over 50 films and was buried wearing it in 1984. Which luchador's mask appeared in the most films?
hints: His real name was Rodolfo Guzmán Huerta.
He was nicknamed “the Man in the Silver Mask” («el Enmascarado de Plata»).
His ring name sounds like someone you'd find on a church altar.
questions.description: A piece of clothing he never took off, not even for the trip to the afterlife.
questions.fun_fact: In several films, El Santo ate and even slept with his mask on so his face would never be seen.

questions.question: Eiza González became famous with the telenovela “Lola, érase una vez”. Which country made the original series it was a remake of?
hints: The original came from a production company famous for teen series full of music.
The original was called “Floricienta”.
It's the country of Buenos Aires.
questions.description: Before fighting giant monsters in Hollywood, she lived in a telenovela fairy tale.
questions.fun_fact: Eiza González later acted in “Hobbs & Shaw” and “Godzilla vs. Kong”.

questions.question: A stop-motion Pinocchio set in Mussolini's Italy won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2023. Which Mexican directed it?
hints: He's from Guadalajara.
He loves monsters and fantastic creatures.
He also directed “The Shape of Water”.
questions.description: A wooden boy whose nose kept growing… and so did his director's trophy shelf.
questions.fun_fact: The movie's puppets were animated frame by frame, moved just a tiny bit for each photo.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this gets snapped shut in front of the camera before every take. What is it called?
hints: It has the scene and take numbers written on it.
An assistant holds it in front of the lens and calls out the scene before the director says “Action!”.
Its name sounds just like the noise it makes.
questions.description: It makes more noise than a round of applause, and nobody ever tells it to be quiet.
questions.fun_fact: The snap of the clapperboard is used later to sync the sound with the picture.

questions.question: Alejandro González Iñárritu made “Amores perros” and later “Babel”. Which film did he make between those two?
hints: It was his first English-language film.
It stars Sean Penn and Naomi Watts.
Its title is a number and a unit of weight.
questions.description: A trilogy where every path crosses… except the ones in this question.
questions.fun_fact: Those three films, all written with Guillermo Arriaga, are known as the “trilogy of death”.

questions.question: My face, with a white suit and a little goatee, is on buckets of fried chicken. Which US state is in my chain's name?
hints: The chain is known by three letters.
The state is famous for racehorses and a race called the Derby.
KFC stands for “… Fried Chicken”.
questions.description: A gentleman in a white suit who spent his whole life thinking about chicken.
questions.fun_fact: Sanders was never a real colonel: “Colonel” was an honorary title given to him by the state of Kentucky.

questions.question: “Sólo con tu pareja” (1991) is a comedy about a lovesick ad man. Which future Oscar winner made his directing debut with it?
hints: He co-wrote it with his brother Carlos.
Years later he directed “Y tu mamá también”.
He also made “Gravity” and “Roma”.
questions.description: A debut so good its director ended up collecting golden statuettes.
questions.fun_fact: The star of “Sólo con tu pareja” is Daniel Giménez Cacho.

questions.question: Production designer Eugenio Caballero created the sets for three of these films. Which one is NOT his?
hints: He won the Oscar for Best Art Direction for a Guillermo del Toro film.
He worked with Cuarón on a black-and-white film.
The one that isn't his takes place almost entirely off Earth.
questions.description: Building worlds is his job; winning awards is his hobby.
questions.fun_fact: For “Roma”, Eugenio Caballero's team rebuilt whole streets of 1970 Mexico City.

questions.question: You're watching Iñárritu's “Birdman,” which looks like one single unbroken shot inside a theater. What city is that theater in?
hints: The main character is an actor who wants to make it in serious theater.
He used to be famous for playing a winged superhero in the movies.
It's the city of the Statue of Liberty.
questions.description: A movie where it seems nobody remembered to yell “cut.”
questions.fun_fact: The cinematographer of “Birdman,” Mexico's Emmanuel Lubezki, won three Oscars in a row.

questions.question: On Día de Muertos, candles are lit on the ofrenda next to the photo of a loved one who has passed. By tradition, what are they for?
questions.answer: To guide the souls to the ofrenda
wrong_answers: To keep the ofrenda's food warm
To keep the flowers from wilting
hints: It has to do with the special visitors who arrive that night.
Those visitors come from very far away and need to find their way.
They do the same job a lighthouse does for ships.
questions.description: A little light that works overtime every November.
questions.fun_fact: Many ofrendas also have a little path of cempasúchil petals, whose color and scent help the souls find their way.

questions.question: Its purple flowers are boiled, sweetened with honey and drunk warm. What do Mexican grandmas drink bugambilia (bougainvillea) tea for?
hints: People drink it mostly in the cold season.
It's a remedy for the throat and chest.
It calms what makes you go “hack, hack” all night.
questions.description: The plant that decorates garden walls and also works as a nurse.
questions.fun_fact: Bougainvillea is named after French explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville; the plant was described during his voyage around the world.

questions.question: You've just spent all afternoon ironing and go to wash your hands. According to Mexican grandmothers, what will happen if you get them wet?
questions.answer: You'll get rheumatism in your hands
hints: The belief says the trouble is going from hot to cold.
The damage is felt in the joints.
It's a pain older people often feel in their bones.
questions.description: A house rule even stricter than no snacks before dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors say wetting your hands after ironing doesn't cause rheumatism: arthritis has other causes, such as age or the immune system.

questions.question: You're watching a Pedro Infante movie on TV and everything is in black and white. When do you think it was filmed?
hints: Your grandparents or great-grandparents could have seen it at the movies.
Back then, filming in color was very hard and expensive.
It isn't new, but it isn't from the time of castles either.
questions.description: A movie so old that even the colors went on vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In the Golden Age, almost all Mexican movies were in black and white; color only became common in the 1960s.

questions.question: You walk into a vecindad like the one in “El Chavo del 8” or “Nosotros los pobres”. What will you NOT find there?
questions.answer: A swimming pool in every home
hints: Many families with little money live in a vecindad.
Almost everything is shared among the neighbors.
Look for what would be a luxury.
questions.description: Here everyone hears about everything before it even happens.
questions.fun_fact: Many vecindades in Mexico City’s historic center were once grand colonial mansions split up into rooms.

questions.question: I'm an early movie showing; my name comes from the French word for “morning”, and kids looked forward to me every Sunday. What am I?
hints: You didn't have to dress up to go.
It played before the evening shows.
In French, “matin” means “morning”.
