questions.description: For anyone who just couldn't wait until nighttime to see a movie.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican movie theaters had “permanencia voluntaria”: you paid for one ticket and could stay to watch several showings in a row.

questions.question: Croquettes, small breaded and fried bites that are golden outside and creamy inside, get their name from the French verb “croquer”. What does it mean?
hints: It has to do with a sound.
Think of the first bite.
The French word imitates a sound, a bit like “crack” or “crisp”.
questions.description: A little snack that vanishes from the party tray before anyone even sees it.
questions.fun_fact: The same French word gave its name to the “croque-monsieur”, a hot ham and cheese sandwich.

questions.question: I'm a carpenter in a vecindad, I raise Chachita as if she were my daughter, and my story continues in “Ustedes los ricos” (1948). Who am I?
hints: My first film was “Nosotros los pobres”.
I was played by Pedro Infante.
My nickname is an animal with horns.
questions.description: A hammer, a handsaw and a voice that made the whole neighborhood sigh.
questions.fun_fact: The character got a third film, “Pepe el Toro” (1953), in which he becomes a boxer.

questions.question: In many Mexican homes, that's where you find the tinaco, the laundry hanging out to dry and sometimes even the dog. What is the azotea?
questions.answer: The flat roof of the house
hints: To get there, you almost always have to go up.
From there you can see the neighbors' houses.
It's at the very top of the house, above all the rooms.
questions.description: The spot in the house where the dog lives, the laundry sunbathes, and nobody knows who left that broken chair.
questions.fun_fact: Flat roofs are so common in Mexico that the azotea works as a laundry room, storeroom, garden and even a ball court.

questions.question: You walk past a table at a fonda where someone is eating. To be polite, in Mexico you say…
hints: You say it even if you don't know the person.
It's a good wish for their meal.
It means: may your food do you good.
questions.description: The magic word you give away to any stranger with a full mouth.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's common to say “provecho” even on your way out of a restaurant, to every table you pass.

questions.question: They're on streets all over Mexico, make your car jump if you drive fast and force drivers to slow down. What are they called?
hints: People or the government put them there on purpose.
They're like a small hill in the pavement.
Many are painted yellow so you can see them.
questions.description: Public enemy number one of shock absorbers and of the coffee in your cup holder.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries, topes are called “lomos de burro” (donkey's backs), “muertos” (dead men) or “policías acostados” (lying-down policemen).

questions.question: In this Mexico City colonia, streets are named Homero, Horacio, Aristóteles and Molière, and Avenida Masaryk has luxury shops. Which one is it?
hints: It's on the west side of the city.
It's right next to Chapultepec Park.
It's famous for its pricey restaurants and boutiques.
questions.description: A neighborhood where you need to have read the classics just to ask for directions.
questions.fun_fact: Many of Polanco's streets are named after famous writers, philosophers and scientists from around the world.

questions.question: Leaving a baptism in Mexico, children shout “¡bolo, bolo!” at the godfather. What does he throw into the air?
hints: The children race to pick it up off the ground.
Later they can spend it at the corner store.
It's money, but not bills.
questions.description: The moment at a baptism when the smallest guests turn into Olympic athletes.
questions.fun_fact: Today many godparents also hand out “bolos” as baptism keepsakes: little bags filled with candy.

questions.question: It's sold in the park, the vendor carries it in little bags hanging from a long pole, and it melts in your mouth. What is it?
hints: It's sweet and very fluffy.
It's almost always pink or blue.
It's made by spinning hot sugar in a machine.
questions.description: A cloud you can buy, but it vanishes the moment you bite it.
questions.fun_fact: A big cotton candy is made from just one or two spoonfuls of sugar.

questions.question: Chicharrón preparado from street stalls is a crunchy rectangle topped with cream, cabbage, tomato and avocado. What is that chicharrón made of?
hints: Even though it's called chicharrón, it isn't pork.
It's sold dry and puffs up when it's fried.
It's the same main ingredient as bread and the tortillas of northern Mexico.
questions.description: A street snack so crunchy you can hear it from the next corner.
questions.fun_fact: Flour chicharrón is also called “duro,” and some stalls top it with cueritos (pickled pork skin).

questions.question: At her XV años, like this quinceañera, her dad swaps her flat shoes for high heels. What does it mean?
questions.answer: She's no longer a little girl
hints: It has to do with growing up.
Along with the “last doll,” it marks a new stage of life.
It's a goodbye to childhood.
questions.description: The party with more waltz rehearsals than any wedding.
questions.fun_fact: At many XV años parties, the quinceañera dances a waltz with her chambelanes that they rehearse for weeks.

questions.question: It's the most populous country in Central America, it borders Chiapas, and its name comes from Nahuatl. Which country is it?
hints: Its name is often translated as “place of many trees.”
Its national bird is the quetzal.
Its capital has almost the same name as the country.
questions.description: A neighbor so close it shares a border, tamales and even words.
questions.fun_fact: Besides Spanish, Guatemala recognizes 22 Mayan languages.

questions.question: In “The Jungle Book,” the animals almost never call Mowgli a “boy.” What nickname do they use?
hints: They call him as if he were one of the wolf family, but they also say what he really is.
It's made of two words joined together, and one of them says what species Mowgli is.
The second part is the word for a baby bear, lion or wolf.
questions.description: Raised by wolves, he learns to howl before he learns to say “Mom.”
questions.fun_fact: In Kipling's original book, Mother Wolf calls him “Mowgli the Frog” because the baby had no fur at all.

questions.question: You're looking at a Huichol painting made of colored yarn. What material were the threads pressed into?
hints: It's a natural material that comes from an animal.
It softens in the heat of the sun.
It's made by the insects that make honey.
questions.description: Art so colorful that even a rainbow would ask permission to look at it.
questions.fun_fact: The Wixárika (Huichol) people live mainly in the Sierra Madre Occidental, across Jalisco, Nayarit, Durango and Zacatecas.

questions.question: It's at the end of Zapopan, Tuxpan and Ixtapan. In Nahuatl, what does the ending “-pan” do?
questions.answer: It marks a place: “on” or “on top of”
wrong_answers: It shows that something is very big
It shows that something happened long ago
hints: All three are names of places in Mexico.
It works like an English preposition.
It's the same idea as “the book is ___ the table.”
questions.description: Three letters that have been working hard on Mexico's maps for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Zapopan, in Jalisco, is often translated as “place among the zapotes,” after the trees of that fruit.

questions.question: Juan Diego had a Nahuatl name: Cuauhtlatoatzin. Fill in what it means: “___ that speaks.”
hints: It's an animal on Mexico's coat of arms.
It's the same “cuauh” found in the name Cuauhtémoc.
It's a hunting bird that flies very high.
questions.description: A name so long that the Virgin preferred to call him “Juanito.”
questions.fun_fact: Juan Diego was made a saint in 2002 and is considered the first Indigenous saint of the Americas.

questions.question: Each Mexico City Metro station has a little drawing, like the grasshopper for Chapultepec, so you can recognize it without reading. What is that kind of symbol called?
hints: Mexica codices used lots of them.
Its name joins the ideas of “picture” and “written.”
Public restrooms use one showing a man and a woman.
questions.description: For when you're so sleepy on the Metro that you can't even read anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Many of the Metro icons were designed by Lance Wyman, who also made the symbols for the 1968 Mexico City Olympics.

questions.question: The Apertura ends in December, and in January the Liga MX season's other tournament kicks off. What is it called?
hints: It also ends with a Liguilla, but in the spring.
In Spanish, it's the formal word for the closing of an event or a conference.
It's the opposite of “apertura”.
questions.description: A season in two chapters, like those telenovelas that never end.
questions.fun_fact: Liga MX has used the names Apertura and Clausura since 2002.

questions.question: I'm Argentine and played for River Plate and Lazio. In 2017 I led Chivas past Tigres in the Clausura final. Who am I?
hints: After Chivas, I went to coach in MLS, in San Jose.
They call me “el Pelado” because of my shaved head.
My last name starts with A.
questions.description: A Guadalajara final with a taste of asado and mate.
questions.fun_fact: With that title, Chivas reached 12 league championships and at the time tied América as the most successful club.

questions.question: How many league titles did Chivas's “Campeonísimo” team win between 1956 and 1965?
hints: It was the golden age of the “Rebaño Sagrado.”
They won almost every tournament that decade, but not all of them.
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.description: A trophy case that needed a few extra shelves in the fifties and sixties.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Campeonísimo, Chivas had never won the professional league: its first title came in the 1956–57 season.

questions.question: Estadio Hidalgo is in Pachuca, the “cradle of soccer” in Mexico. Who brought soccer there in the late 19th century?
hints: They came from abroad to work in the region's main industry.
They spoke English
Besides soccer, they brought pastes, the meat-filled pastries Pachuca is now famous for
questions.description: A ship, a suitcase and a ball: that's how a national passion began.
questions.fun_fact: Pachuca, founded in 1901, proudly calls itself the oldest soccer club in Mexico.

questions.question: Complete the nickname of the coach who wildly celebrated Mexico's goals at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil: Miguel “…” Herrera.
hints: As a player, he was a defender for Atlante.
His nickname is something nobody wants to find on their head.
It lives in hair and makes you itch.
questions.description: His celebrations on the bench went around the world faster than the ball.
questions.fun_fact: Herrera won two league titles with América, both in finals against Cruz Azul: Clausura 2013 and Apertura 2018.

questions.question: They ran from 1996 to 2002, Santos Laguna won the first one, and then the names changed. What were these short tournaments called?
hints: They have to do with the weather
They are seasons of the year
One of them was played around Christmas time
questions.description: Mexico's short tournaments once changed names as often as you change jackets.
questions.fun_fact: Santos Laguna won Invierno 96, the very first short tournament, by beating Necaxa in the final.

questions.question: When Sergio Ramos joined Rayados in 2025, he picked a shirt number honoring his famous goal in the 2014 Champions League final. Which one?
hints: It's a two-digit number
It has to do with the minute of the goal
It was a stoppage-time header against Atlético in Lisbon
questions.description: An Andalusian who swapped gazpacho for Monterrey's cabrito.
questions.fun_fact: Ramos scored that goal at 92:48, and it gave Real Madrid its tenth European Cup.

questions.question: This tournament brings together clubs from North and Central America and the Caribbean, has been played since 1962, and its champion goes to the Club World Cup. Which country has won it most?
hints: Its clubs have won more than half of all editions.
It's the country from the region that has played the most World Cups.
América and Cruz Azul are among the biggest winners.
questions.description: A tournament where the neighbors to the north and to the south fight over the same trophy.
questions.fun_fact: From 2006 to 2021, every edition of the tournament was won by a Mexican club.

questions.question: In “la de a caballo,” the wrestler sits on the back of a face-down opponent and pulls their head back. What is it for?
questions.answer: To make the opponent give up
wrong_answers: To throw the opponent out of the ring
To pull off the opponent's mask
hints: It's a submission hold, not a high-flying move.
Bending the back like that hurts a lot.
The opponent ends up tapping the mat or shouting “ya!” (enough!).
questions.description: A hold that turns your opponent into the world's most uncomfortable horse.
questions.fun_fact: In English-language wrestling, this hold is known as the “camel clutch.”

questions.question: You're at an AAA show and they announce Los Psycho Circus. What are its wrestlers dressed as?
hints: They are three masked wrestlers who usually fight together in trios matches.
Their masks are in loud colors and are a little scary.
Each of their names ends in the English word for a circus performer with a red nose.
questions.description: A circus where nobody wants a front-row seat.
questions.fun_fact: Psycho Clown, the most famous of the trio, is the son of the luchador Brazo de Plata, known as Super Porky.

questions.question: In Mexican lucha libre, what is a “técnico”?
questions.answer: The clean wrestler who follows the rules
wrong_answers: The wrestler who always fights unmasked
The heaviest wrestler on the card
The wrestler who trains the rookies
hints: The word describes a fighter's style and attitude in the ring.
The crowd almost always cheers for him.
He is the opposite of a rudo.
questions.description: Colorful masks, shouting from the stands and a referee who never sees anything.
questions.fun_fact: A luchador can switch sides: many famous técnicos started out as rudos.

questions.question: On which day of the week is CMLL's traditional family show at Arena México?
hints: It's a day with no school.
The big Friday shows are at night.
It's the last day of the weekend.
questions.description: The perfect day to boo the rudo with the whole family.
questions.fun_fact: Arena México, in the Doctores neighborhood, is known as “the Cathedral of Lucha Libre.”

questions.question: Complete the nickname of the legendary técnico (good-guy wrestler) Atlantis: “The Idol of the…”
hints: He has been a much-loved técnico since the 1980s.
His lucha libre career has lasted more than four decades.
They're the littlest fans in the arena.
questions.description: A wrestler who comes up from the bottom of the sea to sign autographs.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, at the CMLL anniversary show, Atlantis won Último Guerrero's mask.

questions.question: Which singer, known as “El Lujo de México,” was part of the trio Los Tres Ases before going solo?
hints: He's a bolero singer whose career took off in the 1950s and 1960s.
He was born in Jalisco in the 1930s.
He made the song “Luz y sombra” famous.
questions.description: To sing under a balcony you need a velvet voice and a shawl in case it gets chilly.
questions.fun_fact: Marco Antonio Muñiz was born in Guadalajara in 1933 and kept recording for more than five decades.

questions.question: You're in Zapopan on October 12, and thousands of people walk with the Virgin to her basilica. What is this festival called?
hints: It's a pilgrimage that sets out from Guadalajara Cathedral.
UNESCO listed it as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2018.
Its name sounds like “romero” (rosemary), and also like “Roma.”
questions.description: A walk so long that even your shoes ask for a break.
questions.fun_fact: The Virgin of Zapopan is called “La Generala” (the General), and more than a million people join her romería.

questions.question: This town in southern Jalisco saw the Vargas family's mariachi born in 1897, and its name completes the group's name. Which town is it?
hints: It's not the town known as the “cradle of mariachi.”
The group is known as “the best mariachi in the world.”
Mariachi Vargas de…
questions.description: A small town with a very big musical last name.
questions.fun_fact: Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán is still playing today, more than 125 years after it was founded.

questions.question: Which country is the original Pinocchio book from?
hints: The book came out in Europe in the 19th century.
In the original language, “Pinocchio” means something like “pine nut”, the seed of the pine tree.
It's the country shaped like a boot.
questions.description: A bug who works full-time as a conscience and doesn't charge a single cent.
questions.fun_fact: In the original book the cricket has no name: he's simply “the Talking Cricket”. The name Jiminy Cricket came with the Disney film.

questions.question: Which ranchera singer, born in Chihuahua, was known as “La Grandota de Camargo”?
hints: She was also an actress, in films like “Mecánica nacional.”
She sang many songs by José Alfredo Jiménez.
Her stage name puts together the Spanish words for a kind of wrestling and a town.
questions.description: A voice so big it needed a nickname to match.
questions.fun_fact: Lucha Villa's real name was Luz Elena Ruiz Bejarano.

questions.question: In the movie “Coco,” what is the name of the boy who dreams of being a musician?
hints: He lives in the town of Santa Cecilia.
He's joined by a xoloitzcuintle dog named Dante.
He shares his name with an archangel.
questions.description: A family of shoemakers and a boy who just wants to make beautiful noise.
questions.fun_fact: In “Coco,” Miguel's family has banned music for generations.

questions.question: At my big party I wear a white dress and a veil. I just got married, and the mariachi sings while I dance with my husband. Who am I?
hints: The party is called a wedding.
I just said “I do.”
At the end I toss a bunch of flowers.
questions.description: Today is the most important day, and the mariachi knows it.
questions.fun_fact: At many Mexican weddings, the newlyweds dance “la víbora de la mar” with their guests.

questions.question: Which singer made the ranchera “Volver, volver” famous in the 1970s?
hints: He was born in Jalisco and sang dressed as a charro, with mariachi.
He was known as “El Charro de Huentitán”.
His son Alejandro is also a famous singer.
questions.description: A song that makes the whole room shout along without anyone asking.
questions.fun_fact: “Volver, volver” was written by Fernando Z. Maldonado, not by the singer who made it famous.

questions.question: It began in 2011, falls in November, and for several days stores all over Mexico offer huge discounts. What is it called?
hints: Many people use it to buy gifts before Christmas.
It was inspired by Black Friday in the United States.
Its name plays on the Spanish word for “weekend.”
questions.description: That weekend when your wallet begs for a vacation and the malls are packed tighter than a can of sardines.
questions.fun_fact: The first Buen Fin ran from November 18 to 21, 2011, and many companies pay the year-end bonus (aguinaldo) early so their workers can shop.

questions.question: You see it on prices at the tianguis, before the number, like an S with a line through it. In Mexico, what does that sign mean?
hints: It's a sign with centuries of history, older than many of the currencies that use it today.
American movies use the same sign, but there it means something else.
The sign is thought to come from abbreviating “ps”, the name of Mexico's currency.
questions.description: An S that put a little stick on top to look fancier on price tags.
questions.fun_fact: Many historians think the $ sign came from abbreviating “pesos”, and the United States borrowed it for its dollars.

questions.question: I live at the butcher's and the tianguis; put tortillas or tomatoes on me and I tell you their weight so you know what to pay. What am I?
hints: I care about kilos, not centimeters.
I often have a little tray on top and numbers on a screen.
Many homes also have one of me in the bathroom.
questions.description: The only one that tells you the truth about how many tomatoes you're taking, even if it hurts.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, the consumer agency Profeco checks the scales in markets and shops so nobody sells you less than you paid for.

questions.question: How many 10-centavo coins do you need to make the same amount as one 5-peso coin?
hints: First think how many 10-centavo coins make one peso.
With 10 of them you get one peso.
Multiply 10 by 5.
questions.description: A coin so tiny even the piggy bank complains it weighs nothing.
questions.fun_fact: The 10-centavo coin is still legal money, even though almost nobody uses it to pay anymore.

questions.question: Mexicans working abroad, mostly in the United States, send it to their families, and it reaches countless towns. What is this money called?
hints: It shows up in the economic news almost every month.
Many families pick it up at stores or banks with a code.
Its name comes from a formal verb that means “to send” money or payment.
questions.description: Money that crosses the border faster than any car at the checkpoint.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico receives the second-most remittances of any country in the world, behind only India.

questions.question: Mexico has 1, 2 and 5 peso coins. What is the everyday coin that comes next after the 5?
hints: It's the biggest coin most people carry in their coin purse.
It has a silver center and a gold ring.
It's worth twice the 5-peso coin.
questions.description: The queen of the coin purse: big, heavy and two-toned.
questions.fun_fact: The center of the 10-peso coin shows a design inspired by the Aztec Sun Stone.

questions.question: This black panther found Mowgli as a baby and took him to live with the wolves. What is its name?
hints: It's not the bear who sings or the tiger who hunts Mowgli.
It's the one who keeps telling Mowgli off and urging him to go back to the humans.
Its name starts with B, just like its bear friend's.
questions.description: The jungle's most stylish babysitter, dressed all in black.
questions.fun_fact: Black panthers are leopards or jaguars with lots of dark pigment: in the right light, you can still see their spots.

questions.question: Many people think “Masiosare” is a character in the Mexican anthem, but the lyrics say “mas si osare…”. Who is it that “osare”?
hints: “Osar” means to dare.
It's someone who dares to defile the homeland's soil.
They come from outside, and they're no friend.
questions.description: The anthem's most famous character, who never actually existed.
questions.fun_fact: The mix-up is so well known that “Masiosare” became a popular joke, and some people even draw him as a villain.

questions.question: The 1821 Plan of Iguala gave the Trigarante Flag its three guarantees. Which one was NOT among them?
hints: They gave the Army of the Three Guarantees its name.
Each guarantee had its own color on the Trigarante Flag.
The odd one out is a form of government without a king.
questions.description: Three promises, three colors and a plan named after a town in Guerrero.
questions.fun_fact: Because of the Plan of Iguala, newly independent Mexico had an emperor: Agustín de Iturbide.

questions.question: The music of “¡Patria! ¡Patria! tus hijos te juran” is by Jaime Nunó, who was born in Europe, led military bands and won the 1854 contest. What country was he from?
hints: Before coming to Mexico, he lived in Cuba.
In his home region, people also spoke another language besides his country's official one.
He was born in Catalonia.
questions.description: An anthem so Mexican that its music had to cross the ocean first.
questions.fun_fact: Jaime Nunó spent years forgotten in the United States and was only honored as an old man; his remains now rest in the Rotonda de las Personas Ilustres in Mexico City.

questions.question: On the night of September 15, at the end of the Grito, how many times is “¡Viva México!” traditionally shouted?
hints: It's more than two.
From the balcony of the National Palace it is repeated several times, and the crowd answers each time.
It's the number of stripes on the flag.
questions.description: The night when all of Mexico ends up hoarse and happy.
questions.fun_fact: The bell rung at the National Palace is the Dolores bell, brought from Dolores Hidalgo in 1896.

questions.question: In February, Constitution Day comes first, on the 5th. On what day does Flag Day come next?
hints: It's not Valentine's Day.
It's near the end of the month.
It's four days before the 28th.
questions.description: February is short, but it has a party for the Constitution and for the most beloved piece of cloth.
questions.fun_fact: On February 24, 1821, the Plan of Iguala was announced, which gave rise to the Trigarante Flag.

questions.question: Francisco González Bocanegra's original poem for the National Anthem has how many stanzas, not counting the chorus?
hints: Officially, only four of them are sung.
The original poem is more than twice as long as the version sung today.
It's the number of fingers on your two hands.
questions.description: A poem so long that at ceremonies we only sing the short version.
questions.fun_fact: Legend has it that González Bocanegra's girlfriend locked him in a room until he finished writing the anthem.

questions.question: When you toss a coin in Mexico, you call “¡águila o sol!”. Where does the “águila” (eagle) side get its name?
questions.answer: From the national coat of arms
hints: It's stamped on every Mexican coin.
The same image appears on official documents and government buildings.
It's the same picture that sits in the middle of the flag.
questions.description: A big decision made by throwing money into the air.
questions.fun_fact: The “sol” (sun) side comes from old coins that showed a liberty cap with rays around it, like a sun.

questions.question: Zayu is a jaguar who plays forward and is one of the three mascots of the 2026 World Cup. Which country does he represent?
hints: His country had already hosted two World Cups before.
Jaguars live in the jungles in the south of that country.
It's the home of El Tri.
questions.description: A big cat that swapped its naps for training sessions.
questions.fun_fact: The other two 2026 World Cup mascots are Maple, a moose from Canada, and Clutch, a bald eagle from the United States.

questions.question: You do me with your back to the goal, body in the air, kicking the ball over your head. Raúl Jiménez scored with me against Panama in 2013. What move am I?
hints: It takes a lot of acrobatics.
The player ends up landing on their back on the grass.
In Mexico it's named after the people of a South American country.
questions.description: A move kids try at the park while their parents watch nervously.
questions.fun_fact: That late goal by Raúl Jiménez at Estadio Azteca kept El Tri's hopes alive on the road to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

questions.question: You're filling in the Panini World Cup album and reach Mexico's page. Who is on those stickers?
questions.answer: The players of the Mexican national team
wrong_answers: The characters of El Chavo del 8
The singers of a mariachi band
hints: They wear shorts and soccer cleats.
They play in the World Cup.
They wear El Tri's green jersey.
questions.description: The only book you read with hands covered in glue.
questions.fun_fact: The first Panini World Cup album was made for Mexico 1970.

questions.question: In this stadium, in 2012, El Tri won the Olympic soccer final. Which team did it beat?
hints: It's a South American team.
Neymar played in that final.
It's the team with five World Cups.
questions.description: An arch so big it could pass for the world's widest goal.
questions.fun_fact: Oribe Peralta scored both of Mexico's goals in that final, the first one in the very first minute of the match.

questions.question: It opened in 1966, Pelé and Maradona lifted the World Cup there, and in 2026 it became the first stadium to host three World Cup opening matches. Which is it?
hints: It's in Mexico City.
It's the home of Club América.
Its name recalls an ancient people of Mexico.
questions.description: A stadium that has hosted more World Cups than many countries have played in.
questions.fun_fact: The Azteca hosted the opening matches of the 1970, 1986 and 2026 World Cups.

questions.question: In 2018, Mexico's Under-17 women's team finished runner-up at the World Cup, a first for any Mexican women's team. Which country hosted it?
hints: It was in South America.
Its capital sits on the shores of the Río de la Plata.
The final was played in Montevideo.
questions.description: Some young players who went further than plenty of their bearded colleagues.
questions.fun_fact: Spain beat Mexico 2-1 in that final in Montevideo.

questions.question: In what year did Mexico beat defending champions Germany 1–0 at a World Cup, with a goal by Hirving “Chucky” Lozano?
hints: Germany had won the previous World Cup, in Brazil.
That World Cup was played in Europe.
It was in Russia.
questions.description: A goal celebrated so loudly that even the ground started shaking.
questions.fun_fact: After the goal, sensors in Mexico City picked up a small “earthquake” caused by thousands of fans jumping at once.

questions.question: The Mexico City Grand Prix is raced at a track named after two drivers. Who were they?
hints: They were two Mexican racing drivers from the 1960s.
Both raced in Formula 1, and their names were Ricardo and Pedro.
Their last name is one of the most common in Mexico and ends in “-íguez”.
questions.description: Here you go so fast that not even the traffic on the Periférico could slow you down.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Rodríguez won two Formula 1 Grands Prix: South Africa in 1967 and Belgium in 1970.

questions.question: At Tokyo 2020, Aremi Fuentes won bronze in weightlifting. What is the lift that takes the bar from the floor to overhead in one single pull?
hints: In Olympic weightlifting, only two lifts count.
The other lift is done in two stages: first to the shoulders, then overhead.
Its English name also means to grab something quickly.
questions.description: A sport where saying “I can't handle this” literally means you lose.
questions.fun_fact: Aremi Fuentes won her Olympic bronze in the 76 kg (168 lb) category, adding up her two lifts.

questions.question: At La Quebrada in Acapulco, divers jump from a cliff about 35 m (115 ft) high. Why do they wait for a wave to come in?
questions.answer: To land where the water is deeper
wrong_answers: So the wave carries them to the beach
So the water is a little warmer
hints: Down below, between the rocks, the sea isn't always the same depth.
When the water pulls back, it can get very shallow.
If they jump at just the right moment, the wave fills the gap between the rocks.
questions.description: Even the highest diving board at the pool wouldn't dare look down from here.
questions.fun_fact: Before jumping, many La Quebrada divers pray at a small altar to the Virgin of Guadalupe at the top of the cliff.

questions.question: I'm a US open-wheel racing series; I race on ovals and city streets, and Monterrey's Pato O'Ward is one of my stars. What am I?
hints: My cars have uncovered wheels, not the body of a street car.
Pato O'Ward drives for the Arrow McLaren team.
My most famous race is the Indianapolis 500.
questions.description: A regiomontano who steps on the gas harder than the August sun in Monterrey.
questions.fun_fact: Pato O'Ward has finished second in the Indianapolis 500, one of the most famous races in the world.

questions.question: Fernando Valenzuela is the only player to win Rookie of the Year and the Cy Young in the same season, 1981. Which city did he play for?
hints: It was a US city with a huge number of Mexican fans.
It's the most populous city in California and the second in the United States.
It's the city of Hollywood.
questions.description: He looked up at the sky before every pitch, and half a country looked up with him.
questions.fun_fact: The craze around him was called “Fernandomania,” and in 2023 his team retired his number 34.

questions.question: About how wide can a leaf of the giant Amazon water lily grow?
hints: It's much bigger than the leaf of any plant in your home.
A grown-up could lie down on it, stretched out.
It's about as long as a small car.
questions.description: A plate so big that not even a whole family barbecue could fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The ribs under this leaf inspired the gardener Joseph Paxton when he designed London's Crystal Palace.

questions.question: I'm a tapatío, I drive in Formula 1, and I won races with the Red Bull team. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Guadalajara, Jalisco.
I raced for Red Bull alongside Max Verstappen.
All of Mexico calls me “Checo.”
questions.description: His nickname sounds friendly and cute, but on the track he means business.
questions.fun_fact: Checo Pérez won his first Formula 1 race at the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix after dropping to last place on the first lap.

questions.question: How many medals did diver Osmar Olvera win at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
hints: He competed on the 3-meter springboard, alone and with a partner.
In the pairs event, with Juan Celaya, he took silver.
In the individual event he also made the podium, with bronze.
questions.description: A young man who jumps off the springboard and lands straight on the podium.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico won 5 medals at Paris 2024, and 2 of them were Osmar Olvera's.

questions.question: She was a painter of the Generación de la Ruptura, a pioneer of informal abstraction in Mexico and the wife of Manuel Felguérez. Who is she?
hints: She died young, in 1974.
Her paintings are textures and patches of color, with no figures.
Her first and last names start with L and C.
questions.description: No landscapes, no portraits of Grandma: here the splotches are in charge.
questions.fun_fact: Her husband, Manuel Felguérez, has a museum of abstract art named after him in Zacatecas.

questions.question: In a museum, you see a vocho taken apart: every piece hangs from the ceiling on threads, as if it were exploding. Which Mexican artist made it?
hints: He started his career as a political cartoonist.
He was a student in Gabriel Orozco's workshop.
He shares a last name with the founder of Zara.
questions.description: The world's tidiest mechanic… or the most desperate one.
questions.fun_fact: The work is called “Cosmic Thing” and was first shown in 2002.

questions.question: I was born in 1919, I expelled Diego Rivera in 1929, and David Alfaro Siqueiros was one of my most loyal members. What am I?
hints: My newspaper was called El Machete.
Frida Kahlo joined me too.
My flag was red, with the hammer and sickle.
questions.description: There was a time when paintbrushes and politics carried the same membership card.
questions.fun_fact: El Machete started as the newspaper of the painters' union of Siqueiros and Xavier Guerrero, and later became the party's newspaper.

questions.question: Who is the voice and leader of El Tri, the band once called Three Souls in My Mind?
hints: He was born in Puebla, grew up in Mexico City and shouts “¡Que viva el rocanrol!” at every show.
His wife, Chela, is the band's manager.
His last name has just four letters and starts with L.
questions.description: He's been on stage for so many decades that the stage now charges him rent.
questions.fun_fact: The band started in 1968 as Three Souls in My Mind and at first sang in English.

questions.question: “I started as a child in Timbiriche, my mom was the actress Susana Dosamantes and they call me ‘La Chica Dorada’.” Who am I?
hints: I was a judge on the American show “The X Factor”.
I sang “Y yo sigo aquí” and “Ni una sola palabra”.
My last name is another way of saying “güero” (blond).
questions.description: If she shines this much, it's not the spotlights: she came that way from the factory.

previous.feedback: Hint 3 is false: Omar Chaparro did not voice Pikachu. He played Sebastian, the Charizard trainer, in “Detective Pikachu” and dubbed his own role in the Latin American version. The translation turned the source's vague wording into a specific claim that is wrong. Use: “He's from Chihuahua and played Sebastian, the Charizard trainer, in “Detective Pikachu”.” The source's own wording (“le puso la voz en español a «Detective Pikachu»”) is also misleading; source: it should be clarified the same way. Separately, related q-17307 pairs Omar Chaparro with Martha Higareda in its question text, and q-15670 is built on the same clues as hints 2 and 3, so the overlap is worth checking. Fact check: wrong. Hint 3 is false. Omar Chaparro is from Chihuahua, but he did not voice Pikachu in the Spanish dub. He played Sebastian in the film and dubbed himself in Latin America. Reynolds voiced Pikachu in the original. The answer is right and the film was a big box-office hit.

questions.description: Up on the roof, it's always the first to find out that rain is on the way.
questions.fun_fact: A clothesline in the sun dries clothes for free, and the sunlight also helps take stains out of white clothes.

questions.question: A robot walks on six legs, moving three at a time while the other three hold it up. Which group of animals is it copying?
hints: Look at the number of legs.
Spiders have eight, so it isn't them.
Ants, beetles and cockroaches belong to this group.
questions.description: A robot that would need three pairs of shoes just to leave the house.
questions.fun_fact: Walking with three legs always on the ground makes a tripod, so the robot never loses its balance, just like a cockroach.

questions.question: In El Chavo del 8's vecindad, the kids play there, the barrel sits there and Don Ramón walks through all the time. What place is it?
hints: It's outdoors, right in the middle of the homes.
It's where Don Ramón and Doña Florinda get into their fights.
It's the open space all the neighbors share.
questions.description: It was all “sin querer queriendo,” but everything happened right there.
questions.fun_fact: El Chavo's vecindad was filmed in a Televisa studio, not in a real vecindad.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this animal also appears in Minecraft. In real life, where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in fresh water.
It's in the south of Mexico City.
Colorful trajineras float through there.
questions.description: In Minecraft you carry it around in a bucket; in real life, better not even touch it.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Nahuatl word “axolotl,” which is often translated as “water monster.”

questions.question: It's one of the “big four,” plays its home games in Zapopan and is the only top-division club that fields only Mexican players. Which is it?
hints: Its stadium is shaped like a volcano covered in grass.
Zapopan is right next to Guadalajara.
Its mascot is a goat.
questions.description: A club with a rule as strict as grandma's pozole recipe.
questions.fun_fact: The rule includes players with dual nationality as long as they are Mexican, such as several born in the United States.

questions.question: Only two wrestlers face each other, with no partners to help, and almost always over a personal rivalry. What is this match called?
hints: No partner is waiting in the corner.
Besides the referee, there are only two people in the ring.
Its name repeats the Spanish word for “hand.”
questions.description: In lucha libre, rivalries simmer even slower than Grandma's mole.
questions.fun_fact: Many famous mano a mano matches come with a bet: the loser gives up their mask or their hair.

questions.question: In a tag team match, what are the corners of the ring for?
questions.answer: For the partner to wait in
wrong_answers: For the referee to stand in
For the loser to rest in
For the fans to sit in
hints: In a tag match, not everyone wrestles at the same time.
You need a slap of the hand to enter the ring.
Someone there is ready to jump in as soon as they're called.
questions.description: Four spots in the ring with a better view than the front row.
questions.fun_fact: Wrestlers launch their most spectacular dives from the top of the corners.

questions.question: Many matches are “a dos de tres caídas” (two out of three falls). What is a caída?
questions.answer: A point won by a pin or submission
wrong_answers: Knocking the rival down to the mat
A dive from the top rope
hints: Whoever collects two of them wins the match.
The referee has to see something to award it.
It can be shoulders held to the mat while the count goes “one, two, three”.
questions.description: A question for the fans who yell from the front row every Saturday.
questions.fun_fact: In a two-out-of-three-falls match, whoever wins the first two doesn't need the third.

questions.question: In this lucha de apuestas (bet match), whoever escapes wins, and the last one left inside loses their mask. What match is it?
hints: To get out, you have to climb.
Before it starts, something made of metal is lowered from the ceiling.
Metal bars surround the whole ring, as if it were made for birds.
questions.description: A match where running away isn't cowardly, it's the whole point.
questions.fun_fact: In CMLL cage matches, sometimes more than ten wrestlers go in with their masks on the line.

questions.question: They were a legendary rudo trio in Mexican wrestling who revolutionized six-man trios matches. Who were Los Misioneros de la Muerte?
questions.answer: El Signo, El Texano and Negro Navarro
wrong_answers: Brazo de Oro, Brazo de Plata and El Brazo
Villano I, Villano III and Villano IV
Blue Demon, Huracán Ramírez and Mil Máscaras
hints: The trio formed in the late 1970s.
One of them kept wrestling well into old age and is a master of mat wrestling.
One was named after a state in the southern United States.
questions.description: Three missionaries who definitely weren't here to teach Sunday school.
questions.fun_fact: Negro Navarro debuted in the 1970s and kept stepping into the ring for more than four decades.

questions.question: What nickname is José José, the singer of “El triste,” known by?
hints: He was famous for his romantic ballads in the '70s and '80s.
The nickname shows off how well he sang.
In fairy tales, it's what the king's son is.
questions.description: A nickname so elegant it makes you want to sing in a suit and tie.
questions.fun_fact: José José became famous in 1970 by singing “El triste” at a song festival in Mexico City.

questions.question: Look at this: several musicians in a mariachi band use it. What is it for?
hints: It has stretched horsehair.
It moves back and forth across an instrument.
The instrument rests on the shoulder.
questions.description: It looks like a magic wand, but no wizard would ask to borrow it.
questions.fun_fact: The hairs of a bow are usually horsehair, rubbed with rosin so they make a sound.

questions.question: In which decade did the Roomba, the disc-shaped robot vacuum, first go on sale?
hints: It's younger than your parents, but older than many kids playing today.
It came out before the first iPhone.
It came out in 2002.
questions.description: The only worker in the house who never complains about cleaning the floor, but still gets stuck under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Roomba, iRobot, the company that made it, built robots to explore dangerous places.

questions.question: Why are the mercados sobre ruedas (“markets on wheels”) called that?
questions.answer: Because they set up in a different neighborhood each day
wrong_answers: Because they only sell car parts
Because you shop without leaving your car
Because they set up next to highways
hints: People buy fresh fruit and vegetables from the countryside there.
At the end of the day, the stalls are taken apart and carried away.
Tomorrow it will be somewhere else, and the day after, somewhere else again.
questions.description: Where the marchante lets you taste a bit of mango even if you're not buying anything.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City's mercados sobre ruedas bring farm produce straight to the neighborhoods.

questions.question: The silver Onza Libertad weighs exactly one troy ounce. How many grams is that?
hints: It isn't the same ounce used in the kitchen.
It's a little heavier than the kitchen ounce.
It's almost exactly 31 grams.
questions.description: A coin so fancy it even has its own special way of being weighed.
questions.fun_fact: The troy ounce is used all over the world for gold and silver, and it's heavier than the ordinary kitchen ounce.

questions.question: How many 50-centavo coins do you need to make one peso?
hints: Think about what this coin is worth compared with a peso.
It's a very small number.
That's why people call this coin “medio peso”.
questions.description: A tiny coin with a very simple job.
questions.fun_fact: In 1993 Mexico created the “nuevo peso”, worth 1,000 old pesos: they knocked off three zeros!

questions.question: I won the Under-17 World Cup with Mexico in 2005, shone at Real Sociedad and broke the MLS scoring record with LAFC. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Cancún.
As a teenager I signed with Arsenal in England.
My last name is the Spanish word for “candle,” like the ones on a birthday cake.
questions.description: A striker who taught San Sebastián and Los Angeles to shout “¡gol!” Mexican style.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019 Carlos Vela scored 34 goals for LAFC, an MLS record at the time.

questions.question: El Tri takes the field in its green jersey, like the flag of Mexico. How many colors do the stripes of that flag have?
hints: One of them is green.
Another is the color of snow.
The last stripe is red, like a tomato.
questions.description: A question you could wear to the stadium… literally.
questions.fun_fact: El Tri often pairs a green jersey with white shorts and red socks, so the players wear the whole flag.

questions.question: Three of these teams have played in a Concacaf Nations League final. Which one has NOT?
hints: The United States won the first three editions.
Mexico won the 2025 final.
The missing one is famous for its volcanoes, its beaches and its “pura vida.”
questions.description: A young tournament where the same few faces keep crashing the last party.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico won its first Nations League in 2025, beating Panama 2–1 with two goals from Raúl Jiménez.

questions.question: Ernesto Canto was world champion in 1983, broke the world record in 1984 and won gold in Los Angeles that year. In which event?
hints: His event is held on the streets, not by running laps around the track.
It's an event in which Mexico has won many Olympic medals.
In his event one foot must always touch the ground, and it was the shorter of the two held.
questions.description: A 1984 gold that Mexican families still brag about after Sunday lunch.
questions.fun_fact: At Los Angeles 1984, Raúl González won gold in the 50 km race walk, so Mexico took both race walking events.

questions.question: Plates of a soft material invented in the 19th century are carved with gouges, inked and printed; the Taller de Gráfica Popular used it a lot. What technique is it?
hints: It is a relief print, a bit like carving wood
That material was used to cover kitchen floors
Its name comes from linoleum
questions.description: An art for people with a lot to say and little money for a printing press.
questions.fun_fact: The Taller de Gráfica Popular was founded in Mexico City in 1937, with Leopoldo Méndez and Pablo O'Higgins among its founders.

questions.question: In what year did the artists of the Ruptura found the Salón Independiente, as a protest against an official government exhibition?
hints: It was the decade of the Beatles and the miniskirt
The official exhibition was part of a cultural program tied to a big sporting event
It was the year of the Mexico City Olympic Games
questions.description: When nobody invites you to the party, you throw your own next door.
questions.fun_fact: The Salón Independiente began as a protest against the Exposición Solar, which the government put on for the Cultural Olympiad.

questions.question: Belinda, the star of “Amigos x siempre”, came to Mexico as a child. In which country was she born?
hints: Spanish is also spoken in her home country.
Her home country is in Europe.
She was born in the city of Real Madrid.
questions.description: She came to Mexico with a tiny suitcase and took over the big stage.
questions.fun_fact: Belinda was about 10 years old when she starred in “Amigos x siempre” in 2000.

questions.question: “I started on TV as a little girl, I sing pop and also rancheras with mariachi, and I was married to the singer Mijares.” Who am I?
hints: As a girl I starred in the telenovela “Chispita.”
I made the film “Fiebre de amor” with Luis Miguel.
My name is the Spanish word for a bright star seen at dawn.
questions.description: A star you could see on TV before your parents even had a remote control.
questions.fun_fact: As a girl she was called “Lucerito,” and today her daughter, Lucero Mijares, is a singer too.

questions.question: What nickname has the singer Lucero been known by for decades?
hints: Lucero started singing and acting as a child, and the nickname has followed her since she was very young.
It's an affectionate nickname from her fans and the press.
It's like saying a whole continent wants to marry her.
questions.description: Celebrities don't have names, they have showbiz royal titles.
questions.fun_fact: Lucero is one of the few stars who can switch from pop to rancheras with mariachi without breaking a sweat.

questions.question: Alfonso Herrera played Miguel in “Rebelde”, sang in RBD and acted in the series “Sense8”. What nickname do his fans call him?
hints: It's the usual nickname for his first name.
Like many Mexican nicknames, it swaps a few letters of his first name.
In Mexico, almost every Alfonso gets called this.
questions.description: A telenovela rebel with a cute pet name.
questions.fun_fact: “Rebelde” is the Mexican version of an Argentine telenovela called “Rebelde Way”.

questions.question: In Sinaloa, this instrument is so important that the whole band is also named after it. Which one is it?
hints: It's a percussion instrument.
It's played with a mallet and has a cymbal on top.
Its name sounds like the Spanish word for “drum.”
questions.description: The instrument that makes the glasses shake at every wedding, even three blocks away.
questions.fun_fact: Banda El Recodo, founded in 1938 by Cruz Lizárraga in Mazatlán, is one of the oldest Sinaloan bands still playing.

questions.question: In which decade was the norteño group Calibre 50 formed in Mazatlán?
hints: It’s newer than Los Tigres del Norte or Ramón Ayala.
Their songs were on cell phones and social media from the very start.
It formed when YouTube already existed and the 21st century was about ten years old.
questions.description: A norteño group that measures success in packed stadiums and endless streams.
questions.fun_fact: Their original singer and songwriter, Edén Muñoz, left the group in 2022 to go solo.

questions.question: I'm a Zapotec fiesta from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, with embroidered tehuana dresses and sones all night long. What's my name?
hints: I'm celebrated a lot in Juchitán, Oaxaca, especially in May.
One season has many of me, each with its own name and its own queen.
In Spanish, my name is also a wax object that people light in churches.
questions.description: A fiesta on the Isthmus where nobody goes home early, even with work in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Juchitán holds dozens of velas every season, and some last several days.

questions.question: In Mexico, almost every town has one big fiesta a year, with banda music, fireworks and a procession from the church. Who is it for?
hints: It's a religious celebration.
The celebration leaves the church and goes through the streets carrying an image.
Depending on the town, it may be San Miguel, San Juan or a Virgin.
questions.description: A party with fireworks, banda and jaripeo, and nobody in town remembers sending the invitations.
questions.fun_fact: Many patron saint fiestas end with a “castillo”: a tower of fireworks that spins and sparkles.

questions.question: Los Bukis, Los Temerarios and Bronco packed dance halls in the '80s and '90s with grupera music. Which instruments were their core?
questions.answer: Keyboard, electric bass, drums and guitar
hints: It looked more like a rock band than a banda or a mariachi.
Several of the instruments plug into the wall.
A synthesizer was almost a must.
questions.description: The soundtrack of tardeadas, ballroom dances and your parents' love letters.
questions.fun_fact: Marco Antonio Solís's Los Bukis split up in 1996 and got back together in 2021 for a tour that filled stadiums.

questions.question: What very Mexican expression means “agreed” and seals a deal?
hints: It's how you answer when someone asks «¿nos vemos a las cinco?».
One of its verbs is also used to ask a price: «¿cuánto…?».
Its two verbs rhyme.
questions.description: Mexico's shortest contract: no signature, no lawyer needed.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico a simple «sale» is enough to accept a plan; the «y vale» just ties the deal up tight.

questions.question: In Mexico, if two people are «uña y mugre», it's not because they don't wash their hands. What are they?
hints: Think how hard it is to get dirt out from under a fingernail.
Wherever one goes, the other goes too.
They're always together and tell each other everything.
questions.description: A saying that's begging for a nail brush.
questions.fun_fact: In other places people say «ser uña y carne» (fingernail and flesh) with the same meaning; in Mexico many prefer the version with dirt.

questions.question: In Mexico, what kind of phrase is «¿Qué onda?»?
hints: Young people use it a lot with their «cuates».
People answer it with «nada, aquí nomás» or «todo bien».
It's like saying “hi, how are you?”.
questions.description: The most Mexican question in the world, and almost nobody answers it seriously.
questions.fun_fact: It can also ask about something specific: «¿Qué onda con la fiesta del sábado?» means “What's up with Saturday's party?”.

questions.question: In Mexico, on what day is Independence officially celebrated?
hints: There's no school anywhere in the country that day.
There's a military parade in the Zócalo in Mexico City.
It's in the mes patrio, the day right after the Grito.
questions.description: Everything turns green, white, and red, even the antojitos.
questions.fun_fact: The bell the president rings at the Grito was brought in 1896 from the church in Dolores, Guanajuato.

questions.question: In many Mexican colonias, someone comes by ringing a bell like this one. Who is it?
hints: He comes in a big truck, usually in the morning.
When you hear it, you have to take the bags out fast.
He takes away what you threw in your trash can at home.
questions.description: A little bell that in Mexico has more power than any alarm clock.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican cities, garbage workers sort cardboard, plastic and metal by hand to sell it for recycling.

questions.question: The municipio provides it, it's often billed on the electric bill, and it works at night on streets and in parks. What service is it?
hints: You see it on tall poles.
If it breaks, your street goes dark.
It's the lamps along the sidewalk.
questions.description: The city service everyone only remembers when it stops working.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican municipios have switched their street lamps to LEDs, which use much less electricity.

questions.question: In Mexico, which of these words is NOT a way to talk about a friend?
hints: Three of them are for people close to you.
One of them isn't a person at all, but a thing.
You put it on when it's cold.
questions.description: In Mexico, what you call your friends changes with how close you are.
questions.fun_fact: “Carnal” comes from “carne” (flesh): it's like saying your friend is of your own blood, like a brother.

questions.question: If someone in Mexico tells you “al ratito te marco”, when are they going to call you?
hints: It's not this second.
But it's not a long time from now either.
It's in a little while, that same day.
questions.description: The stretchiest unit of time in the universe.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico even time comes in diminutives: “ahorita”, “al ratito” and even “ahoritita”.

questions.question: His jokes are told all over Mexico, passed from grandparents to grandkids, and they nearly always get him in trouble. Who is Pepito?
hints: His jokes get told at family parties and among friends.
His parents always end up scolding him for what he says.
Many of his jokes start with “The teacher asks him…”.
questions.description: A character who has kept Mexico laughing for decades without charging a single peso.
questions.fun_fact: Other countries have a similar boy: in Spain he's called Jaimito, and in Italy, Pierino.

questions.question: In Mexico, when someone greets you with “¿Qué onda, banda?”, what does “banda” mean?
hints: YouTubers say it at the start of their videos.
It's a way to call a whole group of people.
It's like saying “¿Qué onda, raza?”.
questions.description: A greeting you hear in Mexico more often than “good morning”.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, “la banda” is your gang of friends, while “banda sinaloense” is a style of music with tubas and trumpets.

questions.question: In Mexican memes and chats, when someone loses their game or gets left on read, people write “¡pipipipí!”. What does it imitate?
hints: It isn't a machine noise.
It's used to tease someone who came out the loser.
It's like pretending someone is sobbing.
questions.description: A chat sound sent with a cheeky little grin.
questions.fun_fact: “Pipipipí” often comes with the crying emoji, to tease someone lovingly about their bad luck.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The one source I found says 'pipipi' comes from El Chavo del 8, where Chavo whines after Don Ramón hits him. It is used to mock a loss. No source describes it as a fake cry, though that reading is plausible.

questions.question: In colonial times, Campeche filled up with walls, bastions and lookout towers. What did people want to spot in time?
hints: It was a danger that came by sea.
They attacked the port to steal its riches.
They flew a black flag with a skull, at least in the movies.
questions.description: A whole city that slept with one eye open, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its walls against pirates, Campeche's historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: In what year did the animated series “PAW Patrol” first air?
hints: It's from this century.
It came out when touchscreen phones were already common everywhere.
It first aired the same year the movie “Frozen” hit theaters.
questions.description: Six puppies and a boy with a tablet handle more emergencies than real firefighters.
questions.fun_fact: Its creator, Keith Chapman, also came up with the series “Bob the Builder.”

questions.question: You're in the Palacio Nacional, where the viceroys of New Spain lived. A viceroy ruled in someone's place. Whose?
hints: That person lived on the other side of the ocean.
The Spanish word “virrey” hides that person's title inside it.
He wore a crown, and his kingdom spoke Spanish.
questions.description: The boss was very far away, so he sent someone to take charge for him.
questions.fun_fact: New Spain had more than 60 viceroys in almost three centuries.

questions.question: “Más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando.” In this saying, what does the bird in the hand stand for?
hints: The hundred flying ones could fly off at any moment.
It's advice not to be greedy or take too many risks.
Whatever you hold in your hand is already yours and can't get away.
questions.description: Grandma's advice, feathers and all.
questions.fun_fact: The English version is much more modest: a bird in the hand is worth just “two in the bush”, not a hundred flying.

questions.question: I was a Mexican comedian with a tiny mustache and droopy pants who talked a lot without saying anything. The Royal Spanish Academy accepted a verb made from my name. Who am I?
hints: I was a star of the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.
I acted in the Hollywood film “Around the World in 80 Days.”
My real name was Mario Moreno.
questions.description: Back in the old movie theaters, the laughter could be heard all the way to the candy counter.
questions.fun_fact: For his role in “Around the World in 80 Days” (1956), he won a Golden Globe in Hollywood.

questions.question: I go from mouth to mouth and nobody knows if I'm true, but the saying goes that if I make that much noise, I carry some truth. What am I?
hints: People whisper me at the little corner store.
I love going from neighbor to neighbor.
I almost always start with “Did you hear what happened?”
questions.description: It runs through the whole neighborhood but never gets anyone wet.
questions.fun_fact: The usual saying is “Cuando el río suena, agua lleva” (when the river makes noise, it carries water), and another version says “piedras trae” (it carries stones).

questions.question: Someone played a joke on me, I turned red as a jitomate and slammed the door. According to the saying, who am I?
hints: In Mexico, everyone knows the saying about me.
I'd have been better off laughing at the joke.
The saying says getting angry won't let you win.
questions.description: A rule of the game that nobody wrote down, but everybody follows.
questions.fun_fact: Laughing at a joke instead of getting mad usually takes all the fun out of it for the joker.

questions.question: This notebook has little squares, the school supply list asks for small or large squares, and you line up digits in it to add. Which subject is it for?
hints: It's the subject where you use your ruler and pencil a lot.
There you do subtraction, multiplication and division.
It's the subject of numbers.
questions.description: A page with more little squares than an endless game of tic-tac-toe.
questions.fun_fact: The little squares help keep ones, tens and hundreds in neat columns so they don't get mixed up when you do sums.

questions.question: In Mexico, when do you go to kínder?
hints: You go when you're very little.
There you learn colors and songs, and how to cut paper.
It's the first school you ever go to.
questions.description: The place where you learned that modeling clay is not a snack.
questions.fun_fact: The word kínder comes from the German Kindergarten, which means “garden of children”, just like the Mexican name jardín de niños.

questions.question: It's thick, stiff paper that comes in colored sheets, and the teacher asks for it to make presentation posters. What is it called?
hints: It's thicker than a normal sheet but thinner than cardboard.
It stays standing if you lean it against the board.
Its name sounds like a tiny “cartón”.
questions.description: The hero of every school presentation made the night before.
questions.fun_fact: The word cartulina comes from the Italian “cartolina”, which in Italy today means postcard.

questions.question: Complete it: CONALEP is the Colegio Nacional de Educación…
hints: It is a high-school-level school.
It was founded in the late 1970s.
The P and the T at the end are your clue.
questions.description: A super long name that fits neatly into seven letters.
questions.fun_fact: CONALEP was created in 1978 to train the technicians that Mexican industry needed.

previous.feedback: source: hint 3 is false in the source and in the translation. The acronym CONALEP ends in E-P (Educación Profesional) and has no T, so "the P and the T at the end of the acronym" doesn't match the letters and misleads players. The source needs a corrected hint 3, for example "The acronym stops at the P of Profesional; the full name adds one more word." The translation should then follow it. Fact check: wrong. The answer (Profesional Técnica) and the 1978 founding date are right, and the wrong answers are wrong. But hint 3 is false. The acronym CONALEP ends in E-P (Educación Profesional). It has no T, so 'Técnica' isn't represented in it. The 'P and T at the end' clue doesn't match the letters. I checked this from my own knowledge of the name, not with a search.

source: Hint 3 is false in the source and in the translation. CONALEP stands for COlegio NAcionaL de Educación Profesional, so the acronym ends in P and has no T. The source hint needs fixing first, e.g. "The P at the end of the acronym is the clue." or "The last word describes the kind of skills taught." Then the English hint should follow it. Fact check: wrong. Hint 3 is false: the acronym CONALEP has no T. It stands for Colegio Nacional de Educación Profesional (only P). The 'T' for Técnica is not in the acronym.

questions.question: In Mexico, when you finish sixth grade of primaria, which school do you move on to?
hints: It's the school that comes right after.
You're there from about age 12 to 15.
Its name sounds like “second”.
questions.description: Six years of times tables and then… time to grow up!
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, secundaria lasts three years and has been compulsory since 1993.

questions.question: I have pointy ears, I'm half human and half Vulcan, and I greet people with my fingers split in a V, saying “Live long and prosper.” Who am I?
hints: I travel through space on a ship called the Enterprise.
I'm famous for being very logical and almost never showing emotions.
My show is “Star Trek” and my name has five letters.
questions.description: A hand greeting so tricky that some people practice it in front of the mirror.
questions.fun_fact: Actor Leonard Nimoy based the Vulcan salute on a blessing gesture he saw in a synagogue as a boy.

questions.question: You put Resistol on your card and sprinkle this on top: it sparkles, and the leftovers keep showing up on the floor for weeks. What is it?
hints: It comes in little colored jars.
It's tiny bits that shine like crazy.
In Mexico it's called diamantina.
questions.description: You use it for five minutes and find it in your hair five weeks later.
questions.fun_fact: Regular glitter is made of plastic, which is why biodegradable glitter made from cellulose now exists.

questions.question: For decades, Liconsa has sold one product at a low price to millions of Mexican families. Which one?
hints: It's sold in its own little shops, in bags.
Registered families get a card to buy their weekly share.
Its outlets are called lecherías.
questions.description: The earliest lines in the colonia, bag and card in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Liconsa milk is fortified with iron, zinc and vitamins to fight anemia in children.

questions.question: You can get it at 18, it has your photo and your CURP, and in Mexico it's used as ID for everything. What was the INE card created for?
hints: You have to renew it about every ten years.
It used to be issued by the IFE.
It gets marked when you go to the casilla.
questions.description: The photo where we all look like we just woke up.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico started issuing the voter card with a photo in 1992.

questions.question: In Mexico, you've finished secundaria and want to go to university. Which school do you still need?
hints: It usually lasts two or three years.
When you finish it, you take the university entrance exam.
Its name says it gets you ready for university.
questions.description: The school where you decide what you want to be when you grow up… or at least you try.
questions.fun_fact: UNAM's Escuela Nacional Preparatoria was founded in 1867 in the old Colegio de San Ildefonso.

questions.question: In a Mexican home, “se acabó el cilindro”: the stove won't light, the shower runs cold, and you have to order a full one. What ran out?
hints: The cylinder is made of metal and sits on the azotea or in the patio.
The water heater uses it too.
It's sold from a truck that drives down the street announcing itself.
questions.description: A household tragedy right in the middle of your shower.
questions.fun_fact: LP gas has no smell of its own: a strong odor is added on purpose so you notice if there's a leak.

questions.question: You're on the street and hear someone shout “¡Ey, flaco!”. Literally, what kind of person are they calling?
hints: It's about the body, not the personality.
Clothes almost always look loose on this person.
It's someone with hardly any belly.
questions.description: A nickname people give you without asking, and sometimes it doesn't even fit.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, many people call their partner “flaca” or “flaco” as a pet name, even if they aren't thin at all.

questions.question: If a Mexican teen says “me vale”, what do they mean?
hints: It has nothing to do with money or prices.
People often shrug while saying it.
It's what you answer when something means nothing at all to you.
questions.description: Two words parents hate to hear when they ask about homework.
questions.fun_fact: “Me vale” gave Mexico the word “valemadrismo”, for an attitude where nothing matters to you.

questions.question: “¡Chispas!” is short, even grandparents say it, and you hear it a lot in Spanish-dubbed cartoons. What is it used for?
wrong_answers: To greet someone from far away
To ask someone for a match
hints: It's a word that slips out without thinking.
For example, when your ice cream falls on the floor.
It takes the place of a word you shouldn't say in front of kids.
questions.description: Cartoons have their own dictionary of shouts, and this word is on almost every page.
questions.fun_fact: Many mild exclamations like “¡chispas!” or “¡rayos!” were born so people wouldn't use bad words in front of the family.

questions.question: In Mexico, a pop quiz, being scolded unfairly or getting stood up are all “gachas”. What does “gacho” mean?
hints: None of those things puts you in a good mood.
The opposite would be “padre” or “chido”.
It's something that rubs you the wrong way or looks awful.
questions.description: In Mexico, one little word can sum up your whole day.
questions.fun_fact: To say something is really bad, Mexicans pile it on with “gachísimo”.

questions.question: You hear “¿Qué rollo?” a lot among young people in Mexico, sometimes with a fist bump. What does it mean?
hints: You say it at the start of a chat.
It's a close cousin of “¿Qué onda?”.
You answer it with something like “good, and you?”.
questions.description: Mexican teens have their own language, and this phrase is one of the first you learn.
questions.fun_fact: If someone in Mexico tells you something “es un rollo”, they mean it's long, complicated or boring.

questions.question: You ask where the store is and hear “está cerquita” (it's really close). Which of these does NOT mean the same?
hints: Three of them tell you that you won't walk much.
One would make you grab a bottle of water and your sneakers.
It's the one that talks about a long distance.
questions.description: In Mexico, distances are measured in “cerquitas”, and nobody knows how long one is.
questions.fun_fact: Mexicans love the diminutive so much that they even say “cerquitita” for something even closer.

questions.question: The party is canceled, the cake is gone, it rains on your day off: in Mexico, all of that deserves a “¡chale!”. What does it express?
hints: It doesn't put you in a good mood.
You say it when something didn't turn out the way you hoped.
It's like saying “¡qué mala onda!”.
questions.description: A five-letter word that fits into every one of your Mondays.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Chale!” is also used to show disbelief, like when someone tells you something hard to believe.

questions.question: You say “¡fuchi!” when you smell a dirty sock, see food you don't like or step in something sticky. What does it express?
hints: It's not a nice feeling.
It makes you want to hold your nose.
It's what you feel about something really gross.
questions.description: The official word kids use when they see a plate of vegetables.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, people also say “guácala” about something gross.

questions.question: Which city's soccer team has the nickname “los Xolos”?
hints: It's a city on the border with the United States.
It's in the state of Baja California.
It's very close to San Diego.
questions.description: A hairless dog that became the most soccer-crazy mascot in the country.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname comes from the xoloitzcuintle, a hairless dog already bred by the ancient peoples of Mexico.

questions.question: I'm not from this town, and it shows as soon as I ask for directions. In Mexico, what do people call me?
hints: It's a very common word in Mexican towns for newcomers.
It's the opposite of someone who is from the place.
It starts like “fuera,” the Spanish word for “outside.”
questions.description: He arrived in town, asked for directions, and two minutes later everyone knew his life story.
questions.fun_fact: “Fuereño” is heard mostly in Mexico and Central America, while “forastero” is understood everywhere Spanish is spoken.

questions.question: At Teotihuacan, night is to the Pyramid of the Moon as day is to the Pyramid of the…
hints: Think about what's in the sky during the day.
It gives us light and warmth.
It rises in the morning and sets in the evening.
questions.description: Two neighboring pyramids: one works the day shift, the other the night shift.
questions.fun_fact: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest pyramids in the Americas.

questions.question: Which of these traditions is NOT from Veracruz?
hints: The odd one out is a big festival from a neighboring state.
It's held in July on a hill.
It's the most famous festival in Oaxaca.
questions.description: Three traditions come from the same state, and one crashed the party.
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO added the Papantla Flyers to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.

questions.question: It's from Mexico City, wears yellow and blue and plays the Clásico Joven against Cruz Azul. Which bird is Club América's nickname?
hints: It's a very large bird of prey.
It flies high and has very sharp eyesight.
It's the bird on the flag of Mexico.
questions.description: A team that flies high… or so its fans say.
questions.fun_fact: Club América, founded in 1916, is one of the most successful teams in Mexico.

questions.question: You're at a Chivas game and you hear these nicknames. Which one is NOT a Chivas nickname?
hints: It belongs to another team, from the capital.
It comes from a company that made building materials.
It's Cruz Azul's nickname.
questions.description: Everyone in the stands is shouting, but not everyone is shouting the right thing.
questions.fun_fact: Chivas are famous for playing only Mexican players.

questions.question: I delivered pizza in New York, got frozen on New Year's Eve 1999 and woke up a thousand years later, in the year 3000. Who am I?
hints: My show was made by the same creator as “The Simpsons.”
Now I work for a space delivery company.
My best friend is a robot, and my full name starts with Philip J.
questions.description: The longest nap in history: a thousand years, and the pizza didn't even get cold.
questions.fun_fact: In a time-travel episode of “Futurama,” Fry ends up becoming his own grandfather.

questions.question: This state's baseball team is called the Pericos. Which state is it?
hints: It's in central Mexico, near the capital.
The Popocatépetl volcano sits on its border.
It's famous for mole and chiles en nogada.
questions.description: A team named after a bird that never stops chatting.
questions.fun_fact: The Pericos de Puebla play in the Mexican Baseball League.

questions.question: Which of these telenovelas did Aracely Arámbula NOT star in?
hints: In one of them, her leading man was Eduardo Yáñez.
The odd one out stars another very famous actress.
The odd one out starred Bárbara Mori, and its title is the Spanish name of a gemstone.
questions.description: Get the popcorn and the tissues ready: today we suffer in style.
questions.fun_fact: “Corazón salvaje” had already been made several times in Mexico before Aracely Arámbula's 2009 version.

questions.question: You see a meme online of a woman screaming “¡Maldita lisiada!”. Which telenovela villain is it from?
hints: She was played by Itatí Cantoral in 1995.
She appears in “María la del Barrio”, starring Thalía.
Her surname means “black mountain” in Spanish.
questions.description: Some villains give you nightmares, and some give you memes for life.
questions.fun_fact: Years after “María la del Barrio” premiered in 1995, Soraya Montenegro's scenes became famous memes all over Latin America.

questions.question: In which decade did “La fiera,” the telenovela with Victoria Ruffo and Guillermo Capetillo, premiere in Mexico?
hints: Victoria Ruffo was born in 1962 and was a young lead here.
It came before “Simplemente María” (1989), also with Victoria Ruffo.
It's from the same decade as “Cuna de lobos.”
questions.description: One of those telenovelas your grandma watched with the volume all the way up.
questions.fun_fact: “La fiera” (1983) was produced by Valentín Pimstein, one of Televisa's great telenovela producers.

questions.question: In a 2010 telenovela, Angelique Boyer plays a poor, ambitious young woman who studies law to get out of her vecindad. What is her character's name?
hints: The character's name is also the title of the telenovela.
Sebastián Rulli was one of her leading men.
She shares her name with a famous nun from Calcutta.
questions.description: She had a plan, and the plan did not include staying in the vecindad.
questions.fun_fact: The first version of “Teresa” was made in 1959, starring Maricruz Olivier.

questions.question: Maximilian had it built so Carlota could ride from Chapultepec Castle to downtown, and it was first called Paseo de la Emperatriz. What avenue is it today?
hints: Today it is lined with skyscrapers and traffic circles.
Many of Mexico City's parades and marathons go along it.
The Angel of Independence stands on it.
questions.description: An emperor who skipped the flowers and gave his wife an entire avenue instead.
questions.fun_fact: Maximilian is said to have been inspired by Europe's grand boulevards, such as the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

questions.question: I sell lottery tickets on the street, my name is made of two women's names, and my telenovela aired in 1992. Who am I?
hints: My telenovela is named after me.
Thalía played me.
My second name is also a German car brand.
questions.description: A lottery ticket can change your life, especially if you're the one selling it.
questions.fun_fact: María Mercedes's leading man was Arturo Peniche, as Jorge Luis del Olmo.

questions.question: The telenovela “Ramona” (2000) is set in California just after it stopped being part of Mexico. Which actress starred in it?
hints: Her leading man was Eduardo Palomo.
Years later, she starred in a huge hit series about a woman in drug trafficking, filmed partly in Spain and Morocco.
Her last name means “castle” in Spanish.
questions.description: Love, ranches and a border that moved.
questions.fun_fact: “Ramona” is based on a novel by the American writer Helen Hunt Jackson, published in 1884.
