questions.question: In “La usurpadora,” Paulina falls in love with Carlos Daniel Bracho. Which actor played him?
hints: He was one of Televisa's most famous leading men in the ’90s and 2000s.
He also starred in “Abrázame muy fuerte” (2000).
His last name starts with “Col…”.
questions.description: The only man who didn't notice his wife had suddenly turned nice.
questions.fun_fact: Memes of Paola Bracho, the evil twin, are still going around social media more than 25 years later.

questions.question: The dancers in the Zócalo dance to a drum, with seed rattles on their ankles, and first they light copal. What is copal?
questions.answer: A tree resin burned as incense
wrong_answers: A cacao seed roasted over a fire
A charcoal made from dried corncobs
A volcanic stone that glows when heated
hints: Peoples before the Spanish conquest already used it in their ceremonies.
It's also used on Day of the Dead altars.
It comes from a tree's bark, like a sap that hardens.
questions.description: Before the first drumbeat, even the dancers need their warm-up ritual.
questions.fun_fact: The name copal comes from the Nahuatl word “copalli”, and the Aztecs were already burning it in their temples more than 500 years ago.

questions.question: I'm a lab mouse with a huge head, every night I plan to take over the world, and my buddy keeps shouting “Narf!”. Who am I?
hints: I live in a cage at Acme Labs.
I'm very serious and very smart; my buddy is the total opposite.
My name is the organ you think with.
questions.description: One evil plan a day, every day, for years: now that's dedication.
questions.fun_fact: “Pinky and the Brain” started as a segment of the show “Animaniacs” before getting its own series.

questions.question: At a quinceañera, these are the boys who dance the waltz with the birthday girl, rehearse for weeks and wear matching outfits. What are they called?
hints: They are often the birthday girl's cousins, friends or classmates.
Often the main one is her boyfriend or her best friend.
Their name comes from a post at European royal courts: the man who attended the king.
questions.description: The only boys who rehearse more than the school marching band.
questions.fun_fact: Chambelán dance routines got so elaborate that some choreographers now do nothing but stage quinceañera dances.

questions.question: You're at a party and the sonidero announces a set of cumbias. Which of these songs is NOT a cumbia?
hints: You dance three of them with a partner, doing little spins.
Two are by Los Ángeles Azules and one is by Selena.
The odd one out has a famous “Ay, ay, ay, ay, canta y no llores”.
questions.description: The ultimate test of who's the life of the party and who stays in their seat.
questions.fun_fact: “Cielito lindo” was written by Quirino Mendoza y Cortés around 1882, and it is one of the most sung Mexican songs in the world.

questions.question: The city where the Guelaguetza is held officially carries the surname of a Mexican president. Which one?
hints: He was president in the 19th century.
He led the government during the French intervention and stood up to Emperor Maximilian.
He's famous for the line “Respect for the rights of others is peace.”
questions.description: A city with a first name and a last name, like a kid on the class roll call.
questions.fun_fact: During the French intervention, Juárez carried the government across the country in a horse-drawn carriage, and today even a border city bears his name.

questions.question: Which Cuban musician, nicknamed “the King of Mambo”, made the rhythm famous from Mexico City with “Qué rico el mambo” and “Mambo No. 5”?
hints: He was a pianist and bandleader.
He let out a shout like “Ugh!” in the middle of his songs.
His double surname ends with the Spanish word for “meadow”.
questions.description: A king with no crown, but plenty of trumpets.
questions.fun_fact: Pérez Prado lived much of his life in Mexico and died in Mexico City in 1989.

questions.question: They have a pointed toe, a tall shaft and a high heel, and people stomp out norteña polka in them. Why was the cowboy boot heel invented?
questions.answer: To keep the foot from slipping out of the stirrup
wrong_answers: To make the zapateado sound louder
To keep from sinking in the ranch mud
To make the cowboy look taller
hints: Think about what cowboys did all day.
It has to do with riding a horse.
The stirrup is the loop on the saddle where you rest your foot.
questions.description: Footwear nobody takes off, not even to dance polka all night long.
questions.fun_fact: The pointed toe of the boots also helps slip the foot quickly into the stirrup.

questions.question: The song “La Llorona” is a traditional son from the region where this dress is worn. Which region is it?
hints: There, Mexico's land narrows between two oceans.
Frida Kahlo often wore this dress.
The women from there are called tehuanas.
questions.description: A song so sad that even the onions feel like they have company.
questions.fun_fact: “La Llorona” has dozens of versions and every singer adds verses of their own; Chavela Vargas recorded one of the most famous.

questions.question: In Guerrero, a dancer in a jaguar mask is chased by hunters who want to catch him. What is this dance called?
hints: Nahua communities dance it, in Morelos and Puebla too.
Its name comes from a Nahuatl word for “wild beast”.
That Nahuatl word is “tecuani”.
questions.description: A little mountain kitty nobody wants to run into in the cornfield.
questions.fun_fact: In Nahuatl, “tecuani” means something like “the one who eats people”, the perfect nickname for a jaguar.

questions.question: In 1970s and 1980s Mexico City, many people rode to work in a “combi”. It was a Volkswagen and ran a fixed route. What was it?
hints: It fit more people than a regular car.
It was one of the first kinds of pesero.
Later it was replaced by microbuses, which are bigger.
questions.description: In old Mexico City, getting to work on time meant squeezing in tight and not missing your stop.
questions.fun_fact: Peseros started out as shared taxis that charged one peso per person, and that's where their name comes from.

questions.question: About what year did Uber arrive in Mexico City?
hints: To use it, you need a cell phone with internet.
Smartphones were around, but the pandemic hadn't happened yet.
It was in the early 2010s.
questions.description: You used to hail a taxi with your arm; now you do it with your thumb.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City was the first city in Latin America to get Uber, and over the years it became one of the cities that use it most in the world.

questions.question: For decades, it was a little slip of paper you bought at the ticket booth and fed into the turnstile to enter the Mexico City Metro. What was it?
hints: It used to cost very little, just a few coins.
You bought it before going down to the trains.
You also need one to get into the movies or a big game.
questions.description: A tiny slip of paper that opens the door to the whole city.
questions.fun_fact: Metro tickets have come in hundreds of special designs, and some people collect them.

questions.question: I'm a secret agent in a hat, living with two inventor stepbrothers who don't know my double life. My kind lives wild in only one country. Which?
hints: I'm Perry, from “Phineas and Ferb.”
My kind has a duck's bill and lays eggs, even though it's a mammal.
It's the land of kangaroos and koalas.
questions.description: Lazy pet by day, secret agent in a hat by night: every cat's dream.
questions.fun_fact: The platypus is one of the very few mammals in the world that lay eggs.

questions.question: You're on the pesero (minibus) and you've reached your corner. Which of these will NOT get the driver to stop?
hints: The driver has to know you want to get off.
Three of the options are ways to tell the driver.
One of the options just makes more noise.
questions.description: Getting off a pesero is an art you learn as a little kid.
questions.fun_fact: Many peseros have no stop button, so the famous “¡Bajan!” is the most used bell in the city.

questions.question: I don't drive around looking for riders: I wait at my base and you call me on the phone. What kind of taxi am I?
hints: Many people say I'm safer than the one you hail on the street.
I have a fixed spot where I park with other taxis.
My name comes from the Spanish word for the “place” where I wait.
questions.description: Taxi drivers know every shortcut in the city, even the ones that aren't on any map.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, a taxi you hail on the street is called a «taxi libre», after the “libre” (free) sign it shows when it has no passenger.

questions.question: In which decade did the second deck of the Periférico open in Mexico City?
hints: It's a fairly recent project.
It was built when Andrés Manuel López Obrador was head of government of the D.F.
It was at the start of the 21st century.
questions.description: When the traffic no longer fit on the street, they built it an upstairs.
questions.fun_fact: The second deck runs right over the original Periférico, so some cars drive on top and others below, along the same route.

questions.question: Indios Verdes station, at the end of Metro Line 3, is named after something that stood nearby. What was it?
questions.answer: Two bronze statues that turned green
wrong_answers: A people who painted their faces green
A soccer team with green uniforms
hints: They show two Mexica rulers.
They have stood outdoors for more than a century.
Over time the metal oxidized and changed color.
questions.description: A station with a name straight out of an adventure movie.
questions.fun_fact: The statues show the tlatoanis Itzcóatl and Ahuízotl and were made in the 19th century for Paseo de la Reforma.

questions.question: You pay me to the driver when you get on the pesero. Going farther, I sometimes cost a bit more, and you get change if you need it. What am I?
hints: Without me, you don't ride.
You pay me every time you get on.
It's what the ride costs each passenger.
questions.description: You count it out in coins and lose it in a second.
questions.fun_fact: The word “pesero” comes from the days when the fare cost one peso.

questions.question: I'm an actress and singer, and in 1991 I hosted the music and variety show “La movida” on Televisa. Who am I?
hints: Before that, I hosted another late-night show: “Mala noche... ¡no!”.
I starred in the telenovela “Los ricos también lloran”.
My son Cristian is also a very famous singer.
questions.description: Before streaming series, the nights of the nineties already had their own queen with a microphone.
questions.fun_fact: “Los ricos también lloran”, starring Verónica Castro, was a huge hit even in Russia.

questions.question: La Chilindrina from “El Chavo del 8” is Don Ramón's daughter, has freckles and wears two pigtails. What does she always wear on her face?
hints: It's as much a part of her look as her pigtails.
It's not a costume: she wears it in every episode.
It rests on the nose and the ears.
questions.description: ¡Fíjate, fíjate, fíjate! This question comes from the most famous vecindad on TV.
questions.fun_fact: María Antonieta de las Nieves played La Chilindrina for decades, even as an adult.

questions.question: Who won the first season of “La Casa de los Famosos México” in 2023?
hints: This contestant was already famous on the internet before entering the house.
This contestant's videos went viral on social media.
She's from León, Guanajuato, and shares a last name with Che.
questions.description: Living locked up with cameras everywhere: every nosy mom's dream.
questions.fun_fact: Wendy Guevara became famous for the videos she filmed with her friends “Las Perdidas.”

previous.feedback: Hint 2 says "Her videos", but the source's "Sus videos" doesn't mark gender. Wendy Guevara is the only woman among the options, so the pronoun gives the answer away before hint 3. Make hint 2 gender-neutral, e.g. "This contestant's videos went viral on social media."

questions.question: Azteca Uno is to TV Azteca as Las Estrellas is to…
hints: It's the biggest TV company in Mexico.
Its historic headquarters is in Chapultepec, in Mexico City.
It's the company that aired “El Chavo del 8”.
questions.description: A channel so bright it had to name itself after the night sky.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2016 the channel was called “El Canal de las Estrellas”.

questions.question: My sketch show “XHDRBZ” looked like a TV station's call letters, but it hid my last name. Who am I?
hints: It had characters like Armando Hoyos and el Lonje Moco.
Later I made “La familia P. Luche”.
My last name sounds just like the last letters: D-R-B-Z.
questions.description: A show with a name that looks like a wifi password.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican TV stations have call letters starting with XE or XH, which is why the name looked like a channel.

questions.question: I'm a dog who can stretch, grow huge or tiny, and I go on adventures in the Land of Ooo with my human brother Finn. Who am I?
hints: I'm on a Cartoon Network show.
My friend Finn wears a white hat with little ears.
I'm yellow and my show is “Adventure Time”.
questions.description: The perfect dog: stretches like chewing gum and never needs a walk.
questions.fun_fact: “Adventure Time” started as a short cartoon in 2007, years before it became a series.

questions.question: What is the TV game show where two families try to guess the most popular answers from a survey?
hints: The answers are hidden on a board.
Marco Antonio Regil hosted it for years.
Its name starts with a number.
questions.description: The only game show where answering “mother-in-law” can earn you points.
questions.fun_fact: The show is the Mexican version of “Family Feud,” which started in the United States in 1976.

questions.question: Which Mexican poet wrote “En paz” (“At Peace”), the poem that ends: “Life, you owe me nothing! Life, we are at peace!”?
hints: He was a modernist poet born in Tepic, Nayarit.
He was also a diplomat and died in Montevideo, Uruguay, in 1919.
His last name sounds like the English word “nerve.”
questions.description: A poem for settling accounts with life without asking for a single peso in change.
questions.fun_fact: When Amado Nervo died in Uruguay, a ship carried his body back to Mexico, and every port where it stopped held a tribute to him.

questions.question: Juan Rulfo is to “Pedro Páramo” as Rosario Castellanos is to…
hints: It's a 1957 novel partly told by a little girl.
It takes place in Comitán, Chiapas, among rich families and Indigenous villages.
Its title is the Maya name for Comitán: “nine stars”.
questions.description: A matching game for anyone who has already read the whole middle-school bookshelf.
questions.fun_fact: Rosario Castellanos was also Mexico's ambassador to Israel, where she spent the last years of her life.

questions.question: Which Valeria Luiselli novel follows a family driving from New York to Arizona while migrants try to cross the border?
hints: It came out in 2019, and she wrote it in English rather than Spanish.
The parents record sounds for a living and pack their things in boxes.
In Spanish it is called “Desierto sonoro.”
questions.description: A road trip so long that even the kids stopped asking “Are we there yet?”
questions.fun_fact: Valeria Luiselli worked as an interpreter for migrant children in a New York immigration court, and that experience became her book “Tell Me How It Ends.”

questions.question: Juan, 13, spends a summer with his uncle Tito in a house full of books that move on their own, hunting one that runs from everyone. What novel is it?
hints: It's very common in Mexican middle-school libraries.
It's a 2008 novel by a Mexican writer also famous for his writing about soccer.
The book Juan is looking for is as untamable as an animal from the hills.
questions.description: A library where the books change places faster than your socks do.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Villoro is also famous for his soccer chronicles and is a big fan of the Necaxa club.

questions.question: I was born in Jerez, Zacatecas, in 1888. They call me the poet of the provinces, and in 1921 I wrote a poem to a “flawless and diamond-like” homeland. Who am I?
hints: I died very young, at 33, in 1921.
My most famous poem is recited in schools on national holidays.
That poem is called “La suave Patria”.
questions.description: A poet who wrote to Mexico more tenderly than a grandma writes to her grandchild.
questions.fun_fact: In “La suave Patria”, López Velarde says the Christ Child gave Mexico a stable, and the devil gave it the oil fields.

questions.question: In Carlos Fuentes’s “The Old Gringo,” an elderly American writer crosses into Mexico. In what period is the novel set?
hints: Hollywood made it into a film in 1989 with Gregory Peck and Jane Fonda.
The gringo joins the troops of a general in the north of the country.
Those troops follow Pancho Villa.
questions.description: A man from the United States who comes to Mexico looking for adventure, not tacos.
questions.fun_fact: The gringo is based on Ambrose Bierce, a real writer who disappeared in Mexico around 1914 and was never heard from again.

questions.question: I'm an idler and a drunk from Santa Clara del Cobre, Michoacán, telling my woes from a bell tower. José Rubén Romero put me in a 1938 novel. Who am I?
hints: My story is a Mexican picaresque novel.
On screen I was played by Manuel Medel and, later, by Ignacio López Tarso.
My novel calls my life “useless.”
questions.description: The friendliest guy in town, as long as you're picking up the check.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Clara del Cobre is famous for its artisans who hammer copper by hand, and the town has a statue of Pito Pérez.

questions.question: I was born in Mixcoac in 1914, wrote “The Labyrinth of Solitude” and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990. Who am I?
hints: I was a poet, an essayist and a diplomat in India.
I founded the magazines “Plural” and “Vuelta.”
My last name is the Spanish word for “peace.”
questions.description: A prize so important they hand it out in Sweden and celebrate it all the way to Mixcoac.
questions.fun_fact: Octavio Paz is, so far, the only Mexican to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the brain of the computer, I do billions of calculations per second and I live on a tiny chip. What am I made of inside?
hints: My parts are tiny switches that turn on and off.
Each of my parts lets electric current through or stops it: that's how I count in ones and zeros.
Before chips, these parts came one by one, and they gave their name to your grandparents' portable radios.
questions.description: It thinks faster than you, but it still has no idea where you left your keys.
questions.fun_fact: The transistors in a modern processor are so small that they're tinier than most viruses.

questions.question: The tech region in California where companies like Apple and Google were born has a nickname. Which material is it named after?
hints: It's an element on the periodic table, not something you buy at a hardware store.
It sits right below carbon on the periodic table.
Computer chips are made from it.
questions.description: A valley where, instead of cows grazing, you find engineers drinking coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust, after oxygen: it's in almost all sand.

questions.question: Riddle: I read the tiny lines on your finger to unlock your phone. If only one identical twin registers a finger, what happens when the other twin tries?
hints: Identical twins share their genes, but not everything is genetic.
The lines on our fingers form before we're born, shaped by our movements inside mom's belly.
Not even identical twins have the same fingerprints.
questions.description: Your finger is your password, so don't lend it to anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that they are hard to tell apart.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a space probe. I left Earth in 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and now travel beyond the planets. What do I carry in case aliens find me?
questions.answer: A record of sounds and music from Earth
wrong_answers: A flag from every country in the world
Seeds from plants that grow on Earth
A letter written by children of the world
hints: A team led by the astronomer Carl Sagan put it together.
It comes with drawn instructions showing how to use it.
It's golden and shaped like your grandparents' old vinyl LPs.
questions.description: The slowest letter in the universe, sent with no address and no stamp.
questions.fun_fact: The Voyager Golden Record carries greetings in 55 languages and even the song of a humpback whale.

questions.question: What do the trains run on along most lines of the Mexico City Metro?
hints: It isn't future technology: it has been in use for more than seventy years.
The idea came from the Paris Metro, which wanted quieter trains.
It's the same thing a mechanic pumps up when a car gets a flat.
questions.description: A metro that rolls with more style than you walk.
questions.fun_fact: The little pictures for each Mexico City Metro station were made so that anyone could find their way, even people who couldn't read.

questions.question: In Madrid, you board a train called the AVE, short for “Alta Velocidad Española” (Spanish High Speed). About how fast can it carry passengers at most?
hints: It goes much faster than a car on the highway.
But not as fast as a plane in mid-flight.
It's about the top speed of a Formula 1 car.
questions.description: In Spanish its name means “bird,” and it doesn't just flap around.
questions.fun_fact: The first AVE line, between Madrid and Seville, opened in 1992, the year Seville hosted the World's Fair.

questions.question: At the movie theater, the stadium and the train station, you line up at a window to pay before you go in or travel. What is that window called?
hints: You usually find it near the entrance.
It's often a window with glass and a little gap to pass the money through.
Its name says exactly what you buy there.
questions.description: The place where the line is always longest just when you're in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: At movie theaters and stadiums, the ticket office is often called the box office, which is why a very successful movie is called a “box-office hit”.

questions.question: It's 6 p.m., everyone is leaving work, and the subway is so packed you can't move. What is this time of day called?
hints: It's when the most people travel at the same time.
It's the opposite of off-peak, when trains are almost empty.
The first word of its name also means “to hurry”.
questions.description: The time of day when the subway turns into a can of sardines.
questions.fun_fact: In Tokyo, station staff sometimes help squeeze passengers into packed trains during the morning rush.

questions.question: This is the Big Boy, one of the largest steam locomotives ever built. What was it made for?
hints: A US company built it in the 1940s.
Its huge pulling power mattered more than speed.
It had to pull very heavy trains up the mountains of the western United States.
questions.description: If this were a toy train, you'd need a living room the size of a stadium.
questions.fun_fact: Only 25 Big Boys were ever built, and one of them, No. 4014, ran again in 2019.

questions.question: In the Harry Potter books and films, what do wizards use Platform 9¾ at King's Cross station for?
questions.answer: To catch the train to Hogwarts
wrong_answers: To reach the Ministry of Magic
hints: It's part of the world of Harry Potter.
Students use it at the start of every school year.
A red train leaves from there for a school of magic.
questions.description: A platform where running straight into a wall is part of the plan.
questions.fun_fact: J. K. Rowling has said her parents met on a train leaving King's Cross station.

questions.question: Which luxury train ran from Paris to Istanbul and is the setting of an Agatha Christie novel with Hercule Poirot?
hints: Its route went from Western Europe toward the east.
Istanbul sits at the gateway to Asia.
Its name means “the express to the East”.
questions.description: A luxury train where nobody gets off until a detective has asked them a few questions.
questions.fun_fact: The Orient Express made its first trip in 1883.

questions.question: A paper clip floating on water, an insect walking on a puddle, food coloring fleeing from soap in milk: what do they have in common?
hints: It all happens on the surface of a liquid.
It's as if the water had a very thin “skin”.
Soap “breaks” the tension of that skin on the liquid.
questions.description: An experiment where milk sets off fireworks without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: With whole milk the effect is even more spectacular, because the soap also starts “chasing” the fat in the milk.

questions.question: I'm a famous character. So I never forget a detail, I keep each fact in a room of my “mind palace” and walk through it in my imagination to find it. Who am I?
hints: I'm a detective.
I live in London, and a doctor friend writes down my adventures.
My address is 221B Baker Street.
questions.description: For anyone who can never remember where they left their keys: someone keeps a whole building inside their head.
questions.fun_fact: The mind palace is the ancient “method of loci”, which legend says the Greek poet Simonides invented about 2,500 years ago.

questions.question: The finger trick for the 9 times table gives 27, 63 and 72. What do these results have in common?
hints: Look at each number on its own, one digit at a time.
Try adding: 2 + 7, 6 + 3, 7 + 2.
It always gives you the same number as the times table you're practicing.
questions.description: Ten fingers, one times table and zero calculators: the oldest technology at school.
questions.fun_fact: The trick works because 9 is 10 minus 1: each time you add 9, the tens go up by one and the ones go down by one.

questions.question: With toothpaste and a cloth, you can make something shiny again after it turns black over time. What is it?
hints: It's something that used to be very shiny.
It gets darker because it reacts with the air.
It's a precious metal, cheaper than gold.
questions.description: A bathroom product with a secret second job in the dining room.
questions.fun_fact: Silver turns black because it reacts with sulfur in the air and forms a layer of silver sulfide.

questions.question: I paint puzzling pictures full of uniforms in Leipzig, made windows for Naumburg Cathedral and stage sets for “Lohengrin” in Bayreuth. Who am I?
hints: I am seen as the leading figure of the “New Leipzig School.”
I was born in Leipzig in 1960.
My first name is the Greek word for “new.”
questions.description: A painter whose pictures look like dreams you can't explain at breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: He designed the sets for the 2018 Bayreuth “Lohengrin” together with his wife, the painter Rosa Loy.

questions.question: On Bremen’s Böttcherstraße you visit the world’s first museum dedicated to a woman painter. Which painter?
hints: She lived and painted in the artists’ colony of Worpswede.
The museum opened in 1927.
She died in 1907 at only 31; her very simplified pictures of farm women and children count as early Expressionism.
questions.description: A whole building for just one woman, and it still isn’t her apartment.
questions.fun_fact: She is thought to be the first woman painter to paint herself nude, in a self-portrait from 1906.

questions.question: You are writing a school report on the painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner. Which term does NOT belong in it?
hints: In 1905 Kirchner founded an artists' group in Dresden.
The group you want was centered in Munich.
Its name is made of a color and a person on an animal.
questions.description: A school report where you need to grab the scissors just once.
questions.fun_fact: Kirchner later backdated some of his paintings on purpose, so he would be seen as a pioneer of Expressionism.

questions.question: Schwerin Castle got its present look in the 19th century. What defines the style of this rebuilding?
hints: The rebuilding began around 1845.
One model was the French Renaissance château of Chambord.
The style is called Historicism.
questions.description: A fairy-tale castle on an island where people in suits now vote on laws.
questions.fun_fact: Today Schwerin Castle is home to the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

questions.question: The “Frankfurt Kitchen” is seen as the first modern fitted kitchen. In which year was it designed?
hints: It was made for the housing estates of the “New Frankfurt” program.
It was designed by Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky.
It was the time of the Weimar Republic and the Bauhaus.
questions.description: A room where every move was meant to cost exactly one step.
questions.fun_fact: About 10,000 Frankfurt Kitchens were built into new apartments in the city.

questions.question: I came over the Alps from Italy around 1500, Albrecht Dürer brought me along, and Augsburg's town hall is one of my showpieces. What am I?
hints: I come after the Gothic.
I love the columns and shapes of ancient Greece and Rome.
My name means “rebirth”.
questions.description: An era that got all dressed up just by looking back in time.
questions.fun_fact: Dürer traveled to Venice twice and learned the new Italian way of painting there.

questions.question: Roughly how many Scoville units does pure capsaicin, the substance that makes chili peppers hot, measure?
hints: It's far more than any chili pepper you've ever tasted.
A jalapeño measures only a few thousand units.
It's a number with six zeros.
questions.description: Some spicy things you feel on your tongue, and some you feel in your soul.
questions.fun_fact: Birds don't feel the burn of capsaicin, so they eat chili peppers and spread the seeds everywhere.

questions.question: The Städel in Frankfurt is Germany's oldest museum foundation, set up by a will in 1815. What social class did its founder come from?
hints: Frankfurt had no prince of its own at the time.
Johann Friedrich Städel was born and died in the free city of Frankfurt and left his paintings and fortune to the city.
He was a banker and merchant.
questions.description: A will that still gets visitors every single day.
questions.fun_fact: The Städel's underground extension from 2012 pokes out of the museum garden's lawn with almost 200 round skylights.

questions.question: I studied at the Bauhaus, a bicycle handlebar inspired my tubular steel furniture, and my most famous chair bears the first name of a painter colleague. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Hungary in 1902.
I ran the furniture workshop at the Bauhaus.
My chair is named after Wassily Kandinsky.
questions.description: A designer who saw more than just the road when he went cycling.
questions.fun_fact: Breuer later designed the building of the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York.

questions.question: The Guelph Treasure comes from Brunswick Cathedral, is now in Berlin and is disputed as looted art. What does it mainly consist of?
hints: The pieces were used in church services.
Many are made of gilded silver with enamel.
They held the remains of saints.
questions.description: A treasure fought over by more lawyers than pirates.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, the Guelph Treasure even reached the US Supreme Court.

questions.question: This artwork is the star of the Neues Museum in Berlin. What is it?
hints: It comes from ancient Egypt.
It was found in Amarna in 1912.
It shows the wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten.
questions.description: A museum star that may never leave its glass case, yet still meets thousands of fans every day.
questions.fun_fact: The bust’s left eye is missing its inlaid pupil, and to this day nobody knows for sure why.

questions.question: Which of these German national team players was NOT a goalkeeper?
hints: You are looking for an outfield player.
At the 2022 European Championship, she played in defensive midfield.
Merle Frohms made the saves at that tournament; the player you want won the ball back in front of her.
questions.description: Three of them may grab the ball with their hands without anyone blowing a whistle.
questions.fun_fact: In 2022, Merle Frohms kept goal in the European Championship final at Wembley Stadium in front of about 87,000 people.

questions.question: You're sailing around the world like Boris Herrmann in the Vendée Globe: after the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Leeuwin, which cape comes next?
hints: For centuries, this cape has been seen as a great test for sailors.
Sailors who had sailed around it were once allowed to wear a gold earring.
It is the stormy southern tip of South America.
questions.description: Alone on the open sea, and the nearest bakery is a few thousand kilometers away.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, Boris Herrmann sailed Greta Thunberg across the Atlantic to New York on his yacht.

questions.question: Walter Röhrl from Regensburg was World Rally Champion twice. In which decade?
hints: Back then, he drove for Fiat and Opel, among others.
It was the decade of the wild Group B cars.
The Berlin Wall fell in the same decade.
questions.description: He took corners so smoothly that the trees along the road applauded.
questions.fun_fact: Röhrl won the Monte Carlo Rally four times, with four different car brands.

questions.question: Biathlete Magdalena Neuner won two Olympic golds in 2010, was world champion 12 times and retired at 25. Which German state is she from?
hints: Her hometown is close to the Alps.
Her hometown is in southern Germany, not far from the border with Austria.
In her state, people love to wear Lederhosen and Dirndl.
questions.description: Shoot, run, smile, and do it all on skis.
questions.fun_fact: Because she won so many titles, fans called Magdalena Neuner “Gold-Lena.”

questions.question: “I'm a tennis pro from Hamburg, many call me ‘Sascha’, and in 2021 I won Olympic gold in Tokyo.” Who am I?
hints: He was born in 1997.
His parents are from Russia, and his brother Mischa plays tennis too.
“Sascha” is a pet form of his first name.
questions.description: A serve so fast the ball kids can only stare.
questions.fun_fact: Alexander Zverev is almost 2 m (6 ft 6 in) tall, one of the tallest players on the tour.

questions.question: Haba is based in Bad Rodach in Upper Franconia, was founded in 1938 and is named after the Habermaaß family. What kind of company is it?
hints: Its headquarters are very close to the border with Thuringia.
Kids are the ones who are happiest about its products.
“Obstgarten” and “Tier auf Tier” come from this company.
questions.description: A family name so long that the company boiled it down to four letters.
questions.fun_fact: Haba games like “Obstgarten” have been in German children's rooms for decades.

questions.question: Fruchtzwerge come in small cups in the fridge aisle and, according to the ads, were “as valuable as a little steak”. What are they mainly made of?
hints: It's a dairy product.
People also eat it with boiled potatoes in their skins and linseed oil.
Its name sounds a bit like a duck's “quack”!
questions.description: Small, but with a gigantic advertising budget.
questions.fun_fact: Fruchtzwerge are made by the French food company Danone.

questions.question: Penaten cream was invented in 1904 in Rhöndorf on the Rhine and has a name from ancient Rome. What were the Penates?
hints: The Penates belonged to every ordinary Roman household, not just the emperor's.
The Romans kept the Penates close to the hearth and the pantry.
They watched over family, home and hearth.
questions.description: Babies don't notice, but their bottoms get a little help from antiquity.
questions.fun_fact: The cream was invented by the druggist Max Riese.

questions.question: The Stabilo Boss highlighter has been around since 1971, and the company behind it is based near Nuremberg. What did it start out making in the 19th century?
hints: Nuremberg has been a stronghold of this product for centuries.
Faber-Castell and Staedtler come from the same area.
It has a graphite core inside.
questions.description: The pen that saves the important stuff at school and the unimportant stuff at the office.
questions.fun_fact: The Stabilo Boss is said to be Europe's best-selling highlighter.

questions.question: The VW Bus, the “Bulli”, came out in 1950 and became a cult classic with surfers. Which other VW gave it its engine?
hints: The other car is older than the Bus.
It starred as Herbie in movies.
It's round and named after an insect.
questions.description: A bus that has seen more campfires than any scout.
questions.fun_fact: The idea for the Bulli was sketched in 1947 by Ben Pon, the Dutch importer of VW cars.

questions.question: Bayern and Dortmund played the 2013 Champions League final against each other in this stadium. In which city is it?
hints: The city isn't in Germany.
The stadium is famous for its huge white arch.
The British king lives here.
questions.description: A German derby so big it had to move abroad.
questions.fun_fact: Arjen Robben scored Bayern's 2–1 winner just before the end of the first all-German Champions League final.

questions.question: The Fertile Crescent, shaped like a half-moon and watered by the Tigris and Euphrates, saw farming begin 10,000 years ago. Which countries cover much of it today?
hints: It's in the Middle East, in Asia.
Ancient Mesopotamia was there.
One of these countries has Baghdad as its capital.
questions.description: A half-moon that lives on a map instead of in the sky, and invented the vegetable garden.
questions.fun_fact: Wheat, barley, lentils, peas and chickpeas are among the first plants humans learned to grow in that region.

questions.question: A DFB-Pokal match is tied after 90 minutes. What comes next these days, before the penalty shootout?
hints: The players keep on playing.
It lasts two halves of 15 minutes.
The playing time simply gets longer.
questions.description: For when 90 minutes just weren't enough drama.
questions.fun_fact: In the past, a tie in the DFB-Pokal meant a full replay on another day.

questions.question: FC Bayern fans love to shout “Mia san …”. What does the full saying mean?
hints: In Bavarian, “mia” means “we”.
The saying stands for Bavarian pride and the club's self-confidence.
The full saying is “Mia san mia”.
questions.description: A saying so Bavarian that only a Weisswurst fully understands it.
questions.fun_fact: FC Bayern even made “Mia san mia” its official club motto.

questions.question: From his youth days until 2025, this player played for only one pro club in Germany. Which one?
hints: He won the World Cup in 2014.
The club is from southern Germany.
It's Thomas Müller, and the club plays at the Allianz Arena.
questions.description: A man who would rather read open spaces than the stars.
questions.fun_fact: Müller called himself the “Raumdeuter” (space interpreter) because he is so good at spotting open space on the field.

questions.question: A clock in Hamburg's stadium counted how long HSV had played in the Bundesliga without a break. What did it show at their first relegation in 2018?
hints: HSV had been there since the Bundesliga's very first season.
The Bundesliga started in 1963.
Just count from 1963 to 2018.
questions.description: A clock that frayed more nerves than any alarm clock ever did.
questions.fun_fact: Because of its long Bundesliga run, HSV was nicknamed “the Dino”.

questions.question: Franz Beckenbauer holds the record: how many times was he voted Germany's Footballer of the Year?
hints: It's more than twice.
He won the vote in the 1960s and the 1970s.
Twice in the '60s, twice in the '70s.
questions.description: A Kaiser collects trophies the way other people collect stamps.
questions.fun_fact: Among women, Birgit Prinz holds the record: she was voted Germany's Women's Footballer of the Year eight times.

questions.question: The Bundesliga leader at a certain point can call itself “Herbstmeister” (autumn champion). After which matchday is it decided?
hints: It's usually just before or just after Christmas.
A Bundesliga season has 34 matchdays.
That's when the first half of the season, the “Hinrunde”, is over.
questions.description: A title with no trophy, no party, and often not even any autumn.
questions.fun_fact: Matchday 17 often falls in December or even January, so it's really already winter.

questions.question: This club plays in black and yellow, has a bee named Emma as its mascot and the huge “Yellow Wall” in its stadium. Which club is it?
hints: The club comes from the Ruhr area.
The club was founded in 1909.
The club is named after a city with “Dort” in its name.
questions.description: A club where even the bee has a season ticket.
questions.fun_fact: With about 25,000 places, Dortmund's South Stand is the largest standing terrace in Europe.

questions.question: Bayern players celebrate their titles with the fans on the balcony of this city hall. On which square does it stand?
hints: The square is right in the middle of Munich's old town.
A famous glockenspiel turns in the city hall tower.
The square is named after the mother of Jesus.
questions.description: A balcony that sees more parties than some people's living rooms.
questions.fun_fact: In the tower's glockenspiel, little figures do the coopers' dance (Schäfflertanz) and ride in a knights' tournament.

questions.question: “I was born in Stuttgart, grew up in England and played in Chelsea's youth teams. In 2019 I joined FC Bayern and chose Germany.” Who am I?
hints: He is a young and very fast dribbler.
He could also have played for England.
At Euro 2024 in Germany, his three goals put him among the tournament's top scorers.
questions.description: Two countries wanted him, but only one got to keep him.
questions.fun_fact: Musiala played for England's youth national teams before he chose Germany.

questions.question: Which insects ooze a yellow liquid from their legs when disturbed and are set loose in vegetable gardens to eat aphids?
hints: These insects are hunters.
Farmers use them as a natural way to control pests.
They are usually red with black spots.
questions.description: A tiny bug that drinks your plants' juice without asking first.
questions.fun_fact: Some ants look after aphids like cows, so they can drink the sweet liquid the aphids give off.

questions.question: You bite into a Toffifee: chocolate on top, nougat below, caramel outside. What's right in the middle?
hints: It grows on a bush.
Squirrels love to gather it in the fall.
It's small and round, and nougat is made from it.
questions.description: A little candy cup with more floors than some houses.
questions.fun_fact: Toffifee came out in 1973 and is made by Storck, the company that also makes Werther's Original.

questions.question: You mix a packet of Tortenguss (clear cake glaze) with sugar and juice. About how much liquid goes in?
hints: It's enough for a single fruit tart base.
It's about as much as a large glass.
It's a quarter of a liter.
questions.description: The glue that keeps strawberries from running away from the cake.
questions.fun_fact: Tortenguss often sets thanks to carrageenan, a gelling agent made from red seaweed.

questions.question: Spitzbuben are jam-filled sandwich cookies. But who do you mean when you say “Du bist ein Spitzbube!”?
hints: “Spitz” here is an old word for sharp-witted or cunning, not pointy.
It's a loving name for a child who has been up to mischief.
Think of Max and Moritz, Wilhelm Busch's two troublemakers.
questions.description: Two cookies stuck together with jam so neither one has to be alone.
questions.fun_fact: Many Spitzbuben have a hole in the top cookie so the red jam shows through.

questions.question: You tear open a packet of Brausepulver, and it fizzes on your tongue. What is NOT in it?
hints: What you're looking for is in almost every kitchen cupboard.
It belongs in cake batter more than anything.
It's made from ground grain.
questions.description: A powder that throws a little party on your tongue.
questions.fun_fact: The fizz happens because baking soda and acid react with your saliva to make carbon dioxide, the same gas as in sparkling water.

questions.question: You unwrap a hollow chocolate figure from colorful foil: bushy beard, red hat, sack of presents. Who is it?
hints: He is busiest in winter.
He travels by sleigh.
In many families he brings the presents on Christmas Eve.
questions.description: A man who shrinks around the house faster and faster as New Year's Day gets closer.
questions.fun_fact: Germany makes well over 100 million chocolate Santas every year.

questions.question: You cook apples until soft and mash them, and people love it with potato pancakes or rice pudding. What is it?
hints: You eat it with a spoon.
It's soft like baby food.
At the supermarket it often comes in a jar.
questions.description: Apples that had a very relaxing day.
questions.fun_fact: In the Rhineland, Reibekuchen (potato pancakes) are traditionally eaten with applesauce, and some people prefer Rübenkraut (sugar beet syrup).

questions.question: The Federal President appoints an ambassador. Under the Basic Law, it only counts once someone countersigns it. Who?
hints: With the signature, someone else takes on the political responsibility for the decision.
The rule is in Article 58 of the Basic Law.
For ambassadors, it would be the Federal Foreign Office.
questions.description: At Schloss Bellevue one autograph isn't enough: someone else has to grab a pen too.
questions.fun_fact: The Federal President needs no countersignature for only a few decisions, such as appointing the chancellor.

questions.question: After the euro arrived in 2002, many Germans called the new currency “Teuro”. What did they mean by that?
wrong_answers: The bills are easy to fake
hints: It was a complaint, not praise.
It's about prices in cafés and supermarkets.
The word mixes “Euro” with the German word “teuer”.
questions.description: Goodbye to the Deutsche Mark: many cried over it, some recounted their change.
questions.fun_fact: One euro was worth exactly 1.95583 Deutsche Marks, so many people simply multiplied by two in their heads.

questions.question: In 2021, the traffic light coalition (Ampel) of SPD, Greens and FDP began. In which year did it break up, when Chancellor Scholz fired FDP finance minister Lindner?
hints: The coalition didn't last the full four years.
An early Bundestag election followed.
The new election took place in February of the following year.
questions.description: Red, green and yellow: just like on the road, this traffic light didn't stay green forever.
questions.fun_fact: In the early election in February 2025, the FDP failed to win any seats in the Bundestag.

questions.question: Look at these leaves: they're rich in folic acid, which doctors recommend during pregnancy. What is it for?
questions.answer: Helping the baby's spine and brain form well
wrong_answers: Helping the baby be born with more hair
Helping the baby be born with light eyes
hints: It helps build new cells.
It matters most in the first weeks, when the baby is only just forming.
It has to do with the nervous system.
questions.description: Leaves that work hard for someone who hasn't even been born yet.
questions.fun_fact: “Folic” comes from the Latin “folium”, meaning leaf, because it was discovered in spinach leaves.

questions.question: You want to vote for the CDU in a German state election. In which state is it not on the ballot at all?
hints: A separate sister party runs there instead.
This sister party has an S instead of a D in its name.
It is Germany's largest state by area.
questions.description: A party that can vacation almost anywhere in the country, except in one state.
questions.fun_fact: In the Bundestag, the CDU and CSU sit together as one group known as the “Union.”

questions.question: I have buttons and always the same cut. Angela Merkel wore me in almost every color of the rainbow. What am I?
hints: I'm worn over a blouse or a shirt.
Many people wear me at the office or to a job interview.
I'm a kind of jacket, and my name starts with B.
questions.description: A closet that looks like a box of paints.
questions.fun_fact: A Dutch designer made a color chart from photos of her jackets, and it looks just like a paint swatch card from a hardware store.

questions.question: I was Mayor of Hamburg and Finance Minister. In 2022 I promised a “Doppelwumms” against high energy prices. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Osnabrück.
In the 2021 federal election, I won a constituency in Potsdam.
I am an SPD politician and became Chancellor in 2021.
questions.description: Politics with comic-book sound effects: boom, bang, wumms – and twice over.
questions.fun_fact: Back in 2020, as Finance Minister, he had already talked about a “Wumms” – by 2022 it had to be a double one.

questions.question: Before the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, Germany was divided. Into how many states?
hints: Back then, the Cold War divided all of Europe.
One of them was called the GDR.
The other was called the Federal Republic.
questions.description: A country that finally sat back down at the same table after many years.
questions.fun_fact: On October 3, 1990, the two states became one again, and that date has been German Unity Day ever since.

questions.question: This politician was the CDU and CSU candidate for chancellor in 2021. Which city is he from?
hints: The city is in North Rhine-Westphalia.
It borders Belgium and the Netherlands.
Charlemagne is buried in its cathedral.
questions.description: A man who almost landed in the Chancellery, but would rather nibble gingerbread at home.
questions.fun_fact: Before he ran for chancellor, he was the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia.

questions.question: A chancellor lived in this house in Rhöndorf, near Bad Honnef. Which one?
hints: He governed when Bonn was still the capital.
He was the oldest chancellor in office.
Before that, he was mayor of Cologne.
questions.description: A house on the Rhine where someone grew roses and ran a country on the side.
questions.fun_fact: He was already 73 when he was elected chancellor, and he stayed in office for 14 years.

questions.question: In 2017, the talks on a Jamaica coalition fell apart. Who walked out saying “It is better not to govern than to govern badly”?
hints: He announced the walkout shortly before midnight, live in front of the cameras.
His party had been voted out of the Bundestag in 2013 and came back in 2017.
He led the party whose color is yellow and later became finance minister.
questions.description: A coalition named after a Caribbean flag, sunburn included.
questions.fun_fact: In the end, another grand coalition of the CDU/CSU and the SPD took over.

questions.question: In the song „Der Mai ist gekommen“, the trees burst into leaf. So where does the singer long to go?
hints: The clouds in the sky are his role models.
According to the song, only people with worries stay at home.
He wants to go as far away as he possibly can.
questions.description: Spring fever with a backpack: if you're still on the couch, you didn't get the song.
questions.fun_fact: The words are by Emanuel Geibel; the well-known tune was written by Justus Wilhelm Lyra around 1842.

questions.question: In the lovely month of May, I argued with a bird about which of us sings best. In the end we sang together. Who am I?
hints: I’m not a bird, but I like living on the farm.
My ears are pretty long.
My call sounds like “hee-haw” (in German: “I-A”).
questions.description: The world’s first talent show, sadly with no judges at all.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by Hoffmann von Fallersleben, the same poet who wrote the Deutschlandlied, whose third verse is Germany’s national anthem.

questions.question: In the knee-bouncing rhyme „Hoppe, hoppe Reiter“, the rider falls in at the end and goes “plumps”. Where does he land?
hints: Before that, he already fell into the ditch.
The ground there is wet and muddy.
Frogs feel right at home there; riders, not so much.
questions.description: The only horse race where falling off is the best part.
questions.fun_fact: At “plumps”, you open your knees and the child slides down a little: that's the high point of the game.

questions.question: In the song “Hopp, hopp, hopp, Pferdchen lauf Galopp”, the little horse gallops over sticks and stones. What must it not break?
hints: The little horse needs them to gallop.
A horse has four of them.
In German, the word rhymes with “Steine” (stones).
questions.description: A song every vet would happily play on repeat.
questions.fun_fact: When a horse gallops, all four hooves are briefly in the air at once with every stride.

questions.question: Finish Pippi's German song: “Ich mach mir die Welt, widdewidde wie sie mir …”
hints: Pippi never follows anyone else's rules.
The missing word is about finding something nice.
Pippi makes the world the way it pleases her.
questions.description: Two times three makes four, and if you argue, she puts a horse on your porch.
questions.fun_fact: In German, Pippi's full name is Pippilotta Viktualia Rollgardina Pfefferminz Efraimstochter Langstrumpf.

questions.question: In the finger game “Himpelchen und Pimpelchen”, two climb up a high mountain. Pimpelchen is a dwarf. What is Himpelchen?
hints: He is just as small as Pimpelchen.
Creatures like him are said to have secretly worked at night in Cologne.
His name starts like the first name Heinz.
questions.description: Two little thumbs go mountain climbing, and they don't need any oxygen tanks.
questions.fun_fact: At the end, the thumbs crawl into the fists as if the two were sleeping inside the mountain, and everyone softly snores along.

questions.question: In the children’s song, this animal flies out “in Wald und Heide” (into forest and heath). What is it looking for there?
hints: In the song, the animal is searching for something.
It is looking for “ein Tröpfchen” and “ein Krümchen” (a little drop and a little crumb).
Later it turns this into honey.
questions.description: Small, striped and harder-working than any janitor.
questions.fun_fact: A honeybee beats its wings about 200 times a second, and that’s where the buzzing comes from.

questions.question: I begin with „Heute kann es regnen, stürmen oder schneien“, and Rolf Zuckowski wrote me. Which song am I?
questions.answer: Wie schön, dass du geboren bist
hints: I'm sung once a year for one very special child.
I'm a birthday song.
My chorus goes: „Wir hätten dich sonst sehr vermisst.“
questions.description: Bad weather? Who cares: someone here shines brighter than the sun.
questions.fun_fact: Rolf Zuckowski's song is one of the most-sung birthday songs in Germany.

questions.question: In the counting rhyme “Eins, zwei, Polizei”, someone joins in at “fünf, sechs”. Who?
hints: You know this character from fairy tales.
In fairy tales, this character usually plays the bad guy.
She flies on a broom and likes living in a gingerbread house.
questions.description: Whoever gets counted out mustn't sulk, because the rhyme says so.
questions.fun_fact: The rhyme ends with “neun, zehn, auf Wiedersehn” (nine, ten, goodbye), and whoever it lands on is out.

questions.question: Which feature does NOT fit a typical Wimmelbuch?
hints: Every time you look, you spot something new in the bustle.
You search, discover and tell yourself the stories.
You can enjoy a Wimmelbuch before you can read.
questions.description: So much is going on here that even the dog on page three has its own fan club.
questions.fun_fact: Ali Mitgutsch is seen as the father of the German Wimmelbuch; his first one came out in 1968.

questions.question: Lieselotte the cow lives on a farm, loves to lie in wait and has a favorite moment of the day. What is she waiting for?
hints: It comes to the farm at almost the same time every day.
Lieselotte loves to give a certain person a fright when it comes.
This person delivers letters and packages.
questions.description: A cow with plenty of time, a bush and a clear plan.
questions.fun_fact: The Lieselotte books are by Alexander Steffensmeier, who also draws the cow himself.

questions.question: You’re standing in a bookstore in front of the Carlsen Verlag books. Which series will you NOT find there?
hints: Three of the four series have been bestsellers at Carlsen for years.
The series you’re looking for is published by a Stuttgart publisher.
It’s about three detectives from Rocky Beach.
questions.description: A Hamburg publisher that owns a second shelf in almost every kid’s bedroom.
questions.fun_fact: Carlsen has Danish roots and has been based in Hamburg for decades.

questions.question: In the “Struwwelpeter” story of the Zappelphilipp (Fidgety Philip), how many people sit at the dinner table?
hints: It’s a very small family.
One speaks sternly, one watches in silence.
Dad, Mom and …
questions.description: A dinner after which the tablecloth badly needs a wash.
questions.fun_fact: Heinrich Hoffmann wrote “Struwwelpeter” in 1844 as a Christmas present for his son.

questions.question: Vitamin A is to sight as vitamin K is to…
hints: It's plentiful in leafy greens like spinach and kale.
It has to do with blood.
It helps a cut stop bleeding.
questions.description: Vitamins are named with letters, and this one skipped a big part of the alphabet.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “K” after the German word “Koagulation”.

questions.question: In Michael Ende's “Momo”, which description does NOT fit the gray gentlemen?
hints: The gray gentlemen are the villains of the book.
They talk people into “saving” time.
Master Hora helps Momo against them.
questions.description: Gentlemen with hats, briefcases and a very bad effect on everyone's calendar.
questions.fun_fact: The gray gentlemen smoke cigars made from dried hour-lilies, so they are literally smoking stolen time.

questions.question: The kid detectives of the TV series “Die Pfefferkörner” have their headquarters in an old spice warehouse. In which city?
hints: It's a port city in the north.
It has a whole warehouse district made of red brick.
The city lies on the Elbe River.
questions.description: Kid detectives who solve every case with a pinch of spice.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Pfefferkörner” has been on the air since 1999 and is one of the longest-running children's series on German TV.

questions.question: “I have no borders, a Childlike Empress rules me, and the Nothing is slowly eating me up.” What am I?
hints: I come from a book by Michael Ende.
Atréju travels through me to save me.
I am made of people's dreams and wishes.
questions.description: A vacation spot you don't pack a suitcase for: you just turn the page.
questions.fun_fact: “Die unendliche Geschichte” (The Neverending Story) was first printed in two colors: red for the human world, green for the fantasy land.

questions.question: On Reichenau Island in Lake Constance, men like this one copied books by hand in the Middle Ages. Who were they?
hints: They lived together behind thick walls.
They prayed several times a day.
They lived in a monastery.
questions.description: They had no printer or copier and still ended up with loads of books.
questions.fun_fact: The monastic island of Reichenau has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

questions.question: The children's song goes “Es klappert die Mühle am rauschenden Bach” (the mill clatters by the rushing brook). What was made in a mill like this one?
hints: Afterwards, the miller was often dusted all white.
The result was later taken to the baker.
Bread was baked from it.
questions.description: Nobody reinvented the wheel; they just stood it in a stream.
questions.fun_fact: In England alone, more than 5,000 water mills were already counted in 1086.

questions.question: Marksburg Castle on the Rhine has stood for many hundreds of years. What are its thick walls made of?
hints: It is very hard and heavy.
You find it in mountains and cliffs.
You can throw small pieces of it into a stream.
questions.description: A house where the front yard was allowed to be a moat.
questions.fun_fact: Marksburg is the only hilltop castle on the Middle Rhine that was never destroyed.

questions.question: Valhalla is Odin's huge hall for fallen warriors; legend gives it 540 doors and spears for rafters. What is its roof covered with?
hints: It suits the warriors who live there.
Germanic warriors and Vikings carried these on their arms.
You use them to block sword blows.
questions.description: The after-work pub with the strictest door policy in the whole world of the gods.
questions.fun_fact: The Walhalla hall of fame near Regensburg is named after this legendary hall.

questions.question: This rebuilt tower stands on the Limes, a World Heritage Site since 2005. Who once kept watch here?
hints: They came from a large empire to the south.
Their empire's capital was in Italy.
Their highest ruler was an emperor in Rome.
questions.description: Germany's oldest border post, just without the barrier or the passport stamp.
questions.fun_fact: The Limes in Germany was about 550 km (340 miles) long and had around 900 watchtowers.

questions.question: Above some castle gates hung a small overhanging box with holes in its floor, through which stones or hot water fell. What is it called?
hints: It let defenders hit attackers standing right at the foot of the wall or gate.
It is a small, box-shaped structure that often juts out of the wall right above the entrance.
In German it's called a “Pechnase”: a “pitch nose”.
questions.description: Architecture for visitors you really don't want to invite in.
questions.fun_fact: Pitch was expensive, so defenders mostly dropped stones or poured hot water down instead.

questions.question: Riddle: “I left Lisbon, sailed around Africa past the Cape of Good Hope and was the first European to reach India by sea, looking for pepper.” Who am I?
hints: He was Portuguese.
He reached India in 1498.
His family name starts with G.
questions.description: A really, really long trip just to get something to make dinner tastier.
questions.fun_fact: In the Middle Ages pepper was so expensive that it was sometimes used to pay off debts.

questions.question: The Holy Roman Empire's throne wasn't inherited, so in 1356 the Golden Bull set out who elects the king. Who?
hints: The election was usually held in Frankfurt am Main.
They were powerful lords of the empire themselves, both churchmen and nobles.
In German they're called after the old word “küren”, meaning “to choose”, as in “Kurpfalz”.
questions.description: A royal election with no campaign posters, but a very exclusive voter list.
questions.fun_fact: The Golden Bull is named after its seal made of gold.

questions.question: In the Middle Ages, serfs were firmly bound to their lord. Who was usually NOT a serf?
questions.answer: Citizens of a free imperial city
hints: Serfs mostly lived in the countryside.
Serfdom was passed down from parents to their children.
People said back then: “Stadtluft macht frei” (town air makes you free).
questions.description: An employment contract with no right to quit and no paid vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In Prussia, it took the October Edict of 1807 to begin the end of serfdom.

questions.question: At the big tournament in Kaltenberg, Bavaria, someone like this rides through the arena with a lance. Who is it?
hints: He lived a very long time ago.
He often lived in a castle.
He wears armor made of metal.
questions.description: Fanfares, cheering and an arena full of fans: the big show is about to begin.
questions.fun_fact: The Kaltenberg Knights' Tournament is said to be one of the biggest knights' tournaments in the world.

questions.question: Hildegard von Bingen was a nun about 900 years ago. What was she NOT allowed to do as a nun?
hints: In the convent, nuns make a promise for their whole life.
It has to do with love.
It usually comes with a ring and a big party.
questions.description: A shared house with very strict house rules and an even stricter dress code.
questions.fun_fact: Hildegard von Bingen wrote books about healing herbs and composed music that is still sung today.

questions.question: The German saying “etwas im Schilde führen” (to be up to something) comes from the coats of arms knights painted on their shields. In which century did they start doing that?
hints: It was right in the middle of the age of knights.
Under the new closed helmets, nobody could be recognized anymore.
It was in the time of Emperor Barbarossa.
questions.description: A name tag in XXL size that you'd rather strap to your arm.
questions.fun_fact: In battle, the coat of arms on a knight's shield showed whether he was friend or foe.

questions.question: I'm put together from big concrete parts made in a factory, there are thousands of me in Berlin-Marzahn, and in East Germany I was in high demand. What am I?
hints: I'm a building with lots of apartments.
In East Germany, you often had to wait a long time to get me.
My name tells you what my walls are made of: big, flat panels.
questions.description: In East Germany, waiting for your own four walls could take almost as long as waiting for a Trabi.
questions.fun_fact: Many East German families were happy to move into these buildings, because they had central heating and hot water, which many older buildings lacked.

questions.question: You wake up in West Berlin on August 13, and soldiers are laying barbed wire along the sector border. What year is it?
hints: It was during the Cold War.
Millions of people had already fled from East Germany to the West.
It was in the early 1960s.
questions.description: A city that suddenly became an island, without any sea around it.
questions.fun_fact: The wall around West Berlin was about 155 km (96 miles) long.

questions.question: Who became the first head of the office for the Stasi files in 1990?
hints: Before that, he was a pastor in Rostock.
People called the office by his name.
He later became Federal President of Germany.
questions.description: Millions of files, endless folders, and somebody had to take the keys.
questions.fun_fact: The office was nicknamed after each of its heads in turn: the “Gauck office,” the “Birthler office” and the “Jahn office.”

questions.question: A white palace on the Spree in Berlin's Tiergarten: where is the German president's official residence?
hints: The second official residence is the Villa Hammerschmidt in Bonn.
The palace was built in the late 18th century for a Prussian prince.
Translate “beautiful view” into French.
questions.description: Whoever holds the highest office in the land lives in style, not in a one-bedroom apartment.
questions.fun_fact: When the president's flag flies over Schloss Bellevue, the president is in the building.

questions.question: In June 1961, Walter Ulbricht said: “No one has any intention of building a …” Which word is missing?
hints: He was answering a question from a Western journalist.
Shortly afterwards, exactly what he denied happened in Berlin.
The structure fell in November 1989.
questions.description: A sentence that looked pretty silly just two months later.
questions.fun_fact: Ulbricht used the word even though the question never mentioned any such structure.

questions.question: You put the Gelber Sack (yellow bag) for packaging out on the street. Since which decade has Germany had it?
hints: It arrived after a new packaging law.
It goes with the “Der Grüne Punkt” (Green Dot) symbol.
It arrived around the time of reunification.
questions.description: The great German passion: rinsing out yogurt cups before throwing them away.
questions.fun_fact: Some cities use a Gelbe Tonne (yellow bin) instead of the Gelber Sack for the same packaging.

questions.question: Planes like these flew food and coal into West Berlin in 1948–49. What nickname did Berliners give them?
hints: The Soviet Union had blocked every road, rail and water route into West Berlin.
Some pilots dropped candy for children on tiny parachutes.
The name contains the German word for raisins.
questions.description: Flying visitors that roared instead of buzzing, and still brought something sweet.
questions.fun_fact: During the airlift, at times a plane landed at Tempelhof every few minutes.

questions.question: West Germany's interior minister negotiated the Unification Treaty and signed it on August 31, 1990. Who was he?
hints: At the time he was one of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's closest allies.
Later he spent many years as finance minister and as president of the Bundestag.
After an assassination attempt in October 1990, he used a wheelchair.
questions.description: A treaty so thick that afterwards two countries were only one.
questions.fun_fact: Günther Krause signed for East Germany, and the treaty also made October 3 a public holiday.

questions.question: He drew little men with bulbous noses, invented the stone louse, and had Grandpa Hoppenstedt say “Früher war mehr Lametta”. What is his stage name?
hints: His real name was Vicco von Bülow.
His stage name is the French word for a bird.
In English, that bird is called the golden oriole.
questions.description: A man who turned a bathtub and a breakfast egg into great art.
questions.fun_fact: The stone louse he invented even appears as a joke entry in the German medical dictionary Pschyrembel.

questions.question: You turn on ARD on a Sunday and see Mutter Beimer in “Lindenstraße”. In which year did the first episode air?
hints: Back then there were still two German states.
The show ran for about 35 years.
The last episode aired in 2020.
questions.description: A street in Munich where, for decades, more happened every Sunday than in your whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: When “Lindenstraße” ended in March 2020, one of the longest-running shows on German TV came to a close.

questions.question: I'm an Apache chief, my blood brother is called Ranger, and my twin brother runs the Puder Rosa Ranch. Who am I?
hints: I come from a 2001 Western parody.
Michael Herbig didn't just invent me, he plays me too.
My name starts almost like the Swedish band ABBA.
questions.description: Western heroes with blow-dried hair and a big weakness for puns.
questions.fun_fact: With almost 12 million viewers, “Der Schuh des Manitu” is one of the most successful German movies ever.

questions.question: Which German film award has been given since 1964 without a jury, purely for high box-office attendance?
hints: Cinema owners and the film industry present it.
A film gets it automatically once enough people have bought a ticket.
Its name recalls what the film is shown on in a cinema.
questions.description: An award you don't really need to write a thank-you speech for.
questions.fun_fact: Especially successful films even get the Golden Screen “with Star,” for several million viewers.

questions.question: “Willkommen bei den Hartmanns” is about a refugee from Nigeria living with a Munich family. In which year did the comedy hit theaters?
hints: The film came out in the 2010s.
Shortly before, a particularly large number of refugees had arrived in Germany.
It was one year after Angela Merkel said “Wir schaffen das” (“We can do this”).
questions.description: A Munich family, a new guest room, and a lot to talk about at the dinner table.
questions.fun_fact: It was directed by Simon Verhoeven, the son of Senta Berger, who plays Mother Hartmann in the film.

questions.question: In “Inglourious Basterds”, Michael Fassbender plays a Brit posing as a German officer who gets caught. What gives him away?
questions.answer: How he shows “three” with his fingers
hints: It happens when he orders something in a tavern.
Germans and Brits do it differently.
In Germany, you start with the thumb.
questions.description: An undercover tip: even the smallest habit can spill a secret.
questions.fun_fact: Michael Fassbender was born in Heidelberg and grew up in Ireland.

questions.question: This Berlin-born director moved to Hollywood in 1922. What was his elegant, witty style called there?
hints: He later made the comedy “To Be or Not to Be”.
In his film “Ninotchka” he got Greta Garbo to laugh.
Billy Wilder kept a sign in his office: “How would he have done it?”
questions.description: A Berliner with a secret recipe that all of Hollywood tried to copy.
questions.fun_fact: “Ninotchka” was advertised in 1939 with the slogan “Garbo laughs!”

questions.question: Wim Wenders made a film about a man in Tokyo who cleans buildings like this one every day. What is the film called?
hints: The film came out in 2023.
It was nominated for an Oscar for Japan.
The hero listens to old cassette tapes, and the title recalls a Lou Reed song.
questions.description: A film that proves you can be happy while scrubbing.
questions.fun_fact: The toilets in the film belong to the “Tokyo Toilet” project, for which famous architects designed public restrooms.

questions.question: They're called Sabrina and Amadeus, live on the Martinshof farm and carry Bibi and Tina across meadows and fields. What animals are they?
hints: They like to eat hay and apples.
They sleep in a stable.
You ride them with a saddle and reins.
questions.description: Hex-hex! There's plenty going on at the Martinshof again.
questions.fun_fact: Bibi and Tina started as an audio drama series, long before the movies came out.

questions.question: The movie title “Fack ju Göhte” contains this man's name, misspelled. What is he famous for?
hints: He lived more than 200 years ago, for a long time in Weimar.
In Weimar, he stands as a statue next to his friend Schiller.
He is considered the most famous German poet.
questions.description: A name so famous that you recognize it right away, even when it's misspelled.
questions.fun_fact: In 2013, “Fack ju Göhte” drew more than 7 million people into German movie theaters.

questions.question: This East German state film studio made “The Legend of Paul and Paula” and Westerns starring Gojko Mitić. What was it called?
hints: It was based in Potsdam-Babelsberg.
It was founded in 1946, before East Germany itself existed.
The abbreviation stands for “Deutsche Film-Aktiengesellschaft.”
questions.description: A film studio where even the Wild West came from East Germany.
questions.fun_fact: “Three Wishes for Cinderella” (1973) was also made here, together with a studio in Prague.

questions.question: I made five movies with Werner Herzog and was famous for my fits of rage. In “Fitzcarraldo”, I want to build an opera house in the jungle. Who am I?
hints: In Herzog's 1979 “Nosferatu”, I played the vampire.
Herzog made the documentary “My Best Fiend” about the two of us.
My daughter Nastassja also became an actress.
questions.description: One man, one ship, one mountain, and a director with very strong nerves.
questions.fun_fact: Jason Robards and Mick Jagger were first cast in “Fitzcarraldo”, but both dropped out.

questions.question: Several Winnetou films were shot here in the 1960s. In which present-day country is this place?
hints: Back then, the place belonged to a country that no longer exists.
The country lies on the Adriatic Sea.
Its capital is Zagreb.
questions.description: The Wild West, just with a surprising amount of water and surprisingly little desert.
questions.fun_fact: In “Der Schatz im Silbersee” (“The Treasure of the Silver Lake”, 1962), the Plitvice Lakes play the part of the Wild West.

questions.question: This animal is the mascot of a big German home improvement chain. Which chain is it?
hints: The chain has been around in Germany since 1970.
For decades its ads asked “Wie, wo, was?” (How, where, what?).
The name is meant to remind you of the word “hobby”.
questions.description: He chews on wood all day and would still love a cordless drill.
questions.fun_fact: The name Obi comes from the French pronunciation of the word “hobby”.

questions.question: The Berlin online store Zalando now sells all kinds of fashion. What did it start with in 2008?
hints: In its ads, customers screamed with joy while unpacking.
You always need them in pairs.
You wear them on your feet.
questions.description: A package arrives, someone screams, and the neighbors still don't call the police.
questions.fun_fact: Zalando became famous for its slogan “Schrei vor Glück oder schick's zurück” (“Scream with joy or send it back”).

questions.question: Suits like this one made the fashion brand Hugo Boss famous. In which town was the company founded in 1924?
hints: The town is in southern Germany.
Today it's known for its many outlet stores.
It lies near Reutlingen, at the edge of the Swabian Jura.
questions.description: A suit that fits so well even the coat hanger is jealous.
questions.fun_fact: The brand is named after its founder, the tailor Hugo Ferdinand Boss.

questions.question: I live in a cave under the mountains, eat raw fish, ask a hobbit riddles and call a ring “my precious.” Who am I?
hints: I appear in “The Hobbit” and “The Lord of the Rings.”
I talk to myself, as if there were two of us.
My name used to be Sméagol.
questions.description: The worst roommate ever: lives in a cave, eats raw fish and talks to his jewelry.
questions.fun_fact: The character is called Gollum because of the gulping noise he makes in his throat.

questions.question: What is this ride-on car for small children called?
hints: It has no pedals.
You push yourself along with your feet.
The name starts with “Bobby”.
questions.description: The first car you need no driver's license for, just two strong feet.
questions.fun_fact: The Bobby-Car has been around since 1972 and has zoomed through countless children's rooms since then.

questions.question: The Tempo paper tissue was invented in Nuremberg in 1929. What is it made from?
hints: It's the same material that paper is made from.
The raw material is first ground into a pulp and mixed with water.
It comes from trees.
questions.description: Achoo! From now on, your nose has its own disposable butler.
questions.fun_fact: Many Germans say “ein Tempo” for any tissue, no matter which brand it is.

questions.question: The “button in the ear” is the trademark of which businesswoman's stuffed animals?
hints: She lived in Giengen an der Brenz.
Her company is famous for teddy bears.
Her last name is written on the little button.
questions.description: A cuddly toy wearing an earring was cool before it was trendy.
questions.fun_fact: Margarete Steiff used a wheelchair from childhood and still founded a world-famous company.

questions.question: What would you usually NOT find in a dm drugstore?
hints: A drugstore mostly sells things for your body and your home.
What you're looking for is quite big.
It has two wheels.
questions.description: A store you walk into fresh and walk out of even fresher.
questions.fun_fact: Götz Werner founded dm in Karlsruhe in 1973.

questions.question: The hotel search site Trivago from Düsseldorf became famous with the slogan “Hotel? Trivago!”. In which decade was it founded?
hints: The internet already existed back then, but hardly anyone had a smartphone.
YouTube went online the same year.
In the year it was founded, Angela Merkel became German chancellor for the first time.
questions.description: Two words, one question mark, and suddenly you have vacation plans.
questions.fun_fact: Trivago was founded in Düsseldorf in 2005 and later even went public on the US stock market.

questions.question: It came from the Soviet Union, was based on the Fiat 124 and was a dream car in the GDR, far more wanted than the Trabant. Which car brand is it?
hints: It was built in a city named after an Italian politician.
The factory is called AvtoVAZ and is in Tolyatti.
