A well-known off-road model of the brand is called the Niva.
questions.description: A car that took more patience to get in the GDR than running a marathon.
questions.fun_fact: Tolyatti, the city where the car was built, is named after the Italian communist Palmiro Togliatti.

questions.question: “I had ten grades, almost every child in East Germany went to me, and from grade 7 I sent them regularly into real factories.” Who am I?
hints: I was usually shortened to three letters.
My name links school with technology and work.
The first word of my name means roughly “many techniques.”
questions.description: Ten years of lessons, and every so often it was off to the factory instead of the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: From grade 7 there was “Unterrichtstag in der Produktion”: once a week, students worked in real factories.

questions.question: In East Germany, people spent weekends at the “Datsche”: a garden shed, flower beds and fruit trees, often at the edge of town. What country does this word come from?
hints: The word only became common in everyday East German life after World War II.
There, a country house like this has almost the same name and is still very popular today.
This country's capital is Moscow.
questions.description: On weekends, out of the concrete apartment block and into the cucumber patch.
questions.fun_fact: The Russian word “dacha” is related to the word for “to give”: the tsars used to give away plots of land.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT true about the 1966 DEFA film “Spur der Steine”?
questions.answer: Christa Wolf wrote the novel it is based on
wrong_answers: Manfred Krug plays the lead role
It was pulled soon after its release
hints: The DEFA film tells the story of a work crew on a huge building site.
East Germany's leaders were anything but happy with the film.
The novel was written by Erik Neutsch.
questions.description: A crew of carpenters who would rather build by their own rules than by the plan.
questions.fun_fact: At screenings in 1966, planted audience members heckled the film on purpose before it vanished from movie theaters altogether.

questions.question: In the East German kids' series “Spuk unterm Riesenrad,” three ghost-train figures come to life at a fair like this one. Which three?
hints: You know all three from fairy tales.
As soon as they come to life, the figures run away from the ghost train.
In the series, one of them is called “Rumpel” for short.
questions.description: There's a lot going on at the fair, and far more than planned.
questions.fun_fact: The series aired on East German TV in 1979 and was so popular that it was followed later by “Spuk im Hochhaus.”

questions.question: Who is a stretch of beach with this sign meant for?
hints: The three letters stand for a German word ending in “Kultur” (culture).
It was very common on East Germany's Baltic coast.
Swimsuits and bikinis stay in the bag here.
questions.description: Sand in your shoe, a seagull behind you and a beach chair already taken at six in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1950s, East Germany still wanted to ban nude bathing, but it became hugely popular anyway.

questions.question: In East Germany's “Exquisit” stores, you paid in East German marks instead of Western money, but at very high prices. What did they mainly sell?
hints: The name alone was meant to sound like Western luxury.
Food was sold in separate stores with a different name.
At home, the goods ended up in the closet or on the shoe rack.
questions.description: A store where even the name sounded more expensive than half a month's pay.
questions.fun_fact: For food there was a counterpart: the “Delikat” stores, selling delicacies at equally steep prices.

questions.question: Only students with top grades who were politically reliable got into this East German school. It led to the Abitur. Which school?
hints: It built on the regular ten-grade school.
Its abbreviation has three letters.
Its name says that the Oberschule gets extended here.
questions.description: In East Germany, a spot here was almost as hard to get as a new car.
questions.fun_fact: If you didn't get a place at this school, you could still earn the Abitur in East Germany alongside job training.

questions.question: Many East German families heated their stoves with briquettes like these. What were they pressed from?
hints: The raw material comes out of the ground.
In Lusatia it is dug up in huge open-pit mines.
Its name contains a color.
questions.description: In winter you hauled them up from the basement; in summer you forgot they existed.
questions.fun_fact: At times, East Germany mined more brown coal than any other country in the world.

questions.question: At the 1985 May Day parade in East Berlin, thousands marched past the grandstand. Which SED leader waved to them from there?
hints: He led East Germany until the fall of 1989.
He had taken over the job in 1971.
His wife Margot was Minister of Education.
questions.description: A holiday when waving from up high was a job for the boss himself.
questions.fun_fact: In East Germany, May 1 was officially called the “Day of Struggle and Celebration of the Working People.”

questions.question: In 1980s East Germany, who wore a blue Pioneer neckerchief?
hints: It was about schoolchildren.
The older ones wore a neckerchief of a different color.
They were the youngest members of the Pioneer organization.
questions.description: A piece of cloth you must never, ever forget at home before the flag ceremony.
questions.fun_fact: From 1973, the older Thälmann Pioneers wore a red neckerchief, while the younger ones kept the blue one.

questions.question: Old photos show East Germans in the West buying bananas by the bagful. When were these pictures mostly taken?
questions.answer: After the fall of the Wall in 1989
wrong_answers: When the Wall was built in 1961
hints: Total strangers hugged and cheered in the streets.
Many had just received 100 Deutsche Marks of “welcome money”.
It was in the fall, when the border in Berlin opened.
questions.description: A curved fruit that suddenly made history.
questions.fun_fact: Bananas were rare in East Germany because they had to be bought abroad with scarce foreign currency.

questions.question: People living by the inner German border needed a special pass for their own village. About how wide was this restricted zone?
hints: The zone was set up in 1952 and took in whole villages.
It was much wider than the actual border fence and death strip.
On foot, this distance takes about an hour.
questions.description: A place where even the walk to the bakery needed a stamp.
questions.fun_fact: Even relatives could only visit people in the zone with a pass they had applied for in advance.

questions.question: The houses stood in the East, the sidewalk belonged to the West, and escape helpers dug tunnels here. Which Berlin street is it?
hints: In August 1961, people jumped from their windows into the West here.
In 1964, 57 people escaped through “Tunnel 57” under this street.
Today the main Berlin Wall Memorial stands here.
questions.description: A street where one step could take you into another world.
questions.fun_fact: Escape helpers paid for some tunnels by selling the film rights to US TV networks.

questions.question: In “The Lion King”, Scar bosses the hyenas. In “The Little Mermaid”, the sea witch Ursula bosses two…
hints: They live in the sea.
They are long and look like snakes.
Their names are Flotsam and Jetsam.
questions.description: Every villain needs helpers who laugh at their jokes, even the bad ones.
questions.fun_fact: Scar's hyenas are called Shenzi, Banzai and Ed, and Ed never says a word: he only laughs.

questions.question: In the photo, Willy Brandt meets the head of government of East Germany in Erfurt in 1970. Who was it?
hints: He was Chairman of the Council of Ministers, the head of the East German government.
Erich Honecker only took over the SED in 1971.
His first name sounds almost the same as his guest's from Bonn.
questions.description: A meeting where half the city stood below the windows and shouted.
questions.fun_fact: Outside the hotel “Erfurter Hof,” people shouted “Willy Brandt to the window!” – and the Stasi couldn't stop it.

questions.question: On which day did Hans-Dietrich Genscher tell the GDR refugees at the Prague embassy they could leave?
hints: It happened before the fall of the Wall.
Thousands of refugees had held out for weeks in the embassy garden.
It was the last day of a month.
questions.description: A sentence that was never finished, because the cheering was louder.
questions.fun_fact: Genscher's sentence was drowned out by cheers, and many refugees in the garden never heard its end.

questions.question: The Stasi kept files on millions of people. If you lined up the surviving files, about how long would the row be?
hints: It's far more than would fit in a single building.
The distance is longer than a marathon.
The number is made of three identical digits.
questions.description: An archive that makes every office binder look like a joke.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of sacks of torn-up Stasi files are still being pieced back together, scrap by scrap.

questions.question: This Moscow high-rise housed the RGW, the Eastern Bloc council East Germany joined in 1950. What was it in charge of?
questions.answer: Economic cooperation in the Eastern Bloc
wrong_answers: A joint army of the Eastern Bloc
Sports competitions in the Eastern Bloc
Space programs of the Eastern Bloc
hints: It was founded in Moscow in 1949 by the Soviet Union and several neighboring states.
The military had its own alliance, the Warsaw Pact; Cuba and Vietnam later joined the RGW too.
In the West it was known as “Comecon”.
questions.description: A Moscow high-rise that looks like an open book, but nobody can turn the pages.
questions.fun_fact: The RGW was dissolved in 1991; today its high-rise is used by the Moscow city government.

questions.question: The SED Politburo was the real center of power in East Germany. About how many members did it have in the 1980s?
hints: It was much smaller than the SED's Central Committee.
All its members fit easily around one conference table.
A soccer team plus its substitutes' bench would be about the same size.
questions.description: A club so exclusive it even had its own village in the woods.
questions.fun_fact: Politburo members lived sealed off in the Wandlitz forest settlement, with their own store full of Western goods.

questions.question: East Germany's border strip ran from the Baltic Sea to Czechoslovakia. About how long was the inner German border?
hints: The Berlin Wall alone was only a small part of it.
The border was longer than Germany is from north to south.
It's a few hundred kilometers more than 1,000.
questions.description: A line that traced Germany from top to bottom in barbed wire.
questions.fun_fact: The former border strip became the “Green Belt” (Grünes Band), a refuge for more than 1,000 endangered species of animals and plants.

questions.question: You walk into Dolores Umbridge's office at Hogwarts. Which of these would you NOT find there?
hints: Umbridge's office is pink and overly cute.
Look for the thing that belongs to another teacher.
That animal is the pet of the Hogwarts headmaster.
questions.description: An office so pink that even bubble gum would look dull next to it.
questions.fun_fact: In the movies, the kittens on Umbridge's plates move and meow.

questions.question: You're checking your winter tires in the fall. What is the minimum tread depth required by law in Germany?
hints: It's surprisingly little.
Experts recommend about 4 mm for winter tires, but the law asks for less.
It's thinner than a 1-euro coin.
questions.description: Rubber with grooves: the difference between braking and sledding.
questions.fun_fact: Germans have a rule of thumb for winter tires, “von O bis O”: from Oktober (October) to Ostern (Easter).

questions.question: Complete the German saying: “When you come back from the town hall, you are …”
hints: It's about what you know afterwards.
People say it when someone only gets the right idea later.
It's the opposite of “more foolish.”
questions.description: A building full of mayors, rubber stamps and old sayings.
questions.fun_fact: It really means that hindsight is always clearer, even if you never set foot in a town hall.

questions.question: This space is in the basement and comes with a rented apartment. It often has wooden slat walls and a padlock. What is it?
hints: Bikes, boxes and Christmas decorations often end up here.
You don't share it with the neighbors: each apartment has its own.
In German it's called a Kellerabteil.
questions.description: Moving boxes from 2009 rest here, unopened, in peace.
questions.fun_fact: Whether a basement storage unit comes with the apartment is usually written in the lease, often with its own number.

questions.question: It's yellow, open around the clock and has dozens of lockers that open with a code. What is it?
hints: You pick up something there that you ordered.
The courier brings your delivery there instead of to your front door.
It belongs to DHL and is meant for packages.
questions.description: A closet that never sleeps and still has no socks in it.
questions.fun_fact: The first Packstations opened in 2001 in Mainz and Dortmund.

questions.question: I live in the kitchen. You fill me with dirty plates, I spray hot water and give them back clean. What am I?
hints: After a meal, I have a lot to do.
Inside me there are racks for glasses and cutlery.
Thanks to me, nobody has to scrub plates at the sink.
questions.description: A kitchen gadget that never pays rent and never moves out.
questions.fun_fact: The first truly practical dishwasher was patented by the American Josephine Cochrane in 1886.

questions.question: “Astro-Alex” Gerst spent hours in a spacesuit in a huge water pool in Houston. What was he training for?
questions.answer: Work on the outside of the ISS
hints: In water you feel almost as light as in space.
The pool holds a copy of the place he later flew to.
In 2014 he took part in a spacewalk.
questions.description: Swimming lessons for advanced students, with a helmet, gloves and a 120 kg (265 lb) suit.
questions.fun_fact: In 2018, Alexander Gerst became the first German to command the International Space Station.

questions.question: “The light bulb is to Edison as MP3 is to …?”
hints: MP3 was developed in Erlangen.
The organization is named after a 19th-century optician.
The man it is named after discovered dark lines in the Sun's spectrum.
questions.description: A sound from Franconia that fits in any pocket.
questions.fun_fact: To test MP3, the developers listened to Suzanne Vega's song “Tom's Diner” countless times.

questions.question: This astrophysicist from Munich has explained space and climate on TV for decades. Who is he?
hints: He hosted the show “alpha-Centauri”.
You often see him on “Terra X” on ZDF.
One of his shows is named after him plus the word “Kosmos”.
questions.description: He explains the universe so well that even the TV stops to think for a moment.
questions.fun_fact: Harald Lesch is a professor of astrophysics at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

questions.question: Gutenberg was born here around 1400, printed his famous Bible here, and the university bears his name. Which city?
hints: The city lies on the Rhine.
It is a stronghold of Fastnacht, the local carnival.
It is the capital of Rhineland-Palatinate.
questions.description: The city where books suddenly stopped needing handwriting.
questions.fun_fact: Only about 50 copies of the Gutenberg Bible survive worldwide, and two of them are in the Gutenberg Museum.

questions.question: It hangs on a string in hot water, it's made of thin paper, and the company Teekanne invented a two-chamber version in 1949. What is it?
hints: You throw it away after using it.
Often a small paper tag hangs from the string.
Dried leaves are packed inside it.
questions.description: At five o'clock it's teatime at Grandma's, and there's no arguing about it.
questions.fun_fact: Adolf Rambold's double-chamber bag lets water reach the tea from two sides, so it brews better.

questions.question: Which of these players did NOT become world champion with Germany in 2014?
hints: Three of the four were on the field in the World Cup final against Argentina.
Back then he was playing in Chelsea's youth teams in London.
He was born in 2003.
questions.description: A summer in Brazil that half of Germany remembers wearing a jersey.
questions.fun_fact: In the final against Argentina, Mario Götze scored the winning goal for 1–0 in extra time.

questions.question: Complete the famous German soccer saying: “The round thing must go into the …”
hints: The round thing means the ball.
The saying describes the goal of every attack.
A goal has four corners.
questions.description: Geometry class, the way a soccer coach imagines it.
questions.fun_fact: The saying, “Das Runde muss ins Eckige” in German, is credited to coach Sepp Herberger, who led Germany to its first World Cup title in 1954.

questions.question: At the 2010 World Cup, Paul the octopus from Oberhausen picked a food box with a flag before matches. How many of his picks at that World Cup were right?
hints: Paul became world-famous because he was right so often.
He even correctly predicted Germany's semifinal loss to Spain.
The number matches his arms exactly.
questions.description: A soccer expert who studied mussels instead of tactics.
questions.fun_fact: Paul lived at the Sea Life aquarium in Oberhausen, where a memorial to him stands today.

questions.question: 1966 World Cup final: the ball hits the crossbar, bounces down, and England get a goal that is still disputed today. What is this famous goal called?
hints: The goal came in extra time.
Geoff Hurst took the shot, and the linesman ruled it a goal.
The goal is named after the stadium.
questions.description: A ball that still hasn't figured out where it landed back in 1966.
questions.fun_fact: Most later computer analyses found that the ball was not fully over the line.

questions.question: I won the World Cup as a player and as team manager, and the Ballon d'Or in 1972 and 1976. People called me “the Kaiser”. Who am I?
hints: I mostly played as a sweeper (libero).
I was captain when Germany won the 1974 World Cup.
My first name is Franz.
questions.description: A man who collected golden balls the way other people collect stamps.
questions.fun_fact: In 1990, Beckenbauer led Germany to the title as “team manager” because he didn't have a coaching license.

questions.question: Since 1982, Campino has sung in a Düsseldorf punk band named after a German saying. What does “tote Hose” mean?
hints: You say it about a place or an evening.
People often say it about a village on a Saturday night.
The opposite would be: “This place is buzzing!”
questions.description: A band named after a piece of clothing that is not feeling well at all.
questions.fun_fact: Campino's real name is Andreas Frege.

questions.question: Cro's first big album was called “Raop,” a mix of rap and pop. In what year did it come out?
hints: That same year, his hit “Easy” was playing on every radio station.
That year, the European Championship in soccer was held in Poland and Ukraine.
The Olympic Games were held in London that same year.
questions.description: When two music styles get married, their baby needs a new name.
questions.fun_fact: “Raop” went straight to No. 1 on the German album charts.

questions.question: Complete this: “Lex Luthor is to Superman as Ming the Merciless is to…”
hints: He is a comic-strip hero from the 1930s.
Ming rules the planet Mongo.
In 1980 he got a movie with music by the band Queen.
questions.description: A space emperor with a soap-opera villain mustache and a nickname that doesn't win friends.
questions.fun_fact: Queen's song for the 1980 movie made the shout “Flash! Ah-ah!” famous.

questions.question: The influential Krautrock band Can was founded in 1968. In which city?
hints: Two of its founders had studied with Karlheinz Stockhausen.
The city is on the Rhine.
The city is famous for its cathedral and its carnival.
questions.description: A band whose name you could also find on the soup shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Can bassist Holger Czukay and keyboardist Irmin Schmidt were both students of Karlheinz Stockhausen.

questions.question: Which singer almost always wears a baseball cap, sang “Chöre” and was a coach on “The Voice Kids”?
hints: He comes from the Palatinate region.
He also sang the hit “Sowieso”.
His last name sounds almost like someone who works in the woods.
questions.description: German pop, where every single chorus comes with an earworm guarantee.
questions.fun_fact: Mark Forster’s real name is Mark Ćwiertnia.

questions.question: “Haus am See” by Peter Fox is playing on the radio. In what year did his album “Stadtaffe”, which has this song, come out?
hints: That year, Austria and Switzerland hosted the European Football Championship.
That year, Barack Obama was elected US president.
That same year, the Olympic Games were held in Beijing.
questions.description: A house by the lake sounds lovely, as long as you don't have to mow the lawn.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Fox's real name is Pierre Baigorry, and he also sings in the Berlin band Seeed.

questions.question: For decades, the Westfalenhalle has hosted rock concerts, boxing matches and the techno party “Mayday”. In which city is it?
hints: The city is in the Ruhr area.
A huge soccer stadium stands right next door.
This is the home of BVB.
questions.description: A hall that has seen more bass, boxing gloves and beer cups than any school gym.
questions.fun_fact: The first Westfalenhalle opened back in 1925.

questions.question: Since what year has VOX been airing “Sing meinen Song – Das Tauschkonzert”?
hints: The show is usually filmed in South Africa.
The show's first host was Xavier Naidoo.
It was the year Germany beat Brazil 7–1.
questions.description: Musical clothes swapping: everyone gets to try on someone else's song.
questions.fun_fact: The idea comes from the Netherlands, where the show is called “De beste zangers van Nederland.”

questions.question: In 1977, Kraftwerk named an album after this train, the Trans Europ Express. Who was it first meant for?
hints: Comfort and speed came first.
The trains were meant to get people quickly to meetings in other big cities.
If you wore a suit and had to get from Amsterdam to Paris fast, this was your seat.
questions.description: An album you really shouldn't ride without a ticket.
questions.fun_fact: TEE trains ran from 1957 and linked big cities in several countries of Western Europe.

questions.question: DJs call it a “turntable”: a record spins on it while a needle follows the grooves. What is it called in German?
hints: Grandma probably had one in her living room.
Without it, a record stays silent.
Its German name includes the German word for the thing that sits on it.
questions.description: A machine DJs use to prove that old doesn't have to mean boring.
questions.fun_fact: When DJs scratch, they move the record back and forth by hand so it makes scratching and squeaking sounds.

questions.question: In which Hamburg band did Jan Delay once rap under the name “Eißfeldt”?
hints: The group's name used to be a bit longer.
Their “Liebeslied” was all over the radio in the late '90s.
They used to call themselves “Absolute …”.
questions.description: Before he shone solo with his hat and his nasal voice, this Hamburg artist already had a rap past.
questions.fun_fact: Jan Delay's real name is Jan Phillip Eißfeldt, which is where his rap name “Eißfeldt” comes from.

questions.question: In 1994, Berlin techno DJ Marusha had a big hit with a rave version of which film song?
hints: The original is from 1939.
The film is about a girl from Kansas who ends up in a magical land.
Judy Garland sang the original as Dorothy.
questions.description: Back when techno played at the Love Parade and on cassettes, this Berliner sent a classic through the bass machine.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1990s, Marusha was one of the best-known faces of Berlin's Love Parade.

questions.question: You buy shares in a famous sports shoe company. What do you become?
hints: Now you own a tiny piece of the company.
If the company does well, you might do well too.
The word comes straight from what you bought.
questions.description: Owning a piece of a giant company without ever sitting through a boring meeting.
questions.fun_fact: The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, is considered the first company to sell shares to the public.

questions.question: Which East German athlete won Olympic gold with this piece of equipment in 1972 and 1976?
hints: She was born in Egeln (Saxony-Anhalt) and competed for SC Motor Jena.
Later she went into politics and sat in the Bundestag.
Her surname is the German word for an animal with a bushy tail.
questions.description: A piece of sports equipment that makes you think twice before taking a walk in front of the thrower.
questions.fun_fact: Ruth Fuchs set several javelin world records during her career.

questions.question: “Francesco Friedrich is to bobsled as Felix Loch is to …” Which sport is missing?
hints: Both race down the same ice track.
Felix Loch lies on his back while racing.
Feet go first and the head is at the back, unlike in skeleton.
questions.description: A sport where Germany has won so many medals for decades that the trophy cabinets are running out of room.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2010 Vancouver Olympics, Felix Loch became the youngest-ever Olympic champion in men's singles luge, at age 20.

questions.question: His father came from Sardinia, people called him “Rocky,” and he fought Henry Maske twice. In which city did Graciano Rocchigiani grow up?
hints: The city is one of the largest in Germany.
The city is neither on the Rhine nor in Bavaria.
The city is the German capital.
questions.description: A boxer who could hit hard with his fists, and just as hard with his words.
questions.fun_fact: Rocchigiani was world champion in two weight classes: super middleweight and light heavyweight.

questions.question: I've been rolling out of Wolfsburg since 1974 and took over from the Beetle as the bestseller. A generation is even named after me. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the best-selling cars in the world.
A well-known book by Florian Illies is called “Generation …”.
I share my name with a sport played with clubs and small holes in the grass.
questions.description: A car that seems to be parked outside every other German row house.
questions.fun_fact: The Passat and the Scirocco are named after winds, so VW apparently loved weather maps.

questions.question: Before an autobahn exit there are signs with three, two and one red stripe. How far before the exit is the one-stripe sign?
hints: At 130 km/h (81 mph), you're there in a few seconds.
Each stripe stands for the same distance.
The three-stripe sign stands 300 meters before the exit.
questions.description: A countdown for drivers, with no New Year's fireworks at the end.
questions.fun_fact: The red-and-white signs are officially called Ankündigungsbaken, or “advance warning posts”.

questions.question: What is this machine at the edge of the ski slope?
hints: Without it, many ski slopes would be green instead of white in winter.
It needs water, electricity and cold weather.
It sprays tiny water droplets that freeze in the cold air.
questions.description: This machine often works hard at night, long after every skier has gone to bed.
questions.fun_fact: Artificial snow from a snow cannon is made of tiny ice pellets, so it is harder than real snow.

It asks the same thing from a photo with the same answer, so players who meet both get the answer handed to them. The translation itself is accurate and reads naturally. Keep only one of the two questions, or turn this one into a different question about snowmaking with a real German link.

This duplicates the approved q-4990 (“Look closely at this machine on a ski slope. What is it?” → A snow cannon). English players would get the same photo question with the same answer twice. Drop one of the two from the English pool. The translation itself is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: Green, shiny and set firm: which sweet dish do you see here in a close-up?
hints: You stir it together from powder, sugar and water and let it set in the fridge.
Green kinds often taste of Waldmeister (woodruff).
Its nickname is “Wackelpudding.”
questions.description: A dessert that has to sit and think in the fridge for a good long while before it’s ready.
questions.fun_fact: Götterspeise is usually set with gelatin, but some kinds use agar-agar made from seaweed.

questions.question: Wooden stalls, gingerbread hearts, candied roasted almonds and warm kids' punch: which market is this?
hints: It's only open for a few weeks a year.
It takes place during Advent.
It belongs to the time of year when you write your wish list.
questions.description: Suddenly the whole town center smells of cinnamon and sugar.
questions.fun_fact: Dresden's Striezelmarkt was already around in 1434, and it's seen as one of the oldest Christmas markets in Germany.

questions.question: Which country does the Advent calendar come from?
hints: The Advent wreath also comes from this country.
Families there used to count the days to Christmas with chalk marks on the door.
The first printed Advent calendar came out in Munich.
questions.description: 24 little doors, and behind each one lives impatience.
questions.fun_fact: The first printed Advent calendar was published by Munich publisher Gerhard Lang in the early 20th century.

questions.question: I have no handles and no wicker, but I hold rice, milk, rent and bus fares, and I'm checked every month. What am I for?
questions.answer: To measure how much prices go up
wrong_answers: To work out how much tax you pay
To count how many people live in the country
hints: I'm a list of what a typical household buys.
Economists compare what I cost before with what I cost now.
I'm how inflation gets calculated.
questions.description: The most famous basket in the country, and nobody has ever seen it.
questions.fun_fact: The basket used to measure inflation holds hundreds of goods and services, from potatoes to haircuts.

questions.question: Starting in March 2020, almost all schools in Germany stayed closed for weeks. What was the reason?
hints: It was about everyone's health.
Many children had school only on a computer at home back then.
The virus was called SARS-CoV-2.
questions.description: A spring when the living room was a classroom, an office and a gym all at once.
questions.fun_fact: In March 2020, Merkel said that since the Second World War there had been no challenge where acting together mattered so much.

questions.question: On August 13, 1961, East Germany sealed off the border in Berlin. With what, before the concrete wall went up?
hints: It had to be quick and work in a single night.
You know it from fences around cow pastures.
It has sharp spikes.
questions.description: A building project that started overnight, without asking the neighbors for a permit.
questions.fun_fact: Only in the days that followed did workers gradually replace the wire with walls of stone and concrete.

questions.question: I was a poet and a hunter, and I wrote so much about the heath that people call me the “Heath Poet”. I wrote “Auf der Lüneburger Heide”. Who am I?
hints: I lived from 1866 to 1914.
I died as a soldier in France in World War I.
My first name is Hermann.
questions.description: Purple heather, yellow sun, black ink: this gentleman needed nothing more to be happy.
questions.fun_fact: His grave lies in the middle of the Lüneburg Heath, near Walsrode.

questions.question: You hear “Hey, hey, Wickie!” on TV. What part of the world do Wickie and the strong men come from?
hints: Winters there are cold and dark for a long time.
Wickie's father is Halvar, chief of the village of Flake.
Wickie's people are Vikings.
questions.description: A little boy with big ideas, plus a crew that would rather row than think.
questions.fun_fact: The cartoon was made in Japan in 1974 for the German TV channel ZDF, and the books it's based on were written by the Swede Runer Jonsson.

questions.question: I'm a TV show full of puppets, in Germany since 1973. My song says: “Wer nicht fragt, bleibt dumm!” (“If you don't ask, you'll never learn!”). Who am I?
hints: Kids learn letters and numbers with me.
I originally come from the USA.
Ernie and Bert live with me.
questions.description: Puppets live here who ask more questions than any kindergartner.
questions.fun_fact: Samson the bear and the pink creature Tiffy were invented just for the German Sesamstraße.

questions.question: In first grade, many children in Germany get a “Fibel”. What is this book for?
hints: You need it at the very start of school.
It has lots of colorful pictures and hardly any text at first.
A for Affe (monkey), B for Ball …
questions.description: A book you later find far too thin, but never quite forget.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Fibel” probably comes from children mispronouncing “Bibel” (Bible), the book people once learned to read from.

questions.question: Many picture books about this character are called “… will nicht …” (“… doesn't want to …”), like not wanting to go to bed or to share. Who is it?
hints: The character is an animal.
Its first name is also the name of a star sign.
Its last name ends in the German word for a small, cheeky rodent.
questions.description: A picture-book hero who turns stubborn the moment someone says “bed.”
questions.fun_fact: Leo Lausemaus is originally from Italy, where he is called “Topo Tip.”

questions.question: Which animal is NOT one of Urmel's friends on the island of Titiwu?
hints: On the island, Professor Habakuk Tibatong teaches the animals to talk.
Wawa lives in a seashell.
The animal you want has a great many teeth and lives in the river.
questions.description: An island where animals learn to talk, though not always quite correctly.
questions.fun_fact: Urmel became famous through the Augsburger Puppenkiste puppet theater, and the books were written by Max Kruse.

questions.question: This comic magazine almost always came with a free gadget, most famously brine shrimp you could raise at home. Which magazine was it?
hints: The magazine started in the 1970s.
Its mascot was a kangaroo.
Its name has only three letters.
questions.description: Pets you could buy at the newsstand and raise in a toothbrush cup.
questions.fun_fact: Brine shrimp eggs can survive dry for years and only hatch once they’re in water.

questions.question: When does the Sandmännchen show its bedtime story on KiKA?
hints: After that, it's off to bed.
The Tagesschau news at 8 p.m. comes quite a bit later.
It's on around suppertime, a good hour before the Tagesschau.
questions.description: A little man with a pointy beard and a bag of sand, more punctual than any train.
questions.fun_fact: The Sandmännchen has been around since 1959, starting almost at the same time in East and West Germany.

questions.question: We're brothers, we wear masks and prison numbers, and we keep trying to rob Scrooge McDuck's money bin. Who are we?
hints: We show up in the adventures of DuckTales.
Our mom is a thief too.
Our name comes from a breed of dog, the same breed as Snoopy.
questions.description: A very close family, especially when they're planning something they shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: The Beagle Boys were created by cartoonist Carl Barks and first appeared in a comic book in 1951.

questions.question: In Roman buildings, like those in Trier or at the Saalburg, often only small brick pillars are left of the hypocaust. What did it do?
wrong_answers: It piped water into the house
It cooled food in the cellar
hints: The Greek part “hypo” means “under”.
The second part of the word is linked to “burning”.
It was an early kind of heating.
questions.description: The Romans brought more than roads to Germania: they brought a little luxury too.
questions.fun_fact: At the Saalburg in the Taunus hills, a whole Roman fort has been rebuilt.

questions.question: In August 1948, experts spent two weeks on an island in a Bavarian lake drafting the basis of the Grundgesetz (Basic Law). Which island?
hints: The lake is also called the “Bavarian Sea”.
It is the largest island in its lake.
On the same island, King Ludwig II built a palace modeled on Versailles.
questions.description: If you want to write a constitution, you need peace, lake air and ideally no bridge to the mainland.
questions.fun_fact: The convention met in the Old Palace, not in Ludwig II's grand New Palace next door.

questions.question: In 1988, this tennis player won all four Grand Slam tournaments plus Olympic gold. Who is she?
hints: She won her first Grand Slam title at the 1987 French Open.
She won Wimbledon seven times.
She is married to tennis star Andre Agassi.
questions.description: A ball machine would need overtime to keep up with this tennis year.
questions.fun_fact: Steffi Graf was ranked world number one for a total of 377 weeks, longer than any other woman.

questions.question: This politician was Germany's chancellor for 16 years. Which party does she belong to?
hints: This party has provided the most chancellors so far.
Konrad Adenauer and Helmut Kohl belonged to it too.
Its sister party in Bavaria is called the CSU.
questions.description: Her hand gesture became more famous than many of her government speeches.
questions.fun_fact: Angela Merkel was the first woman to lead a German federal government.

questions.question: Thomas Kretschmann (“The Pianist”, “King Kong”) escaped East Germany on foot across several borders as a young man. In which decade?
hints: He was in his early twenties at the time.
Erich Honecker was ruling East Germany then.
A few years later, the Wall came down.
questions.description: Before playing captains and officers in Hollywood, he went on a rather long walk.
questions.fun_fact: Before becoming an actor, Thomas Kretschmann was a competitive swimmer in East Germany.

questions.question: The company Pelikan was founded in Hanover in 1838. What does it mainly make?
hints: You need these things at school.
Ink and ink cartridges are part of it too.
Fountain pens, paint boxes and watercolors.
questions.description: A bird with a big beak that made it big as a famous German brand.
questions.fun_fact: The pelican in the logo comes from the family coat of arms of Günther Wagner, who took over the company in the 19th century.

questions.question: Which of these sports brands does NOT come from Germany?
hints: The brand you want comes from another continent.
Its logo is a curved check mark.
It comes from the USA.
questions.description: Three of these brands carry a German passport; one is just visiting the playing field.
questions.fun_fact: Puma and Adidas both come from Herzogenaurach and were founded by two brothers who fell out, Rudolf and Adolf Dassler.

questions.question: In which city did Dirk Rossmann open his first drugstore in 1972, Germany's first self-service drugstore?
hints: The city has more than half a million people.
It is in northern Germany.
The world's fair Expo was held here in 2000.
questions.description: A man whose name is on more shopping bags than business cards.
questions.fun_fact: Dirk Rossmann has also written novels, including the bestseller “Der neunte Arm des Oktopus” (“The Ninth Arm of the Octopus”).

questions.question: On an East German vacation, you get to the Baltic beach early in the morning and shovel a sand wall around your spot. What have you built?
hints: It's only meant for one vacation; wind and waves soon flatten it again.
Families often decorated it with shells and stones.
Its German name means something like “beach castle”.
questions.description: Turf wars on the Baltic beach: first to dig is first to lie down.
questions.fun_fact: Many families decorated their Strandburg with shells and spelled out the name of their hometown in stones.

questions.question: He's a billionaire, lives in a mansion in Gotham, and his butler is named Alfred. Where did his fortune come from?
hints: We're talking about the man behind Batman's mask.
He didn't have to earn it all by himself.
His family was already rich and owned a big company before he was born.
questions.description: A butler, a mansion and a secret cave don't come cheap.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce Wayne has appeared on Forbes magazine's lists of the richest fictional characters.

questions.question: In the GDR, Western money was in high demand, for example for shopping at the Intershop. Who did most people get it from?
wrong_answers: From their workplace as a bonus
From the bank at the exchange desk
From school as report card money
hints: The East German state didn't just hand it out.
It often came along with parcels from the West or during visits.
Grandma and Uncle from West Germany were happy to help out.
questions.description: Money that was worth more in the East than in the place it came from.
questions.fun_fact: From 1979 on, Western money had to be exchanged for so-called Forumschecks before you could shop at the Intershop.

questions.question: On October 9, 1989, Kurt Masur and five others called on Leipzig to stay calm. Who was NOT among these signers?
hints: The appeal was read out over the city's loudspeakers.
One of the six usually performed on stage with the “academixer” cabaret.
The “Leipzig Six” came from culture, the church and the party.
questions.description: A conductor who, for once, calmed not just an orchestra but a whole city.
questions.fun_fact: That same evening about 70,000 people marched in Leipzig, peacefully, and nobody stepped in to stop them.

questions.question: About how much used clothing does Germany collect per person each year?
hints: It's much more than a single T-shirt.
It would roughly fill a packed moving box.
Roughly: more than 10 but less than 20 kilograms.
questions.description: This is where your favorite sweater from fifth grade starts a whole new life.
questions.fun_fact: Only part of the used clothing gets worn again; a lot of it is turned into cleaning rags or insulation.

questions.question: In Germany, you call an ambulance by dialing 11… What is the last digit?
hints: It's the same number as for the fire department.
This number reaches emergency services all over Europe.
110 calls the police, and the ambulance number comes right after it.
questions.description: Three digits you hopefully never need but should always know.
questions.fun_fact: 112 is the emergency number in every country of the European Union.

questions.question: At DHL, what makes a Päckchen different from a Paket?
hints: It is the cheaper of the two ways to ship.
It's about what happens if the shipment gets lost.
A lost Paket is covered up to 500 euros, but a Päckchen isn't.
questions.description: The little brother of a big delivery.
questions.fun_fact: A DHL Päckchen may weigh no more than 2 kg (4.4 lb), while a Paket can weigh up to 31.5 kg (about 69 lb).

questions.question: It stood over 110 m (360 ft) tall, sent Apollo 11 to the Moon in 1969 and was built under Wernher von Braun. Which rocket was it?
hints: It had three stages that were dropped one after another.
It is still one of the most powerful rockets ever flown.
Its name is shared with a planet that has rings.
questions.description: A skyscraper with a fiery tail, built to the plans of a man from Wirsitz.
questions.fun_fact: Between 1969 and 1972, the Saturn V carried the twelve people who walked on the Moon.

questions.question: In 1967, a Henkel researcher on a plane saw a woman putting on makeup, which gave him the idea for the glue stick. What was she using?
hints: Many people carry it in their handbag.
You twist it up out of a small tube.
You put it on your mouth.
questions.description: A stick that doesn't write, but still sticks to everything.
questions.fun_fact: The Pritt stick came out in 1969 and is now sold in many countries around the world.

questions.question: This bird stars in the old saying “Grain by grain, the hen fills her crop.” What does the saying teach?
questions.answer: That saving bit by bit adds up
wrong_answers: That food is worth more than money
hints: The hen doesn’t eat everything in one bite.
Think of a piggy bank where you drop in a coin every day.
Lots of small things together make something big.
questions.description: A bird that has been teaching money lessons for centuries without charging a cent.
questions.fun_fact: The crop is a little pouch in a bird’s neck where it stores food before digesting it.

questions.question: In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler made the salt ammonium cyanate into a substance known until then only from living things. Which one?
hints: Today it's found in many skin creams and fertilizers.
Our kidneys get rid of it every day.
Its name comes from the same root as the word “urine”.
questions.description: A chemist who stole the show from the “life force” right in a test tube.
questions.fun_fact: Wöhler wrote excitedly to his teacher that he could make urea “without needing kidneys”.

questions.question: Around 1510, Nuremberg locksmith Peter Henlein is said to have built a small object known as the “Nuremberg Egg”. What was it?
hints: It was a small masterpiece of fine mechanics.
You could carry it around with you.
It showed you what time it was.
questions.description: An egg that no chick will ever hatch from.
questions.fun_fact: The name “egg” probably comes from a misreading: the little clocks were called “Aeurlein”, meaning “little clocks”.

questions.question: In which decade did the very first “Bravo Hits” CD come out?
hints: There were no smartphones back then.
Many people listened to it on the go with a Discman.
The Olympic Games in Barcelona took place the same year.
questions.description: The playlist you used to have to buy in a store.
questions.fun_fact: By 2018, the 100th edition of “Bravo Hits” had already come out.

questions.question: In a kids’ hit that topped the charts in 2005, Schnappi sings that he comes from Egypt, right on the Nile. What kind of animal is Schnappi?
hints: This animal lives both in water and on land.
It has a long snout full of teeth.
It’s a big green reptile with armored skin.
questions.description: An earworm from Egypt that had whole kindergartens in its grip.
questions.fun_fact: “Schnappi” was sung by a little girl, Joy Gruttmann, and the song hit number 1 in the German charts in early 2005.

questions.question: You're in the long line outside the Berlin techno club Berghain. What was the huge concrete building originally?
hints: The building dates from the days of East Germany.
Things got hot in here long before the music arrived.
It once made heat for lots of Berlin apartments.
questions.description: A place where you wait in line for hours just to maybe get turned away.
questions.fun_fact: The name Berghain combines the districts of Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain, on whose border the club sits.

questions.question: We're from Stuttgart, and in 1997 we rapped about a woman whose name reads the same forward and backward. Later we sang “Mit dir” with Joy Denalane. Who are we?
hints: Our best-known hit is a love song.
Our frontman Max Herre is also successful solo today.
Our name means “circle of friends”.
questions.description: Swabian rapping with a big heart and an umbrella.
questions.fun_fact: Max Herre and Joy Denalane, who sang “Mit dir” together, later became a couple in real life too.

questions.question: Karel Gott, the “golden voice of Prague”, sang the German theme song of a cartoon series in 1976. Which one?
hints: The main character is very small.
The main character is not a human.
She flies over the flower meadow, collecting adventures instead of honey.
questions.description: Straight from Prague into every German kid's bedroom, with a single tune.
questions.fun_fact: The series is based on the 1912 children's book “The Adventures of Maya the Bee” by Waldemar Bonsels.

questions.question: Which instrument is shown in the picture?
hints: You blow into it.
It is usually made of wood or plastic.
Many children learn it as their very first instrument at school.
questions.description: An instrument whose first notes are rarely its prettiest.
questions.fun_fact: Recorders already existed in the Middle Ages, long before anyone taught them at school.

questions.question: “I'm made of shiny brass, have three valves and play the highest notes of the brass section in an orchestra.” Who am I?
hints: I belong to the brass instruments.
I'm fairly small and sound bright.
Louis Armstrong made me famous around the world.
questions.description: I'm loud, I'm shiny, and the neighbors don't always love me.
questions.fun_fact: A trumpet is really a tube about 1.5 m (5 ft) long that has simply been bent into loops.

questions.question: M-Pesa, a service for sending money by phone, launched in 2007 in an African country. Which one?
hints: It's a country in East Africa.
It's famous for its safaris and its marathon runners.
Its capital is Nairobi.
questions.description: Sending money by text message before it was cool.
questions.fun_fact: “Pesa” means “money” in Swahili, and the “M” stands for “mobile.”

questions.question: Who is this Schlager singer and TV host?
hints: He comes from Lower Bavaria.
As a child he started out on the Steirische Harmonika, a button accordion.
His last name begins with the German word for a precious metal.
questions.description: He owns more glitter jackets than most people own socks.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, Florian Silbereisen took over as Captain Max Parger on the TV series “Das Traumschiff”.

questions.question: Which statement about the 50:50 lifeline on “Wer wird Millionär?” is NOT true?
wrong_answers: The right answer stays on screen
It can only be used once per game
hints: Three statements describe exactly how the lifeline works.
One statement sounds plausible, but would make the game far too easy.
The computer makes the choice.
questions.description: Half the worries, at least on the screen.
questions.fun_fact: The 50:50 is the only lifeline where no other person helps at all.

questions.question: On “Wer wird Millionär?” it has existed since 1999: a person picked in advance gets 30 seconds to help. Which lifeline is it?
hints: It's one of the lifelines that were already there in the very first show.
Contestants often pick someone who knows a lot for it.
Back then, it usually meant a landline ringing.
questions.description: When your head goes completely silent, maybe someone else can help.
questions.fun_fact: Many contestants pick friends with special knowledge for this lifeline, such as teachers or librarians.

questions.question: I'm a fashion designer, and on VOX I judge how contestants spend 500 euros in four hours on an outfit for a theme. Who am I?
hints: Besides fashion, I also write books.
My show has aired in the early evening since 2012.
My show is called “Shopping Queen”.
questions.description: Get the theme wrong here, and you'll be wearing your mistake on TV.
questions.fun_fact: The designer reveals his scores, up to ten per outfit, only in the last episode of the week.

questions.question: Since 1954 it has aired late on Saturday nights on Das Erste and lasts only a few minutes. Who speaks in “Das Wort zum Sonntag”?
hints: The show is hardly younger than the Tagesschau.
The speakers mainly want to make you stop and think.
The speakers take turns coming from the Protestant and the Catholic Church.
questions.description: Four minutes of quiet thoughts before Saturday night is finally over.
questions.fun_fact: After the Tagesschau, “Das Wort zum Sonntag” is the second-oldest show still running on German TV.

questions.question: In Wolfsburg, two glass towers are filled almost to the top. With what?
hints: The towers belong to the city's best-known company.
Customers come here to pick up their purchase in person.
A robot elevator brings the freshly bought vehicle down.
questions.description: Wolfsburg's answer to the question of where to put everything that no longer fits in the basement.
questions.fun_fact: Each car tower is 48 m (157 ft) tall and holds about 400 cars.

questions.question: Germany's highest railroad bridge opened in 1897 and crosses the river Wupper near Solingen. What is it made of?
hints: In the 19th century, this material was a symbol of the industrial age.
The two halves of the arch grew out from both sides of the valley without supports until they met in the middle.
In hot weather, the bridge's metal expands by a measurable amount.
questions.description: A bridge where a fear of heights is not a good travel companion.
questions.fun_fact: The bridge, about 107 m (351 ft) high, was called the Kaiser Wilhelm Bridge when it opened.

questions.question: A famous legend is set in Hamelin on the Weser River. What did the stranger first play his flute for?
hints: The town had a big problem with animals.
The animals were eating up the townspeople's food supplies.
His German name, “Rattenfänger”, tells you what he caught.
questions.description: A musician who, in the end, collected his fee in a very unusual way.
questions.fun_fact: Hamelin has a lane where, because of the legend, no music may be played to this day.

questions.question: What is the frame of the giant Colossos roller coaster at Heide Park made of?
hints: The material is much older than any roller coaster.
Coasters made of this material rattle and shake much more than modern rides.
It comes from the forest.
questions.description: A roller coaster that makes your knees go weak just from watching.
questions.fun_fact: Colossos opened in 2001 and is one of the tallest wooden roller coasters in Europe.

questions.question: Germany's biggest theme park is in Rust. What are many of its themed areas named after?
hints: The park's name gives a lot away.
For example, there are areas with pizza and gondolas.
In one day you can walk from France to Italy.
questions.description: A day out that leaves even the grandparents completely out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Europa-Park opened in 1975 and belongs to the Mack family, who have been building rides for centuries.

questions.question: Complete this: an umbrella is to rain as an emergency fund is to…
hints: You need an umbrella for something you can't be sure when it will come.
Think of a fridge that breaks down or a trip to the doctor.
It's something you never planned to pay for.
questions.description: Money you put aside for when life decides to play a prank on you.
questions.fun_fact: Many experts say an emergency fund should be big enough to cover three to six months of expenses.

questions.question: “Swag” was Germany’s Youth Word of the Year 2011. Complete the sentence: someone with “swag” has…
hints: It’s about how someone comes across to others.
Back then, rappers all wanted to have it.
You could also say: they’re just cool.
questions.description: A word everyone said in 2011 and that today only parents use to embarrass their kids.
questions.fun_fact: Before “Swag”, the 2010 Youth Word was “Niveaulimbo” (roughly “limbo of standards”), and after it came “YOLO” in 2012.

questions.question: This detail shows a mythical creature from a coat of arms. Which one is it?
hints: It has something of the king of birds and something of the king of beasts.
A university town on the Baltic Sea carries its German name.
It has the head and wings of an eagle and the body of a lion.
questions.description: A heraldic animal you are guaranteed never to have seen at the zoo.
questions.fun_fact: The town of Greifswald is named after the griffin (Greif in German), the heraldic animal of the dukes of Pomerania.

questions.question: It ruled Bavaria until 1918, supplied the Counts Palatine of the Rhine and put the golden Palatinate lion into coats of arms. Which family is it?
hints: One branch of the family even gave Sweden its kings.
The “Fairy-Tale King” Ludwig II was one of them.
Their family seat was a castle near Aichach whose name starts with “W”.
questions.description: A family that left its big cat behind in several German states.
questions.fun_fact: The Wittelsbachs ruled Bavaria for more than 700 years, from 1180 to 1918.

questions.question: France is to blue-white-red as Germany is to …?
hints: You see these colors on flags and jerseys at every soccer World Cup.
The darkest of the three colors is at the very top of the flag.
The top stripe is as dark as the night, the middle one like a strawberry.
questions.description: Three stripes, one country and quite a lot of face paint on fans' cheeks.
questions.fun_fact: Black, red and gold flags were already flying at the Hambach Festival in 1832 as a sign of unity and freedom.

questions.question: I proudly say “Mia san mia”, meaning “We are who we are”. Who am I?
hints: My state is the largest in Germany.
Neuschwanstein Castle is in my state.
My state colors are white and blue.
questions.description: Self-confidence in three words, no grammar lesson needed.
questions.fun_fact: At just over 70,000 square kilometers (27,000 square miles), Bavaria is bigger than all of Switzerland.

questions.question: I was built in England, and on December 7, 1835, I steamed from Nuremberg to Fürth as Germany's first locomotive. What is my name?
hints: The Ludwig Railway I ran on was only just over six kilometers (about 4 miles) long.
My name comes from nature, not from technology.
My name is also the animal on Germany's coat of arms.
questions.description: Six kilometers, lots of steam, and all of Franconia watching with its mouth wide open.
questions.fun_fact: The Adler's first driver was an Englishman: William Wilson.

questions.question: On the Autobahn, yellow lines suddenly replace the white ones, lanes get narrower and the limit is often 80 km/h (50 mph). What is this stretch called?
hints: This stretch only stays for a while, then it's gone again.
You often see excavators and orange-and-white posts there.
People in hard hats are working on the road here.
questions.description: The place where GPS suddenly gets its math wrong and patience snaps.
questions.fun_fact: When yellow and white lines are both there, the yellow ones always win.

questions.question: It often runs next to the sidewalk, is sometimes paved in red, and has its own round blue sign. Who is this path for?
hints: These people sit on a saddle while they ride.
These people often wear a helmet.
They push the pedals.
questions.description: In traffic everyone has their own place – you just have to know which line belongs to whom.
questions.fun_fact: Germany even has bike highways (Radschnellwege), a kind of autobahn just for bicycles.

questions.question: I'm an airline, and my name, QANTAS, is an acronym that starts with “Queensland.” Which country am I from?
hints: My country is in the Southern Hemisphere.
Queensland is a region famous for a huge coral reef.
A red kangaroo is painted on the tail of my planes.
questions.description: An airline whose name sounds like a tongue twister but is really a geography lesson.
questions.fun_fact: Qantas was founded in 1920 and is one of the oldest airlines in the world that is still flying.

questions.question: Children walk through the streets with lanterns singing: “Laterne, Laterne, Sonne, Mond und …” What comes next?
hints: It's something in the night sky.
There are lots and lots of them up there.
They twinkle at night and rhyme with “Laterne”.
questions.description: In November it gets dark early, but some kids bring their own light.
questions.fun_fact: The lantern parade usually takes place around St. Martin's Day on November 11.

questions.question: People once washed clothes on it; today musicians rattle across it wearing thimbles. What kind of instrument is the washboard?
hints: You don't need any breath to play it.
It keeps the rhythm.
Drums and cymbals belong to this group too.
questions.description: Grandma never dreamed her cleaning gear would end up on stage one day.
questions.fun_fact: Washboard players often wear thimbles so the rattle sounds loud and their fingers stay unhurt.

questions.question: In 1969 Michael Holm sang “Mendocino”, based on a song by a band from Texas. Where is the town of Mendocino?
hints: The town is on the Pacific.
It is known for its foggy cliffs and old wooden houses.
From there it's not far to San Francisco.
questions.description: A place half of Germany went looking for on the radio in 1969.
questions.fun_fact: The original “Mendocino” was released by the Sir Douglas Quintet in 1968.

questions.question: It's often taller than an adult, you play it standing up, and it sounds the lowest. What is the largest bowed string instrument in the orchestra?
hints: You play it with a bow or pluck it.
It's even bigger than the cello.
Its name contains the musical word for the lowest voice.
questions.description: An instrument that really ought to get its own seat on the bus.
questions.fun_fact: In folk music and jazz, the double bass is often not bowed at all but plucked.

questions.question: In the children's song, this animal stole the goose. Who will come for it “mit dem Schießgewehr” (with his gun)?
hints: He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He often wears a green hat.
The German line goes: “sonst wird dich der … holen.”
questions.description: This animal has a guilty conscience and one roast goose too many.
questions.fun_fact: The song was written by the teacher Ernst Anschütz, who also gave “O Tannenbaum” the form everyone knows today.

questions.question: “A children's song is about us: we swim on the lake, heads in the water, tails up high.” Who are we?
hints: We have feathers.
We're fairly small and say “quack.”
In the German song we're “alle meine …chen.”
questions.description: A family that doesn't care one bit about its hairdo at bath time.
questions.fun_fact: Many children learn their first notes with “Alle meine Entchen” because the tune simply climbs up the scale.

questions.question: This lively, hopping couple dance in 2/4 time comes from Bohemia and is a must at any Musikantenstadl. What is it called?
hints: It comes from what is now the Czech Republic.
It's faster than the waltz.
It starts with “Pol…”.
questions.description: A dance that makes even Grandpa start hopping again.
questions.fun_fact: Around 1840, the polka was so popular in Paris that people spoke of a real “polkamania”.

questions.question: “I have three corners and sit on your head. In my song, you leave out words one by one and only show them with your hands.” Who am I?
hints: I'm something you wear.
I can be made of felt or straw and often have a brim.
The song goes: “And if it didn't have three corners, it wouldn't be my …”
questions.description: A song where, by the end, only the hands are still singing.
questions.fun_fact: The song's tune comes from Italy: it is known as “The Carnival of Venice”.

questions.question: Navy ships leaving port are often sent off with “Muss i denn zum Städtele hinaus”. Which US star sang it in 1960 as “Wooden Heart”?
hints: He was born in 1935 in the southern United States.
Shortly before, he had been stationed in Germany as a soldier.
People called him the “King of Rock 'n' Roll”.
questions.description: A farewell song from Swabia that made it all the way to Hollywood.
questions.fun_fact: Elvis sang “Wooden Heart” partly in German in the film “G.I. Blues”, and in 1961 the song went to number 1 in the UK.

questions.question: At airports, “BOG” is to Bogotá as “MAD” is to…
hints: These codes appear on luggage tags.
Look at the first letters of the city's name.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.description: Cities have nicknames too, but only three letters long.
questions.fun_fact: Chicago's airport code is ORD because the airport used to be called Orchard Field.

questions.question: Since which decade has “das aktuelle sportstudio” been on ZDF?
hints: The show is almost as old as ZDF itself.
In the first episodes, the TV picture was still black and white.
The first show aired in the same year ZDF went on the air.
questions.description: Saturday night, a sport coat, studio lights, and a ball that simply refuses to go in the hole.
questions.fun_fact: At the famous Torwand (goal wall), guests take three shots each at the lower and the upper hole from about 7 meters (23 ft).

questions.question: You're on “Wer wird Millionär?” and you use the audience lifeline. What happens next?
wrong_answers: The host gives you a tip
You get more time to think
hints: You don't need a phone number for it.
It depends on lots of people at once.
Afterwards, a bar chart with percentages appears.
questions.description: A million in sight, and suddenly you can't even remember the capital of France.
questions.fun_fact: The studio guests cast their votes using small keypads at their seats.

questions.question: On “The Voice Kids”, the classic seasons have the Battles after the Blind Auditions. How many kids sing one song together there?
hints: More kids sing together than in a duet.
In the end, only one of the kids goes through.
People often call it a trio.
questions.description: First the chairs turn, then things get serious, microphone in hand.
questions.fun_fact: In the Blind Auditions, the coaches sit with their backs to the stage and only hear the voice.

questions.question: Who helped people deep in debt on the RTL show “Raus aus den Schulden”, often using a flip chart?
hints: The show started in 2007.
Before that, he worked in Berlin as a debt counselor.
His first name is Peter.
questions.description: A marker, a big sheet of paper, and suddenly your bank balance is on TV.
questions.fun_fact: The three wrong answers were also well-known RTL helpers: for restaurants, homes and parenting.

questions.question: In which decade did the ZDF music quiz show “Erkennen Sie die Melodie?”, with tunes from opera and operetta, begin?
hints: Back then, West Germany had only a very few TV channels.
Its first host was the actor Ernst Stankovski.
The first episode aired in the year of the first Moon landing.
questions.description: Back then, the whole country hummed arias in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: The show ran until the mid-1980s, hosted last by Günther Schramm.

questions.question: Visitors may have a taste from this chocolate fountain in a museum. In which city is it?
hints: The museum sits right on a big river.
The city is famous for its carnival.
Nearby rises a huge cathedral with two towers.
questions.description: A museum where, for once, you may touch the exhibits, as long as you eat them right away.
questions.fun_fact: The Chocolate Museum opened in 1993 and is one of the most visited museums in Germany.

questions.question: You're standing in Munich in front of the two towers of the Frauenkirche. In which century was the church built?
hints: The church is built in the Gothic style.
It took only about 20 years to build, amazingly fast for such a big church.
It was finished a few years before Columbus reached America.
questions.description: Two towers wearing caps that haven't gone out of fashion in centuries.
questions.fun_fact: In the entrance of the Frauenkirche there's a footprint in the floor, the “Devil's Footstep”, with a legend behind it.

questions.question: An amusement park in Sierksdorf sits right on the Baltic Sea coast. Which historical alliance is it named after?
hints: The alliance's most important city was nearby Lübeck.
Its merchants traded across the North Sea and the Baltic in ships called cogs.
Hamburg and Bremen still carry its name in their official city titles.
questions.description: Roller coasters with a sea view: here the cotton candy tastes a little salty.
questions.fun_fact: Before today's park, a Legoland stood on the same spot from 1973.

questions.question: I was born in Lübeck in 1875 and wrote about a merchant family from my hometown. I won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Who am I?
hints: My most famous novel is set in a Hanseatic city on the river Trave.
I also wrote “The Magic Mountain”.
My brother Heinrich was a writer too.
questions.description: Lübeck is famous for marzipan, but some of its sons are much heavier reading.
questions.fun_fact: The Buddenbrook House on Lübeck's Mengstraße once belonged to Thomas Mann's grandparents.

questions.question: You're lying under palm trees at Tropical Islands in Brandenburg, looking up at the ceiling. About how high is the hall?
hints: The hall was originally built for airships.
A skyscraper with about 30 floors would fit inside.
The Statue of Liberty with its pedestal (93 m, 305 ft) could stand upright inside it.
questions.description: A South Seas vacation with no plane ticket, just a very, very big roof.
questions.fun_fact: It's about 26 °C (79 °F) inside the hall all year round, even when there's snow outside.

questions.question: I'm a Caribbean beach where planes land almost right over the swimmers' heads. Which island am I on?
hints: My name is Maho Beach, and I star in lots of viral videos.
My airport is named after a Dutch princess.
My island is split between France and the Netherlands.
questions.description: A place where sunbathing comes with free hair styling by jet engine.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Martin is one of the smallest islands in the world shared by two countries.

questions.question: In which city does this tower stand?
hints: The city is in the south of Germany.
On a clear day, you can see the Alps from the top.
The 1972 Summer Olympics were held at the foot of the tower.
questions.description: A tower that loves sports but just stands around all day.
questions.fun_fact: The Olympiaturm is about 291 m (955 ft) tall and opened back in 1968, four years before the Games.

questions.question: This Kaiser Wilhelm monument stands high above a narrow point in a river. Which river?
hints: The monument is in North Rhine-Westphalia, near Minden.
The river flows into the North Sea at Bremerhaven.
A mountain range right next to the monument is named after the river.
questions.description: An emperor with a view: standing this high up, he never has to worry about wet feet.
questions.fun_fact: The monument opened in 1896 and stands at the narrow gap known as the “Gateway to Westphalia” (Porta Westfalica).

questions.question: What is the outer shell of this Munich stadium made of, the one that can light up in many colors?
hints: The shell is much lighter than it looks.
The material is see-through and only a fraction of a millimeter thick.
Blowers keep pumping air into the parts all the time.
questions.description: A stadium that changes outfits faster than the players in the locker room.
questions.fun_fact: The shell of the Allianz Arena is made of almost 3,000 separate cushions.

questions.question: Pack animals once carried people and sacks. Now I do that, I'm made of metal, and so Germans call me a “wire donkey”. What am I?
hints: I have no engine.
I have spokes and a chain.
You push the pedals to make me go.
questions.description: A pet that never needs feeding, just a little oil now and then.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has almost as many bicycles as people.

questions.question: You're packing your Klamotten into a suitcase. Which of these is NOT part of your Klamotten?
hints: “Klamotten” is another word for something you need every day.
You hear the word more at home and among friends than at school.
Only one of these is something you can just give a hug.
questions.description: The suitcase is full, but there's surely room for one more thing.
questions.fun_fact: “Klamotten” used to mean something like rags or junk, and only later became a word for clothes.

questions.question: German teens love the youth slang word “delulu”. It’s a short form: which English word is behind it?
hints: The word spread mostly on the internet.
People often say it with a wink about their own rather unrealistic hopes.
It describes someone who believes things that just aren’t true.
questions.description: Teenagers shorten words until only half of them is left.
questions.fun_fact: “Delulu” first caught on among K-pop fans and then spread through TikTok.

questions.question: What is someone doing if they „sich zum Affen machen“?
hints: It's about how you come across to other people.
Afterwards, it's often embarrassing.
The others are laughing at you, not with you.
questions.description: No zoo needed: you can pull off this transformation all by yourself.
questions.fun_fact: German has more monkey sayings: someone who is totally surprised says „Ich glaub, mich laust der Affe!“ (“I think the monkey is picking my lice!”).

questions.question: In German slang, “Kohle” (coal) means money. Which of these words does NOT also mean money?
hints: Three of these words could replace “Geld” at the store.
The word you want has to do with a feeling.
You often have it before a hard test.
questions.description: You can grill with it, but you can also pay with it.
questions.fun_fact: “Bammel” means fear, and “Moos” for money probably comes from Yiddish.

questions.question: Hamburg's coat of arms and state flag have exactly two colors. Which ones?
hints: You can see the same colors on many lighthouses along the coast.
One of the two colors is very light, the other is strong.
The background is the color of ketchup.
questions.description: A Hanseatic city that picked its colors centuries ago and never changed its mind.
questions.fun_fact: Red and white are known as the colors of the Hanseatic League: Bremen and Lübeck have them in their flags too.

questions.question: The white lines airplanes leave in the sky form very high up, where it is extremely cold. What are they made of?
hints: They are close cousins of clouds.
The engine releases hot water vapor that cools down all at once.
It’s the same thing that forms frost in a freezer.
questions.description: Airplanes can draw too, but only in straight lines.
questions.fun_fact: When the air is very humid, these trails can last for hours and turn into real clouds.

questions.question: I'm big and brown, I sleep through the winter in a cave and I love licking honey. On Berlin's coat of arms I stand upright. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the biggest predators in Europe.
Lots of kids take a small cuddly version of me to bed.
My friends Pooh and Baloo are famous.
questions.description: Berlin's mascot wears a fur coat, and it wears it all year round.
questions.fun_fact: A bear already appears on a Berlin city seal from 1280.

questions.question: In a German saying, someone who doesn't say a word is “stumm wie ein …” (“as mute as a …”). As mute as what?
hints: This animal lives in water.
It opens and closes its mouth, but you hear nothing.
It has fins and gills.
questions.description: This saying fits everyone who suddenly goes quiet when it's time to do the dishes.
questions.fun_fact: Fish aren't completely silent: some, like the gurnard, grunt using their swim bladder.

questions.question: On the coat of arms of North Rhine-Westphalia, a white wavy band stands for the Rhineland and a white horse for Westphalia. What stands for Lippe?
hints: It's a plant.
It blooms, and its name is also a girl's first name.
People often give it on Valentine's Day.
questions.description: Three regions, one coat of arms, and none of them wanted to give up its picture.
questions.fun_fact: Lippe was a small state of its own until 1947, when it joined North Rhine-Westphalia.

questions.question: In German, what kind of look is a “Basiliskenblick”?
hints: The word comes from a mythical creature.
People said this creature could kill with its eyes.
It's a look you'd rather not get.
questions.description: A mythical creature that made it all the way from old legends into everyday German.
questions.fun_fact: In the Middle Ages, people believed a basilisk hatched from an egg laid by a rooster and kept warm by a toad.

questions.question: In autumn, German children fly kites on a long string. The German word for a kite is also the name of which mythical creature?
hints: The creature can fly.
It has scales and a long tail.
In fairy tales, it breathes fire.
questions.description: A mythical creature that goes for a walk on a leash every autumn.
questions.fun_fact: In English, the toy is called a “kite” after a bird of prey of the same name.

questions.question: This coin has a silver center and a gold rim, and the German side shows the federal eagle. How much is it worth?
hints: It isn't a cent coin.
Its big sister has the colors the other way around.
It is the smaller of the two two-colored euro coins.
questions.description: Small, round and always a welcome guest in any wallet.
questions.fun_fact: A tiny letter on German euro coins (A, D, F, G or J) tells you which city minted it.

questions.question: Until what time of day is Weißwurst traditionally eaten?
hints: An old saying goes that it must not hear a certain ringing of bells.
People like to eat it with sweet mustard and Brezn (pretzels).
By the time the church bells ring at midday, your plate should be empty.
questions.description: This sausage sticks to a stricter timetable than any school bus.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says a Munich innkeeper invented Weißwurst in 1857 because he had run out of the right casings for bratwurst.

questions.question: A message in a bottle is thrown into the Rhine near Basel and keeps drifting downstream. Which sea does it end up in?
hints: On the way, it drifts past Cologne and Düsseldorf.
Just before the end, it floats through the Netherlands.
Sylt and Heligoland are islands in this sea too.
questions.description: Water needs no passport, yet it still travels through several countries.
questions.fun_fact: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometers (764 miles) long and starts in the Swiss Alps.

questions.question: The Brocken, northern Germany's highest mountain, is here, Luther worked in Wittenberg, and the capital is Magdeburg. Which state?
hints: This state was part of East Germany until 1990.
The Elbe flows through the state and through its capital, too.
Its name starts like the name of its neighbor, whose capital is Dresden.
questions.description: Legend says witches dance on the summit here, and reformers knock on church doors.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Bauhaus building in Dessau is also in Saxony-Anhalt and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: Germany's “new states” joined with reunification in 1990. How many are there, not counting Berlin?
hints: These states were part of East Germany until 1990.
One has Erfurt as its capital, another has Dresden.
They include Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia, plus two with long names.
questions.description: In 1990 the map of Germany grew, and every school atlas got detention.
questions.fun_fact: East Germany replaced its states with districts in 1952; they were only founded again in 1990.

questions.question: East and West Germany became one country again. In which year did this reunification happen?
hints: The Berlin Wall had fallen a year earlier.
It happened in the fall, almost a year after the big Monday demonstrations.
The year ends in 0.
questions.description: Two puzzle halves, one country and quite a lot of sparkling wine.
questions.fun_fact: Since reunification, October 3 has been Germany's national holiday.

questions.question: About how many people live in Thuringia?
hints: Thuringia is one of the smaller German states that isn't a city.
It's far fewer than Berlin, with almost 4 million people.
The number is only a little above Hamburg's population.
questions.description: The green heart of Germany, but how many hearts beat inside it?
