questions.fun_fact: The Rennsteig, a hiking trail about 170 km (105 miles) long, runs along the ridge of the Thuringian Forest.

questions.question: Under German law, what must you do if you come across an accident where people are hurt?
wrong_answers: You must ask the police first
You must leave it to professionals
hints: German law has a clear rule about this.
It's the reason every car carries a first aid kit.
It applies to everyone at the scene who is able to help.
questions.description: Bandages, scissors, gauze: the world's smallest first aid shop rides along in the back of the car.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, not helping when you could is actually a crime, called “unterlassene Hilfeleistung” (failure to give help).

questions.question: In Germany, where do you usually find this traffic sign?
hints: Children often play there.
There are lots of houses and little through traffic.
People live right on this street.
questions.description: A sign where even the snails by the roadside can almost keep up.
questions.fun_fact: Germany's first 30 km/h (19 mph) zones were tested in the 1980s, for example in Buxtehude.

questions.question: I'm red, I have eight corners, and when you see me, you have to halt. What am I?
hints: I stand at intersections.
I have four big white letters on me.
My name is another word for “Halt!”
questions.description: The strictest sign on the road: no arguing with me.
questions.fun_fact: At a stop sign you really must come to a full stop, even if there's no car anywhere in sight.

questions.question: In summer 2022, you could travel all over Germany by bus and regional train for three months. How much did the ticket cost per month?
hints: It was much cheaper than a normal monthly pass.
It was followed by the pricier Deutschlandticket.
The price was a single-digit number.
questions.description: The summer when all of Germany suddenly took the regional train.
questions.fun_fact: About 52 million of these tickets were sold in just three months.

questions.question: A long-distance train arrives 60 minutes late. In Germany, who then gets part of the fare back?
hints: The money goes back to where it came from.
They paid money beforehand and had to wait a long time.
They sit on the train and just want to get there.
questions.description: The train will definitely come, just not necessarily on time.
questions.fun_fact: From 60 minutes late you get a quarter of the fare back, and from 120 minutes even half.

questions.question: At an autobahn rest stop, you go through the Sanifair turnstile to the restroom. About how much does it cost?
hints: It isn't free.
A single coin gets you through.
You even get a voucher back for it.
questions.description: Germany's priciest turnstile isn't at a theme park.
questions.fun_fact: For your entry you get a voucher that you can use in the rest stop's shop.

questions.question: Drivers who speed collect points in Flensburg. At how many points do you lose your driver's license?
hints: It's a single-digit number.
In the old system, it used to be 18.
It's double 4.
questions.description: A sticker album in northern Germany that nobody wants to fill up.
questions.fun_fact: They're called “points in Flensburg” because that's where the Federal Motor Transport Authority (Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt) has its offices.

questions.question: I'm four gold stripes on a pilot's sleeves. What am I for?
questions.answer: To show the pilot is the captain
wrong_answers: To count the years spent flying
To show how many languages they speak
To show how many engines the plane has
hints: The stripes change with the job in the cockpit.
The co-pilot usually wears three.
They show who is in charge of the plane.
questions.description: A uniform that speaks without saying a single word.
questions.fun_fact: Pilots' stripes come from navy uniforms, where they also show rank.

questions.question: You see the blue “Autobahn” sign. How fast must a vehicle be able to go, at least, to be allowed on it?
hints: A Mofa (a small moped) isn't allowed here.
A normal small car manages it easily.
It's less than half the recommended autobahn speed.
questions.description: A blue sign that politely says “No, thank you” to slow vehicles.
questions.fun_fact: That's why Mofas and most tractors aren't allowed on the autobahn.

questions.question: A ticket inspector catches you without a valid ticket. How much do you usually have to pay in Germany?
hints: It's a lot more than a normal ticket.
It's less than 100 euros.
It's a round number starting with a 6.
questions.description: Sometimes the most expensive ride is the one you didn't pay for.
questions.fun_fact: Officially this fine is called “erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt”, an “increased transport fare”.

questions.question: You pull it on, it glows yellow or orange, and every car in Germany must carry one. What is it?
hints: You need it when your car breaks down.
It has no sleeves.
Road workers and breakdown crews wear it too.
questions.description: It belongs in the car like a lunchbox in a school bag, except you hopefully never have to unpack it.
questions.fun_fact: Since July 2014, every car in Germany must carry a high-visibility vest.

questions.question: Figure skaters spin very fast on one spot, often on just one leg. What is this move called?
hints: This move also exists in ballet.
You don't jump into the air for it.
The word comes from French and starts with “Pi”.
questions.description: An office chair can do this too, but it looks a lot less elegant.
questions.fun_fact: If you pull your arms in close to your body while spinning, you automatically spin faster.

questions.question: In the photo, an iron is used to put wax on the underside of a ski. Why?
questions.answer: To make the ski glide better
wrong_answers: To make the ski more colorful
hints: Pros do this before almost every race.
The melted wax soaks into the ski's base.
Without wax, the snow slows the ski down more.
questions.description: Ironing in the ski basement: the shirts stay wrinkled, but the skis are delighted.
questions.fun_fact: For the classic style, cross-country skiers often add a grip wax that briefly “sticks” to the snow under the foot when they push off.

questions.question: I sit firmly on the ski and hold your boot. If you fall hard, I let go so your leg stays safe. What am I?
hints: Without me, you would slide out of your ski with every step.
I get adjusted to match your weight and skill.
You “step in” with your boot until you hear a click.
questions.description: On the slopes, every skier needs a partner they can trust blindly.
questions.fun_fact: Before safety bindings existed, boots were simply strapped to the skis with leather straps.

questions.question: You're riding a chairlift, and each chair holds 4 people. How many people fit on 2 chairs?
hints: It's more than 4.
Add 4 plus 4.
It's the number that looks like a snowman.
questions.description: A sofa that hangs in the air and carries you up the mountain.
questions.fun_fact: On many chairlifts, a bubble-shaped cover protects riders from wind and snow.

questions.question: In winter there is snow there. Kids pull their sleds up and then race back down. Where are they?
hints: In summer it is all green there.
The ground slopes down there.
The place is named after what the kids are doing there.
questions.description: Going up is hard work, coming down is all screaming.
questions.fun_fact: The classic wooden sled is often called a “Davoser”, named after the town of Davos in Switzerland.

questions.question: This striker, a Barça star in the 1950s, played for three different national teams, the last one Spain. In which city was he born?
hints: He was born in Central Europe in 1927.
His first national team was Czechoslovakia, his second that of his home country.
It's the capital of Hungary, split by the Danube.
questions.description: A player so good that a new stadium had to be built to fit everyone who wanted to watch him.
questions.fun_fact: The crowds who came to see Kubala were one of the reasons the Camp Nou was built; it opened in 1957.

questions.question: After a run, what does a drink with electrolytes help your body get back?
wrong_answers: The sugar the body uses to sleep
hints: Think about what comes out of your skin when you exercise a lot.
Sweat tastes a little salty.
They are minerals like sodium and potassium.
questions.description: After a race, even the bravest runner stares at the bottle like it's buried treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Sweat tastes salty because it carries sodium, one of the electrolytes a sports drink puts back.

questions.question: Under several Spanish cities there are still tunnels like this one, dug during the Civil War (1936–1939). What were they for?
wrong_answers: To bring water to the fountains
hints: People ran down into them when they heard sirens.
The danger came from the sky.
Warplanes couldn't reach anyone deep underground.
questions.description: Tunnels nobody wanted to spend a vacation in, but everyone was glad to have nearby.
questions.fun_fact: In Barcelona alone, more than 1,000 shelters were dug during the war, many by the neighbors themselves.

questions.question: Brothers Nacho and José María Cano and Ana Torroja formed this 1980s band that sang “Hijo de la Luna”. What city were they from?
hints: Their city is inland, far from the sea.
Their city is right in the middle of the peninsula.
It’s the capital of Spain.
questions.description: Three musicians, one synthesizer and enough hairspray to put another hole in the ozone layer.
questions.fun_fact: “Hijo de la Luna” was so popular that the singer Loona turned it into a dance hit in 1998.

questions.question: This Guardia Civil lieutenant colonel stormed into Spain's Congress, pistol in hand, on February 23, 1981. Who is he?
hints: He was wearing the Guardia Civil's three-cornered tricornio hat.
From the speaker's stand he shouted “¡Quieto todo el mundo!” (“Nobody move!”).
His last name starts with T.
questions.description: One February afternoon, members of parliament found out how uncomfortable it is to hide under their seats.
questions.fun_fact: The session was being broadcast on radio and TVE filmed the storming, so half of Spain watched it later on TV.

questions.question: The donkey Platero, “small, fluffy, soft,” walks with his owner through a town near the Río Tinto and the Doñana marshes. In which autonomous community?
hints: It's an area in southwest Spain, near the Atlantic Ocean.
The town, Moguer, is in the province of Huelva.
It's the region of Seville and Granada.
questions.description: A main character with four legs, soft fur and zero interest in doing homework.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Ramón Jiménez, author of “Platero and I,” won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1956.

questions.question: In July 1909, the so-called Tragic Week broke out in Barcelona. What sparked the revolt?
questions.answer: Sending reservists to the war in Morocco
wrong_answers: A rise in the price of bread
The loss of Cuba and the Philippines
The fall of Alfonso XIII’s monarchy
hints: At the time, Spain was fighting a colonial war.
Many of those soldiers were family men who had already finished their service.
They were being sent to fight in North Africa.
questions.description: A week that no calendar in Barcelona ever wants to circle again.
questions.fun_fact: The revolt ended up bringing down Antonio Maura’s government a few months later.

questions.question: In December 1995, a former minister of Felipe González became Secretary General of NATO. Who was he?
hints: He trained as a physicist and had been Minister of Culture and of Foreign Affairs.
Later he became the EU's first High Representative for Foreign Policy.
His surname is also a Spanish word for a sunny hillside.
questions.description: A politician who ended up with more international meetings in his diary than hours in the day.
questions.fun_fact: Solana had protested against NATO in the 1980s and ended up as its top civilian leader.

questions.question: In 1936, as the Republic's finance minister, this politician arranged for much of the Bank of Spain's gold to be sent to the USSR. Who was he?
hints: He was a doctor and a professor of physiology.
He later became prime minister of the Republic.
He was Severo Ochoa's teacher at university.
questions.description: A shipment so valuable that no delivery company would dare to insure it.
questions.fun_fact: The gold left the port of Cartagena on Soviet ships and reached Odessa before going on by train to Moscow.

questions.question: Born in 1958 in Catalonia, it's shaped like a ball, and its inventor, Enric Bernat, put a stick on it. Why?
questions.answer: So children wouldn't get their hands dirty
wrong_answers: So the candy would last longer
So it could hang on a tree
So it could sell for more in stores
hints: Bernat watched how people ate candy back then.
He wanted to solve a very practical everyday problem.
It meant the end of fingers sticky with sugar.
questions.description: A sweet that comes with its own handle, like any serious tool.
questions.fun_fact: In 1995, some Chupa Chups traveled to space with the cosmonauts of the Mir space station.

questions.question: He painted “Guernica,” invented Cubism with Braque and was named Pablo Ruiz Picasso, but signed “Picasso.” From whom did he get that surname?
hints: In Spain, everyone has two surnames.
“Picasso” was his second surname.
The first one, “Ruiz,” came from his father.
questions.description: A painting genius whose signature hides a little family secret.
questions.fun_fact: His mother was María Picasso López, and his father, José Ruiz Blasco, was a drawing teacher.

questions.question: This singer from Linares represented Spain at Eurovision in 1966 and 1967 and had a hit with “Mi gran noche.” Who is he?
hints: He is famous for his sweeping arm gestures when he sings.
One of his best-known songs is “Escándalo.”
His stage name is the name of a Renaissance painter.
questions.description: A performer with so much energy on stage that the microphone asks for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: At Eurovision 1966 he sang “Yo soy aquel” and came seventh, but the song became a classic.

questions.question: I wear a huge hat, drink tea with a hare and celebrate a “happy unbirthday” with Alice. Who am I?
hints: I live in Wonderland.
My tea party never ends.
My name says what I make… and how things are going in my head.
questions.description: The perfect party: no presents, no cake and no sense at all.
questions.fun_fact: In the book, it is always six o'clock at the Hatter's party: teatime.

questions.question: When my husband was exiled, I stayed with our daughters at the monastery of Cardeña. After he died, I ruled Valencia for a few years. Who am I?
hints: My husband is the hero of Castile's most famous epic poem.
He rode Babieca and fought with the sword Tizona.
I married Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar.
questions.description: Behind every great knight there's someone minding the castle while he wanders off with his sword.
questions.fun_fact: Jimena defended Valencia after El Cid's death until 1102, then took his remains to the monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña, near Burgos.

questions.question: Medieval Christian knights charged shouting “¡Santiago y cierra, España!”. What does “cierra” mean there?
hints: It has nothing to do with doors or city walls.
It was shouted just as they rushed at the enemy.
In old Castilian, “cerrar con el enemigo” meant to charge at them.
questions.description: A battle cry that, heard today, sounds more like a job for the doorman than a cavalry charge.
questions.fun_fact: The Order of Santiago wore a red cross shaped like a sword, the same one Velázquez painted on his own chest in Las Meninas.

questions.question: In which century was the Gothic cathedral of León built?
hints: It's from the age of castles and knights.
The Gothic style belongs to the Middle Ages.
It was the century of Alfonso X the Wise.
questions.description: Stone monsters that have spent centuries working as gutters, in a very bad mood.
questions.fun_fact: León Cathedral has about 1,800 m² (19,400 sq ft) of medieval stained glass, which is why it's called “Pulchra Leonina.”

questions.question: I lived in Córdoba in the 9th century. I made wings of feathers, jumped from a height and glided for a while before a terrible landing. Who am I?
hints: I was an inventor, poet and astronomer at the emir's court.
Too late, I realized I was missing a tail, like the ones birds have.
A bridge in Córdoba and a crater on the Moon are named after me.
questions.description: History's first pilot: no license, no plane and, above all, no landing gear.
questions.fun_fact: Abbas ibn Firnas is said to have hurt his back on landing because his flying machine had no tail to slow him down.

questions.question: You're standing in the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra. In which century was it built?
hints: Granada was still under Muslim rule.
A sultan of the Nasrid dynasty had it built.
It was more than a hundred years before the Catholic Monarchs took Granada.
questions.description: Twelve marble cats that haven't moved in centuries and never complain about the Granada heat.
questions.fun_fact: Sultan Muhammad V had the Court of the Lions built, and its 124 marble columns are said to look like a palm grove.

questions.question: Look at this miniature from a 13th-century Castilian book on chess, dice and “tables” (a backgammon-like game). Which king commissioned it?
hints: He also had laws, chronicles and astronomy books written.
He brought together Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars in Toledo.
His nickname suits someone who writes lots of books.
questions.description: A king who, instead of waging war all day, preferred to spend the afternoon over a good game board.
questions.fun_fact: The original manuscript, finished in 1283, is kept today in the library of the Monastery of El Escorial.

questions.question: You're at the kiosk on the corner. Which of these is NOT usually sold there?
hints: Think of what you buy with your allowance after school.
Three of these fit on the counter next to the newspapers.
To buy this one, you have to go to the shop with the green cross.
questions.description: A tiny shop that holds more stuff than your backpack on a school trip.
questions.fun_fact: The word “kiosk” comes from the Turkish “köşk”, an open pavilion in a garden.

questions.question: Chupa Chups is to lollipops as Facundo is to…
hints: It's a family brand from Palencia.
You eat them one at a time, and in the park they leave piles of shells behind.
They come from a big yellow flower that turns to face the sun.
questions.description: A brand with a grandpa's name, famous for keeping fans busy through entire soccer games.
questions.fun_fact: The Pipas Facundo factory is in Villamuriel de Cerrato, a village in Palencia.

questions.question: bonÀrea is a cooperative based in Guissona that raises its own pigs and chickens and sells them in its stores. Which province is it from?
hints: It's an inland province.
Its capital lies on the Segre River.
It's home to the Seu Vella, the old cathedral on a hill.
questions.description: A supermarket that has personally met the hen that laid your eggs.
questions.fun_fact: bonÀrea grew out of the Guissona Cooperative, founded in 1959 by a handful of local farmers.

questions.question: In the Spanish version of “Heidi”, Grandfather has a huge companion called Niebla who sleeps by the hut. What animal is it?
hints: It's a loyal companion that follows Heidi and Peter through the meadows.
It's very calm and has lots and lots of fur.
It's a Saint Bernard.
questions.description: There's no Wi-Fi in the Alps, but there's plenty of company.
questions.fun_fact: In the original Japanese series, Niebla is called Josef.

questions.question: I'm a fermented milk from the Caucasus, made with little white grains that look like tiny cauliflower. What am I?
hints: My grains are a mix of bacteria and yeasts.
I taste a little sour and a bit fizzy.
My name starts with K and ends with R.
questions.description: A milk that comes with its own little pets.
questions.fun_fact: Kefir grains grow and multiply, so you can give some away for others to make their own kefir.

questions.question: How many points does Patrick, SpongeBob's best friend, have?
hints: He's pink and wears green shorts with flowers on them.
Patrick is a starfish.
Count his arms, his legs and his head.
questions.description: He lives under a rock and is happier than anyone else at the bottom of the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Some real starfish can grow back an arm if they lose one.

questions.question: Doraemon pulls the gorrocóptero (Take-copter) and the Anywhere Door out of it. It's white, small and on his belly. What is it?
hints: He can't take it off: it's attached to his body.
Far more fits inside than you'd think.
It's like a kangaroo's, but full of gadgets.
questions.description: The dream of every parent packing the suitcase for vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In Japanese it's called the “four-dimensional pocket”, because almost anything fits inside.

questions.question: Who made the song «Soy una taza, una tetera, una cuchara y un cucharón» famous among Spanish children?
hints: It's a group that sings and dances in very bright, colorful clothes.
Their videos play nonstop in homes with little kids.
Its name joins the Spanish words for “sing” and “play”.
questions.description: The perfect song to dance to while you empty the dishwasher.
questions.fun_fact: In “Soy una taza” you dance by making your body into the shape of each kitchen item.

questions.question: “My legs are like wire because I'm always hungry, I've lost all my feathers, and I lay eggs in the living room and kitchen but never in the coop.” Who am I?
hints: I'm in a song sung by Los Payasos de la Tele.
The song says I'm truly crazy.
My name rhymes with the Spanish words «muñeca» and «peluca».
questions.description: A barnyard neighbor with a very poor sense of direction.
questions.fun_fact: The song was a hit for Los Payasos de la Tele and, decades later, became a hit again with CantaJuego.

questions.question: Naruto was born there, dreams of becoming its leader, the Hokage, and the Hokage faces are carved into its mountain. Which village is it?
hints: It's surrounded by huge forests.
Sasuke and Sakura live there too.
In Japanese it's called Konoha.
questions.description: A town where even the baker knows how to throw ninja stars.
questions.fun_fact: The Hokage mountain looks a lot like Mount Rushmore, with the faces of four US presidents.

questions.question: In the British “Art Attack”, Neil Buchanan made the crafts. Who made them in the Spanish version?
hints: He also hosted “Megatrix” on Antena 3.
The Spanish version aired on Disney Channel.
He has the same first and last name as a very famous TV chef.
questions.description: More glue was used here than in an entire school in September.
questions.fun_fact: He's not the same Jordi Cruz as the “MasterChef” chef: they just share a name.

questions.question: Miliki greeted children with “¿Cómo están ustedes?” on “El gran circo de TVE”. In which decade did the show start?
hints: Your grandparents or parents watched it as kids.
TV in Spain still had very few channels.
It started a few years before Spain became a democracy.
questions.description: A question so polite that half of Spain still shouts back the answer.
questions.fun_fact: To Miliki's question, the children all answered at once with a very long “¡Bieeen!” (“Great!”).

questions.question: Pieces of the Roman city wall still stand in Barcelona's Gothic Quarter. Roughly how old are they?
hints: It's older than the name “Gothic” itself.
Back then, Barcelona was called Barcino.
It was built when the Roman Empire ruled Hispania, around the start of the Common Era.
questions.description: A neighborhood so old its stones are already collecting a pension.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Gothic bridge on Carrer del Bisbe looks medieval, but it was built in 1928.

questions.question: An emperor who had ruled half the world spent his last years in this monastery of Yuste, in Cáceres. Who was he?
hints: He was King of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor.
He was the grandson of the Catholic Monarchs.
As Holy Roman Emperor he carried a different number: V.
questions.description: The most exclusive retreat in Extremadura: no Wi-Fi, but plenty of monks.
questions.fun_fact: Charles I loved clocks and took a whole collection of them with him to Yuste.

questions.question: This large sculpture by Chillida, the “Elogio del Horizonte,” crowns a hill by the sea. Which city is it in?
hints: It's in northern Spain, facing the Cantabrian Sea.
It's the biggest city in its autonomous community, but not the capital.
It has San Lorenzo beach and the Cimadevilla neighborhood.
questions.description: A concrete sculpture that stares at the sea like someone waiting for the bus.
questions.fun_fact: If you stand in the middle, under the sculpture, the concrete amplifies the sound of the wind and the waves.

questions.question: Strictly speaking, chamomile isn't a tea but an herbal infusion, because it doesn't come from this plant. Which plant is it?
hints: Green, black and white tea all come from it.
It is related to a very popular garden flower.
The second part of its Latin name means “from China.”
questions.description: A family feud: chamomile insists it's tea, and tea says it's no child of hers.
questions.fun_fact: Green and black tea come from the same plant; the difference is how much the leaves oxidize after they are picked.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which building in Madrid is this?
hints: It stands next to the Almudena Cathedral.
It is used for official ceremonies of the head of state.
It is the king's official residence, though he doesn't live there.
questions.description: A house with so many rooms that a game of hide-and-seek could last for years.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Palace has more than 3,000 rooms and is the largest royal palace in Western Europe.

questions.question: Roughly how long is Madrid's Gran Vía from one end to the other?
hints: You can walk it without getting very tired.
It runs from Calle de Alcalá to Plaza de España.
At a relaxed pace, you can walk it in 15 to 20 minutes.
questions.description: A street with “great” in its name… but how great is it in steps?
questions.fun_fact: The Telefónica Building on the Gran Vía was one of the first skyscrapers in Europe when it opened in 1929.

questions.question: In Spanish, what do you call someone born in the city of this basilica?
hints: The basilica stands by the Ebro River.
The city is the capital of Aragon.
It's the Basílica del Pilar.
questions.description: Coming up with names for a city's residents: clearly a job for someone with a lot of imagination.
questions.fun_fact: During the Fiestas del Pilar, thousands of people bring flowers to the Virgin, forming a huge floral cloak.

questions.question: This painted front faces a square in Madrid lined with arcades, with a king on horseback in the middle. Which square is it?
hints: It dates from the early 17th century.
At Christmas it fills with stalls selling nativity scene figures.
The bars around it sell fried squid sandwiches.
questions.description: A square so square it could do its geometry homework all by itself.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's Plaza Mayor has 237 balconies looking onto the square.

questions.question: You're in Benidorm and almost all the foreign tourists you hear come from the same country. What nationality are most of them?
hints: They come from a European country.
To get there, they usually fly across the sea.
Their capital is London.
questions.description: Beach umbrella, towel and an accent that's definitely not from Alicante.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1950s, Mayor Pedro Zaragoza rode a Vespa all the way to Madrid to argue for allowing the bikini in Benidorm.

questions.question: San Fermín is to Pamplona as San Isidro is to…
hints: It's celebrated on May 15.
People dress up as chulapos and dance the chotis.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.description: Every city has its favorite saint, and some throw it a huge party.
questions.fun_fact: San Isidro was a farm worker, and during his fiesta people eat rosquillas “tontas” and “listas” (“silly” and “smart” doughnuts).

questions.question: This hard turrón, made with whole almonds, is named after the city it comes from. Which city?
hints: It's a beach city on the Mediterranean.
It's in the Valencian Community.
Its soft neighbor is turrón de Jijona.
questions.description: A sweet so hard your teeth need a vacation after Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: Turrón de Alicante is the hard one and turrón de Jijona the soft one, and both are made in the same province.

questions.question: It's the largest city in Galicia, faces the Cíes Islands and is famous for its huge Christmas lights. Which city is it?
hints: It lies by the sea, on an Atlantic ría (estuary).
It has one of the biggest fishing ports in Europe.
Its soccer team is Celta.
questions.description: A city whose Christmas lights try to outshine the sun itself.
questions.fun_fact: In 2007, the British newspaper The Guardian named Rodas Beach, on the Cíes Islands, the best beach in the world.

questions.question: The Marqués de Bradomín, “ugly, Catholic and sentimental,” is the hero of the four “Sonatas.” Which writer created him?
hints: The “Sonatas” came out in the early 20th century, between 1902 and 1905.
Each of the four novels is named after a season of the year.
The same author invented the esperpento in “Luces de bohemia.”
questions.description: An aristocrat who describes himself with three adjectives, and none of them is “humble.”
questions.fun_fact: Valle-Inclán lost his left arm after a fight in a Madrid café in 1899, and from then on his long beard and single arm became his trademark.

questions.question: I was the first master of a boy born in the river Tormes. In Salamanca I banged his head against a stone bull, and he got back at me with a post. Who am I?
hints: I'm a character in “Lazarillo de Tormes”.
I made my living saying prayers in exchange for coins.
The boy led me through the streets because I couldn't see.
questions.description: History's first boss to train his intern with knocks on the head.
questions.fun_fact: The stone bull from the story still exists: it's an ancient Vettonian boar-bull statue kept next to Salamanca's Roman bridge.

questions.question: You boil dried hibiscus flowers, called “flor de Jamaica” in Mexico, in water to make a drink. What color does the water turn?
hints: It is a very popular drink in Mexico, served ice cold.
It tastes tart, a bit like cranberry.
It's the same color as a ripe tomato.
questions.description: A flower that jumps into the pot and comes out as a soft drink.
questions.fun_fact: The part of the hibiscus used for the drink isn't the petals but the calyces, the cup of leaves around the flower.

questions.question: I was born in Seville in 1547. In 1599 I published the life of a rogue that was read all over Europe, and in 1608 I sailed to Mexico. Who am I?
hints: My novel came out a few years before Don Quixote.
In Mexico I also published a book on Spanish spelling.
My rogue was called Guzmán de Alfarache.
questions.description: A man from Seville who wrote about rogues and ended up packing his bags for the other side of the ocean.
questions.fun_fact: His novel was such a hit that people simply called it “el Pícaro” (the Rogue), and a fake second part came out before the real one, just as would later happen to Don Quixote.

questions.question: His name was Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, he rode Babieca, and he is buried in his home city's cathedral. Which city was El Cid from?
hints: It is a city in northern Castile.
Its Gothic cathedral is one of the most famous in Spain.
It is in Castile and León, and its name starts with B.
questions.description: A knight so famous that even his horse and his sword have names of their own.
questions.fun_fact: “Cid” comes from the Arabic “sidi”, meaning “lord”, and even his enemies called him that.

questions.question: The “Canción del pirata” begins “Con diez cañones por banda, viento en popa a toda vela…” (“Ten cannons on each side, full sail before the wind…”). Who wrote it?
hints: He was a poet of Spanish Romanticism.
He was a rebel who spent years in exile and wrote “El estudiante de Salamanca”.
His surname starts with E.
questions.description: A poem with more sails, cannons and freedom than a pirate theme park.
questions.fun_fact: The pirate in the poem sings that his ship is called “el Temido” (“the Feared One”) and that his only god is freedom.

questions.question: In 1936, at the University of Salamanca, its rector stood up to General Millán Astray: “Venceréis, pero no convenceréis” (“You will win, but you won't convince”). Who was he?
hints: He was a Basque writer of the Generation of '98.
He wrote “Niebla,” where a character goes to argue with his own author.
He also wrote “San Manuel Bueno, mártir.”
questions.description: A university rector who proved that you can lose the fight and still win the speech.
questions.fun_fact: Unamuno was rector of the University of Salamanca several times, and you can still visit his house-museum next to the university today.

questions.question: “What is poetry?, you ask, as you fix your blue pupil on mine. […] Poetry… is you.” Who wrote these lines?
hints: He is a Romantic poet of the 19th century.
He also wrote spooky legends like “El monte de las ánimas” (“The Mount of Souls”).
He was from Seville and is also famous for “Volverán las oscuras golondrinas” (“The dark swallows will return”).
questions.description: The most romantic answer ever given to an exam question.
questions.fun_fact: Bécquer never saw his “Rimas” published as a book: his friends collected and published them in 1871, a year after his death.

questions.question: Pedro Antonio de Alarcón's novel “El sombrero de tres picos” (1874) became what in 1919?
questions.answer: A ballet with music by Falla
wrong_answers: An opera with music by Verdi
A zarzuela with music by Chapí
hints: It premiered in London with a famous Russian company.
The composer was from Cádiz and also wrote “El amor brujo.”
Picasso designed the sets and costumes, and there is dancing in it.
questions.description: A hat so elegant it wasn't happy staying inside a book.
questions.fun_fact: Picasso designed the sets and costumes for the ballet, which was premiered by Diaghilev's Ballets Russes.

questions.question: Spain's biggest manga and anime convention started in 1995 and is run by Ficomic. In which city is it held?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean Sea.
The same organizers hold the big comics convention there every spring.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: The only place where dressing as a ninja with blue hair doesn't turn any heads.
questions.fun_fact: The Barcelona manga convention draws more than 150,000 visitors every year, many of them dressed as their favorite characters.

questions.question: It's a short text, often rhyming, that describes something without saying its name so you can guess it. What is it called?
hints: Kids play it a lot at school and on car trips.
At the end, someone always asks “What am I?”
Many start with “What has…”, like “What has keys but can't open locks?”
questions.description: The best cure for “Are we there yet?” in the back seat of the car.
questions.fun_fact: Riddles are so old they already appear in Greek myths, like the famous riddle of the Sphinx.

questions.question: Which cartoonist created Makinavaja, “el último choriso” (the last petty crook), in the magazine El Jueves?
hints: He was Catalan and died in 1993.
His real name was Ramón Tosas.
His pen name has only three letters and an accent.
questions.description: A neighborhood pickpocket with more bar-stool philosophy than money in his pocket.
questions.fun_fact: Makinavaja reached the movies in 1992, played by Andrés Pajares.

questions.question: I'm about 5 mm (0.2 in) long, I raise a colorful fan on my abdomen and dance for the female. What spider am I?
hints: I live in Australia, and videos of my dances go viral online.
I'm a jumping spider: I don't spin webs to hunt, I pounce on my prey.
I'm named after a blue and green bird that spreads its tail like a fan.
questions.description: An eight-legged dancer with zero shyness and plenty of sparkle.
questions.fun_fact: If his dance doesn't win the female over, the male has to run fast, or he could end up as her lunch.

questions.question: People say it's cast just by looking, without touching, and that babies are the most at risk. In folk belief, what is the mal de ojo?
questions.answer: Bad luck caused by an envious look
wrong_answers: An infection caught by looking at someone
A punishment for spying on the neighbors
An illness from staring at the sun
hints: People use charms like the higa or a red ribbon to protect against it.
It's a superstition about bad luck, not a disease of the eyes or the body.
It's as if jealousy could bring bad luck.
questions.description: Some looks say it all, and according to Grandma, some say far too much.
questions.fun_fact: In Galicia, babies are traditionally given a higa made of jet to protect them from the mal de ojo.

questions.question: Which fairy-tale character sings “I'm in the ox's belly, where it doesn't snow or rain”?
hints: He's so tiny that his family couldn't find him.
He walked down the street singing so nobody would step on him.
He's named after the legume that stars in cocido stew.
questions.description: A boy who got lost and ended up in the coziest spot in the barn.
questions.fun_fact: In 1945, “Garbancito de la Mancha” came out; it's considered Europe's first full-length animated film in color.

questions.question: What is the name of the story that never ends, used to tease children?
hints: Parents and grandparents in Spain have played it with children for generations.
It starts with “¿Quieres que te cuente…?” (“Do you want me to tell you…?”).
Its name has something in it that you snack on in the park, from a sunflower.
questions.description: Get ready for the most annoying question of the afternoon, and not because it's hard.
questions.fun_fact: The trick is to answer every reply with “I didn't ask you to say yes, I asked if you want me to tell you the cuento de la buena pipa.”

questions.question: I'm a group of volcanic islands in the Atlantic, off the coast of Africa. Greeks and Romans said life on me was free of sorrow. What did they call me?
hints: Today I'm one of Spain's autonomous communities.
My highest peak is the Teide.
My ancient name is about good luck.
questions.description: A place with weather so nice that even the ancients gave it five stars.
questions.fun_fact: Pityusic and Gymnesian were Greek names for the Balearic Islands: the first for Ibiza and Formentera, the second for Mallorca and Menorca.

questions.question: You're singing “Estaba el señor don Gato”. Which of these does NOT happen in the song?
wrong_answers: He comes back to life when he smells fish
hints: Something sad happens, but it ends well.
At the end, the funeral passes through the fish market street.
Don Gato doesn't catch anything in the whole song.
questions.description: The life of a cat with more drama than all nine lives put together.
questions.fun_fact: “Don Gato” is an old ballad that has been sung in Spain for centuries, and in many countries of the Americas too.

questions.question: They meet at night at the aquelarre, brew potions in a cauldron, and the Zugarramurdi cave is their most famous spot. Who are they?
hints: They often wear a pointy hat.
They fly around on a broomstick.
A very famous one gave Snow White a poisoned apple.
questions.description: Neighbors who throw their parties in a cave and never invite anyone.
questions.fun_fact: In Zugarramurdi, in Navarre, there is a Witches' Museum very close to the famous cave.

questions.question: In Basque legends they call me iratxo, and I roam at night near the farmhouses. What am I?
hints: I'm small and not very harmful.
I love playing pranks and messing everything up.
I'm related to the trasgo of other regions.
questions.description: A farmhouse neighbor who never pays the building fees.
questions.fun_fact: In Basque mythology, the pagan giants are the jentilak, the witches are the sorginak and the dragon is the herensuge.

questions.question: Galician tradition says they live underground, guard treasures and built the castros (hillforts) and mámoas (burial mounds). Who are they?
hints: Almost anything ancient of unknown origin was credited to them.
Their enchanted women comb their hair beside springs.
Their name sounds almost like the Spanish word “moros” (Moors).
questions.description: Galicia's first builders, and they never asked for a building permit.
questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, the mouros of legend aren't Muslims: they're a magical people from a very distant past.

questions.question: Our Lady of Covadonga is to Asturias as Our Lady of Montserrat is to…
hints: Her shrine sits on a mountain of strangely shaped rocks.
Her monastery has a famous boys' choir, the Escolanía.
People fondly call her “la Moreneta”, and her mountain is near Barcelona.
questions.description: Even patron saints have a favorite home region.
questions.fun_fact: The Escolanía de Montserrat is one of the oldest boys' choirs in Europe, with more than 700 years of history.

questions.question: Why does Ratoncito Pérez come to children's homes?
questions.answer: To swap a baby tooth for a gift
wrong_answers: To eat the crumbs in the kitchen
hints: He comes when something happens in a child's mouth.
He looks under the pillow.
One falls out and you save it for him.
questions.description: The only mouse that's welcome in the house.
questions.fun_fact: Father Luis Coloma invented him in 1894 for the young King Alfonso XIII, and on Calle del Arenal in Madrid there's a plaque where he “lived”.

questions.question: They go in the belén (nativity scene), they're sold at the Christmas market in Madrid's Plaza Mayor, and the classic ones are hand-painted. What are they usually made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from the earth.
Before they're painted, they're baked in a kiln.
It's the same wet earth used to make botijos and water jugs.
questions.description: Shepherds, sheep and a river of tinfoil: the smallest town in all of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: The nativity scene Francisco Salzillo made in Murcia in the 18th century has more than 500 figures.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The description (teaser) says 'the smallest town in all of Spain', which has nothing to do with the question about belén figures and is not true of anything in it. The answer (clay) and the other content are fine.

questions.question: One player counts facing the wall while the others look for a good spot where they won't be seen. What game is it?
hints: Behind a curtain or under the bed is a good spot.
The one who counted then has to find everyone else.
At the end of the count, someone shouts “Ready or not, here I come!”
questions.description: Recess always ends sooner than it takes to decide what to play.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, a player who reaches the base without being caught shouts “¡Por mí y por todos mis compañeros!” to free everyone.

questions.question: In “escondite inglés”, the player who is “it” turns around and shouts “Un, dos, tres…”. How does it go on?
hints: It's a small animal.
It's the baby of a farm bird.
Its mother is the hen.
questions.description: A game where standing as still as a statue is the best plan.
questions.fun_fact: In England this game is called “Grandmother's Footsteps”.

questions.question: At Spanish village fiestas, people race like this. What fabric are these sacks traditionally made of?
hints: It's a rough, cheap fabric.
It's a little itchy and lets air through.
It's what potato sacks have always been made of.
questions.description: The only race where hopping your way to the finish is completely normal.
questions.fun_fact: In many villages the sack race shares the fiesta program with the greasy pole and tug-of-war.

questions.question: Two teams in rows, each player with a number. The person in the middle calls a number, and the two players with it race to grab… what?
hints: The person in the middle holds it out at arm's length.
Years ago almost everyone carried one every day.
You can also blow your nose with it.
questions.description: A two-person race where everything comes down to who has the faster reflexes.
questions.fun_fact: If you step over the center line before the other player grabs the object, you're out.

questions.question: What is this hook-tipped needle used for?
hints: Grandmothers used to do this a lot.
The hook catches the thread and makes loops.
It makes the doilies that sit on top of the mesa camilla (a round table with a heater underneath).
questions.description: A needle that got tired of being straight and decided to become a fishhook.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word “ganchillo” comes from “gancho” (hook), after the curved tip of the needle.

questions.question: You draw me with two lines standing up and two lying down. One player draws X's, the other O's, and three in a row wins. What game am I?
hints: I have nine squares.
Only two people play.
My name is three short words joined by hyphens.
questions.description: For when a Sunday afternoon drags on longer than the line at the doctor's.
questions.fun_fact: If neither player ever makes a mistake, the game always ends in a draw.

questions.question: Mix orujo (a strong grape spirit) with coffee and sugar and you get licor café. Which region of Spain is it typical of?
hints: It's a very rainy land in the northwest.
Queimada is also made there with orujo.
Its capital is Santiago de Compostela.
questions.description: A coffee that decided breakfast was too small for it.
questions.fun_fact: At Galician festivals it's common to end the meal with a shot of licor café, as dark as coffee itself.

questions.question: In a bar in Spain, what happens if you order a «jarra» of beer instead of a «caña»?
questions.answer: You get more, in a big glass with a handle
wrong_answers: You get less, in a small glass
You get it mixed with lemon
hints: It has to do with the amount.
You hold the glass in a special way.
It usually holds about half a liter.
questions.description: At a Spanish bar counter, ordering is almost a language of its own.
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the bar and the city, a caña can be around 200 ml (7 fl oz), while a jarra is usually over half a liter.

questions.question: In which city was Estrella Damm beer born in 1876?
hints: It's a big city with an important port.
Its founder came from Alsace, in France.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: A star you've never seen through a telescope, but you've seen it on plenty of café terraces.
questions.fun_fact: Estrella Galicia, from A Coruña, has nothing to do with Estrella Damm, even though both have the word “Estrella” in their names.

questions.question: When a male peacock spreads its tail like a fan, about how many long feathers does it show off?
hints: That's far more than all the fingers in your whole family put together.
Many of them have a colorful “eye” at the tip.
It's more than a hundred, but less than a thousand.
questions.description: The only animal that carries its own fan wherever it goes.
questions.fun_fact: Every year the peacock loses its long tail feathers, and they grow back again.

questions.question: Old Spanish chocolate pots were tall and narrow, with a hole in the lid. What was that hole for?
questions.answer: To fit a wooden whisk for frothing
wrong_answers: To add milk without opening it
hints: A wooden stick went through it.
It was spun between the hands to make foam.
In Spain this tool is called a “molinillo”, like a small coffee mill.
questions.description: A pot with a hole in its head, and not because it's absent-minded.
questions.fun_fact: In the 17th and 18th centuries, drinking frothy chocolate was a fashion among the Spanish nobility.

questions.question: Finish the classic Spanish toast: «Arriba, abajo, al centro y…»
hints: You say it while moving your glass.
It's the last thing you do with the drink.
It tells you where the drink ends up: in your mouth.
questions.description: The shortest dance routine at any Spanish party.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain it's also customary to look each other in the eye when toasting and say «¡Chinchín!» as the glasses clink.

questions.question: Fruit like the one in the photo is squeezed into fresh juice for breakfast. Which Spanish region is famous for it?
hints: It's in the east of the peninsula.
It has three provinces and two official languages.
Its capital has the same name as the region.
questions.description: Round orange balls that get squeezed and never complain.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the biggest orange exporters in the world.

questions.question: You stroll through a medieval market among costumed blacksmiths, falconers and minstrels. Which era came right after the one they imitate?
hints: The era they imitate is the age of castles and knights.
It began around the time Columbus reached the Americas.
It's the age of the printing press, the Renaissance and the great voyages of discovery.
questions.description: Here you pay in euros, but everyone acts as if phones had never been invented.
questions.fun_fact: The Middle Ages lasted about a thousand years, from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 to the late 15th century.

questions.question: On the Día de los Santos Inocentes, many children stick a “monigote” on other people's backs. What is a monigote?
hints: You can make one at home with scissors.
It usually has a head, arms and legs.
It's a cut-out drawing shaped like a person.
questions.description: The one day of the year when checking your back is a matter of survival.
questions.fun_fact: Every December 28, many Spanish newspapers and TV news shows run a fake story as a prank, or “inocentada.”

questions.question: In this Valencian town, on the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other in the world's biggest food fight. Which town is it?
hints: The fiesta began in the mid-20th century, almost by accident.
The fiesta is called the Tomatina.
Its name starts with B.
questions.description: The one place where getting your T-shirt dirty is the whole point.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2013 you need a ticket for the Tomatina, and afterwards the streets are washed clean with hoses.

questions.question: You're in the square, facing the town hall balcony, and a well-known person reads the pregón of the fiestas. When does this happen?
questions.answer: At the start, to open the fiestas
wrong_answers: On the last day, to close them
Midway through, on no fixed day
hints: In the old days, a pregonero (town crier) called out the news in the streets.
Each year the town hall picks a different person to read it.
Right after it, the music, the verbenas and the fireworks begin.
questions.description: A speech from a balcony that nobody fully hears because of the firecrackers.
questions.fun_fact: Many towns invite a famous local as pregonero each year: actors, athletes or chefs.

questions.question: Look at the photo: dancers in traditional Galician dress and bagpipers. What is the most typical dance of Galicia called?
hints: It's usually played on bagpipes and tambourine.
Its name comes from the Galician word for “mill.”
It sounds a bit like «muñeca», the Spanish word for doll, but that's not it.
questions.description: A dance with so many jumps that even the bagpipes run out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Tradition says people danced it at the mills while they waited for their grain to be ground.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in the village of El Rocío, the Virgin is lovingly called “la Blanca…”
hints: This nickname turns up in many sevillanas sung on the pilgrimage.
The romería takes place at Pentecost, the feast of the Holy Spirit.
It's the bird that stands for peace.
questions.description: A nickname so lovely that nobody uses her full name.
questions.fun_fact: The village of El Rocío has sand streets so that carts and horses can pass.

questions.question: Look at the photo: underneath this Holy Week paso, hidden behind its skirts, many men carry and move it. What are they called?
hints: You can't see them during the procession.
They carry the weight on the back of their necks and shoulders.
Their name comes from the sack, or “costal,” they wear on their heads for protection.
questions.description: A procession with more hidden feet than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: Some of Seville's pasos weigh more than 2,000 kg (4,400 lb) and are carried by about 40 or 50 costaleros.

questions.question: You're at the Entierro de la Sardina, the parade that sends off Carnival in Madrid and other places. What day is it usually held?
hints: It's right when Carnival ends.
Lent begins that day.
At Mass that day, they mark your forehead.
questions.description: A funeral with a brass band for a fish that never did anything wrong.
questions.fun_fact: In Murcia, the Entierro de la Sardina is different: it takes place after Holy Week and hands out thousands of toys.

questions.question: I'm a fair booth full of prizes: you buy a ticket, open it, and if you win, you take home a stuffed animal or a ham. What am I?
hints: You don't need good aim here.
It all comes down to luck.
Marisol had a song and a film with my name.
questions.description: The spot at the fair where the giant stuffed animal always goes to someone else.
questions.fun_fact: The 1962 film “Tómbola” starred Marisol, who also sang the song of the same name.

questions.question: You're on the Alameda in Valencia, and people on the floats throw thousands of flowers at you in the Batalla de Flores. In which month is it held?
hints: It isn't during the Fallas.
It's the last event of a fair named after its month.
It's usually on the last Sunday of the month.
questions.description: A war where the ammunition smells better than the enemy.
questions.fun_fact: Valencia's Batalla de Flores was first held in 1891, and it closes the Feria de Julio.

questions.question: You're in a caseta at the Seville Fair, dancing sevillanas. What season of the year is it?
hints: Seville's worst heat hasn't arrived yet.
It takes place shortly after Holy Week.
It's the season when the orange trees blossom and the streets smell of azahar.
questions.description: Paper lanterns, rebujito and sevillanas until your feet fall asleep.
questions.fun_fact: Many casetas at the Seville Fair are private: you only get in if a member or a friend invites you.

questions.question: You're at a beach bar in Málaga and Chambao, the “flamenco chill” band, is playing. In which decade did they become known?
hints: The band is much more recent than Camarón or Paco de Lucía.
They mixed flamenco with relaxed electronic music.
Their first album came out just as euro cash started to be used.
questions.description: Flamenco in flip-flops, with sand on your feet and zero rush.
questions.fun_fact: In Andalusia, a «chambao» is a shelter of reeds put up on the beach for shade.

questions.question: Niña Pastori, whose real name is María Rosa García, mixes flamenco and pop and was born in the same Cádiz town as Camarón. Which one?
hints: It's in the province of Cádiz, very close to the city of Cádiz.
It has salt flats, marshes and a long navy tradition.
There's a clue in Camarón's own name: “de la Isla”.
questions.description: As a little girl she already sang louder than the whole family's alarm clock.
questions.fun_fact: San Fernando used to be called Isla de León, which is why Camarón was known as “de la Isla” (of the Island).

questions.question: This city in Cádiz is proud of its bulerías, has a famous school of equestrian art, and its name gave English the word “sherry”. Which is it?
hints: It's the biggest city in its province.
Every year it hosts a major flamenco festival and a motorcycle Grand Prix.
Its wine has the same name as the city, without “de la Frontera”.
questions.description: A city where even the horses keep the rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: “Sherry” comes from the way the English pronounced “Xerez”, the city's old name.

questions.question: Complete: “Sandal is to footwear as bun is to…”
hints: Think about what kind of thing a sandal is: a type of footwear.
Think about where on the body a bun goes.
Ponytails and braids belong to the same group.
questions.description: Before dancing, the bailaora ties a knot… but not in her stomach.
questions.fun_fact: Flamenco dancers pull their hair up into a bun so it doesn't cover their face when they spin.

questions.question: This Spanish song genre has dramatic love lyrics, was a hit in the 1940s and was sung by Lola Flores and Rocío Jurado. What is it?
hints: It's sung with deep feeling, backed by an orchestra or a guitar.
Its roots are in Andalusia.
Its singers are called tonadilleras.
questions.description: Impossible loves, jealousy and handkerchiefs: a whole drama in three minutes.
questions.fun_fact: Copla is also known as “canción española” (Spanish song), and its singers as tonadilleras.

questions.question: One of flamenco's oldest palos, it's sung with no guitar at all, and its family includes the martinete and the debla. Which is it?
hints: It's cante jondo: serious and solemn.
Its family is linked to work in blacksmiths' forges.
Its name sounds like the word “tonada” (tune).
questions.description: A song so deep you need a diving suit to reach the bottom.
questions.fun_fact: In the martinete, sometimes the only accompaniment is a hammer striking an anvil.

questions.question: Its team plays in yellow, won the Europa League in 2021 and is nicknamed the “Yellow Submarine”. Which city is it from?
hints: It's quite a small city to have a top-flight team.
It's in the province of Castellón.
Its club plays at the Estadio de la Cerámica.
questions.description: A team that sails underwater without getting its shirt wet.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname comes from the Beatles song “Yellow Submarine”, which fans started singing in the 1960s.

questions.question: Which of these players never won the European Golden Shoe?
hints: All four won the Spanish league at least once.
This award goes to the top goalscorer in Europe's leagues in one season.
He was a midfielder and scored the goal that won the 2010 World Cup.
questions.description: A shoe so shiny that nobody dares to wear it for a match.
questions.fun_fact: Messi holds the record for Golden Shoes: he won six, all of them with Barça.

questions.question: Unai Emery won three Europa Leagues in a row as Sevilla's coach. In which years?
hints: It came after Sevilla had won its first two UEFA Cups.
He won the last of the three in Basel, against Liverpool.
It was in the middle of the 2010s.
questions.description: A coach who treated the Europa League like a yearly spring tradition.
questions.fun_fact: Emery won another Europa League in 2021 with Villarreal, making him the coach with the most titles in this competition.

questions.question: It wears green and white, plays at the Benito Villamarín and its fans shout “¡manque pierda!”. Which club is it?
hints: It's a club from Andalusia.
Its great rival is Sevilla FC.
Its full name starts with “Real”, followed by a word beginning with B.
questions.description: A club that sometimes loses, but whose fans never seem to notice.
questions.fun_fact: The full chant is “¡Viva el Betis manque pierda!”: in everyday Andalusian speech, “manque” means “even if”, so it's “Long live Betis, even if they lose!”.

questions.question: It's a single match, played in August, and it opens the European season. Who plays in the UEFA Super Cup?
questions.answer: The Champions League and Europa League winners
wrong_answers: The Spanish and English league champions
The Champions League and Club World Cup winners
The two finalists of the last Champions League
hints: It's often the first trophy handed out in the season.
One of them lifted “La Orejona”, the big-eared trophy.
The other won Europe's second club competition.
questions.description: August: beach, flip-flops and a trophy played for before your ice cream melts.
questions.fun_fact: Real Madrid and Barça are among the clubs that have won the most UEFA Super Cups.

questions.question: With his famous volley in the 2002 final, Zidane won Real Madrid what fans call “La…” what?
hints: It refers to a European Cup.
The final was in Glasgow against Bayer Leverkusen.
Twelve years later the next one came, the most famous of all.
questions.description: A volley so good that it's still playing on a loop on some TV somewhere.
questions.fun_fact: Zidane's volley came from a looping cross by Roberto Carlos, and many call it the best goal ever scored in a Champions League final.

questions.question: In the first years of the European Cup, Di Stéfano's Real Madrid won it several times in a row. How many?
hints: It was in the second half of the 1950s.
They won every edition from the very first one.
As many as the fingers on one hand.
questions.description: When winning once just isn't enough, the best thing is to repeat... and repeat.
questions.fun_fact: The fifth, in 1960, ended 7–3 against Eintracht Frankfurt in Glasgow: Puskás scored four goals and Di Stéfano three.

questions.question: In this cave in Asturias, people honor a Virgin who, legend says, helped Don Pelayo. What loving nickname do Asturians give her?
hints: It's a word in Asturian.
It has the little ending Asturians add to almost any word to make it sound loving.
It ends in “-ina”, like “guapina” (pretty).
questions.description: A cave with a view, its own waterfall and a very beloved neighbor.
questions.fun_fact: Below the cave is the Fountain of the Seven Spouts; tradition says a young woman who drinks from it will marry within a year.

questions.question: In Spain's public health system, up to what age does the health center's pediatrician usually see you?
hints: The pediatrician is the children's doctor.
They still see you after you've finished primary school.
Roughly when you finish 2.º de la ESO (second year of secondary school).
questions.description: The only doctor whose waiting room has more toys than magazines.
questions.fun_fact: The word “pediatrician” comes from the Greek “paidós”, which means “child”.

questions.question: Look at this 1-cent euro coin. It is copper-colored on the outside, but what metal is it on the inside?
hints: It is a cheap and very strong metal.
Nails, screws and beams are made from it too.
That's why a magnet can pick the coin up.
questions.description: The coin nobody picks up off the ground, but everyone misses when the price gets rounded.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish side of the 1, 2 and 5 cent coins shows the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.

questions.question: In Spain, if you work for yourself with no boss and pay a monthly fee to the Seguridad Social, what are you?
hints: Nobody pays you a salary at the end of the month.
Lots of plumbers, taxi drivers and bar owners are one.

questions.description: Mondays, paperwork, coffee and more paperwork: Spanish working life in one word.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has more than 3 million autónomos (self-employed workers).

questions.question: In 2010 Spain had about 45 cajas de ahorros (savings banks). How many still work as a caja today?
hints: The financial crisis of those years changed everything.
Most merged or turned into banks, like La Caixa becoming CaixaBank.
The ones left are small: one in Ontinyent and one in Pollença.
questions.description: They kept your savings in a giant piggy bank, until someone bumped the shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Every October 31, World Savings Day, many cajas used to give piggy banks to children.

questions.question: With a Spanish DNI you can travel to many countries without a passport. Where can you travel with just the DNI?
hints: You cross some borders, but not an ocean.
France and Portugal are on the list.
It's the club of countries with a blue flag and twelve stars.
questions.description: A little booklet that collects stamps more eagerly than your grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: Since October 2021, a DNI is no longer enough to enter the United Kingdom: you need a passport.

questions.question: In “Money Heist” (La casa de papel), after the Royal Mint of Spain, the gang raids the Bank of Spain. In which part does that heist begin?
hints: The first heist fills the start of the series.
Netflix released that part in 2019.
It comes right after the first two parts.
questions.description: A building with more gold inside than a pirate's chest, and better locks.
questions.fun_fact: The Bank of Spain building, on Madrid's Plaza de Cibeles, opened in 1891.

questions.question: It arrives at home in a letter, it can come from a speed camera, and if you pay within 20 days you get half off. What is it?
hints: It's sent by the DGT or the town hall.
It usually comes after driving too fast or parking badly.
Sometimes you also lose points from your driver's license.
questions.description: The only letter nobody is in a hurry to open.
questions.fun_fact: That 50% discount for paying early is called “pronto pago” (prompt payment).

questions.question: Today, unemployment benefits in Spain are handled by the SEPE. What was this agency called before?
hints: That name lasted from 1978 to 2003.
Its acronym has four letters.
It stood for Instituto Nacional de Empleo.
questions.description: An office with a new name and the same old queues.
questions.fun_fact: Many people still say “apuntarse al INEM” (signing up at the INEM), even though the agency changed its name in 2003.

questions.question: Plaça de Catalunya is the big crossroads in the center of Barcelona. Which of these streets does NOT start there?
hints: Three of them leave from the corners of the square.
The one you want is among Barcelona's longest streets and crosses the city from end to end.
Its name says that it cuts across the Eixample at a slant.
questions.description: Barcelona's living room, where everyone meets “at the plaza” and nobody finds each other.
questions.fun_fact: Several metro and train lines cross under Plaça de Catalunya, making it one of the busiest spots in the city.

questions.question: Every year thousands of pilgrims walk to a cathedral in Galicia where, by tradition, an apostle is buried. Which one?
hints: He was one of Jesus's twelve apostles.
He is the patron saint of Spain.
The cathedral's city carries his name in Spanish.
questions.description: Hundreds of kilometers on foot to visit someone who hasn't answered the door in centuries.
questions.fun_fact: To get the “Compostela,” the pilgrim's certificate, you must walk at least the last 100 kilometers (62 miles).

questions.question: They date from the 11th century, are in Jaén and are among the largest surviving Arab baths in Europe. Why did they survive so intact?
questions.answer: Because a palace was built on top
wrong_answers: Because they were used as a church
hints: For centuries, nobody knew they were there.
They were rediscovered in the early 20th century.
Today you enter them through the Villardompardo Palace.
questions.description: A spa almost a thousand years old without a single bad review.
questions.fun_fact: The same Villardompardo Palace also houses a museum of naïve art.

questions.question: “I hang in Santiago Cathedral, weigh over 50 kg (110 lb), eight men pull my rope and I swing side to side full of incense.” What am I?
hints: The men who swing me are called tiraboleiros.
I can fly over the worshippers at almost 70 km/h (43 mph).
My name in Galician means “smoke-spreader.”
questions.description: The biggest and fastest air freshener in all of Galicia.
questions.fun_fact: One theory says the botafumeiro also helped cover the smell of the pilgrims who slept in the cathedral.

questions.question: It's in Burgos, its Romanesque cloister is famous for a cypress, and in 1994 its monks sold millions of albums. What music did they sing?
hints: It's very old church music.
It's sung in a single melody line, with no instruments.
It's named after a pope called Gregory.
questions.description: Monks who made the charts without ever changing out of their robes.
questions.fun_fact: The album by the monks of Santo Domingo de Silos climbed into the top five of the US album charts.

questions.question: Velázquez painted this picture as a young man in Seville, but it isn't in the Prado. In which city can you see it today?
hints: It got there as a gift from a Spanish king.
It was given to a foreign general who fought against Napoleon in Spain.
It hangs in the Duke of Wellington's house.
questions.description: A boy from Seville hands out cool water and ends up a tourist abroad forever.
questions.fun_fact: Joseph Bonaparte was carrying it as he fled after the Battle of Vitoria in 1813; Wellington recovered it, and Ferdinand VII later gave it to him as a gift.

questions.question: In which year did Velázquez paint his famous portrait of Pope Innocent X in Rome?
hints: It was during his second trip to Italy.
He painted it a few years before “Las Meninas”.
It was right in the middle of the 17th century.
questions.description: A pope who posed looking so grumpy he nearly asked to speak to the painter's manager.
questions.fun_fact: The pope supposedly exclaimed “Troppo vero!” (“Too true!”) on seeing the portrait, and centuries later Francis Bacon painted dozens of versions of it.

questions.question: This painting by Goya, “Fight with Cudgels”, is in the Prado. Which group of works does it belong to?
hints: It isn't a print: it's painted in oil.
Goya painted it when he was old and deaf, for his own house.
They were on the walls of the Quinta del Sordo.
questions.description: Two men settling their differences without going through the residents' association.
questions.fun_fact: Goya painted these works straight onto the walls of his house, and around 1874 they were moved onto canvas to save them.

questions.question: In which decade was surrealism born, the art movement that Dalí, Miró and Buñuel joined?
hints: The poet André Breton founded it in Paris, wanting to set the unconscious mind free.
Dalí painted his famous melting clocks, “The Persistence of Memory”, in 1931, when he was already part of the group.
It was the decade of the “Roaring Twenties”.
questions.description: An art movement that took dreams as seriously as you take your alarm clock.
questions.fun_fact: In 1929 Buñuel and Dalí made the surrealist short film “Un Chien Andalou” (“An Andalusian Dog”), which doesn't have a single Andalusian dog in it.

questions.question: You're in the Prado in front of “Queen Isabella the Catholic Dictating Her Will”, a large history painting from 1864. Who painted it?
hints: He was a 19th-century painter from Madrid who died young.
Today a Madrid boulevard carries his surname.
His surname is the Spanish word for rose bushes.
questions.description: A queen writing her last wishes with a bigger audience than a lawyer on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: This painting won him a first-class medal at Spain's 1864 National Exhibition and later a gold medal at the 1867 World's Fair in Paris.

questions.question: Velázquez painted it around 1632. It has a black background, and Unamuno wrote a long poem about it. How many nails hold its crucified Christ?
hints: Velázquez followed the ideas of his father-in-law and teacher, Francisco Pacheco.

Each foot has its own nail.
questions.description: A hardware store question right in the middle of the Prado Museum.
questions.fun_fact: He painted it for the convent of San Plácido in Madrid, which is why it is also called the “Christ of San Plácido.”

questions.question: Complete it: Velázquez is to “Las Meninas” as Claudio Coello is to…

questions.question: Elías García Martínez painted it in 1930 in a sanctuary in Borja, and in 2012 a local woman “restored” it and it went around the world. What is it painted on?

questions.question: Which of these natural areas in Spain has NO large beech forests?

questions.question: Ferns have no flowers, spread by spores and need lots of moisture. In which part of Spain are they most common?

questions.question: Look at the map: this small region, full of vineyards, gives its name to one of Spain's most famous wines. Which is it?

questions.question: You're at the Alhambra, the palace of the old Nasrid Kingdom of Granada. In what year did the Catholic Monarchs conquer it?

It was the year of Christopher Columbus's first voyage.

questions.question: Balearic Islands Day is in March, marking when the region's 1983 Statute of Autonomy came into force. Which day of March?

questions.question: This is the coat of arms of Bilbao. Which church appears next to the bridge?

questions.question: Which of these old kingdoms does NOT appear on Spain's coat of arms?

questions.question: I'm made of gold and precious stones, King Alfonso II gave me to Oviedo Cathedral in 808, and I'm on the city's coat of arms. Which cross am I?

questions.question: For more than 30 years, this Renfe station had a big tropical garden under its old iron roof. Which station is it?

questions.question: Which autonomous community of Spain does this flag belong to?

questions.question: It was approved by referendum in 1978, has 169 articles, and its anniversary on December 6 is a public holiday. What is it?

questions.question: I secretly married my cousin Ferdinand, together we conquered Granada, and I paid for Christopher Columbus’s voyage. Who am I?

questions.question: In the schoolyard, you pick who's “it” with “Pito, pito, gorgorito”. Which of these is NOT another counting-out rhyme?

previous.feedback: This asks the same fact as the approved q-9398 ("The sole is worn through and the heel has broken off.
