questions.fun_fact: Alexia won the Ballon d'Or two years in a row, in 2021 and 2022, and Aitana Bonmatí won it after her.

questions.question: It reached the 1980 Copa del Rey final and lost 6–1 to its own senior team. Which reserve team is it?
hints: With that win, its senior team completed the league and cup double.
On the way to the final, it knocked out several top-flight teams.
Its stadium is named after Alfredo Di Stéfano.
questions.description: A little brother who one day dared to take on the big one.
questions.fun_fact: By reaching the final, Castilla qualified for the European Cup Winners' Cup and played against West Ham.

questions.question: In 2006, Joaquín Sánchez left Betis for the first time. Which club did he play for next?
hints: He kept playing in La Liga's top division.
His new club has a bat on its crest.
His new team played at Mestalla.
questions.description: A winger who ran up and down the touchline and across TV studios.
questions.fun_fact: Joaquín later went back to Betis and retired there in 2023, aged 41, after winning the 2022 Copa del Rey.

questions.question: It's in Vigo, it's Celta's home and it hosted games at the 1982 World Cup. What is this stadium called?
hints: It's in Galicia, but it isn't Deportivo's.
It stands next to the Lagares River.
It's named after the Vigo neighborhood where it stands.
questions.description: A stadium where it sometimes rains more than it scores.
questions.fun_fact: At the 1982 World Cup, Italy played its first-round games at Balaídos… and went on to win the whole tournament.

questions.question: “I was finished in 1929 on Madrid's Gran Vía, and at almost 90 m (295 ft) I was the tallest building in Spain.” What am I?
hints: I was one of the first skyscrapers in Europe.
A communications company built me.
My name is that of the company that put in Spain's telephone lines.
questions.description: A Madrid skyscraper that was tall before being tall was cool.
questions.fun_fact: Hemingway and other reporters went up to its top floors during the war, because international calls went out from there.

questions.question: The Monastery of Leyre, in Navarre, was very important to the first kings of Pamplona. What did they use it for?
wrong_answers: As the seat of the Cortes
hints: Its Romanesque crypt dates from the 11th century and sits next to the Yesa Reservoir.
The kings of Pamplona showered it with gifts and privileges.
In its church, a wooden chest holds the remains of those kings.
questions.description: A monastery in Navarre with reservoir views any hotel would envy.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Abbot Saint Virila stopped to listen to a bird in the Leyre woods, and when he got back, 300 years had passed.

questions.question: This stained-glass skylight crowns the main hall of a modernista building in Barcelona. Which one?
hints: It is one of Lluís Domènech i Montaner's most famous works.
It opened in 1908 and hosts concerts.
It was built for the Orfeó Català, a famous choir.
questions.description: A ceiling so beautiful that nobody remembers to look at the floor.
questions.fun_fact: It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, and its skylight looks like a huge drop of light hanging over the audience.

questions.question: Which king had the Aljafería Palace in Zaragoza built in the 11th century?
hints: He was king of a taifa, one of the kingdoms al-Andalus split into.
He ruled the taifa of Zaragoza.
His other name, Abu Ja'far, sounds a lot like the palace's name.
questions.description: A Zaragoza palace built for joy that ended up full of politicians.
questions.fun_fact: Today the Aljafería is home to the parliament of Aragon, and it's where Verdi's opera “Il trovatore” begins.

questions.question: Euro banknotes went into circulation in 2002. Which of these currencies was NOT replaced by the euro?
hints: It belongs to a country that joined the European Union after 2002.
That country is in the European Union but still has its own currency.
Its capital is Budapest.
questions.description: In 2002, half of Europe emptied its wallets and started over with brand-new money.
questions.fun_fact: Hungary joined the European Union in 2004, but people there still pay in forints.

questions.question: The Museo Picasso Málaga opened in 2003 in a Renaissance palace in the painter's hometown. Who donated most of its works?
hints: Hardly anything had to be bought at auction.
The donors weren't institutions or companies, but private individuals.
They were his daughter-in-law Christine and his grandson Bernard.
questions.description: A gift to Málaga so generous it puts every Secret Santa to shame.
questions.fun_fact: The museum is in the Palacio de Buenavista, and Phoenician and Roman remains were found in its basement during the building work.

questions.question: This print opens Goya's series “The Disasters of War”. Which technique was used to make it?
hints: It's drawn on a metal plate.
An acid “bites” the lines into the copper plate.
Its Spanish name, «aguafuerte», means “strong water”, an old name for nitric acid.
questions.description: Goya had a dark period too, and it wasn't because his studio was short on light.
questions.fun_fact: Goya never saw the series published: it came out in 1863, 35 years after his death.

questions.question: Picasso and Braque created it around 1907, and it shows an object from several sides at once. What are its figures made of?
hints: It's a 20th-century avant-garde movement.
One of its first great paintings is Picasso's “Les Demoiselles d'Avignon”.
The movement's name comes from a shape with six faces.
questions.description: Art for anyone who looks at a guitar and thinks: it could do with being taken apart a bit.
questions.fun_fact: The name came from a critic who, looking at paintings by Braque, said he reduced everything to “cubes”.

questions.question: Julio González, an avant-garde sculptor from Barcelona, taught his technique to Picasso. What material did he sculpt with?
hints: He came from a family of goldsmiths and metalworkers.
He didn't cast his pieces in molds: he welded them.
It's the metal of railings and horseshoes.
questions.description: The sculptor who got Picasso, at almost fifty, to go back to taking lessons.
questions.fun_fact: He is seen as one of the fathers of welded iron sculpture, which he described as “drawing in space.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: this mushroom-shaped rock is the most famous one in a natural site in Spain. What is the site called?
hints: Water and wind carved these limestone rocks over millions of years.
It's in the hills of the province famous for its Hanging Houses.
Its name says it's a city… but a bewitched one.
questions.description: Here the rocks have been posing for photos for millions of years without moving an inch.
questions.fun_fact: Scenes from the movie “Conan the Barbarian” were filmed in the Ciudad Encantada.

questions.question: When muddy rain falls in Spain, which desert does the dust usually come from?
hints: It's very close to Spain, just across the sea.
It's the largest hot desert in the world.
It covers much of North Africa.
questions.description: The day you washed the car and the sky said no.
questions.fun_fact: Sahara dust crosses the Atlantic and helps fertilize the Amazon rainforest.

questions.question: I'm a storm with a woman's name. In January 2021 I covered Madrid in snow, and people skied down the Gran Vía. Who am I?
hints: It was Madrid's biggest snowfall in about 50 years.
I arrived a few days after Three Kings' Day.
Of these names, mine is the only one with four syllables.
questions.description: Madrid's snowmen still send it thank-you cards.
questions.fun_fact: Some parts of Madrid got about 50 centimeters (20 inches) of snow.

questions.question: Vegetta777, Willyrex, Rubius and other YouTubers had adventures in a town called Karmaland. What was Karmaland?
hints: You didn't have to leave home to visit Karmaland.
Each YouTuber recorded it while playing on their own computer.
In that world everything, even the houses and trees, is made of cubes.
questions.description: A town where all the neighbors are famous and nobody pays taxes… or so they say.
questions.fun_fact: Karmaland ran for several seasons, and its YouTubers handed out roles as if they were neighbors in a real town.

questions.question: León's coat of arms has a lion, just as Castile's has a castle. What color is that lion?
hints: It's one of the rarest colors in heraldry: it hardly ever shows up on coats of arms.
It was the color of Roman emperors' cloaks.
It's close to violet, like dark grapes.
questions.description: A lion that doesn't roar or eat, and has been posing for the same photo for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: The castle of Castile and the lion of León also appear on Spain's coat of arms.

questions.question: At the top of Valencia's coat of arms sits a “rat penat.” What animal is it?
hints: It's an animal that comes out at night.
By day it hides in caves and dark corners.
It hangs upside down to sleep.
questions.description: The upstairs neighbor of the coat of arms, living there rent-free for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: The same animal appears on the crest of Valencia CF, the city's soccer club.

questions.question: In a New York store, prices are marked with $. If € stands for the euro, $ stands for the…
hints: Its name comes from an old European silver coin, the “thaler”.
Scrooge McDuck has millions of them.
Its most famous banknote is green.
questions.description: An S that got a stripe and suddenly became a millionaire.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before the dollar, and today both use it.

questions.question: A heraldic color is named after a Black Sea city famous for a reddish earth used as paint. Which city?
hints: Today it belongs to Turkey.
Today that heraldic color is green.
The philosopher Diogenes, the one who lived in a big jar, was born there.
questions.description: A color that turned its coat halfway through the Middle Ages.
questions.fun_fact: At first sinople was red, like the earth of Sinope, and only over time did it come to mean green.

questions.question: In 1979, the shield on the flag of Gipuzkoa lost some objects that recalled a battle against Navarre. What were they?
hints: There were twelve of them.
Tradition says they were captured at the Battle of Velate in 1512.
They are pieces of artillery.
questions.description: A coat of arms that did a big clear-out in 1979, like emptying the garage.
questions.fun_fact: Today the Gipuzkoa shield still shows the king with his sword and the three yew trees above the water.

questions.question: You're in a class that never ends. According to the Spanish saying, it's longer than a day without what?
hints: In many homes, it's bought almost every day.
The saying comes from a time when, if this was missing from the table, the day felt endless.
It can be a long barra or a round hogaza.
questions.description: A question for anyone who checks the clock every two minutes.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, bread was the basis of every meal in Spain, so a day without it felt endless.

questions.question: In Spain, people say someone is in «la edad del pavo». Who is it usually said about?
hints: It has nothing to do with Christmas.
It's the time when your voice changes and your mood comes and goes.
It usually starts at around 12 or 13.
questions.description: A stage of life with more feathers than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: The name is said to come from the awkward, gangly stage young turkeys go through as they grow, and «pavo» also means a silly, scatterbrained person.

questions.question: In an exam, you knew the answer, but suddenly you can't remember a thing. What do people in Spain say has happened to you?
hints: It's the opposite of a head full of ideas.
Think of a sheet of paper with nothing written on it.
It's the color of snow and milk.
questions.description: That moment when your brain goes on vacation without telling you.
questions.fun_fact: Nerves can block your memory for a while, which is why taking a deep breath helps you remember.

questions.question: If someone in Spain «te echa una mano», what are they doing?
hints: It's an expression: don't take it literally.
It comes in handy when you're carrying too many bags.
It makes your job easier.
questions.description: A question that gets very hands-on.
questions.fun_fact: Lots of languages use the hand to talk about helping: in English you “give someone a hand.”

questions.question: Which mountaineer became the first Spanish woman to climb Everest without bottled oxygen, in 1999?
hints: She is from Galicia.
She reached the summit by the north face, from Tibet.
Her surname is the Spanish word for a body of fresh water.
questions.description: Climbing to where planes fly and barely breathing: a terrible plan for anyone but her.
questions.fun_fact: Chus Lago has also crossed vast stretches of polar ice alone, pulling her own sled.

questions.question: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca was shipwrecked in Florida and crossed the south of North America on foot. Which waterfalls was he the first European to see?
hints: He saw them around 1541, years after his great walk.
At the time, he was governor of the Río de la Plata region.
Argentina and Brazil share them.
questions.description: A man who walked so much that today he'd get a sneaker sponsorship.
questions.fun_fact: After his shipwreck, Cabeza de Vaca spent about eight years walking and living with Native peoples until he reached Mexico.

questions.question: Complete: engineer Manuel Jalón, a pioneer of the disposable syringe in Spain, is even more famous for inventing the…
hints: It's an invention found in almost every home in Spain.
It saved people many hours on their knees scrubbing floors.
In Spain it's called the “fregona”.
questions.description: A Spanish engineer who deserves a thank-you card from millions of homes.
questions.fun_fact: Manuel Jalón developed the fregona in Zaragoza in 1956.

questions.question: Karlos Arguiñano is to cooking as Jesús Calleja is to…
hints: His TV shows are filmed far away from any studio.
He has climbed Everest.
On “Planeta Calleja” he takes celebrities to extreme places.
questions.description: A man who can't sit still, not even on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Jesús Calleja was born in Madrid but grew up in León, the place he always calls home.

review.feedback: Source: the fun fact says Jesús Calleja was born in Madrid. As far as I know he was born in León in 1965, as the rater also noted. The source's fun fact needs correcting first, for example to say he was born and raised in León, and then the translation should follow it. Otherwise the translation is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: The Eiffel Tower is to Paris as the Red Fort is to…
hints: It's in Asia.
It's a city in India.
The country's capital is there.
questions.description: A fort so red that even its name is blushing.
questions.fun_fact: The Red Fort in Delhi appears on the back of India's 500-rupee banknote.

questions.question: In 1788, the Royal Cabinet of Natural History in Madrid mounted the first fossil skeleton in history, brought from Argentina. What animal was it?
hints: It was a giant mammal, not a dinosaur.
Its relatives today hang from trees in the rainforest.
It was a sloth the size of an elephant.
questions.description: A pile of bones so big it didn't fit on any of the king's shelves.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Bautista Bru mounted the skeleton, and Cuvier named the animal from Bru's drawings without ever seeing the bones.

questions.question: Which naturalist drove the creation of the Doñana Biological Station in 1964, in marshes like these?
hints: He was a zoologist who studied the birds of the Guadalquivir marshes.
He is called “the father of Doñana”.
He was born in Valladolid and was the first director of the Biological Station itself.
questions.description: Marshes where flamingos get more room than you do on a rush-hour train.
questions.fun_fact: Valverde got foreign naturalists to buy land in Doñana, and that campaign helped found the WWF.

questions.question: In 1935, Emilio Herrera, an engineer from Granada, designed a pioneering suit. What was it for?
questions.answer: Going up to the stratosphere by balloon
hints: It was never used because the Spanish Civil War broke out.
It had to protect against extreme cold and lack of air.
It is seen as a forerunner of the astronaut's spacesuit.
questions.description: An engineer from Granada who designed work clothes for a very unfriendly place.
questions.fun_fact: Emilio Herrera went on to lead the government of the Spanish Republic in exile.

questions.question: Who directed the 1953 film in which a whole village sings “Americanos, os recibimos con alegría” (“Americans, we welcome you with joy”)?
hints: The film is “Welcome Mr. Marshall!”.
The director was from Valencia and portrayed the Spain of his time with humor and big casts of characters.
He also directed “The Executioner” and “The National Shotgun”.
questions.description: A whole village dresses up to impress some visitors who are in quite a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The film was shot in Guadalix de la Sierra (Madrid), which became Villar del Río in the story, a village dressed up as Andalusian.

questions.question: Mario Casas played Hache, a rebel boy with a motorcycle, in this 2010 movie based on a novel by Italian writer Federico Moccia. Which is it?
hints: It's a teenage love story between Hache and Babi.
Its sequel was called “Tengo ganas de ti”.
The title describes a distance high above the clouds.
questions.description: A movie that made half of Spain want a leather jacket and a motorcycle.
questions.fun_fact: The sequel to Moccia's novel, “Ho voglia di te” (“I Want You”), made the habit of hanging love locks on Rome's Milvian Bridge famous in Italy.

questions.question: Look at the hoof on this ham. Which animal does a ham with a hoof like this usually come from?
hints: It's a pig raised mostly in the southwest of the peninsula.
Many spend the fall outdoors, eating acorns under the oak trees.
Because of that hoof, people call it “pata negra”.
questions.description: A leg that hangs from the ceiling for years, and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: A good jamón ibérico can spend more than three years curing before it reaches the table.

questions.question: It's a simple, old-school place serving stews, cocido and a cheap menú del día. What is this type of place called?
hints: Some places like this in Spain are over a hundred years old.
They're common in traditional Madrid, often with checkered tablecloths.
Its name sounds like “the house where you eat”.
questions.description: Where Grandma would cook if she had a business license.
questions.fun_fact: Sobrino de Botín in Madrid opened in 1725 and is listed by Guinness as the oldest restaurant in the world.

questions.question: We lived in the Middle Ages and slipped away from court to hunt in northern mountains. When people looked for us, they said “Está en Babia”. Who are we?
hints: Today “estar en Babia” means being absent-minded, but Babia is a real place.
Babia is a mountain area in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula.
Babia is in the province whose coat of arms shows a lion.
questions.description: Some places you can visit without ever getting off the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Babia really exists: it is an area in the north of the province of León, famous for its mountain pastures.

questions.question: When someone in Spain wants you to stop beating around the bush and get to the point, they say “Ve al…” what?
hints: The word is something very small.
Hens peck it off the ground.
Rice and wheat both come in tiny pieces of this; think of a single seed.
questions.description: This question won't beat around the bush, promise.
questions.fun_fact: The idea is to get past the useless husk, the chaff, to the seed that actually feeds you.

questions.question: What is this glass container, so typical of Spain, used for?
questions.answer: Drinking wine in a thin stream
hints: It gets passed from hand to hand at fiestas and group meals.
Nobody puts their lips on it: you lift it and tip it.
It is very typical of Catalonia and Aragon, and it is usually filled with red.
questions.description: A container that tests your aim and the patience of whoever washes your T-shirt.
questions.fun_fact: Drinking from a porrón takes skill: you start close to your mouth and slowly move it away to make the stream longer without spilling.

questions.question: Alejandro Malaspina was born in Italy, sailed for the Spanish Crown and led a great scientific expedition from 1789 to 1794. Where is the huge glacier named after him?
hints: His expedition sailed the Pacific coast from end to end.
In 1791 he sailed far north, looking for a passage between the Pacific and the Atlantic.
The glacier is in a territory that Russia sold to the United States in 1867.
questions.description: Some people get a street named after them; this sailor got something that moves very, very slowly.
questions.fun_fact: The Malaspina Glacier is the largest piedmont glacier in the world: it covers more ground than some Spanish provinces.

questions.question: I'm an engineer at Spain's CSIC and created the world's first exoskeleton for children, so kids who can't walk can take their first steps. Who am I?
hints: My specialty is robotics.
My exoskeleton helps children with spinal muscular atrophy.
My second surname is the Spanish word for a navy.
questions.description: Science that doesn't stay in the lab: it walks right out the door.
questions.fun_fact: Her children's exoskeleton is called ATLAS, and she founded the company Marsi Bionics to bring it to hospitals.

questions.question: I circle the Earth nonstop, astronauts from many countries live in me, and in 2003 I welcomed Spain's Pedro Duque. What am I?
hints: Several countries built me by joining pieces together in space.
I go all the way around the Earth in about 90 minutes.
People call me by the initials ISS.
questions.description: A home with spectacular views, but the front door is a bit of a trek.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Duque first went to space in 1998 on the space shuttle Discovery, alongside the veteran John Glenn.

questions.question: Miguel de la Quadra-Salcedo was a TVE reporter who created the Ruta Quetzal. In 1956 his spinning throw, like in the Basque barra, was banned. In which event?
hints: In the other throwing events, you are allowed to spin.
The thing you throw is long and ends up stuck in the ground.
It was a hunting and war weapon in ancient times.
questions.description: Sometimes you're so good they change the rules just to stop you winning.
questions.fun_fact: His way of throwing became known as the “Spanish style,” and it reached distances far beyond the world record of the time.

questions.question: Which Spanish city is known as the capital of the navaja (folding knife) and knife-making?
hints: It's in Castilla-La Mancha.
It has a Knife Museum.
It has a big fair every September, and its soccer club is nicknamed “Queso Mecánico”.
questions.description: An object that opens, closes and has been slicing cheese out in the countryside for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, knife sellers waited for trains at this city's station to sell their knives to travelers through the windows.

questions.question: It was 2009, for a supporting role in a Woody Allen film shot in Barcelona, and no Spanish actress had done it before. What award did Penélope Cruz win?
hints: This award has a category for supporting roles.
It's given by a film academy whose members vote, not by a festival jury.
It's a golden statuette of a man holding a sword; Javier Bardem had won one the year before.
questions.description: From Alcobendas all the way to the top, without ever taking off her heels.
questions.fun_fact: The film was “Vicky Cristina Barcelona,” where Penélope Cruz acted alongside Javier Bardem, whom she married in 2010.

questions.question: “Lawrence of Arabia” shot desert scenes in Almería and used the Plaza de España in Seville. In which decade did it come out?
hints: It's a huge British production that won the Oscar for Best Picture.
Its director, David Lean, soon came back to Spain to shoot “Doctor Zhivago”.
It came out the same year as the first James Bond film.
questions.description: Almería put on a turban, and nobody in Hollywood noticed the difference.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, the Plaza de España in Seville stood in for buildings in Cairo and Jerusalem.

questions.question: Which of these trophies is NOT given at any film festival in Spain?
hints: Three of them are given in Málaga, San Sebastián and Valladolid.
A biznaga is a little bunch of jasmine flowers typical of Málaga.
The odd one out is given in Venice.
questions.description: At film festivals, gold comes in every shape except a bar.
questions.fun_fact: The Málaga Film Festival is devoted to Spanish-language cinema, and its awards are called biznagas, like the jasmine bunches sold in the city's streets.

questions.question: The Goya Awards ceremony, once held in Madrid, has traveled all over Spain. In which of these cities has it NEVER been held?
hints: Three of them hosted the ceremony between 2019 and 2023.
One of the cities that did host it did so two years in a row, in 2020 and 2021.
The odd one out is in the Basque Country.
questions.description: Spanish cinema's big night packs its bags more often than a touring theater company.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021 the ceremony was held from Málaga with almost no audience, and many nominees accepted their awards from home by video call.

questions.question: With the mother away on a trip, the father is home alone with all the kids. In the first “Padre no hay más que uno”, how many kids does he have?
hints: There are more of them than fit in a normal car along with their parents.
They include a teenage daughter and a very little girl.
In the second movie, another baby joins the family.
questions.description: A house where the only adult doesn't even know where the washing machine is.
questions.fun_fact: The movie is a Spanish version of the Argentine film “Mamá se fue de viaje”, and Santiago Segura both directs it and plays the lead.

questions.question: The Spanish children's song “La farolera” goes: “six and two are eight, and eight sixteen, and eight twenty-four, and eight…”. What number comes next?
hints: The song keeps adding the same number.
Each step adds 8 to the number before.
It's 24 plus 8.
questions.description: A song where someone falls down and, instead of getting up, starts doing math homework.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric light bulbs, there were people whose job was to light the street lamps by hand every night.

questions.question: I played a TV reporter trapped in a Barcelona building in “REC” and won the Goya for Best New Actress. Who am I?
hints: The 2007 movie was shot as if a TV camera recorded everything.
Before that, I had been a TV presenter.
I'm the niece of TV presenter Concha Velasco.
questions.description: The reporter who only wanted a quiet story about firefighters.
questions.fun_fact: “REC” was such a hit that Hollywood made its own version, “Quarantine”, just one year later.

questions.question: Snack time in Spain: a sándwich is to sliced bread as a bocadillo is to…
hints: You buy it at the bakery, almost every day.
It's long, and its crust is crunchy.
You ask for “una…” and sometimes carry it home under your arm.
questions.description: An after-school snack with more history than the school bell.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, people often buy fresh bread every day, and the barra is the best-selling bread.

questions.question: It comes before lunch, it's often a vermouth with olives, and its name comes from the Latin “aperire”. What does that word mean?
hints: Think about what it's for, just before the meal.
It's meant to get your appetite going.
It's the opposite of “to close”.
questions.description: The moment on Sunday when you eat before you eat.
questions.fun_fact: In many Spanish cities, going for “el vermut” on Sunday means the same as going out for an aperitivo.

questions.question: Which of these cured sausages does NOT contain pimentón?
hints: Look at the color of each one.
Pimentón dyes them red.
The one you're looking for has visible black peppercorns.
questions.description: Four sausages walk into a bar, and one of them is undercover.
questions.fun_fact: Salchichón de Vic, from Catalonia, has Protected Geographical Indication status.

questions.question: This bivalve with a ridged shell is eaten from a can with lemon and gathered by hand in the rías at low tide. Which region has the most famous ones?
hints: It's on the Atlantic coast.
It's a region in the northwest, with lots of rain and lots of rías.
The Ría de Noia is one of its best-known spots.
questions.description: A tiny shellfish that comes to the table in its own fancy can.
questions.fun_fact: Cockles live buried in the sand and breathe through two little tubes that poke up to the surface.

questions.question: You walk into a bodega in La Rioja and it smells of oak barrels. What is made there?
hints: It's made from fruit.
It's often left to age for years before it's sold.
It's made from grapes.
questions.description: A cool, dark cellar that grown-ups are never in a hurry to leave.
questions.fun_fact: “Bodega” comes from the Greek “apothēkē”, a storehouse, the same root as the English word “apothecary”.

questions.question: It opened in 1991, hosted the Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix every year until 2025, and also hosts MotoGP. In which town is it?
hints: It's in Catalonia.
It's about 20 km (12 miles) from Barcelona, in the Vallès Oriental area.
Its name starts with “Mont”.
questions.description: A quiet town where, one weekend a year, nobody respects the speed limit.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2026 the Spanish Grand Prix has been held in Madrid, and Montmeló still has its own race: the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

questions.question: Yellow is to the Tour de France as pink is to the Giro d'Italia, and … is to the Vuelta a España.
hints: It's the color worn by the leader of the overall standings.
The leader has worn it since 2010, the year Spain won the soccer World Cup.
It's the color of the Spanish national soccer team's shirt.
questions.description: Three races, three jerseys, and a cyclist who dresses according to who's winning.
questions.fun_fact: Before red came back in 2010, the Vuelta leader wore yellow for a while, and later gold.

questions.question: In a futsal match, how many players from each team are on the court at once, counting the goalkeeper?
hints: Fewer than in the regular outdoor game.

questions.question: On Antena 3's “¡Boom!”, four friends won more than 6 million euros, a Spanish TV record. What was their team called?

questions.description: A drink that comes in its own cup, and you need a machete to open the cup.
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese sailors gave the coconut its name, “coco”, because its three little spots looked like a funny face to them.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this icy drink, sweet and a little spicy, is served with a straw coated in tamarind. What is it called?
hints: It has chamoy and chile powder.
Its main fruit is yellow and has a big pit.
Its name starts with the name of that fruit.
questions.description: Sweet, spicy, chile-dusted and icy: a drink that can't make up its mind, and thank goodness.
questions.fun_fact: Chamoy is said to have been inspired by the salted plums that Asian immigrants brought to Mexico.

questions.question: This small yellow mango with almost no fibers is named after the farmer who grew it. Which state does it come from?
hints: Mangoes need heat and tropical rain.
That state borders Guatemala.
Its Soconusco region, around Tapachula, holds the designation of origin.
questions.description: A mango with a first and last name, as if it were about to get its own ID card.
questions.fun_fact: It's named after Ataúlfo Morales Gordillo, on whose land in Tapachula the original tree was found in the mid-20th century.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these little black, wrinkly fruits are a must in Christmas ponche. Which fruit are they, once dried?
hints: They're not the tiny raisins in arroz con leche.
Fresh, it's purple and juicy and has a pit.
In ponche people call them “pasas,” but they're bigger than raisins.
questions.description: Fruits that got way too much sun and ended up more wrinkly than a happy grandma.
questions.fun_fact: They're famous for helping digestion, thanks to their fiber and sorbitol, a natural sugar.

questions.question: A pregnant woman's belly is pointy, sticking straight out in front. According to popular belief, what will she have?
hints: The belief guesses something about the baby just by looking at the belly.
If the belly were round and wide, they'd say the opposite.
They say it will be a little varoncito.
questions.description: Aunts seem to have X-ray eyes when they look at a pregnant belly.
questions.fun_fact: The shape of the belly depends on the mom's muscles and how the baby is lying, not on whether it's a boy or a girl.

questions.question: Which of these does Grandma NOT do with Vicks VapoRub?
questions.answer: Give it to you with water for a tummy ache
wrong_answers: Rub it on your chest for a cough
Put it in your stuffy nose
Rub it on your mosquito bites
hints: Lots of Mexican grandmas really do three of these things.
It has a very strong smell of menthol and eucalyptus.
It should never be swallowed.
questions.description: The little blue jar that cures everything at Grandma's house… well, almost everything.
questions.fun_fact: Vicks VapoRub was invented by a pharmacist in the United States in the late 1800s.

questions.question: This is azabache (jet), the stone on little bracelets worn against the evil eye. What is it really?
hints: It isn't a mineral like quartz: it comes from something that was once alive.
It formed millions of years ago, buried under great pressure.
Before it was stone, it was part of a tree.
questions.description: A little black stone older than all your grandparents put together.
questions.fun_fact: Black volcanic glass is obsidian, which the Mexica used to make knives and mirrors; azabache is much lighter.

questions.question: You just ate and want to jump in the pool. According to many Mexican moms, what can you get?
hints: They say you have to wait a good while before getting in the water.
It has to do with the food you're still digesting.
The same word is used when your nose is all stuffed up.
questions.description: Mom's rule that turns the pool into a no-go zone for a whole hour.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors say swimming after eating isn't dangerous: at most you might get a cramp or feel heavy.

questions.question: María Félix made her film debut in 1943 in “El peñón de las ánimas,” with Jorge Negrete. Who directed that first film of hers?
hints: He was a very busy Golden Age director who also wrote and produced many of his films.
Years later he directed several Pedro Infante films.
His last name starts with Z.
questions.description: Before she was “La Doña,” somebody had to shout “Action!” at her for the very first time.
questions.fun_fact: On the set of “El peñón de las ánimas,” María Félix and Jorge Negrete couldn’t stand each other; years later they got married.

questions.question: Alberto Gout directed “Aventurera,” the great classic of rumbera films, starring Ninón Sevilla. In what year was it released?
hints: It was during Miguel Alemán’s six-year presidential term.
That same year, Luis Buñuel released “Los olvidados.”
It was exactly the middle of the 20th century.
questions.description: Sequins, feathers and a director who knew exactly when to start the bongos.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1990s, “Aventurera” became a hugely successful stage musical starring Edith González.

questions.question: You do it with both hands, it makes noise, and the song “If You're Happy and You Know It” asks you to do it. What is it?
hints: The audience does it at the end of a show.
Your hands hit each other.
People say “Give them a big hand!” just before doing it.
questions.description: A song that turns being happy into a workout.
questions.fun_fact: In later verses, the song also asks you to stomp your feet and shout “Hooray!”

questions.question: Ernesto Alonso, a leading man of the Golden Age, was nicknamed “Mr. Telenovela”. Why?
questions.answer: He produced dozens of famous telenovelas
wrong_answers: He was the first announcer on television
He wrote TV reviews in the newspaper
He sold the first television in Mexico
hints: His most famous work wasn't in front of the camera.
He was behind classics like “El maleficio”.
He decided which melodramas got made and with whom.
questions.description: If your family cries in front of the TV at nine at night, you can blame this man.
questions.fun_fact: Before TV, Ernesto Alonso starred in Luis Buñuel's “The Criminal Life of Archibaldo de la Cruz” (1955).

questions.question: In Age of Empires II, it's the Aztecs' unique unit: it fights on foot and is very good against other infantry. What is it called?
hints: It's based on a real order of elite Mexica warriors.
In Tenochtitlan they formed one of the two most respected military orders.
They wore the skin of the largest wild cat in the Americas.
questions.description: To win this video game, building isn't enough: you also have to dress the part.
questions.fun_fact: In Age of Empires II, Aztec villagers answer in Nahuatl when you give them orders.

questions.question: In Nahuatl I'm called “atl,” and I hide in place names like Atlixco and Atlacomulco. What am I?
hints: Without me there would be no chinampas in Xochimilco.
In Mexica codices I was painted blue, with little shells.
You drink me when you're thirsty.
questions.description: A tiny Nahuatl word that sneaks like a stowaway into very long town names.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Atlantic” doesn't come from Nahuatl: its likeness to “atl” is pure coincidence.

questions.question: “Splinter” is to wood as “tepalcate” is to…
hints: Archaeologists find millions of tepalcates at their digs.
A tepalcate is a piece of something that broke.
It’s the material of traditional ollas and jarritos.
questions.description: What’s left over when someone in the kitchen says “it just slipped.”
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Nahuatl “tapalcatl,” and in Mexico it’s also used to say something is old or useless.

questions.question: The meat is cooked in a pit in the ground, wrapped in maguey leaves, and many families eat it on Sundays with consomé. What is it?
hints: Hidalgo and the State of Mexico are famous for it.
It's almost always made with lamb.
A very similar word is used in English for grilling meat outdoors.
questions.description: The official reason the uncles show up right on time for Sunday lunch.
questions.fun_fact: The word “barbacoa” comes from the Taíno language of the Caribbean, where it meant a frame of sticks for cooking.

questions.question: In the Leyendas film where Leo San Juan faces mummies rising from the cemetery, in which city does the story take place?
hints: It's a colonial mining city in the Bajío region.
It has underground streets and the famous Callejón del Beso.
The city has the same name as its state, and it has a real mummy museum.
questions.description: A movie where the dead get up early, and not to go to school.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody made Guanajuato's real mummies on purpose: the bodies mummified on their own because of the cemetery's soil and climate.

questions.question: According to legend, a rider in a charro suit like this one, but all black, offers gold coins to travelers. Who is he really?
hints: The gold he gives away is never free.
In exchange for the coins, he takes your soul.
He's the same one who has horns and a tail in the pastorelas.
questions.description: The best-dressed rider on the road, but you'd better not even accept a ride from him.
questions.fun_fact: In many versions, the Charro Negro rides a black horse with fire in its eyes and appears only on lonely roads at night.

questions.question: A very famous team from Guadalajara is nicknamed after this animal. Which animal is it?
hints: It loves climbing hills and rocks.
It has a little beard and horns.
In Mexico it's also called a chiva.
questions.description: In Guadalajara, some people lose their voices every weekend shouting for it.
questions.fun_fact: A baby goat is called a kid, and roasted kid, known as cabrito, is one of Monterrey's most famous dishes.

questions.question: In the Apertura 2006 final, Chivas beat Toluca and became champion. How many years had it gone without winning the league?
hints: The fans had waited many tournaments to celebrate a title again.
It was less than a decade.
Its previous title was the Verano 1997.
questions.description: Some droughts last so long that not even the weather forecast remembers them.
questions.fun_fact: With that title Chivas reached 11 league championships and became the most successful team in Mexico at that time.

questions.question: This club was founded in 1927 by workers at a cement plant in Hidalgo, wears blue and ended a 23-year title drought in 2021. What is its most famous nickname?
hints: It's a Mexico City team, one of the “big four.”
In 2021 it finally won “la novena,” its ninth title.
The full nickname adds the color “celeste.”
questions.description: A team whose fans suffer so much that people invented a verb for it.
questions.fun_fact: The club was born in Jasso, Hidalgo, and its name comes from the cement brand of the cooperative where its founders worked.

questions.question: What nickname is this Mexican coach known by?
hints: He coached the Mexican national team more than once.
He also played in a World Cup for Mexico, in 1986.
The nickname comes from his family's roots in a region of northern Spain famous for the beret and jai alai.
questions.description: Some coaches shout from the bench, and then there's this one, who turns every match into a full-volume pep talk.
questions.fun_fact: Javier Aguirre coached Mexico at the 2002 and 2010 World Cups, and he also managed Spanish clubs like Osasuna, Atlético Madrid and Mallorca.

questions.question: Which red-and-black Guadalajara club ended a 70-year wait for a league title in 2021?
hints: It is Chivas' rival in the Clásico Tapatío.
Its only earlier title came in 1951.
Its nickname is «los Zorros» (the Foxes).
questions.description: Its fans' patience deserves a trophy of its own.
questions.fun_fact: After waiting 70 years, Atlas won again the very next tournament and became back-to-back champions in 2022.

questions.question: In what year was Club América founded?
hints: It was before Mexico had a professional league.
It was founded by young students from schools in Mexico City.
It was founded on October 12, and that's why it picked its name.
questions.description: A club with so much history that its birth certificate belongs in a museum.
questions.fun_fact: The name “América” was chosen because the club was founded on October 12, the day that marks Columbus's arrival in the Americas.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican goalkeeper who started out at América. At the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, I stopped everything Neymar tried and became a meme. Who am I?
hints: Besides playing in Mexico, I spent several years at clubs in Europe.
My full first name is Guillermo.
They call me “Memo” and my last name starts with O.
questions.description: Some people catch balls, and some catch the attention of the whole internet.
questions.fun_fact: Memo Ochoa was called up to several World Cups with Mexico, starting with Germany 2006.

questions.question: In lucha libre, if a wrestler throws a low blow, who can disqualify him?
hints: This person is in the ring for the whole match.
This is also the person who counts when a wrestler is flat on his back on the mat.
Usually wears a light-colored shirt and enforces the rules.
questions.description: A blow that hurts your pride the most… well, no, it hurts most down there.
questions.fun_fact: Rudos often throw low blows just when the referee is distracted, and the crowd yells it at the referee.

questions.question: Look at this tag team match. If one show has a tag team match and then a trios match, how many wrestlers get in the ring in total?
hints: First count the wrestlers in each match separately.
A tag team match has two teams of two.
A trios match has two teams of three.
questions.description: Math class, but with headlocks and kicks.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, trios matches are also called “relevos australianos” (Australian relays).

questions.question: How is a traditional pro wrestler's mask fastened at the back?
hints: They're tightened by hand before heading out to the ring.
In the middle of a match, a sneaky opponent can loosen them with one tug.
They criss-cross through little eyelets at the back.
questions.description: It's the part of the mask nobody sees… until a rudo gets mischievous.
questions.fun_fact: Untying the laces of an opponent's mask is a classic rudo dirty trick.

questions.question: In “Coco”, Imelda, Miguel's great-great-grandmother, banned music in her family. What trade did the family take up after that?
hints: Imelda started this business to get by on her own.
It uses leather, thread and a hammer.
What they make, you wear on your feet.
questions.description: A great-great-grandma with more fire than a habanero pepper.
questions.fun_fact: “Coco” won the Oscars for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song, for “Remember Me”.

questions.question: During Mexico's Independence Day celebrations, from the balcony of which building does the president give the Grito de Independencia?
hints: It's in the historic center of Mexico City.
It faces the Zócalo, the biggest plaza in the country.
Inside, it has Diego Rivera's famous murals about the history of Mexico.
questions.description: A balcony with a bigger crowd than any concert all year.
questions.fun_fact: The bell rung during the Grito is the original one from Dolores Hidalgo, brought to Mexico City in 1896.

questions.question: Look at this pipe at the back of a vehicle. What comes out of it when the engine is running?
hints: It comes from what the engine has already used and doesn't need anymore.
Sometimes it looks gray or white, especially on cold mornings.
It smells bad and you shouldn't breathe it in.
questions.description: Even cars need somewhere to let out what didn't agree with them.
questions.fun_fact: The exhaust system has a muffler that makes the engine sound much quieter.

questions.question: This is a detail of the most famous Maya book in existence, painted on bark paper. In which city is it kept today?
hints: It's very far from the Yucatán Peninsula, in Europe.
The book is named after the city where it's kept.
It's a German city on the Elbe River.
questions.description: A library book more than 800 years overdue.
questions.fun_fact: The Dresden Codex got wet during the bombing of the city in 1945, and some of its pages were damaged.

questions.question: Look at the photo: an ofrenda like this one always has a glass of water. According to tradition, what is it for?
questions.answer: So the souls can quench their thirst
wrong_answers: So the living and dead can toast
hints: It's for the visitors who arrive that night.
It has to do with how tiring the journey back is.
The departed arrive thirsty after a long road.
questions.description: One night a year, the house fills with guests nobody sees but everyone expects.
questions.fun_fact: Salt is also placed on the ofrenda; according to tradition it purifies the souls so they stay pure on their journey.

questions.question: If you looked up through your eclipse glasses on April 8, 2024, in which of these cities could you NOT see the total solar eclipse?
hints: The Moon's shadow entered Mexico from the Pacific Ocean.
Then it crossed the country toward the northeast, heading for the United States.
The right city is on the Caribbean, far away from that path.
questions.description: The day the Sun took a nap in the middle of the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Mazatlán was the first big city on the mainland of the whole continent to see totality during that eclipse.

questions.question: This head of a Maya king from Palenque is modeled in stucco. What was that material made from?
hints: The Yucatán Peninsula is made almost entirely of this kind of rock.
To make it, the stone was burned in kilns and then mixed with water.
It's the same white powder used to nixtamalize corn for tortillas.
questions.description: Long before cement, someone already knew how to give a wall a quick touch-up.
questions.fun_fact: Burning limestone took huge amounts of firewood, so stucco may have helped clear the forest around Maya cities.

questions.question: This facade, the Codz Poop, is covered with hundreds of masks of the rain god. At which archaeological site in Yucatán is it?
hints: It is a Puuc-style city in southern Yucatán.
A white Maya road linked it to its neighbor Uxmal.
A lone arch stands at the start of that road, and the site's name has five letters.
questions.description: A wall with more noses than a clown convention.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya name Codz Poop is often translated as “rolled mat,” after the shape of the masks' noses.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this temple at Chichén Itzá called, with a chac mool on top and a forest of columns at its feet?
hints: It stands right on the main plaza, next to El Castillo.
The columns below form the so-called Group of the Thousand Columns.
Hundreds of armed men are carved into those columns.
questions.description: A temple with so many columns that nobody has dared to really count them.
questions.fun_fact: Inside this temple, archaeologists found an older one, built first and then covered by the new one, like a Russian nesting doll.

questions.question: You're on a beach in Oaxaca, releasing newborn sea turtles into the ocean. How many flippers does each one have?
hints: It uses its flippers both to crawl across the sand and to swim.
The front flippers are much bigger and do almost all the work when swimming.
It's an even number, smaller than five.
questions.description: They swim from the day they're born and never took a single swimming lesson.
questions.fun_fact: Female sea turtles often return to lay their eggs on the same beach where they hatched.

questions.question: As an ancient Maya, you wouldn't bathe or leave home during Uayeb. How many days did it last at the end of the 365-day year?
hints: The other months of the year had 20 days each.
There were 18 of those months.
Do the math: 365 minus 360.
questions.description: The unluckiest days of the year: even grandma wouldn't go out to the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica also had 5 unlucky days at the end of their year: they called them nemontemi.

questions.question: This Maya priest and healer from Yucatán leads the Ch'a Cháak rain ceremony and tells the future with a crystal stone. What is he called?
hints: He is part of life in the Maya farming villages of Yucatán.
There are still some today in the Maya villages of Yucatán.
His name in Maya means roughly “the one who knows” or “the one who does”.
questions.description: In the villages of Yucatán, some jobs aren't taught at any university.
questions.fun_fact: The crystal stone the h-men uses to tell the future is called a sastún.

questions.question: A cyclist’s legs are to the pedals as an engine’s pistons are to…
hints: Pedals turn an up-and-down push into a spin.
In the engine, this part takes the push from the pistons and turns it into rotation.
It’s a long metal shaft bent into a zigzag of elbows.
questions.description: A cyclist and a gasoline engine have more in common than you’d think.
questions.fun_fact: A bicycle’s pedal arms work like a tiny crankshaft, which is why bike mechanics call that part the “crankset”.

questions.question: Look at the photo: at the spring equinox, a serpent seems to crawl down this Maya pyramid's stairs. What is its body made of?
hints: It only appears on sunny afternoons.
If a cloud comes by, the serpent disappears.
They are triangles the Sun makes as it hits the corners of the pyramid.
questions.description: A serpent that shows up on time every year and never needs an entry ticket.
questions.fun_fact: Every equinox, thousands of people dressed in white go to Chichén Itzá to watch Kukulcán come down and soak up its energy.

questions.question: At the tiendita you pay for a 17-peso bag of chips with a 20-peso bill. Which coins give you the exact change?
hints: First work out how much is left over.
From 17 to 20 is only a few pesos.
They have to give you back 3 pesos.
questions.description: The most important math of childhood: the math at the tiendita.
questions.fun_fact: At many tienditas, if they're out of change, they make up the difference with a candy or a piece of gum.

questions.question: Pure gold is 24 karats, and the Mexican Centenario is about 21.6. What does having fewer karats tell you?
questions.answer: It has another metal mixed in
hints: For gold, karats don't measure weight.
They measure how pure the metal is.
The Centenario got a bit of copper to make it tougher.
questions.description: A number that can make gold look great or not so great.
questions.fun_fact: The Centenario was first minted in 1921 to celebrate 100 years since Mexico's independence was won.

questions.question: You eat at a fonda (a small family restaurant) and the bill is 200 pesos. How much is it customary to tip in Mexico?
hints: It's a small part of the bill, but more than a few loose coins.
It's worked out as a percentage.
The usual amount is between 10 and 15%.
questions.description: Money you leave on the table on purpose, and nobody gives it back.
questions.fun_fact: In supermarkets, the kids and older folks who bag your groceries are called “cerillitos,” and they work for tips.

questions.question: Banco de México has made the silver Onza Libertad since 1982. What percentage of pure silver does it contain?
hints: It's a coin for investing and collecting, not for paying.
Its purity matches the most famous silver investment coins from other countries.
Its purity is written as “.999”.
questions.description: A coin so pretty it feels wrong to spend it at the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: The Onza Libertad shows the winged Victory from the Angel of Independence, with the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes in the background.

questions.question: White shorts, red socks and an eagle on the chest: that's the classic home kit of Mexico's national soccer team. What color is the shirt?
hints: Fans call the team by a nickname that comes from its colors.
It's the color of the grass on a soccer field.
It's the color of a nopal cactus.
questions.description: When the team plays at home, half the country wears the same shirt and nobody calls them copycats.
questions.fun_fact: Estadio Azteca is the first stadium to host matches at three World Cups: 1970, 1986 and 2026.

questions.question: We are six students in white gloves. We march at the Monday honores a la bandera, and one of us carries the flag. Who are we?
hints: We are often chosen for having good grades.
We march in step while drums and bugles play.
The one who carries the flag is called the abanderado.
questions.description: White gloves, shoes shined like mirrors, and zero plans to start off on the wrong foot.
questions.fun_fact: Being in the escolta is such an honor that many students practice their march for weeks.

questions.question: What color is the middle stripe of this flag?
hints: It's a very light color.
The eagle from the coat of arms sits on that stripe.
It's the color of snow.
questions.description: On September 16, this flag waves at every school, every home and even at the elote stand.
questions.fun_fact: The three stripes of the Mexican flag are vertical and exactly the same width.

questions.question: Finish what kids learn in school: the red on Mexico's flag stands for “the blood of the…”
hints: They're people, not animals.
They fought for the homeland.
Hidalgo and Morelos are among the most famous.
questions.description: A color with so much attitude even the chiles are jealous.
questions.fun_fact: On the Trigarante flag of 1821, red stood for union.

questions.question: There are three of them, a 1984 law says how they must be used, and one is sung while another is raised. What are they called together?
hints: You see them at school every Monday.
One has an eagle, and another begins “Mexicanos, al grito de guerra”.
They are the flag, the coat of arms and the anthem.
questions.description: A trio more famous than any rock band: they never miss the Monday ceremony.
questions.fun_fact: The law that protects them is called the Law on the National Coat of Arms, Flag and Anthem.

questions.question: You sit behind the wheel of a car with a manual gearbox. How many pedals are at your feet?
hints: One of them makes the car go faster.
Another one makes the car stop.
Besides those two, there is one you press to change gears: the clutch.
questions.description: Driving a car with gears means your feet have to know how to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Automatic cars have no clutch pedal, just an accelerator and a brake.

questions.question: I was the last tlatoani of the Mexica and defended Tenochtitlan to the end. Every February 28, the flag flies at half-mast in my memory. Who am I?
hints: I was very young when I became tlatoani.
I came after Cuitláhuac.
A borough (alcaldía) of Mexico City bears my name.
questions.description: A man with his own date on the calendar: every February, the flag bows its head for him.
questions.fun_fact: In Nahuatl, the name Cuauhtémoc means “descending eagle.”

questions.question: The World Cup that Mexico hosted with the United States and Canada opened with El Tri playing at Estadio Azteca. In which month?
hints: It was right in the middle of the rainy season in Mexico City.
Many kids weren't out of school for summer vacation yet.
It's the month when summer begins.
questions.description: The whole country said “ahorita empieza,” and for once it really did start right away.
questions.fun_fact: The 2026 World Cup was the first in history with 48 teams.

questions.question: I coached the Under-23 team that won Olympic bronze at Tokyo 2020, and in 2023 I lifted the Gold Cup with the senior team. Who am I?
hints: As a player, I was a midfielder for Pumas and for El Tri.
I took over the senior team in 2023, after an Argentine coach who didn't last long.
Fans call me “Jimmy.”
questions.description: From the youth bench to the big bench, with no layovers.
questions.fun_fact: In the bronze medal match at Tokyo 2020, Mexico beat host Japan 3-1.

questions.question: At the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, this player scored a left-footed stunner against Mexico. Who is he?
hints: He's from South America.
He wears number 10 for his national team.
He was the captain who won that same World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: A night in Qatar that El Tri's fans would rather erase from memory.
questions.fun_fact: After beating Mexico, Argentina kept going all the way to beating France in the 2022 World Cup final.

questions.question: This El Tri striker, son of a former Argentine soccer player, became famous scoring goals for Feyenoord. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Argentina but chose to play for Mexico.
His dad, “el Chaco,” played for Cruz Azul.
His nickname is “el Bebote.”
questions.description: A striker who could have worn another color, but his heart beat for green.
questions.fun_fact: Santiago Giménez could have played for Argentina, where he was born, but he chose to wear Mexico's jersey.

questions.question: At France 1998 I wore the Aztec calendar jersey and made a move famous: hopping between two opponents with the ball trapped between my feet. Who am I?
hints: I was an idol at Club América.
Years later I became governor of Morelos.
The move is named after me: the “cuauhtemiña”.
questions.description: Some jerseys just look nice, and some look like they came straight out of the Anthropology Museum.
questions.fun_fact: Cuauhtémoc Blanco showed off the “cuauhtemiña” at the 1998 World Cup against South Korea.

questions.question: In the London 2012 Olympic final, at what point in the match did Oribe Peralta score Mexico's first goal?
hints: It was in the first half.
Many fans were still settling into their seats.
Not even the first minute had passed.
questions.description: A goal replayed in Mexico more often than Saturday morning cartoons.
questions.fun_fact: Oribe Peralta also scored the second goal, and Mexico won the final 2–1.

questions.question: Argentina, captained by Maradona, beat West Germany 3–2 in the final at the Estadio Azteca. In what year?
hints: The mascot of that World Cup was Pique, a chili pepper with a mustache and a sombrero.
At that tournament, Maradona scored his famous “Hand of God” goal.
It was the second World Cup in Mexico, 16 years after the first.
questions.description: An Argentine victory party with a taste of tortilla.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico hosted that World Cup because Colombia, the country first chosen, pulled out.

questions.question: I'm an Olympic sport: I win if I lift more weight over my head. In me, Soraya Jiménez became Mexico's first female Olympic gold medalist. What am I?
hints: Athletes compete in categories by body weight.
It uses a long bar with plates on the ends.
In Spanish it's called “halterofilia” or “levantamiento de pesas”.
questions.description: A sport where shouting helps even more than when you're moving house.
questions.fun_fact: Soraya Jiménez won at Sydney 2000 in the 58 kg (128 lb) category, Mexico's first gold since Los Angeles 1984.

questions.question: This windshield cracked, but it didn’t shatter into pieces. What is it made of?
hints: It isn’t a single piece: it has several layers.
Between two layers of glass there is a sheet of plastic.
Its name is the same word used for sealing a paper ID card in clear plastic.
questions.description: A glass that breaks but flatly refuses to fall apart.
questions.fun_fact: Side windows are usually made of tempered glass, which breaks into lots of small pieces without sharp edges.

questions.question: This yellow sculpture on Paseo de la Reforma, known as “El Caballito,” is by Sebastián. In which state was this sculptor born?
hints: It's a state in northern Mexico.
It's the largest state in the country.
It shares its name with its capital and with a tiny dog breed.
questions.description: A horse that has never tasted a carrot, but has had plenty of yellow paint.
questions.fun_fact: Sebastián's real name is Enrique Carbajal; his artist name comes from a painting of Saint Sebastian.

questions.question: Dr. Atl invented solid painting sticks, the “Atl-colors,” that worked on paper, canvas or even rock. What were they made of?
hints: You didn't need water or any mixing on the spot to paint with them.
They are more like a crayon than a watercolor.
Bees make one of the ingredients; another comes from the sticky sap of trees.
questions.description: When no color from the art store will do, the artist invents his own and names it after himself.
questions.fun_fact: Dr. Atl watched the Paricutín volcano being born in 1943 and painted it again and again.

questions.question: Rosa Rolanda, a California-born artist married to Miguel Covarrubias, had several careers. Which one was NOT one of them?
hints: She came to Mexico after making it big on the New York stage.
In Mexico she was friends with Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera.
Her art was about movement and images, not her voice.
questions.description: An artist with so many jobs that her business card needed its own business card.
questions.fun_fact: Her real name was Rosemonde Cowan; “Rosa Rolanda” was her stage name.

questions.question: The film “Frida” (2002), starring Salma Hayek, won two Oscars: one for Best Original Score. What was the other?
hints: Salma was nominated, but she didn't win that night.
The film was also nominated for Best Costume Design, but didn't win that one.
It has to do with wigs, face paint and prosthetics.
questions.description: Hollywood went to Coyoacán and came back with golden statuettes in its suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: With this role, Salma Hayek became the first Mexican woman nominated for the Best Actress Oscar.

questions.question: In 1995 I wrote the introduction to Frida Kahlo’s diary, but I was already famous for novels like “Aura” and “Where the Air Is Clear.” Who am I?
hints: I’m a novelist, not a poet or a chronicler.
I was born in Panama, the son of a Mexican diplomat.
I also wrote “The Death of Artemio Cruz.”
questions.description: Reading someone else’s diary is wrong… unless it’s published with a fancy introduction.
questions.fun_fact: Frida’s diary, full of color drawings, was published in full for the first time in 1995.

questions.question: After her accident, Frida Kahlo painted her first self-portraits lying down, looking into a mirror. Where was it placed?
questions.answer: In the canopy above her bed
wrong_answers: On the floor next to her bed
hints: She couldn't get up.
She had to see herself without turning her head.
Lying on her back, all she could see was what was above her.
questions.description: An old-school selfie: no phone, no filters and loads of patience.
questions.fun_fact: Frida painted about 55 self-portraits and said she painted herself because she was the subject she knew best.

questions.question: Which people carved the huge stone heads found in Veracruz and Tabasco?
hints: It is one of the oldest cultures in Mesoamerica, much older than the Mexicas.
Many call it the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica.
Its name comes from Nahuatl and means “people of the rubber country.”
questions.description: Faces so big that no mirror in the world could fit them.
questions.fun_fact: Some Olmec heads weigh more than 20 metric tons (about 22 US tons), and the stone was moved from mountains tens of kilometers away, with no pack animals or wheels.

questions.question: I'm orange, my Nahuatl name means “twenty flowers,” and my scent guides the dead to the ofrenda. What am I?
hints: You see me everywhere in late October and early November.
My petals are used to make paths from the front door to the altar.
I'm the Day of the Dead flower.
questions.description: The favorite decoration of the visitors who arrive every November from very, very far away.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is where cempasúchil first came from; today it's grown in many countries, even to make egg yolks a deeper color.

questions.question: This bright light shines in the sky before dawn. According to legend, it was born from a god's heart. Which god?
hints: The god went away to the east, and there his heart rose into the sky.
This god was also the Feathered Serpent.
The Maya called him Kukulcán.
questions.description: A light in the sky that gets up even earlier than your dad on market day.
questions.fun_fact: The “morning star” isn't a star at all: it's the planet Venus, the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon.

questions.question: In the Mexica myth of the Five Suns, in which era did people turn into monkeys?
hints: It was the second of the five suns.
Right after this era came one in which people turned into turkeys.
People held on to the trees so the hurricanes wouldn't carry them away.
questions.description: An era so wild that people ended up hanging from the trees.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya Popol Vuh also has men who turn into monkeys: the men made of wood, one of the gods' failed attempts at making people.

questions.question: Three of these luxury car brands were founded in Germany. Which one wasn't?
hints: The one we want was founded in another European country.
It was founded in 1906 by two partners, Charles and Henry.
It's as British as afternoon tea.
questions.description: Four luxury cars walk into a party, and one of them doesn't speak the same language as the others.
questions.fun_fact: The little silver statue on the hood of every Rolls-Royce is called the “Spirit of Ecstasy.”

questions.question: At the Sacred Cenote of Chichén Itzá, the Maya threw in jade, gold and pottery. Why?
wrong_answers: To pay taxes to the king
hints: Yucatán has almost no rivers, and water was everything.
Their food depended on a good harvest from the milpas (cornfields).
This Maya god was in charge of clouds, lightning and water for the milpas.
questions.description: A natural swimming pool where nobody went for a swim, out of respect.
questions.fun_fact: In the early 20th century, divers and dredges pulled thousands of jade, gold and copal objects out of the Sacred Cenote.

questions.question: This life-size clay sculpture of an eagle warrior was found in Mexico City. At which archaeological site?
hints: It was found in a building called the House of the Eagles.
It's right in the Historic Center, next to the Cathedral and the Zócalo.
It was the main temple of Tenochtitlan, dedicated to Tláloc and Huitzilopochtli.
questions.description: A warrior with a beaked helmet and wings, ready for a photo for 500 years now.
questions.fun_fact: The eagle warriors and the jaguar warriors were the two elite military orders of the Mexica.

questions.question: Listen: this wind instrument plays alongside the accordion in norteño music from Chihuahua. What is it?
hints: It’s made of metal, but it has a mouthpiece with a reed, like the wooden ones.
It’s curved, like the letter J.
It’s named after its inventor, Adolphe Sax.
questions.description: In Chihuahua the accordion never dances alone: it always brings a partner to the party.
questions.fun_fact: The saxophone was invented in Belgium around 1840, and today it’s a must in Chihuahua norteño and in duranguense music.

questions.question: If you count the strings on the bajo sexto Cornelio Reyna played in Los Relámpagos del Norte, how many are there?
hints: Don't be fooled by the word “sexto”.
Its strings come in pairs, tuned together.
There are six pairs of strings.
questions.description: The accordion's best buddy in any norteño cantina worth the name.
questions.fun_fact: Cornelio Reyna and Ramón Ayala formed Los Relámpagos del Norte in Reynosa, Tamaulipas, in the 1960s.

questions.question: The marimbol is a wooden box the musician sits on to play the bass in son jarocho. What do the fingers pluck to make it sound?
hints: Despite its name, it isn't played like a marimba.
It's related to the African kalimba.
They are thin metal strips that vibrate when you let go.
questions.description: An instrument you can sit on without anyone telling you off.
questions.fun_fact: The marimbol comes from African instruments like the mbira and is also played in Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico.

questions.question: Look at this keyboard: in pasito duranguense it plays the bass lines that another instrument plays in a Sinaloa-style banda. Which one?
hints: It’s a wind instrument.
It’s the biggest and deepest instrument in the band.
It’s made of metal, and the musician almost hugs it.
questions.description: A keyboard covering for a bandmate who skipped rehearsal.
questions.fun_fact: Pasito duranguense exploded in the early 2000s among migrants from Durango living in Chicago.

questions.question: Los Tucanes de Tijuana recorded it in the ’90s, it’s a must at weddings, and in it a man complains his wife won’t stop dancing. Which song is it?
hints: The title is a woman’s nickname.
It’s a short name ending in “a”.
It’s a popular nickname for Encarnación.
questions.description: The song that gets even the most serious uncle onto the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: In 2018 “La Chona” became a hit again in Mexico and the US thanks to an online challenge where people filmed themselves dancing to it.

questions.question: I sing banda and corridos, they call me “El Toro del Corrido,” and my sister was “La Diva de la Banda.” Who am I?
hints: I was born in California, into a family of Mexican musicians.
My last name belongs to a famous family of singers.
My sister was Jenni.
questions.description: A singer with more attitude than a rodeo bull.
questions.fun_fact: The Riveras are a family of singers: Lupillo, Jenni, Juan, and their dad Pedro Rivera all recorded albums.

questions.question: In which decade did the duranguense group K-Paz de la Sierra pack dance floors with “Pero te vas a arrepentir”?
hints: It wasn’t that long ago: people already had cell phones.
Pasito duranguense took off at the turn of the century.
It was the first decade of the 21st century.
questions.description: Pointy boots, synthesizers and the pasito: an era nobody forgets.
questions.fun_fact: K-Paz de la Sierra started in Chicago, like many groups of the duranguense boom.

questions.question: At Paris 2024, Sinaloa boxer Marco Verde went further than any other Mexican boxer. What did he take home?
hints: In Paris he won more fights than he lost.
His last fight was against a boxer from Uzbekistan.
Mexico won no gold at all at Paris 2024.
questions.description: Sinaloa sent a boxer to Paris, and he came home with a really good souvenir.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico finished Paris 2024 with five medals: three silver and two bronze, and no gold.

questions.question: You're in Matsumoto, Japan, in front of one of the country's oldest castles. Which bird gives it its nickname?
hints: The nickname comes from the color of its walls.
Himeji Castle, all white, is nicknamed after a white bird: the heron.
It's a black, clever, noisy bird, and its bigger cousin, the raven, guards the Tower of London in legend.
questions.description: A Japanese castle with a bird for a nickname, just like athletes who get named after animals.
questions.fun_fact: Matsumoto Castle still has its original wooden main tower from more than 400 years ago, which is very rare in Japan.

questions.question: At a boxing gym in Mexico, they teach you to move your head or upper body so the punch goes right past. What is this move called?
hints: You don't need your gloves to do it.
The opponent's glove only hits air.
It's the same word as losing your footing on a wet floor.
questions.description: A move practiced at the gym more than dancing at a wedding.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Manuel Márquez was famous for slipping punches and countering almost in the same motion.

questions.question: In pro boxing, it's the heaviest division of all, with no upper weight limit. What is it called in Mexico?
hints: The biggest, tallest boxers fight in it.
Mike Tyson and Muhammad Ali fought in it.
Its name says the weight is whole, with nothing missing.
questions.description: The division where the scale asks for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In English it's “heavyweight” and in Spain it's “peso pesado”, but in Mexico it's known as “peso completo”.

questions.question: Which boxer won Mexico a bronze medal in the bantamweight division at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
hints: His teammates also won bronze in basketball and in polo.
Mexico had to wait more than 30 years for an Olympic gold in boxing.
His first name is the same as that of the Cuban revolutionary Castro.
questions.description: A bronze so old it was won when your great-grandparents still wore hats every day.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's first boxing golds only came in 1968, at home, with Ricardo Delgado and Antonio Roldán.

questions.question: They come in a little Bimbo bag and are tiny, some dusted with sugar and others covered in chocolate. What are they called?
hints: They're a school-lunch favorite for recess.
They have a little hole in the middle.
Their big version is Homer Simpson's favorite treat.
questions.description: Small, sweet and dangerous: nobody eats just one.
questions.fun_fact: Bimbo was founded in 1945 in Mexico City and is now one of the biggest bread companies in the world.

questions.question: You take your dog for a walk on a leash. In the yo-yo trick called “walk the dog”, what plays the leash?
hints: In this trick the yo-yo rolls along the floor.
It's tied to your hand.
It winds around the yo-yo.
questions.description: A trick for taking out a pet that never eats dog food.
questions.fun_fact: When a yo-yo stays spinning at the bottom without coming back up, it's said to be “sleeping”.

questions.question: I crouch down in the schoolyard and the others jump over my back; if someone misses the jump, they take my place. Who am I?
hints: You have to hold up everyone else's weight.
The game has versions like “castigado” or “dieciséis”.
I'm named after a long-eared animal that brays.
questions.description: In this recess game, one kid gets to be the schoolyard furniture.
questions.fun_fact: In “burro dieciséis”, each jump comes with its own phrase or challenge you have to complete.

questions.question: Each player picks a word, both throw out fingers at the same time, and you add them up. In “pares o nones”, what are the “nones”?
hints: It's about whether a number can be split into two equal piles.
If you add 2 and 3 fingers, the nones win.
1, 3, 5 and 7 belong to this group.
questions.description: At recess, even math is played with your hands.
questions.fun_fact: If both players throw one to five fingers at random, the evens have a tiny edge over the odds (52% to 48%).

questions.question: Which of these telenovelas did NOT star Verónica Castro?
hints: The one you’re looking for premiered in the mid-1990s.
Its lead actress came from the teen pop group Timbiriche.
It’s part of Thalía’s famous trilogy of telenovelas.
questions.description: A TV queen so famous that people on the other side of the world cried along with her.
questions.fun_fact: “Los ricos también lloran” was a huge hit in Russia, where Verónica Castro became a real celebrity.

questions.question: On TV Azteca's celebrity show “Ventaneando,” what does it mean to “ventanear” a star?
hints: No celebrity likes having it done to them.
The show is famous for its showbiz gossip and feuds.
It's airing their dirty laundry.
questions.description: Pati Chapoy has a verb all her own, and she's not afraid to use it.
questions.fun_fact: “Ventaneando” has been on the air since the 1990s, and Pati Chapoy has hosted it for almost all of that time.

questions.question: When the castle was attacked, soldiers gathered in me: open to the sky and surrounded by walls. What am I?
hints: I'm inside the walls, but I have no roof.
Many cities in the Americas, like Lima and Cusco, have a main square, the “Plaza de Armas”, named after the same idea.
Big houses and schools often have one of me too: an open space in the middle of the building.
questions.description: The only place in the castle where nobody complained there was no room for the horse.
questions.fun_fact: The “Plazas de Armas” (“squares of arms”) of many Latin American cities got their name because troops gathered there in colonial times.

questions.question: In Manolo Caro’s Netflix series, what business does the De la Mora family run?
hints: It’s a long-standing family business in Mexico City.
They make arrangements there for weddings and funerals.
The business has the same name as the series.
questions.description: A family that looks perfect on the outside, with more secrets than drawers.
questions.fun_fact: Paulina de la Mora’s slow way of talking turned into one of the show’s most famous memes.

questions.question: What is the Televisa comedy, produced by Eugenio Derbez, about the squabbles between people living in the same condo building?
hints: Its title is a single word.
It premiered in the mid-2000s.
Its title is the Spanish word for the people who live right next door.
