questions.description: Thin walls, thick gossip.
questions.fun_fact: “Vecinos” premiered in 2005 and, years later, came back to TV with new seasons.

questions.question: “Luvina,” “Macario” and “No oyes ladrar los perros” are stories by Juan Rulfo, published together in 1953. In which book?
hints: It's not a novel but a book of short stories.
It came out two years before his most famous novel.
Its title is about a field on fire.
questions.description: A skinny little book more famous than plenty of fat ones.
questions.fun_fact: Rulfo is famous mainly for two thin books, and both are classics of Spanish-language literature.

questions.question: In Mexico it's a very well-known brand, born near Torreón, with trucks delivering all over the country. If someone asks for “a Lala,” what do they want?
hints: Lots of people have it at breakfast.
You keep it in the fridge.
You drink it with chocolate powder or pour it on cereal.
questions.description: A name so catchy you want to sing it: la, la, la.
questions.fun_fact: The name Lala comes from La Laguna, the Comarca Lagunera region where the company was born.

questions.question: At the posadas, people serve a hot drink made with tejocote, guava and sugarcane. What is it called?
hints: It's served hot, in a clay mug or a cup.
Besides fruit, it has cinnamon and piloncillo.
Its name looks like “poncho” with just one letter changed.
questions.description: A pot so big that in December it needs its own spot on the stove.
questions.fun_fact: The tejocote, the star fruit of ponche, is native to Mexico and looks like a little yellow apple.

questions.question: A huge, crispy tortilla spread with asiento (pork lard) and beans, topped with cheese. Which state is the tlayuda from?
hints: It's a state in southern Mexico.
It makes the country's most famous mezcal.
It's the home of the Guelaguetza.
questions.description: A tortilla that hit the gym and came out the size of a pizza.
questions.fun_fact: Tlayudas are toasted on a comal or over hot coals, and many are folded in half to eat.

questions.question: On November 20, schools and cities all over Mexico hold sports parades. What does the day remember?
hints: It happened in the early 20th century.
In the parades, many kids dress up in wide-brimmed hats and crossed bandoliers.
It began in 1910 against the government of Porfirio Díaz.
questions.description: The day half the class shows up to school with a painted-on mustache.
questions.fun_fact: The Adelitas remember the soldaderas, women who traveled with the troops and also fought alongside them.

questions.question: At the fiestas patrias, people toss rolled-up paper strips into the air that unroll as they fly. What are they called?
hints: They're sold in little rolls.
In September, many come in green, white and red.
Their Spanish name comes from an animal that coils up.
questions.description: What's still hanging from the trees days after the party.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish they're called “serpentinas” because they wiggle like a serpent as they unroll.

questions.question: In 1910, Francisco I. Madero called on Mexicans to take up arms and end a long period of rule. What is it called?
hints: It lasted more than 30 years.
Its leading figure was a general from Oaxaca who was reelected many times.
Its motto was “Order and Progress.”
questions.description: A government so long that even the calendar was begging it to leave.
questions.fun_fact: During that period, thousands of kilometers of railroad track were built in Mexico.

questions.question: In Mexico, on which day of May is Mother's Day celebrated?
hints: It's in the first half of the month.
It isn't Labor Day or the day of the Battle of Puebla.
It falls exactly five days before Teacher's Day.
questions.description: The day with the most flowers, hugs and school shows per square meter.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, Mother's Day is always on May 10, whatever day of the week it falls on.

questions.question: What are the colorful, confetti-filled surprises called that people crack on each other's heads at parties?
hints: They are filled with something inside.
They are painted bright colors and sealed with tissue paper.
Before being decorated, each one held an egg.
questions.description: A party where no hairstyle makes it out alive.
questions.fun_fact: Cascarones are filled with confetti, and people say cracking one on someone's head brings good luck.

questions.question: Look at this detail from a portrait. Who is this hero of Mexican Independence?
hints: He was already about 57 when the war began, older than almost all the other rebel leaders.
He was a priest.
He was the parish priest of Dolores and rang his church bell before dawn.
questions.description: A face you've seen in more textbooks than your teacher's.
questions.fun_fact: The bell Hidalgo rang now hangs in the National Palace, and the president rings it every night of the Grito.

questions.question: In Chichén Itzá there is a round building with a spiral staircase inside and small windows up high. What did the Maya use it for?
hints: What mattered was up above, not inside.
Maya priests kept very precise calendars.
The windows point to where certain stars and planets rise.
questions.description: A building shaped like a seashell, but nowhere near the beach.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya recorded the cycles of Venus in the Dresden Codex, one of the few Maya books that survived.

questions.question: With “La ley de Herodes”, Luis Estrada and Damián Alcázar began a series of political satires. Which of these films is NOT part of it?
hints: Damián Alcázar acts in the one you're looking for, but Luis Estrada didn't direct it: he directed the other three.
The film you're looking for was directed by Carlos Carrera in 2002.
Its star is Gael García Bernal as a young priest.
questions.description: A town where the law is applied depending on who's holding the rulebook.
questions.fun_fact: In 1999 there was a scandal over attempts to stop the release of “La ley de Herodes”, which made it even more famous.

questions.question: Which movie theater format, created in South Korea, moves the seats and hits you with wind, water and smells?
hints: Here you don't just watch the movie: you feel it in your body.
Cinépolis has theaters with this name in many cities in Mexico.
Its name hints at “four dimensions”.
questions.description: A theater where the popcorn is in more danger than the movie's heroes.
questions.fun_fact: 4DX theaters can release bubbles, fog and even fake snow during the movie.

questions.question: Which movie did Alfonso Cuarón direct right after “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001)?
questions.answer: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
hints: It was a leap from a road movie to a blockbuster.
It came out in 2004.
It has wizards, a hippogriff and dementors.
questions.description: From a trip in a beat-up car to a much stranger trip, with no stops in between.
questions.fun_fact: Cuarón asked the Harry Potter actors to write an essay about their characters before filming.

questions.question: Eulalio González, “El Piporro,” made all of Mexico laugh by imitating the speech and ways of one group of people. Which one?
hints: His favorite music had an accordion in it.
He sang “El taconazo” and “Chulas fronteras.”
He was born in Nuevo León himself.
questions.description: A man who got laughs just by opening his mouth.
questions.fun_fact: His nickname comes from a character in the radio drama “Ahí viene Martín Corona,” which he later took to the movies with Pedro Infante in 1952.

questions.question: You're watching Disney and Pixar's “Coco”, and Miguel crosses a bridge of orange flowers. Which Mexican holiday is the movie set during?
hints: For this holiday, people set up altars with family photos.
People eat a special bread and little sugar skulls.
It is celebrated on November 1 and 2.
questions.description: The world's most famous mouse took a trip to Mexico and came back with a guitar.
questions.fun_fact: “Coco” won two Oscars in 2018: Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song for “Remember Me”.

questions.question: Ninón Sevilla, María Antonieta Pons and Rosa Carmina were famous “rumberas.” What was a rumbera in Mexican cinema?
questions.answer: An actress who danced tropical rhythms in cabaret films
wrong_answers: An actress who danced jarabe tapatío in charro films
An actress who danced the waltz in period films
An actress who danced ballet in theater films
hints: Her films usually took place at night, in the city.
Her costumes had sequins, feathers and ruffles.
The rhythm she is named after comes from Cuba.
questions.description: If your grandma knows every single step, you know which movies she was watching.
questions.fun_fact: Several of the great rumberas of Mexican cinema were born in Cuba, including Ninón Sevilla and María Antonieta Pons.

questions.question: “—¿Vamos por unos tacos? —¡Órale!” What did the person who answered “órale” mean?
hints: They said it with lots of enthusiasm.
It's also used to cheer someone on: “¡Órale, tú puedes!”
It's like saying “you bet!” or “deal!”
questions.description: A little Mexican word that works for almost everything.
questions.fun_fact: Many people think “órale” comes from “ahora” (now), as if saying “now we're talking, let's go!”

questions.question: It starred Jorge Negrete, was directed by Fernando de Fuentes in 1942, and was the first Mexican film with this new feature. What was it?
hints: Hollywood already had it in the 1930s.
Audiences were amazed by the landscapes and costumes of Jalisco.
Before this, all Mexican films were in black and white.
questions.description: Jorge Negrete singing, the sarape showing off, and the audience with their eyes wide open.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Así se quiere en Jalisco!” was filmed in a system called Cinecolor, cheaper than Hollywood's Technicolor.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Cast and director are right (Negrete, Fernando de Fuentes, 1942, ¡Así se quiere en Jalisco!). The 'first Mexican color feature' claim is widely repeated, but English Wikipedia only says it 'was commented' to be the first. The Cinecolor detail in the fun fact is not stated in any source I found. The only support is a Wikipedia category tag. Color shorts such as Novillero and Extravaganza mexicana existed, so the hint 'all Mexican films were black and white' is slightly overstated. Sound and 3D are clearly wrong, and widescreen is almost certainly wrong too.

questions.question: “Ahuacatl” is to “aguacate” as “mizquitl” is to…
hints: Look at what happens to the end of the Nahuatl word.
Just like “aguacate,” the answer is a word that comes from Nahuatl.
It's a thorny tree from northern Mexico.
questions.description: When Spanish met Nahuatl, lots of words lost their little tails.
questions.fun_fact: Tomate, cacahuate, tecolote and guajolote all lost the Nahuatl “-tl” ending on their way into Spanish.

questions.question: It’s spoken in the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, its speakers call themselves “ayuuk,” and their sacred mountain is Zempoaltépetl. Which language is it?
hints: It is not the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Oaxaca.
Its towns, like Tlahuitoltepec, are famous for their brass bands.
Its name looks like that of another Oaxacan language, but it’s shorter.
questions.description: A language that lives so high up it can almost chat with the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: “Ayuuk” is often translated as “the language of the mountain” or “the flowery word.”

questions.question: A thunderclap booms in a storm: the Mexica said it was the rain's helpers breaking their water jars. Where did these helpers come from?
hints: It is a Mexica afterlife, full of water and green plants.
People who drowned or were struck by lightning went there.
Its name comes from the rain god, Tlaloc.
questions.description: Helpers so clumsy that every time they break something, the whole valley hears it.
questions.fun_fact: In Teotihuacan there is a famous mural, at Tepantitla, that many scholars identify as a painting of Tlalocan.

questions.question: It's a night bird with a white, heart-shaped face, and in the villages they say it's a witch. Where in churches does it like to nest?
hints: It looks for a high, quiet place to sleep during the day.
From there it can see the whole town.
It's the spot that rings out to call people to Mass.
questions.description: A neighbor who sells tortillas by day, and at night nobody knows where she goes.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish this bird is also called “lechuza de campanario,” the “bell-tower owl,” because of its habit of living in church towers.

questions.question: You misbehave and someone says, “¡Te va a llevar el chamuco!” Who is the chamuco?
hints: “Chamuco” is just one of his many nicknames in Mexico.
In Mexico he's also called “el Patas” or “el Maligno.”
He has horns and a tail.
questions.description: A character with such a bad reputation that grown-ups use him to make kids finish their soup.
questions.fun_fact: “Chamuco” is a Mexican word: in other Spanish-speaking countries hardly anyone uses it.

questions.question: In the villages of Yucatán they say a Maya sorcerer turns into an animal at night to scare people. What is this spook called?
hints: It's a Maya legend from the Yucatán Peninsula.
It's a kind of nahual: a person who changes shape.
Its name mixes a Maya word with the Spanish name of an animal with horns and a beard.
questions.description: A neighbor who's perfectly normal by day, and at night you'd better not look out the window.
questions.fun_fact: “Huay” comes from the Maya word “way”, meaning something like to transform or sorcerer, so Huay Chivo is the “goat sorcerer”.

questions.question: Ronaldinho, a World Cup winner with Brazil, ended up playing for Querétaro's Gallos Blancos. In what year did he arrive?
hints: He had already left Barcelona and AC Milan.
He came to Mexico after playing for Atlético Mineiro.
It was the same year as the World Cup in Brazil.
questions.description: Even the roosters of the Bajío learned to dance with the ball.
questions.fun_fact: With Ronaldinho, Querétaro reached the Clausura 2015 final, which they lost to Santos Laguna.

questions.question: In 2020, during the pandemic, Liga MX created the Liga de Expansión. What did it suspend in exchange?
hints: The decision made the weakest teams happy.
The move was meant to ease the clubs' money troubles during the crisis.
The last-place team no longer dropped down a division.
questions.description: A year so strange that even Mexican soccer changed its own rules.
questions.fun_fact: Before the pause, relegation was decided by the “tabla de cocientes”, which averaged a team's points over its last few seasons.

questions.question: Its giant stones fit together without mortar, it watches over Cusco, and Inti Raymi is celebrated there. What language does the name Sacsayhuamán come from?
hints: It's the language of the people who built it.
It was the main language of the Inca Empire.
Millions of people in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador speak it today; English got words like “llama” and “puma” from it.
questions.description: A stone puzzle put together so well that not even a sheet of paper fits between its pieces.
questions.fun_fact: Its name is often translated as “satisfied falcon”, though experts argue about other meanings.

questions.question: Pierre de Coubertin is to the modern Olympic Games as Salvador Lutteroth is to…
hints: Lutteroth was a businessman who put on shows in Mexico City in the 1930s.
The company he founded in 1933 is still running and is the oldest of its kind in the world.
He had the Arena México built, in the Colonia Doctores.
questions.description: Every great show has a dad who brought it into the world.
questions.fun_fact: Salvador Lutteroth is known as “the father of Mexican lucha libre.”

questions.question: Which of these names is NOT a hold or move in Mexican lucha libre?
hints: The other three are done to the opponent's body.
This one is done with the feet, but without touching anyone.
It's a soccer trick: kicking the ball with one leg crossed behind the other.
questions.description: The fans shout three of these names in the arena; the fourth one snuck in without a ticket.
questions.fun_fact: The huracarrana is named after the luchador Huracán Ramírez, who made it famous.

questions.question: What is it called when you bring a mariachi band at night to sing to someone outside their house?
hints: Lots of moms get one on May 10.
The person being celebrated usually leans out of the window.
In Mexico it's also called “llevar gallo.”
questions.description: A very romantic way to keep the neighbors awake.
questions.fun_fact: The word “serenata” comes from Italian and is linked to “sereno,” the cool night air.

questions.question: He rode a horse, sang to his sweetheart with a mariachi band and was a hero of 1940s Mexican cinema. What classic character was he?
hints: He was a hero of the Mexican countryside on the big screen.
He dressed like the traditional horsemen of Jalisco, with a wide sombrero and silver buttons.
Jorge Negrete and Pedro Infante were the most famous ones.
questions.description: The old-time movie heartthrob: mustache, intense gaze and a voice like thunder.
questions.fun_fact: The film “Allá en el Rancho Grande” (1936) made the cinema of charros and rancheras famous around the world.

questions.question: The Maya saw the three hearthstones of creation in Orion, with the smoke of the fire between them. What is that smoke really?
hints: Through binoculars it looks like a small, fuzzy white smudge.
It is a huge cloud of gas and dust inside our own galaxy.
New stars are being born there, and it is known as M42.
questions.description: Even up in the sky, the Maya had something cooking on the fire.
questions.fun_fact: In many Maya kitchens, people still cook over a three-stone hearth, just like the one in the constellation.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: the main job of the Banco de México is to keep down…
hints: It has to do with the prices of everything you buy.
If it climbs a lot, the same money buys you less and less.
It's when prices keep going up and up over time.
questions.description: The bank of all banks has a mission, and it isn't guarding your piggy bank.
questions.fun_fact: The Banco de México sets an inflation target of about 3% a year.

questions.question: In Mexico, what is a “miscelánea”?
hints: They sell lots of different things there.
It has chips, candy, milk and sometimes fruit.
People also call it “la tienda de la esquina.”
questions.description: A fancy word for a place you've known your whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has hundreds of thousands of neighborhood tienditas; they are among the most common businesses in the country.

questions.question: According to the most common explanation taught in school, what does the green stripe of the Mexican flag stand for?
hints: It's a feeling.
It has to do with what you wish for the future.
A popular saying calls it the last thing you ever lose.
questions.description: If colors could talk, this stripe would have a lot to say.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican law doesn't say what each color means; on the Trigarante flag of 1821, green stood for independence.

questions.question: It's a nickname, it comes from the colors of the flag, and fans shout it when Mexico's national soccer team plays. What is it?
hints: Its full name is longer, but the fans shorten it.
It has to do with a number.
Green, white and red: that makes three.
questions.description: When Mexico plays, the whole country shouts the same thing.
questions.fun_fact: “El Tri” is short for “el Tricolor”, after the green, white and red of the flag.

questions.question: In what year did María del Rosario Espinoza, from Sinaloa, win Olympic gold in taekwondo?
hints: She is the first Mexican woman with medals at three Olympic Games.
That gold came at her first Olympics, when she was 20.
Those were the Beijing Games, famous for the “Bird's Nest” stadium.
questions.description: Kicks so precise that even the calendar remembers them.
questions.fun_fact: Espinoza won gold at Beijing 2008, bronze at London 2012 and silver at Rio 2016: one medal of each color.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a fairy-tale castle in Germany. Which king, nicknamed “the Swan King”, had it built?
hints: He ruled a region in the south of Germany.
He was a huge fan of Wagner's operas.
The capital of his kingdom was Munich.
questions.description: A king who spent more on dreams than on armies.
questions.fun_fact: Neuschwanstein inspired Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.

questions.question: Archer Alejandra Valencia, an Olympic medalist at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, was born in Hermosillo. What state is she from?
hints: It's a state in northwestern Mexico.
It borders the United States and has a coast on the Gulf of California.
It's famous for carne asada, coyotas and its huge desert.
questions.description: An arrow, a target and a whole lot of northern pride.
questions.fun_fact: Alejandra Valencia won mixed team bronze at Tokyo 2020 and women's team bronze at Paris 2024.

questions.question: How many teams play in the Liga Mexicana del Pacífico, the winter baseball league?
hints: It's a regional league, not a national one.
Most of its teams are from Sonora and Sinaloa.
They include the Tomateros, Naranjeros, Venados and Charros.
questions.description: Baseball in winter: because in the northwest, cold is just a matter of opinion.
questions.fun_fact: The Liga Mexicana del Pacífico champion represents Mexico in the Caribbean Series.

questions.question: Complete it: Usain Bolt is to the 100 meters as Ana Gabriela Guevara is to…
hints: She was born in Sonora and also played basketball when she was young.
It's a longer distance than Bolt's, but still a sprint.
Guevara became world champion in this event in Paris in 2003.
questions.description: The woman from Sonora who got all of Mexico up off the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Ana Gabriela Guevara, from Nogales, Sonora, won Olympic silver at Athens 2004.

questions.question: The bronze sculpture “La Giganta” stands in the courtyard of a museum in the Centro Histórico named after its maker. Who made it?
hints: He was a rebellious draftsman who harshly criticized the muralists in the 1950s.
In 1967 he painted an “ephemeral mural” in the Zona Rosa that lasted only a short time.
His surname is the Spanish word for dark places under the ground.
questions.description: A bronze lady so tall she never needs a step stool to reach the top shelf.
questions.fun_fact: The José Luis Cuevas Museum is housed in the former Convent of Santa Inés, in Mexico City's Centro Histórico.

questions.question: Two studio houses, one blue and one red and white, joined by a rooftop bridge, designed by Juan O'Gorman in San Ángel. What museum are they today?
questions.answer: Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Studio House
hints: They were built in 1931–1932, when “functionalist” houses were brand new.
A very famous painter couple lived there, each in their own house.
He painted in the big house; she painted in the blue one.
questions.description: Architecture so modern for its time that more than one neighbor in San Ángel thought it was a factory.
questions.fun_fact: The fence around the houses is made of organ pipe cactus, a very Mexican living wall.

questions.question: A house in Polanco was the studio of a muralist who gave it to the public in 1969 and left his work there. Whose was it?
hints: As a young man, he was a soldier in the Mexican Revolution.
He experimented with spray guns and industrial car paint.
His name is on the Polyforum on Avenida Insurgentes.
questions.description: Some people leave their house to their kids; others leave it to the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Siqueiros kept painting even while he was locked up in Lecumberri prison.

questions.question: According to the Mexica, the first sun was called Nahui Océlotl. Fill in what its name means: “Four ___”.
hints: Each sun was named after a date in the calendar: a number and a sign.
Tezcatlipoca ruled that first world, and giants lived in it.
At the end of that age, the giants were eaten by the same animal that gives the sun its name.
questions.description: Four worlds came before this one, and none of them came with an extended warranty.
questions.fun_fact: On the Sun Stone, the four earlier suns appear around the central face, each in its own box.

questions.question: For the Maya, the ceiba was a sacred tree at the center of the world, linking several levels of the universe. How many?
hints: The Maya pictured the universe in layers, from bottom to top.
Its roots sank into the underworld.
Its branches reached the sky, and its trunk stood in the world of humans.
questions.description: A tree with more connections than your home Wi-Fi.
questions.fun_fact: The ceiba is Guatemala's national tree, and in many Maya villages it is still respected and never cut down.

questions.question: In a legend said to be Maya, the gods carved a tiny jade arrow, blew on it, and the hummingbird was born. What job did they give it?
hints: That's why people say no one should ever catch one.
Its job is to go back and forth from one place to another.
They say that if a hummingbird comes close to you, someone is thinking of you.
questions.description: The tiniest bird in the jungle, with the most important job.
questions.fun_fact: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute while it flies.

questions.question: At a son jarocho fandango, what is the wooden tarima for?
questions.answer: To stomp on so it sounds like a drum
wrong_answers: For the musicians to sit on while playing
To hold the town's food offerings
For the verse singers to read their coplas
hints: At a fandango, the dance is also part of the music.
The hollow wood booms with every hit.
Dancers mark the rhythm on top of it with their heels.
questions.description: A piece of wood that is the most important guest at a Veracruz party.
questions.fun_fact: At many fandangos the tarima counts as one more instrument, and the dancers “play” it with their feet.

questions.question: It's a French word, it's on many wine labels, and there are hundreds along the Loire River. What does “château” mean?
hints: It's a large building.
Many French kings and nobles lived in one.
It comes from the Latin “castellum”, just like the English word for it.
questions.description: A word that sounds super fancy just because it's in French.
questions.fun_fact: In Bordeaux, many wineries call themselves “château” even if they only have a country house and not a single tower.

questions.question: Complete the name of the band founded by Gilberto Gutiérrez that has revived jarocho fandangos since 1977: Mono…
hints: It was a key band of the jarana movement in Veracruz.
Its founder was born in southern Veracruz.
It's the color of traditional jarocho clothing.
questions.description: A band with a name straight out of the zoo and a fandango soul.
questions.fun_fact: Mono Blanco helped bring son jarocho back to community fandangos, not just concert stages.

questions.question: I'm a saying: if someone loves you and treats you kindly, I remind you to give the same back. Which saying am I?
wrong_answers: Obras son amores y no buenas razones
Ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente
hints: I talk about giving back what you receive.
I sound like paying a bill, but with the heart instead of money.
My most important word shows up twice and starts with A.
questions.description: A saying you hear at weddings, anniversaries and in Valentine's Day cards.
questions.fun_fact: Many loving sayings in Mexico come from centuries-old Spanish proverbs that lived on in the Americas.

questions.question: Which Spanish saying warns that if you take on too many things at once, you won't do any of them well?
questions.answer: El que mucho abarca poco aprieta
wrong_answers: No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano
Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
El que con lobos anda a aullar se enseña
hints: It isn't about schedules or bad company.
It compares someone trying to carry too many things with someone who can no longer hold them tight.
Its first verb means to wrap your arms around something: “abar…”.
questions.description: For people who want to be at every party at the same time.
questions.fun_fact: “Abarcar” comes from Latin, and its root has to do with arms: to “abarcar” is to wrap your arms around something.

questions.question: Look at the map: the torta ahogada, a sandwich drowned in chili sauce, was born in this state's capital. Which state is it?
hints: Its capital is one of the biggest cities in Mexico.
It's the home of mariachi and tequila.
People from its capital are called tapatíos.
questions.description: A lonche that jumped into a pool of salsa and never made it out.
questions.fun_fact: The torta ahogada is made with birote salado, a hard-crusted bread that soaks up the sauce without falling apart.

questions.question: Look at the map: the highlighted state is the smallest in Mexico. Which one is it?
hints: It is in the center of the country, very close to the capital.
It borders Puebla, which almost surrounds it.
Its capital has the same name as the state.
questions.description: A state so tiny you can cover it on the map with a coin.
questions.fun_fact: Online, there is a famous joke that “Tlaxcala doesn't exist,” even though it is one of the states with the most history in the country.

questions.question: In a classic telenovela, the truth comes out and the villain gets what she deserves. What scene usually closes the last episode?
hints: It's a party with lots of guests.
There's almost always a cake with several tiers.
The heroine walks to the altar dressed in white.
questions.description: A hundred episodes of tears, secrets and slaps… all just to get to this.
questions.fun_fact: Some telenovelas have filmed alternate endings so that nobody could leak how the story ends.

questions.question: “Nada personal”, a political thriller with Ana Colchero and Demián Bichir, was one of TV Azteca's first big hits. In what year did it premiere?
hints: It's from the 1990s.
It premiered before “Mirada de mujer” (1997), from the same production company.
The year 2000 was still four years away.
questions.description: Politics, intrigue and romance: the combo that made the competition sweat.
questions.fun_fact: It was produced by Argos, Epigmenio Ibarra's company, which made “Mirada de mujer” the following year.

questions.question: Verónica Castro and Guillermo Capetillo starred in “Rosa salvaje”, still remembered for its theme song. In what year did it premiere?
hints: It was in the '80s, the decade of the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
It premiered after that World Cup.
It premiered one year after that World Cup.
questions.description: A flower with thorns, a lioness's mane and ratings through the roof.
questions.fun_fact: Verónica Castro didn't just star in it: she also sang the theme song.

questions.question: Danna Paola was a little girl when she starred in the children's telenovela “María Belén.” What year did it premiere?
hints: Danna Paola was born in the mid-1990s.
It premiered before “Amy, la niña de la mochila azul.”
It was the year the 21st century began.
questions.description: Before filling stadiums, this star was already making half of Mexico cry in the kids' time slot.
questions.fun_fact: A few years later, Danna Paola starred in another children's telenovela: “Amy, la niña de la mochila azul” (2004).

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actress, and in 1997 I played a young woman born blind who was swapped at birth for a baby boy. Who am I?
hints: My telenovela was named after a green gemstone.
My leading man was Fernando Colunga.
I share my last name with former president Felipe Calderón.
questions.description: A melodrama that made half the planet cry, all the way to the other side of the world.
questions.fun_fact: “Esmeralda” is a remake of a 1970 Venezuelan telenovela written by Delia Fiallo.

questions.question: It goes under the skirt, and folk dancers wear it with lots of holanes (ruffles). What is the enagua for?
questions.answer: To give the skirt volume and swing
wrong_answers: To mark the rhythm of the zapateado
To protect the feet from the floor
To hold the rebozo at the waist
hints: You notice it most when the dancer spins and swirls her skirt.
For centuries, women also wore it under their everyday skirts, not just for dancing.
It makes the skirt look wider and fluffier.
questions.description: The secret garment nobody sees, but that works harder than the dancer herself.
questions.fun_fact: The word “enagua” comes from “nagua”, a word from Taíno, the language the Spanish first met in the Caribbean.

questions.question: Many dance masks from Guerrero are made by hand and painted in bright colors. What are they usually made of?
hints: Each craftsman gives it his own style, and no two masks ever come out the same.
The mask is light and gets several coats of paint and varnish.
It comes from a tree trunk.
questions.description: Faces that dance once a year and spend the rest of the time resting on the wall.
questions.fun_fact: Many dance masks are handed down from parents to children and danced in for decades.

questions.question: Look at the photo: many Mexican dancers wave this while they dance. What is it used for at home?
hints: You can keep it in your pocket.
You use it when you have a cold.
You hold it up to your face when you sneeze.
questions.description: A little square of cloth that's for flirting on the dance floor and for something far less elegant at home.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican sones, dancers wave a handkerchief to flirt with their partner.

questions.question: It's a famous huapango sung in falsetto. In “Malagueña salerosa,” what does she have that's pretty, according to the first line?
hints: It's on the face.
The lips come later in the song, in “besar tus labios quisiera” (I'd like to kiss your lips).
According to the lyrics, they're “debajo de esas dos cejas” (beneath those two eyebrows).
questions.description: A song with notes so long the singer needs the lungs of a deep-sea diver.
questions.fun_fact: When singing “Malagueña salerosa,” many singers hold very long falsetto notes to show off.

questions.question: In Mexico, having a job is «tener chamba». Which of these words is NOT used in Mexico to talk about work?
hints: You'd hear three of them in any Mexican repair shop or market.
The odd one out is very common on the other side of the ocean.
It's how people say “work” in Spain.
questions.description: Some words get up early, clock in and come home really tired.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, «talacha» is also a quick repair job, like when someone changes your car's flat tire.

questions.question: You're invited out with a group that's always getting into trouble, and you'd rather stay home. «Más vale solo que…»
hints: It's a very old saying that grandparents use to give advice.
The ending starts with the same word as «malo».
It's the opposite of «bien acompañado».
questions.description: A night in pajamas on the couch can also be the best decision of the week.
questions.fun_fact: This saying already appeared in Spanish collections of proverbs from the 16th century.

previous.feedback: Hint 2 (“The ending is about who you're with.”) gives the answer away: “Mal acompañado” is the only option about company, so the hint points straight to it. The source's hint only narrowed it to the two “Mal…” options. Hint 2 needs a vaguer replacement that doesn't point to company, for example one that says the ending has two words and rhymes with nothing in particular, or one about the tone of the warning.

questions.question: When you finally understand something, you say «¡ya me cayó el veinte!». That veinte was a 20-centavo coin. What did it drop into?
hints: It was a machine you found out on the street.
Sometimes the coin got stuck, and you had to wait for it to drop.
Before cell phones, people lined up on the corner to use it.
questions.description: There was a time when understanding things cost exactly twenty centavos.
questions.fun_fact: Sometimes the coin was slow to drop, so you had to wait or give the machine a little tap, which is why people say the veinte “took a while to drop.”

questions.question: Look at the map: this state is home to Janitzio Island, famous for its Noche de Muertos with candles and canoes. Which state is it?
hints: It is a state in western Mexico with a Pacific coast.
The island is in Lake Pátzcuaro, where people fish with butterfly-shaped nets.
Its capital is Morelia.
questions.description: A night when nobody goes to bed early, not even those who are already gone.
questions.fun_fact: At the top of Janitzio stands a giant statue of José María Morelos, about 40 meters (130 feet) tall, and you can climb inside it up to its fist.

questions.question: It's served in a deep bowl, topped with lettuce, radish and oregano, and is a must at the fiestas patrias. What is pozole?
hints: You eat it with a spoon.
It's served nice and hot.
It has meat and lots of liquid, like a soup.
questions.description: The dish that gets the whole family to sit down at the table at the same time every September.
questions.fun_fact: In Guerrero there's white, red and green pozole, and many restaurants celebrate “jueves pozolero” (pozole Thursday).

questions.question: The Macroplaza, said to be one of the largest squares in the world, has an orange tower called the Faro del Comercio. Which city is it in?
hints: It is a city in northern Mexico.
It is an industrial city surrounded by mountains.
Its nickname is “la Sultana del Norte.”
questions.description: A square so big you need a bus to get from one bench to the next.
questions.fun_fact: At night, the Faro del Comercio shoots a green laser beam across the city sky.

questions.question: Darth Vader is to a black helmet as a Star Wars stormtrooper is to…
hints: Think of the Empire's soldiers marching in rows.
Their suit covers them from head to toe and makes them all look the same.
They look like they're made of plastic the color of snow.
questions.description: A thousand identical soldiers and not one can aim: the great mystery of the galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: The name “stormtrooper” was borrowed from German shock troops of World War I.

questions.question: On a map of Mexico, you cover Chihuahua, the largest state, with your hand. Roughly what part of the country did you cover?
hints: Mexico is split into 32 parts, 31 states plus Mexico City, and Chihuahua is just one of them.
It's much less than half, but much more than an average state.
If you put about eight Chihuahuas together, you'd cover the whole country.
questions.description: A state so huge that the tiny dog named after it would never finish walking across it.
questions.fun_fact: Chihuahua covers about 247,000 km² (95,000 sq mi), more than entire countries like the United Kingdom.

questions.question: When did work begin on Mérida's Paseo de Montejo, the avenue inspired by the Champs-Élysées in Paris?
hints: Mexico was already an independent country.
Porfirio Díaz was in power, and he loved all things French.
The mansions were paid for with henequen money, before 1900.
questions.description: A Mérida avenue that wanted to dress up in French style.
questions.fun_fact: The Paseo de Montejo was first laid out in 1888, when henequen made Yucatán one of the richest places in Mexico.

questions.question: You're sailing in the northern Sea of Cortez, the only place on Earth where the smallest cetacean lives. What is it?
hints: It's related to dolphins and whales.
It's about 1.5 m (5 ft) long and has dark rings around its eyes.
Its Spanish name sounds like a farm animal.
questions.description: A sea so full of life that Jacques Cousteau called it “the aquarium of the world.”
questions.fun_fact: The vaquita is one of the most endangered species on the planet, and Mexico has protected areas to look after it.

questions.question: Angelique Boyer and Sebastián Rulli starred in “Lo que la vida me robó”. In what year did it premiere?
hints: Smartphones and social media were already around.
It premiered three years after “Teresa”, which also starred Angelique Boyer.
It was the year before the World Cup in Brazil.
questions.description: A telenovela whose title sounds like a police report about a stolen life.
questions.fun_fact: It adapts the novel “Bodas de odio” by Caridad Bravo Adams, the same story that inspired “Amor real” (2003).

questions.question: Hogwarts is to Harry Potter as the Elite Way School is to…
hints: It's a teen telenovela from 2004.
Its stars formed a band that became famous in many countries.
That band was called RBD.
questions.description: A private school where the uniform matters more than the homework.
questions.fun_fact: It was the Mexican version of the Argentine telenovela «Rebelde Way» (2002).

questions.question: On a Friday, your telenovela episode ends with “To be continued…”. When will you see the next episode?
hints: Think about which days telenovelas air on regular broadcast TV.
On weekends, the TV schedule changes.
You have to wait for the new week to start.
questions.description: The cruelest words that can ever appear on a screen.
questions.fun_fact: Many writers save the biggest cliffhanger for Friday, so you won't switch channels on Monday.

questions.question: You're watching a black-and-white Mexican movie and everyone is dancing the cha-cha-chá. In which decade did it become popular?
hints: It was invented in Cuba by the violinist Enrique Jorrín.
It was the golden age of mambo and Pérez Prado.
It was the same decade that rock and roll was born.
questions.description: A dance named after a sound effect, with feet that never stop talking.
questions.fun_fact: The name is said to copy the sound of feet shuffling during the step: cha-cha-chá.

questions.question: Long before the Spanish arrived, why did the Mexica (Aztecs) perform their dances?
wrong_answers: To earn money at the market
To train for war with Spain
hints: They danced in temples and at great festivals.
The dances had to do with the Sun, the rain and the harvests.
It was a way of praying with your whole body.
questions.description: Long before concerts existed, some people were already dancing for the most important audience of all.
questions.fun_fact: “Conchero” dancers get their name from their guitar, made from an armadillo shell.

questions.question: It spins the rehilete, lifts the papalote and moves the laundry hanging in the yard. What is it?
hints: It's part of the weather and changes from day to day.
It blows harder when a storm is coming.
It's air that moves.
questions.description: An afternoon of papalotes and laundry on the line: the yard turns into quite a show.
questions.fun_fact: A papalote's long tail helps it stay upright in the air.

questions.question: Which of these Star Wars characters is NOT a Sith?
hints: Three of them are villains from the dark side of the Force.
The one we want sat on the Jedi Council.
He uses a purple lightsaber.
questions.description: Dark Side Club: cape, yellow eyes and a bad attitude required.
questions.fun_fact: Under the “Rule of Two” in Star Wars, there can only be two Sith at a time: a master and an apprentice.

questions.question: When someone in Mexico shouts “¡chin chan pu!” and puts out a hand, what game are they playing?
hints: It's played with just one hand.
Each player makes a shape with their fingers.
A closed fist beats two open fingers.
questions.description: Three magic words that settle arguments faster than a judge.
questions.fun_fact: The game as we know it today spread from Japan, where it's called “janken”.

questions.question: You're playing Lotería and the caller sings “¡El Gallo!”, which is on your board. What do you traditionally place on the card?
hints: It comes from the kitchen.
It's small and doesn't slide off the board.
It's also used to make tasty refritos.
questions.description: When the caller sings out the cards, the whole table holds its breath, ready to shout “¡Lotería!”.
questions.fun_fact: Classic Mexican Lotería has 54 cards, each with its own number and picture.

questions.question: It's shouted before a coin toss to decide who goes first, and each word is one side of the coin. What do people say in Mexico?
hints: Other countries say it differently.
One side of the coin has the national coat of arms.
One of the words is a bird that's on the flag.
questions.description: The Mexican science of deciding who gets the front seat of the car.
questions.fun_fact: The “sol” part comes from old coins that showed a cap with rays, like a sun.

questions.question: In Mexico, what word is used for the smiling skeletons on Day of the Dead toys and figures?
hints: You see lots of them at the markets in November.
It's shaped like what we all have under our skin.
La Catrina is the most elegant of them all.
questions.description: A toy that's nothing but skin and bones, minus the skin, and still dances happily.
questions.fun_fact: José Guadalupe Posada made skeleton figures famous with his prints, including the one of La Catrina.

questions.question: A Mexican Lotería card shows a woman rowing a canoe full of flowers, like in Xochimilco. What is the card called?
hints: The woman is sitting down and holding an oar.
In its traditional verse, a girl named Lupita goes “rema y rema” (rowing and rowing).
It's also the name of a snack from Puebla.
questions.description: A card that comes with its own Sunday outing included.
questions.fun_fact: In Puebla, a chalupa is also a small tortilla topped with salsa, shredded meat and onion.

questions.question: Online, people jumped out of moving cars to dance to “La Chona” by Los Tucanes de Tijuana. What year did it go viral?
hints: It was in the late 2010s.
It copied another challenge done to Drake’s song “In My Feelings.”
It was the summer of the World Cup in Russia.
questions.description: Some viral challenges start with a moving car and end with the whole neighborhood dancing.
questions.fun_fact: “La Chona” came out in the 1990s, more than 20 years before it went viral.

questions.question: In “El Chavo del 8,” what kind of outfit does Quico always wear?
hints: Long ago, it was what well-dressed boys wore to parties.
It has a wide collar and comes with a little cap.
It's what people who work on a ship wear.
questions.description: The vecindad's biggest show-off never changes clothes, yet always looks brand new.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Villagrán, the actor who played Quico, was already a grown man when he played a kid in the vecindad.

questions.question: El Escorpión Dorado is the masked character who interviews celebrities in his car on YouTube. Which comedian plays him?
hints: He got famous mostly on the internet, not on TV.
In his videos his face is almost always hidden by the mask, so many people don't recognize him without it.
His last name starts with “Mont…”.
questions.description: A wrestler with no ring who prefers the driver's seat.
questions.fun_fact: Wearing his gold mask, El Escorpión Dorado has given rides to singers, soccer players and even politicians.

questions.question: Which of these shows is NOT from Televisa?
hints: It airs on a network that used to be public TV until the government sold it in 1993.
The show started in 2002.
It's a singing reality show from Televisa's big rival.
questions.description: A channel war where the remote control is the referee.
questions.fun_fact: “La Academia”, which started in 2002, launched singers such as Yuridia.

questions.question: In what year did Carmen Aristegui’s team break the story of President Enrique Peña Nieto’s “Casa Blanca”?
hints: It was roughly halfway through his six-year term.
It was the same year as the World Cup in Brazil.
The next year, Aristegui left her news show on MVS.
questions.description: Some houses end up in home decor magazines, and others end up on the evening news.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving MVS in 2015, Aristegui kept reporting through her own website, Aristegui Noticias.

questions.question: You're driving the DeLorean in “Back to the Future”. What speed must you reach for the flux capacitor to send you through time?
hints: The speed is in miles, not kilometers.
It's about 141 km per hour.
The number is two eights in a row.
questions.description: A car that runs on a calendar instead of gasoline.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the speed, the flux capacitor needs 1.21 gigawatts of power, which Doc gets from plutonium or a bolt of lightning.

questions.question: On Netflix, you watch Diego Boneta sing as El Sol de México in “Luis Miguel: The Series”. In what year did it premiere?
hints: It was in the second half of the 2010s.
Its final season came out three years later.
It was the year Andrés Manuel López Obrador won the presidency.
questions.description: A life so full of telenovela drama that it had to become a series.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Boneta recorded the show's songs himself, imitating Luis Miguel's voice.

questions.question: You wake up early and Chabelo is on TV with “En Familia”. What day of the week is it?
hints: It's a day with no school.
Many families watched it before the big family lunch.
It's the last day of the weekend.
questions.description: Every kid's best friend, who took a very, very long time to grow old.
questions.fun_fact: “En Familia con Chabelo” was on the air for about 48 years, from 1967 to 2015.

questions.question: The 2025 series about the life of Roberto Gómez Bolaños is called “Chespirito: …”. How does the title go on?
hints: It's a line from El Chavo del 8.
He said it when something went wrong and he swore it wasn't his fault.
It uses the verb “querer” (to want) twice.
questions.description: A series about the man who made a whole continent laugh with a barrel.
questions.fun_fact: One of the creators of the series is Roberto Gómez Fernández, Chespirito's son.

questions.question: Ricardo Garibay wrote “Beber un cáliz” and “Las glorias del gran Púas,” a chronicle about a boxer. He was born in 1923. In which state?
hints: His home state is in central Mexico, just north of Mexico City.
His home state borders San Luis Potosí and Veracruz.
He was born in Tulancingo, in the land of pastes and the miners of Real del Monte.
questions.description: A writer who knew all about punches, though he only threw them on his typewriter.
questions.fun_fact: “Las glorias del gran Púas” tells the life of Mexican boxer Rubén “Púas” Olivares, a world bantamweight champion.

questions.question: I was born in Puebla in 1949. In 1997 I became the first woman to win the Rómulo Gallegos Prize, with my novel “Lovesick”. Who am I?
hints: My novels often star women from Puebla.
My first novel was made into a film starring Ana Claudia Talancón.
I wrote “Tear This Heart Out”.
questions.description: A writer who brought back more than arepas from Venezuela.
questions.fun_fact: The Rómulo Gallegos Prize was created in Venezuela, and its first winner was Mario Vargas Llosa, for “The Green House”.

questions.question: As Secretary of Education, the poet Jaime Torres Bodet pushed for free textbooks. In what year was the commission that makes them created?
hints: Torres Bodet was Secretary of Education twice.
It happened under President Adolfo López Mateos.
It was one year before the 1960s began.
questions.description: Books that landed in your backpack without anyone paying a single peso.
questions.fun_fact: Before that, Torres Bodet was Director-General of UNESCO.

questions.question: Proceso magazine was founded in 1976 by Julio Scherer García and journalists who had been forced out of a daily paper. Which one?
hints: It was a blow against the press under President Luis Echeverría.
Scherer was the editor of that paper.
Founded in 1917, this paper was called “the newspaper of national life.”
questions.description: Journalists who were shown the door and came back through the newsstand.
questions.fun_fact: Proceso went on sale in November 1976, a few months after Scherer was pushed out of his old paper.

questions.question: You’re reading a story where the flooded river carries off Serpentina, Tacha’s cow. Who wrote it?
hints: The story is called “We’re Very Poor”.
Its author was from Jalisco and was also a photographer.
He wrote the novel set in Comala.
questions.description: A story where the rain brings nothing good, not even a day off school.
questions.fun_fact: The cow was a gift from her dad so that Tacha would have something to marry with.

questions.question: The author of “Muerte sin fin” (1939) belonged to the Contemporáneos group and wrote “Canciones para cantar en las barcas.” Which state was he from?
hints: The poet is José Gorostiza.
His state is a land of rivers and cacao.
He was born in Villahermosa.
questions.description: A poem so long that its title warns you it never ends.
questions.fun_fact: The central image of “Muerte sin fin” is water taking the shape of the glass that holds it.

questions.question: It has Gungans living underwater, Padmé was its queen and its capital is Theed. Which planet is Palpatine from?
hints: It's a green planet with lakes and elegant palaces.
Jar Jar Binks comes from there too.
It appears at the start of “The Phantom Menace”.
questions.description: A very friendly senator with big weekend plans: taking over the galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: The scenes in the palace on Naboo were filmed at the Royal Palace of Caserta in Italy.

questions.question: In what year did Octavio Paz publish the first edition of his poetry book “Libertad bajo palabra” (Freedom on Parole)?
hints: Paz was about 35 years old.
A year later, “The Labyrinth of Solitude” came out.
It was just before the middle of the 20th century.
questions.description: A book with a title fit for a lawyer, but full of poems.
questions.fun_fact: Paz revised this book so much that the 1960 version is very different from the first one.

questions.question: Amado Nervo was born in 1870, became a diplomat and died in Montevideo in 1919. In which present-day state is his hometown?
hints: His state is one of the youngest in Mexico.
It is on the Pacific coast, north of Puerto Vallarta.
He was born in Tepic.
questions.description: A poet who traveled so much that even his final goodbye needed a passport.
questions.fun_fact: His body was brought back from Uruguay to Mexico by ship, and he rests in the Rotonda de las Personas Ilustres.

questions.question: In Juan Pablo Villalobos’s “Down the Rabbit Hole”, the boy Tochtli wants an animal like this one. From which country?
hints: In the wild, this small hippo lives in thick, humid forests near rivers.
It is a country in West Africa.
Its capital is Monrovia.
questions.description: A boy who asks for a present that won’t fit in any box.
questions.fun_fact: A pygmy hippo weighs about ten times less than a common hippo.

questions.question: Chewbacca is to Wookiee as the furry little bears of the moon of Endor are to…
hints: They appear in “Return of the Jedi”.
They live in little houses up in the forest trees.
One of them is named Wicket.
questions.description: Cuddly toys with spears that won a war against an empire.
questions.fun_fact: The forest of Endor was filmed among the giant redwoods of California.

questions.question: In which decade did Stanisław Lem publish his novel “Solaris”?
hints: It's about scientists on a space station studying a planet covered by a living ocean.
It came out the same year Yuri Gagarin flew into space.
Tarkovsky turned it into a film in 1972, a decade later.
questions.description: A planet that's all ocean and reads your mind too: a terrible vacation spot.
questions.fun_fact: “Solaris” has two famous films: Andrei Tarkovsky's (1972) and Steven Soderbergh's with George Clooney (2002).

questions.question: In which US state is Area 51?
hints: It lies deep in the desert of the American West.
It borders California and was home to a famous nuclear test site.
Its largest city is Las Vegas.
questions.description: The most secret base in the world, which somehow everyone has heard of.
questions.fun_fact: The US government only officially admitted that Area 51 exists in 2013.

questions.question: Joseph Lister introduced it in 1867. It used carbolic acid and keeps wounds from getting infected. What is it called?
hints: It has to do with killing germs.
The alcohol and iodine you put on a cut do exactly this.
Its name means “against rotting.”
questions.description: Before this, surgeons operated in the same stained coat they wore last week.
questions.fun_fact: Listerine mouthwash is named in honor of Joseph Lister.

questions.question: In an animated film, food like this falls from the sky thanks to a young inventor's machine. What is his name?
hints: He lives in a small town on an island.
His machine turns water into food.
The film is called “Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs.”
questions.description: Today's weather forecast: grab an umbrella and a fork.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, Flint's machine has a very long name, shortened to FLDSMDFR.

questions.question: Henry Cavendish discovered it in 1766, called it “inflammable air,” and it is the lightest element there is. What is it?
hints: It's a gas.
Stars like the Sun are made mostly of it.
It's the H in H₂O.
questions.description: A scientist so shy he left notes for his housekeeper so he wouldn't have to talk to her.
questions.fun_fact: Cavendish also “weighed” the Earth with an experiment using lead balls and a thin wire.

questions.question: In which century did Hippocrates, the Greek known as the father of medicine, live?
hints: It was before the birth of Christ.
It was around the same time as Socrates.
It was about a hundred years before Alexander the Great.
questions.description: The doctor every doctor swears an oath to, even though none of them ever met him.
questions.fun_fact: Hippocrates was one of the first to say that diseases have natural causes and are not punishments from the gods.

questions.question: I was the first dog to circle the Earth, aboard a Soviet satellite in 1957. Who am I?
hints: Before I was famous, I lived on the streets of Moscow.
I traveled on Sputnik 2.
My name means something like “barker” in Russian.
questions.description: A little dog who went farther than any ball anyone ever threw for her.
questions.fun_fact: Laika was the first animal to orbit the Earth, more than three years before the first human.

questions.question: Which German physicist discovered that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance?
hints: He published his law in 1827.
Today the unit of electrical resistance is named after him.
That unit is written with the Greek letter omega.
questions.description: A law that puts up resistance, but only to the current.
questions.fun_fact: When Ohm published his law, many fellow scientists dismissed it, and he lost his job as a teacher.

questions.question: Oppenheimer led the lab that tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In which year?
hints: It happened during the Second World War.
The United States built it in secret as part of the Manhattan Project.
It was in the middle of the 20th century, in the 1940s.
questions.description: A scientist Hollywood gave three hours of film and zero minutes of jokes.
questions.fun_fact: The test was called “Trinity”, and its flash was seen more than 200 km (124 miles) away.

questions.question: In which decade was “A Beautiful Mind”, the movie about mathematician John Nash, released?
hints: The lead actor is Russell Crowe.
It won the Oscar for Best Picture.
It came out the same year as the first Harry Potter movie.
questions.description: A movie where the equations have more suspense than the villains.
questions.fun_fact: John Nash won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994 for his ideas on game theory.

questions.question: In which century did Washington Irving publish “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” the tale of the Headless Horseman?
hints: Irving was one of the first famous writers from the United States, a country born in 1776.
It was the same century the telephone was invented.
It came out in 1820, one year before Napoleon died.
questions.description: A rider who lost his head long before there were phones to distract him.
questions.fun_fact: Irving published the story in the same book as “Rip Van Winkle,” the man who slept for 20 years.

questions.question: A 2004 British comedy with zombies in London and a plan to hide out at the local pub. Which film is it?
hints: Its director later made “Baby Driver.”
Its star is Simon Pegg, Scotty in the newer “Star Trek” films.
Its title is a play on “Dawn of the Dead” and the hero's name.
questions.description: The world is ending, and plan B is going out for a drink.
questions.fun_fact: George A. Romero, the father of zombie films, liked it so much that he invited its creators to play zombies in “Land of the Dead.”

questions.question: What is this classic Christmas tree star made of?
hints: It grows in fields.
It's what's left over when grain is harvested.
In the barn, it's spread out as bedding for horses and cows.
questions.description: This star doesn't shine; at most it crackles a little.
questions.fun_fact: Straw stars are meant to recall the straw in the manger where baby Jesus lay.

questions.question: You crack three walnuts with a nutcracker, and each one breaks into two halves. How many shell halves are there?
hints: Each nut makes two pieces.
Count along: two, four …
It's twice as many as three.
questions.description: A wooden soldier who bares his teeth for a living.
questions.fun_fact: The first soldier-shaped nutcracker from the Erzgebirge is said to have been carved on a lathe by Wilhelm Friedrich Füchtner of Seiffen around 1870.

questions.question: In the New Year's Eve classic “Dinner for One”, Miss Sophie is celebrating her birthday. Which one?
hints: She's older than most grandmas.
Her butler James isn't exactly young either.
It's a round birthday between 80 and 100.
questions.description: Same procedure as every year, only the candles on the cake keep multiplying.
questions.fun_fact: In Britain, where the sketch is set, hardly anyone knows it, yet in Germany it's on TV every New Year's Eve.

questions.question: When do most German families have the Bescherung (the handing out of presents)?
hints: It's already dark outside.
Before it, many families go to church for the nativity play.
This day is called Heiligabend.
questions.description: The moment when wrapping paper ends its short career.
questions.fun_fact: In the UK and the US, children usually don't unwrap their presents until the morning of December 25.

questions.question: I'm recited by heart on St. Nicholas Day, I rhyme, and whoever knows me might get something from the sack. What am I?
hints: I have verses.
A well-known example begins with “Lieber, guter Nikolaus” (“Dear, good Nicholas”).
You learn me like a song without a tune.
questions.description: Stage fright in front of a man with a very long beard.
questions.fun_fact: “Von drauß' vom Walde komm ich her” (“From out of the forest I come”) was written by Theodor Storm and lets Knecht Ruprecht speak for himself.

questions.question: People say it between Christmas and New Year's Eve, often when saying goodbye, and it has nothing to do with icy roads. What does “Guten Rutsch” wish you?
questions.answer: A good start to the new year
hints: It's about a change from one thing to the next.
At midnight, the moment arrives.
It begins on January 1.
questions.description: A good wish with a built-in slide, supposedly.
questions.fun_fact: It's often said that “Rutsch” comes from the Hebrew “rosh” (beginning), but language experts think it more likely comes from the old word “rutschen”, meaning “to travel”.

questions.question: You open the very last door on the Advent calendar. What number is on it?
hints: That's the day of Christmas Eve.
The number starts with a 2.
It's two dozen.
questions.description: Chocolate with a built-in countdown.
questions.fun_fact: One of the first printed Advent calendars came out in Germany around 1904.

questions.question: I'm the monster in a 2006 animated film: my door is my mouth, my rug is my tongue, and I swallow balls. What am I?
hints: I don't walk: I never leave my street.
I have windows that look like eyes.
I have a roof, a chimney and a yard that nobody dares to enter.
questions.description: The grumpiest grumpy neighbor in the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: “Monster House” was produced by Steven Spielberg and Robert Zemeckis and was nominated for the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

questions.question: In a Bavarian custom, people go from house to house between Christmas and Epiphany to praise the hosts' Christmas tree. What do they get in return?
hints: The thicker you lay on the praise, the more it pays off.
The host usually has the reward ready in the cupboard.
Afterwards you say “Prost”, and kids don't get any.
questions.description: Rarely has a compliment to a fir tree paid off so well.
questions.fun_fact: “Christbaumloben” (praising the Christmas tree) is most common in Old Bavaria, for example in the Bavarian Forest and the Upper Palatinate.

questions.question: I sizzle over charcoal at the Christmas market. I'm long and thin, and I lie in a bread roll with mustard. What am I?
hints: I'm made of meat.
Nuremberg and Thuringia are especially proud of me.
In Nuremberg, people order me in threes: “Drei im Weggla” (three in a bun).
questions.description: The secret star right next to the Glühwein stand.
questions.fun_fact: Real Nürnberger Rostbratwürste may only be made in Nuremberg, and they are just 7 to 9 cm (about 3 to 3.5 in) long.

questions.question: This writer wrote “The Flying Classroom”, a Christmas story set at a boarding school. Who is it?
hints: He came from Dresden.
He also wrote “Lisa and Lottie” and “Dot and Anton”.
His most famous young detective is called Emil.
questions.description: A classroom with airplane mode, long before anyone had a phone.
questions.fun_fact: The book came out in 1933 and is set during the last school days before Christmas at a secondary school in Kirchberg.

questions.question: Opel started out in Rüsselsheim in 1862 making sewing machines. How many years later did Opel build its first car?
hints: Carl Benz's first car took to the road in 1886.
In between, Opel also built bicycles.
The first Opel car rolled out of the factory just before the year 1900.
questions.description: First needle and thread, then steering wheel and horn: a company with a very twisty résumé.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1920s, Opel was the biggest bicycle maker in the world.

questions.question: Sebamed came out in 1967 as a soap-free cleansing bar. What pH does it have, the same as healthy skin?
hints: The number is printed large on the package.
Healthy skin is slightly acidic, so a bit below the neutral value of 7.
The value is between 5 and 6.
questions.description: For everyone who'd like a little chemistry lesson while washing their hands.
questions.fun_fact: Regular soap is alkaline and usually has a pH of around 9 to 10.

questions.question: These Christmas star cookies are baked with no flour at all. What makes up most of their dough instead?
hints: This ingredient grows on trees.
It's also in marzipan.
Squirrels collect them for the winter.
questions.description: These stars don't shine in the sky; they sit in the cookie tin.
questions.fun_fact: The white glaze on Zimtsterne is made of beaten egg whites and powdered sugar.

questions.question: At a German fair, you buy a gingerbread heart that says “Ich hab dich lieb.” What are the colorful letters made of?
hints: The letters are sweet and turn hard.
They are piped on from a bag.
You make it by stirring powdered sugar with a little liquid.
questions.description: Love letters you can eat afterwards.
questions.fun_fact: Gingerbread hearts are often baked so hard that many people don't eat them at all but hang them up as souvenirs.

questions.question: What are these thin, crunchy discs mainly made of?
hints: They turn golden brown and shiny when baked.
The underside is often coated in chocolate.
Sugar, honey and cream are cooked together with nuts.
questions.description: Crunchy discs with an Italian name that still love to sit on German Christmas cookie plates.
questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, nobody is sure whether Florentines really come from Florence.

questions.question: About how fast does a bumper car go at the Kirmes?
hints: It's faster than someone walking.
A person out jogging goes at about the same speed.
Faster than walking pace, but slower than a car driving through town.
questions.description: The one place where bumping into other drivers is actually welcome.
questions.fun_fact: A bumper car gets its power through its pole from the metal net on the ceiling.

questions.question: At the Rosenmontag parade, people at the roadside shout “Kamelle!”. Who throws candy in return?
wrong_answers: The mayor at the town hall
hints: These people move through the streets with the parade.
They're in costume and stand higher up than you.
They ride on big, colorfully decorated wagons.
questions.description: The one day of the year when you're allowed to beg for sweets in the street at the top of your lungs.
questions.fun_fact: At the Cologne Rosenmontag parade, hundreds of tons of candy fly into the crowd every year.

questions.question: Toggo, Toggolino for the little ones and Toggo Radio: which TV channel does this kids' brand belong to?
hints: It's a private channel, not a public one.
The channel is based in Cologne.
Its name contains a big German private broadcaster with three letters.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a magic spell, and yet it works every single afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: Super RTL went on air in 1995 and for many years was run jointly by RTL and Disney.

questions.question: “I'm the often grumpy neighbor in “Löwenzahn”, grumbling about Peter Lustig and later about Fritz Fuchs. Who am I?”
hints: I always find something wrong with my neighbor.
I care a lot about keeping my garden in order.
My name starts with “Pa…”.
questions.description: Every street has one, but only this one made it onto TV.
questions.fun_fact: Herr Paschulke was played by Helmut Krauss, who is also well known as a voice actor.

questions.question: A girl reads a magic book, turns into an elf with wings and rides unicorns. What is the world in “Mia and Me” called?
hints: Elves, unicorns and nasty Munculus live there.
The name sounds a bit like “century”, from a word for hundred.
It starts with “Cento…”.
questions.description: A magic book you definitely won't find in the school library.
questions.fun_fact: “Mia and Me” was created by Gerhard Hahn from Berlin and mixes live-action scenes with computer animation.

questions.question: This lighthouse stands in the Baltic Sea resort of Warnemünde. Which city is Warnemünde part of?
hints: The city has one of the oldest universities in Northern Europe.
It is an old Hanseatic city in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
The river that flows into the sea at Warnemünde is called the Warnow.
questions.description: A lighthouse, a round building and lots of wind: here even the seagulls have to book a Strandkorb.
questions.fun_fact: The curvy round building next to the lighthouse is called the “Teepott” (teapot).

questions.question: You're on a trip to Neuschwanstein Castle. Where are you NOT?
hints: The castle is in the far south of Germany.
High mountains rise all around the castle.
You're looking for a place in the far north, with low and high tides.
questions.description: A castle so fairy-tale that even the princesses in cartoons want to move in.
questions.fun_fact: Neuschwanstein is said to have inspired the Sleeping Beauty Castle at Walt Disney's parks.

questions.question: You bike the Berlin Wall Trail all the way around former West Berlin. Roughly how long was the Wall there?
hints: The Wall enclosed half of a big city.
From east to west, Berlin is about 40 km (25 miles) wide.
The route is longer than three marathons put together.
questions.description: A bike ride you once would have needed a very good reason for.
questions.fun_fact: Today, in many places in Berlin, a double row of cobblestones shows where the Wall used to stand.

questions.question: Hamburg's Reeperbahn, where the Beatles once played, is named after old craftsmen. What were “Reeper”?
hints: The street is long and very straight, which is exactly what these craftsmen needed.
Ships in the port of Hamburg needed what they made.
The English word for what they made sounds a lot like “reep”.
questions.description: A street where things were pulled tight long before the Beatles showed up.
questions.fun_fact: The Beatles played in Hamburg clubs from 1960 to 1962, before they became world-famous.

questions.question: Speyer Cathedral was begun in 1030 by the Salian dynasty and holds the tombs of eight emperors and kings. It is the largest surviving church of which style?
hints: The style is older than the great cathedrals with pointed arches.
It is known for thick walls and round arches.
The style's name recalls ancient Rome.
questions.description: Eight crowned heads rest here, and not one of them complains about the view.
questions.fun_fact: Emperor Conrad II, who started the building, is himself buried in the cathedral's crypt.

questions.question: “Vampyr” (1932) is a classic vampire movie. Which country was its director, Carl Theodor Dreyer, from?
hints: It's a Scandinavian country.
Its capital has a famous statue of a little mermaid by the sea.
It's the home country of Lego.
questions.description: Long before vampires sparkled, there were vampires who barely said a word.
questions.fun_fact: The lead actor in “Vampyr” was a baron who paid for the movie and acted under a fake name.

questions.question: Above the coal mines of the Ruhr, tall towers with big wheels rose into the sky. What were they for?
questions.answer: Lifting coal and miners up from deep down
hints: The wheel turned a thick steel cable.
Below it, a shaft went many hundreds of meters into the earth.
The cage on the cable moved like an elevator.
questions.description: Ferris wheels all over the Ruhr, but not a single stick of cotton candy.
questions.fun_fact: The former Zollverein coal mine in Essen is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: They're only as long as a finger, grilled over beech wood, and legend says they were sold through keyholes at night. What are they?
hints: They are seasoned with lots of marjoram.
People often eat three of them in a bread roll.
They come from the city of the famous Christkindlesmarkt.
questions.description: Small but mighty: a handbag-sized sausage.
questions.fun_fact: Real Nürnberger Rostbratwürstchen may only be 7 to 9 cm (about 3 to 3.5 in) long and weigh no more than 25 grams (under 1 oz).

questions.question: In which city is this soccer stadium?
hints: The city lies right in the middle of the Ruhr area.
The club that plays here wears royal blue.
The club is named after a district called Schalke.
questions.description: Where tens of thousands sing on Saturdays as if the whole world depended on one penalty kick.
questions.fun_fact: The arena's entire field can be rolled out of the stadium so the grass gets sunlight.

questions.question: These thin sausages are warmed in hot water and named after the city with Germany's tallest skyscrapers. Which city?
hints: The city lies on the Main River.
It has Germany's biggest airport.
Because of all its bank towers, people also call it “Mainhattan.”
questions.description: They usually come in pairs and love a hot bath.
questions.fun_fact: In Austria these sausages are called “Frankfurter,” while in Germany they're often called “Wiener.”

questions.question: This grand Baroque building with a large courtyard stands in Dresden. What is it called?
hints: It was built for Augustus the Strong.
It stands very close to the Semperoper.
Its name once meant the space between two city walls.
questions.description: Pomp, pavilions and putti: whoever built this didn't skimp on anything.
questions.fun_fact: The picture gallery at the Zwinger holds Raphael's “Sistine Madonna” with its two famous little angels.

questions.question: About how far is it from Flensburg to the border with Denmark?
hints: Flensburg is Germany's northernmost larger city.
Many Danes come to Flensburg to go shopping.
By bike, you get there in less than an hour.
questions.description: Way up at the top of the map, where “Moin” already counts as a conversation.
questions.fun_fact: Flensburg has a Danish minority with its own schools and its own newspaper.

questions.question: Which of these characters is NOT part of Rolf Kauka's comic “Fix und Foxi”?
hints: The character comes from a different German magazine of the postwar years.
It has spines instead of fur.
This hedgehog was the mascot of the TV guide magazine “Hörzu”.
questions.description: Back in the day, a few Groschen of pocket money bought you whole adventures in a magazine at the newsstand.
questions.fun_fact: Kauka's magazine started in 1953 as “Till Eulenspiegel” and was only called “Fix und Foxi” from 1955 on.

questions.question: He is Karl May's narrator and Winnetou's blood brother. What is his Wild West name?
hints: His real first name is the same as the author's.
He owns the Henry rifle and the “Bear Killer” gun.
His name says what his fist does to an opponent's jaw.
questions.description: A man from Saxony in the Wild West who would rather ride across the prairie than fill out forms.
questions.fun_fact: Winnetou calls his friend “Scharlih,” after his first name, Karl.

questions.question: At night in the forest, the poor girl from the Grimm fairy tale has given away even her last little shirt. What falls from the sky now?
hints: With these, the girl will never go hungry again.
Before, they were something that shines in the sky.
The tale's name, “Sterntaler,” gives it away.
questions.description: If you give everything away, you end up with nothing… or do you?
questions.fun_fact: The girl also gets a new little shirt made of the very finest linen.

questions.question: Maik and Tschick drive through eastern Germany in a car like this in Wolfgang Herrndorf's novel. Which model is it?
hints: Tschick “borrows” the car without asking first.
This car handles dirt tracks and fields with ease.
The model came out in the Soviet Union in 1977.
questions.description: A road movie with no driver's license, but plenty of summer vacation.
questions.fun_fact: “Tschick” came out in 2010 (in English as “Why We Took the Car”), and Fatih Akin turned it into a film in 2016.

questions.question: I scare people in their dreams and wear a red-and-green striped sweater, a hat and a glove with blades. Who am I?
hints: I'm a movie villain from the 1980s.
Director Wes Craven created me.
My first name is short for Frederick.
questions.description: Counting sheep won't help you one bit against this gentleman.
questions.fun_fact: Wes Craven is said to have picked red and green for the sweater because those two colors clash and are hard on the eye when put together.

questions.question: In which year was Cornelia Funke's novel “Inkheart” published?
hints: The book is newer than “The Neverending Story”.
The movie version came out a few years later.
It was in the first decade of the 21st century.
questions.description: Careful when reading aloud: sometimes a villain climbs right out of the book.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2008 movie, Brendan Fraser plays the father, Mo, known as “Silvertongue”.

questions.question: This man turned the legend of the Flying Dutchman into an opera. Who is he?
hints: He lived in the 19th century.
