He had his own festival theater built for his operas.
His works are performed in Bayreuth every summer.
questions.description: A ghost ship that sails forever, and a man who turns it into hours and hours of music.
questions.fun_fact: Wagner knew the legend from a story by Heinrich Heine, and a stormy sea voyage is said to have inspired him too.

questions.question: You're in Braunschweig at the premiere of Lessing's “Emilia Galotti”. What year is it?
hints: Lessing was working as a librarian in Wolfenbüttel at the time.
The performance was held for a duchess's birthday.
It was in the early 1770s.
questions.description: A prince, a schemer and a father with very strict principles: theater for advanced audiences.
questions.fun_fact: The premiere on March 13, 1772, celebrated the birthday of Duchess Philippine Charlotte of Brunswick.

questions.question: He was born in 1898, wrote “All Quiet on the Western Front”, and his hometown gives out a peace prize in his name. Where was he from?
hints: The city is in Lower Saxony.
Part of the Peace of Westphalia was signed here in 1648.
The city lies near the border with Westphalia and starts with “O”.
questions.description: A writer who fiddled with the spelling of his last name until it sounded French.
questions.fun_fact: His real name was Erich Paul Remark, and he picked the French-looking spelling himself.

questions.question: In the Grimm fairy tale, the eldest son gets a little table like this one after his apprenticeship. Who did he learn from?
hints: His master works with wood himself.
His brothers get a gold donkey and a cudgel.
This craftsman builds tables, cupboards and chairs.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that beats any food delivery app.
questions.fun_fact: The middle son learns from a miller and gets the donkey that spits out gold coins when you say “Bricklebrit”.

questions.question: A merchant's son travels with actors, a harpist goes with him, and Mignon sings “Do you know the land where the lemon trees bloom?”. Which work is it?
hints: As a child, the hero loved his puppet theater.
It is seen as the model of the German coming-of-age novel, the Bildungsroman.
The title names the hero and his years of training.
questions.description: A young merchant's son would rather go on stage than into the family office, and parents know how that goes.
questions.fun_fact: Mignon's song was set to music by Beethoven, Schubert and Schumann, among others.

questions.question: In Frank Schätzing's novel “The Swarm,” whales attack boats and worms set off a tsunami. What are the beings behind it called?
hints: They live in the deep sea.
They are made of countless single-celled organisms that think together.
Their name is very short, only three letters.
questions.description: The ocean has had enough, and now it's fighting back.
questions.fun_fact: “The Swarm” came out in 2004 and was made into an international TV series in 2023.

questions.question: You have it in the beer tent, at Fasching and when you go sledding. In Bavaria they say: “Des war a Gaudi!” What does “Gaudi” mean?
hints: Most people go home in a good mood afterwards.
There's a lot of laughing.
It's the opposite of boredom.
questions.description: This question has nothing at all to do with architecture in Barcelona. Honestly.
questions.fun_fact: “Gaudi” comes from the Latin “gaudium”, meaning “joy”.

questions.question: Low German says “Water”, “Appel” and “maken”, but standard German says “Wasser”, “Apfel” and “machen”. What caused this difference?
hints: It's about consonants, not vowels.
The change happened roughly between the 6th and 8th centuries and only reached the south.
Its best-known boundary is the Benrath Line, and it wasn't the first shift of its kind.
questions.description: Low German and standard German order the same apple and still can't understand each other.
questions.fun_fact: The Benrath Line, which separates “maken” from “machen”, crosses the Rhine at Benrath in Düsseldorf.

questions.question: You say it when you leave, often with a wave, and it's the opposite of “Hallo”. Which German word is it?
hints: You say it when you head home.
It's a word for saying goodbye.
It starts with “Tsch”.
questions.description: A little word parents remind their kids to say a hundred times a day.
questions.fun_fact: “Tschüss” comes from old goodbyes like “adieu” and “adiós”, which literally mean “to God”.

questions.question: Who composed the famous two-note theme from “Jaws” (1975)?
hints: He is American and has worked with Spielberg on almost all of his films.
He composed the music for “Jurassic Park”.
He also wrote the famous march from “Star Wars”.
questions.description: Two notes were enough to make sure nobody ever swam calmly in the sea again.
questions.fun_fact: That music won John Williams the Oscar for Best Original Score.

questions.question: A “Dappes” is a clumsy fool; the word is related to “tappen” (to fumble along). Where do people use this insult?
hints: It's a region in western Germany.
The Rhine and the Main meet there.
People there like to drink Ebbelwoi and Riesling.
questions.description: A word for anyone who just tripped over their own feet.
questions.fun_fact: In Hesse the fool is often called a “Dabbes”, with a soft “b” but the same meaning.

questions.question: Anglers wish each other “Petri Heil”. Which of these greetings does NOT belong to a particular job or hobby?
hints: Miners, hunters and ninepin bowlers have their own greetings.
One greeting is used by everyone in a whole region.
You hear this greeting on the North Sea coast at any time of day.
questions.description: Greetings that tell you right away who didn't catch anything today.
questions.fun_fact: “Petri” refers to the Apostle Peter, who was a fisherman, and the reply is “Petri Dank”.

questions.question: At a German supermarket, a water bottle says “Medium”. What does that mean?
hints: It's about something you feel on your tongue.
Next to it you'll often find “Classic” and “Still”.
It tingles, but only a bit.
questions.description: In Germany, mineral water has more settings than some washing machines.
questions.fun_fact: Few countries drink as much bottled mineral water as Germany: on average well over 100 liters (26 gallons) per person a year.

questions.question: In Germany, what is “Leitungswasser”?
hints: It doesn't come in a bottle.
In German restaurants, you often have to ask specially if you want it.
“Leitung” is German for a pipe or line.
questions.description: The cheapest drink in the whole house is waiting inside the wall for its big moment.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, tap water is one of the most strictly tested foods of all.

review.feedback: Now that the translation asks what “Leitungswasser” means, two things give the answer away that didn't in the source, where the question itself already said the water comes from the tap. First, the description ("waiting inside the wall") states the answer's defining trait: of the four options, only tap water waits inside the wall. Rewrite it to joke about water or drinks in general without saying where it comes from. Second, the kept illustrative image (a glass being filled at a kitchen tap) is shown sharp and shows the answer. Replace it with a decorative image, or with a neutral one such as a glass of water on a restaurant table.

questions.question: People drink Viez in Trier and along the Saar, often from a china mug called a “Porz”. The name may come from Latin “vice” (instead of). What is Viez?
hints: It used to replace wine for poor people.
It's made from a fruit that grows on trees.
In Frankfurt it's called “Ebbelwoi”.
questions.description: A drink with a Latin name that everyone along the Moselle still understands.
questions.fun_fact: Trier holds its own Viez festival every year, right in the middle of the old town.

questions.question: For this drink, German brandy and sugar are flambéed in a special cup, then coffee, whipped cream and chocolate shavings are added. What is it called?
hints: It was invented in Germany in 1957.
Its home is a wine town on the Rhine.
It is named after a wine town in the Rheingau.
questions.description: A coffee that bursts into flames before you even get to drink it.
questions.fun_fact: TV chef Hans Karl Adam invented it in 1957 to make Asbach, the brandy from Rüdesheim, better known.

questions.question: “In 1924, I founded a coffee business in Bremen. The first syllables of my name became a brand that later joined Tchibo.” Who am I?
hints: The brand sold coffee by mail and in its own stores.
Take the first syllable of the first name and of the last name.
The brand sounds like “Edu-Scho”.
questions.description: Bremen has smelled of fresh-roasted coffee forever, so somebody must have started it.
questions.fun_fact: Eduscho and Tchibo were fierce rivals for decades, until Tchibo bought the company in 1997.

questions.question: “I arrived in November 1923, one trillion paper marks were swapped for one of me, and Hjalmar Schacht watched over me as currency commissioner. What am I?”
hints: I ended the hyperinflation almost overnight.
I was supposed to be backed by the land of farms and industry.
The first part of my name is the German word for a pension.
questions.description: When a bread roll cost billions, Germany badly needed something new in its wallet.
questions.fun_fact: People called it the “miracle of the Rentenmark”; it even stayed legal tender alongside the Reichsmark until 1948.

questions.question: Who founded the Bauhaus art school in Weimar in 1919?
hints: He was an architect and later taught at Harvard University.
He designed the famous Bauhaus building in Dessau.
For a while he was married to Alma Mahler.
questions.description: Suddenly chairs, lamps and houses could do without a single frill.
questions.fun_fact: Gropius ran the Bauhaus until 1928; after him came Hannes Meyer and then Mies van der Rohe.

questions.question: The 1918 armistice was signed in the Forest of Compiègne. Which country had to sign in the same railroad car in 1940?
hints: Hitler wanted to reverse the defeat of 1918 as a symbol.
In 1918, the car had served as Marshal Foch's office.
It is the country where Compiègne is.
questions.description: A railroad car where world history was signed not once, but twice.
questions.fun_fact: Hitler had the original car taken to Berlin; the car in Compiègne today is one of the same series.

questions.question: This Reich chancellor called for passive resistance to the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923. Who was he?
hints: He belonged to no party and had run the HAPAG shipping line.
His successor called off the resistance in September 1923.
His last name has only four letters.
questions.description: A strike where the boss himself says: please don't work!
questions.fun_fact: The state kept paying the strikers' wages with freshly printed money, which fueled the hyperinflation.

questions.question: What are the small brass plaques in the sidewalk called that honor people persecuted by the Nazis outside their former homes?
hints: The artist Gunter Demnig has been laying them since the 1990s.
They often say “Hier wohnte” (“Here lived”) followed by a name.
The name means you should stumble over them in your mind, not with your feet.
questions.description: A work of art you won't find in a museum, only by looking down at your own shoes.
questions.fun_fact: With more than 100,000 stones in many European countries, they are seen as the world's largest decentralized memorial.

questions.question: In 1888, this woman drove her husband's motor car from Mannheim to Pforzheim, the first long car trip ever. Who is she?
hints: On the way, she bought fuel at a pharmacy in Wiesloch.
Her husband had filed a patent for the car in 1886.
Today her last name is on millions of cars.
questions.description: The world's first joyride, and she didn't ask her husband first.
questions.fun_fact: Her sons Eugen and Richard came along, and the route is now called the “Bertha Benz Memorial Route.”

questions.question: After Hindenburg died, Hitler merged the office of Reich President with that of Reich Chancellor. In which year?
hints: That same summer, soldiers had to swear an oath to Hitler personally.
Hindenburg died in August at the age of 86.
It was one year after the Nazis took power.
questions.description: Two boss's chairs, and only one man left sitting in both.
questions.fun_fact: In 1945, Karl Dönitz held the title of Reich President once more, for just a few weeks.

questions.question: In which year did the Nazis set up the Dachau concentration camp near Munich?
hints: It later served as a model for other camps.
At first, mainly political opponents were locked up there.
It was the year Hitler became chancellor.
questions.description: A place that shows why remembering is never a small thing.
questions.fun_fact: Since 1965, the site has been a memorial visited by people from all over the world.

questions.question: In which year did the Allies ban the Nazi Party (NSDAP) and all its sub-organizations?
hints: It was done by a law of the Allied Control Council.
Germany was split into four occupation zones at the time.
The Second World War in Europe ended that same year.
questions.description: The winners cleaned house, and one party ended up on the scrap heap of history.
questions.fun_fact: Control Council Law No. 2 of October 10, 1945, dissolved the party and seized its property.

questions.question: At Oktoberfest you see a man wearing a green Trachten hat. What is usually NOT found on a hat like this?
hints: Three of these are small hat decorations.
One of them is even tied together from animal hair.
At the fair, you'd rather hang this thing around your neck.
questions.description: A hat with more decorations than some Christmas trees.
questions.fun_fact: A big, real Gamsbart made from the back hair of a chamois can cost several thousand euros.

questions.question: I wrote the novel about a snowy haunted hotel that Stanley Kubrick made into a film in 1980, though I didn't like his version. Who am I?
hints: I'm American and I live in Maine.
I wrote “Carrie” and “Misery”.
I also wrote “It”, the one with Pennywise the clown.
questions.description: A vacation at a mountain hotel: what could possibly go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: Stephen King disliked Kubrick's version so much that in 1997 he made his own TV miniseries of “The Shining”.

questions.question: Candles are burning on the birthday cake. You blow them all out at once and say nothing. What did you secretly think up?
hints: You keep it all to yourself.
They say that if you tell anyone, it won't come true.
In fairy tales, the good fairy often grants three of them.
questions.description: Once a year, you're officially allowed to blow all over your food.
questions.fun_fact: In many German families, a bigger candle called the “Lebenslicht” (light of life) stands in the middle of the birthday ring.

questions.question: After a storm, lots of tiles are missing from the top of your house. Which tradesperson do you call?
hints: The tiles sit at the very top of the house.
This tradesperson often works on ladders and scaffolding.
The name of the job tells you exactly what gets fixed.
questions.description: A job with the best view in town, and a healthy respect for wind.
questions.fun_fact: On steep roofs, roofers secure themselves with harnesses and ropes, almost like mountain climbers.

questions.question: What is a godparent's real job?
questions.answer: To guide the child in life and faith
wrong_answers: To choose the child's first name
To fill the font with water
hints: The godparent is usually a close relative or a friend of the family.
During the baptism, the godparent makes a solemn promise.
They are meant to be someone the child can turn to and look up to for life.
questions.description: A baptism brings cake, candles and one person looking extra solemn.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Pate” (godparent) comes from the Latin “pater”, meaning “father”.

questions.question: What are the straps on these Lederhosen for?
hints: Without them, something might slide down.
They go over the shoulders.
In German they're called Hosenträger, “pants carriers.”
questions.description: Two strips of leather that spend their whole lives on someone's shoulders.
questions.fun_fact: The crosspiece between the straps of Lederhosen is often embroidered with edelweiss or deer.

questions.question: St. Martin cut his cloak with his sword to share it with a freezing beggar. Into how many pieces?
hints: He kept one piece for himself.
The beggar got just as much as Martin did.
He cut it right down the middle.
questions.description: Sharing is caring, especially when you have a sword handy.
questions.fun_fact: The legend says Martin kept one half because it belonged to the Roman army.

review.feedback: This duplicates approved q-10835 ("In the song “Sankt Martin ritt durch Schnee und Wind”, Martin cuts his cloak with his sword. Into how many pieces?", answer 2). It asks the same fact with the same answer, and the added "with his sword" makes the wording even closer. The German source has the same overlap (source:). One of the two should be dropped, or this one should ask a different St. Martin fact.

previous.feedback: This duplicates approved q-10835 ("In the song “Sankt Martin ritt durch Schnee und Wind”, Martin cuts his cloak with his sword. Into how many pieces?" → 2). Both ask the same fact with the same answer, so one of the two should be dropped from the English pool. Note that the duplicate is also in the German source pool.

questions.question: What is this game called? Children love to play it at Easter and on school field days.
hints: You need a spoon for it.
If you drop something, you have to go back.
The spoon carries something a hen has laid.
questions.description: Easter is when kids are suddenly officially allowed to play with their food.
questions.fun_fact: To keep anything from breaking, many people use wooden eggs or potatoes instead of real ones.

questions.question: In Germany, this lucky charm is a popular gift on New Year's Eve. How many leaves does it have?
hints: Just count them.
Normal clover has one less.
It's the same number as a dog's legs.
questions.description: A plant that got luckier than its brothers and sisters.
questions.fun_fact: Only about one in 5,000 to 10,000 clovers grows four leaves naturally.

questions.question: How long after Easter Monday does Whit Monday come?
hints: It falls in May or June.
Pentecost is celebrated about 50 days after Easter.
Divide 49 days by 7.
questions.description: A day off on a Monday that really likes to keep you waiting.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Pfingsten”, like the English “Pentecost”, comes from the Greek “pentekoste”, meaning “the fiftieth day”.

questions.question: The Easter Bunny hid 4 eggs under a bush and 3 eggs in the grass. How many Easter eggs is that?
hints: Add up both hiding places.
It's more than 6.
Work out 4 plus 3.
questions.description: Math with bunny paws.
questions.fun_fact: The Easter Bunny bringing eggs was first mentioned in Germany in 1682.

questions.question: A baby gets water poured on its head, a priest says its name and the godparents stand nearby. Where does this usually happen?
hints: It's usually quiet and solemn there.
The water is in a big stone basin.
The building often has a tall tower with bells.
questions.description: A party where the baby gets wet and everyone still smiles.
questions.fun_fact: Godparents are meant to stand by the child and help it for its whole life.

questions.question: “Found footage” films pretend to be real recordings discovered later. Which of these movies is NOT in that style?
hints: Look for the one that seems like a normal movie, with no handheld camera.
In [REC], everything is filmed by a TV reporter.
The one you want is about the paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren.
questions.description: Movies shot as if the camera operator had never heard of a tripod.
questions.fun_fact: “The Blair Witch Project” cost about $60,000 to make and earned more than $240 million.

questions.question: Under blooming fruit trees like these, a big festival with fruit wine has been held near Potsdam since 1879. In which town?
hints: It is one of the biggest folk festivals in eastern Germany and draws lots of Berliners.
The town's old center sits on an island in a river.
The same river also flows through Potsdam and Spandau.
questions.description: A festival where the trees are in full bloom before the guests are even out of bed.
questions.fun_fact: Werder was long known as “Berlin's orchard” and shipped its fruit to the capital by boat.

questions.question: What is NOT part of a classic snowman?
questions.answer: A bicycle helmet as a hat
hints: Three of these things show up in old picture books.
The one you're looking for belongs to a very different hobby than snow.
You wear the one you're looking for when riding a bike.
questions.description: A man who only feels like going outside in winter.
questions.fun_fact: Snowmen used to get coal eyes because almost every house was heated with coal.

questions.question: Which poet made the legend of Doctor Faust, who makes a pact with the devil, famous around the world?
hints: He was also a minister in Weimar.
He also wrote “The Sorrows of Young Werther.”
His last name starts with G.
questions.description: A man who knew you should never do business with the devil, but you can always write poetry about it.
questions.fun_fact: Goethe kept coming back to his “Faust” for about 60 years.

questions.question: In Heinrich Heine's “The Harz Journey” it says: “I am Princess Ilse.” What is the Ilse in the Harz in real life?
hints: It starts on the Brocken.
The town of Ilsenburg at the edge of the Harz is named after it.
It rushes down over rocks into the valley.
questions.description: Nobility has its duties, even in the middle of the Harz.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Princess Ilse lives inside the Ilsenstein, a huge rock above the Ilse valley.

questions.question: An apprentice miller, a mill in the Koselbruch marsh, and journeymen who turn into ravens: what kind of legend is Otfried Preußler’s “Krabat” based on?
hints: The story is set in eastern Germany.
The region is Lusatia (Lausitz).
The people there speak their own West Slavic language.
questions.description: Grinding, magic and keeping your mouth shut: the toughest apprenticeship in literary history.
questions.fun_fact: Preußler worked on “Krabat” for about ten years before the book came out in 1971.

questions.question: “I collected legends in Thuringia, my uncle studied birds, and my fairy-tale book was once more popular than the Grimms’.” Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 19th century and worked in Meiningen.
I wrote the “Deutsches Sagenbuch” (German Book of Legends).
My last name sounds like a famous piano brand.
questions.description: Before streaming services, there were men with very thick books.
questions.fun_fact: Bechstein’s bat is named after his uncle, the forester Johann Matthäus Bechstein.

questions.question: The Little Ghost of Eulenstein Castle has 13 keys and only haunts at midnight. What does it climb out of then?
hints: Where it sleeps is up in the attic.
You can flip the lid open.
In the old days, people kept treasure and linens in one.
questions.description: Even ghosts need a cozy bed, just a very old one.
questions.fun_fact: Once, when the Little Ghost haunts at noon, the sun turns it completely black.

questions.question: She lived at the Wartburg, secretly brought bread to the poor and got caught. According to legend, what was suddenly in her basket?
hints: It was something completely harmless and beautiful.
It smelled lovely.
It has thorns.
questions.description: A picnic basket with a built-in surprise.
questions.fun_fact: St. Elizabeth’s Church in Marburg is considered one of the oldest purely Gothic churches in Germany.

questions.question: “I was fired from a barrel, and a baron famous for his tall tales jumped on me and rode over the enemy city.” What am I?
hints: I am round and very heavy.
I am made of iron.
My barrel sits on wheels and goes “BOOM!”
questions.description: The first budget flight: no seat, no seatbelt, no honesty.
questions.fun_fact: The real Baron Münchhausen lived in Bodenwerder on the Weser River.

questions.question: Which fairy-tale character dances around a fire singing “Ach, wie gut, dass niemand weiß …” (“Oh, how good that nobody knows …”)?
hints: He can spin straw into gold.
The queen has to guess his name.
In the end he stamps his foot deep into the ground in rage.
questions.description: A little man with a big secret and an even bigger temper tantrum.
questions.fun_fact: In German, when someone jumps up and down in a rage, people still say they are raging like Rumpelstilzchen.

questions.question: In “Madagascar 3,” the zoo animals join a circus in Europe. Which of these characters is NOT in that movie?
hints: Three of them lived in the New York zoo.
The odd one out comes from another movie series about prehistoric animals.
He's a mammoth from “Ice Age.”
questions.description: A zoo that ran away from home to do acrobatics in Europe.
questions.fun_fact: In “Madagascar 3,” Marty the zebra sings the catchy song “Afro Circus.”

questions.question: In the evening you want a newspaper, some gum and a cold soda from the little booth on the corner. What is that kind of shop called in Germany?
hints: Things are often sold through a small window.
In Berlin, one version is called a “Späti”.
The word comes from Turkish and first meant “garden pavilion”.
questions.description: The place where your change often comes back with a friendly “The usual, then?”
questions.fun_fact: In the Rhineland it is lovingly called a “Büdchen”, and in the Ruhr area a “Bude” or “Trinkhalle”.

questions.question: Karstadt was founded in Wismar in 1881, later merged with Kaufhof and is now called Galeria. What kind of business is it?
hints: Its stores are usually right in the middle of downtown.
You often ride an escalator from floor to floor.
From fashion to toys to cooking pots, it has everything under one roof.
questions.description: A classic name from the pedestrian zone that has been renamed more often than some soccer clubs.
questions.fun_fact: Back in 1881, Rudolph Karstadt already used fixed prices and cash payment instead of haggling with customers.

questions.question: It's pink, made of china and has a slot in its back. What do you put into this pig?
hints: You often find it in a kid's bedroom.
When you shake it, it jingles.
Later you can buy something with what's inside.
questions.description: The only pig that looks sad when its tummy is empty.
questions.fun_fact: In German, “slaughtering” your piggy bank (das Sparschwein schlachten) doesn't hurt it at all: it just means taking all the coins out.

questions.question: This colorful sealed bag is sold at the kiosk. It holds candy and a small toy, but you don't know which one beforehand. What is it called?
hints: The exciting part is the surprise.
There's often a sticker or a little plastic figure inside.
The first part of its name means “miracle” or “wonder”.
questions.description: Buy it, rip it open, be amazed, and sometimes be a little disappointed.
questions.fun_fact: The idea is a bit like the Kinder Surprise egg: there, too, you don't know which toy is inside until you unwrap it.

questions.question: I know every customer by name and sometimes let them pay later. Small corner shops are named after me. Who am I?
hints: I sell flour, milk and candy from big glass jars.
Supermarkets have pushed shops like mine almost out of business.
I'm related to you: I'm your mother's or father's sister.
questions.description: Long before delivery apps, there was a memory that knew exactly which milk you wanted.
questions.fun_fact: Small village shops are making a comeback: many are now run by the villagers themselves as cooperatives.

questions.question: When shopping, kids are often given a free slice of sausage like this one. Who gives it to them?
hints: He stands behind a glass counter.
He often wears a white apron.
He's the one who sells you schnitzel and sausages.
questions.description: A smile, a “Would you like one?”, and the kid is in a great mood for the rest of the shopping trip.
questions.fun_fact: The “Kinderscheibe” (kid's slice) is usually Fleischwurst or Gelbwurst, and many adults still remember exactly how it tasted.

questions.question: Passing it on is a crime. The Bundesbank says you can spot it with “Feel – Look – Tilt”. What is it?
hints: The police hunt for the people who make it.
Real bills have a hologram and a watermark instead.
In everyday German, such bills are called “Blüten”.
questions.description: A topic the Bundesbank looks at very closely, and even touches.
questions.fun_fact: If you accidentally take a “Blüte”, you don't get your money back: it has to be handed in to the police or a bank.

questions.question: These leaves are shown on the German 1, 2 and 5 cent coins. Which tree do they come from?
hints: The old pfennig already showed this tree.
It is seen as a typically German tree and can live to a great age.
Wild boars love its nuts with their little caps.
questions.description: The smallest money in your wallet carries a little piece of forest around with it.
questions.fun_fact: A cent isn't made of pure copper but of steel with a thin copper coating, which is why it sticks to a magnet.

questions.question: Why do many rented apartments have this small device on the radiator?
questions.answer: It records usage for the heating bill
wrong_answers: It lets air out of the radiator
It warns when the air is too dry
hints: It gets read once a year, these days often by radio.
That way one bill can be split fairly among all the tenants in the building.
The result ends up in the yearly statement of extra housing costs.
questions.description: A device that has a lot more to do in winter than in summer.
questions.fun_fact: Older heat cost allocators have a small tube of liquid that slowly evaporates with the heat.

questions.question: He wears a costume of colorful diamonds and a black mask, and he was born in Italian comedy theater. Who is he?
hints: He is a playful, very nimble servant.
His costume looks like it's made of colorful patches.
His name starts with “Harle-”.
questions.description: The character who made diamonds fashionable four hundred years ago.
questions.fun_fact: A pattern of colorful diamonds is still called a “harlequin” pattern.

questions.question: This folk song dates from 1844. In it, the water, the wheels and even the stones go wandering, and it's a school-trip classic. Which song is it?
hints: The singer first learns to wander from the water.
The wheels and stones belong to a workshop by a stream.
The trade in the song's title grinds grain into flour.
questions.description: An earworm that has been wearing hiking boots for almost 200 years.
questions.fun_fact: The words are by Wilhelm Müller, whose poems Franz Schubert set to music in “Die schöne Müllerin”.

questions.question: You're on a summit with the sun behind you and fog in front. A giant shadow with a ring of light appears in it. What is this called?
hints: The shadow is your own.
It's named after a mountain in the Harz.
The highest peak in the Harz is in the name.
questions.description: Crawl out of your sleeping bag at dawn for the summit view, and sometimes you get a free surprise too.
questions.fun_fact: The colored ring of light around the shadow is called a glory and is made by tiny water droplets in the fog.

questions.question: I wind down a hillside, made of steel or plastic. I don't need snow: you zoom down me into the valley on small sleds with wheels. What am I?
hints: You ride alone or in pairs and do your own braking.
In winter you'd ride down me on a real sled.
My name gives away the season when I'm the most fun.
questions.description: In summer, many a mountain turns into a giant playground.
questions.fun_fact: On many summer toboggan runs you zoom down at up to about 40 km/h (25 mph), braking with a lever on the sled.

questions.question: Zugspitze is to the Wetterstein range as Kampenwand is to …?
hints: The Kampenwand is in Upper Bavaria, near Aschau.
From the summit you look down on a large lake.
That lake is also called the “Bavarian Sea”.
questions.description: Bavarian mountains have family names, and this is a bit of family-tree research.
questions.fun_fact: The Kampenwand is about 1,669 m (5,476 ft) high and has one of the largest summit crosses in the Bavarian Alps.

questions.question: Nördlingen lies in a crater made by an asteroid about 15 million years ago. Roughly how wide is it?
hints: A whole town plus villages fits inside it.
From Nördlingen, the crater rim only shows as a distant line of hills.
Crossing it by bike would take about an hour.
questions.description: A town that took a direct hit from outer space.
questions.fun_fact: In 1970, Apollo 14 astronauts practiced rock studies for the Moon in the Ries crater.

questions.question: You're standing at the very top of the Zugspitze, next to the golden summit cross. About how tall is the cross?
hints: It's taller than a grown-up.
It's much smaller than a church tower.
About three adults standing on each other's shoulders would be that tall.
questions.description: You finally reach the top, and someone is already waiting with open arms.
questions.fun_fact: The first summit cross went up the Zugspitze in 1851; porters carried it up in pieces.

questions.question: I lie between the Main and the Neckar, I'm shared by Hesse, Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, and I have a famous Felsenmeer (sea of rocks). Which low mountain range am I?
hints: On my western edge, along the Bergstraße, the almond trees bloom early.
Heidelberg lies on my southern edge.
My name begins like a kind of poem.
questions.description: A forest that gets not just trees but three German states to agree.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Siegfried was murdered at a spring in the Odenwald during a hunt, and several towns argue over which spring it was.

questions.question: Which German state was the first to let 16-year-olds vote in its state parliament election?
hints: It's a city-state.
It is made up of two cities that are separate from each other.
This is where the four animal musicians in the Grimm fairy tale were headed.
questions.description: Here you're old enough at 16 for the ballot box, but still too young for a driver's license.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2011 state election, Bremen became the first place in Germany where 16-year-olds could help elect a state parliament.

questions.question: When you turn 14 in Germany, you become “religionsmündig”. What does that mean?
wrong_answers: You must start paying church tax
You may get married in church
hints: It has to do with the freedom of religion in the Basic Law.
Before this age, parents usually decide.
From this age you can, for example, join or leave a church on your own.
questions.description: At 14, German teens get more say than some parents would like.
questions.fun_fact: Already at 12, a child in Germany can no longer be raised in a different faith against their will.

questions.question: You get a letter with the German federal eagle in the letterhead. Who can it NOT be from?
hints: The federal eagle stands for the federal government, meaning all of Germany.
Towns, cities and states have their own coats of arms.
You're looking for someone from city hall.
questions.description: Mail with a bird on it: either it's important, or it's from the pigeon-racing club.
questions.fun_fact: The Bundestag, the Bundesrat and the Federal Constitutional Court each use their own, slightly different version of the eagle.

questions.question: The Wallendas are a famous circus family who walk on wires high up in the air, like in the photo. What are these performers called?
hints: Their secret is never losing their balance.
Sometimes they carry a long pole so they don't fall.
Their name describes exactly what they do: step along a stretched line.
questions.description: A family that walks to school on a wire instead of the sidewalk.
questions.fun_fact: Nik Wallenda walked across Niagara Falls on a wire in 2012.

questions.question: In what year did Angela Merkel become the first woman to serve as Germany's chancellor?
hints: It was in the first decade of the 21st century.
Her predecessor was Gerhard Schröder.
The year after, Germany hosted the World Cup known as the “Sommermärchen” (summer fairy tale).
questions.description: For decades, this job only ever came with a tie.
questions.fun_fact: Angela Merkel governed for 16 years, almost exactly as long as Helmut Kohl.

questions.question: My title comes from the Latin word for “servant.” The chancellor proposes me, and I run areas like finance or health. Who am I?
hints: I am appointed by the federal president.
Together with the chancellor, I make up the federal government.
I sit at the cabinet table and run my own ministry.
questions.description: A top job whose name originally sounds more like fetching the coffee.
questions.fun_fact: The Latin “minister” is the opposite of “magister”: one serves, the other is the master.

questions.question: Since 1996, which day has been Germany's Day of Remembrance for the Victims of National Socialism?
hints: A federal president declared this day of remembrance.
The United Nations marks it as an international day of remembrance.
On this day in 1945, the Auschwitz camp was liberated.
questions.description: A date in the Bundestag's calendar when nobody cracks jokes.
questions.fun_fact: Federal President Roman Herzog proclaimed the day of remembrance on January 3, 1996.

questions.question: The Bundestag passes laws, the government carries them out, and the courts check both. What is this principle called?
hints: It sets the legislative, executive and judicial branches apart.
The Frenchman Montesquieu made the idea famous.
The power of the state is split among three branches.
questions.description: So nobody gets to decide everything alone, just like siblings cutting a cake.
questions.fun_fact: Some people jokingly call the press the “fourth estate” because it keeps an eye on the other three.

questions.question: The principle of subsidiarity is in Germany's Basic Law and in the EU treaties. What does it require?
questions.answer: What a smaller level can handle, it handles itself
wrong_answers: The federal government always outranks the states
The state funds all non-profit associations
Important laws need a public referendum
hints: The idea comes from Catholic social teaching.
It decides how tasks are shared between the EU, the federal government, the states and local towns.
Only when the lower level can't cope does the higher one step in.
questions.description: A Latin-sounding word that comes up in Brussels more often than rain.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin “subsidium”, meaning reserve or help, the same root as the English word “subsidy”.

questions.question: Here and in the Bundesrat, this needs two thirds of the votes in each. What for?
hints: It's about something that is meant to be very well protected.
No government should be able to do this with just a simple majority.
It's about the German constitution.
questions.description: Sometimes half isn't enough in politics, and then you have to win over a whole lot of people.
questions.fun_fact: Under the “eternity clause”, some principles, such as human dignity, can't be abolished even with a two-thirds majority.

questions.question: Before an international match, a second anthem is played along with the German one. Who is it for?
hints: In an international match, two countries play each other.
Every country has its own anthem.
The players on the other side sing along to it.
questions.description: Before the ball starts rolling, everyone sings first, even the people who can't sing.
questions.fun_fact: At home games, the visitors' anthem is usually played first, then the hosts' anthem.

questions.question: If you think the state has violated your basic rights, you can take me to Karlsruhe, no lawyer needed. What am I?
hints: Anyone in Germany may file me.
As a rule, I cost nothing.
I end up at the highest court for the Basic Law.
questions.description: For everyone who said as a kid: “That's unfair, I'm going all the way to the top!”
questions.fun_fact: Every year thousands of complaints arrive in Karlsruhe, but only a small share of them succeed.

questions.question: What is the left column on this Bundestag election ballot for?
questions.answer: Choosing a person in your own district
wrong_answers: Choosing a party for all of Germany
hints: The left column is called the Erststimme (first vote).
It lists the names of people from your area.
For this, Germany is split into almost 300 areas.
questions.description: One slip of paper, two columns, and a whole lot of ballpoint pens every four years.
questions.fun_fact: For the Bundestag election, Germany is divided into 299 electoral districts.

questions.question: How many federal states (Bundesländer) make up Germany?
hints: There are more than ten.
Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen count too.
It's twice as many as eight.
questions.description: A country pieced together like a puzzle from lots of little countries.
questions.fun_fact: Bremen is made of two separate parts: the city of Bremen and Bremerhaven, about 60 km (37 miles) away.

questions.question: Germany's women lost the Euro 2022 final 2–1 after extra time. The winners were the hosts and took their first major title. Which country?
hints: The tournament took place in July, in the middle of a heat wave.
The final was played in its capital city.
That's where the famous Wembley Stadium stands.
questions.description: A summer evening when all of Germany crossed its fingers until they hurt.
questions.fun_fact: 87,192 people watched the final in the stadium, more than at any European Championship before, men's tournaments included.

questions.question: Before Germany's game, you get black, red and gold painted on your cheeks. What is the right thing to use?
hints: It has to stay on the skin well and wash off again later.
Kids also use it for their costumes at Fasching.
Clowns use it to paint their faces.
questions.description: The one day of the year when parents actually want their faces painted.
questions.fun_fact: Good fan face paint is made especially for skin, so it comes off with soap and water after the final whistle.

questions.question: Germany wears a star for every World Cup title; the fourth came in Brazil in 2014. In which country was the very first won?
hints: The first title came in 1954.
There's a famous movie about the final with “Miracle” in its title.
The final was played in the city of Bern.
questions.description: Above the eagle, the sky gets a little more crowded with every title.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1954 final, Germany beat a Hungary team thought to be unbeatable 3–2, after losing to them 8–3 in the group stage.

questions.question: At Germany's first international match in 1908, how many players were on the field at kickoff, not counting the referee?
hints: Two teams play against each other.
Think of one team's lineup: goalkeeper, defense, midfield and attack.
Each team has eleven players.
questions.description: Two countries, one ball, and neither wants to give it up.
questions.fun_fact: Germany lost that first international match in Basel in 1908 to Switzerland, 5–3.

questions.question: This player scored for Germany in the 1974 and 1982 World Cup finals. Who is it?
hints: He started out as a defender and later played in midfield.
In the 1974 final, he scored from the penalty spot.
He played for FC Bayern and Real Madrid and had an afro and a full beard.
questions.description: A hairstyle as legendary as his shots from the penalty spot.
questions.fun_fact: Breitner is one of the few players who scored in two different World Cup finals, alongside names like Pelé and Zinédine Zidane.

questions.question: Cold fog hangs in the valley, while on the mountain above the sun shines and it's warmer. What is this kind of weather called?
hints: Normally it gets colder the higher you go.
Here it's the other way round: warmer above than below.
The name comes from the Latin word for “turning upside down”.
questions.description: When the weather decides the textbook is more of a suggestion.
questions.fun_fact: In this kind of weather, smog gets stuck in valleys and cities because the warm layer above acts like a lid.

questions.question: When it gets very hot in summer, Germany sometimes has “Hitzefrei”. Who gets to go home early?
hints: It usually happens by late morning.
Whether it happens is usually decided by someone in charge on site.
Classes are canceled for the rest of the day.
questions.description: The most beautiful word a thermometer ever came up with.
questions.fun_fact: Each German state sets its own rules for Hitzefrei, and usually the school principal makes the call.

questions.question: Since 2021, Germans pay an extra charge per metric ton of a greenhouse gas when they buy fuel or heat their homes. It makes climate-harming things cost more. What is it called?
hints: The charge goes up with the amount of exhaust gas.
It means the gas that forms when gasoline, heating oil and natural gas are burned.
The name contains the chemical formula of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: A price tag for something you can't even see.
questions.fun_fact: When it started in 2021, one metric ton of CO2 cost 25 euros in Germany.

questions.question: Listen: an old weather saying claims that when this bird flies low, rain is coming soon. Which bird is it?
hints: It likes to build its nest in barns or under the edges of roofs.
In the fall, it flies all the way to Africa.
It has a forked tail.
questions.description: A weather report with feathers, no app or satellite needed.
questions.fun_fact: The saying has some truth to it: in damp air, insects fly lower, and the swallows chase after them.

questions.question: It's sweet, full of cream, and clowns smash it into each other's faces. What is it?
hints: You can buy it at a bakery.
It's a dessert that you usually cut into slices shaped like wedges.
In old silent films, comedians threw them at each other's faces.
questions.description: The most wasted dessert in the history of comedy.
questions.fun_fact: Silent comedy films made the pie in the face famous, and a single scene once used up thousands of pies.

questions.question: In which season does Germany get the most thunderstorms?
hints: Thunderstorms need warm, humid air.
They often come after a hot, muggy day.
It's the season of the long school break.
questions.description: When the sky plays the drums and brings its own flashlight.
questions.fun_fact: You can estimate how far away a storm is from the gap between lightning and thunder: three seconds is about one kilometer (about five seconds per mile).

questions.question: “April, April, der macht, was er will” (April does whatever it wants): what weather is NOT typical for April in Germany?
hints: The saying describes weather that keeps changing.
In April, winter often isn't quite over yet.
This is more likely in the middle of summer.
questions.description: A month that flips a coin every morning.
questions.fun_fact: In April, cold polar air and warm air from the south often still collide over Germany, which is why the weather changes so fast.

questions.question: Hamburg Wadden Sea National Park includes islands that belong to the city of Hamburg. Which island does NOT belong to Hamburg?
hints: Three of these islands lie off the mouth of the Elbe near Cuxhaven.
The island you want lies far out in the open sea.
It is known for its red cliffs and the rock pillar “Lange Anna”.
questions.description: Hamburg has more than a port and the Elbe: it also owns a few piles of sand in the North Sea.
questions.fun_fact: At low tide, you can ride from Cuxhaven to Neuwerk in a horse-drawn carriage straight across the mudflats.

questions.question: “Es schüttet wie aus Eimern” means it's pouring with rain. Which German saying does NOT mean heavy rain?
hints: You're looking for a saying where it can stay dry.
It's about air, not water.
You'd say it when the window and the door are both open.
questions.description: German has more words for bad weather than for a good mood.
questions.fun_fact: “Es zieht wie Hechtsuppe” describes a strong draft, and where the saying comes from is still argued about today.

questions.question: On July 12, 1984, a hailstorm hit a big German city and caused the country's most costly insurance damage up to then. Which city was it?
hints: The city is in the south of Germany.
The storm came in from the foothills of the Alps.
The city is famous for Oktoberfest.
questions.description: Ice cubes falling from the sky, but sadly not for your lemonade.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the hailstones were as big as tennis balls and smashed countless roofs and car windows.

questions.question: You find these tiny red fruits at the edge of the forest in summer. What are they?
hints: You can eat them straight off the plant.
Their big relatives grow in pick-your-own fields.
They're the tiny wild cousins of a fruit people love to dip in chocolate.
questions.description: Small but mighty: these fruits have more flavor than their big relatives from the supermarket.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny seeds on the outside of a strawberry are actually the plant's real fruits.

questions.question: These berries grow on a prickly evergreen shrub with needles. What have Germans long used them for?
questions.answer: As a spice for sauerkraut and game
hints: You don't eat them on their own; they're quite bitter.
They often go into the same pot as bay leaves.
A venison roast or Sauerbraten would be only half as good without them.
questions.description: Small, blue-black and wrapped in so many prickles that you think twice before reaching in.
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, juniper berries aren't berries at all but tiny cones whose scales have grown together.

questions.question: I'm yellow like egg yolk, smell a bit like apricot and grow in moss. Germans say a worthless person “isn't worth one of me.” What am I?
hints: I'm an edible mushroom.
Under my cap I have no true gills, only ridges.
In Bavaria I'm also called “Reherl”.
questions.description: Anyone sneaking into the woods at dawn with a basket and a knife won't reveal their favorite spot, not even to their own grandma.
questions.fun_fact: Chanterelles are almost impossible to farm, so nearly all the ones you can buy come from wild forests.

questions.question: This fir is Germany’s most popular Christmas tree. Which mountain region does it originally come from?
hints: Its name is misleading: it has nothing to do with the north.
Its home lies between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
The country of Georgia is there.
questions.description: It doesn’t shed, it hardly pokes, and every December it moves into the living room.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Finnish naturalist Alexander von Nordmann, who discovered it in the Caucasus in the 19th century.

questions.question: What is this cone from a conifer made of?
hints: It opens up in dry weather.
The seeds sit between its parts.
The parts overlap like roof tiles.
questions.description: Every kindergarten's favorite craft supply in the fall.
questions.fun_fact: You almost never find true fir cones on the ground: they fall apart up in the tree, so the cones in the forest mostly come from spruces.

The translation itself is faithful and reads naturally. Fact check: uncertain. The answer and hints are correct. Silver fir cones do disintegrate in the tree. I did not search to check this.

questions.question: What material is this circus tent made of?
hints: It's a very thick, strong fabric.
It keeps the rain out without letting water through.
It's also used for awnings and camping tents.
questions.description: A roof that folds up, packs away and goes on tour.
questions.fun_fact: Old circus tents were made of cotton; today they're made of polyester canvas coated with PVC.

questions.question: I work in the forest with an ax and a saw and shout “Timber!”. In the fairy tale, Hansel and Gretel’s father is one of us. Who am I?
hints: I don’t need a gun.
I bring tree trunks out of the forest.
My name says what I do with the wood.
questions.description: A job where the end of the workday starts with a loud crash.
questions.fun_fact: Today, giant machines called harvesters often fell trees in the forest and strip off their branches in just a few seconds.

questions.question: Which vegetable is this typical German dish made from?
hints: It's a kind of cabbage.
The cabbage is finely shredded and left to ferment with salt.
The head of this cabbage is pale and has smooth leaves.
questions.description: Without this side dish, many a bratwurst would feel pretty lonely on the plate.
questions.fun_fact: In southern Germany, “Kraut” is simply another word for cabbage, which is how sauerkraut got its name.

questions.fun_fact: Germany lies between a maritime climate in the west and a continental climate in the east, which is why winters in Brandenburg are usually colder than on the Lower Rhine.

questions.question: Listen: an animal in Berchtesgaden National Park makes this shrill whistle to warn its family about eagles. Which animal is it?
hints: It lives in burrows under mountain meadows.
It likes to sit up on its back legs in front of its burrow.
It sleeps through a very long winter.
questions.description: A furry alarm system that keeps watch high up in the mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Marmots hibernate for up to six months a year, snuggled up close together in their burrow.

questions.question: Take a close look: what is this berry made up of?
hints: The surface isn't smooth.
Each little part has a tiny seed inside.
You can see lots of round, red little bubbles.
questions.description: A fruit that in the garden usually lands in your mouth faster than in the basket.
questions.fun_fact: Each little ball of a raspberry is actually its own tiny fruit with its own seed.

questions.question: What is this nut called?
hints: It grows on a big tree, often in gardens.
Its green husk stains your fingers brown.
The kernel inside looks like a little brain.
questions.description: Squirrels hide them, forget them, and plant trees by accident.
questions.fun_fact: Both the German and the English name come from old words meaning “foreign nut”: the Romans brought it north from the south.

questions.question: You'll find one in many German homes at Easter. What is an “Osterstrauß”?
wrong_answers: Sweet braided bread shaped like a flower
A basket full of chocolate bunnies
hints: You decorate it yourself.
It often stays up as decoration until after the holidays.
You hang blown-out, painted eggs on it.
questions.description: Easter without this thing? Unthinkable for many families.
questions.fun_fact: If you bring the branches into a warm home early enough, they often grow green leaves or blossoms by Easter.

questions.question: “Babo” became Germany's Youth Word of the Year in 2013, made famous by Haftbefehl's song “Chabos wissen, wer der Babo ist”. What does it mean?
hints: Everyone wants to be it; nobody wants to be last.
The word goes back to a word for “dad”.
It means the one who calls the shots in the group.
questions.description: A word that leaves parents frowning in confusion at the dinner table.
questions.fun_fact: Haftbefehl comes from Offenbach am Main and made the city famous in German rap.

questions.question: Which prince had this monument, with its giant statue and water cascades, built from 1701?
hints: He ruled for about 60 years.
The hill park around it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2013.
He held the title of landgrave.
questions.description: A muscleman who has been standing guard on a hill for 300 years.
questions.fun_fact: The copper statue is over 8 m (26 ft) tall and copies the ancient “Farnese Hercules”.

questions.question: A wise Jew, Sultan Saladin and a young Templar meet in Jerusalem. With which objects does Nathan explain which religion is the true one?
hints: The 1779 play is a major work of the Enlightenment.
A father has three sons and doesn't want to favor any of them.
You wear this object on your finger.
questions.description: An argument between religions, settled with a bedtime story.
questions.fun_fact: Lessing took the Ring Parable from Boccaccio's “The Decameron”, but it had been told long before that.

questions.question: In 1806, 16 German princes, among them Bavaria and Württemberg, founded the Confederation of the Rhine. What was it for?
wrong_answers: An alliance for the emperor in Vienna
An alliance for a shared currency
hints: Soon after, Francis II gave up the crown of the Holy Roman Empire.
Its members had to send troops to fight in other people's wars.
Its protector was an emperor who ruled from Paris.
questions.description: Sixteen princes, one signature and a mountain of paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: In 1806, with Napoleon's help, Bavaria and Württemberg became kingdoms.

questions.question: Which name is NOT another name for Kalter Hund, the cookie cake set in the fridge?
hints: The three real names come from different parts of Germany.
The name you want belongs to a separate, well-known cake of German coffee tables.
That cake is full of buttercream and nut brittle and is named after a city in Hesse.
questions.description: A dog that doesn't bark, doesn't bite and belongs in the fridge.
questions.fun_fact: Kalter Hund isn't baked at all: butter cookies and chocolate cream are layered and set in the fridge.

questions.question: In the Palatinate they make “Grumbeersupp” from it, in Saarland “Dibbelabbes”. What is a “Grumbeere”?
hints: Despite the “Beere” (berry) in its name, it isn't a berry at all.
It grows underground.
The word comes from “Grundbirne”, a “pear from the ground”.
questions.description: Palatinate dialect for beginners, lesson one: lunch.
questions.fun_fact: The French call it “pomme de terre”, an “apple of the earth”, and some Germans say “Erdapfel” too.

questions.question: In Mainz and the Palatinate, people love to celebrate with “Worscht, Weck un Woi”. What's on the table?
hints: You can slice a “Weck” open and fill it.
The third word grows on vines in the Palatinate.
At a bakery in Hesse, you buy “Weckche” in the morning.
questions.description: Three words, one starting letter and zero calorie counting.
questions.fun_fact: The Palatinate is one of Germany's largest wine-growing regions.

questions.question: Parchment like this was made from animal skin. In an old belief behind a German saying, who wrote people's sins on a cowhide?
hints: The writer was said to sit unseen in church and note down people's chatter during Mass.
When the cowhide was full, he supposedly stretched it with his teeth.
He has horns and lives in hell.
questions.description: A notepad with fur on it, and some very bad news.
questions.fun_fact: A whole cowhide holds a lot of writing, so when Germans say something “geht auf keine Kuhhaut” (won't fit on any cowhide), it really is outrageously much.

questions.question: I've been on the air since 1963, and little men in pointy hats pop up between my commercials. Who am I?
hints: I am a public broadcaster.
My little men are called Mainzelmännchen.
My name begins with “Zweites Deutsches”.
questions.description: A TV channel older than almost every remote control in the living room.
questions.fun_fact: ZDF went on the air on April 1, 1963, and the Mainzelmännchen first appeared on its second day, April 2.

questions.question: Herbert Köfer and Helga Göring played the married couple Paul and Anna Schmidt in it. The East German series started in 1978. What is it called?
hints: The series aired on East German TV and was a family comedy.
It tells the story of the Schmidts and their family's everyday life with gentle humor.
The title says that retired people are always busy.
questions.description: A TV comedy from the East, where the living-room wallpaper was guaranteed to have a pattern.
questions.fun_fact: Herbert Köfer was still acting on stage at over 90 and lived to be 100.

questions.question: Anyone who watches “Ein Fall für zwei” knows detective Josef Matula. What was his job before he became a private detective?
hints: In the series, he helps a lawyer in Frankfurt.
He already knows his way around investigations from his past.
He had to leave his job with the Kripo.
questions.description: Two men, one case, and a résumé with an interesting gap.
questions.fun_fact: Claus Theo Gärtner played Matula for over 30 years and worked alongside several different lawyers along the way.

questions.question: I've worked Tatort cases in Cologne since 1997, my partner is Freddy Schenk, and after a case there's often currywurst by the Rhine. Who am I?
hints: I'm played by Klaus J. Behrendt.
Before Cologne, I was an assistant in Düsseldorf.
My first name is the same as one of the two rascals in “Max und Moritz”.
questions.description: A detective who deserves a sausage with a cathedral view after every case.
questions.fun_fact: The sausage stand with a view of Cologne Cathedral isn't a real snack bar but a film set, and fans love it anyway.

questions.question: Vinzenz Geiger became Olympic champion in the Nordic combined individual event. In which year did he win this gold?
hints: At the Games before, he had already won gold, but with the team.
The host city had already held the Summer Olympics in 2008.
It was the Winter Games in Beijing, during the COVID pandemic.
questions.description: First fly, then run, and with luck end up on the top step.
questions.fun_fact: Vinzenz Geiger comes from Oberstdorf, the town where the Four Hills Tournament starts every year.

questions.question: When you're cold, tiny bumps appear on your arms and the little hairs stand up. What did this do for our hairy ancestors?
questions.answer: Trapped warm air in their fur
hints: A cat does something similar and looks fluffier.
Birds fluff up their feathers in winter for a similar reason.
The raised hair worked like a coat.
questions.description: Your skin doing a goose impression, and nobody asked it to.
questions.fun_fact: You can also get goosebumps from hearing a song that really moves you.

questions.question: Hans-Jürgen Bäumler skated to many wins with Marika Kilius. Which title did the pair NEVER win?
hints: At one big event, they only managed second place twice.
The two took silver in both 1960 and 1964.
The title you're looking for only comes around every four years.
questions.description: Two on the ice, one heart, and later even a record of their own.
questions.fun_fact: Kilius and Bäumler were also pop stars: in 1964 they had a hit with “Honeymoon in St. Tropez”.

questions.question: Which of these do you NOT pack in your lunch box as a school snack?
hints: You eat a school snack with your hands.
One of these would leak all over your school bag.
You need a spoon and a bowl for it.
questions.description: The lunch that gets shaken around in a school bag all morning long.
questions.fun_fact: In different parts of Germany, the school sandwich has different names, like “Stulle” in Berlin or “Kniffte” in the Ruhr area.

questions.question: What kind of baked good is this roll?
hints: The crust is shiny because the dough is briefly dipped in a liquid before baking.
The pretzel belongs to this family too.
The liquid the dough is dipped in is a diluted sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.description: A roll with a suntan, and no vacation needed.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says a Munich baker invented lye pastry by accident in 1839, when he brushed lye instead of sugar water onto his pretzels.

questions.question: The sausage maker from Bad Zwischenahn, which now also sells lots of veggie sausage, is called “Rügenwalder …” what?
hints: The company was run by the same family for many generations.
The company logo shows a building in the countryside.
It has big sails that turn, and you often see one in Holland.
questions.description: Here everything revolves around sausage – sometimes with no meat at all.
questions.fun_fact: The name recalls Rügenwalde in Pomerania, where the company was founded in 1834 – the town is now called Darłowo and is in Poland.

questions.question: A Brötchen is crispy outside, soft inside and fresh from the bakery. What is it mainly baked from?
hints: It's made from grains.
It's usually white and gets dusty when you bake.
The grains are ground for it in a mill.
questions.description: Small, round, crispy – and in big demand early on a Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the region, Germans also call a Brötchen a Schrippe, Semmel, Weck or Rundstück.

questions.question: Which food group does the topping on this roll belong to?
hints: The topping is yellow and sometimes has holes.
This group also includes something you drink cold or pour over your cereal.
Yogurt and butter belong to this group too.
questions.description: The secret star of every lunch box in the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: To make 1 kg (2.2 lb) of hard cheese, you need about 10 to 12 liters (around 3 gallons) of milk.

questions.question: This bread roll is topped with “Nordseekrabben” (North Sea crabs). What group of animals do they really belong to?
hints: The name on the roll is a bit misleading.
They have a long tail and swim instead of walking sideways.
They are the classic star of a cocktail served in a glass with pink sauce.
questions.description: Harbor air and screaming seagulls, squeezed between two halves of a bread roll.
questions.fun_fact: Many North Sea shrimp are trucked all the way to Morocco to be peeled, then driven back to the German coast.

questions.question: Which animal does this bacon usually come from?
hints: This animal lives on a farm.
It loves rolling around in mud.
It has a curly tail and goes “oink”.
questions.description: Sizzling in the pan, it sings its own little song.
questions.fun_fact: In German, the ring of suburbs around a big city is called the „Speckgürtel“, the “bacon belt”.

questions.question: What type of sausage is the sausage on this bread?
hints: You need a knife, but not for cutting.
Teewurst also belongs to this type.
You put it on bread the same way you put on butter.
questions.description: A sausage with a reputation for sulking.
questions.fun_fact: Germans say a sulking person is “playing the offended liverwurst” (“die beleidigte Leberwurst spielen”), because people once believed feelings lived in the liver.

questions.question: What is this dish called?
hints: It is made in a frying pan.
The potatoes are sliced, not grated.
Onions and bacon often sizzle along with them.
questions.description: When the kitchen smells like this, the whole family suddenly sits down at the table without being called.
questions.fun_fact: Many cooks use potatoes boiled in their skins the day before, because cold slices get extra crispy in the pan.

questions.question: I'm oily, I come from tiny glands attached to each hair, and when there's too much of me, pimples appear. What am I for?
hints: Without me, your skin would crack like dry ground.
When there's too much of me, hair looks shiny and greasy very quickly.
I work like a natural cream.
questions.description: The oil your face makes for free, and nobody ever thanks it.
questions.fun_fact: This oil is called sebum, the Latin word for tallow: the animal fat once used to make candles.

questions.question: This tower of Trendelburg Castle is known as Rapunzel's tower. In the Brothers Grimm tale, who is the first to call “Rapunzel, let down your hair”?
hints: The king's son only overhears the call in secret and copies it.
This person took Rapunzel in as a baby.
In the Grimms' tale she is called Frau Gothel.
questions.description: The world's oldest elevator: no electricity, but lots and lots of conditioner.
questions.fun_fact: “Rapunzel” is also an old German name for lamb's lettuce, the very plant Rapunzel's mother craved from the enchantress's garden.

questions.question: In the Bible, God tests people „auf Herz und Nieren“ (on heart and kidneys). What did the kidneys stand for back then?
hints: Back then, organs were thought to hold things you can't see.
In the Hebrew Bible, the heart stood more for the mind.
It's about the things you don't tell anyone.
questions.description: An organ inspection that's far older than any car.
questions.fun_fact: In German today, the phrase is mostly used for checking used cars „auf Herz und Nieren“, even though a car has neither one.

questions.question: Which of these German words do people NOT use when they are really, really hungry?
hints: Look at the first part of each word.
One of the animals in these words doesn't fit a big hunger.
You're looking for the word with the smallest animal.
questions.description: The growling you hear isn't the dog, it's someone's stomach.
questions.fun_fact: In the fall, a brown bear eats until it has a thick layer of fat, so it can make it through its winter rest.

questions.question: Once a year the whole class lines up for me, tall kids in back, small ones in front. Then every child takes me home. What am I?
hints: Years later, people look at me and laugh at old hairstyles.
The teacher usually stands at the edge, in it too.
Someone calls out: “Everybody smile, please!”
questions.description: A date for which Mom lays out your scratchy Sunday sweater, just for the occasion.
questions.fun_fact: Photographers often line children up by height so every face can be seen afterward.

questions.question: In Germany, school is required for every child, usually from age six for nine or ten years. So what is banned there, unlike in many countries?
hints: It's about the place where children learn.
Private schools are clearly allowed in Germany.
In some countries, parents teach their children entirely at home.
questions.description: Nine years of required attendance, and a sore throat won't get you out of it. Well, almost never.
questions.fun_fact: Required schooling for all of Germany has been in the law since the Weimar Constitution of 1919.

questions.question: The school bell rings and the lesson begins. How long is a normal school lesson in Germany?
hints: A double lesson is twice as long.
It's shorter than a real hour.
It's three quarters of an hour.
questions.description: A sound a whole class waits for more eagerly than for Santa Claus.
questions.fun_fact: A school lesson is called a “Stunde” (hour) in German, but it's a quarter of an hour shorter than a real one.

questions.question: In the past, children in the countryside got time off school in the fall to help with this harvest. What is being harvested here?
hints: They grow underground.
They are yellowish or reddish.
French fries and mashed ones are made from them.
questions.description: There used to be no school in the fall, but definitely not so you could laze around.
questions.fun_fact: That's why fall break in the countryside was often called “Kartoffelferien” (potato vacation).

questions.question: It lives in your Ranzen, you write down in it what's due tomorrow, and sometimes parents sign it. What is it?
hints: You usually get a new one at the start of the school year.
Each weekday has its own line or page.
In it you'll find, for example: “Math, page 12, number 3”.
questions.description: The little book that knows more about your afternoons than you do.
questions.fun_fact: Many schools design their own Hausaufgabenheft, with holiday dates and school rules inside.

questions.question: After lessons, many German primary school children go to the Hort. Who usually looks after them there?
hints: This job is often learned at a Fachschule (vocational college).
They play with the children and help with homework.
The same people also work in kindergartens.
questions.description: When school ends at twelve but Mom doesn't finish work until five.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Hort” actually means “treasure” or “safe place”, as in the Nibelungenhort, the treasure of the Nibelungs.

questions.question: In the schoolyard, you draw it on the ground in chalk. What kind of game is “Himmel und Hölle”?
hints: You need a small stone for it.
The boxes are numbered.
You jump on one leg from square to square.
questions.description: A game where you can end up at the very top or the very bottom, right in the middle of the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, the folded paper fortune teller that you open and close with your fingers is also called “Himmel und Hölle”.

questions.question: Roughly how many muscles does the human body have?
hints: There are many more muscles than bones.
An adult body has 206 bones.
It's a three-digit number.
questions.description: A whole gym hidden under your skin.
questions.fun_fact: The smallest muscle in the body, the stapedius, sits inside the ear and is just over 1 millimeter long.

questions.question: The whole class goes away with the teachers for a few days, sleeps in a Jugendherberge and chats secretly at night. What is it called?
hints: You pack a suitcase for it.
It often goes to the sea or the mountains.
You set off by bus or by train.
questions.description: Three days without your parents, but with the math teacher in pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: The world's first permanent youth hostel opened in 1912 at Altena Castle in the Sauerland.

questions.question: A child sees another child misbehaving and runs straight to the teacher to tell. What is the German word for that?
hints: It often happens in the schoolyard.
It has to do with giving someone away.
In English, you would call it “tattling.”
questions.description: Everyone who just got caught has very strong feelings about this word.
questions.fun_fact: A child who does this a lot quickly gets called a “Petze” in the schoolyard.

questions.question: Many German towns have a Bolzplatz. What is it mainly for?
hints: It is often surrounded by a high fence.
It usually has two small metal goals.
“Bolzen” means to kick a ball hard.
questions.description: Here, scraped knees are a badge of honor.
questions.fun_fact: “Bolzen” is soccer slang for kicking the ball hard, without much technique.

questions.question: In which month does Christmas break usually end in Germany?
hints: New Year's Eve falls in the middle of the break.
The new year has already begun.
It is the first month of the year.
questions.description: The tree is dropping its needles, the cookie tin is empty, and then the alarm clock rings again.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, each federal state sets its own school vacation dates.

questions.question: In Munich, what do people call a vain, elegant ladies' man like Monaco Franze?
hints: The word is in the subtitle of Helmut Dietl's series.
The subtitle is “Der ewige …”.
The word has five letters and rhymes with the German word “Lenz” (spring).
questions.description: A man from Munich who is never home on time, thanks to all the pretty women.
questions.fun_fact: Helmut Fischer played Monaco Franze so well that many people in Munich just called him “Monaco” until he died.

questions.question: Tatort inspectors Paul Stoever and Peter Brockmöller stepped down in Hamburg in 2001. Which inspector took over there next?
hints: The successor stayed in Hamburg until 2008.
He was played by an actor many knew as a teacher from a ZDF series.
His last name sounds almost like a place name ending in “-dorf”.
questions.description: Two Hamburg detectives who were happier singing a duet than grilling a suspect.
questions.fun_fact: As Stoever and Brockmöller, Manfred Krug and Charles Brauer sang songs together in many episodes and even released records.

questions.question: In which year did Ivo Batic have his first case in the Munich “Tatort”?
hints: The team solved cases in Munich for a very long time.
By 2016, the duo had been on the job for more than 25 years.
The year is exactly one year after German reunification.
questions.description: Two detectives who were a team for so long that they bickered like an old married couple.
questions.fun_fact: Miroslav Nemec and Udo Wachtveitl worked together as Batic and Leitmayr for more than three decades, longer than almost any other Tatort team.

questions.question: It's part of the criminal police, investigates the most serious crimes against life, and nearly every Tatort inspector works for it. What is it called in German?
hints: Its officers usually wear plain clothes and get called at any time of day or night.
Without it, there would be no Sunday-night crime show.
Its name starts with the German word for murder.
questions.description: The department nobody calls just to wish them a nice day.
questions.fun_fact: In “Tatort” the Mordkommission is almost always in charge, but in real police work it's only a small part of the job.

questions.question: I'm a TV channel that shows “The Simpsons” and “Germany's Next Topmodel”. Who am I?
hints: I'm based in Unterföhring, near Munich.
My number is red.
My number comes right after six.
questions.description: Whoever holds the remote holds the power, at least until Mom walks into the living room.
questions.fun_fact: ProSieben has been showing The Simpsons since the 1990s, and it is one of the channel's most repeated shows.

questions.question: In which year did the ZDF series “Unser Lehrer Doktor Specht” start?
hints: The show ran until the end of the decade it started in.
Its lead actor later played a police inspector on TV.
It was in the early 1990s.
questions.description: A teacher named after a woodpecker, who still never drilled his students too hard.
questions.fun_fact: The lead role was played by Robert Atzorn, who later investigated as an inspector in the Hamburg “Tatort”.

questions.question: When the Tagesschau gong sounds at 8 p.m., about how many minutes does the show last?
hints: The evening movie often starts right after it.
It's shorter than a school lesson.
It's exactly a quarter of an hour.
questions.description: The gong that suddenly makes parents go very quiet.
questions.fun_fact: The Tagesschau has been on since 1952, making it the oldest news show still running on German TV.

questions.question: In what year did the RTL II series “Köln 50667” first air?
hints: The series is younger than the smartphone.
It started in the 2010s.
The following year, Germany won the soccer World Cup.
questions.description: A zip code that made it all the way to prime time.
questions.fun_fact: The number in the title is a real Cologne postal code from the city center.

questions.question: It's the central criminal police office for all of Germany, based in Wiesbaden, with a three-letter short name. What is it?
hints: It works for the whole country, not for a single state.
Its name contains the word “Kriminal”.
Its short name is BKA.
questions.description: An agency you'd rather see on TV than outside your own front door.
questions.fun_fact: The Bundeskriminalamt was founded in 1951 and has offices in Berlin and Meckenheim as well as Wiesbaden.

questions.question: I'm a car, blue and silver in Germany, with a blue light on my roof, and police officers drive me around town. What am I called in German?
hints: When I come, you hear “Tatütata.”
Inside sit people in uniform who keep things in order.
The first part of my name means “stripes.”
questions.description: A car that just plays music in a traffic jam until everyone moves out of the way.
questions.fun_fact: German police cars used to be green and white; only from about 2005 did they slowly turn blue and silver.
