questions.question: Fill in the blank: Giant slalom is called that because, compared to slalom, the … are farther apart.
hints: It's something the racers have to go around on the course.
They are made of poles with colorful flags.
If a racer misses one, they are disqualified.
questions.description: Same slope, same skis, just everything one size bigger.
questions.fun_fact: Because the gates are farther apart, pros race much faster in giant slalom than in slalom.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many ski poles does this skier have?
hints: Count the poles in his hands.
There is one for each hand.
It's the same number as your hands.
questions.description: For pushing off, for leaning on, and for waving after the run.
questions.fun_fact: Here's how to find the right pole length: hold the pole upright in front of you on the ground, and your arm should make roughly a right angle.

questions.question: Oberwiesenthal in the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) is Germany's highest town. Roughly how high up is it?
hints: The Ore Mountains are low mountains, not part of the Alps.
The Fichtelberg, right above the town, is just over 1,200 m (3,900 ft) high.
The town sits just below the 1,000-meter mark.
questions.description: Here the air is thinner and the snow sticks around longer than anywhere else in Germany.
questions.fun_fact: The Fichtelberg cable car in Oberwiesenthal has run since 1924 and is Germany's oldest aerial cableway.

questions.question: Since when have almost all ski jumpers flown in the V-style, with their ski tips spread apart?
hints: Jens Weißflog had to switch to the new technique in the middle of his career.
It was invented by the Swedish jumper Jan Boklöv.
It caught on shortly after German reunification.
questions.description: Ski jumpers used to keep their skis neatly together, until someone pulled them apart.
questions.fun_fact: At first Jan Boklöv lost points for his V-style because judges thought it looked “ugly”, even though it made him fly farther.

questions.question: When is the Biathlon auf Schalke in Gelsenkirchen's arena traditionally held?
questions.answer: between Christmas and New Year's Eve
hints: The race needs a whole lot of snow.
Many people have time off then and go with their family.
The presents are already unwrapped, but the fireworks are still to come.
questions.description: A soccer stadium that pretends once a year that it's up in the mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, hundreds of tons of snow are trucked into the soccer stadium for the race.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says "hundreds of metric tons" of snow, but sources give about 3,000–4,000 cubic metres, which is well over 1,000 tonnes. The fact check is uncertain and I can't confirm the tonnage either. Correct the fun fact in the German source, for example to "thousands of cubic metres of snow (from the Neuss ski hall)", and then translate it again. Fact check: uncertain. The date is right (late December, e.g. 28–30 Dec). The fun fact gives snow in 'hundreds of metric tons', but sources give about 3,000–4,000 cubic metres, which weighs far more than that. I found no figure in tonnes. The snow comes from the Neuss ski hall.

questions.question: When learning to ski, you do the “snowplow”: ski tips together, ski tails wide apart. What does it do?
hints: Beginners learn this technique at the very start.
It matters for getting down the hill safely.
The angled skis push snow in front of them and hold you back.
questions.description: A plow that never digs up a field, yet still moves snow.
questions.fun_fact: Many ski instructors call the snowplow “pizza” with kids, because the skis look like a slice of pizza.

questions.question: How many Olympic gold medals did lugers Tobias Wendl and Tobias Arlt each win from 2014 to 2022?
hints: They competed at three Olympic Games: Sochi, Pyeongchang and Beijing.
Besides the doubles, they also raced in the team relay every time.
Every time they competed, they simply won everything there was to win.
questions.description: Two Tobiases, one sled and a pretty crowded trophy cabinet.
questions.fun_fact: In the luge world, the two Bavarians are simply known as “the Tobis”.

questions.question: At ski school, you step onto the “magic carpet.” What is it for?
questions.answer: It carries you up the slope.
wrong_answers: It stops you at the bottom.
hints: It is a long belt that moves.
It works a bit like the belt at the supermarket checkout.
With it, you don't have to trudge up the practice slope.
questions.description: A carpet that could fly, but would rather stay on the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The magic carpet is a conveyor belt in the snow, like the one at the supermarket checkout, only for little skiers.

questions.question: You're inside a dolmen, like the ones at Antequera. Which of these is NOT true about it?
questions.answer: It was built to store grain
wrong_answers: It was usually a shared tomb
It is made of huge stone slabs
hints: Three of the sentences are true; look for the one that doesn't fit its purpose.
Inside dolmens, archaeologists have found bones and grave goods.
It was a place for the dead, not a storeroom.
questions.description: Stones so huge that even the toughest moving company wouldn't dare touch them.
questions.fun_fact: The Dolmen de Menga faces the Peña de los Enamorados, a mountain shaped like a face lying on its back.

questions.question: In 1879, someone first spotted the bison painted on the ceiling of the Altamira cave. Who was it?
hints: It was someone who went into the cave with a family member.
A father was searching the floor of the cave for prehistoric remains and didn't look up.
Her name was María, and she was very young.
questions.description: The first graffiti in history, and nobody gave it a fine.
questions.fun_fact: As the story goes, María shouted “Look, Daddy, oxen!” when she saw the bison on the ceiling.

questions.question: You're reading a newspaper in Spanish. Roughly how many of its words come from Latin?
hints: Spanish grew out of the Latin spoken in Roman Hispania.
It's a large majority.
More than 70%.
questions.description: The Romans left, but they forgot to take their dictionary with them.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word «hablar» (to speak) comes from the Latin «fabulari», which meant to chat or tell stories.

questions.question: This Iberian sculpture, the Lady of Baza, was found in Granada in 1971. In which museum is it shown today?
hints: It isn't in the province where it was found.
It's in Madrid.
It's the same museum that holds the Lady of Elche.
questions.description: She's been sitting for over 2,000 years and still hasn't been given her favorite chair.
questions.fun_fact: The Lady of Baza was a funeral urn: it held the remains of a cremation inside.

questions.question: On an Andalusian beach you find a murex shell, once used to make purple dye. Which people, whose Greek name came from that color, made the dye?
hints: They were great sailors and traders of the Mediterranean.
They came from cities like Tyre and Sidon, in today’s Lebanon.
They founded Gadir, today’s Cádiz.
questions.description: Some sea snails that ended up dressing kings and emperors.
questions.fun_fact: It took thousands of snails to dye a single tunic, which is why purple was the color of the powerful.

questions.question: In 153 BC, the Roman consul Nobilior attacked Numantia with elephants. One was hit on the head by a stone. What happened?
questions.answer: The elephants panicked and trampled the Romans
wrong_answers: The Numantians surrendered when they saw the animals
The elephants knocked down Numantia’s walls
The Romans took the city that same day
hints: The elephants came from North Africa, sent by Masinissa, king of Numidia.
Think about how a huge animal reacts when something hurts.
The Romans ended up running away.
questions.description: The biggest secret weapon ever seen around Soria.
questions.fun_fact: Numantia held out against Rome for about 20 years, until Scipio surrounded it with a siege in 133 BC.

questions.question: Look at the Tower of Hercules in A Coruña. Why did the Romans build it?
hints: It stands by the sea.
The Romans shipped lots of goods along the Atlantic coast.
It helps sailors keep from crashing into the coast.
questions.description: Almost 2,000 years standing, and not one complaint about the damp Galician weather.
questions.fun_fact: It is the oldest Roman lighthouse in the world that still works, and it has been a World Heritage Site since 2009.

questions.question: Elisabeth Farnese had it built as a widow, in a Segovia forest full of fallow deer, and today it holds a hunting museum. Which palace is it?
hints: It's in the province of Segovia, a few miles from a much more famous royal palace.
Work on it began in 1751, when Ferdinand VI was already king.
In Spanish, its name means “cold river”.
questions.description: A widow with a big budget and a strong wish to stay out of her stepson's sight.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso XII shut himself away in this palace to mourn after the death of his young wife, María de las Mercedes.

questions.question: There were twelve of us, set up in the Roman Forum about 2,500 years ago for everyone to read. What was written on us?
hints: Before us, only a few people really knew what was forbidden.
We said what punishment someone got for stealing or hurting others.
Judges had to follow what we said.
questions.description: Before social media, the Romans posted the important stuff in the town square.
questions.fun_fact: Roman children learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart at school.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this countess from A Coruña championed naturalism and was Spain's first woman university professor. Who is she?
hints: She wrote mostly novels and short stories, not poetry.
Her most famous novel is set in a Galician manor house.
She wrote “The House of Ulloa”.
questions.description: A countess who liked the pen more than the crown.
questions.fun_fact: She applied to the Royal Spanish Academy several times and was always turned down for being a woman.

questions.question: Which painter was expelled from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando in 1926 for saying no professor was fit to examine him?
hints: In Madrid he lived at the Residencia de Estudiantes.
There he became friends with Lorca and Buñuel.
He is famous for his melting clocks and his curled-up mustache.
questions.description: Some students fail their exams; others fail their teachers.
questions.fun_fact: The Academy, founded in 1752 under Ferdinand VI, holds paintings by Goya, who was once one of its directors.

questions.question: Ferdinand VII was nicknamed “el rey Felón”. What does “felón” mean?
hints: At first, the people called him “el Deseado” (the Desired One).
He swore to uphold the Constitution in 1820 and later abolished it.
It's someone who breaks their word and betrays those who trust them.
questions.description: A nickname you won't find on any greeting card.
questions.fun_fact: He was called “el Deseado” because, during the war against Napoleon, he spent six years held in France while Spaniards waited for his return.

questions.question: Look at the portrait: this king is called “the best mayor of Madrid” because he paved and lit its streets. Who is he?
hints: Before reigning in Spain, he was king of Naples.
The Puerta de Alcalá was built during his reign.
He was the son of Felipe V and the half-brother of Fernando VI, whom he succeeded.
questions.description: A king who wasn't happy just giving orders: he wanted clean streets too.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos III brought streetlamps, sewers and garbage collection to a Madrid where people threw their waste out the window.

questions.question: You hear someone shout “¡Viva la Pepa!”. In what year was the Constitution that the phrase comes from approved?
hints: It was approved in Cádiz during the war against Napoleon.
It was approved on March 19, Saint Joseph's Day, which is why it got the name “la Pepa” (Pepa is short for Josefa).
It's the same year Napoleon invaded Russia.
questions.description: A certain Pepa who gets more cheers than a pop star.
questions.fun_fact: Today “¡viva la Pepa!” describes someone carefree, though it started out as a liberal battle cry.

questions.question: In the collegiate church of La Granja you see the tomb of Philip V and his second wife, Elisabeth Farnese. Which of her sons later ruled Spain?
hints: He first ruled in Naples.
He took the throne after his half-brother died.
He was the Italian queen's first son.
questions.description: An Italian mother who moved all of Europe to find jobs for her sons.
questions.fun_fact: Elisabeth Farnese fought so hard for her sons that one became King of Spain and another Duke of Parma.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this politician from Málaga brought the Bourbons back with Alfonso XII and took turns in power with Sagasta. Who is he?
hints: He led the Conservative Party.
He was the main author of the 1876 Constitution.
His surname includes the Spanish word for a castle.
questions.description: A politician who turned government into a chore chart, like taking turns washing the dishes.
questions.fun_fact: The Cánovas–Sagasta turn-taking relied on elections rigged by each town's local bosses, the caciques.

questions.question: Which of these characters does NOT appear in José Zorrilla's “Don Juan Tenorio”?
hints: Three of them are Don Juan's love, his rival and his beloved's father.
The odd one out comes from an older novel.
She is the lady Don Quixote falls in love with.
questions.description: A seducer with more ghosts than a Scottish castle.
questions.fun_fact: Zorrilla sold the rights to the Tenorio for very little money and regretted all his life not getting rich from it.

questions.question: From the port of Marseille you can see a small island with a fortress: the Château d'If. What was it used as for centuries?
hints: The fortress was built in the 16th century on the orders of King Francis I.
A famous French writer set part of an adventure novel there.
Edmond Dantès spent fourteen years there in “The Count of Monte Cristo.”
questions.description: A tiny rock in the middle of the sea that took the whole castle thing very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Dantès never existed, but tourists at the Château d'If can still visit a “Monte Cristo cell” today.

questions.question: This car is a SEAT Ibiza, named after a Spanish island. Which archipelago does that island belong to?
hints: It's in the Mediterranean Sea.
Its capital is Palma.
It shares the archipelago with Mallorca and Menorca.
questions.description: A car with a vacation name, for driving to work while dreaming of the beach.
questions.fun_fact: The first SEAT Ibiza, from 1984, was designed by the Italian Giorgetto Giugiaro.

questions.question: Iberdrola was born in 1992 when Hidroeléctrica Española merged with another company that had a river in its name. Which river?
hints: Listen carefully to how “Iberdrola” sounds.
The other company was based in Bilbao and had dams in Castile and León.
The river flows through Soria, Zamora and Porto.
questions.description: Before becoming a big power company, there was a wedding between two firms.
questions.fun_fact: The Aldeadávila Dam, on the Duero next to the Portuguese border, is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in Spain.

questions.question: Dinosaurus cookies are shaped like prehistoric animals. Which of these was NOT a dinosaur?
hints: It lived much later than the other three.
Its body was covered in long hair against the cold.
It had huge tusks and looked like a hairy elephant.
questions.description: Jurassic breakfast: bite it before it bites you.
questions.fun_fact: On an island in Siberia, mammoths were still alive after the Egyptian pyramids had already been built.

questions.question: Traditionally, on what day do the summer sales start in Spain?
hints: They start soon after school lets out.
It's the first day of a month.
It's the day many people start a whole month of vacation.
questions.description: The time of year when a swimsuit costs less than an ice cream.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2012, each shop can choose when to hold its sales, so many now start in late June.

questions.question: A Donut has a hole in the middle. Which of these things does NOT have one?
hints: It's something to eat.
Lots of people dip it in milk.
It's round, flat and has no gap in it.
questions.description: For breakfast, for an afternoon snack and, if nobody's looking, for dinner.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, Donuts is a brand: Panrico launched it in Barcelona in 1962.

questions.question: Campofrío was founded in Burgos in 1952 and is famous for its Christmas ads. What does it mainly sell?
hints: It goes great inside a bocadillo.
You find its products in the refrigerated section of the supermarket.
Turkey, chorizo and cooked ham.
questions.description: A company that every December gets half the country teary-eyed over a commercial.
questions.fun_fact: Its 2011 Christmas ad, “Cómicos”, brought together many Spanish comedians from several generations.

questions.question: Here you buy notebooks, pens and erasers, and in September it fills up with families. What store is it?
hints: In September, school starts.
They also sell folders, printer paper and pencil cases.
Its Spanish name comes from the material your notebook pages are made of.
questions.description: The place where you find out there are 200 different kinds of marker.
questions.fun_fact: The word “paper” comes from “papyrus”, the plant the ancient Egyptians wrote on.

questions.question: Look at this detail from a belén (nativity scene): by tradition, where are these little shepherds going?
hints: An angel told them the news while they were looking after their flock.
Mary and Joseph are waiting for them there.
That's where the manger with the Baby Jesus is.
questions.description: Characters with very little pay and a starring role every December.
questions.fun_fact: Many nativity scenes show dozens of tiny trades: bakers, blacksmiths, washerwomen, fishermen...

questions.question: Which of these does NOT bring presents on Christmas Eve?
hints: They arrive almost two weeks after the others.
They come by camel, not by sleigh.
Their night is January 5.
questions.description: Holiday delivery drivers with very different work shifts.
questions.fun_fact: Olentzero is a charcoal maker from the Basque Country and Navarre who, by tradition, comes down from the mountains with presents on Christmas Eve.

questions.question: Before bed, you leave your shoes by the window so presents get left next to them. Who comes that night?
hints: They come from very far away.
They travel by camel.
Their night is January 5.
questions.description: For one night, the shoes by the door turn into a mailbox.
questions.fun_fact: Before it became popular to leave shoes by the tree, the Spanish tradition was to put them on the balcony or by the window.

questions.question: The poinsettia is to Christmas as which flower is to All Souls' Day?
hints: It's one of the best-selling flowers in Spain in early November.
Many families take it to the cemetery on those days.
Its name comes from Greek and means “golden flower.”
questions.description: A question for people who never forget to bring flowers.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan the chrysanthemum is the symbol of the imperial family, and its throne is called the “Chrysanthemum Throne.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: according to tradition, this star guided the Three Wise Men to a city. Which one?
hints: It's in the Middle East.
It's a small town, very close to Jerusalem.
Jesus was born there, in a stable.
questions.description: History's first GPS only worked at night, and with no signal at all.
questions.fun_fact: Some astronomers, like Kepler, thought the star might have been Jupiter and Saturn meeting in the sky around 7 BC.

questions.question: They dress in Eastern-style robes, walk beside the parade floats and help the Three Kings. Who are they?
hints: They aren't kings, but they work for them.
Their name comes from the boys who served in palaces.
They're Their Majesties' official helpers.
questions.description: Without them, Their Majesties would have to carry everything by themselves.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, a page was a young boy who served a noble while learning good manners.

questions.question: You set up the nativity scene and put the mule and the ox by the manger. By tradition, who do they keep warm with their breath?
hints: It was a cold night in a stable in Bethlehem.
His figure sits at the center of the scene.
He's the baby in the nativity scene.
questions.description: The two nativity guests who never complain about sleeping in a stable.
questions.fun_fact: The Gospels never mention the mule or the ox: tradition added them later, partly inspired by a passage from the prophet Isaiah.

questions.question: Three of these words are used to greet someone when you arrive. Which one is NOT?
hints: Think about when in a visit each word is said.
The odd one out is said at the end of a visit or a phone call.
In Spanish it would be “adiós”.
questions.description: Welcome to the party of Spain's languages, where every guest says hello in their own way.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalan you can also say “a reveure”, which literally means “until we see each other again”.

questions.question: Look at the map: how is the name of the highlighted autonomous community written in its own language?
hints: It is in the northeast corner of the peninsula.
It borders France and Andorra.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.description: Every region has one name for home and another one for guests.
questions.fun_fact: In Aranese, the language of the Val d'Aran, Catalonia is called “Catalonha”.

questions.question: In their regions, Catalan, Galician and Basque have the same status as Spanish, as the 1978 Constitution allows. What are they called?
hints: That's why you see signs written in two languages.
They can be used with public offices and in schools just like Spanish.
It has the prefix “co-”, as in “copilot”.
questions.description: Sharing is caring, even when two languages have to share one road sign.
questions.fun_fact: Article 3 of the Constitution says that the richness of Spain's different languages is a cultural heritage that deserves special respect and protection.

questions.question: In which of these cities do people NOT usually speak with an Andalusian accent?
hints: Andalusian Spanish is spoken in the south of Spain.
One of these cities is far to the north, on the Bay of Biscay.
It's the city of the Guggenheim Museum.
questions.description: A trip where they swap your s's but never your smile.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Andalusia, the final “s” gets so soft that «los niños» can sound like «lo niño».

questions.question: In Galicia, the tender leaves of the turnip are called “nabizas”. What are they called once the turnip grows its flowering stalks?
hints: They are eaten mostly at the end of winter.
They go with lacón in a typical Carnival dish.
Their Galician name starts with “gre-”.
questions.description: A vegetable that changes its name as it grows up, like little “Pepito” turning into “Don José”.
questions.fun_fact: Grelos have their own Protected Geographical Indication: “Grelos de Galicia”.

questions.question: In lawyer movies, you sometimes hear someone ask for “habeas corpus.” What is it?
questions.answer: A prisoner's right to be brought before a judge
wrong_answers: Bail paid to get out of jail
A DNA test taken from a suspect
hints: It protects people from being locked up without explanation.
In Latin, it means something like “you may have the body.”
It forces the authorities to present the arrested person so a court can check whether the arrest is legal.
questions.description: Two Latin words that sound like a magic spell in lawyer movies.
questions.fun_fact: England made it law with the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679.

questions.question: You buy something in a shop and the cashier says “gràcies”. Who is the cashier most likely to be?
hints: Their region speaks another language as well as Spanish.
They speak a language from eastern Spain.
Their language is Catalan.
questions.description: Good manners travel in many languages, but always with a smile.
questions.fun_fact: “Gràcies” is the same word in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and the Valencian Community.

questions.question: Which ocean washes the coasts of Galicia and Portugal?
hints: Christopher Columbus crossed it to reach America.
It lies between Europe and America.
Its name comes from Atlas, a giant from Greek myths.
questions.description: So much water that not even Grandma's fullest bathtub could compete.
questions.fun_fact: The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean in the world; only the Pacific is bigger.

questions.question: You're on a boat in the Strait of Gibraltar and see bottlenose dolphins jumping. What is this animal NOT?
hints: It breathes air through a hole on top of its head.
Its babies drink their mother's milk.
It doesn't have gills like a sardine does.
questions.description: It smiles in every photo without anyone telling it to say “cheese”.
questions.fun_fact: Bottlenose dolphins sleep with half their brain awake so they never stop breathing.

questions.question: A famous beach in San Sebastián, facing Santa Clara Island and with a white railing, is named after the shape of its bay. What does that shape look like?
hints: It is in the Basque Country
It's something you can find in the sand on any beach
Hold one to your ear and they say you can hear the sea
questions.description: A bay so pretty that even the seagulls stop to take pictures of it.
questions.fun_fact: Its white iron railing has stood along the promenade for more than a hundred years and is a true symbol of San Sebastián.

questions.question: This column with a statue on top stands by the harbor in Barcelona. Who does the statue show?
hints: The monument was unveiled for the 1888 World's Fair
His arm points out to sea
He reached America in 1492
questions.description: It has been standing by the harbor for over a century and still hasn't asked for a chair.
questions.fun_fact: Many people think it points towards America, but the statue actually points out over the Mediterranean.

questions.question: Look at the map: Spain's most famous banana, the one with little black spots, grows on the islands marked. Which are they?
hints: They are in the Atlantic Ocean
They are very close to Africa
Mount Teide is there
questions.description: Monkeys' favorite snack… and half of Spain's too.
questions.fun_fact: The little black spots on a Canary Islands banana mean it is ripe and sweet.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which sea animal is this, the one that sometimes stings swimmers in summer?
hints: It is almost see-through
It has no bones and no brain
It has long tentacles and floats like a wobbly dessert
questions.description: It looks like a flan, but don't have it for dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Jellyfish have no brain and no heart, and they have been in the seas for more than 500 million years.

questions.question: You're on the coast with the Peñón de Ifach, and Europe's largest palm grove, in Elche, is close by. Which coast are you on?
hints: It's in the Valencia region.
Its big city is Alicante.
Its name is the color of snow.
questions.description: Miles of beach umbrellas, and there's always someone who forgot the sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: The Peñón de Ifach, in Calpe, is about 332 m (1,089 ft) tall and rises almost straight out of the sea.

questions.question: What is the name of the coast of the province of Málaga, famous for its beaches?
hints: It's in Andalusia.
Marbella and Torremolinos are there.
Its name refers to the star that keeps us warm.
questions.description: Here, people lay out their towels at eight in the morning to save a spot.
questions.fun_fact: Málaga boasts about 300 days of sunshine a year.

questions.question: It's small and silvery, fried whole in Málaga and also served in vinegar. What is a boquerón?
questions.answer: The same fish as the anchovy
hints: It's an oily fish
When it's cured in salt, it changes its name
Canned in oil, the Cantabrian kind is world-famous
questions.description: The little big star of the paper cone at the chiringuito.
questions.fun_fact: People from Málaga are affectionately nicknamed “boquerones”.

questions.question: I sparkle with diamonds, I'm kept in the Tower of London, and I only come out on very special occasions. Who wears me on their head?
hints: I'm golden and round.
I'm put on during a big ceremony.
The person who wears me lives in a palace.
questions.description: A piece of jewelry so important it has its own tower and its own guards.
questions.fun_fact: In 1671, a man named Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels and squashed the crown flat to hide it.

questions.question: Christopher Columbus is to the Santa María as Juan Sebastián Elcano is to the…
hints: It left Sanlúcar de Barrameda in 1519
It was the only ship of the expedition to make it back to Spain, in 1522
Its name means “triumph”
questions.description: The longest trip in history without being able to ask “Are we there yet?”
questions.fun_fact: A replica of this ship also sailed around the world between 2004 and 2006.

questions.question: This Galician cape has a famous lighthouse and is the end of the Camino for many pilgrims. What does its Latin name mean?
hints: It's on the Costa da Morte
The Romans watched the sun set into the sea there
For the Romans, nothing known lay beyond it
questions.description: A place with a view that beats even the best phone wallpaper.
questions.fun_fact: It's often called the westernmost point of mainland Europe, but that honor actually goes to Cabo da Roca in Portugal.

questions.question: What is the coast of the province of Girona called, the one that reaches the border with France?
hints: It faces the Mediterranean Sea.
Tossa de Mar and Cadaqués are there.
Its name means “wild,” because of its cliffs.
questions.description: Cliffs, coves and pine trees leaning over the water as if they wanted a swim.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Costa Brava” was coined by the journalist Ferran Agulló in 1908.

questions.question: These colorful blocks protect the harbor of Llanes, in Asturias. Which artist painted them?
hints: He also painted a whole forest in the Basque Country
That forest is the Oma forest, in Biscay
His surname starts with “I”
questions.description: The breakwater that got tired of being gray and went full rainbow.
questions.fun_fact: The work is called “Los Cubos de la Memoria” (The Cubes of Memory) and is one of the most photographed sights in Asturias.

questions.question: Which of these Francisco Ibáñez characters does NOT work at the T.I.A.?
hints: Ibáñez created many characters besides Mortadelo and Filemón’s crew.
He is short and can barely see.
He mixes everything up: he might say hello to a lamppost, thinking it’s a neighbor.
questions.description: A spy agency so secret that even some comic-book neighbors are left outside.
questions.fun_fact: Rompetechos is so nearsighted that he mistakes people for mailboxes, lampposts or animals, and that’s where all his trouble starts.

questions.question: She’s a girl who hides a book of magic, travels to other times with her spells and was created by German author Knister. What is she called in Spain?
hints: She has a little brother called Dani.
Her adventures also reached the cinema and a cartoon series.
Part of her Spanish name sounds like a superhero’s.
questions.description: A girl who does her homework with a magic wand… and it never turns out the way she planned.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany she’s called “Hexe Lilli”, and her books have been translated into dozens of languages.

questions.question: The photo shows the stage of Resurrection Fest, a big metal festival. In which Galician coastal town is it held every summer?
hints: It's in the north of Galicia, on the Mariña coast.
It belongs to the province of Lugo.
Its name starts with “Vi”, and it's also famous for its Holy Week.
questions.description: Three days of electric guitars at full volume, and the seagulls can't get their afternoon nap.
questions.fun_fact: Resurrection Fest began in 2006 as a small local concert and is now one of the biggest metal festivals in Europe.

questions.question: Ana Mena, this singer from Estepona, is also a star in another country, where she sings summer hits in its language. Which one?
hints: It's a neighbor across the Mediterranean.
She has sung at the Sanremo Festival.
There, her summer songs are full of “ciao” and “amore”.
questions.description: A girl from Málaga who has summer so well organized she celebrates it in two countries.
questions.fun_fact: As a child, Ana Mena was an actress and played the young Marisol in a TV miniseries.

questions.question: This singer, Manuel Carrasco, came out of Operación Triunfo and is from Isla Cristina. Which province is his hometown in?
hints: It's an Andalusian province by the sea.
It borders Portugal.
It's the home of Doñana and of strawberries.
questions.description: A singer with so much southern flair that even his ballads smell of the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Manuel Carrasco was on the second season of Operación Triunfo in 2002, and today he fills whole stadiums.

questions.question: Who is this singer, who came out of Operación Triunfo 2017 and went to Eurovision 2018 with Amaia?
hints: He's Catalan, from El Prat de Llobregat.
Besides singing, he plays the trombone.
He sang “Tu canción” in Lisbon.
questions.description: At the academy you learn to sing, to dance… and not to shake in front of all of Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Alfred and Amaia sang “Tu canción” at Eurovision 2018 in Lisbon, after winning the public's hearts in the OT academy.

questions.question: Today, what is the longest a Test match, cricket's classic format, can last?
hints: It is much longer than a soccer game.
It is played over several days in a row, with breaks for lunch and tea.
It lasts about as long as a school week.
questions.description: A sport where they stop for tea, and that's no joke.
questions.fun_fact: A Test match can go on for five days and still end in a draw.

questions.question: Chanel sang “SloMo” at Eurovision 2022 in the city in this photo. Which city?
hints: That year the contest was held in Italy.
It's a city in northern Italy, at the foot of the Alps.
It's the home city of Juventus.
questions.description: A performance so fast that its title asked for the exact opposite.
questions.fun_fact: Chanel came third with “SloMo”, Spain's best Eurovision result since 1995.

questions.question: The photo shows Arenal Sound, a festival held next to a beach in Burriana. Which province is it in?
hints: It's in the Valencian Community.
It's the northernmost province of that region.
The Benicàssim festival is in the same province.
questions.description: A tent, sunscreen and zero hours of sleep: the full summer package.
questions.fun_fact: Arenal Sound started in 2010 and is famous because many fans camp just a few steps from the beach.

questions.question: The singer of “Quédate”, his huge hit with Bizarrap, grew up on the island in this photo. Which one?
hints: It’s the third-largest island in the archipelago.
Seen from the air, it’s almost round.
Its capital is Las Palmas.
questions.description: A song begging you to stay, from an island nobody wants to leave.
questions.fun_fact: Quevedo was born in Madrid but moved to Gran Canaria as a small child, which is why he sings with a Canarian accent.

questions.question: Shakespeare is to English as Cervantes is to…
hints: Cervantes was born in Alcalá de Henares.
He wrote Don Quixote in this language.
It's spoken in Spain and in most of Latin America.
questions.description: Two geniuses of the pen who said goodbye to the world almost at the same time, in 1616.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes and Shakespeare died just days apart in April 1616, which is why April 23 is World Book Day.

questions.question: This girl, a daughter of Philip IV, posed for Velázquez many times. Who is she?
hints: Her little brother was Charles II, the last Spanish Habsburg king.
She married an emperor and moved to Vienna.
She's the blonde girl in the center of “Las Meninas.”
questions.description: She posed for Velázquez more times than you've posed for school photos.
questions.fun_fact: Many of her portraits ended up in Vienna because they were sent to her future husband, Emperor Leopold I, so he could see her growing up.

questions.question: I met on and off for 18 years in a northern Italian city, answered Luther and set the rules of the Counter-Reformation. What am I?
hints: I began in 1545, in the time of Charles I of Spain.
Philip II made my decrees law in his kingdoms.
My city lies in the Italian Alps, on the Adige River.
questions.description: The longest work meeting in history, and not even a coffee machine.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish theologians such as Domingo de Soto played a big role at the council, and Philip II made it law in Spain in 1564.

questions.question: Which of these people did NOT take part in Hernán Cortés's conquest of Mexico?
hints: Look for the one who lived much farther south.
The odd one out was an Inca emperor.
Francisco Pizarro captured him in Peru.
questions.description: A historic guest list with one gatecrasher who wasn't invited.
questions.fun_fact: La Malinche was Cortés's interpreter: she spoke Nahuatl and Maya and learned Spanish very quickly.

questions.question: The Duke of Alba was sent to Flanders at the head of the tercios to crush the rebellion. In which century?
hints: It was in the time of the Spanish Habsburgs.
It was the same century as the Battle of Lepanto.
He reached Flanders in 1567.
questions.description: A duke with such a bad name in Flanders that they still scare children with him.
questions.fun_fact: The same duke led the conquest of Portugal in 1580, which joined the two crowns under Philip II.

questions.question: Isabella the Catholic fought Joanna la Beltraneja for the throne. The war ended in 1479 with a treaty. Which one?
wrong_answers: The Treaty of the Bulls of Guisando
hints: The Catholic Monarchs ratified it in Toledo in 1480.
It also split up the Atlantic: the Canary Islands went to Castile.
Its name begins with “Alca”.
questions.description: Aunt against niece: the family feud that cost Castile the most.
questions.fun_fact: Joanna la Beltraneja stayed in Portugal, where people called her “the Excellent Lady”.

questions.question: Huge ruffs like the one in this portrait were banned in Spain in 1623. Which king ordered it?
hints: He was a 17th-century king of the House of Habsburg.
Velázquez was his court painter.
He was succeeded by his son Charles II.
questions.description: When fashion makes you eat dinner with your head served on a platter.
questions.fun_fact: Instead of the ruff, the golilla became fashionable: a plain, starched collar that was much cheaper.

questions.question: It's long, round and made of wood or aluminum, and in baseball it's used to hit the ball. In cricket it's flat. What is it?
hints: You hold it with both hands.
The player trying to send the ball far away uses it.
The player who swings it is named after it.
questions.description: The sport where running in circles (well, a diamond) earns you points.
questions.fun_fact: Professional baseball bats are made from woods like maple or ash.

questions.question: In which century did Philip II make Madrid the seat of the royal court?
hints: It was in the time of the Habsburgs.
It was the century of the Battle of Lepanto.
It happened a few years after Philip II came to the throne in 1556.
questions.description: The most important move in Spain's history, and not a moving truck in sight.
questions.fun_fact: Before that, the court traveled from city to city, and Philip III even moved it to Valladolid for a while, from 1601 to 1606.

questions.question: Before “La Revuelta” on La 1, David Broncano hosted a late-night show on Movistar Plus+. What was it called?
hints: It was on the air from 2018 to 2024.
He always asked the guest how much money they had in the bank.
Its name is the Spanish word for holding out and never giving up.
questions.description: A tall comedian raised in Jaén who interviews people with questions no mother would ever dare to ask.
questions.fun_fact: Broncano was born in Santiago de Compostela, but grew up in Orcera, a village in Jaén, and made his name with stand-up comedy and radio.

questions.question: I have stoves, a huge pantry and a clock that shows no mercy. Here amateurs and kids cook for three very strict judges. What place am I?
hints: It's a TV show.
The contestants wear aprons.
In the end, one of them wins the title of best amateur cook.
questions.description: Here potatoes get peeled with more nerves than on a final exam.
questions.fun_fact: MasterChef started in the UK in 1990 and came to Spain's La 1 in 2013.

questions.question: Which of these clothing brands is NOT Spanish?
hints: One of them comes from northern Europe.
It was founded in 1947, in a country famous for flat-pack furniture.
Its country is ABBA's country.
questions.description: Fitting rooms, hangers and a question with a hidden passport.
questions.fun_fact: H&M started in Sweden in 1947 under the name Hennes, which means “hers” in Swedish.

questions.question: Victor Arguinzoniz cooks everything over the grill in a farmhouse in Bizkaia. His restaurant was second in The World's 50 Best 2024. Which is it?
hints: It's in the Atxondo valley, at the foot of the mountains.
The chef designs his own grills and makes his own charcoal.
It's on the square of the village of Axpe.
questions.description: Here smoke isn't a problem: it's the main ingredient.
questions.fun_fact: Every day, Arguinzoniz makes his own charcoal from holm oak and fruit tree wood.

questions.question: Look: these two pieces are tied to the fingers with a cord. What are they used for?
wrong_answers: To crack nuts in the kitchen
hints: They make a noise when they hit each other.
Flamenco dancers use them a lot.
They go “clack, clack, clack” to the beat of the song.
questions.description: Two little wooden shells that are never seen apart.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish they're called castañuelas because their shape looks like castañas, chestnuts.

questions.question: The chotis is the dance of Madrid's chulapos. Which of these neighborhoods is NOT in Madrid?
hints: Three of them are in the center of the capital.
The odd one out sits beside an Andalusian river.
It is a Seville neighborhood across the Guadalquivir from the old town.
questions.description: A dance so proudly old-Madrid that you can dance it on a single floor tile without stepping on your neighbor.
questions.fun_fact: The name “chotis” comes from the German “schottisch,” which means “Scottish.”

questions.question: Look at these huge figures dancing through the streets at fiestas in many Spanish towns. What are they called?
hints: Inside, a person carries the figure on their shoulders.
They come with shorter figures that chase the kids.
Their name is about their size and their heads.
questions.description: Gentlemen so tall they'd never fit through your front door.
questions.fun_fact: In Pamplona during San Fermín, the giants dance to the sound of the gaita and the tamboril, a small drum.

questions.question: Look at this dress: what is it called?
hints: You see it a lot at the ferias in April and May.
Many women and girls wear it with a flower in their hair.
It's worn to dance sevillanas.
questions.description: For this party, showing up in jeans is almost a crime.
questions.fun_fact: The traje de flamenca grew out of the simple clothes women wore to livestock fairs.

questions.question: A hanger is to a coat as what is to a mantilla?
hints: It's the thing that holds the mantilla up.
It's pushed into the hair bun.
It looks like a big, curved comb.
questions.description: A treasure from Grandma's closet that only comes out for a walk during Semana Santa.
questions.fun_fact: Old peinetas were made from tortoiseshell; today they're usually plastic.

questions.question: In cricket and baseball, what word is used when a batter is dismissed?
hints: It's a very short word.
It has only three letters.
It's the opposite of “in.”
questions.description: The saddest word anyone holding a bat can hear.
questions.fun_fact: In cricket, the umpire signals that a batter is out by raising one index finger.

questions.question: Flamenco dancers tie a pañuelo de lunares around their neck. What does that scarf look like?
hints: Look at the pattern on the fabric, not at the sky.
The same shape repeats all over the fabric.
Often small white spots on a red background.
questions.description: At the feria, going without this scarf around your neck is like going without shoes.
questions.fun_fact: “Lunar” is also the Spanish word for the little dark spots on the skin, known as moles.

questions.question: A pandereta has a frame, little metal jingles and a tight surface you hit. What was that surface traditionally made of?
hints: It has to take hits without breaking.
It's the same as on a drum.
It came from animals like goats.
questions.description: An instrument that jingles more than a cat wearing a bell collar.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, the part you hit on a pandereta or a drum is called the “parche”; in English it's the “head”.

questions.question: Look at this detail: what is this wide-brimmed, flat-topped hat called?
hints: Flamenco dancers and Andalusian riders wear it.
It's typical of southern Spain and made of felt.
Its name comes from a city with a famous mosque.
questions.description: A hat so flat you could serve coffee on top of it.
questions.fun_fact: The sombrero cordobés is made of felt and is also worn at fairs on horseback.

questions.question: I was a Barça defender and won the World Cup in 2010. That year I met Shakira while filming the “Waka Waka” video. Who am I?
hints: I'm Catalan, and for Spain I wore the number 3 shirt.
Years later I founded the Kings League.
After we split up in 2022, Shakira wrote a song about me that everyone talked about.
questions.description: A World Cup, a catchy song and love at first sight on a video shoot.
questions.fun_fact: Piqué and Shakira share a birthday, February 2, exactly ten years apart.

questions.question: In this stadium with the great arch, Spain beat Germany 1–0 in the 2010 World Cup semifinal. In which city is it?
hints: It lies on the shore of the Indian Ocean.
It's the big city of the KwaZulu-Natal province.
Its name starts with D.
questions.description: An octopus saw this one coming before anyone else.
questions.fun_fact: Carles Puyol scored the semifinal goal with a header from a corner taken by Xavi.

questions.question: You're watching Spain's national team, who play in red. Which Spain player does NOT wear the red shirt?
hints: His shirt has to look different from his teammates' shirts.
He's the player closest to his own goal.
He wears gloves to stop the ball.
questions.description: Ten of them match, and one dressed for a different party.
questions.fun_fact: The rules of the game say the goalkeeper must wear a color different from the other players and from the referee.

previous.feedback: The translation is accurate, but it asks the same fact as the approved base question q-6292 ("which player must wear a shirt of a different color from all the teammates?" → the goalkeeper). English players of the spain bundle also get base questions, so they could meet both, and one gives the other away. The only Spanish touch is the red shirt. Consider dropping this item, or replacing the source with a question that really needs Spain.

source: This asks the same fact as approved q-6292 (the goalkeeper is the player who must wear a different color from the teammates); only the Spain framing differs, so in the English pool one gives the other away. The translation itself is faithful and natural; the overlap comes from the source question, which should be dropped or replaced with a different Spain-specific fact.

questions.question: This Basque goalkeeper started for Spain when it won Euro 2024. Who is he?
hints: He is from Álava.
His club is Athletic Bilbao.
He shares his first name with the coach Emery.
questions.description: A man who spends 90 minutes begging everyone to keep their stuff out of his net.
questions.fun_fact: He played every game of Euro 2024 except one: against Albania, David Raya was in goal.

questions.question: Iago Aspas, a left-footed striker born in Moaña, is the all-time top scorer of one club. Which one?
hints: It's a club from Galicia.
Its fans sing «A Rianxeira» in the stands.
It plays at the Balaídos stadium.
questions.description: Some go far away to make it big, others would rather become a legend at home.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2018 World Cup, Aspas scored a back-heel goal against Morocco in stoppage time.

questions.question: Olga Carmona scored in both the semifinal and the final of the 2023 Women's World Cup. Which team did Spain beat in the semifinal?
hints: The match was played in Auckland and ended 2-1.
Their shirt is yellow with blue details.
It's a Nordic team whose capital is Stockholm.
questions.description: Before lifting the trophy, there was one last exam to pass.
questions.fun_fact: All three goals in that semifinal came in the last ten minutes of the match.

questions.question: Spain vs. Portugal at the 2018 World Cup ends 3–3, and all three Portuguese goals come from the same player. Who?
hints: He was one of Real Madrid's biggest stars.
The third goal was a stunning free kick near the end.
He wears number 7 and celebrates by shouting “Siuuu!”
questions.description: The same heartbreak three times, like a song stuck on repeat.
questions.fun_fact: For Spain, Diego Costa scored twice and Nacho once, with a spectacular volley.

questions.question: In cricket, players shout “Howzat!” (“How's that?”) to ask for the batter to be given out. Who do they shout it at?
hints: It's someone who doesn't play for either team.
It's the person who decides whether the batter is out or not.
They raise a finger when the answer is yes.
questions.description: A shout that's half question, half begging, and all cricket.
questions.fun_fact: If nobody shouts “Howzat”, the umpire can't give the batter out, even if they saw it happen.

questions.question: This Barça midfielder from the Canary Islands is one of the stars of Spain's national team. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Tegueste, on Tenerife.
He was named Young Player of the Tournament at Euro 2020.
His nickname is a short form of Pedro.
questions.description: He has more dribbling moves than you have excuses for not tidying your room.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021 he won the Kopa Trophy, awarded to the best young player in the world.

questions.question: In Spanish villages, the pig slaughter, the matanza, traditionally began on a saint's day. Which saint?
hints: It was done once the cold arrived, so the meat would keep well.
His day is November 11.
A Spanish saying goes “a cada cerdo le llega su…” (every pig gets its…).
questions.description: In Spanish villages, winter had its own calendar, and it wasn't exactly vegetarian.
questions.fun_fact: The saying “a cada cerdo le llega su San Martín” means that sooner or later, everyone gets what's coming to them.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this fruit falls from the holm oaks in the dehesas. What is it famous for in Spain?
hints: They fall in autumn in the holm oak pastures of western Spain.
The season when they are put to use in the dehesa is called the montanera.
The best jamón ibérico carries its Spanish name on the label.
questions.description: Small, wears a little cap, and has a bad habit of jumping out of trees.
questions.fun_fact: An Iberian pig can eat about 10 kg (22 lb) of acorns a day during the montanera.

questions.question: Look closely at this photo: which kitchen herb is it?
hints: It's chopped very fine and goes into the green sauce for hake (merluza en salsa verde).
At Spanish greengrocers they sometimes throw it in for free with your shopping.
In Spain, a busybody who meddles in everything is called this herb “of every sauce”.
questions.description: The green stuff that decorates the plate and that half the world pushes aside with a fork.
questions.fun_fact: Chewing parsley after eating garlic helps hide bad breath.

questions.question: It's a sauce of oil, vinegar, bay leaf and paprika that preserves mussels, bonito or partridge. What is it called?
hints: The vinegar is what lets the food keep for a long time.
It's sold in cans in every supermarket in Spain.
The cans say “mejillones en…”.
questions.description: A luxury pool where mussels soak for months without getting wrinkly.
questions.fun_fact: The word “escabeche” comes from Arabic, and the recipe was already used in the Middle Ages to preserve fish.

questions.question: Look at this close-up photo: what food is it?
hints: It's carved by hand with a long, thin knife.
It comes from a pig's leg.
The priciest kind comes from pigs that eat acorns.
questions.description: Slices so thin you can almost see the plate through them.
questions.fun_fact: A good jamón ibérico de bellota can cure for more than three years before it reaches the table.

questions.question: Oregano grows wild on the hillsides, smells strong and nearly everyone likes it. What does “no todo el monte es orégano” mean?
questions.answer: That not everything will be easy
wrong_answers: That you must look after nature
That good things should be shared
That it pays to get up early
hints: People say it when something starts well but then gets harder.
The oregano is the pleasant part; the rest of the hillside, not so much.
It warns you there will be tough or unpleasant parts too.
questions.description: A herb that smells like pizza and gives out life lessons.
questions.fun_fact: Oregano is one of the favorite herbs for pizza, and it grows wild all around the Mediterranean.

questions.question: They come wrapped in paper, melt in your mouth and are eaten at Christmas. Besides flour, sugar and lard, which nut is in classic polvorones?
hints: It's the same nut as in the most famous turrón.
Its trees bloom white and pink in late winter.
It's also the base of marzipan.
questions.description: A sweet that crumbles even faster than your January diet.
questions.fun_fact: Many people squeeze a polvorón in their hand before unwrapping it so it doesn't fall apart into a thousand crumbs.

questions.question: According to the saying used in Spain, how many lives does a cat like this one have?
hints: English speakers give a cat more lives than people in Spain do.
It's an odd number that many people think of as magic or lucky.
It's a number between 6 and 8.
questions.description: An animal that has carried around a reputation it never earned for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain cats have seven lives, but in the English-speaking world they have nine.

questions.question: In Bécquer's legend “El monte de las ánimas”, Alonso climbs the mountain to find Beatriz's blue sash. On which night does it happen?
hints: The legend takes place in Soria and is about the old Knights Templar.
The story begins after a hunt, and that night the church bells toll without stopping.
It falls in early November, right after All Saints' Day.
questions.description: A mountain hike that no tour guide would ever recommend.
questions.fun_fact: The legend takes place in Soria, and its Mount of Souls is real: it stands across the Duero River from the city.

questions.question: In Galicia, people jumping the San Juan bonfire shout “¡Meigas fóra!”. Who are they telling to get out?
hints: “Fóra” means “out”, like “fuera” in Spanish.
In Galicia they say: “I don't believe in them, but they do exist.”
They fly on broomsticks.
questions.description: Doing an extreme sport one night a year to scare off whoever shouldn't be around.
questions.fun_fact: In many Galician villages, people jump the bonfire an odd number of times, often seven or nine, so the spell works.

questions.question: “We're a TV comedy duo, famous for the Móstoles empanadillas sketch, named after Spain's unlucky day.” Who are we?
hints: For years they made Spain laugh on New Year's Eve specials.
The saying about the unlucky day goes: “don't get married or set sail.”
Their name is a day of the week plus a number.
questions.description: If nothing goes right for you one day, maybe the calendar is to blame.
questions.fun_fact: In many countries the unlucky day is Friday the 13th, but in Spain it's Tuesday, the day of Mars, the god of war.

questions.question: In the 19th century, Rosalía de Castro, Curros Enríquez and Eduardo Pondal gave Galician back its literary prestige. What is that movement called?
hints: It's a late Romantic movement, like similar ones elsewhere in Europe.
Its counterpart in Catalonia has another name, though it means almost the same.
Its name in Galician means “resurgence.”
questions.description: Once upon a century, a language woke up from its siesta itching to write.
questions.fun_fact: Galician Literature Day is celebrated on May 17 because Rosalía de Castro's “Cantares gallegos” was published on that day in 1863.

questions.question: I was born in Cuba in 1814, wrote “Sab,” a novel against slavery, and had a hit in Madrid with the play “Baltasar.” Who am I?
hints: I was a writer of the Romantic era.
I was born in Puerto Príncipe, today's Camagüey.
My friends called me “Tula.”
questions.description: She crossed the Atlantic and took over Madrid's theaters without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: In 1853 the Royal Spanish Academy turned down her bid to join because she was a woman.

questions.question: I was born in San Sebastián in 1959 and have lived in Germany since the eighties. My novel “Patria” became an HBO series. Who am I?
hints: “Patria” tells how ETA terrorism broke the friendship between two families.
With that novel I won Spain's National Prize for Narrative in 2017.
My surname starts with “A”, but I didn't write “Obabakoak”.
questions.description: Two families, one village and a novel that half of Spain read on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Fernando Aramburu has lived in Germany since 1985 and writes his novels in Spanish far from his homeland.

questions.question: “Longa noite de pedra” (1962) became a symbol of Galician poetry against the dictatorship. Which poet wrote it?
hints: He belongs to Galician social poetry.
He was born in 1912 in a town in the province of Ourense.
His first name is shared with a famous Roman writer, Celsus.
questions.description: A night so long and so hard that no alarm clock could ever end it.
questions.fun_fact: Celso Emilio Ferreiro was born in Celanova and lived for some years as an emigrant in Venezuela.

questions.question: “Obabakoak” by Bernardo Atxaga was the first book in Basque to win Spain's National Prize for Fiction. In which decade was it published?
hints: It came out after Spain had become a democracy.
Unified Basque, or Batua, had been created about twenty years earlier.
It came out the same year as the Seoul Olympics.
questions.description: A made-up village with more stories than a building full of gossiping neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: “Obabakoak” means “the ones from Obaba” and has been translated into more than twenty languages.

questions.question: In Javier Cercas’s “Soldados de Salamina” (Soldiers of Salamis), a soldier spares the life of a writer on the run. When does it happen?
hints: The writer who was spared, Rafael Sánchez Mazas, was a real person.
The writer survives a firing squad for prisoners and hides in a forest near the French border.
It is the same conflict as in “Las bicicletas son para el verano”.
questions.description: A title that sounds like ancient Greece but misleads more than an upside-down map.
questions.fun_fact: The title refers to the Battle of Salamis, where the Greeks beat the Persians in 480 BC.

questions.question: “The Shadow of the Wind” is to Carlos Ruiz Zafón as “The Time in Between” is to…
hints: It was its author's first novel, published in 2009.
Its author was a professor of English philology at the University of Murcia.
She was born in Puertollano, in the province of Ciudad Real.
questions.description: A novel that got half of Spain staring at sewing patterns and thimbles.
questions.fun_fact: The heroine, the seamstress Sira Quiroga, spends much of the novel in Tetouan, during the Spanish Protectorate in Morocco.

questions.question: It's a four-masted brigantine schooner launched in 1927 that trains the Spanish Navy's midshipmen. What is its home port?
hints: It's in the south of the peninsula.
Its home city is the same one where it was built, in an Andalusian shipyard.
It's the city of the 1812 Constitution, “la Pepa.”
questions.description: A classroom with a sea view and no chance of going out at recess.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Juan Sebastián Elcano, the sailor who completed the first voyage around the world in 1522.

questions.question: You see a car with a license plate like “1234 BCD”, with no province letters. Since what year has Spain used these?
hints: Before, plates started with letters like M for Madrid or B for Barcelona.
The change came shortly before euro cash started being used.
It came right at the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: License plates: the ID card that cars wear stuck to their bumper.
questions.fun_fact: Today's Spanish plates have no vowels, so the letters can't spell out words.

questions.question: I'm a composer and military musician. In 1997 a Royal Decree made my arrangement the official version of the Marcha Real. Who am I?
hints: I conducted the Music Unit of the Royal Guard.
I'm from Valencia, and my harmonization replaced the one from the early 20th century.
My first name is the Spanish form of the name the Argentine pope chose.
questions.description: An anthem with no words, but plenty of footnotes.
questions.fun_fact: That same year the Spanish state bought the anthem's rights from the heirs of Bartolomé Pérez Casas, who had harmonized it in 1908.

questions.question: Which writer appears on the Spanish 10, 20 and 50 cent coins?
hints: He lived more than 400 years ago.
In his portrait he wears a white pleated collar called a ruff.
He wrote the adventures of a knight and his squire Sancho.
questions.description: A writer so famous he fits in your coin purse.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish 1 and 2 euro coins show the king's face, and the 1, 2 and 5 cent coins show the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.

questions.question: At the October 12 parade in Madrid, which unit usually closes the march on foot, with a goat as its mascot?
hints: They march much faster than everyone else.
They wear open-necked shirts and a cap with a tassel.
Their anthem is “El novio de la muerte”.
questions.description: A parade where even the mascots march in step.
questions.fun_fact: The Legion marches at about 160 steps per minute, much faster than the other units.

questions.question: This small country's anthem has no official lyrics. It is surrounded by Italy and is a very old republic. Which is it?
hints: It is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
It sits high on a mountain, Monte Titano.
A motorcycle Grand Prix carries its name, even though it is raced in Italy.
questions.description: Anthems you can hum without any fear of forgetting the words.
questions.fun_fact: San Marino claims to be the oldest republic in the world: according to tradition, it was founded in the year 301.

questions.question: I was born in Alcoy, played Jesus in the 1975 Spanish version of “Jesucristo Superstar” and sang “Perdóname” and “Algo de mí”. Who am I?
hints: I was one of the most famous Spanish ballad singers of the 1970s.
I didn't just star in the musical, I also produced it.
My stage name joins a first name and a word that sounds like the Spanish for “sixth”.
questions.description: Flowing mane, velvet voice and broken hearts all over Spain.
questions.fun_fact: To stage “Jesucristo Superstar” in Madrid, Camilo Sesto paid a big part of the cost out of his own pocket.

questions.question: The singer of “Desátame” and “Sobreviviré”, born in Figueres, is nicknamed “la ___ de Figueres”. Which animal fills the blank?
hints: She was a hit in the 1990s with a hugely powerful, very dramatic voice.
She's known for her dark mane of hair and her power on stage.
It's a black feline, like Bagheera in “The Jungle Book”.
questions.description: A diva with so much voice that the microphones ask for a vacation after every concert.

questions.question: Fito Cabrales and Uoho played in this Bilbao band, and one of its albums was called “Hay poco rock & roll”. Which band is it?

questions.question: This singer sang “Piensa en mí” and “Un año de amor” in Almodóvar's “High Heels”. Which region of Spain is she from?

questions.question: Hatzegopteryx, a huge flying reptile, probably hunted small dinosaurs on an island in what is now Romania. In which period did it live?

questions.question: In “A quién le importa” by Alaska y Dinarama, she sings: “Yo soy así, y así seguiré, nunca…”. What comes next?
hints: The song is about being yourself, no matter what people say.

questions.question: He's Julio Iglesias's son, grew up in Miami and debuted in 1995 with “Si tú te vas”. In which city was Enrique Iglesias born?
hints: He was born in 1975, in Spain.

questions.question: In the 1980s, Olé Olé, with Marta Sánchez, covered a German song that soldiers on both sides sang in World War II. Which one?
hints: The original song is about a girl waiting under a streetlamp.

questions.fun_fact: “Lili Marleen” grew out of a poem written in 1915 by a German soldier, Hans Leip.

questions.question: Which journalist took over from Antonio Herrero as host of COPE's “La Mañana” in 1998?
hints: He is from Teruel and also writes opinion columns for newspapers.

questions.question: Under Franco, every radio station in Spain had to connect to Radio Nacional to broadcast me. My name came from the Civil War. What was I called?
hints: It was the official news bulletin, and no station could skip it.

questions.question: It has four red bars on a yellow background, a blue strip next to the pole and a crown on top. What is this flag called?
hints: It's the official flag of an autonomous community on the Mediterranean.
Tradition says its blue strip comes from privileges the kings of Aragon gave to its capital.
It hangs from the balcony of Valencia City Hall every October 9.

questions.fun_fact: Every October 9 the Real Senyera is lowered from the balcony of Valencia City Hall without ever bowing to anyone, not even the king.

questions.question: One Spanish city has a flag of black and white triangles that's almost the same as Lisbon's. Which city?
hints: It's a port city.
It was Portuguese before it was Spanish, until the 17th century.
It's in North Africa, across from Gibraltar.
questions.description: A flag that plays chess with triangles instead of squares.
questions.fun_fact: Ceuta kept the flag and coat of arms from its Portuguese era, which began in 1415, and that's why it looks so much like Lisbon's.

questions.question: In heraldry, what is the “field” of a coat of arms?
questions.answer: The background the figures sit on
hints: It's the largest part of the shield.

questions.question: This dog is a natural symbol of Gran Canaria. What breed is it?
hints: It's a strong dog with short hair and a broad head.
In the old days it was used to guard livestock and farms.
In Spanish, its name means “Canarian catch dog”.

questions.question: I'm shaped like an X, I fly white on blue on the flag of Tenerife, and I do the same on the flag of Scotland. What am I?
hints: I'm also called a “saltire”.

questions.description: A cross that lay down on its side for a little rest.
questions.fun_fact: The flag of Tenerife grew out of the flag used in the 19th century to register ships from the maritime province of the Canary Islands.

previous.feedback: This overlaps heavily with q-9607 ("Scotland's flag, the Saltire, is a white diagonal cross on a blue background. Whose cross is it?" → Saint Andrew). Both ask which cross is a white X on blue, so seeing one gives away the other. In English, hint 1 also gives it away: "saltire" is the everyday English name for Scotland's flag, which points straight to Saint Andrew. Dropping Scotland from the question text helps, but the core fact is still the same. Either keep this item out of the English pool or move the question to a Tenerife-only fact, and in hint 1 use a neutral word such as "diagonal cross" instead of "saltire".

questions.question: In heraldry, tinctures are divided into metals, colors and furs. What are the two metals?
hints: On shields they are combined with colors like gules (red) and azure (blue).

questions.fun_fact: A classic rule of heraldry says never to put metal on metal or color on color, so the shield can be seen clearly from far away.

questions.question: The Romans put this animal on coins from Hispania because there were so many of them. Which animal is it?

questions.question: There are hundreds in Galicia and Asturias, like the one at Santa Tecla, and many are older than the Romans. What is a castro?
questions.answer: A walled village on a hilltop

questions.fun_fact: Many place names in northern Spain, like Castro or Castrillo, recall these ancient villages.

questions.question: The Romans ruled the peninsula for about 600 years. Which Latin name does the word “España” come from?
hints: It was the name the Romans gave to the whole peninsula.
The other three names were Roman provinces, smaller parts of the peninsula.

questions.description: A country that inherited its name the way you inherit grandpa's house.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans probably took the name “Hispania” from the Phoenicians, who were already trading on these coasts.

questions.question: These ruins in Mérida form a track over 400 m (1,300 ft) long. What Roman building were they?
hints: It isn't round or oval: it's very long.

questions.description: A spot in Mérida where the crowd yelled louder than at a cup final.
questions.fun_fact: The circus of Mérida could hold about 30,000 people, more than many of today's sports stadiums.

questions.question: In 1951, Cuétara opened a factory in Reinosa (Cantabria). What is made there?
hints: Lots of people have them with their breakfast milk.

questions.description: The Spanish pantry hides many secrets, and this one started being made in Cantabria.
questions.fun_fact: Before opening the Reinosa factory, the Gómez Cuétara brothers had already set up a cookie factory in Mexico.

questions.question: I arrive days before the Kings, sit on a throne in the town square and collect children's letters to take them to the East. Who am I?
hints: I dress like an Eastern prince.

questions.fun_fact: In Alcoy, home to one of the oldest Three Kings parades in Spain, the pages climb ladders up to balconies to leave the presents.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this chocolate-filled pastry called in Spain?
hints: People often have it for breakfast or an afternoon snack.

questions.question: In Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs, the mammoths face Rudy, a Baryonyx. In real life, how much time separates Baryonyx from the first mammoths?

questions.question: Listen: which bird makes this sound?

questions.question: I'm a young-adult novel by Carlos Ruiz Zafón. My hero, Óscar Drai, sneaks out of his Barcelona boarding school and meets a mysterious girl. What's my title?

questions.question: I'm an Iberian warrior from Spanish comics who fights the Romans, joined by the giant Taurus and the poet Fideo de Mileto. Who am I?

previous.feedback: Source: hint 3 ("Hace frontera con Barcelona por el norte") looks wrong. Badalona borders Sant Adrià de Besòs, Santa Coloma de Gramenet, Montgat and Tiana, but not Barcelona itself, and it lies to the northeast across the Besòs. The source should change it to something like "It lies just northeast of Barcelona, across the Besòs river." Separately, in the translation, "right next to Barcelona" is stronger than the source's "muy cerca" and also fits L'Hospitalet, which really does border Barcelona; it should read "very close to Barcelona".

questions.question: In the Christmas carol “Hacia Belén va una burra”, what is the donkey carrying?
