It's caught with boats and nets.
Here you'll find hake, sardines and shrimp.
questions.description: A shop where everything is super fresh first thing in the morning and nobody asks for a gift receipt.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the countries in the world where people eat the most fish per person.

questions.question: This show on the Cuatro channel has aired since 2005, covers ghosts, UFOs and mysteries, and is hosted by Iker Jiménez. What is it called?
hints: It airs on Sunday nights, quite late.
Before TV, its host did a similar show on the radio.
Its name sounds like the name of the channel it airs on.
questions.description: If you hear strange noises late at night, it might just be your neighbor's TV.
questions.fun_fact: Iker Jiménez trained as a journalist and hosts the show with his wife, Carmen Porter.

questions.question: Coca with pine nuts and candied fruit, cava, and firecrackers until dawn: that's the typical Saint John's Eve party in which region of Spain?
hints: There, June 24 is a public holiday.
There, besides Spanish, another official language is spoken.
In its language, the party is called “revetlla”.
questions.description: One night when the firecrackers get less sleep than the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word “verbena” for this party comes from a plant (vervain) that was picked on that very night, because people believed it had magical powers.

questions.question: In Laura Gallego’s «Memorias de Idhún», Victoria carries the spirit of the last of our kind, who gives out magic. What are we?
hints: Jack, the other hero, carries a different creature inside him.
In many legends we are white and only show ourselves to the pure of heart.
Our horn grows right in the middle of our forehead.
questions.description: Legendary creatures with more fans than most soccer players.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, the «Memorias de Idhún» trilogy became an animated Netflix series.

questions.question: It’s a 1997 novel by Antonio Muñoz Molina, filmed by Imanol Uribe, and its title is a learned Spanish word for the full moon. What is it?
hints: The word comes from Latin.
Its author was born in Úbeda (Jaén) and is a member of the Royal Spanish Academy.
Its first part shares the Latin root of “plenty” and “plenary”.
questions.description: A word so fancy only poets and werewolves with a dictionary use it.
questions.fun_fact: In 1998, «Plenilunio» won France’s Prix Femina for the best foreign novel.

questions.question: Elvira Sastre, a poet from Segovia, fills concert halls with her readings. In which decade was she born?
hints: She is one of the poets who sell thousands of books in Spain.
She won the Biblioteca Breve Prize in 2019 with her first novel, “Días sin ti”.
She was born early in the most recent of these four decades.
questions.description: Poems that get shared more than cat memes.
questions.fun_fact: Elvira Sastre started out sharing her poems on a blog while she was still a teenager.

questions.question: Elvira Lindo is to “Manolito Gafotas” as Jordi Sierra i Fabra is to…
hints: It’s a young adult novel widely read in Spanish high schools.
It’s about a girl who ends up in the hospital after a night out.
Its title mentions a red fruit.
questions.description: A writer so fast his books come out before his ideas do.
questions.fun_fact: Jordi Sierra i Fabra has published over 400 books and was once a famous music journalist.

questions.question: I was a political journalist on radio and TV. My first novel, in 2004, was a thriller about the Holy Shroud, and “Dime quién soy” became a TV series. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Madrid.
I also wrote “Historia de un canalla”.
My surname is almost the name of a region in northern Spain.
questions.description: From the radio microphone to the top of the bestseller list.
questions.fun_fact: The series “Dime quién soy”, starring Irene Escolar, premiered in 2020.

questions.question: I was a war reporter, I created a Golden Age swordsman who fights in Flanders, and I hold a seat in the Royal Spanish Academy. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Cartagena in 1951.
My swordsman is called Diego Alatriste.
I also wrote “The Queen of the South” and “The Club Dumas”.
questions.description: Swords, wide-brimmed hats and mustaches that would make a musketeer jealous.
questions.fun_fact: In the film “Alatriste” (2006), the captain was played by Viggo Mortensen, Aragorn from “The Lord of the Rings”.

questions.question: I'm a private detective in Barcelona, a great cook, I burn books in my fireplace and my assistant is Biscuter. Who am I?
hints: A writer and journalist from Barcelona created me in the 1970s.
One of my novels won the Planeta Prize in 1979.
My surname is spelled the same as the Portuguese word for “oak.”
questions.description: A detective who solves cases on a full stomach and an empty wallet.
questions.fun_fact: Italian writer Andrea Camilleri named his Inspector Montalbano in honor of Vázquez Montalbán.

questions.question: Look at this coat of arms of Spain. Which old kingdom does the red piece with green leaves at the bottom stand for?
hints: It was the last kingdom the Catholic Monarchs conquered.
Its conquest ended in 1492.
The piece is a fruit whose Spanish name is the same as the kingdom's.
questions.description: A coat of arms with so many pieces it looks like a jigsaw puzzle of Spanish history.
questions.fun_fact: The pomegranate (in Spanish, “granada”) was added to the coat of arms after the Nasrid kingdom was conquered in 1492, and it is shown split open with its red seeds.

questions.question: A one-euro coin shows a portrait of King Felipe VI on its national side. Which country is it from?
hints: Felipe VI has been king since 2014.
His father is King Juan Carlos I.
This country's capital is Madrid.
questions.description: A coin with blue blood: here even the money is royalty.
questions.fun_fact: Each euro country puts its own design on one side, but the coins are worth the same in all of them.

questions.question: This band from Vigo had Iván Ferreiro as its singer, hit big with “Promesas que no valen nada” and split up in 2004. What was it called?
hints: It was one of the key bands of Galician pop rock in the '90s.
It was one of the best-loved bands of Spanish indie in the late '90s.
Their name brings to mind sea raiders with eye patches and treasure maps.
questions.description: A Galician band that got half of Spain singing along with a broken heart.
questions.fun_fact: After the split, Iván Ferreiro went solo and kept singing “Promesas que no valen nada” at his concerts.

questions.question: In heraldry, what do you call a shield divided by one vertical and one horizontal line, like Spain's?
hints: Count how many parts two crossing lines make.
A shield with only the vertical line is called “per pale”.
Its name comes from the fraction of the shield that each of its parts takes up.
questions.description: A shield split into more rooms than a student apartment.
questions.fun_fact: A shield split into eight triangles also has its own name in heraldry: “gyronny”.

questions.question: Every October 25, “Euskadi Eguna” marks the 1979 referendum on the Basque Statute. What does “Eguna” mean?
hints: Think about what you celebrate on a specific date on the calendar.
“Aberri Eguna” is another Basque celebration: “aberri” is the word for “homeland”.
“Egun on”, the Basque way to say good morning, literally means “good …”.
questions.description: A Basque word every Basque uses without thinking, and maybe you will too after this question.
questions.fun_fact: The referendum of October 25, 1979 approved the Statute of Gernika, which still governs Basque self-government today.

questions.question: The flag of the Region of Murcia has four gold castles and seven crowns on a red field. What does its Statute of Autonomy call that red?
hints: It's a deep, intense red.
The Statute also calls it “Cartagena red.”
It's the same word used for a very elegant red theater velvet.
questions.description: Giving a color a paint-catalog name was very serious business in this Statute.
questions.fun_fact: The Region of Murcia is one of Spain's seven autonomous communities made up of a single province.

questions.question: Every fall, shepherds and thousands of sheep cross the center of a city along an ancient drovers' road. Which city?
hints: The sheep walk down streets that are full of traffic the rest of the year.
The shepherds pay a symbolic toll in old coins at City Hall.
It is the capital of Spain.
questions.description: There are car traffic jams, motorbike traffic jams, and then there's this traffic jam, which goes “baaa.”
questions.fun_fact: The shepherds pay 50 maravedís to the city, in memory of a 1418 agreement that let them pass through.

questions.question: This park in Valencia, about 9 km (5.6 miles) long, runs under lots of bridges. What was there before?
hints: Look at the bridges: something used to pass under them.
After a big flood in 1957, it was moved out of the city.
It was called the Turia and carried water to the sea.
questions.description: A park so long that you need to pack a lunch to walk all of it.
questions.fun_fact: After the 1957 flood, there were plans to build a highway in the old riverbed, but the people of Valencia asked for a garden, and they got it.

questions.question: I was born in 1918 and I have a canyon with the Cola de Caballo waterfall. Which national park am I?
hints: I am one of the two oldest national parks in Spain.
I am in the Pyrenees of Huesca, right on the border with France.
The name of my most famous mountain means “lost”.
questions.description: A place so pretty that in 1918 they protected it before anyone could show up in flip-flops.
questions.fun_fact: Monte Perdido, at 3,355 m (11,007 ft), is the highest limestone mountain in Western Europe.

questions.question: I'm the colored ring in your eyes, blue, green or hazel, and I share my name with the Greek goddess of the rainbow. What am I?
hints: It's why some people have green eyes and others have dark eyes.
It surrounds the little black dot in the middle of the eye.
It's also the name of a flower that comes in many colors.
questions.description: A goddess whose eyes follow you everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: The iris flower is also named after the rainbow goddess, because it comes in so many colors.

questions.question: The Nerja Cave, in Málaga, was discovered in 1959. Who found it?
hints: It happened in the middle of winter, on January 12.
They went in through a hole, following some bats.
They were young people from the area out on an adventure.
questions.description: A place where it's always night and the ceiling drips very, very slowly.
questions.fun_fact: The Nerja Cave hosts a music and dance festival inside one of its huge chambers.

questions.question: According to the most popular explanation, what was the «ocho» (eight) in the saying «más chulo que un ocho»?
hints: The story is set in Madrid in the early 20th century.
It was something people climbed onto.
According to the story, it took Madrid people dressed as chulapos to the verbenas (street fairs).
questions.description: A saying with a chulapo cap and a carnation in its lapel.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's last classic tram stopped running in 1972, but the saying is more alive than ever.

questions.question: If people in Spain say someone «es más fresco que una lechuga» (is fresher than a lettuce), what do they mean?
hints: It has nothing to do with temperature.
It's about how that person behaves.
This person does whatever they like without a hint of embarrassment.
questions.description: A vegetable used more often to describe people than to make salads.
questions.fun_fact: Lettuce is about 95% water, which is why it feels so fresh when you bite into it.

questions.question: “I'm from Alcaraz, and in 1587 a book came out under my name saying that sorrow and joy affect your health.” Who am I?
hints: My book was called “New Philosophy of the Nature of Man.”
For centuries, people argued over whether the book was mine or my father's.
My first name is the Spanish word for the fruit of the olive tree.
questions.description: A woman from La Mancha who was talking about stress four centuries before the word existed.
questions.fun_fact: Her book argued that sadness could make the body ill, an idea that psychosomatic medicine studies today.

questions.question: Who created the TVE show “Al filo de lo imposible” and directed it for more than 20 years?
hints: He was a journalist and mountaineer who traveled with many expeditions.
He organized and filmed Himalayan expeditions with Spanish climbers.
His surname is also a very common Spanish first name.
questions.description: A man who spent almost thirty years filming people hanging from ropes, and not at the gym.
questions.fun_fact: “Al filo de lo imposible” won dozens of international awards at mountain and adventure film festivals.

questions.question: Which slang verb do people in Spain use when something blows their mind, like an amazing magic trick?
hints: Young people say it a lot, in phrases like «estoy …ando».
Whoever does it usually opens their eyes wide and says “I can't believe it!”.
It starts with «fli-».
questions.description: A verb that has been hanging around school playgrounds for decades and has no plans to retire.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Spanish Academy's dictionary includes «flipar» and says it comes from the English “to flip”, meaning to get really excited.

questions.question: In Spain, if you call someone a «pesado», what do you mean?
questions.answer: They're annoying and won't let up
hints: It's not a compliment.
Spending time with someone like this wears you out.
They keep repeating the same thing until you're worn out.
questions.description: A word that has nothing to do with the bathroom scale, even if it sounds like it does.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, someone who just won't stop nagging is “más pesado que una vaca en brazos”: more tiresome than carrying a cow in your arms.

questions.question: In 1981, José Luis Garci gave Alfredo Landa a serious role in “El crack”: Germán Areta. What was the character's job?
hints: The film is a film noir, Hollywood style.
Areta used to be a police officer.
People hired him to look into disappearances.
questions.description: When the king of Spanish summer comedies decided it was time to get serious, for real.
questions.fun_fact: Landa played Germán Areta again in “El crack II” (1983), and in 1984 he shared the Cannes acting award with Paco Rabal for “The Holy Innocents”.

questions.question: Lucas Eguibar, from San Sebastián, became snowboard world champion in 2017 in Sierra Nevada. In which event?
hints: He doesn't race only against the clock: he goes down at the same time as his rivals.
The course has jumps, banked turns and tight bends, and the first one to the bottom wins.
It's like motocross on snow, but with a board.
questions.description: A board, a mountain and a guy from San Sebastián: the strange part is that there are no waves.
questions.fun_fact: Eguibar won that world title at home, in Sierra Nevada (Granada).

questions.question: What medal did canoeist Maialen Chourraut win at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics?
hints: She raced in K1, the single kayak event in whitewater.
She couldn't repeat the Olympic title she won at Rio 2016.
She finished just one place below the top of the podium.
questions.description: A trophy cabinet that fills itself: you just have to wait four years between shelves.
questions.fun_fact: Maialen Chourraut won gold at Rio 2016 at the age of 33, already a mother.

questions.question: How many world titles did Jorge Lorenzo win in MotoGP, the premier class?
hints: He had already been 250cc champion twice.
He won them all with Yamaha, between 2010 and 2015.
It's the number of sides of a triangle.
questions.description: A Mallorcan who overtook so wide he nearly drove off the map.
questions.fun_fact: Lorenzo was nicknamed “Por Fuera” (“On the Outside”) for passing rivals around the outside of corners.

questions.question: Dani Pedrosa was 125cc champion in 2003 and 250cc champion in 2004 and 2005, then won 31 MotoGP races. How many MotoGP titles did he win?
hints: He raced in the top class from 2006 to 2018, always with Honda.
He finished second in the championship several times.
He is known as the best rider in history never to win a MotoGP title.
questions.description: A rider who is small on the ground and huge on a motorcycle.
questions.fun_fact: Pedrosa won at least one MotoGP race in 12 seasons in a row.

questions.question: This volcano, with one side cut away by an old quarry, last erupted more than 10,000 years ago. In which autonomous community is it?
hints: It's not on an island.
It's in the northeast of the peninsula, not far from the Pyrenees.
Its province is Girona.
questions.description: A volcano that let itself be sliced open to show what's inside.
questions.fun_fact: Croscat is one of the youngest volcanoes in the Iberian Peninsula, and the area has more than 40 volcanic cones.

questions.question: You're hiking in the Sierra de Guadarrama National Park. Which of these peaks is NOT in it?
hints: Three of them can be seen from Madrid on a clear day.
The odd one out is the highest in the whole Sistema Central.
It is in the Sierra de Gredos, in Ávila.
questions.description: Sunday hike: sandwich, water bottle and one peak that snuck onto the list.
questions.fun_fact: The Sierra de Guadarrama National Park was created in 2013 and lies between the regions of Madrid and Castilla y León.

questions.question: Complete: Spain's first Parador, opened in 1928 high in the mountains, was the Parador de…
hints: It was chosen by King Alfonso XIII, who went hunting there.
It is in the province of Ávila.
It is the highest mountain range of the Sistema Central.
questions.description: Long before all-inclusive wristband hotels, someone had an idea with a mountain view.
questions.fun_fact: In 1978, several of the “fathers” of the Spanish Constitution met at the Parador de Gredos to work on the text.

questions.question: According to a well-known Spanish saying, when a river is churned up like the one in the photo, who comes out ahead?
hints: The saying is about profiting from chaos.
These people are happy when the water isn't clear.
In muddy water, the fish can't see the hook.
questions.description: When everything's upside down, someone is always rubbing their hands together.
questions.fun_fact: The saying is used for anyone who profits from a confusing situation, even if it has nothing to do with fish.

questions.question: This is Lake Ercina, which with its neighbor, Lake Enol, forms a famous pair. What are the two known as?
hints: They are in Picos de Europa National Park.
The Vuelta a España often finishes mountain stages there.
They are named after a nearby shrine in Asturias.
questions.description: Two lakes so inseparable that people always name them together.
questions.fun_fact: The Vuelta first finished at the Lagos de Covadonga in 1983, and it has been one of the race's most legendary climbs ever since.

questions.question: The Tajo (Tagus) is the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula. About how long is it?
hints: It crosses almost the whole peninsula, from east to west.
It rises in the Sierra de Albarracín and reaches the sea at Lisbon.
By car, it would take you about ten hours to cover that distance.
questions.description: If you want to walk the whole thing, you'd better pack a lot of sandwiches.
questions.fun_fact: The Tajo wraps almost all the way around the city of Toledo, as if it were giving it a hug.

questions.question: Tantalus is to the water he can never drink as Sisyphus is to…
hints: His punishment takes place on a hill.
He always gets close to the top, and then it all starts over.
Albert Camus wrote an essay about him pushing something heavy uphill.
questions.description: Some punishments are worse than going to bed without dessert, and this question proves it.
questions.fun_fact: Albert Camus ended “The Myth of Sisyphus” (1942) by saying we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

questions.question: This lake formed when a big dam was built across a river. What is it usually called in Spain?
hints: It stores water for drinking and irrigation.
It fills up with the rain and drops a lot in droughts.
Its technical name is “embalse”.
questions.description: A lake that wasn't there until someone put in a plug.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the countries with the most large dams in the world.

questions.question: Which of these tributaries of the Ebro does NOT start in Spain?
hints: It starts on the other side of the Pyrenees.
It flows through the city of Lleida.
Its source is in the French part of Cerdanya.
questions.description: Four rivers that end up in the same place, but one of them arrived with a passport.
questions.fun_fact: The Segre carries more water than any other tributary of the Ebro and joins it at Mequinenza.

questions.question: I work from sunrise to sunset in high summer, and what I sell then lasts me all year. “Hacer el agosto” comes from me. Who am I?
hints: Think of the countryside, not the sea.
Long ago, August was harvest month.
I work with a sickle, among ears of wheat.
questions.description: A month when some people go to the beach and others make a fortune without leaving home.
questions.fun_fact: Today anyone who makes a lot of money all at once “hace el agosto”, like a beach bar in summer.

questions.question: You're staring out the window in class and the teacher says you're “en las nubes”. Which of these does NOT mean the same?
hints: Three of the phrases describe someone who has no clue what's going on.
The odd one out describes someone who knows exactly what's going on.
Someone like this knows all the secrets of the matter.
questions.description: For whoever looks out the window more than at the blackboard.
questions.fun_fact: “Estar en el ajo” (literally “to be in the garlic”) means being involved in something and knowing all about it, the opposite of having your head in the clouds.

questions.question: In Spain, when it pours, they say “llueve a cántaros”. But what exactly is a cántaro?
hints: Homes used to keep them in the old days.
It was used to carry water from the fountain.
Potters made it, just like the botijo.
questions.description: When the sky decides to empty its whole pantry at once.
questions.fun_fact: A traditional cántaro can hold more than 10 liters (2.6 gallons) of water, and it was carried on the hip or on the head.

questions.question: A huge clap of thunder in the middle of the night makes your … stand on end. What completes the phrase?
hints: You have it almost all over your body.
Cats puff it up when they're scared.
When it rises, you get goosebumps.
questions.description: Storms at night have a special talent for waking up the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: Tiny muscles lift your hair: for our hairy ancestors, it helped them look bigger or stay warm.

questions.question: In Spanish, “tirar la toalla” means to give up. Which of these expressions does NOT also mean giving up?
hints: One of them means exactly the opposite.
Whoever does it holds nothing back.
It means giving it everything, with all your strength.
questions.description: Three phrases that surrender and one that has no plans to.
questions.fun_fact: The phrase comes from boxing: the trainer throws the towel into the ring to stop the fight, and English says “throw in the towel” too.

questions.question: You're getting married on a Tuesday and someone says “ni te cases ni te embarques”. “Martes” (Tuesday) is named after a Roman god. God of what?
hints: He also gives his name to a planet.
It's the red planet, the one NASA's robots explore.
Roman soldiers prayed to him before battle.
questions.description: The day of the week with the worst reputation among brides, grooms and sailors.
questions.fun_fact: Mars gave his name to “martes”, which is why it was seen as a day of fights and bad luck, not a good day for weddings or journeys.

questions.question: This submarine, launched in 1888 and now on display in Cartagena, ran on electric batteries. Which inventor designed it?
hints: He was a naval officer, a lieutenant in the Spanish Navy.
He was born in the same city where his submarine is on display today.
A modern Spanish Navy submarine, the S-81, carries his full name.
questions.description: Long before submarines starred in movies, one was already cruising around Cartagena.
questions.fun_fact: The Peral submarine spent decades on display outdoors at the port of Cartagena before it moved into a museum.

questions.question: You walk past the Royal Seminary of Bergara, where the Elhuyar brothers first isolated tungsten. In what year did that happen?
hints: It happened in the century of the Enlightenment.
In those years, Charles III was king of Spain.
It happened just six years before the French Revolution.
questions.description: A Basque school where the homework ended up on the periodic table.
questions.fun_fact: Tungsten is often called the only chemical element discovered in Spain, and the filaments of old light bulbs were made of it.

questions.question: “I was born in Barcelona in 1767, disguised myself as a Muslim prince and in 1807 entered Mecca, one of the first Europeans to do so.” Who am I?
hints: I traveled through Morocco, Egypt and Syria under a false name.
My real name was Domingo Badía.
My Arabic traveler's name starts with “Ali.”
questions.description: The king of disguise, long before costume parties existed.
questions.fun_fact: His travel books were published in Paris and translated into several European languages.

questions.question: What is this clay jug, so typical of Spain, used for?
hints: You see it a lot in the countryside and in summer.
It has a round belly, a handle on top, a wide mouth for filling and a thin spout.
The clay lets a little liquid seep out, and as it evaporates it cools what's inside.
questions.description: A clay jug that has been keeping watch over village summers since your great-grandparents' day.
questions.fun_fact: The botijo cools water without electricity: the water seeping through the clay evaporates and takes heat with it.

questions.question: Which two climbing brothers from Vitoria scaled big walls on all seven continents?
hints: Their names are Eneko and Iker.
Their project was called “7 walls, 7 continents.”
Their surname has only three letters.
questions.description: Two brothers who never fight over the top bunk: they always go for the top of the world.
questions.fun_fact: The Pou brothers have opened climbing routes in places as different as Greenland, Madagascar and Antarctica.

questions.question: Born in 1758, he founded Madrid's School of Civil Engineering and died working for the tsar in Saint Petersburg. On which island was Agustín de Betancourt born?
hints: It's an island in the Atlantic.
His hometown was Puerto de la Cruz.
His island is home to Spain's highest peak.
questions.description: An islander who ended up building things where the snow sticks around even in spring.
questions.fun_fact: In Russia, Betancourt led projects such as the great Moscow Manege riding hall and became a general in the Russian army.

questions.question: Which Spanish poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1956?
hints: When he got the prize, he was living in exile in Puerto Rico.
He was born in Moguer, in Huelva.
He wrote the story of a little donkey who is “small, fluffy, soft”.
questions.description: Four poets with golden verses, but only one took home the real medal.
questions.fun_fact: “Platero and I” has been translated into dozens of languages and is one of the most widely read Spanish books in the world.

questions.question: In 1949, a teacher from Ferrol patented an early forerunner of the e-book. Who was she?
hints: She didn't want her students to carry so many books.
Her invention worked with spools, compressed air and magnifying glasses.
Her first name was Ángela.
questions.description: Long before tablets, someone already wanted to make school backpacks lighter.
questions.fun_fact: A prototype of her “Mechanical Encyclopedia” is kept at the National Museum of Science and Technology in A Coruña.

questions.question: Which material is NOT used to make a bota, the wine bag you see at San Fermín?
hints: Shepherds and travelers have carried it for centuries.
The inside used to be coated with a sticky substance so it wouldn't leak.
If it fell on the ground, this material would break.
questions.description: A bag that carries the fiesta's liquid snack instead of keys and coins.
questions.fun_fact: Bota makers used to coat the inside with pitch, a pine resin that kept the wine from leaking out.

questions.question: When someone exclaims «¡Caramba!», what are they usually showing?
hints: People often say it with their eyes wide open.
It's what you feel when you see something you didn't expect.
It's a bit like saying «¡Anda!» or «¡Vaya!».
questions.description: A word that has been escaping from grandparents' mouths for centuries without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: «¡Caramba!» is a softened version of a much ruder exclamation, which is why it shows up so often in comics and cartoons.

questions.question: If you think a video game is «guay», what do you think of it?
hints: It's a word heard in Spanish school playgrounds for decades.
You say it with a smile.
It means the same as saying «¡qué pasada!».
questions.description: A word that sneaks into every chat about video games between friends.
questions.fun_fact: «Guay» was already very popular among young people in Spain in the 1970s and 1980s.

questions.question: It was named after a Greek god, it launched on a Saturn V rocket, and in 1969 it reached its big goal. What was that goal?
wrong_answers: Putting the first satellite in orbit
hints: Its destination can be seen in the sky almost every night.
Astronauts left footprints and a flag there.
Neil Armstrong said there: “That's one small step for man…”
questions.description: A Greek god who traveled farther than all the others put together.
questions.fun_fact: The astronauts' footprints are still on the Moon, because there is no wind there to blow them away.

questions.question: I'm shouted in flamenco tablaos and in the stadium when your team strings together lots of passes. What word am I?
hints: It's shouted all together, with lots of rhythm.
You also hear it along with the clapping.
I have three letters and an accent at the end.
questions.description: A word with so much flair it almost dances by itself.
questions.fun_fact: At Spanish matches, the crowd chants an «¡olé!» for every pass when their team keeps the ball for a long time and the other side can't win it back.

questions.question: At school, who usually keeps a student in from recess as a punishment?
hints: This person works inside the school.
You see them every day in your classroom.
In Spain, kids call them «profe».
questions.description: Losing recess is the worst news a soccer ball eager to play could ever get.
questions.fun_fact: Decades ago, in many schools a punished student was made to stand facing the wall in a corner of the classroom.

questions.question: It has desks, a blackboard and recess in the middle of the morning. What is this place called in Spain, in its short form?
hints: You go there almost every day.
It's where you learn to read and write.
It's the short word for «colegio».
questions.description: The place where your backpack weighs more on Monday than on Friday.
questions.fun_fact: «Zoo», «súper» and «pelu» are shortened words too: from zoológico, supermercado and peluquería.

questions.question: In Spain you might say «¡Tío, qué pasada!» to a friend. But in the family, who is your tío?
hints: He's from your parents' generation.
His children are your primos (cousins).
He's a brother of one of your parents.
questions.description: In Spain you have loads of tíos, even if the family only has two.
questions.fun_fact: Calling anyone «tío» goes back a long way: in Spanish villages, an older neighbor was called «el tío Paco» even if he wasn't family.

questions.question: «¡Qué rollo!» is to “boring” as «¡Qué chulo!» is to…
hints: «Chulo» is one of the slang words kids in Spain use most.
People say it a lot about clothes or a drawing.
It's the opposite of “ugly.”
questions.description: Schoolyard slang that any kid in Spain translates without blinking.
questions.fun_fact: «Chulo» has two sides: if a thing is chulo it's pretty or cool, but if a person gets chulo, they're showing off.

questions.question: “Klaus,” the 2019 animated film, came out on Netflix and was nominated for an Oscar. In which city is the studio that made it?
hints: The studio is Spanish and belongs to Sergio Pablos.
It's in a city with no beach.
It's the most populous city in Spain.
questions.description: A mailman, a toymaker and a studio that didn't need to travel to the North Pole to find Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: “Klaus” swept the 2020 Annie Awards for animation, winning seven, including Best Feature.

questions.question: This actress played Babi, the girl who falls for Hache in “Three Steps Above Heaven.” Who is she?
hints: She is from Madrid.
She played the role again in “I Want You.”
Her surname sounds like the Spanish for “green valley.”
questions.description: A motorbike, a rebel boy and a girl from a posh school: the recipe that made half of Spain cry in 2010.
questions.fun_fact: María Valverde had already won the Goya for Best New Actress for “The Weakness of the Bolshevik” before she played Babi.

questions.question: Before it was the 1966 film starring Paco Martínez Soria, what was «La ciudad no es para mí» (“The City Is Not for Me”)?
hints: Paco Martínez Soria was already playing the same role before filming began.
It was written by Fernando Ángel Lozano.
It was performed night after night with a curtain and footlights.
questions.description: A village grandpa takes on the traffic lights of Madrid, and grandpa wins by a landslide.
questions.fun_fact: The title became a popular Spanish saying for anyone who prefers the calm of the village to the noise of the city.

questions.question: You're in Alicante, at the film studios where “Asterix at the Olympic Games” and scenes of “The Impossible” were shot. What are they called?
hints: The Valencian regional government was behind them.
They have huge water tanks for shooting scenes at sea.
In English, their name is the famous nickname of Paris.
questions.description: Hollywood went looking for sunshine and found the Costa Blanca.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012 the European Commission ruled that the public money the studios received was illegal state aid, and they ended up closing.

questions.question: San Sebastián is to the Golden Shell as the Huesca Film Festival is to the…
hints: Huesca is a short film festival.
The award recalls a tradition from the San Lorenzo fiestas.
Its name comes from the people who dance at those fiestas.
questions.description: A festival where the films are shorter than the line for popcorn.
questions.fun_fact: The Huesca Festival, founded in 1973, is one of the oldest short film festivals in Spain.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT the subtitle of any Torrente film?
hints: The films are by Santiago Segura.
The second one takes place on the Costa del Sol.
The one about betting and casinos does exist.
questions.description: “The dumb arm of the law” has had more missions than a secret agent, and a lot less style.
questions.fun_fact: With the first “Torrente” (1998), Santiago Segura won the Goya for Best New Director.

questions.question: This director from Bilbao made “The Day of the Beast”, “Common Wealth” and “The Witches of Zugarramurdi”. Who is he?
hints: Before directing films, he drew comics.
He was president of the Spanish Film Academy.
His last name contains the Spanish word for “church”.
questions.description: If there's an apocalypse, a bar nobody can leave or a bunch of witches on the loose, he probably filmed it.
questions.fun_fact: “The Day of the Beast” won six Goya Awards, including Best Director.

questions.question: In which year did Javier Bardem win the Oscar for playing a killer in “No Country for Old Men”?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
It was one year before Penélope Cruz won one.
It was the same year as the Beijing Olympics.
questions.description: A haircut so strange it should get an award of its own.
questions.fun_fact: Bardem was the first Spanish actor to win an Oscar; his mother, Pilar Bardem, was an actress too.

questions.question: I'm a Catalan point guard, I captained Spain's women's basketball team and won Olympic silver at Rio 2016 at age 36. Who am I?
hints: My job was running the offense more than scoring points.
I also won European gold with Spain in 2013 and 2017.
My first name is very Catalan and starts with L.
questions.description: She had the ball in her hands and the whole game in her head.
questions.fun_fact: Laia Palau kept playing for the national team until the Tokyo Games, past the age of 40.

questions.question: Alejandro Valverde, “el Bala”, holds the all-time record of five wins in one Belgian one-day classic. Which one?
hints: It's raced in spring, in the Belgian Ardennes.
It finishes at the top of a brutally steep wall in the town of Huy.
Its name refers to Wallonia, the French-speaking region of Belgium.
questions.description: Some cyclists climb hills; others practically take ownership of them.
questions.fun_fact: Valverde won four Flèche Wallonnes in a row, from 2014 to 2017.

questions.question: I'm from Mallorca, I won Roland Garros in 1998, I was the first Spanish world No. 1, and years later I coached Rafa Nadal. Who am I?
hints: I reached ATP No. 1 in 1999.
I had long flowing hair and was one of the most popular tennis players of the '90s.
My surname has four letters, with an accent on the last one.

questions.fun_fact: Moyá and Nadal had known each other since Rafa was a kid: they used to train together in Mallorca.

review.feedback: Source: "the first Spanish world No. 1" is false as written. Arantxa Sánchez Vicario reached WTA No. 1 in February 1995, four years before Moyá. Moyá was the first Spanish man to be world No. 1. The source should say “first Spanish man to be world No. 1” (“primer español” reads as men only in Spanish, but the English loses that), and then the translation should follow it.

questions.question: How many times did Sergi Bruguera win the Roland Garros tournament?
hints: His titles came in the early 1990s.
He won them in back-to-back years.
They were in 1993 and 1994.
questions.description: In Paris the clay has a good memory, and some surnames stick to it.
questions.fun_fact: Bruguera also won Olympic silver at Atlanta 1996 and later captained Spain in the Davis Cup.

questions.question: Sergio García made his debut in it at 19, in 1999, and nobody in its history has scored more points. What competition is it?
hints: It's a team event played every two years.
It pits two continents on either side of the Atlantic against each other.
Seve Ballesteros won it both as a player and as Europe's captain.
questions.description: A tournament where golf, the sport of silence, turns into one of shouting and flags.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, Sergio García overtook Nick Faldo as the top points scorer in Ryder Cup history.

questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Mireia Belmonte become Spain's first female Olympic swimming champion?
hints: She had already won two silvers at the previous Games.
She won the 200 meters butterfly.
They were the first Games held in South America.
questions.description: A swimmer who spent her life copying a butterfly, and it turned to gold.

questions.question: You're making baked apples and you cut out the core before they go in the oven. What is that hole for?
questions.answer: To fill it with sugar and butter
wrong_answers: To hang them from a string
To make them float in water
hints: Think about how the dessert tastes, not how it looks.
Whatever you put in the hole melts in the heat of the oven.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is an ice pop like this one made of?
hints: Leave it in the sun and it ends up as a little puddle.
It's almost see-through when the light hits it.
You can make one at home with juice and the freezer.
questions.description: The only stick everyone wants to lick in August.
questions.fun_fact: The ice pop was invented by accident in 1905, when an American boy left a cup of soda with a little stick in it outside on a very cold night.

questions.question: You feel like having a lollipop. Where would you usually NOT find one for sale?
hints: Three of these places sell sweets.
One of them smells a lot like the sea.
That's where you buy hake and sardines.
questions.description: A candy with a built-in handle, so nobody gets sticky fingers.
questions.fun_fact: There are lollipops shaped like hearts and spirals, and even giant ones bigger than a child's face.

questions.question: It's black, looks like a rock and shows up on January 6, but carbón dulce (candy coal) is edible. What is it mostly made of?
hints: It's crunchy and melts in your mouth.
Its black color is just food coloring.
It's the same ingredient people stir into their coffee to sweeten it.
questions.description: The tastiest punishment in the history of punishments.
questions.fun_fact: Carbón dulce is made by beating sugar with egg white and food coloring, which is why it ends up full of little holes, just like a real rock.

questions.question: Classic crunchy chocolate turrón is sweet and dark, and it crunches when you bite it. What's inside that makes it crunch?
hints: It's a grain.
The grains are puffed up and full of air.
It's the same grain used in paella, only puffed.
questions.description: A Christmas bar that makes noise when you bite it, like stepping on dry leaves.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate turrón is much newer than Jijona or Alicante turrón, which have been made with almonds and honey for centuries.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a half moon, made of flaky pastry with lots of butter, and my name comes from French. Who am I?
hints: People often eat me for breakfast, sometimes toasted on the griddle.
My name means “crescent” in French, like the moon.
I have two curved tips.
questions.description: The pastry with more layers than an onion, and none of them make you cry.
questions.fun_fact: Although its name is French, many say the croissant comes from the Viennese “kipferl.”

questions.question: Look at this bird from Spain's rivers. Where does it build its nest?
questions.answer: In a tunnel it digs in the riverbank
wrong_answers: High up in a poplar by the river
Among the reeds, floating on the water
Under the roof tiles of a village house
hints: It looks for a place that snakes and foxes can't reach easily.
The male and female build the nest together.
Its chicks hatch in the dark, at the end of a hole in the earth of the bank.
questions.description: A professional fisher in a blue sequined suit who has never bought a fishing rod.
questions.fun_fact: The kingfisher uses its beak to dig a tunnel up to 1 m (3 ft) long in the earth of the riverbank.

questions.question: According to the popular Spanish saying, in which months is seafood at its best?
hints: The saying looks at how the names of the months are spelled.
It has to do with when shellfish breed.
From September to April, every month has the same letter in it.
questions.description: A Galician seafood restaurant where even the calendar has claws.
questions.fun_fact: The saying makes sense: in the warm months many shellfish breed and their meat is poorer, and some have a closed fishing season.

questions.question: Look at this Iberian wolf. Which domestic animal is descended from the wolf?
hints: It's the oldest tame animal of all.
It has lived with people for thousands of years, since long before farms existed.
It barks, wags its tail and takes the family for walks.
questions.description: A wild grandpa whose grandchildren now sleep on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The Iberian wolf is called “signatus,” meaning “marked,” because of the dark stripes on its front legs.

questions.question: Look at this bird from Spain's rivers and marshes. Which group of birds does it belong to?
hints: Look at how long its legs are.
Storks and flamingos belong to the same group.
In Spanish they're «aves zancudas», birds on «zancos» (stilts).
questions.description: It stands so still in the water that fish mistake it for a stick.
questions.fun_fact: The gray heron flies with its neck folded into an S shape, unlike storks and cranes, which stretch theirs out.

questions.question: In Spain, someone who keeps reminding you what's right is called «un Pepito Grillo». Who did that cricket give advice to?
hints: He's a character from an Italian story.
He was a wooden puppet who wanted to be a real boy.
Whenever he told a lie, his nose grew.
questions.description: An insect in a top hat who scolds you more than your teacher does.
questions.fun_fact: In Carlo Collodi's original story the cricket has no name, just “the Talking Cricket”; the name Pepito Grillo (Jiminy Cricket in English) comes from the 1940 Disney film.

questions.question: Look at this insect. Where do its young live before they learn to fly?
wrong_answers: In the cells of a beehive
hints: You'll always see it flying near one kind of place.
Its young breathe like fish.
When they grow up, they climb up a reed, leave the water and grow wings.
questions.description: A tiny helicopter with glass wings.
questions.fun_fact: Dragonfly young can spend years underwater, and as adults they sometimes live only a few weeks.

questions.question: Roughly how many degrees can a barn owl turn its head?
hints: Much farther than a person can.
But not all the way around.
Three quarters of a full turn.
questions.description: A white-faced neighbor who never needs a rearview mirror.
questions.fun_fact: The barn owl turns its head so far because its eyes can't move: they're fixed in place like two headlights.

questions.question: Look at these espetos: sardines on skewers, grilled in the sand. Which city are they typical of?
hints: It's a city on the Mediterranean.
It's on the Costa del Sol.
It's the city where Picasso was born.
questions.description: Sardines with fishing rods… but stuck right through the middle.
questions.fun_fact: Traditionally, espetos are grilled in old fishing boats filled with sand, right on the beach.

questions.question: They come out after rain, eat leaves in the vegetable garden and have eyes on little horns. Where do these animals lay their eggs?
questions.answer: In a hole in the ground
wrong_answers: In the water of a pond
In a nest in a tree
hints: They look for a damp, hidden spot.
They lay dozens of small eggs together, in spring or autumn.
The eggs, white like pearls, end up buried.
questions.description: It carries its house on its back and is never in a hurry to get anywhere.
questions.fun_fact: Snails hatch with a tiny, almost see-through shell that grows along with them.

questions.question: Look at this salmon leaping upriver. Which rivers in Spain does it swim up to lay its eggs?
hints: It looks for cold, very clean water.
It comes in from the Atlantic Ocean.
Asturias, Cantabria and Galicia are its territory.
questions.description: A fish that refuses to go downstream like everybody else.
questions.fun_fact: In Asturias, the first salmon of the season is called «el campanu» and is auctioned off every year.

questions.question: Juan Gabriel wrote “Amor eterno,” one of Mexico's most beloved songs. Who did he dedicate it to?
hints: He said she was the most important person in his life.
Her name was Victoria Valadez, and the song is about how much he missed her.
In Mexico, she is celebrated every May 10.
questions.description: The Divo of Juárez arrives in sequins, with a handkerchief to dry your tears.
questions.fun_fact: In 1990 Juan Gabriel filled the Palacio de Bellas Artes, and some critics got angry because almost only classical music was performed there.

questions.question: He was a jalapeño pepper with a mustache and a sombrero, and the mascot of the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. What was his name?
hints: His sombrero was a charro hat.
He almost always appeared with a ball at his feet.
His name is the Spanish word for the sting a hot chili leaves on your tongue.
questions.description: The spiciest mascot in World Cup history.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico was the first country to host two World Cups: in 1970 and in 1986.

questions.question: I was born in Álamos, Sonora, and became a star of the Golden Age of film. My role in “Doña Bárbara” earned me the nickname “La Doña.” Who am I?
hints: She was famous for her beauty and her spectacular jewelry.
Diego Rivera painted her portrait.
Agustín Lara wrote “María bonita” for her.
questions.description: A diva so commanding that even the cameras asked her permission.
questions.fun_fact: Cartier made her a famous necklace shaped like two crocodiles covered in precious stones.

questions.question: It was the first Olympic host city in Latin America, and at 2,240 m (7,350 ft) its thin air helped break records in 1968. Which city?
hints: It also hosted two World Cup finals.
Its Olympic stadium is in Ciudad Universitaria.
It is the country's capital.
questions.description: Games where the athletes could almost touch the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: There, Bob Beamon long-jumped 8.90 m (29 ft 2½ in), a world record that stood for almost 23 years.

questions.question: I'm a warrior princess from a '90s TV series: I throw a chakram and travel with my friend Gabrielle. Where do most of my adventures take place?
hints: My world is an ancient, mythical age, full of kings and warlords.
The places I travel through are near the Aegean Sea.
Zeus and the gods of Olympus show up there too.
questions.description: A heroine with a battle cry loud enough to wake up the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Although “Xena: Warrior Princess” is set in Greece, it was filmed in New Zealand.

questions.question: Listen: this soft cooing is heard on patios and power lines all over Mexico. Which bird is it?
hints: It eats seeds that it pecks from the ground.
In romantic songs it is a symbol of love.
It looks like a pigeon, but smaller and slimmer.
questions.description: A bird that gets up even earlier than the gas truck guy.
questions.fun_fact: Like pigeons, doves feed their chicks a kind of “milk” made in their crop.

questions.question: Listen: which Mexican animal makes this sound?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl, just like the names of the other options.
It's a wild relative of the dog.
In cartoons it chases the Road Runner and never catches him.
questions.description: A night-time singer who never asks the neighbors for permission.
questions.fun_fact: The word “coyote” comes from the Nahuatl word “cóyotl”.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico this bird is called a guajolote. Which language does that word come from?
hints: More than a million people in Mexico still speak it.
The words “chapulín” and “cacahuate” come from the same language.
It was the language of the Mexica (Aztecs).
questions.description: Before it starred in mole, it starred in this photo.
questions.fun_fact: The guajolote was tamed in Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, and from there it traveled to Europe.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this crustacean with long, spiny antennae is caught off the coast of Quintana Roo. What is it?
hints: It's one of the most expensive seafood dishes in Cancún's restaurants.
Unlike its European relative, it has no big claws.
It's the star of Puerto Nuevo in Baja California, served with flour tortillas and beans.
questions.description: An armored critter that costs more than your beach hotel.
questions.fun_fact: The Caribbean spiny lobster defends itself with a squeak it makes by rubbing the base of its antennae.

questions.question: They live inside the maguey plant, get eaten in tacos and sometimes turn up in mezcal bottles. What are “maguey worms” really?
hints: They aren't real worms.
If you let them grow, they get wings.
Before they fly, they wrap themselves up in a cocoon.
questions.description: The snack with the most protein and the fewest fans at the table.
questions.fun_fact: Red maguey worms, called chinicuiles, turn into moths; the white ones turn into butterflies.

questions.question: Look at these quetzal feathers. Among the Mexica (Aztecs), who could wear them in their headdresses?
hints: These feathers were worth more than gold.
The famous headdress said to be Moctezuma's is made with them.
Only the most powerful people were allowed to wear them.
questions.description: Long before designer sneakers, people found other ways to show off.
questions.fun_fact: The headdress said to be Moctezuma's has hundreds of quetzal feathers and is kept today in a museum in Vienna.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this reptile lives in the forests and mangroves of Veracruz and Oaxaca. As an adult, what kind of eater is it?
hints: It doesn't need to hunt for its food.
It spends hours up in the branches of trees.
Its menu is leaves, flowers and fruit.
questions.description: It looks like a dragon, but it doesn't breathe fire or pay rent.
questions.fun_fact: The green iguana can dive into the water from high branches and swim with no trouble.

questions.question: Gillnets set for totoaba fish trap the vaquita in the Gulf of California. About how many vaquitas were thought to be left in 2024?
hints: It is the most endangered marine mammal in the world.
In 1997 there were thought to be about 570.
They would all fit in a single small boat.
questions.description: A very efficient net… at catching everything it shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: The vaquita lives only in the northern Gulf of California and is the smallest porpoise in the world.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in 1996, Mexico blamed the chupacabras for attacking animals like these goats. Where did its legend begin?
hints: The first reports came out in 1995, a year before Mexico's.
It's an island in the Caribbean.
It's the land of the coquí frog and Ricky Martin.
questions.description: The 1990s news shows' favorite monster.
questions.fun_fact: In 1996 the chupacabras got so famous in Mexico that it inspired songs, toys and T-shirts.

questions.question: Adidas is to three stripes as Nike is to…
hints: Look at the sneakers of someone near you.
It looks like the mark a teacher draws when an answer is right.
It's like a comma lying on its side.
questions.description: A Greek goddess who now lives on the feet of half the planet.
questions.fun_fact: Nike is named after the Greek goddess of victory, and its logo is often described as one of the goddess's wings.

questions.question: I'm white and fluffy, I wear a baker's hat and apron, and I'm on bags of sliced bread. Who am I?
hints: My brand makes bread, snack cakes and much more.
I've been on my brand's packages for decades.
My brand starts with B and rhymes with “Mimbo.”
questions.description: A mascot so cute you want to hug the package.
questions.fun_fact: Bimbo was founded in Mexico City in 1945 and is now one of the biggest bakeries in the world.

questions.question: Emperador cookies by Gamesa come in a long pack, and each one is two cookies stuck together. What's in the middle?
hints: The middle part is soft, and you can lick it.
The most famous flavor is chocolate.
It's the same kind of sweet layer a birthday cake has on top.
questions.description: A cookie named after an emperor deserves a throne in your lunchbox.
questions.fun_fact: Lots of people pull the two halves of an Emperador apart to eat the filling first.

questions.question: At the corner store you ask for some Chaparritas. Which of these words does NOT mean the same as «chaparrito»?
hints: In Mexico it's a word people use fondly to talk about someone.
The odd one out describes a different thing about body shape.
The answer is about being thin, not about height.
questions.description: What comes out of the corner store fridge right at recess time.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, a short person is fondly called «chaparrita» or «chaparrito».

questions.question: At the Monday flag ceremony you sing “Mexicanos, al grito de guerra.” In which century was that anthem first sung?
hints: Mexico was already an independent country when it premiered.
The lyrics were chosen in a contest called by President Antonio López de Santa Anna.
It premiered in the 1850s.
questions.description: Every Monday at school: hundreds of kids with a hand on their heart, and one looking for his sweater.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Francisco González Bocanegra wrote the lyrics because his girlfriend locked him in a room until he finished.

questions.question: In downtown Mexico City people call it a “cilindro”. It plays when you turn a crank, and a man in a brown uniform plays it. What is it?
hints: You don't play it with your fingers or with sticks.
While one man plays it, his partner walks around asking for coins.
Its player is called an “organillero”.
questions.description: A giant music box that needs a strong arm and a cap for the coins.
questions.fun_fact: Many of the barrel organs still playing in Mexico were built in Germany more than 100 years ago.

questions.question: In the song «Mi pollito amarillito» (My Little Yellow Chick), what does the chick do when it wants to eat bugs?
questions.answer: Scratches the ground with its little feet
wrong_answers: Opens its little beak very wide
Hops around in the palm of your hand
Runs off to go find its mommy
hints: It uses a part of its body that isn't its beak.
The little bugs are down in the dirt.
It uses the same body parts it walks on.
questions.description: A yellow friend who fits in the palm of your hand and never stops saying “peep.”
questions.fun_fact: Hens and chicks scratch the dirt to uncover hidden seeds and little bugs.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. I could not open the lyrics text. Search summaries confirm the song is about a yellow chick that fits in the palm of a hand, eats bugs and fears a hawk. I could not verify the line about what it does to get the bugs. From memory, the answer (scratching the ground with its feet) is plausible, and the wrong answers look wrong. The fun fact about hens scratching for seeds and bugs is generally true. The title is also ambiguous because several versions exist (Gallina Pintadita, El Reino Infantil, Lunacreciente).
Fact check: uncertain. Song summaries confirm the chick scratches the ground for bugs, but I couldn't see the exact lyrics. The wrong answers look plausible as wrong.

questions.question: In the song, Pin Pon washes his face and combs his hair without crying. When the little stars come out, what does he do?

questions.question: It's black and thick. Cartoonists put it over pencil drawings with a nib pen or brush, and once dry, water won't smear it. What is it?
hints: It's a liquid, not a solid.
It goes over the pencil lines to make them final before coloring.
Its name sounds like a country in Asia.
questions.description: Without it, the monitos would stay shy little pencil sketches.

questions.question: I'm a 2006 Mexican animated film that grew out of some internet shorts. My hero dreams of becoming a chicken. What's my name?
hints: My hero doesn't want to end up as breakfast.

questions.description: Proof that a silly internet video can end up on the big screen.
questions.fun_fact: It had sequels such as “Otra película de huevos y un pollo” (2009).

questions.question: The cartoonist behind the little drawings in the margins of MAD magazine grew up in Mexico and studied at UNAM before moving to New York. In what country was he born?
hints: He came to Mexico as a child, fleeing a war.
Before reaching Mexico, his family lived for a while in France.
