questions.description: An artist who never respected margins, least of all the ones on the page.
questions.fun_fact: Sergio Aragonés joined MAD in 1963 and drew his “marginals” for decades, almost without using words.

questions.question: This Ghost Rider from a Mexican family, created in 2014, drives a race car instead of a motorcycle and looks after his little brother. Where is he from?
hints: He lives in the United States.
His neighborhood is famous for its Chicano community.
It's in California.
questions.description: A motorcyclist from the underworld who traded two wheels for four.
questions.fun_fact: Robbie Reyes also appeared in the series “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.”, played by Gabriel Luna.

questions.question: You open the paper and see the day's political cartoon. The word comes from the Italian “cartone”. What was a “cartone” originally?
questions.answer: A sketch on heavy paper for painting a fresco
wrong_answers: A box for storing old newspapers
A theater poster pasted up in the street
A deck of playing cards for gambling
hints: It comes from “carta”, Italian for paper.
It served as a template before the final work.
It was traced onto a wall or a tapestry.
questions.description: A word that ended up mocking politicians after a long trip from Italy.
questions.fun_fact: In 1843 the British magazine Punch mocked some sketches for murals in Parliament, and ever since “cartoon” has meant a funny drawing.

questions.question: You're watching a marathon of El Santo films against vampire women and mummies. In which decade did the lucha libre film boom peak?
hints: Many of these films are in black and white.
El Santo made his first film in the late 1950s.
“Santo vs. the Vampire Women” came out in 1962.
questions.description: Silver masks, capes and mummies that just won't stay down.
questions.fun_fact: El Santo starred in more than 50 films and never took off his mask on screen.

questions.question: He's a hopelessly clumsy barbarian who ruins everything he touches, travels with his dog Rufferto and was created by Sergio Aragonés. Who is he?
hints: His comic has been published in the United States since the 1980s.
His nickname says he never stays in one place for long.
He's known as “the Wanderer.”
questions.description: A warrior whose sword is extremely dangerous, especially to his friends.
questions.fun_fact: Groo has a famous obsession: cheese dip.

questions.question: The satirical newspaper “El Padre Cobos”, which mocked 19th-century governments, was founded by the grandfather of a Mexican writer. Which one?
hints: The grandson was a poet and essayist.
He wrote “The Labyrinth of Solitude”.
He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990.
questions.description: A grandpa who made fun of the government, and a grandson who won prizes for writing.
questions.fun_fact: The grandfather, Ireneo Paz, was also a soldier and novelist, and his grandson grew up surrounded by his huge library in Mixcoac.

questions.question: If people say someone «pasó a mejor vida», even though they never moved house, what happened to them?
hints: It's a gentle way of saying something sad.
People say it quietly, with a serious face.
It's similar to saying someone now “rests in peace.”
questions.description: A saying so optimistic it sounds like an ad for a travel agency.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish has loads of funny ways to say it, like “colgar los tenis” (hang up your sneakers) or “estirar la pata” (stretch out your leg).

questions.question: Look at the photo: many kids carry something like this to “pedir calaverita” in late October. What do they hope to get in it?
hints: It's something you can hand over quickly at the door.
It fits in a child's hand and doesn't need cooking or lighting.
Kids love it, dentists not so much.
questions.description: The one time of year when knocking on strangers' doors in costume is perfectly polite.
questions.fun_fact: Many kids ask for their calaverita with a line like “¿Me da mi calaverita?” (“Can I have my calaverita?”).

questions.question: In “Coco,” when does Miguel sing “Remember Me” to his great-grandmother Mamá Coco?
questions.answer: At the end, when he gets back home
wrong_answers: At the start, on his birthday
At the music contest in the plaza
While crossing the bridge of petals
hints: It's the most moving scene in the whole film.
Miguel plays the guitar, and Mamá Coco starts to smile and sing.
Through the song, Mamá Coco remembers her papa.
questions.description: A song so catchy it can wake even a great-grandma from her nap.
questions.fun_fact: “Remember Me” won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2018.

questions.question: I'm white, I live in your kitchen, and on the ofrenda I sit in a little dish to purify souls on their journey. What am I?
hints: I'm on almost every table at mealtime.
People put me on elotes, potatoes and popcorn.
I come from the sea.
questions.description: The ingredient no kitchen is ever without, and in November it also works for the afterlife.
questions.fun_fact: Sometimes the salt is shaped into a cross on the ofrenda, so the soul is not corrupted on its way.

questions.question: I run the fashion magazine Runway, and Meryl Streep played me in the movie. Which real person is my character said to be based on?
hints: She is a British woman who worked in New York for decades.
For many years she was the editor of the US edition of Vogue magazine.
She is famous for her straight bob with bangs and her dark sunglasses.
questions.description: A boss so demanding that even her coffee is scared of her.
questions.fun_fact: Lauren Weisberger, who wrote the novel “The Devil Wears Prada,” had worked as Anna Wintour's assistant.

questions.question: A huge parade of skulls and catrinas appeared in a 2015 James Bond film, and since 2016 a real one has been held. In which city?
hints: The film is called “Spectre.”
The parade goes along huge avenues and ends in a famous square.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: Fiction once copied Mexico, and then Mexico copied fiction.
questions.fun_fact: Before the film, Mexico City had no big Day of the Dead parade: it was invented for the screen and then became a tradition.

questions.question: Calaveritas literarias are written in November: funny pieces about Death taking someone away. What form are they written in?
hints: Every year newspapers publish them and kids write them at school.
Many poke fun at teachers, classmates or politicians.
The words at the end of the lines sound alike.
questions.description: Death has a sense of humor too, and every November it puts it in writing.
questions.fun_fact: Calaveritas literarias began in 19th-century newspapers as a way to make fun of politicians and famous people.

questions.question: Finish the sentence: a strawberry licuado is strawberries blended with…
hints: It's white.
Cows give it.
You also pour it on your breakfast cereal.
questions.description: The breakfast that makes a racket in the kitchen first, then behaves itself in the glass.
questions.fun_fact: At Mexican markets, many strawberry licuados also get banana or oats added to make them more filling.

questions.question: At what time of year do stands in Mexico fill up with agua de mango, because it's mango season?
hints: First the mango trees bloom, and a few months later the fruit ripens.
It lines up with Semana Santa and the end of the school year.
April, May and June are the big months.
questions.description: When the vitrolero turns yellow, you know the calendar has moved on.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the biggest mango exporters in the world.

questions.question: It's orange inside, has a pile of little black seeds in the middle, and blended with milk it's a breakfast classic. What fruit is it?
hints: It's long, and green or yellow on the outside.
People say it helps with digestion.
In Mexico it's very often sold as the “Maradol” variety.
questions.description: A fruit that wakes up the blender every morning before the rest of the family.
questions.fun_fact: Papaya is native to Mesoamerica, so people in Mexico have been eating it for a very long time.

questions.question: In many Mexican villages, a baby girl's belly button stump is buried by the fogón (hearth) so she grows up a homebody. How far back does this custom go?
hints: It is much older than the arrival of the train in Mexico.
The fogón has been the heart of Mexican kitchens for centuries.
The Mexica did it too: a baby boy's belly button was taken to the battlefield.
questions.description: Some people leave their roots back in the village, and some leave their belly button there, literally.
questions.fun_fact: This is where the Mexican saying «ahí tengo enterrado el ombligo» (“my belly button is buried there”) comes from, used for the place where you were born.

questions.question: It's made with 1 liter (about 1 quart) of boiled water and sipped slowly during diarrhea to prevent dehydration. What two other things go in suero casero?
hints: They're cheap and found in any Mexican kitchen.
They replace what the body loses with diarrhea: minerals and energy.
One makes food taste like the sea, the other makes coffee sweet.
questions.description: The cheapest remedy in the medicine cabinet: you make it yourself in the kitchen in two minutes.
questions.fun_fact: Oral rehydration solution is considered one of the most important medical advances of the 20th century: it has saved millions of children's lives around the world.

questions.question: I'm a little mouse: when you lose a baby tooth, you leave it under your pillow and I swap it for a coin. Who am I?
hints: I work at night while you sleep.
In other countries, a fairy does my job.
My last name is the same as lots of people's.
questions.description: The only collector in the world who pays for used teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Ratón Pérez was born in a story the writer Luis Coloma wrote in 1894 for the young King Alfonso XIII of Spain.

questions.question: In this game, one player covers their eyes and counts while the others run off, then goes looking for them. What is it called in Mexico?
hints: At the end of counting, the seeker shouts “¡Ahí voy!” or “¡Listos o no, ahí voy!”
The runners look for places where they can't be seen: behind a car, under the table…
In other Spanish-speaking countries it's called “el escondite.”
questions.description: One player counts to a hundred and everyone else vanishes like socks in the washing machine.
questions.fun_fact: There are hide-and-seek championships for adults: Italy has hosted a world championship of the game for years.

questions.question: Look at the photo: sugar skulls, orange flowers and candles. Where does all this go in early November?
hints: It's set up at home to remember family members who are gone.
It holds photos, pan de muerto and cempasúchil flowers.
It shows up a lot in the movie “Coco.”
questions.description: Early November: the time of year when the whole house dresses up for a party.
questions.fun_fact: People say the smell and orange color of cempasúchil help the souls find their way home.

questions.question: It was Mexico City's most famous taxi: green and white, no front passenger seat so riders could climb in, and made in Puebla. Which car was it?
hints: Its engine was in the back.
It had a small, round, bubble-like shape.
In Mexico it's called the “vocho.”
questions.description: A taxi so tiny they had to take out a seat just to fit you in.
questions.fun_fact: The Volkswagen plant in Puebla was the last in the world to make the original vocho, until 2003.

questions.question: In Mexico, what do you call the woven plastic bag with colorful stripes that you take to the market?
hints: You use it again and again; you don't throw it away.
You carry the household's food home in it.
It's named after the errand Mom sends you on to buy things.
questions.description: Every market trip's loyal sidekick: it carries jitomates, potatoes and even a kilo of tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: Because it gets reused for years, the bolsa del mandado is now seen as an eco-friendly choice compared to throwaway plastic bags.

questions.question: I was an insurgent who switched to the royalist side. In March 1811, at Acatita de Baján, Coahuila, I ambushed and captured Hidalgo and Allende. Who am I?
hints: My name went down in history as a byword for betrayal.
I was a captain in the northern provinces, not a great general of the viceroyalty.
I share my first name with Allende.
questions.description: An oasis in the desert that turned out to be the worst stop of the trip.
questions.fun_fact: Acatita de Baján was a spot with water wells in the middle of the desert: the insurgents stopped there to look for water.

questions.question: Guadalupe Victoria was the first on the list, in 1824. Of which office in Mexico?
wrong_answers: Head of Government of Mexico City
hints: This office still exists today.
It is elected every six years.
Benito Juárez and Porfirio Díaz also held this office.
questions.description: First in line, and nobody cut in front of him.
questions.fun_fact: His real name was José Miguel Ramón Adaucto Fernández y Félix; he changed it to honor the Virgin of Guadalupe and victory.

questions.question: Which Independence hero, famous for the bandana on his head, was on the old 50-peso bill?
hints: He was a priest, just like Hidalgo.
He wrote the “Sentimientos de la Nación” (Feelings of the Nation).
He was born in Valladolid, a city that now carries his last name in his honor.
questions.description: Long before it was trendy, he was already rocking his paliacate.
questions.fun_fact: It is said that Morelos wore the bandana to ease his bad headaches.

questions.question: During the Grito on September 15, people shout “¡Viva!” for the heroes of Independence. Who do they NOT cheer for?
hints: He arrived in Mexico long before 1810.
He came from Spain in the 16th century.
He conquered Tenochtitlan.
questions.description: The only party where shouting at midnight makes you a patriot instead of a bad neighbor.
questions.fun_fact: Hidalgo gave his famous cry in the early hours of September 16, 1810, not on the night of the 15th.

questions.question: He succeeded Juárez in 1872, opened the Mexico City–Veracruz railway and was overthrown by Porfirio Díaz. As a Spanish adjective, what does his surname mean?
hints: His brother Miguel wrote a famous law of the Reform era.
His first name was Sebastián, and he had a double surname.
It's what people call someone who takes a long time to understand things.
questions.description: His surname rode first class on the train to Veracruz.
questions.fun_fact: In 1873, Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada made the Reform Laws part of the Constitution.

questions.question: Paseo de la Reforma honors the Reform Laws, which gave their name to a war between liberals and conservatives. When was that war?
hints: It was in the middle of the 19th century.
It began shortly after the Constitution of 1857.
It ended just before the French arrived.
questions.description: Liberals versus conservatives: the tensest family carne asada of the 19th century.
questions.fun_fact: During that war, Juárez governed from Veracruz, where he issued the Reform Laws in 1859.

questions.question: A green flag with a harp flew on Mexico's side in the 1846–1848 war against the United States. Who carried it?
hints: Many of them had deserted from the US Army.
They were Catholic, like the Mexicans.
Their battalion was named after the saint of the shamrock.
questions.description: A flag that brought its own musical instrument to the battlefield.
questions.fun_fact: Every September 12, they are honored in San Ángel, in Mexico City.

questions.question: Versace's famous 1994 black dress, covered in gold safety pins, took its idea from a 1970s street style. Which one?
hints: It was a rebellious style born in London and New York.
Its fans wore colorful mohawks and leather jackets.
The band Sex Pistols was its great symbol.
questions.description: A luxury dress held together by what your grandma keeps in her sewing box.
questions.fun_fact: Actress Elizabeth Hurley became famous overnight after wearing that dress to a movie premiere.

questions.question: This is the bell Hidalgo rang in Dolores in 1810. Where does it hang today?
wrong_answers: At the parish church of Dolores Hidalgo
hints: It was moved to another city in 1896.
It's in Mexico City.
It hangs above the main balcony, facing the Zócalo.
questions.description: A bell that woke up a whole country, and not for Sunday Mass.
questions.fun_fact: Every September 15, the president rings it after giving the Grito.

questions.question: I'm spoken in Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca; my speakers can talk from hill to hill by whistling, and the healer María Sabina spoke me. Which language am I?
hints: I'm a tonal language: the pitch changes what a word means.
My region is in northern Oaxaca, by the Miguel Alemán dam and near the borders with Puebla and Veracruz.
My name sounds a bit like the city of Mazatlán, though I have nothing to do with Sinaloa.
questions.description: A language so musical it sometimes doesn't even need words.
questions.fun_fact: Mazatec whistling copies the language's tones, so whole sentences can be said without speaking a word.

questions.question: It’s the most widely spoken indigenous language in Mexico, and words like “chocolate,” “tomato” and “avocado” come from it. Which is it?
hints: The Mexica spoke it in Tenochtitlan.
Today more than 1.5 million people in Mexico speak it.
The word “Mexico” comes from it too.
questions.description: Every time you order a hot chocolate, you speak a little of this language without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: “Chicle” (gum), “cacahuate” (peanut) and “papalote” (kite) also come from Nahuatl.

questions.question: Purépecha is spoken around Lake Pátzcuaro. In which of these places is it NOT the traditional Indigenous language?
hints: Three of these places are in Michoacán.
The odd one out is on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.
In that place, people speak Zapotec, in Oaxaca.
questions.description: A language so unique it has no known relatives, not even distant cousins.
questions.fun_fact: Purépecha is a language isolate: no link to any other language has ever been proven.

questions.question: This green glazed clay pottery is typical of a town in Oaxaca. Which one?
hints: It's in the Central Valleys, very close to the city of Oaxaca.
Next to the town is an archaeological site linked to Monte Albán.
Its name starts with “Santa María”.
questions.description: Pots that look as fresh as a just-picked head of lettuce.
questions.fun_fact: Nearby towns have other specialties: Coyotepec is famous for its black pottery and Tilcajete for its alebrijes.

questions.question: In this sahumerio (incense burner), a tree resin is burned that gives off white, fragrant smoke. What is it called?
hints: It is used in ceremonies, limpias and Day of the Dead altars.
The Mexica already burned it for their gods.
Its name comes from the Nahuatl word “copalli”.
questions.description: The perfume of ancient temples, served on a glowing piece of charcoal.
questions.fun_fact: Chicle is also a tree resin, but people chew that one instead of burning it.

questions.question: In “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever,” Namor's underwater people come from a region of Mexico full of sinkholes like this one. Which region?
hints: The Maya lived there and still do.
It's a very flat region with no rivers on the surface.
Cancún and Chichén Itzá are there.
questions.description: Marvel went looking for villains at the bottom of the water… and found a very Mexican one.
questions.fun_fact: The Talokan actors spoke Yucatec Maya in the film, and Namor was played by Mexican actor Tenoch Huerta.

questions.question: It’s a Mayan language of northern Chiapas, from towns like Tila and Tumbalá, and a close relative of the language of the Palenque inscriptions. Which is it?
hints: Its speakers also live in parts of Tabasco.
It is one of the most spoken Mayan languages in Mexico, after Yucatec Maya, Tseltal and Tsotsil.
Its name has just one syllable and an apostrophe.
questions.description: A language that has been chatting next to some very famous pyramids for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Experts who read the Maya glyphs of Palenque use Ch’ol to better understand that ancient language.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a name of the woman who was Hernán Cortés's interpreter?
hints: The Spaniards gave her one of the names when they baptized her.
Another carries the Nahuatl suffix of respect “-tzin”.
The odd name out belonged to a daughter of Moctezuma.
questions.description: A woman with more names than someone with three social media accounts.
questions.fun_fact: Her name gave Mexico the word “malinchista”, used for someone who prefers anything foreign.

questions.question: The song “La Llorona” is said to come from the land of the women who wear this dress. What are they called?
hints: It's a son from southern Mexico.
It comes from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, in Oaxaca.
Frida Kahlo painted herself in this dress many times.
questions.description: A song so sad that even the skeletons in Coco sing it.
questions.fun_fact: In “Coco,” Mamá Imelda sings “La Llorona” on a stage in the Land of the Dead.

questions.question: The Hermès silk scarf is 90 cm (35 in) on each side, and Grace Kelly once wore one as a sling for a broken arm. Which country is the brand from?
hints: Hermès started in 1837 making harnesses and saddles for horses.
Its main store is on an elegant street in the country's capital.
That capital has a very famous iron tower.
questions.description: A little square of silk that costs more than plenty of coats.
questions.fun_fact: Hermès launched its first silk scarf in 1937, exactly 100 years after the company was founded.

questions.question: Look at this pyramid in the State of Mexico. Who built it?
hints: It's much older than Tenochtitlan.
When the Mexica arrived, the city had already been abandoned for centuries.
It's the Pyramid of the Sun.
questions.description: Climbing its steps already counts as your workout for the whole week.
questions.fun_fact: It was the Mexica who named Teotihuacan, “the place where the gods are born,” centuries after it was abandoned.

questions.question: Which of these peoples of Mexico did NOT have a writing system with glyphs?
hints: The other three left behind stelae, carved stones or codices.
The people you're looking for live in the mountains of Chihuahua.
They are famous for running huge distances in huaraches.
questions.description: Before text messages, there were messages carved in stone.
questions.fun_fact: The Rarámuri, or Tarahumara, are famous for races of many, many kilometers in which they kick a wooden ball.

questions.question: The Central de Abasto in Iztapalapa opens before dawn and gets trucks from all over the country. What is it?
hints: Many fondas and corner shops go there to stock up.
«Abasto» comes from «abastecer»: to supply what's needed.
They sell fruit, vegetables and meat by the ton.
questions.description: A place that wakes up before the roosters do.
questions.fun_fact: It's one of the biggest wholesale markets in the world, covering more than 300 hectares (about 740 acres).

questions.question: I was a ripe red jalapeño. They dried and smoked me until I was brown and wrinkly, and my smoky taste goes into creams and salsas. What am I?
hints: My name comes from Nahuatl and has to do with smoke.
I'm often sold in a can, in adobo sauce.
You can find mayonnaise with my flavor at the supermarket.
questions.description: A chile with a green past and a wrinkly present.
questions.fun_fact: “Chipotle” comes from the Nahuatl word chilpoctli, meaning “smoked chile.”

questions.question: Complete the Mexican saying: “Es bueno el ___, pero no tanto.” Which herb is missing?
hints: It's a green herb with delicate leaves.
Its dried seeds are also used as a spice.
It goes chopped with onion on top of tacos.
questions.description: Some advice about not overdoing it, kitchen edition.
questions.fun_fact: To some people cilantro tastes like soap, because of a gene they inherited.

questions.question: It's big, round and brown, and you put it in water with toothpicks so it sprouts. In an avocado, what is the «hueso»?
hints: A whole new tree can grow from it.
It sits right in the middle of the fruit.
Plants use it to make new plants.
questions.description: It's named after part of a skeleton, but it lives inside a fruit.
questions.fun_fact: An avocado tree grown from a «hueso» can take 5 to 13 years to give fruit.

questions.question: The Palacio de los Deportes, with its copper dome, was built for the 1968 Olympic Games. About how many people does it hold?
hints: It's an indoor venue, not an open-air soccer stadium.
It holds far more people than a movie theater, but far fewer than Estadio Azteca.
Think of a five-digit number that starts with 2.
questions.description: Here you've heard baskets, concerts and screaming fans; what you never hear is silence.
questions.fun_fact: Félix Candela and other architects designed its dome, and because of its shape and covering many people call it “el Domo de Cobre” (the Copper Dome).

questions.question: Look at this model of the Templo Mayor of the Mexica. How many temples did it have on top?
hints: Look closely at the top of the pyramid.
Each temple at the top was dedicated to a different god.
One was for the rain god and the other for the god of war.
questions.description: A stone building with a penthouse for gods.
questions.fun_fact: One temple was dedicated to Tláloc, god of rain, and the other to Huitzilopochtli, god of the sun and war.

questions.question: There's a stadium inside the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez: Formula 1 cars drive through it, and since 2023 it's named after an insurance company. What was it called before?
hints: It's famous for huge open-air concerts.
The Diablos Rojos del México used to play baseball there.
Its name had to do with the star that gives us daylight.
questions.description: A place where one day the engines roar and the next day a packed stadium roars along to the songs.
questions.fun_fact: At the Mexican Grand Prix, the drivers celebrate on the podium inside the stadium, surrounded by thousands of fans.

questions.question: The Torre Latinoamericana opened in 1956 in the Historic Center and stands on piles driven into soft ground. What made it famous in 1957 and 1985?
hints: Its engineers designed it with ideas that were very new for the time.
On September 19, 1985, many nearby buildings collapsed, but it stayed standing.
In Mexico they're called “sismos.”
questions.description: A skyscraper with nerves of steel, literally.
questions.fun_fact: From its lookout on the top floors you can see all of Mexico City and, on clear days, even the volcanoes.

questions.question: In which decade did Madonna wear her famous cone-shaped corset, designed by Jean Paul Gaultier, on tour?
hints: Madonna was already a worldwide star by then.
The tour was called “Blond Ambition”.
It started right at the beginning of that decade, the same year as the World Cup in Italy.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so pointy it almost needs a “Caution” sign.
questions.fun_fact: Gaultier said that as a boy he made a cone corset for his teddy bear, Nana.

questions.question: Look at this Olmec head: some weigh more than 20 tonnes (44,000 lb). What is it made of?
hints: It has lasted thousands of years without rotting or rusting.
It is a very hard, very heavy material.
It comes from what pours out of a volcano and then cools.
questions.description: A face so serious it hasn't smiled in about 3,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: The stone, a basalt, came from the Tuxtlas mountains, and the Olmecs moved it dozens of kilometers without using the wheel.

questions.question: These huge human figures, painted in red and black in a cave, have been a World Heritage Site since 1993. In which Mexican state are they?
hints: They are in a mountain range, in a state with lots of desert.
The state has a huge amount of coastline.
El Vizcaíno, where gray whales come every year, is nearby.
questions.description: Murals so old that their artists left no signature and no phone number.
questions.fun_fact: Missionaries heard a legend that the Cochimí people said the paintings had been made by giants.

questions.question: Dogs like this one, the breed of Dante in “Coco”, roam the gardens of the museum with the most works by Diego Rivera. In which part of Mexico City is it?
hints: The museum is in an old hacienda.
The area is famous for its canals.
That's where you ride a trajinera.
questions.description: A museum where the security guards don't have a single hair.
questions.fun_fact: The museum is named after Dolores Olmedo, a collector and friend of Diego Rivera, who also gathered many works by Frida Kahlo.

questions.question: This bronze Christ with open arms stands on top of a hill that many consider the center of Mexico. Which state is it in?
hints: It's a state in the Bajío region.
The hill is near Silao and León.
It's the state of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas.
questions.description: A statue with the best view in the country whose arms never get tired.
questions.fun_fact: The hill is called Cubilete because its shape looks like the cup used to shake dice.

questions.question: Look at this street sign from one of the longest avenues in Mexico City. Who is it named after?
wrong_answers: Those who fought in the Revolution
hints: It was a fight that began in the 19th century.
Hidalgo and Morelos were among them.
It began with the Grito de Dolores in 1810.
questions.description: An avenue so long that if you walk the whole thing, you arrive a year older.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City's first Metrobús line runs along Avenida Insurgentes, and it opened in 2005.

questions.question: The towns at the foot of this volcano lovingly call it “Don Goyo.” Where does that nickname come from?
questions.answer: From Saint Gregory, whose feast day brings offerings to it
wrong_answers: From Diego de Ordaz, the first Spaniard to climb it
From the “goyo, goyo” sound its steam vents make
From a president of Mexico who once visited it
hints: The nickname comes from a person's name.
In Mexico, “Goyo” is the usual nickname for a certain first name.
That name is Gregorio, and every March 12 the people of Santiago Xalitzintla climb up to celebrate it.
questions.description: A neighbor who smokes, rumbles now and then, and still everyone calls him “sir.”
questions.fun_fact: In Santiago Xalitzintla, tradition says Don Goyo shows up as a little old man to warn people when the volcano is about to get angry.

questions.question: The manatee, a chubby, calm plant-eater, lives in Chetumal Bay. It's also called a “… cow.” Fill in the blank.
hints: It always lives in the water.
It's called a cow because it spends the day eating plants, like a cow in a field.
It's a cow, but one that lives in the ocean.
questions.description: It grazes underwater all day and has never given a single glass of milk.
questions.fun_fact: Manatees can spend up to eight hours a day eating water plants.

questions.question: This is what the mangroves on the coasts of Nayarit, Tabasco and Yucatán look like. How do they help the coast when a hurricane hits?
questions.answer: They slow the waves and protect the coast
wrong_answers: They pull the rain out toward the sea
They warm the water and push storms away
They soak up the wind with their leaves
hints: Think about what their tangled roots do in the water.
Their roots hold the sand and mud of the shore in place.
Where they are cut down, the sea gets into seaside towns more easily.
questions.description: Trees that live with wet feet and never complain about their aching joints.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries with the most mangroves in the world, and Marismas Nacionales in Nayarit is one of the largest mangrove areas on the Pacific.

questions.question: This river takes in the waters of the Moctezuma, marks the border between Veracruz and Tamaulipas and reaches the Gulf next to Tampico. Which river is it?
hints: It flows into the Gulf of Mexico, on the northern part of the coast.
It gives its name to a town in Veracruz founded by the Spanish in the 16th century.
Its name starts with P, and it isn't the Papaloapan.
questions.description: A river that winds through the Huasteca and reaches the sea smelling of crab.
questions.fun_fact: The Pánuco basin begins far away, near the Valley of Mexico, and the water from the capital's deep drainage system reaches the sea through it.

questions.question: It was the largest lake in the Valley of Mexico, Tenochtitlan was founded on one of its islands, and a new airport was going to be built there. Which lake is it?
hints: Its water was salty.
It shares its name with a municipality in the State of Mexico.
The airport project was canceled in 2018, and today there is an ecological park there with its name.
questions.description: A lake so famous that it barely exists anymore, yet it keeps showing up in the news.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica built the Albarradón de Nezahualcóyotl, a dike about 16 km (10 miles) long, to keep the lake's salty water apart from the fresh water.

questions.question: With a needle, thread, scissors and a tape measure, I sew dresses to fit my customers. Who am I?
hints: I work with fabrics of many colors.
I often use a sewing machine.
If your dress is too big, I can fix it.
questions.description: A professional who knows exactly how big your waist is and never tells anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Coco Chanel started her career making hats before she became one of the most famous dressmakers in the world.

questions.question: In which of these states does the olive ridley turtle (golfina) NOT nest?
hints: Olive ridleys come ashore in huge groups called “arribadas”.
La Escobilla, one of the beaches with the most olive ridleys in the world, is in one of the wrong states.
Olive ridleys nest on Pacific beaches; the right answer faces the Caribbean.
questions.description: A turtle that shows up at the beach with thousands of friends and no invitation.
questions.fun_fact: During the “arribadas” at La Escobilla beach in Oaxaca, tens of thousands of olive ridleys can come ashore to lay eggs in just a few days.

questions.question: They're pink, they eat tiny shrimp, and their biggest nesting colony in Mexico is at Ría Lagartos. In which state?
hints: It's a state on the Gulf of Mexico coast.
It's on a peninsula famous for its cenotes.
Its capital is Mérida.
questions.description: Birds that stand on one leg and still never fall out of the photo.
questions.fun_fact: Flamingos are born gray: their pink color comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.

questions.question: Look at this: in Paracho, Michoacán, many craftspeople work at this trade. What do you call a person who does it?
hints: They work with wood, but they don't make furniture.
What they build has strings: guitars, violins, vihuelas.
The name comes from an old string instrument called the lute.
questions.description: A craft where patience is worth more than any tool in the workshop.
questions.fun_fact: Paracho is known as Mexico's guitar capital, and every year it holds a national guitar fair.

questions.question: Look at this photo: this singer grew up in Veracruz and brought back classic Latin American songs on her “Musas” albums. Who is she?
hints: She has won several Grammy Awards.
She sang “Remember Me” from “Coco” at the Oscars.
Her last name sounds French.
questions.description: A voice that treats old boleros like Grandma's treasures.
questions.fun_fact: Natalia Lafourcade recorded “Musas” with Los Macorinos, the guitarists who used to play with Chavela Vargas.

questions.question: “My dad was the Charro de Huentitán, I also sing rancheras with mariachi, and my nickname is a young horse.” Who am I?
hints: I'm from Jalisco.
My dad sang “Volver, volver”.
They call me “El Potrillo”.
questions.description: Like father, like son… or rather, like stallion, like foal.
questions.fun_fact: Alejandro Fernández made his stage debut as a child next to his dad, Vicente Fernández.

questions.question: It comes from Nahuatl and means to pick things up off the ground one by one. People who do it with recyclable trash have a name based on it. Which verb is it?
hints: You can do it with beans, coins or cans.
People who do it at garbage dumps have a special name for it.
It ends in “-nar”.
questions.description: The favorite verb of hens, can collectors and anyone looking for a lost earring in the carpet.
questions.fun_fact: “Pepenar” comes from the Nahuatl “pepena”, which means to choose or to pick up.

questions.question: The Tenayuca pyramid in the State of Mexico is surrounded by a wall of more than 130 stone serpents. What is this kind of wall called?
hints: It is a Nahuatl word made of two parts.
It joins the name of the animal carved on the wall with a word meaning row or wall.
The first part, “coatl”, means serpent.
questions.description: A fence so scary that even burglars would think twice, and it's only made of stone.
questions.fun_fact: Tenayuca was enlarged many times: it has several layers built one on top of another, like an onion.

questions.question: You're in a museum looking at Mexica clothing, like the tilmatli, a cloak knotted at the shoulder. Which of these words does NOT name a piece of clothing?
hints: One of them is something hard that you can't wear.
It is also one of the day signs of the calendar.
It is a flint knife.
questions.description: A Mexica fashion show, with a stone runway and dressing rooms without mirrors.
questions.fun_fact: The word “tilma” comes from “tilmatli”, as in Juan Diego's famous tilma in the Basilica of Guadalupe.

questions.question: The Nahuas' word for poetry was a pair of words: “in xóchitl in cuícatl”. What does it mean?
hints: One of the words comes from nature.
The other has to do with music.
“Xóchitl” is a name many girls in Mexico have today.
questions.description: When the Nahuas wanted to say something beautiful, they used two beautiful words at once.
questions.fun_fact: By contrast, “water and fire” (“in atl in tlachinolli”) was the Nahuatl way of saying war.

questions.question: If you look up the year Hernán Cortés reached the coast of Mexico in a codex, what name does it have in the Mexica calendar?
hints: Years were named with a number and one of four signs.
It was the same name as the date linked to Quetzalcoatl.
In Nahuatl it's “Ce Ácatl.”
questions.description: A date so full of prophecies that even astrologers would get nervous.
questions.fun_fact: The four signs that named the years were reed, flint, house, and rabbit, and they repeated in 52-year cycles.

questions.question: On shows like “Project Runway,” designers test a dress in cheap fabric before cutting the expensive one. What is this test version called?
hints: It's a usual step in haute couture workshops and fashion schools.
It's often made of muslin, a plain white cotton fabric.
In French, the word simply means “cloth.”
questions.description: The rough draft of a dress, so nobody ruins the million-dollar fabric.
questions.fun_fact: In some haute couture houses, a single dress goes through several toiles before it reaches the final fabric.

questions.question: This human skull, covered in turquoise mosaic, is a Mixtec-Mexica work now in the British Museum. Which god does it represent?
hints: In the myths he was the great rival of Quetzalcóatl.
He was the god of night and fate, and in pictures he is missing a foot.
His name in Nahuatl means “smoking mirror”.
questions.description: A skull that dressed up more than you did for a quinceañera.
questions.fun_fact: Its shiny eyes are pyrite set in rings of shell, and the inside is lined with leather so it could be worn as a mask or ornament.

questions.question: About 700 years ago, birds like this were raised in adobe pens in a desert city, and their feathers were traded far to the north. Which city was it?
hints: It was the great trading center of northern Mexico.
Its adobe houses had T-shaped doorways.
It is in Chihuahua, next to the town of Casas Grandes.
questions.description: A luxury feather farm in the middle of the desert: not even Instagram had this much color.
questions.fun_fact: At Paquimé, archaeologists found the remains of hundreds of macaws and the adobe nests where they were raised, with stone plugs at the entrance.

questions.question: Between 1917 and 1922, a Mexican anthropologist uncovered this temple in Teotihuacan's Ciudadela and studied the whole valley in depth. Who was he?
hints: He was a student of Franz Boas at Columbia University.
He's called the father of Mexican anthropology; he also studied Mexican migration to the United States.
In 1914 he found the first remains of the Templo Mayor, decades before its big excavation.
questions.description: Someone had to dust off the Feathered Serpent, and it wasn't done with a broom.
questions.fun_fact: His work “The Population of the Valley of Teotihuacan” (1922) was groundbreaking because it studied the ruins, the history and the lives of the people living there all together.

questions.question: The Mixtecs painted codices like this one. In which state is most of their homeland, the Mixteca?
hints: It's in the south of the country, on the Pacific Ocean.
The Zapotecs of Monte Albán lived there too.
It's famous for its moles, its mezcal and the Guelaguetza.
questions.description: Comic book artists who were drawing their stories centuries before newsstands existed.
questions.fun_fact: The Mixtecs call themselves Ñuu Savi, which means “people of the rain.”

questions.question: This hunched old man carved in stone, found in Teotihuacan, is one of the oldest gods of Mesoamerica. What is he the god of?
hints: The Mexica called him “the old god.”
The vessel he carries on his head was used in temple ceremonies.
In homes he was honored at the hearth.
questions.description: The oldest grandpa in Mesoamerica, and he still carries things on his head.
questions.fun_fact: His Nahuatl name, Huehueteotl, means “old god,” and he was already being carved in Cuicuilco more than 2,000 years ago.

questions.question: You're at the market in Juchitán and hear people speaking Zapotec. How many people in Mexico speak a Zapotec language?
hints: It's one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages in Mexico.
It's far more than the people of one town, but fewer than all of Oaxaca.
The number is close to half a million.
questions.description: A language that came down from the clouds and settled in the Isthmus for good.
questions.fun_fact: The Isthmus Zapotecs call themselves binnizá, which translates as “people of the clouds.”

questions.question: Every 52 years, the Mexica put out every fire, broke their pots and lit a new flame on the Cerro de la Estrella. What were they hoping for?
questions.answer: That the Sun would keep rising
wrong_answers: That rain would fall on the corn
To announce the start of a war
hints: On that day their two calendars lined up again.
Priests waited at night for a group of stars, the Pleiades, to cross the sky.
They feared that if the flame didn't catch, the night would never end.
questions.description: A birthday party held every 52 years that started with smashing the dishes.
questions.fun_fact: The last New Fire ceremony was held in 1507, just a few years before the Spanish arrived.

questions.question: I cover central and southern Mexico and part of Central America; in me people grew corn, played the ball game and used a 260-day calendar. What am I?
hints: The Olmecs, the Maya and the Mexica flourished here.
I am not the dry north of the hunter-gatherers.
My name means “Middle America.”
questions.description: A region so big it won't fit in one country or on one school map.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Mesoamerica” was proposed by the anthropologist Paul Kirchhoff in 1943.

questions.question: This gold jewel is part of the treasure found in 1932 in Tomb 7 at Monte Albán. Which archaeologist discovered it?
hints: He spent much of his life studying Oaxaca and the Mixtec codices.
He was the first director of the National Indigenous Institute.
His brother Antonio was a famous Mexican philosopher.
questions.description: A Mixtec treasure that hid in someone else's house: a Zapotec tomb.
questions.fun_fact: Tomb 7 was Zapotec, but the Mixtecs reused it and left hundreds of pieces of gold, silver, jade and turquoise inside.

questions.question: Which of these archaeological sites in Mexico is NOT a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
hints: The answer is a very popular archaeological site.
It sits right by the Caribbean Sea.
It's the walled Maya city facing the beach, in Quintana Roo.
questions.description: Even the most famous ruins can miss out on their international diploma.
questions.fun_fact: Tulum isn't on the UNESCO list, but the nearby Sian Ka'an reserve has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

questions.question: It's the first test model of an invention, built before mass production to find mistakes. What is it called?
hints: New car models get one before they reach the showrooms.
The Wright brothers built several before they managed to fly.
The word starts with “proto”, which means “first”.
questions.description: The dress rehearsal before an invention steps on stage.
questions.fun_fact: James Dyson says he made 5,127 prototypes before he got his bagless vacuum cleaner right.

questions.question: She was born in Mexicali and won vault bronze at the 2018 World Championships, Mexican gymnastics' first world medal. Who is she?
hints: Her sport uses a beam, bars and a vaulting table.
At Tokyo 2020 she finished fourth on vault, just short of the podium.
Her first name is the same as a famous voice assistant that answers questions.
questions.description: A girl from Baja California who flies higher than the price of tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: At Tokyo 2020, Alexa Moreno got the best Olympic result by a Mexican gymnast up to then: fourth place on vault.

previous.feedback: Source: the claim "Mexican gymnastics' first world medal" is wrong. Daniel Corral won pommel-horse silver at the 2013 World Championships, so Moreno's 2018 vault bronze was the first world medal for a Mexican woman (female gymnast). The source needs this correction ("first world medal for a Mexican woman gymnast"), and the translation should then follow it.

questions.question: Its baseball team has won the most Mexican Pacific League titles, it's a state capital, and summers top 45 °C (113 °F). Which city is it?
hints: It's in the northwest of the country, near the desert.
It's the capital of Sonora.
Its team is named after people who grow or sell oranges.
questions.description: A city so hot that even the baseballs break a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: The Naranjeros have also won the Caribbean Series, for example in 2014.

questions.question: In diving, the springboard is a flexible board that bounces. Which of these events does NOT exist at the Olympics?
hints: The springboard bounces; the platform is fixed like a floor.
The Olympics have eight diving events: four for men and four for women.
The platforms are the high ones; Olympic springboards are much lower down.
questions.description: The favorite sport of anyone who forgot what the pool ladder is for.
questions.fun_fact: Rommel Pacheco and Yahel Castillo won Mexico many international medals on the 3-meter springboard.

questions.question: Before he became a Mexican citizen and played for Mexico in the 2023 World Baseball Classic, what nationality was Randy Arozarena?
hints: He was born on an island.
Before reaching Mexico, he left his country in a small boat.
The capital of his home country is Havana.
questions.description: An outfielder with two homelands and a cannon for an arm.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, with the Tampa Bay Rays, Arozarena hit 10 home runs in a single postseason, a Major League record.

questions.question: This ballplayer from Chihuahua, nicknamed “the Mexican Babe Ruth,” chose to stay in Mexico rather than play in the major leagues. Who is he?
hints: He was a star in the 1960s and 1970s
He shone with the Sultanes de Monterrey in summer and the Naranjeros in winter
Hermosillo's baseball stadium carried his name for decades
questions.description: A hitter who sent the ball so far you had to take a bus to go get it.
questions.fun_fact: Counting both the summer and winter leagues, Héctor Espino is credited with more than 700 home runs in Mexican baseball.

questions.question: Which border city is Érik “El Terrible” Morales from, the first Mexican boxer to be world champion in four divisions?
hints: It's in the far northwest of the country
It's in Baja California
It's next door to San Diego
questions.description: A guy with a cartoon villain's nickname, but a real-life champion.
questions.fun_fact: His three fights against Marco Antonio Barrera are among the most famous rivalries in Mexican boxing.

questions.question: I'm a tiny self-portrait by Frida, painted on aluminum and surrounded by flowers painted on glass. The French government bought me in 1939. Which painting am I?
hints: I reached France through an exhibition organized by André Breton.
Today I hang in the Centre Pompidou in Paris.
My name is about what surrounds my portrait.
questions.description: A self-portrait that went to Paris and never wanted to come home.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first work by a 20th-century Mexican artist to be bought by the Louvre.

questions.question: These concrete columns and staircases, which lead nowhere, belong to a Surrealist garden in the middle of the jungle. Where is it?
hints: It was built by the English poet Edward James, a friend of the Surrealists.
It's in the Huasteca, surrounded by waterfalls and pools.
The garden is called Las Pozas.
questions.description: A garden where the stairs go up… to nowhere at all.
questions.fun_fact: Edward James filled the garden with orchids and even kept exotic animals there.

questions.question: Who is this Mexican painter, famous for her unibrow and the flowers in her hair?
hints: She lived in the Casa Azul in Coyoacán.
She married the muralist Diego Rivera.
She painted lots of self-portraits and appears in the movie “Coco”.
questions.description: Eyebrows so close they never fight.
questions.fun_fact: Frida didn't pluck her unibrow: she made it stand out in her self-portraits as part of who she was.

questions.question: Alberto Gironella, a painter of the Ruptura generation, spent years repainting and distorting one Spanish queen. Which painting did he take her from?
wrong_answers: “The Family of Charles IV,” by Goya
hints: The original portrait hangs in the Prado Museum.
The original painter worked at the court of Philip IV.
He is the same painter who made “Las Meninas.”
questions.description: A queen who never asked for this many visits from the painter.
questions.fun_fact: Gironella also made collages with bottle caps and was a friend of the filmmaker Luis Buñuel.

questions.question: My painted walls sleep in the jungle. Rina Lazo, a Guatemalan painter and Diego Rivera's assistant, copied me life-size for the National Museum of Anthropology. What place am I?
hints: I am a Maya city.
I am in Chiapas, near the Usumacinta River.
My name means “painted walls” in Maya.
questions.description: A place that has a life-size twin in the big city.
questions.fun_fact: Rina Lazo also painted “Venerable abuelo maíz” (Venerable Grandfather Corn), the mural in the Maya Hall of the National Museum of Anthropology.

questions.question: A Mexican artist sliced a car like this one lengthwise, took out the middle strip and joined it back together, narrower. Who was he?
hints: The work is called “La DS”, and he showed it in Paris in 1993.
He also made a ping-pong table with a pond in the middle.
He shares a surname with a great muralist from Jalisco.
questions.description: A car that went on a diet… a very serious one.
questions.fun_fact: At the 1993 Venice Biennale, Gabriel Orozco showed an empty shoebox lying on the floor.

questions.question: These insects live on the nopal cactus and give a red dye that was worth a fortune in colonial times. Which state was its great producer?
hints: The dye is called grana cochinilla, or cochineal.
It was New Spain's second most valuable export, after silver.
It's the state of alebrijes and the Guelaguetza.
questions.description: Tiny bugs that dress in white on the outside and in red on the inside.
questions.fun_fact: Cochineal is still used to color some yogurts, candies and lipsticks red.

questions.question: Tradition says this image appeared on Juan Diego's tilma. What flowers did he carry wrapped inside it?
hints: They were flowers that shouldn't grow in December on a dry hill.
He picked them on Tepeyac hill to take to the bishop.
They're the red flowers people give on Valentine's Day.
questions.description: A miracle that arrived wrapped like a last-minute gift.
questions.fun_fact: The original tilma is kept in the Basilica of Guadalupe, one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world.

questions.question: This Mexican cactus is called “viejito” (little old man) for its long white hairs. What are they for?
questions.answer: To protect it from sun and cold
hints: It lives in dry, very sunny ravines in Hidalgo.
The hairs work like a blanket wrapped around the whole cactus.
It's like wearing a cap and sunscreen at the same time.
questions.description: A cactus that refuses to dye its gray hair.
questions.fun_fact: The viejito grows very slowly, but in the wild it can grow taller than 10 m (33 ft).

questions.question: It's green, has a huge pit, and Mexico grows more of it than any other country in the world. What fruit is it?
hints: Inside, it's soft and creamy.
People spread it on tortas and tostadas.
It's what guacamole is made from.
questions.description: A fruit so Mexican it has fans all over the planet.
questions.fun_fact: The Hass variety, the best-selling avocado in the world, came from a single tree planted in California in the 1920s.

questions.question: Corn, beans and squash are planted together: the beans climb the corn stalks and the squash covers the ground. What is this field called?
hints: It's a way of farming that comes from Mesoamerica.
Its name comes from Nahuatl.
It's the word farmers use for their cornfield.
questions.description: Three plants that share a home and actually get along.
questions.fun_fact: Corn, beans and squash grown together are also known as “the three sisters.”

questions.question: In what year did Café Tacvba's song “Eres” come out?
hints: Phones already had cameras, but the iPhone didn't exist yet.
It was on the album “Cuatro caminos,” which came after “Revés/Yo soy.”
It was in the early 2000s, shortly after the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: The song that plays at weddings right when your uncle gets all emotional.
questions.fun_fact: “Eres” was written by Emmanuel “Meme” del Real, Café Tacvba's keyboard player.

questions.question: We're two sisters born in Lake Charles, Louisiana, we mix pop with country and sing “Lo aprendí de ti.” What group are we?
hints: We started singing as little girls in the United States.
Our name combines the first names of the two sisters.
Our names are Hanna and Ashley.
questions.description: Two sisters, one mic each, and zero fights over the bathroom… in theory.
questions.fun_fact: The name Ha*Ash comes from the first letters of Hanna and Ashley Pérez.

questions.question: Before going solo and starring in “Marimar”, which youth group did Thalía sing in?
hints: It started in the early eighties as a kids' group tied to TV.
Paulina Rubio and Sasha Sokol also sang in it.
They recorded “Tú y yo somos uno mismo”.
questions.description: Before she was queen of the telenovelas, she had to practice her dance steps on another stage.
questions.fun_fact: Before Timbiriche, Thalía already sang as a little girl in the kids' group Din-Din.

questions.question: Thomas Jefferson is said to have owned one of the first swivel chairs. In which century did he use it?
hints: Jefferson was one of the founders of the United States.
He is said to have used it while the US Declaration of Independence was being written.
It was around the same time as the French Revolution.
questions.description: The favorite chair of anyone who likes to go around in circles without getting up to work.
questions.fun_fact: Charles Darwin put wheels on his chair to move faster between his specimens, an early ancestor of the office chair.

questions.question: Finish the name: Café Tacvba's singer has called himself Cosme and Anónimo, but his real name is Rubén…
hints: He is one of the founders of the band from Ciudad Satélite.
His last name isn't shared by any other member of Café Tacvba.
His last name starts with “Al” and ends in “-rrán.”
questions.description: A singer who changes his name more often than you change your profile picture.
questions.fun_fact: Rubén Albarrán has used a huge number of stage names over Café Tacvba's career.

questions.question: Which song was the big 1980s hit of Flans, the trio of Ilse, Ivonne and Mimí?
hints: It was written by Nacho Cano of the Spanish band Mecano.
Its lyrics tell someone to stop policing how she dresses and who she goes out with.
The title starts with “No.”
questions.description: Three girls, same dress, same hairdo: not even their moms could tell them apart.
questions.fun_fact: Nacho Cano of Mecano wrote “No controles,” and in Mexico it became a Flans anthem.

questions.question: Born in Mexico City in the '80s, with acoustic guitar and harmonica, its manifesto written by Rockdrigo González. Which movement is it?
hints: Its musicians played in small venues, plazas and even on the street.
Its name shows off a simple, almost primitive kind of music.
In Spanish, its name is the word used for paintings on cave walls.
questions.description: Rock with no cables, no lights and no cash for the amp.
questions.fun_fact: Rockdrigo González was nicknamed “el Profeta del Nopal” (the Prophet of the Nopal).

questions.question: You're eating a paste in Real del Monte, Hidalgo. Miners from Cornwall, England, brought it there. In which century did they arrive?
hints: Mexico was already an independent country when they arrived.
They came a few years after the War of Independence ended.
It was in the 1820s.
questions.description: A snack that crossed the ocean in a few miners' lunchboxes.
questions.fun_fact: Decades later, the Cornish mining community also brought soccer to Pachuca, which is why it's called the “cradle of Mexican soccer.”

questions.question: Enmoladas are tortillas filled with chicken and covered in mole. Which little seeds are traditionally sprinkled on top?
hints: They're small, flat seeds with a pale color.
You also see them on top of lots of hamburger buns.
In Mexico they're called ajonjolí.
questions.description: The fancy cousins of enchiladas, all dressed up for the party.
questions.fun_fact: Sesame isn't native to the Americas: it came to Mexico with the Spanish, and today mole is never without it.

questions.question: In Yucatán, mucbipollo is made for Hanal Pixán; its name is half Maya, half Spanish. What does it mean?
hints: The Maya part of the name is about how it's cooked.
It's cooked in a very special oven that isn't in the kitchen.
The oven is a hole in the ground covered with earth.
questions.description: A giant tamal cooked by a most mysterious method.
questions.fun_fact: Mucbipollo is cooked in a “pib,” the same underground oven that gives cochinita pibil its name.

questions.question: It has corn, carrots, zucchini and a good marrow bone, and it's called caldo de res. Which animal does carne de res come from?
hints: It's a big farm animal.
It eats grass all day in the fields.
It also gives us milk.
questions.description: The soup that cures every ache, even a broken heart.
questions.fun_fact: Marrow is the soft part inside the bone, and lots of people fight over it in the soup.

questions.question: Mole de olla is a thick, spicy broth that is very popular in central Mexico. What does it NOT have in it?
hints: It's a classic at the fondas and the comida corrida of central Mexico.
It's served with tortillas, lime and chopped onion.
What it doesn't have lives in the sea.
questions.description: A mole so humble it doesn't need a metate: a big pot does the job.
questions.fun_fact: Mole de olla often gets xoconostle, a sour prickly pear that gives it a tangy kick.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what are these carnival dancers from Morelos called?
hints: They dance with little hops to the beat of a brass band.
They wear masks with beards that point upward and huge hats.
They are the symbol of the carnival in Tepoztlán, Yautepec and Tlayacapan.
questions.description: Guys who jump so much they should get paid as gym trainers.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the chinelos began as Indigenous people's way of mocking the bearded Spaniards who wouldn't let them celebrate carnival.

questions.question: I live in huge vitroleros, I'm served over ice, and I come in jamaica, horchata or tamarind. What am I?
hints: People drink me ice-cold, especially when it's hot out.
El Chavo del 8 sold me at a stand in the vecindad.
I'm made with water, sugar and fruit, flowers or seeds.
questions.description: After three elotes and a cotton candy, the fair still has something to keep you company.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican horchata is made with rice and cinnamon, while other countries make it with other seeds.

questions.question: In charrería, Mexico's national sport, which animals take part in the events?
hints: It's held in a lienzo charro, a dirt arena.
Charros rope and ride big ranch animals.
One is what the charro rides; the other gives milk or meat.
questions.description: The national sport where the hat matters as much as the score.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, UNESCO named charrería part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: At the Veracruz and Mazatlán carnivals, “carros alegóricos” parade by. Why are they called “alegóricos”?
questions.answer: Because they represent a theme or an idea
wrong_answers: Because a Mr. Alegre invented them
hints: The name has nothing to do with being happy, even though it sounds like “alegría”.
An allegory is a way of showing something through figures and symbols.
Each float tells something: a story, a character or the carnival's theme.
questions.description: A car that needs no driver's license, just tons of glitter.
questions.fun_fact: The Veracruz Carnival boasts of being “the happiest in the world” and lasts several days, with parades along the malecón (seafront).

questions.question: In California, seismologist Charles Richter created the magnitude scale that bears his name. In what year?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was before the Second World War.
It was in the middle of the 1930s.
questions.description: A scale for telling how hard the ground shook, without exaggerating like your uncle does.
questions.fun_fact: Today Mexico's National Seismological Service uses the “moment magnitude,” created in 1979, because it measures big earthquakes better.

questions.question: On September 19, 1985, a magnitude 8.1 earthquake brought down buildings in Mexico City. What has been held every September 19 since then?
wrong_answers: A day off school and work
hints: An alarm sounds in many cities at the same time.
Schools and offices go out into the street to practice.
It's a rehearsal so you know what to do if a real one hits.
questions.description: A day on the Mexican calendar nobody forgets, even if they try.
questions.fun_fact: The Torre Latinoamericana, one of the city's tallest buildings back then, came through the 1985 earthquake still standing.

questions.question: When rain fell on the jungle, the ancient Maya thanked a god for it. Which one?
hints: He was painted holding a stone axe or a lightning bolt.
Masks of him with a long, curved nose cover the walls of buildings at Uxmal and Kabah.
His name is short and starts with “Ch”.
questions.description: A god nobody wanted to upset during planting season.
questions.fun_fact: At the Codz Poop in Kabah, Yucatán, an entire front wall is covered with hundreds of Chaac masks.

questions.question: Watch the video: in rainy season, many streets in Mexico flood like this. What clogs the storm drains and makes it worse?
hints: It's something you can prevent yourself.
It should end up in a trash can, but sometimes it doesn't make it.
Bags, bottles and wrappers.
questions.description: When the sky gets generous and the street turns into a swimming pool.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City is built on an old lake bed, which is why rainwater has such a hard time draining away.

questions.question: For the first time, a strong earthquake hit Mexico City on the very anniversary of the 1985 quake. In what year?
hints: Just days earlier that same month, an even stronger quake had struck off the coast of Chiapas.
It had a magnitude of 7.1, and its epicenter was between Puebla and Morelos.
It came exactly 32 years after the 1985 earthquake.
questions.description: A date in Mexico known for celebrating its birthday with a little shaking.
questions.fun_fact: By pure coincidence, another strong earthquake hit Mexico on September 19 in 2022.

questions.question: On April 8, 2024, the shadow of the total eclipse first reached land at a Mexican Pacific port famous for its malecón and its carnival. Which one?
hints: It faces the southern tip of Baja California.
It's in Sinaloa.
Its name comes from Nahuatl and has to do with deer.
questions.description: The day the Sun took a few minutes off and half of Mexico put on funny glasses.
questions.fun_fact: In Mazatlán, total darkness lasted about 4 minutes and 20 seconds.

questions.question: You can see your breath, you put on a jacket and scarf, and someone says “¡qué friazo!”. What does it mean?
wrong_answers: That the air is very dry
hints: The ending “-azo” makes things bigger.
It's like “calorón”, but the other way around.
It's much more than a pleasant little chill.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a punch but doesn't hurt.
questions.fun_fact: In winter, temperatures in the mountains of Chihuahua can drop below −20 °C (−4 °F).

questions.question: Watch the video: you're on a beach like this one and the tsunami alarm goes off. Where should you go?
questions.answer: To a hill or high ground
wrong_answers: To the shore, to watch the waves
To the pier, next to the boats
hints: The danger comes from the sea.
Tsunami waves can reach far inland.
Follow the “evacuation route” signs that lead uphill.
questions.description: A beach tip that matters more than sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: Before a tsunami, the sea sometimes pulls back suddenly and leaves the beach bare: that's a signal to run.

questions.question: I am Antoni Gaudí's great work in Barcelona, and construction on me began in 1882. What am I?
hints: I am a basilica full of pointed towers.
I have been under construction for more than 140 years.
My name refers to Jesus, Mary and Joseph.
questions.description: The world's most patient building site: not even traffic jams last this long.
questions.fun_fact: Gaudí is buried in the crypt of the Sagrada Família itself.

questions.question: During a heat wave, which of these is NOT a tip from Protección Civil?
questions.answer: Leave your pet in the closed car
wrong_answers: Drink water even if you're not thirsty
Stay out of the midday sun
hints: Three of them help you stay cool.
One would make someone overheat very fast.
A car in the sun turns into an oven within minutes.
questions.description: When the May sun decides to stay over for several days in a row.
questions.fun_fact: On a hot day, the inside of a closed car in the sun can go above 50 °C (122 °F) in less than an hour.

questions.question: In much of Mexico, heavy afternoon downpours are typical of one time of year. Which one?
hints: In those months the countryside turns green and the milpa grows.
It overlaps with hurricane season.
It starts soon after the hottest days of May.
questions.description: When the sky turns on the faucet at five in the afternoon, right on time.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico this season is called «las aguas» (the waters): when the downpours begin, people say «ya entraron las aguas».

questions.question: In the Maya Popol Vuh, Huracán, Heart of Sky, sent a great flood to wipe out some failed first humans. Which ones?
hints: They could talk, but had no souls and didn't remember their makers.
According to the book, their descendants are the monkeys.
They were made of something that comes from trees.
questions.description: A wind god who had no patience for prototypes.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Popol Vuh, the humans who finally turned out right were made from corn dough.

questions.question: “Bésame mucho” became so famous that a British band played it at a 1962 audition, before they were stars. Which band?
hints: There were four of them.
They came from a port city in the north of England.
One of them was Paul McCartney.
questions.description: A song so romantic it crossed the Atlantic without a passport.
questions.fun_fact: Consuelo Velázquez said she wrote it very young, before she had even had her first kiss.

questions.question: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, Felipe “el Tibio” Muñoz won gold in the 200 m breaststroke. How old was he?
hints: He won at home, in the Olympic pool built for those Games.
His gold is still Mexico's only Olympic medal of that color in swimming.
He was born in 1951.
questions.description: Not cold, not hot: this swimmer was just like his nickname.
questions.fun_fact: He was called “Tibio” (lukewarm) because his dad was from Aguascalientes (“hot waters”) and his mom from Río Frío (“cold river”).

questions.question: Walking through Morelia, you see a plaque to the “Niños de Morelia,” children who arrived by ship under Lázaro Cárdenas. What war were they fleeing?
hints: They came from Europe.
They traveled on a French ship called the “Mexique.”
In their country, the Republicans were fighting Franco's side.
questions.description: A very long boat trip for passengers in short pants.
questions.fun_fact: There were about 456 children, and many of them stayed in Mexico for the rest of their lives.

questions.question: The ocelot nearly disappeared from Mexico in the 1960s and 1970s. Why was it hunted?
hints: It had nothing to do with food.
The same thing happened to the jaguar.
Its spots ended up on coats.
questions.description: A wild cat that sees better at night than you do with glasses on.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1960s, hundreds of thousands of ocelot furs were sold around the world every year.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT mentioned in the circle song “Naranja dulce”?
hints: It's sung in a circle, holding hands.
One line asks for something very lovingly.
At the end you sing “adiós, señora, yo ya me voy” (goodbye, ma'am, I'm leaving now).
questions.description: A playground circle song so old your grandparents already knew it by heart.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the song, someone goes off “a su casita de sololoy,” a word that comes from “celluloid,” an old kind of plastic.

questions.question: On a Day of the Dead ofrenda, toys are set out for certain departed souls. What are they traditionally called?
hints: They are the smallest visitors to the ofrenda.
They get sweets, milk and toys because they died as children.
Their name brings to mind little beings with wings and halos.
questions.description: The ofrenda guests with the sweetest menu in the whole graveyard.
questions.fun_fact: On many ofrendas, the food for the angelitos has no chile, so it isn't too spicy for the children.

questions.question: These jets of glowing gas shot out by newborn stars carry the surnames of an American astronomer and a Mexican one. Who is the Mexican?
hints: He worked at the Tonantzintla Observatory in Puebla.
He discovered them almost at the same time as George Herbig, in the early 1950s.
He was married to the writer Elena Poniatowska.
questions.description: Baby stars throwing tantrums, one jet at a time.
questions.fun_fact: In 1971, Guillermo Haro founded the National Institute of Astrophysics, Optics and Electronics (INAOE) in Tonantzintla.

questions.question: Pastel fridges with rounded corners, radios with knobs and new record players that copy the 1950s. What style is this?
hints: It looks to the past, not to the future.
It's like your grandparents' clothes, but freshly made.
Its name comes from Latin and means “backwards”.
questions.description: Something new that dresses up as old to look more interesting.
questions.fun_fact: “Retro” comes from the Latin word for “backwards”, as in “retrospective” or “retrograde”.

questions.question: The Mondragón rifle, one of the world's first semi-automatic rifles, was adopted by the Mexican army. In which period?
hints: It was made in Switzerland for the Mexican army.
It was in the early 20th century.
It was adopted in 1908.
questions.description: A Mexican invention that was ahead of its time and ended up flying over Europe.
questions.fun_fact: In World War I, Germany used Mondragón rifles on some of its airplanes.

questions.question: Jalisco proudly calls itself the birthplace of mariachi. Of today's mariachi instruments, which was the last to join, in the 20th century?
hints: It became popular in the era of radio and Mexican cinema.
At first, some traditional musicians thought it was far too loud.
It's the only one of the four without strings.
questions.description: A serenade that kept getting more and more guests showing up over the years.
questions.fun_fact: Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán, one of the most famous mariachi groups in the world, helped make the trumpet a must in mariachi.

questions.question: It has a mast, moves only with the wind, and cartoon pirates sail on it. It's also on Campeche's coat of arms. What is it?
hints: It travels across the sea.
It needs no gasoline and no oars.
It has big pieces of cloth that fill up with air.
questions.description: The favorite ride of anyone with an eye patch and a parrot on their shoulder.
questions.fun_fact: Campeche put ships on its coat of arms because its port was one of the most important in New Spain.

questions.question: Look at the area marked on the map. Until 2016 it had a different official name. What was it?
hints: It's the seat of the country's government.
Today it's called Mexico City.
Its initials are D.F.
questions.description: A place that changed its name in 2016, like someone trying out a new haircut.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2016 its official name has been Mexico City, but many people still say “el De Efe.”

questions.question: These towers are the great symbol of a Mexican city. Which city is it?
hints: It is one of the biggest cities in Mexico.
Its people are called tapatíos.
The Chivas play there.
questions.description: Two towers so pointy they look like pencils fresh out of the sharpener.
questions.fun_fact: The cathedral's original towers fell in an earthquake in 1818, and the pointy ones you see today were built afterward.

questions.question: Look at this bread topped with candied fruit. Who is it named after?
hints: They arrive on a camel, an elephant and a horse.
There are three of them, and they brought gifts to the baby Jesus.
Their names are Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
questions.description: A bread so big the whole family lines up with a knife in hand.
questions.fun_fact: People say the candied fruit on the rosca stands for the jewels on the kings' crowns.

questions.question: On Mexican highways, what is the “caseta”?
questions.answer: The place where you pay to use the highway
wrong_answers: The place where you fill up with gas
The place where you wait for the bus
The place where you stop to enjoy the view
hints: You always have to stop there, even if just for a moment.
A TAG is a sticker that lets you drive through without taking out your wallet.
It's also called a “caseta de cobro”.
questions.description: Family road trip: three hours of highway and forty rounds of “are we there yet?”
questions.fun_fact: Toll highways are called “autopistas de cuota” because you pay a “cuota” (fee); the ones that don't charge are called “libres” (free).

questions.question: The ride app Cabify came to Mexico around 2012, long before DiDi. In what country was it founded?
hints: It isn't from the Americas.
Its home city has a very famous soccer team that plays in white.
It was born in Madrid.
questions.description: An app that takes you everywhere, but first had to make the trip from its own home.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico was one of the first countries outside its home country where Cabify started running.

questions.question: In Mexico City, I hold the graves of Diego Rivera, Siqueiros, Agustín Lara and Rosario Castellanos. What is my name?
questions.answer: La Rotonda de las Personas Ilustres
hints: I opened in the 19th century.
Mexicans who stood out in art, science or politics are buried here.
My old name only mentioned “hombres ilustres” (illustrious men).
questions.description: The most exclusive neighborhood in the capital: to move in, you need a very impressive résumé.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2003 it was called the Rotonda de los Hombres Ilustres; the name was changed so it would include women too.

questions.question: The clay catrinas of Capula, Michoacán, copy the “Calavera Garbancera,” a famous print. When was that print published?
hints: It was printed on cheap sheets sold in the street.
It made fun of people who showed off European clothes and hid their roots.
It's from the time the Mexican Revolution began.
questions.description: A clay lady so elegant she never leaves the house without her huge feathered hat.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Catrina” came later from Diego Rivera, when he painted her in his mural “Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central.”

questions.question: Raymond Loewy, the great industrial designer, created the colors of this US presidential plane. In which country was he born?
hints: He fought in the First World War before he emigrated.
He arrived in New York in 1919.
He was born in Paris.
questions.description: The man who dressed the most important plane in the world in blue-and-white pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Loewy also redesigned the Shell logo and the Coca-Cola soda fountain dispenser.

questions.question: In “Coco,” Miguel is trapped in the Land of the Dead. Before what moment must he return so he doesn't stay there forever?
hints: He only has one night.
As time passes, Miguel slowly turns into a skeleton.
He must get back before the sun comes up.
questions.description: A boy allowed to visit his great-great-grandparents, but with a curfew.
questions.fun_fact: To go back, Miguel needs a blessing from a family member.

questions.question: It has blenders lined up and mountains of oranges and carrots, and serves you a glass made on the spot. What kind of shop is it?
hints: There's almost always one in the markets.
What they sell there comes in a glass, not on a plate.
Its name comes from what they squeeze there.
questions.description: Oranges go in whole and come out as breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican juguerías will offer you your juice “con todo y huevo crudo” (with a raw egg in it), an old habit for a hearty breakfast.

questions.question: This Mexican soda has no alcohol, is dark red, and its label says “Señorial”. Which drink inspired it?
hints: The original drink is for grown-ups.
That original drink is made with red wine and fruit.
That drink comes from Spain.
