questions.description: A soda with manners so fine it even earned itself a fancy last name.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it's called sangria, this soda is for the whole family: it doesn't have a single drop of wine.

questions.question: I'm a cool drink from Colima and Jalisco, made with toasted, ground chan seeds and sweetened with piloncillo syrup. What am I?
hints: People drink me ice-cold on hot afternoons.
My seeds look like chia and come from a wild plant.
My name is the Spanish word for a baseball bat.
questions.description: A drink so local that even the state next door needs it explained.
questions.fun_fact: Chan is a relative of chia, and its seeds also turn jelly-like when they get wet.

questions.question: Look at this little clay jarrito. What drinks is it traditionally used for in Mexico?
questions.answer: Hot drinks, like café de olla
wrong_answers: Fizzy sodas, like the bottled ones
Iced licuados, like a strawberry one
Milkshakes with ice cream, like vanilla
hints: It's sold at craft markets, next to the clay pots.
It's the classic cup at fondas and tamal stands.
One of those drinks is made with cinnamon and piloncillo.
questions.description: A cup so traditional it still smells like Grandma's kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Many people say café de olla tastes better in a clay jarro because the clay gives it an earthy flavor.

questions.question: On the night of December 31, many Mexicans put a coin or a bill somewhere and keep it there all night so they never run out of money. Where?
hints: You carry it with you while you dance at the party.
It's closer to the floor than to your head.
Your socks go there too.
questions.description: A money plan for the whole year that you won't find in any economics book.
questions.fun_fact: It's just one of many New Year's rituals in Mexico, along with eating 12 grapes, sweeping the house and walking around the block with a suitcase.

questions.question: The palm of your hand itches. The belief says that if it's one hand, it's coming to you, and if it's the other, it's leaving. What is it?
hints: This belief is also told in many other countries.
That's why some people are happy to scratch their hand.
You count it in pesos.
questions.description: An itch that Grandma reads better than any skin doctor.
questions.fun_fact: Which hand brings and which takes away depends on the family: in some homes the left hand receives, in others the right.

questions.question: It's made to Saint Jude or the Virgin, and many fulfill it by walking to the shrine or arriving on their knees. What is a manda?
questions.answer: A promise in exchange for a favor
wrong_answers: An order given by the parish priest
A prayer said nine days in a row
hints: First you ask for something, and then you keep your word.
People make one when someone is sick or has a big problem.
If the saint grants you the miracle, you do what you promised.
questions.description: A custom that leaves more than a few knees begging for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Every December, millions of pilgrims arrive at the Basilica of Guadalupe, many of them to fulfill a manda.

questions.question: Grandma rubs your belly with oil, pulls the skin on your back until it “pops” and gives you some tea. What is all that for?
hints: It's one of the most common ailments in children, and many families treat it at home.
You can tell because you feel heavy, with a bloated belly and no appetite.
It hits whoever ate too much or ate something heavy.
questions.description: One of Grandma's recipes you won't find in any medical book.
questions.fun_fact: Pulling the skin on the back is called “tronar el empacho”, and many grandmothers swear the snapping sound means it's cured.

questions.question: After singing Las Mañanitas, everyone shouts “¡Que le muerda, que le muerda!” (“Bite it!”). What does the birthday person have to bite?
hints: It's something sweet, and in the end every guest wants a piece.
Someone almost always pushes the person's head in, and they end up with a messy nose.
It has candles and frosting.
questions.description: The moment at the party when everyone pulls out their phone to record.
questions.fun_fact: Pushing the birthday person's face into the frosting is so typical in Mexico that many bite with their eyes closed, just in case.

questions.question: Many Mexican town plazas have a kiosco in the middle. What traditionally goes on there on Sundays?
hints: Many people stroll in circles around it in the evening.
That's why its floor is raised, like a stage.
You hear drums, trumpets and tubas.
questions.description: A little house with a roof and no walls where the whole town meets without sending invitations.
questions.fun_fact: Many of Mexico's kioscos were built in the late 1800s and early 1900s, in the time of Porfirio Díaz, following European fashion.

questions.question: You go up to the rooftop and see a cement basin with a ridged board for scrubbing clothes by hand. What is it called?
hints: Before washing machines, almost every house had one.
There's usually a clothesline next to it.
You wash things there, but not the dishes.
questions.description: An arm workout that came free with the house.
questions.fun_fact: In many old vecindades the lavaderos were shared, and neighbors gathered there to chat while they scrubbed.

questions.question: In September 1910, Porfirio Díaz organized huge celebrations all over Mexico. What were they celebrating?
wrong_answers: The victory of Cinco de Mayo
hints: It was a round-number anniversary.
The celebrations lasted the whole month, and guests came from many countries.
It has to do with the Grito de Dolores.
questions.description: Don Porfirio never missed a good party, especially one he threw himself.
questions.fun_fact: The Angel of Independence on Paseo de la Reforma was unveiled for those celebrations, on September 16, 1910.

questions.question: During the Porfiriato, peons bought on credit at the tienda de raya and ended up in debt. Who owned that store?
hints: The owner profited twice: from the peons' work and from their shopping.
Sometimes the peons were paid in tokens that could only be spent at that store.
He was the patrón, the boss of the whole estate.
questions.description: Buying on credit sounded great, until the bill got passed down from parents to kids.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's 1917 Constitution banned paying workers in tokens or vouchers and forcing them to shop at the boss's stores.

questions.question: You're in the Sierra Tarahumara and a Rarámuri runner takes pinole out of his bag. What does he use it for?
questions.answer: To drink with water for energy
wrong_answers: To heal blisters on his feet
To paint his face before running
To light a campfire at night
hints: Long before the Spanish arrived, travelers and messengers carried it.
It's made from toasted, ground corn, sometimes with cinnamon and piloncillo.
It's mixed with water and drunk or eaten.
questions.description: In the sierra, a shoulder bag is pantry, first-aid kit and toolbox all at once.
questions.fun_fact: The word «pinole» comes from the Nahuatl «pinolli», meaning toasted corn flour.

questions.question: I'm a very elegant skull with a hat of flowers and feathers, and you see me on altars and in parades in early November. Who am I?
hints: I appear at the holiday when people remember those who have passed away.
Lots of people paint their faces to look like me.
José Guadalupe Posada was the first to draw me.
questions.description: Nothing but bones, yet always dressed to the nines.
questions.fun_fact: Posada called her “La Calavera Garbancera,” and it was Diego Rivera who made her famous as the Catrina.

questions.question: What are the feather-crowned dancers called who play a mandolin made from an armadillo shell?
hints: They dance a lot at the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
On their ankles they wear seeds that rattle with every step.
Their name comes from “concha,” as that shell is called.
questions.description: Feathers, rattles and feet that never get tired.
questions.fun_fact: The rattling seeds on their ankles are called ayoyotes, and they are the shells of a tree’s fruit.

questions.question: This Nahuatl word names a bird, and its final “tl” became “te” in Mexican Spanish. What animal is a “tecolotl”?
hints: It eats mice and insects.
It is a bird of the night.
It can turn its head almost all the way around.
questions.description: A word that moved into Spanish and lost its tail along the way.
questions.fun_fact: Ajolote, chocolate, tomate and aguacate also lost their Nahuatl “tl” in Spanish, yet English kept it in “axolotl”.

questions.question: It's one of the 20 day signs of the Mexica calendar. What does “itzcuintli” mean?
hints: It's the tenth of the 20 day signs.
It's an animal people keep as a pet.
It's part of the name of the breed of Dante, Miguel's companion in “Coco.”
questions.description: A stone calendar with more animals than a zoo.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica believed a dog helped souls cross a river to reach Mictlán, the land of the dead.

questions.question: Look at this fruit: Mexico grows it mostly in one southeastern state full of rivers and rainforest. Which one?
hints: It lies on the Gulf of Mexico.
The Olmec culture flourished there.
Its capital is Villahermosa.
questions.description: A fruit that is the grandfather of every chocolate bar.
questions.fun_fact: Tabasco produces more than half of all the cacao grown in Mexico.

questions.question: I'm a red and white soup can. In 1962 an artist painted me 32 times and I became art. Which art movement am I a symbol of?
hints: This movement turned things from the supermarket and TV into art.
It began in Britain and the United States in the 1950s and 1960s, and also used comics and famous faces like Marilyn Monroe.
The artist was Andy Warhol, the one with the silver wig.
questions.description: A soup nobody ever ate, yet it hangs in museums.
questions.fun_fact: Warhol painted 32 cans because Campbell's sold 32 kinds of soup at the time.

questions.question: Pickled red onion goes with this Yucatán pork dish made with achiote and cooked wrapped in banana leaves. What is it?
hints: Its name mixes Spanish and Maya.
It's traditionally cooked in a pit in the ground.
The first word of its name means “little female pig.”
questions.description: An onion that turned pink from embarrassment… or from all that acid.
questions.fun_fact: Achiote, which gives the dish its red color, comes from the seeds of a shrub native to the Americas.

questions.question: Chepil is mixed into tamal dough and added to rice and broth, mostly in Oaxaca and Chiapas. What is it?
hints: You buy it in little bunches at the market.
It grows in the milpa, among the corn.
It's a quelite, like verdolagas.
questions.description: An ingredient that sounds like a luchador's nickname.
questions.fun_fact: Chepil is related to beans: it's a legume.

questions.question: This cloister belonged to the old convent that gave the Mercado de La Merced its name. Why was its friars' order founded?
hints: The order was born in Barcelona in the 13th century.
It was a time of constant wars between Christian and Muslim kingdoms around the Mediterranean.
Some friars promised to stay behind as prisoners so others could go free.
questions.description: Long before the market cries of “¡Pásele, güerita!”, all you heard here were quiet prayers.
questions.fun_fact: The cloister of La Merced is considered one of the most beautiful from the colonial era in Mexico City.

questions.question: La Bufadora shoots jets of seawater several meters into the air. Which Mexican state is it in?
hints: It's on the Pacific, in northwest Mexico.
It's part of a long, narrow peninsula.
It's the northern half of that peninsula, where Ensenada is.
questions.description: The sea sneezes so hard that tourists pay to watch.
questions.fun_fact: La Bufadora roars because waves rush into a sea cave and the squeezed air blasts the water upward.

questions.question: In 1970, Cancún was almost all jungle and beach, with very few people. Why did the government decide to build a city there?
questions.answer: To attract tourists from all over the world
wrong_answers: To drill for oil in the sea
To have a big fishing port
hints: The Bank of Mexico helped choose the spot.
What it had most were white beaches and turquoise water.
Today it's full of hotels and gets millions of visitors every year.
questions.description: A city made to order, like a birthday cake.
questions.fun_fact: The site for Cancún was chosen in the late 1960s using Bank of Mexico studies that compared beaches all over the country.

questions.question: It's by José Alfredo Jiménez, it plays at lots of weddings, and it promises to move “a un mundo nuevo” with the one you love. Which song is it?
hints: It's not a heartbreak song or a cantina song.
It's about loving someone your whole life.
Its title sets a condition: that other people allow it.
questions.description: The song that makes more wedding guests cry than the catering bill makes the hosts cry.
questions.fun_fact: José Alfredo Jiménez couldn't read music or play an instrument: he wrote his songs by whistling or singing them.

questions.question: “I'm tight-fitting with two legs, and down the outside of each runs a row of silver buttons, from waist to ankle.” Which part of the charro outfit am I?
hints: Mariachis wear me at every show.
I almost always match the short jacket, in the same color.
Without me, the charro would be walking around in his underwear.
questions.description: A piece of clothing that shines brighter than a freshly mopped floor.
questions.fun_fact: That row of silver ornaments on the charro suit is called the “botonadura”.

questions.question: Which ranchera singer became famous as a child with the song “La de la mochila azul”?
hints: He is from Guadalajara.
He also starred in the telenovela “Hasta que el dinero nos separe”.
He has the same last name as “El Potrillo”, but they aren't related.
questions.description: A singer who was carrying hits before he was carrying a backpack to middle school.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Fernández recorded “La de la mochila azul” when he was about 7 or 8, and he also appeared in the movie of the same name.

questions.question: It comes from the collagen in animal skin and bones, and it makes gummy candies chewy. What is it?
hints: It comes from animals, not plants.
It is sold as a powder or as clear, thin sheets.
It's what makes that wobbly dessert sold in little boxes of fruit-flavored powder.
questions.description: An ingredient that went from a pot of boiling bones to a bag of candy, and nobody noticed.
questions.fun_fact: Because of gelatin, many gummy candies aren't vegetarian, so some brands use pectin from fruit instead.

questions.question: I'm round and flat, made of clay or metal. I sit over the fire and tortillas get warmed on me. What am I?
hints: My name comes from Nahuatl.
Quesadillas get browned and chiles get toasted on me too.
My name starts with “co”.
questions.description: The only kitchen object that gets along better with tortillas than with any person.
questions.fun_fact: The word “comal” comes from the Nahuatl “comalli”, and the Mexica were already cooking their tortillas on clay comales.

questions.question: Every afternoon, the cuicacalli, the Mexica “house of song”, opened its doors to teach songs and dances. Who did it teach?
hints: The festivals of the gods needed lots and lots of singers and dancers.
Students started going there at around age 12.
You didn't have to be a noble, a priest or a warrior, and girls went too.
questions.description: A school where failing meant dancing badly in front of the gods.
questions.fun_fact: Young people went to the cuicacalli at sunset and could dance and sing until late into the night.

questions.question: Which of these was Nezahualcóyotl NOT?
hints: His face has appeared on Mexican banknotes.
His poems about flowers and how short life is are still read today.
His city formed the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan.
questions.description: A king with more hobbies than a freshly retired grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: His name means “hungry coyote” or “fasting coyote.”

questions.question: “Apapachar” comes from the Nahuatl “papachoa,” and in Mexico today it means to hug lovingly. What did “papachoa” originally mean?
questions.answer: To soften something by squeezing it
wrong_answers: To rock a baby to sleep
hints: It was an everyday word, not only about affection.
It was also used in the kitchen.
It was done with the fingers, like when you knead something.
questions.description: Grandma's favorite word the moment you walk through her door.
questions.fun_fact: People like to say “apapachar” means “to hug with the soul,” but that's a modern myth: the Nahuatl word was about squeezing something with your fingers.

questions.question: Fresh water reached Tenochtitlan through a stone aqueduct from a hill with springs on the mainland. Which hill was it?
hints: The Mexica lived there before founding Tenochtitlan.
Today it is one of the biggest parks in Mexico City.
Today there is a castle on its top.
questions.description: A city in the middle of a salty lake and still thirsty: the Mexica irony.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica rulers, the tlatoanis, had their portraits carved into the rocks of that hill.

questions.question: In Nahuatl, 400 had its own name, centzontli, and 8,000 was called xiquipilli. In groups of how many did the Mexica count?
hints: It's not the system we use today.
The Maya counted the same way as the Mexica.
It's the total number of fingers and toes.
questions.description: Math so old it was handing out homework before notebooks existed.
questions.fun_fact: Many Indigenous languages of Mexico still count in 20s; in Nahuatl, 20 is cempōhualli, “one count.”

questions.question: This courtyard of carved pillars stands next to the Plaza of the Moon in Teotihuacan. What building is it?
hints: Priests or rulers are believed to have lived there.
The figures carved on its pillars had obsidian eyes.
Its name mixes a precious bird and a butterfly.
questions.description: A building so elegant that even its pillars dressed up for the photo.
questions.fun_fact: The palace was rebuilt in the 1960s using the original stones found fallen at the site.

questions.question: Which diver from Guadalajara won Olympic silver in synchronized diving at London 2012 alongside Germán Sánchez?
hints: He was only 18 in London
His specialty is the 10-meter platform
His last name is one of the most common in Mexico and starts with G
questions.description: Two divers falling at the same time, like you and your brother at the pool, but without the splash.
questions.fun_fact: In synchronized diving, the judges score each diver's form and also how evenly the two hit the water.

questions.question: José Clemente Orozco painted his mural “The Trench” in a building in Mexico City. Which one?
hints: Today it is a UNAM museum.
It is in the Historic Center, a short walk from the Templo Mayor.
The building was once the Jesuit college of San Ildefonso.
questions.description: Walls that have been in a fight for almost a hundred years without breaking a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: In that same building, Diego Rivera painted “Creation” in 1922, one of the very first murals of Mexican muralism.

questions.question: Leopoldo Méndez and other artists founded it in 1937, and US sculptor Elizabeth Catlett, who stayed in Mexico, worked there. What was it called?
wrong_answers: Liga de Escritores y Artistas Revolucionarios
hints: They made cheap posters and prints for ordinary people.
Pablo O'Higgins was also one of its founders.
Its name says it was a workshop of graphic art for the people.
questions.description: Artists whose hands were always stained, but whose consciences were spotless.
questions.fun_fact: Elizabeth Catlett became a Mexican citizen in 1962 and lived in Cuernavaca until her death in 2012.

questions.question: On the glycemic index, pure glucose is the reference. What value does it have?
hints: It is a round number.
Foods that raise blood sugar very fast have values close to it; slow ones are much lower.
It is the perfect score on many tests.
questions.description: A leaderboard where sugars race to see who reaches your blood first.
questions.fun_fact: Lentils have a low glycemic index: they release their sugar into the blood little by little.

questions.question: Manuel Manilla, who came before José Guadalupe Posada, engraved many calaveras. When did he make those prints?
hints: He worked for the publisher Antonio Vanegas Arroyo.
Porfirio Díaz was ruling Mexico.
It was in the same decades the telephone was invented.
questions.description: Skulls older than your grandpa and still grinning from ear to ear.
questions.fun_fact: José Guadalupe Posada took Manilla's place at Vanegas Arroyo's print shop and made the calaveras famous forever.

questions.question: Frida painted me in 1944, wearing a steel corset, with my body split open down the middle. Which painting am I?
hints: Frida appears alone, in front of a cracked, barren landscape.
There are tears on her face and nails all over her skin.
My name speaks of something that cracked inside.
questions.description: Frida in front of the mirror once again, and once again not smiling.
questions.fun_fact: Frida wore corsets for much of her life, and she painted and decorated some of them herself.

questions.question: In 1954, Frida Kahlo painted some watermelons and wrote a phrase on one of them; it is one of her last works. What phrase did she write?
hints: She wrote it on the red flesh of one of the watermelons.
Next to the phrase she wrote “Coyoacán” and the year.
Coldplay used it as the title of their 2008 album.
questions.description: A painter who said goodbye with fruit instead of flowers.
questions.fun_fact: Chris Martin of Coldplay said he saw the phrase on Frida’s painting and loved it for the album.

questions.question: Look at these leaves: they're quelites, like verdolaga (purslane). In Mexico, what are they mainly used for?
hints: Many grow on their own among the corn in the milpa.
They're sold fresh in bunches at the tianguis, next to the chiles and tomatoes.
They're cooked a lot like spinach.
questions.description: Little green leaves with a Nahuatl name and loads of cousins.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, people eat hundreds of kinds of quelites, such as quintonil, pápalo and huauzontles.

questions.question: Jaime López wrote it, and Café Tacvba made it famous in 1996 on its covers album “Avalancha de éxitos”. Which song is it?
hints: The lyrics paint a picture of life in the capital.
The lyrics are full of Mexico City street slang and play with the same sound from start to finish.
The title joins the word for people from the capital with the slang for “a group of buddies”.
questions.description: A song Café Tacvba borrowed and, it seems, never gave back.
questions.fun_fact: The lyrics play with the “ch” sound almost from start to finish, like a tongue twister you can dance to.

questions.question: You're at an RBD concert in 2006. Who is NOT on stage singing with the group?
hints: RBD had six members: three girls and three boys.
The missing one was also a teen star, but never acted in “Rebelde”.
She had her own solo career with “Bella traición”.
questions.description: If you ever wore a loose red tie to school, this question is yours.
questions.fun_fact: RBD was born from the telenovela “Rebelde” and ended up filling real stadiums in several countries.

questions.question: These little tortillas fried in lard, topped with green or red salsa, shredded meat and onion, are typical of one city. Which one?
hints: It's a city in central Mexico, famous for its Talavera pottery.
People there also show off their mole and chiles en nogada.
Every May 5, people remember the famous battle won in this city.
questions.description: Small, golden and drenched in salsa: the queens of the evening snack under the arcades.
questions.fun_fact: Chalupas get their name from their shape, which looks like the canoes of the old canals.

questions.question: At the beach, one of the most popular dishes is “mojarra al mojo de…”. How does the name end?
hints: It's a basic ingredient in many Mexican salsas and stews.
Its smell stays on your hands after you chop it.
In legends, it scares off vampires.
questions.description: A fish that arrives at the table wearing its own perfume to win you over.
questions.fun_fact: The word “mojo” is also the name of the classic sauces of the Canary Islands, made with garlic and oil.

questions.question: It's a brothy tomato soup, and its thin pasta strands are browned in oil before the broth goes in. Which pasta is it?
hints: It's one of the soups most often served first at fondas (small family restaurants).
Sometimes it comes rolled up in little nests in the package.
It's long and very thin, and it slips right off your spoon.
questions.description: The soup your grandma serves before the main dish, without asking if you're hungry.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, brothy soup is called «sopa aguada» (wet soup), and red rice is called «sopa seca» (dry soup).

questions.question: In “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” Augustus Gloop is to the chocolate river as Violet Beauregarde is to…
hints: Violet never stopped chewing.
She tried something she shouldn't have and swelled up like a blueberry.
You chew it, but you don't swallow it.
questions.description: A factory where kids vanish faster than candy from a piñata.
questions.fun_fact: Roald Dahl wrote the book in 1964, and as a boy he got to taste-test new chocolates that a factory sent to his school.

questions.question: Pozole is to tostadas as shrimp cocktail is to…
hints: They're brought to the table with the limes and the salsa.
They come in little packets, and sometimes you crumble them on top.
They're square and thin, with salt on top.
questions.description: At a Mexican table nobody eats alone: every dish arrives with its loyal sidekick.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican shrimp cocktail has ketchup, lime, onion, cilantro and avocado, and is served in a goblet or a tall glass.

questions.question: I'm finely chopped raw fish “cooked” in lime juice, mixed with tomato, onion and cilantro, and served on a tostada. What am I?
hints: I don't need a stove, just lime and patience.
People order me a lot at the beach when it's hot.
Peru also shows me off as its national dish.
questions.description: A beach dish that has seen more lime than a lemonade stand.
questions.fun_fact: The acid in lime juice changes the fish's proteins, which is why it turns white as if it were cooked.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a part of the charro saddle?
hints: All four have to do with charrería.
On one part of the saddle, the charro ties his reata.
The odd one out goes on the heel of the rider's boot.
questions.description: A seat with more pieces than flat-pack furniture.
questions.fun_fact: On a charro saddle, the horn is called the “cabeza” (head): it's the knob at the front where the charro ties his reata to rope.

questions.question: At the fair they sell “raspados” in tamarind, grosella and lime, eaten with a spoon from a cup. What are they?
hints: You really crave them when it's hot out.
The man at the stand scrapes a big block with a tool.
It's very cold, and they pour a colorful liquid on top.
questions.description: The fair treat that leaves your tongue painted in bright colors.
questions.fun_fact: Many raspados are served “con lechera”: a drizzle of sweetened condensed milk on top of the syrup.

questions.question: You're in Mexico and you call 911 for an emergency. Who of these is NOT sent to help you?
hints: Three of them show up with sirens.
The odd one out doesn't put out fires or treat injuries.
The odd one out delivers letters.
questions.description: Three digits nobody wants to dial, but everyone should know.
questions.fun_fact: Before 2017, Mexico's general emergency number was 066; since then it has been 911.

questions.question: Many Mexican tables have this object at mealtime. What is it for?
hints: It goes in the middle of the table at mealtime.
It's always there when there are tacos or a guisado.
What it holds comes off the comal and is made of corn dough.
questions.description: The most loyal guardian of the Mexican table at mealtime.
questions.fun_fact: Many families line their tortillero with a hand-embroidered cloth napkin so the heat lasts longer.

questions.question: Its Paraninfo hall has murals by José Clemente Orozco, its soccer team is the Leones Negros, and it runs the world’s biggest Spanish-language book fair. Which university is it?
wrong_answers: The Autonomous University of Nuevo León
hints: Its book fair takes place every year between November and December.
Orozco painted those murals in his home state.
It is named after the city of the torta ahogada.
questions.description: A school where even the lions go to the library.
questions.fun_fact: The Guadalajara International Book Fair welcomes hundreds of thousands of visitors every year.

questions.question: This is the Multifamiliar Miguel Alemán from 1949, Mexico's first large apartment complex. Which architect designed it?
hints: He was one of the most important architects of modern Mexico.
He studied in Paris and founded the magazine “Arquitectura/México”.
He led the master plan for Ciudad Universitaria and designed its Rectory Tower.
questions.description: A small city stacked up inside a single building.
questions.fun_fact: The Multifamiliar Alemán had more than a thousand apartments, plus a swimming pool, a school and stores inside the same complex.

questions.question: It was born in Morelia, Michoacán, has VIP theaters with waiters, and is the largest movie theater chain in Latin America. Which one is it?
hints: Its most famous film festival is also in Morelia.
It has 4DX theaters where the seats move.
Its name joins “cine” with the Greek word for “city.”
questions.description: Where the popcorn costs almost as much as the movie.
questions.fun_fact: Cinépolis has theaters in countries as far away as India and Spain.

questions.question: I'm a civil engineer and my father came to Mexico from Lebanon. I own Telcel and Sanborns, and from 2010 to 2013 I was the richest man in the world. Who am I?
hints: I studied at the UNAM.
I also own Telmex.
I built a museum named after my wife, Soumaya.
questions.description: If you've ever paid a cell phone bill, you may have paid this man.
questions.fun_fact: The Museo Soumaya is free to enter and holds one of the largest Rodin collections outside France.

questions.question: It's the team of the Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León, it wears yellow, and it plays in the stadium nicknamed “El Volcán”. What is its nickname?
hints: Its big rival plays in the same city and wears blue and white.
Its nickname is a big cat.
It's a big cat with black and orange stripes, like Tigger, Winnie the Pooh's friend.
questions.description: In Monterrey, a Sunday of soccer is even more sacred than the carne asada.
questions.fun_fact: The match between Tigres and Rayados is called the “Clásico Regio”, and it brings all of Monterrey to a standstill.

questions.question: At the bottom of Mexico's national coat of arms, two branches form a half wreath around the eagle. What trees are they from?
hints: The branches are tied with a ribbon in the three national colors.
One stands for strength and the other for victory.
One of them was used to crown champions in ancient Greece.
questions.description: The eagle shows off its snake, but the trim at the bottom has a story too.
questions.fun_fact: On the coat of arms, the oak stands for strength and the laurel for victory.

questions.question: It uses accordion and bajo sexto, Ramón Ayala and Intocable play it, and people dance to it at parties in Monterrey. What genre is it?
hints: It has no trumpets and no tambora drum.
It was born near the border with the United States.
Its name tells you which part of Mexico it comes from.
questions.description: Music for dancing in boots and a cowboy hat, with a carne asada sizzling in the background.
questions.fun_fact: The accordion reached northern Mexico with European immigrants in the 19th century.

questions.question: The meridanos live in the capital of the state marked on the map. Which state is it?
hints: It's in southeastern Mexico.
It shares a peninsula with two other states.
Its capital is Mérida, the White City.
questions.description: It's so hot here that even the hammocks ask for shade.
questions.fun_fact: Mérida is called “the White City,” and cochinita pibil is its star dish.

questions.question: The culiacanenses live in the capital of a Mexican state. Which state?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
It's famous for its tomatoes and for banda music with tambora.
Mazatlán is in this state too.
questions.description: A name for locals so long you have to stop for a breath halfway through.
questions.fun_fact: Culiacán's baseball team is called the Tomateros, in honor of the tomatoes grown in the region.

questions.question: In “Camino de Guanajuato,” José Alfredo Jiménez sings that he stays in his “beloved town,” the one in this photo. Which is it?
hints: It's the songwriter's hometown.
A great moment in Mexican history began at its church.
Mexico's Grito of independence was first shouted here in 1810.
questions.description: A song that is a map, a road trip and a dose of nostalgia, all in one.
questions.fun_fact: José Alfredo Jiménez's tomb in Dolores Hidalgo is shaped like a charro hat and a sarape.

questions.question: Look at these leather shoes. Which Mexican city proudly calls itself the “shoe capital of the world”?
hints: It's in the Bajío region.
It's the largest city in Guanajuato.
Its soccer team has the same name as the city and is nicknamed “La Fiera”.
questions.description: A city where “What's your shoe size?” is practically a way to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: León has so many shoe and leather workshops that whole shopping areas there sell nothing but shoes.

questions.question: Take a close look at this pastry. What is it called in Mexico?
hints: Its name comes from English.
At the panadería it usually comes glazed or covered in chocolate.
It's the Mexican Spanish spelling of the English name for this treat.
questions.description: A pastry so round and shiny it looks fresh out of the car wash.
questions.fun_fact: The word “dona” is a Mexican adaptation of the English “donut”; in some other Spanish-speaking countries it's called a “rosquilla”.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican candy brand: Panditas, Bubulubu and Kranky all come out of my factories. Who am I?
hints: I was born in 1970.
For decades I belonged to the same company that makes Bimbo bread.
My name is a cute little version of the Spanish word for “tasty”.
questions.description: A craving factory your dentist knows by heart.
questions.fun_fact: Ricolino was born in 1970 inside Grupo Bimbo and was sold to the company Mondelez in 2022.

questions.question: These white flowers are used to make a liquid that perfumes pan de muerto. What is it?
hints: These flowers grow on a citrus tree.
That tree gives the fruit for your morning juice.
Its Spanish name comes from the Arabic “az-zahr”, meaning “the flower”.
questions.description: The perfume your grandma puts on the bread, not on herself.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, many brides wore crowns of orange blossoms on their wedding day.

questions.question: Take a close look at this slice of pie. What flavor is it?
hints: Its fruit is sour.
It's green and round on the outside.
It's the fruit you squeeze over tacos.
questions.description: The dessert that's always gone before the uncle who showed up late gets any.
questions.fun_fact: Homemade Mexican pay de limón often isn't even baked: the lime juice thickens the condensed milk.

questions.question: You squeeze the tube of a classic Pelón Pelo Rico and sweet, spicy little “hairs” come out. Which fruit are they made from?
hints: This fruit is also used to make agua fresca.
Its pulp is brown and sticky.
It grows inside hard brown pods.
questions.description: The only candy that comes with its own hairdo.
questions.fun_fact: Tamarind is a star of Mexican candy, but it actually came from Africa.

questions.question: It's a brown, pig-shaped bread from the bakery that smells of cinnamon. What sweetens it and gives it its color?
hints: It also sweetens café de olla.
It's made from boiled sugarcane juice.
It's sold in hard little brown cones.
questions.description: The only little piggy that fits whole into your afternoon snack.
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the region, this bread is called marranito, cochinito or puerquito.

questions.question: Mexico City's green vocho taxis had the front passenger seat removed so you could get in easily. How many doors did the vocho have?
hints: To get in the back, you had to tip the front seat forward.
That's why they removed the passenger seat: so you could get in without acrobatics.
It had one door on each side, that's all.
questions.description: Small, round and with more lives than an alley cat.
questions.fun_fact: The world's last vocho rolled out of the Volkswagen plant in Puebla in 2003.

questions.question: It sits on the taxi's dashboard, starts at the banderazo (the base fare) and goes up with distance and time. What is it called?
hints: It tells the passenger how much to pay.
App taxis don't use it: the price shows up on your phone.
Its name starts the same as the vehicle it rides in.
questions.description: A little gadget that counts faster than you do when there's traffic.
questions.fun_fact: The word “taxi” actually comes from “taximeter,” a device invented in Germany in 1891.

questions.question: A Mexico City Metro station has a song by El Tri and a cannon as its icon, for 1913 fighting at a nearby building. Which building?
hints: The station is Balderas, where Lines 1 and 3 cross.
The 1913 fighting is known as the Decena Trágica (Ten Tragic Days).
Today the building is a large library, near a crafts market with the same name.
questions.description: A station with a rock song and a fighting spirit.
questions.fun_fact: The song “Metro Balderas” was written by Rockdrigo González, and El Tri turned it into a Mexican rock anthem.

questions.question: Mexico City's Tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada is a top-up card you tap on a reader. Where can you use it?
wrong_answers: Metro, toll booths, gas stations and parking lots
Metro, intercity buses, planes and trains
hints: “Integrada” means “integrated”: it joins several things into one.
It works on the transit run by the city government.
One of them hangs from cables up in the air.
questions.description: A card that gets along with everybody… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: You can also use the same card to pay for Ecobici bikes.

questions.question: What is the thick, dark syrup left over from refining cane sugar, used to make almost all rum?
hints: It's a by-product, not the main product.
It's also used as feed for farm animals.
It gives gingerbread and brown sugar their dark color and rich flavor.
questions.description: What's left in the pot after sugar gets all fancy.
questions.fun_fact: In 1919, a giant wave of molasses flooded the streets of Boston.

questions.question: I'm in chocolate, I'm named after the cacao tree, and I'm the reason dogs shouldn't eat it. What substance am I?
hints: Humans break it down quickly; dogs do it very slowly.
There's much more of it in dark chocolate than in milk chocolate.
The cacao tree's scientific name starts with “Theobroma”.
questions.description: A substance that makes chocolate off-limits for the furry members of the family.
questions.fun_fact: Despite its name, theobromine contains no bromine: it comes from “Theobroma”, Greek for “food of the gods”.

questions.question: I’m a yellow canary who lives in a cage, and I always say “I tawt I taw a puddy tat!”. Which cat chases me?
hints: He is a Looney Tunes character, just like Bugs Bunny.
He is black and white, with a red nose.
He sprays spit when he talks and never manages to catch the little bird.
questions.description: A chase that has gone on for decades and still has no happy ending for anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The first cartoon that paired the two, “Tweetie Pie” from 1947, won an Oscar.

questions.question: Which writer created Phileas Fogg and his loyal servant Passepartout?
hints: He was French and wrote adventure stories in the 19th century.
He also wrote about a journey to the center of the Earth.
His most famous novel with this pair lasts exactly 80 days.
questions.description: An English gentleman so punctual that even his watch was scared of him.
questions.fun_fact: In Jules Verne's novel, Phileas Fogg never travels by balloon; that scene was added by the 1956 film.

questions.question: In the Pixar film “Monsters, Inc.”, which actor voices Sulley, the big furry monster?
hints: He is a big American actor with a deep voice.
Billy Crystal voices his partner Mike.
He also played Fred Flintstone in the 1994 film.
questions.description: Scaring kids is serious work, and somebody has to do the voice.
questions.fun_fact: To make Sulley look real, Pixar had to animate more than 2 million hairs on his body.

questions.question: In which century was “Pride and Prejudice”, the novel about Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy, published?
hints: Back then, people traveled by carriage and wrote with quill pens.
Its author, Jane Austen, died in 1817.
It came out two years before the Battle of Waterloo.
questions.description: A love story that began with “I can't stand him” in the middle of a ball.
questions.fun_fact: Jane Austen published the novel without her name: the title page only said “By the author of Sense and Sensibility.”

questions.question: You're having an arepa with cheese for breakfast. The arepa is made from corn, just as cheese is made from…
hints: It's a liquid.
It's white.
Cows give it.
questions.description: Colombia's most stable couple shows up at breakfast every single morning.
questions.fun_fact: It takes about 10 liters (2.6 gallons) of milk to make 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds) of cheese.

questions.question: In which decade did Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detect the background radiation, the “echo” of the Big Bang?
hints: The discovery later won them the Nobel Prize in Physics.
They used a giant antenna at Bell Labs.
They published it in 1965.
questions.description: Two scientists blamed some pigeons for a noise that came from the beginning of the universe.
questions.fun_fact: Before they understood the noise, they cleaned pigeon droppings out of the antenna, thinking those were the cause.

questions.question: In which decade did the Kellogg brothers invent the cereal flakes we now call corn flakes?
hints: It was in the 19th century.
They worked at a health resort in Battle Creek, Michigan.
It was a few years before 1900.
questions.description: Two brothers forgot about some wheat dough and changed the world's breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The Kelloggs' first flakes were made of wheat, not corn, and came from a dough they left sitting by accident.

questions.question: Who was the singer of the British duo Eurythmics, alongside Dave Stewart?
hints: She is Scottish.
She was famous for her short hair, dyed orange.
She sang “Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This).”
questions.description: Sweet dreams are made of this, and who are we to disagree?
questions.fun_fact: Annie Lennox won an Oscar for Best Original Song for a song from “The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King.”

questions.question: You're watching X-Men and Magneto looks familiar: the same actor also played Gandalf. What's his name?
hints: He is a British actor, very famous on stage for his Shakespeare roles.
He was knighted, so people call him “Sir”.
His last name starts with “Mc”.
questions.description: A wizard and a magnetic villain fight over the same white beard.
questions.fun_fact: Ian McKellen was nominated for an Oscar for playing Gandalf in “The Fellowship of the Ring”.

questions.question: At what age does a hobbit come of age?
hints: Much later than humans do.
Frodo reached it at the same party where Bilbo turned 111.
It's a two-digit number with both digits the same.
questions.description: In the Shire, you stay “the baby of the family” for a very, very long time.
questions.fun_fact: On their birthdays, hobbits don't get presents: they give presents to their guests!

questions.question: The writing on the One Ring appears when the ring is heated in a fire. What language is it written in?
hints: The letters may look Elvish, but the language is not.
Sauron invented it for his servants.
It is the language of the land where Mount Doom stands.
questions.description: The fine print on a contract nobody should ever sign.
questions.fun_fact: When Gandalf read the inscription out loud at the Council of Elrond, everyone present shuddered.

questions.question: I'm the new bow of the Fellowship's elf, a gift in the golden forest of Lothlórien. Who gave me?
hints: It was a farewell gift, one of many for the Fellowship.
She gave Frodo a little glass vial filled with starlight.
She is known as the Lady of the Wood.
questions.description: The best farewell gift ever: no socks, just adventure gear.
questions.fun_fact: The bow of the Galadhrim was longer and stronger than the one Legolas had brought from Mirkwood.

questions.question: I walk barefoot on big, hairy feet, and I live in a round hole under a hill. What land am I from?
hints: It's a green, peaceful place full of gardens and farms.
Bilbo and Frodo lived there.
Its name is an old English word for a county, like Yorkshire or Hampshire.
questions.description: A place where shoe stores go out of business in a week.
questions.fun_fact: Hobbits hardly ever wear shoes because the soles of their feet are as tough as leather.

questions.question: I am the lord of horses, swift as the wind, and I carry Gandalf with no saddle or reins. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the Mearas, the noble horses of Rohan.
My coat is silvery white.
My name begins with the dark shape that follows you on a sunny day.
questions.description: A luxury taxi for wizards: no saddle, no reins and no meter running.
questions.fun_fact: The Mearas let only the kings of Rohan ride them… until Shadowfax chose Gandalf.

questions.question: I served King Théoden as his esquire, and years later I was called “the Magnificent” and became Master of Buckland. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the four hobbits in the Fellowship.
My best friend became a guard of Gondor.
My full name is Meriadoc Brandybuck.
questions.description: A very short hobbit with a very long résumé.
questions.fun_fact: Merry and Pippin drank the Ents' special drink and ended up the tallest hobbits in history.

questions.question: I'm the line “Fly, you fools!”, shouted on a bridge in the Mines of Moria. Who shouted me?
hints: He was the oldest member of the Fellowship.
Just before, he had shouted “You shall not pass!”
Later he came back dressed in white.
questions.description: The most dramatic travel advice in movie history.
questions.fun_fact: In “Fly, you fools!”, the word “fly” is used in its old meaning of “flee,” not “fly through the air.”

questions.question: I'm a coffee chain with a mermaid in my logo, and my name comes from a sailor in “Moby-Dick”. In which city was I born?
hints: I was born in 1971, in a market by the sea.
My city is in the northwest of the United States and famous for its rain.
I'm the largest city in Washington State, but not its capital.
questions.description: A coffee chain that owes its name to a book about a giant whale.
questions.fun_fact: Starbuck is the first mate of the whaling ship Pequod in the novel “Moby-Dick”.

questions.question: I was a little girl; my dad sold cars and gave my name to the brand with the three-pointed star. What is my name?
hints: The brand is German and makes luxury cars.
My name is Spanish, even though my family was Austrian.
In Spanish, my name means “mercies” or “favors.”
questions.description: Some dads give their daughter a doll; this one gave her a whole car brand.
questions.fun_fact: Emil Jellinek, Mercedes's dad, raced cars in Nice under the nickname “Monsieur Mercedes.”

questions.question: Etsy's founder said the name came from hearing “eh, sì” in an Italian movie. Who directed that movie?
hints: It was a black-and-white Italian movie from the early 1960s about a film director who has run out of ideas.
His movies are full of circuses, clowns and dreamlike parades.
He was born in Rimini, and his last name became an adjective for dreamlike, over-the-top scenes.
questions.description: A shop for handmade things whose name came to someone watching a movie on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Rob Kalin wanted a word with no clear meaning so he could build the brand from scratch.

questions.question: Around 1910, Kirchner and Nolde painted green faces and red skies, which the Nazis later called “degenerate.” What were the wild colors for?
hints: What mattered was not how the world looks, but how it feels.
Edvard Munch’s “The Scream” was a big role model.
The art movement is named after the Latin word for “expression.”
questions.description: When the sky is red and the face is green, either the printer broke or someone painted it that way on purpose.
questions.fun_fact: Emil Nolde’s real name was Emil Hansen, and he named himself after his home village of Nolde.

questions.question: Who painted this yellow cow in 1911, which now hangs in a museum in New York?
hints: The painter loved animals and painted them in bold, imaginary colors.
He founded “Der Blaue Reiter” (The Blue Rider) with Wassily Kandinsky.
He is also famous for his blue horses.
questions.description: Milk is white, but who says the cow has to be too?
questions.fun_fact: For Franz Marc, colors had meanings: yellow stood for gentleness and cheer, blue for the spiritual.

questions.question: Who is this artist from the Rhineland, who was almost never seen without his felt hat?
hints: He liked to work with fat, felt and honey.
For documenta 1982, he had 7,000 oak trees planted in Kassel.
He said “Everyone is an artist.”
questions.description: Some people need a hat to look good, others to make art history.
questions.fun_fact: In 1986, cleaning staff at the Düsseldorf Art Academy cleaned away his “Fettecke” (Fat Corner) because they thought it was dirt.

questions.question: On a boat trip along the Spree in Berlin, you see three giant aluminum men in the water: the “Molecule Man”. How tall is it?
hints: It is much taller than a four-story apartment building.
It is about as tall as a ten-story building.
The American artist planned it at 100 feet.
questions.description: Three men have been standing in the middle of the Spree for years, and nobody has called the lifeguard.
questions.fun_fact: Jonathan Borofsky put up the figures in 1999 at the spot where the Berlin districts of Treptow, Friedrichshain and Kreuzberg meet.

questions.question: In 1905, Kirchner, Heckel and Schmidt-Rottluff founded “Die Brücke” (The Bridge), the first group of Expressionist artists. In which city?
hints: In summer, the artists painted at lakes around a nearby Baroque palace.
Today the city is the capital of a German state.
The city lies on the Elbe and is famous for its Frauenkirche.
questions.description: Four architecture students would rather paint than build, and still managed to put up a bridge.
questions.fun_fact: In 1911 the artists moved to Berlin, where the group broke up in 1913 after a quarrel over Kirchner's chronicle of the group.

questions.question: Translating brand names: “Volkswagen” is to “people's car” as “Samsung”, in Korean, is to…
hints: The founder wanted something big, many in number and lasting forever.
Look up at the sky at night.
“Sam” means “three” in Korean.
questions.description: Brand names that, once translated, sound like a poem or a government announcement.
questions.fun_fact: Samsung started in 1938 selling dried fish, vegetables and noodles, long before it made phones.

questions.question: Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof now shows contemporary art. For how long did trains once leave from there?
hints: The station opened in the 1840s.
It quickly became too small for the growing traffic.
Train service ended as early as 1884.
questions.description: Nobody waits for the train here anymore, at most for someone to explain the artwork.
questions.fun_fact: From 1906 the building was a transport and building museum; contemporary art only moved in in 1996.

questions.question: I was the best-known woman in Berlin Dada, glued photomontages from magazines and made “Cut with the Kitchen Knife”. Who am I?
hints: I came from Gotha in Thuringia.
My partner was the Dadaist Raoul Hausmann.
My last name sounds like the German word for “high”.
questions.description: Scissors, glue, magazines: what kindergarten calls crafts was called revolution in 1919.
questions.fun_fact: Hannah Höch got through the Nazi years in a small house in Berlin-Heiligensee, where she saved many Dada works from being destroyed.

questions.question: I tested roofs with soap films, built Germany's pavilion in Montreal in 1967 and won the Pritzker Prize in 2015. Who am I?
hints: My specialty was light tent and net roofs.
I worked on the curving roof of Munich's Olympic Park.
My first name is the German word for the opposite of “captive”.
questions.description: For most people a roof is just the thing on top; for this person it was a life's work.
questions.fun_fact: Frei Otto died in March 2015, one day before his Pritzker Prize was publicly announced.

questions.question: Which German threw one of these 97.76 m (320 ft 9 in) in Chorzów, Poland, in 2020, the second-longest throw of all time?
hints: He became world champion in London in 2017.
He comes from Dresden but competed for LG Offenburg.
He has the same first name as the composer Brahms.
questions.description: A sport where you really don't want to stand in the way.
questions.fun_fact: Only Jan Železný of the Czech Republic has thrown farther: 98.48 m (323 ft 1 in) in 1996.

questions.question: Blind cross-country skier and biathlete Verena Bentele raced with a guide. How many Paralympic gold medals did she win?
hints: She competed at the Paralympics from 1998 to 2010.
In Vancouver in 2010 alone, she won five golds.
It's exactly a dozen.
questions.description: She couldn't see the ski trail, but she got to know the winners' podium very well.
questions.fun_fact: Verena Bentele later became the German government's Commissioner for People with Disabilities and president of the social welfare association VdK.

questions.question: On a sled like this one, how many Olympic gold medals did Natalie Geisenberger win?
hints: Her first Olympic medal was bronze in Vancouver in 2010.
After that, she came out on top at three Winter Games in a row.
Sochi, Pyeongchang and Beijing: gold each time in the singles and in the team relay.
questions.description: Feet first, head back, and down the icy chute you go.
questions.fun_fact: No female luger has won more Olympic gold than Natalie Geisenberger.

questions.question: The Michelin Guide, famous for its restaurant stars, was created by a tire company. From which country?
hints: It first appeared in 1900, when there were very few cars on the streets.
Its mascot is a white figure made of tires.
The founding brothers came from Clermont-Ferrand.
questions.description: A restaurant guide created by people who wanted you to drive more and wear out more tires.
questions.fun_fact: In its early years, the Michelin Guide was given away for free to drivers.

questions.question: In 2024, a German woman won the women's Ironman World Championship in this city. Who was she?
hints: An Ironman: 3.8 km (2.4 mi) swimming, 180 km (112 mi) cycling, 42.195 km (26.2 mi) running.
The city is on the French Riviera.
Her last name sounds like a man's first name.
questions.description: First swim, then bike, then run – and all of it before dinner.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024, the women's world championship was held in Nice for the first time, while the men raced in Hawaii.

questions.question: Wrestler Wilfried Dietrich won Olympic gold in 1960 and in 1972 threw a giant weighing over 170 kg (375 lb). His nickname: the … of Schifferstadt?
hints: Think of machines, not animals.
You can find one on almost every building site.
It has a long arm and a hook.
questions.description: Schifferstadt in the Palatinate had a man you'd better not hug.
questions.fun_fact: His throw against the American Chris Taylor at the Munich Olympics is seen as one of the most famous moments in wrestling history.

questions.question: At the edge of the pool, you time Lukas Märtens' 2025 world record in the 400 meter freestyle. Roughly what does the clock show?
hints: The best swimmers do 100 meters freestyle in under 50 seconds.
Over the longer distance you get slower, but not by much.
It is just under four minutes.
questions.description: Eight lengths, a swimmer from Magdeburg and a stopwatch that can barely keep up.
questions.fun_fact: In Paris in 2024, Märtens became the first German man since 1988 to win Olympic gold in the pool.

questions.question: Michael Schumacher won 91 Formula 1 races. How many did his younger brother Ralf win?
hints: Ralf raced in Formula 1 for eleven years, but rarely in the best car.
He drove for Jordan, Williams and Toyota, among others.
It's fewer than ten.
questions.description: When your big brother already has almost every trophy on the shelf …
questions.fun_fact: In Canada in 2001, Ralf and Michael finished first and second, the first one-two by brothers in Formula 1.

questions.question: Germany won the 2014 World Cup final in this stadium. How many World Cup stars did the jersey have after that?
hints: Before 2014, Germany had already been world champion several times.
Germany won its first title in 1954 with the “Miracle of Bern.”
One more than before the tournament.
questions.description: The cheering that night in Rio was supposedly so loud you could hear it all the way to the Baltic Sea.
questions.fun_fact: The winning goal was scored by Mario Götze in extra time, after a cross from André Schürrle.

questions.question: “Quick, go get the Edding!” What are you supposed to get?
hints: The company behind it was founded in Hamburg in 1960.
It comes in many colors, but black is the best known.
People use it to label moving boxes, and it hardly ever comes off.
questions.description: A brand that made it from the company sign all the way into everyday words.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Carl-Wilhelm Edding, who co-founded the company in Hamburg in 1960.

questions.question: How many different flavors do the Goldbären in the classic Haribo bag in Germany have?
hints: It's more than three.
Lemon, orange and apple are among them, plus a few more.
As many as the highest number on a regular die.
questions.description: Tiny bears, big family question: who gets the red ones?
questions.fun_fact: The Goldbären were born in 1922 as “Tanzbären” (dancing bears), invented by Hans Riegel in Bonn.

questions.question: Which of these supermarket chains is NOT a discount store?
hints: Discount stores sell a smaller range of goods at especially low prices.
The one you're looking for often has a big fresh counter with cold cuts and cheese.
Its short name has the letter E in it twice.
questions.description: No haggling here, just shopping: sometimes on a budget, sometimes at the deli counter.
questions.fun_fact: Rewe belongs to the same group of companies as the discount chain Penny.

questions.question: Burgers are to McDonald's as iPhones are to…
hints: It's a tech company.
The company started in a garage in California.
Its logo is an apple with a bite taken out of it.
questions.description: A brand whose fans wait in line all night just to get a new phone.
questions.fun_fact: The first Apple Stores opened in the United States in 2001, and many people thought they would fail.

questions.question: Haribo's German slogan starts “Haribo macht Kinder froh” (Haribo makes kids happy). Who else does it make happy?
hints: The second half of the slogan was added decades after the first.
It makes the slogan cover a much bigger group than just kids.
Mom and Dad count too.
questions.description: A slogan that has been stuck to every kids' birthday party for decades.
questions.fun_fact: “Haribo macht Kinder froh” goes back to the 1930s; the grown-ups were only added in the 1960s.

questions.question: Which of these personal care brands is NOT sold at dm, but at Rossmann?
hints: Three of the four are store brands of the same drugstore chain.
Balea is dm's best-known brand for shower gel and shampoo.
The brand you're looking for sounds a bit like a girl's name starting with “I”.
questions.description: Shower gel shelf knowledge for true drugstore pros.
questions.fun_fact: Store brands are only sold in their own chain, so if you want Balea, you have to go to dm.

questions.question: It's usually made of wood, has a handle at each end, and you use it to roll dough flat. What is this kitchen tool called?
hints: You need it when you bake Christmas cookies.
It looks like a thick roller.
In German it's called a “Nudelholz”, which means “noodle wood”.
questions.description: In cartoons Grandma swings it around; in real life it mostly lives in a drawer.
questions.fun_fact: In southern Germany, many people say “Wellholz” instead of Nudelholz.

questions.question: You use tin cutters to cut stars, hearts and moons out of Plätzchen dough. At what time of year do most families do this?
hints: It's usually cold outside and gets dark early.
At this time, people like to spend cozy afternoons indoors.
The cookies later end up on the bunter Teller, the plate of treats under the tree.
questions.description: The kitchen smells of butter, and there's more flour on the floor than in the dough.
questions.fun_fact: To keep dough from sticking to the cookie cutter, just dip the cutter in flour now and then.

questions.question: Which treat hides a yellow plastic capsule with a small toy under its chocolate?
hints: The chocolate is brown outside and white inside.
It is wrapped in brightly printed foil.
Its shape is a perfect fit for Easter.
questions.description: Chocolate with a built-in bonus level.
questions.fun_fact: Kinder Eggs are banned in the US because candy there may not enclose parts you can't eat.

questions.question: In the Middle Ages, this was the main sweetener in Germany. It isn't grown but harvested, and it almost never goes bad. What is it?
hints: Lebkuchen used to be sweetened almost only with it.
In the Middle Ages, men called Zeidler gathered it from hollow trees in the forest.
Busy insects make it and store it in little wax cells.
questions.description: Even a knight in full armor sometimes just had a craving for Lebkuchen.
questions.fun_fact: The forest around Nuremberg was once called “the bee garden of the Holy Roman Empire” because so many Zeidler worked there.

questions.question: At the Wiesn, you order beer by the Maß. How much does a full Maßkrug hold?
hints: It's a lot more than a normal glass holds.
It's a nice round amount, no decimal point.
Exactly as much as a big carton of milk in a German supermarket.
questions.description: Go big or go home, and make sure it has a handle.
questions.fun_fact: A full glass Maßkrug, beer included, weighs about 2.3 kilograms (5 lb).

questions.question: A Christmas tree is to Christmas as costumes and streamers are to …?
hints: This festival is celebrated in winter, usually in February.
People dress up as princesses, pirates or cowboys.
In Cologne, this festival is called Karneval.
questions.description: The one time of year when Dad can walk to the bakery dressed as a bee and nobody asks why.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Bavaria, people eat Krapfen at Fasching: the same jam doughnuts that other Germans call Berliner.

questions.question: I wear a dirndl, often carry ten full Maß mugs at once and bring them through the beer tent to the tables. Who am I?
hints: I work while everyone else celebrates.
I take orders and collect the money.
In Bavaria, people just call me “Bedienung”.
questions.description: A gym? She doesn't need one, she has two weeks of Wiesn.
questions.fun_fact: In a Bavarian beer tent, people usually just call the waitress “Bedienung”.

questions.question: In Bavaria, someone celebrating Fasching is a “Narr.” If you celebrate Karneval in Cologne, what are you called there?
hints: The word is short and has only one syllable.
In Kölsch, the same word also works as an adjective meaning “crazy.”
A Cologne saying goes: “Jeder … ist anders” (“Every … is different”).
questions.description: In Cologne, being a little crazy isn't an insult. It's a title of honor.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, Cologne's carnival season starts on November 11 at 11:11 a.m.

questions.question: In 2017, Apple admitted that an update slowed down some iPhones on purpose. Which ones?
hints: It had nothing to do with where or when they were bought.
Apple said it did this so they wouldn't suddenly shut down.
It's the part that wears out after many charges.
questions.description: Your phone isn't tired: someone pulled the handbrake.
questions.fun_fact: After the scandal, Apple cut the price of battery replacements and had to pay millions of dollars in settlements.

questions.question: You're at the top of a drop tower, and then the holders let go. About how long is the free fall before the brakes kick in?
hints: It feels much longer than it is.
You barely have time for one deep breath.
Count slowly: one, two, three, and it's over.
questions.description: The fastest way down, safety bar included.
questions.fun_fact: After 3 seconds of free fall, you're already going faster than 100 km/h (60 mph).

questions.question: Long ago, the funny man at the king's court wore me. I have colorful points, and a little bell jingles on each one. What am I?
hints: You wear me on your head.
Today you often see me at Fasching and carnival.
My owner was the court fool.
questions.description: Headwear often tells you more about its wearer than any résumé.
questions.fun_fact: Court jesters were often allowed to tell the king the truth without being punished, and Germans still call that kind of freedom “Narrenfreiheit”.

questions.question: This Cologne band has been around since 1972 and sang “Viva Colonia”. Its name is Kölsch dialect. What does it mean?
hints: In standard German the word sounds almost the same, with just one vowel changed.
They are animals you find on many farms.
They lay eggs.
questions.description: When it's carnival in Cologne, half the city sings along with this band, no lyrics sheet needed.
questions.fun_fact: The Höhner song “Wenn nicht jetzt, wann dann?” became the anthem of the 2007 Handball World Championship in Germany.

questions.question: ARD and ZDF's children's channel went on air in 1997. In which city is KiKA based?
hints: The city lies almost exactly in the middle of Germany.
Its medieval old town has a bridge with houses built on it.
A large cathedral and St. Severus' Church stand side by side on a hill there.
questions.description: Here the chatting, playing and waving goes on live until the camera breaks a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: Statues of KiKA stars such as Bernd das Brot and the Sandmännchen stand on the city's streets.

questions.question: The ARD fairy-tale series is called “Sechs auf einen Streich” (“Six at One Blow”). What number is on the brave little tailor's belt in the Grimm tale?
hints: The number is bigger than six.
He swatted that many flies on his slice of bread with jam.
That's how many dwarfs live with Snow White beyond the mountains.
questions.description: A tailor, a belt and a number worth bragging about.
questions.fun_fact: The series got its name because exactly six fairy-tale films aired when it started in 2008.

questions.question: Rüdiger lives in a crypt with his sister Anna and brother Lumpi and makes friends with Anton. What is his vampire family called?
hints: The name sounds like goosebumps.
It has to do with shaking with fear.
It contains the German word “schlottern”, to tremble.
questions.description: A family that sleeps in all day and only really wakes up at night.
questions.fun_fact: Angela Sommer-Bodenburg published the first book about the little vampire in 1979.

questions.question: When I leave, children sing: “… goodbye, parting hurts. But your parting makes my heart laugh.” Who am I?
hints: I'm a season.
The song is almost 200 years old and is still sung in kindergartens today.
Snowdrops and crocuses come after me.
questions.description: Someone who gets sent out the door every year with drums and songs.
questions.fun_fact: “Ade” comes from the French “adieu”, and “Winter ade” was written by Hoffmann von Fallersleben, who also wrote the words of the German national anthem.

questions.question: It holds half a liter (about a pint), has round dimples all over and is often filled with wine spritzer. Where do people drink from a “Dubbeglas”?
hints: The region is one of Germany's biggest wine-growing areas.
The German Wine Route runs through it.
Kaiserslautern and Ludwigshafen are in this region.
questions.description: A glass with so many dents it's almost impossible to drop.
questions.fun_fact: In the local dialect, “Dubbe” means “dots”, and the dimples stop the glass from slipping out of your hand.

questions.question: In southern Germany it's what you call a fool, and it's also the last name of the actor who played Jack Sparrow. What's the word?
hints: It's a short word, and in Bavaria it has a cute “little” form too.
The same actor also played Edward Scissorhands and Willy Wonka.
The word rhymes with “step”.
questions.description: An insult that made it all the way to Hollywood, at least as a name.
questions.fun_fact: In Bavaria the small form is “Depperl”, and it sounds almost loving.

questions.question: At O. J. Simpson's trial, his lawyer said: “If it doesn't fit, you must acquit.” What didn't fit?
hints: It was a piece of clothing found as evidence.
Simpson tried it on in front of the jury.
You wear it on your hand.
questions.description: Fashion can decide a trial too, if the size is wrong.
questions.fun_fact: The 1995 trial was shown on TV, and millions of people followed it like a soap opera.

questions.question: What is the Low German (Plattdeutsch) word for a girl?
hints: The word comes from the coast.
In Hamburg people fondly say “lütte …” (little …).
The word sounds a bit like “Dirn”.
questions.description: This one is about someone on the coast who doesn't want to be called “Fräulein”.
questions.fun_fact: “Deern” is related to “Dirn”, and the Bavarian word “Dirndl” also first meant simply “girl”.

questions.question: What is a Bavarian “Oachkatzlschwoaf”?
hints: It belongs to an animal.
The animal lives in trees and collects nuts.
“Oachkatzl” is the Bavarian word for “Eichhörnchen”.
questions.description: A word that ties newcomers' tongues in knots every single time.
questions.fun_fact: Bavarians use the word as a tongue-twister test to check whether someone can really speak Bavarian.

questions.question: What do you get when you stir classic Kaba powder into milk?
hints: The drink turns brown.
Kids love it at breakfast.
It tastes like chocolate.
questions.description: A powder that turns boring milk into a breakfast hero.
questions.fun_fact: Kaba was invented in 1929 by Bremen merchant Ludwig Roselius, who also founded Kaffee HAG.

questions.question: At home, someone makes you a hot lemon with honey. What is it a home remedy for?
hints: You'd usually drink it in winter.
You're often lying in bed when you drink it.
You have a runny nose and a scratchy throat.
questions.description: Sour, hot and a classic from Grandma's medicine cabinet.
questions.fun_fact: Vitamin C doesn't like strong heat, so it's better to let the water cool a little before adding the lemon.

questions.question: Picking grapes has a long tradition along the Moselle. Who planted the first large vineyards there?
hints: That was almost 2,000 years ago.
Back then, the city of Trier on the Moselle was one of their important cities.
They also built the Limes wall and spoke Latin.
questions.description: Whoever cuts grapes here is walking in very, very old footsteps.
questions.fun_fact: In the Moselle village of Neumagen, people found a stone Roman ship loaded with wine barrels, called the “Neumagen wine ship”.

questions.question: Fill the gap: in Germany, a bottle that is rinsed and refilled after you return it is called a “…flasche”.
hints: The bottle doesn't get thrown away.
It makes its trip many times.
The opposite is “Einweg”.
questions.description: A bottle that comes back more often than a boomerang.
questions.fun_fact: A glass Mehrweg bottle can be refilled up to 50 times.

questions.question: I was born in Augsburg in 1898, wrote “The Threepenny Opera” with Kurt Weill and invented epic theater. Who am I?
hints: I mostly wrote plays and poems.
The song “Mack the Knife” comes from my “Threepenny Opera”.
Later I ran the Berliner Ensemble in East Berlin.
questions.description: Theater where you are very much supposed to remember you're sitting in a theater.
questions.fun_fact: “The Threepenny Opera” premiered in 1928 at Berlin's Theater am Schiffbauerdamm and was an instant smash hit.

questions.question: Who was the first woman to speak in the Weimar National Assembly on February 19, 1919, and founded the Arbeiterwohlfahrt?
hints: She was a Social Democrat and fought for women's right to vote.
The Arbeiterwohlfahrt (Workers' Welfare), or AWO for short, still exists today.
Her last name starts with “Ju”.
questions.description: A speaker's stand that until then had only ever known men's shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Juchacz began her speech with “Gentlemen and ladies,” which made the assembly laugh.

questions.question: It's made up, it looks real, and people forward it on WhatsApp without checking it. What is it called?
hints: It copies what you see in newspapers.
Before you share it, check who published it.
Its two-word name tells you it isn't true and pretends to be a headline.
questions.description: It runs faster than the truth, and the truth hasn't even left the house yet.
questions.fun_fact: An MIT study found that on Twitter, false news stories spread faster than true ones.

questions.question: In 1918, Rosa Luxemburg wrote a line that is still often quoted: “Freedom is always the freedom of …” How does it end?
hints: She wrote it in prison while thinking about the revolution in Russia.
The line is about free speech and tolerance.
It means people who hold a different opinion.
questions.description: A line that has appeared on more protest signs than any pizza ad.
questions.fun_fact: The line comes from her essay “The Russian Revolution,” in which she criticized none other than Lenin.

questions.question: Emil Tischbein's money is stolen on the train. With Gustav and lots of other kids, he chases the thief through which city?
hints: Emil is actually on his way to visit his grandmother.
Emil travels from a small town to a huge city.
Today it is Germany's capital.
questions.description: A big-city adventure where the grown-ups are just extras.
questions.fun_fact: “Emil and the Detectives” came out in 1929, and the first film of it followed as early as 1931.

questions.question: The silent film “The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari” is famous for its crooked, painted sets. In which year did it reach theaters?
hints: Germany was a young republic at the time.
Movie theaters didn't have sound films yet.
The First World War had ended only a little over a year before.
questions.description: A film where even the houses look like they had a bad night's sleep.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the slanted shadows and lights in “Caligari” were simply painted onto the sets.

questions.question: This general was Reich Chancellor from December 1932 to January 1933, the last one before Hitler. Who is he?
hints: Before that, he was Minister of the Reichswehr (the army).
He was in office for barely two months.
His surname comes from the German verb for sneaking up quietly.
questions.description: A chancellor who barely had time to hang up his name plate.
questions.fun_fact: Schleicher wanted to bring together trade unions and part of the Nazi Party, an idea called the “Querfront” (cross-front).

questions.question: About what percentage of the energy in its fuel did Rudolf Diesel's first working engine use in 1897?
hints: Most of the energy was lost as heat.
The steam engines of his time managed only about 10 percent.
It was roughly a quarter.
questions.description: An engine that squeezes air until it gets too hot to handle.
questions.fun_fact: Diesel's first test engine nearly exploded in 1893: a pressure gauge flew just past his head.

questions.question: Who played the clay giant in the 1920 silent film “The Golem: How He Came into the World” and also directed it?
hints: He had already made a first Golem film in 1915.
He was a celebrated stage star at Max Reinhardt's Deutsches Theater.
He shares his first name with Beatle McCartney.
questions.description: A man of clay with a hairdo not even a hurricane could mess up.
questions.fun_fact: The film's crooked Prague alleys were designed as a studio set by the architect Hans Poelzig.

questions.question: Fritz Lang made “Die Nibelungen”, with Siegfried's fight against the dragon, as a two-part silent film. In which era was it made?
hints: In the same decade, Lang also made “Metropolis.”
World War I was already over.
The film came out in 1924.
questions.description: A dragon, a hero, and not a single spoken word.
questions.fun_fact: The dragon was a huge model, moved by several men hidden inside it.

questions.question: This actress from Lower Saxony played the beautiful Helen in “Troy”. Who is she?
hints: She first worked as a model in Paris.
For Fatih Akin's “In the Fade” she won Best Actress at Cannes in 2017.
In “Inglourious Basterds” she played the actress Bridget von Hammersmark.
questions.description: From a village near Hildesheim to Troy is farther than any GPS thinks.
questions.fun_fact: She was born Diane Heidkrüger in Algermissen, near Hildesheim.

questions.question: In 1960, Berlin-born Horst Buchholz played young Chico in a Hollywood Western about hired gunmen. What is the group called?
hints: The film is a remake of a Japanese samurai classic.
Yul Brynner and Steve McQueen were in it.
The group has as many members as a week has days.
questions.description: A Berliner rides into the Wild West and luckily brings enough colleagues along.
questions.fun_fact: A year later, Buchholz played a young communist in Billy Wilder's Berlin comedy “One, Two, Three.”

questions.question: Who founded FTX, the cryptocurrency exchange that collapsed in 2022 and landed him in prison for fraud?
hints: He is a young American, the son of two law professors.
He became famous for going everywhere with messy hair and wearing shorts.
His initials are SBF.
questions.description: A crypto genius whose fortune turned out to be even more virtual than the coins.
questions.fun_fact: He was once one of the youngest billionaires in the world, and in 2024 he was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

questions.question: Which literary critic was to receive the German Television Award for lifetime achievement in 2008 and turned it down on stage?
hints: He was born in Poland.
He was nicknamed the “Pope of Literature”.
He hosted “Das Literarische Quartett” on ZDF.
questions.description: The rarest acceptance speech in German TV history: “No, thank you.”
