questions.fun_fact: Afterwards, Thomas Gottschalk had a separate talk with him about television, which ZDF aired shortly after.

questions.question: This actress from the Weimar “Tatort” also sings in a band. Which one?
hints: She first became known as an MTV host.
The band is a trio: her and two men.
The band's name is a capital city on the Vltava river.
questions.description: Detective by day, microphone in hand by night: free time is overrated.
questions.fun_fact: Nora Tschirner became famous in cinemas alongside Til Schweiger in “Keinohrhasen”.

questions.question: Every year on “Tag der Republik,” East Germany celebrated its founding with parades in East Berlin. What was the date?
hints: The day fell in the fall.
In 1989 it was celebrated for the 40th time, about a month before the Berlin Wall fell.
The date is four days after today’s Day of German Unity.
questions.description: A birthday party for a whole country, only with flags in place of candles.
questions.fun_fact: For the 40th anniversary in 1989, Mikhail Gorbachev came to East Berlin, and just one month later the Wall fell.

questions.question: You're standing on Alexanderplatz in Berlin. What rises 368 m (1,207 ft) into the sky there, topped by a silver sphere?
hints: It is the tallest structure in Germany.
Inside the sphere there is a restaurant that slowly turns.
From here, pictures were broadcast to the television sets of East Germany.
questions.description: Alexanderplatz is where tourists, pigeons and a good helping of East Berlin nostalgia all meet.
questions.fun_fact: When the sun shines on the sphere, a bright cross appears on it, and Berliners called this “the Pope's revenge.”

questions.question: The East German wall unit often filled a whole living room wall, with a glass cabinet and a bar compartment. What was it usually made of?
hints: The material was cheap and easy to mass-produce.
It came from big furniture combines and was also used in kitchens and kids' rooms.
It was covered with a thin layer of wood veneer or decorative foil.
questions.description: The piece of furniture where the good china only woke up for Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: The “MDW” modular furniture from Dresden-Hellerau could be extended again and again like building blocks.

questions.question: On Men's Day, often called “Herrentag” in East Germany, men head out pulling Bollerwagen (wooden handcarts). Which holiday does it fall on?
hints: It is always on a Thursday.
It comes 39 days after Easter Sunday.
The holiday remembers Jesus going up into heaven.
questions.description: The day when Bollerwagen cover more miles than in the whole rest of the year.
questions.fun_fact: In East Germany, Ascension Day stopped being a public holiday in 1967, but many people celebrated Herrentag anyway.

questions.question: From 5th grade on, East German kids had to learn Russian. Which script is Russian text like in the photo written in?
hints: It is named after a saint.
Bulgarian, Serbian and Ukrainian use it too.
It is named after a monk who lived in the 9th century with his brother Methodius.
questions.description: For many East German kids, their first vocabulary words looked like a secret code.
questions.fun_fact: Anyone who can read Cyrillic knows that the Russian “PECTOPAH” simply means “restaurant”.

questions.question: You find an old radio made by “VEB Stern-Radio Berlin”. In what year did such East German companies stop being VEBs?
hints: A law passed by East Germany's parliament, the Volkskammer, turned them into corporations.
In the same year, the Deutsche Mark arrived in the East.
It is the year of German reunification.
questions.description: People's property had an expiry date; it just wasn't printed on the package.
questions.fun_fact: From 1990, the Treuhandanstalt agency was tasked with privatizing more than 8,000 state-owned companies.

questions.question: In 1633, Galileo was put on trial for saying the Earth goes around the Sun. Which of these scientists did NOT believe that?
hints: Three of them lived between the 15th and 18th centuries.
The odd one out lived in ancient times, in Alexandria.
His model kept the Earth still at the center of the universe.
questions.description: Galileo learned that telling the truth can sometimes get you grounded.
questions.fun_fact: In 1992, the Catholic Church officially admitted it had been wrong about Galileo.

questions.question: What was NOT in East Germany's first constitution of 1949?
questions.answer: The leading role of the SED
hints: The 1949 constitution was meant to look democratic and was modeled on the Weimar constitution.
The missing point was only added with the new constitution of 1968.
It's about the party that called the shots anyway.
questions.description: A constitution from the other side that later got a thorough makeover.
questions.fun_fact: On paper, the 1949 constitution even guaranteed every citizen the right to emigrate.

questions.question: In the GDR I was a crime: whoever committed me left the country without permission, over the Wall, across the Baltic or through a tunnel. What did state and party call me?
hints: Especially in the 1950s, the word was everywhere in newspapers and speeches.
West German newspapers often put the word in quotation marks.
You turned your back on the “Deutsche Demokratische …”.
questions.description: The suitcases were packed, but you weren't allowed to tell anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Wall went up in 1961, about 2.7 million people left the GDR.

questions.question: Strike leaders were put on trial, and East German schoolbooks gave June 17, 1953, a name. What was it?
hints: The term shows the party's official view, not the strikers' view.
The SED wanted to deny that workers had risen up against their own workers' state.
A word from before 1945, plus a failed seizure of power.
questions.description: The art of renaming a workers' strike until it fits the party handbook.
questions.fun_fact: Bertolt Brecht mocked it at the time in a poem, saying the government should simply elect another people.

questions.question: At the 1973 World Festival of Youth and Students in East Berlin, the US civil rights activist in the photo was celebrated like a star. Who is she?
hints: She was a philosopher and an open communist.
Her trial in the US was a big topic in East German schools in the early 1970s.
Her big Afro hairstyle became the symbol of a whole movement.
questions.description: A summer festival that suddenly made East Berlin very colorful.
questions.fun_fact: East German children sent her huge numbers of rose postcards in prison, in a campaign called “A Million Roses for Angela.”

questions.question: In 1961, East Berlin's grand boulevard Stalinallee got a new name. What is its stretch of wedding-cake-style buildings called to this day?
hints: After Stalin's death, his name was no longer welcome, even in the GDR.
The new name honored a thinker whose ideas the SED claimed to follow.
He wrote “The Communist Manifesto” together with Friedrich Engels.
questions.description: Wide sidewalks, tiled palaces and a street sign that didn't last long.
questions.fun_fact: The eastern part of the old Stalinallee is now called Frankfurter Allee.

questions.question: The “Ständige Vertretung” (Permanent Mission) on Hannoversche Straße in East Berlin opened in 1974, first led by Günter Gaus. What was it?
questions.answer: Bonn's stand-in for an embassy in East Germany
wrong_answers: The seat of East Berlin's mayor
The United Nations office in East Germany
The meeting place of East Germany's parliament
hints: It came about after the Basic Treaty of 1972.
West Germany didn't want to recognize East Germany as a foreign country.
Its head was practically an ambassador, but wasn't allowed to be called one.
questions.description: A building in East Berlin whose door sign took longer to negotiate than most house rules.
questions.fun_fact: Today, the Berlin pub “Ständige Vertretung” recalls the Bonn years by serving Kölsch beer.

questions.question: You're watching Miss Universe 2015: they announce Miss Colombia, then correct it. Which country was the real winner from?
hints: Before she won, the winner had already entered her country's beauty pageant twice.
It is a country made up of thousands of islands.
It is in Asia and its capital is Manila.
questions.description: The shortest crown in history: about four minutes on the throne.
questions.fun_fact: Host Steve Harvey read the card wrong and had to apologize live in front of millions of people.

questions.question: Who was East Germany's Minister of Education from 1963 to 1989?
hints: Because of the tint of her hair, people called her the “purple witch” (lila Hexe).
After reunification she lived in Chile until her death.
Her husband led East Germany from 1971 to 1989.
questions.description: She decided what was learned in East German classrooms, and for quite a long time.
questions.fun_fact: Margot Honecker died in Santiago, Chile, in 2016.

questions.question: The Standesamt (registry office) issues this document shortly after birth. It lists your name, place of birth and parents. What is it?
hints: You need it later, for example when you want to get married.
It puts one very specific day on paper.
It officially records when and where you came into the world.
questions.description: The very first paper of your life, and you didn't even sign it yourself.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, a birth must be reported to the Standesamt within one week.

questions.question: It grows in damp corners when rooms aren't aired out enough, is often black or green, and likes old bread too. What is it?
hints: Regular Stoßlüften (opening the windows wide for a few minutes) helps against it.
You often find it behind wardrobes or in the bathroom.
It is a fungus and forms a fuzzy layer on forgotten food.
questions.description: A roommate who never pays rent but still takes over every corner.
questions.fun_fact: In German, “Schimmel” is also the word for a white horse.

questions.question: For Stoßlüften, you open the windows wide for a few minutes instead of leaving them tilted open for a long time. Why?
questions.answer: So damp air gets out but the walls stay warm
wrong_answers: So the dust blows off furniture and shelves
So no insects fly into the home
hints: It's about the air and the heating.
It has to do with cooking, showering and breathing indoors.
It's meant to stop mold while still saving heating energy.
questions.description: German homes follow a breathing routine stricter than any gym.
questions.fun_fact: In winter, experts recommend doing Stoßlüften several times a day for about five to ten minutes.

questions.question: In an apartment building, it leads from the front door to the apartments. The mailboxes often hang here, and the light goes off after a few minutes. What is it?
hints: Every resident walks through it every day.
Sometimes shoes or a stroller stand here.
You pass through it before unlocking your own apartment door.
questions.description: All the neighbors meet here, but nobody stays a second longer than they have to.
questions.fun_fact: The switch that turns off the hallway light by itself has its own long German name: Treppenlichtautomat.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The question is based on the German "Treppenhaus" (stairwell). "Hallway" is ambiguous. It could mean the flat's own entrance hall or a floor corridor. The fun fact also mistranslates: "Treppenlichtautomat" means a stairwell light timer, not a hallway one. I did not run a web search, so this rests on my own knowledge of German.

questions.question: Lots of people keep a small plastic token like this on their key ring. What is it for?
hints: You get it back afterwards.
You push it into a small lock.
Then you can push something with wheels away.
questions.description: The tiniest VIP on your key ring: looks worthless, but sometimes nothing works without it.
questions.fun_fact: Most of these locks also take a 1-euro coin instead of a token.

questions.question: At this table full of instruments, the first nuclear fission was achieved in Berlin in 1938. Who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it?
hints: He was a chemist, not a physicist.
His colleague Lise Meitner explained the result in terms of physics.
In German, his last name means “rooster.”
questions.description: A workbench where more happened than on any kitchen table in the world.
questions.fun_fact: The chemical element meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner, who was the first to explain nuclear fission in terms of physics.

questions.question: On your charger and your weather app you meet units named after scientists. Which one is NOT named after a German?
hints: Three of the scientists spoke German, one spoke Italian.
Fahrenheit came from Danzig, even though Americans use his scale the most today.
You're looking for the inventor of the first battery.
questions.description: Units are like street names: everyone uses them, nobody asks who's behind them.
questions.fun_fact: For the zero point of his scale, Fahrenheit used the lowest temperature he could reach with a mix of ice, water and ammonium chloride.

questions.question: For years, Ranga Yogeshwar explained science on WDR in the show “Quarks & …”. How does the title end?
hints: The show started on WDR in 1993.
You often see it in company names, too.
It's short for “Compagnie”, or company.
questions.description: A TV show you won't find in the dairy aisle, even though its name sounds like it belongs there.
questions.fun_fact: Ranga Yogeshwar was born in Luxembourg and studied physics in Aachen.

questions.question: Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci researched cancer treatments at their Mainz company BioNTech. What made it world-famous with Pfizer in late 2020?
hints: It has to do with the pandemic.
It is based on a technique called mRNA.
You got it as a shot in the upper arm.
questions.description: A company from Mainz that got famous in 2020 faster than any Fastnacht band.
questions.fun_fact: Şahin and Türeci are a married couple, and they are said to have gone straight back to the lab after their wedding.

questions.question: An emigrant mechanic is said to have built light bulbs like this one in New York before Edison. Which town near Hanover was he from?
hints: His name was Heinrich Göbel.
The town lies at the foot of the Deister hills.
Its name sounds like the German command “jump!”.
questions.description: A story that shines so brightly you can hardly see the holes in it.
questions.fun_fact: No proof of Göbel's invention was ever found: the story mostly came up in patent fights against Edison around 1893.

questions.question: The Watzmann is the highest peak in Berchtesgaden National Park. About how high is it?
hints: The Zugspitze is higher, at 2,962 meters (9,718 ft).
It is said to be the highest mountain that lies entirely on German soil.
The number is just over 2,700.
questions.description: A mountain with a family: his wife and kids stand right next door, all made of stone.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Watzmann was a cruel king who was turned to stone along with his wife and children.

questions.question: Heinrich Heine's Lorelei poem begins: “I don't know what it means that I am so …” Which word is missing?
hints: Next, the speaker can't get “a fairy tale from ancient times” out of his mind.
The boatman hears the Lorelei's song, forgets the reef and goes down.
It's the opposite of merry.
questions.description: A rock that distracts boatmen more than a phone distracts drivers.
questions.fun_fact: The well-known tune for Heine's poem is by Friedrich Silcher and was published in 1837.

questions.question: About 150 million years ago, the Swabian Alb was the sea floor, and today it is full of caves. What rock is it mostly made of?
hints: You can find fossil ammonites and shells in it.
Rainwater slowly dissolves this rock, and that's how caves form.
Chalk and marble are close relatives of it.
questions.description: Where Swabians now scrape their Spätzle, very different locals once swam.
questions.fun_fact: Caves in the Swabian Alb held the oldest known musical instruments in the world: flutes made of bone and ivory, about 40,000 years old.

questions.question: This animal was released back into the wild in a German low mountain range starting in 2000. In which range?
hints: The range lies in Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
It is also home to northern Germany's highest mountain.
A steam train runs up the Brocken.
questions.description: This cat has paintbrushes on its ears but never paints a thing.
questions.fun_fact: By 2006, about two dozen lynxes had been released in the Harz, and today their descendants roam as far as Hesse and Thuringia.

questions.question: The Middle Rhine Valley is to clifftop fortresses as the Münsterland is to…?
hints: There are hardly any hills in the Münsterland.
Instead of cliffs, people there protected themselves with wide ditches.
Burg Vischering and Burg Hülshoff are famous examples.
questions.description: If you're looking for a mountain here, better get on a bike and be ready for a long search.
questions.fun_fact: The poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff was born at Burg Hülshoff in the Münsterland in 1797.

questions.question: In this kind of cave, stone spikes grow from the ceiling and the floor, very slowly over thousands of years. What is it called?
hints: The spikes form from water that slowly falls down.
Every drop of water leaves a tiny bit of lime behind.
The name says what the water does from the ceiling.
questions.description: A room where the decorations have been growing for thousands of years, no watering can needed.
questions.fun_fact: In the Atta Cave in the Sauerland, one of Germany's largest dripstone caves, they even age cheese.

questions.question: Mac computers play a famous chord when they start up. In which country is the company that makes them based?
hints: It's a very large country in the Americas.
People there mainly speak English and pay with dollars.
Its flag has 50 stars.
questions.description: A computer that greets you with a chord before it asks for your password.
questions.fun_fact: Apple removed the startup sound from Macs in 2016 and brought it back in 2020 because many users missed it.

questions.question: These rocks in the Teutoburg Forest are called the Externsteine. What kind of rock are they made of?
hints: It's a rock made of tiny grains that settled and were pressed together.
Wind and rain have washed out the softer layers.
You know the grains from the beach.
questions.description: These rocks have stood in the forest so long that they let the weather cut their hair.
questions.fun_fact: One of the rocks has a carving about 900 years old that shows Jesus being taken down from the cross.

questions.question: How long ago did a volcano last erupt in the Eifel?
hints: No history book tells of it.
It was at the end of the last Ice Age.
People already lived in Europe then, but there were no farmers yet.
questions.description: The ground here is only sleeping, and sometimes it even bubbles in its sleep.
questions.fun_fact: The Ulmener Maar is thought to be the Eifel's youngest volcano, and today it is a small, round lake.

questions.question: A river flows into the Danube at Kelheim and past the rocks called the “Zwölf Apostel” (Twelve Apostles). Which valley does it run through?
hints: The valley is in Bavaria.
In quarries near Solnhofen and Eichstätt, people found fossils of the earliest bird.
The river's name contains the German word for a mill.
questions.description: A river that is never in a hurry, yet still gathers apostles on its banks.
questions.fun_fact: The Altmühl flows so gently that it is said to be one of the slowest rivers in Bavaria.

questions.question: After the final whistle, each of Germany's eleven starters swaps his jersey with an opponent. How many jerseys change hands in total?
hints: Each swap sends two jerseys across the field.
Count both teams together.
Eleven plus eleven.
questions.description: The only deal where both sides walk away sweaty and still happy.
questions.fun_fact: One of the first jersey swaps is said to be from a 1931 game: France beat England, and the French players wanted the English shirts as souvenirs.

questions.question: I was born in Poland, had a rocket of a left foot, and I'm still the darling of Cologne's fans. My nickname is a short form of my last name. Who am I?
hints: In 2014 I became world champion with Germany.
The club closest to my heart is 1. FC Köln.
Everyone just calls me “Poldi”.
questions.description: A left foot like a hammer and a good mood like at Carnival.
questions.fun_fact: Besides soccer, Podolski runs his own döner kebab chain called “Mangal Döner”.

questions.question: It has yellow and black stripes, comes for the plum cake in late summer and stings if you swat at it. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It has six legs.
Bees and ants belong to this group too.
The group's name begins with “In…”.
questions.description: It invites itself to every coffee-and-cake afternoon in the garden.
questions.fun_fact: Only female wasps have a stinger – the males can't sting at all.

questions.question: In the garden you find a bumblebee nest in an old mouse hole. About how many bumblebees live in it?
hints: A bumblebee colony is much smaller than a honeybee colony.
A honeybee colony has tens of thousands of bees in summer.
It's more than 100 but fewer than 1,000.
questions.description: Buzzes like a mini helicopter and loves to rent a room from a mouse.
questions.fun_fact: Bumblebees warm up by shivering their flight muscles, so they can fly on cool spring days when honeybees stay in the hive.

questions.question: It's long and pink, has no legs, loosens the garden soil and crawls out of the ground after a rain shower. What is it?
hints: It lives under the ground in the garden.
Blackbirds love to pull it out of the lawn.
Its name tells you where it lives: in the soil.
questions.description: A gardener with no hands, no feet and no garden shears.
questions.fun_fact: Earthworms have no eyes, but they can sense light through their skin.

questions.question: This beetle lives only a few weeks as an adult. How long did it spend before that as a larva in rotting wood?
hints: The larva eats its way very slowly through old, rotting oak wood.
Its time as a larva is much longer than its life as a beetle.
This time is counted in years, but not in decades.
questions.description: It wears antlers, but you'll never hear it roar in the fall.
questions.fun_fact: The stag beetle is the largest beetle in Germany, and only the males have the antler-like jaws.

questions.question: Its slogan is “The Best a Man Can Get,” its founder was named King, and it made disposable razor blades popular. Which brand is it?
hints: It's a brand for getting rid of your beard.
It has models called Mach3 and Fusion.
The brand is named after its founder's last name, which starts with G.
questions.description: A sentence that promises a lot at six in the morning in front of the mirror.
questions.fun_fact: King wasn't a title: it was the first name of King Camp Gillette, who patented his razor in 1904.

questions.question: You meet this animal on the mudflats of the North Sea. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It has a hard shell and two claws.
Lobsters and shrimp belong to this group too.
The zodiac sign Cancer is drawn as one of these animals.
questions.description: A beachgoer with no swimsuit, but a season pass to the mudflats.
questions.fun_fact: If a shore crab loses a claw, it grows back over its next few molts.

questions.question: It has a black head with white cheeks, a yellow chest and calls “zee-zee-bah”. Where does it prefer to build its nest?
questions.answer: In tree holes or nest boxes
wrong_answers: On the ground in tall grass
In the reeds by a lake
As a mud nest under the eaves
hints: It's a common garden bird from the tit family.
It stays all year round and likes to visit bird feeders in winter.
Many people hang wooden boxes with a small entrance hole in their gardens for it.
questions.description: It wears a tie every day and still has never had an office job.
questions.fun_fact: A pair of great tits flies to its chicks with caterpillars several hundred times a day.

questions.question: Listen: which bird is singing here in the garden?
hints: It often sings at dawn from rooftops and TV antennas.
It likes to hop across the lawn and pull out worms.
The male is black and has a yellow-orange beak.
questions.description: A free garden concert: no entry fee, no tickets, and still sold out every day.
questions.fun_fact: Only the male blackbird is black – the female is brown.

questions.question: It has short legs and a long body, and it was once meant to crawl into badger dens. What kind of animal is a Dackel?
hints: It comes from Germany and is also called a Teckel.
It is one of the most popular pets in Germany.
It barks when the doorbell rings.
questions.description: A sausage on four legs that you must never put on the grill.
questions.fun_fact: A colorful Dackel named “Waldi” was the mascot of the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich.

questions.question: You'll find big mounds of needles and twigs like this one in German forests. Which animals built it?
hints: The builders are tiny, but there are hundreds of thousands of them.
They can spray acid to defend themselves.
They crawl on six legs and drag needles into their nest.
questions.description: A high-rise with no elevator, but with very hard-working residents.
questions.fun_fact: Red wood ants are protected by law in Germany, so you're not allowed to destroy their mounds.

questions.question: Which German musician goes by the nickname “Panikrocker”?
hints: He comes from Gronau in Westphalia.
He has lived for decades in Hamburg's Hotel Atlantic.
He almost always wears a hat and sunglasses, and he sang “Sonderzug nach Pankow”.
questions.description: Some nicknames sound a lot scarier than the people who wear them.
questions.fun_fact: Before he became famous, Udo Lindenberg played drums, including in Klaus Doldinger's band Passport.

questions.question: Which Berlin band, founded in 1982, calls itself, tongue in cheek, “the best band in the world”?
hints: The band has three members.
One hit asks: “Junge, warum hast du nichts gelernt?”
Its members are Farin Urlaub, Bela B. and Rodrigo González.
questions.description: Modesty is a virtue, but this band gets along just fine without it.
questions.fun_fact: The band split up in 1988 and got back together in 1993.

questions.question: The electro duo D.A.F., with Gabi Delgado and Robert Görl, sang “Der Räuber und der Prinz” in 1981. What does D.A.F. stand for?
hints: The name is meant ironically and refers to the postwar era.
The “F” stands for something you share between friends.
The second word refers to the country of the Statue of Liberty.
questions.description: Three letters, two musicians and quite a lot of synthesizer.
questions.fun_fact: D.A.F. is seen as a pioneer of Electronic Body Music, or EBM for short.

questions.question: Which of these hip-hop groups is NOT from Hamburg?
hints: The group you're looking for has been active since the late 1980s.
It comes from Baden-Württemberg.
Its hit “Die Da!?” came out in 1992.
questions.description: Hamburg has a harbor, fish sandwiches and apparently a whole lot of microphones.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Da!?” by Die Fantastischen Vier was one of the first big German rap hits in the charts, in 1992.

questions.question: I'm a Japanese sports shoe brand, and my name is a Latin acronym: “a healthy soul in a healthy body.” Who wrote the original line?
hints: He was a Roman poet famous for his satires.
He lived under the emperors Trajan and Hadrian.
The original line reads “mens sana in corpore sano.”
questions.description: A shoe brand that went to Latin class and actually remembered everything.
questions.fun_fact: In his satire, Juvenal said the only thing worth asking the gods for is a healthy mind in a healthy body.

questions.question: Who has sat on the judging panel of “Deutschland sucht den Superstar” for the most seasons since 2002?
hints: He is also a music producer and songwriter.
In the 1980s he was part of Modern Talking.
He is known for his brutally blunt remarks about the contestants.
questions.description: A judges' desk where big singing dreams have been decided for decades.
questions.fun_fact: With Modern Talking he scored the 1984 hit “You're My Heart, You're My Soul”.

questions.question: The line “Ich muss nur noch kurz die Welt retten” (“I just have to quickly save the world”) comes from a Tim Bendzko hit. From which decade?
hints: By then, lots of people already had a smartphone.
In the song, he still wants to check 148 emails.
Shortly before, Lena had won the Eurovision Song Contest.
questions.description: Even superheroes have appointments, and some of them are pretty short.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, Tim Bendzko won the Bundesvision Song Contest for Berlin with “Wenn Worte meine Sprache wären”.

questions.question: NDW singer Markus sang “Ich will Spaß, ich geb Gas” (“I want fun, I step on the gas”). In what year did the hit come out?
hints: Back then there were still two German states.
The Neue Deutsche Welle was at its peak.
That same year, Nicole won the Eurovision Song Contest with “Ein bisschen Frieden”.
questions.description: A song for everyone who thinks speed limits are just a friendly suggestion.
questions.fun_fact: In the song, his Maserati does 210 km/h (about 130 mph), and the police didn't even see it.

questions.question: Three of these words have won Germany's Youth Word of the Year. Which one has NOT?
hints: The word was nominated but never won.
You shout it when something amazes you.
People often stretch it out like a long hiss.
questions.description: A few words made it onto the winners' podium; one is still waiting for its trophy.
questions.fun_fact: “Cringe” won in 2021, and “Sheesh” went home empty-handed despite lots of votes.

questions.question: Rap songs from Berlin-Kreuzberg often mention the “Kotti”. What is it?
questions.answer: A square with a subway station
wrong_answers: A basketball court by the canal
A park on an old airfield
hints: Almost everyone in Kreuzberg passes by it nearly every day.
Its full name ends in “Tor”.
The U1 and U8 lines stop there.
questions.description: A nickname so short you'd think it belonged to a pet.
questions.fun_fact: “Kotti” is short for Kottbusser Tor, one of the best-known squares in Kreuzberg.

questions.question: We started in 1994 with “Hyper Hyper” and later got thousands of people yelling “Maria (I Like It Loud)”. Who are we?
hints: We are a techno band from northern Germany.
Our frontman is known for his bleached-blond hair.
We share our name with a small two-wheeler, pushed with one foot or run by a small motor.
questions.description: Louder, faster, blonder: quiet is so yesterday.
questions.fun_fact: Scooter had more than 20 top-10 hits in Germany, more than almost any other band.

questions.question: DJs call records “vinyl”, fans collect it again, and around 1950 it replaced shellac. What is vinyl, actually?
hints: It is made in a factory and doesn't grow in nature.
It bends more easily and breaks far less often than shellac.
Floor coverings and some rain jackets are made of PVC, a material of this kind.
questions.description: Black, round, full of grooves, and Grandma still has a whole cabinet of them.
questions.fun_fact: Shellac, the material of the old records, comes from the secretions of tiny lac bugs.

questions.question: It comes from Arabic and shows up in lots of German rap lyrics. Why do people say “Wallah”?
questions.answer: To swear that something is true
hints: You say it when someone doesn't believe you.
Word for word, it means “by God”.
A typical use: “Wallah, it wasn't me!”
questions.description: A word heard in schoolyards more often than “homework”.
questions.fun_fact: Lots of German teens say “Wallah” even though they don't speak a word of Arabic themselves.

questions.question: Who made the 1513 engraving “Knight, Death and the Devil”?
hints: The artist lived at the time of the Reformation.
His self-portrait in a fur-trimmed coat is world-famous.
His monogram is a big A with a D underneath.
questions.description: Back then, the printer was still a person with an engraving tool and a very steady hand.
questions.fun_fact: In copper engraving the picture is cut into the plate in mirror image, and mistakes can hardly be fixed.

questions.question: Which German woman won Olympic gold in this event at Tokyo 2021?
hints: She comes from near Heidelberg.
She was also world champion in 2019 and 2022.
Her first name means “angel” in Swahili.
questions.description: Run-up, takeoff, sandbox, all at world-class level.
questions.fun_fact: Malaika Mihambo's father is from Tanzania.

questions.question: An ad ends with “The Power of Dreams,” the slogan of a Japanese brand named after its founder. Who founded it?
hints: The brand makes cars and motorcycles seen all over the world.
It created ASIMO, a famous humanoid robot.
The logo on its cars is a big H.
questions.description: A slogan for daydreamers, but with your seatbelt fastened.
questions.fun_fact: After World War II, Soichiro Honda got his start by fitting small engines to bicycles.

questions.question: Which supermarket chain belongs to the Schwarz Group like Lidl does, and is known for its especially large stores?
hints: The company is based in Neckarsulm, Baden-Württemberg.
Its logo is a red rectangle with a white letter.
The name joins the German words for “buy” and “country”.
questions.description: A store so big you almost need GPS to find the fruit section.
questions.fun_fact: Kaufland has stores not only in Germany but also in Poland, Czechia, Romania and other European countries.

questions.question: Which German carmaker started out building aircraft engines?
hints: The company was founded during the First World War.
The company is based in Bavaria.
The name is short for “… Motoren Werke”.
questions.description: Four wheels, lots of sheet metal and a company history with a surprising start.
questions.fun_fact: People often think the blue-and-white logo shows a spinning propeller, but the colors actually come from the Bavarian flag.

questions.question: This two-seater fits sideways into a parking space and was made with a Swiss watchmaker. Which car brand is it?
hints: The watchmaker is known for colorful plastic watches.
For a long time, the brand belonged to Mercedes-Benz.
The name hides Swatch, Mercedes and “Art”.
questions.description: A car with a trunk about the size of a grocery bag.
questions.fun_fact: The first Smart Fortwo was only about 2.5 m (8.2 ft) long, barely more than half the length of a normal family car.

questions.question: The hazelnut-nougat wafer has been around since 1959, and its name “Hanuta” is short for a German word. Which one?
hints: The name joins the main ingredient to a second word.
The second word has to do with the wafer's shape.
It's the same word you'd use in German for a bar of chocolate: “Schokoladen…”.
questions.description: Two wafers, one filling and a name that saved itself a few letters.
questions.fun_fact: Hanuta is made by Ferrero, the same candy company that makes Nutella.

questions.question: Which ride at the Kirmes does this horse belong to?
hints: It's fine even for very small children.
Besides horses, it often has carriages and little fire trucks too.
Playgrounds have a small version that you push around.
questions.description: A horse that never eats hay but still carries kids every day.
questions.fun_fact: The word “carousel” comes via French from the Italian “carosello”, an old game played on horseback.

questions.question: In the Rhineland, the carnival season begins at 11:11 a.m. On which day does it end?
hints: For many Jecken, it's a rather sad day.
After it, Lent begins, the time of fasting before Easter.
In church on this day, people get a cross marked on their forehead.
questions.description: Every party ends sometime. This one even has a fixed date for it.
questions.fun_fact: An old carnival hit goes: “Am Aschermittwoch ist alles vorbei” (“On Ash Wednesday, it's all over”).

questions.question: At the lottery booth, you unroll your ticket and read “Niete”. What does that mean?
hints: It's no reason to cheer.
Most tickets in the drum are like this.
The opposite of it is a “Treffer”.
questions.description: Luck at the Kirmes is like the weather: you never know beforehand what's coming.
questions.fun_fact: “Niete” comes from the Dutch word “niet”, which means “nothing”.

questions.question: Complete the “Fliegerlied”: “Und ich flieg, flieg, flieg wie ein Flieger, bin so stark, stark, stark wie ein …”
hints: It's an animal.
It's a big wild cat.
It has orange and black stripes.
questions.description: A song where no arm stays down.
questions.fun_fact: The “Fliegerlied” started out as a children's song by Donikkl before it became a party hit at carnival and après-ski.

questions.question: Until 2006, kids' teams from Germany, Austria and a third country played on “1, 2 oder 3”. Which country?
hints: Many areas there speak German too.
The country borders Lake Constance.
The country is famous for the Alps, watches and chocolate.
questions.description: Whether you're really standing on the right spot, you'll see when the light comes on, and this time you don't even have to jump.
questions.fun_fact: “1, 2 oder 3” started in 1977, and its first host was Michael Schanze.

questions.question: In the morning I buy Schrippen at the bakery, and I say “wat” for “was” and “icke” for “ich”. Where am I from?
hints: I live in a big city.
The Spree River flows through my city.
I live in Germany's capital.
questions.description: A dialect where even the little word “ich” sounds pretty cheeky.
questions.fun_fact: 1990 World Cup winner Thomas Häßler was born in Berlin, and his nickname is “Icke”.

questions.question: A fast-food chain that sold tacos and burritos told people to “think outside the bun.” Which country does that food come from?
hints: It is a country in the Americas.
The Day of the Dead is celebrated there.
Its capital city shares the country's name.
questions.description: An invitation to drop the burger and fold the tortilla instead.
questions.fun_fact: The chain behind the slogan, Taco Bell, is actually American: Glen Bell founded it in California in 1962.

questions.question: I often wear a striped shirt, I know all about knots, and I shout “Ahoy!” to greet another ship. Who am I?
hints: I don't work on land.
My workplace can rock quite a bit.
I go to sea.
questions.description: Every job has its own greeting, and this one sounds like adventure.
questions.fun_fact: Alexander Graham Bell wanted people to answer the phone with “Ahoy”, but “Hello” won.

questions.question: Many businesses in Germany call themselves a “Kelterei”, from the verb “keltern”. What does such a business mainly do?
hints: It is busiest in the fall, at harvest time.
Winemakers do the same with grapes.
In the end, something liquid flows out of a big press.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a Celtic tribe but has nothing to do with Asterix.
questions.fun_fact: Before machines, grapes were often trodden with bare feet; the wine press (Kelter) later took over that job.

questions.question: In many places, beer mixed with lemon soda is called “Radler”. In which city is it traditionally ordered as “Alsterwasser”?
hints: The name comes from a river.
The river the drink is named after forms two lakes right in the middle of the city.
The Elbphilharmonie stands there.
questions.description: A drink that changes its name from region to region like a secret agent.
questions.fun_fact: Legend has it that an innkeeper invented the Radler in 1922 when he ran out of beer with crowds of cyclists stopping by.

questions.question: Cloves go into Glühwein. Their names, “Nelke” in German and “clove” in English, both come from old words for…
hints: It's about the shape of the clove.
It has a thin stem with a round head on top.
You hit these into the wall with a hammer.
questions.description: A spice with a name older than Grandma's spice rack.
questions.fun_fact: Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tree that first came from the Moluccas in Indonesia.

questions.question: On Vatertag (Father's Day), many German men pull Bollerwagen (handcarts) through the countryside. On which weekday is it always?
hints: In Germany it's a public holiday, so most people have the day off.
It falls on Ascension Day, 39 days after Easter Sunday.
Many people take the next day off for a long weekend.
questions.description: The day when handcarts get their big moment.
questions.fun_fact: Because Ascension Day is always 39 days after Easter Sunday, German Father's Day always falls on a Thursday.

questions.question: It's made of colorful plastic, has a handle and 12 or 20 slots, and people love to stack it. What usually goes in the slots?
hints: When it's full, it's really heavy.
At parties and family gatherings, there are often several of them standing around.
When they're empty, you take them back and get your Pfand (deposit) back.
questions.description: A colorful plastic block that has a home in almost every German basement.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany you usually get a deposit back for the crate itself too, often 1.50 euros.

questions.question: Around 1902, the toy company Steiff from Giengen brought out a stuffed animal that is still world-famous today. Which one?
hints: It has round ears and soft fur.
After the Leipzig toy fair in 1903, it became a huge hit in America.
It is named after the nickname of US President Theodore Roosevelt.
questions.description: A cuddly toy that has been helping children fall asleep for more than 100 years.
questions.fun_fact: Margarete Steiff, who founded the company, used a wheelchair from childhood and sewed her first stuffed animals herself.

questions.question: Hermann Göring helped found the Gestapo in 1933, was the only “Reichsmarschall” and from 1935 led which branch of the Wehrmacht?
hints: This branch of the Wehrmacht was only officially unveiled in 1935.
In World War I, Göring led Richthofen's former squadron.
This branch fought in the air.
questions.description: A man with more titles than medals, and he had a lot of medals.
questions.fun_fact: Göring had a huge country estate built in the Schorfheide north of Berlin and called it “Carinhall”.

questions.question: In Erich Kästner's book, Luise and Lotte find out at summer camp that they are twins. What must they change to secretly swap places?
hints: The book is “Das doppelte Lottchen” (in English, “Lottie and Lisa”).
At first, one of the sisters isn't happy about the change at all.
It's about what a hairdresser does.
questions.description: A plan meant to fool even their own parents.
questions.fun_fact: “Das doppelte Lottchen” came out in 1949 and was later made into the Hollywood film “The Parent Trap.”

questions.question: You're watching “The Simpsons” in German and hear Anke Engelke. Which character has she voiced since 2006?
hints: The character is an adult.
She appears in almost every episode.
Her hair is a tall blue tower.
questions.description: In Springfield's German version, some voices sound suspiciously like “Ladykracher.”
questions.fun_fact: Before Anke Engelke, Elisabeth Volkmann voiced this role for many years.

questions.question: I'm a solid dome: no one can go inside me, and pilgrims walk around me. The first ones held the ashes of a great teacher. Whose?
hints: He was a spiritual teacher born about 2,500 years ago in what is now Nepal.
His followers pray alongside monks in orange robes.
Many statues show him sitting cross-legged in meditation, with a calm smile.
questions.description: A dome so tightly sealed that even the world's best locksmith would give up.
questions.fun_fact: The Great Stupa at Sanchi, in India, was begun in the 3rd century BC and is one of the oldest stone buildings in the country.

questions.question: Which of these films does Katja Riemann NOT appear in?
hints: The film you want covers just 20 minutes.
The heroine has bright red hair.
Franka Potente plays the lead, and Tom Tykwer directed it.
questions.description: Katja Riemann has been in a huge number of films, just not every single one.
questions.fun_fact: Katja Riemann won Best Actress at the Venice Film Festival in 2003 for “Rosenstraße”.

questions.question: This actor became famous with “Good Bye, Lenin!” and later played in a Marvel film. In which city was he born?
hints: He grew up in Cologne.
His mother is from Spain.
His birth city is famous for the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: A face that watched the Wall fall on screen and hatched dark plans for Marvel.
questions.fun_fact: In Berlin he ran a tapas bar called “Bar Raval”, named after a neighborhood in his birth city.

questions.question: You're reading an old GDR menu: “Broiler” is to roast chicken as “Sättigungsbeilage” is to …?
wrong_answers: Pudding, stewed fruit or ice cream
hints: Without it, the plate would look pretty empty.
It usually sits right next to the meat.
Boiled potatoes were the classic choice.
questions.description: Officialese on the plate: even lunch had a job title.
questions.fun_fact: The GDR word “Broiler” comes from English, where “to broil” means to grill.

questions.question: Trabant is to car as Barkas B 1000 is to …?
hints: It was built in Saxony, with the Wartburg's engine.
You saw it as an ambulance, a mail van and a fire truck.
In the West, its counterpart was the VW Bus.
questions.description: A vehicle from Saxony that hardly anyone in the West knew by name.
questions.fun_fact: The Barkas B 1000 was built from 1961 to 1991, about 30 years with almost no changes.

questions.question: In Berlin, you walk straight from the Brandenburg Gate through the Tiergarten to the Victory Column. Which street are you on?
hints: New Year's Eve parties and soccer fan zones take place here.
The street runs west from the gate, not east.
Its name recalls the 1953 uprising in East Germany.
questions.description: Berlin's widest party zone is, on any ordinary day, just a street with lots of traffic.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1990, June 17 was a public holiday in West Germany, called the “Day of German Unity.”

questions.question: Prisoners called the windowless basement cells of the Stasi prison in Hohenschönhausen simply “the …”. What was the nickname?
hints: The name fits cramped, dark rooms with no daylight at all.
It makes you think of tight space, damp and being shut off.
It dives under water.
questions.description: A nickname that sounds like an adventure, but certainly wasn't one.
questions.fun_fact: On GDR city maps the prison grounds in Hohenschönhausen weren't drawn in, just left as a blank spot.

questions.question: Mayors have existed since the Middle Ages. Today they work in the town hall. What is their job?
questions.answer: To run the town or city
hints: They are elected by the people who live there.
They take care of local things like schools, streets and playgrounds.
They are the bosses of the local administration.
questions.description: Being the boss without ever getting to wear a crown.
questions.fun_fact: In Berlin and Hamburg, the mayor is also the head of government of a whole federal state.

questions.question: It sits at the top of a column, joins it to what it holds up, and the Greeks decorated it with spirals or leaves. What is it called?
hints: It's not the long middle part or the bottom part.
Its name comes from the Latin “caput”, meaning head.
It's spelled just like the word for a country's “head” city.
questions.description: The hat columns put on to look elegant.
questions.fun_fact: The three classical Greek orders (Doric, Ionic and Corinthian) are told apart mostly by looking at this part of the column.

questions.question: People used to push me with muscle power, but today I often hum along with a motor. I keep the grass in the yard short. What am I?
hints: People use me outside in the yard.
I have sharp blades that spin.
In Germany, I'm not allowed to run on Sundays.
questions.description: Best friend of every German who simply must have the tidiest front yard on the street.
questions.fun_fact: The first lawn mower was invented by Englishman Edwin Budding in 1830.

questions.question: He carries a big bag and comes almost every weekday. What does the mail carrier bring?
hints: He puts something in your mailbox.
He often rides a yellow bike or drives a yellow van.
Sometimes your name is written on the envelope.
questions.description: He rings your doorbell more often than your friends do.
questions.fun_fact: The word “post” comes from the Italian “posta,” a station where messengers used to get fresh horses.

questions.question: I came from Hamburg, traveled across the Sahara and the Sahel for five years, reached Timbuktu in 1853 and wrote five thick volumes about it. Who am I?
hints: My journey began in Tripoli with a British expedition.
I had studied the ancient world and spoke many languages.
My last name sounds just like the German word for beard.
questions.description: A Hamburger who cared more about sand than about fish sandwiches.
questions.fun_fact: In Timbuktu, you can still visit the house where Heinrich Barth stayed.

questions.question: In 1866, Werner von Siemens built a machine that turns motion into electricity. Its name comes from the Greek word for power. What is it called?
hints: It works exactly the opposite way from a motor.
Huge versions of it spin in power plants.
A small version powers the light on a bicycle.
questions.description: Mr. Siemens tinkered a bit, and today a whole global company carries his name.
questions.fun_fact: A unit of physics is even named after Werner von Siemens: the siemens, for electrical conductance.

questions.question: Complete the word: to this day, many call the 2006 home World Cup Germany's “Sommer…”.
hints: The word makes that summer sound too good to be true.
Sönke Wortmann made a documentary film about the World Cup with this word in its title.
Think of the Brothers Grimm: “Once upon a time…”
questions.description: Black, red and gold on every balcony, and nobody wanted to go home.
questions.fun_fact: Germany didn't win the 2006 World Cup, but after a 3–1 win over Portugal in Stuttgart, fans celebrated third place as if it were the title.

questions.question: I wear a jersey, fans voted on my name, and I was the mascot of Euro 2024 in Germany. Who am I?
hints: Of course I was there for the opening match in Munich.
My name is a well-known first name with an animal built into it.
Sounds like Albert, only a bit more bear-like.
questions.description: Finally, a mascot you're allowed to cuddle after the game.
questions.fun_fact: In the name vote, Albärt beat other names such as “Bärnardo” and “Herzi von Bär”.

questions.question: In what year did the pink-and-purple away jersey of Germany's national team make headlines?
hints: It was only a few years ago.
A European Championship was held that year.
That summer, Germany was the host itself.
questions.description: Real men wear pink, at least for away games.
questions.fun_fact: The pink jersey was so popular that many sizes sold out soon after it went on sale.

questions.question: For his tireless man-marking, fans called World Cup winner Berti Vogts simply “the …”. What was his nickname?
hints: Vogts was rather small, but he never let go of the player he was marking.
“Kaiser” was his teammate Franz Beckenbauer; Vogts's nickname sounded less royal.
A small, stubborn breed of dog.
questions.description: A defender that strikers couldn't shake off even in the shower.
questions.fun_fact: As Germany's head coach, Berti Vogts won the 1996 European Championship in England.

questions.question: Bird catchers once smeared branches with a sticky paste made from tree resin. Which German word comes from this way of catching birds?
hints: The word describes a person, not an animal.
A bird that got stuck there had really bad luck.
Its opposite is a “Glückspilz”.
questions.description: A word with feathers that nobody wants to be called.
questions.fun_fact: The German saying “jemandem auf den Leim gehen” (to fall for someone's trick, literally “to go onto someone's glue”) also comes from catching birds with glue-covered twigs.

questions.question: Listen: which animal native to Germany is calling here?
hints: It lives with its family in a pack.
It looks like a big gray dog.
In the fairy tale, Little Red Riding Hood meets it in the woods.
questions.description: A traveler who came home with no suitcase, but with plenty of singing.
questions.fun_fact: In 2000, the first wolf pups born in Germany in over 100 years arrived in Lusatia, in Saxony.

questions.question: In Roman baths, the caldarium was the hot room and the tepidarium the warm one. What was the cold room called?
hints: The names follow the temperature of the water.
Think of a kitchen appliance that keeps things cold.
Its name sounds like “frigid” and “refrigerator”.
questions.description: A spa from 2,000 years ago: no phones, but plenty of gossip.
questions.fun_fact: The Baths of Caracalla in Rome could hold more than 1,500 bathers at the same time.

questions.question: Herring gulls have a red spot on their beak. What happens when a chick pecks at it?
hints: For the parents, the pecking is a signal.
Newly hatched chicks can't look after themselves yet.
Afterwards, the chick is full.
questions.description: Press the button and the show begins, no remote control needed.
questions.fun_fact: The scientist Niko Tinbergen showed that gull chicks will even peck at cardboard beaks with a red spot.

questions.question: Complete the old New Year's Eve custom: “If you carry a carp scale with you, in the new year you'll have …”
hints: People often get the scale from eating carp on New Year's Eve or Christmas Eve.
It's meant to work as a little good-luck charm all year long.
You keep it in your wallet so it never runs empty.
questions.description: A fish that used to enjoy a little vacation in the bathtub before the holidays.
questions.fun_fact: In parts of Germany, Austria and the Czech Republic, carp is a traditional dish on Christmas Eve or New Year's Eve.

questions.question: Which publisher picks Germany's Youth Word of the Year (Jugendwort des Jahres) every year?
hints: The publisher was founded in Berlin in the 19th century.
It is best known for foreign-language dictionaries.
Its dictionaries are usually yellow with a big blue letter on the cover.
questions.description: Adults love saying they don't understand it, yet one publisher makes a big deal of it every year.
questions.fun_fact: The very first Youth Word of the Year, in 2008, was “Gammelfleischparty” (literally “rotten meat party”), meaning a party for people over 30.

questions.question: I sit on your ears and play music just for you. DJs use me to secretly listen to the next song. What am I?
hints: I keep music so quiet that nobody else can hear it.
I have two ear cups and a band over the top of your head.
You put me on your head and listen through me.
questions.description: A concert just for you, and the neighbors never notice a thing.
questions.fun_fact: DJs often hold just one ear cup to their ear, so the other ear can hear what's playing in the club.

questions.question: The rocks of the Elbe Sandstone Mountains contain fossil shells. What did this sandstone form from about 100 million years ago?
questions.answer: Sand on the floor of a sea
hints: Back then, the land in Saxony looked completely different.
Rivers washed in sand, which settled layer by layer.
The shellfish lived right where the sand came to rest.
questions.description: These rocks are so old that even Grandpa looks like a baby next to them.
questions.fun_fact: Dresden's Frauenkirche was also built from Elbe sandstone.

questions.question: On a map of Lake Constance, you see the word “Obersee.” What does it mean?
questions.answer: The large main part of Lake Constance
wrong_answers: A small mountain lake high above the shore
The part of the lake west of Konstanz
A reservoir on the Alpine Rhine
hints: Lake Constance is made up of two main parts.
The other part is called the Untersee.
Friedrichshafen, Lindau and Bregenz lie on this part.
questions.description: At Lake Constance, even the water needs its own map.
questions.fun_fact: To this day, Germany, Austria and Switzerland have never agreed on a shared border in the water of the Obersee.

questions.question: Columbus is said to have stood an egg on its tip at a banquet. What is an “Egg of Columbus”?
hints: Afterwards, everyone else said: “I could have done that too!”
He simply pressed the tip of the egg in a little.
It's a trick you have to think of first, but then it's child's play.
questions.description: Breakfast and world history in a single egg cup.
questions.fun_fact: The story appears in a 1565 book by the Italian Girolamo Benzoni, but a similar tale was told even earlier about the architect Brunelleschi.

questions.question: The German saying “auf großem Fuß leben” (to live on a big foot) is said to come from pointed medieval shoes like these. Who wore the longest tips?
hints: You could hardly work in these shoes.
There were even rules about who could wear tips of what length.
Someone who “lives on a big foot” spends a lot of money.
questions.description: In the Middle Ages, a giant shoe size had nothing to do with your feet.
questions.fun_fact: Some tips were supposedly so long that they had to be tied to the leg with little chains.

questions.question: Which of these words do German teens NOT use as a casual way to address their buddies?
hints: You can hear all four words in German schoolyards.
The word you're looking for describes something rather than calling someone.
You say it when something is super embarrassing.
questions.description: In the schoolyard nobody has a name, but everybody has a nickname.
questions.fun_fact: “Cringe” was voted Germany's Jugendwort des Jahres (youth word of the year) in 2021.

questions.question: Look at the top of this column, decorated with leaves. Which order of classical architecture does it belong to?
hints: It is the most decorated of the Greek orders.
The leaves come from a plant called acanthus.
Its name comes from a Greek city famous for its wealth, near a canal.
questions.description: A column that did its hair with its best leafy hairstyle.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Roman writer Vitruvius, the Corinthian order was born when a sculptor saw a basket surrounded by acanthus leaves on a tomb.

questions.question: You don't follow the news, think smartphones are newfangled and have never heard of today's hits. Where do you live, says a German saying?
hints: The place isn't on Earth.
You can see it in the night sky.
It has a side we never get to see from Earth.
questions.description: A dead zone deluxe, with a view of the stars.
questions.fun_fact: There really is a side of the moon we never see, because the moon always turns the same face towards Earth.

questions.question: Since 1998, I've explained technology, food and everyday life on ProSieben in the early evening. My first host was Aiman Abdallah. What am I?
hints: I usually air just before the 8:15 p.m. prime-time slot.
On my show, you often see how food is made in big factories.
I share my name with a scientist who pointed a telescope at Jupiter in 1610.
questions.description: The show that suddenly makes you an expert on French fries at dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Galileo Galilei, the show's namesake, discovered Jupiter's four large moons with his telescope.

questions.question: Swivel chair is to “The Voice of Germany” as full-body costume is to…?
hints: In this show, at first you don't know who is actually singing.
The panel tries to guess which celebrity is inside the costume.
At the end of each round, a mask comes off.
questions.description: Saturday night: popcorn on the couch, and the whole family singing loudly along with the TV.
questions.fun_fact: The idea for the show originally comes from South Korea.

questions.question: For decades, families have watched the Tagesschau news in front of the „Glotze“ (the TV). In which decade was its first broadcast?
hints: Back then, the pictures were still black and white.
Few families owned a TV then; many watched at the neighbors' or in a pub.
It was just after Christmas, in the same decade Germany first won the World Cup.
questions.description: A box that whole generations have spent their evenings staring at.
questions.fun_fact: The first Tagesschau aired on December 26, 1952; „Glotze“ comes from „glotzen“, meaning to stare.

questions.question: The state flag of Baden-Württemberg is black and gold. From the coat of arms of which old duchy do these colors come?
hints: The three black lions in the state coat of arms come from there.
The Staufer family were dukes there before they became emperors.
People there like to say “Schaffe, schaffe, Häusle baue” (work, work, build a little house).
questions.description: A German state that clearly borrowed its color scheme from the bumblebees.
questions.fun_fact: The three black lions on gold in the state's greater coat of arms are the old arms of the Staufer family.

questions.question: The father is called a boar and the mother a sow. Which animals are we talking about?
hints: They live on a farm.
They are often kept in a barn.
They oink and have a curly tail.
questions.description: A farm family where everyone has a different name, even though they all belong to the same species.
questions.fun_fact: German hunters have their own words for wild boars: the male is a “Keiler” and the mother a “Bache”.

questions.question: I leap, white on a red background, on the coat of arms of Lower Saxony. Which animal am I?
hints: I have hooves.
You can ride on me.
In Lower Saxony I'm also called the Sachsenross.
questions.description: This animal has been leaping on a coat of arms for centuries and still hasn't landed.
questions.fun_fact: A white horse leaps on the coat of arms of North Rhine-Westphalia too: the Westfalenross.

questions.question: In Saarland, the grill that hangs from a tripod has the same name as the man who runs it. What is the word?
hints: Locals use the same word, as a verb, for the grilling itself.
The meat on it is usually marinated pork neck steak.
The word comes from swinging the grill grate back and forth.
questions.description: Here, grilling isn't a hobby, it's a way of life.
questions.fun_fact: In Saarland, even the meat on the grill is often just called a “Schwenker”.

questions.question: What do people in Germany say when they've just been lucky?
hints: You say it after a stroke of luck, not before.
The animal in the saying is a popular gift on New Year's Eve.
The animal oinks.
questions.description: Sometimes in life you just need a beast of a lucky break.
questions.fun_fact: One explanation: at old contests, the last-place finisher often got a piglet as a consolation prize, so they had “had pig”.

questions.question: With honey it becomes cough syrup; warmed in a small bag on the ear, it's said to ease earache. Which vegetable is it?
hints: It's almost always in the kitchen.
It's made of many layers.
Cutting it often makes your eyes water.
questions.description: Grandma's pharmacy was usually in the vegetable drawer.
questions.fun_fact: When you cut an onion, it releases a substance that rises into the air and makes your eyes water.

questions.question: I'm an ice hockey club from the “City of Velvet and Silk,” and I became German champion in 2003. Who am I?
hints: The city lies on the Lower Rhine, northwest of Düsseldorf.
In the 2003 final, it beat the Kölner Haie.
Its mascot wears a tailcoat and can't fly.
questions.description: This club is cut from finer cloth than its rivals.
questions.fun_fact: Krefeld was once so famous for its silk fabrics that it is still called the “City of Velvet and Silk” today.

questions.question: You're on the beach at Büsum at low tide. About how long until the water is at its highest again?
hints: The water comes in twice a day.
From one high tide to the next takes a little over half a day.
It's roughly a quarter of a day.
questions.description: The North Sea keeps a strict schedule, and it actually sticks to it.
questions.fun_fact: Because the Moon drives the tides, low and high tide come almost an hour later each day.

questions.question: An old German hit song goes “Pack die Badehose ein … und dann nischt wie raus nach Wannsee”. In which city is the Wannsee?
hints: Young Conny Froboess sang the song in 1951.
The word “nischt” (instead of “nichts”) gives away the local dialect.
It is the capital of Germany.
questions.description: Swimsuit on, picnic basket packed: now you just need the right S-Bahn train.
questions.fun_fact: Strandbad Wannsee, the lake's big public beach, opened in 1907 and is one of the largest inland lake beaches in Europe.

questions.question: This river rises in Vorarlberg, plunges over a waterfall near Füssen and flows through Augsburg to the Danube. Which is it?
hints: For long stretches it separates Swabia from Old Bavaria.
In 955, Otto the Great defeated the Hungarians by this river.
The town of Landsberg carries the river's name as part of its own.
questions.description: A river that sets off in Austria and makes its career in Swabia.
questions.fun_fact: Augsburg lies west of the Lech, so it belongs to Swabia, not to Old Bavaria.

questions.question: What is this long, grassy bank on the North Sea coast for?
questions.answer: It protects the land from the sea
wrong_answers: It is a pasture just for sheep
It is a sledding hill in winter
It holds the sand on the beach
hints: It matters most during storms.
Without it, many fields and villages would get wet.
High waves and storm surges can't get over it.
questions.description: Long, green, full of sheep, and still not a golf course.
questions.fun_fact: Sheep on the dike keep the grass short and press the soil firm with their hooves.

questions.question: In a flood, helpers usually fill sandbags like these only about two-thirds full. Why?
questions.answer: So they mold together and close the gaps
wrong_answers: So they float on top of the water
So the sand lasts for more bags
So they dry out faster afterward
hints: A bag stuffed full is as hard as a rock.
Gaps stay open between hard, round bags.
A bag that isn't quite full can be pressed flat and shaped.
questions.description: Heavy to haul, but wanted by everyone when the river tries to leave its banks.
questions.fun_fact: A filled sandbag weighs about 15 kg (33 lb), and a long wall needs thousands of them.

questions.question: Where in Germany are you most likely to find pieces like these on the beach after a storm?
hints: The pieces are so light that the waves easily wash them ashore.
Long ago, traders carried them on long journeys all the way to Rome.
Rügen and Usedom lie in it.
questions.description: Golden treasures you can find without a treasure map.
questions.fun_fact: Amber isn't a stone at all: it's tree resin that hardened over millions of years.

questions.question: What do you call this triangular part at the top of a temple's front, above the columns?
hints: It is neither round nor curved.
In Greece, people filled it with statues of gods.
Smaller copies of it often sit above the doors and windows of grand old buildings.
questions.description: Greek temple roofs have a pointy side too.
questions.fun_fact: The pediment of the Parthenon had sculptures telling the story of Athena's birth.

questions.question: A raindrop falls into the Danube in Ulm. Which sea does it end up in?
hints: The Danube flows east.
It passes through ten countries.
Its delta is in Romania.
questions.description: A raindrop on a long journey, without any luggage.
questions.fun_fact: On its way, the Danube flows through four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

questions.question: Thousands of curly little sand piles like these lie on the Wadden Sea mudflats. What are they?
questions.answer: Sand pooped out by a worm
wrong_answers: Sand swirls shaped by the wind
Eggs laid by a kind of clam
hints: An animal made them.
It lives buried in the mud and eats sand.
Whatever it can't digest comes out the back end.
questions.description: An art show on the seabed that reopens after every high tide.
questions.fun_fact: A lugworm eats sand, digests the tiny living things in it and leaves the clean sand behind.

questions.question: At low tide you walk barefoot across the seabed, usually with a guide and sometimes all the way to an island. What is this called?
hints: People do this mainly on the North Sea coast.
The ground is muddy and full of tiny creatures.
The name contains the German word for the muddy seabed.
questions.description: A day trip where shoes just get in the way and mud is very much welcome.
questions.fun_fact: From Cuxhaven you can walk about 10 km (6 miles) across the mudflats to the island of Neuwerk.

questions.question: When was the pirate Klaus Störtebeker causing trouble on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea?
hints: The Hanseatic League was especially powerful at the time.
It was in the late Middle Ages.
Christopher Columbus was born only about 50 years later.
questions.description: A sea robber who kept Hamburg's merchants up at night.
questions.fun_fact: Every summer on the island of Rügen, the Störtebeker Festival in Ralswiek acts out his story on stage.

questions.question: Which German saying fits when someone ties a double knot in their shoe or locks the door twice?
hints: It's about caution and safety.
There's a number hidden in it, if not in plain sight.
Twice is safer than once.
questions.description: For people who rattle the door once more after locking it.
questions.fun_fact: At school you often hear it when a teacher explains something a second time.

questions.question: You're in class, and the teacher is about to say what's on the test. According to a German saying, what do you “sharpen”?
hints: It's about listening very carefully.
Dogs and horses really do this when they hear something.
You have two of them, one on each side of your head.
questions.description: Be very quiet now, things are about to get exciting.
questions.fun_fact: Cats can turn each ear on its own to find exactly where a sound is coming from.

questions.question: In German, someone who hits „ins Schwarze“ (into the black) is exactly right. Where does the saying come from?
hints: Here people compete for points, and sometimes for prizes.
“The black” was a painted spot meant to be seen from far away.
The center of the target used to be black.
questions.description: Get this one right and you can be the know-it-all for the rest of the evening.
questions.fun_fact: On many old shooting targets, the black circle was in the middle so it was easy to see from far away.

questions.question: I am a queen and want to be the fairest in all the land. Every day I ask something hanging on my wall. Who am I?
hints: Something hanging on the wall answers me.
One day a girl beyond the mountains is fairer than I am.
The girl lives with seven dwarfs.
questions.description: If you can't stand coming in second, don't hold a beauty contest in your own castle.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brothers Grimm's first version, it was Snow White's own mother; only later did she become the stepmother.

questions.question: I'm a comedian from Berlin, my catchphrase is “Kennste? Kennste?”, and in 2008 I filled Berlin's Olympic Stadium. Who am I?
hints: On stage, my favorite stories are about my girlfriend.
On RTL, I have my own show exposing where tax money gets wasted.
My first name is the same as that of a famous video game plumber.
questions.description: A man who filled a whole stadium with his relationship talks.
questions.fun_fact: With almost 70,000 people watching, his show at the Olympic Stadium entered the Guinness World Records as the biggest comedy show in the world.

questions.question: In the middle of the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra, twelve marble lions stand in a circle. What are they there for?
questions.answer: To spout water from their mouths
wrong_answers: To hold up the courtyard's roof
To serve as an altar for offerings
hints: It was a very important element in the palaces of Muslim Spain.
They make noise, but they don't roar.
They are part of a fountain.
questions.description: Twelve big cats that haven't moved or complained in centuries.
questions.fun_fact: After years of work, the fountain was fully restored and started running again in 2012.

questions.question: You're sitting across from Günther Jauch and just got the 125,000-euro question right. How much is the next question worth?
hints: The jump is bigger than at any step before.
After that, only one more question stands between you and the million.
The amount is exactly half of a million.
questions.description: This is where the chair starts to sweat – and the contestant even more.
questions.fun_fact: The first person to win the million with Günther Jauch was historian Eckhard Freise, in 2000.

questions.question: Which of these women did NOT win “Germany's Next Topmodel”?
hints: She's known more for her voice than for the runway.
In 2010 she won a big European music contest.
Her winning song was called “Satellite”.
questions.description: Runway, photo shoots, tears, and in the end only one gets the photo.
questions.fun_fact: The very first winner of the show, in 2006, was Lena Gercke, so a Lena did win after all!

questions.question: On ProSieben, until 2015, I challenged contestants in up to 15 games. The celebrity version of my show is “Schlag den Star”. Who am I?
hints: I also make music and have performed at the Eurovision Song Contest.
For years I hosted the show “TV total”.
My own show was called “Schlag den …” followed by my last name.
questions.description: Anyone who wanted to beat this man needed muscles, brains and the patience to sit through a very long night.
questions.fun_fact: Some episodes of “Schlag den Raab” lasted more than five hours and ran late into the night.

questions.question: A family in need goes away, a team completely rebuilds their house, and Eva Brenner hosts. What is this RTL II show called?
hints: At the end there is a big, tearful reunion in front of the house.
Interior designers and builders finish the makeover in about a week.
The title links your own home with great happiness.
questions.description: One week of vacation, and afterwards you don't recognize your own living room.
questions.fun_fact: The show has been on RTL II since 2005.

questions.question: On “Dalli Dalli,” Hans Rosenthal jumped in the air and shouted “Das war Spitze!” In which decade did the ZDF show start?
hints: Color TV was still fairly new in West Germany at the time.
Hans Rosenthal had long been a popular quizmaster on the radio before.
In the same decade, Germany won the soccer World Cup for the second time.
questions.description: A quizmaster so happy he briefly took off.
questions.fun_fact: Rosenthal's jump was frozen on screen, so he seemed to float in the air for a moment.

questions.question: In German comics, “Haha” stands for laughing. What's written there when someone gets hurt?
hints: Little kids often shout it at the playground.
An ice pack often helps afterwards.
It has only three letters and starts with A.
questions.description: A word that usually comes right before a bandage and a cookie to cheer you up.
questions.fun_fact: In English you shout “Ouch,” and in French “Aïe.”

questions.question: In German, who is lovingly called a “Frechdachs”?
hints: It’s usually not meant in a mean way.
People often grin when they say it.
This child probably has a big mouth.
questions.description: An animal that sleeps all day and still has a bad reputation.
questions.fun_fact: Real badgers are quite shy and usually leave their burrows only at dusk.

questions.question: Which German word do you shout with glee while rubbing one index finger along the other?
hints: Kids say it when they've won and the other one hasn't.
People often stick out their tongue as well.
It's often followed by “bätsch”.
questions.description: Sometimes gloating fits into a single word.
questions.fun_fact: In some regions the finger gesture is called “Rübchen schaben”, which means “scraping little turnips”.

questions.question: Germans call repeated picking on someone “Mobbing.” It sounds English. What word do people in England mostly use for it?
hints: In English, “mobbing” is more about an angry crowd.
It's linked to the word for a schoolyard tyrant.
It begins like the word for a male cow.
questions.description: An English word that hardly anyone in England uses this way.
questions.fun_fact: “Handy” is similar: in England hardly anyone uses it to mean a phone, but Germans do.

questions.question: In German you say “Hatschi” when you sneeze. When do you say “Hoppla”?
hints: It happens very suddenly.
Afterwards you often grab hold of something.
Your feet are to blame.
questions.description: A word that comes out faster than you can think.
questions.fun_fact: There's even an old song called “Hoppla, jetzt komm ich!”, which means “Whoops, here I come!”.

questions.question: Kalush Orchestra won Eurovision 2022 with “Stefania”. Which country, shown on the map, did they represent?
hints: It's an Eastern European country on the Black Sea.
It's the largest country that lies entirely within Europe.
Its flag is blue and yellow.
questions.description: A song for a mom that ended up winning over a whole continent.
questions.fun_fact: Kalush Orchestra is named after Kalush, its leader's hometown, and their song mixes rap with traditional flutes.

questions.question: I'm white, have a long curved neck and glide across Hamburg's Alster lake. A fairy-tale castle in Bavaria bears my name. Who am I?
hints: I'm a water bird.
I'm much bigger than a duck.
In the fairy tale, the ugly duckling grows up to become one of me.
questions.description: In Hamburg, this bird even has its own dad with an official boat.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries Hamburg has had a “Schwanenvater” (swan father) who takes the Alster swans to a warm winter home every year.

questions.question: What you see here is also in the German saying for something totally baffling: “ein Buch mit sieben …” (a book with seven …). What is it?
hints: Letters and documents used to be closed with them.
Kings pressed their ring into hot wax to make one.
The saying comes from the Book of Revelation in the Bible.
questions.description: Once the best way to stop nosy siblings from reading your letters.
questions.fun_fact: Anyone who broke a seal showed right away that they had secretly opened the letter.

questions.question: Which of Germany’s neighbors is marked on this map?
hints: It lies south of Germany.
Lake Constance and a stretch of the Rhine lie between the two countries.
Famous for mountains, pocket knives and cheese with holes.
questions.description: A neighbor where you can see mountain peaks right over the garden fence.
questions.fun_fact: Switzerland has four national languages, and German is the most widely spoken of them.

questions.question: This is Hamburg's coat of arms. How many towers does the castle on it have?
hints: Count very carefully from left to right.
The tower in the middle is the tallest.
It's more than two but fewer than four.
questions.description: A coat of arms straight out of a knight movie, just with a harbor around the corner.
questions.fun_fact: Hamburg's name goes back to the Hammaburg, a castle from the 9th century.
