questions.question: You paddle the whole Main River, from Upper Franconia to where it meets the Rhine at Mainz. Roughly how far is that?
hints: On the way, you pass Würzburg and Frankfurt.
Paddling it would take you a few weeks.
It's the Rhine's longest right-hand tributary, but much shorter than the Rhine itself at about 1,200 kilometers (750 miles).
questions.description: A paddling trip where you'd better pack a great many sandwiches.
questions.fun_fact: The Main is seen as the line between northern and southern Germany, which is why people jokingly call it the “Weißwurstäquator” (white sausage equator).

questions.question: Bremerhaven is about 60 km (37 miles) from Bremen, in the middle of Lower Saxony, but belongs to the state of Bremen. What record does this state hold?
wrong_answers: Longest sea coast of all states
hints: The record has nothing to do with people.
It's about a number measured in square kilometers.
On a map of Germany, you almost need a magnifying glass to find it.
questions.description: Two cities, one state, and a whole lot of Lower Saxony in between.
questions.fun_fact: At the Klimahaus in Bremerhaven, you can travel around the world through different climate zones in a single day.

questions.question: Which animal is NOT one of the Town Musicians of Bremen?
hints: In the fairy tale, four old animals set off for Bremen.
In Bremen, they stand on top of each other as a statue.
The rooster is at the very top, with the cat, the dog and the donkey below.
questions.description: A band whose members are all a little bit wild.
questions.fun_fact: The bronze statue in Bremen has stood there since 1953, and touching the donkey’s front legs is said to bring good luck.

questions.question: Which of Germany's neighbors is marked on this map?
hints: It lies to the south and borders Bavaria.
It is very narrow in the west and wide in the east.
Its capital is Vienna.
questions.description: On the map, it looks like someone rolled out a piece of dough.
questions.fun_fact: Germany shares a longer border with Austria than with any other neighbor: about 800 kilometers (500 miles).

questions.question: Which of these countries did NOT take part in Eurovision 2022 because it was banned from the contest?
hints: It has won Eurovision only once, in 2008.
Its capital has a famous square called Red Square.
It is the largest country in the world.
questions.description: A party where one guest got turned away at the door.
questions.fun_fact: The European Broadcasting Union announced the ban in February 2022, just days after the invasion of Ukraine.

questions.question: In the Rhineland, on the night before May 1, young men set up a decorated birch tree in front of a house. Who is it for?
hints: The birch stays up for a whole month.
It's about a feeling, not about someone's job.
The tree often has a heart hanging on it with a girl's name.
questions.description: A tree that delivers an important message without a single word.
questions.fun_fact: In leap years, in many places it's the women's turn to set up a maypole for the men.

questions.question: It rises in the Giant Mountains in the Czech Republic, flows through Dresden and Magdeburg, and reaches the North Sea at Cuxhaven. Which river?
hints: It's one of the longest rivers in Central Europe.
Hamburg's huge port lies on it.
Its name has only four letters and starts with E.
questions.description: A river that drops in on several state capitals on its way to the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Dresden's Elbe Valley lost its World Heritage status in 2009 because a new bridge was built there.

questions.question: You're on the parade route in Cologne on Rosenmontag. Who does NOT march in the parade?
hints: This group has its big moment back in January.
They sing at front doors and collect donations.
They write C+M+B in chalk above the door.
questions.description: Kamelle, confetti and a crowd so packed that even sardines would be jealous.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, hundreds of tons of candy are thrown into the crowd at Cologne's Rosenmontag parade.

questions.question: After a math test, someone sighs: “Da mache ich drei Kreuze!” (“I'll make three crosses!”). What do they mean?
wrong_answers: They want to retake the test
hints: The crosses originally come from church.
People used to cross themselves like this when a danger had passed.
You take a deep breath and think: “Phew, done!”
questions.description: A saying with more crosses than a filled-in lottery ticket.
questions.fun_fact: The saying probably comes from the custom of gratefully crossing yourself after getting through something.

questions.question: I'm a black bird with a loud croak. In German, someone who always has bad luck is called an “Unglücks…” after me. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the cleverest birds in the world.
In German, parents who take poor care of their children are named after me.
In Wilhelm Busch's story, one of us is called Hans Huckebein.
questions.description: Dressed in black, loud and grumpy, like a teenager on a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: Young ravens are lovingly cared for by their parents, so the German insult “Rabeneltern” (raven parents) is actually a mistake.

questions.question: Here, people are clinking glasses. According to superstition, which drink should you never toast with?
hints: It's the simplest drink of all.
Sailors in particular found it spooky.
It comes straight out of the tap.
questions.description: Cheers! But pick the right glass, or things could get awkward.
questions.fun_fact: An old sailors' superstition says that toasting with water brings bad luck at sea.

questions.question: According to folk belief, who does a bulb of garlic hung over the door keep away?
hints: These creatures are out and about at night.
They sleep in a coffin during the day.
Count Dracula is the most famous of them.
questions.description: Great in the sauce, bad for a first kiss, and for certain creatures of the night.
questions.fun_fact: Garlic has been used as a medicinal plant for thousands of years, for example in ancient Egypt.

questions.question: You want to make elderflower syrup and need the white blossoms. In which month does elder usually bloom in Germany?
hints: It's already warm.
Strawberries are ripe at the same time.
The longest day of the year falls in this month.
questions.description: A shrub people turn into syrup, tea and a whole lot of folk belief.
questions.fun_fact: People used to say a good spirit lived in the elder, so you should take off your hat in front of the shrub.

questions.question: In German folk belief, the Geisterstunde (“ghost hour”) begins at midnight. At what time does it end?
hints: The name already tells you how long it lasts.
It lasts exactly 60 minutes.
The tower clock then strikes only a single time.
questions.description: When even ghosts show up to work on time.
questions.fun_fact: In many legends, ghosts must vanish by the first crow of the rooster at the latest.

questions.question: Sun in the morning, hail at noon, rain in the evening: which month do Germans say “does whatever it wants”?
hints: It's in spring.
Easter often falls in this month.
On its first day, you're allowed to play tricks on people.
questions.description: A month with more moods than a cat in front of an empty bowl.
questions.fun_fact: In spring, warm and cold air masses often clash, which is why the weather changes so fast then.

questions.question: You win at dice three times in a row. What do Germans call you then?
hints: The word praises you for chance, not for skill.
You get called this too when you find a coin on the street.
A red-and-white fly agaric mushroom is a lucky symbol.
questions.description: Dice, lottery, card games: some people just always win.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany the poisonous fly agaric mushroom is a popular good-luck charm, for example on New Year's Eve cards.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many blades does this pair of ice skates have in total?
hints: Count the boots first.
Under each boot there is a metal blade.
One boot, one blade, and there are two boots.
questions.description: Shoes you should never wear on the sidewalk.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago, people tied animal bones under their feet to glide across the ice.

questions.question: On the Kandahar run in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, ski racers speed down at over 100 km/h (60 mph). What is the fastest event in alpine skiing?
hints: It has only a few gates.
Its course is the longest in alpine skiing.
Its English name simply describes heading down the mountain.
questions.description: Here people leave the mountain faster than kids leave the classroom before vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In a World Cup race in Wengen, a skier was once clocked at almost 162 km/h (about 100 mph).

questions.question: You ski down it from the top of the mountain. Easy ones are marked blue, medium ones red and hard ones black. What is it?
hints: Every ski resort has them.
The lift takes you up, and then you go back down on it.
In German it's called “Piste,” a word borrowed from French.
questions.description: The widest path in the world, and nobody ever walks on it.
questions.fun_fact: The German and British word “piste” comes from French and first meant “track” or “trail.”

questions.question: In the biathlon sprint, athletes shoot twice. The first time, they lie on their stomachs. How do they shoot the second time?
hints: The second position is harder than the first.
The rifle doesn't rest on the ground.
The athletes simply stay upright on their skis.
questions.description: First a cozy lie-down, then things get serious, a bit like Sunday morning.
questions.fun_fact: In prone shooting the target is only 4.5 cm (1.8 in) wide; in standing shooting it's 11.5 cm (4.5 in).

questions.question: In 2017, Johannes Rydzek from Oberstdorf became the first Nordic combined athlete to win four golds at one World Championships. Where?
hints: The place is in northern Europe.
No other place has hosted the Nordic World Ski Championships as often.
Its name has five letters and starts with L.
questions.description: Four gold medals in one suitcase: that's excess baggage on the flight home.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2018 Olympics, Rydzek, Fabian Rießle and Eric Frenzel took a German one-two-three in the large hill individual event.

questions.question: At the Four Hills Tournament you hear “hill HS 142.” Which measure replaced the old K-point as the hill's official rating?
hints: The measure describes the whole hill, not just one point on the slope.
It is measured from the takeoff table to the end of the landing area.
It tells you how big the hill is, in two words.
questions.description: Two letters that tell you how much courage to bring along.
questions.fun_fact: The K in K-point first stood for “kritischer Punkt” (critical point); today it officially means “Konstruktionspunkt” (construction point).

questions.question: I don't make a single turn. Both ski tips point straight down the valley, and I keep getting faster. What am I called?
hints: Braking is not part of me.
The path goes straight down the fall line.
My name is the German word for a shot.
questions.description: Ski school in the morning, Germknödel at lunch, waiting in line for the lift all afternoon: the perfect ski day.
questions.fun_fact: During a schuss, downhill racers crouch into a tuck so the wind slows them down less.

questions.question: The Münchner Haus is Germany's highest mountain hut, at almost 3,000 m (9,800 ft). On which mountain does it stand?
hints: The mountain is in Bavaria.
The border with Austria runs over its summit.
A golden cross stands on its summit, and it is near Garmisch-Partenkirchen.
questions.description: A hut where the walk to the snack stand is rather steep.
questions.fun_fact: Right next to the Münchner Haus, a weather station of the German Weather Service measures wind and snow.

questions.question: You're in Motril, on the coast of Granada, where sugarcane was grown for centuries. Who first planted it there?
hints: It was in the Middle Ages.
The Spanish word “azúcar” comes from their language.
Their story began when Islam arrived on the peninsula in 711.
questions.description: Before it could sweeten your coffee, this plant had a very long trip to make.
questions.fun_fact: Centuries later, sugarcane traveled the other way: Columbus took it to the Americas on his second voyage, in 1493.

questions.question: Olivia Newton-John, Sandy from “Grease”, sang at Eurovision for the United Kingdom. In which decade?
hints: It was a few years before she filmed “Grease”.
It was the same year ABBA won with “Waterloo”.
It was in 1974.
questions.description: Before she put on a leather jacket for the movies, she put on a dress for a song contest.
questions.fun_fact: Olivia came fourth at Eurovision 1974, the famous year ABBA won with “Waterloo”.

questions.question: In which century did Granada first become the capital of its own kingdom, the Zirid taifa?
hints: It happened after the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart.
The Zirids were Berbers from North Africa who came to al-Andalus as soldiers of the caliphate.
It's the same century in which El Cid conquered Valencia.
questions.description: A city that put on a crown before anyone asked it to.
questions.fun_fact: Abd Allah, the last Zirid king of Granada, wrote his memoirs in exile, something very rare for a king of his time.

questions.question: When you say “¡Ojalá apruebe!” (“I hope I pass!”), you're naming someone without realizing it. Who?
hints: The word comes from the Arabic spoken in al-Andalus.
It meant something like “if … wills it.”
In Arabic, that name is “Allah.”
questions.description: A word you've been saying with your fingers crossed for more than a thousand years.
questions.fun_fact: “Ojalá” comes from the Arabic expression “law sha Allah,” meaning “if God wills.”

questions.question: All of these people lived in Muslim Zaragoza except one. Who is it?
hints: One of them lived about four centuries after the others.
Al-Muqtadir had the Aljafería palace built.
The one you want was the last king of a taifa in the south.
questions.description: A palace guest list with one gatecrasher from another city.
questions.fun_fact: El Cid spent several years in exile working for the Muslim kings of Zaragoza.

questions.question: Tradition says the Reconquista began here, with the battle of Don Pelayo. What place is this?
hints: It is in the north of Spain.
There is a cave with a very famous statue of the Virgin Mary.
It is in Asturias, near some mountain lakes.
questions.description: Eight centuries of history, and it all started among some very green mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Tradition places the Battle of Covadonga in the year 722, though historians still argue about the exact date.

questions.question: What is this vegetable called?
hints: You eat the inside, the most tender part.
It has tough leaves that you pull off one by one.
In Spain, its name is also used for a shower head.
questions.description: A vegetable that dresses in layers as if it were going skiing.
questions.fun_fact: Its Spanish name comes from Andalusi Arabic “al-jarshúfa.”

questions.question: Maimonides was born Jewish in Córdoba in 1138 and had to flee with his family when he was young. Who came to power and forced them out?
hints: Look at the date: these were the days of al-Andalus.
They were very strict Muslims who came from North Africa.
They are the same people who built the Giralda in Seville.
questions.description: A doctor from Córdoba who moved house more often than a moving truck.
questions.fun_fact: Maimonides ended up as a doctor at Saladin's court in Egypt, and today he has a statue in Córdoba's Jewish quarter.

questions.question: You're in Salas de los Infantes, in Burgos, named after the Seven Infantes of Lara. In which century is their legend set?
hints: Castile was still a county, not a kingdom.
The powerful Almanzor appears in the legend.
It is the century of the Caliphate of Córdoba.
questions.description: Seven brothers, a spiteful uncle and a town that won't forget them.
questions.fun_fact: In the legend, the infantes are avenged by Mudarra, their half-brother, son of their father and a woman from Córdoba.

questions.question: The Almohads who built the Giralda in Seville also built this twin tower. In which city is it?
hints: It's in North Africa.
The tower is the minaret of the Koutoubia Mosque.
Jemaa el-Fnaa square is right next to it.
questions.description: The Giralda has a sister who lives across the Strait of Gibraltar.
questions.fun_fact: The Almoravids founded Marrakesh around 1070, and many say the name “Morocco” comes from it.

questions.question: The three fleurs-de-lis in the center of Spain's coat of arms stand for the royal family, the Bourbons. Which king was NOT a Bourbon?
hints: The Bourbons arrived in Spain in 1700.
Before them, another family ruled: the Habsburgs (“los Austrias”).
He is the king who had El Escorial built.
questions.description: A family so flowery it wears the garden on its coat of arms.
questions.fun_fact: The fleur-de-lis arrived with Philip V, grandson of the French king Louis XIV.

questions.question: It's a town south of Madrid. In 1808 its mayor, Andrés Torrejón, signed a proclamation calling on Spaniards to rise up against the French. Which town?
hints: The proclamation was signed on May 2 itself, as soon as news came of what had happened in Madrid.
Today it is a large city in the Community of Madrid.
The mayor is so famous that people nearly always call him by his job title and his town.
questions.description: A mayor who signed the most famous proclamation in history, and it wasn't even about the town festival.
questions.fun_fact: The proclamation began “The homeland is in danger” and was passed from town to town all the way to Andalusia.

questions.question: Sandie Shaw won Eurovision 1967 singing “Puppet on a String” barefoot. Which country did she represent?
hints: Sandie Shaw was a pop star of the 1960s, the decade of the miniskirt.
It is an island country in northwestern Europe made up of several nations.
Its capital is London.
questions.description: A puppet on a string that moved a whole continent, sung by someone who didn't even bother with shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Sandie Shaw was the first British winner of Eurovision, and she often sang barefoot on stage.

questions.question: In what year did Santiago Ramón y Cajal win the Nobel Prize in Medicine?
hints: It was early in the 20th century.
It was a few years after the Nobel Prizes were first awarded, in 1901.
It happened the same year as the great San Francisco earthquake.
questions.description: A man from Aragon who saw things nobody else could see, and had a microscope to prove it.
questions.fun_fact: Cajal shared the Nobel with the Italian Camillo Golgi, who disagreed with him about how nerve cells work.

questions.question: After Isabella II was driven out in 1868, General Prim looked for a new king for Spain. Which country did the one he finally brought in come from?
hints: The king's name was Amadeo.
He belonged to the House of Savoy.
He was the son of the first king of a country that had only just been unified.
questions.description: A very strange job interview: wanted, one king, experience optional.
questions.fun_fact: Amadeo I reigned for only two years: he gave up the throne in 1873, and the First Republic was declared soon after.

questions.question: You're walking through Madrid's Royal Botanical Garden, next to the Prado Museum. In which century was it set up there?
hints: It was during the Age of Enlightenment.
It was moved there by the same king who had the Puerta de Alcalá built.
It was a few years before the French Revolution.
questions.description: A spot in the middle of Madrid where the plants have more surnames than you do.
questions.fun_fact: The garden moved to the Paseo del Prado in 1781 and received plants from scientific expeditions to the Americas and Asia.

questions.question: After Spain lost its last colonies, a group of writers reflected on the “problem of Spain”. What are they known as?
hints: The lost colonies were Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines.
Unamuno, Baroja and Azorín were among them.
Their name recalls the year of the defeat.
questions.description: Some writers who got very serious because the country was feeling down.
questions.fun_fact: It was Azorín who made the name “Generation of '98” popular, in some articles from 1913.

questions.question: Look at the portrait: an archipelago in Asia, Spanish until 1898, is named after this king. Who is he?
hints: The islands are the Philippines.
They got the name in 1543, when he was still a prince.
His father was Emperor Charles V, known in Spain as Charles I.
questions.description: Some people put their name on a mug; this one put his on thousands of islands.
questions.fun_fact: The name came from explorer Ruy López de Villalobos, who called the islands of Leyte and Samar “Felipinas”.

questions.question: In Valencia people say “When harm comes from Almansa, it reaches everyone.” Which decrees did Philip V issue after that 1707 battle?
hints: It was during the War of the Spanish Succession.
They ended the fueros (local laws) of Valencia and Aragon.
In Spanish, their name sounds like gardening, though they were laws.
questions.description: A saying from Valencia with more history in it than many textbooks.
questions.fun_fact: After Almansa, Philip V had Xàtiva burned, and the town's museum still hangs his portrait upside down.

questions.question: Look at this detail of the painting of the proclamation of the 1812 Constitution. Its defenders gave the world a political name. Which one?
hints: They opposed those who wanted the king to have absolute power.
They stood for freedom of the press and national sovereignty.
The word comes from “libertad” (liberty).
questions.description: An invention from Cádiz that was exported to half the world, and it isn't pescaíto frito.
questions.fun_fact: “Liberal” as a political name was born in the Cortes of Cádiz and from there passed into English and French.

questions.question: In Japan it's called “Captain Tsubasa”, and in Spain it's known as “Oliver y Benji”. In which decade did the anime first air in Japan?
hints: It was long before everyone had a cell phone.
The author was inspired by watching the 1978 World Cup in Argentina on TV.
It first aired in the same decade as the World Cup in Spain.
questions.description: A match so long the field seems to go on forever without a goal in sight.
questions.fun_fact: Yoichi Takahashi started the Captain Tsubasa manga in 1981, and many pro soccer players say this series made them want to play as kids.

questions.question: In the Pocoyó cartoons, who is his friend, the pink elephant who loves to dance?
hints: The show has a completely white background.
She's pink from trunk to tail.
Her name sounds like the start of the word “elephant”.
questions.description: A whole gang that fits on one blank white screen.
questions.fun_fact: Pocoyó was created in Spain, premiered in 2005, and has been watched in a huge number of countries around the world.

questions.question: In which decade did “D'Artacán y los tres mosqueperros” (Dogtanian and the Three Muskehounds), the cartoon by Spanish studio BRB, first air?
hints: It was made together with a Japanese animation studio.
Later, the same studio made “Around the World with Willy Fog”.
It came out around the time Spain hosted the soccer World Cup.
questions.description: One for all, all for one, and a bone for each one.
questions.fun_fact: The series was made with the Japanese studio Nippon Animation and is based on Alexandre Dumas's “The Three Musketeers”, only with dogs.

questions.question: I'm Greek, but in 1963 I sang at Eurovision for Luxembourg, and my black glasses are famous. Who am I?
hints: I have sold hundreds of millions of records in many languages.
I also recorded many songs in Spanish.
My stage name starts with “Nana”.
questions.description: Glasses so famous they deserved their own passport.
questions.fun_fact: Nana Mouskouri recorded songs in more than a dozen languages, including Spanish.

questions.question: In the Spanish version of “Inside Out” («Del revés»), what is the red emotion with fire shooting from his head called?
hints: He's short, square and wears a tie.
He blows up the moment something seems unfair.
His Spanish name has only three letters.
questions.description: Five very different tenants live inside a girl's head, and none of them pays rent.
questions.fun_fact: In Latin America the film was called «Intensa-Mente», and this emotion was named Furia.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in Euskera, “Euskadi” is the name for…
hints: There, Euskera is an official language alongside Spanish.
It is an autonomous community with three provinces.
Those provinces are Álava, Bizkaia and Gipuzkoa.
questions.description: A name whose K looks like it was typed in a hurry on a phone.
questions.fun_fact: Sabino Arana made up the word in the late 19th century, and back then it was spelled “Euzkadi”.

questions.question: Many shops in Barcelona hang up a sign saying “tancat per vacances”. In which month do you most often see it?
hints: “Tancat” means “closed”.
It's the month when half of Spain is on vacation.
It's the month right after July.
questions.description: A sign that leaves you with your nose pressed against the glass.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalan, “open” is “obert”, the sign you'll see on that same shop for the rest of the year.

questions.question: Its Basque name is Donostia. It has La Concha beach, a famous film festival and the tamborrada. Which city is it?
hints: It's in Gipuzkoa.
Its tamborrada drum parade is held every January 20.
Its Spanish name is the name of a saint.
questions.description: A city with two names and one pintxos bar that everybody wants to conquer.
questions.fun_fact: “Donostia” comes from “Done Sebastiane”, which in old Basque means exactly “Saint Sebastian”.

questions.question: In this Catalan tradition, it gets covered with a blanket, “fed”, and hit with sticks at Christmas so it drops presents. What is the caga tió?
hints: It usually shows up at home on December 8, the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, and from then on the children look after it.
It usually wears a barretina (a red Catalan cap) and has a painted face.
Before it became a Christmas tradition, this kind of thing was used to keep the fireplace going.
questions.description: The only Christmas where the presents come out of the last place you'd expect.
questions.fun_fact: While they hit it, the children sing it a song that starts with the words “Caga tió”.

questions.question: It's Galician, you say it to someone you'll see again soon, and it sounds a lot like Spanish. Which phrase is it?
hints: Two of the others are Catalan and one is Basque.
It looks like the Portuguese “até logo”.
Its first word means “until”.
questions.description: A goodbye that comes with rain, bagpipes and empanada.
questions.fun_fact: In Galician, people also often say goodbye with “adeus”.

questions.question: In Catalan, “porta” means “door”. And “carrer” means…
hints: You see it on the signs on corner buildings in Barcelona.
Your house number is on it.
Avenue, square, boulevard… it's the most common of them all.
questions.description: A word with so many r's it sounds like a motorbike revving up.
questions.fun_fact: On signs and in addresses, “carrer” is often shortened to “C/”, just like Spanish “calle”.

questions.question: Eivissa is the Catalan name of a Balearic island famous for its sunsets. What is it called in Spanish?
hints: It's the third-largest of the Balearic Islands.
Its walled old town, Dalt Vila, is a World Heritage Site.
In Spanish, its name starts with “I”.
questions.description: Sun, salt and sea: the starter kit of any self-respecting Balearic island.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans called it Ebusus, a name they took from the Phoenicians.

questions.question: “I go from fair to fair across Galicia with my copper pot, cut tentacles with scissors and serve them on a wooden plate with paprika.” Who am I?
hints: My dish has the same name as the market where I work.
What I cut used to have eight arms.
I make the famous “pulpo á feira”.
questions.description: At Galician markets there's someone with scissors and a whole lot of flair.
questions.fun_fact: Every August, O Carballiño (Ourense) holds a very famous Festa do Pulpo (octopus festival).

questions.question: At a toast with cava, you're handed a «flauta». What is it?
wrong_answers: A clay jug with a handle
hints: It's named after its shape.
It has a stem, like other wine glasses.
Because it's so narrow, the cava's bubbles last longer.
questions.description: A musical instrument that makes no music, but you hear it when you make a toast.
questions.fun_fact: The wide, shallow “pompadour” glass was once popular for cava, but bubbles escape from it faster.

questions.question: Complete the Spanish expression for when you're all muddled up: “Tengo un cacao…”
hints: It's what you say when nothing makes sense to you.
People often say it before an exam or when too much happens at once.
It has to do with the mind.
questions.description: A cup of milk so lumpy that no spoon can stir the lumps out.
questions.fun_fact: In everyday Spanish in Spain, “cacao” on its own can also mean a mess or a commotion.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Asturias, cider is poured like this, from high up. Why?
hints: It has nothing to do with temperature.
When it hits the glass, the cider changes.
People say the cider “breaks” and fills with air.
questions.description: A waiter with Olympic aim and one arm high above his head.
questions.fun_fact: Pouring cider this way is called «escanciar», and Asturias even holds contests for the best pourers.

questions.question: The Valor brand, famous for its thick drinking chocolate, began as a small workshop in Alicante. In which century?
hints: It's much older than it looks.
Back then there were no cars on the streets yet.
It was about twenty years before the 20th century began.
questions.description: A chocolate bar older than all your great-grandparents put together.
questions.fun_fact: Valor was born in 1881, when Valeriano López Lloret began making chocolate by hand and selling it from village to village.

questions.question: Water comes out of me by itself, from deep inside the earth, with no one pulling it up or pumping it. Many rivers start at me. What am I?
hints: You find me in the mountains or the countryside.
Water has to be pulled up out of a well, but not out of me.
My water bubbles up out of the rock all on its own.
questions.description: The oldest tap in the world, and it never sends a water bill.
questions.fun_fact: Many bottled waters in Spain are sold as “agua de manantial” (spring water) because they are collected right where the water comes out of the ground.

questions.question: Take a close look at these small, wrinkly tubers. What refreshing summer drink is made from them?
hints: It's a sweet, white drink.
It's typical of Valencia and is enjoyed with fartons.
These tubers are called chufas.
questions.description: They look like chickpeas that spent the whole summer sunbathing.
questions.fun_fact: Valencian horchata de chufa has a protected designation of origin, and most chufas are grown in the farmland around Valencia, in towns like Alboraya.

questions.question: This daughter of the Catholic Monarchs married Henry VIII and became Queen of England. Who is she?
hints: She was first married to Arthur, Henry's older brother.
She was born in Alcalá de Henares in 1485.
Henry VIII broke with the Pope so he could divorce her.
questions.description: A princess from Alcalá who ended up with an English father-in-law and lots of paperwork with Rome.
questions.fun_fact: In 1507 her father made her Spain's ambassador to England, something almost unheard of for a woman at the time.

questions.question: I was born in Toledo, married an archduke called “the Handsome” and spent almost fifty years locked up in Tordesillas. Who am I?
hints: I was a daughter of the Catholic Monarchs.
My son was the emperor Charles.
My nickname says I lost my mind.
questions.description: A royal wedding that got every court in Europe talking.
questions.fun_fact: Even though she lived locked away, she remained queen of Castile, at least on paper, until her death in 1555.

questions.question: In which century did chocolate arrive in Spain from the Americas?
hints: It came thanks to the voyages and conquests in the Americas.
It was in the time of Emperor Charles I.
It was shortly after Hernán Cortés conquered Mexico.
questions.description: Half of Spain's afternoon snack had to cross an ocean before it could keep the churros company.
questions.fun_fact: At first it was drunk as a bitter, spicy drink; in Spain it became fashionable to sweeten it with sugar.

questions.question: You're watching Eurovision and a country announces “douze points” for a song. How many points is it giving?
hints: “Douze” sounds a bit like an English word.
It's the highest score each country gives.
It's a dozen.
questions.description: French gets a lot easier when all you need is the numbers.
questions.fun_fact: At Eurovision each country hands out 1 to 8, 10 and 12 points, so a single country never gives 9 or 11.

questions.question: In 1571, ships from Spain, Venice and the Pope fought at Lepanto, in Greece, where Cervantes lost the use of one hand. Against whom?
hints: The enemy controlled much of the eastern Mediterranean.
Its capital was Constantinople.
Today that city is called Istanbul.
questions.description: One day at sea that cost a famous writer a hand.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes called Lepanto “the greatest occasion the centuries have seen” and was proud of his wound.

questions.question: The Spanish Inquisition kept a strict eye on whether people followed the rules of one religion. Which one?
hints: It was the religion of the king and of almost all of Spain.
Its places of worship are called churches.
It's the religion of the Pope.
questions.description: A court with no sense of humor and a great many questions.
questions.fun_fact: Its coat of arms showed a cross between an olive branch and a sword.

questions.question: What is mainly kept inside this famous building in Madrid?
hints: It's a very famous museum.
The statue at the entrance is of a painter.
“Las Meninas” hangs there.
questions.description: A building where you can look all you want but touch nothing.
questions.fun_fact: The Prado owns about 8,000 paintings, but it can only hang some of them in its galleries at any one time.

questions.question: This knight dedicated his great deeds to Dulcinea del Toboso, whom he imagined as a fine lady. What was she really?
hints: She wasn't noble and didn't live in a palace.
She worked with her hands in her village in La Mancha.
Her life was out in the fields, among the harvests.
questions.description: A love story where only one of the two had been told about it.
questions.fun_fact: In the novel, Dulcinea's real name is Aldonza Lorenzo.

questions.question: After losing the war for the throne of Castile to Isabella the Catholic, in which kingdom did Joanna la Beltraneja spend the rest of her life?
hints: She had married a foreign king who was also her uncle.
That kingdom was famous for its sailors and voyages of exploration.
Its capital was Lisbon.
questions.description: A family fight over a crown that ended worse than an argument over the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: Until her death in 1530, she kept signing her letters “Yo la Reina” (“I, the Queen”).

questions.question: Picado is a flamenco guitar technique. Which of these is NOT part of picado?
wrong_answers: Resting the finger on the next string
hints: Picado is used to play scales and melodies at top speed.
It's a right-hand technique, like the one classical guitarists use for their scales.
The correct option is the usual way to play chords, sweeping the hand across the strings; in picado, each stroke sounds just one note.
questions.description: Fingers racing along the strings faster than you when the school bell rings.
questions.fun_fact: Paco de Lucía was famous for a picado so fast and clean that many classical guitarists studied it.

questions.question: Which artist made the copla “Ay, pena, penita, pena” famous in the 1950s?
hints: She was from Jerez de la Frontera.
Besides singing it, she starred in a film with the same title as the song.
She was known as “la Faraona”.
questions.description: A song so sad that even the tissues ask for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The film “¡Ay, pena, penita, pena!”, starring Lola Flores, came out in 1953 and was partly shot in Mexico.

questions.question: I'm a flamenco dancer born in San Fernando in 1971. My mother ran a dance school, and my show “Voces” paid tribute to Paco de Lucía. Who am I?
hints: My hometown is in the province of Cádiz.
I have my own company, which has taken flamenco around the world.
My last name starts with B.
questions.description: Heels that make more noise than a renovation in the apartment upstairs.
questions.fun_fact: Sara Baras learned to dance at her mother Concha Baras's academy in San Fernando.

questions.question: Almost every flamenco guitarist carries one, Paco de Lucía used one all the time, and it can be wood or metal. What is a cejilla?
questions.answer: A piece that presses all the strings at one fret
wrong_answers: A rest to raise your foot on
A cloth to mute the strings
hints: It goes on the neck of the guitar.
It raises the key to suit the singer's voice.
In other styles it's called a “capo”.
questions.description: Its name means “little eyebrow”, but it has nothing to do with your face.
questions.fun_fact: By moving the cejilla, a guitarist can play the same chord shapes in another key without changing the fingering.

questions.question: You're at a wedding and Rosalía's “Despechá” comes on. In which decade did the song come out?
hints: It's a fairly recent song.
It came out the same year as the album “Motomami”.
It was a hit in the summer of 2022.
questions.description: A song that has been to more weddings than the village priest.
questions.fun_fact: “Despechá” mixes pop and mambo, and it was one of the most-streamed songs in Spain in 2022.

questions.question: The band Ketama, famous for “No estamos lokos”, was formed by members of a Gypsy family of guitarists from Granada. Which one?
hints: The Ketama members' surname was Carmona.
Their fathers, Juan and Pepe, were highly respected guitarists.
The family nickname is the Spanish name of a legume.
questions.description: Some cousins who said they weren't crazy, and the audience agreed.
questions.fun_fact: Ketama blended flamenco with pop, salsa and even African music, and was key to the “nuevo flamenco” of the '80s and '90s.

questions.question: Lolita is the eldest of Lola Flores's children. How many children did Lola Flores have in total?
hints: Lolita isn't the only one of her siblings who went into music.
Their father was the guitarist Antonio González, “El Pescaílla”.
Lolita, Antonio and Rosario.
questions.description: A family where even the dog can clap along in perfect rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: Lolita became a star at just 17 with the song “Amor, amor”.

questions.question: My name is Antón Álvarez, my album “El madrileño” mixes rumba and flamenco, and I sang “Tú me dejaste de querer” with Niña Pastori. Who am I?
hints: I started out in rap.
La Húngara also sings on that song.
My stage name starts with a letter and a period.
questions.description: A guy from Madrid who went looking for flamenco and came back with an album under his arm.
questions.fun_fact: The video for “Tú me dejaste de querer” was shot as a big family party with flamenco artists from several generations.

questions.question: A common superstition in Spain says that when your ears ring, someone is to blame. Who?
questions.answer: Someone who is talking about you
wrong_answers: A ghost who wants to talk to you
A relative who is coming to visit
hints: It's nobody who is with you at that moment.
That person doesn't even know you can hear them.
They might be criticizing you… or saying nice things about you.
questions.description: Your ears have Wi-Fi, and someone just connected without asking.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors call that ringing tinnitus, and nearly everyone has noticed it at some point.

questions.question: In Spain, when a tenant stops paying rent and a judge orders them to leave the apartment, what is that called?
hints: It comes up a lot in the news about housing.
It's when someone is removed from their home by court order.
The word starts with “des-”, like “deshacer” (to undo).
questions.description: A word no landlord wants to use and no tenant wants to hear.
questions.fun_fact: An “embargo” is something else: it's when your belongings or money are seized to pay off a debt.

questions.question: Your autonomous community gives it to you, it has your patient number, and you show it at the health center and the pharmacy. What is it?
hints: It's a plastic card.
It's for the public health system.
With it, the doctor sees your medical history and the pharmacy sees your prescriptions.
questions.description: The VIP pass to the doctor's waiting room.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, each autonomous community has its own design for the tarjeta sanitaria.

questions.question: In Spain, which of these places is NOT usually run by the ayuntamiento (town council)?
hints: Three of them are paid for and looked after by your town.
The odd one out isn't paid for by any town council, but by a body for all of Spain.
In Spain almost all of them are run by a state company called Aena, and millions of suitcases pass through them.
questions.description: The mayor doesn't pay for everything, even if it looks that way at ribbon cuttings.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has more than 8,100 ayuntamientos, one for each municipality.

questions.question: You put one 2-euro coin and three 1-euro coins into your piggy bank. How many euros have you saved?
hints: First add up the 1-euro coins.
Three 1-euro coins make 3 euros.
Now add the 2 euros from the other coin.
questions.description: A little pig that gets fatter without eating a single bite.
questions.fun_fact: For years, Spain celebrated Savings Day (Día del Ahorro) on October 31, and banks gave piggy banks to children.

questions.question: In Spain, the A license is for riding motorcycles. Which letter is the regular license for driving a car?
hints: It's the license most people get.
C is for trucks and D is for buses.
It's the letter right after the motorcycle one.
questions.description: The most nerve-racking alphabet there is, especially at driving school.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's driver's license uses points: new drivers start with 8 and can build up to 15.

questions.question: Before singing, I was a youth goalkeeper for Real Madrid; in 1970 I sang “Gwendolyne” at Eurovision. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the best-selling Latin singers of all time.
My son is a famous singer too.
My son's name is Enrique.
questions.description: From stopping shots to stealing hearts: all it took was a change of stage.
questions.fun_fact: Julio Iglesias started singing after a car accident ended his career as a goalkeeper.

questions.question: The Vía de la Plata runs through western Spain from south to north, from Seville to Astorga. When was it built as a road?
hints: It is much older than the Camino de Santiago.
It passes through a city once called Emerita Augusta.
It was built by the same people who built the aqueduct of Segovia.
questions.description: A road so old it doesn't have a single traffic light.
questions.fun_fact: Its name has nothing to do with silver (“plata”): it probably comes from the Arabic word “balat,” meaning paved road.

questions.question: Los Millares, in Almería, is one of the oldest walled settlements in Europe. How long ago did people live there?
hints: It's older than the Romans and the Phoenicians.
The people who lived there already knew how to work copper.
It's from roughly the same time as the first pyramids of Egypt.
questions.description: A gated community, long before anyone invented the homeowners' association.
questions.fun_fact: Its people worked copper from the nearby Sierra de Gádor, which is why this period is called the Copper Age.

questions.question: Salvador Dalí designed a red sofa shaped like lips, inspired by the actress Mae West. In which decade?
hints: Mae West was a Hollywood star in the early years of talking pictures.
It was before World War II, at the height of Surrealism.
The collector Edward James ordered it around 1936 or 1937.
questions.description: The only sofa that blows you a kiss when you sit down.
questions.fun_fact: Dalí based it on one of his own paintings, in which Mae West's face turns into a room, with her lips as the sofa.

questions.question: I was born in Brussels, was the first professor of landscape painting at the San Fernando Academy, and painted the Picos de Europa. Who am I?
hints: I was the great reformer of realist landscape painting in 19th-century Spain.
One of the other three names was my student.
My surname looks Dutch because my family moved to Málaga when I was a child.
questions.description: A teacher who taught with no desks, no blackboard and sometimes no roof.
questions.fun_fact: Haes painted quick outdoor sketches on small wooden panels, and today they are seen as almost more modern than his big paintings.

previous.feedback: Source problem, carried over faithfully into the translation. First, hint 3 states something false: Haes's surname doesn't look Dutch "because" his family moved to Málaga; it is Flemish because he was born to a Belgian family. The hint should give the two facts separately, for example "My surname isn't Spanish: my family moved from Belgium to Málaga when I was a child." Second, check "first professor of landscape painting": Jenaro Pérez Villaamil is usually named as the first holder of the landscape chair at San Fernando. Haes won that chair in 1857, at the new Escuela Especial.

questions.question: This colorful building, designed by Ricardo Bofill in 1973, is a hit on social media. Where is it?
hints: It stands on a cliff by the Mediterranean.
It's in the Valencian Community.
The Peñón de Ifach rises very close by.
questions.description: A building so photogenic it has more photos than many celebrities.
questions.fun_fact: Bofill took inspiration from the kasbahs of North Africa, and the blue tones of the courtyards are meant to blend with the sky and the sea.

questions.question: Santa María del Naranco, in Oviedo, was built as a palace for the Asturian king Ramiro I. In which century?
hints: It's older than the Romanesque style.
The Kingdom of Asturias arose after the Muslims arrived in the peninsula in the 8th century.
It's from the same era as Charlemagne and his sons.
questions.description: A king who built himself a palace with a view long before real estate agents existed.
questions.fun_fact: At first it was the king's leisure palace; later it was turned into a church.

questions.question: Goya painted this dog straight onto the wall of a house on the outskirts of Madrid. What was the house called?
wrong_answers: La Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida
hints: Goya bought it late in life, in 1819, near the Manzanares River.
The Black Paintings were born there.
The name didn't come from Goya, though it fit him perfectly too.
questions.description: Wall decor that no interior designer would ever suggest for your living room.
questions.fun_fact: Around 1874 the Black Paintings were moved from the walls onto canvas, and that's how they reached the Prado.

questions.question: The painter Santiago Rusiñol turned this seaside house into his studio and museum, the Cau Ferrat. Which town is it in?
hints: It's in the province of Barcelona.
Rusiñol held the Modernista Festivals there in the 1890s.
Today the town is famous for its fantasy and horror film festival.
questions.description: A house with so much wrought iron you could build an army of window grilles.
questions.fun_fact: The Cau Ferrat has two paintings by El Greco that Rusiñol bought in Paris and carried in a procession through the town's streets.

questions.question: Around 1927, the sculptor Alberto Sánchez and the painter Benjamín Palencia walked to a hill outside Madrid in search of a new art. What was their group called?
hints: It began on the edge of Madrid, before the Spanish Civil War.
The hill they walked to is in a neighborhood in the southeast of Madrid.
Today that neighborhood is famous for its soccer team, Rayo.
questions.description: Artists who walked their way to the avant-garde, no car or tram needed.
questions.fun_fact: They renamed the Almodóvar hill “cerro Testigo” (Witness Hill), and Maruja Mallo and poets like Alberti joined them there too.

questions.question: Goya painted this clash between people of Madrid and Napoleon's horsemen on May 2, 1808. Where in Madrid did it happen?
hints: It's one of the most central spots in the city.
It's a half-moon-shaped square where several streets meet.
It's the square with the clock whose chimes ring in the New Year.
questions.description: A horse traffic jam right downtown, and not a single traffic light.
questions.fun_fact: The horsemen in the painting are Mamelukes, soldiers recruited in Egypt whom Napoleon had added to his army.

questions.question: In which century did Charles Darwin publish his famous book “On the Origin of Species”?
hints: It was the same era when steam trains were spreading around the world.
His ideas came from a long voyage around the world that stopped at the Galápagos Islands, and he waited many years to publish them.
The book came out in 1859.
questions.description: A book so controversial that half the world looked in the mirror searching for the monkey.
questions.fun_fact: The first printing of “On the Origin of Species” sold out on the very day it went on sale.

questions.question: Julio Romero de Torres painted “La chiquita piconera”, was on the 100-peseta note, and a copla remembers him for painting “the dark woman”. Which city was he from?
hints: He was from Andalusia.
The Guadalquivir River flows through his city.
His museum is on the Plaza del Potro, the square Cervantes mentions in “Don Quixote”.
questions.description: A painter who got more publicity from a song than from any gallery.
questions.fun_fact: “La chiquita piconera” was one of his last paintings: he painted it in 1930, the same year he died.

questions.question: This carving of the Sacrifice of Isaac, now in the National Museum of Sculpture in Valladolid, is by a sculptor who trained in Italy studying Michelangelo. Who?
hints: It's from the Renaissance, the first half of the 16th century.
His father was a painter too, and worked in Ávila.
He made it for the altarpiece of San Benito el Real in Valladolid.
questions.description: A carving so restless it looks ready to jump out of the altarpiece.
questions.fun_fact: Berruguete was in Italy when the Laocoön was dug up in 1506, and his twisting figures recall that statue.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says Berruguete was in Italy when the Laocoön was unearthed in 1506. That is doubtful. He is first documented in Florence around 1507–08. Vasari tells of him making a wax copy of the Laocoön for Bramante's contest, but that came after the discovery. The source fun fact needs changing, for example to "Berruguete spent about a decade in Italy, and his twisting figures recall the Laocoön and Michelangelo." Then the translation should follow it. Fact check: wrong. The fun fact is doubtful. The Laocoön was unearthed in January 1506, but Berruguete (b. c.1488) is generally thought to have gone to Italy around 1507–08, so he was probably not there at the discovery. The answer, wrong answers and hints check out.

Fact check: uncertain. Answer, distractors and hints are right. The fun fact says Berruguete was in Italy when the Laocoön was dug up in 1506, but sources date his Italian stay differently (c. 1504/08, or leaving in 1506). None confirms he was there at the discovery. Britannica does link his work to the Laocoön.

questions.question: It's Spain's great Romanesque cathedral, and Master Mateo carved its Portico of Glory. Which city is it in?
hints: Work on its cathedral began in the 11th century.
The city is the capital of its autonomous community.
It's the goal of thousands of pilgrims every year.
questions.description: A doorway with so many carved people it looks like the line at a bakery on a Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: Master Mateo carved his name into the lintel of the portico, along with the date 1188.

questions.question: You're in the Hospital de la Caridad in Seville, in front of Valdés Leal's “In ictu oculi”, with a skeleton putting out a candle. In which century was it painted?
hints: It is a Baroque painting.
Its painter lived at the same time as Murillo.
It comes from Spain's Golden Age, the time of Velázquez.
questions.description: A painting that reminds you every party ends, and not because it's closing time.
questions.fun_fact: Murillo is said to have joked that you had to look at Valdés Leal's paintings “holding your nose.”

questions.question: This painting by Antonio Gisbert shows General Torrijos and his men being executed in 1831. On which city's beaches did it happen?
hints: It's on Andalusia's Mediterranean coast.
Torrijos had sailed there from Gibraltar.
It's the city where Picasso was born.
questions.description: A beach that made it into the Prado but never into the holiday brochures.
questions.fun_fact: The government ordered the painting in 1886 for the Prado, as a tribute to the defense of freedom.

questions.question: In a famous painting by Goya, a man in a white shirt raises his arms high. Who is standing in front of him?
hints: The painting remembers what happened in Madrid in May 1808.
It marked the start of what Spain calls its War of Independence.
Their emperor was Napoleon.
questions.description: A white shirt that has become more famous than many runway shows.
questions.fun_fact: On the right hand of the man in the white shirt there is a mark like a stigma, as if he were a martyr.

questions.question: I was born in Granada in 1944, and in March 1982 I recorded a legendary live double album in Madrid. Its title joins the genre and my surname. Who am I?
hints: He is one of the pioneers of rock in Spain and was already singing in the 1960s.
In 1969 he had a hit around the world with a sung version of Beethoven's Ninth.
The album is called “Rock & …”, and the second word is his surname.
questions.description: An album so loud that the speakers in some 1982 living rooms are still shaking.
questions.fun_fact: “Rock & Ríos” was recorded at Real Madrid's indoor arena and is one of the best-selling live albums in the history of Spanish rock.

questions.question: In “19 días y 500 noches”, Sabina sings that their love lasted as long as “two fish of ice in a whiskey on the rocks”. What figure of speech is that?
hints: It's a figure of speech you learn about in literature class.
It puts one thing next to another so you see how they're alike.
It's a kind of comparison, and it often uses the word “like” or “as”.
questions.description: How long love lasts according to Sabina: not long, cold and on the rocks.
questions.fun_fact: “19 días y 500 noches” gave its name to a 1999 album that many consider Sabina's best.

questions.question: In which decade did Rosendo Mercado form the trio Leño, pioneers of Madrid's “rock urbano”?
hints: It was before the Movida madrileña took off.
Back then, Spain had just come out of Franco's dictatorship.
The band was born in 1978, the same year as Spain's Constitution.
questions.description: A rocker so Madrid that even his guitars order a bocadillo de calamares.
questions.fun_fact: Leño's song “Maneras de vivir” became an anthem that crowds still sing together at rock concerts.

questions.question: “El baile de los pajaritos” was a hit in Spain with María Jesús and her accordion, and at weddings you dance it copying a bird. Which three parts do you copy?
hints: Young and old dance it in a circle, at weddings and street parties.
Each move goes with a short phrase of the music.
You open and close your fingers, flap your elbows as if to fly and wiggle your bottom.
questions.description: The only dance where acting like a silly goose is encouraged… even if it's a different bird.
questions.fun_fact: The tune was written in the 1950s by Swiss accordion player Werner Thomas, and in German it's called “Ententanz”, the duck dance.

questions.question: “El sitio de mi recreo” by Antonio Vega is on the radio. Before going solo, which Movida band did he sing in?
hints: It was a Madrid band from the late 1970s and the 1980s.
He founded it with his cousin Nacho García Vega.
Its biggest hit was “La chica de ayer”.
questions.description: Before going solo, even the best need someone to argue with in the tour van.
questions.fun_fact: “La chica de ayer”, written by Antonio Vega, has often been voted one of the best songs in Spanish pop.

questions.question: Which singer-songwriter from a village in Cuenca wrote and sang “¿Y cómo es él?” and “Un velero llamado Libertad”?
hints: Besides singing, he wrote many hits for other artists.
He was born in Castejón, in the province of Cuenca.
His surname sounds like the Spanish word for pear trees.
questions.description: A singer-songwriter so calm that even his songs travel by sailboat.
questions.fun_fact: Perales also wrote “Porque te vas”, Jeanette's big hit that was featured in the film “Cría cuervos”.

questions.question: Marea formed in 1997, has Kutxi Romero's raspy voice up front and is a big name in Spanish street rock. Which region is the band from?
hints: It's a region in northern Spain.
It borders France and the Basque Country.
Its capital is famous for its running of the bulls in July.
questions.description: A band that rises and falls like the sea, but mostly just turns the volume up.
questions.fun_fact: Marea comes from Berriozar, a town right next to Pamplona.

questions.question: What city is Hombres G from, the band behind “Devuélveme a mi chica”?
hints: The members were very young friends when they started the band in the early '80s.
Their singer, David Summers, is the son of a well-known film director.
It's the capital.
questions.description: A song that has been asking for the same thing since the '80s, and very politely too.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1980s, Hombres G even starred in their own films, which played in movie theaters all over Spain.

questions.question: It's the most famous song by Héroes del Silencio, Enrique Bunbury's band, released in 1990 on “Senderos de traición”. Which is it?
hints: It opens with a guitar riff that half of Europe recognizes.
The lyrics are about someone who is torn and won't let you breathe.
Its title is about being halfway between two places.
questions.description: An anthem so epic you sing it with your eyes closed and your hair blowing in the wind, even if you have no hair.
questions.fun_fact: Héroes del Silencio were very successful in Germany and Italy, even though they always sang in Spanish.

questions.question: Spain's first two national parks, Covadonga and Ordesa, were created in the same year. In which century?
hints: Cars and airplanes already existed.
It was a few years after the Titanic sank.
It was in 1918.
questions.description: Mountains so beautiful that someone decided nobody could ever take them home.
questions.fun_fact: The Covadonga park was created in 1918 to mark 1,200 years since the Battle of Covadonga, and today it is part of Picos de Europa.

questions.question: In a Doñana lagoon you see a black bird with a white plate on its forehead and, above it, two little red knobs in breeding season. What bird is it?
hints: It's related to a black bird that's very common on park ponds.
In Spain it's critically endangered, and there are programs to reintroduce it.
Its common cousin has no red knobs, and its Spanish name points to North Africa.
questions.description: A bird that puts on its best earrings just in time for dating season.
questions.fun_fact: The crested coot lives mainly in Morocco and southern Spain, and Andalusia breeds birds to release into lagoons.

previous.feedback: Source: the fun fact is wrong. The crested (red-knobbed) coot lives mainly in eastern and southern Africa. Morocco and southern Spain are only the northern edge of its range. The translation copies this error faithfully, so the source needs correcting first. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: These are the Lagunas de Ruidera. Which river, famous for “appearing and disappearing,” starts in this area?
hints: It flows through La Mancha and Extremadura.
Near its end it forms the border with Portugal and flows into the Atlantic.
In Spain, someone who keeps showing up and vanishing is said to be “like the…”
questions.description: A river with more magic tricks than a magician at a birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the Guadiana's water seeps underground and comes back up further on, at the so-called Ojos del Guadiana (Eyes of the Guadiana).

questions.question: I'm a walking route over 50 km (31 miles) long, marked with a white stripe above a red one painted on rocks and trees. What am I?
hints: Other, shorter routes are marked in white and yellow.
One of the most famous crosses the whole Pyrenees from end to end.
In Spain I go by two letters, a G and an R.
questions.description: To walk all of me, you'll need sandwiches, bandages and lots of willpower.
questions.fun_fact: A white and a red stripe crossed in an X mean “not this way.”

questions.question: This waterfall on the Costa da Morte, in Galicia, drops almost straight into the sea. What is it called?
hints: It's in the town of Dumbría, in A Coruña.
It's formed by the Xallas River as it reaches the Atlantic.
Its name starts with É, and in summer it's lit up at night.
questions.description: A Galician river in such a hurry it didn't wait for a beach.
questions.fun_fact: The waterfall's flow is controlled by a hydroelectric plant, so on some days it pours down much harder than on others.

questions.question: Along the cañadas reales, flocks crossed Spain from north to south every year. A medieval law fixed their width. How wide?
hints: Thousands of sheep passed through at the same time.
They were much wider than a normal street.
They measured 90 Castilian varas, a bit less than the length of a soccer field.
questions.description: Sheep had highways too, and with no tolls.
questions.fun_fact: Every fall, during the Fiesta de la Trashumancia, a flock of sheep crosses central Madrid along an old cañada.

questions.question: It was once a hunting ground of the Dukes of Medina Sidonia, is now a national park and is Spain's largest wetland. What is it?
hints: It's in Andalusia, between Huelva and Seville.
The Iberian lynx lives there.
Its name comes from a lady: doña Ana.
questions.description: A place where flamingos make a stopover like at an airport.
questions.fun_fact: Every winter, hundreds of thousands of birds from northern Europe come to Doñana to escape the cold.

questions.question: Spain's first marine reserve (1986) surrounds an island off Alicante settled by families from Genoa in the 18th century. Which island?
hints: It lies off Santa Pola.
King Charles III brought the families there.
It is named after an island off Tunisia where those families came from.
questions.description: An island with an accent that came from very, very far away.
questions.fun_fact: Tabarca is the smallest inhabited island in Spain, and its Posidonia seagrass meadows are protected.

questions.question: It came out in 1987, Opera Soft published it, and its hero is a friar investigating in an abbey. What computer was “La abadía del crimen” first made for?
hints: It was an 8-bit computer very popular in Spanish homes in the 1980s.
The brand was British, and the model had a 3-inch floppy disk drive.
The brand's founder, Alan Sugar, put his own initials in its name.
questions.description: A mystery of monks and pixels, solved with no Wi-Fi and a lot of patience.
questions.fun_fact: The game was programmed by Paco Menéndez, with graphics by Juan Delcán, and was inspired by Umberto Eco's “The Name of the Rose”.

questions.question: When something really funny happens on a livestream, the chat types: “Clip, clip!” What is a clip?
questions.answer: A short piece of the stream
hints: You can share it on social media in no time.
It usually lasts just a few seconds.
It's like cutting a tiny piece out of the video.
questions.description: That moment when the chat goes wild and everyone types in all caps.
questions.fun_fact: Many Spanish streamers became famous because their funniest clips went viral outside Twitch.

questions.question: In a Spanish livestream chat, what does it mean to «banear» someone?
questions.answer: To kick them out so they can't post
wrong_answers: To give them a surprise prize
To say hi to them live
hints: Nobody wants it to happen to them.
It's done when someone insults or annoys others.
It comes from the English word “ban”, meaning “to forbid”.
questions.description: Thousands of strangers typing at once: a live chat is like a playground with no bell.
questions.fun_fact: Fundéu, a Spanish language foundation, recommends «bloquear» or «vetar» instead of «banear», though almost nobody on Twitch listens.

questions.question: You send me from the chat with a message, the streamer reads your name out loud and you give money for nothing in return. What am I?
hints: Sometimes an alert pops up on screen when I arrive.
At charity events, thousands of us add up.
I'm like a gift or a tip.
questions.description: When the streamer pulls a surprise-party face in the middle of the stream.
questions.fun_fact: Some charity marathons by Spanish streamers have raised hundreds of thousands of euros for good causes.

questions.question: Chipirones en su tinta is a black dish typical of the Basque Country. What animal is a chipirón?
hints: It's a sea animal that squirts ink to escape.
It has tentacles, but not eight long, equal arms.
When it's big, it's cut into rings, battered and fried “a la romana”.
questions.description: A dish so black it looks like it was written with a quill and an inkwell.
questions.fun_fact: Squid ink is also used to make black rice and even black pasta.

questions.question: I'm long and ridged, I come out of the frying pan, and people dip me in hot chocolate. What am I?
hints: I am sold at stalls and in cafés.
I am made from a dough of flour and water, and sometimes I have sugar on top.
My chubbier brother is called a porra.
questions.description: The favorite breakfast of late-night partygoers and schoolkids alike.
questions.fun_fact: A churro's ridges come from the star-shaped nozzle of the churrera, and they help it fry evenly.

questions.question: Look closely at this photo. Which tapa is it?
hints: It's one of the most-ordered tapas in Spanish bars.
They're coated in breadcrumbs and fried.
Inside they have béchamel, and they come with ham, chicken or salt cod.
questions.description: Crunchy on the outside, soft on the inside: just like a grumpy grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: Croquetas were born as a way to use up leftovers from cocido (a Spanish stew) or roast chicken.

questions.question: Columbus thought he had reached Asia, so the Spanish called the Americas “the Indies.” What name set them apart from the Asian ones?
hints: The name has to do with a compass direction.
From Spain, you had to sail toward the sunset to get there.
The ones in Asia were the East Indies.
questions.description: Columbus's GPS was a little out of date: by about half a planet.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that mistake, the native peoples of the Americas were called “Indians,” even though they had never been to India.

questions.question: Cabrales sauce is made with this blue cheese. Which autonomous community is it from?
hints: It's a region in the north, on the Cantabrian Sea.
The cheese ripens in caves in the Picos de Europa.
People there drink cider and eat fabada.
questions.description: A cheese with more blue veins than a road map.
questions.fun_fact: Cabrales cheese ripens in natural caves, where the damp and cold help its blue mold grow.

questions.question: It's shaped like a ring, topped with candied fruit, and hides a little figure and a bean. It's eaten every January 6. What sweet is it?
hints: It's made from a sweet yeast dough, like bread.
It's often filled with whipped cream or custard.
Whoever finds the bean has to pay for it.
questions.description: The Three Kings have left, but they left something behind for breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: Tradition says whoever finds the little figure wears the crown, and whoever finds the bean pays for the roscón.

questions.question: Which of these dishes does NOT use tomate frito?
hints: Tomate frito is the red sauce in lots of pasta and meat dishes.
Think of which dish would have nothing red in it.
It has cinnamon sprinkled on top.
questions.description: The red sauce that rescues every last-minute dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas in the 16th century, and at first many people grew them only as decorative plants.

questions.question: White rice, a fried egg, tomato sauce and fried plantain or banana: in Spain, this dish has a country in its name. Which one?
hints: It's a country in the Americas.
It's an island in the Caribbean.
Its capital is Havana.
questions.description: The emergency dinner of every student with a frying pan and not much patience.
questions.fun_fact: The name is thought to date from when Cuba was a Spanish colony, where rice with fried plantain was a common meal.

questions.question: I'm a white, creamy dessert with cinnamon on top, and in a children's song I want to marry a young lady from San Nicolás. What am I?
hints: I am cooked slowly with lemon peel.
I am made with a very small, white grain.
My name tells you my two main ingredients.
questions.description: A dessert so romantic it even looks for a partner in songs.
questions.fun_fact: In Asturias, arroz con leche is often served with the sugar on top burned, like a crema catalana.

questions.question: I'm stretchy and round, I wait on your wrist until you need me, and in the nineties they covered me in fabric. I hold ponytails. What am I?
hints: I go on your head, but I'm not a hat.
I stretch and shrink back; stretch me too far and I snap.
In Spain many people call me a “coletero” or a “gomilla”.
questions.description: It disappears more often than socks, and nobody knows where it goes.
questions.fun_fact: The fabric-covered hair ties that were all the rage in the nineties are called scrunchies in English.

questions.question: In parts of southern Spain and the Canary Islands, people at the movies ask for a tub of “rosetas”. What are they asking for?
hints: You eat them by the handful while you watch the movie.
They're made by heating corn kernels.
When heated, each kernel bursts open like a little white flower.
questions.description: The official background noise of every movie.
questions.fun_fact: They're called “rosetas” because a popped corn kernel opens up like a small flower.

questions.question: «Casita», «perrito», «cochecito»: what are words called that make things smaller or cuter?
hints: You learn about them in language class.
The opposite would be «casona» or «perrazo».
The name sounds a lot like “diminish”.
questions.description: Words that shrink themselves just so you'll like them more.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the diminutive ending changes from region to region: -ito, -ico, -ín, -iño, -illo…

questions.question: A Spanish stereotype says people here answer everything with “depende” (it depends), and on a staircase you can't tell if they're going up or down. Where?
hints: It's in the north of Spain.
It rains a lot there, and people eat a lot of octopus.
Its capital is Santiago de Compostela.
questions.description: A question whose answer is… well, it depends how you look at it.
questions.fun_fact: Many Galicians take the stereotype with humor and even wear it printed on T-shirts.

questions.question: It's a knock on the head, often with the knuckles, that hurts but doesn't draw blood. What is it called in Spanish?
hints: It's not on the back of the neck or on the feet.
It's given with a closed hand.
Its name starts with «cos-».
questions.description: A knock-knock that nobody wants to hear on their own head.
questions.fun_fact: A coscorrón given with a knuckle is also called a «capón».

questions.question: In the Canary Islands, if you order «papas» with mojo, what do you get?
hints: It's one of the islands' most typical dishes, served with red or green sauce.
They're boiled in their skins with lots of salt.
They're what goes into a Spanish tortilla.
questions.description: A food that changes its name when it crosses the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Papas arrugadas are boiled in water so salty that their skins come out white and wrinkly.

questions.question: I greet everyone with “¡Miarma!”, my way of saying “mi alma” (my soul), and I brag about my river. Who am I?
hints: I speak with a southern accent.
My river is the Guadalquivir.
In April I go to the Feria and look up at the Giralda.
questions.description: Someone who showers you with affection without knowing you at all.
questions.fun_fact: “Miarma” is so typical of Seville that people even use it with total strangers.

questions.question: The pale is a vertical stripe covering a third of a shield, and in heraldry the bars of Aragon are four pales. What group of figures does it belong to?
hints: It isn't a color, and it isn't a stand-alone figure like a lion or a castle.
Its group also includes the fess, the bend and the chevron.
In Spanish they're also called “piezas de primer orden”, and the English name starts like a title for a judge.
questions.description: In heraldry, even a stripe painted on a shield needs its own paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: When a pale is narrower than usual, heralds call it a “pallet”.

questions.question: The Kingdom of Toledo was born when Alfonso VI conquered the city and its taifa. In what year did that happen?
hints: It was in the 11th century.
It happened a few years before El Cid conquered Valencia.
It was more than half a century after the Caliphate of Córdoba ended.
questions.description: A city so old it changed owners more often than it changed swords.
questions.fun_fact: After the conquest, Toledo was for centuries a city where Christians, Jews and Muslims lived side by side, famous for its School of Translators.

questions.question: This green and white flag, the “arbonaida,” was approved at the 1918 Ronda Assembly. Who was behind it?
hints: He was a notary and a politician who championed Andalusian identity.
He was also behind his region's anthem and coat of arms.
He's called the “father of the Andalusian homeland.”
questions.description: Two colors, a very unusual name and a lot of pride waving in the wind.
questions.fun_fact: The green and white of the arbonaida have been linked to the colors of the Umayyads and the Almohads.

questions.question: José Serrano, the musician from Sueca, composed the music of a regional anthem. For which region?
hints: José Serrano also composed zarzuelas such as «La canción del olvido».
He was born in a land of rice fields, near a famous lagoon.
Its lyrics begin «Per a ofrenar noves glòries a Espanya».
questions.description: A musician, an anthem and a brass band that can't keep up.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem was composed for the 1909 Regional Exhibition, with lyrics by Maximiliano Thous.

questions.question: The four Moors' heads on Aragon's coat of arms recall the Battle of Alcoraz in 1096. In legend, which saint helped the Christians?
hints: His cross is red on a white background.
He's the patron saint of Aragon and Catalonia.
He's usually shown slaying a dragon.
questions.description: A coat of arms with more heads than a residents' meeting.
questions.fun_fact: Aragon Day is celebrated on April 23, its patron saint's feast day.

questions.question: On the Spanish flag you can see two columns with a “Plus Ultra” ribbon, the emblem of Charles V. In which century did he reign?
hints: It was after Columbus's voyage.
He was the grandson of the Catholic Monarchs.
It was the century of Philip II and El Escorial.
questions.description: A Latin motto that has spent centuries urging people to go a bit further.
questions.fun_fact: The columns are the Pillars of Hercules, which legend says marked the end of the known world at the Strait of Gibraltar.

questions.question: The blue border of the City of Madrid's coat of arms, around the bear and the strawberry tree, has silver stars. How many?
hints: The flag of the Community of Madrid has the same number of stars.
They recall a constellation.
They are the stars of the Great Bear, also called the Big Dipper.
questions.description: A bear, a tree and a whole sky thrown in for free.
questions.fun_fact: The statue of the Bear and the Strawberry Tree in the Puerta del Sol is one of Madrid's most famous meeting spots.

questions.question: These volcanic Spanish islands lie in the Atlantic off Africa, and the clock there is one hour behind Madrid. Which are they?
hints: Eight of them are inhabited.
They're much closer to Africa than to mainland Spain.
Mount Teide is on one of them.
questions.description: A trip where the suitcase holds more swimsuits than sweaters.
questions.fun_fact: On Spanish radio, the hourly time check always ends with “una hora menos en Canarias” (“one hour less in the Canaries”).

questions.question: Which of these islands was NOT settled by Polynesian sailors before Europeans arrived?
hints: Three of them form the great “Polynesian Triangle.”
The right answer is much closer to South America.
Darwin studied finches and giant tortoises there.
questions.description: Sailors who crossed the ocean with no compass, just stars, waves and birds to show them the way.
questions.fun_fact: The Galápagos had no human inhabitants when Spanish sailors found them by accident in 1535.

questions.question: Which of these people did NOT live in the time of the Catholic Monarchs?
hints: Three of them dealt with Isabella and Ferdinand in person.
Isabella died in 1504 and Ferdinand in 1516.
The odd one out wrote a very famous book about a slightly crazy knight.
questions.description: A couple with so many kingdoms they needed two crowns and a very packed calendar.
questions.fun_fact: Isabella and Ferdinand married almost in secret in Valladolid in 1469, when she was 18.

questions.question: Look at this cocido madrileño. Which legume is the base of the dish?
hints: They are round and beige.
They are soaked overnight before cooking.
Hummus is made from them.
questions.description: A dish you eat in chapters, like a TV series with three seasons.
questions.fun_fact: Cocido madrileño is served in three “vuelcos” (courses): first the soup, then the chickpeas with vegetables, and finally the meats.

questions.question: It rises in Cantabria, flows through Logroño and Zaragoza and forms a big delta on the Mediterranean. Which river is it?
hints: It is the longest river that flows entirely within Spain.
It flows past the Basílica del Pilar.
Its delta, in Tarragona, is full of rice fields.
questions.description: It has been traveling for centuries without a ticket and has never once gotten off at a station.
