questions.fun_fact: The ancient Greeks called it “Iber”, and that is where the name of the Iberian Peninsula comes from.

questions.question: I cross Spain diagonally from La Rioja to near Valencia, the Douro River starts in me, and my highest peak is Moncayo. What am I?
hints: I separate the central plateau from the Ebro valley.
I pass through the provinces of Soria and Teruel.
My name comes from the ancient Iberians, just like the peninsula's name.
questions.description: A mountain range that always comes out crooked when you draw it in your geography notebook.
questions.fun_fact: The Douro starts in the Picos de Urbión, in this range, and reaches the sea at Porto, in Portugal.

questions.question: This yellow arrow is painted on walls and stones in many Spanish villages. What is it for?
hints: People who follow it usually carry a backpack and wear boots.
Many people follow it for weeks, on foot.
It leads to a cathedral in Galicia.
questions.description: The cheapest road sign in Europe: one can of paint and a brush.
questions.fun_fact: Elías Valiña, the parish priest of O Cebreiro, started painting the arrows in the 1980s with yellow paint left over from road works.

questions.question: This crown of gold and sapphires was found in 1858 near Toledo, in the Treasure of Guarrazar. What period is it from?
hints: Back then, Toledo was the capital of a kingdom.
It is older than the arrival of the Muslims in 711.
Letters hanging from it spell the name of King Recceswinth.
questions.description: Gold, sapphires and a field near Toledo that was hiding more than it seemed.
questions.fun_fact: Another crown from the treasure, King Swinthila's, was stolen from the Royal Palace of Madrid in 1921 and has never been found.

questions.question: These 1950s cars still drive around the largest island in the Caribbean, which was Spanish until 1898. Which island is it?
hints: It's about 150 km (90 miles) from Florida.
It grows the tobacco for some world-famous cigars.
Its capital is Havana.
questions.description: Here cars never retire: they become grandparents and keep on working.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain people say “más se perdió en Cuba” (“more was lost in Cuba”) to play down a problem, a saying born after 1898.

questions.question: You're converting prices from pesetas to euros. When the euro arrived in 2002, how many pesetas was one euro worth?
hints: It was not a round number; it had decimals.
One euro was worth quite a bit more than a 100-peseta coin.
It is between 150 and 200.
questions.description: A sum your grandparents still work out in their heads every time they go to the supermarket.
questions.fun_fact: The exact rate was 166.386 pesetas to the euro, and the peseta had been born in 1868.

questions.question: It was born in Cádiz in 1811, during the war against Napoleon, and today its most famous draw is at Christmas. Why was the Lotería Nacional created?
questions.answer: To raise money without raising taxes
wrong_answers: To elect the members of the Cortes
To share out land among peasants
hints: The country was at war and needed a lot of money.
The idea was copied from a lottery that already existed in New Spain, in the Americas.
The Treasury keeps part of what people bet.
questions.description: A Cádiz invention that gets the San Ildefonso children singing every December.
questions.fun_fact: The first draw was held in Cádiz on March 4, 1812, just days before the Constitution was approved.

questions.question: Ana Belén and Víctor Manuel sang about a Madrid monument: “Ahí está, ahí está…”. Which king had it built?
hints: The monument is the Puerta de Alcalá.
It was finished in 1778, at the height of the Enlightenment.
Before ruling Spain, he was king of Naples.
questions.description: There it is, there it is, watching time go by… and now watching this question too.
questions.fun_fact: The Puerta de Alcalá was designed by the Italian architect Francesco Sabatini, and each side has a different facade.

questions.question: They're in Indonesia, Magellan set out to reach them, and the Dutch controlled them for centuries. What were Europeans after there?
hints: They are the Maluku Islands, also called the Moluccas.
What they wanted was used to give food flavor.
They were known as “the Spice Islands.”
questions.description: Tiny islands that empires fought over like kids fighting over the last piece of cake.
questions.fun_fact: In 16th- and 17th-century Europe, nutmeg cost many, many times more than on the islands, and only the rich could afford it.

questions.question: A Benedictine monk in Oviedo, he wrote the “Teatro crítico universal”, and Ferdinand VI banned attacks on his books. What did Feijoo fight against?
hints: He was one of the first Spanish thinkers of the Enlightenment.
His essays were huge bestsellers in the 18th century.
His other great work is called “Cartas eruditas y curiosas”.
questions.description: A monk who swapped the silence of the cloister for a good argument.
questions.fun_fact: In 1726 Feijoo also argued that women were just as capable as men, a very bold idea for his time.

questions.question: The Simpsons has been on Spanish TV at lunchtime for decades. In which decade did the show first air in Spain?
hints: Before getting their own show, they appeared in shorts on another American program.
It reached Spain very soon after its US premiere, first on TVE.
It premiered in Spain in 1991.
questions.description: The yellow family that's been eating lunch with us for decades and never brings dessert.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, The Simpsons aired on Antena 3 for more than two decades, almost always at lunchtime.

questions.question: In the Basque Country and Navarre you often hear the word “ikastola”. What is an ikastola?
hints: Almost every Basque town has one, and many people go there nearly every day.
Children spend many weekday mornings there.
It comes from “ikasi”, which means “to learn” in Basque.
questions.description: A Basque word that sounds far more mysterious than it really is.
questions.fun_fact: In Basque, “ikasle” means “student” and “irakasle” means “teacher”: the one who makes you learn.

questions.question: Many Catalan towns have a “Plaça Major”. What is a “plaça”?
hints: It often has benches and a fountain.
The town hall is often there.
It's an open space with houses all around it.
questions.description: A word with a little tail on its c to make it look extra fancy.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalan the letter “ç” is called “ce trencada” (broken c), and French and Portuguese use it too.

questions.question: In a Spanish bar, which coffee comes in a small cup, with no milk, no water and no liquor?
hints: Look closely at what each one is called.
It's the shortest and strongest coffee on the menu.
Its name says it comes with no company.
questions.description: At a Spanish bar counter, ordering a coffee is almost a language of its own.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, if you order a café solo with a splash of brandy or anise, you get a “carajillo”.

questions.question: The Inquisition made some convicted people wear this yellow tunic with painted crosses, later hung in the village church. What was it called?
hints: It was a garment that shamed whoever wore it in public.
Convicted people wore it during the autos-da-fé.
In Spain, people still say someone has been “hung with the …” when they get stuck with a bad name.
questions.description: A uniform nobody wanted to wear, not even at a clearance sale.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from “San Benito” (Saint Benedict), because the penitent's robe looked like the Benedictine scapular.

questions.question: What were the soldiers of the tercios who carried this weapon called?
hints: The weapon fired lead balls.
It was fired with a match cord that had to be kept burning.
The soldier's name comes straight from the weapon's name.
questions.description: The tercios had more specialists than a hospital.
questions.fun_fact: Because it worked with a burning match cord, an arquebus could fail to fire on rainy days.

questions.question: Silver from a mountain in the Andes became millions of pieces of eight, the coin of half the world. Which city is that mountain next to?
hints: The Spanish mined it from the 16th century on.
The city lies more than 4,000 m (13,000 ft) above sea level.
In Spain, something very valuable is said to be “worth a …”.
questions.description: A mountain with more money inside than a whole shelf of piggy banks.
questions.fun_fact: The piece of eight was used so widely that it became the model for the US dollar.

questions.question: Antonio Cruz García, a great flamenco singer who won the Llave de Oro del Cante in 1962, went by Antonio Mairena. What is “Mairena”?
questions.answer: The town near Seville where he was born
wrong_answers: The name of a flamenco style
hints: It has nothing to do with the singing itself.
His brother Manuel, also a singer, used the same name.
Today that place, near Alcalá de Guadaíra, holds a flamenco festival named after him.
questions.description: A stage name with more roots than a hundred-year-old olive tree.
questions.fun_fact: Mairena del Alcor holds the Antonio Mairena Cante Jondo Festival every year, one of the oldest in Andalusia.

questions.question: It comes from the Moriscos and takes place in the caves of Granada's Sacromonte. What is a zambra?
questions.answer: A party with singing and dancing
hints: It involves music.
Today you can see it in cave venues for tourists in Granada.
Its most famous dances are done by women with shawls and castanets.
questions.description: Living inside a hill facing the Alhambra: the dream home no real estate agent will ever list.
questions.fun_fact: The Sacromonte is famous for its cave houses dug into the hillside, right across from the Alhambra.

questions.question: In the legends of Asturias, what is a xana?
hints: It appears in tales told by the fire in Asturian villages, and it's usually kind.
It lives in springs and rivers and combs its long hair with a golden comb.
It's like the nymphs of Greek myths.
questions.description: An Asturian character so shy that nobody has managed to take a photo of it yet.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that on the morning of San Juan, xanas lay out skeins of golden thread in the sun beside the springs.

questions.question: Many people hang it on their chair in bars, because a superstition says that if it touches the floor, your money runs away. What is it?
hints: It's something many people carry with them all day.
You can buy special hooks to hang it from the edge of the table.
You carry it on your shoulder or in your hand.
questions.description: A superstition that puts your savings at risk without you even leaving the bar.
questions.fun_fact: This superstition isn't only Spanish: it's also very common in many Latin American countries.

questions.question: You take out 50 euros from an ATM at a Spanish bank. Which of these does the ATM NOT give you?
wrong_answers: A receipt, if you ask for one
hints: Think about what comes out of each slot on the ATM.
The smallest money doesn't come out of the slot for bills.
What it doesn't give jingles in your pocket; for that you go to a shop or the bank counter.
questions.description: A machine in the wall that spits out money, but only if you tell it the password.
questions.fun_fact: The world's first ATM was installed in London in 1967.

questions.question: You live on the 4th floor in Spain, there's no entresuelo (mezzanine) and the elevator is broken. From the ground floor, how many floors do you climb?
hints: The ground floor doesn't count as a floor.
You climb one floor to reach the 1st, another to the 2nd...
It's the same number as your floor.
questions.description: The elevator has gone on vacation, and your legs have to work overtime.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the ground floor is also called “el bajo”, and on many elevators its button shows a “B” or a “0”.

questions.question: It takes place every January 6 and is the biggest lottery draw after the Christmas one. What is it called?
hints: It's run by Loterías y Apuestas del Estado, not by the ONCE.
It falls on the day of the Reyes Magos (Three Kings).
Its name is about a baby.
questions.description: No luck in December? Life gives you a second chance, with roscón.
questions.fun_fact: The Sorteo del Niño pays out its money just as the January sales begin.

questions.question: Look at this Spanish coin. How much is it worth?
hints: The side you see is designed by each country; the other side is the same all over Europe.
It has two colors: silver on the outside and gold on the inside.
Two of these make €4.
questions.description: Finding one in the pocket of your old jeans makes your whole day.
questions.fun_fact: Before 2002, people in Spain paid in pesetas, and 1 euro was worth about 166 pesetas.

questions.question: On the ceiling of the Altamira cave in Cantabria, red and black bison were painted about 14,000 years ago. What were those colors made from?
hints: They used things that don't spoil over the years.
One of the colors is the shade of a brick or of something rusty.
The red was an earth called ocher.
questions.description: The first artists in history had no pencil case, but they managed just fine.
questions.fun_fact: When a girl named María spotted the bison on the ceiling in 1879, many experts didn't believe they were so old.

questions.question: Four heralds carry this tomb, holding remains of Christopher Columbus, on their shoulders. Which cathedral is it in?
hints: The city lies on a river that ships once sailed down on their way to America.
It is one of the largest Gothic cathedrals in the world.
Its bell tower is the Giralda.
questions.description: History's most famous traveler took centuries to find a place to finally stay put.
questions.fun_fact: Columbus's remains traveled from Valladolid to Seville, Santo Domingo and Havana before returning to Seville in 1899.

questions.question: Look at these horseshoe arches in the Mosque of Córdoba. What two materials make up their red and white stripes?
hints: Neither of them is a metal.
They're ordinary building materials, nothing fancy.
The red stripes are made of a material made from baked clay.
questions.description: Striped arches, as if the mosque had put on its favorite team's jersey.
questions.fun_fact: The prayer hall has more than 800 columns, many reused from Roman and Visigothic buildings.

questions.question: Look at the Alcazaba of Málaga: when it was built in the 11th century, stones and columns were taken from an older building at its foot. Which one?
hints: That building is about 2,000 years old.
It was built by the people who built the aqueduct of Segovia.
Plays were performed there in front of an audience.
questions.description: Recycling is trendy now, but in Málaga they were doing it almost a thousand years ago.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman theater lay buried and forgotten until 1951, when it turned up during construction work.

questions.question: Look at this courtyard of the Alcázar of Seville. Who stays on its upper floors when they visit the city?
hints: Nobody votes for them in an election.
Their role passes from parents to children.
Today they are Felipe VI and Letizia.
questions.description: A palace with a thousand years of history and a guest room that's always ready.
questions.fun_fact: It's considered the oldest royal palace still in use in Europe, and parts of “Game of Thrones” were filmed in its gardens.

questions.question: This glass-slat facade belongs to a bullet-shaped tower in Barcelona designed by Jean Nouvel. What is it called today?
hints: At night it lights up with thousands of colored lights.
It was the headquarters of Barcelona's water company.
It used to be called Torre Agbar.
questions.description: In Barcelona, even the skyscrapers have shapes that get people talking.
questions.fun_fact: Jean Nouvel said he was inspired by Montserrat mountain and by a geyser shooting upward.

questions.question: A pavilion in the Retiro was built in 1887 to show plants brought from the Philippines, and today it hosts contemporary art. What is it made of?
hints: It stands beside a small pond in the park.
The plants needed lots of light, so inside it almost feels like you're outdoors.
Its name gives away one of the two materials.
questions.description: A palace whose first guests had neither mouths nor feet.
questions.fun_fact: Ricardo Velázquez Bosco designed it, taking inspiration from the Crystal Palace built in London for the Great Exhibition of 1851.

questions.question: Joaquín Sabina, from Úbeda, often comes on stage in a hard black hat with a low, rounded crown. What hat is it?
hints: It's a classic type of hat.
Charlie Chaplin wore one too, along with his cane.
English bankers wore it, and Americans call it a derby.
questions.description: Some singers have their own style, and some have a very, very small closet.
questions.fun_fact: In 2007, Sabina and Joan Manuel Serrat toured together on a tour called “Dos pájaros de un tiro” (“Two Birds with One Stone”).

questions.question: “Corazón partío,” the huge 1997 hit, was played at every wedding. Which style does it mix with pop?
hints: It's a style closely tied to southern Spain.
It comes with Spanish guitar, singing and dancing with stamping heels.
Camarón de la Isla and Paco de Lucía are its great legends.
questions.description: The song that turns any uncle at a wedding into the star of the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: The album “Más,” which included “Corazón partío,” is one of the best-selling albums ever in Spain.

questions.question: Anabel Conde sang “Vuelve conmigo” at Eurovision 1995 in Dublin. What place did Spain finish in?
hints: That year Norway won with a song that had almost no lyrics.
It was Spain's best result since 1979.
Only one song, Norway's entry by Secret Garden, got more points.
questions.description: Dublin, 1995: a night when half of Spain stayed glued to the TV counting points.
questions.fun_fact: Since 1995 no Spanish entry has finished second again; Chanel came third in 2022.

questions.question: Madrid band Dover was a huge hit in 1997 singing in English with “Devil Came to Me”. Who were the band's front pair?
hints: They were an unusual front pair for Spanish rock in the 1990s.
They had known each other all their lives: they grew up in the same house.
Their names are Cristina and Amparo, and they share a surname: Llanos.
questions.description: A band from Madrid named after an English port: the musical Brexit came early.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006 Dover swapped guitars for an electronic sound on the album “Follow the City Lights”.

questions.question: You're walking around Cap de Creus in Girona, among twisted rocks that inspired some very famous paintings. By which painter?
hints: He painted strange things, as if straight out of a dream.
His house was in Portlligat, next to Cadaqués.
He had an extremely long mustache with the tips curled upward.
questions.description: Here the wind has been sculpting rocks for centuries without charging a single euro.
questions.fun_fact: Cap de Creus is the easternmost point of the Iberian Peninsula: the sun rises there before anywhere else on the peninsula.

questions.question: It's the largest protected area in Spain, it's in Jaén, and the Guadalquivir River starts there. What is it called?
hints: It's full of pine forests, deer, Spanish ibex and bearded vultures.
Its full name also includes the Sierra de Segura and Las Villas.
It shares its name with a Jaén town with a castle, and the name sounds a bit like «cazar» (to hunt).
questions.description: A park so big that if you get lost, they find you in another province… or not.
questions.fun_fact: This natural park covers more than 200,000 hectares (about half a million acres), and bearded vultures breed there again.

questions.question: Next to the pink lagoon of Torrevieja there are white mountains that aren’t made of snow. What are they made of?
hints: The lagoon sits right next to the sea.
The sun and wind dry up the water and leave this on the ground.
You sprinkle it on your food, and too much makes you thirsty.
questions.description: A lake that dyed itself bubble-gum pink without a trip to the hair salon.
questions.fun_fact: The pink color comes from tiny algae and bacteria that live in very salty water.

questions.question: According to a famous story, who made an egg stand on its end by crushing its tip, to silence his critics?
hints: His critics said anyone could have done his great feat.
His feat had to do with crossing an ocean.
He reached the Americas in 1492.
questions.description: The easiest solution in the world… once someone shows it to you.
questions.fun_fact: Today an idea that seems hard but turns out very simple once you know how is called an “egg of Columbus”.

questions.question: They wear uniforms, drive off-road vehicles and can give fines. What is the main job of Spain’s forest rangers?
questions.answer: To watch over and protect the countryside
wrong_answers: To cut down trees and sell the wood
hints: Their work has to do with nature.
If they see smoke in the forest, they’re among the first to raise the alarm.
They make sure no one harms the forests or their animals.
questions.description: Their office has trees instead of walls and birds instead of printers.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, forest rangers are officers of the law, like the police, and can report anyone who damages the countryside.

questions.question: Which Spanish autonomous community has the most national parks?
hints: It has four.
None of its national parks shares land with another community.
One of them is Teide.
questions.description: A collecting contest where every trading card is a whole landscape.
questions.fun_fact: The four Canary Islands national parks are Teide, Timanfaya, Garajonay and Caldera de Taburiente.

questions.question: If you live in Trujillo, you hear the lesser kestrels at the church again when they return from Africa to breed. When is that?
hints: They arrive before many other migrating birds.
They want their chicks ready when there are lots of insects.
They come back while it's still cold, before spring begins.
questions.description: Neighbors who take very long vacations and always come back to the same bell tower.
questions.fun_fact: Lesser kestrels nest in colonies in gaps in roofs, churches and castles, and eat mostly grasshoppers.

questions.question: Las Ratitas are two Spanish sisters, Gisele and Claudia, with millions of YouTube followers. What videos do they post?
hints: Most of their fans are very young.
They appear in the videos themselves, with costumes and surprises.
It's what kids do at recess, but on camera.
questions.description: Two sisters who skip the cheese but nibble up millions of views.
questions.fun_fact: Las Ratitas started making videos when they were very little, and theirs is one of the most-watched kids' channels in Spain.

questions.question: On FM radio in Spain, as in almost every country, between which numbers do you tune in to stations?
hints: They are measured in megahertz.
There are about twenty units between the lowest and highest numbers.
The highest number is just over a hundred.
questions.description: A wheel of numbers where Los 40, the SER and your favorite car station all live.
questions.fun_fact: FM stands for “frequency modulation”, and it sounds better than AM, though its waves don't travel as far.

questions.question: I was a hit in 1950s and '60s Spain: daily episodes, actors who only lent their voices, sound effects made by hand. My biggest hit was “Ama Rosa”. What am I?
hints: Families gathered around the set so as not to miss a single episode.
Horses and rain were imitated with coconut shells or crumpled paper.
I'm like a telenovela, but you listen to me.
questions.description: Tears, impossible love affairs and fake slamming doors… and half of Spain was hooked at the same hour.
questions.fun_fact: “Ama Rosa”, written by Guillermo Sautier Casaseca for Cadena SER, left the streets half empty while it was on the air.

questions.question: This radio network was founded in 1990 by ONCE, now belongs to Atresmedia and airs the show “Más de uno”. Which is it?
hints: It's a private station, not RTVE's public one.
It has the same owner as the TV channels Antena 3 and laSexta.
Its name includes the Spanish word for a number that means “nothing”.
questions.description: A station that keeps you company at breakfast, in traffic jams and on the way home.
questions.fun_fact: Onda Cero was formed in 1990 by merging stations ONCE had bought, such as those of the old Cadena Rato.

questions.question: Look closely at this paella. What kind of paella is it?
hints: Take a good look at what's on top of the rice.
Look at the dark shells peeking out of the rice.
It has prawns, mussels and langoustines.
questions.description: A dish so big you need the whole family around it to finish it.
questions.fun_fact: For many people from Valencia, the original paella has no seafood at all, just chicken, rabbit and green beans.

questions.question: Look at this photo. What is this dish called?
hints: They're made with ground meat, egg and bread.
They're cooked in a sauce that you mop up with bread.
Their name starts with “al-”, like many Spanish words that come from Arabic.
questions.description: Little balls that have kept grandparents and grandkids happy for generations.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish bars, albóndigas are one of the most-ordered tapas, especially in tomato or almond sauce.

questions.question: Look at this tapa. What is it called?
hints: It's one of the most famous tapas in Spain.
You order it to share at the bar, pick it up with a toothpick, and every bar boasts about its own sauce.
Its name says these potatoes have a fierce temper.
questions.description: That little plate in the middle of the table that friends fight over down to the last piece.
questions.fun_fact: Brava sauce usually contains hot pimentón (paprika), and many bars boast about their own secret recipe.

questions.question: On which date do many Latin American countries celebrate the Día de la Raza, which marks Columbus's arrival in the Americas?
hints: It's in the second half of the year.
It falls in the month of Halloween.
It's the 12th of that month.
questions.description: A holiday that shows up on time every year, unlike a ship that set out looking for Asia.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the same day is called Día de la Hispanidad, and in some other countries it is the Day of Cultural Diversity.

questions.question: It's a thick white sauce from Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, served with black rice. What does its name, alioli, mean?
hints: Its name is two words joined together.
“Oli” sounds a bit like “oil”.
One of the ingredients is bought in heads and split into cloves.
questions.description: Two ingredients that met in a mortar and never split up again.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional alioli is made just by crushing garlic in a mortar and slowly adding oil, with no egg at all.

questions.question: Latin American seseo, saying «casa» (house) just like «caza» (hunt), came mostly with settlers from one Spanish region. Which?
hints: It's a region in the south of the peninsula.
Ships bound for the Americas sailed from its ports.
You also hear «miarma» and «quillo» there.
questions.description: An S that crossed the ocean and decided to stay for good.
questions.fun_fact: People in the Canary Islands use seseo too, and many ships heading to the Americas stopped there on the way.

questions.question: In Spain, when rain is on the way, you often hear “coge el chubasquero”. What is a chubasquero?
hints: You use it when the weather turns bad.
A “chubasco” is a short, heavy shower.
It's a jacket that keeps the water out.
questions.description: What your mom makes you take “just in case”, even when the sun is blazing.
questions.fun_fact: Many chubasqueros fold up small enough to fit in a pouch the size of a fist.

questions.question: “Una pechá de gente” means “a whole lot of people”. In which region of Spain do you mostly hear this expression?
hints: People there are known for swallowing letters when they speak.
It's the region of Spain with the most people.
It's the region of Seville, Málaga and Granada.
questions.description: A word that says “loads” with hardly any letters.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish dictionary defines “pechada” as “hartazgo” (a bellyful), so “una pechá” is literally a bellyful.

questions.question: I live by the Segura river, among irrigation ditches and lemon trees, and my way of speaking is called panocho. Who am I?
hints: I work the land in a fertile valley in southeast Spain.
My festival is held in Murcia just after Holy Week.
My name comes from the place where I grow my vegetables.
questions.description: Someone who gets up even earlier than the tomatoes.
questions.fun_fact: During the Bando de la Huerta, Murcia fills with people wearing the traditional huertano costume.

questions.question: In Spain, if a grown-up says to a child “¡Ven aquí, renacuajo!”, what is the child being called?
hints: It's an affectionate nickname.
A “renacuajo” is a baby frog: a tadpole.
It has to do with size.
questions.description: A pet name that came straight out of the pond.
questions.fun_fact: “Renacuajo” comes from “rana” (frog), and Spaniards also use it for a small person or a little kid.

questions.question: In Madrid or Catalonia they're called “bambas”, and elsewhere “tenis” or “playeras”. What are they?
hints: You wear them on your feet.
You wear them in gym class.
They're made for running and have laces.
questions.description: Something with more names than a king.
questions.fun_fact: In many places they're called “tenis” because they first became popular for playing tennis.

questions.question: Antón García Abril, who wrote the music for the nature series “El hombre y la Tierra”, composed the official anthem of which Spanish region?
hints: It's an inland region with no coastline.
The region has three provinces.
García Abril was born in Teruel, and the Ebro River flows through this region.
questions.description: A composer whose tunes reached more living rooms than most TV hosts.
questions.fun_fact: García Abril also wrote the theme tunes of TV series such as “Fortunata y Jacinta” and “Anillos de oro”.

questions.question: You're on a beach on the east side of Fuerteventura, looking out to sea. Roughly how far away is the coast of Africa?
hints: It is the Canary Island closest to Africa.
A passenger plane would cross it in less than a quarter of an hour.
It's roughly two and a half marathons back to back.
questions.description: An island so windy that even the dunes comb their own hair.
questions.fun_fact: Calima, a haze of dust from the Sahara Desert, sometimes reaches Fuerteventura on the wind.

questions.question: Which people sailed longships, long boats with a dragon's head on the prow?
hints: They came from northern Europe.
They hung round shields along the sides of their ships.
Like Hiccup's dad in “How to Train Your Dragon.”
questions.description: A ship with a face that says “stay away,” literally.
questions.fun_fact: The Vikings reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.

questions.question: These limestone mountains lie between Asturias, Cantabria and León, and the Naranjo de Bulnes rises among them. What are they called?
hints: They are part of the Cantabrian Mountains.
They became Spain's first national park, in 1918.
Their name includes the name of a continent.
questions.description: Mountains where the cows graze with better views than a five-star hotel.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that they got their name because they were the first land sailors saw on their way back from the Americas.

questions.question: Mérida is to Extremadura as… which city is to Galicia?
hints: We're looking for the region's capital.
It's not the Galician city with the most people.
The Camino, the famous pilgrims' route, ends there.
questions.description: A matching game played with the map of Spain's regions spread out on the table.
questions.fun_fact: Its cathedral has a giant incense burner, the botafumeiro, which weighs about 53 kg (117 lb) and swings from side to side.

questions.question: In Spain, someone who talks nonstop and never lets you get a word in “habla por los…” what?
hints: You have two of them.
They're on your arm.
You rest them on the table, even when you're told not to.
questions.description: Some people have too much to say to fit it all through one mouth.
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese has the same saying: “falar pelos cotovelos”, which also means talking through your elbows.

questions.question: In Spain, when you're introduced to someone, how many kisses on the cheek do people usually give?
hints: It's a small number.
In some parts of France they give more than in Spain.
One on each cheek.
questions.description: A Spanish custom that leaves your face more greeted than a striker after a goal.
questions.fun_fact: In France the number of kisses depends on the region: two in some areas, three or even four in others.

questions.question: In “Game of Thrones,” the islet of San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, in Biscay, became another place. Which one?
hints: It's where one of the main characters was born, and she returns there years later.
Daenerys welcomes Jon Snow there in season seven.
It's the fortress of House Targaryen, and its name joins a rock with a fire-breathing beast.
questions.description: When a fantasy series goes house hunting for a sea view, it calls a Spanish location agency.
questions.fun_fact: To reach the hermitage on Gaztelugatxe, you have to climb about 241 steps.

questions.question: I was born in Mahón, Menorca, in 1992, and became world number 1 in a paddle sport played in pairs inside glass walls. Who am I?
hints: My sport was born in Mexico and is a huge hit in Spain.
I'm the big Balearic star of women's padel.
My last name starts with “Tr”.
questions.description: A woman from Menorca who spends all day hitting things against walls, and people clap for it.
questions.fun_fact: Padel was invented by Enrique Corcuera at his home in Acapulco, Mexico, in 1969.

questions.question: The Barcelona Olympics ended on August 9, 1992. In which month did the Paralympics start there?
hints: They started after the Olympics, not before.
Only a few weeks passed between the two.
It was around the time Spanish kids go back to school.
questions.description: Barcelona put out the Olympic flame, but it still had a second party ready.
questions.fun_fact: The archer who lit the Olympic cauldron in Barcelona, Antonio Rebollo, was a Paralympic athlete.

questions.question: Spain has 17 autonomous communities. Which of these places is NOT one of them?
hints: All four are in the north of the Iberian Peninsula.
Three of them have their own regional parliament and president within Spain.
It's in the Pyrenees and is an independent country.
questions.description: Seventeen sisters who share a house and never agree on who holds the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the 17 communities, Spain has two autonomous cities: Ceuta and Melilla.

questions.question: This is Madrid's M-30. What kind of road is it?
hints: Many big cities have one or more roads of this kind.
It doesn't leave Madrid for another city.
It loops all the way around the city center.
questions.description: A Madrid road where traffic jams have season tickets.
questions.fun_fact: Part of the M-30 runs through tunnels under the Madrid Río park, next to the Manzanares river.

questions.question: Which Andalusian city built a large network of bike lanes in just a few years and filled up with cyclists?
hints: It is one of the biggest cities in Spain.
The Guadalquivir River flows through it.
The Giralda tower is there.
questions.description: A city where the pedal beat the car horn fair and square.
questions.fun_fact: Seville has a public bike rental service called Sevici, running since 2007.

questions.question: Spain has “rotondas” everywhere. What is a “rotonda”?
questions.answer: A round junction that cars drive around
wrong_answers: A bridge that crosses over a river
A covered stop where buses pick you up
A tunnel that goes through a mountain
hints: It's on the road, at ground level.
Many have gardens or statues in the middle.
Its shape is like a circle.
questions.description: The place where drivers prove whether they really learned the rules of the road.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, the car already driving inside a rotonda (roundabout) has the right of way.

questions.question: Which architect designed the Bilbao metro, with its famous curved glass entrances?
hints: He is a very famous architect outside Spain.
He did not design the city's Guggenheim Museum.
He is British and designed the London skyscraper nicknamed “the Gherkin”.
questions.description: Giant glass shells that swallow the people of Bilbao every morning and spit them out in the evening.
questions.fun_fact: Locals call these glass entrances “fosteritos” (little Fosters), after their architect.

questions.question: In which version of TVE's “MasterChef” does the winner give the prize money to a charity instead of keeping it?
hints: It's not the version where kids cook.
The contestants were already on TV before they joined.
The name includes a word for a famous person.
questions.description: A kitchen where the nerves sneak right into the frying pan.
questions.fun_fact: The first season of “MasterChef Celebrity” premiered on TVE in 2016.

questions.question: Jordi Cruz, a “MasterChef” judge, was one of Spain's youngest chefs to win a Michelin star. In which city is his restaurant ABaC?
hints: The restaurant has three Michelin stars.
The city is on the Mediterranean coast.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: If he frowns at you on TV, imagine what happens when you burn the fish in his kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Jordi Cruz won his first Michelin star at 24, at the restaurant L'Estany Clar.

questions.question: It was Spain's first private nationwide TV channel and started broadcasting in January 1990. Which channel is it?
hints: Its name has a number in it.
Today it airs “El Hormiguero”.
It also airs “La ruleta de la suerte” and “Pasapalabra”.
questions.description: Before it arrived, channel-surfing in most of Spain meant picking between two channels.
questions.fun_fact: Antena 3 started broadcasting on January 25, 1990, after some test broadcasts at Christmas 1989.

questions.question: On “Supervivientes”, celebrities live on an island in Honduras. What do they usually win in the reward challenges?
hints: It's what they miss most on the island.
Without it, they only have rice and whatever they catch.
It could be a pizza or a sandwich.
questions.description: A vacation on a tropical island where nobody wants to stay.
questions.fun_fact: Many “Supervivientes” contestants leave the island several kilos lighter than when they arrived.

questions.question: You get up really early to do your homework. According to the Spanish saying, who helps those who rise early?
hints: In Spanish, the saying begins “A quien madruga…”.
He appears in lots of other Spanish sayings and expressions.
Many religions say he lives in heaven.
questions.description: The alarm goes off at six and you're already bargaining for five more minutes.
questions.fun_fact: Another Spanish saying argues the opposite: “No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano” (getting up early won't make the sun rise sooner).

questions.question: Complete the Spanish comparison for someone who can't hear a thing: “Más sordo que una…” (deafer than a…)
hints: It has no ears, of course.
It's made of mud or stone.
It's a wall around a vegetable garden or a farmyard.
questions.description: You talk, you shout, you sing… and nothing, not even a blink.
questions.fun_fact: A tapia is a wall of packed earth: many houses and farmyards in Spanish villages were built this way.

questions.question: Where did the expression “salvado por la campana” (saved by the bell) come from?
hints: The phrase dates from the 19th century.
The person saved was in real trouble, and a sound, not a person, came to the rescue.
There, the bell marked the end of each round.
questions.description: A ding-dong just in time got you out of something really big.
questions.fun_fact: A popular myth says it comes from coffins fitted with little bells, but experts trace it to 19th-century boxing.

questions.question: By the most popular explanation, who spent the night awake dressed in white, giving rise to “pasar la noche en blanco”?
questions.answer: Young men about to become knights
hints: It happened in the Middle Ages.
It was the night before a very important ceremony for them.
They kept watch over their weapons before being dubbed with a sword.
questions.description: No counting sheep, no herbal tea, nothing: eyes wide open until sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: Don Quixote also kept watch over his weapons all night, though in the yard of an inn.

questions.question: If someone “está de mala uva”, what's wrong with them?
hints: It has nothing to do with eating fruit.
Better not ask them for a favor right now.
They grumble, complain and slam doors.
questions.description: A grape that hears everyone talking about it and has no idea why.
questions.fun_fact: It's usually explained this way: bad grapes make sour wine, just as a bad mood turns people sour.

questions.question: Seafood for 300 guests, fireworks and a live band: as they say in Spain, the hosts threw… what out of the window?
hints: The saying means spending a huge amount of money on something.
It's far too big to fit through a window.
It's where you live.
questions.description: A party where even the confetti was luxury.
questions.fun_fact: It's said to come from lottery winners, who threw their old furniture out of the window to buy new things.

questions.question: It's summer, you're at the town pool and you've just eaten. Many grandparents say if you jump in now, what can you get?
hints: That's why they tell you to wait a good while before swimming.
It has to do with the food still in your tummy.
Spanish grandparents call it a “corte de…” something.
questions.description: The summer warning that has saved more sandwiches than swimmers.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors say the “corte de digestión” isn't the real danger: it's jumping suddenly into very cold water with a hot body, called hydrocution.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Spain, which group of sweets does this one belong to?
hints: People eat it mostly when it's cold out.
It sits on the table next to the polvorones and the marzipan.
It's a classic at Nochebuena dinner.
questions.description: A sweet with so many almonds that any squirrel would call it a dream come true.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's most famous turrón comes from Jijona, in Alicante, which even has a museum all about it.

questions.question: On a report card in Spain, from what grade up do you get a “sobresaliente”?
hints: The “notable” comes just below it.
It's almost the top grade.
Only a 10 beats it, and that's a sobresaliente too.
questions.description: The piece of paper that travels from school to home slower than any other, especially if it holds surprises.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, grades go from 0 to 10: a 5 is a pass, a 6 is a “bien”, and a 7 or 8 gets you a “notable”.

questions.question: They look after you while you eat at school, help you peel your fruit and watch the playground afterward, but they aren't your teachers. Who are they?
hints: You only see them if you stay at school for lunch.
They work during lunchtime.
Their name includes the place where you eat with your classmates.
questions.description: Heroes without capes who somehow get kids to finish their lentils.
