questions.fun_fact: Benito and Manolo came back in 2006 with their own series, “Manolo y Benito Corporeision”.

questions.question: A Basque chef has said it on TV since the 1990s, tasting his dishes between jokes. Which phrase is it?
hints: The chef is Karlos Arguiñano.
His cooking show airs at midday on Antena 3.
It repeats the same word twice at the start.
questions.description: A catchphrase so tasty they should sell it at the supermarket.
questions.fun_fact: Karlos Arguiñano has his restaurant and a cooking school in Zarautz, in Gipuzkoa.

questions.question: It's a private Mediaset channel that has aired “Gran Hermano”, “La que se avecina” and “Sálvame”. Which channel is it?
hints: It's the older sibling of the channel Cuatro.
Its name has a number in it.
The number in its name comes right after four.
questions.description: A channel named after a number that has never had to do the math.
questions.fun_fact: Telecinco started broadcasting in 1990, shortly after private channels arrived in Spain.

questions.question: In what year did La 1 first air “El cazador”, the quiz show where an expert chases the contestants down a board?
hints: It's a fairly recent quiz show.
It's the Spanish version of the British show “The Chase”.
It came to TV the same year as the pandemic.
questions.description: A quiz show where you run faster than you would for the last bus, without ever leaving your chair.
questions.fun_fact: The show's chasers are star contestants from Spanish TV quiz shows, known by their nicknames.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT part of «Allá tú», Jesús Vázquez's quiz show?
wrong_answers: A phone to talk to the banker
hints: It was the Spanish version of “Deal or No Deal”.
The contestant picked boxes and opened them.
The odd one out belongs to another quiz show, the one with letters and puzzle boards.
questions.description: A quiz show for people who can't even decide what to order at a bar.
questions.fun_fact: «Allá tú» came from a format born in the Netherlands that has aired in dozens of countries.

questions.question: Risto Mejide became famous in Spain as the toughest judge on “Operación Triunfo”. In which decade was that?
hints: “Operación Triunfo” started with the new century.
It was the show's fifth season.
It was in 2006.
questions.description: Sunglasses indoors in a TV studio: a sure sign this is going to hurt.
questions.fun_fact: After “Operación Triunfo”, Risto Mejide was also a judge on “Got Talent España”.

questions.question: Hugo Sánchez was nicknamed “Hugol” for his goals in Spain. About how many did he score in the Spanish league?
hints: He played there for many years, for Atlético and Real Madrid.
He was that league's top scorer for five seasons.
More than 200, but fewer than 300.
questions.description: He yelled “goal” so often they even changed his name.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1989–90 season he scored 38 goals, and it's said every one of them was a first-touch finish.

questions.question: In 1968, rector Javier Barros Sierra flew the flag at half-mast at UNAM and led a march to defend me. What am I?
hints: It has to do with who's in charge inside the university.
That summer the army entered university campuses.
UNAM has had it since 1929.
questions.description: A rector who put his job on the line to defend his school.
questions.fun_fact: Barros Sierra was a civil engineer and served as Secretary of Public Works before becoming rector.

questions.question: Agustín Lara, the “Flaco de Oro,” wrote “Solamente una vez” and “Granada.” About how many songs did he write in his life?
hints: He composed for more than 40 years.
That's far more than would fit on ten albums.
It's several hundred.
questions.description: A skinny man who never ran out of sweet words for anyone.
questions.fun_fact: He wrote “Granada” without ever having set foot in Spain.

questions.question: From the 1930s to the 1950s, Pedro Infante, Jorge Negrete and Dolores del Río packed theaters and Mexico ruled Spanish-language film. What is that era called?
hints: It was the brightest period of Mexican film.
World War II helped, because Hollywood and Europe were making fewer films.
It's the metal of the first-place medal.
questions.description: Back when going to the movies meant watching your grandma fall in love with a charro.
questions.fun_fact: “Allá en el Rancho Grande” (1936) took the Mexican ranchera comedy all over Latin America.

questions.question: This orange train car is from Mexico City. What kind of transit is it?
hints: It has rubber tires even though it runs on tracks.
Many of its stations are underground.
Every station has a little picture so you can recognize it.
questions.description: Millions of chilangos ride it every day, and almost all of them have seen it at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: It opened on September 4, 1969, and every station has an icon so that even people who can't read can recognize it.

questions.question: Diego Rivera painted “Man at the Crossroads” in New York; it was destroyed for showing Lenin, and he repainted it at Bellas Artes. Under what name?
hints: The new title is grander than the original.
The man in the center operates a huge machine.
It's no longer about a crossroads, but about the whole cosmos.
questions.description: A mural so unlucky that the very people who ordered it had it wiped out.
questions.fun_fact: The original mural was in Rockefeller Center and was smashed to pieces with hammers in February 1934.

questions.question: On September 19 in both 1985 and 2017, Mexico City shook badly because its soft ground was once the bottom of… what?
hints: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island.
The Spanish drained it little by little.
It shares its name with a municipality in the State of Mexico.
questions.description: A date chilangos watch with one eye on the calendar and the other on the ceiling lamp.
questions.fun_fact: In 2022 another strong quake hit on September 19: the third on that date!

questions.question: The IMSS National Medical Center was badly damaged in the 1985 earthquake. When it was rebuilt, what name was added to it?
hints: It isn't the name of a person or of a date in Mexican history.
It stands on Avenida Cuauhtémoc, in the Doctores neighborhood.
It's a century written in Roman numerals.
questions.description: A building that had to get back on its feet after a really big shake.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City has two other national medical centers: La Raza, run by the IMSS, and 20 de Noviembre, run by the ISSSTE.

questions.question: Lázaro Cárdenas created it in 1937; it puts up poles all over the country and sends you the electric bill. What does CFE stand for?
hints: The “E” is for what runs through the wires.
The “F” is about the whole country, not one state.
The “C” isn't for compañía.
questions.description: The three letters that make your family shudder every two months.
questions.fun_fact: In 1960, President Adolfo López Mateos nationalized Mexico's electricity industry.

questions.question: Finish the phrase: at the taquería, ordering your tacos “con todo” means with onion and…
hints: It's a green herb.
It's chopped fine, very fine.
People love or hate its smell, and its name starts with “ci.”
questions.description: The most important question of the day, and it's the taquero asking, not your teacher.
questions.fun_fact: Some people think cilantro tastes like soap because of a variant in their genes.

questions.question: He's called Strider, he's the heir to a lost kingdom, and he falls in love with the elf Arwen. Which people is Aragorn from?
hints: He is not immortal, though he lives longer than usual.
His people were given nine rings of power.
He is the same species as you.
questions.description: A king who spent years as a wanderer before he ever tried on a crown.
questions.fun_fact: In Tolkien's story, Aragorn lives to 210 thanks to the blood of the Dúnedain in his veins.

questions.question: I'm a potato cut into long strips, fried until golden, and I always come with the burger. What am I?
hints: You eat me with your hands.
I love ketchup.
My name includes a European country.
questions.description: The most famous couple in fast food, and it's not the burger.
questions.fun_fact: Belgium and France still argue over which of the two countries invented these fries.

questions.question: The bolillo is long, crusty outside and soft inside. According to Mexican tradition, what is eating a piece of one good for?
hints: People say it after a bad moment.
It's given to someone who looks pale and shaken.
There's a saying: “un bolillo para el…”.
questions.description: The most serious bread in the bakery: no sugar and no jokes.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico people even say “un bolillo para el susto” after a big scare during a soccer game.

questions.question: You're eating beans and there's no cutlery. In Mexico, a folded piece of tortilla works as a…
hints: It's something you use at the table every day.
It's used to lift food.
You use it to eat soup.
questions.description: In Mexico, the food comes with its own edible helper.
questions.fun_fact: A tortilla folded for eating is sometimes called “the Mexican spoon,” because you eat it along with whatever it scoops up.

questions.question: In which city do people throw and smash the clay plate after eating a buñuelo with honey in December, for good luck?
hints: It's a city in southern Mexico.
The Noche de Rábanos is also celebrated there.
It's famous for its mole negro and the Guelaguetza.
questions.description: A Christmas tradition where breaking the dishes is good manners.
questions.fun_fact: The Noche de Rábanos (Night of the Radishes) is held every December 23 with figures carved from giant radishes.

questions.question: You're in Oaxaca and you unwrap an Oaxacan tamal with mole negro. What is it wrapped in?
hints: It's not what Mexico City's tamal verde comes wrapped in.
It's a big, green, shiny leaf.
It comes from a plant that grows a yellow fruit.
questions.description: A present you unwrap with an empty stomach.
questions.fun_fact: The banana leaf is passed over a flame before use so it softens and doesn't tear.

questions.question: At the fair it's sold on a stick, coated in fried batter and topped with ketchup and mustard. What's inside a classic banderilla?
hints: It's salty, not sweet.
It's meat, and it comes already cooked in a package.
It's long and pink.
questions.description: The fair snack you walk around holding hands with, like in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: In the US, the banderilla is known as a “corn dog,” because its batter is made with cornmeal.

questions.question: I'm from Jalisco, and as a kid I was nicknamed after a sweet spice because of my reddish hair. Today I'm Mexico's most famous boxer. Who am I?
hints: He was born in Guadalajara, so he's a tapatío.
His great rival was Gennady Golovkin from Kazakhstan.
His nickname is the Spanish word for the spice you put in café de olla.
questions.description: He has a nickname like grandma's dessert, but he hits like a truck with no brakes.
questions.fun_fact: Saúl Álvarez is the youngest of eight siblings, and six of them also became boxers.

questions.question: In boxing, a “technical knockout,” or TKO, gives a fighter the win. What does it mean?
questions.answer: The referee stops the fight: a boxer can't go on
wrong_answers: The winner knocked him out with a punch to the neck
The judges give the win on points
The opponent missed the weigh-in time
hints: Nobody has to count to ten.
It happens when a boxer can no longer defend himself properly.
The person who decides is the one walking between the two fighters.
questions.description: In boxing the punches hit hard, but the abbreviations hit even harder.
questions.fun_fact: It is also a technical knockout when a boxer's corner throws in the towel to give up.

questions.question: What are these little cookies called?
hints: They're tiny, and lots of them come in one bag.
Each one has a different shape.
You might find an elephant or a lion among them.
questions.description: Cookies so brave they jump into the glass of milk all by themselves.
questions.fun_fact: Animal-shaped cookies were already being baked in England in the 1800s.

questions.question: I have fangs, I hate sunlight, and I march in armies for the Dark Lord. Which writer made me famous?
hints: He was a professor at the University of Oxford.
He studied languages and invented whole new ones, like the languages of the elves.
His most famous work is “The Lord of the Rings.”
questions.description: Monsters who have never once been to the dentist.
questions.fun_fact: Since Tolkien, orcs have shown up in countless video games and role-playing games.

questions.question: Sponch are Marinela cookies with a pink or white marshmallow on top. What is that marshmallow covered with?
hints: It feels a little scratchy on your tongue.
It comes from a fruit with a very hard shell.
It comes from the hairy fruit that grows on palm trees.
questions.description: A cookie that dresses up in pink to go to the party.
questions.fun_fact: The marshmallow is named after a plant, the marsh mallow, whose root was once used to make it.

questions.question: The owner of the vecindad is called Señor Barriga. What part of the body is a “barriga”?
hints: It’s a part of the body.
That’s where you feel it when you’re hungry.
Your navel sits right in the middle of it.
questions.description: The one neighbor everyone runs from when he shows up: he’s here to collect the rent.
questions.fun_fact: Édgar Vivar played Señor Barriga and also his son Ñoño.

questions.question: I'm Doña Florinda's niece and Quico's cousin, I talk with a nasal voice and always carry my doll Serapia. Who am I?
hints: I'm played by Florinda Meza, the same actress who plays my aunt.
I go to school with Profesor Jirafales.
My name is also Mexican slang for “posh” or “fancy.”
questions.description: A visitor to the vecindad who never shows up without her best friend made of rags.
questions.fun_fact: Florinda Meza played both Doña Florinda and her niece, la Popis.

questions.question: Which of these characters was NOT played by Rubén Aguirre?
hints: Rubén Aguirre played the vecindad's famous teacher.
That character was played by Chespirito himself.
He's a very old doctor who gets angry if you call him old.
questions.description: An actor so tall he had to duck to get into any character.
questions.fun_fact: Rubén Aguirre was about 1.96 m (6 ft 5 in) tall, which is why his character is called Jirafales, from “jirafa” (giraffe).

questions.question: On the night of January 5, Mexican children leave out their shoes. Before going to sleep, what do they usually put inside?
questions.answer: Their letter to the Three Kings
hints: They get it ready right before going to bed.
The Kings check it before leaving the presents.
In it they say how well they behaved and which toys they want.
questions.description: The Kings have to stick their noses where nobody else dares.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, some children also tie their letter to a helium balloon and let it go, so it flies all the way to the Kings.

questions.question: You're setting up the nacimiento and the Niño Dios is already in his manger. Who does NOT belong there?
hints: Three of them are part of the story of Bethlehem.
One arrives by sleigh from the North Pole.
The one dressed in red who says “Ho, ho, ho.”
questions.description: A manger with more visitors than Grandma's house at Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican homes the nacimiento stays up until February 2, the Día de la Candelaria (Candlemas).

questions.question: In a nativity scene, the angel hangs above the stable. In the story of Bethlehem, what did the angel do that night?
hints: It happened the same night Jesus was born.
It appeared in the fields, at night.
It told some men looking after sheep that the Baby had been born.
questions.description: The nativity decoration that spends all Christmas hanging from the ceiling without complaining.
questions.fun_fact: In many nativity scenes, the angel holds a ribbon with the Latin words “Gloria in excelsis Deo”.

questions.question: At the end of a posada, you get a little bag called an “aguinaldo”. What is usually inside?
hints: Kids can't wait to get it after the singing.
It may have peanuts and a mandarin orange.
It has colorful sugar candies and other sweets.
questions.description: Your reward for singing outside in the cold, begging for a place to stay.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, “aguinaldo” is also the extra year-end pay that workers get in December.

questions.question: At a fonda in Mexico City, you order a huarache with beans, salsa and cheese. What do you get?
questions.answer: A long corn-dough base with toppings
wrong_answers: A round sweet bun with a sugar crust
A tamale wrapped in a banana leaf
A tortilla soup with pasilla chile
hints: It's an antojito made of masa, like sopes and tlacoyos.
Its name comes from its shape.
It's flat and oval, like the sole of a sandal.
questions.description: At the fonda, hunger is the boss, and sometimes the menu speaks in code.
questions.fun_fact: The huarache as a dish is said to have been born in Mexico City in the 1930s, at a stand by the La Viga canal.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what do people call this huge square in the center of Mexico City?
hints: It hosts concerts, parades and the September 15 celebration.
The Cathedral and the National Palace stand right next to it.
Its official name is Plaza de la Constitución.
questions.description: The biggest living room in the country, and it doesn't even have a couch.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the Zócalo because for years it only had the base (in Spanish, “zócalo”) of an Independence monument that was never finished.

questions.question: Look at this embroidery: which traditional garment of Mexico's Indigenous women is it?
hints: Frida Kahlo wore it in many of her self-portraits.
It's a blouse or tunic without long sleeves, with an opening for the head.
It's widely worn in Oaxaca, Chiapas and Yucatán, and its name comes from Nahuatl.
questions.description: A garment that takes months to embroider and two seconds to win over Frida Kahlo.
questions.fun_fact: In many towns, the designs on a huipil show which community the person wearing it comes from.

questions.question: When Mexico's national team wins, fans go to celebrate at a monument on Reforma. Complete its name: the Angel of…
hints: The monument is a column topped by a golden figure with wings.
It honors the heroes who fought against Spain.
It's celebrated every September 16.
questions.description: When Mexico scores, the whole city knows exactly where to go and shout.
questions.fun_fact: The golden Angel statue fell during the 1957 earthquake and had to be restored.

questions.question: You're at the Portal de Zevallos in Córdoba, Veracruz, where the treaties recognizing Mexico's independence were signed. In what year?
hints: It was in the early 19th century, when Mexico stopped being New Spain.
They were signed by Agustín de Iturbide and Juan O'Donojú.
That same year, the Army of the Three Guarantees marched into Mexico City.
questions.description: One signature in Veracruz that saved Mexico several more chapters of war.
questions.fun_fact: The Treaties of Córdoba were signed on August 24, 1821, but Spain didn't accept them until years later.

questions.question: Complete the name of the wrestler from San Luis Potosí who took Mexican lucha libre to Japan and the United States: “Mil ___.”
hints: He was also a star of wrestler movies from the 1960s on.
On the big screen he teamed up with El Santo and Blue Demon.
They say he had so many that he almost never entered the ring wearing the same one.
questions.description: A man from San Luis Potosí who made half the world cheer from the ring ropes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012 he entered the WWE Hall of Fame, one of the first Mexican wrestlers to do so.

questions.question: He's a charro rooster from Jalisco with a huge sombrero, and in 1944 he sang in a Disney film with Donald Duck and a Brazilian parrot. What's his name?
hints: The film is called “The Three Caballeros.”
His parrot friend is named José Carioca.
His last name sounds like the guns he fires into the air when he gets excited.
questions.description: A feathered fellow who wakes up the whole ranch, mariachi band included.
questions.fun_fact: In the story, his full name is Panchito Romero Miguel Junípero Francisco Quintero González III.

questions.question: The Museo de la Caricatura, on Calle de Donceles in Mexico City's historic center, is in a colonial building. What was it originally?
hints: It was founded in the early 17th century.
A rich man founded it with money he left in his will.
Young people who couldn't afford their studies lived there.
questions.description: A colonial building that today can't take anything seriously.
questions.fun_fact: The museum is run by the Sociedad Mexicana de Caricaturistas, the guild of Mexico's cartoonists, the “moneros”.

questions.question: Comics are full of onomatopoeias, words that imitate sounds. Which of these groups are NOT onomatopoeias?
hints: An onomatopoeia sounds just like the noise it imitates.
A punch, a rooster or a clock sound like this in comics.
Look for the words you say to cheer someone on or when you're surprised, not to imitate a noise.
questions.description: Pow! Zap! This question comes with sound effects included.
questions.fun_fact: Dogs don't “say” the same thing in every language: in English they bark “woof” and in Japanese “wan wan”.

questions.question: I'm a brave egg from a Mexican animated movie, and my best friend is a strip of bacon named Willy. Who am I?
hints: In my world, food talks and goes on adventures.
My name has only four letters, and I'm a boy, not a girl.
My name rhymes with “photo”.
questions.description: A character who loves coming out of his shell… but not getting into the frying pan.
questions.fun_fact: Willy the bacon was voiced by Mexican actor and comedian Carlos Espejel.

questions.question: A palm hat is to palm as a huarache is to…
hints: Think about what each thing is made of.
A huarache is a sandal woven by hand.
It comes from the skin of cows.
questions.description: Ranch fashion: handmade from head to toe.
questions.fun_fact: In Becal, Campeche, many palm hats are woven in damp caves so the fiber doesn't crack.

questions.question: It's a gem that flashes many colors, ranges from yellow to red and is mined in Querétaro. What is it?
hints: Tequisquiapan, in Querétaro, is famous for selling it.
It has a little water trapped inside.
Its name brings flames to mind.
questions.description: The jewel that took on the colors of a sunset over the semi-desert.
questions.fun_fact: Opal holds water inside, so it can crack if it dries out too much.

questions.question: Look at this chicken and vegetable soup. When does Grandma make it for you as a remedy?
hints: It's when you're stuck in bed and don't feel like doing anything.
Here come the runny nose and the sneezing.
It's that illness with chills, a cough and a stuffy nose.
questions.description: Grandma's hug, served in a deep bowl.
questions.fun_fact: A study from 2000 found that chicken soup may slightly reduce swelling in the nose and throat.

questions.question: You stir it into warm water, gargle without swallowing, and it's the classic remedy for a sore throat. What goes in the water?
hints: Every home has it in the kitchen.
It isn't sweet.
The sea tastes like this.
questions.description: A remedy that sounds like you're drowning on purpose.
questions.fun_fact: Salty water draws fluid out of a swollen throat and brings the swelling down a little.

questions.question: I'm a baby illness: they say I come if you lower a baby too fast, the soft spot on its head sinks, and some hang babies by their feet to cure me. What am I?
hints: It isn't a tummy illness or one caused by a look.
It has to do with the baby's head.
“Mollera” is what people call the soft spot on a baby's head.
questions.description: An illness so strange that its cure looks like a circus act.
questions.fun_fact: For doctors, a sunken soft spot can be a sign of dehydration, so the baby needs fluids and a trip to the doctor.

questions.question: Look at this sugar skull. On a Day of the Dead ofrenda, who is it placed for?
questions.answer: For family members who have died
wrong_answers: For kids who have a birthday
hints: It's a way to remember someone who is no longer here.
Their photos go on the ofrenda too.
They're the grandparents, great-grandparents and other loved ones who are gone.
questions.description: A candy that smiles even without lips.
questions.fun_fact: Alfeñique, the sugar technique used to make the little skulls, came to Mexico from Spain in colonial times.

questions.question: Look: when entering the church, people dip their fingertips here and make the sign of the cross. What's inside?
hints: It's special water for believers.
A priest prepares it with a prayer.
It's also used to bless houses and cars.
questions.description: The little fountain where nobody makes a wish, but everyone dips their fingers.
questions.fun_fact: In many churches in Mexico, people bring little bottles to take holy water home.

questions.question: In a shop you see a curved, cone-shaped charm hanging up, filled with corn, beans, rice and coins and renewed every year. What is it called?
wrong_answers: The sábila with a red ribbon
hints: It's a very old symbol, much older than Mexico.
It also appears on the coats of arms of several countries.
Its name promises you'll never be short of anything.
questions.description: The favorite decoration of every hopeful shopkeeper.
questions.fun_fact: In Greek mythology it was the horn of the goat Amalthea, who nursed the baby Zeus.

questions.question: On New Year's Eve, many Mexicans wear new underwear in one color to attract love and another for money. Which colors?
questions.answer: Red for love and yellow for money
wrong_answers: Yellow for love and red for money
Blue for love and black for money
Purple for love and brown for money
hints: This custom is also followed in other Latin American countries.
Both colors are warm, like fire.
One is the color of hearts and the other the color of gold.
questions.description: The thing you really wear brand new on December 31, and nobody sees it.
questions.fun_fact: In Brazil the tradition is different: people dress in white to welcome the new year.

questions.question: At family meals, Grandma won't let single women sit in one spot: the belief goes they won't marry for seven years. Where?
questions.answer: At the corner of the table
wrong_answers: At the head of the table
hints: It's a spot on the table itself.
It's at the edge of the table, but it isn't the place of honor.
It's where the table comes to a point.
questions.description: A seat at the table that no single aunt wants.
questions.fun_fact: The same belief exists in Russia: there, too, they say whoever sits at the corner of the table won't marry for seven years.

questions.question: For a cough, Grandma gives you a spoonful of honey with a few drops of a green, very sour fruit. Which one?
hints: It's small and round.
You squeeze it over tacos.
It's so sour that biting into one makes you scrunch up your face.
questions.description: A syrup that comes from the pantry, not the pharmacy.
questions.fun_fact: Honey should never be given to babies under one year old, so this remedy is for older kids.

questions.question: In Mexico they say that if you point at a rainbow, you'll get a “mezquino”. What is a mezquino?
hints: It shows up on your skin.
It's a small hard bump that sometimes appears on your hands.
A virus causes it, and a dermatologist can remove it.
questions.description: A warning from Grandma: the sky has its own rules of good manners.
questions.fun_fact: Warts are caused by a virus that spreads through touch, not by rainbows.

questions.question: It opened in 1974 in Mexico City, it preserves and screens films, and in 1982 a fire destroyed much of its archive. What is it?
hints: It isn't a film studio: no movies are shot there.
It has theaters showing film series from all over the world, in the Xoco neighborhood on Avenida México-Coyoacán.
Its Spanish name blends “cine” with the idea of a library, plus the country's adjective.
questions.description: For Mexican cinema, popcorn is optional; passion is a must.
questions.fun_fact: After the fire, the Cineteca reopened in 1984 at its current home in Xoco, on Avenida México-Coyoacán.

questions.question: It was the title of a 1930s film, it's used to brag that one state always wins, and many add “y cuando pierde, arrebata”. Which saying is it?
hints: It's a saying of pure bragging, not of bravery.
Chivas fans shout it when their team wins.
It says that state never gets beaten.
questions.description: Some phrases can only be said with your charro hat firmly on your head.
questions.fun_fact: In 1941 Jorge Negrete starred in “¡Ay, Jalisco, no te rajes!”, another film that brought Jalisco pride to the big screen.

questions.question: You hear Pedro Infante sing “Amorcito corazón” in the movie “Nosotros los pobres”. In which decade did it come out?
hints: Your great-grandparents could have seen it at the movies when they were young.
It’s in black and white, like almost all films of the Golden Age.
It came out about three years after the end of World War II.
questions.description: A song so sweet it could sweeten even a cup of café de olla.
questions.fun_fact: “Amorcito corazón” was written by Manuel Esperón and Pedro de Urdimalas, and in the movie Pepe el Toro sings it to Celia, “la Chorreada.”

questions.question: This is Ninón Sevilla, queen of the rumberas of Mexican cinema. In which country was she born?
hints: She wasn't born in Mexico, though she made her whole film career there.
Her country is an island in the Caribbean.
She was born in the capital famous for its Malecón and its old classic cars.
questions.description: Dancing hips that arrived in Mexico on a one-way ticket.
questions.fun_fact: French critics such as François Truffaut were big admirers of Ninón Sevilla's cabaret films.

questions.question: “La perla”, by Emilio “el Indio” Fernández, was shot in Spanish and English, based on a novel by John Steinbeck. In which year was it released?
hints: It starred Pedro Armendáriz, at the height of the Golden Age.
World War II had already ended.
It came out in the late 1940s.
questions.description: Finding a treasure in the sea sounds awesome… until you see it in black and white.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriel Figueroa's cinematography in “La perla” won a Golden Globe.

questions.question: In many Mexican homes, when something goes missing and then turns up somewhere else, people say a mischievous someone hid it. Who?
hints: It's very, very small.
It loves playing pranks, not scaring people with screams.
Some people leave it candy so it gives things back.
questions.description: The real reason you can never find the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican stories, duendes live in old houses and at night make noises or move things around.

questions.question: Grupo Omnilife, the company that owns Chivas, was founded by a businessman who bought the club in 2002. Who?
hints: He was from Guadalajara and sold nutritional supplements.
Today the club is run by his son Amaury.
His last name starts with V.
questions.description: A shake company that ended up running a herd of goats.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Vergara pushed for Estadio Akron, which opened in 2010 and is shaped like a grass-covered volcano.

questions.question: Which of these nicknames does NOT belong to Puebla FC?
hints: Three of these nicknames are from Puebla.
One comes from a typical Puebla sweet, and another from the stripe on the jersey.
The odd one out belongs to a team from Querétaro.
questions.description: Soccer nicknames are like grade-school nicknames: one of them snuck in where it doesn't belong.
questions.fun_fact: Puebla is called “La Franja” because of the blue band that runs diagonally across its white jersey.

questions.question: In the stands you hear the chants of La Monumental. Which team does this supporters' group cheer for?
hints: It's a team from the capital.
Its fans dress in yellow.
They're called the Águilas.
questions.description: A fan group that sings so loud the neighbors don't even bother turning on the TV.
questions.fun_fact: La Monumental is one of the biggest and best-known supporters' groups in Mexican soccer.

questions.question: Which of these legendary luchadores did NOT wear a mask?
hints: He won many bet matches against masked wrestlers and for opponents' hair.
He was born in Zacatecas and was one of the most feared rudos of the '70s and '80s.
His ring name includes the Spanish word for an animal that barks.
questions.description: Three kept their secret under the fabric, and one showed his face from day one.
questions.fun_fact: His son, Perro Aguayo Jr., was also a famous rudo and founded the group Los Perros del Mal.

questions.question: Look at this tall Egyptian crown, shaped like a bowling pin. What did it stand for?
hints: Egypt began as two kingdoms that later joined together.
It was called the “hedjet,” and its partner was a red crown.
It was the crown of the southern kingdom, up the Nile River.
questions.description: A hat shaped like a bowling pin, but with political power.
questions.fun_fact: Once the two kingdoms were united, the pharaoh wore the white crown set inside the red one: the double crown, or “pschent.”

questions.question: Plain walls below, stone mosaics above, full of masks of the god Chaac: it's the style of Uxmal, Sayil and Labná. What is it called?
hints: It is found in the hilly part of Yucatán.
Its Maya name means “hills” or “hill country.”
A tourist route with this name runs from Uxmal to Labná.
questions.description: Maya architects nobody ever told that less is more.
questions.fun_fact: In this style, facade stones were cut like puzzle pieces and set onto a core of Maya concrete.

questions.question: It's a tall stone slab that stood in plazas, carved with a ruler and dates in glyphs. Calakmul has over a hundred. What is it?
hints: It always stands upright, like a little wall all on its own.
It often had a low, round stone in front of it.
Its name comes from Greek, and it's also used for monuments in Egypt and Greece.
questions.description: The social media profile of Maya kings: a picture, a date and lots of bragging.
questions.fun_fact: Calakmul, in Campeche, is the Maya city with the most known stelae: about 120.

questions.question: The tzolkin, the sacred Maya calendar, lasts 260 days, was used for ceremonies and naming babies, and is still used today. How is it made up?
hints: One of the numbers is the base of the Maya number system.
The other is the number of heavens in Maya cosmology.
Each day pairs a number from 1 to 13 with a sign such as Imix or Ik.
questions.description: A calendar that's no help at all for knowing when the quincena gets paid.
questions.fun_fact: 260 days is roughly the length of a pregnancy, and some researchers think that's why the number was chosen.

questions.question: The Great Ball Court at Chichén Itzá is the largest in Mesoamerica. Roughly how long is it?
hints: It's longer than a soccer field.
Its side walls are very tall: the stone rings sit far above a player's head.
It's more than 100 meters long, but less than 200.
questions.description: A field where not even Chicharito could score with his feet.
questions.fun_fact: The court has a famous echo: someone speaking at one end can be heard at the other.

questions.question: The Mesoamerican ballgame was played with rubber balls. Which ancient people has a Nahuatl name meaning “rubber people”?
hints: They lived on the Gulf of Mexico coast, in Veracruz and Tabasco.
They are called the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica.
One of their great cities was La Venta, and they carved jade figures with jaguar features.
questions.description: It was bouncing thousands of years before sneakers were invented.
questions.fun_fact: Mesoamericans mixed latex from the rubber tree with the juice of a vine to make their balls bounce better.

questions.question: The pyramid of the Temple of the Inscriptions in Palenque has as many stepped levels as the Maya underworld had layers. How many is that?
hints: The Maya heavens numbered 13, but the underworld had fewer.
It's an odd number.
It's 3 squared.
questions.description: A pyramid with a secret basement and a staircase straight out of a movie.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spent about four years clearing the hidden staircase that leads to Pakal's tomb, which he found in 1952.

questions.question: In Maya numbers, digits are stacked in levels. If you put a dot on top and the zero symbol below, what number is it?
hints: The bottom level is the ones.
Each level is worth more than the one below, like in our numbers.
The Maya counted in twenties.
questions.description: A number with a ground floor and an upstairs.
questions.fun_fact: Europe didn't use zero until the Middle Ages, centuries after the Maya were already carving it in stone.

questions.question: You're swimming in a cenote in Yucatán. Which people does the word “cenote” come from?
hints: They wrote with glyphs and created a very precise calendar.
The original word is ts'ono'ot.
They are the same people who built Chichén Itzá.
questions.description: You're taking a dip right in the middle of the dictionary.
questions.fun_fact: Almost 800,000 people speak Yucatec Maya today: it's the second most spoken Indigenous language in Mexico, after Nahuatl.

questions.question: Your job sets it up for you, you use it at the ATM and the supermarket, and your pay lands on it every quincena. What is a “tarjeta de nómina”?
hints: It's made of plastic and a bank gives it to you.
With it, you never end up owing the bank anything.
You only spend what's already in your account: it's the opposite of a credit card.
questions.description: Payday comes and the money appears like magic… on a little piece of plastic.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's very common to be paid by the quincena: once in the middle of the month and again at the end.

questions.question: You buy a 6,000-peso TV on a credit card at 12 months interest-free. How much do you pay each month?
hints: Interest-free: you pay exactly the price, just in parts.
Divide the price by the number of months.
It's exactly half of 1,000.
questions.description: Take it home today and suffer just a little each month.
questions.fun_fact: With interest-free months you don't pay extra, but if you miss a payment the bank can still charge you interest.

questions.question: This president promised to defend the peso “like a dog,” and in 1982 the peso was devalued. Who is he?
hints: He governed from 1976 to 1982.
In 1982 he also nationalized the banks.
People nicknamed his houses in Cuajimalpa “la Colina del Perro” (Dog Hill).
questions.description: A promise with lots of barking and very little biting.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that phrase, people nicknamed his houses in Cuajimalpa “la Colina del Perro” (Dog Hill).

questions.question: My boyfriend didn't want to enter the anthem contest, so I locked him in a room until he slid the verses under the door. Who am I?
hints: This story happened in 1853, in Mexico City.
My boyfriend, who later became my husband, was Francisco González Bocanegra.
People called me “Pili,” and I shared a last name with my boyfriend.
questions.description: The most romantic method ever invented for curing a poet's laziness.
questions.fun_fact: Bocanegra won the contest, and the anthem was first performed on September 15, 1854.

questions.question: The flag of Mexico starts with a green stripe. Which of these foods is NOT green?
hints: Three of them could paint the first stripe.
It's not a cactus, and it's not the base of guacamole.
It's red and used to make salsa.
questions.description: A question you read from left to right, just like the flag.
questions.fun_fact: The flag's three colors also show up in guacamole made with tomato and onion.

questions.question: The anthem's chorus says “Mexicanos, al grito de guerra / el acero aprestad y el bridón”. What is that “acero” (steel)?
hints: It's made of metal.
It gets ready because a war cry was heard.
You wear it at your waist, and it has a sharp edge.
questions.description: You may have sung it every Monday since kindergarten, but did you ever stop to think about what it means?
questions.fun_fact: The “bridón” in the same line is a horse, saddled and ready for battle.

questions.question: When the flag passes during a ceremony, which of these groups does NOT give the civil salute with a hand on the chest?
hints: Three of the groups are civilians.
The one you're looking for has its own salute.
Their salute is raising the hand to the forehead.
questions.description: Monday, 8 a.m., sun in your eyes, and everyone standing at attention.
questions.fun_fact: The civil salute is made with the right hand held flat across the chest, over the heart, palm facing down.

questions.question: It has three vertical stripes, green, white and red in that order, just like Mexico's, but no coat of arms. Which flag is it?
hints: It belongs to a European country.
That country is shaped like a boot.
It's the country of pizza and pasta.
questions.description: The European cousin who always shows up to the party in the same outfit.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's flag is longer: it is 4 high by 7 long, while Italy's is 2 by 3.

questions.question: In Mexico it's called “400 metros planos”. Which group of track races does it belong to?
hints: It's a single lap of the track.
Runners go all out and don't ease off to save energy.
It's the longest race in Usain Bolt's group.
questions.description: One full lap of the track with nothing to jump over, but with lungs on fire.
questions.fun_fact: It's the longest distance in track and field where every runner stays in their own lane from start to finish.

questions.question: I was born in San Luis Potosí and play on an indoor court where the ball bounces off the walls. I was world number one in racquetball for many years. Who am I?
hints: My sport isn't in the Olympics, but it is in the Pan American Games.
I've won a huge number of gold medals at the Pan American Games.
My last name starts with the English word “long”.
questions.description: A ball that bounces off the ceiling, the walls and the other player's patience.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the world's great racquetball powers, along with the United States.

questions.question: At London 2012, Aída Román won silver in women's individual archery. Which other Mexican woman won bronze in that event?
hints: She's from Monterrey and was only 18 at London 2012.
Before London 2012 she had already won medals at the Pan American Games.
Her first name begins with María, the Spanish name of the Virgin Mary.
questions.description: Two Mexican women on the same podium: good aim must be catching, like a cold.
questions.fun_fact: They were Mexico's first Olympic medals in archery, and two came on the same day.

questions.question: Complete: Alejandra Orozco is to the platform as Osmar Olvera is to…
hints: Both are Mexican Olympic medal-winning divers.
Osmar dives from lower than Orozco's 10 meters.
At Paris 2024 he won medals in the 3-meter event.
questions.description: A question to show off at the pool, with or without a splash.
questions.fun_fact: Alejandra Orozco was only 15 when she won Olympic silver at London 2012.

questions.question: Guillermo Pérez from Michoacán won taekwondo gold at Beijing 2008. How many gold medals did Mexico win in total at those Games?
hints: It wasn't many.
Guillermo Pérez wasn't Mexico's only champion in Beijing.
It's the same as the number of legs on a chicken.
questions.description: A kick from Uruapan that was heard all the way to China.
questions.fun_fact: Guillermo Pérez is from Uruapan, Michoacán, a place famous for its avocados.

questions.question: These shiny black pieces are made in San Bartolo Coyotepec, Oaxaca. What material are they made of?
hints: They are shaped by hand and then fired.
It's the same material as jarritos and kitchen cooking pots.
It's wet earth that hardens in the kiln.
questions.description: So black and shiny they look like they came from another planet, but they're very down to earth.
questions.fun_fact: The shine was invented by Doña Rosa Real in the mid-20th century: she polished the pieces with a quartz stone before firing them.

questions.question: Next to a drawing of my feet, I wrote in my diary: “Feet, what do I need you for if I have wings to fly?” Who am I?
hints: I was a painter, and I kept my diary until the end of my life.
Shortly before I wrote it, one of my legs had to be amputated.
I lived in the Blue House in Coyoacán with Diego Rivera.
questions.description: A line so famous it now flies on its own across mugs, T-shirts and market tote bags.
questions.fun_fact: Frida wrote that line in 1953, a year before she died, and her full diary wasn't published until 1995.

questions.question: You're looking at a Siqueiros mural painted with pyroxylin, a lacquer used on cars. In which decade did he start using it?
hints: In the 1920s he was still painting in fresco.
He began experimenting with industrial materials outside Mexico.
It was around the time of his experimental workshop in New York.
questions.description: A muralist who walked into an auto shop and came out with a masterpiece.
questions.fun_fact: In his 1936 New York workshop, Siqueiros let the lacquer drip and mix on its own; a young Jackson Pollock took part.

questions.question: In which decade did Orozco paint “Man of Fire” in the dome of the Hospicio Cabañas in Guadalajara?
hints: Orozco was already a famous muralist when he painted it.
He painted it after coming back to Mexico from several years of painting murals in the United States.
Orozco died in 1949, ten years after finishing it.
questions.description: A dome so hot it should come with a fire extinguisher.
questions.fun_fact: The Hospicio Cabañas is a World Heritage Site, and many visitors lie down on special benches to see the dome without hurting their necks.

questions.question: You're at the market and you buy some tunas, green or red. What are they for?
hints: They grow along the edges of the nopal pads.
You have to peel them carefully because of their tiny spines.
They're sweet, juicy and really good when cold.
questions.description: It comes from the nopal and has its own built-in security system.
questions.fun_fact: On the coat of arms of Mexico's flag, the eagle stands on a nopal, the cactus that gives us tunas.

questions.question: Roughly how many kernels does an ear of corn have?
hints: Far more than fit in your two hands.
An ear of corn has about 16 rows of kernels.
Each row has about 50 kernels.
questions.description: Counting them by hand is the perfect punishment for a boring Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: The rows of kernels on an ear of corn are almost always an even number.

questions.question: Fruit cups with chile and lime have a bit of everything. Which of these is NOT a fruit, but a root?
hints: Think about which one grows hidden underground.
It's white inside, crunchy and juicy.
It looks like a giant turnip with brown skin.
questions.description: A cup of fruit with chile and lime is hiding an impostor.
questions.fun_fact: Jícama is a relative of the bean: it's the root of a climbing plant in the legume family.

questions.question: The chile de árbol is thin, red and pointy. In some places it is also called “pico de…” (“… beak”). Which word finishes it?
hints: Think about its shape: skinny, a little curved and with a sharp tip.
It's an animal that flies.
It's very small, it sings and it builds nests in trees.
questions.description: A chile named after a tree with a nickname from the animal kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: It's also called “cola de rata” (“rat's tail”) because it is so long and thin.

questions.question: I'm braided, I was tied to the chin with a strap, and even Queen Hatshepsut wore me. What was I for?
wrong_answers: To cover the face at funerals
hints: Pharaohs usually shaved their faces.
You can see it on many statues and on Tutankhamun's gold mask.
It was a fake beard: a symbol of sacred power.
questions.description: The accessory a pharaoh wore to look wiser, even at 9 years old.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, the beard fell off Tutankhamun's mask and was badly glued back with resin; experts later restored it.

questions.question: Pimienta gorda is grown in Veracruz and Tabasco, smells of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg, and isn't related to black pepper. What is it?
questions.answer: The dried fruit of a tree
wrong_answers: The dried bark of a shrub
The dried root of an herb
The dried flower of a vine
hints: It's used in moles, escabeches and Caribbean cooking.
It's picked green and dried in the sun.
It grows on the branches of a tropical tree, like a berry.
questions.description: They call it “gorda” (chubby), but nobody complains, because it smells delicious.
questions.fun_fact: In English it's called allspice, because its smell seems to mix all the spices in one.

questions.question: Mamey has rough brown skin, creamy orange flesh and a shiny black pit. In Mexico, what is its flesh mostly used for?
questions.answer: For shakes, ice cream and desserts
hints: Its flesh is sweet and soft like butter.
It's almost never cooked: the flesh is used raw and cold.
It gets mixed with milk in the blender.
questions.description: On the outside it looks like a potato; on the inside it looks like a sunset.
questions.fun_fact: The roasted mamey pit, called pixtle, is used to make tejate, a traditional drink from Oaxaca.

questions.question: You're setting up the Day of the Dead ofrenda at home. What goes on it?
questions.answer: Photos, candles, pan de muerto and flowers
wrong_answers: Ornaments, lights and a pine tree
hints: It's for remembering the people who are gone.
It goes up in early November.
Orange cempasúchil blossoms are a must.
questions.description: A buffet for guests who come back from the beyond once a year.
questions.fun_fact: People say the smell of cempasúchil and the light of the candles guide the souls back home.

questions.question: In Mexico, what do you call a whole ear of young corn, boiled or grilled, with mayonnaise, cheese and chili?
hints: It's sold from street carts.
You eat it by biting the kernels straight off the cob.
Cut the kernels off and serve them in a cup, and it becomes esquite.
questions.description: The street-cart treat that leaves your cheeks covered in mayo.
questions.fun_fact: The word “elote” comes from the Nahuatl word “élotl”.

questions.question: Roughly how many years does a blue agave take before its heart, the piña, is ready to harvest for tequila?
hints: It's much longer than corn takes.
A child born when it's planted is already in elementary school when it's harvested.
It's between 5 and 10 years.
questions.description: A bluish plant that keeps all of Jalisco busy.
questions.fun_fact: The agave landscape of Tequila, Jalisco, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.

questions.question: Look at this plant: it decorates homes all over the world in December. Which country does it come from?
hints: It's a warm country, not a snowy one.
There it grows wild and can become a bush several meters tall.
In that country it's called “nochebuena”, after Christmas Eve.
questions.description: It dresses in red for the holidays and makes the Christmas tree jealous.
questions.fun_fact: Its English name, “poinsettia”, comes from Joel Poinsett, a US diplomat who brought it home from Mexico.

questions.question: A stuffed poblano chile, covered in walnut sauce and topped with pomegranate and parsley, is a chile en…
hints: It's a classic dish from Puebla.
People eat it mostly in September.
Its name comes from the tree that gives walnuts, the “nogal”.
questions.description: A chile that arrives at the table stuffed to the brim and dressed for a gala.
questions.fun_fact: Its colors, green, white and red, are those of the Mexican flag, and it's eaten mostly during the September Independence celebrations.

questions.question: The xoconostle is a tuna (prickly pear) from central Mexico. It's rarely eaten fresh and is added to mole de olla. What does it give the broth?
hints: It isn't sweet like other tunas.
Its Nahuatl name has to do with its taste.
It's more like a lime than a prickly pear.
questions.description: The tuna's cousin that would rather be in the kitchen than at the fruit stand.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Nahuatl: “xoco” means sour and “nochtli” means tuna (prickly pear).

questions.question: If you put a bean on wet cotton inside a glass, about how long does it take to grow a tiny root?
hints: It doesn't happen while you're watching.
You can see it within the same week.
You'll see something before the weekend.
questions.description: The most famous school experiment fits inside a glass.
questions.fun_fact: Beans have been grown in Mexico for thousands of years, together with corn and squash.

questions.question: This Mexica goddess “ate the filth” of confessed sins, watched over childbirth and wore cotton spindles in her headdress. What is her name?
hints: She was a goddess from the Huasteca region whom the Mexica adopted.
She was linked to weaving, cleaning and purification.
Her name starts with “Tlazol-,” which in Nahuatl has to do with filth.
questions.description: A goddess who never turned up her nose at cleaning what nobody else wanted to touch.
questions.fun_fact: People could confess a serious wrongdoing to Tlazolteotl only once in their life to be made clean.

questions.question: Which of these names is NOT used for the two volcanoes in the legend of the warrior and the princess?
hints: Three of these are nicknames that people use fondly.
The smoking volcano is called by a nickname for a man named Gregorio.
The answer is another volcano, in Tlaxcala.
questions.description: Two neighbors from Puebla who haven't gotten off the couch in centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Popocatépetl is called “Don Goyo” because nearby villages honor it on Saint Gregory's Day, March 12.

questions.question: In a Mexica legend, Quetzalcóatl turned into this little animal to bring something to people. What did he go looking for?
hints: He found it hidden inside a mountain.
The gods wanted it so the new humans would have something to eat.
Tortillas are made from it.
questions.description: History's first delivery guy was also tiny and very reliable.
questions.fun_fact: In the myth, a red ant showed Quetzalcóatl where the corn was hidden: inside Tonacatépetl, the “mountain of sustenance.”

questions.question: I'm a giant from the Popol Vuh who lifts mountains. I killed 400 boys, and twins tricked me with a fake crab to crush me under a hill. Who am I?
hints: My brother didn't lift mountains; he knocked them down with earthquakes.
My dad was a show-off bird who claimed to be the Sun.
My name starts with Z.
questions.description: A big guy who could carry hills but couldn't resist some good seafood.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Popol Vuh, the 400 boys Zipacná killed rose into the sky and became the Pleiades.

questions.question: According to the Mexica, Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed and defeated his 400 brothers, the Centzon Huitznáhuac, on a hill. Which one?
hints: His mother, Coatlicue, lived there.
The brothers were led by Coyolxauhqui.
Its name means “serpent hill.”
questions.description: Four hundred brothers against one: the worst family reunion in history.
questions.fun_fact: The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan stood for that hill, which is why the Coyolxauhqui stone lay at the foot of its stairs.

questions.question: Because of the carving on his tomb lid, some people claim the Maya king Pakal was… what?
hints: It's a very popular theory online, though archaeologists reject it.
They say he's sitting at the controls of a machine.
According to them, he traveled through space.
questions.description: A Maya king who died centuries ago and is still trending on weird-theory forums.
questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists say the carving shows Pakal entering the underworld at the foot of the ceiba, the sacred Maya tree.

questions.question: At the center of this stone is Nahui Ollin, the sun we live in according to the Mexica. Which number sun is it?
hints: The earlier suns all ended in destruction.
It's an odd number.
Around the center are four panels, one for each sun that has already passed.
questions.description: Careful: according to the Mexica, this world is a version that has already been updated several times.
questions.fun_fact: “Ollin” means movement, and it was said that this sun would end with great earthquakes.

questions.question: It's said that when Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519, Moctezuma thought he was a god who had promised to return from the east. Which god?
hints: This god had left Tollan by sea.
He was shown with a beard, like the Spaniards.
He's the Feathered Serpent.
questions.description: A god who said “ahorita vengo” and everyone took him at his word.
questions.fun_fact: Many historians think this story was told and spread only after the Conquest.

questions.question: Listen: a Sinaloan banda is never without this instrument. Which one is it?
hints: It's a percussion instrument.
It's shaped like a shiny golden disc.
You play them by crashing two together.
questions.description: The perfect instrument for waking up the whole neighborhood in one second.
questions.fun_fact: In a Sinaloan banda, the cymbal player crashes them right on the beats of the tambora, as if they were one instrument.

review.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The snare drum (tarola) is a standard part of the banda sinaloense, so it is arguably also a correct answer. The 'never without' claim fits the tambora, with cymbals mounted on it, better than the cymbals alone. Cymbals are usually mounted on the tambora and are not always a separate instrument.

questions.question: In the corrido “Contrabando y traición,” Camelia la Texana and Emilio Varela cross the border by car. Which Mexican city were they coming from?
hints: Los Tigres del Norte made the song famous.
It is a border city in Baja California.
It sits right next to San Ysidro, California.
questions.description: A road trip with more drama than a prime-time telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Camelia la Texana became so famous that she starred in movies and even a TV series.

questions.question: The Colossi of Memnon are two giant statues of a pharaoh in Egypt. About how old are they?
hints: They date from the time of the pharaohs.
Tutankhamun lived at roughly the same time.
They are older than the Roman Empire, but not from the Stone Age.
questions.description: Two giants sitting and waiting for a bus that never comes.
questions.fun_fact: After an earthquake, one of the statues “sang” at sunrise, and travelers in ancient times came to hear it.

questions.question: You hear me all the time in corridos, and I'm how you call a buddy. I come from what a baptized baby's parents and godfather call each other. What word am I?
hints: I'm the short piece of a longer word.
That longer word has to do with a baptism.
The woman in that relationship is called “comadre”.
questions.description: A word you hear more at a carne asada than at an office meeting.
questions.fun_fact: “Cuate” comes from the Nahuatl word “cóatl”, which means both snake and twin.

questions.question: In the ’90s, Banda Machos got half of Mexico dancing to “La culebra” and “Al gato y al ratón.” What dance became a craze with their music?
hints: People danced it in cowboy boots and hats.
Couples did acrobatic spins and jumps.
The woman leaned so far back she looked like she might break (“quebrarse”).
questions.description: The ’90s: tight jeans, a cowboy hat and energy for the whole night.
questions.fun_fact: Banda Machos comes from Jalisco and earned the nickname “La Reina de las Bandas” (The Queen of the Bands).

questions.question: Many norteño groups today play with a drum kit. Which of these is NOT part of a drum kit?
hints: Three of them are hit with sticks or a pedal.
The odd one out has keys and buttons.
It opens and closes like a bellows.
questions.description: The only place where hitting things makes you an artist.

questions.question: Import substitution lasted from the 1940s until the 1982 crisis. Which model then opened Mexico up to foreign trade?
hints: Under it, many state-owned companies were sold off.
Mexico joined GATT in 1986 and later signed NAFTA.
Its name sounds like a renewed liberalism.
questions.description: When the country decided homemade is always better… until it changed its mind.
questions.fun_fact: During stabilizing development, the Mexican economy grew more than 6% a year.

questions.question: On October 17, 1953, under Adolfo Ruiz Cortines, Mexican women finally won suffrage nationwide. What is “suffrage”?
hints: It's a right you use every few years.

You use it with a ballot at a polling station.

questions.question: It's sold at the corner store, kept in the freezer, and in Mexico it's called a “boli.” What is it?
questions.answer: A flavored ice in a little bag
wrong_answers: An ice pop on a stick
hints: It's cold and sweet.
It has no stick and no cone.
It comes in a long, thin bag.
questions.description: The frozen treasure that costs less than a bus ride.
questions.fun_fact: In some parts of Mexico, bolis are called “congeladas” or “hielitos.”

questions.question: I'm a rolled, fried tortilla, longer than a taco dorado, served with crema, lettuce and cheese. What am I?
hints: I'm very crunchy.
I'm filled with chicken or potato.
My name is Spanish for a wind instrument.
questions.description: A snack that comes by the order, neatly lined up in a row.
questions.fun_fact: Flautas and taquitos dorados are so alike that in many parts of Mexico both names mean the same thing.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this white sauce gets spread on elotes. What ingredient is it made from, whisked with oil?
hints: It comes from a farm animal.
At the market you buy it by the dozen.
A hen lays it.
questions.description: The white sauce that makes the cheese stick to your elote.
questions.fun_fact: To make homemade mayonnaise, all you need is egg yolk, oil, a little lime juice or vinegar, and salt.

questions.question: They come in a bag, crunch when you bite them, and in Mexico many people call them “sabritas.” What are the classic ones made of?
hints: It's a vegetable.
It grows underground.
It's also boiled and mashed as a side dish.
questions.description: The bag that makes noise before you even open it.
questions.fun_fact: Sabritas started in Mexico City in the 1940s and is part of PepsiCo today.

questions.question: In the concheros dances, what is the atecocolli used for?
hints: It comes from the sea.
It's a large shell.
It sounds loud and deep, like a trumpet.
questions.description: An object with a Nahuatl name that's harder to pronounce than to use.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica also blew conch shells from the tops of temples to mark the hours of their ceremonies.

questions.question: In the movie “Cleopatra” (1963), Elizabeth Taylor set a costume record. How many times did she change outfits?
hints: It was a Guinness World Record for an actress in a single film.
It's more outfits than you'd wear in a normal week.
It's more than 50 but less than 100.
questions.description: A queen of Egypt with more outfits in her closet than years on the throne.
questions.fun_fact: “Cleopatra” cost so much that it nearly bankrupted the studio that made it.

questions.question: I was born in the 1960s with novels by José Agustín and Gustavo Sainz, full of rock music and teen slang. What movement am I?
hints: My readers were mostly young people in Mexico City.
“De perfil” and “Gazapo” are among my most famous works.
My name comes from the greeting “¿Qué…?” that young people used with each other.
questions.description: Literature that sounded like an electric guitar and kids chatting on the street corner.
questions.fun_fact: José Agustín published “La tumba” at age 20, and it kicked off this youth literature.

questions.question: Which of these early 20th-century literary avant-garde movements was NOT born in Europe?
hints: Its poets loved machines, noise and the modern city.
Its first manifesto appeared in 1921 as a sheet posted on the city’s walls.
It was founded by the poet Manuel Maples Arce in Mexico City.
questions.description: Artists who wanted to break everything, starting with the rules of poetry.
questions.fun_fact: The Stridentists turned Xalapa, Veracruz, into their “Estridentópolis” with the support of Governor Heriberto Jara.

questions.question: Martín Luis Guzmán is to “The Shadow of the Strongman” as Vicente Leñero is to…
hints: It is a crime novel that won the Biblioteca Breve Prize in 1963.
The story takes place in a building under construction.
Its characters work with bricks and mortar.
questions.description: Two Mexican novelists, one comparison, zero spoilers.
questions.fun_fact: Leñero also wrote the screenplay for “The Crime of Padre Amaro” and worked as a journalist at Proceso magazine.

questions.question: After his surprise win over Anthony Joshua in New York, Andy Ruiz Jr. agreed to a rematch. In which country was it held?
hints: It was in an outdoor ring built just for that night.
The fight was nicknamed “Clash on the Dunes.”
It is the country where Mecca is.
questions.description: After the upset of the century, nobody wanted to miss the sequel, popcorn in hand.
questions.fun_fact: In the rematch, held in Diriyah, Joshua won on points and took back the belts Ruiz had taken from him.

questions.question: In 1938, Nestlé launched a coffee in Switzerland that you make without a coffee maker or a pot. What kind of coffee is it?
hints: In many offices there's a jar of it next to the big water jug.
In Mexico many people call it “Nescafé” even when it's another brand.
Just one teaspoon and hot water, and it's ready.
questions.description: What your parents need before they can hold a conversation in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Nescafé was created because Brazil's government asked Nestlé for a way to use up its huge piles of leftover coffee.

questions.question: I come sliced in a plastic bag, and you make sandwiches with me. Which bread am I?
hints: You can put me in the toaster.
My slices are almost square.
My Spanish name comes from the rectangular, box-like pan I'm baked in.
questions.description: The best friend of ham, cheese and mayonnaise.
questions.fun_fact: Bimbo opened in Mexico City in 1945, and its white bread was one of its first products.

questions.question: Complete it: Shakespeare is to “Hamlet” as Chespirito is to…
hints: Look for a show that Chespirito wrote and starred in.
He's a very clumsy superhero.
He has little antennae and a bump on his head.
questions.description: Two writing geniuses: one with a goose-feather pen, the other with a huge sense of humor.
questions.fun_fact: “Chespirito” is a Spanish nickname meaning “little Shakespeare”: he got it for his writing talent and because he was short.

questions.question: You're in the park on a hot day and hear cicadas singing. Which of these is NOT true about them?
questions.answer: They sing by rubbing their legs

They leave empty skins on trees
hints: Three of these statements are true.

questions.description: The loudest summer concert around, and nobody bought a ticket.
questions.fun_fact: Some North American cicadas spend 17 years underground before they come out to sing.

previous.feedback: source: Hint 3 says crickets rub their legs to sing, which is wrong. Crickets rub their wings together; grasshoppers (chapulines) rub their hind legs against their wings. The Spanish source has the same error, and the translator and rater both flagged it. The source needs a corrected hint 3, for example: “Grasshoppers make their sound by rubbing their back legs against their wings.” Then the translation can be redone from it.

questions.question: Where does the “Ocho” (eight) in the name “El Chavo del Ocho” come from?
wrong_answers: The number painted on his barrel
hints: It has to do with how people watched the show in the 1970s.

questions.description: An eight that worked harder than the whole cast put together.

questions.question: Besides the vecindad, where else do El Chavo, Quico, Ñoño and la Popis almost always get together?
hints: Ñoño is almost always the one who knows all the answers.

questions.description: A gang of kids who get into trouble both inside and outside the vecindad.
questions.fun_fact: Edgar Vivar, who played Ñoño, was an adult dressed up as a kid, just like the actors who played El Chavo and Quico.

questions.question: In which decade were the famous episodes filmed where El Chavo's neighbors go on vacation to Acapulco?

Your grandparents or parents may have watched them on TV as kids when they first aired.

questions.description: The whole vecindad went to the beach, and not even Señor Barriga came to collect the rent.

previous.feedback: Source: the description is false, and it is the same in the source. It says Señor Barriga didn't come to collect the rent, but in the Acapulco episodes he does come for it, finds the vecindad empty and takes El Chavo to Acapulco himself. Fix the source description, for example: “The whole vecindad went to the beach, and Señor Barriga ended up there too.” Then translate it again. Fact check: wrong. Answer (1970s) is right (aired May–June 1977), and the fun fact is right. But the description is false: Señor Barriga does come to collect rent. He finds the vecindad empty and takes El Chavo to his favorite hotel in Acapulco, so he is in the episodes.

questions.question: My little vinyl antennae sense when the enemy is near, and I wear a heart with two letters on my chest. Who am I?
hints: I was played by Roberto Gómez Bolaños, “Chespirito.”
I fight with my chipote chillón, a squeaky hammer.
My suit is red, and people call me when they ask “¿Y ahora quién podrá defenderme?”
questions.description: Homemade costumes and cardboard special effects: Chespirito’s TV in all its glory.
questions.fun_fact: The letters “CH” on his chest stand for “Chapulín,” and the character first appeared on TV in 1970.

questions.question: On the night of January 5, many children leave grass and water next to their shoes for the Three Kings' most famous animal. Which one is it?
hints: It comes across the desert.
It can go many days without drinking water.
People call it “the ship of the desert”.
questions.description: Room service for guests arriving from very, very far away.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, people say the Three Kings arrive on three different animals: a horse, a camel and an elephant.

questions.question: Mazamitla, a Pueblo Mágico in Jalisco, has pine forests, wooden cabins and mountain cold. What is its nickname: “the ___ of Mexico”?
hints: The nickname compares the town to a European country.
That country is famous for its cheese and chocolate.
It's the country of watches, the Alps and Heidi.
questions.description: Fog, a fireplace and wood-fired bread: here a jacket is not optional.
questions.fun_fact: The name Mazamitla comes from Nahuatl and means “place where arrows are made to hunt deer”.

questions.question: This mosaic of colored stones covers all four walls of a famous building. Where is it?

At the National Museum of Anthropology
hints: The mosaic tells the story of Mexico, from pre-Hispanic times to modern science.
Juan O'Gorman made the mosaic in the 1950s.
It's in the south of Mexico City, next to the stadium where the Pumas play.
questions.description: A building that decided to wear its history homework as an outfit.
questions.fun_fact: The Central Library mosaic is made of natural colored stones brought from different parts of Mexico.

questions.question: Every winter, millions of monarch butterflies fly from Canada to the forests of Michoacán. About how many kilometers do they fly?
hints: They cross almost the whole United States.
It's more than crossing Mexico from end to end.
It's a few thousand kilometers, not tens of thousands.
questions.description: Travelers with no suitcase, no map and no GPS, and yet they never get lost.
questions.fun_fact: No single butterfly makes the whole round trip: the ones that reach Mexico each fall are the great-grandchildren or great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left in spring.

questions.question: I'm a comic: my hero is a mischievous boy who goes to school with Ernestillo, Carlangas and Ricardo, and in 2005 I was on postage stamps. What am I?
hints: I was born in the 1940s in a comic magazine.

questions.description: A comic your grandma secretly read under her school desk.

questions.question: What was the name of Yolanda Vargas Dulché's comic magazine where “Yesenia,” “Rarotonga” and “María Isabel” appeared?
hints: It came out every week at newsstands, and its readers were mostly women.

questions.description: A magazine people read at the beauty salon while their hair dye set.
questions.fun_fact: “Yesenia” and “María Isabel,” two of its stories, were turned into telenovelas and movies.

questions.question: In what year did “La Garrapata”, the political humor magazine by Rius, Naranjo and other cartoonists, subtitled “el azote de los bueyes”, first appear?

questions.question: The Great Migration of wildebeest makes a full loop every year. How many countries does it pass through?

questions.question: This colorful flower embroidery comes from Zinacantán, in the Chiapas Highlands. Which Indigenous people embroiders it?

San Juan Chamula, famous for its church, is also one of their towns.
Their name means “bat people.”

questions.question: It has yellow flowers, gets soaked in alcohol and is sold as an ointment in any pharmacy. What do you use árnica for?

hints: It doesn't only happen to pregnant women: it can happen to you too.

questions.question: I directed “El gendarme desconocido” in 1941, with Cantinflas as agent 777, and then almost all his films for four decades. Who am I?
hints: I'm not an actor: I worked behind the camera.

questions.question: André-Pierre Gignac, the French striker and Tigres idol: what number does he wear on his back?

questions.question: Who is the all-time top scorer of Mexico's national team?
hints: He took the record from Jared Borgetti.

questions.question: In Liga MX, what is the final stage called, with home-and-away matches, that decides the champion?

questions.question: He played for Toros Neza, and as a coach he won titles with Xolos, América and Monterrey. What country is “Turco” Mohamed from?

questions.question: In the Liga MX rules on foreign players, what does the acronym NFM stand for?

questions.question: Outside the arenas, they sell lucha libre masks for kids. What are they almost always made of?

It is reddish and turns green over time, like the Statue of Liberty.
questions.description: An artist who worked with acid without being a chemist.
questions.fun_fact: In etching, the acid “bites” the metal only where the artist scratched away the varnish with a needle.

questions.question: He painted one of the first frescoes of Mexican muralism at San Ildefonso, then went to teach art in Hawaii. Who is he?
hints: He came to Mexico from Europe.
He was born in Paris in 1898.
His fresco shows “The Massacre in the Templo Mayor.”
questions.description: At San Ildefonso, not every paintbrush carried a Mexican passport.
questions.fun_fact: Jean Charlot was one of the first to make José Guadalupe Posada's prints known to the world.

questions.question: This Mixtec codex, now kept in the British Museum, tells the life of a great warrior lord. Who is he?
hints: He ruled in the Mixteca, in what is now Oaxaca.
His name comes from the calendar day he was born on.
His name combines a number, an animal with antlers and a big cat's claw.
questions.description: A comic book from centuries ago, with no speech bubbles but plenty of action.
questions.fun_fact: The codex is read in a zigzag, following red lines that guide the reader from one side of the page to the other.

questions.question: Chaya is a Yucatán shrub the Maya already grew; its leaves are used in tamales and with eggs. Why should you cook them before eating?
questions.answer: Because raw they can be toxic
wrong_answers: Because raw they stain your mouth purple
Because raw they taste like soap
Because raw they make you very sleepy
hints: Something similar happens with some raw beans.
When it boils, a substance escapes with the steam.
Raw, it contains substances that can harm you.
questions.description: The spinach of the Maya, and Popeye has nothing on it.
questions.fun_fact: Chaya is a relative of cassava, which also has harmful substances that are removed by cooking.

questions.question: This Mexica codex tells the journey from Aztlán, with footprints marking the way. What is it called?
hints: It is a long strip of amate bark paper that folds like an accordion.
It carries the surname of an 18th-century Italian collector.
It is also known as the Tira de la Peregrinación (Strip of the Pilgrimage).
questions.description: The very first Google Maps, with little footprints instead of arrows.
questions.fun_fact: The Codex Boturini is more than 5 m (16 ft) long and is kept at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City.

questions.question: In the Mexica myth of the suns, the people of the first sun ate acorns and were finally eaten by jaguars. Who were they?
hints: In each sun, people were transformed or destroyed in a different way.
Beings like these also show up in European tales, sometimes with just one eye.
They were called quinametzin, and they were the same kind of being as Goliath.
questions.description: The world had a few test versions before the final release came out.
questions.fun_fact: People used to say that the huge bones of prehistoric animals found in Mexico were the remains of those giants.

questions.question: In a Mexica legend, the warrior Huitzilin returns as a bird to the flower his beloved Xóchitl became. What does “huitzilin” mean?
hints: It is also the first part of the name of the god Huitzilopochtli.
It can hover in place in the air by beating its wings incredibly fast.
It is the smallest bird in Mexico and drinks nectar from flowers.
questions.description: A pre-Hispanic romance with a garden ending.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, when the bird touched the yellow flower, it opened into the petals of the cempasúchil (Mexican marigold).

questions.question: Since the 1950s, the Ballet Folklórico de México has danced sones and jarabes from all over the country at Bellas Artes. Who founded it?
hints: She was a dancer and choreographer.
She started the company with just a handful of dancers.
Her last name is one of the most common in Mexico.
questions.description: Skirts that spin like pinwheels and shoes that sound like drums.
questions.fun_fact: The Ballet Folklórico de México started in 1952 with only eight dancers.

questions.question: With “Inténtalo,” the Monterrey trio 3BallMTY popularized a genre famous for its pointy boots. Besides electronic music, what does it mix?
hints: One ingredient is a rhythm Mexico adopted as its own.
The other recalls drums and flutes from before the Spanish Conquest.
The genre is called tribal guarachero.
questions.description: A dance floor where the boots were longer than the song.
questions.fun_fact: 3BallMTY won the Latin Grammy for Best New Artist in 2012.
