questions.question: In Cuchillo Parado, Chihuahua, Toribio Ortega took up arms before the date Madero had set. On what day?
hints: Madero had called for the uprising to begin one November day at six in the evening.
Ortega jumped the gun by less than a week.
It was six days before Revolution Day.
questions.description: Some people show up early to the party, and some show up before the invitations go out.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that early uprising, Cuchillo Parado calls itself “the cradle of the Revolution.”

questions.question: The Winchester 30-30 carbine was one of the revolutionaries' favorites. Which country did it come from?
hints: Its name comes from the surname of the owner of the company that made it.
The same carbine shows up in lots of cowboy movies.
It came from the neighbor to the north.
questions.description: The corridos sing about it so fondly it sounds like part of the family.
questions.fun_fact: The corrido “Carabina 30-30” made this rifle so famous that its name lives on in Mexican folk music.

questions.question: Mariano Azuela first published his novel “Los de abajo” in installments in a newspaper in El Paso, Texas. In what year?
hints: Azuela served as a doctor with the revolutionary troops.
He wrote it while the Revolution was still going on.
It was the same year as the battles of Celaya.
questions.description: A novel written with the dust of the road still on its shoes.
questions.fun_fact: At first almost nobody read “Los de abajo”. It only became famous in 1925, ten years later.

questions.question: After the oil expropriation of 1938, Mexico created a government company to run its oil. What is it called?
hints: Its name is a short form.
For many years it was the only company selling gasoline in the country.
Its name joins “Petróleos” and “Mexicanos”.
questions.description: One March 18, the black gold changed owners, and someone had to take care of the inheritance.
questions.fun_fact: After March 18, 1938, thousands of people donated jewelry, chickens and even wedding rings to help pay for the expropriation.

questions.question: About how long is an adult Egyptian cobra?
hints: It's much longer than a pencil or a ruler.
But it's not as gigantic as an anaconda.
Stretched out, it would be as long as a tall person (about 6 ft).
questions.description: The snake that pharaohs wore as decoration on their foreheads.
questions.fun_fact: The cobra on the pharaohs' headdress is called the “uraeus,” and it stood for royal protection.

questions.question: In 1920, the Plan of Agua Prieta refused to recognize a president of Mexico. Which one?
hints: The plan was launched by men from Sonora who had once been his allies.
He was the “First Chief” of the Constitutionalist Army.
The Constitution of 1917 was passed while he was in power.
questions.description: A president whose own friends showed him the door.
questions.fun_fact: After the Plan of Agua Prieta, Carranza fled the capital by train, heading for Veracruz.

questions.question: Like the tortoise in the fable, this saying favors going slow and steady over rushing ahead. Which saying is it?
questions.answer: Más vale paso que dure y no trote que canse
wrong_answers: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda
A caballo regalado no se le mira el colmillo
hints: It fits long tasks, like studying for a test or going on a long hike.
It warns you not to use up all your energy at the start.
It names two of a horse's gaits: a slow one and a faster one.
questions.description: A saying that crosses the finish line without breaking a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: Horses have several gaits, or ways of moving: the walk, the trot and the gallop are the best known.

questions.question: You arrive at the party and greet everyone. Which of these Mexican phrases does NOT work as a greeting?
hints: Three of them are ways to start chatting with someone who just arrived.
The odd one out is said when something surprises you or you can't believe it.
It's what you'd reply if someone told you a dog learned to drive.
questions.description: Four phrases walk into the vecindad, but one didn't come to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: “¿A poco?” shows surprise or doubt, a bit like saying “Really?”.

questions.question: In Mexico, “hacer un bisne” means making a little deal to earn some money. Which language does the word “bisne” come from?
hints: Many words used every day in Mexico come from this language.
The same language gave Mexican Spanish words like “lonche” and “troca”.
It's the language spoken in Mexico's neighbor to the north.
questions.description: A word that arrived without a passport and opened its own little stand.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican Spanish is full of words adapted from English, like “bisne”, “checar” (from “check”) or “parquear” (from “to park”).

previous.feedback: The translation glosses “bisne” as “a little business deal”, so the English word “business” sits right next to “bisne” in the question and gives the answer away. The source's “negocito” gave nothing away. Gloss it without the word “business”, for example “making a little deal on the side” or “a small money-making deal”.

questions.question: If something in Mexico is “chiquitito”, what is it like?
hints: It's a word with a double diminutive ending, the kind said with affection.
It comes from the word “chico”.
An ant is like this.
questions.description: A word Mexican grandmas say with tons of love.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, diminutives can pile up: “chico”, “chiquito”, “chiquitito” and even “chiquititito”.

questions.question: In Mexico, who gets called “regio”?
hints: It comes from a longer word for the people of a city.
It's a northern city, famous for carne asada and its mountains.
Its symbol is the Cerro de la Silla.
questions.description: A short nickname for people who never stop bragging about their hometown.
questions.fun_fact: “Regio” comes from “regiomontano”, which sounds like Latin for “king's mountain”, just like Monterrey.

questions.question: In a very famous TV vecindad (a shared housing courtyard), which character always dreamed of a ham torta?
hints: The show was created by Chespirito and has aired all over Latin America since the 1970s.
He always said “fue sin querer queriendo” (“I didn't mean to, but I did”).
He used to hide inside a barrel.
questions.description: There's hungry, and then there's vecindad hungry.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico a torta is a stuffed sandwich roll, but in many other Spanish-speaking countries “torta” means a cake.

questions.question: “Amor real”, starring Adela Noriega and Fernando Colunga, is a period telenovela. In which century is it set?
hints: Mexico was already an independent country.
It takes place a few decades after Independence.
It is the same century as Benito Juárez.
questions.description: A love story of long dresses, horse-drawn carriages and not a single cell phone.
questions.fun_fact: In “Amor real”, Adela Noriega plays Matilde Peñalver y Beristáin, a young woman from an aristocratic family.

questions.question: It plays polkas, redovas and corridos, and it was born in northern Mexico. What is a “conjunto norteño”?
questions.answer: A band with accordion and bajo sexto
wrong_answers: A band with trumpets, violins and guitarrón
A band with tuba, clarinets and tambora
A guitar trio with a requinto
hints: Its main instrument arrived in northern Mexico with European immigrants.
Los Tigres del Norte and Ramón Ayala are famous examples.
Its star instrument has bellows and buttons.
questions.description: The official soundtrack of any self-respecting carne asada in Monterrey.
questions.fun_fact: The accordion reached northern Mexico in the 19th century with German and Czech immigrants, which is why so many polkas are danced there.

questions.question: It's reddish, it comes out of a hippo's skin, and it isn't blood. Which human product does it act like?
hints: Hippos spend many hours under the African sun.
Their skin is delicate and cracks easily.
You'd put it on at the beach so you don't get burned.
questions.description: The hippo has its own beauty line, and it refuses to sell it.
questions.fun_fact: This “red sweat” also helps keep the hippo's wounds from getting infected.

questions.question: After the Revolution, José Vasconcelos had Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros paint history on the walls of public buildings. Mainly for whom?
hints: The murals were painted in schools, markets and palaces, where anyone could see them.
In those years, most Mexicans had never gone to school.
You can understand a mural just by looking at it, without any words.
questions.description: When the notebook gets too small, history class goes up on the wall.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Rivera's mural on the staircase of the Palacio Nacional has hundreds of figures and took him several years to finish.

questions.question: Álvaro Obregón grew chickpeas, never lost a battle and was president from 1920 to 1924. Which state was he from?
hints: It is in the northwest of the country, a state with a lot of desert.
His state borders Arizona, in the United States.
A city in his home state carries his last name: Ciudad Obregón.
questions.description: Before he commanded armies, this general was in charge of sacks of chickpeas.
questions.fun_fact: Obregón's memory was said to be so good that he could remember a whole deck of cards after seeing it just once.

questions.question: Leonor Villegas de Magnón founded it in Laredo in 1913, and its nurses cared for wounded soldiers on Carranza's side. What was it called?
hints: Its name sounds like a much more famous international organization.
It cared for Constitutionalist soldiers on the border.
Its color is the same as the flag you wave to ask for peace.
questions.description: When there's no hospital nearby, someone has to invent one out of bandages and courage.
questions.fun_fact: Leonor Villegas de Magnón wrote a memoir, “The Rebel,” which came out decades after her death.

questions.question: Emiliano Zapata was a farmer with a huge mustache who fought with his army of the south. What did he want to give back to the farmers?
hints: The farmers lived by growing corn and beans.
Big hacienda owners had taken what once belonged to the villages.
He asked for it in the Plan de Ayala: the haciendas had to return the fields where the villages grew their crops.
questions.description: A mustache so big it even had its own army.
questions.fun_fact: Even as a young man, Zapata was famous as a great rider who knew a lot about horses.

questions.question: You're in a theater in Querétaro, listening to deputy Francisco J. Múgica argue for secular education for everyone. What years are these?
hints: A Constitutional Congress met in that theater.
Venustiano Carranza was the leader of the country.
The Constitution written there is still in force in Mexico.
questions.description: A trip back in time to a theater where the show ran for weeks and the script was a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, Múgica helped Lázaro Cárdenas write the speech announcing the oil expropriation.

questions.question: What did NOT travel on the trains of the División del Norte?
hints: A whole army moved on those trains, with everything it needed.
People even rode on the roofs of the cars.
That armored machine with caterpillar tracks first appeared in Europe, in World War I.
questions.description: The most crowded train in the world was not the subway at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: Some of Villa's trains had hospital cars with doctors to care for the wounded.

questions.question: The “Apostle of Democracy” came from a rich landowning family, studied in France and wrote “La sucesión presidencial en 1910”. Which state was he from?
hints: It is a state in the north of the country.
He was born in Parras, a place famous for its vineyards.
Its capital is Saltillo.
questions.description: An apostle without a long beard, but with a book that made a president shake.
questions.fun_fact: Madero practiced spiritism and said the spirits encouraged him to go into politics.

questions.question: Who directed “¡Vámonos con Pancho Villa!” (Let's Go with Pancho Villa!), a classic of 1930s Mexican cinema?
hints: The same director made “El compadre Mendoza.”
He also directed “Allá en el Rancho Grande,” which paved the way for the comedia ranchera.
His surname is the Spanish word for the fountains in a town square.
questions.description: A movie so expensive it nearly bankrupted the people who made it.
questions.fun_fact: The film cost so much that it nearly ruined the studio, and for years it was seen as a box-office flop.

questions.question: Pancho Villa was called “el Centauro del Norte” (the Centaur of the North), after a creature that is half man, half horse. Which mythology does it come from?
hints: These myths are thousands of years old and were told around the Mediterranean Sea.
Creatures like this appear in Disney's “Hercules.”
It comes from the country of the first Olympic Games.
questions.description: There are good riders, great riders, and riders where you can't tell where the horse ends.
questions.fun_fact: Villa was born in Durango, and his real name was José Doroteo Arango Arámbula.

questions.question: I was born in 1907, but said 1910 so I'd be a daughter of the Revolution. I married Diego Rivera and painted a lot from my bed. Who am I?
hints: I'm a Mexican painter and lived in Coyoacán.
My house is blue and is now a museum.
I loved dressing like a Tehuana and painting myself.
questions.description: Some people take years off their age; others swap them to match history.
questions.fun_fact: Frida could paint lying down thanks to a mirror fixed to the canopy above her bed.

questions.question: Which animals can pull in their claws when they walk, so their footprints almost never show claw marks?
hints: Tucked away, the claws don't wear down on the ground and stay sharp.
They hunt by creeping up quietly and then pouncing on their prey.
They belong to the same family as the lion and the leopard.
questions.description: Claws that fold away by themselves, like a pocketknife.
questions.fun_fact: The cheetah is the exception: it can't fully pull in its claws, and it uses them like cleats when it runs.

questions.question: It’s the night of September 15 and you’re in the plaza. At the end of the Grito, how many times is “¡Viva México!” shouted?
hints: Before that, people shout “¡Viva!” for the heroes of Independence.
At the end the phrase is repeated several times in a row, louder each time.
It’s as many times as there are colors in the flag.
questions.description: One night a year the whole country practices shouting at the same time, and somehow nobody loses their voice before midnight.
questions.fun_fact: The Grito remembers the early morning of September 16, 1810, when Miguel Hidalgo called on the people of Dolores to rise up.

questions.question: Someone shows up super dressed up, and people tell them: «Aunque la mona se vista de seda…». How does it end?
hints: The saying means clothes don't change who you are.
People say it when someone tries to look like something they're not.
It ends by saying the monkey doesn't change: she stays just as she is.
questions.description: A saying with more style than a fashion show in the middle of the jungle.
questions.fun_fact: Silk is made by silkworms, which spin their cocoons from a single thread that can be hundreds of meters long.

questions.question: The saying goes: “Amigo en la adversidad, amigo de verdad.” What is “adversidad”?
hints: It's in the same word family as “adverso”.
The saying is about the moment you find out who your real friends are.
It's when things go badly.
questions.description: Grandmas have a saying for everything, and this one is about friends.
questions.fun_fact: “Adversidad” comes from the Latin “adversus”, meaning “turned against”.

questions.question: You say it to someone distracted so they wake up and try harder, and it comes from what a TV remote needs to work. What Mexican expression is it?
hints: You hear it a lot at school before a test.
Toys and flashlights need them too.
Without them, the remote won't turn on the TV.
questions.description: A phrase that works better than coffee, and you don't even have to plug it in.
questions.fun_fact: The Italian Alessandro Volta invented the first electric battery around 1800, and the word “volt” comes from his name.

questions.question: It has a shell and four legs, can live over 100 years, and a very slow person is called “slower than” it. What animal is it?
hints: It's a reptile.
Some kinds live in the sea and others on land.
In the fable, it beats the hare in a race.
questions.description: For this animal, getting there matters more than getting there fast.
questions.fun_fact: Some giant tortoises have lived more than 150 years.

questions.question: In Mexico you say it about a party, a movie or some tacos, and it has nothing to do with hair. What does «estar de pelos» mean?
hints: It's a compliment.
You say it when you loved something.
It's like saying something is «padrísimo».
questions.description: A phrase with plenty of hair and zero haircuts.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican Spanish has lots of ways to say something is great: «está padre», «está chido» or «está de pelos».

questions.question: At school, November 20 is to the Revolution parade as March 21 is to which parade?
hints: On that day, kindergarten kids dress up in costumes.
Around that date a new season begins.
Here come the flowers and the butterflies.
questions.description: Parents filming on their phones, and not a single kid marching in step.
questions.fun_fact: March 21 is also the birthday of Benito Juárez, who was born in 1806 in Oaxaca.

questions.question: In Mexico, if you go to a CBTIS after secundaria, what kind of school are you in?
hints: It belongs to the SEP, and there are hundreds across the country.
The students there are about 15 to 18 years old.
The T in its initials stands for “Tecnológico”.
questions.description: You survived secundaria and the entrance exam; now it's time for a brand-new uniform.
questions.fun_fact: CBTIS stands for Centro de Bachillerato Tecnológico Industrial y de Servicios, and many of its students also graduate as technicians.

questions.question: You check the SEP school calendar. About how many days of class are in a school year?
hints: There are summer, winter and Holy Week vacations.
Saturdays and Sundays don't count.
It's about 38 weeks of Monday to Friday.
questions.description: A question about counting the days, just like every student does in June.
questions.fun_fact: The SEP was founded in 1921, and its first secretary was José Vasconcelos.

questions.question: It has 18 characters, it's on your birth certificate, and schools ask for it when you sign up. What is the CURP for?
hints: You get it when you're still a baby.
It's made from letters of your name, your date of birth and the place where you were born.
The U in its acronym stands for “Única” (unique).
questions.description: Eighteen characters that say more about you than your horoscope.
questions.fun_fact: In your CURP, the 11th character is H or M (hombre or mujer) depending on your sex, and the next two show the state where you were born.

questions.question: In a museum, you see a huge elephant bird egg. Which of these labels does NOT fit it?
hints: It was a giant bird that walked, like an ostrich.
It no longer exists: it died out centuries ago.
It lived in the forests and fields of an island, not at sea.
questions.description: A bird so big that even its name seems too small for it.
questions.fun_fact: One elephant bird egg could hold the contents of more than 100 chicken eggs.

questions.question: You shout me when someone tells you something unbelievable. I sound like I'm calling them a liar, but I only show surprise. What expression am I?
hints: You hear it all the time among Mexican teens.
It's a close cousin of “¡No manches!”.
Its verb is the thing Thomas Edison was famous for doing.
questions.description: This phrase shoots out every time someone shares the gossip of the year.
questions.fun_fact: “¡No inventes!” works for good and bad surprises alike: winning a prize or a pop quiz.

questions.question: In Mexico, what fond nickname do people give someone with no hair at all?
hints: The nickname describes the head.
Newborn babies sometimes get called this too.
It sounds like the word “pelo” (hair) with a bigger ending.
questions.description: A nickname that saves a lot of money on shampoo.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican nicknames, “chino” has nothing to do with China: it's what you call someone with curly hair.

questions.question: When something goes wrong or surprises you, people say “¡híjole!” all the time. In which country is this word so typical?
hints: It's a country in the Americas.
It shares a border with a much bigger neighbor to the north.
Its capital is one of the biggest cities in the world.
questions.description: Your ice cream just hit the ground, and this is the only word that comes out.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Híjole!” comes from “hijo” (son), and you can stretch it out as long as you like: “¡híjoleeee!”.

questions.question: It's super short, you say it when you drop your taco or forget something, and it saves you from saying a bad word. Which word is it?
hints: You say it when something small goes wrong.
Many people use it to avoid a ruder word that starts the same way.
Its cousin is “¡chale!”.
questions.description: A word so tiny it fits right into the moment you remember you forgot your homework.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico “¡Aguas!” means “Watch out!”, and people say it comes from the days when dirty water was thrown out of windows.

questions.question: It's said when you're fed up, it's classic Mexico City slang, and it ends with the nickname for women named Soledad. What expression is it?
hints: You use it to ask someone to stop doing something.
It's said in a tired voice, stretching out the last word.
It starts with “ya” and ends with a name.
questions.description: A chilango phrase that sounds like someone just greeted their aunt in the middle of the street.
questions.fun_fact: “Chole” is the traditional nickname for Soledad, just as “Lupe” is for Guadalupe and “Chucho” for Jesús.

questions.question: Which TV show is the famous “vientito” from, the little breeze that blows when a miracle is about to happen?
wrong_answers: Mujer, casos de la vida real
hints: It is a Televisa show that has been on the air since 2008.
Each episode tells a different story about a problem that seems to have no solution.
After the vientito, a white flower appears.
questions.description: An air conditioner with heavenly powers that always shows up at just the right moment.
questions.fun_fact: The vientito became so famous that there are thousands of memes and parodies of it on social media.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actress and singer. In 1996, as a child, I starred in “Luz Clarita” as a cheerful, mischievous little orphan. Who am I?
hints: I was born in the late 1980s.
As a teenager, I kept acting in telenovelas for young viewers.
My last name is also the name of an Argentine city famous for its basilica.
questions.description: A ’90s child star who was actually allowed to make mischief in prime time.
questions.fun_fact: “Luz Clarita” is a remake of the 1979 Argentine telenovela “Andrea Celeste.”

questions.question: What year did “Cuna de lobos,” the telenovela of Catalina Creel and her famous eye patch, premiere?
hints: It premiered the same year Mexico hosted a soccer World Cup.
It's from the same decade as “La fiera” and “Rosa salvaje.”
That World Cup was the one with Maradona's “Hand of God.”
questions.description: A family so close-knit you'd be scared to sit down to dinner with them.
questions.fun_fact: Catalina Creel was played by María Rubio, and her eye patch became a symbol of the great telenovela villains.

questions.question: Which Mexican singer-songwriter wrote “Te sigo amando,” the theme song of the telenovela with the same name?
hints: He's one of the most famous songwriters in Mexican music.
He wrote “Amor eterno” and “Querida.”
He was nicknamed “El Divo de Juárez.”
questions.description: A song so good that a whole telenovela took its name.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Gabriel wrote more than 1,500 songs, and many of them were recorded by other artists.

questions.question: “Kangaroo” is to “jumping forward” as “sifaka” is to “jumping…”
hints: The sifaka is a lemur from Madagascar that lives in the trees.
When it comes down to the ground, it looks like it's dancing.
It moves like a crab, with its arms up in the air.
questions.description: A lemur that dances like nobody's watching.
questions.fun_fact: The name “sifaka” copies the alarm call this lemur makes: “shi-fak!”

questions.question: The notary arrives at the mansion and the whole family sits in silence. Finish the cliché: “Now begins the reading of the…”
hints: It decides who gets the fortune.
There is almost always a surprise: someone nobody expected gets everything.
It's the paper where someone writes down what each relative inherits.
questions.description: The moment in a telenovela when every relative suddenly becomes very loving.
questions.fun_fact: In many telenovelas, a surprise inheritance is what turns the poor girl into a millionaire.

questions.question: Which of these actors was NOT in the telenovela “Soy tu dueña” (2010)?
hints: The heroine was a rich, tough, distrustful woman named Valentina.
The villain was the Venezuelan actress who had earlier played twins in “La usurpadora”.
The one missing is the star of “María Mercedes”.
questions.description: A ranch, a heartthrob and enough villains to fill the corral.
questions.fun_fact: “Soy tu dueña” is a remake of “La dueña”, a 1995 Mexican telenovela starring Angélica Rivera.

questions.question: I was born in Álamos, Sonora, in 1950. My “Danzón No. 2” premiered in 1994, and Gustavo Dudamel took it around the world. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four composers; I started composing in the second half of the 20th century.
My most famous work was inspired by the dance halls of Veracruz and Mexico City.
My last name starts with the same three letters as the red planet Mars.
questions.description: A whole orchestra in evening dress, trying to sound like a dance hall on a Saturday night.
questions.fun_fact: The UNAM commissioned “Danzón No. 2”, and today it is one of the Mexican works orchestras play most around the world.

questions.question: In many Mexican dances of Moors and Christians, the hero rides a white horse and defeats the Moors, as in this image. Which saint is he?
hints: He is one of the twelve apostles of Jesus.
The Spanish shouted his name as they charged into battle.
He is also called “Matamoros”.
questions.description: A saint who never shows up to the dance on foot.
questions.fun_fact: Many towns in Mexico are named Santiago in honor of this apostle, such as Santiago Tuxtla and Santiago de Querétaro.

questions.question: In Puebla and Veracruz, people perform the dance of the Twelve Peers of France. Which emperor did those twelve knights serve?
hints: He ruled a large part of Western Europe.
Among his knights was Roland, hero of a famous medieval epic poem.
He was crowned emperor in the year 800.
questions.description: Twelve knights who crossed the ocean without a ship, armed only with masks and wooden swords.
questions.fun_fact: The stories of the Twelve Peers reached Mexico in the books of chivalry that the Spanish brought with them.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which dancers wear this on their heads?
hints: They dance to the beat of a big drum.
You often see them in the Zócalo in Mexico City.
They're also called “Aztec dancers.”
questions.description: Feathers that have never seen a bird fly up close.
questions.fun_fact: Conchero headdresses often have pheasant or ostrich feathers, which can sway a lot during the dance.

questions.question: Octavio Paz collected the poems he wrote during his years in Asia in “Ladera este.” In what year was it published?
hints: It came after “Sunstone.”
The book collects poems he wrote while he was Mexico's ambassador to India.
It came out the same year humans first walked on the Moon.
questions.description: A poetry book that faced the sunrise, and not because the poet was an early bird.
questions.fun_fact: Paz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990, the first Mexican ever to receive it.

questions.question: He was a modernist poet, published “Lascas” in 1901 and was known for picking fights. In what city was Salvador Díaz Mirón born?
hints: He was born in 1853 and was also a journalist and a congressman.
His hometown was founded by the Spanish in the 16th century.
It is the most important port in Mexico's history, and it shares its name with its state.
questions.description: A poet with velvet verses and a sandpaper temper.
questions.fun_fact: Díaz Mirón spent several years in prison after a fight, and he kept writing poetry there.

questions.question: In Francisco Hinojosa's book, the worst lady in the world is so mean that everyone flees the town. What is the town called?
hints: The book begins by saying she lived in the north of this town.
It isn't a real town: the author made it up.
Its name starts with T and has three syllables.
questions.description: If you're house hunting, don't move onto this lady's street.
questions.fun_fact: “La peor señora del mundo” (The Worst Lady in the World) came out in 1992 and is one of the Mexican children's books most read in schools.

questions.question: I was born in Zapotlán el Grande, Jalisco, in 1918. I wrote “Confabulario” and a story about a traveler waiting for a train that may never come. Who am I?
hints: My hometown is now called Ciudad Guzmán.
I was well known on television for my theatrical way of speaking and for playing chess.
I have two first names, and my last name starts with A.
questions.description: Mexican short stories are like tacos: they're gone fast and you always want another one.
questions.fun_fact: “El guardagujas” (“The Switchman”) is read as a satire of Mexico's railroads and its red tape.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT linked to Antonieta Rivas Mercado or her family?
hints: Antonieta was a patron of the Contemporáneos group and of experimental theater.
Her father, Antonio Rivas Mercado, was the architect of a famous monument on Paseo de la Reforma.
The odd one out was built in the 1930s, after her death, on the frame of an unfinished legislative palace.
questions.description: A woman whose life in 1920s Mexico reads like the script of a period telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Antonieta paid for the Teatro de Ulises, where Xavier Villaurrutia and Salvador Novo acted in and translated avant-garde plays.

questions.question: Which Mexican band turned “Battles in the Desert” into the song “Las batallas”, on their album “Re” (1994)?
hints: The band comes from Ciudad Satélite, in the State of Mexico.
They also sing “Eres” and “Ojalá que llueva café”.
Their name recalls a famous café in Mexico City’s Centro Histórico.
questions.description: When a short novel turns into a karaoke song with friends.
questions.fun_fact: The song repeats the name of Mariana, young Carlitos’s impossible love in José Emilio Pacheco’s novel.

questions.question: Which of these works is NOT by José Emilio Pacheco?
wrong_answers: “No me preguntes cómo pasa el tiempo”
hints: Pacheco won the Cervantes Prize in 2009.
The odd one out is a novel written by a woman.
The odd one out was written by Ángeles Mastretta from Puebla.
questions.description: A stowaway with a fake ID has sneaked onto this bookshelf, and nobody has checked the cover.
questions.fun_fact: Pacheco also translated great poets and wrote the column “Inventario” for decades.

questions.question: I'm a tiger: to everyone else, a stuffed toy; to my friend Calvin, a real one. I share my name with an English philosopher. Who am I?
hints: I appear in a newspaper comic strip, not in a movie.
My creator is Bill Watterson.
My name is that of the philosopher who wrote “Leviathan”.
questions.description: A stuffed toy that has read more philosophy than most grown-ups.
questions.fun_fact: Calvin is named after a thinker too: the theologian John Calvin.

questions.question: Saint Augustine is to “Confessions” as Thomas Aquinas is to…
hints: It is a huge work that was never finished.
He wrote it in the 13th century.
Its title says it is a “summary” of what is known about God.
questions.description: A book so long that not even its author got to the end of it.
questions.fun_fact: Because he was quiet and heavyset, his classmates nicknamed Thomas Aquinas “the Dumb Ox.”

questions.question: This 1787 painting shows a famous Greek philosopher surrounded by his students. Who is he?
hints: He was Plato's teacher.
He is credited with the saying “I know that I know nothing”.
A way of teaching by asking questions is named after him.
questions.description: A get-together of friends where nobody asked for popcorn.
questions.fun_fact: David painted Plato as an old man at the foot of the bed, even though Plato was actually young at the time.

questions.question: I'm a 19th-century German philosopher who wrote “Phenomenology of Spirit” and spoke of “absolute spirit”. Who am I?
hints: I lived at the same time as Napoleon.
When I saw Napoleon in Jena, I called him “the world soul on horseback”.
As a young man, Karl Marx was one of my most famous followers.
questions.description: A philosopher so hard to follow that even his students asked for subtitles.
questions.fun_fact: Hegel finished “Phenomenology of Spirit” in Jena just as Napoleon was winning a battle there in 1806.

questions.question: The Florentine Marsilio Ficino named it after a Greek philosopher, and it means love for someone you idealize. What is it called?
hints: It shows up in countless songs and soap operas.
The Greek philosopher was a student of Socrates.
That philosopher wrote “The Symposium”, a dialogue about love.
questions.description: That crush who never knew you existed, now with a philosophy diploma.
questions.fun_fact: For Ficino, platonic love wasn't love that goes unreturned, but a love of beauty that lifts the soul toward the divine.

questions.question: I seem logical, but I lead to something absurd: thanks to me, Zeno said, swift Achilles never catches a tortoise. What am I?
hints: Zeno of Elea came up with several of them to defend his teacher Parmenides.
Another very famous one is the sentence “This sentence is false.”
My name starts with “para-”.
questions.description: Why you're never on time, explained by an ancient Greek.
questions.fun_fact: Math untangled the puzzle centuries later: infinitely many tiny pieces of a path can add up to a finite distance.

questions.question: A track switch lever like this one is the star of a famous moral dilemma. What is that dilemma called?
hints: It became a hugely popular internet meme.
You must decide whether to change the path of a vehicle with no brakes.
The vehicle runs on rails through a city.
questions.description: A lever that has ruined more family dinners than politics.
questions.fun_fact: British philosopher Philippa Foot came up with this dilemma in 1967.

questions.question: Inside an igloo you can stay warmer than outside. What job does the packed snow of its walls do?
hints: Packed snow is full of tiny trapped air bubbles.
It does the same job as the wool in a good winter coat.
It barely lets your body heat escape to the outside.
questions.description: A house made of ice that, against all odds, is not a refrigerator.
questions.fun_fact: Inside an igloo, with nothing but the warmth of the people in it, the temperature can be tens of degrees higher than outside.

questions.question: Complete: one hertz equals one vibration or oscillation per…
hints: The hertz measures frequency: how often something repeats.
It is the basic unit of time in the International System of Units.
A clock shows it with its fastest hand.
questions.description: A unit with a German last name that buzzes more than a phone on silent.
questions.fun_fact: Human ears hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and dogs can hear much higher frequencies.

questions.question: In what year did the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius propose his temperature scale?
hints: It was after Galileo built his first thermoscopes, around 1600.
It was before the French Revolution.
It was in the middle of the 18th century.
questions.description: A Swede who got half the world talking about the weather in his own numbers.
questions.fun_fact: Celsius's original scale was upside down: water boiled at 0 degrees and froze at 100.

questions.question: You drop a stone and a flat sheet of paper at the same time, and the stone lands first. What slows the paper down most?
hints: If you crumple the sheet into a ball, it falls much faster.
On the Moon, both would land at the same time.
A parachute uses the very same thing.
questions.description: A race between a stone and a sheet of paper, and everyone already knows how it ends.
questions.fun_fact: In 1971, an Apollo 15 astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and they hit the ground at the same time.

questions.question: In what year did Albert Einstein publish his theory of special relativity?
hints: Einstein was only about 26 years old.
At the time, he worked in a patent office in Switzerland.
It was early in the 20th century, before the First World War.
questions.description: A year so busy that even time started to stretch.
questions.fun_fact: People call 1905 Einstein's “miracle year”: he published four papers that changed physics.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a cone: speak into my narrow end and your voice comes out louder and carries far. What am I?
hints: People use me at marches, sports games and fire drills.
Many of me run on batteries and have a trigger.
My name starts with “mega”, which means big.
questions.description: The best friend of every gym teacher on a school field trip.
questions.fun_fact: Before they had batteries, megaphones were just simple cones of cardboard or metal, and they still worked pretty well.

questions.question: Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, it measures electrical resistance, and body fat scales use it. Which unit is it?
hints: It is named after a German physicist.
It tells you how hard it is for current to flow through something.
Its symbol looks like a horseshoe: Ω.
questions.description: A unit that resists everything, even being easy.
questions.fun_fact: Fat carries electricity less well than muscle does, which is how those scales can estimate how much body fat you have.

questions.question: The Koch snowflake is built by repeating the same step over and over. What shape does it start from?
hints: At each step, every side grows a little spike in the middle.
After the first step, the shape looks like a six-pointed star.
The starting shape has three equal sides.
questions.description: A snowflake that never melts, but never finishes being drawn either.
questions.fun_fact: The Koch snowflake has an infinitely long edge, yet the area inside it is finite.

questions.question: It has one point, one curved edge and two equal straight edges: a party hat, unrolled and flattened. What shape is it?
hints: The bottom edge of the hat is round, so the flat shape can't be made of straight lines only.
It looks like a slice of pizza.
It's a piece of a circle cut out from the center.
questions.description: The accessory that turns any serious adult into a birthday unicorn.
questions.fun_fact: From the same circle of cardboard you can make taller or wider hats, depending on how big a slice you cut out.

questions.question: Pentagon, hexagon, heptagon… keep going and you reach the dodecagon. How many sides does it have?
hints: “Dodeca” comes from Greek.
It has more sides than a decagon, which has 10.
It's the number of eggs in a dozen.
questions.description: A shape with so many corners it almost thinks it's a circle.
questions.fun_fact: The British one-pound coin in use since 2017 is shaped like a dodecagon.

questions.question: These shapes have the same form and the same size, and they match exactly when you put one on top of the other. What are they called?
hints: Looking alike isn't enough: they must also be the same size.
Similar shapes have the same form, but they can be different sizes.
The word starts with “con”.
questions.description: Two shapes so alike that even their mom can't tell them apart.
questions.fun_fact: Fold a sheet of paper in half and cut out a shape through both layers: the two pieces you get are congruent.

questions.question: An open umbrella hangs under the leaky roof. What is this famous painting called?
hints: The picture was painted in 1839, in the Biedermeier period.
It belongs to the collection of the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.
It was painted by Carl Spitzweg.
questions.description: When the rain comes in, you don't need a roofer, just imagination.
questions.fun_fact: Carl Spitzweg was actually a trained pharmacist and taught himself to paint.

questions.question: In which museum does the painting this detail comes from hang?
hints: Caspar David Friedrich painted it around 1818.
The museum stands right next to a big main train station.
The city has a large port on the Elbe River.
questions.description: A man with a view who hasn't come down off the wall in decades.
questions.fun_fact: The Hamburger Kunsthalle also owns Friedrich's “The Sea of Ice”, with a wrecked ship among slabs of ice.

questions.question: The architect Buckminster Fuller made this dome built from triangles popular. What is it called?
hints: It is very light and strong for its size.
Disney's Epcot park has a giant sphere built the same way.
Its name shares a root with the science that measures the shape of the Earth.
questions.description: A roof that is all triangles and zero tiles.
questions.fun_fact: Ball-shaped carbon molecules are called “fullerenes” in honor of Buckminster Fuller.

questions.question: In Kassel, basalt stones like these stand next to trees, part of an artwork that began in 1982. Who came up with it?
hints: The artwork started at the documenta art show.
Every tree planted comes with a stone.
The artist almost always wore a felt hat.
questions.description: An artwork you have to water instead of dust.
questions.fun_fact: The last of the 7,000 trees was planted in 1987 by Beuys's son, a year after the artist died.

questions.question: Max Braun founded his company in 1921, and Dieter Rams later designed devices there that inspired Apple's designers. In which city did it all begin?
hints: At first the company made radio parts, not shavers.
Today the company is based in nearby Kronberg im Taunus.
The city is home to the European Central Bank.
questions.description: These shavers and radios looked so good that they now stand in museums instead of bathrooms.
questions.fun_fact: Dieter Rams summed up good design in ten principles; one says: “As little design as possible.”

questions.question: You're standing in Berlin's Lustgarten in front of the Altes Museum with its 18 columns. Who designed this building?
hints: He was Prussia's most famous architect of the 19th century.
He also designed the Schauspielhaus on the Gendarmenmarkt.
His last name sounds almost like the German word for ham.
questions.description: Columns, columns, columns: the ancient world had a big fan in Prussia.
questions.fun_fact: The Altes Museum opened in 1830 and was Berlin's first public museum.

questions.question: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed this chair in 1929. What is it called?
hints: Seen from the side, its steel frame crosses in an X.
It stood in the German pavilion at a world's fair.
The city lies on the Mediterranean and has the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: A chair that needed a world stage before anyone was allowed to sit on it.
questions.fun_fact: Mies van der Rohe was the last director of the Bauhaus, from 1930 to 1933.

questions.question: You're fetching Brötchen on Sunday. Which word is NOT a regional name for a bread roll?
hints: Three of the words are used for bread rolls in Berlin, Bavaria and Swabia.
The word you're looking for also comes from Berlin.
It means a slice of bread with something on it, like a school snack.
questions.description: Sunday morning, pajama pants under your jacket, and off to the bakery.
questions.fun_fact: In Hamburg, a bread roll is called a “Rundstück”, and in Saarland a “Weck”.

questions.question: For an Apfeltasche, you put apple filling on puff pastry, fold it over and press the edges with a fork. Why?
questions.answer: So the filling doesn't leak out
hints: It's about the edge, not the middle.
In the oven, the filling gets hot and runny.
Without a sealed edge, you end up with apple stuck to the baking sheet.
questions.description: A pocket you're allowed to bite into without getting in trouble.
questions.fun_fact: Steam builds up inside while it bakes, so people often cut a few small slits in the top.

questions.question: It sells cream cakes and chocolates, often has a small café, and its master was once called a “Zuckerbäcker” (sugar baker). What is the shop called?
hints: Bread and rolls aren't the main thing here.
The job there is a trade of its own, with its own master's exam.
The master here is the Konditor.
questions.description: Here, every calorie is carefully decorated with whipped cream.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Konditor” comes from the Latin “condire”, meaning “to preserve” or “to season”.

questions.question: In the song “In der Weihnachtsbäckerei”, many a “Knilch” makes a huge mess. Between which two ingredients?
hints: The song is by Rolf Zuckowski.
In the German line, one of the ingredients rhymes with “Knilch”.
One is a white powder, the other comes from the cow.
questions.description: A Christmas song that always leaves the kitchen looking like a snowstorm hit it.
questions.fun_fact: Rolf Zuckowski released “In der Weihnachtsbäckerei” in 1987, and today it is one of the best-known German Christmas songs.

questions.question: Long ago, people cut cookies into stars and hearts, poked a hole in them before baking and threaded a ribbon through. What for?
questions.answer: As decorations for the Christmas tree
hints: The cookies were meant to be looked at for a while before being eaten.
They were hung up somewhere.
Today, mostly glass balls and tinsel hang there.
questions.description: Cookies that refuse to be eaten right away.
questions.fun_fact: Before glass ornaments existed, Germans decorated Christmas trees with apples, nuts and baked treats.

questions.question: What kind of dough is this pastry made from?
hints: The dough is cooked in a pot on the stove first.
In the oven, steam puffs it up into a hollow ball.
Eclairs and Spritzkuchen are made from it too.
questions.description: A pastry that's hollow inside but still never shows off.
questions.fun_fact: In German, calling someone a “Windbeutel” means they're a show-off: big on the outside, nothing but air inside.

questions.question: The track in the photo, near Barcelona, first hosted Formula 1 in 1991. Who won that race?
hints: At that point he had never been world champion.
The next year he would win his only world title.
He was a British driver with a famous mustache who raced wheel to wheel with Senna down the main straight in that race.
questions.description: A racetrack so Catalan that even its corners have an accent.
questions.fun_fact: In that 1991 race, Mansell and Senna raced down the straight with their wheels almost touching at more than 300 km/h (186 mph).

questions.question: You lift the DFB-Pokal high after the final in Berlin. Roughly how heavy is it?
hints: A single player can lift it easily.
It's much heavier than a full carton of milk.
It weighs about as much as six 1-liter cartons of milk.
questions.description: A trophy that makes arms shake in Berlin every year.
questions.fun_fact: The DFB-Pokal is about 52 centimeters (20 in) tall and holds about eight liters (2 gallons).

questions.question: You're standing in the Frankfurt fan section. Which nickname for Eintracht will you NOT hear there?
hints: One real Frankfurt nickname comes from the animal on the club crest.
One of the names belongs to a club from the Lower Rhine.
It's Borussia Mönchengladbach's nickname.
questions.description: Here every win is celebrated like an Äppelwoi festival on the Main.
questions.fun_fact: At Eintracht home games, a real golden eagle named Attila is often in the stadium.

questions.question: You're celebrating Frankfurt's 2022 Europa League win in Seville. When had Eintracht last won a European trophy before that?
hints: Back then the competition was still called the UEFA Cup.
Their opponent in the final was Borussia Mönchengladbach.
It was more than 40 years earlier.
questions.description: A city that waited so long for this night that its cheers had started gathering dust.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2022 final against Rangers, Kevin Trapp saved Aaron Ramsey's kick in the penalty shootout.

questions.question: A player gets a yellow card in a match. How many yellow cards does he need in total before he is sent off?
hints: Then the referee shows two colors at once.
In Germany this card is called “Gelb-Rot” (yellow-red).
The very next yellow card is enough.
questions.description: A small piece of cardboard that can make grown men sulk.
questions.fun_fact: The Bundesliga has only had the yellow-red card since the 1991/92 season.

questions.question: In 2013, Bayern Munich became the first German club to win the treble. In which year did they do it a second time?
hints: The Champions League final was played in Lisbon.
In the final, Bayern beat Paris Saint-Germain 1–0.
The coach at the time was Hansi Flick.
questions.description: Three trophies, one team bus and a bus driver with a very wide grin.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2019–20 Champions League season, Bayern won all eleven of their games – no team had done that before.

questions.question: On a German soccer field, he's called “Schiri” for short. What is the full word?
hints: He carries a whistle.
He shows yellow and red cards.
The second half of the word, “Richter”, means “judge”.
questions.description: A word that gets yelled on the field much shorter than it's spelled.
questions.fun_fact: A Bundesliga referee runs about 11 kilometers (7 miles) per game.

questions.question: When “Der Klassiker” is on in the Bundesliga, which teams are playing each other?
hints: It's the clash of the two most successful clubs of recent decades.
This match often helps decide who becomes German champion.
One of the teams is from Munich.
questions.description: A match hyped about as much as “Dinner for One” on New Year's Eve.
questions.fun_fact: The name is modeled on Spain's “El Clásico” between Real Madrid and FC Barcelona.

questions.question: A defender deliberately handles the ball inside his own penalty area. What does the referee give?
hints: The attacking team is very happy.
It becomes a duel: one shooter against the goalkeeper.
The ball is placed on a spot inside the box.
questions.description: Soccer is played with the feet – not every arm seems to know that yet.
questions.fun_fact: In German a penalty is called “Elfmeter” (eleven-meter), because the spot is exactly 11 meters (12 yards) from the goal.

questions.question: How many euros a month did the Deutschlandticket cost when it started in May 2023?
hints: It was much cheaper than most old monthly passes.
It cost a lot more than a movie ticket, but much less than many old monthly passes for local transit.
Many people named it after its price: the “…-euro ticket”.
questions.description: Pay once and roam the whole republic for a month, as long as the trains play along.
questions.fun_fact: The Deutschlandticket is valid on all buses and local trains across Germany, but not on the ICE or IC.

questions.question: I was foreign minister twice, moved into Schloss Bellevue as Federal President in 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the SPD.
In 2010, I donated a kidney to my wife.
My last name starts with the German word for “stone”.
questions.description: First jetting around the world, then settling down in a Berlin palace.
questions.fun_fact: Frank-Walter Steinmeier comes from Brakelsiek near Detmold and is the son of a carpenter.

questions.question: At a Formula 1 pit stop, how long does a good team take to change all four tires?
hints: About twenty people work at the same time.
It's less time than it takes you to say your full name.
You could barely blink twice.
questions.description: Faster than Mom slipping on her sandals to run out the door.
questions.fun_fact: In 2023, McLaren changed all four tires in just 1.80 seconds, a record at the time.

questions.question: How many times did Angela Merkel take the chancellor's oath of office in the Bundestag?
hints: Each time she was elected chancellor again, she had to take the oath again.
She governed for 16 years.
A term in parliament lasts four years.
questions.description: Raise your hand, recite the words, and please do it all again every few years.
questions.fun_fact: The phrase “So help me God” is optional in the oath; Gerhard Schröder left it out in 1998.

questions.question: Parties like Die Linke are called “left-wing”. Where does this label originally come from?
questions.answer: The seating in the French parliament
wrong_answers: The hand you use to mark your ballot
The left column on the ballot paper
Where the party offices are in Berlin
hints: The story doesn't begin in Germany.
It goes back to the Revolution of 1789.
It's about where the members took their seats.
questions.description: In politics, “left” has nothing to do with your turn signal.
questions.fun_fact: In the Bundestag, too, Die Linke sits furthest to the left as seen from the chair.

questions.question: I chair the sessions of the Bundestag, ring a bell, call members to order and rank second in the state's protocol. Who am I?
hints: The members of parliament elect me from among themselves.
Only the head of state ranks above me in protocol.
My office carries the name of the parliament itself.
questions.description: Get too loud in the Bundestag and you'll have to deal with the lord of the bell.
questions.fun_fact: The first woman to lead the Bundestag was Annemarie Renger of the SPD, in 1972.

questions.question: I wrote children's books with my wife, served as economy minister and ran as the Greens' candidate for chancellor in 2025. Who am I?
hints: I come from the far north and was a minister in Schleswig-Holstein.
I was vice chancellor in the traffic-light coalition.
My first name is Robert.
questions.description: Writing children's books is good practice for writing party platforms.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Habeck has a doctorate in philosophy and also wrote novels together with Andrea Paluch.

questions.question: I became Minister-President of Bavaria in 2018 and CSU leader in 2019, and I love posting photos of döner and bratwurst online. Who am I?
hints: I come from Nuremberg in Franconia.
In 2021 I wanted to be the Union's candidate for Chancellor, but Armin Laschet got the job.
My first name is Markus.
questions.description: A politician whose social media feed is more menu than party manifesto.
questions.fun_fact: The CSU only runs in elections in Bavaria and forms a joint group with the CDU in the Bundestag.

questions.question: Shortly after Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022, Olaf Scholz announced an extra 100 billion euros. Who got the money?
hints: Scholz announced it on a Sunday, in a special session of the Bundestag.
For years, many had complained that the equipment there was old or broken.
This means Germany's soldiers.
questions.description: Suddenly there's a fat package of money, and everyone wonders who gets to unwrap it.
questions.fun_fact: The money is officially called a “Sondervermögen” (special fund), even though it is really debt.

questions.question: Germany's first democracy began in 1918, had Friedrich Ebert as its first president and ended in 1933. What is it called?
hints: It came after the end of the German Empire.
It is named after a city in Thuringia.
Goethe and Schiller also lived in that city.
questions.description: Germany's first try at democracy: lots of courage, not much luck.
questions.fun_fact: In 1919 the National Assembly met in Weimar because Berlin was too unsettled.

questions.question: Who made this way of holding the hands famous as a trademark?
hints: This person led Germany for a very long time.
This person grew up in East Germany.
She was the first woman to become chancellor.
questions.description: Ten fingers, one shape, and suddenly it's an election poster.
questions.fun_fact: In 2013 a giant CDU poster in Berlin showed just these hands, made up of many small photos.

questions.question: Little Bear and Little Tiger go looking for the land of their dreams. Finish Janosch's book title: “Oh, wie schön ist …”
hints: The two friends find a crate that smells of bananas.
The country is in Central America.
A famous canal between two oceans runs through this country.
questions.description: Two friends, one signpost and a pretty big detour.
questions.fun_fact: In the end the two walk in a circle and land back at their own home, which suddenly seems wonderful to them.

questions.question: I wear a red bow in my hair, I have a cat named Mau and a little brother named Jakob. Who am I?
hints: My books are published by Carlsen Verlag.
In my books I learn new things, like riding a bike or swimming.
My name starts with “Con”.
questions.description: This heroine has had more “first times” than a whole kindergarten.
questions.fun_fact: The first Conni picture books came out in the early 1990s.

questions.question: Little Red Riding Hood is to the wolf as the bunny children in the picture book “Die Häschenschule” are to which animal?
hints: The bunny teacher warns the children about this enemy.
This animal also likes to sneak up on henhouses at night.
In fables it is often called Reynard.
questions.description: A school with no phone ban, but with suspiciously long ears.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Häschenschule” (“The Bunny School”) first came out in 1924 and is still in print today.

questions.question: Who wrote the picture book “Das Neinhorn”, about a unicorn that says no to everything?
hints: He is also a comedian and songwriter.
He wrote books about a kangaroo that moved in with him.
“The Kangaroo Chronicles” are his.
questions.description: A fairy-tale creature with its own built-in toddler tantrum phase.
questions.fun_fact: In the Heart Forest, the Neinhorn meets more creatures with pun names, such as the WasBär, the NaHund and the KönigsDochter.

questions.question: In Michael Ende's “Der Wunschpunsch”, the cat is to the wizard Irrwitzer as which animal is to the witch Tyrannja Vamperl?
hints: The animal is a bird.
In the story it is scruffy, frozen and rather grumpy.
Its name is Jakob Krakel.
questions.description: A magic potion whose name takes two breaths to say.
questions.fun_fact: The cat Maurizio and Jakob Krakel are secretly spies for the High Council of Animals.

questions.question: I'm an old sea dog in a captain's cap. I tell my three grandchildren wild tall tales, and my sailor is called Hein Blöd. Who am I?
hints: The cartoonist Walter Moers created me.
I was often on “Die Sendung mit der Maus.”
My fur is the color of the sea.
questions.description: A sailor whose stories are best taken with a whole bucket of seawater.
questions.fun_fact: In 1999 Walter Moers even wrote a thick novel about him: “Die 13½ Leben des Käpt'n Blaubär” (“The 13½ Lives of Captain Bluebear”).

questions.question: With a good audio play, you see everything even though you only listen. Germans call this “Kino im …”, cinema in the what?
hints: The pictures come from your imagination.
It's a part of the body.
It's where your brain is.
questions.description: A movie with no screen, no projector and no popcorn crumbs on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The first German radio play was broadcast as early as 1924, long before cassettes existed.

questions.question: Bibi rides Sabrina, Tina rides Amadeus. In which decade did the first “Bibi und Tina” cassette come out?
hints: Bibi Blocksberg already had her own audio dramas before that.
Back then, cassettes were still more popular than CDs.
It started shortly after German reunification.
questions.description: Two horses, two girls and a farm with more adventures than hay.
questions.fun_fact: “Bibi und Tina” is a spin-off of “Bibi Blocksberg”, and its first episode came out in 1991.

questions.question: Rostock is the biggest city in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Roughly how many people live there?
hints: Rostock has a university, a large port and a streetcar network.
Hamburg has almost 2 million inhabitants.
The number is between 100,000 and 300,000.
questions.description: A city with Baltic Sea views, cruise ships and more seagulls than anyone wants to count.
questions.fun_fact: The University of Rostock was founded in 1419 and is one of the oldest universities in Northern Europe.

questions.question: The Pied Piper of Hamelin wasn't paid for his work. Who did he then lead out of town with his pipe?
hints: Afterwards, Hamelin was very quiet.
According to the legend, the procession left through a town gate on a summer feast day, June 26, 1284.
According to the legend, 130 of them disappeared.
questions.description: A pest controller with a musical instrument and very strict payment terms.
questions.fun_fact: To this day, no music may be played on Bungelosenstraße in Hamelin, because the procession is said to have gone down that street.

questions.question: This photo shows part of a famous building in Germany. Which one is it?
hints: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It was built from 1248 to 1880, with long breaks.
It stands right next to the train station of a city on the Rhine.
questions.description: That's an awful lot of pointy tops for just one building.
questions.fun_fact: When Cologne Cathedral was finished in 1880, it was the tallest building in the world for a few years.

questions.question: You walk across the Stone Bridge (Steinerne Brücke) over the Danube in Regensburg. About how old is it?
hints: It is older than the discovery of America.
But the Romans didn't build it.
It was built in the time of knights and the Crusades.
questions.description: A bridge that has seen more feet than any shoe store.
questions.fun_fact: The Wurstkuchl right next to the bridge is said to be one of the oldest sausage kitchens in the world.

questions.question: The Imola racetrack in Italy is named after the founder of a famous sports car brand and his son. What is their last name?
hints: This brand is the oldest team in Formula 1.
Its factory is in Maranello, in the same region of Italy as Imola.
Its cars are famous for being red.
questions.description: A racetrack named after a family, like Grandpa's farm.
questions.fun_fact: Its official name is Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari.

questions.question: In 1775, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe moved to Weimar and lived there until he died. In which city was he born?
hints: He only studied in Leipzig and Strasbourg.
The house where he was born is now a museum on the Großer Hirschgraben.
The city has Germany's tallest skyscrapers.
questions.description: A poet on the move: boxes full of poems and no moving truck in sight.
questions.fun_fact: In front of the National Theater in Weimar, Goethe and Schiller stand side by side as a statue, holding one laurel wreath together.

questions.question: Atlas is to map as … is to spelling?
hints: In arguments about capital letters, people often quote this book.
The first edition came out in 1880.
You'll find the yellow volume in almost every German classroom.
questions.description: Family dinner arguments need a referee, and some referees are made of paper.
questions.fun_fact: The first Duden in 1880 had about 27,000 entries; today it has well over 100,000.

questions.question: One Saturday, a cheeky creature with a snout-like nose moves in with Mr. Taschenbier. Who came up with this story?
hints: He was born in Schweinfurt in 1937.
He also wrote “Lippels Traum” (Lippel's Dream).
His most famous book is “Eine Woche voller Samstage” (A Week Full of Saturdays).
questions.description: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday… and then the week suddenly gets very strange.
questions.fun_fact: The Sams grants wishes with the blue dots on its face, and each wish costs one dot.

questions.question: When did Matthias Claudius write the evening song “Der Mond ist aufgegangen”?
hints: Goethe was still a young poet back then.
Carriages, candles and wigs were part of everyday life.
It was printed a good ten years before the French Revolution.
questions.description: The lullaby that sent whole generations to sleep before the last verse ever came.
questions.fun_fact: In the last verse, Claudius also asks for peaceful sleep for “unsern kranken Nachbar” (our sick neighbor).

questions.question: One winter I knocked on the door of two sisters, slept by their fire and was really an enchanted prince. Who am I?
hints: I have a thick, shaggy coat.
An evil dwarf had put a spell on me.
The two girls are called Snow-White and Rose-Red.
questions.description: A winter guest who can hardly be moved away from the fireplace.
questions.fun_fact: In the end, Snow-White marries the prince and Rose-Red marries his brother.

questions.question: Jacob Grimm moved house many times in his life. In which of these cities did he NOT live?
hints: He was born in a town on the Main River.
He spent his last years in the capital of Prussia.
The city you're looking for is in Bavaria.
questions.description: A fairy-tale collector with more moving boxes than fairy tales.
questions.fun_fact: Jacob Grimm died in 1863 while working on the great German dictionary; he had just reached the word “Frucht” (fruit).

questions.question: Goethe staged the premiere of Kleist's comedy “The Broken Jug” in Weimar, and it flopped. In which year?
hints: Kleist was still alive at the time.
Napoleon ruled half of Europe at the time.
The Holy Roman Empire had come to an end only two years earlier.
questions.description: A court case about a few broken pieces, with a judge who seems oddly nervous.
questions.fun_fact: Goethe split the single long act into three parts, and many think that's exactly why the play felt so slow.

questions.question: I poured water on a stone at a magic spring, married the widow of the lord I defeated, and a lion became my companion. Who am I?
hints: I sit at King Arthur's Round Table.
Hartmann von Aue told my story in Middle High German around 1200.
My French model, by Chrétien de Troyes, is called “Yvain.”
questions.description: A knight who learns too late how much a calendar matters.
questions.fun_fact: At Rodenegg Castle in South Tyrol, 13th-century wall paintings show scenes from this story; they are considered the oldest non-religious murals in the German-speaking world.

questions.question: Which character does NOT appear in Michael Ende's “The Neverending Story”?
hints: The character you're looking for still comes from the same author.
He lives on a tiny island with two mountains.
He travels with Luke the Engine Driver.
questions.description: A book you should really never close.
questions.fun_fact: In the book the text is printed in two colors: red for Bastian's world and green for Fantastica.

questions.question: A teacher starts me in his class to show how easily a dictatorship can begin. I have a salute and a logo. What am I called?
hints: Morton Rhue wrote the book based on a real experiment in California.
In 2008 it was made into a movie, with Jürgen Vogel as the teacher.
My salute copies a movement of the sea.
questions.description: A school project that gets out of hand very, very fast.
questions.fun_fact: The real experiment was run by the teacher Ron Jones at a school in Palo Alto in 1967.

questions.question: It's shown to a driver about to be lapped, asks them to let the faster car pass, and the back of the field sees it most. Which flag is it?
hints: It doesn't warn of danger or a crash.
It's also shown at the pit exit when cars are coming down the track.
It's the color of Italy's national soccer team shirt.
questions.description: The color of good manners on the track, even if the driver isn't one bit amused.
questions.fun_fact: If a driver ignores the blue flag several times, the race stewards can give them a penalty.

questions.question: In the Grimm fairy tale “Briar Rose”, the princess pricks her finger on a spindle. What happens next?
hints: A good wise woman was able to soften a wicked curse.
The whole castle joins in, even the cook in the kitchen.
Only after a hundred years does a kiss wake her.
questions.description: A party for a newborn princess where one invitation too few went out.
questions.fun_fact: The whole castle falls asleep along with her, even the fire in the stove and the flies on the wall.

questions.question: In TKKG, each letter stands for a member: Tim, Karl, Gaby and the chocolate fan. What is his name?
hints: His real name is Willi Sauerlich.
He shares a room with Tim at boarding school.
He's a bit round, like a little dumpling (a “Kloß”).
questions.description: Four letters, one dog and an astonishing amount of chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: TKKG has been around since 1979, first as books by Stefan Wolf and soon after as audio dramas too.

questions.question: Which word does NOT fit Karl May's Winnetou?
hints: Karl May made him up in the 19th century.
He rides through the Wild West on his horse Iltschi.
He has nothing to do with ships or treasure maps.
questions.description: A man from Saxony wrote about lands he had never seen, and everyone believed him.
questions.fun_fact: In the Winnetou films of the 1960s, the lead role was played by a Frenchman: Pierre Brice.

questions.question: Müller is the most common last name in Germany. About how many people have it?
hints: In the old days, almost every village had a mill and a miller.
It's far more people than live in a city like Göttingen.
It's about as many people as live in Frankfurt am Main.
questions.description: A name that clatters, grinds and fills page after page of every phone book.
questions.fun_fact: In second and third place come Schmidt and Schneider, which are also old trades.

questions.question: Along the Limes you find many remains of Roman “Kastelle”. A Kastell was a …
hints: The Limes was the border of the Roman Empire.
Hundreds of men lived there behind walls and gates.
The word comes from the same Latin root as the English word “castle”.
questions.description: A place where Romans on the Rhine were supposed to feel at home, with the stress on “supposed to”.
questions.fun_fact: The Saalburg in the Taunus hills is a Kastell rebuilt around 1900 at the wish of Emperor Wilhelm II.

questions.question: You could pull up this bridge in front of the castle gate. Why?
wrong_answers: To protect it from the rain
To save space in the courtyard
hints: Many castles had a deep ditch in front of them.
When pulled up, it also blocked the gate.
Uninvited guests were meant to stay outside.
questions.description: A bridge with moods: sometimes it's there, sometimes it isn't.
questions.fun_fact: Drawbridges were moved with chains and counterweights, so just a few men could pull them up quickly.

questions.question: Around 387 BC, Celts sacked Rome. Which Germanic people were the next to do it, in 410?
hints: This people had a brother people with an almost identical name.
Their king was called Alaric.
Their kingdom later lay in Spain; their brothers in the east ruled Italy.
questions.description: Rome wasn't built in a day – and it wasn't sacked in a day either.
questions.fun_fact: Gothic architecture is named after the Goths, even though they had nothing to do with Gothic cathedrals.

questions.question: Charlemagne had his palace chapel built here, he is buried here, and in 2014 researchers measured his bones here. Which city is it?
hints: The city lies in the far west of Germany, near Belgium and the Netherlands.
It is home to Printen, a spiced gingerbread-like cookie.
In 1978 its cathedral became the first German site on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
questions.description: An emperor so great that, 1,200 years later, someone wanted to measure him again.
questions.fun_fact: The study found Charlemagne was about 1.84 m (6 ft) tall, a giant for his time.

questions.question: You're standing in Naumburg Cathedral in front of Uta, the famous stone figure of a cathedral founder. About how old is she?
hints: She dates from the Gothic period.
Her sculptor worked at the time of the Crusades.
She was made around the year 1250.
questions.description: She's been posing as a model forever and has never once complained about cold feet.
questions.fun_fact: Uta is known as “the most beautiful woman of the Middle Ages”, and Naumburg Cathedral has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018.

questions.question: First page, then squire, then knight. At about what age did a boy in the Middle Ages become a squire?
hints: Before that, he had already been a page for some years.
He had to be strong enough to carry his lord's armor and lance.
He was about the age of a teenager in middle school today.
questions.description: A knight-in-training whose full-time job is polishing armor.
questions.fun_fact: A squire was usually only made a knight at around age 21.

questions.question: In classic 35 mm film, each photo is 36 × 24 mm, like a “full-frame” sensor. What does that “35 mm” measure?
questions.answer: The total width of the film strip
wrong_answers: The focal length of the lens
hints: It has nothing to do with the lens, only with the film itself.
The name came from movies, long before anyone talked about photo sizes.
Lay the strip flat and measure it from one edge to the other: that's exactly the number.
questions.description: The little roll Grandpa's camera used to swallow, which today costs more than a restaurant lunch.
questions.fun_fact: 35 mm film came from the movies, and Oskar Barnack's Leica brought it to still photography in the 1920s.

questions.question: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale, who spins straw into gold on a wheel like this one?
hints: He helps a miller's daughter.
He is a small, strange little man.
The queen has to guess his name.
questions.description: A wheel that keeps turning without anyone going anywhere.
questions.fun_fact: In German, he is called “Rumpelstilzchen,” which roughly means “little rattling stilt.”

questions.question: It's made of metal, protects a knight from head to toe and is really heavy. What is it called?
hints: In castle museums it often stands on a stand.
It clanks when you walk.
Fairy tales talk about a “knight in shining …”.
questions.description: A pair of pajamas nobody would ever want to sleep in.
questions.fun_fact: A full suit of plate armor usually weighed about 20 to 25 kg (44 to 55 lb), less than many people think.

questions.question: Half-timbered houses like those in Quedlinburg have dark wooden beams in the walls, with clay or bricks between them. What are the beams for?
questions.answer: They hold up the whole house
hints: The panels between the beams are called “Gefache” in German.
When building, carpenters set up the beams first and only filled the panels afterward.
The beams are like a skeleton.
questions.description: A house that proudly shows off what other houses prefer to plaster over.
questions.fun_fact: Because the beams carry the weight, some half-timbered houses could be taken apart and rebuilt somewhere else.

questions.question: This glass dome has sat on top of the Reichstag building in Berlin since 1999. Which architect designed it?
hints: The architect is from Great Britain.
He also built the pickle-shaped London tower known as “The Gherkin.”
His last name is also an English word for caring for a child who isn't your own.
questions.description: A parliament with a bald head would look boring, so it got a glass hat.
questions.fun_fact: A cone of 360 mirrors inside the dome reflects daylight down into the Bundestag's main debating chamber.

questions.question: 2006 World Cup, quarterfinal against Argentina, penalty shootout in Berlin: goalkeeper Jens Lehmann pulled a note out of his sock. Why?
questions.answer: It said where the penalty takers usually shoot
wrong_answers: It listed the order of Germany's penalty takers
It was a good-luck letter from his kids
It had the tactics for extra time
hints: Germany won the shootout 4–2.
Goalkeeping coach Andreas Köpke had prepared it.
Lehmann wanted to know which corner to dive toward.
questions.description: Germany's most famous cheat sheet was never used in a classroom.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006 the note was auctioned for 1 million euros for charity, and today it is kept at the Haus der Geschichte museum in Bonn.

questions.question: “I'm about 7.5 cm (3 in) tall, almost twice the size of a Lego figure. I always smile and have no nose.” What am I?
hints: I'm made of plastic and have hands that can hold things.
I come as a knight, a firefighter, a pirate and much more.
I come from Zirndorf near Nuremberg and love playing in castles and on farms.
questions.description: A toy that has been in a good mood for decades, even when it's stuck under the sofa.
questions.fun_fact: The first Playmobil figures came out in 1974: a knight, a Native American and a construction worker.

questions.question: A red-haired kobold got stuck to the glue pot in master carpenter Eder's workshop. What did this do to Pumuckl?
questions.answer: He became visible to Meister Eder
wrong_answers: He could no longer make rhymes
He grew as big as a human
hints: The glue pot changed his life forever: from then on, he stayed in the workshop.
Under kobold law, he has belonged to Meister Eder ever since.
Before that, no human could see him.
questions.description: In a Munich workshop, getting stuck once turned out to be a stroke of luck.
questions.fun_fact: Ellis Kaut created Pumuckl in 1962, and at first he could only be heard on the radio.

questions.question: At the peak of the Berlin Airlift in 1949, about how often did a plane land in West Berlin?
hints: More than 2 million people had to be supplied by air.
Pilots flew on a tight, fixed schedule through three air corridors.
You could barely count to 60 before the next plane came in.
questions.description: Berlin once had raisins falling from the sky instead of raindrops.
questions.fun_fact: The blockade ended on May 12, 1949, but the flights kept going until September, just to be safe.

questions.question: When Germany reunited on October 3, 1990, one man became the first chancellor of the united country. Who?
hints: He came from Ludwigshafen in Rhineland-Palatinate.
He was in power for 16 years in total, from 1982 to 1998.
People also called him the “Chancellor of Unity”.
questions.description: Two become one: a sum that changed a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: The big celebration for the Day of German Unity takes place in a different German state every year.

questions.question: Which of these places in Germany saw big protests that were NOT against nuclear power?
hints: The protests there were about a different kind of energy.
It was about a village in the Rhineland.
The village was to make way for an open-pit lignite mine.
questions.description: Construction fences, banners and a great many people in rubber boots.
questions.fun_fact: Despite huge protests, Lützerath was cleared in January 2023.
