questions.question: Which of these photography books is NOT by the Brazilian Sebastião Salgado?
hints: Salgado spent years on huge projects shot around the world, always in black and white.
The odd one out is a famous 1950s book about a road trip.
It was made by the Swiss photographer Robert Frank while traveling across the United States.
questions.description: An economist who swapped numbers for black-and-white photos.
questions.fun_fact: Salgado and his wife Lélia replanted millions of trees on the family farm in Brazil, which had lost its forest.

questions.question: Evening TV: about how long does one episode of “Unser Sandmännchen” last?
hints: After it, children are supposed to go to bed.
It's longer than a TV commercial.
It's just long enough for a short story and a goodnight wish.
questions.description: The only TV star who puts the audience to sleep on purpose.
questions.fun_fact: The Sandmännchen first aired on East German TV on November 22, 1959.

questions.question: This is how the lying baron rode the cannonball. Who played him in the 1943 UFA color film “Münchhausen”?
hints: He was one of the biggest UFA stars of the 1930s and 1940s.
He sang “La Paloma” and “Auf der Reeperbahn nachts um halb eins”.
He was nicknamed “der blonde Hans” (blond Hans).
questions.description: Pulling yourself out of a swamp by your own hair takes a leading man with strong arms.
questions.fun_fact: The screenplay was written by Erich Kästner, who was banned from writing at the time, under the pen name Berthold Bürger.

questions.question: For actor Hardy Krüger, “Hardy” was just a short form. What was his real first name?
hints: Krüger was born in Berlin in 1928 and later made films in Hollywood too.
It's an old Germanic name, and “-hard” in it means something like “strong”.
The first part of the name is the German word for a male wild boar.
questions.description: A Hollywood name just sounds cooler than what's written in the baptism register.
questions.fun_fact: Hardy Krüger made “Hatari!” with John Wayne and for many years owned a farm in Tanzania at the foot of Mount Meru.

questions.question: You're at the movies watching Fatih Akin's “Head-On” (“Gegen die Wand”), fresh from winning the Golden Bear. What year is it?
hints: It was in the 2000s.
That same summer, Greece won the European soccer championship.
It was the year Facebook was founded.
questions.description: A love story that skips the gentle approach and goes straight for impact.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first German film in 18 years to win the Golden Bear at the Berlinale.

questions.question: Jella Haase was born here, played an ex-Stasi assassin here in the series “Kleo,” and filmed a Döblin adaptation here. Which city?
hints: The series “Kleo” is set around the fall of the Wall.
Alfred Döblin's most famous novel has a square in this city in its title.
The Brandenburg Gate stands here.
questions.description: An actress who never has to leave home for long to get to work.
questions.fun_fact: In “Berlin Alexanderplatz” (2020), Jella Haase played the character Mieze.

questions.question: This replica submarine stands at Bavaria Filmstadt. Who used it to shoot the 1981 film “Das Boot”?
hints: The director later moved to Hollywood.
He also made “The NeverEnding Story”.
His last name sounds northern German and ends in “-sen”.
questions.description: A place where you can dive down without getting wet.
questions.fun_fact: Wolfgang Petersen later made Hollywood films such as “Air Force One” and “Troy”.

questions.question: Max Ophüls, namesake of Saarbrücken's award for young filmmakers, directed three of these films. Which one did he NOT?
hints: The film you're looking for was made at the very start of sound film.
It is based on a novel by Heinrich Mann.
Director Josef von Sternberg made Marlene Dietrich world-famous with it.
questions.description: An award for young filmmakers, named after a man with a particularly elegant eye behind the camera.
questions.fun_fact: Max Ophüls was born in Saarbrücken in 1902 – that's why the festival takes place there.

questions.question: This German film star won the very first Oscar for Best Actor in 1929. In which country was he born?
hints: Surprisingly, it isn't Germany.
His birthplace lies on Lake Constance.
He was born in Rorschach.
questions.description: A man who carried the very first Best Actor Oscar home – but where exactly was home?
questions.fun_fact: Emil Jannings won his Oscar for two films at once: “The Way of All Flesh” and “The Last Command”.

questions.question: Three of these camera shots show a person at least down to the knees. Which one does NOT?
hints: Look for the closest shot.
It's the one soap operas use when someone cries.
It shows the face and little else.
questions.description: It's all about distance: some show all of you, others get close enough to count your pores.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain and France, the medium long shot is called the “American shot”, after Hollywood westerns, where it showed the cowboy's gun at the hip.

questions.question: Ravensburger has sold this card game since 1959. What is it called?
hints: It is often one of the very first games small children play with their family.
You always turn over two cards and look for matching pictures.
Even in Germany, its name is an English word for what your brain keeps.
questions.description: A game where grandparents suddenly lose to five-year-olds.
questions.fun_fact: A Swiss man, William Hurter, brought the idea for Memory to Ravensburger.

questions.question: I opened a small workshop in Stuttgart in 1886. Today my last name is on dishwashers and green power drills. Who am I?
hints: The company is also a huge supplier of car parts.
One of its early successes was an ignition device for engines.
The last name starts with B.
questions.description: A man whose name now shows up more often in kitchens and basements than in history books.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Bosch brought in the eight-hour workday at his company as early as 1906.

questions.question: Fressnapf is to dog food as Media Markt is to …?
hints: It's about what the store mainly sells.
The store's slogan is “Ich bin doch nicht blöd” (“I'm not stupid”).
People watch movies on it in the evening.
questions.description: A store where grown-ups stand in front of the shelves as long as kids do in front of the candy aisle.
questions.fun_fact: The first Media Markt opened in Munich in 1979.

questions.question: I was a pharmacist in Bielefeld and sold baking powder in little packets. Today my name is on pudding and frozen pizza. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 19th century.
On the packages, a doctor's title stands before my name.
My brand is called “Dr. …”
questions.description: A pharmacist who preferred making cakes rise to handing out pills.
questions.fun_fact: His baking powder “Backin” has been around since 1893.

questions.question: In 1932, I came up with a chocolate bar that fits into any jacket pocket without breaking. Who am I?
hints: My company is based in Waldenbuch, near Stuttgart.
The bar was meant to be handy for athletes and day-trippers.
My last name is the German word for “knight”.
questions.description: A woman who got chocolate into shape, quite literally.
questions.fun_fact: The slogan “Quadratisch. Praktisch. Gut.” (Square. Practical. Good.) was only added in 1970.

questions.question: Schleich from Schwäbisch Gmünd is known for figures like these. From the 1960s on, comic characters from Belgium made it famous. Which ones?
hints: The comics come from the artist Peyo.
They live in mushroom houses.
They are small and blue.
questions.description: A company whose shelves hold more animals than some zoos.
questions.fun_fact: Schleich has made hundreds of millions of Smurf figures.

questions.question: This inventor founded a telegraph company in Berlin in 1847 that still bears his name. Who is he?
hints: His company is today one of Germany's largest technology groups.
He discovered the principle of the dynamo.
The company was first called “… & Halske”.
questions.description: A gentleman with sideburns who sent messages racing through wires while others were still feeding carrier pigeons.
questions.fun_fact: In 1879, Werner von Siemens built the world's first electric railway for an exhibition in Berlin.

questions.question: Like Adolf Hennecke in 1948, you mine almost four times your daily quota. What were such model workers called in East Germany?
hints: Hennecke became the model for a whole movement, on the Soviet pattern.
The word describes someone full of energy and drive, eager to get things done.
The movement named after Hennecke was also called the “… movement”, with the word you're looking for in front.
questions.description: A man who turned one shift of coal into a whole movement.
questions.fun_fact: On October 13, 1948, Hennecke mined 24.4 cubic meters of coal in one shift; the quota was 6.3.

questions.question: You live in Dresden in 1985, and your antenna picks up no West German TV. What was the area mockingly called because of this?
hints: The name pokes fun at what people supposedly missed out on.
The region was too far from the TV towers in the West.
Anyone who didn't watch Western news supposedly had no idea what was going on.
questions.description: An area where only the East came out of the TV in the evening.
questions.fun_fact: People joked that the TV channel ARD stood for “Außer Raum Dresden”, meaning “except the Dresden area”.

questions.question: In a scene like this, with a very bright sky and very dark areas, what is your phone's HDR mode for?
questions.answer: To show detail in highlights and shadows at once
wrong_answers: To zoom in without losing quality
To make the photo file smaller
To take photos in black and white
hints: Without it, the sky turns white or the ground turns black.
The phone takes several photos with different amounts of light and combines them.
The letters stand for “high dynamic range.”
questions.description: Three letters your phone turns on when the sky and the shadows can't agree.
questions.fun_fact: As early as the 1850s, Gustave Le Gray combined two negatives to capture both the sky and the sea in one picture.

questions.question: A factory often built me, sometimes with columns like a palace. My hall hosted dances, theater, Jugendweihe and painting clubs. What am I?
hints: I was there for all ages, not just for children.
In many East German towns, I was the center of free-time life.
My name tells you I was all about art, music and the stage.
questions.description: A building where in one weekend you could dance, paint and officially become a grown-up.
questions.fun_fact: Many former Kulturhäuser in eastern Germany are now protected historic monuments.

questions.question: After the Thälmann Pioneers, most GDR teenagers joined the Free German Youth (FDJ). At what age did they usually join?
hints: By then they had already been Pioneers for several years.
It was roughly the age of the Jugendweihe.
It usually happened in 8th grade.
questions.description: A blue shirt instead of a red neckerchief: the fashion changed as you got older.
questions.fun_fact: The FDJ's blue shirt had a rising sun badge on its sleeve.

questions.question: East German apartment ads often said “Zweiraumwohnung,” typical for Plattenbau blocks and still common in the East. What does it mean?
questions.answer: Two rooms plus kitchen and bathroom
hints: In the West people usually just call it something else.
The two counts something every apartment has.
In the West it would be called a “Zweizimmerwohnung.”
questions.description: A word every real estate agent in the East understands and everyone in the West has to do the math on first.
questions.fun_fact: In the East people often say “Raum” where Westerners say “Zimmer,” though both simply mean “room.”

review.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The answer is correct: a Zweiraumwohnung has two living or sleeping rooms plus a separate kitchen and bathroom, the same as a Zweizimmerwohnung. The wrong answers are wrong and the fun fact is fine. The problems are in the hints and description. Hint 2 ('the two counts something every apartment has') is misleading, because the 'two' does not count the kitchen and bathroom that every apartment has. Hint 1 is vague. Hint 3 almost gives the answer away. The description says Westerners 'have to do the math', but the term is simply equivalent to Zweizimmerwohnung, so no calculation is needed.

questions.question: Pastor Christian Führer held a peace prayer every Monday, and in 1989 it grew into Leipzig's Monday demonstrations. In which church?
hints: The church stands right in the center of Leipzig.
It is not the church where Bach was Thomaskantor.
It is named after the saint whose day is December 6.
questions.description: A pastor who drew so many people to church on Mondays that afterwards they didn't want to go home.
questions.fun_fact: A sign outside the church read “open to all”, and that was Führer's whole program.

questions.question: At the Leipzig Monday demonstrations, “Wir sind das Volk” (We are the people) later became “Wir sind ein Volk” (We are one people). When did the new chant start?
hints: The new chant called for reunification.
First the border had to be open.
It was a few weeks after November 9.
questions.description: Change one tiny word, and suddenly it's about all of Germany.
questions.fun_fact: On October 3, 1990, the wish came true: the GDR joined the Federal Republic.

questions.question: With “Zersetzung” (“decomposition”), the Stasi secretly unsettled opponents instead of jailing them. Since when had the Stasi had its own directive for this?
hints: East Germany wanted to look good internationally at the time.
Many Western countries had just recognized East Germany, and it had joined the United Nations.
Honecker had already been in power for a few years.
questions.description: If your favorite mug is suddenly in the wrong cupboard, maybe it wasn’t your roommate.
questions.fun_fact: Directive 1/76 listed methods such as spreading targeted rumors, damaging reputations and arranging failures at work.

questions.question: This boot print was photographed in 1969. Where exactly was it made?
hints: It was on the Moon, during Apollo 11.
The Moon’s “seas” are dark plains without a single drop of water.
The landing site was named after that same sea.
questions.description: The most famous footprint in the universe, and it isn’t on any Walk of Fame.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Aldrin photographed his own footprint to study how moon dust packs down, not for the family photo album.

questions.question: I was born in Romania, outsmarted the limit of the light microscope in Göttingen and won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Who am I?
hints: My method is called STED microscopy.
I make structures in living cells visible that are smaller than half the wavelength of light.
My last name is the German word for “bright”.
questions.description: A scientist who proved that “impossible” sometimes just means “not yet”.
questions.fun_fact: At first he found no job in Germany for his idea, so he did his research for some years in Turku, Finland.

questions.question: In Göttingen, Max Born explained the wave function of quantum mechanics as a probability. In which decade was that?
hints: It was before the Nazis forced Born into exile.
Heisenberg and Schrödinger put forward their theories in the same decade.
It was the decade Germans call the “Golden Twenties.”
questions.description: A physicist who stopped trusting electrons.
questions.fun_fact: Max Born's granddaughter was the singer Olivia Newton-John, famous from the film “Grease.”

questions.question: The Nuremberg Chronicle, with over 1,800 woodcuts, was printed in Nuremberg. In which year?
hints: It is one of the incunabula, the books from the earliest days of printing.
Gutenberg's Bible was almost 40 years old by then.
It was one year after Columbus reached America.
questions.description: An encyclopedia from a time when links were still carved out of wood.
questions.fun_fact: Many cities in the book share the same woodcut: the printers simply reused one picture for several places.

questions.question: I lived in Hanover, and in 1703 I described a number system made only of 0 and 1. Every computer uses it today. Who am I?
hints: I lived at the same time as Isaac Newton and argued with him.
I invented calculus independently of Newton.
A famous butter cookie from Hanover bears my name.
questions.description: Thanks to him, the whole world could do its math on two fingers.
questions.fun_fact: Leibniz saw 1 and 0 as a picture of creation: God and nothingness.

questions.question: You open the door, cold air hits you, and inside are milk and butter. Which kitchen appliance is this?
hints: Almost every kitchen has one.
Yogurt stays fresh in here for a long time.
Munich engineer Carl von Linde invented the cooling machine inside it.
questions.description: The kitchen: the only room kids happily tiptoe into in the middle of the night.
questions.fun_fact: Carl von Linde's cooling machine first cooled breweries' beer cellars, long before kitchens had refrigerators.

questions.question: German kids learn the planets with “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel.” Which planet does “Nachthimmel” stand for?
hints: “Nachthimmel” is the last word of the sentence.
The order goes outward from the Sun.
The first letter of each word is also the first letter of a planet.
questions.description: A sentence dads say without ever having owned a telescope.
questions.fun_fact: Neptune was discovered in 1846 at the Berlin Observatory: Johann Gottfried Galle found it right where Le Verrier had calculated it would be.

questions.question: It flickers over the moor at night, lures walkers off the safe path, and old legends call it a restless soul. What is it?
hints: Today it is explained by gases rising from the swamp.
If you follow it, you are sure to get lost.
Its German name, Irrlicht, means a light that leads you astray.
questions.description: A night light you’d rather not put in a child’s bedroom.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists think swamp gases such as methane, catching fire by themselves, are behind the will-o’-the-wisp.

questions.question: According to legend, in which mountain range does the mountain spirit Rübezahl play his tricks?
hints: Today these mountains lie on the border between Poland and the Czech Republic.
Their highest peak is the Schneekoppe.
Their German name fits a spirit of gigantic size.
questions.description: Count turnips out loud around here and you're asking for trouble.
questions.fun_fact: In the legend, “Rübezahl” was a mocking nickname, and anyone who called him that risked the mountain spirit's anger.

questions.question: I'm an old imperial city that grew rich from silver in my mountain. On my guild house squats a little man who poops out gold coins. Who am I?
hints: I lie on the northern edge of the Harz Mountains.
My Rammelsberg mine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
My name comes from the little Gose River.
questions.description: Here the saying “money doesn't smell” is meant quite literally.
questions.fun_fact: One theory says the Dukatenmännchen on the Kaiserworth house is a reminder of the city's right to mint its own coins.

questions.question: This figure with a pointed cap stands in many German gardens. What is it called?
hints: He's pretty small.
He often holds a shovel, a lantern or a wheelbarrow.
In legends, his relatives work deep down in mines.
questions.description: The only garden resident who never has to mow the lawn.
questions.fun_fact: The first clay garden gnomes were made around 1872 in Gräfenroda in Thuringia.

questions.question: I was the first human to travel to space, and from up there I said: “The Earth is blue.” Who am I?
hints: My trip was in 1961, before anyone had walked on the Moon.
I came from the Soviet Union.
My first name starts with Y, and my spaceship was called Vostok 1.
questions.description: The first tourist who looked out the window and found out home had a whole new paint job.
questions.fun_fact: Gagarin's trip around the Earth lasted only about 108 minutes.

questions.question: It hits suddenly when you bend down or lift something heavy, and people used to think witches shot it at you. Where does a Hexenschuss hurt?
hints: It usually strikes with no warning, after one clumsy move.
Many people find that warmth helps, like a hot-water bottle.
It usually sits low down, just above your bottom.
questions.description: A witch's curse that needs no broomstick and no magic wand.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors call a Hexenschuss “lumbago,” from the Latin word “lumbus,” meaning loin.

questions.question: I don't live in the sea but in rivers and ponds, and I have long hair and a fish tail. Who am I?
hints: I love to sing and comb my hair on the bank.
My sisters in the sea are called mermaids.
My name begins with N.
questions.description: Fairy-tale creatures sadly don't carry ID cards, so you have to recognize them some other way.
questions.fun_fact: In old legends, you can spot a nixie who comes on land to dance by the wet hem of her skirt.

questions.question: I'm invisible, I slam doors, knock plates off the shelf and rumble through the whole house. Who am I?
hints: Above all, I do one thing: make noise.
I don't live out in nature but with people.
In German, “poltern” means to crash and bang about, which is exactly what I do.
questions.description: A roommate who never pays rent and still knocks everything over.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Poltergeist” was taken into English without any change.

questions.question: You're standing in front of the Imperial Crown, the most important piece of the regalia of the Holy Roman emperors. About how old is it?
hints: It comes from the Middle Ages.
It was probably made in the time of the Ottonian emperors.
It was made around the turn of the first millennium.
questions.description: A hat that's a lot older than anything in your grandma's closet.
questions.fun_fact: For almost 400 years, from 1424 to 1796, the imperial regalia were kept in Nuremberg.

questions.question: The Basic Law was proclaimed on May 23, 1949, in the city with this monument. Which city is it?
hints: The city lies on the Rhine.
The monument shows a famous composer who was born here.
For decades it was the capital of West Germany.
questions.description: A city that had its moment on the big stage and stayed modest anyway.
questions.fun_fact: In Bonn, the Parliamentary Council met in a former teacher-training college that later became part of the Bundeshaus, the federal parliament building.

questions.question: Until 1918, Prussia's noble upper chamber met in this building on Leipziger Straße in Berlin. Today the Bundesrat meets there. What was it first called?
hints: The name tells you who used to get a seat there.
Members got in by birth or were appointed by the king, not elected.
This chamber had no place for ladies.
questions.description: A house that used to be full of nobles and is now full of states.
questions.fun_fact: Its elected counterpart, the Prussian House of Representatives, stands right next door, and Berlin's state parliament meets there today.

questions.question: You're in front of the Reichstag building, reading “Dem Deutschen Volke” (To the German People). Which emperor is said to have long blocked the inscription?
hints: He openly made fun of the new parliament building.
He was a grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.
He was the last German emperor.
questions.description: Giant letters that one emperor spent years steering clear of.
questions.fun_fact: A Berlin family firm cast the bronze letters, supposedly from cannons captured in the wars against Napoleon.

questions.question: In 1985, German President Richard von Weizsäcker called May 8 a “day of liberation”. What does this day mark?
questions.answer: The end of World War II in Europe
wrong_answers: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The founding of the Federal Republic
The end of World War I
hints: Weizsäcker was speaking on the 40th anniversary.
He meant liberation from National Socialism.
On this day, the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht took effect.
questions.description: A date whose name Germany had to think about for decades.
questions.fun_fact: Berlin made May 8 a one-off public holiday twice: in 2020 and 2025, for the 75th and 80th anniversaries.

questions.question: For a Bundestag election, the polling card must arrive in your mailbox at least how many days before election day?
hints: You should have enough time to apply for a mail-in vote.
Just a few days ahead would be far too tight for voting by mail.
It's exactly three weeks.
questions.description: Mail that smells like an election campaign but still isn't junk mail.
questions.fun_fact: If you lose your polling card, you can still vote: just bring your ID card.

questions.question: In which century was the book published that begins “Somewhere in La Mancha, in a place whose name I do not care to remember…”?
hints: It is a Spanish novel about a knight who reads too many books.
It came out more than a hundred years after Columbus reached America.
Its first part came out in 1605.
questions.description: A place so famous that its author didn't even want to say its name.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes and Shakespeare died in 1616, only one day apart by their official dates.

questions.question: Which flowers is this chain woven from?
hints: This flower blooms in the lawn almost all year round.
It has white petals and a yellow center.
Its English name comes from “day's eye”, because it opens with the morning sun.
questions.description: Jewelry you don't buy at a jeweler's: you just pick it off the lawn.
questions.fun_fact: Daisies close their flowers at night and when it rains.

questions.question: In high summer, the risk of forest fires in Germany is often high. Who in the forest is doing something wrong?
wrong_answers: A hiker with a water bottle
A cyclist on the forest trail
A family with a picnic blanket
hints: It's about something that can burn.
Dry grass and leaves catch fire very quickly.
Someone is about to toast Stockbrot (bread dough on a stick).
questions.description: The forest gets very thirsty in summer, and some visitors don't make things any easier.
questions.fun_fact: In many German states, open fires are banned even up to 100 meters (330 feet) from the edge of a forest.

questions.question: Corn like this grows in many fields in Germany. What is it mostly grown for there?
wrong_answers: Corn on the cob for grilling
hints: People eat only a small part of it.
Often the whole plant is chopped into small pieces.
Cows in the barn are happy about it.
questions.description: Huge green walls in the fields, and hardly anyone asks who eats all of it.
questions.fun_fact: A large part of the rest of the corn ends up in biogas plants, where it is turned into electricity.

questions.question: If you touch this plant, you get itchy bumps on your skin. What is it called?
hints: It often grows along paths and fences.
Peacock butterfly caterpillars love to eat its leaves.
Its full English name tells you what it does to your skin.
questions.description: A plant that fights back if you get too close.
questions.fun_fact: You can make tea and soup from nettles, and long ago people even made cloth for clothes from them.

questions.question: You pick some fresh dandelions. For which pets are they NOT a typical food?
hints: Three of these animals eat plants.
One of these animals mostly needs food other than greens.
This pet purrs.
questions.description: A yellow lion that would rather live on the lawn than on the savanna.
questions.fun_fact: The dandelion got its name from its jagged leaves, which are said to look like lion's teeth (French “dent de lion”).

questions.question: This cake has shortcrust pastry, a meringue topping and sour, green, slightly hairy berries the size of marbles. Which berries?
hints: These berries grow in many German gardens.
The bush pricks you when you pick them.
Their English name hides a farm bird.
questions.description: A cake that makes you pull a face at the first bite, out of joy, of course.
questions.fun_fact: Gooseberries don't only come in green, but also in yellow and even red.

questions.question: This flower used to turn whole grain fields red. What is it called?
hints: It likes to grow alongside the blue cornflower.
Its petals are as thin as tissue paper.
The seeds of its relatives end up on bread rolls.
questions.description: A flower that loves to join the summer party in the fields without being invited.
questions.fun_fact: Its German name, Klatschmohn, probably comes from the clapping sound (“Klatsch”) a petal makes when you slap it on your hand.

questions.question: Champignons are sold in almost every German supermarket. What are they?
hints: You can eat them raw or fried.
You usually find them in the vegetable section.
They have a cap and a stem.
questions.description: Sounds like a champion, but just lies there quietly in the supermarket.
questions.fun_fact: “Champignon” is simply the French word for “mushroom.”

questions.question: My real name was Ralph Möbius. With Ton Steine Scherben I sang “Keine Macht für Niemand,” later “Junimond” solo. Who am I?
hints: My band formed around 1970 in West Berlin.
As a solo artist, I sang that I wanted to be “König von Deutschland.”
My stage name sounds like a city in Brazil.
questions.description: A man who trusted authority so little that he even got rid of his own name.
questions.fun_fact: From the mid-1970s, Ton Steine Scherben lived together on a farm in Fresenhagen in North Frisia.

questions.question: In 1983, Peter Schilling sent Major Tom floating “völlig losgelöst” (completely detached). Which 1969 song did this character first appear in?
hints: The original song is by a British pop star.
It came out shortly before the first Moon landing.
David Bowie sang it, and its title hints at something strange in space.
questions.description: A man in a spacesuit who'd rather ignore the radio link to Earth.
questions.fun_fact: The English version, “Major Tom (Coming Home),” even made it into the US charts.

questions.question: At my farewell match I said: “I made mistakes and I paid for them, but the ball doesn't get stained.” Who am I?
hints: I said goodbye at Boca Juniors' stadium, in 2001.
I was a World Cup champion in Mexico in 1986.
I became famous for “the Hand of God” and the “Goal of the Century.”
questions.description: A ball with more dignity than plenty of the people who kick it.
questions.fun_fact: Maradona's farewell match was at La Bombonera in November 2001, in front of a packed stadium.

questions.question: Which band from Magdeburg had a number-one hit in 2005 with “Durch den Monsun”? Its singer has a twin brother on guitar.
hints: The band members were still teenagers back then.
The twins are called Bill and Tom Kaulitz.
The band's name contains a Japanese city and a place to stay.
questions.description: A weather report that played in every kid's bedroom in 2005.
questions.fun_fact: Bill Kaulitz was only 15 when “Durch den Monsun” came out.

questions.question: In 1984, Klaus Lage sang: “Tausendmal berührt, tausendmal ist nix passiert … und es hat Zoom gemacht.” What does “Zoom” mean here?
questions.answer: Two people suddenly fall in love
hints: It's about two people who have known each other for a long time.
After a thousand nights, suddenly everything is different.
It's about butterflies in your stomach.
questions.description: A chorus that has been stuck in German heads since 1984, like gum under a school desk.
questions.fun_fact: The lyrics were written by Diether Dehm, who later became a member of the German parliament.

questions.question: Germany won this music contest with Nicole in 1982 and with Lena in 2010. What is it called?
hints: Here, countries compete against each other.
The show airs once a year in spring and has well over 100 million viewers.
Lena won it with “Satellite” in Oslo.
questions.description: A TV night full of glitter, wind machines and suspense until the very last second.
questions.fun_fact: Lena competed again in 2011 as the defending champion and finished tenth.

questions.question: Smudo has been rapping since the late 1980s in one of Germany's first big hip-hop groups. Which of these hits is NOT by his band?
hints: Smudo's band has four members.
The song you're looking for is by a band from Hamburg.
It's by Fettes Brot.
questions.description: A rapper who also puts the pedal to the metal on the racetrack.
questions.fun_fact: Smudo also races cars, including in the 24-hour race at the Nürburgring.

questions.question: Posters were stuck all over Berlin's buildings until Ernst Litfaß put up his columns in 1855. Who could post notices on them for free?
hints: Litfaß could only put up his columns because the authorities agreed to it.
This group wasn't selling anything. It wanted to tell all Berliners about official orders.
They got to post their official notices for free as thanks for the permission.
questions.description: A column that carries more paper than a student's backpack right before summer break.
questions.fun_fact: During the war of 1870, Litfaß posted the latest news on his columns as special editions, and Berliners crowded around to read them.

questions.question: “We're full of witches, wolves and princesses. The Brothers Grimm collected us over 200 years ago.” What are we?
hints: We often begin with the same words.
“Once upon a time …”
Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel and Gretel are among us.
questions.description: Two brothers, one hobby: listening to other people and writing everything down.
questions.fun_fact: The Brothers Grimm also started a huge dictionary that wasn't finished until 1961, more than 120 years after they began.

questions.question: The French philosopher Voltaire spent a few years as the guest of Frederick the Great in Potsdam. When did this stay begin?
hints: Frederick was already king by then.
Frederick reigned from 1740.
It was shortly before the Seven Years’ War.
questions.description: A king and a mocker under one roof: what could possibly go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: The friendship ended in a quarrel: in 1753, Frederick had Voltaire detained in Frankfurt on his way home.

questions.question: At Easter, children build it from moss or grass in the yard so the Easter Bunny can put something in it. What is it?
hints: It is round and soft and padded inside.
On Easter morning, there are colorful eggs in it.
Birds build something like this for their eggs, but from twigs.
questions.description: For a bunny that never lays a single egg, he sure hands out a lot of them.
questions.fun_fact: The egg-bringing Easter Bunny was already written about in Germany in the 17th century.

questions.question: The “Bundschuh” was a secret alliance of rebel peasants on the Upper Rhine. Which group, by contrast, was NOT an alliance of rebel peasants?
hints: The group you're looking for had powerful members.
It was founded in 1531 to defend the new faith.
Its members were Protestant princes and cities.
questions.description: Secret societies armed with pitchforks instead of passwords.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Bundschuh” comes from the laced peasant shoe that the plotters painted on their banner.

questions.question: In 1521, Luther was told to take back his writings before Emperor Charles V, refused and was outlawed. What is this assembly called?
hints: The assembly met in an old bishop's city with a large cathedral.
Luther is said to have declared there: “Here I stand, I can do no other.”
The city lies in Rhineland-Palatinate, not far from Mannheim.
questions.description: A monk against an emperor: who will blink first?
questions.fun_fact: On his way home, his own prince had him fake-kidnapped and hidden at Wartburg Castle.

questions.question: The monk Tetzel sold them, and people said: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.” What did Luther aim his theses against?
hints: It was about money and sins.
People believed it let them buy their way out of punishment for their sins.
The slips of paper were called Ablassbriefe.
questions.description: A note on a church door that turned a whole country upside down.
questions.fun_fact: Money from these sales was also meant to help pay for the new St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.

questions.question: You're in Munich having a classic Weißwurst breakfast. What traditionally does NOT belong on the table?
hints: Three of the four are almost a must at a Weißwurst breakfast.
The answer is a side dish you'd rather eat with Schweinshaxe or Bratwurst.
It's sour and made from white cabbage.
questions.description: A breakfast where the Bavarian alarm clock goes off, without mercy, at twelve o'clock.
questions.fun_fact: An old rule says Weißwürste must not “hear the noon bells,” so you eat them before midday.

questions.question: At a German snack stand, what meat is the breaded schnitzel in a Schnitzelbrötchen like this one usually made from?
hints: Real Wiener Schnitzel is NOT made from it.
In Germany it's the cheapest and most common meat for schnitzel.
The animal goes “oink.”
questions.description: A hot lunch dressed up as a packed sandwich.
questions.fun_fact: A pork schnitzel may not be called “Wiener Schnitzel,” only “Schnitzel Wiener Art” (Viennese-style).

questions.question: It cooks in a pot with the lid shut, gets a crispy salt crust on the bottom and comes with wine sauce in the Palatinate. What is a Dampfnudel made of?
hints: Dampfnudeln are popular in Bavaria too, and people eat them sweet or savory.
The same dough is used for Buchteln or for the base of a Bienenstich.
This dough often needs a small cube from the refrigerated section that makes it grow.
questions.description: A specialty where the pot lid is holier than the Sunday roast.
questions.fun_fact: If you lift the lid too early while making Dampfnudeln, they may collapse.

questions.question: Swabian potato salad is lukewarm, glossy and juicy, with no mayonnaise. What is poured in with the vinegar and oil instead?
hints: It's poured over the potatoes while warm.
It's often served on its own as a soup with noodles or dumplings.
It's simmered from beef, bones and soup vegetables.
questions.description: A salad that has to be “schlonzig” in Swabia, or there's trouble.
questions.fun_fact: “Schlonzig” is Swabian for nicely slippery and juicy, which is exactly how the salad must be.

questions.question: Which country's national anthem begins with the words “Gloria al bravo pueblo” (“Glory to the brave people”)?
hints: It is a neighbor of Colombia.
Simón Bolívar was born there.
Its capital is Caracas.
questions.description: An anthem that opens by congratulating everyone, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: “Gloria al bravo pueblo” became the official national anthem in 1881, though the song dates from the time of independence.

questions.question: What traditionally goes inside a Bratapfel like the one in the photo?
hints: A Bratapfel is a dessert.
The filling tastes sweet and like Christmas.
It contains dried grapes.
questions.description: An apple that would rather spend the winter in the oven than on the tree.
questions.fun_fact: Tart varieties like Boskop are popular for Bratäpfel because they turn soft in the oven without falling apart.

questions.question: It's baked flat on a sheet pan, has little dimples filled with sugar and almonds, and is served at weddings in northern Germany. Which cake is it?
hints: It's made from yeast dough and has no filling.
You press the dimples into the dough with your finger.
Into the dimples go little flakes of a yellow spread.
questions.description: A cake where you're allowed to poke holes with your finger without getting in trouble.
questions.fun_fact: In northern Germany, Butterkuchen was also served at funerals, so it was sometimes called “Beerdigungskuchen” (funeral cake).

questions.question: It's baked in a two-part mold, dusted with powdered sugar and often carries a little flag. What is this Easter lamb made of?
hints: It sits on the table at Easter breakfast.
You eat it in slices, like marble cake.
It's mixed from butter, sugar, eggs and flour.
questions.description: A lamb that never stood in a meadow but still loves a coat of powdered-sugar snow.
questions.fun_fact: The little flag on the Easter lamb is an old Christian symbol of the Resurrection.

questions.question: You order it at stalls in Nuremberg, it fits in one hand, and mustard goes with it. What do you get with “Drei im Weggla”?
questions.answer: Three bratwursts in a bread roll
wrong_answers: Three Lebkuchen in a paper bag
hints: “Weggla” is Franconian for something from the bakery.
It's savory, not sweet.
The sausages are only as long as a finger.
questions.description: An order in Franconian dialect that leaves newcomers at the stall scratching their heads.
questions.fun_fact: Nürnberger Rostbratwürste are protected and may only be made in Nuremberg.

questions.question: At a beer garden you order “Wurstsalat Schweizer Art.” Besides sausage, onions and vinegar, what goes into it?
hints: The name points to a country famous for one particular food.
This ingredient often has holes.
Emmentaler is the usual choice.
questions.description: A salad that knows vegetables mostly from hearsay.
questions.fun_fact: The classic Bavarian Wurstsalat uses Regensburger or Lyoner sausage, cut into strips or slices.

questions.question: Prussian soldiers dug this silver tableware out of the ground near Hildesheim in 1868. Where does it come from?
hints: The treasure is about 2,000 years old.
Many pieces show gods and mythical creatures from ancient legends.
On one bowl sits Minerva, the goddess from Rome.
questions.description: Digging for a shooting range and finding Grandma’s good silverware is lucky. Except this never belonged to any grandma.
questions.fun_fact: The Hildesheim Treasure is considered the largest find of Roman silver outside the Roman Empire, and today it is kept in Berlin.

questions.question: In 1999, Andreas Gursky photographed a discount store in Los Angeles with endless colorful shelves. What is the picture called?
hints: Gursky belongs to the Düsseldorf School of Photography.
A print of the picture sold at auction in 2007 for over 3 million US dollars.
Everything in this store cost less than a dollar.
questions.description: Endless shelves, razor sharp, and the picture itself costs a few million.
questions.fun_fact: Gursky studied in Düsseldorf under Bernd and Hilla Becher, famous for their photos of water towers and mine winding towers.

questions.question: I was the second man to walk on the Moon, and I called it “magnificent desolation.” Who am I?
hints: I flew on Apollo 11 in 1969.
I stepped onto the Moon a few minutes after my crewmate.
A famous toy from “Toy Story” has my first name.
questions.description: A five-star review for a place with no air, no water and no Wi-Fi.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Lightyear from “Toy Story” was named after Buzz Aldrin.

questions.question: Easter is to Osterlamm as a wedding is to …?
hints: You're looking for a bake for a big celebration.
It's often white and richly decorated.
It often has several tiers, and the couple cut it together.
questions.description: A bake most people order only once in their life. Hopefully, anyway.
questions.fun_fact: An old custom says that whoever has their hand on top when cutting the cake will be the boss in the marriage.

questions.question: Its short-passing game was called the “Kreisel” (spinning top), and its six titles from 1934 to 1942 made it the top club of that era. Which club?
hints: The club comes from the Ruhr area.
Its fans also call themselves “Knappen”.
It plays in a big arena in Gelsenkirchen.
questions.description: A club that was winning titles back when Grandpa still played ball in short pants.
questions.fun_fact: The “04” in the name stands for the year the club was founded: 1904.

questions.question: What was this glass building in Dresden opened for in 2001?
hints: People inside worked on wooden parquet floors instead of concrete.
Customers could watch their own ordered piece being finished.
First the Phaeton luxury sedan was made here, later electric Golfs.
questions.description: A workplace where you really can't hide anything.
questions.fun_fact: For years, parts arrived on a special freight tram, the “CarGoTram”, right across Dresden.

questions.question: The church tower in Bad Frankenhausen leans more than the one in Pisa. Which rock in the ground beneath it is to blame?
hints: The tower stands by the Kyffhäuser hills in Thuringia.
Hollows form under the tower because groundwater washes something away.
Bad Frankenhausen is a spa town known for its salty healing water, the “Sole”.
questions.description: A church tower that has clearly been standing on one leg for too long.
questions.fun_fact: The tip of the tower hangs more than 4 m (13 ft) off vertical, and steel structures keep it standing.

questions.question: In Stuttgart there's a silver museum with a star on its roof. You ride up and walk down spiral ramps. What does it show?
hints: Stuttgart is a city of engineers and factories.
The star is the logo of a famous company from Stuttgart.
One of the first motor vehicles, built by Carl Benz, is on display there too.
questions.description: A museum you visit from the top down, like a cake you eat cream first.
questions.fun_fact: The museum's shape is based on a double helix, like DNA.

questions.question: Here you see part of a famous bridge. In which city does it stand?
hints: Huge container ships pass underneath the bridge.
The bridge spans one arm of a big river.
The city on the Elbe likes to call itself the “Gateway to the World”.
questions.description: A bridge so high that even giants don't have to duck.
questions.fun_fact: The Köhlbrand Bridge opened in 1974 and is about 3.6 km (2.2 miles) long.

questions.question: What major event was this tent roof in Munich built for?
hints: A whole new park, with its own subway connection, was built for the event.
Next to it stands a TV tower almost 300 m (nearly 1,000 ft) tall.
Athletes from all over the world competed here for gold, silver and bronze.
questions.description: A roof that looks like a giant spider went on vacation in Munich.
questions.fun_fact: The tent roof was designed by Günter Behnisch and Frei Otto and is made of thousands of acrylic glass panels.

questions.question: Hamburg's port has huge cranes as tall as high-rise buildings. What are they mainly used for?
wrong_answers: Lifting ships out of the water
hints: They stand right at the water's edge, next to big ships.
They work day and night so the ships can leave again quickly.
They lift big, colorful metal boxes full of goods from all over the world.
questions.description: Steel giants that never clock out, not even on Sundays.
questions.fun_fact: The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest seaport.

questions.question: In a car, the pedal farthest to the right is pressed with the right foot. What happens when you press it?
wrong_answers: The car turns on its lights
hints: On the Autobahn you need this pedal especially often.
The engine hums louder.
Afterward, the speedometer shows a higher number.
questions.description: Down in the footwell, a little thing is waiting for its big moment.
questions.fun_fact: People say “step on the gas” even in electric cars, which don't burn any gas at all.

questions.question: A road is closed for construction, and yellow signs with arrows point another way. What is this other way called?
hints: You still reach your goal, just not the usual way.
This way often takes a bit longer.
It leads you around the construction site.
questions.description: When your GPS suddenly gets grumpy and has to recalculate everything.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, temporary detours, for example around construction, are usually marked with yellow signs so they stand out right away.

questions.question: Which video game character has the motto “Gotta go fast!”?
hints: He runs so fast he curls up into a little ball.
He collects golden rings.
He is a blue hedgehog.
questions.description: Someone who has never once had to wait for anything to load.
questions.fun_fact: Sonic is blue because that was the color of the logo of Sega, the company that created him.

questions.question: A defender accidentally kicks the ball into his own goal. Who does the goal count for?
hints: The referee lets this goal stand.
The scorer's team is definitely not cheering.
It's an unwanted gift to the opponents.
questions.description: A goal after which the scorer would love to sink into the grass.
questions.fun_fact: An own goal is not credited to any player of the team that benefits, so it never shows up in the top scorer list.

questions.question: July 1990: Helmut Kohl, in a cardigan, meets Mikhail Gorbachev in the Caucasus. Which alliance may a united Germany then belong to?
hints: With this, Gorbachev made a big concession to the West.
The alliance was founded in 1949.
A military alliance based in Brussels.
questions.description: World history in a wool sweater: knitwear can do more than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: The meeting took place in Arkhyz, a small village in the Caucasus.

questions.question: The twins Silvania and Dakaria move to Germany with their family. Their mother is human, their father isn't. What are the two girls?
hints: The book series is by Franziska Gehm.
The family moves to a small German town and tries to fit in with normal people.
Their father sleeps in a coffin, and they can't stand garlic.
questions.description: Two sisters who bring more than just cardboard boxes when they move.
questions.fun_fact: The series was also made into a movie in 2012.

questions.question: Pixi books are square. About how wide is a Pixi book?
hints: It fits easily in a jacket pocket.
Pixi books are made for small children and often sit by the supermarket checkout.
It is about as wide as an adult's palm.
questions.description: Square, practical, good, but sadly not made of chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: The Carlsen publishing house has been making Pixi books since 1954.

questions.question: Die drei ???, TKKG and Hanni und Nanni: which audio drama label released these cassettes?
hints: The label has been around since the 1960s.
Benjamin Blümchen and Bibi Blocksberg came out on a different label.
The label shares its name with a continent.
questions.description: More crimes were solved on tape here than at any police station.
questions.fun_fact: Die drei ??? are far more successful in Germany than in the USA, where the books come from.

questions.question: This giant wine barrel sits in the cellar of a famous castle. Which one?
hints: Today's barrel was built in 1751.
Down in the town below, the Neckar River flows.
The town has Germany's oldest university.
questions.description: Someone clearly ordered way too much wine and couldn't fit it in the fridge.
questions.fun_fact: The Great Barrel holds about 220,000 liters (58,000 gallons), and in front of it stands a figure of the court jester Perkeo, who is said to have guarded it.

questions.question: This golden figure stands on a column in the heart of Munich. Who does it show?
hints: An elector had the column put up as a thank-you during the Thirty Years' War.
The square is also home to the New Town Hall with its Glockenspiel.
Munich's Frauenkirche is dedicated to her as well.
questions.description: She has stood at the very top for centuries and never once got scared of heights.
questions.fun_fact: The Mariensäule (Mary's Column) has stood on the square since 1638.

questions.question: He founded Munich, made Braunschweig his seat and put up a famous bronze statue there. What was Duke Henry's nickname?
hints: He lived in the 12th century and quarreled with Emperor Barbarossa.
“The Proud” was his father.
His nickname is an animal known as the king of the beasts.
questions.description: A duke who picked a fight with the emperor and still shapes a whole city today.
questions.fun_fact: Braunschweig still calls itself the “Löwenstadt” (Lion City), and the bronze statue on the Burgplatz is a copy: the original is inside Dankwarderode Castle.

questions.question: In which book series does Mortimer Morrison bring children talking companions, each one belonging to exactly one child?
hints: The animals come from a mysterious pet shop.
Since 2021, the stories have also been in movie theaters.
The stories take place at Winterstein School.
questions.description: Reading for everyone who secretly hopes their stuffed animal will talk back one day.
questions.fun_fact: As soon as strangers look, the animals freeze and look just like ordinary stuffed animals.

questions.question: From 375 on, the Huns pushed into Europe, the Vandals went as far as North Africa and the Lombards moved to Italy. What is this time called?
hints: It happened at the end of antiquity.
Many Germanic tribes left their old homelands.
Its name describes whole peoples moving to new homes.
questions.description: An era when Europe's map had to be redrawn again and again.
questions.fun_fact: The word “vandalism” comes from the Vandals, but it was only coined in France in 1794.

questions.question: I wore braces on my legs until a friend shouted, “Run!” Later I ran across the United States. Who am I?
hints: My movie came out in 1994.
Tom Hanks plays me.
My mama always said life is like a box of chocolates.
questions.description: The man who turned a bit of playground advice into the longest jog in movie history.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Forrest runs for three years, two months, fourteen days and sixteen hours.

questions.question: In 1138, Conrad III became king, the first of a new royal dynasty that also included Frederick Barbarossa. Which one?
hints: Their family castle stood on a mountain in Swabia.
Barbarossa's grandson Frederick II was one of them too.
They are named after the Hohenstaufen mountain near Göppingen.
questions.description: A family business with a crown, a beard and quite a lot of Italy.
questions.fun_fact: Of the family castle on the Hohenstaufen, only a few bits of wall remain today.

questions.question: The film title “Kokowääh” is the name of a dish, said the way a child says it. Which country does the dish come from?
hints: The dish is chicken cooked slowly in wine.
The country is famous for croissants and baguettes.
The dish's proper name is “coq au vin”.
questions.description: A film title that's best said with your mouth full.
questions.fun_fact: The daughter in “Kokowääh” was played by Til Schweiger's real daughter, Emma.

questions.question: A comedian from Mülheim an der Ruhr sang “Katzeklo”. Apart from comedy, what does he mainly perform as?
hints: He has toured with big live shows for decades.
He has recorded many albums and plays in concert halls.
His music is full of improvisation, like Louis Armstrong's.
questions.description: A man who never lets you know whether he means something seriously or not.
questions.fun_fact: Helge Schneider plays more than a dozen instruments and taught himself many of them.

questions.question: Hans Liebherr founded his company in Kirchdorf an der Iller in 1949. Today it also makes refrigerators. What did it all start with?
hints: After the war, many houses in Germany had to be rebuilt.
Liebherr was a trained bricklayer.
This machine lifts heavy loads high above the building site.
questions.description: Before this was about cold milk, it was about something completely different.
questions.fun_fact: His first crane could be set up and taken down quickly, and it made Hans Liebherr successful in the years of rebuilding after the war.

questions.question: This discount supermarket comes as “Nord” and “Süd” because its two founding brothers split it up. Which one is it?
hints: The two brothers came from Essen.
The founders were named Karl and Theo.
Take the first two letters of Albrecht and of Discount.
questions.description: A family feud that split Germany into two shopping halves.
questions.fun_fact: The Albrecht brothers split their company into Aldi Nord and Aldi Süd in 1961.

questions.question: From 1927, Berlin's KaDeWe belonged to a department store group whose name later became “Hertie.” Who was it named after?
hints: At first, the group carried one man's full name.
This man was the uncle and financial backer of the actual founder, Oscar.
“Hertie” is made from the first syllables of his first and last name.
questions.description: A department store name that sounds like something you'd call your sweetheart.
questions.fun_fact: His nephew Leonhard Tietz founded the chain that later became Kaufhof.

questions.question: Sigmund Jähn flew into space in 1978. In East Germany he wasn't called an astronaut but a cosmonaut. Which language did that word come from?
hints: In spaceflight, East Germany stayed close to its big ally.
Jähn flew into space on a Soyuz rocket from Baikonur.
It's Yuri Gagarin's native language.
questions.description: A man from Saxony who got farther from home than any vacationer on the Baltic coast.
questions.fun_fact: Sigmund Jähn spent almost eight days in space, making him the first German in space.

questions.question: From 1979, East Germans had to exchange their D-marks at the bank for Forumschecks. What were these checks for?
wrong_answers: Paying for trips to the West
hints: In East Germany, paying directly with Western money was no longer supposed to be allowed.
Where you cashed them in, there was Western coffee, jeans and cosmetics.
These stores were often at border crossings, train stations and hotels.
questions.description: A piece of East German paper that collectors love more today than the bank ever did.
questions.fun_fact: Forumschecks even came in pfennig amounts, as a stand-in for Western coins.

questions.question: From 1964, I served in uniform in East Germany but never carried a weapon. Who am I?
hints: I was a way out for young men whose conscience would not let them shoot.
East Germany had no real civilian service without a uniform.
My work was often building barracks and roads.
questions.description: A soldier the drill instructor waited for in vain at shooting practice.
questions.fun_fact: In 1989, many former Bausoldaten were active in East Germany's peace movement.

questions.question: Diamant was the best-known bicycle brand in East Germany and still builds bikes in Saxony today. Since when have Diamant bicycles existed?
hints: When the brand began, bicycles were still a real luxury.
It is seen as one of the oldest bicycle brands in Germany that still exists.
The first bike went on sale while Germany still had a Kaiser.
questions.description: A gemstone that half of East Germany pedaled to work on.
questions.fun_fact: The Diamant works are near Chemnitz, which was called Karl-Marx-Stadt in East Germany.

questions.question: Radeberger was a sought-after export beer in East Germany. Which Dresden building appears in its famous TV ad?
hints: The ad links the beer with culture.
People sing in this building, but not at church services.
It is named after its architect, Gottfried.
questions.description: A beer that dresses up rather fancy for its commercials.
questions.fun_fact: Radeberg is only about 15 km (9 miles) northeast of Dresden.

questions.question: Hans Modrow chaired it in 1989/90. Which body formed the government of the GDR?
hints: It was not the GDR's collective head of state.
It was not a body of the SED party itself either.
The GDR's ministers sat on it.
questions.description: Long meetings, thick files and plenty of rubber stamps: East Berlin office life at its finest.
questions.fun_fact: Real power in the GDR lay not with the Council of Ministers but with the SED's Politburo.

questions.question: In September 1989, Bärbel Bohley and others founded the New Forum (Neues Forum) in Grünheide. How many signed its founding appeal there?
hints: The meeting had to be kept secret from the Stasi.
The founders were mostly well-known dissidents who already knew each other.
The number has two digits.
questions.description: A painter who, in 1989, would rather repaint a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Within a few weeks, over 200,000 people signed the appeal, and Bohley was called the “Mother of the Revolution.”

questions.question: This planned town on the Oder was named after Stalin in 1953, after his death, and got a new name in 1961. What is it called today?
hints: It lies in Brandenburg, on the border with Poland.
From 1950 it was built as a model socialist town next to a big new works.
In German, its name today tells you what is made there.
questions.description: A town that wanted to get rid of its name faster than an old sweater.
questions.fun_fact: In 1961, Stalinstadt was merged with the neighboring town of Fürstenberg (Oder) to form the new town.

questions.question: You're at a party in the United States and everyone is dancing to rock and roll, which was just born. What decade is it?
hints: It was a few years after World War II.
It's the time of cars with tail fins and jukeboxes in diners.
Elvis Presley became famous in that decade.
questions.description: A time when parents were shocked because young people moved their hips way too much.
questions.fun_fact: Bill Haley's song “Rock Around the Clock” became a worldwide hit in 1955 after it was played in a movie.

questions.question: It's 1975 and you drive your Trabi through a red light in Leipzig. Who waves you over with a signal paddle?
hints: This is about ordinary road traffic.
These people kept order on the roads in the GDR.
Their name sounds like a police force for the whole people.
questions.description: Paddle up, Trabi pulls over, and papers, please.
questions.fun_fact: In the West, GDR police officers were called “Vopos” for short.

questions.question: What was the name of the Dresden combine that built most of the GDR's computers?
hints: Many GDR typewriters carried this name too.
The combine was formed in 1969 from several office machine and electronics firms.
It sounds like a word for mechanical people.
questions.description: A computer from the East: slower than today's, but it came with a five-year plan.
questions.fun_fact: The name lives on today in a Dresden software company.

questions.question: These ruins in Turkey are thought to be the legendary city of Troy. Which German merchant began digging here in 1871?
hints: He got rich as a merchant and learned many languages.
He found a gold treasure he called “Priam's Treasure.”
His last name starts with “Sch” and ends in “-mann.”
questions.description: A man who took bedtime stories a little too literally.
questions.fun_fact: Schliemann dug so roughly that he destroyed layers from the time of Homer's Troy.

questions.question: Artur Fischer from the Black Forest invented this gray plastic part in 1958. Why do you put it into a drilled hole?
questions.answer: So a screw holds in the wall
wrong_answers: So no water seeps through the wall
So electricity flows safely through the wall
So the drill bit doesn't break
hints: You often need it when you hang up a shelf.
It spreads apart inside the hole.
Without it, a screw would barely grip in concrete or plaster.
questions.description: Small, gray, and plain, yet a superstar at the hardware store.
questions.fun_fact: Over his lifetime, Artur Fischer filed more than 1,100 patents.

questions.question: In the game “Wer hat Angst vorm schwarzen Mann?” (Who's afraid of the bogeyman?), you get caught. What are you then?
hints: In the end, only one child is left.
Everyone starts on one side and has to run across to the other side.
From now on, you help chase the others.
questions.description: A playground classic where running away is not just allowed but required.
questions.fun_fact: In many groups, the last child left gets to be the bogeyman in the next round.

questions.question: Article 5 of the Grundgesetz lets you openly criticize the government. What is this basic right called?
hints: The same article also protects freedom of the press.
You can use it in the school newspaper, too.
It's about your own view, which you're allowed to say out loud.
questions.description: The right that gets argued about the loudest at the dinner table.
questions.fun_fact: Freedom of expression applies to children too, not just from age 18.

questions.question: The Parliamentary Council that wrote “Men and women shall have equal rights” into the Basic Law in 1949 had 65 members. How many were women?
hints: There were very few.
Today they are called the “Mothers of the Basic Law”.
You can count them on one hand and still have a finger to spare.
questions.description: A room full of men, where luckily a few women got very loud.
questions.fun_fact: Elisabeth Selbert pushed the equal-rights sentence through, backed by protest letters from all over the country.

questions.question: It is the holiest day in Judaism, spent fasting, and in 1973 it gave its name to a war. Which day is it?
hints: Its name is in Hebrew.
It is also called the Day of Atonement.
Its name starts with “Yom”, which means “day”.
questions.description: A day so serious that even a war ended up taking its name.
questions.fun_fact: In 1973, Egypt and Syria attacked Israel on exactly that day, when almost the whole country was fasting and the streets were empty.

questions.question: In Germany, polling stations close at 6 p.m. Right after, the votes are counted in public on the spot. Who counts them?
hints: Anyone is allowed to watch.
Counting usually happens in a nearby school or gym.
Instead of a wage, they only get a small allowance.
questions.description: A Sunday evening when suddenly every single slip of paper matters.
questions.fun_fact: Poll workers get paid “Erfrischungsgeld” for their help, which really means “refreshment money”.

questions.question: In Mittenwald in Bavaria, which instrument has been made from sycamore maple and spruce for over 300 years?
hints: A monument in Mittenwald honors the man who brought this craft there.
You play it with a bow.
It has four strings and is tucked under the chin.
questions.description: A tree with music in its wood, even though all it can do itself is rustle.
questions.fun_fact: Mittenwald has its own school for violin making and a violin museum.

questions.question: In his song “Nur noch kurz die Welt retten”, Tim Bendzko just has to save the world first. What does he then want to check 148 of?
hints: You get some every day, often far too many.
He does it on a computer or phone.
Their addresses have an @ in them.
questions.description: A superhero who squeezes in some office work before the big mission.
questions.fun_fact: “Nur noch kurz die Welt retten” came out in 2011 and made Tim Bendzko famous almost overnight.

questions.question: In Oberammergau, the whole village performs the story of Jesus' suffering and death every ten years. Where does this tradition come from?
questions.answer: From a vow made during the plague
wrong_answers: From a bet between two farmers
From a gift from the king
hints: The tradition began in the middle of the Thirty Years' War.
In a time of great need, the villagers turned to their faith for help.
Back then, many people all over Europe were dying of a disease.
questions.description: A play that only runs every ten years: buying tickets really pays off.
questions.fun_fact: The vow dates from 1633, and the people of Oberammergau still keep it today: hundreds of amateur actors from the village take part.

questions.question: Which of these fairy tales is NOT in the Brothers Grimm's “Children's and Household Tales”?
hints: A single writer made up this story himself.
Its author came from Denmark.
Hans Christian Andersen wrote it.
questions.description: Two brothers who collected stories instead of stamps.
questions.fun_fact: The first volume of “Children's and Household Tales” came out in 1812, just before Christmas.

questions.question: It's eaten cold with eggs and potatoes, and in Frankfurt seven small greenhouses honor it. What is “Grie Soß”?
hints: “Grie” is Hessian dialect and names a color.
Each of the greenhouses stands for one ingredient.
It contains borage, chervil, cress, parsley and chives, among others.
questions.description: A Frankfurt classic whose recipe some grandmas guard like a state secret.
questions.fun_fact: Real Frankfurt Grüne Soße needs exactly seven herbs: borage, chervil, cress, parsley, salad burnet, sorrel and chives.

questions.question: “Arme Ritter” is an old dish made from leftovers. Which leftover is used?
hints: It's usually eaten sweet, often with cinnamon and sugar.
The leftover is dipped in egg and milk and fried in a pan.
In the US, the dish is called “French toast.”
questions.description: A dish for heroes whose armor has seen better days.
questions.fun_fact: The name is said to come from poor knights who couldn't afford fresh white bread.

questions.question: You order a Bockwurst at a German Imbiss (snack stand). How is it warmed up there?
hints: It doesn't get any brown grill marks.
If it bursts open, it got too hot.
At home, people warm Wiener sausages the same way.
questions.description: Mustard on top, a roll on the side, and lunch is ready to eat on the go.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Bockwurst got its name from Bock beer, which it was served with in Berlin in 1889.

questions.question: The Sandinista Revolution won in this country in 1979. Which country is it?
hints: It is in Central America.
It has the largest lake in Central America.
Its capital is Managua.
questions.description: A land of lakes and volcanoes that changed hands almost overnight in 1979.
questions.fun_fact: The Sandinistas took their name from Augusto César Sandino, a rebel fighter who fought against US Marines in the 1920s and 1930s.

questions.question: I stand at train stations and on street corners, I smell of fries and currywurst, and people eat at me standing up. What am I?
hints: I'm usually small and have a deep fryer.
I serve quick food you can eat on the go.
Another German name for me is “Pommesbude”.
questions.description: No silver cutlery here, just a tiny wooden fork.
questions.fun_fact: Currywurst is said to have been invented in 1949 by Herta Heuwer at her snack stand in Berlin.

questions.question: In the south, people also say “Wurscht”. What does “Das ist mir Wurst” mean?
hints: People often say it with a shrug.
You say it when either choice is fine with you.
The opposite would be “That matters to me”.
questions.description: Germany loves its sausage so much that it even shows up in everyday sayings.
questions.fun_fact: A well-known German saying goes: “Alles hat ein Ende, nur die Wurst hat zwei” (“Everything has an end, only the sausage has two”).

questions.question: In the children's song “Ein Männlein steht im Walde”, the little man wears a crimson cloak and a black cap. What is he?
hints: People like to sing about the little man in the fall.
It grows on a prickly bush.
It's the fruit of the rose, used to make tea and jam.
questions.description: A riddle with a false bottom: not everything here is what it seems.
questions.fun_fact: Many people picture a fly agaric mushroom while singing, but that one has white spots and no black cap.

questions.question: Listen: which brass instrument from the brass band is this?
hints: It sounds lower than a trumpet but higher than a tuba.
Its notes can glide smoothly into each other.
You push a long slide in and out to change the note.
questions.description: In a brass band things get loud, and this instrument is right in the middle of the noise.
questions.fun_fact: Many Protestant parishes in Germany have a Posaunenchor (literally “trombone choir”), even though trumpets and tubas play in it too.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: You hear it in orchestras, brass bands and jazz.
You blow into it, and a single thin reed on the mouthpiece vibrates.
In “Peter and the Wolf”, this instrument plays the cat.
questions.description: Your ears have to do all the work here; your eyes get the day off.
questions.fun_fact: Jazz musician Benny Goodman became so famous on the clarinet that people called him the “King of Swing”.

questions.question: “I sit in a hollow, asleep. In the children's song, they ask if I'm sick because I can't hop anymore.” Who am I?
hints: My song is a game song that everyone joins in.
I have soft fur and just a tiny stub of a tail.
I have long ears and bring the eggs at Easter.
questions.description: A nap that causes quite a stir in kindergarten.
questions.fun_fact: At “Häschen, hüpf!” (“Bunny, hop!”), all the children who were crouching down jump up into the air.

questions.question: What is Germany's oldest private TV channel? It went on air on January 1, 1984, in Ludwigshafen, one day before RTL plus.
hints: At first, the channel was still called “PKS”.
For many years, it showed the Bundesliga soccer league on its show “ran”.
Its name contains a short form of the word “satellite”.
questions.description: Before private TV came along, the remote control didn't have much to do.
questions.fun_fact: At first it broadcast only through a cable TV pilot project in Ludwigshafen that very few homes could receive.

questions.question: Forensic teams look for it: the object used to commit a crime. What is it called in German?
hints: You can put it in an evidence bag.
In the board game Clue (Cluedo), there are six of them, such as a candlestick.
The second part of the word also describes a sword or a spear.
questions.description: In a crime show the detective knows everything by the end; here, a single word is enough.
questions.fun_fact: In the board game Clue (Cluedo), there are six possible weapons, including a candlestick and a rope.

questions.question: In which year did the ARD series “Um Himmels Willen”, with Fritz Wepper as Mayor Wöller, first air?
hints: The series is set in a small Bavarian town with a convent.
Before that, Fritz Wepper played Harry Klein in “Derrick” for decades.
It started shortly after euro coins and bills came into use.
questions.description: A mayor against a convent full of nuns: guess who usually wins.
questions.fun_fact: Wöller's first rival was Jutta Speidel as Sister Lotte; later Janina Hartwig took over as Sister Hanna.

questions.question: Cold War spies hid microfilm everywhere. In which century was microfilm invented?
hints: It's older than it looks.
It was invented soon after photography.
Back then, steam trains were running, but the electric light bulb didn't exist yet.
questions.description: The tiniest thing a spy could hide inside a hollow coin.
questions.fun_fact: During the Siege of Paris in 1870, thousands of messages on microfilm were sent tied to carrier pigeons.

questions.question: This quiz show airs on Saturday nights on Das Erste: celebrities answer questions from kids, and short films explain the answers. What is it called?
hints: The show is based on a famous children's TV program.
That program also features an elephant and a duck.
The orange animal from that program is in the show's name.
questions.description: Finally, a place where grown-ups can admit they don't know how gummy bears are made.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Sendung mit der Maus”, where the idea of kids' questions comes from, has been on the air since 1971.

questions.question: To have fresh Brötchen in the morning, someone gets up in the middle of the night. Who?
hints: This person works with flour and dough.
Their most important tool is a hot oven.
Their shop smells of fresh bread every morning.
questions.description: While you're still fast asleep, someone's shift started long ago.
questions.fun_fact: Many bakers start work around 2 or 3 a.m. so the Brötchen are fresh from the oven in the morning.

questions.question: In some parts of Germany, the lunch box is also called a “Brotbüchse”. Where do kids usually pack it in the morning?
hints: You carry it on your back.
Notebooks and the pencil case go in it too.
You take it with you to class every morning.
questions.description: A plastic treasure that often comes home in the evening with half a banana inside.
questions.fun_fact: In the Ruhr area, a school sandwich is often called a “Knifte”, and its box is a “Kniftendose”.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is plausible and the wrong answers are clearly wrong. I did not verify the fun fact that 'Knifte' and 'Kniftendose' are used in the Ruhr area.

questions.question: At the deli counter, the clerk asks: “Darf's ein bisschen mehr sein?” (“Is a little more okay?”). What has usually just happened?
wrong_answers: The sausage is on sale today
The store is about to close
hints: The question comes just before the cold cuts are wrapped.
Say you ordered 200 grams.
The scale might show 230 grams.
questions.description: A classic behind the glass, right next to the Fleischwurst.
questions.fun_fact: The line “Darf's ein bisschen mehr sein?” is so well known in Germany that it's almost a saying.

questions.question: What did Schlager singer Wolfgang Petry wear by the dozen on both wrists when he performed?
hints: He liked to wear them with checked lumberjack shirts.
Fans gave him many of them as gifts.
You give them to people you're especially fond of.
questions.description: One man, one mustache, one mane of curls, and wrists that were never bare.
questions.fun_fact: When Petry's hit “Wahnsinn” plays at parties and in soccer stadiums, crowds still roar “Hölle, Hölle, Hölle” along with it.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: Without this instrument, a brass band has no bass.
It is made of shiny brass and is very big and heavy.
It is the trumpet's big, chubby brother.
questions.description: Without this instrument, a beer tent would just be a tent with beer.
questions.fun_fact: If you unrolled the tubing of a large tuba, it would be about 5 meters (16 feet) long.

questions.question: It's jokingly called a “Quetschkommode” (squeeze dresser): you wear it in front of your belly, pull it apart and push it together. What is it?
hints: You often hear it at folk festivals and the Schützenfest.
It has keys or buttons and bellows that pump air.
A close relative is called the Ziehharmonika.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that makes music if you squeeze it hard enough.
questions.fun_fact: The Hohner company in Trossingen, Baden-Württemberg, has been making accordions and harmonicas for more than 100 years.

questions.question: At almost every German wedding, everyone sings along: “Atemlos durch die …” What comes next?
hints: Helene Fischer made it famous in 2013.
It's a time when almost everyone is usually asleep.
It's the opposite of day.
questions.description: A song that leaves even Uncle Herbert gasping for air on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: The lyrics of “Atemlos durch die Nacht” were written by the singer Kristina Bach.

questions.question: In a crime show, a suspect needs an alibi: proof that he was somewhere else when the crime happened. What does NOT help him?
hints: Three of these show where he was at the time.
One of them actually speaks against him.
It's a trace he left behind himself at the scene of the crime.
questions.description: “It wasn't me!”: the most popular line in every crime show.
questions.fun_fact: “Alibi” is Latin and simply means “elsewhere”.

questions.question: In 1956 this yacht carried Fidel Castro and Che Guevara from Mexico to Cuba, and today Cuba’s official newspaper bears its name. What was it called?
hints: It set sail from Tuxpan, on the Gulf of Mexico.
It was a pleasure yacht bought from an American.
Its English name was a fond nickname for a grandmother.
