questions.description: An overloaded little boat that ended up giving its name to a whole province.
questions.fun_fact: The yacht was built for about 12 people, but 82 men squeezed aboard for a week-long trip.

questions.question: Detectives dust powder on a glass and see a pattern of fine lines. Every person has their own. Which body part does it come from?
hints: You use this body part many times a day.
With it, you can feel especially well whether something is soft or rough.
You sometimes use it to unlock your phone screen.
questions.description: No culprit is so careful that detectives can't find a trace of them somewhere.
questions.fun_fact: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

questions.question: Which character is NOT part of “Stromberg”, the office comedy series set at the Capitol insurance company?
hints: Three of these characters work in Stromberg's department.
The character you're looking for became famous on a completely different comedy show.
He was created by Hape Kerkeling.
questions.description: An office where the coffee machine is the most sensible coworker.
questions.fun_fact: For the 2014 “Stromberg” movie, fans raised about 1 million euros through crowdfunding.

questions.question: Reporter is to interview as detective is to…?
hints: It's all about questions and answers.
The one being questioned is a suspect or a witness.
In crime shows, it often happens in a bare room with a table.
questions.description: In crime shows, the truth usually comes out just before the end credits.
questions.fun_fact: In real German police work, the official word is usually not “Verhör” but “Vernehmung”.

questions.question: Which of these vehicles does NOT drive with blue flashing lights in Germany?
hints: Blue lights are only for vehicles that must get somewhere very fast.
The vehicle you're looking for drives slowly and stops all the time.
It empties the trash cans.
questions.description: When the street suddenly gets loud and all the cars pull over.
questions.fun_fact: Blue lights have only been required in Germany since 1938; before that, fire trucks mostly warned people with bells.

questions.question: I'm a show on Das Erste, and on early Saturday evenings I show the Bundesliga goals. What am I?
hints: I've been around since the 1960s.
I'm not on ZDF, and not on private TV either.
My name is “Sport” plus the German word for “show”.
questions.description: At six on Saturdays, many living rooms go quiet, except when someone scores.
questions.fun_fact: The Sportschau first aired back in 1961, making it one of the oldest shows on German TV.

questions.question: Whistle is to referee as … is to judge on “Das Supertalent”?
hints: The judges press it with their hand.
When all of them light up red, the act is over.
There's even a golden version of it.
questions.description: Nervous contestants, stern faces and a man making music with spoons.
questions.fun_fact: With the golden buzzer, a judge can send an act straight to the final.

questions.question: From 1959 to 1987 I read the Tagesschau news, for many years as chief newsreader, and people called me “Mister Tagesschau.” Who am I?
hints: I was already reading the Tagesschau in its early years.
In 1987 a colleague took over my post as chief newsreader.
My first name is a double name, and my last name starts with “K.”
questions.description: Back then, TV still had a face, and it was the same one every night at eight.
questions.fun_fact: Köpcke was the Tagesschau's chief newsreader from 1964 to 1987.

questions.question: Which comedian from the Cologne area got her own comedy show on Das Erste, named after her?
hints: Before that, she already had her own satire show on WDR.
She is a huge carnival fan and started her own women's carnival show.
Her last name starts with “K” and is quite unusual.
questions.description: One woman, one microphone, and a TV channel that gets a bit more complaint mail afterwards.
questions.fun_fact: With “Deine Sitzung”, Kebekus runs a carnival show where almost only women are on stage.

questions.question: Three of these Gothic churches only got their towers finished in the 19th century. Which one's tower was already complete in the Middle Ages?
hints: The tower you're looking for is in Baden-Württemberg.
Its openwork spire looks like lace carved from stone and is about 116 m (381 ft) high.
The city sits at the edge of the Black Forest and is known for its “Bächle”, little streams along the streets.
questions.description: Some building sites take even longer than Berlin's new airport, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: The historian Jacob Burckhardt called it “the most beautiful tower in Christendom”.

questions.question: What is this building in Berlin used for today?
hints: The building stands in the old eastern part of Berlin, near Alexanderplatz.
It gets its nickname from the color of its bricks.
Not all of Germany is governed from here, only Berlin itself.
questions.description: A brick building so red you want to offer it some sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Rotes Rathaus” (Red City Hall) comes from its red clinker bricks, not from politics.

questions.question: In what year did the US and the Soviet Union sign the START I treaty to cut their nuclear weapons?
hints: On the Soviet side, it was signed by the leader who launched perestroika.
On the US side, it was signed by George H. W. Bush, president since 1989.
It was just a few months before the Soviet Union ceased to exist.
questions.description: A treaty for fewer bombs, signed at almost the last minute.
questions.fun_fact: It was signed in July 1991, and in December of that same year the Soviet Union ceased to exist.

questions.question: In 1907, Carl Hagenbeck opened a zoo in Hamburg with deep moats and fake rocks. What were the moats for?
hints: Before then, zoo animals mostly lived in small cages.
The animals were meant to look like they were in the wild.
The moats are too wide to jump across, so there's no need for cages anymore.
questions.description: A zoo where the lions are so close you almost want to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: Hagenbeck even patented his idea of enclosures without bars, and zoos around the world copied it.

questions.question: This ancient structure now stands in a Berlin museum. What was it once used as?
questions.answer: An altar for offerings to the gods
hints: It comes from an ancient Greek city in what is now Turkey.
On its frieze, gods fight against giants.
Priests climbed its great staircase to offer animals to the gods.
questions.description: Archaeologists moved a whole building to Berlin, without a single moving box.
questions.fun_fact: From 1878 on, the altar was dug up and shipped to Berlin piece by piece.

questions.question: Knut the polar bear was born in December 2006 and became world-famous. How much did he weigh at birth?
hints: Polar bear cubs are born blind and almost hairless.
Adult polar bears weigh hundreds of kilos, but their babies are tiny.
Knut weighed less than a small bag of flour.
questions.description: A polar bear star whose first meals came from a bottle.
questions.fun_fact: Zookeeper Thomas Dörflein raised Knut with a bottle because his mother didn't take care of him.

questions.question: The exhibition building of the Porsche Museum in Stuttgart seems to float. How many supports does it rest on?
hints: There's a big open square under the building.
There are surprisingly few supports.
There are fewer supports than a normal table has legs.
questions.description: A building that clearly doesn't feel like touching the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The Porsche Museum in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen opened in 2009.

questions.question: The Deutsches Museum in Munich stands on an island in the river Isar. What is mainly on display there?
hints: An engineer founded it in 1903.
Inside there is a rebuilt mine and real airplanes.
You can see machines, engines, rockets and experiments there.
questions.description: You can spend a whole day here and still not see everything.
questions.fun_fact: The Deutsches Museum is one of the largest museums of science and technology in the world.

questions.question: You wear it on your head when cycling, it has air holes and a strap under the chin. What is it for?
questions.answer: It protects your head in a fall
wrong_answers: It keeps your hair nice and tidy
It makes the bike go faster
hints: In many families, kids have to put it on before they're allowed to ride off.
It's soft on the inside and hard on the outside.
When you fall over, you're glad you had it on.
questions.description: A piece of headwear that gets argued about before every bike ride.
questions.fun_fact: After a crash you should replace a bike helmet, even if you can't see any damage on the outside.

questions.question: A gray box stands by the roadside. If you drive past too fast, you see a red flash. What usually happens next?
questions.answer: A letter with a fine arrives
wrong_answers: The next traffic light turns red
hints: The box has taken a photo.
It comes a few days or weeks later.
It lands in your mailbox with bad news.
questions.description: A roadside photographer who never asks for your permission.
questions.fun_fact: Many speed cameras use infrared light, so you can barely see the flash, or not at all.

questions.question: I'm a street. Cars may only drive on me in one direction, and my sign is blue with a white arrow. What am I?
hints: You often find me in narrow lanes in an old town.
Cyclists are sometimes still allowed to ride the other way.
My name has the number one in it.
questions.description: City traffic: someone's honking here, someone's been hunting for a parking spot for twenty minutes there.
questions.fun_fact: In many German cities, cyclists may ride the wrong way down a one-way street if an extra sign allows it.

questions.question: To jump-start a car, you connect two car batteries with cables. How many volts does a normal car battery have?
hints: It's much more than a small battery for the remote control.
It's much less than a wall socket.
The number is a dozen.
questions.description: When a car won't wake up in the morning, it needs a cup of coffee from the car next door.
questions.fun_fact: When jump-starting, the red cable always goes on the plus terminal, and the black one on the minus terminal or on bare metal on the engine.

questions.question: Long-distance trains cross at Berlin Hauptbahnhof. On how many levels, one above the other, do trains run there?
hints: The trains don't all run at the same height.
One line runs up high, the other deep underground.
One direction is east–west, the other north–south.
questions.description: A train station that loves stacking things as much as a kid with building blocks.
questions.fun_fact: Berlin Hauptbahnhof opened in 2006, just before the soccer World Cup in Germany.

questions.question: The CIA is the famous secret service of the United States. What does the “I” in CIA stand for?
hints: The word describes the agency's job: secretly finding out what other countries are planning.
It is also a word used for spying in general.
It is what an IQ test measures.
questions.description: Three letters that always show up in dark sunglasses in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: The CIA was founded in 1947, just as the Cold War was beginning.

questions.question: You're in the car with Mom, Dad and Grandma. How many people need to buckle up?
hints: The rule applies in the front and in the back.
Kids have to buckle up too.
Don't forget to count yourself!
questions.description: One click, and you're ready for the big trip.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, wearing a seat belt in the front became the law in 1976, but you only got fined for skipping it starting in 1984.

questions.question: In which grade do children in Germany usually take the cycling test (Fahrradprüfung)?
hints: It's still in elementary school.
The kids have been riding bikes for a few years and now learn the traffic rules properly, with a written and a riding test.
Soon afterwards, many move on to a secondary school.
questions.description: Your very first license, no engine required.
questions.fun_fact: For the cycling test, children often practice with the police at a children's traffic training ground (Jugendverkehrsschule).

questions.question: This metal rail runs along many autobahns. What is it for?
questions.answer: To keep cars from leaving the road
wrong_answers: To keep deer from running onto the road
To keep the traffic noise down
To measure how fast cars are going
hints: It's about safety.
You often find it on bridges and in sharp curves, too.
Its German name, Leitplanke, says that it “guides” cars.
questions.description: A very long piece of metal that would love to have nothing to do all day.
questions.fun_fact: Guardrails are built to bend when a car hits them, soaking up part of the force of the crash.

questions.question: A tow truck lifts the front wheels of a broken-down car. How many wheels is the car still rolling on?
hints: A car has four wheels in total.
Only the front ones are in the air.
It's the two back wheels.
questions.description: A car that gives other cars a piggyback ride when they can't go on.
questions.fun_fact: Some tow trucks have a bed that tilts, so the whole car can be pulled up onto it.

questions.question: It runs in Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, and its sign is blue with a white letter. What does the “U” in U-Bahn stand for?
hints: It has to do with where it mostly runs.
You often walk down stairs to get to it.
It mostly runs through tunnels beneath the streets.
questions.description: One letter that gets millions of commuters to work on time every morning (usually).
questions.fun_fact: Germany's first U-Bahn opened in Berlin in 1902, and most of it actually ran up high on an elevated track.

questions.question: It was born on Calle Preciados in Madrid and is now Spain's most famous department store chain. What was the “corte inglés” it is named after?
hints: The name comes from the small shop where it all began.
That shop was a tailor's.
It has to do with jackets and pants made to measure in the London style.
questions.description: A department store where you go in for socks and come out with a TV, a cake and a trip to Rome.
questions.fun_fact: El Corte Inglés started as a small tailor's shop that Ramón Areces turned into a company in 1940.

questions.question: In the prologue of the 1989 Tour de France, Perico Delgado, the previous year's winner, was late for his own start. By how much?
hints: It was enough to lose the Tour, but not enough to be disqualified.
Longer than it takes to tie your shoes.
Less than three minutes.
questions.description: The most expensive alarm clock in the history of Spanish cycling.
questions.fun_fact: Despite that slip, Perico fought back and finished third in the 1989 Tour.

questions.question: Which cyclist broke the hour record in Bordeaux in 1994 and won Olympic gold in Atlanta in 1996?
hints: He was a great time trial specialist.
Abroad they called him “Big Mig.”
He won five Tours de France in a row.
questions.description: A cyclist who pedaled as if the bike owed him money.
questions.fun_fact: In that hour record he rode 53.040 km (about 33 miles) in 60 minutes.

questions.question: He was called “la Saeta Rubia” (the Blond Arrow), won five European Cups in a row with Real Madrid and played for several national teams. Where was he born?
hints: He was born in South America.
He started out playing for River Plate.
He was born in Buenos Aires.
questions.description: A soccer player with more national team shirts than boots in his closet.
questions.fun_fact: Di Stéfano played for both Argentina and Spain, yet never played in a single World Cup.

questions.question: You're at the Zona Franca factory in Barcelona, watching the first SEAT 600s roll out. Which decade is it?
hints: Franco was already ruling Spain.
It was before people landed on the Moon.
It was 1957.
questions.description: A car so small it fit four people, one suitcase and the dreams of a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: About 800,000 SEAT 600s were built, and many Spanish families took their first trip to the beach in one.

questions.question: Who is this singer, still called “the King”?
hints: He lived in Memphis, in the United States, and became famous there.
He lived in a mansion called Graceland.
His first name starts with E, and he is known as “the King of Rock and Roll”.
questions.description: A singer whose hips were censored on television.
questions.fun_fact: Elvis did his military service in West Germany from 1958 to 1960, in the middle of the Cold War.

questions.question: It started broadcasting in 1956, had La Primera and the UHF channel, and for decades was Spain's only TV broadcaster. What is it?
hints: It is a public broadcaster.
At first its signal only reached Madrid and the area around it.
Its initials have three letters.
questions.description: Grandma's TV, back when there was only one channel and nobody fought over the remote.
questions.fun_fact: TVE's first broadcasts came from a small house on Paseo de la Habana in Madrid.

questions.question: We were short and strong, with a big bony brow; we left bones at El Sidrón (Asturias) and vanished about 40,000 years ago. Who are we?
hints: We were a different human species from yours.
Our name comes from a valley in Germany.
We lived alongside your species, and you still carry some of our genes.
questions.description: The first neighbors in Asturias, long before anyone made fabada.
questions.fun_fact: A Neanderthal skull was found in Gibraltar in 1848, eight years before the one from the German valley that gave them their name.

questions.question: It was oval, had seating all around the arena, and gladiators fought in it; remains survive in Mérida and Tarragona. Which Roman building was it?
hints: Fights with wild animals also took place there.
Chariot races were held in a different building.
The Colosseum in Rome is the most famous one of this kind.
questions.description: A stadium with a big crowd, lots of sand and no referee.
questions.fun_fact: Tarragona's amphitheater sits right by the beach, and you can see the Mediterranean from its seats.

questions.question: The Vía de la Plata linked Mérida to Astorga. Legions and carts used it, and parts survive after 2,000 years. How was it built?
questions.answer: With layers of stone, gravel and slabs
hints: It had to stand up to centuries of rain and wheels
The Romans used materials they found near the road
Flat stones, fitted tightly together, went on top
questions.description: The highway of 2,000 years ago: no tolls, no rest stops.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Vía de la Plata” (Silver Road) probably has nothing to do with the metal: it is thought to come from the Arabic “balat”, meaning paved road.

questions.question: It began as the “Marcha Granadera” of Charles III's soldiers, has no official lyrics and is played before Spain's national team games. What is it?
hints: It is an official symbol of Spain.
People stand for it at state events and sports finals.
It is Spain's national anthem.
questions.description: A trumpet sounds in the stadium, and suddenly even the guy munching sunflower seeds stands as straight as a grenadier.
questions.fun_fact: The Marcha Real is one of the few national anthems in the world with no official lyrics.

questions.question: Look at the painting: Goya showed people fighting Napoleon's soldiers on May 2, 1808. In which city did it happen?
hints: It was the city where the royal family lived.
Today May 2 is a public holiday in that autonomous community.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.description: A day in May when the neighbors poured into the streets, and not for a pre-lunch snack.
questions.fun_fact: Goya painted this picture in 1814, six years after the events, together with “The Third of May 1808”.

questions.question: I was born in 1844, under Isabella II, and my officers patrol roads and villages wearing a patent-leather tricorn hat. Who am I?
hints: I was founded by the Duke of Ahumada.
My uniform is green.
My three-cornered hat is famous all over Spain.
questions.description: A hat so unusual it has stayed in fashion for more than a century and a half.
questions.fun_fact: The patent-leather tricorn is now worn only at formal events; day to day, officers wear a cap.

questions.question: Pablo Iglesias Posse founded it in 1879 in a Madrid tavern, and its symbol is a fist holding a rose. What does PSOE stand for?
wrong_answers: Plataforma Social de Obreros del Estado
hints: It was founded to stand up for workers.
The O stands for “Obrero” (worker).
The S stands for “Socialista.”
questions.description: Four letters, almost a century and a half of history, and not a word search it can't beat.
questions.fun_fact: Casa Labra, the tavern where it was founded, is still open in Madrid and is famous for its cod croquettes.

questions.question: Look at the painting: Goya painted this king with his whole family around 1800. Which king is it?
hints: His favorite prime minister was Manuel Godoy.
His son took the throne from him after the Mutiny of Aranjuez.
He was the son of Charles III.
questions.description: A family photo with no phone: everyone had to pose for weeks.
questions.fun_fact: Goya painted himself into this picture, standing in the shadows on the left, just as Velázquez did in “Las Meninas.”

questions.question: In what year did Narcís Monturiol test his first submarine, the Ictíneo, in the port of Barcelona?
hints: It was during the reign of Isabella II.
It was in the middle of the 19th century.
It was about 30 years before Isaac Peral's submarine.
questions.description: A Catalan who wanted to see the fish up close without getting wet.
questions.fun_fact: Monturiol started thinking about a submarine after seeing how dangerous the work of coral divers in Cadaqués was.

questions.question: The Cádiz Constitution was nicknamed “la Pepa” because it was passed on Saint Joseph's Day. What day of March is that?
hints: It falls in the second half of the month.
It is the day the Fallas of Valencia end.
In Spain it is also Father's Day.
questions.description: A constitution with a pet name, as if it were a cousin from the village.
questions.fun_fact: The Cortes that passed it met in Cádiz because it was one of the few cities the French never managed to capture.

questions.question: You're in Soria, where Antonio Machado taught French and wrote “Campos de Castilla”. In which century was this poet born?
hints: He was part of the Generation of '98.
He was already an adult when Spain lost Cuba.
He was born in Seville in 1875.
questions.description: A poet who became famous for walking, though he never owned a step counter.
questions.fun_fact: His brother Manuel was a poet too, and the two of them wrote plays together.

questions.question: It came after the Baroque and before Romanticism, trusted reason and science, and Jovellanos stood for it in Spain. What movement was it?
hints: It was in the 18th century.
In France it produced Diderot's great “Encyclopédie”.
It was called “the Age of Lights”.
questions.description: A century when thinking became trendy, and nobody had an encyclopedia on their phone.
questions.fun_fact: The Prado Museum building was first planned under Charles III as a natural history museum.

questions.question: Look at this detail: which famous painting is it from?
hints: It hangs in the Prado Museum.
It shows French soldiers shooting people from Madrid after the uprising against Napoleon.
Its title is a date: the day after the Madrid uprising.
questions.description: A white shirt that has become more famous than plenty of runway shows.
questions.fun_fact: The man in the white shirt has a mark on his hand like a stigma, as if he were a martyr.

questions.question: “The Nude Maja” earned Goya a summons from the Inquisition. Which of these paintings did he NOT paint?
hints: Three of them are in the Prado and are by the same painter from Aragon.
The one you want is almost 150 years older.
Velázquez painted it and it hangs in London.
questions.description: A painting so daring that its painter ended up explaining himself to the Inquisition.
questions.fun_fact: Both of Goya's majas belonged to Manuel Godoy, Charles IV's favorite, who kept them in his private collection.

questions.question: They're made by the toy company Famosa, fit in the palm of your hand, and you can change their hair and clothes. What are Pinypon?
hints: They're for playing, not for eating or drawing.
They have big heads and round eyes.
They have little houses, cars and even pets for making up stories.
questions.description: The thing you find most often under the sofa, after the bread crumbs.
questions.fun_fact: Pinypon first appeared in 1983, so your parents may have played with them too.

questions.question: They're round, have a hole in the middle and come in a tube. What are Filipinos made of?
hints: They crunch when you bite them.
You can dip them in milk, but not for too long.
They're made by Artiach, the same brand as Dinosaurus.
questions.description: The only ring you can wear on your finger and then eat.
questions.fun_fact: Artiach, the brand behind Filipinos, was founded in Bilbao in 1907.

questions.question: I was born in Vigo in 1960, and my ships froze fish out at sea. Today I live in the supermarket freezer with my fish sticks and hake. Which brand am I?
hints: I'm a Galician brand.
I don't sell cans, just frozen food.
My name joins the Spanish word for fishing and the Galician word for “new”.
questions.description: A brand that gets colder than a penguin in January.
questions.fun_fact: Pescanova was a pioneer in freezing fish on board its own ships, far from the coast.

questions.question: You pour yourself a glass of Puleva milk at breakfast. Where does the brand name come from?
questions.answer: From “pura leche de vaca” (pure cow's milk)
wrong_answers: From “puerta de Levante” (gateway to the East)
hints: It's a hidden acronym.
Each syllable is the start of a word.
The last two syllables are the start of the Spanish words for the drink and the animal that gives it.
questions.description: Three syllables hiding a whole phrase, like a secret message on the milk carton.
questions.fun_fact: Puleva was born in Granada in the 1950s.

questions.question: In Spain, what is the shop that sells screws, hammers, wrenches and nails called?
hints: This is where you go when a faucet breaks
Nails used to be sold there by weight
Its name comes from a very hard metal
questions.description: Paradise for anyone who says “I'll fix that myself in a minute.”
questions.fun_fact: “Ferretería” comes from “hierro,” Spanish for iron (in Latin, “ferrum”), because almost everything sold there used to be made of that metal.

questions.question: ElPozo was born in Alhama de Murcia, gives its name to a famous futsal team and turns up in lots of school-break sandwiches. What does it sell?
hints: It isn't sweet
Once opened, it goes in the fridge
Its turkey breast and “york” come in thin slices
questions.description: Murcia doesn't just grow lemons: it also grows brands named after a hole in the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The ElPozo Murcia team has won several Spanish futsal league titles.

questions.question: Luis Cernuda, the poet from Seville who wrote “La realidad y el deseo”, belongs to which group of poets?
hints: Almost all the members of his group were born around 1900.
It’s the group of Lorca, Alberti and Dámaso Alonso.
Its name recalls a tribute to Góngora on the 300th anniversary of his death.
questions.description: Poets, metaphors and a literature exam getting dangerously close.
questions.fun_fact: Cernuda spent his last years in exile and died in Mexico City in 1963.

questions.question: In which centuries were the ballads of the Romancero viejo, like the one about Count Arnaldos, composed?
hints: They were born before the printing press reached Spain.
Many come from the old medieval epic songs.
It’s the Late Middle Ages, just before the Catholic Monarchs.
questions.description: Poems that went from mouth to mouth long before anyone could hit “forward”.
questions.fun_fact: Many of these ballads were written down in the 16th century in the “Cancionero de romances”, printed in Antwerp.

previous.feedback: Source: hints 1 and 3 are factually off, and the translation carries both over faithfully. Printing reached Spain around 1472, and many 15th-century ballads (the frontier ballads about the Granada war, for example) were composed after that. The Catholic Monarchs reigned from 1474, inside the 15th century, so the ballads did not all come "just before" them. Fix it in the source (for example, hint 1: "They were passed on by word of mouth and mostly written down in the 16th century"; hint 3: "It's the late Middle Ages"), then re-translate. Fact check: wrong. The answer (14th and 15th centuries) is fine, and so is the Cancionero de romances fun fact (Antwerp, c. 1547). But hint 1 is false: printing reached Spain in the 1470s, and many 15th-century ballads were composed after that. Hint 3 is also off, since the Catholic Monarchs reigned 1474–1516, within the 15th century, so the ballads were not 'just before' them.

questions.question: In what year was the first known edition of “La Celestina,” by Fernando de Rojas, published?
hints: It comes from the early days of printing in Spain.
It was still published in the 15th century.
It was a few years after Columbus's first voyage.
questions.description: A matchmaker, two lovers and an author who hid his name like buried treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Rojas hid his name in an acrostic: the first letters of some verses in the book spell out who wrote it and where he was born.

questions.question: Which of these Spanish adjectives does NOT come from a character in Spanish literature?
hints: Three of them come from works written in Spain.
The odd one out comes from a giant who loved to eat.
That giant was created by the French writer Rabelais.
questions.description: Some characters got so famous they retired into the dictionary as adjectives.
questions.fun_fact: «Quijotesco» describes someone who fights for noble ideals even when they seem impossible, like battling windmills.

questions.question: In a poem, “casa” and “cama” rhyme, but only the vowels match from the last stressed syllable on. What is this rhyme called?
hints: The consonants don't count here.
It is the typical rhyme of Spanish romances (ballads).
Its name comes from the Latin for “sounding similar”.
questions.description: When words only sound a tiny bit alike, but just enough to look good.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish romances (ballads) rhyme the even lines in assonance and leave the odd lines unrhymed.

questions.question: Which institution publishes the “Diccionario de la lengua española”, the one people check to see if a Spanish word exists?
hints: It was founded in the 18th century.
Its motto is «Limpia, fija y da esplendor» (“It cleans, sets and gives splendor”).
In Spanish, it goes by three letters: R, A and E.
questions.description: The official guardians who make sure nobody gets away with a word that's been made up.
questions.fun_fact: Each academician has a chair marked with a letter, in uppercase and lowercase, like “A” and “a”.

questions.question: Which of these words is NOT used for a name someone uses instead of their real one?
hints: Three of them can apply to a person.
Two of the four words end in a Greek root meaning “name”.
“Madrid” and “Guadalquivir” are examples of this word.
questions.description: Signing with another name: many writers' favorite disguise.
questions.fun_fact: “Clarín” and “Azorín” are pseudonyms: their real names were Leopoldo Alas and José Martínez Ruiz.

questions.question: Gloria Fuertes, the children's poet, was on Spanish TV in the 1970s and '80s with short hair, always wearing something at her neck. What?
hints: Back then, it was something mostly men wore.
It is knotted under the shirt collar.
Many men put one on to go to a wedding or the office.
questions.description: A poet whose style was so much her own that you knew her before she read a single line.
questions.fun_fact: Gloria Fuertes recited her poems on TVE children's shows like “Un globo, dos globos, tres globos.”

questions.question: Which creatures run Gringotts, the wizarding bank?
hints: They are short, very clever and brilliant with gold and metalwork.
One of them, Griphook, helps Harry get into a vault.
They have long fingers, pointy ears and very grumpy faces.
questions.description: The only bank where nobody complains about the line, because complaining looks like a bad idea.
questions.fun_fact: To reach the deepest vaults at Gringotts, you ride down in little carts that race along like a roller coaster.

questions.question: On the news, you see the King presenting the Cervantes Prize in Alcalá de Henares. What day of the year is it usually?
hints: It's in spring.
It's the date linked to Cervantes's death.
It's the same day as World Book Day.
questions.description: A ceremony so formal that even the morning coats get nervous.
questions.fun_fact: The first Cervantes Prize, in 1976, went to the poet Jorge Guillén.

questions.question: Pío Baroja's “El árbol de la ciencia” shows Spain before the defeat that gave his generation its name. What year was that defeat?
hints: It is at the end of the 19th century.
Spain lost a war against the United States.
That year Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines.
questions.description: A medical student who ends up with more doubts than class notes.
questions.fun_fact: The novel is by Pío Baroja, and its hero, Andrés Hurtado, studies medicine in Madrid at the end of the 19th century.

questions.question: Spanish is called “the language of Cervantes.” Which of these writer–language pairs is NOT correct?
hints: Each language is named after its most famous writer.
Think of the country where each writer was born.
The wrong writer wrote “Faust” in Germany.
questions.description: Every language has its star writer, just like every Spanish town has its fiesta.
questions.fun_fact: The Instituto Cervantes is named after the author of Don Quixote and teaches Spanish all over the world.

questions.question: After “The Art of Flying”, about his father, Antonio Altarriba and Kim made another graphic novel about his mother. What is it called?
hints: The title follows the flying idea of the first book.
It's about a woman with an injury she hid for almost her whole life.
It's the part of a bird that, when hurt, keeps it from flying.
questions.description: A family album in comic panels: first the father, then the mother.
questions.fun_fact: “The Art of Flying” won Spain's National Comic Award in 2010.

questions.question: Who created “El héroe” (The Hero), the graphic novel that tells the labors of Hercules as a superhero comic?
hints: He is a Galician author born in the 1970s.
He also turned the poem “Beowulf” into a comic with Santiago García.
He shares his first name with the Bible king who beat Goliath.
questions.description: Twelve labors, one cape and lots of panels: a demigod's workout plan.
questions.fun_fact: “El héroe” came out in two volumes and was also published in the United States.

questions.question: I was born in Madrid in 1941, spent part of my childhood in postwar boarding homes and told the story in “Paracuellos”. Who am I?
hints: I started publishing “Paracuellos” in the 1970s.
Later I told the story of my teenage years in another series called “Barrio”.
My first name is Carlos.
questions.description: A cartoonist who turned his school memories into comics you can't forget.
questions.fun_fact: “Paracuellos” became one of the most awarded Spanish comics and has been translated into several languages.

questions.question: You open a comic and see a building cut open from top to bottom, with all its neighbors on show: it's «13, Rue del Percebe». In which decade did it start?
hints: It's one of Francisco Ibáñez's first series.
It appeared soon after Mortadelo y Filemón, born in 1958.
It started in 1961.
questions.description: An apartment building with no front wall and zero privacy.
questions.fun_fact: Every page of «13, Rue del Percebe» showed what was happening on every floor at once, from the doorman's lodge to the rooftop.

questions.question: Geryon had three bodies and ruled an island near Gadir, today's Cádiz. Hercules beat him in one of his twelve labors. What did he take?
hints: It was something alive that grazed and moved around.
Hercules had to drive it on foot all the way to Greece.
They were reddish animals with horns.
questions.description: Having three bodies doesn't help much when the most famous strongman in Greece knocks on your door.
questions.fun_fact: In A Coruña, legend says Hercules buried Geryon's head and built the Tower of Hercules on top of it.

questions.question: The giant Caraculiambro, lord of the isle of Malindrania, would have to kneel before a lady. In which book does he appear?
hints: It's a Spanish book from the Golden Age.
That giant exists only in the hero's imagination.
The lady in question is called Dulcinea.
questions.description: A giant whose name is scarier than his size.
questions.fun_fact: Caraculiambro shows up in the very first chapter: he's just an imagined giant the hidalgo dreams of defeating.

questions.question: In the Colegio del Patriarca in Valencia hangs a “dragon” that is really a stuffed reptile. According to legend, who killed it?
hints: He was no nobleman and no famous hero.
He wore armor covered in mirrors to confuse the beast.
In return for killing it, he was promised something very precious: his freedom.
questions.description: A dragon that has been hanging around for centuries without a single complaint.
questions.fun_fact: The famous “dragon” of the Patriarca is really a stuffed crocodile or caiman.

questions.question: I'm a Hogwarts subject: in my class, students read tea leaves, and a centaur teaches by watching the planets. What am I?
hints: My main teacher lives at the top of a tower full of incense.
That teacher is Sybill Trelawney, who keeps predicting terrible things for Harry.
My goal is to see the future.
questions.description: A class where you can get top marks if you already know what's on the test.
questions.fun_fact: The centaur Firenze teaches this subject in a classroom that looks like a forest, with moss on the floor.

questions.question: The Asturian trasgu wears a red cap, limps and has a hole in one hand. What task do you give him to get rid of him?
hints: The trasgu loves to show off and never turns down a job.
The trick is to make him tired of it so he leaves forever.
The container is full of holes.
questions.description: A lodger who pays no rent and still moves your things around.
questions.fun_fact: One story says a trasgu loved his family so much that when they moved house, he rode along with them in the cart.

questions.question: Legend says that if you're rowing back to port tired in Cantabria, tiny green-winged beings help you. What are they called?
hints: They are kind beings, not mischievous at all.
They mostly help the oldest fishermen.
They travel on the sea breezes.
questions.description: The smallest helpers in the fishing fleet, and the worst paid.
questions.fun_fact: Ventolines are said to be air spirits that come down from the sky to quietly push the boats along.

questions.question: The Asturian cuélebre is a huge winged serpent that lives in caves and springs, and its scales harden with age. What does it guard?
hints: What it guards is hidden underground.
Lots of people would like to take it from him to get rich.
Water fairies live next to what it guards.
questions.description: A security guard with scales and a really bad temper.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that when the cuélebre grows old, it flies off to the sea and keeps guarding treasures there.

questions.question: In Santa Marta de Ribarteme, in Pontevedra, people who escaped death parade inside coffins. On what day is it held?
hints: It's held in summer.
It's the feast day of the saint the parish is named after.
It's late in the month that comes after June.
questions.description: A procession where some people would rather lie down than walk.
questions.fun_fact: The people in the parade are thanking Saint Martha for helping them through a serious illness or an accident.

questions.question: This singer in the photo was one of the favorites at the first Benidorm Fest with “Ay mamá”. Who is she?
hints: She’s from Barcelona and used to work as a voice actress for dubbing.
Her stage name sounds Italian, but it isn’t.
Her real name is Paula Ribó.
questions.description: A singer who shouts for her mom, and half the country sings backup.
questions.fun_fact: Paula Ribó picked “Rigoberta” after Rigoberta Menchú and “Bandini” after a character in a John Fante novel.

questions.question: Pepe Rodríguez is from Illescas (Toledo), and his Michelin-starred restaurant El Bohío reinvents the dishes of his home region. What cuisine does he cook?
hints: Look at where Toledo is on the map.
Think of pisto, aged cheese and migas.
It's the land of Don Quixote.
questions.description: The judge who laughs a lot on TV, but in his kitchen nobody laughs at the lamb.
questions.fun_fact: El Bohío started out as the Rodríguez family's simple local eatery.

questions.question: You're watching FIFA videos on YouTube and the most famous Spanish YouTuber for them shows up, a big Real Madrid fan. Who is it?
hints: His videos are almost always about soccer.

His name has two i's in a row.
questions.description: A controller, a virtual ball and a goal scream heard across the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: DjMaRiiO's YouTube channel has more than 10 million subscribers.

questions.question: I started as a reporter on “Caiga quien caiga”, played Julián in “Camera Café”, and on “¡Ahora caigo!” contestants drop through a trapdoor. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Valencia.
I also hosted “Mask Singer” on Antena 3.
My surname sounds almost like the Spanish word for a waltz.
questions.description: A whole life on TV, jumping from set to set without a hair out of place.
questions.fun_fact: On “Mask Singer”, hosted by Arturo Valls, celebrities sing in costume and you have to guess who they are.

questions.question: Which streamer runs La Velada del Año, the boxing event between content creators?
hints: He's Basque.
He's famous for his live streams with guests and his contagious laugh.
He's known just by his first name, which means “river” in Basque.
questions.description: One night when streamers put down the keyboard and put on the gloves.
questions.fun_fact: Between fights, La Velada has live shows by singers.

questions.question: “Sálvame”, Telecinco's celebrity gossip show, said goodbye in June 2023. In what year did it start?
hints: It ran for more than a decade.
It started two years after the first iPhone came out.
It ended after 14 years on air.
questions.description: Whole afternoons of shouting, exclusives and someone yelling “That's not how it happened!”.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the afternoon show, it had a special Friday night edition: “Sálvame Deluxe”.

questions.question: Mikecrack, El Trollino and Timba Vk form a group famous for their videos and adventure books. What is it called?
hints: Their adventures usually take place in Minecraft.
Their books fill the libraries of many schools.
Their name is a friendly way of saying “compañeros” (companions).
questions.description: Three friends, a world made of blocks and a stack of books on your shelf.
questions.fun_fact: The Los Compas books have sold millions of copies in Spain and Latin America.

questions.question: In which decade did the film where Lola Flores sings “A tu vera” come out?
hints: The film is already in color, not black and white.
It was the same decade in which the Beatles became famous.
The film is “El balcón de la Luna”, from 1962.
questions.description: A copla so catchy it sticks to you like glue.
questions.fun_fact: “A tu vera” means ‘by your side,’ and it is one of the most covered coplas ever.

questions.question: You're at a flamenco-jazz concert. Complete this: “Paco de Lucía is to the guitar as Jorge Pardo is to…”
hints: It's a wind instrument.
You hold it sideways and blow across a hole.
Pardo played this silver instrument for years in Paco de Lucía's sextet.
questions.description: A question for people who'd never miss a concert, even if it rained indoors.
questions.fun_fact: Paco de Lucía's sextet also had Rubem Dantas, the percussionist who helped bring the Peruvian cajón into flamenco.

questions.question: I was born in Córdoba in 1969, danced with the Spanish National Ballet, and with “Pasión gitana” I filled theaters worldwide dancing shirtless. Who am I?
hints: I'm a flamenco dancer, not a singer.
I even appeared in a Pedro Almodóvar film.
I share my surname with the conquistador who reached Mexico.
questions.description: A question that walks on stage stamping hard and without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Joaquín Cortés appeared in Pedro Almodóvar's film “The Flower of My Secret” (1995).

questions.question: Which of these songs was NOT made famous by Manolo Escobar?
hints: The odd one out is from the 1990s.
It was sung by a duo from Seville and has a dance with arm moves.

questions.fun_fact: “Y viva España” was first released in 1971 by a Belgian singer, Samantha, before Manolo Escobar made it his own.

questions.question: Café de Chinitas was a famous 19th-century flamenco café, and Lorca sang about it in a folk song. In which city was it?

questions.question: How many brothers make up the band Estopa?

questions.fun_fact: Estopa's first album, from 1999, sold more than a million copies in Spain.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who is this French player, the all-time top scorer of Atlético de Madrid?

His last name starts with “G” and fans call him “Grizi”.
questions.description: He celebrates his goals by dancing, and he's had plenty of chances to practice.

questions.question: Which of these teams does NOT play in red-and-white striped shirts?

Its shirt is all white.
questions.description: A shirt that looks like a candy cane.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that Atlético de Madrid began as a branch of Athletic Bilbao, which is why it shares the red-and-white stripes.

questions.question: Sergio Ramos was born in Camas, on the Guadalquivir, and made his debut for the club of his province's capital. Which province?
hints: It's a province in Andalusia.
Its capital is the biggest city in Andalusia and also the capital of the region.
The Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán stadium is there.
questions.description: A defender with more tattoos than a sticker album has stickers.
questions.fun_fact: Sergio Ramos has played more games for Spain's national team than anyone else: 180.

questions.question: I was Quidditch captain and Keeper, and I cried with joy when we won the cup in my last year. Which Hogwarts house was I in?
hints: My name is Oliver Wood.

My house has a lion as its symbol.
questions.description: A captain who talks about Quidditch even in his sleep.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Hogwarts, Oliver Wood signed with the reserve team of Puddlemere United.

questions.question: Andrés Iniesta won this trophy with Spain, and you can see part of it. Which one is it?
hints: It's the biggest trophy a national team can win.
It's golden, and figures hold up the globe.
Iniesta won it by scoring in South Africa in 2010.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who wears an armband like this one during a soccer game?
hints: It's one of the team's players.

The armband often has a letter “C” on it.
questions.description: A little strip of cloth that weighs more than a whole pair of cleats.

previous.feedback: The fun fact gets the toss rule wrong and doesn't match the source. Since the 2019 Laws of the Game, the team that wins the toss chooses either which goal to attack or to take the kickoff. Translate the source faithfully: “At the coin toss before the match, the captains are the ones who choose the end or the kickoff.”

questions.question: England is to the Premier League as Spain is to…

questions.question: Which of these is NOT on the Real Madrid crest?

questions.question: They pay a fee, carry a card and vote to elect the president of Barça, Real Madrid, Athletic and Osasuna. What are they called in Spain?
hints: These four clubs have no single owner.

In everyday Spanish, the same word also means business partners.
questions.description: They shout louder than the coach and pay for the privilege.
questions.fun_fact: Barça, Real Madrid, Athletic and Osasuna are the only professional clubs in Spanish soccer that never became “sociedades anónimas deportivas” (sports companies owned by shareholders).

questions.question: How many European Cups (Champions League titles) did Carlo Ancelotti win as Real Madrid coach?
hints: More than one.
One of them was the famous “Décima”.
He won them in 2014, 2022 and 2024.
questions.description: An Italian who lifts trophies with a single raised eyebrow.
questions.fun_fact: Ancelotti also won two European Cups as coach of AC Milan, so he has five in total.

questions.question: This curly-haired player won Euro 2024 with Spain. Which part of the team does he play in?
hints: His main job is to stop the other team from scoring.
He plays close to the left touchline.
He's a left back.
questions.description: A hairstyle so famous it has more fans than some teams.
questions.fun_fact: In the Euro 2024 final, Cucurella gave Oyarzabal the pass for the winning goal.

questions.question: David Silva, the Canary Islander who became a Manchester City hero, won how many major tournaments with Spain's national team?
hints: He played in Spain's golden era, between 2008 and 2012.
Count the Euros and World Cups from those years.
Two Euros and one World Cup.
questions.description: A wizard from the Canary Islands who made defenders vanish without a wand.
questions.fun_fact: Manchester City put up a statue of David Silva next to its stadium in 2021.

questions.question: Messi, Sergio Busquets, Jordi Alba and Luis Suárez all ended up at Inter Miami. How many of them are Spanish?
hints: Think about which national team each one played for at the World Cup.
Busquets won the World Cup with Spain in South Africa in 2010.
The Spaniards are the midfielder and the left back.
questions.description: A Barça class reunion, but with palm trees.
questions.fun_fact: Inter Miami plays in an eye-catching pink jersey.

questions.question: The 2030 World Cup will have three matches in South America for its 100th anniversary, but almost all of it will be in Spain and two other countries. Which ones?
hints: The bid brought together countries that are very close to each other.
One is on the other side of the Strait of Gibraltar.
The other shares the Iberian Peninsula with Spain.
questions.description: A birthday party so big it needs several houses.
questions.fun_fact: The 2030 World Cup will be the first one played on three continents: Europe, Africa and South America.

questions.question: This Spain forward came up through the youth academy of a big club from his home region, then joined Manchester City and Barça. Where is he from?
hints: His nickname is “el Tiburón” (the Shark).
He was born in a town near the Mediterranean coast.
He made his top-flight debut with the club that plays at Mestalla.
questions.description: A striker with a sea-creature nickname who can't swim through defenders… or can he?
questions.fun_fact: Ferran Torres celebrates his goals by making a shark fin with his hands, a nod to his nickname.

questions.question: Legend says that when the hand carved on this gate's arch reaches the key on the inner arch, the building will fall. Where is it?
hints: It's a monument from al-Andalus, Muslim Spain.
Many people see the carved hand as a Hand of Fatima, a symbol of protection.
It's the Nasrid palace that looks out at the Sierra Nevada.
questions.description: A gate with a carved hand: clearly someone wanted to lend a hand.
questions.fun_fact: The Gate of Justice was built in 1348, in the time of the Nasrid sultan Yusuf I.

questions.question: You’re watching “La lengua de las mariposas” (Butterfly’s Tongue): Moncho’s school year in his Galician village ends when the Civil War breaks out. What year is it?
hints: It’s before the Second World War.
The war began in summer and lasted until 1939.
It’s the same year the Spanish Civil War broke out.
questions.description: A school year nobody would ever forget, even if they wanted to.
questions.fun_fact: José Luis Cuerda’s movie is based on a short story by Manuel Rivas, first written in Galician.

questions.question: I'm a hairy giant from Basque and Navarrese mythology who protects the forests, and the “invisible guardian” in Dolores Redondo's novel. Who am I?
hints: I live in the forests of the Baztán valley.
My name in Basque means something like “lord of the forest.”
My name starts with “basa.”
questions.description: A forest neighbor who never goes to the barber.
questions.fun_fact: The Baztán Trilogy, with Inspector Amaia Salazar, was filmed in Elizondo and its forests.

questions.question: Ildefonso Falcones’s «La catedral del mar» (Cathedral of the Sea) is set while Barcelona’s Santa Maria del Mar church is built. In which century?
hints: It’s right in the Middle Ages.
The church is Gothic.
Building work began in 1329.
questions.description: A building project so slow the bricklayers retired before seeing the roof.
questions.fun_fact: The bastaixos, the port’s dockworkers, carried the church’s stones on their backs, and they still appear carved on its doors.

questions.question: In Maite Carranza’s “El clan de la loba”, Anaíd lives in a village in the Pyrenees and finds out she has powers. What is she?
hints: Don’t trust the title: she doesn’t turn into an animal.
She comes from a long line of women who cast spells.
The trilogy is called “La guerra de las…”, “The War of the…”.
questions.description: A teenager who learns her family keeps more secrets than Grandma does with her cocido recipe.
questions.fun_fact: Maite Carranza’s trilogy has been translated into more than twenty languages.

questions.question: I interviewed the key figures of Spain's transition to democracy for El País, wrote “La loca de la casa” and created the replicant detective Bruna Husky. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Madrid and I still write for newspapers.
My Bruna Husky novels are science fiction set in a future Madrid.
I won Spain's National Prize for Letters in 2017.
questions.description: A pen that moves just as well in the newsroom as in the future.
questions.fun_fact: “The madwoman of the house” was Saint Teresa's name for the imagination, and Rosa Montero borrowed it for her book.

questions.question: In «El tiempo entre costuras» (The Time in Between), Sira opens her workshop in the capital of the Spanish protectorate in Morocco. Which city?
hints: It’s in northern Morocco.
Sira gets there after a stay in Tangier.
Its white medina is very close to Ceuta.
questions.description: Needle, thread, spies and a city as white as a brand-new sewing pattern.
questions.fun_fact: The Antena 3 series, with Adriana Ugarte as Sira, was partly filmed in Tetouan itself.

questions.question: I wrote “Fariña”, about smuggling in Galicia’s rías; a judge pulled it from bookstores in 2018, and later it became a series. Who am I?
hints: I’m a Galician journalist.
The book was my debut, published in 2015.
My first name is a nickname for Ignacio.
questions.description: A book that was grounded for a while and not allowed out of the house.
questions.fun_fact: After the court ban, the book sold out and became one of the most requested of the year.

previous.feedback: Source: the timeline is wrong in both versions. The Antena 3 series “Fariña” premiered in late February 2018, and the judge ordered the book pulled from stores in early March 2018, so “a judge pulled it… and it later became a TV series” gets the order backwards. The source should say something like “it became a TV series, and a judge pulled it from bookstores in 2018”, and then the translation should follow it. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: What is the magic game, a bit like marbles, where the pieces squirt a smelly liquid at a player who loses a point?
hints: Harry sees other students playing it at Hogwarts.
Snape's mother, Eileen Prince, was captain of this game's club at Hogwarts.
Its name ends with what the pieces are usually made of.
questions.description: Marbles, but with really bad manners.
questions.fun_fact: The pieces of this game can be made of stone or even solid gold.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is right. The smelly squirt, the marbles comparison and Eileen Prince as club captain are confirmed. Two claims are not supported. Rowling's site says the stones may be made of 'precious metals', not specifically 'solid gold'. I also found no source for 'Harry sees other students playing it at Hogwarts'. The Gobstones Club first appears in Order of the Phoenix.

questions.question: Which of these writers did NOT win Seix Barral's Biblioteca Breve Prize?
hints: The winners of the 1960s helped launch the Latin American Boom.
One won with “The Time of the Hero” and another with “Últimas tardes con Teresa.”
The odd one out published his masterpiece in Buenos Aires in 1967.
questions.description: A prize named after a small bookshelf, with some very big winners.
questions.fun_fact: The prize stopped being awarded in 1972 and didn't come back until 1999.

questions.question: Which character does NOT belong to the El Barco de Vapor book series?
hints: El Barco de Vapor is a Spanish series of children's books.
It is published by SM and aimed at children starting to read on their own.
The odd one out is an English wizard with glasses.
questions.description: A steamboat that sails bookshelves instead of the sea.
questions.fun_fact: El Barco de Vapor books are sorted by color according to age: white, blue, orange and red.

questions.question: Which of these novels did Carlos Ruiz Zafón NOT write?
hints: All four novels are set in Barcelona.
The odd one out is much older: it came out in the 1940s, before Ruiz Zafón was born.
Its title is the Spanish word for “nothing”.
questions.description: A Barcelona bookshelf with an intruder from the same city.
questions.fun_fact: “The Shadow of the Wind” is one of the best-selling Spanish novels ever, with millions of copies sold worldwide.

questions.question: You're walking around Las Setas in Seville, the huge wooden structure on Plaza de la Encarnación. What is NOT there?
hints: Three of the options really are under, inside or on top of Las Setas.
Old mosaics turned up while the foundations were dug, and up top there's a walkway with views.
The missing one would need a big sand ring, and Seville already has a famous one by the river.
questions.description: Giant mushrooms in the middle of the city, and nobody dares to put them in the stew.
questions.fun_fact: Las Setas opened in 2011 and are among the largest wooden structures in the world.

questions.question: You're standing in front of Almudena Cathedral, facing the Royal Palace of Madrid. How long did the cathedral take to finish?
hints: Building work started in the 19th century.
For decades only the crypt was finished and in use, while the church above it kept waiting.
The first stone was laid in 1883.
questions.description: Home renovations always take longer than planned, but some building projects really take their time.
questions.fun_fact: In 2004, today's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia got married in the Almudena.

questions.question: Barça's stadium opened in 1957. What does its name, “Camp Nou,” mean in English?
hints: It's in Catalan.
“Camp” comes from the same Latin word as the English “campus.”
“Nou” is the opposite of “old.”
questions.description: A stadium so big that from the back row the players look like ants in cleats.
questions.fun_fact: Before its big renovation it held almost 100,000 people, more than any other stadium in Europe.

questions.question: On the Arch of Santa María in Burgos, surrounded by Castilian heroes like El Cid and Fernán González, one king takes center stage. Which one?
hints: The front of the arch was rebuilt in the 16th century.
It was made to win back the king's favor after the Revolt of the Comuneros.
He was also Holy Roman Emperor, under the name Charles V.
questions.description: A city gate with more celebrities on its front than a red carpet.
questions.fun_fact: The arch also shows Nuño Rasura and Laín Calvo, the legendary judges of Castile.

questions.question: The Generalife gardens, next to the Alhambra in Granada, are still watered by their old channels. About how old are they?
hints: The Nasrid sultans built them.
They are older than the Catholic Monarchs' capture of Granada in 1492.
They were laid out in the early 14th century.
questions.description: A garden where even the fountains pose for the tourists' photos.
questions.fun_fact: The name Generalife is often translated as “the architect's orchard” or “garden of paradise.”

questions.question: It lies between the Royal Palace and the Teatro Real, with Philip IV on horseback and statues of kings all around. Why is it called Plaza de Oriente?
questions.answer: Because it is east of the Royal Palace
wrong_answers: Because spices from Asia were sold there
Because an emperor of Japan once visited
hints: The name has nothing to do with Asia.
“Oriente” is the side where the sun rises.
Its name says where it lies compared to the biggest building next to it.
questions.description: A Madrid square where stone kings stand guard, and one even pulls off a balancing act on horseback.
questions.fun_fact: Galileo Galilei helped work out the balance of that statue, where the horse rests only on its back legs.

questions.question: Every December 22, a big drum spins while children sing out numbers and prizes. Which draw is it?
hints: It takes place just before the school winter break starts.
Its most famous prize is called «el Gordo».
Its name holds the same holiday as the tree and the nativity scene.
questions.description: A December morning when half of Spain is glued to the TV with fingers crossed.
questions.fun_fact: The Christmas draw was held for the first time in 1812, in Cádiz.

questions.question: You're at an army barracks, and at sunset the soldiers lower the flag. When will they raise it again?
hints: It happens every single day.
The flag flies during the daylight hours.
It goes up when the day begins and the bugle plays reveille.
questions.description: A piece of cloth with a stricter schedule than your school.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, raising the flag has its own verb, «izar», and lowering it is «arriar».

questions.question: You're in Park Güell, which Eusebi Güell asked Gaudí to build as a luxury housing estate. What inspired Güell?
hints: Güell greatly admired a very industrialized country of his time.
It was a model of suburb mixing houses with lots of nature, fashionable in the late 19th century.
It's the country of Big Ben and afternoon tea.
questions.description: A patron so rich he ordered whole neighborhoods the way you'd order a pizza.
questions.fun_fact: It was meant to have about 60 houses, but only two were sold, and Gaudí himself bought one of them.

questions.question: This Madrid-born painter, a student of Carlos de Haes, painted the Guadarrama mountains and wrote a famous book on Velázquez. Who is he?
hints: Besides painting, he was a lawyer and a member of parliament.
He was a close friend of Joaquín Sorolla.
His son, who had the same name, went on to run the Prado Museum.
questions.description: A painter who swapped the bustle of Madrid for the fresh mountain air, brush in hand.
questions.fun_fact: His friend Joaquín Sorolla painted a portrait of him that now hangs in the Prado Museum.

questions.question: I was Real Sociedad's goalkeeper until an injury ended it, then became a sculptor, and my steel combs comb the wind in San Sebastián. Who am I?
hints: I was born in San Sebastián in 1924.
My house-museum is in an old farmhouse in Hernani, surrounded by sculptures in a meadow.
I also have a big work in Gijón: the “Elogio del horizonte”.
questions.description: From stopping balls to bending steel: the strangest transfer in art history.
questions.fun_fact: Each steel piece of the Comb of the Wind weighs about 10 tonnes (11 tons).

questions.question: At a peace march you see a banner with a simple white dove drawn in a few lines. Which painter made it famous on a 1949 poster?
hints: It was for a peace congress held in Paris.
His daughter was born that same year, and he named her Paloma, Spanish for “dove”.
He painted “Guernica”.
questions.description: A bird that flew from a poster around half the world without flapping its wings.
questions.fun_fact: Picasso named the daughter he had in 1949 Paloma, Spanish for “dove”, the same year as the famous poster.

questions.question: Look at this photo of Terminal 4 at Madrid-Barajas Airport. Which British architect designed it with Estudio Lamela?
hints: He won the Pritzker Prize in 2007.
Earlier, he had designed the Pompidou Center in Paris with Renzo Piano.
In London he built the Lloyd's building, with its pipes on the outside.
questions.description: A place where people run with suitcases, staring at the ceiling without knowing it's a work of art.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006 the T4 won the Stirling Prize, the most prestigious award in British architecture.

questions.question: You're in the Royal Palace of Madrid, looking at ceilings by a court painter of Charles III, born in Bohemia and a great champion of Neoclassicism. Who is he?
hints: Before coming to Spain, he worked a lot in Rome.
He was a friend of the art historian Winckelmann.
His middle name is that of a great painter of the Italian Renaissance.
questions.description: A painter who came to Madrid to decorate ceilings and ended up ruling the taste of a whole royal court.
questions.fun_fact: Mengs and Tiepolo were working in the Royal Palace at the same time, and they were rivals in style.

questions.question: My house and studio in Madrid, with a garden inspired by Seville and Granada, is now my museum. My wife, Clotilde, left it to the state. Who am I?
hints: People called me the painter of light.
I was born in Valencia in 1863.
I painted lots of children swimming at Malvarrosa beach.
questions.description: An artist who never had to commute: his work lived in his living room.
questions.fun_fact: The Sorolla Museum opened in 1932 and keeps the studio almost exactly as the painter left it.

questions.question: Francisco Pacheco is to Velázquez what Velázquez is to Juan Bautista Martínez del Mazo. What is the relationship?
hints: All three were painters in 17th-century Spain.
Their bond was both from the workshop and from the family.
Velázquez married Juana, Pacheco’s daughter.
questions.description: In the Golden Age, paintbrushes traveled from Seville to Madrid and reached the Prado without losing their shine.
questions.fun_fact: Martínez del Mazo, Velázquez’s pupil, married his daughter Francisca, just as Velázquez had married his own teacher’s daughter.

questions.question: Which of these artists was NOT part of the Dau al Set group, founded in Barcelona?
hints: The group began in 1948 and published a magazine with the same name.
The one you're looking for founded another group almost ten years later, in Madrid.
That other Madrid group was called El Paso.
questions.description: A group of artists who rolled the die and got a side that doesn't exist.
questions.fun_fact: “Dau al Set” is Catalan for “die on seven”, a side no die has.

questions.question: I'm an object: if you write on my pages, the ink disappears and a young man named Tom Riddle writes back. What am I?
hints: I appear in “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.”
Ginny Weasley found me and wrote her secrets in me.
Harry destroyed me with a basilisk fang.
questions.description: An object that keeps secrets… and talks back.
questions.fun_fact: The letters of “Tom Marvolo Riddle” can be rearranged to spell “I am Lord Voldemort.”

questions.question: Look at this painting by Jusepe de Ribera, with its black background and strong light from one side. Where did this style come to Spanish painting from?
hints: It arrived from Italy in the early 17th century.
Ribera lived and painted in Naples.
It was created by an Italian painter with a very wild life, who painted “The Calling of Saint Matthew.”
questions.description: Painters who worked as if someone had switched off the lights and left them only a flashlight.
questions.fun_fact: Ribera, born in Xàtiva, lived in Naples, where Italians called him “lo Spagnoletto,” the little Spaniard.

questions.question: The cathedrals of Burgos, León and Toledo are Gothic. Where does the name “Gothic” come from?
questions.answer: From the Goths, a Germanic people
wrong_answers: From the German town of Gotha
From the Latin word “gutta”, a drop
From a French monk named Gautier
hints: The name was given centuries later, in the Renaissance.
It was invented by Italian artists who preferred the classical style of ancient Rome.
In Spain, schoolchildren learn about the Visigoths, one of their branches.
questions.description: Cathedrals so tall their builders must have had permanently stiff necks.
questions.fun_fact: The Goths never built a single Gothic cathedral: the style was born in France centuries after them.

questions.question: Look at the photo: every July, this plant turns the fields of Brihuega, in Guadalajara, purple. What is it?
hints: Its scent is in lots of soaps and air fresheners.
It's put into little cloth bags to make clothes smell nice.
Its name comes from the Latin word for “to wash”.
questions.description: A landscape so purple it looks like someone went overboard with a phone filter.
questions.fun_fact: Every summer Brihuega holds a festival with concerts right in the middle of its purple fields.

questions.question: I'm a field full of water that shines like a mirror. In Valencia I surround the Albufera, and the grain for paella comes from me. What am I?
hints: Herons walk through me looking for food.
A small white grain grows in me.
I'm named after the main ingredient of paella.
questions.description: A field so tidy it looks like it was combed with a ruler.
questions.fun_fact: Many of the Albufera's rice fields are flooded in winter and become a shelter for thousands of birds.

questions.question: The cardo (thistle) has prickles and purple flowers and grows by the roadside. In Spain, what does it mean if someone “es un cardo”?
hints: Think about how it would feel to touch that plant.
It's the opposite of someone warm and cuddly.
That person won't even let you hug them.
questions.description: Some plants get used as insults, and nobody asked them first.
questions.fun_fact: The artichoke is a farmed cousin of the thistle: the part we eat is its flower before it opens.

questions.question: Which of these trees, very common in Spain, is NOT native and came from another continent?
hints: It was planted widely in Galicia for timber and paper.
Its leaves smell like cough drops.
It's the koala's favorite food.
questions.description: A forest can look like it's always been there and still hide a secret.
questions.fun_fact: Eucalyptus came to Spain from Australia in the 19th century and now covers hundreds of thousands of hectares in Galicia.

questions.question: Its grain plains turn golden in summer, it's called “the granary of Spain,” and it grows more wheat than any other region. Which is it?
hints: It's the largest region in Spain.
The Duero River flows through it.
Valladolid, Burgos and Salamanca are there.
questions.description: Where bread starts its life, long before it reaches the bakery.
questions.fun_fact: The Canal de Castilla was built starting in the 18th century to carry Castilian wheat toward the northern ports.

questions.question: Which Spanish streamer founded the esports club KOI in 2021?
hints: Before becoming a streamer, he was a commentator for League of Legends matches.
Every year he puts on La Velada del Año, an event where creators box each other.
He is from Bilbao and his first name starts with “I”.
questions.description: A club named after a pond fish that has never swum a stroke in its life.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024 KOI joined forces with Movistar Riders and the club was renamed Movistar KOI.

questions.question: Before La Velada del Año, Ibai posts posters and teasers for weeks. Why does he do it?
hints: He wants people counting down the days.
He wants everyone excited and eager for it.
It's a short word for big buzz and high expectations.
questions.description: Weeks of posters, teasers and countdowns for something that lasts one night.
questions.fun_fact: The word “hype” was used for over-the-top advertising long before streamers existed.

questions.question: Which of these radio stations does NOT belong to the COPE group, as Rock FM does?
hints: The COPE group's stations are linked to the Spanish Bishops' Conference.
The odd one out belongs to the PRISA group, like the newspaper El País.
The odd one out began as a hit-music chart on Cadena SER.
questions.description: Three sisters on the dial and one neighbor who sneaked into the family photo.
questions.fun_fact: Rock FM plays almost nothing but rock classics, from the Beatles to AC/DC.

questions.question: In heraldry, what do you call a shield split from top to bottom by a vertical line into two halves, like this one?
hints: All four terms are real, and each names a different way to divide a shield.
The one split by a horizontal line is called “per fess”.
Its name comes from the Latin “palus”, a wooden stake or fence post.
questions.description: A shield that can't make up its mind, so it keeps both options at once.
questions.fun_fact: A shield split both per pale and per fess ends up in four parts: that's called “quarterly”.

questions.question: The coat of arms of Galicia shows a gold chalice on a blue background, surrounded by crosses. What rises above the chalice?
hints: It's white or silver.
It has to do with Mass.
In church it's called the Sacred Host.
questions.description: A shield so blue it looks like the Galician sky on its one sunny day.
questions.fun_fact: The seven crosses on the Galician coat of arms stand for the seven provinces of the old Kingdom of Galicia.

questions.question: I was born in Ponteceso in 1835, was a poet of the Galician Rexurdimento, and wrote the lyrics of “Os Pinos”, Galicia's anthem. Who am I?
hints: People called me “the bard of Bergantiños”.
My great book of poems is called “Queixumes dos pinos”.
My surname starts with “Pon”, like my hometown.
questions.description: Someone who sang so much about pine trees that he ended up writing the words for a whole nation.
questions.fun_fact: “Os Pinos” was first sung as an anthem in Havana, in 1907.

questions.question: The bear and the strawberry tree are to Madrid's coat of arms as which crowned animal, on a red background, is to Zaragoza's?
hints: It's an animal that doesn't live in Aragon.
It also appears on the crest of Real Zaragoza.
It's called the king of the jungle.
questions.description: Every city has its official mascot, and not all of them are as calm as a bear snacking on fruit.
questions.fun_fact: The lion on Zaragoza's coat of arms is gold and wears a crown, on a red field.

questions.question: Which autonomous community does this flag belong to?
hints: It's a region in the north, with a coastline.
It's a land of green valleys and dairy cows, famous for its sobaos.
It's where people eat the famous rabas, and it's home to the Altamira caves.
questions.description: Some balconies show off more flags than flowerpots during the fiestas.
questions.fun_fact: The flag of Cantabria has the same colors in the same layout as the flag of Poland.

questions.question: Its Basque name means “the four in one,” and it joined the arms of Álava, Gipuzkoa, Biscay and Navarre in one shield. What is it called?
hints: It was a very popular symbol in the 19th century.
A similar motto unites seven territories on both sides of the Pyrenees.
In Basque, “lau” means four.
questions.description: An emblem that was doing “all for one” long before the Musketeers.
questions.fun_fact: “Zazpiak bat” (“the seven in one”) adds the three Basque territories in France to these four.

questions.question: How wide is “The Persistence of Memory”, Dalí's famous painting of the soft clocks?
hints: Many visitors are surprised when they see it in person.
It's much smaller than most people imagine from the posters and postcards.
It's roughly the size of a large sheet of paper.
questions.description: Some clocks that are late for everything because they melt on the way.
questions.fun_fact: The 1931 painting hangs in MoMA in New York and measures about 24 by 33 centimeters (about 9.5 by 13 inches).

questions.question: In Alange (Badajoz), people still use thermae built by the Romans. What were thermae for?
hints: They had cold, warm and hot rooms.
Today we would call it a spa.
The word is related to “thermal” springs.
questions.description: The Romans’ favorite afternoon plan, and no phone needed.
questions.fun_fact: Romans went to the thermae almost every day: besides bathing, they exercised, read and made business deals.

questions.question: You pass through the Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos) and see dozens of archaeologists digging, as they do every year. What month is it, almost certainly?
hints: Winters in Burgos are very cold.
Many of the diggers are students with no classes.
It falls during the longest school vacation.
questions.description: A job that takes a shovel, a brush and endless patience.
questions.fun_fact: Each Atapuerca dig season brings together hundreds of researchers for a few weeks between June and July.

questions.question: This atrium with a pool in the middle was the heart of a Roman domus, like those in Mérida or Itálica. What was a domus for?
questions.answer: A home for a wealthy family
hints: The pool collected rainwater from the roof
It had bedrooms, a dining room and a kitchen
The English word “domestic” comes from this Latin word
questions.description: A pool right in the middle of the building: every Roman frog's dream.
questions.fun_fact: The House of the Mithraeum in Mérida still has a mosaic of the whole universe, with the sky, the winds and the rivers.

questions.question: Dr. Dre co-founded the headphone brand Beats. In which decade was it founded?
hints: It came after Dr. Dre was already a 1990s rap legend.
The iPod already existed, but the iPhone hadn't come out yet.
It was founded in the middle of the decade when the 21st century began.
questions.description: Headphones so expensive they should come with their own bodyguard.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, Apple bought Beats for about $3 billion.

questions.question: In Spain's Restoration, the party whose turn it was always won. What was the trick of secretly stuffing and removing ballots called?
hints: It came in very handy during the turns between Cánovas and Sagasta.
Today the word is used for any kind of election fraud.
Its name comes from «puchero», a clay cooking pot.
questions.description: An election where the winner knew the result before anyone had voted.
questions.fun_fact: Conservatives and Liberals took turns in government by agreement, in what was called the «turno pacífico» (peaceful turn).

questions.question: You open a can of Calvo tuna. Why is the brand called that?
wrong_answers: After a character from an old ad
