hints: It has nothing to do with hair
Its story begins with a family from Carballo, in Galicia
The man who created it was named Luis
questions.description: A brand that has never needed a comb.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Calvo Sanz founded the company in 1940 in Carballo (A Coruña).

questions.question: It came out in 1605, is credited to Francisco López de Úbeda, and its heroine is a girl from Mansilla de las Mulas (León). What book is it?
hints: It came out the same year as the first part of Don Quixote.
It's a picaresque novel with a woman in the lead role.
The title gives the girl's name and calls her a pícara (a rogue).
questions.description: A girl who got by in life with more smooth talk than a fairground salesman.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes made fun of its author in “Journey to Parnassus”, where he shows him arriving sweaty and in a rush.

questions.question: When was “La gran aventura de Mortadelo y Filemón”, the first live-action film of Ibáñez’s characters, released?
hints: By then Mortadelo had been in the comics for more than 40 years.
It was directed by Javier Fesser, who made “El milagro de P. Tinto”.
It came out early in the 21st century.
questions.description: Two T.I.A. agents step off the comic page and find out the bumps hurt just as much on the big screen.
questions.fun_fact: The film came out in 2003, starring Benito Pocino and Pepe Viyuela, and won several Goya awards.

questions.question: If someone tells you “tienes más cuento que Calleja”, what are they saying?
questions.answer: That you exaggerate or make up excuses
wrong_answers: That you read a huge number of books
That you talk far too loudly
hints: It’s not a compliment.
It’s what people say to someone who pretends to be sick to skip school.
Here, “cuento” means something that isn’t true.
questions.description: A publisher so famous that he ended up in one of grandma’s sayings.
questions.fun_fact: Saturnino Calleja, born in Burgos, sold very cheap illustrated storybooks from his Madrid publishing house so that every child could read.

questions.question: At night you see little blue flames floating over a field: the fuego fatuo, or will-o'-the-wisp. In Spanish folk tradition, what were they?
hints: Many people said a prayer when they saw them.
They were often seen in graveyards.
People believed they were the spirits of people no longer alive.
questions.description: Little night lights with no plug and no batteries.
questions.fun_fact: Science explains them as gases from rotting remains that catch fire on their own when they touch the air.

questions.question: The xanas of Asturias, the Basque lamias and the Galician mouras comb their hair by the water. What kind of comb do they use, according to legend?
hints: Many legends say these beings guard treasures.
Legends say anyone who tried to steal it got into serious trouble.
It's the same metal as pirates' coins.
questions.description: An open-air hair salon with river views, no appointment needed.
questions.fun_fact: In Asturian legends, the xanas also spin skeins of golden thread beside the springs.

questions.question: The Diablos de Luzón blacken their faces with soot and oil, wear cowbells and horns, and put in potato teeth. Which province are they from?
hints: It's a province in the interior of Spain.
Luzón is near the Señorío de Molina.
It belongs to Castilla-La Mancha.
questions.description: A carnival where the makeup comes off with lots of soap and even more patience.
questions.fun_fact: The devils of Luzón come out at carnival and smear black on anyone who crosses their path.

questions.question: I was born in Málaga in 1989, started out posting videos on YouTube, then sang “Solamente tú” and “Saturno”. Who am I?
hints: He’s a singer-songwriter who plays piano and guitar.
His first album, in 2011, was a smash hit in Spain.
His surname is also the name of an island and a sea in the Mediterranean.
questions.description: From singing in his bedroom to filling stadiums, with a stopover on a computer screen.
questions.fun_fact: Kelly Rowland declared herself a Pablo Alborán fan on Twitter while he was still posting videos on YouTube.

questions.question: This singer from Majorca has hits with urban songs like “A mí” and “cómo dormiste?”. Who is he?
hints: He started out rapping before moving on to more melodic songs.
His real name is Daniel Heredia.
His stage name is short and ends in a single letter.
questions.description: Songs for texting to someone in the small hours of the night.
questions.fun_fact: Rels B started out rapping in Majorca and is one of the most streamed Spanish artists in Latin America.

questions.question: At a party, the DJ moves the record back and forth so it goes “wikka-wikka.” In which decade was this trick invented?
hints: It was invented in the Bronx, New York, when hip hop was being born.
It was the same era as disco music and mirror balls.
A teenager invented it in the middle of that decade, while his mother was scolding him about the volume.
questions.description: A record getting pushed back and forth like it's being told off.
questions.fun_fact: Scratching was discovered by Grand Wizzard Theodore when he was about 12, as he stopped a record with his hand while his mother was talking to him.

questions.question: In 2018, “Lo malo” came second in the show that picked Spain’s Eurovision song. Which song won?
hints: It’s a romantic ballad sung as a duet.
Its singers were classmates on Operación Triunfo 2017.
It was sung by Amaia and Alfred.
questions.description: Some finals are decided by text message and then sung at every wedding.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it lost that night, “Lo malo” became an anthem and one of the most-played songs of 2018 in Spain.

questions.question: The chorus “Aserejé, ja, de jé, de jebe tu de jebere…” isn’t a made-up language. What is it really copying?
questions.answer: An English rap sung by ear
wrong_answers: A Latin prayer sung by ear
A Romani copla sung by ear
A Sanskrit mantra sung by ear
hints: The song tells the story of a guy called Diego who walks into a nightclub.
The original came out in 1979, and the singers copied its sounds without knowing what the lyrics said.
It’s “Rapper’s Delight” by the Sugarhill Gang.
questions.description: The secret language everyone sang in 2002 without understanding a single word.
questions.fun_fact: “Aserejé” hit number one in more than twenty countries, and half the world learned its hand dance.

questions.question: Rosalía won the Latin Grammy for Album of the Year with “El mal querer”. In which year?
hints: It was in the 2010s.
The album had come out the fall before, with “Malamente”.
It was just before the year of the pandemic.
questions.description: A golden gramophone that understands Spanish too.
questions.fun_fact: “El mal querer” began as Rosalía's final degree project at the Catalonia College of Music (ESMUC).

questions.question: If on Operación Triunfo the contestants live in “the Academy”, on Gran Hermano they live in…
hints: It’s a place full of cameras everywhere.
It has a living room, a kitchen and a diary room.
It’s the place contestants get “evicted” from every week.
questions.description: A school where the exams are sung and every grade is a musical note.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Gran Hermano” (Big Brother) comes from George Orwell’s novel “1984”, where Big Brother watches everything.

questions.question: The rosco is the final round of “Pasapalabra”: it's shaped like a wheel and each right answer turns green. What is in each circle?
hints: You have to guess one word for each circle.
What's in the circles is also on your computer keyboard keys.
Each word starts with what its circle shows, or contains it.
questions.description: A wheel worth more than a car, if you complete it.
questions.fun_fact: If nobody completes the rosco, the jackpot grows every day, and it has gone over 2 million euros.

questions.question: On which TV cooking show has Samantha Vallejo-Nágera been a judge since 2013?
hints: The contestants are amateur cooks, not professionals.
The format began on British TV in 1990.
It has a Junior version where kids do the cooking.
questions.description: A judge who tells you “I wouldn't serve this at my catering” and ruins your whole day.
questions.fun_fact: Before TV, Samantha started her own catering company in Madrid.

questions.question: The Kings League is a 7-a-side soccer league that Gerard Piqué launched in 2023. Who are the presidents of its teams?
hints: The matches are mostly streamed live on Twitch.
Some presidents never played professionally, but they have millions of followers.
Ibai and Iker Casillas are team presidents.
questions.description: A league where the rules change faster than the score.
questions.fun_fact: The Kings League has “secret cards” that can, for example, give a team an extra penalty.

questions.question: Look at this artist at the tablao. Which part of flamenco is she doing?
hints: Look at her mouth.
She uses her voice, not her hands or feet.
The person who does it is called a cantaor or cantaora.
questions.description: She's been at the tablao all night and still isn't tired.
questions.fun_fact: The cantaor usually sings sitting down, and the guitarist follows the voice to accompany it.

questions.question: Complete the name of Spain's big knockout cup for club teams, played since 1903: the Copa del…
hints: It has to do with who hands over the trophy at the final.
Over the years, the name changed depending on who was ruling Spain.
In Spain today, that's Felipe VI.
questions.description: A trophy so big it takes two captains to lift it and a whole squad to kiss it.
questions.fun_fact: The trophy is handed over by the monarch or another member of the Royal Family, and the women's tournament is called the Copa de la Reina.

questions.question: Which long item in the team's colors do fans wear around their necks and hold up in the stands with both hands?
hints: It's worn a lot in winter.
It's long and narrow.
You wear it in the snow with a hat and gloves.
questions.description: In the stands you sing, you suffer and you show off your colors until your voice is gone.
questions.fun_fact: Many fans hold their scarves up with arms stretched out while the club anthem plays.

questions.question: I'm a video series by an Argentine DJ in a cap and dark glasses; Shakira sang about Piqué in me. What am I called?
hints: Each video has a number, and the guest singer sits facing the producer in his small studio.
Quevedo, Nathy Peluso and Residente have also been guests.
Its name starts with the consonants of the producer's nickname: B, Z, R, P.
questions.description: A producer who hides behind his sunglasses and makes everyone else famous.
questions.fun_fact: Bizarrap got his start uploading edited videos of freestyle rap battles from his bedroom.

questions.question: Barça, Levante and Eibar all wear “azulgrana”. What colors are those?
hints: You already know the first part.
The second part is a color that used to be made from an insect.
It's a very dark red, like red wine.
questions.description: One word that's really two colors glued together.
questions.fun_fact: “Grana” is a dark red; Barça is known as “el club azulgrana” and its fans as “culés”.

questions.question: Dani Carvajal played the 2012–13 season for Bayer Leverkusen before going back to Real Madrid. Which country is that club in?
hints: This country has won four World Cups.
It hosted Euro 2024, which Spain won.
Its capital is Berlin.
questions.description: A kid from Madrid who went on a study-abroad year, but in cleats.
questions.fun_fact: Carvajal is one of the few players in history with six European Cups, level with legends like Gento and Modrić.

questions.question: A widespread superstition in Spain says spilling salt on the table brings you what?
hints: It makes superstitious people nervous when it happens.
To undo it, some people throw a pinch over their left shoulder.
They say a black cat brings the same thing.
questions.description: A small slip at the table that some people take very, very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's “The Last Supper”, a tipped-over salt cellar sits next to Judas's elbow.

questions.question: In the old days, the village curandero (folk healer) made remedies for the neighbors. What did he mostly make them from?
hints: He found them out in the countryside.
Many were boiled to make herbal teas.
Chamomile and rosemary were among his favorites.
questions.description: Before there was a pharmacy on every corner, there was one neighbor the whole village went to for advice.
questions.fun_fact: Many of today's medicines, like aspirin, started out as substances found in plants.

questions.question: It's made of iron, a horse once wore it on its hoof, and it brings luck to the home. By tradition, where do you hang it?
hints: You hang it in a place everyone passes by.
It has to be in sight of whoever comes in.
You'd see it if you looked up just before walking in.
questions.description: The horse doesn't need it anymore, but your house does.
questions.fun_fact: Horseshoes were traditionally nailed on with seven nails, another number that is thought to be lucky.

questions.question: Who wrote «El pirata Garrapata», the hopeless pirate of children’s books?
hints: His books are full of zany humor.
His books came out in the El Barco de Vapor series in the 1980s.
He also created Fray Perico and his faithful donkey.
questions.description: A ship, an eye patch, a parrot and someone with a lot of imagination at the wheel.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Muñoz Martín was a schoolteacher for many years before his children’s books took off.

questions.question: What is Pupi, the curious little hero of María Menéndez-Ponte's books?
hints: He isn't a human being.
Everything on Earth seems new and surprising to him.
He comes from another planet.
questions.description: A new neighbor who didn't arrive by train or by car.
questions.fun_fact: The Pupi books are published in the El Barco de Vapor series, one of the most read by children in Spain.

questions.question: Which singer-songwriter wrote the bestselling poetry book “Todos mis futuros son contigo”?
hints: He was born in Madrid.
He mixes his concerts with readings of his own poems.
He goes by his first name only, which is of Arabic origin.
questions.description: Someone who tunes his guitar and his verses at the same time.
questions.fun_fact: Marwan is one of the bestselling poets in Spain, which is very rare for poetry.

questions.question: Don Quixote is to knight as Gurb, from “No Word from Gurb”, is to…
hints: Gurb arrives in Barcelona and gets lost.
His companion searches the whole city for him, writing everything down in a diary.
He isn't from Earth.
questions.description: A missing person who never shows up on any “wanted” poster.
questions.fun_fact: Eduardo Mendoza first published the novel in installments in the newspaper El País in 1990.

questions.question: At a military flag oath (jura de bandera) in Spain, which of these do the soldiers taking the oath NOT do?
hints: It is a ceremony where the flag is treated with huge respect.
One by one, those taking the oath walk up to the flag and touch it with their lips.
Nobody pulls out a pen during the whole ceremony.
questions.description: A ceremony where everyone swears in style and nobody crosses their fingers behind their back.
questions.fun_fact: Charles III chose the red and gold colors in 1785 so Spanish ships could be easily recognized at sea.

questions.question: The wide middle stripe of Spain's flag is the color called “gualda”. What color is that?
hints: It isn't the color of the stripes at the top and bottom of the flag.
It's the color of an egg yolk.
It's the color we use to paint the sun.
questions.description: A color with a name so strange it sounds like it came out of a book about knights.
questions.fun_fact: Gualda is a plant (weld) that people once used to dye cloth yellow.

questions.question: Because of the color of its shirt, what nickname does Spain's national soccer team have?
hints: Think of the color of the shirt it wears at home games.
It's the same color as the stripes at the top and bottom of the flag.
It's the color of strawberries and tomatoes.
questions.description: Eleven players who share a locker room, an anthem and a nickname.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname “La Roja” became hugely popular at Euro 2008, the first of the three European Championships Spain has won this century.

questions.question: Around 1580 I painted a gentleman dressed in black, with a white ruff and his right hand on his chest. Today it's in the Prado. Who am I?
hints: I lived and worked in Toledo.
I wasn't born in Spain: I came from Italy.
Everyone knows me by a nickname that says which country I come from.
questions.description: A gentleman who has been swearing to something for over 400 years, and nobody knows what.
questions.fun_fact: A restoration in 1996 removed a dark background that had been added later and revealed that the original background was light gray.

questions.question: In which village in the province of Zaragoza, with about 150 residents, was Francisco de Goya born in 1746?
hints: It's in the Campo de Belchite, a dry area south of Zaragoza.
You can visit the house where the painter was born there.
In Spanish, its name seems to promise a fountain for everyone.
questions.description: A village with fewer residents than a small concert, but with a local boy who filled the Prado.
questions.fun_fact: Fuendetodos has a museum of Goya's prints, right next to the house where he was born.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these white windmills on a hill are among the most famous in Spain. Which autonomous community are they in?
hints: It's in the center of the peninsula.
A very famous sheep's milk cheese is made there.
Its capital is Toledo.
questions.description: Very calm giants that only move when the wind blows.
questions.fun_fact: The Consuegra windmills were used to grind grain into flour.

questions.question: It's a music station from Atresmedia, sister to Onda Cero, and for years it aired “Levántate y Cárdenas”. Which station is it?
hints: It belongs to the same group as Antena 3 and laSexta.
It plays mostly pop hits, and its name ends in “FM”.
It's named after the continent Spain is in.
questions.description: A station for singing along in the car, even when you don't know the words.
questions.fun_fact: Europa FM is in the same group, Atresmedia Radio, as Onda Cero and Melodía FM.

questions.question: On the night of July 24, the eve of Galicia's national day, the Obradoiro square fills up for the “fogos do Apóstolo”. What are the “fogos”?
hints: You look up to watch them.
They make a lot of noise and fill the sky with color.
The cathedral's front lights up with their bursts of light.
questions.description: On the eve of Galicia's big fiesta, nobody in Santiago wants to go to bed early.
questions.fun_fact: July 25 is the feast of Saint James the Apostle, patron saint of Spain, and also Galicia's national day.

questions.question: According to tradition, Doñana National Park is named after a woman who lived there. Who was she?
hints: In the past, “doña” was the title for important ladies.
She was the daughter of a famous princess at the court of Philip II.
Her name is the second half of the word.
questions.description: A park named after a lady, with feathered neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: Doña Ana de Silva y Mendoza, daughter of the Princess of Éboli, retired in the 16th century to a palace in these woods, which ended up taking her name.

questions.question: The Tagus is to my north and the Guadiana to my south, and among my hills lies Cabañeros, “the Spanish Serengeti.” Which mountain range am I?
hints: I'm almost entirely in Castilla-La Mancha, with a small piece in Extremadura.
In the fall you can hear my red deer roaring in the rut (the “berrea”).
I share my name with a city famous for its swords and its cathedral.
questions.description: A safari with no lions, and you never leave the Spanish plateau.
questions.fun_fact: Cabañeros is called the “Spanish Serengeti” because its wide grasslands full of deer look like the African savanna.

questions.question: The Iberian ibex lives in Gredos, Cazorla and Sierra Nevada, but its scientific name, “Capra pyrenaica”, points to another mountain range. Which one?
hints: It's a mountain range on a border.
It lies between Spain and France.
Look closely at the second word of the scientific name.
questions.description: A pro climber: no rope, no harness, just horns.
questions.fun_fact: The bucardo, the Pyrenean ibex, died out in 2000, and in 2003 a clone of it was born that lived only a few minutes.

questions.question: I'm a street dance, named for the “pop” the body makes. What move am I based on?
wrong_answers: Spinning on your head on the floor
Tapping your feet in metal-soled shoes
Jumping nonstop with a jump rope
hints: When you watch me, the dancer looks a bit like a robot.
The move happens in the arms, legs, neck and chest, like tiny jolts.
It means tightening your muscles all at once, as if something taps you from inside.
questions.description: A dance where your body seems to have the hiccups, but with style.
questions.fun_fact: Popping was born in the 1970s in Fresno, California, with a group called the Electric Boogaloos.

previous.feedback: Hint 1 ("When you watch me, the dancer can look like a robot.") keeps the first-person voice of the source riddle ("Soy un baile…"). The English question isn't in the first person, so "me" doesn't refer to anything. Reword it, e.g. "Watching it, the dancer can look like a robot."

questions.question: In ancient times, the Ebro River was called the “Iber”. Which name is thought to come from it?
hints: It's a very big name, bigger than a region.
It covers Spain and Portugal.
It sounds almost like “Iber”.
questions.description: A river so influential it named the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: The Ebro carries more water than any other river in Spain.

questions.question: You're watching “Planet 51”, and the planet's green locals run in terror from a visitor who has just arrived from space. Who is it?
hints: In this movie, the usual roles are turned upside down.
He arrives sure that nobody lives on the planet.
He's a human, just like you.
questions.description: A planet of green neighbors who watch far too many scary movies.
questions.fun_fact: “Planet 51”, made by Ilion Studios in Madrid, was once the most expensive animated movie in Spanish film history.

questions.question: In the comedy “Ocho apellidos catalanes”, which region of Spain is NONE of the main characters from?
hints: The male lead is from Seville.
The bride and her father come from the first movie, “Ocho apellidos vascos”.
The missing region is in the northwest of Spain.
questions.description: A wedding where the in-laws need an interpreter for each other's customs.
questions.fun_fact: “Ocho apellidos vascos” is the highest-grossing Spanish movie ever in Spain.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this tennis player won the French Open in 2016 and Wimbledon in 2017. In which country was she born?
hints: She wasn't born in the country she played for.
Her father is Basque and her mother is from another country.
She was born in Caracas.
questions.description: Grass in London, clay in Paris and a passport with a lot of history.
questions.fun_fact: Garbiñe Muguruza won Wimbledon in 2017 by beating Venus Williams in the final.

questions.question: Rudy Fernández played six Olympic Games in a row and said goodbye at Paris 2024. In what year were his first Games?
hints: The Games are held every four years.
He was only 19.
They were held in Athens.
questions.description: Twenty years on the national team makes for a lot of team photos.
questions.fun_fact: Rudy was the first male basketball player to play at six Olympic Games.

questions.question: It's an old-style place serving wine, sometimes from the barrel, with a little something to nibble. Madrid still has 100-year-old ones with tiled fronts. What is it?
hints: It's not on the beach, and it doesn't serve trendy mixed drinks.
Behind its wooden or zinc bar stands the same owner as always.
The person who runs it is called the “tabernero”.
questions.description: Here the wine flows from the barrel and the chatter never stops.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) was founded on May 2, 1879, in Casa Labra, a Madrid taberna that opened in 1860.

questions.question: Look at this dish from a bar. Which part of the chicken is it?
hints: A chicken has two and flaps them when it runs.
Birds use them to fly.
On Spanish bar menus they're called “alitas”.
questions.description: A dish you eat with your hands that goes back to the kitchen with spotless bones.
questions.fun_fact: Every chicken wing has three parts: one that looks like a tiny drumstick, the middle part and the little tip.

questions.question: Look at this photo. What is this part of a bar called?
hints: It's inside the bar, not out on the street.
The waiter stands on one side and the customers on the other.
In Spain it's called la barra, just like a long loaf of bread.
questions.description: This is where people order drinks, share their troubles and argue about soccer.
questions.fun_fact: The word “bar” first meant the barrier, the counter, that separated the bartender from the customers.

questions.question: Many Spanish bars write their “menú del día” on a chalkboard. What does it usually include?
questions.answer: Two courses, dessert, bread and a drink
wrong_answers: A sandwich, fries and a coffee
Three tapas of your choice and a beer
Breakfast, lunch and an afternoon snack
hints: It's served at midday, on weekdays.
You choose from several dishes for each course.
There's a first and a second course, and at the end something sweet or a coffee.
questions.description: The only chalkboard that's actually a pleasure to read.
questions.fun_fact: The menú del día grew out of the “menú turístico” that the Spanish government created in the 1960s to offer tourists meals at a fixed price.

questions.question: In a bar you order “un bocata de jamón”. What do you get?
questions.answer: A ham sandwich in a roll
hints: You don't need a plate or a spoon.
The ham goes between two pieces of bread.
“Bocata” is the short form of a longer word.
questions.description: A short word for something very filling.
questions.fun_fact: “Bocata” is a casual word, just like “finde” is for “fin de semana” (weekend).

questions.question: I'm a party right in the street of a Bronx neighborhood; DJs plugged their speakers into the lampposts. What am I called?
hints: I'm a bit like a neighborhood street fair.
The whole street was closed to traffic so people could dance on it.
My name comes from the stretch of city street between two crossroads.
questions.description: A party where the neighbors can't complain about the noise, because they're all invited.
questions.fun_fact: Many people date the birth of hip hop to a back-to-school party that DJ Kool Herc played in the Bronx in August 1973.

questions.question: This regional TV channel first went on air on February 28, 1989, its region's own holiday. Which region is it from?
hints: It is the autonomous community with the most people in Spain.
Its flag is green and white.
The channel is called Canal Sur.
questions.description: A TV channel that blew out its first candle on the very day its whole region was out partying.
questions.fun_fact: Canal Sur's headquarters are in San Juan de Aznalfarache, a town right next to Seville.

questions.question: Celebrities sing in head-to-toe costumes, the judges guess who's inside, and whoever is voted off takes the costume off. Which Antena 3 show is it?
hints: It premiered on Antena 3 in 2020.
The costumes cover the whole head too.
The title names what hides the singers' faces.
questions.description: A show where even the biggest star might turn out to be a giant unicorn.
questions.fun_fact: This format was born in South Korea before traveling all over the world.

questions.question: On Antena 3 Noticias, what does Roberto Brasero report on every day?
hints: He stands in front of a map of Spain.
He talks about storms, high pressure and temperatures.
He helps you know if it will rain tomorrow.
questions.description: A TV presenter whom strangers stop in the street to ask about his work.
questions.fun_fact: Roberto Brasero is so popular that he has written books of weather sayings and weather curiosities.

questions.question: Finish the title of the La 1 show that visits Spaniards living in other countries: “Españoles en el…”.
hints: It has aired on TVE since 2009.
Each episode travels to a different city, on any continent.
The word means the whole Earth.
questions.description: A show with more air miles than any flight attendant.
questions.fun_fact: In every episode, the Spaniards who live there act as the guides and show off their own city.

questions.question: A game show of crazy challenges to storm a castle began on my TV and became a hit in Spain thanks to its joke-filled dub. Which country am I?
hints: In Spain the show was called «Humor amarillo».
The original show was hosted by comedian Takeshi Kitano.
My capital is Tokyo.
questions.description: Contestants who went flying without a plane ticket.
questions.fun_fact: Back home the show was called «Takeshi's Castle» and aired from 1986 to 1990.

questions.question: Seville's iron Triana Bridge opened in 1852 as a copy of a bridge that no longer exists. Where was that bridge?
hints: It was in a European capital.
The original bridge was torn down in the 1930s and replaced by another one.
The original bridge crossed the Seine.
questions.description: Iron, river and art: this bridge has more history than your grandma's photo album.
questions.fun_fact: Its official name is the Isabel II Bridge, but hardly anyone in Seville calls it that.

questions.question: If you live on the island of the Roque de los Muchachos observatory, one of the world's best places for stargazing, what are you called after your island?
hints: It's an island in the west of the Canaries.
Its island is called “la Isla Bonita”.
Your island shares its name with the capital of Mallorca.
questions.description: Neighbors with a sky cleaner than your freshly washed glasses.
questions.fun_fact: Since 1988, the so-called “Sky Law” has limited lighting on the island so the lights don't hide the stars.

questions.question: The Turia, the river of Valencia, starts in mountains like the ones in the photo. In which province?
hints: It's inland, far from the sea.
It's one of the least populated provinces in Spain.
Its capital is famous for a pair of medieval lovers.
questions.description: A river from the inland hills that left home to see the beach.
questions.fun_fact: In its upper course it's called the Guadalaviar, a name from Arabic that means “white river.”

questions.question: This huge rock, Roque Bentayga, was a sacred place for the ancient Canary Islanders. Which island is it on?
hints: It stands in the middle of an almost round island.
From it you can see Roque Nublo.
The island's capital is Las Palmas.
questions.description: A rock with more visitors than many museums, and no gift shop.
questions.fun_fact: It is part of the Risco Caído and the Sacred Mountains landscape, a World Heritage Site since 2019.

questions.question: This black Virgin, “La Moreneta,” is the patron saint of Catalonia. On which mountain is her monastery?
hints: It's near Barcelona.
Its rocks are shaped like the teeth of a saw.
Its name means “sawn mountain.”
questions.description: A lady so loved that people wait in line for hours just to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: The monastery is home to the Escolania de Montserrat, one of the oldest children's choirs in Europe.

questions.question: Along many Spanish rivers stand ruins of buildings whose wheels were turned by water. A saying says water that has passed no longer turns them. What are they?
hints: The saying means there's no point crying over what's already happened.
People used to bring their grain there on a donkey's back.
Don Quixote fought some that were turned by the wind.
questions.description: The perfect saying for when you're still upset about last week's game.
questions.fun_fact: Many Spanish towns have “Molino” or “Molinos” in their name, after the ones that stood on their rivers.

questions.question: This is Roque Nublo, one of the symbols of the Canary Islands. What type of rock is it made of?
hints: The Canary Islands rose from the seabed in a very explosive way.
Before it was rock, it was something extremely hot.
It came out of a volcano.
questions.description: A monolith named after a cloudy day, with plenty of attitude.
questions.fun_fact: Roque Nublo stands about 80 m (260 ft) tall from its base, and its top is 1,813 m (5,948 ft) above sea level.

questions.question: These snowy mountains separate Madrid from Segovia, and in winter you can see them from the capital. Which mountain range is it?
hints: It's part of the Sistema Central.
It has been a national park since 2013.
Its name starts with “Guada”, like the names of many rivers.
questions.description: The mountains where people from Madrid escape when the city gets too much.
questions.fun_fact: Many of Madrid's rivers, like the Manzanares, rise in these mountains.

questions.question: You go down into the mines of Almadén (Ciudad Real), a World Heritage Site. What metal was dug out here for centuries?
hints: Almadén produced more of this metal than any other mine in the world.
It used to be inside thermometers.
It shares its name with the planet closest to the Sun.
questions.description: Going down a mine in La Mancha without hunting for a single giant dressed up as a windmill.
questions.fun_fact: About a third of all the mercury humans have ever used is thought to have come from Almadén.

questions.question: To keep cosmic rays from spoiling its dark matter experiments, a Spanish lab was dug under hundreds of meters of rock. Where?
wrong_answers: Under the Picos de Europa, in Asturias
hints: Its first experiments took place in the 1980s.
It made use of an old railway tunnel that was no longer in service.
Next to it stands the huge international station of Canfranc.
questions.description: Scientists who climb into a hole to look at the universe.
questions.fun_fact: The Canfranc Underground Laboratory sits next to the old Somport railway tunnel, which once crossed under the mountain into France.

questions.question: Severo Ochoa isolated it in 1955, it was used to make RNA in a test tube for the first time, and it won him the 1959 Nobel. Which enzyme is it?
hints: At first it was thought to be the one that copies RNA in cells, but it wasn't.
It joins nucleotides without needing a template.
Its name combines “polynucleotide” with the phosphate group.
questions.description: A microscopic chef who cooks up recipes with the letters of the code of life.
questions.fun_fact: Ochoa shared the Nobel with Arthur Kornberg, who years earlier had worked in his lab in New York.

questions.question: Basque engineer Alejandro Goicoechea, the “G” in Talgo, tested the first prototype of his light articulated train. In which decade?
hints: Spain still had many steam train lines.
It was about fifteen years before the SEAT 600 hit the roads.
The first prototype, the Talgo 0, was tested in 1942.
questions.description: An engineer who signed his invention with the first letter of his last name, like carving your initial into a school desk.
questions.fun_fact: Talgo stands for “Tren Articulado Ligero Goicoechea Oriol”: Goicoechea Oriol Light Articulated Train, after the engineer and José Luis Oriol, who paid for it.

questions.question: Fausto Elhuyar, born in Logroño in 1755, isolated a chemical element with his brother. Why did the Crown send him to New Spain in 1788?
wrong_answers: To search for the Northwest Passage
hints: His work had to do with what lies underground.
Much of the Empire's silver came from Mexico.
He rose to director general of the Mining Tribunal.
questions.description: From Logroño to the other side of the ocean, with the periodic table in his suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico City he pushed forward the Royal Seminary of Mining, whose building, the Palacio de Minería, still stands.

questions.question: “I was born in Palos, I was a rich sailor, and with my brother I helped Columbus; on his first voyage I captained the Pinta.” Who am I?
hints: I came from the province of Huelva.
My brothers were famous sailors too.
In Spanish, my surname is also the word for a small bird, the finch.
questions.description: A captain who crossed the ocean without any GPS.
questions.fun_fact: His brother Vicente Yáñez Pinzón captained the Niña on that same 1492 voyage.

questions.question: In which decade did “The Sea Inside” come out, the film that won Belén Rueda the Goya for Best New Actress?
hints: By then, people in Spain were already paying in euros.
The film also won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.
Its star was Javier Bardem, a few years before he won his own Oscar in 2008.
questions.description: An actress who spent years in everyone's living room before making the jump to the big screen.
questions.fun_fact: Belén Rueda won the Goya for “new” actress at 39, after becoming a TV star in “Médico de familia”.

questions.question: Eminem's “Lose Yourself” was the first rap song to win an Oscar. In which decade did it come out?
hints: It came out when people still bought music on CDs.
The 21st century had already begun.
It came out just a couple of years after the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: A song that tells you that you only get one shot, so think carefully about your answer.
questions.fun_fact: Eminem didn't go to collect his Oscar: reportedly he was asleep at home.

questions.question: Old legends say I'm a human-shaped root that screams when pulled up. In “Pan's Labyrinth”, Ofelia looks after me under a bed. What am I?
hints: Healers used me in the Middle Ages, and people told terrible stories about me.
In “Harry Potter”, students repot me while wearing earmuffs.
My name starts with “mandr…”.
questions.description: A plant with so much personality that witches' tales always give it the lead role.
questions.fun_fact: The mandrake belongs to the same family as the tomato, the potato and the eggplant: the nightshades.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in “Perdiendo el norte” (2015), two highly qualified young Spaniards move to this city looking for work. Which one?
hints: The tower in the photo has a big silver ball and is the tallest structure in the country.
It's the most populous city in its country.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: Degrees, master's and three languages, only to end up serving kebabs: the European dream.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, the two leads end up working at a kebab shop run by a Turkish man.

questions.question: In “Capture the Flag” (“Atrapa la bandera”), a boy travels to the Moon to save the flag in this photo, left there by a famous 1969 mission. How many astronauts were on that mission?
hints: Only some of them walked on the Moon.
One stayed behind, circling in the spacecraft while the others went down.
They were Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins.
questions.description: A boy, his grandpa and a millionaire who badly wants to plant his own flag in the lunar neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: “Capture the Flag”, by Enrique Gato, won the Goya for Best Animated Film in 2016.

questions.question: In “The Holy Innocents”, Paco Rabal's character Azarías looks after a bird he calls “¡milana bonita!”. What bird is it?
hints: It follows him everywhere and eats from his hand.
It belongs to the crow family, but it's small.
Its English name starts with a common boy's name.
questions.description: The most beloved pet in Spanish cinema, and it neither barks nor meows.
questions.fun_fact: Paco Rabal and Alfredo Landa shared the Best Actor award at the 1984 Cannes Film Festival for this film.

questions.question: Paco Plaza co-directed “[REC]” (2007) with Jaume Balagueró. How many films in the “[REC]” saga did Plaza direct?
hints: The saga has four films in total.
They directed the first two together.
Then they split them up: one each, and the last one was Balagueró's alone.
questions.description: A saga proving that worse things can happen in an apartment stairwell than a residents' meeting.
questions.fun_fact: Plaza directed “[REC]³: Genesis” (2012) on his own, and it moves the horror to a wedding banquet.

questions.question: The Goya Awards statuette is a bust of the painter they're named after. In which of these cities did he NOT live?
hints: He was born in a village in Aragon.
He was a court painter in the capital and died in France.
The answer is in another country on the Iberian Peninsula.
questions.description: The most big-headed trophy in Spanish film: it's nothing but head.
questions.fun_fact: The bronze statuette weighs about 3 kg (6.6 lb), so giving your thank-you speech is also a workout.

questions.question: At the 1955 Salamanca Conversations, who called Spanish cinema “politically ineffective, socially false, intellectually worthless, aesthetically void and industrially stunted”?
hints: That same year he released “Death of a Cyclist.”
He had co-directed “That Happy Couple” with a friend from Valencia.
His nephew won an Oscar in 2008.
questions.description: A university conference where Spanish cinema looked in the mirror and did not like what it saw one bit.
questions.fun_fact: The Conversations were organized by a young Basilio Martín Patino, who later became a film director himself.

questions.question: Alberto Contador won the Tour de France in 2007 and 2009. On which famous avenue did the last stage finish?
hints: The riders do several laps on it before the final sprint.
At one end there is a big square with an Egyptian obelisk.
Its name recalls the paradise of the Greek heroes.
questions.description: Three weeks of pedaling around France, only to end up sightseeing by bike.
questions.fun_fact: Contador was nicknamed “el Pistolero” (the Gunslinger) because he celebrated his wins by firing an imaginary pistol.

questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Ruth Beitia, from Cantabria, win gold in the high jump?
hints: She won it at 37, an age when many athletes have already retired.
They were her fourth Olympic Games.
They were held in Brazil.
questions.description: Some people set the bar high, and then there's this woman from Cantabria.
questions.fun_fact: Ruth Beitia was the first Spanish woman to become Olympic champion in track and field.

questions.question: Weightlifter Lydia Valentín finished fourth at London 2012. Years later, after doping disqualifications, which medal did that place become?
hints: She didn't move up just one step.
More than one rival who finished ahead of her lost her result.
All three lifters who beat her were disqualified.
questions.description: Some medals arrive years late, like letters that got lost in the mail.
questions.fun_fact: Something similar happened at Beijing 2008: Lydia Valentín finished fifth and ended up getting silver.

questions.question: Its bass makes you move, James Brown was its big star, and its drum beats fed hip hop. What genre is it?
hints: It was born in the United States in the 1960s.
DJs in the Bronx looped its drum parts so people could dance.
George Clinton's band Parliament and bassist Bootsy Collins were also huge stars of this style.
questions.description: Music that makes even your grandpa shake his shoulders without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: The drum break in James Brown's “Funky Drummer” is one of the most sampled pieces of music in history.

questions.question: Ricky Rubio is the youngest player ever to debut in Spain's Liga ACB. How old was he?
hints: He was still in high school.
His birthday was only a few days away.
He hadn't turned 15 yet.
questions.description: While other kids studied for their math test, he was handing out assists to professionals.
questions.fun_fact: Ricky debuted in 2005 with Joventut de Badalona, a few kilometers from his hometown of El Masnou.

questions.question: How many Olympic medals did race walker María Pérez, from Granada, win at the Paris 2024 Games?
hints: She shared one of them with a teammate.
She won gold in the mixed relay with Álvaro Martín.
She also made the podium in the individual 20 km.
questions.description: Running was against the rules, yet she still beat almost everyone to the finish.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2023 World Championships in Budapest, María Pérez won gold in both the 20 km and the 35 km race walk.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this forward from Madrid starred with Adam Sandler in the Netflix film “Hustle”. Who is he?
hints: His brother also plays for the Spanish national team.
His mother was a European champion with Spain's women's team.
His brother is the center Willy.
questions.description: From the hardwood to the big screen without a single acting class.
questions.fun_fact: In “Hustle”, Juancho plays a Spanish player discovered on a street court in Mallorca.

questions.question: An athlete born in Talavera de la Reina won Olympic gold at Tokyo 2020 at age 39, in a sport held only at those Games. Which sport?
hints: It's a martial art from Japan.
She won it in kata, with no opponent in front of her.
Daniel LaRusso learned it from Mr. Miyagi.
questions.description: She showed up late to the Olympic party and still left with the biggest slice of cake.
questions.fun_fact: Because karate wasn't held at Paris 2024, Sandra Sánchez is still Spain's only Olympic champion in this sport.

questions.question: Alejandro Valverde is to “el Bala” as tennis player Juan Carlos Ferrero is to…
hints: It's an animal.
He got it for being thin, fast and tireless.
It's an insect that bites and buzzes.
questions.description: In Spanish sports, if you don't have a nickname, you haven't won anything.
questions.fun_fact: Ferrero won Roland Garros in 2003 and years later, as a coach, helped Carlos Alcaraz become world number 1.

questions.question: I was born in New York in 1997, grew up in Barcelona, won Indian Wells in 2021 and reached world number 2. Who am I?
hints: I'm from a recent generation.
My parents worked in fashion in New York.
My last name starts with B.
questions.description: A racket with a skyscraper passport and a Mediterranean accent.
questions.fun_fact: Paula Badosa moved with her family from New York to Barcelona when she was seven.

questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Galician canoeist David Cal win his only gold?
hints: They were his first Olympics.
That same year he also won a silver in the 500 meters.
They were held in Greece.
questions.description: A Galician who paddled alone, on his knees, and still finished first.
questions.fun_fact: With five medals, David Cal was for years the Spanish athlete with the most Olympic medals.

questions.question: In a neighborhood bar in Spain, what do you call the person who serves you behind the counter?
hints: They carry trays, glasses and cups back and forth.
They ask you “¿Qué te pongo?”.
The word starts with “cama…” (Spanish for bed), but it has nothing to do with sleeping.
questions.description: The only place where they know your name, your nickname and how you take your coffee.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Latin America, a waiter is called a “mesero” or a “mozo” instead.

questions.question: Look at these black olives. What are they really?
hints: They grow hanging from the branches of a tree.
That tree is the olive tree, and they have a pit like cherries.
They're in the same group as plums and peaches.
questions.description: Small, shiny and always on the little plate next to your drink at the bar.
questions.fun_fact: Many canned black olives are actually green olives that turn dark from exposure to air while they're being processed.

questions.question: I'm hard, I live inside an olive, and if nobody takes me out, I end up spat onto a little plate. What am I?
hints: I'm right in the middle.
In stuffed olives, they take me out to make room for something else.
Cherries and peaches have one too.
questions.description: The guest nobody wants to swallow by mistake.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, olive pits are sold as fuel for stoves and boilers.

questions.question: I'm a very tall hairstyle from the court of Versailles. I carried ships, gardens and birds, and Marie Antoinette made me fashionable. What am I?
hints: It was typical of 18th-century France, before the Revolution.
It was built with pads, wire, fake hair and lots of powder.
My name sounds like a low, padded footstool.
questions.description: Up there, there was room for everything except modesty.
questions.fun_fact: One of the most famous poufs carried a tiny warship to celebrate a French naval battle.

questions.question: In a bar, small is to tapa as big and for sharing is to…
hints: You order it for the whole table.
You can also order a “media” one.
“Una ___ de calamares, por favor.”
questions.description: A question of size, like when you ask for “just a tiny slice” of cake.
questions.fun_fact: If a ración is too much, many bars let you order a “media ración” (half portion).

questions.question: Look at what's being made in this churrería. What is churro dough made with?
hints: It's a very simple dough, the kind you could make with what's in almost any kitchen.
One of its ingredients is also used to make bread.
The sugar goes on top at the end, not inside.
questions.description: A treat that takes a lot of twists and turns before it reaches your cup of hot chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: The San Ginés chocolatería in Madrid has been serving chocolate with churros since 1894.

questions.question: When it's time to pay in a bar in Spain, everyone grabs a wallet and shouts “¡Quita, quita, que hoy…!”. How does it end?
hints: Everyone wants to do the same thing at once.
It's a fight between good friends.
Whoever says it wants to pay for everyone.
questions.description: A wrestling match where the prize is ending up with no money.
questions.fun_fact: When everyone pays their own share instead of one person treating, in Spain they call it “pagar a escote”.

questions.question: In “The Ministry of Time” («El Ministerio del Tiempo»), which century does the soldier Alonso de Entrerríos come from?
hints: He fights with a sword and has no idea what a cell phone is.
He served with the Spanish tercios in Flanders.
It's the century when Charles I and Philip II ruled Spain.
questions.description: Some coworkers clock in late, and then there's this one, who is very, very late.
questions.fun_fact: His patrol partner Amelia Folch comes from 1880, when it was very hard for a woman to get into a university.

questions.question: This actor played a TVE police officer who solved crimes in late-19th-century Madrid. Which character was it?
hints: The series aired on La 1 in the mid-2010s.
It is based on the novels by Jerónimo Tristante.
The series is named after the character, and his last name has only three letters.
questions.description: No fingerprints on a phone and no security cameras here: this case gets cracked with a magnifying glass, a hat and lots of patience.
questions.fun_fact: The actor, Carles Francino, is the son of a well-known radio journalist who has exactly the same name.

questions.question: Which of these characters did NOT live in the building in «Aquí no hay quien viva»?
hints: The odd one out comes from another comedy by the same creators.
That other series premiered on Telecinco in 2007.
He sells seafood wholesale and lives in Mirador de Montepinar.
questions.description: A group of neighbors so nosy they'd spot a gatecrasher in seconds.
questions.fun_fact: Many actors from «Aquí no hay quien viva» returned in «La que se avecina», but as new characters.

questions.question: I clean houses, I live in the Esperanza Sur neighborhood with my family and my brother Luisma, and I first appeared in «7 vidas». Who am I?
hints: My series aired on Telecinco from 2005 to 2014.
Mauricio Colmenero's bar is in my neighborhood.
Carmen Machi plays me, and the series is named after me.
questions.description: A woman who cleans other people's homes while her own life is a total mess.
questions.fun_fact: The character started as a supporting role in «7 vidas» and ended up with her own series for almost ten years.

questions.question: This actor played Iñaki, the Basque man who ends up living in Seville, in the series «Allí abajo». Who is he?
hints: He's neither Basque nor Andalusian: he was born in the Canary Islands.
He starred in the film «La novia» with Inma Cuesta.
His surname is the most common one in Spain.
questions.description: A man who swapped txakoli for rebujito without anyone asking his opinion.
questions.fun_fact: «Allí abajo» played on the clichés about Basques and Andalusians, just like the film «Ocho apellidos vascos» (“Spanish Affair”), released a year earlier.

questions.question: Which actor played Julio Olmedo, the waiter searching for his missing sister in «Gran Hotel»?
hints: Before that, he was a student in «El internado».
Later he worked on «Las chicas del cable» (Cable Girls).
His first name is Basque and has only three letters.
questions.description: A waiter who serves tea with one hand and hunts for clues with the other.
questions.fun_fact: The show's luxury hotel was filmed at the Palacio de la Magdalena in Santander.

questions.question: Mauricio Colmenero is to the bar in «Aída» as Emilio Delgado in «Aquí no hay quien viva» is to…
hints: Emilio works in the same building where everyone lives.
He knows who comes in and who goes out.
He hands out the mail and lives on the ground floor with his father.
questions.description: Every busybody needs a good lookout post.
questions.fun_fact: Fernando Tejero, who played Emilio, worked with the same creators again as Fermín Trujillo in «La que se avecina».

questions.question: The series «Mar de plástico» is set among greenhouses like these, which can be seen even from space. Which province are they in?
hints: It is a province in Andalusia.
It is home to the Tabernas Desert, where Western movies were filmed.
Its capital has a huge Moorish fortress, the Alcazaba, looking out over the Mediterranean.
questions.description: A sea with no fish, but more tomatoes than you could ever give away.
questions.fun_fact: These greenhouses grow a large share of the vegetables Europe eats in winter.

questions.question: Every December 31 at midnight, TV broadcasts them, and in Spain people eat one grape with each of the twelve. What are they called in Spain?
hints: They ring out from a very famous clock in Madrid.
They go “dong, dong, dong”… twelve times.
Bells make them.
questions.description: The one moment of the year when all of Spain chews to the same beat.
questions.fun_fact: Many people buy seedless or even peeled grapes so they can swallow all twelve in time.

questions.question: TV3 is the public regional TV channel of one of Spain's autonomous communities. Which of these cities is NOT in that community?
hints: TV3 broadcasts mostly in Catalan and is based in Barcelona.
Three of these cities are provincial capitals of Catalonia.
The city you're looking for has its own regional channel, À Punt.
questions.description: A TV channel that says good morning with a “bon dia”.
questions.fun_fact: TV3 started regular broadcasts in 1984 and was one of Spain's first regional TV channels.

questions.question: If you were a celebrity and won “Mira quién baila” on TVE, who would get the prize money?
hints: The celebrity didn't keep the money.
Each contestant danced for something they cared about.
The prize went to help other people.
questions.description: Sequins, spins and celebrities sweating buckets in front of all of Spain.
questions.fun_fact: “Mira quién baila” was hosted by Anne Igartiburu, who has also presented TVE's New Year's Eve chimes many times.

questions.question: In 2010, if you had an old TV without a decoder, your channels went blank. What signal was switched off in Spain to make way for TDT?
hints: It had come through the rooftop antenna for decades.
People called the switch “el apagón” (the blackout).
It's the opposite of digital.
questions.description: The day lots of grandmas learned the word “decoder”.
questions.fun_fact: The analog switch-off across all of Spain happened on April 3, 2010.

questions.question: I'm tiny, red with black dots, I eat aphids on plants, and in Mexico my name sounds like a woman's name. What do people there call me?
hints: I'm a beetle.
I hide my wings under a colorful shell.
My name sounds almost the same as “Catalina.”
questions.description: An insect that dresses up for a party every day of the year.
questions.fun_fact: A single catarina can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime, which is why gardeners love it so much.

questions.question: Dante, the dog in “Coco”, is a hairless Mexican breed and one of the oldest in the Americas, over 3,000 years old. Which breed is it?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
The Mexica believed it guided souls to Mictlán.
Lots of people lovingly call it “xolo”.
questions.description: A dog so bald it never has to go to the groomer.
questions.fun_fact: Because it has almost no hair, a xolo's skin feels warm, and people once used it to warm up the sick.

questions.question: The American badger lives in northern Mexico and belongs to the weasel family. Which of these animals is NOT in that family?
hints: The answer has a ringed tail.
It's a close relative of the raccoon.
In many parts of Mexico this animal is also called “tejón”.
questions.description: A case of mistaken identity worthy of a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: The American badger sometimes hunts as a team with the coyote: one digs into the burrows and the other catches the prey that runs out.

questions.question: The founder's son created it in 1896, with flowers and the letters LV. Why was the Louis Vuitton pattern invented?
wrong_answers: To hide stains on the leather
To win a contest in Paris
hints: The brand already had a problem that it still has today.
In 1888 the brand had tried a checkered design, but it didn't solve that problem.
Think of the knockoff bags sold on the street.
questions.description: Letters so famous that even people who can't read know them.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Vuitton started out making flat travel trunks, which stacked better than the ones with curved lids.

questions.question: This black bird has a bald head, circles in the sky looking for dead animals, and its Mexican name comes from Nahuatl. What is it?
hints: It has no feathers on its head so it stays clean while eating.
You see groups of them over garbage dumps and highways.
In English it's called the black vulture.
questions.description: A bird that never makes it onto the postcards, but works harder than anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Its stomach juices are so acidic that they kill germs that would make almost any other animal sick.

questions.question: It's in Campeche, protects Mexico's largest tropical forest and holds an ancient Maya city with huge pyramids. Which reserve is it?
hints: It's a World Heritage Site for both its nature and its history.
Jaguars, pumas and howler monkeys live there.
Its Maya name means “two mounds side by side.”
questions.description: A place where the jaguars have stone neighbors more than a thousand years old.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first place in Mexico that UNESCO named a Mixed World Heritage Site, natural and cultural at the same time.

questions.question: In northern Mexico the roadrunner is also called “paisano.” It runs at about 30 km/h (20 mph) across the desert. What does it catch with that speed?
hints: It eats meat.
Its food has scales.
It even takes on rattlesnakes.
questions.description: In cartoons it only says “beep beep,” but in real life it's very hungry.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it prefers running, the roadrunner can fly, just not very far.

questions.question: Complete the name of the famous show on Mexican free-to-air TV that airs fights on Saturdays: “Box…”
hints: The name comes from Mexico's pre-Hispanic past.
It is the best-known name for the people who founded Tenochtitlan.
Mexico City's most famous stadium has carried the same name for decades.
questions.description: The Saturday night plan: popcorn, the couch, and someone yelling “He's down!”
questions.fun_fact: Former boxers like Juan Manuel Márquez and Jorge “Travieso” Arce have worked as commentators on boxing broadcasts on Mexican TV.

questions.question: I always come in pairs, I go on your hands, I'm padded, and in the ring I protect both boxers. What am I?
hints: I'm put on before stepping into the ring.
I'm often red or blue and fastened with laces or Velcro.
Without me, fists would go in bare.
questions.description: They're like pillows, but nobody wants to sleep with them.
questions.fun_fact: Gloves for professional fights usually weigh only about 230 to 280 grams (8 to 10 oz) each.

questions.question: The bell rings and professional boxers go to their corners to rest. How long is that break?
hints: It's much shorter than school recess.
There's barely time to drink some water and listen to the coach.
It's 60 seconds.
questions.description: Just enough time for a sip of water, a quick scolding and back into the ring.
questions.fun_fact: In men's professional boxing each round lasts 3 minutes, and in women's it usually lasts 2.

questions.question: In boxing, you use your “guard” all the time, and the coach yells “Raise it!” when you drop it. What is it?
questions.answer: The position of your fists to protect yourself
wrong_answers: The referee who watches over the fight
The break between one round and the next
The belt the champion takes home
hints: It has to do with your arms.
If you drop it, your face is left open.
Fists near the face and elbows tight to the body.
questions.description: Your coach yells for it, and no, you don't need to call security.
questions.fun_fact: A left-handed boxer usually fights in a “southpaw” stance, with the right hand and right foot in front.

questions.question: The day before a fight, boxers step on a scale in front of the press and fans. What is this weigh-in for?
questions.answer: To check they make their division’s weight
wrong_answers: To decide who walks out to the ring first
To work out how much money each one earns
To choose the color of their gloves
hints: Boxing has strawweight, lightweight, middleweight, heavyweight...
If a boxer comes in too heavy, he can lose the title or pay a fine.
It’s about how many kilos are allowed.
questions.description: The only time a boxer is more scared of a scale than of the other guy.
questions.fun_fact: After the weigh-in, many boxers put several kilos back on before stepping into the ring the next day.

questions.question: I was born in Sonora, grew up in Culiacán, went almost 90 fights without losing and filled Estadio Azteca with over 130,000 people. Who am I?
hints: I was a legend in the '80s and '90s.
My sons became boxers too.
People call me “JC,” and I share my name with a Roman emperor.
questions.description: The man who kept half of Mexico up late on Saturday nights.
questions.fun_fact: Chávez's 1993 fight against Greg Haugen drew about 132,000 people, a record crowd for a boxing match.

review.feedback: Source: hint 3 says Chávez shares his name with a Roman emperor, but Julius Caesar was a general and dictator, never an emperor. The translation copies this faithfully, so the source hint needs correcting first (e.g. “a famous Roman general and dictator”), then the English should follow it. Fact check: wrong. Hint 3 says the name is shared with a Roman emperor. Julius Caesar was a dictator and never an emperor. The rest checks out: born in Ciudad Obregón, Sonora; raised in Culiacán; unbeaten in his first 89 fights; the 1993 Haugen fight at Estadio Azteca drew about 132,000.

previous.feedback: source: Hint 3 says Julio César Chávez is named after a "Roman emperor". Julius Caesar was a Roman dictator, never an emperor; the empire began with Augustus after his death. Fix the source hint (e.g. "a famous Roman dictator" or "a famous Roman leader") first. The translation will then follow it. Fact check: wrong. The third hint says he is named after a Roman emperor. Julius Caesar was never an emperor. He was a Roman dictator, and the empire began after his death with Augustus. The rest checks out from memory: Chávez was born in Ciudad Obregón, Sonora, and grew up in Culiacán. He was unbeaten for his first 89 fights, losing the 91st to Frankie Randall. The 1993 Haugen fight at Estadio Azteca drew about 132,000. His son Julio César Chávez Jr. is a boxer. The wrong answers are other Mexican boxers.

questions.question: In the ring, when is the best time to throw an uppercut, the punch that comes from below?
questions.answer: When you're very close to your opponent
wrong_answers: When you're far away, across the ring
When your opponent is down on the canvas
hints: It usually aims at the opponent's chin.
It's thrown up under the opponent's guard.
It works when the two boxers are almost touching.
questions.description: A punch that goes up faster than the price of tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: Hitting an opponent who is down on the canvas, or after the bell, is against the rules and can get a boxer disqualified.

questions.question: Gilberto “Zurdo” Ramírez is from Sinaloa, and in 2016 he became the first Mexican super middleweight world champion. Which city is he from?
hints: It's a city by the sea.
It's famous for its malecón (seaside boardwalk) and its carnival.
It's called “the Pearl of the Pacific.”
questions.description: His nickname tells you which hand he hits with, but not where he comes from.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, “Zurdo” moved up in weight and also became a cruiserweight world champion.

questions.question: A lightweight boxer puts on a few kilos and moves up to the next division. Which one is it?
hints: Above lightweight, the divisions go up just a few kilos at a time.
The limit for this division is about 63.5 kg (140 lb).
Put a superhero’s prefix in front of the old division’s name.
questions.description: A few tacos too many and suddenly you’re in a different classroom.
questions.fun_fact: Julio César Chávez was a world champion at super featherweight, lightweight and super lightweight.

questions.question: It's sung softly, asks the baby to fall asleep and promises something for when they wake up. In “Duérmete mi niño,” what will the baby get?
hints: It's something to drink.
It's served nice and warm in a clay mug (jarro).
It's made with corn dough and is sometimes flavored like champurrado.
questions.description: A bedtime bribe so the baby finally closes those little eyes.
questions.fun_fact: People in Mexico have been drinking atole since before the Spanish arrived.

questions.question: In Cri-Cri's «Marcha de las letras», the general orders the books left open. Who are the five that march in the parade?
hints: Notice the number in the song.
You learn them very early in elementary school.
A, E, I, O, U.
questions.description: A military parade where the soldiers march straight out of a notebook.
questions.fun_fact: Francisco Gabilondo Soler, the creator of Cri-Cri, taught himself most of what he knew about music.

questions.question: In the lullaby “Este niño lindo”, the baby wants to be taken for a ride in a car. When was he born?
hints: It’s a lullaby to put the baby to sleep.
In Spanish, the answer rhymes with “coche” (car).
It’s when the moon and stars come out.
questions.description: A newborn baby who already wants a driver.
questions.fun_fact: In another verse, the baby who was “born in the daytime” wants to be taken to the candy shop.

questions.question: In this southeastern state it's so hot that many families sleep in hammocks, Maya is widely spoken, and Chichén Itzá is there. Which state is it?
hints: It's on a peninsula.
It's famous for cochinita pibil.
Its capital is Mérida.
questions.description: A place where the bed hangs from the ceiling and nobody panics.
questions.fun_fact: The word “hamaca” (hammock) comes from the Taíno language of the Caribbean and was one of the first words from the Americas to enter Spanish.

questions.question: The Nao de China crossed the Pacific every year between Acapulco and the city with these walls. Which city is it?
hints: It was on an island chain ruled by Spain.
That island chain is named after King Philip II.
Today it is the capital of the Philippines.
questions.description: The colonial delivery service: you ordered silk and it showed up six months later.
questions.fun_fact: The return trip, from Manila to Acapulco, could take up to six months, and the ships came loaded with silk, porcelain and spices.

questions.question: In 1692, a corn shortage sparked a riot in Mexico City, and part of the Viceroy's Palace burned. The authorities blamed a drink and banned it. Which one?
hints: It was the most popular drink among the capital's poor.
It is made by fermenting the sap of a plant.
It comes from the aguamiel of the maguey.
questions.description: When the tortillas run out, the whole capital gets cranky.
questions.fun_fact: During the riot, the scholar Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora saved documents from the city council's archive from the fire.

questions.question: You're in Otumba, where Cortés and his men, fleeing after the Noche Triste, defeated a huge Mexica army. In what year was it?
hints: It was in the 16th century.
Cortés had arrived in Mexico the year before.
Tenochtitlan fell the following year.
questions.description: A retreat that ended with a gold medal.
questions.fun_fact: According to the chronicles, the battle was decided when Cortés brought down the Mexica captain carrying the battle standard.

questions.question: You're in the Palacio Nacional, where the viceroys lived. About how many years did viceroys rule New Spain?
hints: There were more than 60 viceroys, one after another.
It began a few years after the fall of Tenochtitlan and ended with Independence.
The first viceroy arrived in 1535, and Independence was won in 1821.
questions.description: He ruled like a king, but the real king was on the other side of the ocean.
questions.fun_fact: The first viceroy, Antonio de Mendoza, arrived in 1535 and years later was sent to govern Peru.

questions.question: In the 1920s, party dresses were straight and short, and they swung when people danced the Charleston. What were they usually decorated with?
hints: The decoration had to move with every dance step.
It sparkled under the lights of the jazz clubs.
Thin hanging strips, like on a curtain or a poncho.
questions.description: A decade when even the clothes wanted to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Some 1920s dresses had so many glass beads that they weighed more than a kilogram (over 2 lb).

questions.question: In the patio process, invented in Pachuca around 1555, what was ground ore mixed with to separate out the silver?
hints: Mules and horses trampled the mixture for weeks.
It was scarce and expensive, the Spanish Crown controlled its trade, and much of it came by ship from Spain.
In colonial times it was called “azogue”.
questions.description: A patio where the mules worked harder than kids do at recess.
questions.fun_fact: The method was invented by Bartolomé de Medina from Seville, and it helped silver from New Spain travel across half the world.

questions.question: I was born in Oaxaca, led one of the first painting academies in New Spain and painted series of casta paintings. My portrait of Sor Juana is the most famous one. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 18th century.
I wrote “Maravilla americana”, a book about the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
I share my first name with the boy from “Coco”.
questions.description: He painted so well that even the saints sat perfectly still for him.
questions.fun_fact: In 1751, Cabrera was one of the painters who examined the tilma of the Virgin of Guadalupe up close.

questions.question: This name belongs to the last Mexica tlatoani, a borough of Mexico City and a famous soccer player. It means “descending eagle.” Which language is it from?
hints: Today more than 1.5 million people in Mexico speak it.
Many Mexican place names ending in “-tlán,” like Mazatlán, come from it.
It was the language of the Mexica.
questions.description: A name with wings that lands on streets, boroughs and soccer fields.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City's Historic Center is in the Cuauhtémoc borough.

questions.question: You're watching “Instructions Not Included” (2013). Which of these actors is NOT in the movie?
hints: Three of them make up the family in the story.
The movie starts in Acapulco and then moves to Los Angeles, where Valentín works as a stuntman.
The missing one became famous with “Y Tu Mamá También” and isn't in this comedy.
questions.description: A baby that shows up with no manual, no warranty and, worst of all, no gift receipt.
questions.fun_fact: “Instructions Not Included” became the highest-grossing Spanish-language movie ever in the United States.

questions.question: In Carlos Enrique Taboada's “Veneno para las hadas”, a girl convinces her friend that she's a witch. In which decade did it come out?
hints: Taboada had already scared Mexico with “Hasta el viento tiene miedo” in 1968.
It's one of his last films as a director.
It came out in the same decade as the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: Two girls, a book of spells and the worst idea ever for a sleepover.
questions.fun_fact: In “Veneno para las hadas” you almost never see the adults' faces: everything is filmed from the girls' height.

questions.question: I was born in Guadalajara, and with a love story between a mute woman and an amphibian man I won the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director in 2018. Who am I?
hints: I love monsters and dark fairy tales.
I also directed “Pan's Labyrinth”.
My surname contains the Spanish word for the animal of the bullring.
questions.description: A love story that isn't afraid to get wet.
questions.fun_fact: “The Shape of Water” won four Oscars, including Best Picture.

questions.question: I was born in Barcelona but grew up in Guanajuato, and with “Heli,” a drama shot there, I won Best Director at Cannes in 2013. Who am I?
hints: Before that, I directed “Sangre” and “Los bastardos.”
A year earlier, another Mexican won that same prize at Cannes, and I had worked as his assistant.
Later I made “The Untamed,” and my first name starts with A.
questions.description: A French prize that flew straight to Guanajuato.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico won Best Director at Cannes two years in a row: Carlos Reygadas in 2012 and Amat Escalante in 2013.

questions.question: In the movie Coco, a giant alebrije with wings, a big cat's body and bright colors looks after Mamá Imelda. What's its name?
hints: She's the Rivera family's spirit guide in the Land of the Dead.
She's not the little Xolo dog who goes everywhere with Miguel.
Her name sounds like the pumpkin seeds people eat with lime and chili.
questions.description: If your pet had wings, claws and more colors than a market in Oaxaca, this would be it.
questions.fun_fact: Pepita mixes parts of several animals: a jaguar's body, an eagle's wings and a ram's horns, just like a real alebrije.

questions.question: What is the clay jug with a narrow mouth and a wide belly, carried on the shoulder to fetch water, called?
hints: It's used for liquids, not for grinding or for heating tortillas.
A Spanish saying says it goes to the water so often that it finally breaks.
In Mexican lotería it shows up with a diminutive name.
questions.description: Before plastic water jugs, water traveled in a clay belly.
questions.fun_fact: “El cantarito” is one of the cards in Mexican lotería.

questions.question: I reach the market dry and wrinkled; they boil me, strain me and sweeten me, and with ice I'm agua fresca. They call me a flower, but they use my calyx. What am I?
hints: I'm almost always served with the comida corrida at the fondas.
I turn the water a deep red color.
I share my name with Usain Bolt's home country.
questions.description: A flower that ended up in the pitcher instead of the vase.
questions.fun_fact: What's sold as jamaica “flower” is really the calyx, the fleshy part that wraps around the plant's fruit.

questions.question: In a museum you see a 1960s dress made of small plastic discs joined with metal rings. Which designer invented it?
hints: He said he made “unwearable dresses.”
He was born in the Basque Country, in Spain, and made his name in Paris.
Today his name is famous for perfumes shaped like a gold bar.
questions.description: A dress that rattles like a cookie tin every time you take a step.
questions.fun_fact: He made his metal dresses with pliers and a blowtorch, working more like a jeweler or a blacksmith than a tailor.

questions.question: In Mexico, Bonafont is a well-known brand of…
hints: You drink it, you don't eat it.
It's sold in small bottles and also in big garrafones.
It's what you crave most after running in the sun.
questions.description: A name you see in every corner tiendita, even if you've never stopped to read it.
questions.fun_fact: Bonafont belongs to Danone, the same French company that makes many of the yogurts at the supermarket.

questions.question: Which of these sodas is NOT apple-flavored?
hints: The one you're looking for tastes like citrus.
Its fruit looks like a big, slightly bitter orange.
It tastes like grapefruit.
questions.description: Three sodas agreed to bring the same fruit to the party, and one didn't read the group chat.
questions.fun_fact: Squirt was born in the United States in 1938, but it got so popular in Mexico that many people think it's Mexican.

questions.question: Look at this fruit: in Mexico, even its peel gets used. What for?
hints: It's a drink that's left to sit for several days.
It's sweetened with piloncillo.
At tianguis markets it's sold from barrels or in a little bag with a straw.
questions.description: A fruit wearing a crown, and not even its peel goes to waste.
questions.fun_fact: Tepache was already drunk before the Spanish arrived, though back then it was made from corn.

questions.question: It's a little white flower with a yellow center, drunk as a tea for a tummy ache, and in Mexico its name, manzanilla, means “little…”. Little what?
hints: Listen closely to how the word manzanilla begins.
It's a fruit that can be red or green.
Snow White bit into a poisoned one.
questions.description: The little flower that hides a fruit inside its name.
questions.fun_fact: It got that name because its flowers smell a little like apples.

questions.question: In Mexico it goes into albóndigas and chicken broth, and its tea is drunk for an upset tummy. What is hierbabuena?
hints: Its leaves are green and smell very fresh.
It's related to the flavor of a lot of chewing gum.
It tastes like the little candies people suck to freshen their breath.
questions.description: An herb so proud of itself that its Spanish name calls it “good.”
questions.fun_fact: Hierbabuena belongs to the same plant family as oregano, basil and rosemary.

questions.question: If someone asks you “¿Qué te pasa, calabaza?”, how does the answer “Nada, nada…” end?
hints: It has to rhyme with “nada”.
It's a cool drink for hot days.
It's made with water, sugar and a sour green fruit.
questions.description: A question that tastes like the garden and an answer that tastes like an ice-cold pitcher.
questions.fun_fact: Squash is native to Mesoamerica and has been grown in Mexico for about 10,000 years.
