questions.question: Ismael Rodríguez is to “Nosotros los pobres” as Matilde Landeta is to…
hints: It's a film from the late 1940s.
It's based on a novel by Francisco Rojas González.
Its heroine, an Afro-Mexican woman, rises to colonel in the Revolution.
questions.description: A director analogy where one side won the director's chair from an entire union.
questions.fun_fact: Before she could direct, Matilde Landeta spent years as a script supervisor and assistant director, because the union didn't want a woman in charge.

questions.question: “Aventurera” (1950), with Ninón Sevilla dancing in a cabaret, is the great classic of the rumbera films. Where does its title come from?
questions.answer: From a bolero by Agustín Lara
wrong_answers: From a novel by Juan Rulfo
From a play by Rodolfo Usigli
From a comic by Gabriel Vargas
hints: Before 1950, the title was already very well known in Mexico.
In the film, Pedro Vargas performs it.
Its author was known as the “Flaco de Oro”.
questions.description: Cabaret nights, sequins and a rumbera who kept dancing until sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: In 1997 the film became a stage musical in Mexico City, starring Edith González.

questions.question: I was born in Guanabacoa, Cuba, and was nicknamed “La Única”. In Mexico I played Mercé, the nanny in “Angelitos negros”, with Pedro Infante. Who am I?
hints: I was a singer, pianist and actress.
I was one of the first to record “El manisero” (“The Peanut Vendor”).
My last name sounds a bit like “mountaineer”.
questions.description: A Cuban star who crossed the Gulf of Mexico to shine in Mexican cinema.
questions.fun_fact: The great Bola de Nieve started his career as her accompanying pianist.

questions.question: My husband crowned himself emperor, I made high-waisted dresses fashionable, and I loved the roses in my garden. Who am I?
hints: I lived in France in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
That style of dress is still called the “Empire style”.
My husband was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to an island.
questions.description: Behind every great emperor stood a woman with an even greater wardrobe.
questions.fun_fact: Josephine is said to have spent fortunes on clothes and owned hundreds of cashmere shawls.

questions.question: Which actor, born in Mexico City in 1920, made it big in Hollywood and played Khan, the villain of “Star Trek”?
hints: He made films in Mexico in the 1940s before moving to the United States.
On TV he was the elegant host of “Fantasy Island.”
In “Spy Kids 2” and “Spy Kids 3-D” he played the kids' grandfather.
questions.description: A chilango who started in Mexican studios and ended up causing trouble in another galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: On “Fantasy Island” he played Mr. Roarke, always dressed in white, for seven seasons.

questions.question: Libertad Lamarque, “La novia de América”, made dozens of films in Mexico. In which country was she born?
hints: She was born in a city on the banks of the Paraná River.
Before coming to Mexico, she was already a tango star.
Its capital is Buenos Aires.
questions.description: The sweetheart of a whole continent, who ended up spending her honeymoon with Mexican cinema.
questions.fun_fact: At 90, she acted in the Mexican telenovela “La usurpadora” (1998).

questions.question: A recording blares down your street: “Se compran colchones, tambores, refrigeradores…” Who is coming by?
questions.answer: The man who buys scrap metal
hints: He isn't coming to sell you anything.
He wants to take away the old things you no longer use.
The recording also offers to buy washing machines, microwaves and anything made of metal you want to sell.
questions.description: Mexico's catchiest song isn't on the radio: it plays down your street at eight o'clock on a Saturday morning.
questions.fun_fact: The voice on the most famous recording belongs to María del Mar Terrón, who recorded it as a young girl at her dad's request.

questions.question: People gather in the condo courtyard, vote on the maintenance fee and complain about the dog in 3B. What is that meeting called?
hints: There's no piñata and no music.
The people who go live in the same building or on the same street.
Its name says who attends: the people who live next door.
questions.description: Where people argue passionately about who left the trash by the front gate.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican condos, the law calls these meetings “asambleas de condóminos,” though everyone just calls them juntas.

questions.question: Many old buildings in Mexico City have small rooms on the rooftop, each with its own bathroom. Who were they built for?
hints: Someone who worked in the building lived there.
That person helped the family with cleaning and cooking.
On the building plans they were called “cuartos de servicio.”
questions.description: The room with the best view in the house, though nobody brags about it.
questions.fun_fact: Today many of these rooftop rooms are rented to students or have become small artists' studios.

questions.question: Finish the children's ring song: “A la rueda, rueda de San Miguel, San Miguel, todos traen su caja de…”
hints: It's something you eat.
It's sweet and sticky.
Bees make it.
questions.description: A ring game where everyone spins around until someone ends up facing backward.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the song everyone sings “que se voltee de burro,” and the child named has to turn around and keep playing facing backward.

questions.question: In many Mexican homes, a garrafón like this one is bought every week. What is its water mostly used for?
hints: It's purified water, pricier than tap water.
That's why it isn't wasted on cleaning.
It's the water poured into your glass and used to make meals.
questions.description: It weighs as much as a grade-schooler and always arrives on someone's shoulder.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries that drinks the most bottled water per person in the world.

questions.question: Rows of identical houses, a guard booth at the gate and sometimes a shared pool. What is this kind of neighborhood called in Mexico?
hints: It's very common on the edges of cities.
A builder splits a big piece of land into many lots.
Its name comes from dividing something into fractions.
questions.description: Where every house is a twin and the guard knows your license plate by heart.
questions.fun_fact: In northern Mexico, many fraccionamientos have English names or names of faraway places, like “Villas de Toscana”.

questions.question: It's danced with a huge round headdress of ribbons that spins like a wheel, by Nahua and Totonac dancers, and is famous in Cuetzalan. Which state is it from?
hints: It's danced in a mountain range in east-central Mexico.
This state borders Tlaxcala.
It's the state of mole and Talavera pottery.
questions.description: A dance that needs more ribbons than a sewing shop.
questions.fun_fact: The headdress of the Danza de los Quetzales can be more than 1 meter (3 ft) across, and it stands for the sun.

questions.question: She is a traditional Nahua healer from Jalisco, and in 2018 she sought to be the first Indigenous independent candidate for president. What is she known as?
hints: She was the spokeswoman of the Indigenous Governing Council.
She was backed by the National Indigenous Congress and the Zapatistas.
Her nickname comes from her name, María de Jesús.
questions.description: A woman who took her medicinal herbs all the way to the ballot… or almost.
questions.fun_fact: Marichuy was born in Tuxpan, Jalisco, and for years treated people with medicinal plants at a health house.

questions.question: They call themselves Tének, their language is related to Maya, and they live between San Luis Potosí and Veracruz. In which region do they live?
hints: It is a warm region near the Gulf of Mexico.
Zacahuil, a giant tamale baked in a wood-fired oven, is made there.
In Spanish, the Tének are called huastecos.
questions.description: Distant cousins of the Maya who moved quite far away from the rest of the family.
questions.fun_fact: Tének is the only Mayan language spoken far from southeastern Mexico, hundreds of kilometers from its relatives.

questions.question: The Guelaguetza is Oaxaca's most famous festival, held in July on the Cerro del Fortín, and its name comes from Zapotec. What does it mean?
hints: The festival is also known as “los Lunes del Cerro” (Mondays on the Hill).
Each group arrives with something typical of its region for the audience.
It's what you bring to a party to chip in.
questions.description: Oaxaca's biggest festival has a tongue-twister of a name, and it means something lovely, too.
questions.fun_fact: In Zapotec towns, guelaguetza is also the custom of helping a neighbor with their fiesta, knowing they'll help you later.

questions.question: The recipe says: “First, tatema the jitomates and the chiles.” What does tatemar mean?
questions.answer: Roasting them right on the comal or flame until charred
wrong_answers: Boiling them in salted water until they go soft
Grinding them in the molcajete with garlic and onion
Stuffing them with cheese and frying them in egg batter
hints: The word comes from Nahuatl.
Cooks do it to give salsa a smoky flavor.
It happens on the comal or open fire, with no water and no oil.
questions.description: A word that smells like fresh salsa and grandma's kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: “Tatemar” comes from the Nahuatl “tlatemati,” and those charred spots are what give salsa its smoky flavor.

questions.question: It's Mexico City's most populated borough, home of the Central de Abasto, and its Nahuatl name speaks of stone slabs in the water. Which is it?
hints: It's on the east side of the city.
It has almost 2 million people, more than many Mexican states.
Its name starts with “Izta”, like the volcano Iztaccíhuatl.
questions.description: If all its residents stood in line, the line would reach another state.
questions.fun_fact: Iztapalapa has more people than entire states such as Colima, Campeche or Baja California Sur.

questions.question: You're in Palenque, in front of a stone tablet full of glyphs. About how many different signs does Maya writing have?
hints: It has far more signs than our alphabet.
It combined signs for syllables with signs for whole words.
Several hundred, but fewer than a thousand.
questions.description: Maya scribes had no eraser: every mistake stayed carved in stone forever.
questions.fun_fact: Maya writing could write the same word with a single glyph or spell it out in syllables, like a puzzle.

questions.question: In Nahuatl, “México” was said with an “sh” sound, and the people who first wrote it in Latin letters used an x. Who were they?
wrong_answers: Insurgents of the War of Independence
hints: It was shortly after Hernán Cortés arrived.
The same people wrote the first dictionaries and grammars of Nahuatl.
In the Spanish of that time, the x sounded like “sh.”
questions.description: A letter with a centuries-old secret identity: it looks like an x but sounds like a Spanish j.
questions.fun_fact: That's why the x in Xola, Xoco or Mixquic still sounds like “sh,” while in México it ended up sounding like the Spanish j.

questions.question: They're folded tortillas with queso fresco and cream, covered in tomato sauce instead of chile sauce. What is this dish called?
hints: Look closely at what the sauce is made of.
Its name comes from the sauce's main ingredient, not from chile.
Its name hides the Spanish word for tomato.
questions.description: The family of sauce-covered tortillas has lots of cousins, and all their last names start with “en-.”
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has a whole family of dishes named this way: enchiladas, enfrijoladas, enmoladas and entomatadas.

questions.question: I'm an egg-shaped tomato, firm to the touch and not very juicy; at the market people ask for me for salsas. What am I called?
hints: I'm grown a lot in Sinaloa and in greenhouses all over Mexico.
I'm a favorite for salsa roja and stews.
My name sounds a little French, and a little like salad.
questions.description: A tomato that was born to end up in the molcajete.
questions.fun_fact: The saladet is one of the most grown tomatoes in Mexico because it holds up well on long trips.

questions.question: I'm a Latin name: I group the jalapeño, the habanero and the bell pepper, and Mexico has grown me for thousands of years. Which plant genus am I?
hints: Botanists put all chiles under my name.
I'm not the one for black pepper or the one for onions.
The substance that makes chiles hot is named after me.
questions.description: A Latin last name shared by one very spicy family.
questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin, the stuff that makes chiles hot, takes its name from the genus Capsicum.

questions.question: I wear a uniform with blue, yellow and red stripes, a plumed helmet and a spear, and I protect the Pope. Who am I?
hints: I work in the smallest country in the world.
I live in the Vatican, inside Rome.
My name includes a country famous for its chocolate and its watches.
questions.description: The most colorful bodyguards on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: People often say Michelangelo designed their uniform, but that's a myth: today's version dates from 1914.

questions.question: You finish your elote and you're left with the olote, the hard core with no kernels. In the countryside, what has it traditionally been used for?
hints: It has no kernels left, so it's no good for making masa.
Once dry, it becomes light and hard.
It burns well along with firewood.
questions.description: What's left of the elote when there's no elote left.
questions.fun_fact: The word «olote» comes from Nahuatl, just like «elote».

questions.question: «Miel de agave» is sweet and thick like honey, but it isn't bee honey. Why not?
questions.answer: Because it comes from a plant
wrong_answers: Because it comes from the sea
hints: No animal makes it.
It's harvested in the fields, in places like Jalisco, not in a hive.
It comes from the same plant tequila is made from.
questions.description: A honey so strange that no bee wants to take the credit.
questions.fun_fact: An agave plant can take several years to grow before it's harvested.

questions.question: At a market in Tlaxcala in 1545, a big tomato cost one cacao bean. How many did a guajolota (turkey hen) cost?
hints: A bird is worth much more than a tomato.
But nobody carried giant sacks of cacao to buy food.
It's a round three-digit number.
questions.description: A market where they gave you your change in chocolate that wasn't made yet.
questions.fun_fact: According to the same price list, a turkey egg was worth three cacao beans.

questions.question: Take a close look: this plant tastes like anise, and in Morelos people make crosses from its flowers on September 28. What is it called?
hints: Its flowers are small and yellow.
It's a cousin of cempasúchil, but it isn't the Day of the Dead flower.
The crosses go up on the eve of Saint Michael's Day to protect homes and milpas.
questions.description: A flower that guards the door better than a watchdog.
questions.fun_fact: Pericón is also called “Mexican tarragon” because it tastes a lot like tarragon.

questions.question: Every first Friday in March, I gather on the shore of a lagoon in Veracruz. Curanderos and tourists come for limpias. What am I?
hints: The lagoon is Catemaco, in Los Tuxtlas.
There are limpias, amulets and even a “black mass.”
The people who go there practice magic and sorcery.
questions.description: An event where the dress code is a cape and a nice big bunch of rue.
questions.fun_fact: The Congreso de Brujos in Catemaco began in 1970, organized by Gonzalo Aguirre, known as the “Brujo Mayor” (Chief Sorcerer).

questions.question: I'm a huge dog with red eyes. In Chiapas and Central America they say I follow drunks at night, and there's a good white one and a bad black one. Who am I?
hints: I appear on lonely roads late at night.
My white version protects travelers; my black one wants to hurt them.
My name starts with “Ca”.
questions.description: Man's best friend… as long as the man gets home early.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the legend, the white Cadejo watches over drunks so they get home safe and sound.

questions.question: Which Spanish-born actor played Count Lavud in the Mexican horror film “El vampiro” (The Vampire, 1957)?
hints: He was almost unknown when he took the role.
He was born in Gijón and moved to Mexico as a young man.
His last name is the Spanish word for oak trees.
questions.description: An actor who worked nights and slept all day, strictly because the role demanded it.
questions.fun_fact: Germán Robles was one of the first movie vampires to show fangs, a year before Christopher Lee's British Dracula.

questions.question: In the legend of El Charro Negro, anyone who takes his gold coins makes a pact with him and sells him their…
hints: It's not something you can see or touch.
Many religions say it lives on after you die.
People pray for it to rest in peace.
questions.description: A deal with fine print that nobody read before signing.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions, El Charro Negro's coins turn into charcoal or worms once the pact is fulfilled.

questions.question: I left the world's oldest wrestling company in 1992 to start my own, and in 1993 I filled the Plaza de Toros México with the first Triplemanía. Who am I?
hints: He wasn't a star wrestler: he was a promoter who used to work at CMLL.
The company he founded has a name of three identical letters: AAA.
His last name is the Spanish word for a big rock.
questions.description: One night a year when even your grandma wants to see someone fly off the top rope.
questions.fun_fact: About 48,000 people came to the first Triplemanía at the Plaza de Toros México in 1993.

questions.question: You're dressing up as a wrestler like El Santo for a party. What do you put on your head to cover your face?
hints: Wrestlers take great care of it.
If they lose it in a bet, everyone sees their face.
It has holes for the eyes and mouth.
questions.description: How to show up at the party as a ring champion without spending a single day at the gym.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, kid-sized wrestling masks have been sold outside Mexican arenas.

questions.question: I shine like a pirate's gold, but inside I'm sweet. If you leave me in the sun, what happens to me?
hints: Inside, I'm not made of metal.
I'm made of something brown that kids love.
The same thing happens to ice cream on a hot day.
questions.description: The only pirate treasure you can eat without a trip to the dentist… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: The gold foil on chocolate coins copies real gold coins, and in many countries people give them as gifts at Christmas.

questions.question: In lucha libre, where does a wrestler dive headfirst when doing a “tope suicida”?
questions.answer: Out of the ring, between the ropes
wrong_answers: Into the center of the mat
Onto the top rope in his corner
hints: He gets a running start inside the ring.
His opponent waits for him down below, close to the crowd.
He goes through the gap between the second and top ropes.
questions.description: Its name already warns you not to try it on your parents' bed.
questions.fun_fact: The tope suicida is so risky that the wrestler sometimes ends up landing on the front rows of the crowd.

questions.question: On November 20, many girls dress up as Adelitas, with belts of bullets crossed over their chest. What are those belts called?
hints: They copy what the soldaderas of the Revolution wore.
They were used to carry bullets for the rifle.
Change one letter in “bananas” and you have it.
questions.description: A school costume with more history than many textbooks.
questions.fun_fact: Many soldaderas of the Revolution didn't just cook and nurse the wounded: they also carried rifles and fought.

questions.question: Falsetto, that leap of the voice up to its highest notes, is the trademark of the huapango and son of one region of Mexico. Which one?
hints: People dance zapateado there on a wooden platform.
It covers parts of San Luis Potosí, Veracruz, Hidalgo and Tamaulipas.
Its son is played with violin, jarana and huapanguera.
questions.description: A voice that jumps over the fence without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Miguel Aceves Mejía was called “the king of falsetto”, even though he was from Chihuahua, far from the Huasteca.

questions.question: We ride sidesaddle, in wide skirts and sombreros, and perform figures at a gallop in the lienzo charro. Who are we?
hints: We are the women's event of charrería.
We ride as a team: eight riders who almost brush past each other as we cross.
Our name is also the Spanish word for a skirmish between soldiers.
questions.description: They don't come to the lienzo charro to watch: they come to steal the show.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, UNESCO added charrería to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Look at this charro piteado belt. What is the shiny thread in its embroidery made of?
hints: It shines a lot, but it isn't metal.
It comes from the leaves of something that grows in the countryside.
It gives the embroidery its name: pita.
questions.description: A belt that takes itself so seriously it needs weeks to get dressed.
questions.fun_fact: Pita is a plant from the pineapple family, and embroidering a good piteado belt can take weeks.

questions.question: At the end of “Coco”, we learn that Héctor, the skinny, mischievous skeleton, is related to Miguel. How?
hints: He's been part of the family for many generations.
He's Mamá Coco's dad.
He's Mamá Imelda's husband.
questions.description: A family tree with more bones than leaves.
questions.fun_fact: For “Coco”, the Pixar team traveled to Mexico several times to study how Día de Muertos is celebrated.

questions.question: In 1944 in New York, I formed one of the most famous bolero trios in the world and gave bolero its small, high-pitched guitar, the requinto. Who am I?
hints: People called me “el Güero.”
My trio was called Los Panchos.
My last name has three letters.
questions.description: A man who gave bolero its squeakiest little voice… on guitar.
questions.fun_fact: The requinto is smaller than a regular guitar and sounds higher, which makes it perfect for the fancy runs in a bolero.

questions.question: You hear it shouted between mariachi songs, at charreadas and at Mexico's national team games. What is “¡ajúa!”?
hints: Nobody gets mad when they hear it.
You often hear it right after a famous line of a ranchera.
It's a cousin of “¡ay, ay, ay!” and “¡viva!”.
questions.description: At a Mexican party, the lungs work harder than the trumpets.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexican grito is so loved that many Independence Day parties hold contests to see who can let out the best one.

questions.question: I spoke Nahuatl and Maya, learned Spanish and was Hernán Cortés's interpreter. Who am I?
wrong_answers: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
hints: I lived during the Conquest, in the 16th century.
The Spanish called me doña Marina.
My name gave rise to the word “malinchismo.”
questions.description: Before translation apps, one person did the whole job.
questions.fun_fact: At first, La Malinche translated from Nahuatl to Maya, and Jerónimo de Aguilar went from Maya to Spanish for Cortés.

questions.question: Which of these cities was NOT part of the Triple Alliance that ruled central Mexico before the Spanish Conquest?
hints: Today this city is a borough of Mexico City.
For years the Mexica paid tribute to this Tepanec city.
The alliance was formed precisely to defeat it, in 1428.
questions.description: Three friends teamed up for a school project, and one got left out.
questions.fun_fact: Before 1428, the Mexica paid tribute to Azcapotzalco, the very city they later defeated.

questions.question: How many legs does a molcajete have?
hints: It's carved from volcanic stone and stays steady even on an uneven floor.
It's an odd number.
It's the same number of legs as a camera tripod.
questions.description: It's made of stone, weighs as much as your backpack and makes the best salsa on the block.
questions.fun_fact: The little stone used to grind in a molcajete is called a tejolote.

questions.question: Look at this wooden weapon with stone blades along its sides. Who used it in battle?
hints: In battle they preferred to capture enemies rather than badly wound them.
Its blades were made of obsidian, a volcanic stone.
In Nahuatl it was called the macuahuitl.
questions.description: It looks like a baseball bat, but nobody wanted to step up to the plate against it.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish wrote that the macuahuitl cut so well it could wound a horse.

questions.question: The word “tlapalería” comes from the Nahuatl word “tlapalli.” What does “tlapalli” mean?
hints: At first, these shops mostly sold one kind of thing.
Mexica codices were full of it.
It's what paint has.
questions.description: You walk in for one screw and walk out with half a workshop in a bag.
questions.fun_fact: Tlapalerías started out selling paints, and over time they filled up with nails, pipes and tools.

questions.question: The Mexica called it chalchihuitl. It's a green stone, and they valued it more than gold. Which stone is it?
hints: It was made into necklaces, masks and ear ornaments for nobles.
Its color reminded people of water and young corn.
It is also very famous in Chinese art.
questions.description: For the Mexica, gold was nice, but this was the real treasure.
questions.fun_fact: When the Spaniards asked for gold, the Mexica were surprised that they didn't value jade as much.

questions.question: The tonalámatl, the Mexica “book of fates,” recorded a ritual calendar. How many days did that calendar have?
hints: It’s shorter than a solar year.
The Maya had a calendar with the same number of days: the tzolkin.
It combines 20 day signs with the numbers 1 to 13.
questions.description: A horoscope so serious they painted it by hand, with priests as witnesses.
questions.fun_fact: The 260-day calendar was called the tonalpohualli, and it was used to choose babies’ names.

questions.question: In Nahuatl it was called ichcatl. It is white and fluffy, and the Mexica wove it into cloaks that worked as money. What is it?
hints: It comes from a plant, not an animal.
It grew in hot lowlands and reached Tenochtitlan as tribute.
Today almost all T-shirts are made from it.
questions.description: Before credit cards, the Mexica paid with something nice and soft.
questions.fun_fact: Mexica warriors wore padded cotton armor called ichcahuipilli.

questions.question: Which tlatoani ruled Tenochtitlan when Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519?
hints: He was the ninth tlatoani of the Mexica.
Two tlatoanis had his name, and he was the second.
His name lives on in a joke about tourists with an upset stomach.
questions.description: An emperor who welcomed some visitors who never left.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish he is Moctezuma, in English often Montezuma, but in Nahuatl his name was Motecuhzoma.

questions.question: Huitzilíhuitl, the second tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, was the son of the first. What was his father's name?
hints: He ruled from the late 14th century.
His name means “handful of reeds.”
His name starts with “A” and ends in “-tli.”
questions.description: Before becoming king, every tlatoani was just the kid getting scolded at home.
questions.fun_fact: The name Huitzilíhuitl means “hummingbird feather.”

questions.question: You're at Estadio Azteca and El Tri beats Brazil 4–3 in the Confederations Cup final. What year is it?
hints: Cuauhtémoc Blanco was already El Tri's big star.
It was in the 1990s.
It was one year after the 1998 World Cup in France.
questions.description: The afternoon the Azteca taught the Brazilians themselves how to samba.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first FIFA title ever won by Mexico's senior national team.

questions.question: Which of these has NOTHING to do with Maradona at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico?
hints: Look for the one that happened at a different World Cup.
Two of them were goals against England at the Estadio Azteca.
The odd one out happened in Rio de Janeiro, in 1950.
questions.description: A short man who worked miracles in '86, plus a bit of mischief.
questions.fun_fact: The “Hand of God” and the “Goal of the Century” came in the same match, just four minutes apart.

questions.question: I'm made of paper and you pay with me. I was invented over 1,000 years ago in a country in Asia. Which one?
hints: That country also invented paper.
Gunpowder and the compass were invented there too.
It's the country with the Great Wall.
questions.description: A little piece of paper worth more than all your school notebooks put together.
questions.fun_fact: When Marco Polo told people in Europe that the Chinese paid with paper, many found it hard to believe.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who is this El Tri midfielder, who scored the winning goal in the 2025 Gold Cup final?
hints: He made his debut with Club América.
He played for Ajax in the Netherlands and West Ham in England.
His nickname is “El Machín”.
questions.description: A wall with legs that plants itself in the middle of the field.
questions.fun_fact: Edson Álvarez was born in Tlalnepantla, State of Mexico, in 1997.

questions.question: For years, fans dreamed of seeing El Tri play “el quinto partido” (the fifth game) at a 32-team World Cup. What did that mean?
hints: Count the group-stage games.
After the three group games comes one knockout game.
It's the round right after the round of 16.
questions.description: A curse so famous it deserves its own telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico went out in the round of 16 at seven World Cups in a row, from 1994 to 2018.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who is this left-footed midfielder who played at five World Cups with El Tri?
hints: He was born in Guadalajara.
He played for Atlas, PSV and Real Betis.
His nickname is “El Principito”.
questions.description: A lefty with a crown who never wanted to leave El Tri.
questions.fun_fact: Guardado said goodbye to El Tri in 2023 as the player with the most games in its history.

questions.question: I'm in northern Honduras, I'm the country's biggest stadium, and I made El Tri sweat through qualifiers in the blazing afternoon sun. Which stadium am I?
hints: My city is the industrial capital of Honduras.
I'm not in Tegucigalpa.
I'm in San Pedro Sula.
questions.description: A sauna with grass, goalposts and thousands of voices shouting against you.
questions.fun_fact: It opened in 1997 and holds about 37,000 people.

questions.question: The clay “caritas sonrientes” (smiling faces) from central Veracruz, in the El Tajín region: from which era are they?
hints: They are from the same time as El Tajín at its peak.
They were made several centuries before the Spanish arrived, but long after the Olmecs.
They are between 1,100 and 1,400 years old.
questions.description: The ancient figures that always look good in photos.
questions.fun_fact: Many have open mouths and raised arms, as if singing or dancing, and nobody knows for sure why they smile.

questions.question: Oasisamerica was the region of desert farming peoples between northwestern Mexico and the southwestern US. Which cultures made it up?
hints: They weren't Mesoamerican cultures or nomadic hunters.
One of them dug big irrigation canals in what is now Arizona.
Another built houses in cliffs and is an ancestor of the Pueblo peoples.
questions.description: When the desert gives you sand, make irrigation canals.
questions.fun_fact: The Hohokam dug hundreds of kilometers of canals, and some of their routes were reused centuries later in Phoenix.

questions.question: Every March 21, thousands of people dressed in white come to Teotihuacan, stand in front of the Pyramid of the Sun and raise their arms. Why?
questions.answer: To soak up the Sun's energy
hints: Spring begins on that day.
That's why many dress in white and stretch their hands toward the sky.
They believe the Sun “recharges” them like a battery.
questions.description: A party where everyone wears the same outfit and nobody gets upset about it.
questions.fun_fact: This custom of “charging up with energy” is modern: there is no evidence that the people of ancient Teotihuacan ever did it.

questions.question: The Mogollon culture, which influenced Paquimé, is named after some mountains. Where are those mountains?
hints: The mountains carry the last name of an 18th-century Spanish governor.
The Gila River begins in these mountains.
They are in the US state whose capital is Santa Fe.
questions.description: An ancient culture that ended up with a governor's last name.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollón governed New Mexico from 1712 to 1715, and his last name ended up naming a mountain range and an entire culture.

questions.question: The Toltecs called their capital, today's Tula, Hidalgo, Tollan. Which plant does that name come from?
hints: It is a plant that grows in lakes and marshes.
People weave petates (sleeping mats) and chair seats from it.
A famous tree in Oaxaca is named after it.
questions.description: Some cities are named after saints; this one preferred the garden.
questions.fun_fact: For the Nahuas, “Tollan” came to mean “great city,” so they also used it for Teotihuacan and Cholula.

questions.question: A farmer from Mata Ortiz, Chihuahua, taught himself to copy the Paquimé pots he found in the hills and started a whole tradition. Who was he?
hints: Today hundreds of potters in his town make a living from hand-painted pottery, made without a wheel.
He received Mexico's National Prize for Arts and Sciences.
His initials are J. Q.
questions.description: From picking up tepalcates (pottery shards) in the hills to filling museums with pots.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Quezada spent years testing clays and brushes made from children's hair until he matched the finish of the ancient pieces.

questions.question: The bank gives you money, you pay it back bit by bit, and at the end you pay a little extra. What is that called?
hints: The money isn't yours forever.
That “little extra” is called interest.
It's just like when someone lends you something and you have to give it back.
questions.description: Money that arrives fast, leaves fast, and comes back… with little friends.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Mesopotamia, people were already lending barley and silver more than 4,000 years ago, and they wrote the deals down on clay tablets.

questions.question: The Teotihuacan archaeological site is in the municipality of San Juan Teotihuacán. About how far is it from downtown Mexico City?
hints: It is in the State of Mexico, next to the capital.
By bus it takes a little over an hour.
It's less than 100 km (62 mi), but more than 20 km (12 mi).
questions.description: A Sunday day trip with pyramids included.
questions.fun_fact: At its peak, Teotihuacan may have had more than 100,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time.

questions.question: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325. Around when did the Olmec culture begin to flourish?
hints: They came long before the Classic Maya and the Mexica.
They are called the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica.
It was more than a thousand years before Christ.
questions.description: Get out your timeline, because you'll need the whole thing for this one.
questions.fun_fact: When the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan, the Olmec cities had been abandoned for more than 1,500 years.

questions.question: At the National Museum of Anthropology you see the “pretty ladies” of Tlatilco, very old clay figurines. Who first found them, in the 1930s?
hints: Tlatilco is now in Naucalpan, in the State of Mexico.
They found them by accident while doing their everyday work.
Their job was making blocks of baked clay for building.
questions.description: Pretty for three thousand years, and no filters needed.
questions.fun_fact: The painter Miguel Covarrubias collected and studied these figurines and made them famous around the world.

questions.question: At sunrise, dozens of balloons float over the pyramids of Teotihuacan. What's inside them that makes them rise?
hints: Something similar happens with the smoke from a campfire.
Above the basket there's a gas burner that shoots out flames.
When it heats up, it weighs less than the air around it.
questions.description: The slowest, prettiest and earliest-rising way to see some pyramids.
questions.fun_fact: The first crewed hot air balloon flight took place in Paris in 1783, in a balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers.

questions.question: This museum holds the second most important archaeological collection in Mexico, including several Olmec colossal heads. In which city is it?
hints: It is in the capital of a state on the Gulf of Mexico.
Its halls step down a hillside full of gardens.
It is run by the Universidad Veracruzana.
questions.description: A museum where nobody ever loses their head: these ones weigh tons.
questions.fun_fact: Its star piece is Colossal Head 1 from San Lorenzo, nicknamed “El Rey” (The King).

questions.question: It's by Maldita Vecindad, it came out on the 1991 album “El Circo,” and it's slow and tropical, with a saxophone. What's it called?
hints: It's one of the best-loved songs of 1990s Mexican rock.
Its title is repeated over and over in the chorus.
Its name sounds like “cumbia,” but it starts with a K.
questions.description: A song for slow dancing up close, even in the middle of a rock concert.
questions.fun_fact: “El Circo” is considered one of the most important albums in Spanish-language rock.

questions.question: You're at the Tianguis del Chopo among leather jackets and El Tri records. What were the young neighborhood rockers of the 1980s called?
hints: The name comes from what they called each other: their crew of buddies.
Their music was the rock urbano heard in the working-class neighborhoods of Mexico City.
The word for “gang of friends” comes right after “chavo”.
questions.description: Long before memes, neighborhood rockers were already inventing their own language.
questions.fun_fact: The Tianguis Cultural del Chopo has been held every Saturday since the 1980s and is a meeting point for rockers.

questions.question: “I'm the voice of Hello Seahorse!, the band from Mexico City, and my nickname is Lo Blondo.” Who am I?
hints: The band has been making indie pop since the mid-2000s.
One of its best-known albums is called “Bestia”.
My last name is one of the most common in Mexico and starts with G.
questions.description: A voice that swims through synthesizers like a fish… or something close to one.
questions.fun_fact: Hello Seahorse! has an English name, but it sings mostly in Spanish.

questions.question: In which decade did Pandora, the trio behind “¿Cómo te va mi amor?”, release their first album?
hints: It's a trio made up only of women.
People were still listening to music on cassettes and vinyl records.
They started around the same years as Timbiriche and Flans.
questions.description: Three voices opened a box… and out came ballads.
questions.fun_fact: Pandora was formed by Isabel Lascurain and the sisters Mayte and Fernanda Meade.

questions.question: The telenovela “Rebelde,” which gave us RBD, is the Mexican version of another teen series. Which country is the original from?
hints: The original premiered in 2002.
It's a South American country.
Its capital is Buenos Aires.
questions.description: A telenovela in a red tie that came from very far away.
questions.fun_fact: The original series was called “Rebelde Way” and was created by Cris Morena.

questions.question: The shekel, which gives its name to Israel's currency today, began as a weight of silver in Mesopotamia. How long ago?
hints: Its name comes from an ancient word meaning “to weigh.”
It already appears in the Code of Hammurabi.
Mesopotamia is the same region where writing was invented.
questions.description: A currency older than your grandpa's oldest joke.
questions.fun_fact: At first the shekel wasn't a coin but a unit of weight: people weighed silver on a scale to pay.

questions.question: “I'm a 1999 Carlos Santana album, I have “Smooth” and “Corazón espinado” with Maná, and I won eight Grammys in one night.” Which album am I?
hints: It was Santana's big comeback after years without a huge hit.
It has lots of collaborations with other singers.
My name describes things beyond the natural world, like ghosts and magic.
questions.description: An album that showed up at the Grammys and took home almost everything except the red carpet.
questions.fun_fact: With “Supernatural,” Santana tied Michael Jackson's record of eight Grammys in a single night.

questions.question: I crunch when you bite me, at the market they sell me in huge sheets, and in salsa verde I turn soft. What am I?
hints: People eat me with lime and salsa.
I come from the pig.
I'm its skin, fried until golden and puffed up.
questions.description: The noisiest snack at the corner store: you can hear it from down the block.
questions.fun_fact: Chicharrón en salsa verde is one of the favorite fillings for tacos de canasta and tacos de guisado.

questions.question: This warm soup is the home remedy when you catch a cold. Which bird's meat goes in it?
hints: It's a farm bird.
It lays eggs almost every day.
It's the mother of the little chicks.
questions.description: Grandma's medicine: it doesn't come from the drugstore, it comes in a deep bowl.
questions.fun_fact: Caldo de gallina is often tastier than chicken soup because a hen is an older bird, and its meat cooks slowly.

questions.question: The penca is long, thick and spiny along the edges; it's roasted to wrap barbacoa, and its fibers are used for weaving. What part of the maguey is it?
hints: It grows above the ground and you can easily see it.
A maguey has many of them, arranged like a rosette.
It's the green part the plant uses for photosynthesis.
questions.description: A plant that gives you a drink, a blanket for the barbacoa and even thread.
questions.fun_fact: Fibers from maguey pencas were woven into ayates, like the cloak bearing the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe.

questions.question: Mole coloradito is brick red, made with ancho chile, plantain and chocolate, and is one of its state's classic moles. Which state?
hints: It's a southern state on the Pacific, with many Indigenous peoples and languages.
Its capital shares the state's name, and the ruins of Monte Albán are nearby.
The Guelaguetza is held there, and it boasts seven moles, like the black and the yellow.
questions.description: A mole that turned red, but not from embarrassment.
questions.fun_fact: In Oaxaca, mole is sold as a paste in the markets: at home you just dissolve it in broth and you're done.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: no party is complete without tostadas de… shredded meat with tomato, onion and chipotle chile.
hints: It's a classic stew from Puebla.
It's almost always made with shredded chicken.
Its name has five letters and starts with “tin.”
questions.description: The shredded meat that makes tostadas work overtime at every party.
questions.fun_fact: The original tinga poblana was made with pork and chorizo; the chicken version became famous later.

questions.question: La Sandunga, danced in the traje de tehuana on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, is sung in Spanish and in…
hints: It's the language of an Indigenous people of southern Mexico.
It's the most widely spoken language in Oaxaca's Central Valleys and Isthmus.
Monte Albán was a great city of this people.
questions.description: A son so elegant that even the embroidered skirts get nervous when it starts.
questions.fun_fact: La Sandunga has a slow three-beat rhythm, a lot like a waltz.

questions.question: At the feria you buy a bag of chicharrones de harina. What does almost everyone put on them before eating?
hints: It's not sweet at all.
It's a little spicy and a little sour.
The same thing many people put on peanuts and potato chips.
questions.description: A little wheel so crunchy you can hear it from the other end of the fair.
questions.fun_fact: Chicharrones de harina start as small, hard wheat-flour pellets that puff up in seconds when they hit hot oil.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this fair treat is coated in red candy and has a stick. What fruit is underneath?
hints: It's a fruit that grows on trees in orchards.
It can be red, green or yellow.
Snow White bit into a poisoned one.
questions.description: A treat so shiny it looks like it just came back from the hair salon.
questions.fun_fact: At Mexican fairs, apples aren't only coated in candy: they're also sold covered in chamoy and chili.

questions.question: At weddings in Veracruz, the couple dances La Bamba and uses their feet to tie a ribbon into a bow. What does the bow stand for?
hints: Think about what a bow is for.
Remember what a wedding celebrates.
Two ends that end up tied together.
questions.description: A dance where the feet do arts and crafts.
questions.fun_fact: La Bamba is a traditional son jarocho from Veracruz, and Ritchie Valens made it famous around the world as a rock song in 1958.

questions.question: I'm a colorful glass bead, and in Africa people used me as money. Which European city did the finest of us come from?
hints: It's a city in southern Europe, by the sea.
It was the capital of a powerful trading republic in the Mediterranean.
In this city, people get around by gondola.
questions.description: Costume jewelry that, for centuries, was worth more than plenty of real jewels.
questions.fun_fact: The glassmakers of Murano guarded their secrets so closely that for centuries they were forbidden to leave the republic.

questions.question: Some pilgrims cover the last stretch to the Basilica on their knees, even though it hurts. Why do they do it?
wrong_answers: To ask for a job at the church
hints: It's a sacrifice that comes from their faith.
They do it to give thanks for a favor they received.
It's a promise made to the Virgin or to a saint.
questions.description: Some trips are made by car, some by bus… and some on your knees.
questions.fun_fact: The Basilica of Guadalupe is one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world, with millions of pilgrims every December.

questions.question: At the feria you throw plastic pieces so they land around the neck of a bottle and win a prize. What is the game called?
hints: There are no rifles or corks.
What you throw is round and hollow in the middle.
It's like a tiny hula hoop.
questions.description: A game for people who always brag about their aim… until they reach the stand.
questions.fun_fact: The bottles in this game usually stand very close together and the ring barely fits over the neck: that's why it's so hard to win.

questions.question: In many Mexican towns, a family takes on the role of mayordomo for one year. What does that role involve?
questions.answer: Paying for and organizing the saint's fiesta
hints: It's not a job for the government or the priest.
It has to do with the town's patron saint.
It covers the food, the band and the fireworks.
questions.description: An honor so big that the whole family ends up working for the town for an entire year.
questions.fun_fact: In many communities, families sign up years in advance to hold the mayordomía, because it's a great honor.

questions.question: It's huge and round, turns slowly and lifts you up high in little cabins so you can see the whole fair. Which ride is it?
hints: It doesn't go fast.
It turns from bottom to top, not along the ground.
It looks like a giant bicycle wheel.
questions.description: Colored lights, cotton candy and screaming kids: welcome to the town fair.
questions.fun_fact: The first big wheel of this kind was built by George Ferris for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.

previous.feedback: This asks the same fact as approved q-9381 (“What is this ride called?” → Ferris wheel), so it duplicates a question already in the English pool. Source: it also has no link to Mexico, so it doesn't belong in the mexico bundle. The rater flagged both problems.

questions.question: In Tonalá and Zapopan, Jalisco, dancers with masks and long manes play the peoples who fought Saint James. What are they called?
hints: Their big fiesta is in July, on Saint James's Day.
Their name comes from the Nahuatl word “tlatoani,” meaning ruler.
They're characters from Jalisco, not from Morelos or Chiapas.
questions.description: Characters with so much hair that no barber dares to come near them.
questions.fun_fact: In the dance, Saint James rides a horse and the masked dancers challenge him again and again in a staged battle.

questions.question: Every October 28, thousands of people visit St. Jude Thaddeus at the church of San Hipólito. What do they pray to him for?
hints: His followers are very faithful and all arrive with the same hope.
His images show him in a green robe with a medallion on his chest.
He is the patron of things that seem to have no solution.
questions.description: The saint with the busiest schedule in Mexico, especially on the 28th.
questions.fun_fact: Many devotees go to San Hipólito on the 28th of every month, not just in October.

questions.question: José Sulaimán led it from 1975, and today his son Mauricio runs it. Which boxing organization is it?
hints: It is one of the four major organizations in world boxing.
Its headquarters are in Mexico City.
Its champion's belt is green and carries the flags of many countries.
questions.description: A family business where whoever inherits the chair also inherits all the champions.
questions.fun_fact: The World Boxing Council was founded in 1963 in Mexico City.

questions.question: On a Mexican Independence Day weekend, Canelo knocked down Puerto Rico's Edgar Berlanga and beat him on points in Las Vegas. In what year?
hints: He had already been undisputed super middleweight champion, though by then he had lost the IBF belt.
It came after his third fight against Gennady Golovkin.
It was the year Claudia Sheinbaum won Mexico's presidential election.
questions.description: September in Las Vegas: green, white and red flags, mariachi, and a Puerto Rican on the canvas.
questions.fun_fact: Berlanga had won his first 16 pro fights by knockout in the first round.

questions.question: In the tongue twister “Pablito clavó un clavito”, where did Pablito hammer the little nail?
questions.answer: On the bald head of a little bald man
wrong_answers: On the top of a little table
On the door of a little house
On the leg of a little chair
hints: The place wasn’t a piece of furniture.
Someone there surely complained.
In Spanish, the place sounds almost like “clavito”.
questions.description: Hammer in hand and tongue in a knot: the playground’s favorite tongue twister.
questions.fun_fact: Tongue twisters like this one are used to practice pronunciation, especially sounds like “cl” and “bl”.

questions.question: You rock a baby on your lap and sing “Aserrín, aserrán, los maderos de…”. Where is the wood from?
hints: It's a saint.
This saint's feast day is June 24.
The capital of Puerto Rico is named after him.
questions.description: Some hungry carpenters who get nothing but bad luck on the menu.
questions.fun_fact: “Aserrín” is the fine dust that comes off wood when you saw it, and the song copies the back-and-forth of a saw.

questions.question: There were 450 of us. On Mount Carmel, we begged our god all day to send fire, but it never came. Who are we?
hints: The prophet Elijah challenged us.
We worshipped a Canaanite god of rain and storms.
Our god's name starts with B.
questions.description: History's first cooking contest held without a stove.
questions.fun_fact: In the story, Elijah soaked his altar with water three times before the fire came down, so no one could doubt the miracle.

questions.question: In Morelos there are ruins of colonial works where sugarcane was ground to make sugar. What were they called in Spanish?
hints: Hernán Cortés founded one of the first ones near Cuernavaca.
Huge fields of sugarcane were planted next to them.
The same Spanish word also means “cleverness”, like the English word “ingenious”.
questions.description: Where sugarcane went in whole and came out ready for dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Many old sugar haciendas in Morelos are now hotels and gardens for parties.

questions.question: In casta paintings and baptism records of New Spain, the word “mulato” appears. Who did it refer to?
questions.answer: Child of a Spaniard and an African
wrong_answers: Child of a Spaniard and an Indigenous person
Child of an Indigenous person and an African
Child of Spaniards born in the Americas
hints: Thousands of people brought from Africa arrived in New Spain.
The child of a Spaniard and an Indigenous person had another name: mestizo.
One parent came from Europe and the other from Africa.
questions.description: A family portrait where the label mattered more than the face.
questions.fun_fact: Veracruz and the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca are regions of Mexico with a strong Afro-Mexican heritage.

questions.question: Martín Hernández has worked on almost every Iñárritu film since “Amores Perros” and was Oscar-nominated for “Birdman” and “The Revenant”. What is his field?
hints: The cinematography of “Birdman” and “The Revenant” was done by Emmanuel “El Chivo” Lubezki.
In “The Revenant”, the forest, the wind and a bear all had to feel real.
His work goes in through your ears.
questions.description: A Mexican who knows the end credits by heart because he's always in them.
questions.fun_fact: For “Birdman”, drummer Antonio Sánchez recorded almost the whole score on just his drum kit.

questions.question: It's a fragrant tree from Guerrero; its wood is used for Olinalá lacquer boxes that perfume the clothes stored inside. What is it called?
hints: Its oil was also used to make perfume.
It's not Mexico's national tree.
Its name sounds like the lacquer town's name: Olinalá.
questions.description: The only wooden box that smells better than your closet.
questions.fun_fact: Linaloe boxes can keep their scent for many years.

questions.question: It grows along riverbanks, and people weave baskets and make flutes from it. What is carrizo?
wrong_answers: The fiber taken from the maguey
The dried leaf of the palm
The bark of the amate tree
hints: It's a plant from the grass family.
Its stem is long and thin, with joints.
It looks a lot like what pandas eat.
questions.description: A plant that's just as good for carrying tortillas as for playing a tune.
questions.fun_fact: Carrizo is also used to build the frames of papalotes (kites) and mojigangas, the giant parade puppets.

questions.question: In 1936, a Fernando de Fuentes film starring Tito Guízar was Mexican cinema's first big international hit and founded a genre. Which one?
hints: Jorge Negrete and Pedro Infante later made it huge.
Its heroes were usually charros who sang and fell in love on the hacienda.
Its name comes from life in the countryside and on ranches.
questions.description: When movies learned to talk, in Mexico they started singing right away.
questions.fun_fact: In 1938 the film won a cinematography award at the Venice Film Festival, thanks to the work of Gabriel Figueroa.

questions.question: The founders of the “La Michoacana” ice pop shops came from a town in Michoacán now called “the land of the paleta.” Which town?
hints: It's a small town, far less known than the state's tourist cities.
A giant paleta stands as a monument at its entrance.
Its name starts with “To.”
questions.description: Ice pops so famous that their name is almost an address.
questions.fun_fact: Families from this town opened paleterías all over Mexico and even in the United States, which is how “La Michoacana” became a name everyone knows.

questions.question: In Mexico, people eat 12 grapes at midnight on December 31, one for each chime of the clock. Who did Mexico inherit this custom from?
hints: The custom came from across the ocean.
In its home country, people follow the chimes on TV, watching the clock on a famous square.
It's the country that conquered Mexico in the 16th century.
questions.description: Twelve wishes, twelve chimes and a mouth so full you can't say a word.
questions.fun_fact: The custom caught on in Spain in the early 1900s; one popular story says it was because a harvest left far too many grapes.

questions.question: Take a close look at this craft of colorful yarn woven in a diamond shape over two crossed sticks. What is it called?
hints: Peoples of the Sierra Madre Occidental make it to protect children.
A diamond is often added for each year of the child's life.
Its name says someone is watching you from the sky.
questions.description: A colorful craft that decorates the room and works as a bodyguard too.
questions.fun_fact: In the Wixárika language, the Ojo de Dios is called «tsikuri».

questions.question: What is the cold drink of fermented corn, served with lime, salt and a scoop of lime nieve (sorbet)?
hints: It's typical of Jalisco and western Mexico.
It's made with corn masa and piloncillo.
Its name starts with “te”, but there's no pineapple in it.
questions.description: On a hot afternoon, nothing beats something that first had to go a little sour.
questions.fun_fact: Tejuino comes from a ceremonial drink of peoples of the west and north, such as the Wixárika (Huichol) and the Rarámuri.

questions.question: I'm made of wood, I turned into a snake in the desert, and with one strike I made water flow from a rock. What am I?
hints: My owner looked after sheep before he became a leader.
I was held out over the Red Sea.
I'm a long stick you can lean on when you walk.
questions.description: The most useful thing to carry in the desert, after a water bottle.
questions.fun_fact: Moses was a shepherd, so his famous staff was really just a shepherd's walking stick.

questions.question: In 1995, Indigenous peoples of the Montaña and Costa Chica regions set up a community police force, with unpaid neighbors chosen by assembly. In which state?
hints: It is a southern state on the Pacific coast.
Nahuatl, Mixtec, Tlapanec and Amuzgo are spoken there.
Its most famous port is Acapulco.
questions.description: Guards who don't get paid, but sure get respect.
questions.fun_fact: This community police force is coordinated by the CRAC, which also delivers justice that aims to repair the harm, not just punish.

questions.question: In Mexica society, the “macehualtin” were the majority, paid tribute, and their name lives on in “macehual.” Who were they?
hints: They were not the ones in charge.
They worked the land and served in war when called.
They were the opposite of the nobles.
questions.description: A word from Tenochtitlan that outlived the empire itself.
questions.fun_fact: On the Yucatán Peninsula, many Maya speakers still call themselves “masewal,” a word related to “macehual.”

questions.question: It’s a 16th-century Nahuatl account, credited to Antonio Valeriano, of the Virgin of Guadalupe and Juan Diego. What does its title, “Nican Mopohua,” mean?
hints: They are the first words of the text.
It is not the name of a person or a place.
“Nican” means “here.”
questions.description: A title that sounds like a tongue twister but says something really simple.
questions.fun_fact: The Nican Mopohua was first published in 1649, inside a book by the priest Luis Lasso de la Vega.

questions.question: Take a close look at these salsas, one red and one green. Where do you find them on every table?
hints: They're hot salsas.
You spoon them onto something made with a tortilla.
There they ask you: “¿Con todo, joven?”
questions.description: Two bowls that decide whether your dinner will be calm or full of tears.
questions.fun_fact: Many taquerías keep their salsa recipe as a family secret.

questions.question: Look at this salsa borracha, made with chile pasilla. Which drink does it traditionally contain?
hints: Its name already tells you the drink has alcohol.
It's a thick, white drink.
It comes from the maguey and was sold in pulquerías.
questions.description: A salsa nobody lets drive home.
questions.fun_fact: Salsa borracha is the classic partner of barbacoa, especially in central Mexico.

questions.question: In traditional Mexican medicine, what can happen to you if you walk past a cemetery or a cave at night?
hints: It brings chills, headaches and even a crooked mouth.
It is cured with a limpia using an egg, rue or pirul branches.
They say it's caused by something invisible floating in those places.
questions.description: An illness that never shows up in any lab test.
questions.fun_fact: To cure it, some curanderos “sweep” the sick person with branches of pirul or basil and then throw them away far from the house.

questions.question: Guillermo del Toro's movie “El espinazo del diablo” has a body part in its Spanish title. What is the “espinazo”?
hints: It's part of the skeleton.
In Mexico it's eaten in stews, like pork espinazo with verdolagas (purslane).
It runs from the neck down to the hips.
questions.description: A movie title with a real bone to pick.
questions.fun_fact: Del Toro has said “The Devil's Backbone” and “Pan's Labyrinth” are sister films, both set in Spain during and after the Spanish Civil War.

questions.question: What name did CMLL's great masked idol of the mid-2000s, famous for his flying moves, use before he left for WWE?
hints: He's a técnico and almost always wrestled at Arena México.
He debuted in CMLL in the early 2000s and was its biggest star within a few years.
In WWE they gave him a name about having no face.
questions.description: He dresses in silver and gold, yet no one has ever seen him in a jewelry store.
questions.fun_fact: The original Místico wrestled in WWE as Sin Cara, and CMLL gave the name Místico to another wrestler.

questions.question: Look at this young Mexican music singer. Who is her dad, also a ranchera music star?
hints: Her family has been singing ranchera for several generations.
He made “Por mujeres como tú” famous.
She has the same last name as her dad and her grandfather Antonio.
questions.description: When your family sings “Las Mañanitas” with a professional mariachi.
questions.fun_fact: Ángela Aguilar was born in Los Angeles, California, in 2003, and has been singing on stage since she was a little girl.

questions.question: This Mexico City Metro station joins Lines 8 and B, and its name pairs a mariachi plaza with a famous market. What is it called?
hints: It's downtown, north of the Alameda.
The market in its name is famous for its Sunday antiques.
The plaza bears the last name of an Italian hero.
questions.description: A station where even the turnstiles get emotional.
questions.fun_fact: La Lagunilla market is named after a small lagoon that was in the area centuries ago.

questions.question: Rocío Dúrcal made famous a Juan Gabriel song heard at many farewells and on Día de Muertos. Complete the title: “Amor…”
hints: Juan Gabriel wrote it thinking of his mother.
Juan Gabriel also sang it at his famous concert at Bellas Artes.
It means “lasting forever.”
questions.description: A Spaniard who could cry a ranchera better than plenty of Mexicans.
questions.fun_fact: Rocío Dúrcal was born in Madrid, but Mexico loved her so much they called her “la Señora.”

questions.question: At the 2024 Concacaf W Gold Cup, Mexico's women's team beat the United States 2-0 in California. In what year was their previous win against the US?
hints: It was a knockout match on the road to a Women's World Cup.
It was played in Cancún.
It was the same year as the men's World Cup in South Africa.
questions.description: The day the neighbor to the north had to put the party on hold.
questions.fun_fact: The 2024 win in Carson, California, was Mexico's first ever women's victory over the United States on US soil.

questions.question: For the Centennial of Independence in 1910, this Teotihuacan pyramid was rebuilt. Who led the work?
hints: He worked under the government of Porfirio Díaz.
He was the country's inspector general of archaeological monuments.
His last name starts with B.
questions.description: A pyramid that got an early-20th-century facelift.
questions.fun_fact: Many archaeologists today criticize him because the rebuilding stripped several meters off the pyramid's original outer layer.

questions.question: They live in the Sierra Tarahumara of Chihuahua, are also called Tarahumara, and their language has their name. What is “Rarámuri” said to mean?
hints: It has to do with something they are very good at.
Sports magazines and books around the world have written about their stamina.
They are famous for running huge distances, sometimes in huaraches.
questions.description: A people whose name is almost a résumé.
questions.fun_fact: In the ball race (carrera de bola), Rarámuri runners cover mile after mile kicking a wooden ball.

questions.question: Which of these songs is NOT by Belanova?
hints: Belanova plays electronic pop and comes from Guadalajara.
The odd one out is a rock ballad sung by a man, not a woman.
The odd one out is by a rock band that is also from Guadalajara, but much older.
questions.description: A band from Guadalajara so sweet it should be sold at the candy store.
questions.fun_fact: “Labios compartidos” is by Maná, another band from Guadalajara.

questions.question: Danna Paola is Mexican, sang “Oye Pablo” and played Lucrecia in the series “Elite”. Which country is that series from?
hints: The series premiered on Netflix in 2018.
It takes place at a very exclusive private school called Las Encinas.
The characters keep saying “tío” and “vale”.
questions.description: A Mexican girl who transferred to the most dramatic school on TV.
questions.fun_fact: Before “Elite”, Danna Paola was already famous in Mexico for kids' telenovelas like “Atrévete a soñar”.

questions.question: Kenia Os started out making YouTube videos, then moved into pop; her name comes from her last name, Osuna. Where was she born?
hints: It's a city on Mexico's Pacific coast.
It's in the state famous for banda sinaloense.
It's famous for its carnival and its malecón.
questions.description: From uploading videos on a phone to filling stadiums: every influencer's dream.
questions.fun_fact: Kenia Os was born in 1999, and her full name is Kenia Guadalupe Flores Osuna.

questions.question: After the 1971 Avándaro festival, rock moved to warehouses and vacant lots called “hoyos fonquis”. Around which city were they common?
hints: The name mixes a Spanish word with one that sounds like the English “funky”.
Avándaro is near Valle de Bravo, in the State of Mexico.
Many were in Nezahualcóyotl and other neighborhoods on the east side.
questions.description: Concerts where a stage was optional and dust was mandatory.
questions.fun_fact: “Fonqui” is the Spanish spelling of “funky”, an English word used for anything with lots of rhythm.

questions.question: “We're a romantic duo: Leonel is Mexican and Noel is Argentine. We sing ‘Entra en mi vida’ and ‘Que lloro’.” Who are we?
hints: Our first album came out in the early 2000s.
Our name has two words.
Our name means “without a flag”.
questions.description: Two voices, two countries and a pile of tear-soaked tissues.
questions.fun_fact: “Entra en mi vida” is now a wedding classic, and their debut album won a Latin Grammy.

questions.question: Long before Christmas existed there, the Mexica were already raising the guajolote, the turkey of Christmas dinner. What kind of animal is it?
hints: It hatches from an egg.
It has feathers and wings.
It's a relative of the chicken.
questions.description: The guest of honor at Christmas dinner, even though nobody asked if it wanted to come.
questions.fun_fact: The guajolote was domesticated in Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, and from there it sailed to Europe on Spanish ships.

questions.question: At the wedding at Cana, the wine ran out. According to the Gospel, what did Jesus turn into wine?
hints: It came out of some large stone jars.
Jesus told the servants to fill the jars to the brim.
It has no color and no taste.
questions.description: The trick every waiter wishes they could learn.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Gospel of John, this was Jesus's first miracle, and the new wine turned out better than the first.

questions.question: Complete it: in northern Mexico, on Sundays the family lights the charcoal and makes carne…
hints: It's cooked on a grill.
It needs a charcoal or wood fire.
In Monterrey it comes with tortillas, grilled green onions and salsa.
questions.description: The only Sunday plan that starts with lighting charcoal and ends with everyone asleep.
questions.fun_fact: In Monterrey, carne asada is almost a ceremony: some families make it every weekend of the year.

questions.question: It's tender beef cooked in fat on a domed comal and served with onion and cilantro. Which taco is it?
hints: It isn't cooked on a spit or underground.
It's a classic at Mexico City taquerías.
Its name sounds like the Spanish word “sudar” (to sweat).
questions.description: Meat so tender it melts before you can say “con todo”.
questions.fun_fact: At many taquerías, suadero is mixed with longaniza sausage to make the famous taco campechano.

questions.question: Its flower goes into soup, its toasted seeds are pepitas, and it grew in the milpa with corn and beans. Where was squash domesticated?
hints: It was domesticated thousands of years ago, even before corn.
It's the same region where corn and chile peppers were domesticated.
It covers a large part of Mexico and Central America.
questions.description: A plant that moved into the milpa with corn and beans and never paid rent.
questions.fun_fact: In Guilá Naquitz Cave in Oaxaca, seeds of farmed squash about 10,000 years old were found.

questions.question: I open between April and May, and my dates match the anniversary of the 1862 victory over the French army. Which feria am I?
hints: The battle was fought near the forts of Loreto and Guadalupe.
General Ignacio Zaragoza won that battle.
It's the city of Cinco de Mayo, mole and Talavera pottery.
questions.description: A party that shows off a victory every year as if it happened yesterday.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Puebla is held on grounds next to the forts of Loreto and Guadalupe, where the Cinco de Mayo battle was fought.

previous.feedback: source: the clue ("opens between April and May, dates match the anniversary of the 1862 victory") also fits the Feria de San Marcos, one of the wrong answers. It also runs from late April to early May and spans May 5, as the fact check notes. The source needs a Puebla-only clue (e.g. "held beside the forts where the May 5, 1862 victory over the French was won") or a distractor that isn't held in April–May. The English text is a faithful, natural translation. Fact check: wrong. The answer (Feria de Puebla) and the hints and fun fact are true. The Zaragoza and Loreto/Guadalupe facts check out, and the fair is held at the Centro Expositor next to the forts (24 Apr–11 May 2025). The problem is the distractor "Feria de San Marcos". It also opens in April and runs through early May (19 Apr–11 May 2025), so it also spans 5 May. The riddle's clue ("opens between April and May, dates match the anniversary") therefore doesn't clearly rule it out.

questions.question: The Feria de Xmatkuil has a Maya name, opens every November and sets up on the edge of the “White City.” Which state is it in?
hints: It's on the peninsula in Mexico's southeast.
The “White City” is that state's capital.
Its capital is Mérida.
questions.description: A fair with a name so tricky you should practice it before you ask for a taxi.
questions.fun_fact: Many place names in Yucatán start with “X,” which sounds like “sh” in Maya.

questions.question: At a charreada, they announce that the “floreo de reata” is next. What are you about to see?
questions.answer: A charro doing tricks with a rope
wrong_answers: A charro riding a wild bull
A horse dancing to mariachi music
An escaramuza circling at a gallop
hints: A reata is a rope.
Nobody needs to catch any animal.
He spins the rope in circles and even jumps through them.
questions.description: The lienzo charro announcer drags out the call so long the crowd has already eaten three elotes.
questions.fun_fact: The best charros spin the reata both on foot and on horseback, then use the same rope to catch a horse at full gallop.

questions.question: The ruedo of a lienzo charro, the round arena where many of the events take place, is about how many meters across?
hints: Several horses have to fit in it at a gallop.
It's smaller than a soccer field.
It's a little less than half the length of a soccer field.
questions.description: A field so round that no ball can figure out what it's for.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the ruedo, a lienzo charro has a long lane called the manga, used for events such as the colas, where riders bring down a steer by its tail.

questions.question: In Mexico, students at an Escuela Normal are called normalistas. What are they training to be?
hints: After they graduate, they work with children and teenagers.
Their training happens in front of a group of students.
Soon they'll be taking attendance and giving homework.
questions.description: A school whose name is so plain that no one would guess it's special.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the French «école normale»: a school that taught the «norm», meaning how to teach.

questions.question: You scrape your knee and open the first aid kit. Before you put on a bandage, what should you do?
questions.answer: Wash it with soap and water
wrong_answers: Put ice on top of it
Pour lots of powder on it
hints: The scrape has dirt and tiny bits of stuff in it.
Germs that cause infections can get into a dirty scrape.
It's the same thing you do to your hands before you eat.
questions.description: A box with a cross on it that has saved more knees than any superhero.
questions.fun_fact: Cleaning a scrape well with water is one of the most important things you can do to stop it from getting infected.

questions.question: Frida, the rescue dog, became famous after the 2017 earthquake in Mexico. Which institution did she belong to?
hints: It's part of Mexico's armed forces.
Besides doing rescues, her teammates guard the coasts.
Her human teammates work on ships and in ports.
questions.description: A four-legged hero who wore goggles and little boots to work.
questions.fun_fact: Before the 2017 earthquake, Frida had already helped with rescues in Haiti and Ecuador.

questions.question: Ignacio Chávez was rector of UNAM, founded a national institute in 1944, and is Mexico's great pioneer in his field. What does that institute treat?
hints: His institute is still running today in the south of Mexico City.
It cares for an organ that works day and night without rest.
Its full name is the Instituto Nacional de Cardiología.
questions.description: A doctor so important that even the university students had him as their boss.
questions.fun_fact: The Instituto Nacional de Cardiología, founded by Ignacio Chávez in 1944, was one of the first hospitals in the world devoted only to the heart.

questions.question: Chocolate Abuelita comes in round tablets divided into triangles. What is it mainly used to make?
hints: It dissolves in milk or water.
You whip it with a molinillo (wooden whisk) to make it foamy.
It's perfect with a pan de muerto in November.
questions.description: A grandma so famous she's on the box and never gets any older.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate Abuelita is also used to make champurrado, a thick drink made with corn masa.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Mexico makes a famous antivenom against this animal's sting. Which group does it belong to?
hints: Its body has two main parts, not three.
Count its legs: it has eight.
It's a relative of spiders.
questions.description: A critter that carries its weapon in its tail and doesn't need a license for it.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's scorpion antivenom is made with antibodies from horses and has saved thousands of lives.

questions.question: This state is named after an insurgent who went on to become Mexico's second president. Which state is it?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
Its capital is Chilpancingo.
Acapulco and Taxco are there.
questions.description: A state named after someone who never, ever gave up.
questions.fun_fact: Vicente Guerrero and Agustín de Iturbide signed the Plan of Iguala, which led to Mexico winning its independence in 1821.

questions.question: The Sonoran Desert is home to the “Gila monster.” What is it?
hints: It can go months without eating because it stores fat in its tail.
Its skin has black and orange or pink markings.
It's a four-legged reptile, a cousin of Jalisco's “escorpión.”
questions.description: Its name sounds like a horror movie, but it spends most of the year hiding under a rock.
questions.fun_fact: A diabetes medicine was developed from a substance found in Gila monster saliva.

questions.question: In the movie “Coco” there's one called Pepita. What is an alebrije?
hints: It's a handicraft.
It usually mixes parts of several animals.
It can have wings, horns and fangs, all painted in bright colors.
questions.description: If dreams had a souvenir shop, this is what they'd sell in Oaxaca.
questions.fun_fact: Alebrijes were invented by Pedro Linares in Mexico City in 1936, after he dreamed of strange creatures during a fever.

questions.question: At the Guelaguetza Auditorium on the Cerro del Fortín, groups from the regions of Oaxaca dance. Which of these regions is NOT in Oaxaca?
hints: Oaxaca is officially divided into eight regions.
The odd one out is home to the Tének people.
It stretches across several states near the Gulf of Mexico, such as San Luis Potosí and Veracruz.
questions.description: A stage on top of a hill: the only theater where you're out of breath before the show even starts.
questions.fun_fact: The Guelaguetza is held on the two Mondays after July 16, which is why it's also called “los Lunes del Cerro” (the Mondays on the Hill).

questions.question: A children's rhyme starts with “De tin marín, de do pingüé” and goes on with “cúcara, mácara”. What are those words?
hints: Kids pass it down from one generation to the next, no book needed.
Every country, even every neighborhood, says it a little differently.
Nobody knows what they mean, because they don't mean anything.
questions.description: A schoolyard rhyme everyone knows by heart and nobody learned in class.
questions.fun_fact: The rhyme ends with “títere fue”, and many families add “yo no fui, fue Teté” to stretch out the luck.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico, why is this person by the side of the road holding up a thumb?
wrong_answers: To signal that the car is full
To ask drivers to slow down
hints: People use this gesture on roads all over the world.
This person doesn't have their own car for this trip.
It's the Mexican word for when someone gives you a free ride in their car.
questions.description: On the highway, sometimes one hand is enough to chat with every car.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico people also say “dar raite,” from the English word “ride,” when someone gives you a lift.

questions.question: He has a big mustache, wears a white coat, dances outside drugstores, and fans throw plush toys of him at singers at concerts. Which chain is he the mascot of?
hints: It's one of the biggest drugstore chains in Mexico.
The chain sells generic medicines at low prices.
The mascot is called Doctor Simi.
questions.description: A doctor who never writes you a prescription but dances better than your uncles at parties.
