questions.fun_fact: The Doctor Simi character is based on Víctor González Torres, the founder of Farmacias Similares.

questions.question: At the papelería, you ask for “a dozen” pencils. How many pencils do you get?
hints: It's more than ten.
Eggs are often sold this way too, in cartons.
It's the number of months in a year.
questions.description: In August, with back-to-school season, the papelería gets more packed than the Metro at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: Half a dozen is 6, and a dozen dozens, 144, is called a gross.

questions.question: Look at this Cruz Roja Mexicana vehicle. Who works on board to help people?
hints: They know first aid.
They carry bandages, oxygen and a stretcher.
Their job is a lot like a nurse's, but out on the street.
questions.description: It shows up with a siren, flashing lights and in a big hurry, but never to a party.
questions.fun_fact: The Cruz Roja Mexicana was founded in 1910, and every year it collects money in the streets to pay for its ambulances.

questions.question: Look at this worker. What does he deliver to people's homes?
hints: He carries a big bag over his shoulder.
What he brings sometimes has stamps stuck on it.
He works for the post office.
questions.description: He walks more than anyone in the colonia and always has something for you.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, Mail Carrier Day (Día del Cartero) is celebrated on November 12.

questions.question: Many schools in Mexico have several uniforms. Which of these does NOT normally exist?
hints: Three of them are worn at school.
One is for ceremonies and another for P.E.
Picture going to class in a swimsuit.
questions.description: Mexican schools have clothes for every occasion, except one.
questions.fun_fact: The dress uniform (uniforme de gala) usually has a white shirt and is worn for ceremonies and the Monday flag salute.

questions.question: It's an 11-digit number: you need it for your first formal job and to go to your family clinic. Which institution gives it to you?
hints: It has nothing to do with voting or taxes.
It has clinics and hospitals all over the country.
People call it “el Seguro.”
questions.description: Eleven numbers that follow you from your first job all the way to retirement.
questions.fun_fact: The IMSS was founded in 1943 and is one of the largest health institutions in Latin America.

questions.question: There's a blackout: no TV, the fridge isn't cooling and the lights won't turn on. What can you still use to cook?
hints: Think about how food gets heated in your home.
It runs on a tank or a pipe.
You can light it with a match.
questions.description: Suddenly the whole colonia goes dark and someone yells “¡Se fue la luz!”
questions.fun_fact: Stoves with electric ignition can still be lit with a match when the power goes out.

questions.question: I open at recess, sell tortas, chips with salsa and aguas frescas, and always have a line. What am I?
hints: You don't get sent here for misbehaving.
You need a few coins.
Many people call it “la cooperativa”.
questions.description: The recess bell rings and half the school runs to the same place.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican schools the snack shop (la tiendita) is called the “cooperativa” because school co-ops of students, parents and teachers were set up to run it.

questions.question: Which of these schools does NOT belong to the IPN?
hints: Three of them belong to the Poli, whose mascot is a white donkey.
The odd one out is at the same level as a prepa.
It belongs to the university of the Pumas.
questions.description: The Poli has lots of schools, but one snuck in from the rival university.
questions.fun_fact: The IPN was founded in 1936, while Lázaro Cárdenas was president.

questions.question: Look at the photo: who brought this way of roasting meat on a vertical spit, the trompo, to Mexico?
hints: They arrived in Mexico in the early 20th century, mostly in Puebla.
In their homeland, this meat is traditionally made with lamb, not pork.
Puebla still sells tacos árabes, cousins of tacos al pastor.
questions.description: A pineapple riding shotgun and meat spinning like a fair ride.
questions.fun_fact: Tacos al pastor were born when Mexican taco makers swapped the lamb of shawarma for pork marinated in chile and topped it with pineapple.

questions.question: The prophet Samuel anointed the first king of Israel. Who was he?
hints: He was from the tribe of Benjamin.
He was so tall he stood head and shoulders above everyone.
He was later replaced by the young David.
questions.description: He had to pick a king with no elections, no debates and no polls.
questions.fun_fact: Samuel later anointed David too, while he was still a boy looking after sheep.

questions.question: The Maya solar calendar, the Haab, had 18 months of 20 days each, plus a few extra days at the end. How many days did it have in total?
hints: It followed the journey of the Sun, just like our calendar.
The extra days were very few, and the Maya thought they were unlucky.
It’s the same number of days as a normal year.
questions.description: The Maya had no cell phones, but they never forgot a birthday.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya also had a sacred calendar, the Tzolkin, of 260 days, and they used it together with the Haab.

questions.question: Cacahuates japoneses (“Japanese peanuts”) were invented in Mexico City. Why are they called “Japanese”?
questions.answer: Their inventor was a Japanese immigrant
wrong_answers: A Japanese emperor once tasted them
A Tokyo chef used to sell them
hints: Their inventor arrived in Mexico before World War II.
He started out selling them at the La Merced market.
His last name was Nakatani, and he founded the Nipón brand.
questions.description: A snack with a passport from one side of the world and a birth certificate from the other.
questions.fun_fact: Yoshigei Nakatani based the crunchy coating on a snack from his homeland, yet in Japan almost nobody knows “Japanese” peanuts.

questions.question: In which city is El Trompo, the interactive science and technology museum?
hints: The city is in the north of the country.
It sits right on the border with the United States.
It is the largest city in Baja California.
questions.description: A museum where not touching anything is against the rules.
questions.fun_fact: El Trompo in Tijuana opened in 2008, and its name honors the traditional Mexican spinning top.

questions.question: It's round, made of peanuts, crumbles very easily, and its wrapper has a red rose on it. Which candy is it?
hints: You can buy it at any tiendita, and it falls out of piñatas.
It's a Mexican childhood classic, and each one comes wrapped in cellophane.
Its most famous brand is De la Rosa, from Guadalajara.
questions.description: At the tiendita on the corner, there are always more cravings than coins in your pocket.
questions.fun_fact: There's a famous trick for opening a mazapán without breaking it: squeeze it a little before you take off the wrapper.

questions.question: Students at UPAEP in Puebla built it with NASA's help; it flew on a SpaceX rocket in 2019 and was released from the International Space Station. Which satellite was it?
hints: It's a tiny satellite, the kind called a CubeSat.
It was the first Mexican satellite launched into space from the International Space Station.
Its name plays on the people who founded Tenochtitlan and the word “technology.”
questions.description: Some college students' homework that ended up being turned in from orbit.
questions.fun_fact: AztechSat-1 is about 10 centimeters (4 inches) on each side and weighs just over 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds).

questions.question: You're on the beach in Acapulco watching the sunset. Cancún is to the Caribbean Sea as Acapulco is to the…
hints: Acapulco is on Mexico's west coast.
It's the same water that reaches Puerto Vallarta and Mazatlán.
It's the largest ocean in the world.
questions.description: A bathtub so big that even the most show-off whale can't fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pacific Ocean is so big that all the continents together would fit inside it.

questions.question: Look at the state highlighted on the map: aguachile, raw shrimp soaked in lime juice and chili, comes from here. Which state is it?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
It's famous for its banda music with the tambora drum.
The port of Mazatlán is there.
questions.description: A dish that gets “cooked” with no stove, no oven and not a single match.
questions.fun_fact: The original aguachile is thought to have had no shrimp at all, just dried meat with water and chiltepín chili.

questions.question: You're in Papantla watching the voladores: four men spin down upside down, and each one makes 13 turns. How many turns is that in total?
hints: You need to multiply.
There are four voladores, and each one makes the same number of turns.
It's the same as 4 × 13.
questions.description: A dance that needs no dance floor, just a tall pole and nerves of steel.
questions.fun_fact: The 52 turns stand for the 52 years of one cycle of the Mesoamerican calendar.

questions.question: Cuernavaca is “the City of Eternal Spring.” Roughly how high above sea level is it?
hints: It's not on the coast.
Its mild climate comes from sitting in a valley between mountains, south of Mexico City.
It's lower than Mexico City, which is at about 2,240 m (7,350 ft), but still far above the sea.
questions.description: A city where the jacket and the swimsuit fight over space in your suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its mild weather all year, both Hernán Cortés and Emperor Maximilian had vacation homes in Cuernavaca.

questions.question: What is the name of the garden that Adam and Eve were sent out of?
hints: It is also called paradise on Earth.
The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil grew there.
It starts with E.
questions.description: The only garden you get thrown out of for eating the fruit.
questions.fun_fact: According to the story, God placed cherubim with a flaming sword at the garden's entrance so no one could ever get back in.

questions.question: It's a seed with a thin red skin, coated in chile powder and sold in little bags at the corner store. What is this snack called?
hints: People eat it a lot at the movies, at the stadium and with lime.
The seed inside is also turned into a spread for bread.
Unlike the Japanese-style ones, it has no flour crust.
questions.description: A snack so spicy that even the bag asks for a glass of water.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico peanuts are called cacahuates, from the Nahuatl word tlalcacáhuatl, “cacao of the earth.”

questions.question: My name comes from Arabic and means “date of India.” In Mexico I'm drunk as a brown agua fresca and coated in chili in candies. What am I?
hints: My flavor is sweet and sour.
I grow in hard-shelled pods.
My pulp is brown and sticky, with shiny seeds.
questions.description: A fruit with an Arabic passport and a chili-covered Mexican soul.
questions.fun_fact: Tamarind is native to Africa, but it has been part of Mexican food since colonial times.

questions.question: You're in Tlaxcala, and camadas of huehues dance through the streets in wooden masks with glass eyes and feathered hats. What time of year is it?
hints: It's a movable feast: it falls on a different date every year.
It's celebrated at the end of winter, before a season of fasting.
It ends just before Ash Wednesday.
questions.description: Very elegant gentlemen who haven't aged a day… because their faces are made of wood.
questions.fun_fact: The huehue masks have light skin and beards to make fun of the old Spanish hacienda owners.

questions.question: Every May in Zitlala, Guerrero, men in tiger masks face off in ritual fights. It's a very old custom. According to tradition, why do they do it?
questions.answer: To ask for rain for the milpas
wrong_answers: To celebrate the end of the harvest
To remember a battle against the Spanish
hints: May comes right before planting season starts.
It has to do with the sky and the fields.
The farmers hope water will soon fall from the sky.
questions.description: An open-air gym where everyone is dressed up as a giant cat.
questions.fun_fact: Zitlala's tiger masks are made of hardened leather and sometimes have whiskers made of real bristles.

questions.question: I arrive at the party dressed like a princess, turn a very special age and open the dancing with a waltz. Who am I?
hints: The party usually has a big hall, a cake and lots of family.
Many girls in Mexico dream of this party for years.
I'm not a little girl anymore: I'm turning fifteen.
questions.description: A party where one person wears more dress than all the guests put together.
questions.fun_fact: At many XV años parties, the birthday girl is given her “last doll” as a farewell to childhood.

questions.question: In Saltillo, Chihuahua and other northern cities, hundreds of matachines groups dance each year at their biggest fiesta. On what date is it?
hints: It's a religious holiday, not a patriotic one.
It's the day of Mexico's most beloved Virgin.
Many groups dance in front of the Basilica in Mexico City.
questions.description: Dancers so eager you can hear their rattles from the next block over.
questions.fun_fact: The matachines dance for the Virgin of Guadalupe wearing headdresses and colorful fringed costumes, and shaking rattles.

questions.question: These dancers are part of a January fiesta listed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Which state are they from?
hints: It's a state in southeastern Mexico.
They're called parachicos and wear wooden masks and carry rattles.
Its capital is Tuxtla Gutiérrez.
questions.description: Dancers with wigs so fluffy they look fresh out of the dryer.
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO added the Fiesta Grande of January in Chiapa de Corzo to its list in 2010.

questions.question: Look at this gato (tic-tac-toe) board. How many squares does it have for your X's and O's?
hints: Count the little squares slowly.
It has three rows.
Each row has three squares: 3 + 3 + 3.
questions.description: In Mexico this X and O game is called “gato”, but no cat ever gets hurt.
questions.fun_fact: If neither player ever makes a mistake, a game of gato always ends in a tie.

questions.question: In which decade were the ejes viales built, the big avenues that cross Mexico City from side to side?
hints: It was before the Metrobús existed.
They were built under city regent Carlos Hank González.
They opened in 1979, while José López Portillo was president.
questions.description: Streets numbered like a grocery list: Eje 1, Eje 2, Eje 3… and the traffic is just as bad.
questions.fun_fact: To open the ejes viales, thousands of houses and trees were torn down in a very short time.

questions.question: The ADO bus line started in 1939, running between the capital, Puebla and Veracruz. Which of these cities does it NOT reach?
hints: ADO focuses on one part of the country.
Its initials stand for Autobuses de Oriente (Eastern Buses).
The answer is on the northwest border, far from the Gulf and the Caribbean.
questions.description: Reclining seats, a movie from the nineties and arctic air conditioning: a long-distance bus trip.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexican group that owns ADO also bought Avanza, a bus company in Spain.

questions.question: It carries lots of seated people, has a driver and stops at corners to let people on. In Mexico they call it a camión. What is it?
hints: It travels on the street, not on rails or through the air.
It has a bell you ring to ask to get off.
In other Spanish-speaking countries it's called a «colectivo» or a «guagua».
questions.description: Miss it and you'll get to school late and in a big hurry.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, «camión» can mean a passenger bus or a cargo truck; it all depends on the conversation.

questions.question: I'm a small orange fruit with a pit, and a Mexico City Metro station where three lines cross is named after me. What am I?
hints: My skin is soft, almost velvety.
I look like a durazno (peach), only smaller.
Lines 2, 8 and 9 cross at that station.
questions.description: A Metro station that sounds like one of Grandma's desserts.
questions.fun_fact: The Chabacano station's icon is that very fruit, so anyone can recognize it without reading.

questions.question: I was born in Tijuana, hosted “Atínale al precio” and in 2000 launched “¿Quién quiere ser millonario?” on Televisa. Who am I?
hints: He was one of Televisa's best-known game show hosts around 2000.
Years later he became a motivational speaker and a vegan activist.
His first names are the Spanish form of the Roman general who loved Cleopatra.
questions.description: A man who made you sweat more than a final exam, but with a prize at the end.
questions.fun_fact: On the show, players could use lifelines like the 50:50, phone a friend and ask the audience.

questions.question: Which of these newscasts was NOT on Televisa?
hints: Three of them aired on the Televisa channel known today as Las Estrellas.
The one you want belongs to the rival network, the one based in Ajusco.
Javier Alatorre has hosted it for many years.
questions.description: News shows wear team jerseys too, and one of these plays for the other side.
questions.fun_fact: Jacobo Zabludovsky's “24 Horas” was on the air at Televisa for about 28 years, from 1970 to 1998.

questions.question: The boy who always says sorry with “fue sin querer queriendo” has a favorite hiding place in the vecindad. What is it?
hints: It's from a Chespirito show.
It's round and used to hold things like water or wine.
It's made of wood and has metal hoops.
questions.description: When you break something, it always pays to have a good hiding place.
questions.fun_fact: Many people think El Chavo lives in the barrel, but he actually lives in apartment number 8 of the vecindad.

questions.question: It's Imagen Televisión's morning magazine show, on the air since 2016. What is it called?
hints: Imagen Televisión started broadcasting as a national network in 2016.
Two of the other options are shows on Spanish-language networks in the United States.
Its Spanish name describes what happens in the sky at dawn.
questions.description: For people who eat chilaquiles for breakfast with a side of gossip and horoscopes.
questions.fun_fact: Imagen Televisión was Mexico's first new national free-to-air network in more than 20 years.

questions.question: A dad in San Luis Potosí invited “everyone” by video to his daughter Rubí’s quinceañera, and thousands came. What year was it?
hints: It was back when Facebook videos went viral within hours.
The party was in December, just after Christmas.
It was the same year Donald Trump won his first presidential election.
questions.description: A party with more guests than a ranch wedding… and the whole internet saying it would come.
questions.fun_fact: Rubí’s party, in the village of La Joya, even had a horse race with a cash prize for the winner.

questions.question: Which of these singers has NEVER been a coach on “La Voz México”?
hints: One of the others was a coach from the very first season, in 2011.
The one you want hardly ever gives interviews or goes on TV shows.
His nickname is “el Sol de México”.
questions.description: Four spinning chairs, lots of drama and a red button everyone wants to press.
questions.fun_fact: In the first season of “La Voz México”, in 2011, the coaches were Alejandro Sanz, Lucero, Aleks Syntek and Espinoza Paz.

questions.question: This public TV channel belongs to the Instituto Politécnico Nacional and first went on the air in 1959. Which is it?
hints: It's known for its documentaries and cultural shows.
Its kids' programming block is named after the channel.
Its number is the same as the number of players a soccer team has on the field.
questions.description: A channel that came out of school… and never stopped studying.
questions.fun_fact: Canal Once was the first educational TV channel in Latin America.

questions.question: You're watching Paty Chapoy host “Ventaneando” on TV Azteca. In what year did the show start?
hints: It started a few years after TV Azteca was born.
It started before the year 2000.
It started two years after the World Cup in the United States.
questions.description: This afternoon gossip show is older than many of the celebrities it talks about.
questions.fun_fact: “Ventaneando” is one of the longest-running entertainment news shows on Mexican TV.

questions.question: Samurai is to Japan as… is to the army of ancient Rome.
hints: He was a foot soldier.
In Asterix, Obelix knocks them over by the dozen.
His name comes from the big unit of the Roman army: the legion.
questions.description: Sandals, a helmet and a 30-kilometer (19-mile) walk every day: the least relaxing vacation plan in history.
questions.fun_fact: A legionary carried about 30 kg (66 lb) of gear on his back, including a shovel for digging the camp every night.

questions.question: I started making people laugh on the radio, starred in “No manches Frida” and acted in “Pokémon Detective Pikachu.” Who am I?
hints: I'm a comedian, host, singer and actor from northern Mexico.
In “No manches Frida,” I play a thief who poses as a teacher.
My last name is Mexican slang for a short person.
questions.description: A guy who gets laughs on the radio and on the big screen… and even in Hollywood.
questions.fun_fact: “No manches Frida” (2016) was one of the highest-grossing Mexican films ever.

questions.question: What is the name of TV Azteca's morning variety show?
hints: Every morning it goes head to head with Televisa's show.
Its name invites you to be happy.
Its name starts with a Spanish verb used to call someone over: “¡ven!”.
questions.description: Dancing, cooking and gossip before you finish your coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican morning shows often run for several hours and mix cooking, exercise, music, contests and showbiz news.

questions.question: I owe 14 months' rent, I wear a cap and a black T-shirt, and Doña Florinda slaps me. Who am I?
hints: I live in El Chavo del Ocho's vecindad.
I always hide when the landlord comes to collect the rent.
I have a freckled daughter with two pigtails.
questions.description: A vecindad where gossip runs faster than the water at the washtub.
questions.fun_fact: Don Ramón was played by Ramón Valdés, and the character has the same first name as the actor.

questions.question: It has run in Mexico since 1997, stays on TV for more than a full day and raises money for the CRIT centers. What is it?
hints: At the end, the total amount raised is shown on screen.
The CRIT centers care for children with disabilities.
Its name joins “tele” with the end of “marathon.”
questions.description: That moment when you smash your piggy bank and give it all to a good cause.
questions.fun_fact: The idea came from Chile, where Don Francisco organized the first Latin American Teletón in 1978.

questions.question: Complete: the word “basilica” comes from the Greek basiliké, meaning “the … hall.”
hints: In Rome, a basilica wasn't a temple: people held trials and did business there.
The Greek word “basileús” has to do with whoever ruled.
Basileús meant “king.”
questions.description: Today it's a fancy church, but it started its career as a courthouse and a shopping mall.
questions.fun_fact: The first Christians copied the shape of Roman basilicas for their churches because they were huge halls that could hold lots of people.

questions.question: Palatine, Aventine and Capitoline are three of them, and they give Rome its nickname. What are they?
hints: Rome's nickname comes with the number seven.
Legend says Romulus founded the city on the Palatine.
From the top of each one, you can see the whole city.
questions.description: Rome has more nicknames than Grandma has for you when she can't remember your name.
questions.fun_fact: The word “palace” comes from the Palatine Hill, where the Roman emperors lived.

questions.question: I'm the pilum, the Roman legionary's javelin, and my iron tip bent when it hit something. What was that for?
questions.answer: So it couldn't be thrown back
wrong_answers: So it was lighter to carry
So it could hook walls for climbing
So it wouldn't rust in the rain
hints: Think about what the enemy would do after it landed.
A bent javelin doesn't fly straight.
The enemy couldn't reuse it against the Romans.
questions.description: A weapon designed to break on purpose, like an umbrella on a windy day.
questions.fun_fact: If a pilum stuck in a shield, the shield became so heavy and awkward that many warriors chose to drop it.

questions.question: When graphite was found in England in the 1500s, people thought it was a metal. Which metal, whose name we still use for a pencil's core?
hints: It's a gray, soft and very heavy metal.
That's why people say a pencil tip isn't poisonous: it never had this metal in it.
When your pencil breaks, people say you snapped this metal.
questions.description: A lie so old you've even written with it in your notebook.
questions.fun_fact: Shepherds in Borrowdale used that graphite to mark their sheep long before anyone thought of writing with it.

questions.question: I'm a crunchy, orange, triangle-shaped snack, born at a Disneyland restaurant so leftovers wouldn't go to waste. What am I made of?
hints: My name comes from a Spanish word meaning “little golden ones.”
The restaurant had leftover Mexican tortillas.
It's the same ingredient as in arepas and popcorn.
questions.description: Leftovers that skipped the trash can and went straight to fame.
questions.fun_fact: According to the most popular story, the Casa de Fritos restaurant at Disneyland cut stale tortillas into triangles and fried them instead of throwing them away.

questions.question: This dark blue dye once came from a plant, and today it colors almost all jeans. What is it called?
hints: This dye was so valuable that people called it “blue gold”, and ships carried it across oceans.
The plant's leaves are green: the blue only shows up after you soak them and let the air get to them.
In the rainbow, it sits between blue and violet.
questions.description: A color with a name so fancy it sounds royal, yet it lives in your pants.
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton added this color to the rainbow partly because he wanted seven colors, like the seven notes of the musical scale.

questions.question: The putty that bounces, stretches and copies pictures from the newspaper was an accident in the search for fake rubber. In which decade?
hints: Its inventor worked in the lab of a big US electric company.
Only a few years passed between its discovery and its sale as a toy.
Rubber was scarce because of the war, and in 1950 it went on sale in plastic eggs.
questions.description: A failed experiment that bounces, stretches and never did its job, but kept millions of people busy.
questions.fun_fact: No engineer found a serious use for it, until a salesman packed it in plastic eggs and turned it into a toy.

questions.question: Warfarin, a medicine against blood clots, was discovered by studying this moldy plant that cattle ate. What is it?
hints: Its mold made a substance that kept the blood from clotting.
The research was done at the University of Wisconsin in the 1930s and 1940s.
It is also called melilot.
questions.description: From the cows' field to Grandpa's nightstand: a very unusual journey.
questions.fun_fact: Warfarin was first sold as rat poison, and its name comes from WARF, the University of Wisconsin's research foundation.

questions.question: Which actor took over from Pierce Brosnan as 007 and began by playing poker at a casino in Montenegro?
hints: His first Bond film was “Casino Royale” in 2006.
He is English and was the sixth actor to play Bond in the official series.
He played Bond in five films; the last one was “No Time to Die” in 2021.
questions.description: A spy whose first day on the job starts with a game of cards.
questions.fun_fact: The “Montenegro” scenes in “Casino Royale” were actually filmed in Karlovy Vary, in the Czech Republic.

questions.question: I'm British, I work for the secret service, and I order my vodka martini “shaken, not stirred.” Who am I?
hints: I'm a spy, not a detective.
I work for MI6, and my boss is called M.
My agent number is 007.
questions.description: A very stylish gentleman who is extremely fussy about how his drink is served.
questions.fun_fact: In Ian Fleming's novels, Bond invents his own cocktail and names it the “Vesper,” after a Bond girl.

questions.question: Which of these actresses has NOT played Miss Moneypenny in the James Bond films?
hints: One of them had an even more important job at MI6.
That actress played Bond's boss in several films.
She played M from “GoldenEye” to “Skyfall”.
questions.description: Cinema's most famous secretary, still waiting decades later for a date with 007.
questions.fun_fact: Lois Maxwell played Moneypenny in 14 films, starting with “Dr. No” in 1962.

questions.question: In “You Only Live Twice,” what fish did Blofeld keep in the pool of his secret lair inside a volcano?
hints: They are small fish, not giants.
Blofeld punishes helpers who fail him by sending them into the pool.
They are famous for their sharp teeth and for feeding in groups.
questions.description: A pet no villain should keep in the living room, and yet every one of them wants some.
questions.fun_fact: Red-bellied piranhas make barking-like noises when they are caught.

questions.question: Which actor was the first to drive this car in a James Bond movie?
hints: It's a British sports car that became one of the most famous cars in movie history.
The movie was “Goldfinger,” from 1964.
He was the first actor to play 007 on the big screen.
questions.description: A car with more tricks up its sleeve than a magician at a kids' birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: The DB5 in “Goldfinger” had an ejector seat, machine guns, and revolving license plates.

questions.question: The famous ice rink at Rockefeller Center in New York first opened on Christmas Day of which year?
hints: The rink is older than TV sets in most homes.
Your great-grandparents could already have skated there.
It was a few years before World War II.
questions.description: Skating in New York: the only place where you fall down surrounded by skyscrapers.
questions.fun_fact: The giant Christmas tree next to the rink has been an official tradition since 1933.

questions.question: This treasure of 81 gold vessels and pieces of jewelry came to light near Eberswalde in 1913. Who found it?
questions.answer: Construction workers digging a building pit
hints: Nobody had been looking for it; it was pure chance.
The finders were busy building a house.
Shovels, a foundation and the grounds of a brass works.
questions.description: Gold that played hide-and-seek for almost 3,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Since the end of the Second World War the original treasure has been in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow; Berlin only shows copies.

questions.question: You see photos of jeans hanging over a stair railing and of Concorde jets in the sky. Which German photographer won the Turner Prize in 2000?
hints: He comes from Remscheid in the Bergisches Land region.
In 2016 he designed posters against Brexit.
He has the same first name as Mozart.
questions.description: Nobody had to smile for these photos, not even the laundry.
questions.fun_fact: Tillmans was the first photographer ever to win Britain's Turner Prize.

questions.question: I was Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, and in 1710 I set up Europe's first porcelain factory in Meissen's Albrechtsburg. Who am I?
hints: In Dresden, I also had the splendid Zwinger palace built.
I called my passion for collecting porcelain a disease myself.
My nickname claims I could bend horseshoes with my bare hands.
questions.description: White gold, blue swords and a collector who never had enough.
questions.fun_fact: The porcelain factory stayed in the Albrechtsburg for over 150 years, until it moved to a new building in 1863.

questions.question: I'm a chair of bent steel tubing with no back legs, yet I don't tip over and I gently bounce. What am I called?
hints: The Dutchman Mart Stam built the first one of me in 1926.
Mies van der Rohe and Marcel Breuer also designed famous versions of me.
My name comes from the building term for a beam held up at only one end.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that makes every visit to the waiting room a little sportier.
questions.fun_fact: There was later a court case over who invented this chair, and Mart Stam won.

questions.question: I was an actor and playwright who wanted to copy my plays cheaply, so around 1796 in Munich I invented printing from limestone. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Prague but worked mostly in Munich.
My method relies on the fact that grease and water repel each other.
My invention is called lithography, meaning “stone writing.”
questions.description: When money is tight, you just have to become an inventor.
questions.fun_fact: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s famous Paris posters were also made with Senefelder’s stone printing.

questions.question: I painted glowing poppies and stormy seas, lived in Seebüll on the Danish border and named myself after my home village. Who am I?
hints: For a while I belonged to the Dresden artists' group “Brücke”.
I dropped my birth surname, Hansen, in 1902.
Siegfried Lenz's novel “The German Lesson” tells of a painter who recalls me.
questions.description: A painter who turned colors up as loud as other people turn up their radio.
questions.fun_fact: The painter laid out the paths of his garden in Seebüll in the shape of the letters A and E, for Ada and Emil.

questions.question: You switch on a 1924 Bauhaus table lamp: milk-glass globe, glass base, visible metal tube. Who designed it?
hints: He later became famous mainly for everyday glassware.
He also designed the stackable “Kubus” glass storage containers.
Today the lamp is usually called by his surname.
questions.description: A lamp that gave even designers a bright idea.
questions.fun_fact: He designed the lamp with Carl Jakob Jucker in the metal workshop of the Bauhaus in Weimar.

questions.question: The artist Jonathan Meese, usually seen in a track jacket, with long hair, calls for a form of rule in his manifestos and performances. Which one?
hints: He was once meant to stage Wagner's “Parsifal” in Bayreuth.
In his version nobody gets elected; a single power decides everything.
This form of rule is the opposite of democracy and has no king.
questions.description: Art that makes an announcement, and in capital letters.
questions.fun_fact: Meese often appeared with his mother Brigitte, who acted in his performances and films.

questions.question: They called her “Franzi”: at 14 she won four Olympic medals, and in 2002 in Berlin she set a 200 m world record. In which stroke?
hints: It's the fastest of the four swimming styles.
Almost everyone swims front crawl in it.
In this event, you're actually allowed to swim any way you like.
questions.description: As a teenager, this woman collected more medals than most people collect bottle caps.
questions.fun_fact: Franziska van Almsick won many Olympic medals but never gold, and still became one of Germany's biggest sports stars.

questions.question: “Gerd Müller is to ‘the Bomber’ as swimmer Michael Groß is to the …” Which animal?
hints: The nickname came from his arms: a span of over 2 m (6 ft 7 in).
This animal can fly.
This seabird has the largest wings of any bird.
questions.description: Sports nicknames: where parents no longer get a say.
questions.fun_fact: Michael Groß won three Olympic gold medals in total, in 1984 and 1988.

questions.question: He's from Heppenheim, won 53 races and in 2010 became the youngest Formula 1 world champion ever. Which team was he driving for then?
hints: This is Sebastian Vettel.
He only moved to Ferrari later.
The team belongs to a company that sells energy drinks.
questions.description: Some people finish college at 23; others conquer the world.
questions.fun_fact: Vettel won four world titles in a row with Red Bull, from 2010 to 2013.

questions.question: “I'm awarded anew every day. Whoever wears me at the end in Paris has won it all; in 1997, that was Jan Ullrich.” What am I?
hints: I belong to the Tour de France.
I show who has needed the least time overall.
My color is that of bananas and lemons.
questions.description: A piece of clothing men pedal their legs off for three weeks to get.
questions.fun_fact: The jersey is yellow because the newspaper “L'Auto”, which founded the Tour, was printed on yellow paper.

questions.question: All four push at the start, jump in within seconds and race down at over 140 km/h (87 mph). What are the positions on a four-person bobsled?
questions.answer: A pilot, two pushers and a brakeman
wrong_answers: A pilot, one pusher and two brakemen
Two pilots, one pusher and a brakeman
A pilot, three pushers and no brakeman
hints: Only one of the four steers.
The last one to jump in sits at the very back.
Someone has to stop the sled after the finish line.
questions.description: Four people squeezed into a carbon-fiber bullet, and they volunteered for it.
questions.fun_fact: A four-person bobsled with its crew can weigh up to 630 kg (about 1,390 lb).

questions.question: “My real name was Gustav, I boxed for Berlin in the 1950s and became European champion. All of Germany called me by a name for a little kid.” Who am I?
hints: I was the big boxing star of Germany's postwar boom years (the “Wirtschaftswunder”).
In 1962, I fought for the world title in Berlin.
My nickname is an old German word for “little boy.”
questions.description: A man who threw punches in the ring and still ended up with a cute pet name.
questions.fun_fact: In 1962, Scholz fought Harold Johnson for the world title in front of a huge crowd in Berlin, but lost on points.

questions.question: In 1988, Carl-Uwe “Charly” Steeb beat Mats Wilander in the final in Gothenburg. Which title did this help Germany win for the first time?
hints: It is a men's team competition.
Boris Becker played on the same team.
The competition is named after an American and is more than 100 years old.
questions.description: A weekend in Sweden that still warms the hearts of German tennis fans.
questions.fun_fact: Steeb beat Wilander, then the world number one, in a five-set thriller.

questions.question: Markus Rehm long-jumps with a sports prosthesis like this one. What material is the spring blade made of?
hints: The material is very light yet extremely strong.
It's also used in racing bikes and Formula 1 cars.
It's made of fibers of the chemical element with the symbol C.
questions.description: A leg with the bounce of a trampoline, only more elegant.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, Markus Rehm even became German long jump champion, competing against jumpers without disabilities.

review.feedback: Source: this asks the same fact as approved q-2558 (what running-blade prostheses are made of → carbon fiber). Only the Markus Rehm framing is different, so whichever one players see first gives away the other. The translation itself is accurate and reads naturally. The source question needs a different angle on Rehm, for example his 2014 German long jump title or his Paralympic event, or it should be dropped.

questions.question: Staedtler was founded in Nuremberg in 1835, and its Noris pencil has yellow and black stripes. What is the core of a pencil made of?
hints: Even though people call it “lead”, there's no metal in it at all.
One ingredient is also used for flower pots and mugs.
A form of carbon, mixed with a kind of earth that is fired.
questions.description: The pencil case classic that gets a little shorter every time you sharpen it.
questions.fun_fact: Pencils never contained lead: people once simply mistook graphite for a lead ore.

questions.question: You're spooning your way through a cup of Monte by Zott. Which two layers are inside?
hints: It's a milk dessert that lots of kids love as a snack.
“Monte” is the Italian word for “mountain”.
A bit like a famous bread spread, mixed with milk.
questions.description: A cup from the fridge aisle that brothers and sisters love to fight over.
questions.fun_fact: The Zott dairy is based in Mertingen, in Bavaria.

questions.question: You take a Nimm2 candy. According to its ads for decades, what good stuff is supposed to be inside?
hints: It's also found in fruit.
Oranges are famous for it.
They have letters like A, C or E.
questions.description: Candy with a reputation for being almost sensible.
questions.fun_fact: Nimm2 belongs to Storck, the maker of Werther's Original and Toffifee.

questions.question: Brandt saw the Berlin Wall go up as mayor of Berlin. How many years later did he say “Now what belongs together will grow together”?
hints: The Wall was built in the early 1960s.
The Wall went up in 1961.
The Wall came down in 1989.
questions.description: Today you get math and history in one go.
questions.fun_fact: In 1961, the year the Wall went up, Willy Brandt also ran for chancellor for the SPD for the first time.

questions.question: With the first vote, you choose a candidate in your own constituency. How many constituencies are there in a Bundestag election?
hints: There are far more of them than federal states.
Each constituency has roughly 250,000 to 300,000 people.
Just under 300.
questions.description: Germany cut into pieces, but in a very democratic way.
questions.fun_fact: Constituency number 1 is in the far north: Flensburg – Schleswig.

questions.question: Before federal elections, it's a must: the TV debate. The first one was between Gerhard Schröder and Edmund Stoiber. In which year?
hints: Schröder was already chancellor at the time.
After this election, Schröder stayed in office.
It was the first year people paid with euro bills.
questions.description: Two podiums, two candidates and a whole country on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: In 2002 there were actually two TV debates between Schröder and Stoiber.

questions.question: I'm Lillehammer: I hosted the 1994 Winter Olympics and the 2016 Winter Youth Olympics. Which country am I in?
hints: I'm in Scandinavia.
My country has won more gold medals at the Winter Games than any other.
My capital is Oslo.
questions.description: A tiny town that threw a giant party on the snow.
questions.fun_fact: The mascots of Lillehammer 1994 were two children, Håkon and Kristin: the first Olympic mascots in human form.

questions.question: Which statement about the second vote (Zweitstimme) in a German federal election is NOT true?
questions.answer: You may split it between two parties
wrong_answers: It is on the right side of the ballot
With it, you vote for a party
It decides how the seats are shared out
hints: With the second vote, you choose a party, not a person.
Exactly one cross is allowed in each column of the ballot.
Two crosses in the right-hand column make the vote invalid.
questions.description: The second choice that nobody should treat as second best.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it is called the “second vote”, it matters more than the first vote for how seats in the Bundestag are shared out.

questions.question: I'm a boy from Neustadt and often visit the zoo. My best friend is an elephant who can talk. Who am I?
hints: I'm in lots of audio drama cassettes.
Karla Kolumna and zoo director Tierlieb know me well.
My name reads the same forwards and backwards.
questions.description: Every trunk-wearer needs a best friend with just one nose.
questions.fun_fact: Elfie Donnelly created Benjamin Blümchen in 1977, and the same author also created Bibi Blocksberg.

questions.question: The cassette runs out in the middle of the audio play, and you have to flip it over. How many sides does a cassette have for playing?
hints: There's only one way to flip it over.
As many sides as a sheet of paper.
They're called side A and side B.
questions.description: A little plastic box full of stories, always in danger of turning into tape spaghetti.
questions.fun_fact: You could wind a cassette's tape back in with a pencil, no electricity needed.

questions.question: In “Willi wills wissen”, Willi Weitzel asked his way through farms, fire stations and factories. In which decade did the show start?
hints: The show is younger than “Löwenzahn”.
Back then many people already had a cell phone, but not yet a smartphone.
It started shortly after the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: Asking questions is free, except maybe for a few years of airtime.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009 Willi even made it to the movie theater, with “Willi und die Wunder dieser Welt”.

questions.question: You turn on the WDR show with Shary and Ralph. How does its title “Wissen macht …” end?
hints: The word is very short.
It's the sound you make when a light bulb goes on in your head.
It's an exclamation with only two letters.
questions.description: A show that often leaves your mouth hanging open.
questions.fun_fact: Ralph Caspers also explains things in the “Sachgeschichten” on “Die Sendung mit der Maus”.

questions.question: Before Tobi checked out everything, the BR kids' series started with a different checker. What was his name?
hints: He was already checking things out before 2013.
He also visited experts to find out how things work.
His name is spelled like the English word in “Yes, we ___!”.
questions.description: A job where you get to try out every other job.
questions.fun_fact: Checker Can's full name is Can Mansuroğlu.

questions.question: Until 2021, half of Super RTL belonged to a US company; then RTL took over all of it. Which company was the partner?
hints: The company runs theme parks on several continents.
Its logo shows a castle.
It created Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck.
questions.description: A kids' channel with two parents who split up at some point.
questions.fun_fact: Super RTL went on the air in 1995.

questions.question: I live in the beehive, I'm Maja's best friend, and what I love most is eating and sleeping. Who am I?
hints: I'm quite round and easygoing.
Adventures are often too much work for me.
My name starts with W.
questions.description: Over in the poppy meadow, something buzzes, crawls or hops all day long, so nobody ever gets bored.
questions.fun_fact: The cartoon series “Die Biene Maja” (Maya the Bee) was made in Japan in the 1970s, as a co-production with the German TV channel ZDF.

questions.question: This wooden frame with a ball on top stands on the beach in Cuxhaven. What was it built for?
questions.answer: As a navigation mark for ships
wrong_answers: As a lookout tower for swimmers
As a rack for drying fishing nets
As a mast for weather balloons
hints: You can see it especially well from the water.
Cuxhaven lies where the Elbe flows into the North Sea.
A lighthouse has a similar job, just with light.
questions.description: It has stood on the beach forever and still never goes for a swim.
questions.fun_fact: The Elbe officially ends at the Kugelbake, and the North Sea begins beyond it.

questions.question: You take a trip to St. Pauli in Hamburg. What will you NOT find there?
hints: One of them is in a completely different city.
A club in red and white plays there.
It stands in Munich and glows in bright colors at night.
questions.description: A Hamburg neighborhood that is louder at night than during the day.
questions.fun_fact: FC St. Pauli's stadium is called Millerntor, after one of Hamburg's old city gates.

questions.question: Since when has the Schwebebahn (suspended railway) run above the Wupper River through Wuppertal?
hints: Back then, many horse-drawn carriages still used the streets.
Kaiser Wilhelm II took a test ride himself.
It is older than the Wright brothers' first powered flight.
questions.description: A train that never keeps its feet on the ground.
questions.fun_fact: In 1950, Tuffi the circus elephant jumped out of a Schwebebahn carriage into the Wupper and came out almost unhurt.

questions.question: You're visiting the Autostadt in Wolfsburg, where the Volkswagen Group shows off its brands. Which brand is NOT one of them?
hints: The brand you're looking for is a rival of VW.
It doesn't belong to another group; it runs its own, which also owns Mini and Rolls-Royce.
Its logo is blue and white, and its headquarters are in Munich.
questions.description: A city where even the parking spots are museum pieces.
questions.fun_fact: Wolfsburg was founded in 1938 for the VW factory and only got its current name in 1945.

questions.question: I'm hard, brown and spicy, you break me into pieces, and I come from Charlemagne's city. What am I?
hints: People eat me mostly around Christmas.
I'm a kind of Lebkuchen.
My name sounds almost like the English word “print.”
questions.description: A cookie that keeps dentists nicely in business.
questions.fun_fact: Printen used to be pressed into wooden molds, which is where the name comes from: it means “imprint.”

questions.question: An internet joke from 1994 claims that a city in East Westphalia doesn't exist at all. What is this joke called?
hints: The joke started in an early internet discussion forum.
In 2019, the city offered 1 million euros to anyone who could prove it doesn't exist.
The city's name ends in “-feld”.
questions.description: Solve this one, and you'll never trust a map again.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody claimed the million, and in 2019 the city solemnly declared that it does exist after all.

questions.question: On this covered walkway you can walk a long way around the old town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber. What was it built for?
hints: In the Middle Ages, towns were often in danger.
Through the narrow openings, you could peek outside.
The walkway runs along the top of the town wall.
questions.description: A town where somebody forgot to come and pick up the Middle Ages.
questions.fun_fact: Scenes for “Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows” were filmed in Rothenburg.

questions.question: Which region does the saying “Schaffe, schaffe, Häusle baue” come from?
hints: Here, “schaffe” means “to work”.
The ending “-le” is typical of this dialect.
The region is in Baden-Württemberg, around Stuttgart.
questions.description: A life plan in four words: lots of hard work, little free time, a roof of your own.
questions.fun_fact: The saying goes on: “… und net nach de Mädle schaue” (“and don't look at the girls”).

questions.question: Back home in Baden, this athlete was lovingly called “Bobbele”. Who is he?
hints: He comes from Leimen, near Heidelberg.
His sport is played with a racket and a net.
In 1985 he won Wimbledon at the age of 17.
questions.description: A nickname that sounds like a cuddly toy, but came with a serve that packed a punch.
questions.fun_fact: In 1985, at 17, Boris Becker became the youngest men's singles champion in Wimbledon history.

questions.question: Who would you normally NOT call “Schatzi”?
hints: The word is full of affection.
You say it to someone you love very much.
Three of the answers are part of the family.
questions.description: A word you shouldn't use in every situation, unless you're looking for trouble.
questions.fun_fact: “Schatz” (treasure) is one of the most popular pet names in Germany, often made cuter as “Schatzi”.

questions.question: Three of these Berlin words name something to eat. Which one does NOT?
hints: The word you want has to do with thirst.
People like to order it in a Berlin pub.
It's a glass of beer.
questions.description: A Berlin menu with attitude: three things end up on your plate, one doesn't.
questions.fun_fact: In Berlin, a “Molle mit Korn” is a beer with a shot of schnapps on the side.

questions.question: I went deep underground, wore a helmet with a lamp and brought coal up in the Ruhr region. Who was I?
hints: My workplace was called a “Zeche”.
I greeted people with “Glück auf!”.
People also called me “Kumpel”.
questions.description: After work, you looked like you'd done your makeup with barbecue charcoal.
questions.fun_fact: Miners underground had to rely on each other, so “Kumpel” became the German word for a good friend.

questions.question: In Munich, a mother calls: “Bua, kimm her!” Which of these words does NOT mean “boy”, the way “Bua” does?
hints: Three of the words mean the same as “Bua”.
The word you're looking for is Bavarian too.
It's the counterpart of “Bua”.
questions.description: Four words for the kids' room, but one of them walked through the wrong door.
questions.fun_fact: “Steppke” is Berlin slang for a little boy.

questions.question: Some Germans jokingly say “Tschüssikowski” for goodbye. Which country does this surname ending seem to come from?
hints: Surnames with this ending are quite common in Germany too.
Some footballers from a neighboring country have the ending “-owski”.
The country lies east of Germany.
questions.description: A goodbye that put on a disguise and took a surname.
questions.fun_fact: Many families in the Ruhr area have Polish surnames because many miners from Poland once worked there.

questions.question: “Dahoam” means “at home”, and there's even a TV series called “Dahoam is Dahoam”. Which German state does the word come from?
hints: The state is in the south.
People there also say “Servus”.
Its capital is Munich.
questions.description: A word wearing slippers and leaning back on the sofa.
questions.fun_fact: “Dahoam is Dahoam” is set in the made-up village of Lansing and has been on TV since 2007.

questions.question: Max and Moritz, Emil of Lönneberga and Tom Sawyer are full of pranks. What do people in southern Germany fondly call boys like these?
hints: The word sounds a bit cheeky, but it's meant kindly.
In Bavaria and Austria, grandparents often say it with a grin when a child has been up to something.
The first part is the German word for a tiny critter that makes your head itch.
questions.description: They climb trees, swipe apples and always have an excuse ready.
questions.fun_fact: The Bavarian writer Ludwig Thoma even wrote a whole book called “Lausbubengeschichten” (rascal stories).

questions.question: What do the people of Cologne call their own city in the Kölsch dialect?
hints: You can hear all four words in Cologne.
“Kölsch” is the dialect and the beer, and “Köbes” is the waiter.
The word appears in the song “Mer losse d'r Dom en …”.
questions.description: On the Rhine, even the city has a nickname only locals can say properly.
questions.fun_fact: “Klüngel” is the Kölsch word for cronyism: people doing each other favors.

questions.question: “I sit on a Stövchen (tea warmer) to stay hot, and a tea company from Düsseldorf has my German name.” What am I?
hints: In East Frisia, I'm on the table at every tea time.
I have a lid and a spout for pouring.
The tea is poured from me into the cups.
questions.description: This one is about tea, and about a thing that likes to be the center of attention.
questions.fun_fact: In 1949 the company Teekanne developed the double-chamber tea bag, which is now used all over the world.

questions.question: The “Coffee Cantata” (“Schweigt stille, plaudert nicht”) was performed in a Leipzig coffee house. In which decade was it written?
hints: It is the Baroque era.
Its composer was then the cantor of St. Thomas Church in Leipzig.
It was composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.
questions.description: A piece of music about a passion that keeps every office running today.
questions.fun_fact: In the cantata, a father wants to forbid his daughter Lieschen from drinking coffee, but she sings that coffee is “sweeter than a thousand kisses”.

questions.question: In Scotland, it's good luck when a tall, dark-haired man arrives at your home with coal, salt and bread. When must he arrive?
questions.answer: Just after midnight on New Year's
wrong_answers: On the morning of Christmas Day
hints: He has to be the first person to enter the home on that date.
Scots call this celebration “Hogmanay.”
It's when everyone counts down and the calendar starts over.
questions.description: A surprise visitor that nobody in Scotland wants to see arriving empty-handed.
questions.fun_fact: People often say the visitor shouldn't be blond, because that reminded people of the Viking invaders of long ago.

questions.question: Peppermint tea is drunk hot and made from green leaves. How does your mouth often feel afterwards?
hints: The name tastes different from how it sounds.
Lots of chewing gums have the same flavor.
It feels a bit like a fresh breeze in your mouth.
questions.description: Green leaves, hot water and a little surprise for your tongue.
questions.fun_fact: The cool feeling comes from menthol: it tricks the cold sensors in your mouth, even though the tea is hot.

questions.question: In Germany, what is mineral water called when it goes into the bottle with no fizz at all?
hints: It doesn't hiss when you open it.
It doesn't have a single bubble.
The first word also means “quiet” in German.
questions.description: A drink for anyone who hates surprises while drinking.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has more than 500 different mineral waters from many springs.

questions.question: You're holding a steaming mug of Kinderpunsch. In which month do people drink it most?
hints: It's usually cold outside then.
Strings of lights are glowing everywhere.
It's the month of Christmas.
questions.description: A mug that warms you up, smells great and doesn't make you the least bit sleepy.
questions.fun_fact: Kinderpunsch is often made from fruit tea and juice, with no alcohol at all.

questions.question: On Ascension Day you see a group of hikers pulling a Bollerwagen. What is usually inside?
hints: The day is also called Vatertag (Father's Day).
The group wants to take breaks along the way.
Lots of walking makes you thirsty and hungry.
questions.description: A wagon with no engine, but with very important cargo.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Bollerwagen” comes from the rumbling (“bollern”) of its wheels on bumpy paths.

questions.question: In the photo, Sekt is being poured. What is Sekt made from?
hints: The main ingredient comes from plants that grow on hillsides.
Their fruit is picked in the fall, at harvest time.
Sekt is a bubbly relative of what is pressed from grapes along the Moselle.
questions.description: A drink that arrives at the party with a bang.
questions.fun_fact: Germany's Sekt tax was introduced in 1902 to pay for Kaiser Wilhelm's navy, and it still exists today.

questions.question: When clinking glasses in Germany, people often say “Zum Wohl!”. What are they wishing for each other?
hints: It's a friendly wish.
It has to do with health.
You wish the others all the best.
questions.description: A quick clink, a friendly saying, and then everyone takes a sip.
questions.fun_fact: Other languages also wish people good health when clinking glasses, like “Salud” in Spanish or “Santé” in French.

questions.question: Max Schmeling knocked out Joe Louis in round 12 in 1936. In which round was their 1938 rematch over?
hints: This time Joe Louis won.
By then Louis was world champion and badly wanted revenge.
It hardly gets any faster than this.
questions.description: Revenge is sweet, at least for one of the two boxers.
questions.fun_fact: Schmeling and Louis later became close friends, and Schmeling even helped Louis when he was short of money.

questions.question: In 1891 in Hanover, Hermann Bahlsen launched a butter cookie with a toothed edge, named after a famous scholar. What is it called?
hints: The scholar lived in Hanover for a long time.
The cookie has exactly 52 teeth.
The scholar invented an early calculating machine.
questions.description: A treat with more teeth than your mouth.
questions.fun_fact: Bahlsen first spelled the name “Leibniz Cakes”, because English words were considered fancy back then.

questions.question: Before Walther Rathenau became foreign minister in 1922, he ran the company his father Emil had founded. Which one?
hints: The company had to do with electricity.
It started in Berlin in the 1880s, with a license from a famous American inventor.
It later also made washing machines and refrigerators.
questions.description: First the family business, then the Foreign Office: a career path with plenty of power behind it.
questions.fun_fact: Emil Rathenau bought the German rights to Edison's light bulb and built his company on them.

questions.question: You're sitting in St. Lambert's Church in Münster as Bishop Clemens August Graf von Galen openly preaches against the Gestapo. What year is it?
hints: World War II had already begun.
That same year, Germany attacked the Soviet Union.
It was two years after the war began.
questions.description: A bishop with the nickname of a big cat.
questions.fun_fact: For his courage, von Galen was called the “Lion of Münster”, and in 2005 he was beatified.

questions.question: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed emergency decrees without parliament. Who did it give this power to?
hints: This power was used more and more often in the crisis from 1930 on.
This office was elected directly by the people.
From 1925 to 1934, it was held by Paul von Hindenburg.
questions.description: An emergency exit in the constitution that turned out to be a trapdoor.
questions.fun_fact: In 1919, the National Assembly met in Weimar because Berlin was too unsettled.

questions.question: For how many years did the Bauhaus art school exist in Germany?
hints: It was founded after the First World War.
It had to close under pressure from the Nazis.
It lasted about as long as the Weimar Republic.
questions.description: A school that suddenly made chairs, lamps and houses look very plain and boxy.
questions.fun_fact: The Bauhaus moved twice: from Weimar to Dessau, and finally to Berlin.

questions.question: In Stopptanz (freeze dance), everyone dances wildly. When do you suddenly have to stand stock-still?
hints: Listen carefully!
It has to do with the song.
All at once, it goes completely quiet.
questions.description: A dance for anyone who likes turning into a statue without warning.
questions.fun_fact: Anyone who still moves after the stop is usually out, so the winner is whoever is best at freezing.

questions.question: Which game are the children in this photo playing?
hints: You need neither eggs nor a rope for it.
Your legs are stuck inside something.
You can only move forward by jumping.
questions.description: A race where your legs are grounded.
questions.fun_fact: People used to use old burlap potato or coffee sacks for sack races.

questions.question: Why do people in Germany “press their thumbs” for someone?
hints: People often do it before a test or a game.
You can do it for a friend even when they're far away.
You're hoping everything turns out well for the other person.
questions.description: A finger exercise that's meant to help someone else, even though you do nothing at all.
questions.fun_fact: In many other countries, people cross their fingers instead, but in Germany they press their thumbs.

questions.question: After the wedding, everyone walks out of the church, led by children scattering petals. Who follows right behind them?
hints: The spot right behind the petal-scattering children is the place of honor in the procession.
These people stood up front at the altar during the whole ceremony.
They have just said “I do.”
questions.description: The only guests officially allowed to throw things on the floor.
questions.fun_fact: The scattered petals are meant to symbolically prepare a beautiful shared path through life for the couple.

questions.question: One tradition says that if you fold a thousand paper figures like this one, you can make a wish. Which country is it from?
hints: It's a country made up of islands.
There, the crane is a symbol of long life and good luck.
Its flag is white with a red circle.
questions.description: A bird that will never fly, but grants wishes if you're patient.
questions.fun_fact: The crane was said to live a thousand years, so people fold a thousand of them, and the whole set is called “senbazuru.”

questions.question: Where do you NOT take an empty Pfand bottle if you want your deposit back?
hints: You don't get a receipt there.
You'd better not throw anything in there at night or on Sundays.
It often stands outside, with openings for clear, green and brown glass.
questions.description: In Germany, empty bottles have a surprisingly exciting second life.
questions.fun_fact: A reusable glass bottle can be washed and refilled up to about 50 times.

questions.question: People used to lay a trail of paper scraps for me. Today it's often chalk arrows, and a treasure waits at the end. What am I?
hints: You play it outdoors.
You follow signs from one stop to the next.
My name sounds like a dish, but it has nothing to do with food.
questions.description: Ten kids, a mountain of cake and parents who badly need an hour of peace.
questions.fun_fact: The Schnitzeljagd has nothing to do with Wiener Schnitzel: here “Schnitzel” means small scraps of paper.

questions.question: At the end of a children's birthday party there are often small bags of candy called Mitgebsel. Who gets them?
hints: The birthday child already got presents.
You take the bag home with you.
It's a little thank-you for coming.
questions.description: A party that starts with sugar and ends with a bag full of backup supplies.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Mitgebsel” comes from “mitgeben”, to give someone something to take home.

questions.question: What is the thing this breakfast egg is sitting in called?
hints: It sits on the breakfast table.
It keeps the egg nice and upright.
It looks like a tiny goblet.
questions.description: Sunday morning in Germany: the question of the perfect egg splits whole families.
questions.fun_fact: Some people slice the top off their egg with a knife, others tap the shell open with a spoon, and families love to argue about it.

questions.question: What material are these wedding rings made of?
hints: It shines beautifully.
It's a metal.
Pirates look for it in treasure chests.
questions.description: A piece of jewelry you let someone slip onto your finger in front of everyone.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, most married people wear their wedding ring on the right hand, while in many other countries it goes on the left.

questions.question: About how tall is the Würzburg basketball star Dirk Nowitzki?
hints: In basketball, being over 2 meters is nothing special.
He has to duck to get through most doors, but he's no fairy-tale giant.
He is a little taller than 2.10 meters.
questions.description: A man from Würzburg who never has to push to the front at the town festival.
questions.fun_fact: Nowitzki's famous one-legged fadeaway shot was almost impossible to block because of his height (about 7 ft).

questions.question: World Cup in Italy: final in Rome, winning goal by Andreas Brehme, German reunification still three months away. So which team became world champion?
wrong_answers: A joint East and West German team
A team made up only of Berlin players
hints: At the time of this final, there were still two German states.
East Germany hadn't even qualified for the World Cup.
It was the team that had already won the World Cup in 1954 and 1974.
questions.description: A summer when the map didn't quite match the national anthem yet.
questions.fun_fact: After the win, team manager Franz Beckenbauer said the German side would now be “unbeatable for years to come”.

questions.question: On what day in 1989 did the Berlin Wall fall?
hints: It was in the fall, shortly after big protests in Leipzig.
German Unity Day is a different date.
It was a Thursday, just over a week after Halloween.
questions.description: An evening when Berlin suddenly decided to stop locking the door.
questions.fun_fact: It started with a slip of the tongue: Günter Schabowski told the press the new travel rules applied “immediately, without delay”.

questions.question: Die drei ??? from Rocky Beach are Justus Jonas, Peter Shaw and…?
hints: He is in charge of research and records.
He wears glasses and works in a library.
His first name has only three letters and starts with B.
questions.description: A detective agency that operates out of a trailer in a junkyard.
questions.fun_fact: The radio plays have been running since 1979 and are far more successful in Germany than the books ever were in their home country, the USA.

questions.question: “Human dignity shall be inviolable” is the first article of Germany's Basic Law (Grundgesetz). Since which year has it applied?
hints: It was shortly after the Second World War.
The Federal Republic was founded in the same year.
It was one year after the Deutsche Mark was introduced.
questions.description: Germany's most important sentence would easily fit on a fridge magnet.
questions.fun_fact: The Basic Law was only meant to be temporary, until reunification, yet it still applies today.

questions.question: This little man loaded with tiny objects is a good-luck charm for plenty and wealth. Which region does he come from?
hints: It's a cold region, high above sea level.
His most famous festival, Alasitas, is held in La Paz.
Lake Titicaca is there.
questions.description: A man carrying so many shopping bags he looks like he just left the mall.
questions.fun_fact: At the Alasitas fair, people buy tiny houses, cars or banknotes so the Ekeko will bring them the real, full-size thing.

questions.question: In the early 1980s, Nena, Trio and Extrabreit sang in German, often playful and full of synthesizers. What was this style of music called?
hints: It was only a big trend for a few years.
Trio's “Da da da” belongs to it too.
People shorten it to NDW.
questions.description: Synthesizers, shoulder pads and, finally, German lyrics back on the radio.
questions.fun_fact: “99 Luftballons” reached No. 2 on the US charts, even sung in German.

questions.question: In which year was the Green party (Die Grünen) founded?
hints: It grew out of the environmental and peace movements.
Three years later, it entered the Bundestag for the first time.
It was at the start of the decade of Nena and the Walkman.
questions.description: A party that walked into the Bundestag in sneakers and knitted sweaters.
questions.fun_fact: The Greens were founded in Karlsruhe in January 1980; their symbol is the sunflower.

questions.question: The cult comedy “Lammbock” (2001), starring Moritz Bleibtreu, is about a pizza delivery service. In which Franconian city is it set?
hints: Director Christian Zübert comes from this city.
The city lies on the Main River.
It is famous for its Residence palace and Franconian wine in the Bocksbeutel bottle.
questions.description: A comedy where you'd better not look too closely at the pizza.
questions.fun_fact: A sequel, “Lommbock,” came out in 2017, again with Moritz Bleibtreu.

questions.question: You're at Berlin's Wintergarten on November 1, 1895, watching moving pictures through the “Bioskop.” Who is showing them?
hints: The showmen came from Berlin.
They beat a famous screening in Paris by almost two months.
Their first names were Max and Emil.
questions.description: There was no popcorn yet, but people were amazed anyway.
questions.fun_fact: The program included a short film of a boxing kangaroo.

questions.question: Which of these characters has German voice actor Wolfgang Pampel NOT voiced?
hints: He also acts on stage and has been dubbing for decades.
In the series “Dallas” he was the German voice of Larry Hagman.
The character you're looking for commands the Enterprise.
questions.description: A man millions recognize instantly, even though hardly anyone knows his face.
questions.fun_fact: Pampel was Harrison Ford's German voice for decades, from “Star Wars” to the “Indiana Jones” films.

questions.question: Which of these TV productions did Iris Berben NOT appear in?
hints: For years, Iris Berben played the Berlin detective Rosa Roth.
She performed comedy sketches with Diether Krebs.
The series you want is set in a hospital in the Glottertal valley.
questions.description: A guest in German living rooms for decades, without ever needing a house key.
questions.fun_fact: Iris Berben was president of the German Film Academy from 2010 to 2019.

questions.question: According to tradition, why is this object hung with its ends pointing up?
questions.answer: So the luck doesn't spill out
wrong_answers: So the devil slips off it
So it brings rain to the house
hints: Think about its shape: it looks like a container.
Turn it upside down and whatever is inside falls out.
It works like a cup that holds on to something good.
questions.description: A horse's shoe that retired to hang on a wall.
questions.fun_fact: An English legend says Saint Dunstan, a blacksmith, nailed a horseshoe to the devil's hoof and only took it off once the devil promised never to enter a place where one was hanging.

questions.question: Many new East German apartments had “Fernwärme”: no coal stove was needed, and thick pipes often ran above ground through the area. What was it?
questions.answer: Hot water from a heating plant
wrong_answers: Heat from solar panels on the roof
hints: The heat was not made inside the building itself.
It was delivered through long pipes from some distance away.
A big power plant on the edge of town supplied whole housing estates.
questions.description: Cozy and warm, and still nobody in the building had to haul coal.
questions.fun_fact: To this day, many East German prefab housing estates are heated this way.

questions.question: WBS 70 was the most common prefab housing series in East Germany. About how many apartments of this type were built by 1990?
hints: The first block of this series went up in Neubrandenburg in 1973.
That's far more apartments than a big city like Rostock has.
The number is well over half a million.
questions.description: A house from a building kit, except the blocks weigh a few tons each.
questions.fun_fact: The 70 in the name stands for 1970, the year the series was developed.

questions.question: In 1960, East Germany bought a used ship and named it “Völkerfreundschaft.” In 1956 it had collided with the “Andrea Doria.” Which country did it come from?
hints: It came from Scandinavia.
It used to carry the name of a capital city.
Its earlier name was “Stockholm.”
questions.description: A ship with a past, like a used car with a story behind it.
questions.fun_fact: The ship was built in Gothenburg and from 1948 sailed across the Atlantic to New York for the Swedish American Line.

questions.question: Comedian “Cindy aus Marzahn” made this Berlin district famous across Germany. About how many prefab apartments were built there from 1977?
hints: Marzahn is one of the largest Plattenbau (prefab housing) estates in Germany.
More than 100,000 people live there today.
The number has five digits.
questions.description: A neighborhood that grew faster than any allotment-garden hedge.
questions.fun_fact: Marzahn's Gardens of the World hosted the International Garden Exhibition (IGA) in 2017.

questions.question: In the 1945 land reform in the Soviet zone, all estates over 100 hectares (about 250 acres) were seized. Who got most of the land?
hints: From now on, the land was to be farmed by those who worked it themselves.
The new farms were mostly small, only about 5 to 10 hectares, and people often had to share horses and plows.
Many of them had owned no land before or came as expellees from the East.
questions.description: In 1945, anyone with more than 100 hectares suddenly had to move out in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The land reform's slogan was “Junkerland in Bauernhand”: the nobles' land into farmers' hands.

questions.question: East Germany's Delikat stores sold gourmet food at high prices. In which decade were they introduced?
hints: The Wall was already standing when these stores existed.
Shortly before, the “Exquisit” stores for expensive clothing had opened.
It was under Walter Ulbricht, before Honecker took power.
questions.description: No need to wait in line for canned pineapple here, just dig deep into your pocket.
questions.fun_fact: The pricey stores were meant to soak up people's spare money, since there was hardly anything else to buy with it.

questions.question: On June 11, 1953, you read in “Neues Deutschland” that the SED admits mistakes and is reversing price rises. What was this policy shift called?
hints: The turnaround came under pressure from Moscow, shortly after Stalin's death.
It did not reverse the higher work quotas, though, and a few days later the uprising broke out.
The name sounds like heading off in a new direction.
questions.description: The SED admits mistakes: a sentence you didn't read very often.
questions.fun_fact: Because the higher quotas stayed despite the New Course, construction workers on Stalinallee went on strike on June 16, 1953.

questions.question: You're driving from Hamburg to West Berlin and may not leave the transit autobahn. In which year was the Transit Agreement signed?
hints: It was part of Willy Brandt's new Ostpolitik.
It was signed the same year Erich Honecker replaced Walter Ulbricht.
It came into force the following year.
questions.description: A highway where taking an exit was not a good idea.
questions.fun_fact: From then on, West Germany paid East Germany a yearly lump sum so travelers no longer had to pay tolls each trip.

questions.question: The bride carries it at the wedding, throws it backward at the end, and whoever catches it is next to marry. What is it?
hints: She holds it in her hands as she walks down the aisle.
It smells very nice.
It's made of roses, lilies or other plants.
questions.description: The only throwing sport played in fancy clothes.
questions.fun_fact: It's said that guests once tore little pieces off the bride's dress for good luck, and throwing the bouquet was a way to distract them.

questions.question: Until 1990, West Germany called it “Day of German Unity”. Schools were closed, and it honored protests in East Germany. Which day was it?
hints: It's not the holiday Germany celebrates today.
On this day, construction workers in East Berlin went on strike, and soon people in many other East German cities joined them.
A wide avenue leading to the Brandenburg Gate has this date in its name.
questions.description: No school, sleeping in, bratwurst: public holidays are one of the best ideas politics ever had.
questions.fun_fact: Since reunification, October 3 has been Germany's Day of German Unity.

questions.question: Under the Nazis, I was held in a concentration camp. From 1973 to 1976 I led East Germany's Council of Ministers, then was President of the Volkskammer until 1989. Who am I?
hints: I was a member of the SED Politburo.
After the fall of the Wall, I'm said to have remarked: “We were prepared for everything, except candles and prayers.”
The man before me and the man after me as head of the Council of Ministers was the same person.
questions.description: A man who got two big leather chairs in the same republic.
questions.fun_fact: The Volkskammer met in the Palace of the Republic, which was torn down in 2008.

questions.question: In January, gyms are packed, many people eat fewer sweets and some quit smoking. What's usually the reason?
hints: It has to do with the turn of the year.
At midnight on December 31, people firmly promise themselves something.
These are plans to become a better person.
questions.description: In January everyone's an athlete; February is another story.
questions.fun_fact: Many resolutions only last a few weeks, and a classic one is “exercise more.”

questions.question: Shortly before Easter, everyone in Germany has the day off, public dancing is banned and many people eat fish. Which day is it?
hints: The day falls in Holy Week.
It is two days before Easter Sunday.
