It always falls on the last workday of the week.
questions.description: A day when even the disco takes a break.
questions.fun_fact: The dancing ban on this day applies in every German state, but for different lengths of time.

questions.question: In many parts of Germany, children go from house to house with lanterns, sing songs and get candy for it. When is this?
hints: It's in the fall, when it gets dark early.
It belongs to the feast of a saint with a horse and a cloak.
Carnival season also starts on the same date.
questions.description: Singing for candy: the most honest deal in the world.
questions.fun_fact: In East Frisia, children set out a day early, on November 10, Martin Luther's birthday.

questions.question: On New Year's Eve, German supermarkets sell “Tischfeuerwerk” (table fireworks), and you may even set it off indoors. What is it?
questions.answer: A small popper box with confetti and figures
wrong_answers: Rockets you launch from the dinner table
A festive dish that you flambé
hints: It makes only a small bang.
Afterwards, lots of colorful bits lie on the tablecloth.
Out fly scraps of paper and tiny toys.
questions.description: New Year's Eve for people who'd rather stay in their seats.
questions.fun_fact: Table fireworks often shoot out tiny lucky charms like little pigs or horseshoes.

questions.question: On the second Sunday in May, kids make cards, pick flowers and bring breakfast in bed. For whom?
hints: This person is part of the family.
She has known you since you were a baby.
The day is named after her, and little kids call her “Mommy”.
questions.description: The one day a year when breakfast gets delivered straight to bed.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has celebrated this day for about 100 years; it came over from the USA.

questions.question: On New Year's Eve, people long ago made noise with whips, drums and later firecrackers. What were they trying to chase away?
hints: This custom is much older than fireworks.
People believed they roamed about most in the dark winter.
Today you know them from spooky stories.
questions.description: The one night of the year the neighbors don't complain about the noise.
questions.fun_fact: The nights between Christmas and Epiphany are called “Raunächte”: old folk belief said the spirits were especially wild during them.

questions.question: Finish the wedding tradition for brides: “Something old, something new, something borrowed, something…”
hints: It's a color.
It's not the color of the dress.
It's the color of a clear sky.
questions.description: The most famous shopping list at any wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The full old English rhyme ends with “and a silver sixpence in her shoe”.

questions.question: Which vegetable can you use to dye Easter eggs pink to red, the natural way?
hints: This vegetable grows underground.
Its juice stains clothes and fingers.
The vegetable itself is dark red.
questions.description: Easter eggs that would rather do their makeup with vegetables than with dye from a packet.
questions.fun_fact: Onion skins turn Easter eggs golden brown, and red cabbage even turns them blue.

questions.question: At the lantern parade, your paper lantern is usually lit by a battery stick these days. What used to burn inside it?
hints: It had a real flame.
You often find it on the dinner table when things should feel cozy.
You also put them on birthday cakes.
questions.description: A fall evening, cold noses and a choir of children marching through the streets.
questions.fun_fact: Because paper catches fire quickly, many kindergartens now only allow electric light sticks.

questions.question: Nivea cream has come from Hamburg for more than 100 years. Why is it called that?
wrong_answers: After an island in the North Sea
hints: The name was meant to sound clean and pure.
The name comes from Latin.
The Latin “nix, nivis” falls from the sky in winter.
questions.description: A tin that hasn't left Grandma's handbag in decades.
questions.fun_fact: The famous blue tin only dates from 1925; before that it was yellow and green.

questions.question: A Geiger counter clicks when radioactivity is nearby. Who is it named after?
wrong_answers: A miner from the Ore Mountains
hints: The man it is named after lived in the early 20th century.
He did research with Ernest Rutherford in England.
He was a scientist from Neustadt an der Weinstraße.
questions.description: A gadget that starts chattering nervously as soon as something invisible comes close.
questions.fun_fact: In 1928 in Kiel, he improved the device with Walther Müller, which is why it is also called the Geiger–Müller tube.

questions.question: In 1912, Alfred Wegener claimed that Africa and South America were once joined and then moved apart. What is his idea called?
hints: Wegener noticed that the coastlines fit together.
It is about whole parts of the world that move.
The continents float slowly along, like rafts on water.
questions.description: The Earth has been doing a very slow jigsaw puzzle for millions of years.
questions.fun_fact: Wegener also studied the weather, and in 1906 he and his brother stayed up in a balloon for over 52 hours, a world record at the time.

questions.question: I was a chemist. From 1865, a company in Uruguay used my method to boil beef down into extract, sold with colorful trading cards. Who am I?
hints: The factory stood in Fray Bentos on the Uruguay River.
I taught in Giessen for many years and studied mineral fertilizers.
A condenser found in every chemistry lab is named after me.
questions.description: A whole cow, boiled down to the size of a teaspoon.
questions.fun_fact: The company that made the extract later gave rise to the Oxo brand.

questions.question: Müritz National Park was approved in 1990, while East Germany still existed; its Serrahn section became World Heritage in 2011. Which trees make up this World Heritage site?
hints: They are broadleaf trees.
Their bark is smooth and silvery gray.
Their small, three-sided nuts are a favorite food of squirrels and wild boar.
questions.description: A forest so old and dignified that even UNESCO tips its hat.
questions.fun_fact: At about 117 square kilometers (45 sq mi), the Müritz is the largest lake that lies entirely within Germany.

questions.question: You're swimming in the Titisee in the Black Forest. Roughly how deep is it at its deepest point?
hints: A glacier carved out its basin.
Lake Constance is much deeper.
A ten-story building would just barely disappear in it.
questions.description: A Black Forest swimming lake with more to hide than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: The Titisee formed in the last ice age, when the Feldberg glacier scooped out its basin.

questions.question: On the North Sea coast, what is a “Marsch”?
questions.answer: Fertile land made from sea mud
wrong_answers: A long footpath across the mudflats
Sandy land from the Ice Age
A mound for shelter from storm floods
hints: It usually lies behind the dike.
Cows graze there on lush green meadows.
The sea itself once washed up this soil.
questions.description: On the North Sea the wind blows so hard that even the sheep hold on to their hairdos.
questions.fun_fact: In northern Germany, the sandy, higher land that is the opposite of the Marsch is called the “Geest”.

questions.question: At the New Year's ski jump in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, ski jumpers fly a long way. Which of these athletes was NEVER a ski jumper?
hints: He still spent a lot of time on skis.
Instead of jumping off hills, he raced around gates.
His mother is the skiing legend Rosi Mittermaier.
questions.description: New Year's Day: other people sleep in, but here people fly more than 100 meters (330 ft).
questions.fun_fact: People have been jumping off the hill in Garmisch-Partenkirchen on New Year's Day since 1922.

questions.question: In “The Goonies,” a group of kids hunts for the treasure of the pirate One-Eyed Willy. In which decade did the movie come out?
hints: It's from the time of the Walkman and early console video games.
The series “Stranger Things” pays tribute to it many times.
It's from the same decade as “Back to the Future.”
questions.description: A group of kids with more treasure maps than finished homework.
questions.fun_fact: The story of “The Goonies” was Steven Spielberg's idea, but Richard Donner directed it.

questions.question: You're in a bog holding a piece of peat. What did it form from?
hints: It was once alive.
In wet bog soil there isn't enough oxygen for things to rot completely.
Mosses and grasses didn't fully rot in the wet ground.
questions.description: Brown mush with a very long family history.
questions.fun_fact: A bog grows upward by only about 1 millimeter a year.

questions.question: I was once glowing lava. I'm dark and heavy, and in the Eifel and the Rhön I often stand as six-sided columns. Which rock am I?
hints: I come from volcanoes.
People also use me to pave streets.
My name starts with B.
questions.description: A stone with a fiery youth and a very tidy retirement.
questions.fun_fact: The columns form because lava shrinks as it cools and cracks into regular hexagons.

questions.question: In August and September everything blooms purple here, Heidschnucken sheep graze, and the highest point is the Wilseder Berg. Which landscape is this?
hints: It's in Lower Saxony.
It lies between Hamburg and Hanover.
It's named after an old salt town.
questions.description: In late summer, this landscape puts on its prettiest purple dress.
questions.fun_fact: The heath is not a wild, untouched landscape: it formed because people cut down forests and sheep kept everything grazed short.

questions.question: Many metal boxes at summit crosses hold a summit book. What is mostly written in it?
hints: It stays dry in the box, and when it's full, a new one goes in.
Often the date is written next to it.
It's a bit like a guest book.
questions.description: Burning calves, gasping lungs, and then a view at the top that makes it all worth it.
questions.fun_fact: Old summit books are often kept in archives because they show who was on the mountain and when.

questions.question: This hotel in Oberhof, in the Thuringian Forest, was built in East Germany in 1969. What is its shape meant to show?
hints: The shape has to do with what Oberhof is famous for.
The slanted wings rise steeply.
This is where ski jumpers take off.
questions.description: A holiday hotel from East Germany that simply didn't feel like being a shoebox.
questions.fun_fact: Today Oberhof is best known for biathlon and its luge track.

questions.question: From 1959, the East German flag had a hammer and compass in the middle. Roughly how long did it fly before East Germany ceased to exist?
hints: East Germany ended with reunification.
Shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, East Germany was history.
Reunification was in 1990: count from 1959.
questions.description: Almost exactly like the one in the West, just with a little toolbox in the middle.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1959, the East German flag looked exactly like West Germany's: just black, red and gold, with no emblem.

questions.question: In which year did women in Germany get the right to vote?
hints: It was right after the end of World War I.
Germany became a republic the same year.
Women first voted in January of the following year, 1919.
questions.description: A year when half the population finally got a say too.
questions.fun_fact: In the first election in January 1919, 37 women won seats in the National Assembly right away.

questions.question: In 1950 this poet wrote a “Kinderhymne” (children's anthem), which some people suggested in 1990 as the new anthem for all of Germany. Who is he?
hints: After the war he lived in East Berlin.
He founded the Berliner Ensemble there.
He wrote “The Threepenny Opera.”
questions.description: A song that orders grace and hard work instead of trumpet fanfares.
questions.fun_fact: The Kinderhymne begins “Anmut sparet nicht noch Mühe” (“Spare no grace and spare no effort”) and fits the tune of the Deutschlandlied.

questions.question: The mail carrier brings a letter for your neighbor. Who is allowed to open it?
hints: It's even written in Germany's Basic Law.
The rule's name includes the word “privacy”.
Only the person the letter is meant for may read it.
questions.description: Letters are the grandparents of text messages, just with a stamp.
questions.fun_fact: Privacy of correspondence is protected by Article 10 of the Basic Law, together with the privacy of post and telecommunications.

questions.question: On some days, the flag hangs like this outside the town hall. What is this called?
hints: It's done, for example, when an important person has died.
The flag isn't at the top of the pole.
It hangs about halfway up the pole.
questions.description: The flag just doesn't feel like going all the way up today.
questions.fun_fact: To fly a flag at half-mast, you first raise it all the way to the top and then lower it halfway.

questions.question: Guess: I was born in 1873 for California's miners, I have copper rivets, and on my label two horses try to tear me apart. What am I?
hints: You wear me on your legs.
I'm almost always made of a blue cloth called denim.
I have pockets, a zipper or buttons, and two legs.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so tough that not even the cavalry could beat it.
questions.fun_fact: Levi's has used its two-horse logo since 1886 to show off that not even two horses could tear its jeans apart.

questions.question: In a World Cup prediction game, you guess the scores of Germany's matches. What is the latest you can enter your prediction?
hints: It's about predicting, not looking it up afterwards.
Anyone who already knows the score would have it too easy.
Your guess must be in before the referee blows the whistle for the first time.
questions.description: Looking into the future here, no crystal ball, just lots of gut feeling.
questions.fun_fact: Many German offices and school classes run their own prediction game at every World Cup and Euro, often with a table on the wall.

questions.question: From 2027, Germany's national team will wear Nike instead of Adidas. About how long had Adidas been its supplier?
hints: Even grandparents watched Germany play in Adidas shoes.
The German Football Association (DFB) itself was only founded in 1900.
When Germany won the 1954 World Cup, the players already wore shoes from Herzogenaurach.
questions.description: A change of clothes that got all of soccer-mad Germany worked up.
questions.fun_fact: The news of the switch to Nike in March 2024 was so surprising that even politicians commented on it.

questions.question: In July 2014, fans welcomed the world champions on Berlin's Fanmeile at the Brandenburg Gate. About how many people were there?
hints: The Fanmeile is almost 2 km (1.2 miles) long.
There were far more people than fit into a big stadium.
The number has six digits.
questions.description: Here the living room suddenly stretches the length of a whole street.
questions.fun_fact: Berlin's Fanmeile is on the Straße des 17. Juni, which is closed to cars completely for big games.

review.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The answer is fine (reports say roughly 250,000 to almost 500,000). But hint 1 is off: the Fanmeile is about 1.2 km long (Brandenburg Gate to Siegessäule), not 'almost 2 km'. The '1.2 miles' also mixes up km and miles.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is right: reports put the crowd at the 15 July 2014 welcome at roughly 400,000–500,000, and the other options are far too small. Two things are shaky. The hint 'almost 2 km' is loose, because sources give 1.2–1.5 km for the 2014 Fanmeile (about 2 km only in a 2006 taz article). 'Suddenly the living room is as long as an entire street' is odd for a description. The fun fact that the Straße des 17. Juni is fully closed to cars for big matches is plausible but I did not verify it.

questions.question: The word is in “Autokorso” after Germany wins and in “Blumenkorso”, and it comes from Italian. What does “Korso” mean?
hints: At a Blumenkorso there are no cars and no honking.
It's about how many people move along together.
At carnival, floats move through the streets like this in a long line.
questions.description: Honking, flags, walking pace: the traffic rules are taking a short break.
questions.fun_fact: The Italian “corso” goes back to the Latin “cursus”, which means “run”.

questions.question: I'm from Gelsenkirchen, my last name means roughly “sunrise” in Turkish, and I was captain at the home Euro 2024. Who am I?
hints: I play in midfield and was also captain of Manchester City.
With City I won the Champions League in 2023.
My first name starts with a dotted capital İ.
questions.description: A name that makes it light out early in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Mesut Özil is from Gelsenkirchen too, and both played youth soccer in the Ruhr area.

questions.question: Which of these teams has Hansi Flick NOT coached as head coach?
hints: With one of these teams he won six titles in 2020.
He moved to Spain in 2024.
He went to this team's great rival.
questions.description: A coach with more stops on his journey than a local train.
questions.fun_fact: With FC Bayern, Hansi Flick won all six possible titles in 2020, the sextuple.

questions.question: Which of these titles did Toni Kroos NOT win in his career?
hints: With Real Madrid he won almost everything.
His last tournament for Germany was Euro 2024 at home.
It ended there in the quarterfinal against Spain.
questions.description: A man whose passes arrive more on time than any train.
questions.fun_fact: Toni Kroos won the Champions League six times: once with Bayern and five times with Real Madrid.

questions.question: 2018 World Cup: defending champions Germany are knocked out after losing to South Korea. How many goals did South Korea score?
hints: Germany didn't score in the game.
The goals only came in stoppage time.
For the last goal, Manuel Neuer was far away from his empty net.
questions.description: A night in Kazan that German fans would rather not talk about.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first time Germany had ever gone out in the group stage of a World Cup.

questions.question: Who wore the number 10 shirt for Germany's national team at the home Euro 2024?
hints: He was one of the youngest players in the squad.
He plays for FC Bayern Munich.
He was born in Stuttgart and grew up partly in England.
questions.description: A number on your back that brings more pressure than any math test.
questions.fun_fact: With three goals at Euro 2024, Jamal Musiala was one of the tournament's joint top scorers.

questions.question: These blossoms turn into the fruit eaten most in Germany, ripe in the fall. Which fruit is it?
hints: It grows on trees, not on bushes or low plants.
The Altes Land near Hamburg has huge orchards of it.
A saying claims that one a day keeps the doctor away.
questions.description: In spring the tree wears a wedding dress; in fall it opens a fruit stand.
questions.fun_fact: The Altes Land near Hamburg is considered the largest continuous fruit-growing area in Northern Europe.

questions.question: In the morning, dew sparkles on the meadow even though it didn't rain overnight. What is dew?
hints: Your feet get wet if you walk on it barefoot.
It forms when the night is cool.
It's the same thing that beads up on the outside of a cold glass.
questions.description: The meadow put on glitter makeup overnight.
questions.fun_fact: Dew forms mostly on clear, windless nights, because that's when the ground cools down the most.

questions.question: It has the smallest drops of any kind of rain and falls very quietly, but it still gets you wet. What is it called?
hints: It doesn't pound on the roof. You can barely hear it.
The drops are so fine they almost float.
Its name rhymes with “sizzle”.
questions.description: Germany's favorite small-talk topic has many names, and every one of them is wet.
questions.fun_fact: Drizzle drops are smaller than half a millimeter (0.02 in) and fall so slowly that the wind easily blows them sideways.

questions.question: We’re from Düsseldorf, stand on stage like robots and have made music almost only with synthesizers since the 1970s. Who are we?
hints: One of our albums is called “The Man-Machine”.
We sang about the “Autobahn”.
Our name is the German word for a power plant.
questions.description: For this band, a power outage is the worst stage accident imaginable.
questions.fun_fact: The track “Autobahn” from 1974 runs over 22 minutes on the record.

questions.question: Lou Bega from Munich scored a worldwide hit with “Mambo No. 5”. In which year did it come out?
hints: It was shortly before a new millennium began.
Back then, Germans still paid in Deutsche Marks.
It was the last year of the 1990s.
questions.description: A song that remembers more names than you do at a birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: The original is by Pérez Prado from 1949; Lou Bega wrote new lyrics for it full of women’s names.

questions.question: The Leipzig band Die Prinzen sang “Ich wär so gerne Millionär”. In which decade did the song become a hit?
hints: Several band members sang in famous boys’ choirs as children.
Germany had been reunified shortly before the song came out.
The song came out in 1991.
questions.description: They don’t wear crowns, but they sing like they live in a palace.
questions.fun_fact: Die Prinzen are among the most successful German-language bands of all time.

questions.question: The singer of Die Toten Hosen calls himself Campino. What is his real name?
hints: His father was a judge and his mother was English.
His last name sounds almost like the German word for “question.”
His first name is the same as that of the singer of “Auf uns.”
questions.description: On stage a stage name, on his ID card something completely different.
questions.fun_fact: Campino is a huge fan of Liverpool FC and wrote a book about it called “Hope Street.”

questions.question: The Rock am Ring festival has been held in the Eifel hills since 1985. What does the “Ring” in its name refer to?
hints: It’s loud there even without any bands.
Normally people race each other there in circles.
Racing drivers call the place the “Green Hell”.
questions.description: Three days of mud, music and tent life in the middle of the Eifel.
questions.fun_fact: On the same weekend, its twin festival Rock im Park takes place in Nuremberg with the same bands.

questions.question: The Scorpions formed in 1965, their singer is Klaus Meine, and “Wind of Change” starts with whistling. What city are they from?
hints: The city is in northern Germany.
It is the capital of a German state.
It is the capital of Lower Saxony.
questions.description: The name sounds dangerous, but the only stings come from guitar solos.
questions.fun_fact: “Wind of Change” became the anthem of the years when the Cold War came to an end.

questions.question: Guess who: I have stripes, wear a red scarf around my neck, and on the cereal box I say “They're Gr-r-reat!”. Who am I?
hints: You always see me full of energy and playing sports.
My cereal is sugar-frosted flakes.
I'm orange with black stripes.
questions.description: A breakfast so sugary that even the box is smiling.
questions.fun_fact: Tony the Tiger was born in 1952 and beat a kangaroo named Katy for the mascot job.

questions.question: DSDS started on RTL in 2002, its first winner was Alexander Klaws, and the idea came from abroad. From which country?
hints: The country is in Europe.
People there drive on the left side of the road.
The original show was called “Pop Idol” and started in 2001.
questions.description: Even superstars have role models, and this show found its own abroad.
questions.fun_fact: The format was invented by the British producer Simon Fuller; versions ran in many countries, including the US as “American Idol”.

questions.question: For years, Sarah Connor sang only in English. In which year did her first German-language album, “Muttersprache”, come out?
hints: The album title (“mother tongue”) hints that German is her first language.
That same year, her song “Wie schön du bist” was playing everywhere.
It was one year after Germany won the World Cup in Brazil.
questions.description: First she sang for the whole world, then for Mom in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Sarah Connor comes from Delmenhorst, near Bremen.

questions.question: Bela B. of Die Ärzte plays it. He sits at the very back of the stage and holds two sticks. Which instrument is it?
hints: You play it sitting down.
You play it with your hands and your feet.
It has a snare, toms and cymbals.
questions.description: The loudest piece of furniture in any band, and the neighbors are not fans.
questions.fun_fact: Even so, Bela B. sings many Die Ärzte songs himself, often right from behind his drums.

questions.question: Someone in the schoolyard shouts: “Digga, warte mal!” Which German word did “Digga” come from?
hints: The word comes from northern Germany, especially Hamburg.
It used to be a cheeky but affectionate way for buddies to address each other.
It's the opposite of “Dünner”.
questions.description: A way of addressing someone that makes parents wince and friends smile.
questions.fun_fact: Calling someone “Dicker” usually had nothing to do with weight: it simply meant “good friend”.

questions.question: The rapper in the photo is Marteria. Which Hanseatic city on the Baltic Sea is he from?
hints: The city is in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
It's the largest city in that state.
Its best-known sports club is called Hansa.
questions.description: A rapper who gets around a lot but left his heart in the harbor.
questions.fun_fact: As a teen, Marteria played for Germany's under-17 national team, then worked as a model in New York before becoming a rapper.

questions.question: In rap, what do you call a long fight between rappers that plays out in their songs, like the one between Sido and Bushido?
hints: It's a short word with just one syllable.
Outside rap, teens say it too: “I've got … with him.”
It's also the name for meat from a cow.
questions.description: A fight that isn't settled at the kitchen table, but in the charts.
questions.fun_fact: Sido and Bushido made up in 2011 and even released an album together called “23”.

questions.question: It began in 1989 with about 150 ravers on the Kudamm, motto “Friede, Freude, Eierkuchen” (“peace, joy, pancakes”). Later over a million came. What was it called?
hints: It was founded by a DJ called Dr. Motte.
Later it moved to the Tiergarten, around the Victory Column.
Its name is about the feeling everyone celebrates on Valentine's Day.
questions.description: A demonstration where nobody holds up signs, only their arms.
questions.fun_fact: The first parade took place in July 1989, just four months before the Berlin Wall fell.

questions.question: It was Germany's youth word of the year in 2012, and it's an English abbreviation that means “You only live once”. What is the word?
hints: It's made from the first letters of four English words.
The rapper Drake made it famous in a song in 2011.
It starts with a “Y”.
questions.description: A life motto used to excuse many a shaky idea.
questions.fun_fact: The year before, “Swag” won, and the year after, “Babo”.

previous.feedback: The translation dropped the source's spelled-out meaning (“You only live once”), so the description now carries the clue: calling the word “a life motto” picks out YOLO, because Swag, Babo and Smombie are not mottos. Rewrite the description to joke about youth slang or the yearly vote without saying the word is a motto or saying.

questions.question: This rapper got famous on YouTube, was a judge on “Deutschland sucht den Superstar” and had a No. 1 hit with “Bauch Beine Po”. Who is she?
hints: She comes from Hamburg.
Her first album was called “Supersize”.
Her stage name contains the name of a king from the Bible.
questions.description: From a webcam in her childhood bedroom all the way to the top of the charts.
questions.fun_fact: As a child, Shirin David sang in the children's choir of the Hamburg State Opera and learned violin and piano.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Answer Shirin David is right: she is from Hamburg, was a YouTuber and DSDS juror, and "Bauch Beine Po" (2024) hit #1. Her debut album "Supersize" and the "David" stage-name hint are consistent with what I know. I couldn't confirm the fun fact as written. Sources describe the Hamburger Mädchenchor, the Jugendopernakademie, small acting roles at the Staatsoper, and piano, violin and oboe lessons. None named the Hamburg State Opera children's choir.

questions.question: For years I wore a silver skull mask, rapped about “Mein Block” and later sang “Astronaut” with Andreas Bourani. Who am I?
hints: I come from Berlin.
My block is in the Märkisches Viertel.
My name starts with “S” and ends with “o”.
questions.description: A man who hid his face for years, but never his opinions.
questions.fun_fact: “Astronaut” reached No. 1 in the German charts in 2015.

questions.question: In which century did the hermit Ivan of Rila found the famous Bulgarian monastery that bears his name?
hints: It was in the Middle Ages, long before the Ottomans reached the Balkans.
It happened shortly after Bulgaria became Christian.
It was in the 900s.
questions.description: A hermit wanted to be alone on a mountain and ended up with his country's most visited monastery.
questions.fun_fact: Rila Monastery has appeared on Bulgarian banknotes and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

questions.question: Which band released the 1983 single “Tour de France”, where you can even hear cyclists panting?
hints: The band is from Germany.
Its members often stood almost still on stage, like robots.
Their studio in Düsseldorf was called Kling Klang.
questions.description: A song that makes even the synthesizers break a sweat.
questions.fun_fact: For the race's 100th anniversary in 2003, Kraftwerk released the album “Tour de France Soundtracks”.

questions.question: They crawled through narrow mine tunnels, tied threads on running spinning machines and earned just a few pfennigs. Who worked like this in the 1800s?
hints: Being small was an advantage for this kind of work.
In 1839, Prussia passed a law to protect these workers in factories.
Today they go to school instead.
questions.description: A look back at a time when, for some, quitting time was an unknown word.
questions.fun_fact: Prussia's 1839 regulation banned factory work under age nine and limited teens under 16 to ten hours a day.

questions.question: For the 500th anniversary of Luther's theses, Reformation Day was a one-time day off across all of Germany. In which year?
hints: Many adults still remember this extra day off in the fall.
It was in the 2010s.
Do the math: Luther's theses date from 1517.
questions.description: A day when even the Halloween pumpkins stop to think about church history.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2018, Reformation Day has also been a public holiday every year in Bremen, Hamburg, Lower Saxony and Schleswig-Holstein.

questions.question: In Germany, children go from kindergarten to Grundschule (elementary school). How old are most children when they start school?
hints: In the last year of kindergarten, you're a “Vorschulkind.”
Around this age, the first baby teeth fall out.
One hand full of fingers, plus one.
questions.description: From stacking building blocks to stacking letters is only a small step.
questions.fun_fact: Friedrich Fröbel founded the first kindergarten in Bad Blankenburg in 1840, and that's why English uses the German word “kindergarten.”

questions.question: Night watchmen once walked the dark alleys carrying a halberd. What is a halberd?
questions.answer: A pole weapon with an ax blade and a spike
wrong_answers: A lantern with a candle inside
A signal horn made of brass
A long coat made of wool
hints: It was often more than two meters (6.5 ft) long.
It could keep thieves at a distance.
At the top sat a sharp blade and a point.
questions.description: A job for anyone who can't sleep at night anyway.
questions.fun_fact: Night watchmen called out the time every hour and warned of fires; in Rothenburg ob der Tauber, one still leads tourists through the town today.

questions.question: “Walle! Walle!” When was the ballad of the sorcerer's apprentice who can't stop the bewitched broom written?
hints: It was the age of Weimar Classicism.
The poet and his friend Schiller were competing to write ballads at the time.
Soon after, the 19th century began.
questions.description: Anyone who has ever programmed a robot vacuum knows this feeling.
questions.fun_fact: Paul Dukas turned it into an orchestral piece in 1897, and in Disney's “Fantasia” Mickey Mouse plays the sorcerer's apprentice.

questions.question: Which of these terms does NOT describe a soldier who went to war for money?
hints: Mercenaries fought for whoever paid them.
The one you're looking for was among the most powerful men in the Empire.
He got a vote in choosing the emperor.
questions.description: Fighting for a fixed rate: back then, a perfectly normal business model.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Söldner” (mercenary) comes from “Sold”, meaning pay, and even the word “soldier” goes back to an old coin, the Latin “solidus”.

questions.question: This leather helmet with a spike became a symbol of the German Empire. What kind of outfit was it part of?
hints: It was most common in Prussia.
In World War I, it was swapped for a steel helmet.
It was worn while marching.
questions.description: The only hat that could pop a balloon by accident.
questions.fun_fact: Prussia introduced the Pickelhaube in 1842; from 1916 on, soldiers at the front got the steel helmet instead.

questions.question: Which place is NOT inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, according to tradition?
questions.answer: The grotto where Jesus was born
hints: The church remembers the end of Jesus's life, not the beginning.
The church's name already speaks of a tomb.
That place is in another town: Bethlehem.
questions.description: A church so busy that several Christian communities have to take turns looking after it.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, two Muslim families have kept the keys to the Holy Sepulchre and opened its door every morning.

questions.question: If you're Protestant, at some point you celebrate your confirmation. At what age, usually?
hints: You're not a little kid anymore, but not a grown-up yet either.
Before it, there are usually one or two years of confirmation classes.
You're in about eighth grade.
questions.description: A party with a suit, cake and relatives who say “Look how big you've gotten!”
questions.fun_fact: “Confirmation” comes from the Latin “confirmatio”: the teens confirm their own baptism.

questions.question: Luther translated the New Testament in just eleven weeks, it came out in 1522, and he wrote the way ordinary people talked. Why?
questions.answer: So everyone could read the Bible themselves
wrong_answers: So the Pope could read it
So the emperor could ban it
hints: Until then, church services and Bibles were mostly in Latin.
His motto was “dem Volk aufs Maul schauen”: listen to how people really speak.
He translated it into German.
questions.description: A monk, a desk, eleven weeks, and maybe the most influential book in the German language.
questions.fun_fact: Luther's translation shaped the German language: words like “Lückenbüßer” (stopgap) and “Lästermaul” (blabbermouth) go back to him.

questions.question: In 1924 at the Bauhaus, Marianne Brandt shaped brass, silver and ebony into a design classic with a built-in strainer. What is it?
hints: Brandt was one of the first women in the Bauhaus metal workshop.
The piece stands on a small cross-shaped base and has a handle of dark ebony.
In England, people like to use one at five in the afternoon.
questions.description: Circle, half-sphere, cylinder: geometry class, only shinier.
questions.fun_fact: Marianne Brandt was acting head of the Bauhaus metal workshop from 1928 to 1929.

questions.question: In 1924, Käthe Kollwitz made a poster for a youth rally in Leipzig. Which slogan is on it?
hints: The poster was made ten years after World War I began.
It became one of the best-known images of the peace movement.
Three German words, and the first one is “Nie”.
questions.description: An arm raised high, a promise to the world, but in which words?
questions.fun_fact: In 1919, Käthe Kollwitz became the first woman to join the Prussian Academy of Arts.

questions.question: Which title has basketball player Dennis Schröder NOT won?
hints: He led Germany's national team onto the court as captain.
Germany won its big basketball titles only recently, but he's still missing one.
The tournament in question comes only every four years and has rings as its symbol.
questions.description: A man from Braunschweig with a very full trophy cabinet, just not completely full.
questions.fun_fact: Germany won the 2023 Basketball World Cup without losing a single game.

questions.question: Decathlete Leo Neugebauer set a German record in 2024. About how many points was it?
hints: Each of the ten events earns points.
A top result in a single event earns several hundred points.
Ten times about 900: do the math.
questions.description: Ten sports in two days: that adds up.
questions.fun_fact: In June 2024 in Eugene, Oregon, Neugebauer raised his own German record to 8,961 points, then won silver at the Paris Olympics.

questions.question: From 2021, Franz Wagner played for the Orlando Magic alongside his older brother. What is his brother's first name?
hints: Both brothers are from Berlin.
Both won the 2023 World Cup with Germany.
He shares his name with one of Wilhelm Busch's two young rascals.
questions.description: Basketball in Florida: a family reunion with a hoop.
questions.fun_fact: Franz and Moritz Wagner both played at the University of Michigan before going to the NBA.

questions.question: Nico Rosberg was born in Wiesbaden and became Formula 1 world champion in 2016, like his father Keke in 1982. Which country did Keke race for?
hints: The country borders Russia.
It's famous for thousands of lakes and the sauna.
Mika Häkkinen and Kimi Räikkönen come from there too.
questions.description: Becoming world champion apparently runs in this family.
questions.fun_fact: Nico Rosberg retired just five days after winning the world championship.

questions.question: You tap Ravensburger's tiptoi pen on pictures in books. What does it do then?
wrong_answers: It takes photos of the pages
It makes the pictures light up
hints: It's also made for kids who can't read yet.
For every new book, you first load a matching file from a computer onto the pen.
Tap a lion, and you hear it roar.
questions.description: A pen that can do more than any ballpoint in your pencil case.
questions.fun_fact: The pen reads tiny dot patterns that you can hardly see with the naked eye.

questions.question: Penny is a discount supermarket that belongs to the Rewe Group. Where does its name come from?
hints: The name is meant to sound like low prices.
In Britain, you'd find one in your wallet.
100 of them make a pound.
questions.description: A supermarket name that's shorter than any shopping list.
questions.fun_fact: The first Penny store opened in Germany in 1973.

questions.question: In the 1970s, a German-Brazilian patented his “Stereobelt”. Later, which famous device did he fight over?
hints: The device came out in 1979.
You used it to listen to cassettes on the go, with headphones.
Its name tells you that you can take a stroll with it.
questions.description: The invention that finally let you stop talking to the people around you.
questions.fun_fact: Sony only settled with the inventor, Andreas Pavel, in the early 2000s, reportedly for millions.

questions.question: First cassette recorders, then CD players: which device from a Düsseldorf company now plays audio stories in many kids' rooms?
hints: The device is soft and shaped like a cube.
You control it by squeezing its ears.
You put a small figure on top of it.
questions.description: For today's kids, tangled cassette tape is a real horror story.
questions.fun_fact: The Toniebox came out in 2016; the company behind it was first called Boxine.

questions.question: In Bavaria, your sweetheart is often your “Spatzl”. Which of these Bavarian words is NOT a term of endearment?
hints: You say three of these words to people, and one to an object.
The thing you're looking for sits on the breakfast table in the morning.
You drink your coffee out of it.
questions.description: The way to the heart is through the stomach, but in Bavaria it's mostly through the little “-erl” on the end.
questions.fun_fact: “Spatzl” means “little sparrow” and is one of the most popular pet names in Bavaria.

questions.question: In Hesse, Ebbelwoi (apple wine) is poured from a “Bembel”. What is a Bembel?
wrong_answers: A wooden barrel with a tap
hints: It stands on the table and gets passed around.
It has a round belly and a handle.
It usually has a gray body with blue decorations.
questions.description: Frankfurt's apple wine doesn't come out of a juice carton. It gets to the table in style.
questions.fun_fact: People drink Ebbelwoi from a “Gerippter”, a glass with a diamond pattern.

questions.question: The drink Spezi was invented in Augsburg in 1956. What is it mixed from?
hints: One ingredient is brown and famous worldwide.
The other is a sweet soda made from a fruit of warm countries.
The second ingredient is named after a fruit that is also a color.
questions.description: In 1956, Augsburg set up two drinks on a date, and the marriage is still going strong.
questions.fun_fact: Augsburg's Riegele brewery registered the name “Spezi” as a trademark, so similar mixes from other makers often have other names, such as “Mezzo Mix.”

questions.question: I played the organ in German churches, and the famous “Toccata and Fugue in D minor” is credited to me. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the Baroque era, before Mozart.
I was German and had a huge family, with many children who became musicians.
My surname has only four letters.
questions.description: A musician who worked in church and ended up playing in every villain movie.
questions.fun_fact: As a young man, Bach walked about 400 km (250 miles) to hear the organist Dietrich Buxtehude play.

questions.question: Hot chocolate is brown and made with warm milk. From which beans is its powder made?
hints: The beans grow inside big fruits on trees in warm countries.
The Aztecs already made a bitter, frothy drink from them.
In Germany, the drink is often simply named after this bean.
questions.description: A brown mug of happiness for cold days.
questions.fun_fact: Cocoa beans grow in fruits that hang straight from the trunk of the cacao tree.

questions.question: This person works at big copper kettles where malt boils with water. What is their job?
hints: In the end, the result is filled into bottles and barrels.
Hops are used almost only for a single drink.
At Oktoberfest, the result is drunk from huge Maß mugs.
questions.description: A workplace that smells of grain and gets very steamy.
questions.fun_fact: The Weihenstephan brewery in Freising is one of the oldest still-working breweries in the world.

questions.question: Its brown fruit usually has eight points, tastes like licorice and often floats in Glühwein. Which spice is it?
hints: Each point holds a shiny seed.
It originally comes from China and Vietnam.
From above, it looks like something that twinkles in the night sky.
questions.description: A spice that likes to take a bath in a mug at the Christmas market.
questions.fun_fact: Star anise grows on an evergreen tree in southern China and Vietnam.

questions.question: In Germany, which bottle is normally NOT closed with a crown cap?
hints: You open crown caps with a bottle opener.
The drink inside is for adults and often comes to the table at dinner or at parties.
The bottle you're looking for usually has a cork or a screw cap.
questions.description: A little metal hat with a jagged edge that loves to vanish under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The inventor William Painter patented the crown cap in 1892; today it usually has 21 teeth.

questions.question: What plan of the German Wehrmacht in 1940 was hidden behind the code name “Operation Sea Lion”?
wrong_answers: An attack on the Soviet Union
hints: The plan was never carried out.
First, the Luftwaffe was supposed to knock out the British fighter planes.
Soldiers were to cross the English Channel.
questions.description: An animal with flippers as a code name: military planners apparently have a sense of humor too.
questions.fun_fact: Because the Luftwaffe did not win the air battle, Operation Sea Lion was put off indefinitely in fall 1940 and never carried out.

questions.question: The SPD is Germany's oldest party, and its color is red. Who did it mainly want to stand up for in the German Empire?
hints: Back then, these people had very long workdays and low pay.
They toiled in factories and mines.
Their big holiday is May 1.
questions.description: This party is older than the car, the airplane and every grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: Bismarck banned the Social Democrats in 1878 with the “Anti-Socialist Law”, yet they kept growing stronger.

questions.question: As Reich finance minister in 1919–20, Matthias Erzberger pushed through a major reform. What was it for?
questions.answer: Collecting taxes centrally for the Reich
wrong_answers: Giving women the right to vote
hints: It was about money, but not about new bills.
Before, the states had much more say over the revenue.
The Reich's own tax offices were created back then.
questions.description: A minister who wanted to clean house in the Reich after the war.
questions.fun_fact: The Reich finance administration Erzberger created is a forerunner of Germany's tax offices today.

questions.question: The symbol the Nazis used is an ancient sign in India, where it's called “swastika” and seen on temples. What does it mean there?
hints: In India, many families paint it on their front door.
It's meant to protect the home and the people who live there.
It's a wish that everyone will be well.
questions.description: An ancient sign that got a terrible deal in the 20th century.
questions.fun_fact: The symbol is thousands of years old and is still sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism today.

questions.question: It glows for just a moment in the night sky, and you see lots of them in August. What do you do when you see a shooting star?
hints: It happens very quietly, just inside your head.
People say it won't come true if you tell anyone.
You do the same thing when you blow out your birthday candles.
questions.description: A fireworks show in the sky that costs nothing and lasts one second.
questions.fun_fact: Most shooting stars are tiny specks of space dust burning up in Earth's air.

questions.question: What is the town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee where Peter's house stood and where Jesus lived while preaching?
hints: It's not where Jesus was born or where he grew up.
Today visitors can see the ruins of a white stone synagogue there.
Its name means “village of Nahum” in Hebrew.
questions.description: A fishing village more famous than many of the world's capitals.
questions.fun_fact: A modern church stands on pillars right above the ruins said to be Peter's house, so it looks like a spaceship hovering over them.

questions.question: Which song do German families sing before the candles are blown out, with its first line coming three times?
wrong_answers: Wie schön, dass du geboren bist
hints: People know the tune all over the world.
It's the German version of an English song.
Its title wishes you something a four-leaf clover brings too.
questions.description: The song the candles on the cake wait for impatiently every year.
questions.fun_fact: The tune of “Happy Birthday” comes from Mildred and Patty Hill, two American sisters, in the 19th century.

questions.question: For how many years was Helmut Kohl Chancellor of Germany?
hints: He was the chancellor of reunification.
He became chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence.
He governed from 1982 to 1998.
questions.description: A chancellor who loved serving Palatinate Saumagen (stuffed pig's stomach) even to visiting world leaders.
questions.fun_fact: Kohl governed only about ten days longer than Angela Merkel, so he holds the record by a hair.

questions.question: Nuclear waste in a salt dome, Castor transports, protests in the Wendland under “Atomkraft? Nein danke”: which place was this about?
hints: The fight over this place dragged on for more than 40 years.
A final repository for radioactive waste was supposed to be built here.
It lies on the Elbe in the district of Lüchow-Dannenberg.
questions.description: A smiling sun that wasn't smiling at all about some building projects.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, Gorleben was officially removed from the search for a final repository site.

questions.question: Heinz Badewitz founded this film festival in 1967 and ran it for almost 50 years. Which is it?
hints: It takes place every October.
The town is in Upper Franconia, near the Czech border.
The town's name has only three letters.
questions.description: A festival for everyone who thinks popcorn is a basic food group.
questions.fun_fact: Wim Wenders affectionately called the festival the “Home of Films”, a play on the town's name.

questions.question: Held every summer since 1983, this festival gives out the CineMerit Award and the New German Cinema Award. Which is it?
hints: After the Berlinale, it counts as one of Germany's biggest film festivals.
For a long time, the Gasteig cultural center was a major venue.
The city is also known for its Oktoberfest.
questions.description: Summer, big screen, popcorn: for some, that's the perfect holy trinity.
questions.fun_fact: The CineMerit Award honors people who have done great service to the art of film, often international stars.

questions.question: The “Pionierrepublik Wilhelm Pieck” lay on Lake Werbellin, welcomed children from many other countries too, and bore the name of the GDR's first president. What was it?
questions.answer: A large holiday camp for children
wrong_answers: A boarding school for young athletes
A children's hospital for health cures
hints: Children only stayed there for a few weeks.
It was all about rest, swimming and being together.
They slept in houses by the lake, as was usual in the summer break.
questions.description: A republic with neckerchiefs instead of neckties.
questions.fun_fact: Today the site is once again a place for children and teenagers, as the European Youth Recreation and Meeting Center Werbellinsee.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The fun fact gives the site's current name as 'European Youth Recreation and Meeting Center'. Sources call it the 'Europäische Jugenderholungs- und Begegnungsstätte' (EJB), meaning a meeting 'site', not a 'center'. It now runs as the 'seezeit-resort'. The question and answer are fine.

questions.question: Many East German work brigades filled a thick book with photos and reports on outings, theater trips and parties. What did they mainly need it for?
questions.answer: To earn an honorary title for the brigade
wrong_answers: To apply for a trip to the West
hints: At the end there was often a certificate and a bonus.
The brigade had to show it didn't just work well, but also learned and lived together.
The title was “Collective of Socialist Labor.”
questions.description: A photo album that was more work than the work itself.
questions.fun_fact: Today these brigade diaries are a treasure trove for historians, because they show everyday life at work.

questions.question: I'm a huge building complex in East Berlin. Erich Mielke had his office here, and on January 15, 1990, citizens stormed me. What's my short name?
hints: Surveillance of all of East Germany was run from here.
I wasn't a prison, but the headquarters of a government ministry.
Today I house the Stasi Museum and part of the Stasi Records Archive.
questions.description: A building with a lot of hallways, a lot of files and very little privacy.
questions.fun_fact: Mielke's office in “House 1” is still almost exactly as he left it, and visitors can tour it.

questions.question: The Leipzig building “Runde Ecke” (“Round Corner”) on Dittrichring was occupied by citizens on December 4, 1989. What was it before?
hints: The name comes from the building's curved front.
The occupiers wanted to stop files from being destroyed there.
Mielke's ministry ran the Leipzig district from here.
questions.description: A building that hates sharp edges, yet stands on a corner.
questions.fun_fact: The museum still shows scent samples in jars, which the Stasi used so dogs could track people down.

questions.question: The Maya city of Tulum sits on a cliff above Mexico's Caribbean coast, and its name describes what surrounds it. What does “Tulum” mean?
hints: The name describes something people built around the city.
It protected the city on three sides; the sea guarded the fourth.
It's the same thing that rings the old towns of Cartagena in Colombia and Dubrovnik in Croatia.
questions.description: Ruins with an ocean view: the Maya really knew how to pick a spot.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya seem to have called Tulum “Zamá”, thought to mean “dawn”, because from there you can watch the sun rise over the sea.

questions.question: Many East Germans wore a round badge on their jacket showing two hands shaking, nicknamed the “Bonbon” (candy). What did it stand for?
hints: The badge didn't show a rising sun.
The two hands stand for the merger of the KPD and SPD in 1946.
It means the party that was in charge in East Germany.
questions.description: A Bonbon you'd better not suck on.
questions.fun_fact: The handshake recalls Wilhelm Pieck and Otto Grotewohl shaking hands at the 1946 party merger congress.

questions.question: A couple is celebrating their silver wedding anniversary. How long have they been married?
hints: The golden anniversary comes much later.
The golden anniversary is the same number of years away again.
It's a quarter of a century.
questions.description: An anniversary where everyone hopes nobody plays the wedding video again.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Germany, people decorate the couple's front door with garlands or a wreath for their silver anniversary.

questions.question: September 20 is a public holiday in Thuringia. The rights of which group is this day about?
hints: The day is marked around the world, but only Thuringia gives people the day off.
It is about things like the right to play and to go to school.
You might belong to this group yourself.
questions.description: A holiday that Thuringia keeps all to itself.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2019, this day has been a public holiday in Thuringia, the only German state where it is.

questions.question: What is Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim's topic on YouTube, on ZDF and in her bestselling books?
hints: She has a doctorate herself.
She explains complicated topics in short, fast videos for young people.
Her work is all about studies, research and experiments.
questions.description: A woman with more subscribers than some big cities have people.
questions.fun_fact: Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim earned her doctorate in chemistry.

questions.question: This astronaut from Saarland trained in Cologne and spent about six months on the ISS in 2021 and 2022. Who is he?
hints: He comes from St. Wendel.
He flew to the ISS on a SpaceX spacecraft in November 2021.
In German, his last name is also a trade: bricklayer.
questions.description: A man from Saarland with a very long commute.
questions.fun_fact: Matthias Maurer's mission was called “Cosmic Kiss,” a love letter to outer space.

questions.question: I keep hot tea warm and cold lemonade cold for hours. A Berlin glassblower patented me over 100 years ago. What am I?
hints: People like to take me on hikes or picnics.
I have a double wall with almost no air in the space between.
My name comes from the Greek word for “hot”.
questions.description: A container that can never decide whether it likes summer or winter.
questions.fun_fact: It was modeled on a vacuum flask that the Scottish scientist James Dewar built for lab experiments.

questions.question: Spikes like these hang from the ceilings of many caves in Germany. What are they made of?
hints: Dripping water builds them up very slowly.
Chalk and seashells are made of it too.
The same stuff builds up as scale inside a kettle.
questions.description: Decorations that nature has been crafting for thousands of years.
questions.fun_fact: A stalactite often grows only about 1 cm (less than half an inch) every hundred years.

questions.question: Which of these towns is NOT on the Teutoburg Forest?
hints: The Hermann Monument stands in the Teutoburg Forest.
The town you're looking for lies on the Leine River.
It is known for its Gänseliesel, the goose girl statue.
questions.description: Three towns in Hermann's shadow, and one runaway that got lost.
questions.fun_fact: The Teutoburg Forest cuts right through the middle of Bielefeld, and locals just call it the “Teuto.”

questions.question: This is Mount Tabor, in Galilee. According to Christian tradition, what happened on its summit?
wrong_answers: The giving of the Ten Commandments
hints: It happened during the life of Jesus, not in the Old Testament.
Moses and Elijah appeared there next to Jesus.
The Gospels say his face shone like the sun and his clothes turned white.
questions.description: A nice round mountain that looks like it came out of a pudding mold.
questions.fun_fact: To drive up to the top of Mount Tabor, you take a road full of hairpin bends.

questions.question: Article 3 of Germany's Basic Law begins: “All persons shall be … before the law.” Which word is missing?
hints: Nobody may be favored or put at a disadvantage.
Rich or poor, famous or unknown: the same rules apply to everyone.
The word is the opposite of “different”.
questions.description: A line from the constitution, short enough to fit in a fortune cookie.
questions.fun_fact: Lawyer Elisabeth Selbert fought in 1949 to get “Men and women shall have equal rights” into Article 3 as well.

questions.question: Before some soccer games, everyone stands, the players bow their heads, and the stadium goes completely quiet. What is this called?
hints: It only lasts a very short time.
Nobody says a word.
Going by its name, it lasts exactly 60 seconds.
questions.description: A stadium moment when the drums and horns take a break.
questions.fun_fact: A minute of silence doesn't always last exactly 60 seconds; sometimes it's shorter.

questions.question: In 1991, Lothar Matthäus was the very first to win this FIFA title. What is a “Weltfußballer”?
questions.answer: The best player of the year
wrong_answers: The fairest player of the year
The top scorer at a World Cup
hints: It is an award for one single player.
National team coaches and captains get a vote.
It goes to whoever played best over one year.
questions.description: A title so big it really ought to come with its own globe.
questions.fun_fact: To this day, Lothar Matthäus is the only German man to have won the FIFA World Player of the Year title.

questions.question: Inside a thundercloud, raindrops are tossed up again and again and freeze. What can then come pelting down?
hints: It comes as hard grains of ice.
It can even happen in the middle of summer.
The grains can grow as big as marbles and dent car roofs.
questions.description: A thundercloud that likes to pass its bad moods down to you, loud and clear.
questions.fun_fact: Hailstones often travel up and down inside the cloud several times, growing layer by layer like an onion.

questions.question: People used to keep a tree frog in a jar with a tiny ladder. What was it for?
wrong_answers: To catch flies in the house
As a lucky charm for the harvest
To wake everyone in the morning
hints: In German, some TV presenters are jokingly named after him.
People checked every day how high he sat on the ladder.
People believed he knew whether you'd need an umbrella tomorrow.
questions.description: A green roommate with a ladder and a very important job.
questions.fun_fact: Tree frogs climb higher in warm weather because insects fly higher then, but they could never reliably forecast the weather.

questions.question: Daylight saving time starts in late March: at 2 a.m. that night, the clock jumps straight to …
hints: You get less sleep than usual that night.
A saying to remember it: “Spring forward, fall back.”
The clock is set ahead by exactly one hour.
questions.description: One night in March when the clocks suddenly start doing sports.
questions.fun_fact: Germany introduced daylight saving time as early as 1916, during the First World War, to save coal used for lighting.

questions.question: Which English word was voted Germany's Youth Word of the Year in 2020?
hints: If you are this, you have no clue what's going on.
It's an everyday word that German kids learn early in English class.
It's the opposite of “found”.
questions.description: The jury is old, the words are young, and adults still use them wrong.
questions.fun_fact: The year after, in 2021, “cringe” won.

questions.question: In 2019, Capital Bra broke a German record that the Beatles had held before him. Which one?
hints: It's about the official German charts.
His song “Cherry Lady” is one example.
It counts single songs that made it all the way to the top spot.
questions.description: A Berlin rapper who collects records faster than others collect Pfand bottles.
questions.fun_fact: Capital Bra was born in Siberia, grew up in Ukraine and came to Berlin as a child.

questions.question: “Dissen” is now in Germany's Duden dictionary, and rappers do it to rivals in their songs. What English word is “diss” short for?
hints: It's about putting someone down.
If you do it for a whole song, it's called a “diss track.”
The opposite would be respect.
questions.description: A word that marched straight from the rap stage into the dictionary.
questions.fun_fact: In English, “to diss” has been around since the 1980s; it came from US hip-hop.

questions.question: Frederick the Great had it built on vineyard terraces, and he's buried there too. Which palace is it?
hints: It's in Potsdam.
People often leave potatoes on the king's grave.
Its French name means “without worry.”
questions.description: A king who'd rather play the flute than rack his brains.
questions.fun_fact: Frederick wanted to be buried at Sanssouci, but his wish was only granted in 1991, 205 years after his death.

questions.question: If I don't draw the plans, nobody knows how to build the house. I design houses, buildings and skyscrapers. Who am I?
hints: I work a lot with pencils, rulers and plans on a screen.
My work starts before the first brick is laid.
I went to university to learn how to design buildings.
questions.description: Without this person, buildings would just be piles of bricks with good intentions.
questions.fun_fact: The word “architect” comes from Greek and means something like “chief builder.”

questions.question: What did the lying Baron Munchausen supposedly use his own hair for?
questions.answer: To pull himself out of a swamp
hints: He and his horse were in serious trouble.
He pulled hard, upward.
It was muddy and wet.
questions.description: A man whose stories were even longer than his wig.
questions.fun_fact: The real Hieronymus von Münchhausen did exist: he lived from 1720 to 1797 in Bodenwerder on the Weser River.

questions.question: War-weary soldiers were said to think only of me, because from me they went home. In German, if you don't get anything, you “understand only” me. What am I?
hints: I'm a place where people leave and arrive.
In big cities I often have a huge hall and a big clock.
I have tracks and platforms.
questions.description: The phrase for anyone whose brain quietly switches off in math class.
questions.fun_fact: War-weary soldiers are said to have answered that they understood „nur Bahnhof“ (“only train station”) when people talked about anything other than the trip home.

questions.question: What does the German saying “Ende gut, alles gut” mean?
questions.answer: A good ending makes up for the trouble
wrong_answers: Good things take a lot of time
hints: It's about how something turns out.
You often hear it after an exciting story, when you can finally breathe again.
You say it with relief when everything works out despite the mishaps.
questions.description: For everyone who reads the last page of a mystery novel first.
questions.fun_fact: Shakespeare's play “All's Well That Ends Well” is called “Ende gut, alles gut” in German.

questions.question: People once believed I lived in the heads of confused people. In German, whoever “has” me is thought a bit crazy. What am I?
hints: I'm an animal you often see in the garden.
Drivers sometimes show me to other drivers.

questions.question: I'm from Düsseldorf, I have Polish roots, and I became famous in the early 2010s with beauty and lifestyle videos on YouTube. Who am I?

questions.question: Before Inka Bause hosted “Bauer sucht Frau” on RTL, she became known as a Schlager singer in the 1980s. In which country?

questions.question: In which decade did “Bauer sucht Frau” start on RTL?
hints: Inka Bause has hosted the show since the first season.
The original comes from Britain and started in 2001.
The German version came a few years after the original.

questions.question: You see celebrities crawling through slime in a Dschungelprüfung (jungle trial). Since what year has RTL shown this?
hints: The show is called “Ich bin ein Star – Holt mich hier raus!”.

The first season aired shortly after the turn of the millennium.

questions.question: On “Schlag den Raab”, game 1 is worth one point, game 2 two, game 3 three, and so on. How many points are there in total over 15 games?

questions.question: Twins Lisa and Lena became famous for dance and lip-sync videos on the app musical.ly. What did that app become in 2018?

previous.feedback: The question text reads as translationese and is hard to follow when read aloud. “Eyes wide, often followed by an ‘ey’” is a dangling phrase: it sounds as if the eyes are followed by “ey”. And “say in front of…” sounds like an instruction to say something rather than “for example”. Suggested rewording: “You stand in front of the park's tallest roller coaster, eyes wide, and shout “Boah, ey!”. What does “Boah!” express here?”

questions.question: These carved figures are at Monte Albán in Oaxaca, Mexico. Which people built this city?

questions.question: In German, “usw.” stands for “und so weiter” (and so on). Which of these abbreviations means something quite different?

questions.question: Which German short word means a place with building blocks, nap time and childcare workers, where kids go before school?

questions.question: It sits on the front of the jersey and on the fans' scarves and flags, and at Schalke it holds “S04”. What is it?

questions.question: Saint Peter holds me, I open the gate of heaven, and on Bremen's coat of arms I shine silver on red. What am I?

questions.question: I was an Inca emperor, I turned my people into a great empire, and I had Machu Picchu built. Who am I?

hints: I came from France.

questions.question: I'm white and chubby, and my body is made of stacked tires. Who am I?

questions.question: After the 1898 war against the United States, a saying was born that you still hear: «Más se perdió en Cuba». What is it used for?

questions.question: Look at the photo: it's one of the fountains on Madrid's Paseo del Prado. What gets celebrated there?

questions.question: Look at this castle in Segovia, straight out of a fairy tale. Who lived in it for centuries?

questions.fun_fact: In 1862 a huge fire wrecked the Alcázar, and much of it had to be rebuilt.

questions.question: During Holy Week in Seville, I walk slowly behind the pasos in a robe, with my face covered and a tall pointed hood. Who am I?

My name recalls the town Jesus came from.
