previous.feedback: Source error: the riddle says the nazareno walks "behind the pasos" (source: "tras los pasos"), but in Seville's processions the nazarenos' rows walk in front of each paso, and the paso closes its section. Fix the Spanish source first (e.g. "delante de los pasos" or "acompaño a los pasos"), then re-translate. Otherwise the translation is faithful and natural. Fact check: wrong. The riddle says the nazareno walks 'behind the pasos'. In Seville's processions, nazarenos walk in front of each paso (the paso comes at the end of its section, followed by the band). Answer, wrong answers, hints and fun fact are otherwise fine.

questions.question: You're in Cádiz: the streets are full of costumes and chirigotas singing funny songs. What season is it?
hints: The Three Kings came not long ago.
It usually falls in February.
It's just before Lent, when it's still chilly.
questions.description: Here people dress up in costumes to tell the truth in song.
questions.fun_fact: The chirigotas and comparsas compete for weeks in a contest at the Gran Teatro Falla.

questions.question: People from Bilbao lovingly call their city “el Botxo”. What does that word mean?
hints: It's a Basque word that describes where the city sits.
Bilbao lies in a valley surrounded by mountains.
It's like a pit or a hollow.
questions.description: A pet name, like the nickname your family calls you at home.
questions.fun_fact: The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, opened in 1997, is covered in very thin sheets of titanium.

questions.question: Juanito, a boy in a Mexican sombrero, was the mascot of a FIFA World Cup. Which year?
hints: It was the first World Cup played in North America.
At that World Cup, Brazil and Pelé won their third title.
It came right at the start of a new decade.
questions.description: A boy in a hat who never played a single match but showed up in every sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico hosted the World Cup again in 1986, and that time the mascot was Pique, a jalapeño pepper with a mustache.

questions.question: You walk down Las Ramblas in Barcelona from Plaça de Catalunya all the way to the end. What do you find there?
hints: It's downhill the whole way.
At the end, you can already smell the sea.
It's a very tall column with a sailor on top.
questions.description: A street of living statues, flowers and pigeons: the hard part is reaching the end without stopping.
questions.fun_fact: The Columbus statue doesn't point toward America: it points out over the Mediterranean.

questions.question: I was born in Ávila in 1515, founded many convents of Carmelite nuns and wrote “vivo sin vivir en mí” (“I live without living in myself”). Who am I?
hints: I am a saint and a great mystic writer.
Some egg-yolk sweets typical of Ávila are named after me.
I share my name with a famous nun from Kolkata.
questions.description: A woman from Ávila who traveled more than a suitcase, and without GPS.
questions.fun_fact: The walls of Ávila are about 2.5 km (1.6 miles) long and have almost 90 towers.

questions.question: A British fleet led by Horatio Nelson attacked Santa Cruz de Tenerife and was driven back. In which century?
hints: At that time, Spain and Britain were at war.
Nelson had not yet won the Battle of Trafalgar of 1805.
It was in 1797.
questions.description: A very famous admiral arrived at the island full of confidence and went home very disappointed.
questions.fun_fact: Nelson took a bad memory home from Tenerife: he lost his right arm there.

questions.question: Look at this square in Seville, built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Which architect designed it?
hints: He worked on this square for more than ten years.
He is a key figure of Andalusian regionalist architecture.
His first name is the Spanish form of Hannibal, the Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants.
questions.description: Brick, tiles and little rowing boats: someone had a very inspired day.
questions.fun_fact: The square appeared in “Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones” as a palace on the planet Naboo.

questions.question: In a 16th-century picaresque novel, a blind man and his servant share a bunch of grapes like this one. The blind man takes them two at a time. Who takes them three at a time?
hints: He is the hero and narrator of the novel.
The blind man was his first master.
He was born in a river in Salamanca, and his nickname is a diminutive.
questions.description: Sharing is lovely, until one of you counts and the other keeps quiet.
questions.fun_fact: The blind man worked it out by pure logic: if he was eating two at a time and the boy didn't complain, the boy had to be eating even faster.

questions.question: A poet from Granada published “Romancero gitano” in 1928, with lines like “Verde que te quiero verde.” Who was he?
hints: He belonged to the Generation of '27.
He also wrote plays such as “Yerma”.
His family home, the Huerta de San Vicente, is now a museum in Granada.
questions.description: The moon, the moon, and a poet who stared at it a little too much.
questions.fun_fact: The book was such a hit that its author got fed up with being labeled “the Gypsy poet.”

questions.question: Look at this engraving by Gustave Doré. According to Cervantes, what made this country gentleman's brain dry up?
hints: He spent whole nights reading without sleeping.
His favorite books were full of giants and enchanters.
Because of what he read, he wanted to become a knight-errant.
questions.description: Proof that reading too much can have side effects too.
questions.fun_fact: In chapter 6, the priest and the barber burn almost his whole library, but they save “Amadís de Gaula” for being the best of its kind.

questions.question: In “Count Lucanor”, the count asks for advice and always gets a story with a moral in reply. Who gives the replies?
hints: He is a trusted adviser of the count.
The book was written by Don Juan Manuel in the 14th century.
His name sounds a lot like the word “patron”.
questions.description: History's very first advice column, moral included.
questions.fun_fact: One of its stories, about tricksters who weave invisible cloth for a king, is an early version of Andersen's “The Emperor's New Clothes”.

questions.question: This writer from the Canary Islands published “Fortunata and Jacinta” in 1887. Which literary movement does he belong to?
hints: He wanted to show society just as it was.
The novel is set in the Madrid of his day, with characters from every social class.
The movement’s name comes from the word “real”.
questions.description: Two women, one man and a whole lot of Madrid gossip.
questions.fun_fact: Galdós was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature several times, but never won it.

questions.question: In which century was “The House of Bernarda Alba” written, the play about a mother who shuts her five daughters up at home?
hints: The play is set in an Andalusian village in the middle of summer.
The author finished it a few weeks before the Spanish Civil War.
It premiered in Buenos Aires in 1945.
questions.description: A house with lots of daughters, lots of rules and no key to get out.
questions.fun_fact: Not a single man appears on stage in the whole play: every character is a woman.

questions.question: Before some movies, a little hopping lamp squashes a letter of the logo. Which of these movies does NOT start that way?
hints: The little lamp is the mascot of an animation studio.
That studio belongs to Disney and is based in California.
The answer stars a green ogre from another studio.
questions.description: A desk lamp with more bounce than a kangaroo on coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Pixar's little lamp is called Luxo Jr. and starred in a short film in 1986, before Toy Story even existed.

questions.question: In the 18th and 19th centuries, who sold and recited “pliegos de cordel”, cheap sheets of ballads, in streets and fairs?
hints: They often played a violin or a guitar along with it.
In Madrid they had a brotherhood with a royal privilege to sell certain printed sheets, such as almanacs and gazettes.
In Spanish these ballads were also named after them: “romances de…”.
questions.description: Literature hung up like laundry, only with verses instead of clothespins.
questions.fun_fact: The sheets were called “de cordel” (“of string”) because they hung from a string for people to see, like washing on a line.

questions.question: Every spring, the Madrid Book Fair fills one of the city's famous parks with book stalls. Which park?
hints: It was once a garden kept for the royal family.
It has a big lake with rowing boats and a glass palace.
It's right next to the Puerta de Alcalá.
questions.description: A park where every spring books pop up instead of flowers.
questions.fun_fact: The first Madrid Book Fair was held in 1933, and not in a park at all, but on the Paseo de Recoletos.

questions.question: I'm a thin, early-rising nobleman from La Mancha, about fifty; one day I made myself a knight and changed my name. What's my real name?
hints: At the end of the book I get my sanity and my old name back.
People called me “el Bueno” (“the Good”).
My real surname starts the same way as my knight's name.
questions.description: A man who changed his name without filling in a single form.
questions.fun_fact: At first Cervantes can't decide between Quijada, Quesada and Quejana, and only at the end reveals the name “Alonso Quijano el Bueno”.

questions.question: In 1519, five ships left Sanlúcar de Barrameda to make the first trip around the world. How many years did it take Elcano to get back?
hints: It was a very long voyage, with storms, hunger and lots of adventures.
It lasted more than one year but less than five.
Elcano got back to Spain in 1522.
questions.description: The longest field trip ever, and no stopping for sandwiches at a rest stop.
questions.fun_fact: Of about 240 men who set out, only 18 made it back with Elcano on the ship's return.

questions.question: Mojo picón is a red sauce with pepper, garlic, cumin and oil, and it has a green sister made with cilantro. Where is it from?
hints: It comes from some islands.
Those islands are in the Atlantic Ocean.
Mount Teide is there.
questions.description: A sauce that doesn't bite, but it does bring a little heat.
questions.fun_fact: The word “mojo” probably comes from the Portuguese “molho”, which means “sauce”.

questions.question: You sail along the whole coast of the Bay of Biscay. How many countries' coasts do you pass?
hints: Its coast runs north from Galicia.
North of the Pyrenees, its beaches are famous for surfing.
The French call it the Gulf of Gascony.
questions.description: A bay known for rough seas, where even the bravest captains get seasick.
questions.fun_fact: Sailors know the Bay of Biscay for its storms and its huge waves.

questions.question: They roam free high up on the Rock of Gibraltar, have very skillful hands and can open your backpack to steal your food. What animals are they?
hints: They're mammals and great climbers.
They're the only wild animals of their kind living free anywhere in Europe.
They're distant cousins of chimpanzees.
questions.description: On the Rock, the pickpockets have no pockets, but plenty of nerve.
questions.fun_fact: A legend says that if the monkeys ever leave the Rock, the British will leave too.

questions.question: In the Canary Islands, papas arrugadas are boiled in their skins until the water is gone. What ingredient, used in large amounts, leaves a white crust on them?
hints: It's a mineral people have used for thousands of years to keep food from going bad.
They used to be boiled in seawater.
It's what gives seawater its taste.
questions.description: Potatoes that stayed in the bathtub far too long.
questions.fun_fact: Papas arrugadas are usually eaten with red or green mojo sauce, and always with their skins on.

questions.question: Which of these ingredients do boquerones en vinagre usually NOT have?
hints: It's a dish of shiny white fillets with a touch of green on top.
The odd one out fits better on a pizza or a cold-cut board than with marinated fish.
It goes great with membrillo (quince paste), but not in this dish.
questions.description: Little fish that go to a vinegar spa and come out whiter than white.
questions.fun_fact: Before they're marinated, the anchovies are frozen for a few days for food safety.

questions.question: Which of these Galician rías is NOT part of the Rías Baixas?
hints: The Rías Baixas are on the southern part of the Galician coast.
The odd one out is much further north.
It belongs to the Rías Altas, in the north of A Coruña province, and is famous for its shipyards and naval base.
questions.description: Galicia has more arms of sea than a fairground octopus has arms.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to the mussel rafts (bateas) of the Rías Baixas, Galicia is one of the world's biggest mussel producers.

questions.question: A famous ad says “A Diamond Is Forever.” Which chemical element is this gem made of?
hints: It's the same element found in the graphite of pencils.
It's the basis of the chemistry of all living things.
Its chemical symbol is the letter C.
questions.description: Anything promised “forever” usually comes in a very small box.
questions.fun_fact: Frances Gerety wrote the line for De Beers in 1947, and in 1999 it was named the best advertising slogan of the 20th century.

questions.question: Which of these comics was NOT published by the Barcelona publisher Toray?
hints: Toray was a Barcelona publisher from the 1940s to the 1960s, a rival of the city’s big houses.
The odd one out came from the publisher that also printed “Mortadelo y Filemón”.
Bruguera published it from 1956.
questions.description: Barcelona churned out comics like churros, but not all of them came from the same churro stand.
questions.fun_fact: “Hazañas Bélicas”, drawn by Boixcar, was one of Toray’s biggest hits in the postwar years.

questions.question: The “great inventions of TBO” were signed by a made-up scientist, Professor Franz de… where?
hints: It's a capital in northern Europe.
The Little Mermaid statue is there.
It's the capital of Denmark.
questions.description: An egg-peeling machine that only needs three pulleys, a parrot and a lot of patience.
questions.fun_fact: The TBO inventions were so crazy that in Spain any absurd gadget is called “un invento del TBO”.

questions.question: In what year did the first issue of the humor magazine “El Jueves” come out?
hints: It was born in Barcelona, started by a group of satirical cartoonists.
It was born just as Spain was getting its freedom of the press back.
It was during the Transition, shortly after Franco's death: that same year Spain held its first democratic general election after the dictatorship.
questions.description: A magazine with a serious calendar problem.
questions.fun_fact: “El Jueves” (“Thursday”) proudly calls itself “the magazine that comes out on Wednesdays”.

questions.question: They're sung very softly to send babies to sleep, and a very famous one begins “Duérmete, niño”. What songs are they?
hints: They're sung at home, next to the crib.
Moms, dads and grandparents sing them at night.
In Spain they're called “nanas”.
questions.description: The only concert where the singer is happy when the audience falls asleep.
questions.fun_fact: Federico García Lorca traveled around Spain collecting folk lullabies and gave a famous lecture about them.

questions.question: In the movie “Superlópez” (2018), starring Dani Rovira, the hero arrives as a baby from another planet. Which one?
hints: It isn't Superman's planet: Superlópez is a parody of him.
The planet already appeared in Jan's comics.
Its name is an old Spanish way of saying “hush!”, like the librarian's “shh!”.
questions.description: A superhero who skipped the fancy cape and brought the one from the neighborhood dry cleaner.
questions.fun_fact: The planet Chitón was already in the comics by Jan, Superlópez's creator, long before the movie.

questions.question: “I'm a comic-strip tramp drawn by Josep Escobar. I live under a bridge and always dream of a roast chicken.” Who am I?
hints: I was born after the Civil War, when many people in Spain went hungry.
My stomach is always empty.
My name is also an everyday Spanish word for ravenous hunger.
questions.description: A character with a very simple diet: whatever he can get his hands on.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Spanish Academy's dictionary defines “carpanta” as “violent hunger”.

questions.question: In which decade did the publisher Bruguera, home of Mortadelo and Zipi y Zape, close down?
hints: Its characters lived on with another publisher.
It was after the Transition, when Spain was already a democracy.
Ediciones B took over its characters soon after.
questions.description: Mortadelo's laughter factory had its final chapter too.
questions.fun_fact: Bruguera started in 1910 under another name: El Gato Negro (The Black Cat).

questions.question: You're watching Eurovision 2008, and a man with a pompadour and a toy guitar asks you to dance the “brikindans” and the “robocop”. What's his name?
hints: He was a comedy character, not a real singer.
He was created on Andreu Buenafuente's show.
His song went “Baila el Chiki Chiki”.
questions.description: The day the toy store snuck into Europe's big song contest.
questions.fun_fact: Behind the pompadour was actor David Fernández, and the character was chosen by a public online vote.

questions.question: Las Ketchup, the group behind “Aserejé”, are daughters of a flamenco guitarist. What was their father's nickname?
hints: The group's name is a nod to their father's nickname.
It's a red vegetable.
Ketchup is made from it.
questions.description: A family tree that ends up in the bottle next to the fries.
questions.fun_fact: Las Ketchup's father is the guitarist Juan Muñoz from Córdoba, known as “El Tomate”: if he's the tomato, they're the sauce.

questions.question: Blanca Paloma went to Eurovision in 2023, and Melody in 2025. Who represented Spain in 2024?
hints: It’s a duo from Dénia, in Alicante.
It’s made up of a singer and her husband, who plays keyboards.
Its name sounds like a cloud of gas in space.
questions.description: A Eurovision year with more sparkle than your hometown disco.
questions.fun_fact: Eurovision 2024 was held in Malmö, Sweden, and Nebulossa’s singer, Mery Bas, became an icon with her hand fan.

questions.question: Which of these characters did NOT live in McDonaldland, the fantasy world of McDonald's commercials?
hints: Three of them were Ronald McDonald's friends.
The answer is the mascot of a different burger chain.
She is a red-haired girl with pigtails.
questions.description: A kingdom where hamburgers grow on trees and nobody pays taxes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2023, a purple shake made in honor of Grimace went viral on social media.

questions.question: Charles I is known by a famous phrase: “Charles I of Spain and V of…”. How does it end?
hints: His other number came from his title as emperor, not as king of Spain.
Before him, his grandfather Maximilian of Habsburg had been emperor of that same empire.
It's the country where Berlin and Munich are today.
questions.description: A king with two numbers, like someone with two phones: one for work and one for the empire.
questions.fun_fact: Charles I was born in Ghent, in today's Belgium, and when he arrived in Spain he could barely speak Spanish.

questions.question: Columbus sailed from Palos with the Pinta, the Niña and the Santa María, and one was lost in the Caribbean. How many ships did he bring back to Spain?
hints: Start by counting the ships that set out.
The Santa María was the one that stayed in America.
The Pinta and the Niña came back.
questions.description: The most famous cruise in history, and it didn't even have an all-you-can-eat buffet.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa María ran aground on Christmas Eve 1492, and its wood was used to build a fort called La Navidad.

questions.question: In “The Road to El Dorado,” El Dorado seems to be a city, but at first the name meant something else. Who?
questions.answer: An Indigenous chief covered in gold dust
wrong_answers: A Spanish king with a golden crown
An Inca god with a golden face
An English pirate loaded with gold
hints: His legend drove many conquistadors to set off on expeditions through jungles and mountains.
The conquistadors heard about him in the mountains of what is now Colombia.
In a ceremony, he bathed in a lake with his body coated in gold.
questions.description: Lots of people went looking for gold in the jungle; this question only asks you to dig a little in your memory.
questions.fun_fact: The legend grew from a ritual of the Muisca people at Lake Guatavita, where offerings of gold were thrown into the water.

questions.question: Velázquez's painting is called “Las Meninas”. At court, a menina was a…
questions.answer: Young lady who served the infanta
wrong_answers: Girl who sang in the palace
hints: The word comes from Portuguese.
It was a job at the palace, not a toy or a relative.
In the painting, two of them are tending to little Margarita.
questions.description: A painting so crowded that even the painter squeezed himself in.
questions.fun_fact: Picasso painted 58 pictures inspired by “Las Meninas”, and today they hang in the Museu Picasso in Barcelona.

questions.question: People said the sun “never set” on the Spanish Empire. In which century was that phrase born?
hints: It was in the time of the Habsburg kings.
Charles I and his son Philip II were on the throne.
It's the same century in which Elcano sailed around the world.
questions.description: An empire that never had to say good night.
questions.fun_fact: Under Philip II the empire stretched from the Americas to the Philippines, so it was always daytime in one of its lands.

questions.question: Soldiers of the tercios carried this lance, about 5 m (16 ft) long, called the pike. What was it mainly for?
hints: It was used in groups, with the soldiers forming a block.
Braced on the ground and pointing forward, it made a wall of spikes.
Enemy riders couldn't get close without running into them.
questions.description: A pole so long it wouldn't fit in even the biggest elevator.
questions.fun_fact: Pikemen formed a square bristling with points, and the arquebusiers fired from inside it or beside it.

questions.question: The series “Boundless” tells the story of the first trip around the world, begun by Magellan and finished by Elcano. In which century did it happen?
hints: It was a few years after Columbus's voyages.
Charles I was king of Spain.
They set out in 1519.
questions.description: The longest trip ever made with no GPS and no stops for gas.
questions.fun_fact: Of the five ships that set out, only one came back, the Victoria, with 18 men on board.

questions.question: You're at your village's verbena, dancing to the band in the square. When does a verbena usually take place?
hints: It's the coolest time of day in summer.
The colored light bulbs in the square are switched on.
Many people get home very late, almost at daybreak.
questions.description: A party where your grandma dances better than you, and she knows it.
questions.fun_fact: The party is named after verbena, a plant that people used to pick on the night of San Juan.

questions.question: I'm a narrow street in Pamplona's old town. Every July morning I fill up with runners in white and bulls, and I'm the longest stretch of the encierro. Who am I?
hints: I'm on TV every morning from July 7 to 14.
My name comes from an old post office.
My name starts with E.
questions.description: A street more famous than plenty of soccer players.
questions.fun_fact: An «estafeta» was a post office, and the street took its name from the one that used to be there.

questions.question: Thousands of them hang over the streets of Seville's Feria de Abril: round, colorful and lit up at night. What are the farolillos made of?
hints: They weigh very little and sway in the wind.
Heavy rain ruins them.
Your notebook is made of the same thing.
questions.description: Thousands of colorful moons hanging over your head.
questions.fun_fact: Fair lanterns fold up like an accordion, so they are stored almost flat from one year to the next.

questions.question: In which of these countries does the boa constrictor NOT live in the wild?
hints: The boa constrictor lives on just one continent... well, two that are joined together.
It likes warm, humid tropical jungles and forests.
The answer is in Asia, where pythons take this boa's place.
questions.description: A snake that gives the longest hugs in the world, and nobody asked for them.
questions.fun_fact: The boa constrictor isn't venomous: it catches its prey by squeezing it with its body.

questions.question: Every day of Fallas at 2 p.m., it rumbles for a few minutes in Valencia's city hall square, more heard than seen. What is the mascletà made of?
hints: You can feel the boom in your chest, like a vibration.
Many people listen with their mouths open to protect their ears.
Some kids set these off in the street, but here there are thousands at once.
questions.description: A concert where the best seat comes with your fingers in your ears.
questions.fun_fact: Valencia holds a mascletà in the city hall square every day from March 1 to March 19.

questions.question: Every year, the public picks its favorite Fallas ninot and saves it from the fire: the “ninot indultat”. What happens to it next?
hints: Anyone can see it, all year round.
There it sits next to ninots saved many decades ago.
It goes to a building with glass cases and tickets.
questions.description: A doll with incredible luck and very loyal fans.
questions.fun_fact: Valencia's Museo Fallero has kept the saved ninots since 1934.

questions.question: At noon on July 6, the chupinazo opens the Sanfermines in Pamplona. What is the chupinazo?
hints: It's launched from a balcony.
Each year a different guest, a person or a group, lights it.
It's a kind of firework.
questions.description: The most famous alarm clock in Navarre.
questions.fun_fact: The chupinazo has been launched from the balcony of Pamplona's City Hall since 1941.

questions.question: Kiko Veneno wrote “Volando voy”, but in 1979 a flamenco singer recorded it and made it famous. Who?
hints: He's one of the most famous singers in flamenco history.
He was from San Fernando, in Cádiz, and played with Paco de Lucía.
His stage name means “shrimp of the Island”.
questions.description: A song so light it hasn't landed in more than forty years.
questions.fun_fact: The song was on the album “La leyenda del tiempo”, which sold poorly at first and is now seen as one of the most important flamenco albums ever.

questions.question: In which decade did Manolo Escobar's song “Mi carro” come out?
hints: Spain was still under Franco when it came out.
Back then the SEAT 600 filled the roads.
It was the decade of the Beatles and the first Moon landing.
questions.description: A report of a stolen vehicle that half of Spain knows by heart.
questions.fun_fact: The lyrics begin: “Mi carro me lo robaron anoche cuando dormía” (“My cart was stolen last night while I was sleeping”).

questions.question: Estrella Morente, daughter of the flamenco singer Enrique Morente, was born in the city of this monument. Which one?
hints: It's an Andalusian city at the foot of the Sierra Nevada.
The monument is a Nasrid palace.
It's home to the Alhambra and the Albaicín neighborhood.
questions.description: A singer named after a star, with a palace for a home.
questions.fun_fact: Estrella Morente sang the flamenco version of “Volver” that Penélope Cruz lip-syncs in Almodóvar's film.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT part of the El Rocío pilgrimage in Huelva?
hints: The answer belongs to another very famous Spanish fiesta.
That other fiesta takes place in Valencia in March.
At El Rocío, nobody burns anything at the end.
questions.description: A pilgrimage where the streets are made of sand and nobody misses the asphalt.
questions.fun_fact: The village of El Rocío has sand streets, and many locals still get around on horseback.

questions.question: In flamenco, “pitos” aren't whistles: they're made by snapping your fingers. What are they for?
hints: They're used while others sing or dance.
They do the same job as hand claps, only quieter.
They have to do with rhythm.
questions.description: The only whistles that need neither batteries nor a referee.
questions.fun_fact: In flamenco, hand claps, finger snaps and heel stamping work as percussion, with no drum needed.

questions.question: It's the night of All Souls and you go to the bakery. Which of these sweets is NOT typical for this time of year?
hints: Three of them are sold in late October and early November.
The odd one out has a surprise hidden inside.
It's eaten on January 6.
questions.description: The dead don't eat, but the living make the most of it with a real sweet feast.
questions.fun_fact: Huesos de santo (“saint's bones”) are made of marzipan and traditionally filled with sweet egg yolk cream.

questions.question: In Spain, people say putting bread upside down brings bad luck. According to a popular explanation, who was bread once left that way for?
hints: His was not a job with many friends.
Nobody wanted to get his bread by mistake at the bakery.
He worked for the justice system of the time and often wore a hood.
questions.description: A loaf lying face down on the table, punished for no clear reason.
questions.fun_fact: Another old custom says that if bread falls on the floor, you should pick it up and kiss it.

questions.question: I wrote a story about a girl who admires her father, a doctor who dowses with a pendulum. My partner Víctor Erice filmed it in 1983 as “El Sur”. Who am I?
hints: I am a writer born in Badajoz who grew up in Andalusia.
Later I won the Herralde Prize with “La lógica del vampiro”.
My story was published in 1985 together with another one called “Bene”.
questions.description: A story whose compass needle always points down the map.
questions.fun_fact: Erice could only film the first half of the story: the part set in the south was never shot.

questions.question: Ramón Gómez de la Serna invented them and called them “humor + metaphor”: short, witty sentences. What are they called?
hints: Ramón wrote thousands of them over his lifetime.
They often compare everyday objects in surprising ways.
The word starts with “gre-”.
questions.description: Sentences so short they fit on a café napkin.
questions.fun_fact: Ramón Gómez de la Serna once gave a lecture sitting on a circus trapeze.

questions.question: Blasco Ibáñez published it in 1902. It is set among the fishermen of El Palmar, in Valencia’s Albufera, and TVE made it a series in 1978. Which novel is it?
hints: It belongs to its author’s cycle of Valencian novels.
Its characters live off fishing and the rice fields.
In the Albufera, tall reeds grow on muddy ground.
questions.description: Mosquitoes, boats and rice: the perfect plan for a Valencian in 1902.
questions.fun_fact: Blasco Ibáñez went to live in El Palmar for a while to research the novel before writing it.

questions.question: Inspector Amaia Salazar of the Baztán Trilogy returns to investigate in her home village in Navarre, shown in the photo. Which is it?
hints: It is the main town of the valley that gives the trilogy its name.
The Baztán river runs through it, between houses with wooden balconies.
The village has a family bakery that is key to the Salazar family's story.
questions.description: A lovely village for a stroll, if it weren't for the bodies in the novels.
questions.fun_fact: After the books' success, Elizondo began offering tours of the places in Dolores Redondo's novels.

questions.question: Salvador Espriu was born in Santa Coloma de Farners but grew up in a Maresme town he calls Sinera in his poems. Which town is it?
hints: Espriu is buried in this town's cemetery, the setting of “Cementiri de Sinera”.
It is a coastal town with a fishing harbor.
Read “Sinera” backwards.
questions.description: A town with a secret name, just like a superhero.
questions.fun_fact: “Sinera” is “Arenys” spelled backwards, a trick Espriu used to turn his hometown into a mythical place.

questions.question: What is the 1980s Spanish poetry movement of Luis García Montero and Felipe Benítez Reyes, named after a book by critic Robert Langbaum?
hints: It went for a warm, urban, almost conversational tone.
Its poets wrote about everyday life in the first person.
Langbaum’s 1957 book is about Browning, Tennyson and the dramatic monologue.
questions.description: Poems to read after you’ve paid off the mortgage.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Langbaum published “The Poetry of Experience” in 1957 about English poets, never imagining it would name a Spanish movement.

questions.question: You look at your DNI (ID card) and see you have two last names. Where do they come from?
questions.answer: One from your dad and one from your mom
wrong_answers: One from your town and one from your street
hints: They come from your closest family.
Your parents also have two last names each.
Each of your parents passes one on to you.
questions.description: Your full name doesn't fit in one box, and it's not your fault.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2017, parents in Spain can choose which last name goes first: the dad's or the mom's.

questions.question: Look at this. What is it?
hints: You use it at the post office (Correos).
You stick it in a corner of the envelope.
Without it, the letter doesn't get sent.
questions.description: It's small enough to fit on a fingernail, yet it can travel to the other side of the world.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's first stamp came out on January 1, 1850, and showed the face of Queen Isabella II.

questions.question: The ATM asks for your card's PIN. What do you have to type in?
hints: You type it on a keypad like a calculator's.
It's like your card's password.
They're digits, from 0 to 9.
questions.description: A secret so secret that not even your best friend should know it.
questions.fun_fact: The ATM's inventor wanted a six-digit code, but he chose four because his wife said she could only remember four.

questions.question: Many bank cards have a wave symbol on them, like a Wi-Fi sign lying on its side. What is it for?
questions.answer: To pay by holding it near the card reader
wrong_answers: To connect to the store's Wi-Fi
To charge your phone without a cable
To listen to the radio in the car
hints: You use it in stores.
You don't need to put the card into any slot.
You just hold it close to the little machine at the checkout.
questions.description: Waves so mysterious they seem like magic, yet they live in your wallet.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, when you pay up to 50 euros by holding your card near the reader, you usually aren't asked for your PIN.

questions.question: Listen: this animal is one of the most rescued from illegal wildlife trade in Latin America. What is it?
hints: It's a bird from the rainforest.
It has very bright feathers and a very long tail.
It's a big parrot, sometimes red, blue and yellow.
questions.description: A bird so colorful that smugglers want it, and so do the people who rescue it.
questions.fun_fact: Macaws can live more than 50 years, so a rescued macaw needs care for a very, very long time.

questions.question: You find it at the town hall, the post office or the bank: someone serves you behind glass with a gap, and people line up in front. What is it?
hints: That's where you talk to the person serving you.
Some offices have several with numbers, and a screen tells you which one to go to.
Its Spanish name, «ventanilla», comes from «ventana».
questions.description: The place where patience is measured in ticket numbers.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, «ventanilla» is also the word for the window of a car, a train or a plane.

questions.question: When you get your DNI in Spain, they scan your fingerprints. From how many fingers?
hints: It isn't all the fingers on one hand.
They don't scan your thumbs.
They're the fingers you point with.
questions.description: Your DNI knows you better than your hairdresser: it even knows the little lines on your fingers.
questions.fun_fact: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to ours that they are hard to tell apart.

questions.question: The doctor writes a prescription, and you take it to the pharmacy with the green cross. What does it say?
questions.answer: Which medicine to take and how much
wrong_answers: Which meals to eat each day
How much you weigh and how tall you are
hints: You need one when you're feeling sick.
The pharmacist reads it before giving you something.
It tells you the pills or syrup and how many times a day.
questions.description: A piece of paper famous for handwriting that nobody can read.
questions.fun_fact: The ℞ symbol on prescriptions comes from the Latin word “recipe”, which means “take”.

questions.question: Look at this license plate. Why do cars have one?
wrong_answers: To show how much gas is left
To show that the car is new
hints: Every car has a different one.
Speed cameras take photos of it.
It's like the car's name.
questions.description: The jewelry every car wears on the front and back, even when it doesn't match anything.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2000, Spanish license plates have four numbers and three letters, and never use vowels.

questions.question: You're filling in a EuroMillions ticket (Euromillones) and have marked your 5 numbers. How many stars do you still have to pick?
hints: Fewer than the numbers.
You pick them in a separate, much smaller grid.
Think of a pair of stars.
questions.description: To get rich, all you have to do is look at the sky… and guess right.
questions.fun_fact: EuroMillions started in 2004 with just three countries: Spain, France and the United Kingdom.

questions.question: The DGT puts them beside the road or on bridges, and a sign usually warns you first. What is a traffic radar for?
questions.answer: To measure how fast cars go
wrong_answers: To count the cars going by
hints: When they see one, lots of drivers brake.
If it catches you, a fine arrives at your home.
It has to do with going too fast.
questions.description: It stands perfectly still by the road, yet nothing gets past it.
questions.fun_fact: Spain also has section speed cameras (“radares de tramo”) that work out your average speed between two points on the road.

questions.question: Look at the big building with colorful domes on the Plaza del Pilar in Zaragoza. What was it built for?
hints: Inside there's a very famous statue of the Virgin Mary.
Its towers have bells.
On Sundays it fills up with people going to Mass.
questions.description: A square so big that the pigeons need a map to cross it.
questions.fun_fact: Every October 12, thousands of people bring flowers to this square and build a huge cloak of flowers for the Virgin of the Pilar.

questions.question: “I played for Real Madrid, then was its president for 35 years, and today its stadium bears my name.” Who am I?
hints: I was the club's president from 1943 to 1978.
My first name is the Spanish name of the apostle buried in Galicia.
My surname is heard every time Madrid plays at home.
questions.description: Some people get a street named after them; he got thousands of seats.
questions.fun_fact: When it opened in 1947 it was called Nuevo Estadio Chamartín; it took its president's name in 1955.

questions.question: The Las Ventas bullring in Madrid is the biggest in Spain. About how many people fit inside?
hints: It holds more people than many small soccer stadiums.
That's like the population of a large town.
The number has five digits and starts with a 2.
questions.description: A huge place where the crowd claps, whistles and waves white handkerchiefs.
questions.fun_fact: Las Ventas also hosts concerts: the Beatles played there in 1965.

questions.question: Rafael Moneo, who designed the Kursaal in San Sebastián, was the first Spaniard to win the Pritzker Prize. In which decade?
hints: The prize had already existed for quite a few years when Moneo received it.
By then he had already built the National Museum of Roman Art in Mérida.
He got it in the middle of that decade, about four years after 1992.
questions.description: Some prizes are won in an afternoon; others by building half a country in concrete.
questions.fun_fact: Moneo won the Pritzker in 1996, and in 2017 it went to RCR Arquitectes, a studio from Olot.

questions.question: In 1975, a “pet” that was just a stone in a box went on sale in the United States. About how many were sold?
hints: It was a huge craze, even though it lasted only a few months.
Its inventor became a millionaire.
It was more than a million.
questions.description: The perfect pet: it doesn't eat, doesn't bark and never runs away.
questions.fun_fact: The stone came with a manual explaining how to teach it to “sit” and “play dead.”

questions.question: Which of these buildings is NOT an example of Catalan Modernisme?
hints: Catalan Modernisme loves curves, colorful tiles and shapes from nature.
The odd one out is much older: it dates from the 16th century.
Philip II had it built near Madrid.
questions.description: Over a hundred years ago, Barcelona decided straight lines were just too boring.
questions.fun_fact: The Palau de la Música Catalana and the Sant Pau Hospital, both by Lluís Domènech i Montaner, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: Picasso painted it in Paris in 1907: five women with faces like African masks, the start of Cubism. Which painting is it?
hints: Today it hangs in MoMA in New York.
Its title recalls a street in Barcelona, not a French city.
The title includes the name of a city famous for its bridge and its popes.
questions.description: A painting so groundbreaking that the painter's friends nearly fainted when they saw it.
questions.fun_fact: Picasso didn't choose the title: a friend gave it, and it refers to Carrer d'Avinyó, a street in Barcelona.

questions.question: You're in a museum and see a telephone whose receiver is a lobster. Which Spanish artist made it in 1936?
hints: It's a surrealist work, the kind that puts together things that don't belong together.
The artist was born in Catalonia.
He's the painter of the melting clocks and the long, pointy mustache.
questions.description: A phone that pinches your ear when someone calls.
questions.fun_fact: Dalí made several lobster telephones for the English collector Edward James, who kept them in his house, and they really worked.

questions.question: I carve wood with a gouge, paint my figures' skin so it looks real, and my Christs and Virgins are carried in Holy Week processions. Who am I?
hints: I don't make furniture or work with silver.
My works ride on the pasos, but I don't carry them on my shoulders.
My name comes from “imagen” (image), because I make religious images.
questions.description: A workshop trade, the kind you learn by spending years watching the master's hands.
questions.fun_fact: Gregorio Fernández and Martínez Montañés were two great imagineros of the 17th century, and some of their carvings still go out in processions today.

questions.question: I paint so slowly that the Gran Vía at dawn took me years, and a Víctor Erice film showed me painting a quince tree. Who am I?
hints: My style is so realistic that my paintings look like photos.
I was born in Tomelloso, in the province of Ciudad Real.
I share my first name with Banderas, and my surname is a very common one.
questions.description: If this painter had to paint a snail, the snail would finish the race first.
questions.fun_fact: The film about his quince tree, “El sol del membrillo” (“The Quince Tree Sun”), won the Jury Prize at the 1992 Cannes Film Festival.

questions.question: This detail is from a painting by Juan Bautista Maíno, made in 1635 for the Hall of Realms. Which recaptured place does it celebrate?
questions.answer: Bahia de Todos os Santos, Brazil
hints: It was a victory over the Dutch in 1625.
The place is across the Atlantic, in lands that were Portuguese at the time.
Today the city of Salvador stands there, in northeastern Brazil.
questions.description: Philip IV wanted a hall to show off his victories, and the painters split up the battles like trading cards.
questions.fun_fact: Maíno was a Dominican friar and taught drawing to the young Philip IV.

questions.question: Joan Manuel Serrat started out singing in Catalan and is called “el Noi del Poble-sec,” after the neighborhood where he was born in 1943. In which city was he born?
hints: It's a city by the sea.
It has one of the biggest ports in the Mediterranean.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família and La Rambla.
questions.description: A singer-songwriter with more touring miles than a delivery van, who never forgets his old neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: In 1968 Serrat was set to sing at Eurovision, but he wanted to sing in Catalan, so Massiel took his place and went on to win with “La, la, la.”

questions.question: You're on the beach and someone sings Serrat's “Quizá porque mi niñez sigue jugando en tu playa”. What year did “Mediterráneo” come out?
hints: Franco was still ruling Spain.
It was at the start of a decade.
It came out two years after humans first walked on the Moon.
questions.description: The song that makes even people in inland Teruel miss the beach.
questions.fun_fact: Serrat wrote much of the album “Mediterráneo” in a fishing village on the Costa Brava.

questions.question: You turn on the radio and hear the Los 40 Principales chart, which began as a Cadena SER show. In which decade was it born?
hints: It's older than it seems.
It's older than the compact disc, the CD.
It was back when the Beatles were still together.
questions.description: A chart so famous it has spent decades telling you which song you'll hum in the shower.
questions.fun_fact: Los 40 Principales began in 1966 as a show on Radio Madrid and only became its own station in 1979.

questions.question: Along with Alaska and Carlos Berlanga, which musician founded Alaska y Dinarama and, years later, Fangoria with her?
hints: He isn't a singer: he played bass.
He still plays with Alaska today.
He shares a first name with one of the Mecano members, but he isn't him.
questions.description: In La Movida, people didn't just start bands: they started gangs of friends with a synthesizer.
questions.fun_fact: Alaska and Nacho Canut were already playing together before Dinarama, in Kaka de Luxe and in Alaska y los Pegamoides.

questions.question: This band was led by Pau Donés, had a hit in 1998 with “Depende”, and its name is a Spanish expression for “a beating”. Which city is it from?
hints: It's a city by the sea.
It's the capital of an autonomous community.
It hosted the 1992 Olympic Games.
questions.description: A band named after a home remedy that, luckily, only handed out good songs.
questions.fun_fact: “La flaca”, Jarabe de Palo's first big hit, was inspired by a girl Pau Donés met in Cuba.

questions.question: I was born in Madrid in 1966, my father was an opera singer, and in 1993 I had a solo hit with “Desesperada”. Who am I?
hints: Before going solo, I was the voice of an '80s pop band.
That band was named after the cheer heard at bullfights and flamenco shows, said twice.
I was the singer of Olé Olé.
questions.description: A voice that played in the '90s from every boombox with half-dead batteries.
questions.fun_fact: Marta Sánchez left Olé Olé in 1991, and her first solo album, “Mujer”, was a huge hit.

questions.question: Which word does NOT appear in the chorus of “Ni tú ni nadie” by Alaska y Dinarama?
hints: The chorus talks about something that rings.
The chorus is about how hard it is to admit you were wrong.
“Mil campanas suenan en mi corazón, qué difícil es pedir perdón” (“A thousand bells ring in my heart, how hard it is to say sorry”).
questions.description: A chorus so catchy that nobody, but nobody, can get it out of your head.
questions.fun_fact: “Ni tú ni nadie” came out in 1984 on the album “Deseo carnal” and is one of the anthems of the Madrid Movida.

questions.question: I'm food for sharing, served nice and crispy, and Madrid rocker Ramoncín called himself my king in a song. What am I?
hints: People usually eat me with their hands.
I'm a classic of fast-food chains and takeout.
I'm coated in flour and dropped in hot oil, and I have drumsticks and wings.
questions.description: Some kings have crowns, some have thrones, and some have paper napkins.
questions.fun_fact: Ramoncín was stuck forever with the nickname “el Rey del Pollo Frito” (the King of Fried Chicken), from one of his songs of the late 1970s.

questions.question: In which decade was El Canto del Loco, Dani Martín's band from Madrid, formed?
hints: The members met at an acting school.
Their first album came out right at the turn of the century.
They first got together in the middle of that decade, shortly after the Barcelona Olympics.
questions.description: A band whose name you wouldn't mention in a job interview, but who filled stadiums.
questions.fun_fact: Dani Martín was studying to become an actor when he met his El Canto del Loco bandmates.

questions.question: Two Belgians wrote this song in 1971, and in 1973 Manolo Escobar made it the great anthem of Spanish verbenas. Which song is it?
hints: Tourists sing it at the top of their lungs on the beach.
In the early 1970s it was a summer hit across half of Europe.
The title names Manolo Escobar's country.
questions.description: A song that blasts from the speakers at a verbena (street party) louder than the fireworks.
questions.fun_fact: The original version was in Dutch, sung by the Belgian singer Samantha under the title “Eviva España”.

questions.question: Leo Jiménez was the voice of this Madrid heavy metal band, formed in 1992, with albums like “Vientos de guerra.” What is it called?
hints: It was founded by musicians from 1980s heavy metal bands.
Several singers have fronted the band over the years.
It shares its name with a famous battle of the American Revolutionary War.
questions.description: Long hair in the wind, leather jackets and guitars that don't know how to play quietly.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Saratoga, Leo Jiménez also sang for Stravaganzza and launched his own solo project.

questions.question: The Caldera de Bandama in Gran Canaria is a huge crater almost a kilometer (over half a mile) wide. Roughly how deep is it?
hints: It is much deeper than a five-story building.
From the rim, people at the bottom look like ants, but you can still see them.
It's about as long as two soccer fields placed end to end.
questions.description: A hole in Gran Canaria so big it has held vineyards, houses and even a few lost hikers.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Daniel van Damme, a Flemish merchant who planted vineyards inside the crater in the 16th century.

questions.question: I'm an area whose rocks, fossils and landscapes tell the story of the Earth, and UNESCO gives me its label. Spain has Cabo de Gata and Lanzarote. What am I?
hints: My international label is all about geology.
What matters most to me are stones, volcanoes and fossils.
My name starts with the Greek prefix that means “Earth”.
questions.description: A place where your hiking boots end up dirtier than a kid's knees after recess.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the European countries with the most UNESCO geoparks.

questions.question: Spain's ZEPAs, special protection areas for birds, came from a European Community directive. In which decade was it passed?
hints: It came before Spain joined the European Community.
The well-known Natura 2000 network came more than a decade later.
It was passed the same year Margaret Thatcher came to power.
questions.description: An acronym with wings that flies around half of Spain without paying a single toll.
questions.fun_fact: The Birds Directive dates from 1979 and is one of the oldest nature protection laws in Europe.

questions.question: Look at this crest and those orange cheeks: which group of birds does this bird belong to?
hints: It is a very common pet bird kept in cages.
It raises and lowers its crest depending on its mood.
It is related to some large white birds from Australia with a big crest.
questions.description: A bird that always looks like it just styled its hair with gel.
questions.fun_fact: The cockatiel is the smallest cockatoo in the world, and many males learn to whistle songs.

questions.question: King Alfonso XIII, a big fan of the Sierra de Gredos, created a royal hunting reserve there in 1905 because one species was close to dying out. Which one?
hints: Today, hikers who climb Gredos often see it and take photos of it.
It lives on rocky crags and climbs almost vertical walls.
The males have huge horns that curve backward.
questions.description: A king who went out hunting and came back wanting to save the prey.
questions.fun_fact: It is thought that only a few dozen ibexes were once left in Gredos; today there are thousands.

questions.question: It's a conifer from the juniper family, the trade winds have bent it almost to the ground, and it's the symbol of El Hierro. What tree is it?
hints: It grows in a place called La Dehesa, in the west of the island.
Its fruits look like small berries, like a juniper's.
Its name is also a woman's first name.
questions.description: A tree so famous on its island that it even shows up on tourist souvenirs.
questions.fun_fact: Some of El Hierro's sabinas grow almost sideways, their branches pointing where the wind pushes them.

questions.question: In Ses Salines Natural Park, between Ibiza and Formentera, salt is taken from the sea in large ponds. Since when?
hints: It is far, far older than tourism on the island.
Peoples who sailed all over the Mediterranean were already using it.
The Phoenicians and the Romans already knew these salt flats.
questions.description: A Balearic park where the sea dries up on purpose and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: The seagrass meadows of this park are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: This is the Gruta de las Maravillas, one of the most visited show caves in Spain. Which natural park is it in?
questions.answer: Sierra de Aracena y Picos de Aroche
wrong_answers: Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas
hints: It's in Andalusia, near Portugal.
It's in the same province as Doñana.
Jabugo, famous for its Iberian ham, is in this park.
questions.description: A place so marvelous they even put it in the name.
questions.fun_fact: The Gruta de las Maravillas opened to the public in 1914 and was the first cave in Spain prepared for tourists.

questions.question: In Twitch chat, people use little pictures from each channel, like the famous Kappa, and subscribers unlock more. What are they called?
hints: They look like the emojis on your phone.
They show faces and reactions.
Their name is related to the word “emotion”.
questions.description: When words fail you, the chat has plenty of little faces to spare.
questions.fun_fact: Kappa, one of the most used images on Twitch, is the face of a former employee of the company.

questions.question: In the 1960s, huge vacuum-tube radios gave way to small battery ones, which in Spain were named after their key part. What were they called?
hints: Lots of people took one to the beach to listen to soccer.
It's also the name of a tiny electronic component.
That component was invented in 1947 and replaced vacuum tubes.
questions.description: Grandpa's smartphone, perched on a beach towel.
questions.fun_fact: The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs, and today a phone has billions of them inside.

questions.question: I was born in Collbató in 1871, founded the Orfeó Català with Lluís Millet and wrote the zarzuela “Doña Francisquita”. Who am I?
hints: I'm a Catalan composer who also had big hits in the theaters of Madrid.
Another of my famous zarzuelas is “Bohemios”.
My surname means “you live” in Spanish.
questions.description: A man who spent his life getting half the country to sing, in choirs and on stage.
questions.fun_fact: The Orfeó Català he founded has its home in the Palau de la Música Catalana, which opened in 1908.

questions.question: This is the mocadorà, the traditional sweethearts' gift in Valencia every October 9. What are its little figures made of?
hints: It's given on Sant Donís, the day of Valencia's patron saint of lovers.
They're sweet and colorful, and they come wrapped in a handkerchief.
They're made from ground almonds and sugar.
questions.description: A gift for your sweetheart, wrapped up as if you had a cold.
questions.fun_fact: The two classic figures of the mocadorà are called “piuleta” and “tronaor,” just like two kinds of fireworks.

questions.question: Fabada, Asturias's most famous stew, comes with chorizo and morcilla, and its main ingredient is called “fabes” in Asturian. What are they?
hints: They're a legume.
They're big, soft and pale.
In other parts of Spain they're called “judías blancas.”
questions.description: The dish that makes an Asturian nap mandatory.
questions.fun_fact: The fabes in fabada are so big and buttery that they have their own official quality label: “Faba Asturiana.”

questions.question: Which autonomous community is marked on this map?
hints: It's in the Mediterranean Sea.
It doesn't touch the mainland: it's made up of islands.
Mallorca, Menorca and Ibiza are there.
questions.description: This region went off to sunbathe and never came back to the mainland.
questions.fun_fact: Formentera has no airport: you have to get there by boat, usually from Ibiza.

questions.question: Look at this hill in Rome: it gave its name to capitols around the world. To which god was its great temple dedicated?
hints: He was the most important god in Rome.
His favorite weapon fell from the sky during storms.
He is the Roman version of Zeus.
questions.description: The hill that lent its name to half the world's domed buildings.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the sacred geese of the Capitol woke the Romans with their honking and saved the hill from a night attack by the Gauls.

questions.question: “My name holds a building with towers and walls, and an animal with a mane. I'm Spain's largest autonomous community.” Who am I?
hints: I'm in north-central Spain.
I have nine provinces, such as Burgos and Salamanca.
The animal in my name is the king of the jungle.
questions.description: A region with a name straight out of a tale of knights.
questions.fun_fact: Castilla y León is bigger than whole countries such as Portugal or Austria.

questions.question: Which of these autonomous communities of Spain has NO coastline?
hints: The other three are on the Bay of Biscay or the Atlantic Ocean.
This region borders France across the Pyrenees.
Its capital is Pamplona.
questions.description: Three regions packed their swimsuits, and one packed its hiking boots.
questions.fun_fact: Navarra is only a few kilometers (a few miles) from the sea, but the Basque Country takes up the whole coast between it and the Bay of Biscay.

questions.question: Which of these monuments is NOT in the Community of Madrid?
hints: Three of them are in the center of the capital.
The one you want is many centuries older than the other three.
It is in a city in Castile and León famous for its cochinillo (roast suckling pig).
questions.description: One of these monuments sneaked onto the capital's list without changing its address.
questions.fun_fact: The Aqueduct of Segovia stands without any mortar: its granite blocks are held up by their own weight alone.

questions.question: Look at this athlete standing on a log and chopping it with an axe. Which region of Spain is this rural sport typical of?
hints: It's a region in the north, with lots of forests and mountains.
It grew out of the work of woodcutters in mountain villages, and today it has championships with big crowds.
People there speak Euskera.
questions.description: Athletes who don't need a gym: a log and a lot of grit are all it takes.
questions.fun_fact: Bets between champion aizkolaris (log choppers) have drawn thousands of spectators to a single town square.

questions.question: Look at this Andalusian gazpacho. Which food group are almost all of its ingredients from?
hints: It's made in a blender and served cold.
Its red color comes from its star ingredient.
It has tomato, pepper, cucumber and garlic.
questions.description: A soup that took a vacation and came back nice and refreshed.
questions.fun_fact: Before the tomato arrived from the Americas, gazpacho was white: it was made with bread, garlic, oil and vinegar.

questions.question: This is one of the facades of the Sagrada Família in Barcelona. Whose family is it named after?
hints: It's a church.
This family appears in Christmas nativity scenes.
It's made up of Mary, Joseph and their son.

hints: It's a word people shout a lot to cheer each other on.
In Basque, “gora” is also used to cheer: “Gora!” is like saying “Long live!”.
It's the way you look to see the sky.
questions.description: An anthem so cheerful its title already sounds like a party chant.
questions.fun_fact: The official anthem of the Basque Country, adopted in 1983, has no official lyrics: only its melody is played.

questions.question: Look at this coat of arms. Which Spanish city does it belong to?
hints: It's a city in Castile and León.
It's near Madrid, on the other side of the Guadarrama mountains.
It's famous for its Roman aqueduct and its roast suckling pig.
questions.description: A coat of arms so old it looks like it's made of real stones.
questions.fun_fact: The granite blocks of the Segovia aqueduct hold together without any mortar between them.

questions.question: A philologist from Zamora, a fierce critic of power, wrote the lyrics of the Community of Madrid's anthem in 1983. Who was he?
hints: He was a professor of Latin Philology at the Complutense University.
He was also a poet, playwright and translator of Greek and Latin authors.
His second surname is the Spanish word for “bald.”
questions.description: A regional anthem written by someone who distrusted almost everything official.
questions.fun_fact: The Madrid anthem starts with a very unusual line: “Yo estaba en el medio: giraban las otras en corro” (“I was in the middle: the others spun around me in a ring”).

questions.question: The coat of arms of this autonomous community shows Hercules between two columns, holding two lions. Which one is it?
hints: It's the most populous region in Spain.
It has eight provinces, and its flag is green and white.
Its capital is Seville.
questions.description: A region that hired a mythological strongman as its doorman.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Hercules split Europe from Africa and set two columns at the Strait of Gibraltar.

questions.question: Where does the name of paella, the famous Valencian rice dish, come from?
questions.answer: From the pan it's cooked in
wrong_answers: From the town where it was invented
hints: It comes from Valencian.
In Valencian, it's a very ordinary kitchen word.
It's a wide, flat object with two handles.
questions.description: A dish with so much character that even its name has a story of its own.
questions.fun_fact: In Valencian, “paella” means frying pan, and it comes from the Latin “patella”, a kind of plate or tray.

questions.question: How many provinces does the Region of Murcia have?
hints: It is a region in the southeast.
It is one of the smallest regions on the mainland.
The province has the same name as the region.
questions.description: A region that loves to show off its orchards, its sunshine and its pimentón.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has seven regions with only one province, including Murcia, Madrid and Cantabria.

questions.question: About how deep is El Tajo, the gorge that splits the Málaga town of Ronda in two?
hints: It's much deeper than a house, but not as deep as a mountain is tall.
The Puente Nuevo that crosses it is almost the same height from bottom to top.
It's like a building about 30 stories tall.
questions.description: A town so pretty that someone decided to cut it in half for extra views.
questions.fun_fact: Building Ronda's Puente Nuevo took about 34 years: work began in 1759 and ended in 1793.

questions.question: The griffon vulture has wings about 2.5 m (8 ft) across, flies in groups over canyons and eats dead animals. What does that achieve?
wrong_answers: It spreads seeds across the hills
hints: Its work also helps the cows and sheep that are still alive.
Shepherds like it because it keeps the countryside clean.
A dead animal left to rot can make living ones sick.
questions.description: A bird with a terrible reputation that, deep down, is a very useful neighbor.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is home to the vast majority of all the griffon vultures in Europe.

questions.question: The Patrulla Águila paints the sky with red and yellow smoke. In which Spanish autonomous community is its base?
hints: Its base is on the Mediterranean coast.
It shares its base with the General Air Academy, where Spain's military pilots are trained.
The Mar Menor is very close to the base.
questions.description: Some pilots who go out to party and leave the sky looking like a mural.
questions.fun_fact: The Patrulla Águila was created in 1985 and flies C-101 jets, the same planes Academy students learn to fly in.

questions.question: Rossy de Palma made her film debut with Almodóvar in “Law of Desire.” In which decade?
hints: Franco's dictatorship had already ended.
The Movida madrileña began a few years after Franco's death.
It was the same decade Spain joined the European Community.
questions.description: A one-of-a-kind face that looks like it stepped out of a Picasso painting, and she says so proudly.
questions.fun_fact: Before becoming an actress, Rossy de Palma sang in a Movida band called Peor Impossible.

questions.question: If you board the Tornado-class boat in which Fernando Echávarri and Antón Paz won gold at Beijing 2008, how many hulls does it have?
hints: It is not an ordinary single-hull sailboat.
It has the same shape as many fast ferries and tourist boats.
The Tornado class is a catamaran.
questions.description: A question for anyone who gets seasick just looking at a harbor.
questions.fun_fact: The sailing races of Beijing 2008 weren't held in Beijing at all, but in the coastal city of Qingdao.

questions.question: In 2021, at Torrey Pines (California), Jon Rahm became the first Spanish golfer to win this major. Which one?
hints: It's played in June and has a reputation as the toughest major, with narrow fairways and long grass.
Torrey Pines sits on the Pacific Ocean, near San Diego.
It's the national open of the country California belongs to.
questions.description: A Basque who sends the ball farther than you can throw a slipper.
questions.fun_fact: Jon Rahm won his second major in 2023: the Masters, green jacket included.

questions.question: Ander Mirambell was the first Spaniard to slide head-first and face-down at the Winter Olympics. In which event?
hints: It's raced down an icy track, on a sled.
In luge you lie on your back with your feet in front.
Its name is also the word for all the bones in your body.
questions.description: Racing down a frozen slide at over 100 km/h (62 mph): just what your parents would ban at the playground.
questions.fun_fact: Mirambell made his debut at the Vancouver 2010 Games and went on to compete in four Olympics.

questions.question: Jordi Sánchez is to Antonio Recio as José Luis Gil is to… whom, in «La que se avecina»?
hints: He's a character who lives in Mirador de Montepinar.
He becomes a town councilor and president of the residents' association.
His surname is the Spanish word for someone who looks after sheep.
questions.description: An actor who has spent more hours in a fictional housing complex than in his own home.
questions.fun_fact: José Luis Gil is also the voice of Buzz Lightyear in the Spanish version of «Toy Story».

questions.question: «Arrayán» was Canal Sur's daily series for years. What is an arrayán?
hints: You can see it in many Andalusian gardens.
One of the courtyards of the Alhambra in Granada is named after it.
In English it's called myrtle.
questions.description: A soap opera with a very Andalusian name, even if it doesn't sound like one.
questions.fun_fact: In the Alhambra's Court of the Myrtles, myrtle hedges line a long pool that reflects the Comares Tower.

questions.question: They are old river valleys flooded by the sea, mussels are farmed in them on rafts called bateas, and they split into Altas and Bajas. In which region are they?
hints: It's in northwestern Spain.
Its coast faces the Atlantic Ocean to the north and the west.
It's the land of pulpo a feira and Santiago de Compostela.
questions.description: Where the sea sneaks upriver without asking, and the mussels throw a party.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its bateas, Galicia is one of the world's biggest mussel producers.

questions.question: I flow under the Roman bridge of Mérida, cross Badajoz, form the border with Portugal and reach the sea near Ayamonte. Which river am I?
hints: I cross Extremadura.
I flow into the Atlantic Ocean in the province of Huelva.
My name starts with “Guad”, like another great river in Andalusia, but I'm not the one in Seville.
questions.description: A river with more passport stamps than most tourists.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman bridge of Mérida is about 800 meters (2,600 ft) long, one of the longest bridges the Romans left behind.

questions.question: If you tour the Lagunas de Ruidera Natural Park, how many lagoons in a chain, linked by waterfalls, can you see?
hints: There are more than you can count on the fingers of one hand.
They lie in a row along the upper Guadiana, between Ciudad Real and Albacete.
There are more than 10 but fewer than 20.
questions.description: A water necklace that La Mancha puts on for photos.
questions.fun_fact: In Don Quixote, Cervantes tells how the wizard Merlin turned the lady Ruidera, her daughters and her nieces into lagoons.

questions.question: When someone says “aprovechando que el Pisuerga pasa por Valladolid”, what do they mean?
questions.answer: They're using any excuse to bring up something unrelated
wrong_answers: Something is happening very slowly, with no rush
You should just go with the flow
Something is as old as the river itself
hints: It's said with a bit of irony.
People usually say it right before changing the subject.
It's like grabbing any excuse to raise another topic.
questions.description: A river more famous for a saying than for all the water it carries.
questions.fun_fact: The Pisuerga rises in the Montaña Palentina and ends up flowing into the Duero.

questions.question: It flows through Córdoba and Seville, and its name comes from Arabic. What does “Guadalquivir” mean?
hints: “Guad” comes from an Arabic word meaning river.
It is the main river of Andalusia, and to the Arabs it was the one that mattered most.
It's the opposite of “little river.”
questions.description: The Arabs named it, and Andalusia hasn't wanted to rename it in over a thousand years.
questions.fun_fact: The Guadalquivir is the only big river in Spain that seagoing ships can sail up to an inland city: Seville.

questions.question: A glacier carved it, it's in Zamora, and legend says a sunken village lies at its bottom whose bells ring on St. John's Eve. Which lake is it?
hints: It's the largest lake of glacial origin in the Iberian Peninsula.
It's near the border with Portugal, in Castile and León.
It's inside a natural park in northwestern Zamora, near the Sierra de la Culebra.
questions.description: A lake with so much history underneath that even the fish have a bell tower.
questions.fun_fact: The legend of the sunken village inspired Miguel de Unamuno's novel “Saint Manuel Bueno, Martyr”.

questions.question: Miguel Servet, a 16th-century doctor from Aragon, explained that blood leaves the heart, mixes with air in another organ and comes back redder. Which organ?
hints: You have two of them.
It's inside your chest, very close to your heart.
They fill up every time you breathe in.
questions.description: A doctor who turned blood into a travel agency selling round-trip tickets.
questions.fun_fact: Servet published this in 1553, about 75 years before William Harvey described the full circulation of the blood.

questions.question: INTA runs this huge antenna in Robledo de Chavela, near Madrid. What is it for?
hints: It works day and night, pointing at the sky.
It is part of a network with twin antennas in California and Australia.
It picks up messages from probes heading to Mars or even farther.
questions.description: A giant ear planted in the hills outside Madrid, and no giant is missing it.
questions.fun_fact: Robledo still tracks the Voyager probes, which have already left the solar system.

review.feedback: Source: the fun fact says Robledo tracks "the Voyager probes", but only Voyager 1 is visible from Madrid. Voyager 2 is far south in the sky and can only be reached from Canberra. The source fun fact should name Voyager 1 only ("Robledo still tracks Voyager 1, which has already left the solar system"), and the translation should then follow. Otherwise the translation is faithful and natural.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says Robledo tracks "the Voyager probes", but Voyager 2 is too far south in the sky to be seen from Madrid. Only Canberra can reach it, so only Voyager 1 is tracked from Robledo. questions.question: Thanks to the ONT, founded in 1989, Spain has been a world leader in something for over 30 years. In what?
hints: It takes a lot of generosity.
Hospitals coordinate it, sometimes by helicopter and against the clock.
The T in ONT stands for “trasplantes”.
questions.description: A Spanish world record that isn't won by running or cooking.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has more than 40 donors per million people, over twice the European Union average.

questions.question: In which year did “The Others”, Alejandro Amenábar's ghost movie starring Nicole Kidman, come out?
hints: It was the first movie Amenábar made in English.
It came about five years after “Tesis”, Amenábar's first movie.
It was the same year the first Harry Potter movie and “The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring” came out.
questions.description: A house full of closed curtains and people not quite sure which century they live in.
questions.fun_fact: Although the story is set on the island of Jersey, the mansion in “The Others” is a palace in Las Fraguas, Cantabria.

questions.question: This director from La Mancha made “Volver” (2006), with Penélope Cruz singing a tango. Who is he?
hints: He started making movies in Madrid during the Movida.
He won Oscars for “All About My Mother” and for the screenplay of “Talk to Her”.

questions.fun_fact: In “Volver”, the voice you hear singing the tango isn't Penélope Cruz's but that of flamenco singer Estrella Morente.

questions.question: This Galician actor played Malamadre, the prisoner who leads a riot in “Cell 211”. Who is he?
hints: He was born in the province of Lugo.
He won the Goya for Best Actor for “Take My Eyes” and for “Cell 211”.
His last name starts with T.
questions.description: A Galician with a stare that could start a riot in a whole prison.
questions.fun_fact: “Cell 211” was filmed in the old provincial prison of Zamora and won 8 Goya Awards, including Best Film.

questions.question: In Spain's dub of “Terminator 2,” Schwarzenegger doesn't say “Hasta la vista, baby” but “… baby.” Which word is missing?
hints: They changed it because the original line was already in Spanish, so in Spain it wouldn't have sounded exotic.
The new word had to sound as foreign to a Spaniard as “hasta la vista” does to an American.
It's how you say goodbye in Japanese.
questions.description: A robot from the future who says goodbye in a different language depending on where you watch the film.
questions.fun_fact: The Latin American Spanish dub kept the original “Hasta la vista, baby.”

questions.question: He played Paco in “7 vidas” and the teacher who travels to Almería to meet John Lennon in “Living Is Easy with Eyes Closed.” Who is he?
hints: He was born in La Rioja.
He won the Goya for Best Actor for that English teacher.

questions.description: An actor who has already been through seven lives, and like a cat, still has a few to spare.

questions.question: In “A Monster Calls,” the monster visits Conor at 12:07, tells him three stories and comes from beside the church. What is it?
hints: Before it visits Conor, he sees it every day from his window.
It's very, very old and has stood in the same spot for centuries.
It's a yew that starts to walk.
questions.description: A visitor who never rings the doorbell and always shows up just after midnight.

questions.question: In “I Want You” (2012), Hache returns to Barcelona and meets Gin, a cheerful, cheeky girl. Which actress plays her?
hints: As a child, she starred in “Carol's Journey.”

Her surname is the Spanish word for “lake.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: who is this coach from Vitoria who won two EuroLeagues with Real Madrid's basketball team?

questions.question: I'm from Gipuzkoa. In 1995 I became Spain's first road cycling world champion, in Duitama, Colombia, and I won the 1998 Vuelta. Who am I?

questions.question: In which city on the Ebro River was Teresa Perales born, Spain's swimmer with the most Paralympic medals?

questions.question: Pedro Acosta, “the Shark of Mazarrón”, became world champion in 2021 in his first year in this class. Which one?
hints: He was only 17.

It's the World Championship class with the smallest engines.
questions.description: A shark that prefers asphalt to salt water.

questions.question: I was born in Barcelona in 1933, became a world-famous soprano, and in 1987 sang a song named after my city with Freddie Mercury. Who am I?

questions.question: The Sovereign's Orb is a hollow gold sphere covered in jewels, given to the monarch at the coronation. What sits on top of it?

questions.question: Pau Gasol has two, Marc Gasol has one, and they're worn on a finger. In the NBA, what does “winning a ring” mean?

questions.question: In handball, how many players does each team have on the court, counting the goalkeeper?
hints: More than in basketball.
Fewer than in soccer.
As many as the days of the week.
questions.description: Here, the “no hands allowed” rule stays on the soccer field.
questions.fun_fact: FC Barcelona plays handball at the Palau Blaugrana, right next to the Camp Nou.

questions.question: You're in Badalona in 1992, watching the Dream Team of Jordan, Magic Johnson and Larry Bird. By how many points on average did they win?
hints: Nobody beat them, and hardly anyone came close.

questions.question: They were world champions in 2005 and 2013 and won Olympic bronze at Paris 2024. Which Spanish team is called «los Hispanos»?
hints: In 2013 they became world champions at home, in Barcelona.

Players throw the ball by hand into a goal, on an indoor court.
questions.description: A nickname with plenty of history for a team with plenty of arm.
questions.fun_fact: The women's team has its own nickname too: «las Guerreras» (the Warriors).

questions.question: Pau Gasol reached the NBA through the 2001 draft. Complete: in the draft, NBA teams…

The first one chosen is the “number one draft pick”.

questions.question: In which decade did the Jerez circuit, home of the motorcycle Grand Prix, open?
hints: It opened before the Montmeló circuit near Barcelona.

It opened in the same decade that Spain joined the European Community.
