questions.question: In which year did Antena 3 first air “Física o química”, the series set at Zurbarán High School?
hints: Tuenti and flip phones were already around.

questions.question: You finish the last season of “Vis a vis” and want more of Macarena and Zulema. Which series do you watch next?

questions.question: In which decade did Fórmula V release the original single “Cuéntame”?

questions.question: In what year did Telecinco first air “7 vidas”, the sitcom where the character Aída was born?

questions.question: In «Bienvenidos a Edén», Zoe gets an invite on her phone to an exclusive party on an island. What do the guests later find is behind it?

Its leader wants to build a perfect community.

questions.question: In «El pueblo», some city people move to Peñafría, a nearly empty village. What do people in Spain call the areas that lose people like this?

questions.question: Finish the sentence: Nacho-flavored Doritos taste like…

questions.question: I'm a big bird with red skin hanging from my beak. I go “gobble, gobble”, and on Christmas Eve I'm served roasted and stuffed. Who am I?

questions.question: Which of these characters does NOT appear in the cartoon “El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera”?
hints: The show is set in Miracle City and was created by Jorge R. Gutiérrez and Sandra Equihua.
Heroes, villains and even masked relatives live side by side in the show; the odd one out is none of them.
She is the goddess who rules the Land of the Remembered in “The Book of Life.”
questions.description: Superheroes in wrestling masks guarding a city where almost nobody behaves.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge R. Gutiérrez and Sandra Equihua, the show's creators, are married and later worked together on “The Book of Life” (2014).

questions.question: You're on the banks of the River Thames and see white swans with no markings. By an old tradition, who owns them?
hints: Their owner wears a crown.
Every year they are counted in an official ceremony.
They used to belong to Elizabeth II; today they belong to her son.
questions.description: Some very fancy ducks with a very important owner.
questions.fun_fact: Every summer there is “Swan Upping”, a ceremony where people in boats count and check the swans on the Thames.

questions.question: I wrote “Adelita y las guerrillas,” and from 1952 I published the El Santo comic, mixing photos of the real wrestler with drawings. Who am I?
hints: I was one of the great creators of the golden age of Mexican comics.
My style was photomontage: actors and wrestlers photographed against drawn backgrounds.
My last name is the Spanish word for the symbol on top of many church towers.
questions.description: Cut, paste and draw: the Photoshop of the 1950s.
questions.fun_fact: The El Santo comic was so popular that it helped turn the wrestler into a movie star.

questions.question: You're watching the 1972 film where El Santo and Blue Demon take on the mummies of Guanajuato. Which other masked wrestler fights alongside them?
hints: He's a wrestler from San Luis Potosí who also became famous in Japan and the United States.
He hardly ever wore the same mask twice.
In English, his ring name would be “A Thousand Masks”.
questions.description: A film where the mummies get a good lesson in lucha libre.
questions.fun_fact: The film was shot in Guanajuato, a city famous for its Mummy Museum.

questions.question: El Fisgón is to “La Jornada” as Rogelio Naranjo is to…
hints: Naranjo drew for decades for a weekly political magazine.
That magazine was founded in 1976, after Julio Scherer left “Excélsior”.
Its name is also a legal word in Spanish: what an accused person goes through in court.
questions.description: Every cartoonist has a home, even if the rent is paid in ink.
questions.fun_fact: Naranjo was famous for his portraits of presidents full of fine little lines, drawn with a dip pen.

questions.question: I write science fiction and crime novels, like “Tiempo de alacranes” and “Gel azul”, and I drew William Burroughs's adventures in Mexico. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Mexico City and I'm also a graphic designer.
My comic about Burroughs is called “Uncle Bill”.
My pen name comes from the initials of my real name, Bernardo Fernández.
questions.description: A cartoonist who won't settle for just one way of telling stories.
questions.fun_fact: Bef has won awards for both his novels and his comics.

questions.question: Diego Boneta played the singer in “Luis Miguel: The Series”. How many seasons did the show have?
hints: It premiered in 2018 and ended in 2021.
The last two seasons came out in the same year.
More than two, but fewer than four.
questions.description: Becoming the “Sol de México” took a lot of rehearsing in front of the mirror.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Miguel, the “Sol de México”, was actually born in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 1970.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The answer (3 seasons) is right. But hint 2 is false: season 2 aired in 2019 and season 3 in 2021, so the last two seasons did not come out in the same year. (Season 1 was 2018.)

questions.question: Lila Avilés's “Tótem” follows little Sol during a family party and competed at the Berlin Film Festival. In which year did it come out?
hints: It was Mexico's entry for the Oscar for Best International Feature.
Lila Avilés made it after her first film, “La camarista” (2018).
It came out the same year as “Barbie” and “Oppenheimer”.
questions.description: A whole day of family party, with aunts, balloons and cake included.
questions.fun_fact: “La camarista”, Lila Avilés's first film, takes place almost entirely inside a luxury hotel in Mexico City.

questions.question: Diego Luna played Cassian Andor in “Rogue One” (2016) and came back to the role in the series “Andor”. In what year did that series premiere?
hints: It premiered on Disney+.
It came out well into the 2020s, and its second season followed later.
It premiered six years after “Rogue One”.
questions.description: A rebel from a galaxy far, far away with a Mexico City accent.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Luna and Gael García Bernal have been friends since they were kids, and they starred together in “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001).

questions.question: It's the top prize of the Cannes Film Festival, created in 1955, and “María Candelaria” won its forerunner, the Grand Prix, in 1946. What is it?
hints: It is handed out on the French Riviera.
The other golden prizes are given in Venice, Berlin and San Sebastián.
Its shape looks like the leaf of a tree you find on beaches.
questions.description: A golden trophy handed out at the beach, but no flip-flops allowed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006, Alejandro González Iñárritu won the Best Director award at Cannes for “Babel”.

questions.question: In a museum, you're looking at a Wixárika jícara: a split gourd with bead figures inside. What was it first made for?
hints: Its use has more to do with the sky than the kitchen.
They are left at sacred places during pilgrimages.
A prayer or request to the deities is placed in it.
questions.description: Gluing on thousands of beads one by one: the true extreme sport of patience.
questions.fun_fact: The figures inside the jícara, such as deer, corn or flowers, often show what is being asked of the gods.

questions.question: With a wooden control bar and strings, I make wooden figures dance from above, like Tlaxcala's famous Rosete Aranda company. Who am I?
hints: You almost never see me: I hide above or behind the stage.
My performers are made of wood and can't move on their own.
I work with marionettes.
questions.description: The real boss of the show, even if everyone else gets the applause.
questions.fun_fact: Huamantla, Tlaxcala, the home of the Rosete Aranda company, has a National Puppet Museum.

questions.question: In what year was Charles III crowned at Westminster Abbey?
hints: It was in this decade.
It wasn't the same year he became king.
It was about eight months after the death of Elizabeth II.
questions.description: A king who waited so long for his turn that the line at the bank feels short.
questions.fun_fact: Charles III was 74 when he was crowned, the oldest British monarch ever to be crowned.

questions.question: It's a blue dye, called xiuhquílitl in Nahuatl, and Oaxacan weavers still dye yarn with it. Where does añil (indigo) come from?
hints: Cochineal gives red; this one gives blue.
To get the color, the raw material is left to ferment in big vats of water.
It grows in the fields, like any herb.
questions.description: A blue that had been dyeing things for centuries before jeans existed.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya mixed indigo with a clay to create “Maya blue,” a color that has lasted centuries in their murals.

questions.question: It's October 31, and your family is already setting up the ofrenda, like in “Coco.” How many days until November 2?
hints: October has 31 days.
Tomorrow is already November 1.
It comes the day after tomorrow.
questions.description: A countdown with more sweet bread than rockets.
questions.fun_fact: November 2 is All Souls' Day, a date set in Europe about a thousand years ago.

questions.question: Take a close look: this Day of the Dead decoration is cut from very thin, colorful paper. What is that paper called in Mexico?
hints: It's super thin and tears easily if you pull on it.
It's also used to cover piñatas and wrap presents.
It has the same name as the country of the Great Wall.
questions.description: A decoration made with nothing but scissor snips and chisel taps.
questions.fun_fact: In San Salvador Huixcolotla, Puebla, papel picado is cut with a chisel and hammer, through dozens of stacked sheets at once.

questions.question: In “Coco,” to leave the Land of the Dead, the dead stand in front of a camera and wait for a green light. What does it check?
questions.answer: Whether their photo is on an ofrenda
wrong_answers: Whether they can sing a song
Whether they bought a train ticket
hints: What matters is that someone among the living remembers you.
That's why Héctor never gets the green light.
It has to do with what your family puts on the altar.
questions.description: The strictest customs check in the afterlife, and they don't even look in your suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: The Land of the Dead in “Coco” was partly inspired by the colorful houses stacked up the hills of Guanajuato.

questions.question: In “Coco,” Héctor dresses up as Frida Kahlo, tries to cross the petal bridge and gets caught. Where was he trying to go?
questions.answer: To the Land of the Living
wrong_answers: To the bottom of the sea
hints: He wanted to see someone he loved very much.
It's where Miguel lives with his family.
There, people still have skin and aren't just bones.
questions.description: An escape plan with some very famous eyebrows.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Héctor is actually Miguel's great-great-grandfather, and the one who wrote “Remember Me.”

questions.question: You tap with your fingers on two drums joined together, one smaller than the other, held between your knees, like in the rumbera films. What are you playing?
hints: It comes from Cuba, like many rumberas.
You don't play it with sticks, but with your fingertips.
Its name is the same as an African antelope.
questions.description: Two inseparable little brothers who let themselves get slapped all night long at the cabaret.
questions.fun_fact: The bongos were born in eastern Cuba and came to Mexican cinema with the tropical rhythms the rumberas danced to.

questions.question: The star of “El rey del barrio” (1950) became famous as a pachuco mixing English and Spanish, a border style. In which city did he grow up?
hints: The actor is Germán Valdés, “Tin Tan”.
He started out working at a radio station in that city.
It sits right across from El Paso, Texas.
questions.description: A king with no crown, no castle and very, very baggy pants.
questions.fun_fact: Tin Tan was born in Mexico City, but moved to Ciudad Juárez as a child, where he picked up the pocho slang that made him famous.

questions.question: “La mujer del puerto” (1934), starring Andrea Palma, was remade by Arturo Ripstein. In which decade did the remake come out?
hints: More than fifty years had passed since the original
The script was written by Paz Alicia Garciadiego, Ripstein's longtime collaborator
It came out after the Berlin Wall had fallen
questions.description: A movie so good someone decided to make it again, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: The 1934 film was inspired by “The Port,” a short story by French writer Guy de Maupassant.

questions.question: The Ariel is the top award of Mexican cinema. The Ariel is to Mexico as which award is to Hollywood?
hints: It was first handed out in 1929.
It’s given out every year in Los Angeles, in late winter.
It’s a little golden man holding a sword.
questions.description: Endless speeches, happy tears and the must-have “thanks, Mom.”
questions.fun_fact: The Mexican Academy of Film Arts and Sciences has handed out the Ariel since 1947, right in the middle of the Golden Age.

questions.question: Which of these dancers from the cabaret films was NOT born in Cuba?
hints: She danced Tahitian dances more than rumba
She was famous for a white streak in her hair
She was born in the state of Washington, in the United States
questions.description: Four queens of the dance floor, but one showed up with a different passport.
questions.fun_fact: Tongolele, whose real name is Yolanda Montes, was born in 1932, and her famous white streak was natural.

questions.question: I was king of England, in 1215 I was forced to accept the Magna Carta, and I'm the villain in the Robin Hood stories. Who am I?
hints: I ruled while my brother was far away.
My brother was a king famous for his bravery in the Crusades.
My nickname says I ended up with no land of my own.
questions.description: A king that not even children's stories have a soft spot for.
questions.fun_fact: Only four copies of the 1215 Magna Carta survive today, and two of them are in the British Library in London.

questions.question: Before making his classics in Mexico, Luis Buñuel made a famous surrealist short film with Salvador Dalí. Which one?
hints: It was filmed in France in 1929.
It has a very famous scene with an eye and a razor.
Its title names an animal and a region of Spain.
questions.description: A director so strange his films feel like the dreams you have after a late-night tamale dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Buñuel became a Mexican citizen in 1949 and made classics in Mexico such as “Los olvidados”.

questions.question: It's held every May on the coast of France, today it awards the Palme d'Or, and in 1946 it gave a prize to “María Candelaria”. What is it?
hints: It takes place on the French Riviera
Its red carpet goes up a grand staircase facing the sea
It's named after a French city that starts with C
questions.description: One week a year, movie stars climb stairs slower than ever so the cameras can catch them.
questions.fun_fact: At that same festival, Emilio “El Indio” Fernández's “María Candelaria” also won a prize for Gabriel Figueroa's cinematography.

questions.question: On September 16, there's a military parade, no school, and homes are decorated in green, white and red. Why is it a holiday?
wrong_answers: Because it's Day of the Dead
hints: It remembers something that began in 1810.
The night before, “¡Viva México!” rings out in every plaza.
On that day, Mexico began fighting to stop being ruled by Spain.
questions.description: The one day everyone wakes up after a late night and nobody asks for a note from home.
questions.fun_fact: The war began in 1810, but Mexico didn't win its independence until 1821, eleven years later.

questions.question: Look at the photo. In this city in 1810, a group secretly planned Independence until they were found out. Which city is it?
hints: It's in the Bajío, north of Mexico City.
The corregidor's wife lived here, and she warned the plotters.
Its state has a municipality called Corregidora.
questions.description: A city whose arches are as tall as the secrets once kept there.
questions.fun_fact: The plotters pretended their meetings were literary gatherings so no one would get suspicious.

questions.question: About how old was Miguel Hidalgo when he gave the Grito de Dolores in 1810?
hints: He had already been a priest for many years.
In his portraits he doesn't have much hair left, and what he has is white.
He was born in 1753.
questions.description: A patriotic birthday question, but with no cake and no “Las Mañanitas”.
questions.fun_fact: Before the war, Hidalgo taught the people of Dolores how to raise silkworms and make pottery.

questions.question: September is Mexico's patriotic month. Which place is NOT remembered for something that happened in September?
hints: Three of these places are linked to the Grito, the Niños Héroes and the start of Independence.
The one you want is celebrated in spring.
A famous battle against France was won there.
questions.description: September is so packed with history that you have to spot the gatecrasher at the party.
questions.fun_fact: September also marks the end of the War of Independence: the Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on September 27, 1821.

questions.question: Look at this woman weaving on a backstrap loom. What is the strap around her back for?
questions.answer: To pull the threads tight with her body
wrong_answers: To carry her baby while she weaves
To measure the length of the cloth
To hang up the colored threads
hints: This loom has no legs and no big wooden frame.
When she leans back, something changes in the threads.
One end is tied to a tree or post, the other to her hips.
questions.description: A loom so portable it rolls up like a yoga mat.
questions.fun_fact: The backstrap loom was used in Mesoamerica long before the Spanish arrived, and the weaver is literally part of the loom.

questions.question: These niches are on the Pyramid of the Niches at El Tajín, Veracruz. Which Indigenous people live in that region today?
hints: They live in northern Veracruz and in the Sierra Norte de Puebla.
Their best-known town is Papantla, famous for its vanilla.
The Voladores de Papantla belong to this people.
questions.description: A pyramid with more little holes than a block of Swiss cheese.
questions.fun_fact: The Pyramid of the Niches is said to have 365 niches, one for each day of the year.

questions.question: In Mexico people eat many quelites, like quintonil, pápalo and huauzontle. About how many edible species are there?
hints: Far more than you'd see in a single market.
Every region of Mexico has its own, like chaya in the southeast.
Hundreds, but not thousands.
questions.description: The salad that grows in the milpa all by itself, without anyone inviting it.
questions.fun_fact: The word “quelite” comes from the Nahuatl “quilitl”, which means edible herb.

questions.question: This man appears on every banknote in Vietnam. Who is he?
hints: He was a political leader of the 20th century.
He founded modern Vietnam and was its president.
The old city of Saigon is now named after him.
questions.description: A banknote where the same man always shows up, whatever its value.
questions.fun_fact: Saigon, Vietnam's largest city, has officially been called Ho Chi Minh City since 1976.

questions.question: I'm named after the Tabasco village where I'm spoken, and I'm related to Zoque. In 2011 the press said my last two speakers weren't on speaking terms. What language am I?
hints: I belong to the Mixe-Zoque family.
My village is in the municipality of Jalpa de Méndez.
The village is called Ayapa.
questions.description: Tabasco is so hot that even words melt before they leave your mouth.
questions.fun_fact: The story of the two feuding speakers turned out to be exaggerated: linguists say they simply lived far apart and had little in common.

questions.question: The Lele doll was born in Amealco, Querétaro, wears braids with colorful ribbons and is made by Otomí artisans. What is it made of?
hints: You can hug it without fear of breaking it.
Its body and its dress are made of the same material.
It's stuffed and sewn by hand.
questions.description: A doll with more style than any fashion runway.
questions.fun_fact: In 2018 the Lele doll was declared cultural heritage of the state of Querétaro.

questions.question: Mazatlán, a port in Sinaloa, has a Nahuatl name made of an animal plus an ending. What are they?
hints: The same ending is in Cuautitlán and Aztlán.
The animal is a plant-eater from the hills.
The full name means “land of many of that antlered animal.”
questions.description: A port with a name straight out of a zoo and beaches straight off a postcard.
questions.fun_fact: The ending -tlan shows up in hundreds of place names across Mexico.

questions.question: I stick to the end of Nahuatl names to show respect or affection, like “don” or “-ito” in Spanish. Which ending am I?
hints: Nobles and rulers got me a lot.
I'm in Juan Diego's Nahuatl name.
The Spanish turned me into the “-che” in “Malinche.”
questions.description: The most polite way to talk to a Mexica emperor.
questions.fun_fact: “Malinche” comes from “Malintzin”: the Spanish misheard the ending and changed it.

questions.question: Its name comes from Nahuatl, at the market it's filled with tomatoes or hens, and someone who stops obeying “se salió del huacal.” What is a huacal?
questions.answer: A crate made of wooden slats
hints: It's for carrying and storing things
It has gaps between its parts
It's put together by nailing strips of wood
questions.description: The supermarket cart, traditional market edition.
questions.fun_fact: “Huacal” comes from the Nahuatl word “huacalli,” and people once carried it on their backs with a strap.

questions.question: At the National Museum of Anthropology in Chapultepec, what is mostly on display?
questions.answer: Objects from ancient peoples of Mexico
wrong_answers: Cars and trains from other eras
hints: Anthropology studies human beings and their cultures.
It has halls dedicated to the Maya, the Olmecs and the Mexica.
The great Sun Stone and an Olmec head are there.
questions.description: The perfect place to spend a whole Sunday and still not manage to see everything.
questions.fun_fact: Its courtyard has “El Paraguas” (the Umbrella): a huge roof held up by a single column, with a curtain of water pouring down from it.

questions.question: The Palacio de Minería was designed by Manuel Tolsá, was once a mining school, and has huge meteorites in its lobby. What are they mostly made of?
hints: They are rocks that fell from space and were found in northern Mexico.
They weigh tons even though they aren't that big: they're very dense.
A magnet would stick to them; they're made of the same stuff as Earth's core.
questions.description: A palace where some of the heaviest visitors arrived straight from the sky.
questions.fun_fact: Every year the Palacio de Minería hosts the International Book Fair, one of the oldest book fairs in Mexico.

questions.question: You're walking among the fountains and trees of the Alameda Central, next to Bellas Artes. How long ago was this park created?
hints: It already existed when Mexico was New Spain.
A viceroy ordered it built.
It opened in the late 16th century.
questions.description: Perfect for strolling, eating ice cream, and pretending you're working out.
questions.fun_fact: The Alameda Central is considered the oldest public park in the Americas.

questions.question: Look at this giant stadium in Mexico City, one of the most famous in the world. What sport is almost always played there?
hints: Club América plays its home games there.
Two World Cup finals were played there.
It's played with your feet and two goals.
questions.description: A place where more than 80,000 people scream at once and nobody complains about the noise.
questions.fun_fact: In its early years, Estadio Azteca sometimes held more than 100,000 people for a single match.

questions.question: I'm round, sunk into the ground next to the Estadio Ciudad de los Deportes in Mexico City, and the largest of my kind in the world. What am I?
hints: I opened in 1946.
My concrete stands drop in steep steps toward a single central circle.
Matadors appear here in their suits of lights.
questions.description: A chilango giant that chose to grow down instead of up.
questions.fun_fact: Plaza México opened on February 5, 1946, the same day Mexico celebrates its Constitution.

questions.question: Built by a Franciscan friar in the 16th century, it carries water from Zempoala to Otumba and has the tallest single-tier arcade ever built in an aqueduct. Which is it?
hints: It lies between Hidalgo and the State of Mexico.
UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 2015.
The friar who built it got a nickname that sounds like the Spanish word for shaking.
questions.description: Seventeen years of work so a few towns could get water without walking for miles.
questions.fun_fact: Its tallest arch is about 39 meters (128 ft) high, roughly as tall as a 13-story building.

questions.question: This seabird nests on islands in Mexico's Pacific, and the male dances to show off his blue feet. Why is it called a “booby”?
questions.answer: Because it's clumsy and trusting on land
wrong_answers: Because its call sounds like a whistle
Because of the odd color of its feet
Because it sleeps floating on the sea
hints: Think about how the sailors who landed on its islands saw it
In the water it is a great diver, but on the ground it's another story
It waddles when it walks and hardly runs away from people
questions.description: A bird with clown shoes and a name nobody asked its permission for.
questions.fun_fact: The blue of its feet comes from pigments in the fresh fish it eats: the bluer the feet, the healthier the male looks.

questions.question: The Riviera Maya in Quintana Roo borrowed the word “riviera” from a famous European coast; in that country's language it means “coast”. Which country?
hints: The original coast is on the Mediterranean Sea
Cities like Genoa and Sanremo are there
Its capital is Rome
questions.description: White sand, turquoise water and a name that came from very far away.
questions.fun_fact: Before it was called the Riviera Maya, the area was known as the Cancún–Tulum corridor.

questions.question: Every year, the gray whale swims from the Arctic to the lagoons of Baja California Sur to have its calves. How far does it travel, there and back?
hints: It travels from an icy sea to the Mexican Pacific.
It is one of the longest migrations of any mammal.
It's like going from Mexico to Japan and back.
questions.description: Not even Periférico traffic makes your vacation drive feel this long.
questions.fun_fact: In San Ignacio Lagoon, some gray whale moms swim up to boats on their own and let people touch them.

questions.question: Its lava formed the Pedregal de San Ángel, where Ciudad Universitaria stands today, and buried the round pyramid of Cuicuilco. Which volcano is it?
hints: It isn't one of the giant snowy peaks, but a small volcano
It is in the south of Mexico City, on the slopes of the Ajusco
In Nahuatl, its name is linked to the belly button
questions.description: A neighbor from the south of the city who did the noisiest home makeover in history.
questions.fun_fact: Many people from Cuicuilco are thought to have moved to other parts of the valley, such as Teotihuacan, because of this volcano's eruptions.

questions.question: It collects water from dams like the one at Valle de Bravo, pumps it over the mountains and supplies much of Mexico City. What is it called?
hints: It's all over the news whenever there's a drought
It's named after a river that flows into the Balsas
That river runs along the borders of Michoacán, Guerrero and the State of Mexico
questions.description: Every time you turn on the tap in the capital, this water has traveled farther than you did on vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Cutzamala water is lifted more than 1,000 meters (3,300 ft) by huge pumps before it reaches the capital.

questions.question: You're swimming with sea lions at Los Islotes, off La Paz, and a huge male shows up. How much can he weigh?
hints: He weighs much more than a person
Females weigh around 100 kg (220 lb), and the male is much bigger
He weighs about as much as four adults together
questions.description: A sea dog that barks, swims and has never been to the groomer.
questions.fun_fact: The sea lion pups at Los Islotes are so curious that they sometimes playfully nibble divers' fins.

questions.question: In the Chiapas Highlands, Tzotzil and Tzeltal people tell of the ik'al: a small, hairy being that lives in caves and comes out at night. What does its name mean?
hints: The name comes from the Mayan languages of Chiapas.
Its name comes from an everyday word that Tzotzil children learn when they're very little.
It has to do with a color: the color of the night.
questions.description: A cave-dwelling neighbor nobody ever invites to the posada.
questions.fun_fact: In 1972, anthropologist Sarah Blaffer wrote a whole book about this being: “The Black-Man of Zinacantan.”

questions.question: Alebrije, Don Andrés's sidekick in the animated Leyendas films, is named after figures like this one. In which city were alebrijes born?
hints: The first ones were made of papier-mâché, not carved wood.
They were invented by papier-mâché artisan Pedro Linares after he dreamed of them during a fever.
Linares lived and worked in the country's capital.
questions.description: Half dragon, half rooster, all colorful nightmare.
questions.fun_fact: In 1936, Pedro Linares dreamed of creatures shouting “Alebrijes!”, and that's how the name was born.

questions.question: I was Ecuador's currency until 2000, and I'm named after the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho. Which currency am I?
hints: My hero fought alongside Simón Bolívar.
One of Bolivia's capitals has the same name.
Colombia has a department with my name, and its capital is Sincelejo.
questions.description: A currency named after a hero, which retired as soon as the dollar showed up.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2000, Ecuador has used the US dollar as its official currency.

questions.question: At night in the Mexican countryside, you see balls of fire hopping between the trees and landing on roofs. What do the grandparents say they are?
wrong_answers: A sign that rain is coming
A sign that an earthquake is coming
A sign of a good harvest
hints: The grandparents cross themselves when they see them.
According to the legend, by day they look like ordinary women from the village.
In some villages people pray to make them fall to the ground, so everyone finds out who it is.
questions.description: Lights on the hill that nobody hired for the party.
questions.fun_fact: In some Mexican legends, witches also turn into guajolotes (turkeys) to go out at night without being recognized.

questions.question: Leo San Juan faces the chaneques in his 2023 movie. Which of these beings is NOT tiny like them?
hints: Three of them are the size of a child or even smaller.
By day, the odd one out looks like any ordinary adult.
It's a sorcerer who turns into an animal.
questions.description: Beings so tiny they fit in a huarache, and so naughty they'll hide it from you.
questions.fun_fact: In Yucatán, many Maya families leave food offerings for the aluxes so they will watch over their milpas (cornfields).

questions.question: Which of these wrestlers was NOT one of the famous Hermanos Brazo?
hints: Three of them are sons of the same wrestler, Shadito Cruz.
One of the brothers changed his name and character halfway through his career.
The one you want teamed up with Máscara Año 2000 and Universo 2000.
questions.description: A family that was always ready to lend you an arm.
questions.fun_fact: Súper Porky became a crowd favorite for his dancing and his big belly, and many people forgot he used to wrestle as Brazo de Plata.

questions.question: Look at this detail carved in stone. What writing is it?
hints: It was written in almost square blocks, mixing pictures and sounds.
You can find it at Palenque, Copán and Yaxchilán.
It was used by the same people who built Chichén Itzá.
questions.description: Emojis carved in stone, with no keyboard and no autocorrect.
questions.fun_fact: A key to cracking the Maya glyphs came in 1952 from Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov, who didn't set foot in a Maya ruin until many years later.

questions.question: In the church of San Juan Chamula, in Chiapas, the Tzotzil bring fizzy sodas to their prayers. Why?
hints: The church has no pews, and the floor is covered in pine needles.
It's part of a healing ritual with candles, sometimes led by a healer.
People believe bad things leave the body through the mouth.
questions.description: A church service where the bubbles play a starring role.
questions.fun_fact: Taking photos inside the church of San Juan Chamula is forbidden.

questions.question: People say the steps of the Pyramid of Kukulcán at Chichén Itzá add up to the number of days in a year. How many are there?
hints: Think of the calendar on your wall at home.
Each of its four sides has 91 steps, plus the platform at the top.
It's the number of days in a year that isn't a leap year.
questions.description: A pyramid with more steps than you have excuses to skip the gym.
questions.fun_fact: Inside the Pyramid of Kukulcán there is an older pyramid, with a jaguar throne painted red.

questions.question: Look at this detail of the quetzal-feather headdress said to have belonged to Moctezuma. In which city is it kept today?
hints: It's in a museum in Europe, not in Mexico.
Mexico has asked to borrow it, but it's said to be too fragile to travel.
It's the capital of Austria.
questions.description: A hat so famous it has its own international debate.
questions.fun_fact: The headdress has about 400 long quetzal feathers, from a bird that lives only in the cloud forests of Mesoamerica.

questions.question: “We ruled Uxmal, helped bring down Mayapán, founded Maní and allied with the Spanish in 1542.” Which Maya lineage are we?
hints: They said their ancestors had come from the west, from faraway lands.
Their great rivals were the lords of Sotuta.
Their full name is sometimes written Tutul…
questions.description: A royal family with more feuds than a prime-time telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Their lord Ah Kukum Xiu was baptized with the name of his Spanish ally: Francisco de Montejo Xiu.

questions.question: You leave a piece of jewelry or a device as a guarantee, they lend you money, and if you don't pay on time, they keep it. What is this called?
hints: It's a quick loan that doesn't need a cosigner.
What you leave behind is called the pledge.
It's what people do at the Nacional Monte de Piedad.
questions.description: When payday is hiding and your wallet is crying for help, there are emergency solutions.
questions.fun_fact: The Nacional Monte de Piedad was founded in 1775 by Pedro Romero de Terreros, a wealthy mine owner.

questions.question: I'm Japan's lowest-value coin and I weigh exactly 1 gram. What metal am I made of?
hints: It's a very light, silver-colored metal.
Many drink cans are made of it.
It's also used for the shiny foil that wraps food in the kitchen.
questions.description: A coin so light it nearly flies out of your pocket on its own.
questions.fun_fact: This coin is so light that it can float on water, held up by surface tension.

questions.question: “I'm a low-price supermarket, I'm in almost every town in Mexico, I'm part of the Walmart family and my mascot is Mamá Lucha.” Which store am I?
hints: I have little versions called “Express.”
My name has two words.
The first word of my name is Spanish for a storeroom or warehouse.
questions.description: A very strong lady who wrestles high prices to the ground.
questions.fun_fact: Besides its big stores, it also has small neighborhood shops called “Mi Bodega.”

questions.question: In Mexican schools, which students are traditionally chosen to form the flag's escolta (honor guard)?
questions.answer: The ones with the best grades
wrong_answers: The ones on the soccer team
hints: They aren't picked by lottery or by age.
It has to do with the boleta (report card).
They're the ones who keep getting 10s.
questions.description: Carrying the flag is an honor you don't earn at recess.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican schools, being part of the escolta is one of the most wanted honors of the last year of primary school, sixth grade.

questions.question: On Mexico's coat of arms, the eagle stands on a nopal cactus that has these fruits. What are they called?
hints: They grow on the pads of the nopal.
They have tiny spines on the outside, so you have to peel them carefully.
They come in green and red, and in English they're often called prickly pears.
questions.description: The eagle on the coat of arms has a snack within reach, but it prefers the snake.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Tenochtitlan” is often translated as “place of the prickly pear cactus on the rock.”

questions.question: At the honores a la bandera (flag ceremony), students stand straight, heels together, arms tight at their sides. What is this position called?
hints: It's the opposite of being relaxed.
You're told to stay like this without moving.
In Spanish, the teacher shouts: “¡Fiiir…!”
questions.description: Not even scratching your nose is allowed while the anthem plays.
questions.fun_fact: In the escolta (the flag guard), the command “¡Firmes!” (“Attention!”) is given before the flag enters the schoolyard.

questions.question: Mexico won the 2023 Gold Cup. Which of these teams did it NOT play in that tournament?
hints: One of the opponents isn't even from the Americas: it came as a guest.
Mexico beat a Central American team 1–0 in the final.
The neighbor to the north was knocked out by Panama in the semifinals.
questions.description: A summer tournament with more travel than a family road trip.
questions.fun_fact: Qatar, playing as a guest, beat Mexico 1–0 in the group stage, and El Tri still lifted the trophy.

questions.question: When a commentator says Mexico is about to face “los ticos”, which national team is it playing?
hints: It's a country in Central America.
Its goalkeeper Keylor Navas was a star at Real Madrid.
Its capital is San José.
questions.description: Neighbors to the south who always make life hard for El Tri.
questions.fun_fact: In 2001 this team beat Mexico 2–1 at the Estadio Azteca, a game remembered as the “Aztecazo”.

questions.question: At the 2015 Gold Cup, Mexico beat Panama in the semifinals. Which team did Mexico then face in the final, winning 3-1?
hints: That team knocked out the United States in the semifinals.
That team had never played in a Gold Cup final before.
Its team is nicknamed the “Reggae Boyz.”
questions.description: Thousands of Mexican fans packed a stadium far from home as if it were the Azteca.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first time a Caribbean team had reached the Gold Cup final.

questions.question: I'm the soccer confederation Mexico belongs to, along with the US, Canada, Central America and the Caribbean, and I run the Gold Cup. Who am I?
hints: I'm not the one in charge of the whole world.
South America has its own confederation, and it isn't me.
My name starts like “Confederation” and ends in “caf.”
questions.description: Alphabet soup with a soccer ball thrown in.
questions.fun_fact: This confederation was founded in 1961, at a meeting in Mexico City.

questions.question: Three of these Roman structures are in Italy. Which one is NOT?
hints: One of them is on an island far to the north, where it rains a lot.
It's very far from Rome, in a land the Romans called Britannia.
It runs across the north of England.
questions.description: The Romans built so much that they left things lying around half of Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Some say Hadrian's Wall inspired the giant Wall of ice in “Game of Thrones.”

questions.question: On Mexico's frontón courts people play pelota a mano: you hit the ball with your palm against a wall. Which people brought this game?
hints: It came from Spain with immigrants more than a century ago.
These people live between northern Spain and southwestern France.
Jai alai, a cousin of this game, has a name in Euskera.
questions.description: A sport where the wall always sends back whatever you throw at it, just like Mom when you talk back.
questions.fun_fact: Frontón México, in Mexico City, opened in 1929 and was one of the most famous jai alai courts in the world.

questions.question: In 1991, Mexico's Arturo Barrios broke the world hour record: running as far as possible in 60 minutes. About how far did he go?
hints: A good amateur runner covers about 12 km (7.5 miles) in an hour.
He ran faster than 3 minutes per kilometer for the whole hour.
It's a little more than a half marathon.
questions.description: A race where the finish line doesn't matter, only the clock.
questions.fun_fact: Barrios also held the 10,000 meters world record, which he set in Berlin in 1989.

questions.question: I was born in England in 1917 and came to Mexico fleeing the war. I painted fantastic creatures, and my museum in San Luis Potosí is in an old prison. Who am I?
hints: I was one of the great Surrealist women painters in Mexico.
I also made bronze sculptures of strange beings, and I have another museum in Xilitla.
My first name sounds very English and my last name starts with C.
questions.description: An artist who arrived fleeing a war and stayed to live among cats, witches and floating horses.
questions.fun_fact: Leonora Carrington also wrote stories and novels, like “The Hearing Trumpet,” about a grandma who has wild adventures.

questions.question: Hermenegildo Bustos, a 19th-century painter from Guanajuato, made many small paintings on tin to thank a saint for a miracle. What are they called?
hints: They hang on the walls of churches and shrines.
They usually carry a text telling what happened and who is being thanked.
Their name comes from Latin and means “from a vow.”
questions.description: Tiny paintings that say “thank you” more sincerely than any birthday card.
questions.fun_fact: Bustos taught himself to paint and signed some portraits calling himself an “amateur,” yet today he is seen as a master.

questions.question: Just outside me, in 1933, Siqueiros painted the basement of a country house with Antonio Berni and Lino Enea Spilimbergo. The mural is “Ejercicio plástico.” Which city am I?
hints: Siqueiros came to me after painting in the United States.
Berni and Spilimbergo are great painters from my country.
Today the mural is on display in the Bicentennial Museum, next to the Casa Rosada.
questions.description: A mural so well-traveled it spent almost twenty years packed in boxes before seeing daylight again.
questions.fun_fact: The mural was taken apart in pieces and spent years stored in shipping containers until it was restored and put back together.

questions.question: In which decade did Olga Costa paint “La vendedora de frutas”, the famous painting in Mexico City's Museo de Arte Moderno?
hints: Olga Costa was married to the muralist José Chávez Morado.
By then, Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros were already famous muralists.
It was a few years after the end of the Second World War.
questions.description: A market stall with so much fruit you'll want to order a cup of papaya.
questions.fun_fact: Olga Costa was born in Germany, but she fell so in love with Mexico that her paintings are full of Mexican fruit, flowers and markets.

questions.question: In Thomas Pynchon's “The Crying of Lot 49,” the heroine cries in front of a painting of young women in a tower embroidering the world. Who painted it?
hints: She was a Surrealist painter who lived in Mexico.
She was born in Spain and came to Mexico fleeing World War II.
Her first name is the Spanish word for “remedies.”
questions.description: Young women so busy with their needlework that they don't notice they're stitching the whole planet.
questions.fun_fact: “Embroidering the Earth's Mantle” is part of a 1961 triptych that tells the story of a girl who escapes from the tower.

questions.question: Borola, Regino and his barbershop “El Rizo de Oro” live on Callejón del Cuajo. In which city is this Gabriel Vargas comic set?
hints: The comic is “La familia Burrón.”
It shows life in the vecindades of working-class neighborhoods.
It's the biggest city in the country.
questions.description: A family as broke as it is funny, with hairdos that would make any stylist cry.
questions.fun_fact: “La familia Burrón” was published for more than 60 years, from 1948 to 2009.

questions.question: I show up at the neighborhood dance with huge speakers, play cumbias and send shout-outs over the mic to anyone who asks. What am I?
hints: I'm famous in Mexico City neighborhoods like Tepito or Peñón de los Baños.
My dances get recorded, and the shout-outs travel all the way to Puebla and New York.
My name comes from the Spanish word for “sound.”
questions.description: Here, shout-outs are delivered with more bass than any greeting card could handle.
questions.fun_fact: Recordings of sonidero dances, full of shout-outs, are passed around by families on both sides of the border.

questions.question: Julieta Venegas was born in Long Beach, California, but grew up in a Mexican border city. Which one?
hints: It's in Baja California.
It sits right next to San Diego.
Her first rock band was named after this city, followed by “No!”.
questions.description: Before she could sing “Me voy”, she had to come from somewhere.
questions.fun_fact: Julieta Venegas has a twin sister, Yvonne, who is a photographer.

questions.question: It has white domes, a princess lives there with a tiger, and a genie visited it. Which real monument inspired this Disney palace?
hints: It's in Asia.
It's a white marble tomb.
It's in India.
questions.description: Even cartoon palaces copy someone else's homework.
questions.fun_fact: The story of Aladdin wasn't even in the oldest Arabic versions of “One Thousand and One Nights”: a French translator added it.

questions.question: “I have long black hair and a raspy voice; in the '90s I founded Jaguares and gave Juan Gabriel's “Te lo pido por favor” a rock twist.” Who am I?
hints: My voice is one of the best known in Spanish-language rock of the '80s and '90s.
Before Jaguares, I sang “La negra Tomasa” and “Afuera” with another band.
That other band took its name from the film “Los caifanes.”
questions.description: This rocker wears black even to go buy tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: The name Caifanes comes from “Los caifanes,” a Mexican film from the 1960s.

questions.question: “We're a Mexican pop ballad trio, named after a French painter famous for his colored paper cut-outs.” What's our name?
hints: Our painter was Picasso's friend and rival.
He painted “The Dance”, with red figures dancing in a circle.
His first name was Henri.
questions.description: A band that took the idea of “pop art” very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: In his last years, Henri Matisse made giant works by cutting paper with scissors from his wheelchair.

questions.question: “Todo cambió” is one of the biggest hits by Camila, Mario Domm's band. In which decade did it come out?
hints: Phones already had cameras, but almost nobody had a touchscreen one.
It was the same decade RBD was filling stadiums.
The album came out the same year as the World Cup in Germany.
questions.description: A song that made more wedding guests cry than the padrinos' toast.
questions.fun_fact: The band has a woman's name, even though it was formed by three men.

questions.question: Botellita de Jerez formed in 1983 in Mexico City, mixed rock with sones and albures (double-meaning wordplay), and named its style by joining a dish and the word “rock.” What did it call it?
hints: One of its founders, Sergio Arau, later directed the film “A Day Without a Mexican.”
The dish is made in a molcajete.
It's made with avocado.
questions.description: Chilango rock with more double meanings than a chat at the market.
questions.fun_fact: The band's name comes from the children's saying “botellita de jerez, todo lo que digas será al revés” (“little sherry bottle, whatever you say will mean the opposite”).

questions.question: Reik, the trio behind “Yo quisiera” and “Inolvidable”, formed in a city in northern Mexico. Which one?
hints: It's a state capital.
It's famous for its extreme heat and its Chinese food.
Its name combines Mexico and California.
questions.description: Three buddies from the north who turned heartbreak into a great business.
questions.fun_fact: Reik also moved into reggaeton with hits like “Me niego”, with Ozuna and Wisin.

questions.question: Maldita Vecindad sang about the “Pachuco,” with the baggy suit, chain and hat that Tin Tan made famous. In which decade did that style appear?
hints: It was the golden age of Mexican cinema.
Pachucos danced swing and danzón.
It was during World War II.
questions.description: A style so elegant the pants needed their own zip code.
questions.fun_fact: In English, the pachuco outfit is called the “zoot suit,” which also gave its name to Luis Valdez's 1981 film “Zoot Suit.”

questions.question: I was rich and vain. At the bonfire in Teotihuacan I was scared to jump, so another god went first. I jumped next and became the moon. Who am I?
hints: My name is linked to a sea snail.
The humble god who jumped first became the sun.
So I wouldn't shine as brightly as the sun, they threw a rabbit in my face.
questions.description: A god who showed up late to his own party and ended up with the night.
questions.fun_fact: That's why, according to the myth, you can see the shape of a rabbit on the moon.

questions.question: Xaratanga was a goddess of the moon and fertility, partner of the fire god Curicaueri, worshipped beside a large lake. Which state were her people from?
hints: Her people were never conquered by the Mexica.
Those people are the Purépecha, also called the Tarascans.
Her lake is Lake Pátzcuaro.
questions.description: A goddess who lit up the night and was nowhere to be seen by day.
questions.fun_fact: The Purépecha held out against the Mexica and were among the few peoples who never paid them tribute.

questions.question: On the orders of Hun Camé, lord of Xibalbá, the head of Hun Hunahpú was hung in a tree. Who became pregnant when the head spat into her hand?
hints: She was a young maiden, the daughter of a lord of Xibalbá.
She fled the underworld and went to live with her children's grandmother.
She was the mother of Hunahpú and Ixbalanqué.
questions.description: A tree with the strangest fruit in the whole underworld.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Popol Vuh, the tree filled up with gourds, and no one from Xibalbá was allowed near it.

questions.question: This building was built as a Christian church almost 1,500 years ago. What was its city called back then?
hints: The city lies on a famous strait, where two continents meet.
Later another empire renamed it, and today it is the largest city in its country.
Its name comes from a Roman emperor called Constantine.
questions.description: A city so important it ended up with more names than a dog shared by three families.
questions.fun_fact: Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in the world for almost a thousand years.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this snake has this at the tip of its tail. What does it use it for?
questions.answer: To warn you to stay away
hints: It's made of rings of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
The snake shakes it very fast when someone comes near.
Its sound gave the snake its name.
questions.description: A desert accessory no snake ever leaves at home.
questions.fun_fact: Every time a rattlesnake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to its rattle.

questions.question: I’m from Sinaloa, and in 1965 I founded a band named after my village, El Limón. Today the band also carries my name. Who am I?
hints: The Lizárraga family is almost a dynasty of Sinaloan banda music.
I’m not the founder of Banda El Recodo.
My first name is also part of the name of a big Central American capital.
questions.description: A band with brass so sour you’d want to sprinkle some salt on it.
questions.fun_fact: The village of El Limón de los Ramos, near Culiacán, became famous all over Mexico thanks to its band.

questions.question: At a dance in Matehuala, young guys stomp around in boots with super-long pointy toes. In which decade did these botas picudas become a trend?
hints: People danced in them to tribal guarachero.
Videos of the dancers went viral online.
It came after the pasito duranguense craze.
questions.description: Shoes so long they enter the dance a minute before their owner does.
questions.fun_fact: Some botas picudas from Matehuala had tips more than 1 meter (3 ft) long, decorated with lights and little mirrors.

questions.question: He was called “El Huracán del Valle”, recorded from the 1930s on, and is known as the father of Tejano conjunto music. In which city was Narciso Martínez born?
hints: He was born in 1911, in a border city.
His hometown is in Tamaulipas.
It sits across the border from McAllen, Texas.
questions.description: A hurricane that brought no rain, just plenty of accordion.
questions.fun_fact: Narciso Martínez played the melody on the accordion and left the bass notes to the bajo sexto, the backbone of the norteño sound.

questions.question: Complete the name of the Tijuana band led by Eduin Caz: Grupo…
hints: It started in Baja California in 2014.
It fills stadiums with Mexican regional music.
Its name is the Spanish word for “steady” or “solid.”
questions.description: A band that never gives up, not even in its name.
questions.fun_fact: Grupo Firme has filled Mexico City's Zócalo and huge stadiums in the United States.

questions.question: You tune the radio to a “Regional Mexican” station. What music will you hear?
hints: It's the music of Mexico's towns and regions.
You hear a lot of tuba, accordion and violin.
That's where you'd hear Vicente Fernández or Banda El Recodo.
questions.description: A radio station that comes with a sombrero included.
questions.fun_fact: Regional Mexican music is one of the most-streamed Latin genres in the United States.

questions.question: Banda Jerez comes from a Pueblo Mágico in Zacatecas, was founded by Marco A. Flores and plays a Zacatecas style for weddings and jaripeos. Which one?
hints: It's banda music, with trumpets and saxophones.
Its name comes from the instrument that keeps the beat.
That instrument is a big drum with a cymbal on top.
questions.description: A sound from Zacatecas you can hear before the wedding even arrives.
questions.fun_fact: Jerez, Zacatecas, is also the hometown of the poet Ramón López Velarde.

questions.question: I was born in Long Beach, California, sang banda, filled stadiums in Mexico and the US, and my life inspired the series “Mariposa de barrio.” Who am I?
hints: My parents were Mexican, and my whole family sings.
One of my most famous songs is “Inolvidable.”
I share my last name with a famous painter who was married to Frida Kahlo.
questions.description: A queen who swapped her crown for a banda from Sinaloa.
questions.fun_fact: Jenni Rivera was one of the first women to become a big star singing banda, a genre that was almost all men.

questions.question: Acapulco was the trendy getaway of Hollywood stars, who cruised around its bay. When was it famous for this?
hints: Almost all the photos from that time are in black and white.
It was shortly after the Second World War.
Elvis Presley filmed “Fun in Acapulco” in the early 1960s, when that golden age had already been going for years.
questions.description: Hollywood glamour with sand in its shoes and sunglasses on.
questions.fun_fact: John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy spent their honeymoon in Acapulco in 1953.

questions.question: Most of Mexico sits on the North American Plate, but not all of it. How many tectonic plates is Mexico's territory on?
hints: It's more than two, but you can count them on one hand.
Baja California rides on the Pacific Plate.
Besides the North American and Pacific Plates, there are the Caribbean, Cocos and Rivera Plates.
questions.description: Mexico doesn't stand on solid ground, but on a jigsaw puzzle that keeps moving.
questions.fun_fact: The Cocos Plate slides under the North American Plate off the Pacific coast, which is why Guerrero, Oaxaca and Chiapas have so many earthquakes.

questions.question: You're inside a Gothic cathedral and you don't go out. Which of these parts can you NOT see?
hints: This part does its work on the outside of the building.
It's like a stone arm pushing against the walls.
It's an outside arch that helps hold up the tall walls.
questions.description: Some parts of a cathedral can only be admired by people who skip going inside for Mass.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to those outside arches, Gothic cathedrals could have thinner walls and giant stained-glass windows.

questions.question: It's summer in Mexicali and everyone is saying “¡qué calorón!” How high can the thermometer go in the shade?
hints: It's much more than your body temperature.
But water doesn't boil in the street.
It's a number between 40 and 50.
questions.description: That moment when even the paletas are begging for shade.
questions.fun_fact: Mexicali has topped 50 °C (122 °F), and its motto is “the city that captured the sun.”

questions.question: You step outside and it's drizzling: the famous chipichipi. How big are its tiny drops?
hints: You can barely feel them falling.
They're smaller than the tip of a pencil.
The drops of a real downpour do reach a few millimeters.
questions.description: The rain that doesn't soak you, but still ruins your hair.
questions.fun_fact: Drizzle drops are so light that they fall slowly and sometimes seem to float in the air.

questions.question: It covers parts of Coahuila, Durango and Zacatecas, and crosses the border into Texas and New Mexico. What is Mexico's largest desert?
hints: Roadrunners, coyotes and loads of cacti live there.
It's in the north, between the two Sierra Madres.
It shares its name with Mexico's largest state.
questions.description: A place where the cacti need neither a watering can nor compliments.
questions.fun_fact: It's home to the Bolson tortoise, the largest land tortoise in North America.

questions.question: In May, the hills of Mexico are dry and brown. In June, the rains begin. What color are the hills in August?
hints: With water, plants grow a lot.
Grass and new leaves sprout everywhere.
It's the color of leaves.
questions.description: The most dramatic makeover the hills of Mexico get all year.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Mexico, almost all of the year's rain falls between May and October.

questions.question: I'm a Sabritas corn snack that comes in short, thin strips, flavored with chili and lime. Which snack am I?
hints: I'm not shaped like a triangle.
I'm sold in little bags in every corner store.
My name blends “churro” with the Spanish word for the grain I'm made from.
questions.description: The snack that paints your fingers red and leaves your tongue begging for water.
questions.fun_fact: Corn was domesticated in Mexico about 9,000 years ago from a wild plant called teosinte.

questions.question: I'm a Marinela snack cake: chocolate-covered sponge cake filled with cream and pineapple jam. What am I?
hints: Cut me open and you'll see a spiral inside.
I come two to a pack.
My name puts chocolate together with my roll shape.
questions.description: The snack cake that turns any school lunch into a party.
questions.fun_fact: Marinela, the brand behind Choco Roles, Gansito and Pingüinos, is part of Grupo Bimbo.

questions.question: At the posadas, when do people sing “Entren santos peregrinos”?
questions.answer: When the people inside open the door
wrong_answers: Before setting out with the candles
While the candy bags are handed out
hints: The people outside have already sung for a long time, asking for shelter.
The hosts finally recognize Mary and Joseph.
It's when everyone goes into the house.
questions.description: A party where even the candles know the words by heart.
questions.fun_fact: In the sung litany, the hosts turn the pilgrims away several times before recognizing that they are Mary and Joseph.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actress. In “¿Qué culpa tiene el niño?” (2016) I play Maru, a rich girl who gets pregnant by a guy she barely knows. Who am I?
hints: She has also acted in Hollywood, in a series about lawyers.
She was in “How to Get Away with Murder”.
In “We Are the Nobles” she played Bárbara, the millionaire's spoiled daughter.
questions.description: A comedy where the stork shows up before the engagement ring does.
questions.fun_fact: “¿Qué culpa tiene el niño?” was directed by Mexican filmmaker Gustavo Loza.

questions.question: Complete the title of the 2015 Mexican animated film in which some dogs form a soccer team: “Selección…”
hints: The missing word sounds more like a vet's office than a park.
It's an adjective that comes from Latin.
It looks a lot like the English word for the pointy teeth next to your front teeth.
questions.description: A team where nobody complains that the ball is covered in drool.
questions.fun_fact: “Canino” comes from the Latin “canis”, meaning dog, which is why the pointy teeth are also called canine teeth.

questions.question: Its luxury theaters are called Platino, and it is the big rival of Cinépolis in Mexico. Which movie theater chain is it?
hints: It opened its first theater in the mid-1990s.
In 2013 it bought the theaters a US chain had in the country.
Its name ends like Mexico's internet addresses.
questions.description: The place where the popcorn costs more than the ticket and nobody minds.
questions.fun_fact: In 2013, Cinemex bought the theaters that Cinemark had in Mexico.

questions.question: It stands on an island in the Seine, caught fire in 2019, and a novel has a hunchbacked bell-ringer living in it. What is it?
hints: It's in France.
Disney made a movie about its hunchback.
The hunchback is called Quasimodo, and he lives in Paris.
questions.description: A building with more gargoyles than tourists, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: After the fire, the cathedral opened its doors again in December 2024.

questions.question: It's made of painted wood, with four wheels, a hood and little windows, and you pull it across the floor on a string. What toy is it?
hints: It's a toy for the littlest ones, who are just learning to walk.
It looks like something you see on the street every day.
It's the toy version of a vehicle.
questions.description: Before game consoles, fun came with the string included.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican wooden toys are hand-painted in bright colors like Mexican pink, yellow and green.

questions.question: Besides writing “Pedro Páramo,” Juan Rulfo left a large body of visual work on Mexican villages and farmworkers, now shown in museums. What other art did he practice?
hints: He made these works while traveling Mexico's highways for his job.
He worked almost always in black and white and loved the light and shadows of the countryside.
His favorite tool was a camera.
questions.description: A writer of few words, but with a huge stash of pictures.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Rulfo worked as a traveling salesman for a tire company, and those trips gave him many of his photos.

questions.question: In 1952, Hollywood filmed the life of a leader of the Mexican Revolution, starring Marlon Brando. Who did he play?
hints: The novelist John Steinbeck wrote the movie’s script.
He fought for land for the peasant farmers.
His motto was “Tierra y libertad” (Land and Liberty), and he was born in Morelos.
questions.description: When Hollywood wanted a mustache, a sombrero and a revolution, it put all three on a gringo.
questions.fun_fact: Anthony Quinn, born in Chihuahua, won the Oscar for playing the hero’s brother in that movie.

questions.question: Tin Tan says to his buddy: “¿Qué onda, carnal?”. Originally, what relative was a “carnal”?
hints: Today it's used for a friend so close he's like family
It comes from “of the same flesh”
He has the same parents as you
questions.description: A word that started out in the family tree and ended up on the neighborhood street corner.
questions.fun_fact: Another word for buddies, “cuate”, comes from the Nahuatl “cóatl”, which means “snake” and also “twin”.

questions.question: I was a captain of dragoons in San Miguel el Grande. Before dawn on September 16, 1810, I rode to Dolores to warn that the plot had been discovered. Who am I?
hints: I was a friend and comrade in arms of Allende, also from San Miguel.
There are towns in Chihuahua and Tamaulipas that bear my surname.
My surname starts with A, but I'm not Allende.
questions.description: The most important messenger of 1810, and he didn't even have a cell phone.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to his warning, Hidalgo started the uprising early and called the people to arms that very morning.

questions.question: You're touring the museum at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas in Guanajuato. In what year did the insurgents capture it?
hints: It happened early in the 19th century.
It was in the first weeks of the War of Independence.
That same year, Hidalgo gave the Grito de Dolores.
questions.description: A building made to store corn that ended up storing history.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, a miner nicknamed el Pípila strapped a stone slab to his back so he could get close and set the Alhóndiga's door on fire.

questions.question: Look at this woven palm mat, the petate. What was it mainly used for in homes in the old days?
hints: It was spread out on the floor of the house.
In the morning it was rolled up and stored in a corner.
It was the “bed” of many people in the countryside.
questions.description: Before furniture stores, woven palm took care of almost everything at home.
questions.fun_fact: The word «petate» comes from the Nahuatl «pétatl», meaning mat.

review.feedback: source: the fun fact gives the Nahuatl word as «pétatl», but the Nahuatl word for mat is «petlatl». The source needs correcting first. The English fun fact also uses «» guillemets where house style wants “…”. Fix both in the translation once the source is fixed.

questions.question: Its name comes from the Nahuatl “xacalli”, and it is the traditional little house of the Mexican countryside. What is a jacal made of?
hints: Its materials are gathered in the countryside, without buying anything.
Traditionally, the family builds it themselves, with help from the neighbors.
Its roof is usually made of dry grass or palm leaves.
questions.description: A house with a Nahuatl name that has never been in a home-decor magazine.
questions.fun_fact: The word “jacal” even made it into the English of the US Southwest, where it also means a hut of sticks and mud.

questions.question: It's in downtown Mexico City, it's named after an Italian hero, and at night it fills with people. What do they go there for?
hints: There's a tequila and mezcal museum there.
At night, songs by José Alfredo Jiménez can be heard all over the plaza.
They wear charro suits and play violins, trumpets and guitarrón.
questions.description: A plaza where the party is just getting started when everyone else is going to bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: This marble sculpture is in the Vatican. Who made it?
hints: He was an Italian artist of the Renaissance.
He carved it when he was only about 24 years old.
He also sculpted the famous David in Florence.
questions.description: A sculpture so perfect that its maker just couldn't resist signing it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pietà is the only work Michelangelo ever signed: his name is carved on the sash across the Virgin Mary's chest.

questions.question: I hung in little shops, workshops and kitchens all over Mexico, with Jesús Helguera paintings like the warrior carrying his sleeping love before the volcanoes. What am I?
hints: People hung me on the wall with a little nail.
Shops and businesses gave me to their customers as a gift.
I help you know what day it is.
questions.description: Museum-worthy art that shared the room with dried chilies and the big water jug.
questions.fun_fact: Jesús Helguera was born in Chihuahua in 1910 and spent part of his childhood in Spain.

questions.question: On Popocatépetl's volcanic alert traffic light, what does the yellow light mean?
wrong_answers: The volcano has gone out for good
hints: It works a bit like a street traffic light
It's the color Popo has had most of the time in recent years
It's not time to flee, but it is time to have your emergency backpack ready
questions.description: A traffic light nobody runs, because a volcano is in the driver's seat.
questions.fun_fact: CENAPRED, Mexico's disaster prevention center, watches Popocatépetl day and night with cameras and sensors to decide the light's color.

questions.question: I fall from the sky when Popo gets angry, I turn cars and roofs gray, and I sting your eyes. What am I?
hints: I come from a volcano
I'm gray and very fine, like dust
When I fall, airports sometimes close
questions.description: When Popo sneezes, the whole city finds out.
questions.fun_fact: Volcanic ash isn't left over from something burned: it's made of tiny bits of rock and glass.

questions.question: Every November in Mexico, people write funny rhyming verses where Death comes for someone famous. Where does she usually take them in the end?
hints: These verses are called calaveritas.
It's a place with tombs and crosses.
It's where people bring cempasúchil flowers on Día de Muertos.
questions.description: Poetry so funny that even La Huesuda cracks up.
questions.fun_fact: People have been writing calaveritas literarias since the 19th century, and they started out poking fun at politicians and other important people.

questions.question: I'm a 2021 Netflix animated series. My heroine is a princess who wants to be a warrior and defies the gods. My creator made “The Book of Life.” What am I?
wrong_answers: El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera
hints: It's inspired by the cultures of Mesoamerica, the Caribbean and South America.
Its creator is the Mexican artist Jorge R. Gutiérrez.
The princess's name is also the name of a civilization from Yucatán.
questions.description: An adventure with so many gods that Mount Olympus would get jealous.
questions.fun_fact: The series has only nine episodes, and its voice cast includes Zoe Saldaña and Diego Luna.

questions.question: You're born in a Zapotec village in Oaxaca and, according to the tona belief, an animal will be your double for life. When was that animal born?
questions.answer: On the same day as you
wrong_answers: On the day of your baptism
On the Day of the Dead
hints: It's a very old belief, from before the Spanish arrived.
If something happens to the animal, it happens to you too.
That's why people sometimes spread ash next to a newborn to see what tracks appeared.
questions.description: A companion with feathers, fur or scales that you got without anyone asking you first.
questions.fun_fact: Unlike the nahual, a person with a tona doesn't transform: they only share their fate with the animal.

questions.question: Outside the arena, your hero writes one with a marker on your mask or a photo. What is it called?
hints: Famous people give them to their fans.
It's done by hand, with a pen or a marker.
Its name comes from Greek and means “written by oneself.”
questions.description: Proof that you really saw your hero up close, and not just on TV.
questions.fun_fact: Masked wrestlers sign with their ring name, never their real one, to protect their secret identity.

questions.question: The Maya built it with stones jutting out from each side until they almost meet, capped with a slab and no keystone. What kind of arch is it?
hints: It isn't rounded: it ends in a triangle shape.
Each row of stones sticks out a little farther than the one below.
Its name says it isn't a “true” arch like the Roman one.
questions.description: A stone doorway that has been waiting for visitors in the jungle for over a thousand years.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it is also called the “Maya arch,” because it shows up in so many buildings of that culture.

questions.question: In Mexico, the summer solstice is the longest day of the year. Roughly what date is it?
hints: In Mexico, summer vacation has just started or is about to start.
It's the month right in the middle of the year.
It's exactly six months before the winter solstice, which falls close to Christmas.
questions.description: The favorite day of everyone who hates it when it gets dark early.
questions.fun_fact: After the summer solstice, the days slowly get shorter until December.

questions.question: You pull a bill out of your wallet and it says “Banco de México” at the top. In what year did that bank open?
hints: It came after the Mexican Revolution.
President Plutarco Elías Calles created it.
It turned 100 in 2025.
questions.description: A bank that will never give you a credit card, but signs every one of your bills.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Banco de México existed, several private banks printed their own bills.

questions.question: When a child in Mexico gets their “domingo,” what are they given?
hints: It isn't a day of the week, even though it's named after one.
It almost always comes from parents or grandparents.
It goes into the piggy bank or the wallet.
questions.description: Kids wait for it every week even more eagerly than for recess.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “domingo” (Sunday) because it was traditionally given on that day, to spend on candy or at the fair.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in September, the streets of Mexico are full of these for sale. What are they?
hints: They're green, white and red.
They have an eagle in the middle.
They look like the one raised at school ceremonies, only tiny.
questions.description: In September, street stalls get more patriotic than ever.
questions.fun_fact: Around September 15, many vendors fill the streets with flags, sombreros and pinwheels in the three national colors.

questions.question: On Mexico's civic calendar, on what day is the Oil Expropriation remembered?
hints: It falls early in the year.
Lázaro Cárdenas announced it in 1938.
It's three days before Benito Juárez's birthday.
questions.description: The day black gold decided to stay home for good.
questions.fun_fact: After the 1938 announcement, many people donated chickens, jewelry and even their wedding rings to help pay for the expropriation.

questions.question: In the 2011 Gold Cup final, Giovani dos Santos rounded the goalkeeper and scored with a soft, high touch. What do Mexican commentators call that shot?
hints: It's not done with your back to goal, and it doesn't curve.
The ball floats up slowly and drops into the goal.
It's named after a slippery petroleum jelly for dry skin.
questions.description: A goal that commentators still replay with a trembling voice.
questions.fun_fact: The United States led 2–0 in that final, and El Tri came back to win 4–2 at the Rose Bowl.

questions.question: Mexico co-hosted the 2026 World Cup with the United States and Canada. In which years had it hosted the tournament before?
hints: Both times were in the 20th century, and Estadio Azteca hosted the final.
The first time, Pelé won it with Brazil.
The second time, Maradona scored his famous “Hand of God” goal.
questions.description: Some countries throw a party; others already know by heart where the folding chairs go.
questions.fun_fact: Estadio Azteca was the first stadium to host matches at three World Cups: 1970, 1986 and 2026.

questions.question: The coach of El Tri from 2011 to 2013 was known as “Chepo” de la Torre. “Chepo” is a nickname for which name?
hints: It's one of the most common names in Mexico.
It's the first name of an Independence hero whose last name was Morelos.
It's the name of Mary's husband in the Christmas nativity scene.
questions.description: In Mexico, nobody goes by the name on their birth certificate, and this coach is no exception.
questions.fun_fact: Before coaching El Tri, Chepo won league titles as coach of Chivas and Toluca.

questions.question: Which gymnast won four golds at Mexico 1968 and got married in the Metropolitan Cathedral during the Games?
hints: She was the woman with the most gold medals at those Games.
Her country later split in two: the Czech Republic and Slovakia.
Her first name starts with V and her last name has the letter “č”.
questions.description: She went to Mexico City for medals and came home with a ring as well.
questions.fun_fact: Her wedding to athlete Josef Odložil at the Cathedral drew thousands of curious onlookers to the Zócalo.

questions.question: In what year did the Capitanes de la Ciudad de México make their debut in the G League, the NBA's development league?
hints: Before that, they played a few seasons in the Mexican league, the LNBP.
It was in the 2020s.
They arrived a year late because of the pandemic, the same year as the Tokyo Olympics.
questions.description: A chilango team playing in a gringo league, like the cousin who moved up north.
questions.fun_fact: Their G League debut was planned for a year earlier, but the pandemic pushed it back.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which piece of music plays when the owner of this helmet appears?
hints: A full orchestra plays it, with very loud brass and a marching beat.
You hear it in Star Wars.
Its name is about emperors and armies on parade.
questions.description: When this gentleman walks in, even the soundtrack gets serious.
questions.fun_fact: The Imperial March was first heard in “The Empire Strikes Back” in 1980, not in the first film.

questions.question: In which decade was Lucero the little girl “Lucerito” in the telenovela “Chispita”?
hints: It was the age of Walkmans and shoulder pads.
The first Super Mario Bros. video game came out that decade.
It was the same decade as the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: A little star so small she still fit in a diminutive.
questions.fun_fact: “Chispita” premiered in 1982, when Lucero was only about 13 years old.

questions.question: “My mom is a famous telenovela actress, they call me el Gallito Feliz, and I sang “Azul” and “No podrás.”” Who am I?
hints: I started singing very young, in the early nineties.
My mom starred in “Los ricos también lloran.”
My mom is named Verónica and is one of the great stars of Mexican TV.
questions.description: A rooster who sings ballads instead of waking up the whole ranch.
questions.fun_fact: Cristian Castro made a tribute album to José José called “Mi amigo el Príncipe.”

questions.question: Ixmucané is the grandmother of the twins in the Popol Vuh. She ground yellow and white corn, and the gods used that dough. What did they make?
hints: The gods had already tried this several times before, with no luck.
They had tried mud first, then wood; this time it finally worked.
From that dough they made people's flesh and blood.
questions.description: A grandma who would win every tortilla contest in the universe.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Popol Vuh, the wooden dolls from an earlier attempt ended up turning into monkeys.

questions.question: According to the Mexica, the sons of the creator couple, the Tezcatlipocas, made the world. How many were there?
hints: Each one had his own color.
One of them was Quetzalcóatl, the white Tezcatlipoca.
