Each one watched over one direction of the world: north, south, east and west.
questions.description: A family of gods so big they split the world up like a cake.
questions.fun_fact: The name Tezcatlipoca means “smoking mirror,” after mirrors made of black obsidian.

questions.question: For the Maya, Kinich Ahau, the sun god, crossed the sky by day. At sunset he went down to the underworld. What did he turn into?
hints: He became an animal that hunts at night.
Its spots were like the stars of the night sky.
It's the biggest wild cat in the Americas.
questions.description: A god who works the day shift, then at night changes shifts… and outfits.
questions.fun_fact: At Kohunlich, in Quintana Roo, giant stucco masks show the face of the Maya sun god.

questions.question: In the Mexica Legend of the Suns, the people of one era turned into fish. Which sun was that era?
hints: It is not the era we live in today.
It came right after the sun that ended in fire.
It was the last sun before the current one.
questions.description: An era when people had to learn to swim really fast.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions, only one couple survived the flood by hiding inside a tree trunk.

questions.question: The Olmec “were-jaguar” figures, with a baby face and a cat's mouth, come from which period of Mesoamerica?
hints: The Olmecs were one of the oldest cultures of Mesoamerica.
The Olmecs flourished about 3,000 years ago.
The period's name means “before the Classic.”
questions.description: Half baby, half cat, and a face nobody forgets.
questions.fun_fact: Some scholars think the Olmec were-jaguar is an ancestor of later gods such as Tláloc.

questions.question: This Texas band went viral in 2022 with a norteño version of “No se va,” and in 2023 sang “Un x100to” with Bad Bunny. Who are they?
hints: They play cumbia norteña with an accordion.
“No se va” was first a song by the Colombian band Morat.
Their name refers to the line between Mexico and the United States.
questions.description: Some guys from Texas who got half of Mexico dancing at weddings, quinceañeras and carne asadas.
questions.fun_fact: The members of Grupo Frontera come from the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, just minutes from Tamaulipas.

questions.question: The vibraslap used by modern drummers was invented to copy the sound of a traditional instrument. Which one?
hints: It's heard in the sones of the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca.
It's also very common in Afro-Peruvian music.
It's made from a face bone of a pack animal.
questions.description: An instrument nobody ever bought at a music store.
questions.fun_fact: The jawbone has been played for centuries in the Afro-descendant music of Mexico and Peru.

questions.question: They called me “The Voice” and I sang “New York, New York.” I was born in the US, but my parents came from another country. Which one?
hints: My parents moved to the United States in the early 1900s, like millions of other Europeans.
Many immigrants from that country settled in New York and New Jersey.
It's the country of pizza and pasta.
questions.description: A gentleman so elegant he even sang in a bow tie.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Sinatra was born in Hoboken, a New Jersey city just across the river from New York.

questions.question: In an emergency drill, everyone goes out and waits in a safe spot, away from walls and cables, marked with a green sign. What is that place called?
hints: It's not the door you leave by or the path you follow.
That's where teachers count to make sure nobody is missing.
It's the place where everyone gathers together.
questions.description: The only meeting where showing up late is truly worrying.
questions.fun_fact: A good assembly point is far from buildings, trees, poles and cables that could fall.

questions.question: Which of these people is NOT a capitalino?
hints: A capitalino is someone from the country's capital.
Three of those places are parts of Mexico City.
One of them was born in the capital of Jalisco.
questions.description: Surviving the traffic and the rush-hour metro is the price of bragging about this hometown.
questions.fun_fact: Capitalinos are also called chilangos, a word many now use with pride.

questions.question: What is the most famous nickname of the Toluca soccer team?
hints: It plays its home games at the Estadio Nemesio Díez.
It is one of the clubs with the most league titles in Mexico.
It shares its name with the character in pastorelas (Christmas plays) who pesters the shepherds.
questions.description: A team that plays way up high and still never runs out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Toluca is also called “los Choriceros”, after the city's famous chorizo.

questions.question: Which of these are NOT costeños?
hints: A costeño is someone who lives by the sea.
Three of these cities have beaches.
It's the city of chiles en nogada and mole, far from the sea.
questions.description: A question that smells of sunscreen… for almost everyone.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has more than 11,000 km (6,800 miles) of coastline along the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean.

questions.question: Fill in the nickname of Guadalajara's Atlas: the red-and-blacks are also called “los ___”.
hints: It's a mammal, not a bird.
It's the animal in “The Little Prince” that asks to be tamed.
It's known for being cunning, with a bushy tail and reddish fur.
questions.description: A red-and-black club that has spent decades making its fans suffer, in style.
questions.fun_fact: Atlas is also called “la Academia” for its famous youth academy, which has produced a huge number of players.

questions.question: The people of Mazatlán live in a Sinaloa port whose name comes from Nahuatl and means “place of…” what?
hints: It's an animal of the wild hills.
The Nahuatl word is mazatl.
The city's baseball team is named after this animal.
questions.description: A port with a carnival, a seaside boardwalk and a name that goes way, way back.
questions.fun_fact: The Mazatlán Carnival is one of the oldest and biggest in Mexico.

questions.question: The name Zacatecas comes from the Nahuatl word zacatl. What is zacatl?
hints: It's a plant, not a metal.
It grows on the ground, and cows eat it.
The Mexican word “zacate” for a lawn comes from it.
questions.description: Many Mexican states hide a Nahuatl word in their name, like a secret tucked into a wallet.
questions.fun_fact: In colonial times, Zacatecas was one of the biggest silver producers in the world.

questions.question: Oaxaca, Chiapas and Guerrero are all in the same region of Mexico. Which one?
hints: All three have long coastlines on the Pacific Ocean.
They're famous for their jungles, their mountains and their many Indigenous communities, and it's hot almost all year.
It's the direction you go from Mexico City to reach Guatemala.
questions.description: A question for people who always say “it's over that way…” and point anywhere at all.
questions.fun_fact: Chiapas, in the south, borders Guatemala and has one of Mexico's largest rainforests: the Lacandon Jungle.

questions.question: This Spanish word, used a lot in Spain, jokingly names a very long telenovela full of twists. What is it?
hints: The word comes from an animal.
That animal is very long and has no legs.
It's like a “culebra” (snake), only bigger.
questions.description: A word for telenovelas that last longer than the line at the bank on payday.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from how long the story is: it twists and stretches out like a snake.

questions.question: “Destilando amor” (2007) is the Mexican remake of “Café con aroma de mujer,” minus the coffee, and its heroine Gaviota is a jimadora. In which state is it set?
hints: A jimadora cuts the leaves off the agave plant.
Instead of coffee, the Montalvo family makes a drink famous all over the world.
This state has a town with the same name as the drink, and its capital is Guadalajara.
questions.description: A telenovela where love takes its time, a lot of time, to mature.
questions.fun_fact: The stars of “Destilando amor” were Angélica Rivera and Eduardo Yáñez.

questions.question: Mariachi is to ranchera as cowboy is to…
hints: Its songs are about pickup trucks, horses and broken hearts.
It's sung with guitar, banjo and lots of longing for life out on the land.
Dolly Parton and Johnny Cash are among its biggest stars.
questions.description: Music with boots, a big hat and a whiff of the stable.
questions.fun_fact: Nashville, Tennessee, is so famous for country music that it's nicknamed “Music City.”

questions.question: When La Muerte comes up in lotería, some callers say “la muerte tilica”. In Mexico, what does “tilico” mean?
hints: It's said about people, not things.
It has to do with how someone's body looks.
It's like saying someone is all skin and bones.
questions.description: The card nobody wants to get, but that always shows up in the end.
questions.fun_fact: The La Muerte card shows a skeleton with a scythe, and it's still a favorite for many players.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which Mexico City Metro line has the stations closest to this building?
hints: It crosses the city from north to south.
Its color is olive green.
One of its end stations is Indios Verdes.
questions.description: Every morning, thousands of people get off here with backpacks and not enough sleep.
questions.fun_fact: UNAM's Ciudad Universitaria has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

questions.question: Rosario Castellanos's “Oficio de tinieblas” (1962) tells of an Indigenous uprising. In which Mexican state is it set?
hints: The novel takes place in the highlands, near a colonial city.
Its Indigenous characters are Tzotzil.
Rosario Castellanos grew up in Comitán, in this same state.
questions.description: A novel with church bells, prayers and a rebellion too big to fit in the sacristy.
questions.fun_fact: The novel is based on a 19th-century Chamula rebellion, but Castellanos moved it to the time of President Lázaro Cárdenas.

questions.question: They're poems with humor and a surprise ending, invented by Efraín Huerta, “el Gran Cocodrilo.” What are they called?
hints: They don't come from Japan or Spain: they're a Mexican invention.
Their name joins two words.
One of those words is “mínimo.”
questions.description: Verses to read with a crooked smile and one eyebrow raised.
questions.fun_fact: Efraín Huerta was born in Silao, Guanajuato, in 1914.

questions.question: Jorge Volpi signed a manifesto with Ignacio Padilla and Eloy Urroz in 1996, then made his name with “In Search of Klingsor.” What is his generation called?
hints: They wanted to move away from magical realism.
“In Search of Klingsor” won the Biblioteca Breve Prize in 1999.
Its name sounds like something snapping or breaking.
questions.description: A generation that showed up with a manifesto under its arm, ready to pick a fight with its literary grandparents.
questions.fun_fact: “In Search of Klingsor” is a thriller about physicists like Heisenberg and Einstein, written by a Mexican.

questions.question: These giant saguaros grow in the desert of northwest Mexico, next to the border with Arizona. What are the people of that state called?
hints: The state is famous for its carne asada and its huge flour tortillas.
Its capital is Hermosillo.
The desert where they grow is named after the state.
questions.description: Cacti so tall they seem to wave their arms at everyone driving by.
questions.fun_fact: A saguaro can take about 70 years to grow its first arm.

questions.question: Some Mexican coats of arms show an ear of a plant: yellow, wrapped in leaves, with kernels in rows. Which plant?
hints: Tortillas are made from this plant.
Cooked and topped with mayo and chile, it's sold on the street.
When it's young and tender, Mexicans call it elote.
questions.description: It comes wrapped in leaves like a present, but inside it's nothing but yellow teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Corn was domesticated in Mexico about 9,000 years ago from a wild plant called teosinte.

questions.question: Santos Laguna plays in Torreón and wears green and white. What does the “Laguna” in the club's name refer to?
wrong_answers: A lake next to its stadium
hints: It's much bigger than a stadium.
It covers parts of Coahuila and Durango.
It's an area where the Nazas and Aguanaval rivers once formed old lagoons.
questions.description: A team dressed in green and white, like an Independence Day party that forgot to bring the red.
questions.fun_fact: People from the Comarca Lagunera are called laguneros, even though the lagoons that gave the region its name have almost disappeared.

questions.question: Monterrey's team is called the Rayados (“the Striped Ones”) because of their striped shirts. Which of these animals has NO stripes?
hints: Three of these animals have stripes.
The one you want is very small and red.
It has little black dots instead of stripes.
questions.description: A nickname you can see at a glance, just like a crosswalk.
questions.fun_fact: The Rayados shirt has blue and white stripes.

questions.question: Someone from Jalisco is a jalisciense. Someone from Durango is a…
hints: It follows the same pattern as the demonym of many Mexican states.
A danceable music style from that state, very popular in the 2000s, has the same name.
It ends in -ense.
questions.description: A question with a fancy ending and zero scorpions.
questions.fun_fact: Durango is called “the land of cinema,” because hundreds of Wild West movies were filmed there.

questions.question: This lion tops a famous arch in the Bajío, in the city that shares its name. What are the city's residents called?
hints: The city is known as the shoe capital of the world.
It's the same demonym used for the city of León in Spain.
It ends in -eses.
questions.description: A bronze cat guards the way into the city, though it has never hunted a thing.
questions.fun_fact: The Arco de la Calzada, with its lion on top, is one of the best-loved symbols of León, Guanajuato.

questions.question: You're watching a very young Angelique Boyer as Vico, the wild friend in «Rebelde». In what year did that telenovela premiere?
hints: It was in the middle of the first decade of this century.
Soon after, the band RBD was born and filled stadiums all over Latin America.
It was the same year as the Athens Olympics.
questions.description: A loose necktie, a plaid skirt and a school for rich kids: the recipe for a teen hit.
questions.fun_fact: Angelique Boyer was born in France and moved to Mexico as a child; today she is one of Televisa's most famous leading ladies.

questions.question: I strike the heroine after an accident; because of me she knows the hero only by his voice, not his face, and surgery cures me at the end. What am I?
hints: It doesn't affect the heroine's memory.
The heroine hears the hero perfectly well.
The heroine often wears dark glasses and uses a cane.
questions.description: The writers' favorite trick: take something away from the heroine and give it back in the final episode.
questions.fun_fact: The heroine getting her sight back through surgery near the end is a classic melodrama twist that already showed up in old radio soaps and movies.

questions.question: In what year did “Tú o nadie”, the Televisa telenovela with Lucía Méndez and Andrés García, premiere?
hints: It's from the decade of shoulder pads and big hair.
It premiered around the middle of that decade.
It premiered one year before “Cuna de lobos”.
questions.description: A telenovela whose title leaves no room for a plan B.
questions.fun_fact: Lucía Méndez was both an actress and a singer, and in several of her telenovelas she sang the theme song herself.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actress. In 1989 I was María, a country girl who moves to the capital and succeeds with her sewing machine in “Simplemente María.” Who am I?
hints: People call me one of TV's queens of tears.
My leading man in that telenovela was Manuel Saval.
In 2005 I starred in “La madrastra.”
questions.description: A seamstress, a sewing machine and enough tears to wash the whole neighborhood's laundry.
questions.fun_fact: The first “Simplemente María” was made in Argentina in 1967, but the 1969 Peruvian version was such a hit that it inspired new versions in several countries, including Mexico.

questions.question: You're watching Angélica Aragón as María Inés, a woman who falls for a much younger journalist in «Mirada de mujer». In what year did it premiere?
hints: It premiered before the year 2000 arrived.
It aired on TV Azteca, which had only been on the air for a few years.
It was the same year the movie “Titanic” came out.
questions.description: A telenovela that taught Mexico that love has no expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: «Mirada de mujer» was an adaptation of the Colombian telenovela «Señora Isabel» and dared to take on topics almost nobody touched on TV.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. Alejandro Salas (Ari Telch) is a writer, not a journalist. The 1997 premiere year is correct (June 9, 1997, Azteca Trece).

questions.question: The whole family gathers in front of the TV to watch me, the streets go empty, and the villain finally gets punished. What am I?
hints: After me, there is nothing more.
I come after months of tears and tangled plots.
I'm the very last chapter of the telenovela; after me, the credits roll for good.
questions.description: When I arrive, even grandma turns off her cell phone and nobody answers the door.
questions.fun_fact: Some telenovela finales were so popular that people moved parties and weddings so they wouldn't miss them.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer (the final episode) fits the riddle, and the wrong answers are clearly wrong. The empty-streets effect is documented: Cuna de lobos' finale on 5 June 1987 emptied Mexico City streets and reached about 73 rating points. I couldn't find a source for the fun fact's claim that people moved parties and weddings to catch finales. It's plausible but unverified.

source: the fact check couldn't confirm the fun fact's claim that people moved parties and weddings so they wouldn't miss telenovela finales, and I can't confirm it either. The documented effect is that streets emptied (for example, the 1987 finale of Cuna de lobos). The source's fun fact should be replaced with a documented one, such as the Cuna de lobos finale emptying Mexico's streets. Then the translation can follow it. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and natural. Fact check: uncertain. Answer (the final episode) and wrong answers are fine. Cuna de lobos (1987) finale did empty streets and halt daily life in Mexico. But no source supports the fun fact's claim that people moved parties and weddings. Only the streets and daily-life impact is documented.

questions.question: This US Spanish-language TV network used to be called Spanish International Network and aired Televisa's telenovelas there for decades. Which is it?
hints: It isn't a Mexican network, though its viewers speak Spanish.
It took its current name in 1987 and for years was the most-watched Spanish-language network in the US.
In 2022 it merged with Televisa into a single company.
questions.description: A channel that carried Mexican tears across the border.
questions.fun_fact: Since the 2022 merger, the company has been called TelevisaUnivision.

questions.question: I'm Brazil's most famous festival, with feathers, sequins and giant floats. Who competes by parading in me?
hints: They dance and play drums for hours.
They prepare all year to win the contest.
Their name sounds like a place where kids learn, but there's no homework, only Brazil's most famous dance.
questions.description: A party with more feathers than a henhouse.
questions.fun_fact: The Rio Carnival parades take place in the Sambadrome, an avenue built just for them.

questions.question: You're at recess and everyone's about to play resorte. What is the resorte for in this game?
questions.answer: To jump over and step on with your feet
wrong_answers: To shoot pebbles like a slingshot
To pull on between two teams
To swing around like a jump rope
hints: It's played by three or more kids.
Two of them hold it stretched out and stand still.
Each round it goes higher: ankles, knees, waist.
questions.description: It came out of Grandma's sewing box and ended up as the star of recess.
questions.fun_fact: In English this game is often called “Chinese jump rope”, but kids play it in schoolyards all over the world.

questions.question: In the song “Un elefante se columpiaba”, the first elephant swings on a thin thread that held strong. What animal made it?
hints: It's a tiny animal.
It has eight legs.
It spins webs in the corners of the house.
questions.description: The song that proves physics is optional in the world of children.
questions.fun_fact: It's a counting song: each verse adds one more elephant, and you can keep going until you get tired!

questions.question: One kid chases the others; when they tag someone, they shout a phrase, and now that kid is the chaser. What is this game called in Mexico?
hints: Its name is what you shout when you tag someone.
It's like passing a hot potato with your hand.
When you tag someone, you shout “¡Ahora tú…!”
questions.description: Running until you're out of breath, all so you don't get stuck with it.
questions.fun_fact: In English it's called “tag”, in Argentina «la mancha» and in Spain «pillapilla».

questions.question: I draw the cards one by one, call each with a funny rhyme, and if one is on your board, you put a bean on it. Who am I?
hints: Without me, nobody knows which card came up.
My job is to talk really loud.
My name comes from the Spanish word for shouting.
questions.description: The whole table hangs on every word, with the board almost full and a bean ready in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Many gritones make up their own rhymes, and the best ones get the whole table laughing.

questions.question: You spin a trompo with a string wound around it. Which of these traditional toys is played WITHOUT any string or thread?
hints: It's played on the ground.
You shoot them with a flick of your finger.
They're little glass balls.
questions.description: Some toys are always tied up; others roam free like the wind.
questions.fun_fact: To throw a trompo, you wind the string from the tip upward and then pull it hard.

questions.question: On Sunday mornings, this Mexico City avenue closes to cars so you can ride your bike. Which one is it?
hints: It's one of the most famous and elegant avenues in the city.
It runs next to Chapultepec Park.
The Angel of Independence stands on it.
questions.description: The one day of the week when cars have to ask bikes for permission.
questions.fun_fact: The Sunday ride “Muévete en Bici” started in 2007 and brings out thousands of cyclists, skaters and runners every week.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: to let the driver know you're getting off the bus, you press the ___ next to the back door.
hints: It's a button any passenger can use.
When you press it, it rings so the driver can hear it.
Houses have one too, next to the front door.
questions.description: The politest way to tell the driver “this is as far as I go.”
questions.fun_fact: On many buses, pressing the button lights up a “stop requested” sign so the driver doesn't forget.

questions.question: The Nissan Tsuru, taxi drivers' favorite, stopped being made in Mexico in 2017. About how many years was it on sale?
hints: Your parents knew it, and maybe your grandparents drove one too.
It arrived in Mexico in the 1980s.
It went on sale under that name in 1984.
questions.description: A car that took more people to work than a whole fleet of buses.
questions.fun_fact: “Tsuru” means “crane” in Japanese, a bird that stands for good luck and long life in Japan.

questions.question: It looks like a bus but it's electric: two poles connect it to cables hanging over the street. It has run in Mexico City since 1951. What is it called?
hints: It has rubber tires, like any bus.
If its poles slip off the cables, it stops dead.
One of its lines runs along Eje Central and is called “Cero Emisiones.”
questions.description: A bus that never stops at the gas station, and doesn't miss it one bit.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, the two poles that connect it to the cables are called “troles,” and that's where its name comes from.

questions.question: There are seven of them, they're from South Korea, and in 2020 “Dynamite” made them the first South Korean group to hit No. 1 on Billboard. Who are they?
hints: They are the most famous K-pop group in the world.
Their fans call themselves ARMY.
Their name is just three letters.
questions.description: Seven guys who blew up the charts, literally.
questions.fun_fact: “Dynamite” was the first BTS song sung entirely in English.

review.feedback: Source: the claim is wrong as stated, in both the source and the translation. BTS already reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200 album chart in 2018 with "Love Yourself: Tear". "Dynamite" was their first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, the singles chart. The source should say "Hot 100" (for example "the first all-South Korean act to top the Billboard Hot 100"), and the translation should then follow it.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: the square (and its Metro station) is called Zócalo because only ___ of a monument was ever built.
hints: The monument was meant to celebrate Independence, in the 19th century.
Antonio López de Santa Anna ordered it, but it was never finished.
It's the bottom part a statue would have stood on.
questions.description: A giant square named after something almost nobody ever saw.
questions.fun_fact: The word “zócalo” means pedestal or base, and today many Mexican cities use it as the name for their main square.

questions.question: I never owned a bookstore, but since 1971 a famous Mexican bookstore chain has carried my name. I walked to the sea to make salt. Who am I?
hints: I fought without violence for my country's independence.
My country is India.
The yellow ads of those bookstores are famous all over Mexico City.
questions.description: A leader who never haggled in a bookstore, yet today everyone buys books in his name.
questions.fun_fact: The first Librería Gandhi, founded by Mauricio Achar, opened on Avenida Miguel Ángel de Quevedo in Mexico City.

questions.question: In “News from the Empire” (1987), the empress who lived in this castle tells her story, old and far from Mexico. Who wrote the novel?
hints: The author was born in Mexico City in 1935 and also wrote “Palinuro of Mexico”.
He won the Cervantes Prize in 2015.
He also wrote the novel “José Trigo” (1966) and was a painter and draftsman.
questions.description: An imperial soap opera with over 600 pages and no commercial breaks.
questions.fun_fact: The novel’s voice is Empress Carlota, who in her delusions talks to Maximilian from a castle in Belgium.

questions.question: Which writer created Filiberto García, the tough agent who looks into a supposed plot in Mexico City's Chinatown?
hints: The novel came out in 1969 and is a classic of Mexican crime fiction.
It's called “El complot mongol” (“The Mongolian Conspiracy”).
The author's last name starts with B and ends in “-nal.”
questions.description: An agent so tough that even fortune cookies are scared of him.
questions.fun_fact: “El complot mongol” was made into a movie twice: in 1978 and in 2019.

questions.question: I was a king and a poet. I wrote “I love the song of the cenzontle, bird of four hundred voices,” and my face was on the 100-peso bill. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 15th century, before the Spanish arrived.
I ruled Texcoco, by the great lake in the Valley of Mexico.
My name means “fasting coyote.”
questions.description: A king who skipped the boring speeches and wrote about little birds instead.
questions.fun_fact: “Cenzontle” comes from Nahuatl and means exactly “four hundred voices,” because this bird, the mockingbird, copies many other birds' songs.

questions.question: I was born in the Americas with Rubén Darío; in Mexico, Gutiérrez Nájera and Amado Nervo cultivated me, and I love swans and musical verse. Which movement am I?
hints: I flourished in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
In Mexico I had a famous magazine: the “Revista Azul”.
My name sounds like something new, something “modern”.
questions.description: A movement so elegant its poets wrote wearing bow ties.
questions.fun_fact: Rubén Darío’s book “Azul...”, published in 1888, is considered the great start of modernismo.

questions.question: On TV you’re watching “The Golden Cockerel” (1964), about a poor town crier who gets rich with a rooster. Who wrote the original story?
hints: The author was born in Jalisco and published very few books.
He is also the author of “The Burning Plain”.
He also wrote “Pedro Páramo”.
questions.description: A rooster that doesn’t crow at dawn, but crows victory in the palenque.
questions.fun_fact: The film’s screenplay was adapted by Carlos Fuentes and Gabriel García Márquez.

questions.question: “Where the Air Is Clear,” Carlos Fuentes's first novel, paints the Mexico City of its day. When was it published?
hints: Carlos Fuentes was born in 1928.
Fuentes was still a young writer, around 30, when it came out.
It was during the presidency of Adolfo Ruiz Cortines.
questions.description: A novel with air so clear that today it would need a good filter.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish title comes from Alfonso Reyes: “Traveler, you have arrived at the most transparent region of the air.”

questions.question: I moved from Cancún to Buenos Aires, I deliver food on roller skates and I dream of shining at the Jam & Roller rink. Who am I?
hints: I'm the main character of a Disney Channel series.
The series is named after me.
My first name is the Spanish word for Earth's natural satellite.
questions.description: A girl who can't seem to walk anywhere without wheels under her feet.
questions.fun_fact: Luna was played by Mexican actress and singer Karol Sevilla.

questions.question: They call me a “single,” but I'm not looking for a partner. In music, what am I?
questions.answer: A song released on its own
hints: Artists put me out before their album.
I'm used to promote a record.
On old vinyl records, I often had a B-side.
questions.description: In music, this word has nothing to do with dating apps.
questions.fun_fact: Singles used to be sold on small vinyl records that spun at 45 revolutions per minute.

questions.question: In a black-and-white movie, a dancer in a tailcoat tap-dances with Ginger Rogers. They made 10 movies together. Who is he?
hints: He was a Hollywood star in the 1930s.
He's not the one who dances in the rain with an umbrella.
His stage surname starts with “A”.
questions.description: A man who made the floor look like it was made of clouds.
questions.fun_fact: People say Ginger Rogers did everything he did, but backwards and in high heels.

questions.question: I'm a cheerleader in Seabrook, I hide my white hair under a wig, and I fell in love with Zed, a zombie. Who am I?
hints: I'm in the Disney Channel movie “Zombies”.
My cousin Bucky is the captain of the cheerleaders.
My name starts with “A”.
questions.description: A love story where one of the two needs a wristband to stop craving brains.
questions.fun_fact: The first “Zombies” movie premiered on Disney Channel in 2018 and got several sequels.

questions.question: At a Broadway concert: “Don't Cry for Me Argentina” is to “Evita” as “Memory” is to…
hints: Both musicals are by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
The song is sung by Grizabella, a faded old star.
Its characters have whiskers and tails.
questions.description: Songs so famous that people sing them in the shower, even if they've never seen the show.
questions.fun_fact: The musical “Cats” grew out of a book of poems about cats by T. S. Eliot.

questions.question: Olaf from Frozen is made of snow, loves warm hugs and sings about dreaming of one season. Which one?
hints: It's a season he has never lived through.
He pictures himself on the beach, soaking up the sun.
It's the hottest season of the year.
questions.description: A snowman whose big dream is, honestly, a terrible plan.
questions.fun_fact: In the song, Olaf has no idea what heat would do to snow.

questions.question: In which decade did “Singin' in the Rain”, starring Debbie Reynolds and Gene Kelly, come out?
hints: The film was already in color.
It was the golden age of Hollywood's big studio musicals.
It came out early in that decade, soon after 1950.
questions.description: It was pouring down, and someone still danced happily in the street: that's how cheerful those days were.
questions.fun_fact: Debbie Reynolds was the mother of Carrie Fisher, who played Princess Leia in Star Wars.

questions.question: I played detective Sam Spade in “The Maltese Falcon” and Philip Marlowe in “The Big Sleep”, both film noir classics. Who am I?
hints: I was an American actor of the 1940s.
I also starred in a famous romance set in a café in Morocco.
There I said “We'll always have Paris,” in “Casablanca.”
questions.description: Hat, trench coat, cigarette and zero smiles: the official uniform of the black-and-white detective.
questions.fun_fact: The name “film noir” came from French critics, inspired by a French series of crime novels with black covers.

questions.question: At a trial, “lawyer” is to “defend” as “witness” is to…
hints: A witness is not a judge or a police officer.
They were there when something happened.
Their job at the trial is to use their memory and their voice.
questions.description: Wrong place, wrong time, eyes wide open.
questions.fun_fact: The words “testify” and “testimony” come from the Latin “testis,” meaning someone who is present as a third party.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel where ten strangers are stuck on an island and drop out one by one?
hints: She is an English author.
She created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple.
She is called “the Queen of Crime.”
questions.description: A vacation on a private island that nobody would recommend in a review.
questions.fun_fact: “And Then There Were None” is one of the best-selling novels of all time, with more than 100 million copies sold.

questions.question: I open the mansion door and serve the tea, and in the old mystery-novel joke, I'm always the guilty one. Who am I?
hints: I work in the house, but I'm not part of the family.
I wear a smart suit and white gloves.
I'm the head of the mansion's staff.
questions.description: An English mansion with 40 rooms, three suspects and the same old culprit as always.
questions.fun_fact: The line “The butler did it” is world-famous, but in classic mystery novels the butler is almost never the culprit.

questions.question: One of Van Dine's famous 20 rules for detective novels says: “The detective must never turn out to be the…”
hints: The rules are meant to keep the game fair for the reader.
It would be a huge cheat at the end of the book.
It's exactly the person the detective is hunting for.
questions.description: A rulebook to stop authors from cheating their readers… or at least from cheating too much.
questions.fun_fact: S. S. Van Dine published his 20 rules in 1928, and another one bans the culprit from being a servant.

questions.question: In a mystery novel, a detail makes you suspect the gardener, but the author was tricking you. What is this device called?
hints: It's there to throw the reader off the trail.
It's the opposite of a real clue.
Its name comes from a strong-smelling smoked fish.
questions.description: The author pointed left while the culprit slipped out to the right.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the name comes from using smoked herrings to throw hunting dogs off a scent.

questions.question: I'm an Italian professor, and I wrote a mystery novel set in a medieval abbey, with a friar as the detective. Who am I?
hints: My novel was made into a film starring Sean Connery.
Its title mentions a flower.
I wrote “The Name of the Rose.”
questions.description: A professor who decided the best medieval history lesson was a murder mystery full of monks.
questions.fun_fact: The friar detective in “The Name of the Rose” is called William of Baskerville, a nod to Sherlock Holmes.

questions.question: For years, people believed human cells had 48 chromosomes. In which decade was it shown that they have 46?
hints: It was in the 20th century, when microscopes and staining methods had already improved a lot.
The count was done in a Swedish lab, with a new method that spread the chromosomes out clearly.
It was a few years after the end of the Second World War.
questions.description: For decades, science miscounted and nobody dared to say a word.
questions.fun_fact: Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan found the right number in Sweden in 1955, after more than 30 years of people believing it was 48.

questions.question: In the number 4,725, which place does the 7 sit in?
hints: It's about the position a digit holds inside a number.
Counting from the right, it's the third place.
The 7 in 4,725 is worth 700.
questions.description: Every number lives in a building, and each digit has its own floor.
questions.fun_fact: Our place-value system, with ones, tens and hundreds, came to Europe from India through Arab mathematicians.

questions.question: A normal year of 365 days starts on a Thursday. How many Thursdays does that year have?
hints: Think about how many full weeks fit into 365 days.
52 weeks are 364 days, so exactly one day is left over.
That extra day is the same day of the week the year started on.
questions.description: A whole calendar counted with the 7 times table and a little patience.
questions.fun_fact: That's why in every normal year one day of the week comes up 53 times; in leap years, two days do.

questions.question: Who coined the design motto “Less, but better”?
hints: We're looking for an industrial designer from Wiesbaden.
He wrote “ten principles for good design”.
For decades he designed radios and shavers for Braun.
questions.description: For everyone whose home looks like they just moved in, on purpose.
questions.fun_fact: Rams' designs for Braun are seen as models for the simple look of many Apple products.

questions.question: In 2012, investigators found Cornelius Gurlitt's art collection in Munich's Schwabing district; it later went to Bern. His father was a Nazi-era art dealer. What kind of art was it mostly?
hints: His father dealt in works that the Nazis removed from museums.
Most of the works were made between about 1900 and 1930.
They included Expressionists and other artists the Nazis condemned as “degenerate”.
questions.description: A Munich apartment where the wallpaper was the least important thing on the walls.
questions.fun_fact: The find included works by Max Liebermann, Otto Dix and Henri Matisse.

questions.question: This floating bronze figure hangs in Güstrow Cathedral. Who made it?
hints: The sculptor also carved a lot in wood and wrote plays.
He lived and worked in Güstrow in Mecklenburg.
The Nazis called his art “degenerate”; he died in 1938.
questions.description: An angel that refuses to stay on the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The face has the features of Käthe Kollwitz; the Nazis had the original melted down.

questions.question: This showpiece belongs to a Dresden museum that burglars stole jewels from in 2019. What is the museum called?
hints: It is the treasure chamber of Augustus the Strong.
It is inside the Residence Palace.
Its name sounds like a color plus an arched cellar room.
questions.description: A museum where even the display cases live more grandly than most people.
questions.fun_fact: Before the break-in, the thieves set fire to a power distribution box so the streetlights went out.

questions.question: It began in Cologne in 1967, gallery owners invented it, and it is seen as the oldest of its kind for modern art. What is Art Cologne?
hints: Galleries from many countries come together here.
Collectors and museum people travel to it every year.
It takes place in the exhibition halls on the Deutz bank of the Rhine.
questions.description: Cologne already had a cathedral, but modern art apparently needed something new.
questions.fun_fact: It was founded by gallery owners Hein Stünke and Rudolf Zwirner, back then as “Kunstmarkt Köln.”

questions.question: Three of these were part of Germany's gold-medal eight at London 2012. Who was NOT?
hints: He was already an Olympic champion when the others were still kids.
He didn't need anyone else rowing in his boat.
He won Olympic gold in the single sculls in 1988 and 1992.
questions.description: Rowing is the only sport where you race backward toward the finish and still win.
questions.fun_fact: Thomas Lange won gold for East Germany in 1988 and for reunified Germany in 1992.

questions.question: There's a party in the town square because the city is celebrating its bicentennial. How many years old is it turning?
hints: “Bi” means two, as in “bicycle.”
“Centennial” has to do with a hundred, like “century.”
It's two times a hundred.
questions.description: A birthday cake with so many candles that you need a firefighter to blow them out.
questions.fun_fact: Many countries in Latin America celebrated 200 years of independence between 2009 and 2024.

questions.question: Sailing legend Jochen Schümann won Olympic gold in the Finn dinghy in 1976. In which boat class did he win gold in 1988 and 1996?
hints: It is a keelboat for a crew of three.
The class was part of the Olympics from 1972 to 2000.
Its name sounds almost like a city in North Rhine-Westphalia famous for its knives.
questions.description: Sailing takes wind, patience and a boat with a proper name.
questions.fun_fact: In 2003, Jochen Schümann won the America's Cup as sports director of the Swiss team Alinghi.

questions.question: Here, in 1986, Jürgen Schult threw the discus 74.08 m (243 ft), a world record for almost 38 years. The city lies on Lake Tollense. Which one?
hints: The city is in northeastern Germany.
It has an almost fully preserved medieval town wall with four gates.
Its name is that of a neighboring German state, with a small extra bit in front.
questions.description: A plate that isn't meant for dinner, but for throwing away, as far as possible.
questions.fun_fact: Only in 2024 did Lithuania's Mykolas Alekna beat Schult's world record.

questions.question: “Rudolf Caracciola is to Mercedes-Benz as Bernd Rosemeyer is to …” Which brand is missing?
hints: The company was based in Saxony.
Its race cars had the engine behind the driver.
Its four-ring logo lives on today at Audi.
questions.description: Back when race cars gleamed silver and helmets were made of leather.
questions.fun_fact: In 1937, on the autobahn near Frankfurt, Rosemeyer became the first to go faster than 400 km/h (249 mph) on a public road.

questions.question: “At 18, I equaled the high jump world record in 1980, and in 1984 I won Olympic gold in Los Angeles.” Who am I?
hints: He competed for West Germany.
He jumped for Bayer Leverkusen.

Source: the German fun fact has the same reversed claim and should be fixed too (for example: “The ‘Tag’ in Bundestag means ‘day’: assemblies used to meet on a fixed day, which is where ‘tagen’ (to meet) comes from”).

So it is false that it has nothing to do with "day". The English version makes the claim even stronger ("nothing to do with the German word for 'day'"). Fix the source fun fact first (for example: "The 'Tag' in Bundestag means an assembly; it comes from the old sense of 'Tag' as a day set for a meeting, which is also where 'tagen' comes from"), then translate it again. Fact check: wrong. The fun fact is misleading. "Tag" in Bundestag does mean an assembly or meeting, and "tagen" (to meet) is related. But both come from the ordinary word "Tag" (day), meaning a day appointed for a meeting. So it is not true that it has nothing to do with the word for "day". The answer and the wrong answers are fine.

questions.question: When John F. Kennedy visited West Berlin, people gathered in front of Schöneberg City Hall. About how many?

questions.question: Walt Disney is to cartoons as Lotte Reiniger is to…?

questions.question: In the late 1970s, this singer had the East German hit “Jugendliebe” with the band Elefant. Who is she?
hints: She comes from Weimar.

Her surname means something like “mountain of joy”.
questions.description: A voice that still gets whole beer tents in eastern Germany singing along.

questions.question: In East Germany, you had to order a Trabant and often waited over ten years for it. So what did many families do?

questions.question: After the big Leipzig Monday demonstration on October 9, 1989, things moved fast. When did Erich Honecker step down as SED leader?
hints: The Wall was still standing then.

questions.question: In the Vogelherd Cave in the Lone Valley on the Schwäbische Alb, finds about 40,000 years old rank among the oldest of their kind. What are they?

Afterwards, there are presents under the tree.
questions.description: The simplest holiday dinner in the world, so there's more time for the important stuff.
questions.fun_fact: In surveys, potato salad with sausages comes out as Germany's favorite meal on Christmas Eve.

questions.question: Anselm Kiefer, born in Donaueschingen in 1945, likes to work with straw, ash and lead. Where did he buy tons of old lead from?
hints: The material had been exposed to the weather for decades.
It came from a very famous building.
The building has two huge towers and stands on the Rhine.
questions.description: An artist who makes books nobody can lift.
questions.fun_fact: Kiefer has lived in France since the 1990s and turned an old silk factory in Barjac into a huge art estate.

questions.question: In 1931, Cilly Aussem from Cologne became the first German woman to win this tournament's singles, beating fellow German Hilde Krahwinkel in the final. Which one?
hints: It is one of the four Grand Slam tournaments.
It takes place in Europe.
It is played on grass in London.
questions.description: Back then, women played tennis in long skirts – and still won.
questions.fun_fact: The next German woman to win there was Steffi Graf, not until 1988.

questions.question: People used to write letters on a typewriter. What was a small white bottle like this one for?
hints: A bottle like this used to sit on almost every office desk.
What's inside dries very fast on paper.
A spelling mistake disappears under a white layer.
questions.description: Offices used to sound like clacking keys, ringing bells and clinking coffee cups.
questions.fun_fact: Tipp-Ex didn't start out as a liquid at all, but as small correction sheets you typed over.

questions.question: Zewa's well-known paper towel is called “Zewa Wisch und …”. What is the missing word?
hints: The word describes what happens to the stain.
After wiping, you can't see the stain anymore.
In German, it's the opposite of “da”.
questions.description: A slogan for anyone who has ever knocked over their hot chocolate at breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The name Zewa comes from the pulp factory Zellstofffabrik Waldhof: ZE-llstoff WA-ldhof.

questions.question: Miracoli comes in a box with tomato sauce and a spice mix. What kind of dish is it?
hints: You need a big pot of water to make it.
The name sounds Italian.
The classic box holds long, thin spaghetti.
questions.description: A small miracle from the supermarket shelf that's on the table in ten minutes.
questions.fun_fact: Miracoli has been sold in Germany since 1961.

questions.question: Look at this eye. Most fish sleep with their eyes open because they have no…
hints: You use them many times a minute without noticing.
They are like little skin curtains for the eye.
They come down every time you blink.
questions.description: An eye that will never wink at you.
questions.fun_fact: Some sharks have a special membrane, called the nictitating membrane, that covers the eye when they bite.

questions.question: Lamy from Heidelberg makes the “safari”, which many schoolchildren learn to write with. What kind of writing tool is it?
hints: You need one from elementary school on.
You refill it instead of sharpening it.
You put ink cartridges into it.
questions.description: A school-bag classic that plenty of parents once wrote with too.
questions.fun_fact: The Lamy safari has been around since 1980, and it was designed especially for young people.

questions.question: The Merkel government sealed it for good in 2011, and the last three plants went offline in April 2023. What is this decision called?
hints: In 2011, a tsunami badly damaged a power plant in Fukushima, Japan.
It was about electricity made from uranium.
It meant saying goodbye to splitting atoms for electricity.
questions.description: A farewell after which some cooling towers went quiet forever.
questions.fun_fact: The last three plants, Isar 2, Emsland and Neckarwestheim 2, were shut down on April 15, 2023.

questions.question: Audio dramas used to come on cassette. What had happened when you got “Bandsalat”?
wrong_answers: The tape had played to the end
The player was running too fast
hints: Despite the name, nothing here gets eaten.
In a salad, everything gets tossed and mixed up.
A pencil often helped fix the problem.
questions.description: Some salads fill you up, others just cause trouble.
questions.fun_fact: For Bandsalat, a pencil came to the rescue: you stuck it into the cassette and carefully wound the tape back in.

questions.question: Children jump onto squares, a light comes on, and the host says “Ob ihr wirklich richtig steht …”. What is this show called?
hints: A host asks questions with several answers to choose from.
The show has been running since the 1970s.
The title counts to three.
questions.description: Here there's hopping, nail-biting and staring hard at a little lamp.
questions.fun_fact: The kids' quiz show “1, 2 oder 3” has been on ZDF since 1977 and is one of Germany's longest-running children's shows.

questions.question: This golden figure stands high up on a column in Berlin. Who does it show?
hints: The column was built after wars that were won.
The figure comes from the myths of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
The figure is called Victoria.
questions.description: High above Berlin shines someone who is definitely not afraid of heights.
questions.fun_fact: The figure is over 8 m (27 ft) tall, and Berliners lovingly call her “Goldelse” (Golden Elsie).

questions.question: On this Baltic Sea island, you can walk along the beach into a neighboring country. Which one?
hints: The country lies east of Germany.
The island is called Usedom, and its eastern tip belongs to the neighboring country.
Its capital is Warsaw.
questions.description: For over a hundred years, the rule here has been: rent a Strandkorb and soak up the sun.
questions.fun_fact: The Polish part of Usedom belongs to the city of Świnoujście, called Swinemünde in German.

questions.question: In Heidelberg's Studentenkarzer, the walls are covered in students' scribbles. What was the room used for until 1914?
wrong_answers: A quarantine room for the sick
hints: Nobody went in there by choice.
Anyone who had caused trouble at night ended up there.
The door was locked from the outside.
questions.description: Heidelberg is romantic and cozy, and for some students it used to be a little too cozy.
questions.fun_fact: Many students saw time in the Karzer as a badge of honor, and some even got themselves locked up on purpose.

questions.question: Narrow little water channels like these run through Freiburg's old town. What are they called?
hints: The name comes from the Baden dialect and sounds like a cute, little word.
In the old days, people took water from them to put out fires.
Think of the German word for a stream, made really tiny.
questions.description: If you stroll around the Breisgau, keep an eye on your feet now and then.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that if you step into one by accident, you will marry someone from Freiburg.

questions.question: This aquarium gourami has an organ called the “labyrinth” above its gills. What is it for?
hints: Thanks to it, the fish can live in puddles with little oxygen.
You'll see it swim up to the surface every now and then.
If it can't reach the top, it can drown.
questions.description: A fish with a maze in its head, and somehow it never gets lost.
questions.fun_fact: In many gourami species, the males build a nest of bubbles at the surface for the eggs.

questions.question: North of this dialect line, Germans say “Appel” for apple; south of it, “Apfel”. What is it called?
hints: It separates Central German from Upper German.
It's named after a town in Rhineland-Palatinate.
The town is famous for its huge Romanesque imperial cathedral.
questions.description: An apple doesn't fall far from the tree, but somewhere its pronunciation takes a big leap.
questions.fun_fact: The dialect lines in the Rhineland run so close together that linguists call them the “Rhenish fan”.

questions.question: The medieval German Nibelungenlied begins: “Uns ist in alten mæren wunders vil geseit.” What does “mæren” mean?
hints: Many Middle High German words sound almost like modern ones, but mean something else.
The first line tells the audience what they're about to hear.
Think of the German word “Märchen”.
questions.description: Knights, dragon slayers and castle ladies, talking long before anyone fixed the spelling rules.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Märchen” (fairy tale) is a diminutive of “Mär” and first meant “little tale”.

questions.question: In Cologne, a small 10-liter (2.6-gallon) keg of Kölsch is called a “Pittermännchen”. Which first name is hidden in it?
hints: It's a name from the Bible.
A famous apostle had this name.
The biggest bell of Cologne Cathedral also carries this name in Kölsch: “Decke Pitter”.
questions.description: In Cologne, even the beer barrel has a first name.
questions.fun_fact: Kölsch is traditionally served in narrow 0.2-liter (about 7 oz) glasses called “Stangen”.

questions.question: Missingsch mixes Low German with standard German, and the joke character “Klein Erna” speaks it. Which city is she from?
hints: The city is a German state of its own.
It has Germany's largest port.
This is home to the Elbphilharmonie and the Speicherstadt.
questions.description: Half Platt, half standard German, and all-around good for a chuckle.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Missingsch” probably comes from “meißnisch”, the posh German spoken around the city of Meissen.

questions.question: We were brothers from Hanau, and in 1838 we started a huge German dictionary that wasn't finished until 1961. Who are we?
hints: We were language scholars and professors in Göttingen.
We're better known for a very different collection.
Our collection includes Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel and Gretel.
questions.description: A dictionary that takes more patience than any crossword puzzle.
questions.fun_fact: Jacob Grimm only got as far as the word “Frucht” (fruit) before he died in 1863.

questions.question: From 1876, Georg Wenker had schools translate whole sentences into their dialect. In which city is the “Deutscher Sprachatlas” still based?
hints: The city lies on a tributary of the Rhine.
Its university was founded in 1527 as the first Protestant university.
It is home to St. Elizabeth's Church, one of the oldest Gothic churches in Germany.
questions.description: One man, piles of questionnaires, and sentences all of Germany had to translate into its own dialect.
questions.fun_fact: Wenker's questionnaires went to tens of thousands of school towns; one sentence reads: “In winter the dry leaves fly around through the air.”

questions.question: Which of its borders did Germany accept as final in the 1925 Locarno treaties?
hints: They were borders that the Treaty of Versailles had redrawn.
Gustav Stresemann and Aristide Briand won the Nobel Peace Prize for it.
The demilitarized Rhineland was also part of the deal.
questions.description: Drawing borders is hard; accepting them is sometimes even harder.
questions.fun_fact: A year later, in 1926, Germany was admitted to the League of Nations.

questions.question: You find it on lots of packaging in Germany: what does the Grüne Punkt (Green Dot) mean?
questions.answer: The maker pays for the disposal
wrong_answers: The maker uses no meat at all
The maker plants trees in return
hints: It's not about what's inside, but about the wrapping.
It has to do with sorting your trash.
Packaging like this goes into the Gelber Sack or the yellow bin.
questions.description: A tiny symbol that gets more attention on a yogurt cup than the list of ingredients.
questions.fun_fact: The Green Dot was invented in Germany and is now found on packaging in many European countries.

questions.question: Which city does this blond comedian come from?
hints: He's a true “Nordlicht”, a northerner through and through.
His hometown is on the North Sea, not the Baltic.
Today it has a museum called “Dat Otto Huus”.
questions.description: He turned elephants into art and nonsense into a career.
questions.fun_fact: Otto Waalkes was born in Emden in 1948 and was already drawing his Ottifanten as a schoolboy.

questions.question: In “Finding Nemo”, which shark is NOT in Bruce's club of sharks who promise not to eat fish?
hints: Bruce is the biggest and smiliest member of the club.
One of his friends has a head shaped like a tool.
The missing one is a giant that eats plankton and wouldn't need the club at all.
questions.description: A club full of sharp teeth and very good intentions.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce is named after the mechanical shark from the film “Jaws”, which the film crew nicknamed Bruce.

questions.question: Konrad Adenauer was born in 1876 and became Chancellor in 1949. How old was he when he took office?
hints: Before that, he was mayor of Cologne from 1917 to 1933.
Count from 1876 to 1949.
Up to 1900 is already 24 years, then add 49 more.
questions.description: A math problem from Rhöndorf, no calculator needed.
questions.fun_fact: Adenauer stayed in office until 1963 and was 87 when he stepped down, older than any other German chancellor.

questions.question: Back in the days of the D-Mark, one coin was called a “Groschen”. How many Pfennig was it worth?
hints: It wasn't the smallest coin in your wallet.
It was gold-colored, not silver.
Ten of them made one D-Mark.
questions.description: The coin that regularly made all of Germany go “Aha!”
questions.fun_fact: “Der Groschen ist gefallen” (the Groschen has dropped) comes from vending machines that only started once the coin had dropped in.

questions.question: What is the 2018 German film about a painter from Dresden, loosely based on Gerhard Richter?
hints: It was directed by an Oscar winner who had earlier made a film about the Stasi.
The film was nominated for two Oscars.
Its German title means “Work Without an Author.”
questions.description: A film with lots of paint on its fingers and even more German history in its luggage.
questions.fun_fact: Gerhard Richter himself later clearly distanced himself from the film.

questions.question: Western chocolate is to candy as Western jeans are to …?
hints: You find them in the closet, not in the fridge.
You need them every morning after you get up.
You put them on.
questions.description: In the East, more wanted than any report card.
questions.fun_fact: East Germany sewed its own jeans, for example the “Wisent” brand, but Western jeans sent in family packages were far more wanted.

questions.question: From 1952 the GDR's Barracked People's Police had “police” in its name. What was it really for?
wrong_answers: as a building crew for big projects
hints: West Germany built up something similar a few years later.
In 1956 it became part of a new force.
That new force was called the National People's Army.
questions.description: Some names give away less than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: On March 1, 1956, the KVP officially became the National People's Army.

questions.question: In 1945 Wolfgang Leonhard flew from Moscow to Germany with the Ulbricht Group. How many men were in this group?
hints: It was a small advance party, not an army.
They could all have sat at one long dinner table.
There were as many as you have fingers on both hands.
questions.description: Perhaps the most consequential tour group in Germany's postwar history.
questions.fun_fact: Leonhard recorded Ulbricht saying: “It has to look democratic, but we must have everything in our hands.”

questions.question: From 1963 on, what was the Stasi prison on the Kaßberg in Karl-Marx-Stadt mainly used for?
questions.answer: as a transit stop to the West
wrong_answers: as a prison for young people
as a school for Stasi officers
as a warehouse for seized parcels
hints: Most prisoners stayed here only a short time.
At the end, a bus was waiting, headed for Giessen.
West Germany paid a lot of money for each of them.
questions.description: In Karl-Marx-Stadt, a giant head of Marx was keeping an eye on everything anyway.
questions.fun_fact: From 1963 to 1989, West Germany bought the freedom of more than 33,000 political prisoners from East Germany.

questions.question: The alligator gar, with a crocodile-like snout and scales like armor, is a “living fossil.” How long have its relatives been around?
hints: They are far, far older than humans.
You have to count in millions of years.
They swam in rivers where dinosaurs came to drink.
questions.description: Half fish, half crocodile, and older than all your grandparents put together.
questions.fun_fact: Alligator gar eggs are poisonous to people.

questions.question: Near Münchehagen, about 140 million years ago, a dinosaur left footprints in the mud. What kind of fossil are they?
hints: Experts tell apart the remains of living things from what those living things left behind.
Fossil burrows and fossil poop belong to this group too.
The name is a word for a mark something leaves behind.
questions.description: A dino that never cleaned up after itself, and science is grateful.
questions.fun_fact: In Münchehagen, a large hall protects the real dinosaur tracks from wind and weather.

questions.question: The Höllentalferner lies on the north side of the Zugspitze. What does the Alpine word “Ferner” mean?
hints: The word is used mainly in Bavaria and Tyrol.
It lies high up in a shady bowl below the summit.
On the Zugspitze plateau, a Ferner is partly covered with big tarps in summer.
questions.description: A word everyone in the mountains understands and everyone on the plains takes for a typo.
questions.fun_fact: The Southern Schneeferner has melted so much that it no longer counts as a glacier.

questions.question: The rock wall called the Pfahl runs a long way through the Bavarian Forest. What is it made of, almost entirely?
hints: The Bavarian Forest is ancient bedrock, not a former seabed.
A pocket knife leaves no scratch on this mineral.
Rock crystals are made of exactly this mineral.
questions.description: Eastern Bavaria has its own wall, and nobody had to build it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pfahl stretches about 150 kilometers (93 miles) across eastern Bavaria.

questions.question: Even the government must obey the law, courts are independent, and anyone can defend themselves in court. What is such a state called?
hints: Germany's Basic Law (Grundgesetz) makes this principle part of the constitution.
Nobody is above the law, no matter how powerful.
In German, its name shares a word with “Rechtsanwalt” (lawyer).
questions.description: A principle that sounds more boring than it is, and matters more than you'd think.
questions.fun_fact: Under the Basic Law's “eternity clause”, the rule-of-law principle is one of the rules that can never be abolished.

questions.question: A red carpet is rolled out, a military band plays two anthems, and the Federal President greets a king. What is going on?
hints: The guest comes from another country.
In the evening there is often a festive dinner at Schloss Bellevue.
One head of state travels officially to meet another.
questions.description: An event for which even the lawn in front of the palace gets a fresh mow.
questions.fun_fact: During a state visit, the guest country's anthem is played first, then the German one.

questions.question: Ann-Katrin Berger saved penalties, scored one herself and made a save to secure Olympic bronze in 2024. In which country were the Games held?
hints: The host city had also hosted the Olympics exactly 100 years earlier.
People in the host country speak a Romance language.
The opening ceremony took place on the Seine.
questions.description: A goalkeeper who makes penalty takers wish they'd brought a therapist.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024, Paris hosted the Summer Olympics for the third time, after 1900 and 1924.

questions.question: Manuel Neuer is a goalkeeper, so he wears a different jersey from his teammates. How many players per team wear a goalkeeper jersey on the field?
hints: The goalkeeper usually stands at the very back, in front of the goal.
Only the goalkeeper may play the ball with their hands inside their own penalty area.
The other ten players all wear the same jersey.
questions.description: A jersey that looks like it was meant for a totally different party.
questions.fun_fact: The goalkeeper's colors must be different from all the other players' and from the referee's too.

questions.question: Since 1967, the U 87 by the Berlin company Neumann has stood in recording studios all over the world. What kind of device is it?
hints: You find it in almost every professional recording studio.
It has no keys and no sliders.
Singers stand right in front of it, often with a pop filter in between.
questions.description: A studio classic that's older than most parents.
questions.fun_fact: Georg Neumann founded his company in Berlin back in 1928.

questions.question: Franz Josef Degenhardt was a lawyer and singer-songwriter known as “Väterchen Franz.” Which of his song titles became a saying?
hints: The 1965 song mocks stuffy, narrow-minded parents.
The song is about the posh upper town and the rough lower town.
Parents use it to mean: stay away from the grubby kids.
questions.description: A songwriter with a guitar, a law degree and a sharp pen.
questions.fun_fact: Besides songs, Degenhardt also wrote novels, such as “Brandstellen.”

questions.question: Bettina Wegner wrote “Sind so kleine Hände” and moved to the West in 1983. In which city did she live and sing before that?
hints: Many well-known East German artists and writers lived in her city back then.
The Spree River flows through her city.
Her move to the West took her only a few kilometers, to the other half of the same city.
questions.description: Small hands, big impact, and a move that changed everything.
questions.fun_fact: In 1968 Wegner was arrested for handing out leaflets against the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

questions.question: This rainbow trout is common in the cold rivers of the Andes, but it isn't native there. Where does it originally come from?
hints: It was brought to South America more than a hundred years ago for fishing and fish farming.
Its original home is rivers that flow into the Pacific Ocean.
It's native to places like California, Canada and Alaska.
questions.description: A tourist so well settled in that nobody asks for her passport anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Some rainbow trout travel out to sea and come back to the river much bigger; these are called steelhead.

questions.question: Ski Aggu almost always wears ski goggles, and in 2023 he rapped the hit “Friesenjung” with Joost and Otto Waalkes. Which city is he from?
hints: Despite the song title, he's not a boy from the North Sea coast.
In his hometown, a bread roll is called a “Schrippe”.
That's where the TV tower at Alexanderplatz stands.
questions.description: A rapper who looks ready to hit the slopes even in the middle of summer.
questions.fun_fact: “Friesenjung” is built on an old song by Otto Waalkes, who himself comes from East Frisia.

questions.question: Kaiserschmarrn is torn into pieces with two forks and dusted with powdered sugar. What is it made from?
hints: It's a favorite at mountain huts in Austria and Bavaria.
You whisk it from flour, eggs and milk.
It's runny, can't be kneaded, and is normally poured into a hot pan in thin, flat rounds.
questions.description: The one dish you're allowed to tear apart before it's served, with imperial permission.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Kaiserschmarrn is named after the Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph I.

questions.question: Bavarian Schweinsbraten has a crunchy crust on top. What is it made from?
hints: It's already part of the cut of meat.
It's scored in a diamond pattern before roasting.
In German it's called the Schwarte.
questions.description: A Sunday roast that makes a loud crunch when you cut into it.
questions.fun_fact: In Bavaria, Schweinsbraten usually comes with dumplings and a dark gravy, often made with beer.

questions.question: What kind of dish is the northern German classic Rote Grütze?
hints: It tastes sweet.
It's made by cooking berries and cherries with sugar.
It's often eaten with vanilla sauce.
questions.description: Red, wobbly and straight from the windy northern coast.
questions.fun_fact: For Rote Grütze, red fruits like currants, raspberries and cherries are cooked and thickened.

questions.question: Where do lines with years like these on old house walls by a river come from?
wrong_answers: From the years the house was built
hints: The houses all stand close to the river.
The higher the line, the worse it was back then.
On those days, the river rose all the way up to that spot.
questions.description: This house wall has a pretty good memory.
questions.fun_fact: In Passau in 2013, the water rose almost 13 meters (43 ft), higher than at any time since 1501.

questions.question: You're walking across the mudflats, and a mudflat guide leads the way. What is the guide's job?
questions.answer: Getting the group there and back safely
wrong_answers: Showing ships the way through the mudflats
hints: The mudflats have deep water channels that you need to know about.
The guide knows exactly when the water will come back.
Without one, you could get lost or be caught by the rising tide.
questions.description: A job with wet feet and the best office in the world.
questions.fun_fact: The Wadden Sea on the North Sea coast has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2009.

questions.question: In a German saying, someone who is terribly clumsy is like an elephant. But where?
hints: In this shop you have to be extra careful.
It sells cups, plates and vases.
Whatever falls down in there clinks and shatters.
questions.description: A trunked animal, a tight space and a bill nobody wants to pay.
questions.fun_fact: On the TV show “MythBusters”, real bulls ran through a rebuilt china shop and broke almost nothing.

questions.question: I come before every song, every book and every game. A German saying says I'm always hard. What am I?
hints: Without me, nothing gets going.
After me, things usually get easier.
My opposite is the end.
questions.description: A saying parents love to quote during homework.
questions.fun_fact: Hermann Hesse saw it more kindly: his poem “Stufen” (“Steps”) says that a magic lives in every beginning.

questions.question: Fibbers don't get far, says a German saying, because lies have short… what?
hints: They help you move forward.
A stork often stands on just one of them.
You run and jump with them.
questions.description: Honesty lasts the longest, and fibs have a real problem with that.
questions.fun_fact: Pinocchio's lies give him away differently: his nose grows.

questions.question: In an official agility competition under FCI rules, the dog zigzags through the weave poles. How many poles are there?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than 10.
It's the same as the number of months in a year.
questions.description: A dog that dodges obstacles better than you do at the mall on the first day of a big sale.
questions.fun_fact: Agility was born in England in the late 1970s, inspired by show jumping competitions for horses.

questions.question: Chief Inspector Stephan Derrick solved cases in Munich on ZDF from 1974 to 1998. About how many episodes were there?
hints: Each episode was a complete case of about one hour.
About a dozen new episodes were added each year.
The number is just under 300.
questions.description: A detective who stayed on the job longer than many civil servants.
questions.fun_fact: All 281 Derrick episodes were written by one single author: Herbert Reinecker.

questions.question: Rudi the raven lives in Frau Siebenstein's shop. Which other talking housemate lives there too?
hints: This housemate keeps interrupting Frau Siebenstein.
This thing can be opened up and closed again.
You usually take one of these with you on vacation.
questions.description: A shop where you'd better not say anything rude about the furniture.
questions.fun_fact: “Siebenstein” has been on ZDF since 1988.

questions.question: A theme park in Günzburg has cities, animals and ships made of millions of small, colorful pieces. What kind?
hints: You can snap these pieces together.
They have little bumps on top.
They come from Denmark, and the park is named after them.
questions.description: A park where even the giraffes come straight out of a kid's bedroom.
questions.fun_fact: Legoland Deutschland opened in 2002 in Günzburg, Bavaria.

questions.question: At a wildlife park in Lower Saxony, you drive your car through enclosures with zebras, rhinos and giraffes. What is this kind of tour called?
hints: The word comes from the Swahili language.
People go on one to watch wild animals.
Jeeps and binoculars in the savanna are typical of it.
questions.description: Here nobody honks when a rhino blocks the road.
questions.fun_fact: The park is called Serengeti-Park, is in Hodenhagen and opened in 1974.

questions.question: In Regensburg's old town stand tall tower houses built by rich families in the Middle Ages. What was the main reason?
questions.answer: To show off wealth and power
wrong_answers: To guide ships on the Danube
hints: The families cared a lot about their reputation.
The taller the tower, the better.
Merchants wanted to impress the neighbors with them.
questions.description: Medieval skyscrapers, built long before anyone invented the elevator.
questions.fun_fact: Regensburg's Golden Tower is about 50 m (164 ft) tall and is said to be the tallest medieval tower house north of the Alps.

questions.question: An amusement park in Bottrop has stunt shows and roller coasters about famous heroes. What are its themed areas about?
hints: You usually watch them on a screen.
Popcorn goes well with them.
The park's English name uses the word for what you see at the cinema.
questions.description: A park in the Ruhr area where, for once, the heroes don't work down in the mines.
questions.fun_fact: The park opened in 1996 as “Warner Bros. Movie World” and is now called Movie Park Germany.

questions.question: Leipzig Zoo has a huge hall with rope bridges, tall trees and a boat ride. What kind of landscape is inside?
hints: It rains there very often.
Monkeys and parrots feel right at home here.
You find this kind of landscape along the Amazon.
questions.description: A faraway vacation that only costs you a streetcar ticket in Leipzig.
questions.fun_fact: The tropical hall is called Gondwanaland and opened in 2011.

questions.question: You're on vacation on an East Frisian island like Langeoog or Spiekeroog. What will you NOT find there?
hints: At low tide, you can walk from the island across the mudflats toward the mainland.
Behind the beach, planted marram grass holds the white dunes in place.
The highest point is usually a dune about 20 m (66 ft) high.
questions.description: A vacation with sand in your shoes, sand in your towel and sand in your sandwich.
questions.fun_fact: The East Frisian Islands are slowly moving east: the current washes sand away in the west and drops it again in the east.

questions.question: How old is the rock that makes up the white chalk cliffs on Rügen?
questions.answer: From the age of the dinosaurs
hints: Chalk forms very slowly on the floor of a warm sea.
The rock is made mostly of tiny limestone plates from sea algae.
The rock is about 70 million years old, from a time when T. rex still stomped across the Earth.
questions.description: Whiter than any classroom chalk, and a tiny bit older than your teacher.
questions.fun_fact: People often find fossil sea urchins and flint stones in the chalk of Rügen.

questions.question: I never go out to sea. I carry gravel, coal and containers along rivers and canals, and the captain's family often lives on board. What am I?
hints: You see me all the time on the Rhine.
My name says I stay inside the country.
My home waters are far from the coast, deep inside the land.
questions.description: Here the living room, the kids' room and the workplace are all on the same deck.
questions.fun_fact: A large inland vessel can carry as much cargo as about 100 trucks.

questions.question: The virus behind this dog disease is a cousin of measles. Measles is to child as ___ is to puppy.
hints: Puppies are protected against it by their vaccines.
It often starts with discharge from the nose and eyes.
Cats can get a disease with the same name, though a different virus causes it.
questions.description: A trip to the vet: the only walk no dog ever asks to repeat.
questions.fun_fact: The distemper virus is such a close relative of measles that a measles vaccine was once used to protect dogs.

questions.question: In many Baltic Sea resorts, a long pier like this one leads out into the sea. What was it first built for?
wrong_answers: So that cars could reach islands
So that trains could cross the sea
So that waves would be slowed down
hints: The beach is shallow, so big boats can't come close.
In the past, many vacationers arrived by steamboat.
Even today, tour boats wait at the end of the pier.
questions.description: A bridge brave enough to stop in the middle of nowhere.
questions.fun_fact: At some piers, such as the ones in Sellin and Zingst, you can go down in a diving gondola and watch the Baltic Sea underwater.

questions.question: Why do big ships use this canal straight across Schleswig-Holstein?
questions.answer: To skip the detour around Denmark
wrong_answers: To drain floodwater from the Elbe
To pick up coal from the Ruhr
To avoid the ice in winter
hints: The canal links two seas.
The canal is almost 100 km (62 miles) long and was opened under Kaiser Wilhelm II.
Otherwise the ships would have to sail all the way around the tip of Jutland.
questions.description: Here, ocean giants squeeze past cows and meadows as if it were perfectly normal.
questions.fun_fact: The Kiel Canal opened in 1895 and is said to be the busiest artificial waterway in the world.

questions.question: When you crawl, you're moving “on all fours.” Which animals do NOT walk on all fours?
hints: These animals often live on a farm.
At night, these animals like to sleep on a perch.
They lay eggs and cluck.
questions.description: Some animals have no idea they're part of a figure of speech.
questions.fun_fact: Most babies start crawling on all fours at around eight to ten months old.

questions.question: In class everyone does what they want, and the teacher lets it all happen. In the German saying, where do the kids dance around on him?
hints: The saying describes someone who puts up with everything.
Not much room for dancing there.
You smell with it.
questions.description: A free dance party, paid for by somebody else.
