questions.fun_fact: A related German saying, “jemanden an der Nase herumführen” (to lead someone around by the nose), is said to come from dancing bears led by a nose ring.

questions.question: The doves help Aschenputtel (Cinderella) sort lentils: “Die Guten ins Töpfchen, die Schlechten …” (the good ones into the pot, the bad ones…). Where?
hints: The doves keep the bad lentils for themselves.
The doves peck up the bad lentils.
A part of a bird's neck where food lands before it reaches the stomach.
questions.description: Fairy-tale recycling, with feathered helpers.
questions.fun_fact: The crop is a pouch in a bird's food pipe where doves store grains for later.

questions.question: On your way home from sports practice, you pick up the bread rolls too. In the German saying, how many flies do you swat with one swatter?
hints: It's fewer than the Brave Little Tailor's.
It's an even number.
That's how many things you're getting done at once.
questions.description: Would all insect lovers please cover their ears for a moment.
questions.fun_fact: The “Klappe” in the saying means a Fliegenklappe, an old German word for a fly swatter.

questions.question: According to the German saying, who laughs best?
hints: It's about patience.
Anyone who gloats too early about a prank sometimes learns otherwise.
This person laughs after everyone else.
questions.description: Laughter is contagious, and hopefully this question is too.
questions.fun_fact: English has almost exactly the same saying: “He who laughs last, laughs best.”

questions.question: In which decade did the first episode of “Aktenzeichen XY … ungelöst” air?
hints: Back then, color TV was brand new in Germany.
Its first host, Eduard Zimmermann, presented the show for about 30 years.
In the same decade, the first people landed on the Moon.
questions.description: The show that makes the whole country suddenly lock the front door.
questions.fun_fact: Rudi Cerne, host since 2002, used to be a successful figure skater.

questions.question: Which of these series is NOT a telenovela?
hints: A telenovela is almost always about true love.
The series you're looking for airs on RTL.
On it, cars fly through the air more often than rose petals.
questions.description: Heartbreak in episodes, tissues guaranteed.
questions.fun_fact: “Verliebt in Berlin” with Lisa Plenske was the German version of the Colombian telenovela “Yo soy Betty, la fea”.

questions.question: I'm from Austria, I'd rather wear a shirt than a white coat, and since 2008 I've played ZDF's “Der Bergdoktor”. Who am I?
hints: The show is set at the Wilder Kaiser mountains in Tyrol.
My character is called Dr. Martin Gruber.
My last name has only four letters and starts with S.
questions.description: House calls that come with a climb instead of a waiting room.
questions.fun_fact: Before he became the Bergdoktor, Hans Sigl played a police inspector on the show “SOKO Kitzbühel”.

questions.question: Complete the famous Spanish saying used when people criticize you: “The dogs bark, Sancho, a sign that…”
hints: Sancho Panza travels with a knight-errant.
The saying means that criticism is a sign you are moving forward.
It's what someone does when they are on horseback.
questions.description: A quote so famous that many people swear they read it in a book where it never appears.
questions.fun_fact: Although people credit it to Cervantes, this saying doesn't appear anywhere in “Don Quixote.”

questions.question: This ZDF early-evening series has run since 2002, is set in Upper Bavaria on the Inn River, and the secretary announces: “Es gibt a Leich.” Which series is it?
hints: The town in the show lies between Munich and Salzburg.
The town is known for its big autumn festival.
The title calls the police officers by an English word.
questions.description: Murder with a mountain view and a break for Weißwurst.
questions.fun_fact: Secretary Miriam Stockl's line “Es gibt a Leich” has become the show's trademark.

questions.question: They wear white protective suits, search the crime scene for hairs and fingerprints, and put everything in bags. What is this unit called?
hints: In crime shows, they usually turn up shortly after the detective.
They secure everything a criminal left behind.
In “Tatort”, they're nicknamed “Spusi”.
questions.description: The people who take every crumb more seriously than your mom does when she vacuums.
questions.fun_fact: The white suits keep the investigators from leaving their own hairs or fibers at the crime scene.

questions.question: ARD and ZDF have a free online service that shows programs you missed. What is it called?
hints: You can watch there any time, not just when the show airs.
The word sounds a bit like “Bibliothek”, the German word for library.
The first part of the word sounds like the English word “media”.
questions.description: TV for everyone who had something better to do when the show was on.
questions.fun_fact: In the past, you had to record missed shows on a video cassette with a VCR.

questions.question: In which year did Chief Inspector Frank Thiel have his first case in the Münster Tatort?
hints: It was already in the new millennium.
It was in the first few years after the turn of the millennium.
That same year, euro cash arrived in Germany.
questions.description: A detective from Hamburg among bicycles and know-it-alls.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Thiel is from Hamburg and a big fan of FC St. Pauli.

questions.question: Since which decade has the Bundeskriminalamt stored DNA traces from crime scenes in its own database?
hints: Before that, the police mostly compared classic fingerprints.
DNA fingerprinting was only invented in the 1980s.
It started shortly before the year 2000.
questions.description: An archive where even a single hair gets its own file.
questions.fun_fact: Even tiny flakes of skin can give enough DNA for a trace.

questions.question: This channel shows the Tagesschau and “Die Sendung mit der Maus”, and its logo is a big number one. Which channel is it?
hints: It is paid for by the broadcasting fee, the Rundfunkbeitrag.
Regional broadcasters like WDR and BR are part of it.
It is also called “Das Erste”.
questions.description: In the evening, the remote control is the most fought-over thing in the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: ARD stands for “Arbeitsgemeinschaft der öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunkanstalten der Bundesrepublik Deutschland”, the working group of Germany's public broadcasters.

questions.question: Since what decade have strangers cooked for each other and handed out points on VOX's “Das perfekte Dinner”?
hints: The idea for the show originally came from Britain.
Germany was already paying with the euro back then.
The start year begins with “20”, but it's before 2010.
questions.description: Five strangers, one dinner table and the eternal question of whether the dessert is done yet.
questions.fun_fact: The show is based on the British format “Come Dine with Me”.

questions.question: Younes Zarou became the German TikToker with the most followers. With what kind of videos?
hints: Not everything in his clips would be possible in real life.
He often seems to jump into a phone screen.
He's a kind of magician at the editing desk.
questions.description: One phone, one idea, and suddenly millions are watching.
questions.fun_fact: Because his tricks work without any words, people all over the world follow him.

questions.question: On VOX, contestants shop to a theme and Guido Maria Kretschmer judges them. Since what decade has “Shopping Queen” been on?
hints: When it started, lots of people already had a smartphone in their pocket.
The show was on long before the COVID years.
In its first year, London hosted the Olympic Games.
questions.description: Four hours, one budget and a theme nobody quite understands.
questions.fun_fact: The winner of each week gets €1,000 in prize money.

questions.question: Joko Winterscheidt plays quiz rounds against celebrities, and the winner hosts the next episode. What is the show called?
hints: The show is on ProSieben.
The title is a question.
In the title, someone wants to take something away from the host.
questions.description: Some hosts sleep badly when their guests guess too well.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the celebrities, every episode has one player from the audience, the “Wildcard”.

questions.question: It has no owner, sleeps wherever it can and finds food wherever it can. What word describes this dog?
hints: The word tells you how it lives.
You see it walking along the sidewalks.
The same word means to wander away from where you belong.
questions.description: It has no address, but it knows every address in the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the world's dogs are thought to live not inside a home, but freely on the streets or in the countryside.

questions.question: Mirko Drotschmann explains history and politics on YouTube. How does his channel name “MrWissen…” end?
hints: The ending comes from English.
The name contains a digit that sounds like an English word.
It sounds like a coffee you take with you.
questions.description: For everyone who starts their school presentation the night before.
questions.fun_fact: For ZDF, he also explains history on the Terra X channel “MrWissen2go Geschichte”.

questions.question: Almost every January, German celebrities move into the Dschungelcamp in my country, where it's high summer then. Which country am I?
hints: I'm on the other side of the world from Germany.
The camp is in a rainforest near my east coast.
Kangaroos and koalas live here.
questions.description: Cockroaches for breakfast, and still a crown at the end.
questions.fun_fact: Because of the time difference, the live show airs there in the morning while it's already evening in Germany.

questions.question: This Radio Bremen music show started in 1965, was hosted by Uschi Nerke, and became “Musikladen” in 1972. What was it called?
hints: Its name is in English, even though the show was German.
It recalls the music of the early Beatles era.
The second part of the name is also a word for a golfer's stick.
questions.description: As hair got longer and guitars got louder, Bremen watched very closely.
questions.fun_fact: International stars like Jimi Hendrix also played on “Beat-Club”.

questions.question: In which year did Hans-Joachim Kulenkampff first host the quiz show “Einer wird gewinnen”?
hints: TV was still black and white back then.
ZDF had only been on the air for a short time.
The Olympic Games were held in Tokyo that same year.
questions.description: Back then, a show ran over time with style and a bow tie.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the show, his butler Martin brought him his coat, usually with a dry one-liner.

questions.question: Which of these treasures is NOT in one of the museums on Berlin's Museum Island?
hints: Museum Island sits in the middle of the river Spree.
The treasure you're looking for isn't in Germany at all.
It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
questions.description: An island with no beach, just lots of very old stuff that nobody is allowed to touch.
questions.fun_fact: Museum Island and its five museums have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.

questions.question: It crosses the Rhine in Cologne, thousands of love locks hang on it, and no railroad bridge in Germany carries more trains. Which bridge?
hints: It is named after an old ruling dynasty.
It ends right next to Cologne Cathedral and the main train station.
This dynasty gave Prussia its kings and Germany its emperors.
questions.description: A bridge that carries more declarations of love than any Valentine's Day.
questions.fun_fact: Well over 1,000 trains cross the Hohenzollern Bridge every day.

questions.question: Which German city is shown in this picture?
hints: A great many banks are based here.
The European Central Bank has its headquarters here.
Because of its skyscrapers, the city is nicknamed “Mainhattan”.
questions.description: So many skyscrapers that the pigeons here need an altimeter.
questions.fun_fact: Frankfurt has more skyscrapers than any other city in Germany.

questions.question: Karls Erlebnis-Dorf near Rostock grows one fruit in its fields and makes it the star of the village. Which fruit?
hints: The fruit is red.
Its season is short, and the farm shop sells it as jam and cake.
It grows close to the ground and has tiny seeds on the outside of its skin.
questions.description: A farm where the fun easily beats the farm work.
questions.fun_fact: There are now Karls Erlebnis-Dörfer in several places, for example on the island of Rügen and near Berlin.

questions.question: Here is a close-up of Spätzle from Swabia. What kind of food are they?
hints: They're made from flour, eggs and water.
They're boiled briefly in salted water.
Spaghetti belongs to the same group.
questions.description: Swabians scrape them off a board, and kids shovel them off the plate.
questions.fun_fact: Real Spätzle are traditionally scraped with a knife from a wet wooden board straight into boiling water.

questions.question: It's in Bavaria on the border with Austria, almost 3,000 m (about 9,700 ft) high, and Germany's highest mountain. What is it called?
hints: It belongs to the Wetterstein range in the Alps.
It lies near Garmisch-Partenkirchen.
Its name begins with the German word for “train”.
questions.description: All of Germany looks up to it, and it looks down on all of Germany.
questions.fun_fact: A gilded cross stands on the summit of the Zugspitze.

questions.question: I was Prime Minister of Spain from 1996 to 2004: I came after Felipe González and Zapatero followed me. Who am I?
hints: I was leader of the Partido Popular.
While I was in office, euro coins and bills landed in people's pockets.
Before that, I led the regional government of Castilla y León.
questions.description: Eight years with the keys to the Moncloa in his pocket.
questions.fun_fact: Before moving into the Moncloa, Aznar was president of Castilla y León from 1987 to 1989.

questions.question: Guernica, the Basque town of this tree, was bombed on April 26, 1937. Who carried out the attack?
hints: They were foreign pilots helping one side in the war.
The attack was a test run for air tactics later used in World War II.
They were Franco’s allies, and they were named after a huge bird of the Andes.
questions.description: A tree that has watched Basque history go by for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: The oak tree standing in Gernika in 1937 survived the bombing.

questions.question: Look at this clay jar with two handles and a pointed base: the Romans filled it with wine, oil or garum. What is it called?
hints: It traveled in ships' holds all over the Mediterranean.
The pointed base let it be stuck in sand or wedged between others.
Its Greek name means “carried on both sides”, after its two handles.
questions.description: The Romans' food container, with two handles and no plastic lid to lose.
questions.fun_fact: In Rome there is a hill, Monte Testaccio, made almost entirely of broken amphorae that carried olive oil from Hispania.

questions.question: Remains of woolly mammoths have been found in Padul (Granada). When did these hairy giants live in Spain?
hints: Their very long hair helped them survive terrible cold.
They lived alongside the first humans, who hunted them.
Back then, huge glaciers covered much of Europe.
questions.description: An elephant that refused to leave the house without its coat.
questions.fun_fact: The Padul mammoths lived about 35,000 years ago and are among the southernmost found anywhere in Europe.

questions.question: Look at these trees: in Roman Hispania, their oil was already shipped to Rome. Which Spanish region has the most of them today?
hints: The Romans called this area Baetica, after the Guadalquivir River.
It's in the south of Spain, where summers are very hot.
Jaén, one of its provinces, is famous for its seas of olive trees.
questions.description: The liquid gold that Spaniards pour on everything, even breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The province of Jaén alone has more than 60 million olive trees.

questions.question: Felipe V founded it in 1712. It stands on Madrid's Paseo de Recoletos and keeps a copy of almost everything published in Spain. What is it?
hints: You don't go there to look at paintings, but to read and study.
It holds millions of books, maps, sheet music and newspapers.
It's the place with the most books in all of Spain.
questions.description: A gift from Felipe V that, more than three centuries later, nobody has finished unwrapping.
questions.fun_fact: It shares its Recoletos building with the National Archaeological Museum.

questions.question: In 1808 I defended Zaragoza from the French: when the gunners beside me fell, I grabbed the fuse and fired the cannon myself. Who am I?
hints: I'm a heroine of the Peninsular War.
Goya drew me next to a cannon in a print called “¡Qué valor!” (“What courage!”).
I'm known by the name of the region whose capital I defended.
questions.description: Some people lose their temper; she just lost her patience with the French.
questions.fun_fact: Although she is remembered for Zaragoza, Agustina was born in Barcelona in 1786.

questions.question: The 1766 Esquilache Riot, against a minister of Charles III, is also called the “riot of cloaks and…”. How does the name end?
hints: Esquilache didn't want people in Madrid to be able to hide their faces in the street.
The decree set how long a cloak could be, and it also went after something worn above it.
Along with the long cloak, the chambergo, a wide-brimmed one, was banned.
questions.description: A revolt in which Madrid fashion said “enough is enough.”
questions.fun_fact: Esquilache was Italian, from Sicily, and after the riot Charles III had to dismiss him.

questions.question: Which of these places is NOT Spanish territory?
hints: It's in the south, very close to Africa.
People there pay in pounds, and cars have British license plates.
It has belonged to the United Kingdom since the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.
questions.description: A neighbor so close you can see it from the window, but it asks for a different passport.
questions.fun_fact: Menorca was also British for much of the 18th century, until it went back to Spain in 1802.

questions.question: An old Spanish saying goes: “Once the dog is dead, the rabies is gone.” What does it teach?
questions.answer: Remove the cause and the problem ends
hints: The saying is about solving problems, not about pets.
Think about who spreads the illness in the saying.
If what causes it disappears, so does the trouble.
questions.description: A saying with a nasty bite, but a lot of logic.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Pasteur created the rabies vaccine and first used it successfully on a boy in 1885.

questions.question: The French besieged it from 1810 to 1812, members of parliament took refuge there and Spain's first constitution was born there. Which city is it?
hints: It is in the south of Spain.
It is nicknamed “la tacita de plata” (the little silver cup).
It is the city of chirigotas and Spain's most famous carnival.
questions.description: A city that sat down to write laws while surrounded by French cannons.
questions.fun_fact: The Cortes (parliament) first met in nearby Isla de León, today San Fernando, and moved into the city in 1811.

questions.question: The draft federal Constitution of 1873 split Spain into 17 states, such as Aragon or Catalonia. What for?
questions.answer: So each one would have its own government and laws
wrong_answers: So each one could choose its own king
To spread the army's barracks out better
So Madrid would have even more power
hints: It was a republic, so no kings at all.
Francisco Pi y Margall, one of its presidents, backed it.
Each state would have its own parliament, joined to a shared one for all of Spain.
questions.description: The First Republic had big plans and very little time to carry them out.
questions.fun_fact: Cuba and Puerto Rico were also among those 17 states.

questions.question: I'm a woman lying on a couch in a short jacket and sash. Goya painted my twin in the same pose, but with no clothes on. Which painting am I?
hints: Goya painted me in the early 19th century.
I hang in the Prado Museum, next to my twin.
My title says the exact opposite of my sister's.
questions.description: A painting that always shows up to parties well wrapped up.
questions.fun_fact: Both majas belonged to Manuel Godoy, the powerful minister of Charles IV.

questions.question: You hear children in a ring singing “¿Dónde vas, Alfonso XII, dónde vas, triste de ti?”. In which century did that king live?
hints: He was the son of Queen Isabella II.
His reign began after the First Republic.
He died very young, in 1885.
questions.description: A playground ring song with more drama than an afternoon soap opera.
questions.fun_fact: The song remembers his first wife, Mercedes, who died at 18, only five months after the wedding.

questions.question: Look at the portrait: this queen, wife of Alfonso XII, was the daughter of a sister of Isabella II, the king's mother. What was she to the king?
hints: Draw the family tree in your head.
Their mothers were sisters.
It's what you are to the children of your aunts and uncles.
questions.description: A family tree with more tangled branches than a Galician forest.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso XII married her for love, even though his mother, Isabella II, did not like the match at all.

questions.question: You're in the Royal Palace of El Pardo, where visiting foreign heads of state stay today. Who lived here from 1940 to 1975?
hints: He was a military man.
He ruled Spain for almost forty years.
After his death in 1975, the Transition began.
questions.description: A palace that has changed tenants more often than a student apartment.
questions.fun_fact: It was once a royal hunting lodge, and Carlos III had it enlarged.

questions.question: In class you read Bécquer's “Volverán las oscuras golondrinas” (“The dark swallows will return”). Which literary movement does it belong to?
hints: Bécquer lived in the 19th century.
His poems are about love, dreams and deep feelings.
It's the same movement as Zorrilla's “Don Juan Tenorio”.
questions.description: Some dark swallows that come back every school year, right on time, for the literature exam.
questions.fun_fact: His “Rimas” were published in 1871, a year after his death, thanks to his friends.

questions.question: During the Restoration, whenever Sagasta's Liberal Party left government, its rival, Cánovas's party, always came in. Which party was it?
hints: It was one of the two parties that took turns in power.
It stood for order, the monarchy and the Church.
Its name comes from the verb “to conserve”.
questions.description: A political system with fewer surprises than a fixed match in the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: Cánovas and Sagasta swapped power so many times that the system came to be called “turnismo” (taking turns).

questions.question: I'm made of metal, I look like a small trumpet with no valves, and I used to wake soldiers in their barracks. The author of “La Regenta” wrote under my name. What am I?
hints: I’m a wind instrument.
Leopoldo Alas used my Spanish name as a pen name for his newspaper articles.
My sound is so sharp and clear that my name comes from the word for “clear”.
questions.description: A writer who wanted his reviews heard from the other side of town.
questions.fun_fact: “La Regenta” is set in Vetusta, a made-up city based on Oviedo, which today has a statue of its heroine in front of the cathedral.

questions.question: In “Don Quixote”, Sancho Panza rides across La Mancha on his faithful Rucio. What animal is Rucio?
hints: The skinny horse, Rocinante, belongs to Don Quixote, not to Sancho.
It's shorter than a horse and has very long ears.
When it complains, it brays.
questions.description: Even the most famous squire in literature didn't walk everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: “Rucio” means light brown or grayish: Sancho named his animal after the color of its coat.

questions.question: Canine parvovirus mostly strikes unvaccinated puppies and can survive for months in the ground. Which body system does it harm most?
hints: The puppy stops eating.
The puppy loses a lot of fluid and becomes dangerously dehydrated.
It's the system of the stomach and intestines.
questions.description: A tiny virus that sends shivers through every dog breeder.
questions.fun_fact: Canine parvovirus appeared in the late 1970s, and within just a couple of years it had spread all over the world.

questions.question: Francisco Ibáñez made a comic album about the 1978 World Cup, then more about other World Cups and the Olympics. Who are its stars?
hints: Their comic strips appeared in Bruguera's magazines.
It is Ibáñez's longest-running and most famous series.
One of them is bald, wears glasses and can disguise himself as anything.
questions.description: Kickoff, chaos and a ball that always lands where it shouldn't: a typical Ibáñez match.
questions.fun_fact: Ibáñez kept up the habit for decades: his two agents got albums for many World Cups and Olympic Games.

questions.question: Aleluyas, printed sheets of panels with a rhyming couplet under each one, are grandparents of the Spanish comic. In which century were they most popular in Spain?
hints: They needed a printing press, and a cheap one too.
They sold for very little at fairs and street stalls, next to other cheap prints.
It's the century when the railway arrived in Spain.
questions.description: Before speech bubbles existed, stories were told in verse, and in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: Their name comes from the prints that were thrown to the crowds with a shout of “¡aleluya!” during Holy Week processions.

questions.question: Salvador Bartolozzi drew Pinocchio's Spanish adventures and his rival Chapete for Calleja, then went into exile after the Civil War. In which country did he die in 1950?
hints: It was one of the countries that took in the most Spanish exiles.
Spanish is spoken there.
Its capital is one of the biggest cities in the world.
questions.description: A wooden puppet whose nose grows, and an artist who never took his pencil off him.
questions.fun_fact: Bartolozzi made Pinocchio almost a Spanish character, with dozens of new stories that had nothing to do with the Italian original.

questions.question: The Medusa Festival is an electronic music festival held in summer by the beach in the province of Valencia. In which town?
hints: It's south of the city of Valencia.
It sits at the mouth of the Júcar River, with a castle on top of a hill.
Its name starts with “Cu”.
questions.description: A festival named after a sea creature that, luckily, doesn't sting.
questions.fun_fact: The Medusa Festival started in Cullera in 2014 and brings together DJs from all over the world.

questions.question: She came out of Operación Triunfo 2017 and sings “Teléfono”, “Mon amour” and “Los Ángeles”. What's her name?
hints: She's from Catalonia.
Her name is also the name of a mountain range in Alicante.
Her name starts with “Ai”.
questions.description: A singer who calls you on the phone and won't hang up, not even in summer.
questions.fun_fact: Aitana came second in Operación Triunfo 2017, which was won by her fellow contestant Amaia.

questions.question: Which of these songs is NOT by Vetusta Morla?
hints: The odd one out is also by a Spanish indie band.
The odd one out is by La Casa Azul.
It's the one about a revolution.
questions.description: A band named after a very, very old turtle, and it hasn't fallen behind one bit.
questions.fun_fact: Vetusta Morla takes its name from the giant turtle Morla in “The NeverEnding Story”.

questions.question: Melody sang “El baile del gorila” as a child and went to Eurovision 2025 with “Esa diva”. Which province is she from?
hints: She’s from Andalusia.
She’s from Dos Hermanas, very close to her province’s capital.
Her province is home to the Giralda.
questions.description: From dancing like a gorilla to singing like a diva: a true leap in evolution.
questions.fun_fact: Melody was about 10 years old when “El baile del gorila” became a hit all over Spain.

questions.question: Before dawn on October 12, 1492, after two months at sea, the lookout on the Pinta spotted something far away. What did he shout?
hints: It was exactly what every sailor had been longing to hear for weeks.
What he saw wasn't another ship or a sea monster.
For a tired sailor, it's the opposite of “sea”.
questions.description: Two months staring at water, and finally someone looks up from their phone… sorry, from the horizon.
questions.fun_fact: Tradition says the lookout was called Rodrigo de Triana and never got the reward promised to the first man to sight land.

questions.question: During a long race through the snow, how many calories does a sled dog burn in a day?
hints: Far more than an adult human, who needs about 2,000.
It runs for many hours a day and also has to stay warm.
It's a five-digit number.
questions.description: A furry athlete who eats breakfast like there's no tomorrow.
questions.fun_fact: In races, sled dogs wear fabric booties to protect their paw pads from the ice.

questions.question: She never married, Shakespeare's plays premiered during her reign, and her fleet fought the Spanish Armada in 1588. Which country was Elizabeth I queen of?
hints: Her country is an island… or almost.
Her father was Henry VIII, the one with six wives.
Its capital is London.
questions.description: Philip II's great rival, who left his marriage proposal on read.
questions.fun_fact: Philip II became king consort of England by marrying Mary Tudor, Elizabeth's older half-sister.

questions.question: Founded in Seville in 1503, it controlled the ships and goods sailing to and from the Americas and registered every traveler. What was it?
hints: It was a trade institution of the Catholic Monarchs.
Pilots were also trained and maps drawn there.
Its name sounds like the Spanish for signing contracts.
questions.description: The strictest customs office of the 16th century: nobody left for the Indies without stopping at the counter.
questions.fun_fact: In 1717 it moved to Cádiz, because ever-bigger ships struggled to sail up the Guadalquivir.

questions.question: Martin Luther, a German monk, criticized the sale of indulgences. In 1521, Charles I of Spain made him come to Worms. Why?
questions.answer: To make him take back his ideas
wrong_answers: To make him a royal adviser
To have Luther crown him emperor
To have him lead his troops
hints: Charles I defended the Church of Rome.
Luther's ideas were dividing the Christians of Germany.
The emperor wanted him to back down.
questions.description: A meeting with the boss that didn't exactly end in a promotion.
questions.fun_fact: Luther refused and, later hiding in Wartburg Castle, translated the New Testament into German.

questions.question: I was born because an English king wanted to divorce a daughter of the Catholic Monarchs and the Pope said no. That king became my head. What am I?
hints: It all happened in the 16th century, around the same time Luther was breaking with Rome.
Today the British monarch is still my head.
My name comes from the Latin word for “English”.
questions.description: A divorce so famous it ended up starting its own church.
questions.fun_fact: Before he broke with Rome, the Pope had given Henry VIII the title “Defender of the Faith” for writing against Luther.

questions.question: Don Quixote was one, didn't pay certain taxes, and thought working with his hands was beneath him. What was a hidalgo?
hints: He belonged to the privileged class.
He had no title like duke or count.
The word comes from «hijo de algo», “son of something”.
questions.description: A reader so hooked on novels that he ended up leaving home with a barber's basin on his head.
questions.fun_fact: In “Lazarillo de Tormes”, a hidalgo so poor he had nothing to eat walked the streets with a toothpick in his mouth so people would think he had eaten well.

questions.question: Moctezuma ruled Tenochtitlan when Hernán Cortés arrived. Which city was later built on its ruins?
hints: Today it is a country's capital.
It is one of the most populous cities in the world.
The city has the same name as the country.
questions.description: Moctezuma was expecting visitors, just not gentlemen in armor from across the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco and was bigger than almost every European city of its time.

questions.question: In “Lazarillo de Tormes”, Lázaro serves several masters. Which of these was NOT one of them?
hints: It's a picaresque novel where Lázaro tells his own life story.
Later he also sells indulgences for a pardoner and carries water for a chaplain.
None of his masters ever cut his hair.
questions.description: The unluckiest kid in all of Spanish literature when it comes to picking a boss.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this book, “lazarillo” became an everyday Spanish word for a person or dog who guides a blind person.

questions.question: In 1492, Isabella the Catholic conquered Granada, backed Columbus and signed a decree with Ferdinand. Which group had to convert or leave Spain because of it?
hints: They had lived in Spanish cities for many centuries.
Their descendants are the Sephardim.
They prayed in synagogues.
questions.description: 1492: a year with more headlines than a whole evening news show.
questions.fun_fact: Many Sephardim kept speaking Judeo-Spanish for centuries, a form of the Castilian of that time.

questions.question: I was born in 1848 in the Santa María neighborhood of Cádiz, worked at the slaughterhouse, and famous malagueñas bear my nickname. Who am I?
hints: I'm from the city of chirigotas and Carnival.
My malagueñas sound solemn, almost like a church chant.
My nickname is the Spanish word for a twin.
questions.description: A neighborhood in Cádiz where even the seagulls sing por soleá.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa María neighborhood was also the birthplace of Chano Lobato, famous for his witty, cheerful alegrías.

questions.question: Which of these flamenco artists does NOT have a stage name that is a sea creature?
hints: Three of them could end up in a paella.
One is shellfish with claws, one is small and pink, and one is a fish.
The one you want is a singer from San Fernando whose name starts with “Niña”.
questions.description: A festival poster that could pass for a seafood restaurant menu.
questions.fun_fact: Camarón de la Isla got his nickname as a child because he was very blond and skinny, like a little shrimp (camarón).

questions.question: I'm the oldest written papyrus from Egypt, and I describe the daily work of the inspector Merer. What was his team carrying?
questions.answer: Limestone blocks for the Great Pyramid
wrong_answers: Granite for the obelisks of Karnak
Cedar from Lebanon for royal ships
Gold from Nubia for the pharaoh's treasury
hints: I was found in 2013 at an ancient port on the Red Sea.
I was written in the time of the pharaoh Khufu.
My team crossed the Nile from the Tura quarries to Giza.
questions.description: The world's oldest work notebook, and nobody checked its spelling.
questions.fun_fact: The Diary of Merer shows that the stone reached Giza by boat along canals of the Nile, not dragged across the whole desert.

questions.question: Rodri won the Ballon d'Or in 2024. How many years had it been since a Spanish player last won it?
hints: The previous Spanish winner was playing for Barça when he won it.
It's more than half a century.
It was Luis Suárez Miramontes, in 1960.
questions.description: A trophy Spain waited for even longer than the last bus of the night.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Suárez Miramontes, the previous Spanish winner, was from Galicia and played for Barça when he received it in 1960.

questions.question: In Berlin in 2024, which Spain captain lifted this trophy?
hints: He was a striker.
At the time, he played for Atlético de Madrid.
His surname starts with “mora”, the Spanish word for blackberry.
questions.description: The armband weighs next to nothing, but what you lift with it weighs a ton.
questions.fun_fact: Morata is Spain's all-time top scorer at the Euros, with 7 goals.

questions.question: Spain beat England 2–1 in a European Championship final. In what year?
hints: Spain won every one of its games at that tournament.
The final was played in Germany.
Lamine Yamal was 17 at the time.
questions.description: The country that invented the game is still waiting for it to come home.
questions.fun_fact: England lost two European Championship finals in a row: to Italy in 2021 and to Spain in 2024.

questions.question: I debuted for Atlético at 17 and got a kid's nickname. I scored the winning goal in the Euro 2008 final. Who am I?
hints: He was a fast, blond striker.
He later played for Liverpool and Chelsea.
They called him “El Niño” (the Kid).
questions.description: However much you grow, some nicknames never have a birthday.
questions.fun_fact: Fernando Torres also scored in the Euro 2012 final, becoming the first player to score in two Euro finals.

questions.question: How many seasons did goalkeeper David de Gea play for Manchester United?
hints: He arrived from Atlético de Madrid when he was very young.
He signed in 2011.
He left in 2023.
questions.description: It rains so much in Manchester that goalkeepers should get gloves with built-in umbrellas.
questions.fun_fact: Manchester United fans voted De Gea the club's player of the season four times, a club record.

questions.question: I'm a Barça center-back, born in 2007 in a village in Girona, and I debuted for the first team at 16. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four.
I came up through La Masia.
My first name is Pau.
questions.description: While your friends do their middle school homework, you're stopping strikers in the Champions League.
questions.fun_fact: Cubarsí comes from Estanyol, a tiny village in Girona with only a few hundred people.

questions.question: In Alicante, every June, huge figures made of cardboard and wood go up in the streets and are burned on San Juan night. What is this fiesta called?
hints: It's not the Valencian fiesta in March, even though the two look alike.
The queen of this fiesta gets the title Bellea del Foc.
Its name is the Spanish word for the fires people jump over on the beach on San Juan night.
questions.description: A fiesta where artists spend months on a work that lasts exactly one night.
questions.fun_fact: Alicante's Hogueras have been held officially since 1928, and the burning starts with a burst of fireworks launched from Mount Benacantil.

questions.question: A widespread superstition in Spain says that making a toast with this drink brings bad luck. Which drink is it?
hints: It's the most ordinary drink of all.
It's on almost every table at lunchtime.
It's the one with no sugar, no bubbles and no flavor.
questions.description: Clink that glass… but check what's inside it first.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word “brindis” (toast) comes from the German “bring dir's”, meaning “I offer it to you”.

questions.question: On the night of San Juan, many people write their wishes, or the bad things they want to leave behind, on paper. Where does the paper go?
hints: It's the most widespread ritual of that night, and it's usually done in a group.
Nothing is left of the paper, only smoke.
It's the same thing people jump over that night for luck.
questions.description: A wish list with a very short expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: The night of San Juan falls right next to the summer solstice, the shortest night of the year, and the fire was a way to give strength to the sun.

questions.question: Which of these cities does NOT appear in the title of any book by Antonio Muñoz Molina?
hints: One of his essays travels back to the time of the Umayyad caliphs.
His novel “Winter in…” mixes jazz, love and a Portuguese capital.
The missing city is the one with the Eiffel Tower.
questions.description: A writer from Úbeda with more train tickets than a travel agency.
questions.fun_fact: Muñoz Molina turned his hometown of Úbeda into “Mágina,” the imaginary city of several of his novels.

questions.question: The Semana Negra in Gijón, a crime fiction festival born in 1988, was founded by a writer. Who?
hints: He writes crime novels and also biographies of revolutionaries like Che Guevara.
He was born in Gijón in 1949, but grew up and lives in Mexico.
His detective is called Héctor Belascoarán Shayne.
questions.description: A seaside party where the crimes are on paper and the Ferris wheels are real.
questions.fun_fact: The Semana Negra awards the Hammett Prize for the best crime novel written in Spanish.

questions.question: The famous Drago de Icod in Tenerife is hundreds of years old, over 15 meters (49 ft) tall, and oozes a red liquid. What is it?
hints: Nobody built it.
It grows very slowly, a little more every year.
It has a trunk, branches and leaves.
questions.description: It has stood in the same spot in Tenerife for centuries without ever asking for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The drago's sap turns red as it dries, and long ago it was sold as “dragon's blood.”

questions.question: Look at this Mudéjar tower in Teruel, made of brick and colored tiles. What was it built for?
wrong_answers: To tell the time by the sun
hints: It stands right next to a church.
From the top, it could be heard across the whole city.
It goes “ding, dong” when it's time for Mass.
questions.description: Brick and green tiles: the builders of Teruel had more style than many interior designers.
questions.fun_fact: The Mudéjar architecture of Teruel has been a World Heritage Site since 1986.

questions.question: “I'm a square fortress with four towers, high above a city almost surrounded by the Tagus, and I house the Army Museum.” What am I?
hints: I've been a fortress for centuries and have also been a home for kings.
From my towers you can see a huge Gothic cathedral.
My city is famous for marzipan and for El Greco.
questions.description: A fortress with the best views in the neighborhood and very little desire to move.
questions.fun_fact: The Alcázar of Toledo also houses the Library of Castilla-La Mancha, one of the largest in the region.

questions.question: You're in Terminal 4 of Madrid-Barajas Airport, under its wavy bamboo ceiling. In what year did it open?
hints: The euro already existed.
It was a few years before Spain won its first soccer World Cup.
It opened in the middle of the first decade of the 21st century.
questions.description: A wavy ceiling so long you could miss your flight just staring at it.
questions.fun_fact: In 2006 it won the Stirling Prize, one of the most important architecture awards in the world.

questions.question: Look at this pink stone basilica surrounded by green mountains. Where is it?
hints: It's in northern Spain, near the Picos de Europa.
Some famous lakes are very close by.
It's in Asturias, next to the cave of the Santina.
questions.description: A pink church among green mountains: someone nailed the color palette.
questions.fun_fact: The basilica was built of pink limestone and finished in 1901.

questions.question: Barcelona's red-brick Arc de Triomf was built as the entrance to a World's Fair. In which year?
hints: It was in the 19th century.
It was the first World's Fair ever held in Spain.
It was one year before the Eiffel Tower opened.
questions.description: A triumphal arch with no military parade: here the triumph was a giant fair.
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by the architect Josep Vilaseca, and its red brick is a nod to the Neo-Mudéjar style.

questions.question: Look at these ruins of Medina Azahara, near Córdoba. Who was this palace city built for in the 10th century?
questions.answer: For the caliph and his court
hints: At that time, Córdoba was part of al-Andalus.
It was the seat of the most powerful Muslim ruler on the Iberian Peninsula in his day.
Abd al-Rahman III ordered it built.
questions.description: A whole city built just to show off, with a view of Córdoba thrown in.
questions.fun_fact: Medina Azahara was looted and abandoned less than a century after it was built, and today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: Look at this building by Gaudí in Barcelona, which has been under construction for more than 140 years. What is it for?
wrong_answers: For a king to live in
hints: Thousands of people fit inside, and colored light shines in through the windows.
Its tallest tower, dedicated to Jesus, is topped by a large cross.
It's a church: the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: It's been under construction longer than the street in your neighborhood, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: Gaudí is buried in the crypt of the Sagrada Família.

questions.question: This detail is from “Blind Man's Buff” (“La gallina ciega”), a cartoon Goya painted as a model for a tapestry. In which royal palace was that tapestry meant to hang?
hints: It is on the outskirts of Madrid, next to a forest where the kings went hunting.
Today it hosts foreign heads of state on visits to Spain.
It shares its name with a hilly forest north of Madrid full of holm oaks and deer.
questions.description: A garden game for people with wigs, fans and plenty of free time.
questions.fun_fact: In the painting, the blindfolded boy isn't reaching out with his hands: he's trying to touch the others with a big wooden spoon.

questions.question: Narrow “air shafts” lead out from two chambers inside this pyramid. How many of these shafts are there in total?
hints: The chambers are called the “King's Chamber” and the “Queen's Chamber.”
Each chamber has the same number of shafts.
From each chamber, one shaft heads north and one heads south.
questions.description: Tunnels so narrow that not even a cat would squeeze in, but a robot would.
questions.fun_fact: In 1993, a small robot called Upuaut climbed up one of these shafts and found a tiny stone door with two copper handles.

questions.question: I was born in Zaragoza in 1734, painted frescoes on domes of the Pilar and ceilings of the Royal Palace, and my sister Josefa married Goya. Who am I?
hints: I ended up as director of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando.
My younger brother, Ramón, was a painter too.
Goya worked under me at the Pilar, and we ended up arguing about the way he painted.
questions.description: Being a genius's brother-in-law has its perks… and its arguments at family dinners.
questions.fun_fact: Goya painted his portrait in 1795, the year Bayeu died, and today it hangs in the Prado.

questions.question: I have the shape of a chain hanging from both ends, but flipped upside down. Gaudí found me with models of strings and little bags of shot. What am I?
hints: I appear again and again in the attic of La Pedrera.
Because I only work in compression, I hardly need buttresses.
My name comes from the Latin word “catena”.
questions.description: Clothesline physics applied to the rooftops of Barcelona.
questions.fun_fact: Gaudí hung his models upside down, photographed them and then looked at the photos flipped over to see what the building would look like.

questions.question: Three Eduardo Chillida sculptures are fixed into the rocks where the waves break, at the end of Ondarreta beach in San Sebastián. What are they made of?
hints: They were put there in 1977 and have survived storms ever since.
The sea has turned them a reddish brown.
It's the material of train rails and skyscraper beams.
questions.description: The saltiest hairdo on the whole Bay of Biscay coast.
questions.fun_fact: The square next to the sculptures has holes in the ground, and when the sea is rough, air and water shoot up out of them.

questions.question: RCR, an architecture studio from Olot, won the Pritzker Prize in 2017 and wrapped the Soulages Museum in Rodez, France, in a reddish material. Which one?
hints: This material is also used for bridges and shipping containers.
Its outside is left to weather on purpose.
Its layer of rust protects it and keeps it from rusting on the inside.
questions.description: Three partners from a town of sleeping volcanoes who took home the Nobel Prize of architecture.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Aranda, Carme Pigem and Ramon Vilalta were the first trio to win the Pritzker Prize together.

questions.question: In 1969 Salvador Dalí drew the Chupa Chups logo: red letters on a yellow flower. Which flower is it?
hints: It's a very common flower in meadows.
In the wild it usually has white petals around a yellow center.
People pull off its petals saying “he loves me, he loves me not”.
questions.description: A surrealist painter who also knew how to make kids' lives a little sweeter.
questions.fun_fact: Dalí suggested putting the logo on top of the lollipop so it could always be seen in full.

questions.question: Manolo Millares, of the Art Informel group El Paso, sewed, tore and burned this rough fabric to make his pictures. Which fabric?
hints: Millares was born in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria and was fascinated by Guanche mummies.
It is a rough brown cloth made of jute.
Potato sacks are made of it.
questions.description: Art that isn't painted: it's sewn, torn… and sometimes singed.
questions.fun_fact: Millares called one series of his works “Homunculi,” figures that look as if they were made of patched rags.

questions.question: Jeff Koons's giant dog has guarded the door of the Guggenheim Bilbao since 1997 and is about 12 m (40 ft) tall. What is it covered in?
hints: Its “coat” gets changed a couple of times a year.
Gardeners look after it, not dog groomers.
In spring it gets really colorful, with petunias and pansies.
questions.description: A dog that never needs to be taken for a walk.
questions.fun_fact: Dressing it takes about 38,000 plants, watered by a system hidden inside the sculpture.

questions.question: In which year did Betty Missiego finish second at Eurovision with “Su canción”, backed by a children's choir?
hints: It was in the 1970s.
That year, Eurovision was held in Jerusalem.
It was the last year of that decade.
questions.description: A song so sweet that even the children's choir wanted to move onto the stage for good.
questions.fun_fact: Spain voted last that year, and its points gave the win to Israel, pushing Betty Missiego herself into second place.

questions.question: This band from San Sebastián sang “Rosas” and is named after a body part of the painter Van Gogh. Which one?
hints: Van Gogh has a very famous story about this body part.
The story goes that he cut off a piece of it.
It's the part you hear with.
questions.description: A band that took art history very, very much to heart.
questions.fun_fact: La Oreja de Van Gogh started playing together in San Sebastián in the mid-1990s.

questions.question: We're from Valladolid, we mix rock with bagpipes and fiddles, and we sing “Hola, chata, ¿cómo estás?” in “20 de abril”. Who are we?
hints: Our music sounds like the music of Ireland and Scotland.
The song is a letter written to an old friend.
Our name speaks of an ancient people and of something that isn't long.
questions.description: Bagpipes, fiddles and a letter that arrived many years late.
questions.fun_fact: “20 de abril” is about a date in 1990 and has become an anthem at Spanish fiestas.

questions.question: In which decade did Loquillo y los Trogloditas release “Cadillac solitario”?
hints: The dictatorship in Spain was already over.
It was the time of La Movida.
It was the decade Spain hosted the soccer World Cup.
questions.description: A huge car, a long night and nobody in the passenger seat.
questions.fun_fact: Loquillo is the stage name of José María Sanz, a rocker from Barcelona.

questions.question: It had a tape wound up inside and two sides, A and B; if the tape got tangled, you fixed it with a pen. What was it?
hints: You played it in radios, in the car and in portable players with headphones.
When one side ended, you flipped it over.
It was a small plastic case with two little wheels.
questions.description: Music from the days when your parents wore shoulder pads and impossible hairdos.
questions.fun_fact: The company Philips introduced the compact cassette in 1963.

questions.question: She's from Madrid, a niece of Paco de Lucía, and as a teenager she had a hit in 1998 with “Aprendiz”. Who is she?
hints: She has been a coach on the TV show “La Voz”.
Her stage name has only two syllables.
It starts with M and ends with an accent mark.
questions.description: A voice that learned fast and hasn't stopped giving lessons since.
questions.fun_fact: The song “Aprendiz” was written by Alejandro Sanz.

questions.question: They lie off L’Estartit in Girona, fishing is banned there and huge groupers live there. Why do so many people travel to the Medes Islands?
hints: You need a wetsuit.
It’s done underwater.
You wear a mask and fins, and sometimes an air tank on your back.
questions.description: Islands so small they’d fit on a map the size of a postage stamp.
questions.fun_fact: Since fishing was banned in the early 1980s, the groupers of the Medes have lost their fear and swim right up to divers.

questions.question: The Bellós River carved this landscape in the Pyrenees of Huesca over thousands of years. What is this kind of narrow, deep valley called?
hints: It has very tall rock walls on both sides.
The most famous one in the world is in Arizona, in the United States.
Its name sounds a lot like the big gun that fired iron balls on pirate ships.
questions.description: A river with endless patience and a very, very tiny chisel.
questions.fun_fact: The Añisclo Canyon became part of the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park in 1982.

questions.question: This is the Bolonia dune in Cádiz: it’s about 30 m (100 ft) high and moving into the pine forest. Where does the wind bring its sand from?
questions.answer: From the beach next to it
hints: It doesn’t come from very far away.
The levante wind blows from the sea toward the land.
It’s right in front of it, where people lay down their towels.
questions.description: A mountain that can’t sit still and walks into the forest without asking.
questions.fun_fact: Next to the dune are the Roman ruins of Baelo Claudia, a town that made a famous fish sauce called garum.

questions.question: Hundreds of these birds nest on the cliffs of the Douro River in Arribes, on the border with Portugal. What are they?
hints: They fly in circles very high up, barely moving their wings.
They eat animals that are already dead.
They have long necks with almost no feathers.
questions.description: Neighbors who live on a rock balcony with views of two countries.
questions.fun_fact: The griffon vulture can measure more than 2.5 m (8 ft) from wingtip to wingtip.

questions.question: In the Aiguamolls de l’Empordà wetlands in Girona, there are wooden huts like this one by the water. What are they for?
questions.answer: To watch birds without scaring them
wrong_answers: To sell tickets to the park
hints: It’s best to go in quietly.
The windows are thin and long so you can look out without being seen.
Bring binoculars and look for herons or flamingos.
questions.description: The quietest wooden house in all of Catalonia.
questions.fun_fact: White storks came back to the Aiguamolls after they had stopped breeding in Catalonia.

questions.question: The Valencian Community invented them in 1994, now has hundreds, and other European regions copied the idea. What are micro-reserves?
hints: None of them can be larger than 20 hectares (about 50 acres).
Often they are just one hillside, one ravine or one little strip of coast.
They look after rare species of flora, or ones that grow only in that one spot.
questions.description: A natural park in pocket size.
questions.fun_fact: A micro-reserve can be as small as a piece of cliff: all it takes is one unique species living there.

questions.question: The Timanfaya eruptions began on September 1, 1730, and changed Lanzarote's landscape forever. How long did they last?
hints: It's one of the longest eruptions in the history of the Canary Islands.
It lasted well over a year.
They ended in April 1736.
questions.description: Lanzarote started some home renovations and took a little while to finish them.
questions.fun_fact: The priest of Yaiza, Andrés Lorenzo Curbelo, kept a diary of the first months of the eruption that scientists still study today.

questions.question: Every fall, hundreds of spoonbills like this one stop to feed in the marshes of Santoña, in Cantabria. Where do most of them come from?
hints: They come from northern Europe.
It is a small, very flat country with a lot of coastline.
It is famous for its windmills, its dikes and its land below sea level.
questions.description: A gas station for traveling birds, with the cutlery already included.
questions.fun_fact: Santoña is also famous for something else from the sea: its canned anchovies.

questions.question: It's typed in the chat at the end of an online match, winners and losers use it, and it's just two letters: “GG”. What is it for?
hints: It's short for two words.
It's a sign of good sportsmanship, like shaking hands after a match.
The first G stands for the opposite of “bad”.
questions.description: Two letters you can type faster than you can throw the controller onto the sofa.
questions.fun_fact: Typing “GG” too early, before the match is over, is considered rude in many games.

questions.question: Radio Marca shares its name with a famous Spanish newspaper that has a red masthead. What does it talk about almost all day?
hints: It gets really busy on weekends.
Its listeners care about goals, baskets and transfers.
Real Madrid, Barça and LaLiga come up on almost every show.
questions.description: A station where Mondays get more heated than any family Sunday lunch.
questions.fun_fact: The newspaper Marca was founded in San Sebastián in 1938 and later moved to Madrid.

questions.question: On Twitch I have a little green sword next to my name, I delete nasty messages and I can kick troublemakers out of the chat. Who am I?
hints: I'm usually not the one doing the stream.
The streamer picks me to help keep order.
My name comes from a verb that means to calm things down.
questions.description: Hours and hours inside a live stream, and not one second in front of the camera.
questions.fun_fact: Many moderators for big streamers work for free, just to help their community.

questions.question: You're in the Canary Islands, whose symbol animal is the canary. And which tree is their symbol plant?
hints: It loves sunshine and warm beaches.
Its leaves look like giant feathers and its trunk has no branches.
It's related to the tree that gives us dates.
questions.description: On these islands, even the birds are named after the place.
questions.fun_fact: On La Gomera, the sap of the Canary Island palm is used to make a sweet syrup called “miel de palma” (palm honey).

questions.question: The Tree of Guernica, a symbol of the Basque Country, is a kind of tree that grows acorns. Which kind?
hints: Its leaves have wavy edges with many lobes.
Its wood is so hard it was used for ships and wine barrels.
In Basque it's called «haritza», and squirrels look for it in the woods.
questions.description: A tree that has hosted more important meetings than most offices.
questions.fun_fact: The trunk of the old 18th-century Tree of Guernica is kept under a small pavilion next to the Assembly House.

questions.question: Íñigo Arista lived in the 9th century and is seen as the first king of a Christian kingdom in the north. Which one?
hints: His kingdom lay at the foot of the western Pyrenees.
Centuries later, the kingdom changed its name to that of its territory.
Its capital is famous today for the Sanfermines.
questions.description: Long before castles had gift shops, this king already wore a crown.
questions.fun_fact: Aragon didn't become a kingdom until 1035, almost two centuries after Íñigo Arista.

questions.question: Each part of a divided shield is called a quarter. Look at this coat of arms of Castile and León: how many quarters does it have?
hints: Count the sections with a castle or a lion.
The castles and lions take turns.
It's the same number as a lion's legs.
questions.description: A shield cut into little pieces, but very tidily.
questions.fun_fact: The castles stand for the old Kingdom of Castile and the lions for the Kingdom of León, united in 1230.

questions.question: This is the coat of arms of Barcelona. How many red crosses can you see on it?
hints: Look at the white parts of the coat of arms.
Count only the crosses, not the stripes.
It's the same number as the eyes on your face.
questions.description: A coat of arms all dressed up for a party in red and yellow.
questions.fun_fact: The red cross on white is the cross of Saint George, the saint who, legend says, defeated a dragon.

previous.feedback: source: The essential image is "File:IV Trobada oficial de Biquipedia.jpg". Going by the title, it is a photo of a Catalan Wikipedia meetup, not the Barcelona coat of arms the question asks players to count crosses on. The source's media slot needs a new file, for example the Commons SVG "Escut de Barcelona.svg". The translated text itself is faithful and fine.

questions.question: These are the pyramids of Meroë, in today's Sudan. Which people built them?
hints: They are smaller, steeper and newer than the ones at Giza.
Their kings copied Egyptian customs, like hieroglyphs and burial under pyramids, but they also wrote their own language.
Their kingdom had the name of a son of Ham in the Bible.
questions.description: Pointy pyramids that never make it onto the postcards from Egypt.
questions.fun_fact: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: Meroë alone has about 200.

questions.question: The NO-DO was the newsreel shown in movie theaters under Franco. Which years did his dictatorship last?
hints: It began just as the Civil War ended.
It ended when the dictator died.
Franco died in November 1975.
questions.description: Years when even the news at the movie theater came in black and white.
questions.fun_fact: Movie theaters had to show the NO-DO until 1976, and it kept being made until 1981.

questions.question: In which city is this Santiago Calatrava bridge, held up by cables from one huge leaning mast?
hints: It's in the south of Spain.
The Guadalquivir River flows beneath it.
It's the city of the Giralda.
questions.description: A bridge that seems to be taking a never-ending bow.
questions.fun_fact: The mascot of Expo 92 was Curro, a white bird with a colorful beak and crest.

questions.question: Since 1983, Spain’s tourism logo has been a colorful sun. Which painter created it?
hints: He was a 20th-century Catalan painter.
His paintings are full of stars, moons and bright splashes of color.
He has a large foundation on Montjuïc hill in Barcelona.
questions.description: A logo with more sunshine than a beach towel in August.
questions.fun_fact: In 1980, Miró also designed the logo of La Caixa bank, a colorful star.

questions.question: In the Civil War we defended the government elected in 1936, our flag had a purple stripe and Madrid held out with us. Who are we?
hints: The other side was led by General Franco.
Foreign volunteers of the International Brigades fought with us.
We defended the regime proclaimed in April 1931.
questions.description: Two sides that couldn't agree on anything, not even the flag.
questions.fun_fact: The red, yellow and purple flag was Spain's official flag from 1931 to 1939.

questions.question: Spanish history books often say that military officers «se sublevaron». What does «sublevarse» mean?
hints: The word comes up a lot when studying how the Civil War began.
Whoever does it wants to seize power.
It’s like taking up arms.
questions.description: A word that always brings trouble in history books.
questions.fun_fact: The uprising that started the Civil War began on July 17, 1936, in Melilla and spread to mainland Spain the next day.

questions.question: General Hasdrubal founded it around 227 BC, and today it is a major port in Murcia. Where does the name Cartagena come from?
wrong_answers: From Tarraco, a Roman city in Hispania
From Tartessos, a kingdom in southern Iberia
From Tyre, a Phoenician city in the East
hints: Hasdrubal wasn't Roman: he came from the other side of the Mediterranean.
His people fought against Rome in the Punic Wars.
The Romans later called it “Carthago Nova”, the New…
questions.description: Some cities inherit their mother's eyes; this one inherited her name.
questions.fun_fact: Hannibal set out from Cartagena in 218 BC with his army and his elephants, heading for Italy.

questions.question: Someone doesn't want the last croquette, but won't let anyone else eat it either. According to the Spanish saying, they're like whom?
wrong_answers: Como la gallina de los huevos de oro
Como el lobo con piel de cordero
hints: It is a four-legged domestic animal.
Lope de Vega gave this title to a comedy about a countess who doesn't want her secretary but won't let anyone else have him.
It neither eats nor lets others eat.
questions.description: An animal with very little team spirit when it comes to sharing.
questions.fun_fact: Lope's comedy “El perro del hortelano” was made into a film by Pilar Miró in 1996 and won seven Goya Awards.

questions.question: In Rafael Sánchez Ferlosio's “Industrias y andanzas de Alfanhuí”, to which city does the boy go to learn from a master taxidermist?
hints: It is a provincial capital in Castile.
Today it belongs to Castilla-La Mancha.
The Henares River runs through it, and Alcalá is very close.
questions.description: A boy with eyes like a stone-curlew, stuffed birds and plenty of Castilian poetry.
questions.fun_fact: Sánchez Ferlosio published “Alfanhuí” in 1951, when he was about 24, and won the Cervantes Prize in 2004.

questions.question: In the film “Zipi y Zape y el club de la canica”, the twins start a secret club at a very strict boarding school. What is a canica?
hints: It’s a very small toy.
It’s round and rolls along the floor.
You play by flicking it with your finger to knock into others.
questions.description: Two naughty twins, a very strict boarding school and a club named after a toy.
questions.fun_fact: Little balls for playing have been found in ancient Egyptian tombs: canicas are a toy thousands of years old.

questions.question: Zipi and Zape's father, a very serious professor, is called Don Pantuflo. What is his surname?
hints: His first name and surname go together.
It's a kind of shoe you can also play sports in.
Like his sons' names, it starts with Z.
questions.description: A father so strict that his kids tremble when they hear his footsteps.
questions.fun_fact: Zipi and Zape have real names: they're called José and Zacarías.

questions.question: I'm a giant temple in Nubia, carved into the rock for Ramesses II. In the 1960s, I was cut into blocks and moved up a hill. Why?
questions.answer: A huge dam was going to flood me
wrong_answers: The desert sand was burying me
They wanted to take me to a museum
hints: The problem came from the Nile River.
Something enormous was built at Aswan.
Behind that project, the gigantic Lake Nasser formed.
questions.description: A move so heavy that even calling every cousin you have wouldn't help.
questions.fun_fact: The Abu Simbel temple was cut into more than a thousand blocks and rebuilt about 65 meters (213 feet) higher up.

questions.question: In which Spanish province was Pablo López, the singer and pianist in the photo, born?
hints: He's from Andalusia.
He was born in a very touristy beach town.
His hometown, Fuengirola, is on the Costa del Sol.
questions.description: A singer who'd rather sit at the piano than on the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Pablo López first became known on the talent show Operación Triunfo in 2008, where he made it to the final.

questions.question: Which music style does DJ and producer Juan Magán proudly claim to have created and named?
hints: It was a hit in nightclubs in the early 2010s.
Before singing, he started out playing records in clubs.
The name joins “electronic” with something from Latin America.
questions.description: Some people invent recipes, and some invent a whole new way to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Magán is from Badalona and was a huge hit in 2012 with “Bailando por ahí”.

questions.question: Complete this: “Dani Martín is to El Canto del Loco as Santi Balmes is to…”
hints: It's an indie band from Barcelona.
One of its best-known albums is called “1999”.
It sings “Club de fans de John Boy”.
questions.description: A band with song titles a mile long and concerts packed with thick-rimmed glasses.
questions.fun_fact: Santi Balmes, the singer of Love of Lesbian, also writes children's books.

questions.question: Which band sings “Pan y mantequilla”, the song that gets everyone dancing at parties?
hints: It's a band from the Canary Islands.
They also sing “Cuando me siento bien”.
Their name includes the Spanish word for the hallway of a house.
questions.description: A song so breakfast-themed you'll want to dunk it in your coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Efecto Pasillo is from Gran Canaria, and “Pan y mantequilla” was one of the biggest hits of 2012.

questions.question: I was born in Sos, in Aragon, in 1452. I was King of Aragon, and in 1492 I conquered Granada with my wife. Who am I?
hints: My wedding united two great kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula.
With my wife, I backed Columbus's voyage.
I share my nickname with my wife: the “Catholic Monarchs”.
questions.description: One half of a royal marriage that redrew the map of the Peninsula.
questions.fun_fact: Machiavelli held up Ferdinand as an example of a cunning ruler in his famous book “The Prince”.

questions.question: Philip the Handsome married Joanna, daughter of the Catholic Monarchs, and their son was Charles I. Which dynasty began ruling Spain this way?
hints: It is the dynasty of Philip II and Philip IV.
It ruled Spain for almost two centuries, until Charles II died in 1700.
In Spain, this family is named after the Central European country Philip's family came from.
questions.description: A handsome son-in-law who showed up with a whole dynasty in his suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: Charles I, the son of Philip and Joanna, was born in the Flemish city of Ghent in 1500.

questions.question: A popular Spanish song goes “Échale guindas al pavo”. Look at the photo: what are guindas?
hints: They grow on a tree.
They're small, round and red, with a little stem.
They look a lot like cherries.
questions.description: A turkey with a side dish: now that's a real feast.
questions.fun_fact: A guinda is a sour cherry, and Spaniards say “poner la guinda” for finishing something off, just like “the cherry on top”.

questions.question: At a flamenco tablao, the audience does “jaleo” while someone dances. What is jaleo for?
hints: It's done with joy, never in anger.
Shouts like “¡olé!”, “¡eso es!” or “¡arsa!” are part of it.
It's like fans in the stands shouting to lift their team.
questions.description: When the audience wants its name on the poster too.
questions.fun_fact: Even jaleo is an art: an “¡olé!” that's off the beat really stands out in a tablao.

questions.question: Mikel Merino scored against Germany at Euro 2024 and celebrated by running around something, just like his father did in 1991. What was it?
hints: It's at the edge of the field, not in the middle.
It's a thin object sticking up from the ground.
There are four on the field, one in each corner.
questions.description: Some fathers leave their kids a fortune; others leave them a dance routine.
questions.fun_fact: His father, Ángel Merino, celebrated a goal for Osasuna the same way in Stuttgart, the same city where Mikel scored against Germany.

questions.question: On Spanish mystery shows, a “psicofonía” is a strange voice. Where does it turn up?
wrong_answers: In a stain on a wall
hints: Many mystery shows try to “hunt” them at night.
Ghost hunters leave a device running in an empty house and check it later, calmly.
You can't see it, you hear it, and you need a microphone to catch it.
questions.description: Hunting ghosts in the middle of the night: the favorite hobby of people who can't sleep.
questions.fun_fact: In English this supposed phenomenon is called EVP, or “electronic voice phenomenon.”

questions.question: You're singing the Spanish kids' song “I Had Ten Little Puppies”, and one falls in the snow. How many puppies are left?
hints: It's a really easy take-away sum.
At the start there were ten.
It's the number that comes just before ten.
questions.description: A song where puppies vanish faster than candy from a piñata.
questions.fun_fact: The song helps kids practice counting down: in every verse one puppy goes away, until none are left.

questions.question: The Cross of Caravaca, which many people wear as a lucky charm, has how many horizontal arms?
hints: It's not like the most common cross.
Legend says angels brought it down from heaven in the 13th century.
It's a double cross.
questions.description: A cross so famous it even gave a town its last name.
questions.fun_fact: Caravaca de la Cruz, in Murcia, holds a Jubilee Year every seven years; the last one was in 2024.

questions.question: A poet from Seville wrote some famous letters while recovering his health at the foot of the Moncayo, in Aragon. What are they called?
hints: The poet went there with his brother, who was a painter.
He wrote them at the monastery of Veruela, in the province of Zaragoza.
He is the author of the “Rimas” and the “Leyendas,” and the title speaks of his monk's room.
questions.description: Mail so literary it ended up in schoolbooks.
questions.fun_fact: Bécquer sent the letters to the Madrid newspaper El Contemporáneo, which published them in installments.

questions.question: In 1998 José Hierro published a book of poems called “Cuaderno de…” (“Notebook of…”). Which city?
hints: That same year, Hierro won the Cervantes Prize.
Lorca also devoted a whole book of poems to this city.
The city has skyscrapers and a Statue of Liberty.
questions.description: A poet whose surname means “iron”, yet whose verses are as tender as they come.
questions.fun_fact: Although he was born in Madrid in 1922, José Hierro grew up in Santander and always felt he belonged there.

questions.question: You reach Santiago after walking the last 100 km (62 miles) of the Camino and get the “Compostela”. What is it?
wrong_answers: A pass to the cathedral museum
hints: It is a piece of paper written in Latin.
You get it at the Pilgrim's Office.
It has your name on it and proves you made it.
questions.description: After weeks of blisters, the pilgrim's most longed-for reward finally arrives.
questions.fun_fact: To earn it, you must cover at least the last 100 km (62 miles) on foot or 200 km (124 miles) by bike, getting your pilgrim passport stamped along the way.

questions.question: The Madrid mansion Parque Florido holds thousands of artworks that its owner left to the Spanish state in 1947. Who collected them?
hints: He published a famous literary magazine, “La España Moderna”.
He was born in Beire, in Navarre, in 1862.
The museum now in the mansion bears both of his surnames.
questions.description: Some people collect trading cards, and some people go just a tiny bit overboard.
questions.fun_fact: His treasures include works by Goya and a panel by Hieronymus Bosch, “Saint John the Baptist in Meditation”.

questions.question: It opened in 1914, stands next to Doña Casilda Park and holds Gauguin's “Washerwomen at Arles”. Which city is this Fine Arts Museum in?
hints: The city is in the north of Spain.
An estuary runs through it, and its metro was designed by Norman Foster.
A few steps from the museum, another one shines, covered in titanium.
questions.description: A museum that has been hanging paintings for over a century and still hasn't gotten tired of looking at them.
questions.fun_fact: The park is named after Casilda Iturrizar, a widow who left much of her fortune to the city's charities.

questions.question: I was born in Málaga, starred in “Un rayo de luz” as a child, and later left the spotlight and took back my real name. What was my stage name?
hints: I was a child star of Spanish cinema in the 1960s.
I was famous for my blond hair and cheerful songs.
My stage name joins “Mari” with the Spanish word for something that shines in the sky.
questions.description: A child star who packed 1960s movie theaters with just a smile.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020 she received the Honorary Goya Award for her career, though she chose not to attend the ceremony.

questions.question: Andalusia has used it since 1989, and El Torcal de Antequera, the Tabernas Desert and the Marismas del Odiel all have it. Which protection status is it?
hints: It doesn't include the word “parque”.
In the Valencian Community, town councils have their own “municipal” version.
Its first word is a Spanish way of saying “spot” or “place”.
questions.description: Green paperwork: the Junta stamps it, and the rocks can't move from there anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Dozens of Westerns were filmed in the Tabernas Desert, including scenes from “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly”.

questions.question: Merino sheep are famous worldwide for their super-fine wool. In which country was this breed developed?
hints: For centuries it was forbidden to take these sheep out of the country.
They were moved around by the Mesta, a powerful medieval association of shepherds.
They walked the cañadas reales, from Extremadura to the mountains of León.
questions.description: A sweater on legs that walked hundreds of kilometers.
questions.fun_fact: Today Australia has more merino sheep than any other country, but the first ones there came from Spanish bloodlines.

questions.question: The Torrent de Pareis runs down the Serra de Tramuntana in Mallorca to the beach of Sa Calobra. What is a “torrent” in Mallorca?
questions.answer: A stream bed that only carries water when it rains
wrong_answers: A river that carries water all year round
A cave with a lake inside it
A mule track between two villages
hints: You can walk along it for much of the year.
Its bottom is full of stones and smooth pebbles.
It fills up suddenly during fall storms.
questions.description: Mallorca has beaches, ensaimadas and this word you won't find on postcards.
questions.fun_fact: The road down to Sa Calobra is so twisty that at one point, the “Nus de sa Corbata” (the tie knot), it passes underneath itself.

questions.question: This Spanish Baroque style is full of fancy words and Latin borrowings, and Luis de Góngora was its great master. What is it called?
hints: It belongs to the Golden Age of Spanish literature.
Its great rival was Quevedo's style, which played more with ideas than with words.
Its name comes from the Spanish word “culto”, meaning “learned” or “refined”.
questions.description: Writing so complicated that even the dictionary asks for hints.
questions.fun_fact: Góngora and Quevedo disliked each other so much that they wrote poems to make fun of each other.

questions.question: The Masca gorge in Tenerife is a narrow path between towering rock walls that leads down to the sea. You have to wear a helmet. Why?
questions.answer: To stay safe if rocks fall
wrong_answers: To go diving in the sea
hints: Look up: the walls are very tall.
Every now and then something comes loose from the rocks.
It's the same thing that protects builders on a construction site.
questions.description: A trail with so many bends that even the goats ask for a map.
