questions.fun_fact: Masca was so isolated that until a few decades ago you could only get there on foot or by donkey.

questions.question: Teneguía erupted in 1971 in the south of La Palma, and its black ash fields didn't stay empty. What is mainly grown on them?
hints: Volcanic ash holds moisture, and the plant makes good use of it.
It is harvested at the end of summer and goes straight to the press.
A famous sweet malvasía wine comes from there.
questions.description: A volcano that, after giving everyone a scare, took up farming.
questions.fun_fact: For 50 years, until the 2021 volcano, Teneguía was Spain's last eruption on land.

questions.question: On the coat of arms of Aragon, the Cross of Íñigo Arista is a silver cross pattée. What tincture is its field?
hints: It fills the second quarter, next to the tree of Sobrarbe.
Legend says the cross shone in the sky before a battle.
It's the color of the sky where it appeared.
questions.description: Heraldry for the brave: here the colors have names like magic spells.
questions.fun_fact: The lower arm of this cross ends in a point, as if it were made to be stuck into the ground.

questions.question: I'm the gap between two mountains where the road crosses, and in the Vuelta the cyclists suffer to climb me. What am I?
hints: I'm high up, but I'm not the highest summit.
Road signs show my name and my height in meters.
In Spain my signs say “puerto”, the same word Spaniards use for a harbor.
questions.description: Cyclists' favorite place to turn as red as a tomato.
questions.fun_fact: The Angliru in Asturias is one of the toughest climbs in the Vuelta, with slopes of almost 24 %.

questions.question: The statues in the photo honor the menceyes, the kings of the Guanches. On which island did they rule?
hints: They ruled there before the Castilian conquest, at the end of the 15th century.
The island was split into nine kingdoms, one for each mencey.
It is home to the highest peak in Spain.
questions.description: Bronze kings who have spent years staring at the sea without blinking.
questions.fun_fact: The nine statues in Candelaria stand for the kings of the island's nine old Guanche kingdoms.

questions.question: They shout, threaten and make a big fuss, but in the end they do nothing. What are they, according to a Spanish saying?
hints: The saying has two parts, and the second says what these animals don't do.
It's a pet, not a farm animal.
The saying ends with “… poco mordedores” (bite little).
questions.description: Lots of noise in the playground and then nothing: the story of almost every threat.
questions.fun_fact: English has almost the same saying: “Barking dogs seldom bite.”

questions.question: The saying «Más vale prevenir que curar» means it's better to prevent than to cure. What should you put on before riding a bike, not after?
hints: Think about what helps before something happens and what helps once it has.
Motorcyclists wear one too.
It protects your head.
questions.description: The motto of every grandma who makes you wear a jacket in the middle of August.
questions.fun_fact: The saying has cousins in many languages, like the English “Prevention is better than cure.”

questions.question: TVE aired it from 1974 to 1980, Félix Rodríguez de la Fuente hosted it, and it was filmed in Spain, Venezuela and Canada. What was “El hombre y la Tierra”?
hints: Its host was a great defender of the environment.
It showed lots of wild animals.
Félix showed how wolves, eagles and other animals live in the wild.
questions.description: A gem from your grandparents' TV days that still gives people goosebumps.
questions.fun_fact: Its famous theme music was composed by Antón García Abril, and people still recognize it right away.

questions.question: Pedro Cavadas is a surgeon from Valencia who operates for free in Kenya. In 2008 he did Spain's first double transplant of… what?
hints: It's a part of the body that comes in pairs.
Years earlier, the patient had been injured in an accident at work.
Thanks to the operation, the man could hug people again.
questions.description: A surgeon with hands so steady that watchmakers would be jealous.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011 Cavadas did it again with the world's first transplant of both legs.

questions.question: Sara García Alonso is from León and searches for cancer drugs. In 2022, the European Space Agency picked her. For what role?
hints: She was picked from more than 22,000 applicants from all over Europe.
Before her, Pedro Duque had a similar job.
If she gets the call, she could go to the International Space Station.
questions.description: Her résumé says “laboratory” and, in the fine print, something far more exciting.
questions.fun_fact: Sara García was the first Spanish woman chosen as an ESA astronaut.

questions.question: In which century did Quevedo write his mocking sonnet “Érase un hombre a una nariz pegado” (“Once there was a man stuck to a nose”)?
hints: Quevedo is a figure of the Spanish Golden Age.
It was the time of the Baroque.
Quevedo died in 1645.
questions.description: A poem that poked its nose where nobody asked it to: right into someone's face.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the giant nose in the poem belonged to Quevedo's rival, the poet Luis de Góngora.

questions.question: After winning the 1998 ATP Finals, Àlex Corretja climbed to his best ATP ranking in February 1999. What was it?
hints: 1998 was the best season of his career, with a French Open final and the season-ending title.
He never became No. 1.
Only one player was ranked above him.
questions.description: A player from Barcelona who used tennis balls as steps on a ladder.
questions.fun_fact: Corretja played two French Open finals, in 1998 and 2001, and today he is a well-known voice on tennis broadcasts.

questions.question: I'm a driver from Barcelona: I scored points on my Formula 1 debut in 1999, tested for McLaren and finished second in Hungary in 2006. Who am I?
hints: I made my debut with the Arrows team.
I also raced for Jaguar, Sauber and HRT.
My surname contains the Spanish word for a flower.
questions.description: A man from Barcelona who spent more hours testing cars than many drivers spent racing them.
questions.fun_fact: That second place in Hungary in 2006 was the best result of his Formula 1 career.

questions.question: Ana Peleteiro, from Ribeira, won bronze at the Tokyo 2020 Games. In which track and field event?
hints: It's a jumping event that ends in the sand pit.
At those Games, the gold in this event went to Venezuela's Yulimar Rojas.
You link a hop, a step and a jump.
questions.description: A Galician woman who landed in Tokyo… and not exactly by plane.
questions.fun_fact: In Tokyo, Ana Peleteiro jumped 14.87 m (48 ft 9 in), a new Spanish record.

questions.question: Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote it, and Sarah Brightman and José Carreras sang it at Barcelona '92. Which song is it?
hints: It was performed at the closing ceremony of the Games.
Its title is in Spanish, although the lyrics are almost all in English.
It's about two people who will always stay close.
questions.description: A song so catchy that it hasn't left half of Spain's heads since 1992.
questions.fun_fact: Los Manolos, a Catalan rumba band, recorded a cover that became a big hit in Spain.

questions.question: It's played every spring at the Caja Mágica, Nadal won it five times, and in 2012 its courts were painted blue. What surface is the Mutua Madrid Open played on?
hints: It's the surface of almost all the big European spring tournaments.
Players can slide as they run.
It's the same surface as at Roland Garros.
questions.description: A tournament inside a magic box, and not a rabbit or a top hat in sight.
questions.fun_fact: The blue clay of 2012 was so slippery that Nadal and Djokovic complained, and the next year the red clay came back.

questions.question: Which of these has Pedro Sánchez NEVER done?
wrong_answers: Served as a member of Congress
hints: Three of them are in his life story.
As a young man he liked hoops more than goals.
At Madrid City Hall he was a council member, but he was never in charge.
questions.description: A résumé too long for one page, though it has one suspicious gap.

hints: It's a stone, not something made from clay.
It's polished until it shines, and famous statues are carved from it.
This white stone was brought from Carrara, in Italy.
questions.description: A building so elegant it looks like it dressed up for a night at the opera.
questions.fun_fact: Inside, the theater has a huge glass curtain made by Tiffany that shows the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl.

questions.question: Look at this arch-shaped rock at the tip of a peninsula where two seas meet. Where is it?
hints: It's in northwestern Mexico.
There, the Pacific Ocean meets the Sea of Cortez.
It's at the southern tip of Baja California Sur.
questions.description: A rock that has spent thousands of years pretending to be the gate of a castle in the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Sea lions often lie on the rocks next to the Arch, soaking up the sun.

questions.question: Venice is to gondolas as Xochimilco is to…
hints: They are flat boats pushed along with a long pole.
They are painted in bright colors and carry an arch with a name on it.
Their name starts with “Tra-.”
questions.description: A boat ride with mariachis, elotes and zero seasickness… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: Every trajinera has its name painted on its arch, and many have women's names, like “Lupita” or “Rosita.”

questions.question: I'm in downtown Mexico City, next to Tepito; I sell wedding dresses, and on Sundays I fill up with antiques and piles of old comics. Which market am I?
hints: Comic collectors visit me mostly on Sundays.
My name is a reminder that there used to be water here.
My name means “little lagoon” in Spanish.
questions.description: Here you can buy a wedding dress, your grandpa's record player and a Kalimán comic all in one morning.
questions.fun_fact: La Lagunilla is named after a small lagoon that existed in the area in the days of ancient Tenochtitlan.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in comics, the words the characters say are written inside a speech ___.
hints: It has a little tail pointing at whoever is talking.
When a character is thinking, it's drawn like a cloud.
It shares its name with something you blow up at parties.
questions.description: If comic characters could talk out loud, they wouldn't need it.
questions.fun_fact: When a character shouts, the balloon is often drawn with spikes, like an explosion.

questions.question: In which year was “Calzonzin Inspector” released, Alfonso Arau's film based on Rius's “Los Supermachos”?
hints: The comic it is based on started in the mid-1960s.
It came out in the same decade that El Chavo del Ocho became famous.
It was in the mid-1970s.
questions.description: A government inspector arrives in a small town, and nobody knows whether to laugh or hide.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso Arau, the film's director, later also directed “Like Water for Chocolate”.

questions.question: Two doors, two guards: one always lies, the other never does. You ask one which door the other would say is the exit. What do you do?
hints: It doesn't matter which of the two guards you ask.
The lie passes through the answer exactly once.
The answer always points to the wrong door.
questions.description: Two guards, two doors and one question: harder than picking an ice cream flavor.
questions.fun_fact: This riddle shows up in the film “Labyrinth” (1986), where Sarah faces two guards watching over two doors.

questions.question: It's a comic of just a few panels in a row, it runs in the newspaper and almost always ends with a joke. What is it called?
hints: It takes up very little space on the page.
Its panels sit side by side, like a band.
Its name says it is long and narrow, like a ribbon of paper.
questions.description: The fastest joke in the paper: you finish it before your coffee gets cold.
questions.fun_fact: Many famous comic strips tell their story in just three or four panels.

questions.question: In Rius's comic “Los Supermachos”, who is the clever Indigenous man from San Garabato who makes fun of the authorities?
hints: He is the main character of the comic.
His name recalls an ancient Purépecha ruler.
His surname also appears in the title of a film by Alfonso Arau.
questions.description: In a town where the powerful think they're very smart, there's always someone smarter.
questions.fun_fact: The name Calzonzin recalls Tangáxoan Calzontzin, the last great lord of the Purépecha people.

questions.question: It's each of the boxes in a comic: it has a border, and inside go the drawings and speech bubbles. What is it called?
hints: A comic book page usually has several of them.
The white space between them is called the “gutter”.
It's the same word as a flat section of a door, or a group of experts on stage.
questions.description: Comics live in little rectangular apartments, one next to the other.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish a panel is a “viñeta”, from “viña” (vineyard): in old books, viñetas were ornaments of grape leaves and bunches, the same root as the English “vignette”.

questions.question: I'm made of paper and you use me to buy things. Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz is on one side and monarch butterflies on the other. Which bill am I?
hints: It's one of the bills people use most in daily life.
Its color is reddish.
I'm worth the same as ten 10-peso coins.
questions.description: A nun who travels from wallet to wallet without ever leaving her convent.
questions.fun_fact: Before this bill, Sor Juana had already appeared on the 200-peso bill.

questions.question: Look at this cacao drink. Bernal Díaz wrote that a Mexica tlatoani drank it from gold cups. Who was he?
hints: He ruled Tenochtitlan in the early 16th century.
He was the ninth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan.
His full name ends in Xocoyotzin.
questions.description: Long before coffee shops existed, there was already one very picky customer.
questions.fun_fact: Bernal Díaz del Castillo wrote that Moctezuma was served about fifty large jugs of foamy cacao drink.

questions.question: The Manila galleon brought to Acapulco a very fine fabric made from the thread of cocoons like these. What fabric was it?
hints: It's soft and shiny.
It was used to make very expensive rebozos and dresses.
The little creature that makes these cocoons is called the ___worm.
questions.description: A cargo so fancy it crossed the whole Pacific Ocean just to show off in Acapulco.
questions.fun_fact: The thread of a single silkworm cocoon can be almost 1 kilometer (over half a mile) long.

questions.question: I stand on the Zócalo in Mexico City. I took almost 250 years to finish, I have two towers full of bells, and I'm slowly sinking. What am I?
hints: They started building me in the 16th century.
I'm the most important Catholic church in the country.
I'm the seat of the Archbishop of Mexico.
questions.description: A building project so slow that not even the roadwork on your street can beat it.
questions.fun_fact: It was built between 1573 and 1813 and mixes Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles.

questions.question: José Moreno Villa called the art carved by Indigenous hands in the 16th century “tequitqui”, Nahuatl for “tributary”. Where is it mostly found?
hints: It mixes European symbols with pre-Hispanic forms.
You can see it on stone crosses, church doorways and chapels.
The builders were the same people who were bringing Christianity to the towns.
questions.description: Art with dual citizenship, long before passports existed.
questions.fun_fact: Some tequitqui atrium crosses have a piece of obsidian at the center, like the ancient sacred mirrors.

questions.question: The Mexica could never conquer us, and in 1519 we joined Hernán Cortés to defeat them. Today a state bears our name. Who are we?
hints: We lived very close to Tenochtitlan, surrounded by the Mexica.
First we fought against Cortés, and then we became his allies.
Our state is the smallest in Mexico.
questions.description: Some neighbors who did not get along at all with the people on the island in the lake.
questions.fun_fact: In Nahuatl, Tlaxcala means “place of corn bread”, in other words, of tortillas.

questions.question: These structures, called yácatas, were built by the Purépecha in their capital, Tzintzuntzan. Which present-day state are they in?
hints: They stand next to a large lake.
The island of Janitzio is nearby.
It's the state where the city of Morelia is.
questions.description: Pyramids that chose to be nice and round so they wouldn't look like the neighbors'.
questions.fun_fact: The Purépecha were so strong that the Mexica never managed to conquer them.

questions.question: Which 19th-century English mathematician created an algebra where everything is either true or false, the basis of today's computing?
hints: He worked as a professor in Ireland.
In programming, true-or-false variables are named after him.
Programmers type his surname every day, shortened to four letters.
questions.description: A man who boiled the whole world down to “yes” or “no,” and your phone thanks him for it.
questions.fun_fact: Boole was almost entirely self-taught: he left school very young and learned mathematics on his own while working as a teacher.

questions.question: On the Noche Triste (Sad Night), June 30, 1520, the Spanish fled Tenochtitlan loaded with gold. Who drove them out?
hints: The city belonged to them.
They had founded their city on a small island in the middle of a lake.
Their leader at the time was Cuitláhuac.
questions.description: A midnight move with way too much luggage and zero interest in saying goodbye.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish escaped along the Tacuba causeway, which is still an avenue in Mexico City today.

questions.question: Look at this palace on the Zócalo, where the viceroys once lived. What happens on its central balcony every September 15?
hints: It's a national holiday.
A bell rings and the flag is waved.
At the end everyone shouts “¡Viva México!”
questions.description: A balcony with a bigger crowd than any concert of the year.
questions.fun_fact: Above the central balcony hangs the bell that Miguel Hidalgo rang in Dolores in 1810.

questions.question: Under Mexico's movie ratings, an AA film is understandable for children under what age?
hints: The B rating is already for teens aged 12 and up.
It's fewer than the fingers on two hands.
It's a typical age for a kid in second grade.
questions.description: The letters on the movie listings have their own school rules too.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, an A rating means the film is for all audiences, while AA also signals that it is made to appeal to the youngest viewers.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actress. In “Under the Same Moon” (2007) I played Rosario, a mom working in Los Angeles who calls her son from a pay phone every Sunday. Who am I?
hints: I became very famous in telenovelas.
I was born in Mexico City in 1972.
My last name means “castle” in Spanish.
questions.description: A long-distance call that makes you cry more than the phone bill does.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, young Carlitos crosses the border alone to find his mom, and Eugenio Derbez shows up in a dramatic role.

questions.question: The Guadalajara Film Festival, which gives out the Mayahuel Award, started as a showcase of Mexican cinema. In which decade?
hints: It's older than the “new Mexican cinema” of the nineties.
It started the same year Mexico hosted its second soccer World Cup.
It was 1986.
questions.description: A maguey goddess who hands out trophies instead of pulque.
questions.fun_fact: Today the Guadalajara Film Festival is one of the most important in Latin America, and its trophy honors Mayahuel, the Aztec goddess of the maguey.

questions.question: You're watching “Dragon Ball Z” on TV and Goku shouts with Mario Castañeda's voice. In which decade did he start dubbing adult Goku?
hints: It was before phones could go online.
The series premiered in Japan in 1989; the Spanish dub came later.
It was the same decade the Nintendo 64 came out.
questions.description: A voice so powerful it could turn its own hair gold.
questions.fun_fact: Mario Castañeda is also the Spanish voice of Bruce Willis in many of his movies.

questions.question: In what year did “Don Gato y su pandilla” (Top Cat: The Movie), the Mexican-made animated film about the famous alley cat, come out?
hints: It was already the 21st century.
It came out the same year as “La leyenda de la Llorona”.
It was early in the 2010s.
questions.description: The laziest cat in the alley finally landed a gig on the big screen.
questions.fun_fact: The film was made by the Mexican studio Ánima, and in Mexico the Don Gato cartoon is so loved that he almost became a national character.

questions.question: In which year did “No Manches Frida,” the school comedy with Omar Chaparro and Martha Higareda, come out?
hints: It's from the second half of the 2010s.
Its sequel came out in 2019.
It was the year of the Rio de Janeiro Olympics.
questions.description: A thief who becomes a teacher: every principal's worst nightmare.
questions.fun_fact: “No Manches Frida” is the Mexican version of the German comedy “Fack ju Göhte.”

questions.question: I'm a Mexican filmmaker, son of a producer, and my partner Paz Alicia Garciadiego writes my scripts. In 1994 I filmed the life of Lucha Reyes. Who am I?
hints: I started very young as Luis Buñuel's assistant.
My film “La reina de la noche” competed at Cannes.
I also directed “Profundo carmesí” and “El castillo de la pureza”.
questions.description: A filmmaker who shoots life like a ranchera song: lots of drama and no happy ending.
questions.fun_fact: Lucha Reyes is considered one of the first great ranchera singers in Mexico.

questions.question: You're in a Cinépolis VIP theater. Which of these is NOT part of the experience?
questions.answer: Seats that move and splash you with water
wrong_answers: A waiter who brings you your food
A menu of dishes and drinks
hints: The VIP theater is about being comfortable and relaxed.
There they spoil you with food, not with scares.
Moving and getting wet belongs to another kind of theater, more adventure than rest.
questions.description: You can't go to the movies in pajamas, but here it almost feels like your own living room.
questions.fun_fact: Cinépolis was born in Morelia, Michoacán, and today has theaters in many countries, including India.

questions.question: What do you need to play matatena?
questions.answer: A small ball and pointed pieces
wrong_answers: A spinning top and a string
A small stick and a spool
hints: You play it sitting on the floor.
You go up round by round: first you pick up one at a time, then two at a time…
The pieces look like little metal or plastic stars.
questions.description: A game that tests who has the fastest hand at recess.
questions.fun_fact: Long before metal pieces, matatena was played with pebbles, seeds or little bones.

questions.question: Café de olla is made with cinnamon and piloncillo and served in a traditional jarrito (small mug). What is the jarrito made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from the ground.
It's shaped while wet and then fired in a kiln.
Traditional pots and water jugs are made of the same thing.
questions.description: Grandma's favorite drink, served in her favorite cup.
questions.fun_fact: Many people say the clay gives café de olla an earthy taste it doesn't have in any other cup.

questions.question: They're silver or gold, often filigree, and worn by Tehuana and Mazahua women. Where do you wear arracadas?
hints: They look best with your hair pulled back.
Many are shaped like a hoop or a half-moon.
To wear them, you need piercings.
questions.description: Jewelry so big you can almost hear it when you walk.
questions.fun_fact: The word «arracada» comes from Hispanic Arabic, from a word that meant “earring.”

questions.question: In many Mexican homes, an embroidered cloth napkin goes on the table. What is it mainly for?
hints: It goes on the table at mealtime.
It's used with something eaten at almost every meal.
It keeps in the heat of something fresh off the comal.
questions.description: An embroidered cloth that has a very important job at the Mexican table.
questions.fun_fact: Many of these napkins are cross-stitched: each tiny stitch makes a little X.

questions.question: Look at the photo: by tradition, what does the little ball on top of the pan de muerto stand for?
hints: Its decorations are meant to remember the dead.
The strips across the bread stand for bones.
Think of what sits at the very top of a skeleton.
questions.description: A bread that takes its Day of the Dead costume very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: The strips on pan de muerto are called “canillas” or “huesitos” (little bones), and they often form a cross.

questions.question: A Day of the Dead ofrenda holds many things. Which of these is NOT for eating?
hints: Three of them are real food.
The one you're looking for helps you remember a face.
It goes in a frame.
questions.description: An altar full of food, with just one thing nobody should bite.
questions.fun_fact: The photo is placed so the departed soul knows the ofrenda is meant for them and doesn't go to the wrong house.

questions.question: They're round, made of cempasúchil and other flowers, and families take them to the cemetery on November 2. What are they for?
wrong_answers: To throw them as a game
To put them on the dogs
hints: They stay at the cemetery.
They're a gift for someone who is no longer here.
They go on the headstone or right next to it.
questions.description: They're round, they smell lovely, and nobody serves them at dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Cempasúchil is a flower native to Mexico, and its name comes from Nahuatl.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to Halloween and NOT to Día de Muertos?
hints: Three of them go on the ofrenda.
The one you're looking for comes from Ireland and the United States.
It's orange, has a candle inside, and gets cut-out eyes and a mouth.
questions.description: A party from abroad snuck onto the ofrenda, and you have to spot it.
questions.fun_fact: Before pumpkins, people in Ireland carved faces into turnips and potatoes.

questions.question: It studies what is right and wrong, asks how we should behave, and is a school subject in many places. What is it?
hints: It is a branch of philosophy.
It deals with values like honesty and fairness.
Many doctors and lawyers must follow a professional code named after it.
questions.description: The subject that asks whether it's okay to eat the last slice of cake without telling anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek “êthos”, which means “custom” or “character”.

questions.question: In Mexico, Death goes by many names. Which of these is NOT one of her nicknames?
hints: Death is drawn as a skeleton.
Almost all of her nicknames are about how thin she is.
The one you want means the very opposite of skin and bones.
questions.description: She has more nicknames than a soccer player, and she lives up to every single one.
questions.fun_fact: Death is also called “la Pelona” (the bald one), because a skull doesn't have a single hair.

questions.question: Look at this charro sombrero. What is its extra-wide brim for?
hints: Charros spend many hours outdoors.
It protects the face and neck from the strong sun.
Think of why you stand under a tree on a hot, sunny day.
questions.description: A hat so big it could have its own zip code.
questions.fun_fact: The word “sombrero” comes from the Spanish “sombra,” which means shade: it's literally the thing that shades you.

questions.question: Which of these places is NOT on the Zócalo, the main square of Mexico City?
hints: Three of them surround the huge square with the giant flag.
The odd one out stands in a traffic circle, far from the historic center.
It's a golden column on Paseo de la Reforma, where fans celebrate the national team's wins.
questions.description: A square so big that half the country fits in it on the night of the Grito, but not everything does.
questions.fun_fact: The Zócalo's official name is Plaza de la Constitución (Constitution Square).

questions.question: Which heroine, known as “la Corregidora”, warned in 1810 that the Querétaro conspiracy had been discovered?
wrong_answers: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
hints: Her husband was the corregidor (magistrate) of Querétaro.
Thanks to her warning, Hidalgo moved the Grito de Dolores forward.
Her first name is Josefa.
questions.description: A lady who proved that a good piece of gossip at the right time can change history.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that, locked in her house, she tapped her heel on the floor to alert the jailer Ignacio Pérez.

questions.question: I'm a cold drink of corn and cacao with mamey pit and cacao flower, and my foam floats in gourd bowls in Oaxaca's markets. What am I?
hints: I've been made since pre-Hispanic times, mostly by Zapotec women.
San Andrés Huayápam holds a fair in my honor.
My name starts with the same two letters as “tequila”.
questions.description: A drink you sip through its foam, no straw needed.
questions.fun_fact: Tejate is beaten by hand, and the foam from the cacao flower rises to the top on its own.

questions.question: Mixtec is spoken in Oaxaca, Guerrero and Puebla. It is a tonal language, and its speakers call themselves ñuu savi, “people of the…” what?
hints: The ancient Mixtecs held it sacred.
Their ancient god Dzahui was in charge of it.
Without it, the milpa dries up.
questions.description: A language that sings a little, even when you don't mean it to.
questions.fun_fact: Because of its tones, one Mixtec syllable can mean different things depending on whether you say it higher or lower.

questions.question: It’s a traditional song from Michoacán, sung in the Purépecha language, and UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2010. What is it called?
hints: It can sound slow like a serenade or lively like a son.
It’s sung a lot on the Meseta Purépecha and around Pátzcuaro.
Its singers are called pirériecha.
questions.description: A serenade with a UNESCO passport.
questions.fun_fact: Pirekua joined the UNESCO list one year before mariachi did.

questions.question: Look at these dancers from Oaxaca with huge round headdresses and mirrors. Which dance are they performing?
hints: It's one of the stars of the Guelaguetza.
It tells the story of Moctezuma facing the conquistadors.
Its name refers to what decorates the headdress.
questions.description: A dance where the hairdo weighs more than the steps.
questions.fun_fact: The dancers jump and spin nonstop wearing headdresses that can be more than 1 meter (3 ft) across.

review.feedback: source: The fun fact says the headdresses can be more than 1 meter (3 ft) across. The fact check couldn't confirm this: sources give about 1 m tall and roughly 80 cm wide, or a 60 cm crown. The source's fun fact should be corrected, for example to “The dancers jump and spin nonstop wearing feathered headdresses about 1 meter (3 ft) tall that can weigh over 25 kg (55 lb).” Then the translation should follow it. One small style point while revising: “hairdo” in the description is a literal rendering of “peinado”; “headgear” reads more naturally. Fact check: uncertain. The answer (Danza de la Pluma) is right. The wrong answers are wrong: Venado is Yaqui/Sonora, Viejitos is Michoacán, Voladores is Totonac/Veracruz. The hints are consistent with sources: Guelaguetza, Moctezuma and the conquest, a headdress of feathers and mirrors. The fun fact is not verified. No source gave a headdress diameter of more than 1 m. One travel guide gives about 1 m tall and 80 cm wide, weighing over 25 kg. An artisan catalog lists a 60 cm crown.

questions.question: Natalia Toledo writes in Zapotec, won the Nezahualcóyotl Prize and is the daughter of painter Francisco Toledo. Which city of the Isthmus is she from?
hints: It's in Oaxaca, near the Pacific coast.
It's famous for its velas (big all-night fiestas) and its muxes.
Its official name ends in “de Zaragoza”.
questions.description: A poet who rhymes in a language more than two thousand years old.
questions.fun_fact: Natalia Toledo won the Nezahualcóyotl Prize for Literature in Mexican Languages in 2004 with her poetry book “Olivo negro” (Black Olive).

questions.question: Take away one grain of sand and I stay the same. And another, and another… until one is left. “At which grain did I lose my name?” Which paradox am I?
wrong_answers: The paradox of the Ship of Theseus
The paradox of Achilles and the tortoise
hints: It comes from ancient Greece.
The same goes for someone losing hairs one by one: when do they become bald?
It's about how many grains it takes before you can call something by a certain name.
questions.description: A question that turns a day at the beach into an existential crisis.
questions.fun_fact: It is credited to Eubulides of Miletus, the same Greek philosopher credited with the liar paradox.

questions.question: Zapotec families in Teotitlán del Valle, Oaxaca, weave rugs like these on foot-pedal looms. What are they made of?
hints: It comes from an animal.
It's the same fiber used in many sarapes.
It's sheared once a year.
questions.description: So pretty you'd feel bad stepping on them with muddy shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Many of these rugs are dyed with cochineal, a tiny insect that gives an intense red.

questions.question: Many people believed that, according to the Maya calendar, the world would end on December 21 of a certain year. Which year?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
The Olympic Games were held in London that same year.
It was early in the 2010s.
questions.description: The most announced end of the world in history… which never showed up.
questions.fun_fact: For experts, that day only marked the end of a great cycle of the Maya calendar, like a car's odometer starting over.

questions.question: In the legend of the handsome stranger who asks a girl to dance and turns out to be the devil, which sign does NOT give him away?
hints: Three of the signs are about his body or how he vanishes.
The odd one out comes from a different scary story, from outside Mexico.
In the stories, it's what keeps vampires away.
questions.description: The heartthrob of the party had it all: a sharp suit, smooth moves… and one tiny detail.
questions.fun_fact: In many versions, someone exposes the devil by looking down and seeing rooster feet where his feet should be.

questions.question: You're a patient at night in Mexico City's Hospital Juárez, and a nurse in a spotless uniform cares for you, then vanishes. Who is she, according to legend?
hints: She doesn't cry or scare anyone: she looks after the sick.
Her nickname comes from the way she wears her uniform.
Her clothes never have a single wrinkle.
questions.description: A hospital's employee of the month… for a very, very long time.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, her name was Eulalia, a nurse who kept caring for patients even after she died.

questions.question: Complete the most famous nickname of Club León, the green team from Guanajuato: “La…”
hints: It's a Spanish word for a wild animal.
It goes perfectly with the big cat on the club's crest.
In English, it would be “the Beast.”
questions.description: Guanajuato doesn't just make shoes: it also makes a whole stand roar.
questions.fun_fact: León is also called “Panzas Verdes” (Green Bellies), a nickname for people from León that is much older than the club.

questions.question: In what year did Club Tijuana, the Xolos, win its first First Division league title?
hints: The club was founded in 2007.
It came in an Apertura tournament, with a final against Toluca.
It came just five years after the club was founded.
questions.description: A young team that couldn't wait for its birthday to throw a party.
questions.fun_fact: Club Tijuana moved up to the First Division in 2011 and won the Apertura 2012, in only its third tournament in the top league.

questions.question: In the Clausura regular season, the 18 Liga MX teams each play every other team once. How many games does each team play?
hints: Nobody plays against themselves.
It's one matchday for each opponent.
It's 18 minus one.
questions.description: Math so easy even the referee could do it without VAR.
questions.fun_fact: With 18 teams, every Liga MX matchday has 9 games.

questions.question: At which World Cup did Cuauhtémoc Blanco score a penalty against France, at age 37?
hints: It was his last World Cup.
Spain won that World Cup for the first time.
It was the World Cup of the vuvuzelas.
questions.description: Some people buy a car at 37; he preferred to score against France.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico beat France 2–0 that day; the other goal was scored by Javier “Chicharito” Hernández.

questions.question: Which of these stadiums has NEVER been home to Tigres or Rayados, the rivals of the Clásico Regio?
hints: Tigres has played in the same stadium since the 1960s.
The stadium you're looking for hosted games at the 1970 and 1986 World Cups.
It's in Guadalajara.
questions.description: In Monterrey you share the carne asada, but never the stadium.
questions.fun_fact: Rayados played at Estadio Tecnológico until 2015, when they moved to Estadio BBVA, with a view of Cerro de la Silla.

questions.question: This mistake in arguing uses the conclusion as proof of itself, like “I'm right because I'm never wrong.” What is it called?
hints: The argument gives you no new information.
In Latin it is called “petitio principii.”
The argument ends right where it started, like a wheel.
questions.description: An argument as confident as a kid saying “because I said so.”
questions.fun_fact: In English it is also called “begging the question,” and many people use that phrase as if it meant “raising the question.”

questions.question: The Pumas cheer “¡Goya!” started with UNAM students skipping class. What kind of place did they sneak off to?
hints: The lights go out there.
They sell popcorn there.
It had the painter's name, but instead of paintings it had a screen.
questions.description: A college cheer that was born, like many good ideas, by skipping class.
questions.fun_fact: The Cine Goya was in the Historic Center, near the UNAM schools; the line “¡vámonos al Goya!” (“let's go to the Goya!”) ended up as a stadium chant.

questions.question: In lucha libre, two masked wrestlers fight mask against mask. How many masks does the winner lose?
hints: Think about who ends up with their face showing.
In this match, each one bets their mask against the other's.
The winner leaves the ring just the way they came in.
questions.description: A bet where the only sure thing is that someone is going to need sunglasses.
questions.fun_fact: Whoever loses a mask-against-mask match has to say their real name in front of the crowd.

questions.question: I'm performed with the legs: the wrestler jumps, traps the opponent's neck with them and spins to throw him. Which move am I?
hints: The wrestler barely uses his arms.
While spinning, the wrestler is upside down for a moment.
My name is the Spanish word for something that cuts paper.
questions.description: A lock that opens no door, but sends you straight to the mat.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican lucha has many kinds of tijeras: to the neck, to the waist and even flying ones from the ropes.

questions.question: In this bolero by Armando Manzanero from Yucatán, the man in love finds out the week has more than seven days. What is it called?
hints: It's about everything he discovered thanks to his love.
It says there are “new and better emotions.”
The title says who he learned it all with.
questions.description: A bolero that fixes anyone's calendar.
questions.fun_fact: Armando Manzanero wrote hundreds of songs and started studying music as a child in Mérida.

questions.question: In Tomás Méndez's ranchera “Paloma negra,” who is the black dove the heartbroken singer sings to?
questions.answer: The woman he loved, who left
wrong_answers: His mother, who lives far away
hints: It's a song about love and heartbreak.
The singer asks her “¿dónde andarás?” (where can you be?).
He scolds her for toying with his honor and going out partying.
questions.description: A dove you won't find in any bird book.
questions.fun_fact: Great voices like Lola Beltrán and Chavela Vargas both sang “Paloma negra,” each in her own way.

questions.question: In a mariachi band, which of these instruments does NOT have a wooden sound box?
hints: The sound box is the hollow body that makes the strings sound louder.
The one we're looking for has no strings.
It's made of metal and you play it by blowing.
questions.description: Hollow on the inside, but on the outside they sound like a party.
questions.fun_fact: The guitarrón has such a big sound box that it plays the bass part in a mariachi band.

questions.question: After the Moon, I'm the brightest thing in the night sky. I'm called the morning star, and the Maya tracked my 584-day cycles. What am I?
hints: I'm a planet next door to Earth.
I'm named after the Roman goddess of love.
I'm the second planet from the Sun.
questions.description: A rock star of the sky that, to top it off, isn't even a star.
questions.fun_fact: On Venus a day lasts longer than a year: it takes longer to spin once than to go around the Sun.

questions.question: The traditional Maya house of Yucatán is oval, with walls of sticks and mud. What is its roof made of?
hints: The Maya have used this material for thousands of years and find it close to home.
The roof has to be replaced about every 10 to 15 years.
It's like the roof of beach palapas, and it comes from a tree with big fan-shaped leaves.
questions.description: A house with no corners, so nobody can send you to stand in one.
questions.fun_fact: Its oval shape and high roof let the air flow, so the house stays cool even when it's very hot outside.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this stone ring carved with serpents sits high on a wall at Chichén Itzá. What place is it?
hints: It's a long, open space between two tall, parallel walls.
The ring worked as a goal that was very hard to hit.
The players struck the ball with their hips, not their hands.
questions.description: A stone decoration that took much more work than it looks.
questions.fun_fact: The court has such a curious echo that a single clap is heard repeated several times.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Maya people lives in the jungle and is famous for long white tunics and long hair. Which people is it?
hints: They live in Chiapas, near Bonampak.
They call themselves “hach winik”, “true people”.
They share their name with the jungle where they live.
questions.description: People who dress in white in the middle of the jungle and aren't afraid of a single stain.
questions.fun_fact: Bonampak, the archaeological site with the famous Maya murals, lies in Lacandon territory.

questions.question: “Guacamole” comes from the Nahuatl word “ahuacamolli.” Fill in what it means: “avocado ___.”
hints: Think about how you eat guacamole.
The “molli” part is also in the name of a very Mexican party dish.
It’s like mole: something ground up to pour over food.
questions.description: A green party where the avocado is the guest of honor.
questions.fun_fact: The name of mole comes from that same Nahuatl word, “molli.”

questions.question: “Many peoples who came after us copied our gods, our art and our ballgame; that's why we're called the mother culture.” Who are we?
hints: We are the oldest civilization in Mesoamerica, from more than 3,000 years ago.
We lived on the Gulf of Mexico coast, between Veracruz and Tabasco.
Our most famous cities were San Lorenzo and La Venta.
questions.description: Before there was any abuelita in Mesoamerica, this lady was already around.
questions.fun_fact: The Olmecs were already working jade and rubber centuries before Teotihuacan existed.

questions.question: Lambityeco, in the Central Valleys of Oaxaca, is famous for its stucco masks of the god Cocijo. Around when did it flourish?
hints: It was in the Classic period of Mesoamerica.
Its peak came during the last centuries of Monte Albán's glory.
It was about 200 years after Zapotec culture reached its height at Monte Albán, in the middle of the first millennium AD.
questions.description: A little Zapotec town where the god Cocijo follows you with his eyes from the wall, and he doesn't look friendly.
questions.fun_fact: A tomb at Lambityeco has stucco portraits of a couple, with their names written in the Zapotec calendar.

questions.question: Look at the Temple of the Warriors at Chichén Itzá: it's almost a twin of a temple in a faraway city in central Mexico. Which one?
wrong_answers: The Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan
hints: Both temples have columns carved with warriors and feathered serpents.
The city is in today's state of Hidalgo.
On top of that temple stand huge statues called atlantes.
questions.description: They say architecture has no copies, only “tributes” from hundreds of miles away.
questions.fun_fact: Tula and Chichén Itzá look so alike that archaeologists have argued for over a century about who influenced whom.

questions.question: According to most archaeologists, who do the Olmec colossal heads show?
hints: They were carved about 3,000 years ago.
Each one has different features, like a portrait.
They were very powerful people from their own society.
questions.description: Heads so heavy they wouldn't fit in any elevator, not even one at a time.
questions.fun_fact: Seventeen Olmec colossal heads have been found, and some weigh more than 20 metric tons.

questions.question: “The Mexica admired us so much that they used our name to mean ‘great artist.’ We ruled from a city in Hidalgo.” Who are we?
hints: We lived before the Mexica, in central Mexico.
Our city was very powerful between the years 900 and 1150.
Our capital was called Tollan.
questions.description: Artists so good that their name became a compliment.
questions.fun_fact: For the Mexica, calling someone a “toltécatl” was like calling them a “master craftsman.”

questions.question: Look at this colossal head: today it stands in a park-museum in Villahermosa named after the Olmec site it came from. Which site?
hints: The original site is in Tabasco.
The poet Carlos Pellicer rescued its pieces in the 1950s.
In Spanish, its name means “the sale.”
questions.description: A head that moved house so it wouldn't end up surrounded by oil wells.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Pellicer moved the pieces to Villahermosa in 1958 because oil drilling was threatening the site.

questions.question: The Tomateros are named after the tomatoes grown in the valleys of Sinaloa. Which city is this team from?
hints: They play in the Mexican Pacific League, in winter.
It is the capital of its state.
It is the biggest city in Sinaloa, and the Tamazula River runs through it.
questions.description: A baseball team with a name that belongs in a salad.
questions.fun_fact: The Tomateros play in a stadium named after the team itself: the Estadio Tomateros.

questions.question: The ball court at Chichén Itzá has stone rings high up on its walls. When was the game played there?
hints: When the Spanish arrived, the city was already almost abandoned.
It's much more recent than the pyramids of Egypt.
It was about five centuries before the Spanish arrived, when the Maya had a great city there.
questions.description: A game where scoring was almost as hard as shooting a basket from the moon.
questions.fun_fact: The rings at Chichén Itzá are about 6 m (20 ft) high, and players weren't allowed to touch the ball with their hands.

questions.question: Mexico has won several Olympic medals in this sport: you pull back a string and aim at a colorful target. What is it?
hints: You compete from very far away from the target.
The thing that flies toward the target has feathers.
Merida, the princess from Brave, is an expert at it.
questions.description: A sport where good aim matters more than a good pass.
questions.fun_fact: At the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, Alejandra Valencia and Luis Álvarez won bronze for Mexico in the mixed team event.

questions.question: You're standing in front of a dolmen: big upright stones with a flat slab on top. How long ago were Europe's first ones built?
hints: They are older than the pyramids of Egypt.
They were built in the Neolithic, when people already farmed.
It's thousands of years, but fewer than ten thousand.
questions.description: A table so heavy that the whole family together couldn't move it to sweep underneath.
questions.fun_fact: The word “dolmen” comes from Breton and means “stone table.”

questions.question: This golfer from Guadalajara was world number one for more than three years. Who is she?
hints: Her sport is played on a green course with holes.
She shone between 2007 and 2010.
Her last name starts with O.
questions.description: A tapatía who hit the little ball better than anyone on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: Lorena Ochoa retired in 2010, at 28, while still the world number one.

questions.question: In 1939, Frida Kahlo painted herself twice, sitting hand in hand, with their hearts joined. Complete the title: “The Two…”
hints: One wears a white European dress and the other a Tehuana outfit.
Today you can see it at the Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City.
The title repeats the painter's own name.
questions.description: A painting where nobody ever has to sit alone.
questions.fun_fact: It is one of Frida's biggest paintings: almost 1.75 meters (about 5.7 feet) on each side.

questions.question: They're siblings, they play cumbia with a full symphony orchestra, and their motto says they come from their neighborhood “to the world.” Where are Los Ángeles Azules from?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
It's on the east side of the capital.
It's famous for its Holy Week Passion play on the Cerro de la Estrella.
questions.description: Angels who swapped their harps for a güiro and got half the planet dancing.
questions.fun_fact: Los Ángeles Azules have been playing for more than four decades and now fill festivals with fans of all ages.

questions.question: In what year did Thalía release her hit “Amor a la mexicana”?
hints: It was in the same decade Thalía was a star of her “María” telenovelas.
It came out after her hit “Piel morena,” from 1995.
It was three years before 2000.
questions.description: Tequila, mariachi and a romance spicier than salsa from a molcajete.
questions.fun_fact: The album “Amor a la mexicana” was produced by Emilio Estefan, the same producer who worked with Gloria Estefan.

questions.question: Kauyumari, the blue deer, is a sacred being of the Wixárika (Huichol). Which of these is NOT another of their gods?
hints: Three of them are Grandfather Fire, Father Sun and the Grandmother of Growth.
The odd one out is a god of another people of Mexico.
The Mexica worshipped him to ask for rain.
questions.description: Someone crashed this gathering of gods without an invitation.
questions.fun_fact: For the Wixárika, the blue deer is a messenger who guides pilgrims to Wirikuta, in San Luis Potosí.

questions.question: I'm the goddess of rivers and lakes, and my skirt is made of jade. For the Mexica, I was the sun of an age that ended in a great flood. Who am I?
hints: I'm Tláloc's companion.
I watch over newborn babies and people who travel by water.
My name means “she of the jade skirt.”
questions.description: A goddess who never needed an umbrella, though one might have come in handy.
questions.fun_fact: A huge statue of this goddess was found in Teotihuacan and is now in the National Museum of Anthropology.

questions.question: Look closely: on the national coat of arms, the nopal cactus grows on a rock in the water. Which god told the Mexica to look for this sign?
hints: He was the god of war and the sun.
His name has to do with a hummingbird.
One of the two temples on top of the Templo Mayor, the one painted red, was his.
questions.description: A sign so important that it ended up on every coin in the country.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, that nopal grew from the heart of Cópil, Huitzilopochtli's nephew.

questions.question: Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, lord of the dawn, threw a dart at the Fifth Sun because it wasn't moving. He missed, and the Sun shot back. What did he turn into?
hints: The story is told in the Legend of the Suns.
His new form is called Itztlacoliuhqui, a name linked to obsidian.
It's what covers the fields on the coldest early mornings.
questions.description: Ancient Mexican moral: never throw things at whoever keeps you warm.
questions.fun_fact: Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli was Venus as the morning star, one form of the Feathered Serpent.

questions.question: Which of these characters does NOT appear in the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya?
hints: Three of them are a grandmother, a young woman from the underworld and a vain bird.
The odd one out is a god from another people.
He is the Mexica god of war.
questions.description: Someone opened the wrong book and showed up at the wrong party.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest surviving copy of the Popol Vuh was written by the friar Francisco Ximénez in the early 1700s.

questions.question: In the Popol Vuh, when Tepeu and Gucumatz began creating the world, there was no land, mountains or animals. What lay beneath the sky?
hints: Everything was still and silent.
The creators said “Earth!”, and the land rose up out of it.
It was water, lots of water, with no waves.
questions.description: Before the beginning there was no Wi-Fi, no land, nothing at all.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest surviving manuscript of the Popol Vuh was copied by the friar Francisco Ximénez in the early 18th century.

questions.question: After the gods, a bird and a wild cat leapt into the bonfire at Teotihuacan. The bird's feathers came out scorched black, the cat came out spotted. Which were they?
hints: Neither of them is small.
The bravest Mexica warriors were named after them.
The cat is the largest one in the Americas.
questions.description: Some animals came out a little singed, but with loads of style.
questions.fun_fact: Because of their courage at the bonfire, the elite Mexica warriors were called “eagles” and “jaguars.”

questions.question: In the son jarocho “La bruja”, she grabs the singer, takes him home and turns him into a flowerpot and… what else?
hints: It's a traditional song from Veracruz, and nobody knows who wrote it.
It's not an animal.
It grows in the milpa, it's big and orange, and it's cooked into a sweet “en tacha”.
questions.description: A song where nobody wants to be awake at two in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: In folk ballets, the dancers of “La bruja” often dance with lit candles on their heads.

questions.question: I was a dance rhythm in the 1950s; in Mexico today I'm any lively party, and a party lover is my name plus “-ero.” What word am I?
hints: I'm not a party tied to a special date of the year.
Some people get this nickname because they never miss a dance.
I start with “pa” and rhyme with “ganga.”
questions.description: A word that shows up uninvited and doesn't leave until sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: Pachanga became such a popular dance that its name stuck as a word for any party.

questions.question: Caballo Dorado recorded it, it's a must at weddings and quinceañeras, and it has its own routine. How do you dance “Payaso de rodeo”?
questions.answer: In lines, everyone doing the same steps
wrong_answers: In pairs, holding each other close
One by one, in the middle of the floor
hints: You don't need a partner to dance it.
Everyone faces the same way and then turns together.
It looks like an army of cowboys marching in order.
questions.description: The song that gets even the most serious uncle up from the table.
questions.fun_fact: Caballo Dorado also got Mexico line dancing with “No rompas más mi pobre corazón,” a Spanish version of a country song.

questions.question: Brazil won the 1970 World Cup at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. Which Brazilian star wearing number 10 played in that final?
hints: It was his third World Cup win.
He was called “O Rei,” the King.
His real name was Edson Arantes do Nascimento.
questions.description: A stadium that has seen more goals than a neighborhood pickup game on a Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: The Estadio Azteca was the first stadium to host two World Cup finals: 1970 and 1986.

questions.question: Rubén “Púas” Olivares and Lupe Pintor were both world champions in the same division. Which one?
hints: It is one of boxing's lighter divisions.
Its limit is about 53 kg (118 lb).
It is named after a small breed of chicken.
questions.description: A division so light the scale barely notices anyone is standing on it.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico this division is called “peso gallo”, which means “rooster weight”.

questions.question: Boxers put it in their mouth before every round. It's made of soft plastic and shaped with hot water. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To keep their mouth from drying out
hints: It's also used in rugby, hockey and martial arts.
It sits between the lips and the teeth.
Thanks to it, boxers keep their smile.
questions.description: An accessory nobody shows off, but nobody steps into the ring without it.
questions.fun_fact: Many boxers have a dentist make their mouthguard to measure, using a mold of their mouth.

questions.question: In boxing, what is the punch called where the arm stretches out fully and the fist rotates just at the end?
hints: It's not a defensive move.
It doesn't curve through the air at all.
Its name also describes a line with no curves.
questions.description: A punch that lands before the opponent has finished thinking.
questions.fun_fact: The straight thrown with the front hand is also known as the jab, and it's the most-used punch in a fight.

questions.question: In Mexican boxing gyms, this is called a “costal.” What is it for?
wrong_answers: For the boxer to rest on
hints: It's used in every training session.
It's very heavy and can take a lot of punishment.
Boxers hit it with their fists again and again.
questions.description: They hang it from the ceiling and it takes everything without complaining.
questions.fun_fact: An adult boxing bag can weigh between 30 and 50 kg (66 and 110 lb).

questions.question: This skull, about 430,000 years old, came from the Sima de los Huesos (“Pit of the Bones”) in Spain. Which human lineage did it belong to?
hints: It isn't our species: it's far too old for that.
DNA from these bones links them to humans who later lived in Europe.
They are ancestors of humans with heavy brow ridges who vanished about 40,000 years ago.
questions.description: A pit where the family tree was traced with DNA almost half a million years old.
questions.fun_fact: Remains of at least 28 people turned up in the Sima, and their DNA is among the oldest human DNA ever read.

questions.question: Complete the trio of comic magazines that began the golden age of Mexican comics in the 1930s: “Pepín”, “Chamaco” and “___”.
hints: It is the oldest of the three: it came out in 1934.
Its name is a pet form of a very common Spanish first name.
It comes from “Paco”, with the ending “-ín”.
questions.description: Before the internet, WhatsApp and streaming, kids in the 1930s fought over these at the newsstand.
questions.fun_fact: Comic magazines were so popular that in Mexico people started calling all of them “pepines”, after the magazine “Pepín”.

questions.question: Complete the name of Don Regino's wife in Gabriel Vargas's comic “La Familia Burrón”: Borola ___.
hints: Her full name ends with “de Burrón”.
Her maiden name is also a Mexican slang word for a suit.
It starts with “Ta-” and ends with “-che”.
questions.description: The boldest lady on the Callejón del Cuajo, able to turn any ordinary day into a scandal.
questions.fun_fact: “La Familia Burrón” was published for more than 60 years, from 1948 to 2009, making it one of Mexico's longest-running comics.

questions.question: I fought Porfirio Díaz through the press, and in 1903 I joined the “El Hijo del Ahuizote” protest with the banner “La Constitución ha muerto”. Who am I?
hints: I was an anarchist and founded the newspaper “Regeneración”.
I worked alongside my brothers Enrique and Jesús.
My double surname starts with the Spanish word for “flowers”.
questions.description: A journalist who made Don Porfirio so angry that not even jail could shut him up.
questions.fun_fact: “El Hijo del Ahuizote” took its name from the ahuízotl, a water creature from Aztec mythology.

questions.question: I was born in 1978, I fit in your pocket, and I was one of Mexico's best-selling comics, especially with drivers and workers. Who am I?
hints: I was sold every week at newsstands.
My stories took place far from Mexico, in another country and another century.
My covers show cowboy hats, horses and revolvers.
questions.description: It fits in your jeans pocket and lasts through any long bus ride.
questions.fun_fact: Its stories were set in the American Old West, but Mexican artists wrote and drew them.

questions.question: In lucha libre, what is the “cuadrilátero”?
hints: Its name comes from its shape.
It has ropes on all four sides.
Boxers fight in one too.
questions.description: It has a name straight out of geometry class, but nobody there pulls out a ruler.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish it's called a “cuadrilátero” (four-sided shape), but in English it's a “ring” because fights used to take place inside a circle.

questions.question: Look at this image: it's in millions of homes, markets and cars in Mexico. What is it called?
hints: She wears a green mantle covered in stars.
At her feet are a moon and an angel.
According to tradition, she appeared to an Indigenous man named Juan Diego.
questions.description: She's been in the same place for almost five centuries and has never once asked for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the image appeared in 1531 on a tilma, a kind of cloth cloak worn by Indigenous people.

questions.question: How many Oscar nominations did “Emilia Pérez”, the Mexico-set musical by French director Jacques Audiard, receive?
hints: It was a record for a film not in the English language.
It beat the 10 nominations of “Roma”.
Many people think it's an unlucky number.
questions.description: A French musical about Mexico that sang louder in Hollywood than in Cancún.
questions.fun_fact: It won two of those Oscars: Best Supporting Actress for Zoe Saldaña and Best Original Song for “El Mal”.

questions.question: These bendy willow twigs are woven into baskets, chairs and cradles in Tequisquiapan, Querétaro. What is this material called?
hints: Many bread baskets and picnic baskets are made from it too.
The twigs are soaked in water so they bend without breaking.
Its name rhymes with “kicker.”
questions.description: If your grandma's rocking chair creaks with every bit of gossip, it's probably woven from this.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word for it, «mimbre», comes from the Latin «vimen», meaning “flexible rod.”

questions.question: Take a close look: the potters of Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato, use this to make their pots. What is it called?
hints: It's worked with a foot pedal or a motor.
You put the clay in the center and shape it up with wet hands.
It spins and spins without stopping.
questions.description: Coming home covered in mud and calling it art: now that's talent.
questions.fun_fact: The Talavera pottery of Dolores Hidalgo is painted by hand, piece by piece, before it is fired.

questions.question: A relative of the elephant, it lived in the Americas in the Ice Age, and its Greek name means “nipple tooth.” What animal is it?
hints: It browsed on leaves, twigs and shrubs in forests rather than grazing on open grassland.
Its back teeth had round, cone-shaped bumps.
Its name starts with the same four letters as “masticate.”
questions.description: Its smile was so odd that it got named after its teeth.
questions.fun_fact: French naturalist Georges Cuvier gave it its name in the early 19th century.

questions.question: Which of these women does NOT wear her hair in braids?
hints: Three of them wear their hair braided, sometimes with ribbons or flowers.
The one you want is famous for a TV show, not for traditional clothing.
She's Quico's mom in El Chavo del 8.
questions.description: A question for anyone who always notices other people's hairdos.
questions.fun_fact: Frida Kahlo wrapped her braids around her head like a crown and decorated them with ribbons and flowers.

questions.question: Orange cempasúchil has the color you get by mixing two paints. Which two?
hints: Both are primary colors.
One is the color of the sun.
The other is the color of a tomato.
questions.description: A recipe with no kitchen, just paintbrushes.
questions.fun_fact: Some cempasúchil flowers are yellow, some are orange, and some are almost red.

questions.question: In 1888, Paso del Norte, in Chihuahua, changed its name to honor a president who had lived there. Which one?
hints: He was president in the 19th century, in the time of the Reform Laws.
During the French Intervention, his government traveled the country in a black carriage.
His surname is in the city's current name.
questions.description: A border city that changed its name to say thank you to a very important guest.
questions.fun_fact: Benito Juárez lived in Paso del Norte during the French Intervention, when his government had to move all the way to the border.

questions.question: “I was born in San Miguel el Grande and, after the defeat at Puente de Calderón, I took military command of the insurgents from Father Hidalgo.” Who am I?
hints: I was one of the Querétaro conspirators.
I was the soldier of the movement and argued a lot with Hidalgo about how to fight the war.
My last name starts with “A” and ends in “-llende”.
questions.description: A conspirator who ended up fighting with his partner more than two siblings over the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: San Miguel el Grande changed its name to San Miguel de Allende in 1826 to honor its hero.

questions.question: The Wixárika make pictures full of deer, corn and colorful suns. What are they made with?
hints: No brush is used.
The sticky layer underneath is made by bees.
Strands of wool are pressed in, one by one, until the board is full.
questions.description: Art so detailed it feels wrong to hang it on a nail.
questions.fun_fact: At first, these boards were offerings the Wixárika left at sacred places like Wirikuta, in San Luis Potosí.

questions.question: México, Jalisco and Acapulco all end the same way, in “-co”, an ending inherited from Nahuatl. What does it mean?
hints: The same ending shows up in other places in Mexico, like Texcoco or Tlatelolco.
In Nahuatl it gets stuck onto the end of a word instead of standing alone.
It's like the little word you put before “the house” or “school” to say where you are.
questions.description: Three places that share a last name, and nobody asked their permission.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that ending, one of the best-known explanations says “México” means “in the place of the Mexica”.

questions.question: In Nahuatl, “quetzal” is a bird with precious feathers. Complete Quetzalcóatl's nickname: “the Feathered ___.”
hints: The word “cóatl” is exactly the missing one.
It's an animal with no legs.
It slithers along the ground, and some have a rattle.
questions.description: A god so stylish he dressed in the best of a bird's wardrobe.
questions.fun_fact: “Cóatl” also hides in place names like Coatzacoalcos and Coatepec.

questions.question: The Lecumberri building in Mexico City is said to be haunted. Which of these things is NOT true about it?
wrong_answers: It was a prison for more than 70 years
Today it holds the national archive
hints: Its hallways spread out like a star from a central tower.
From there, the guards could watch all the prisoners at once.
The emperor lived in a castle on a hill, in Chapultepec.
questions.description: A building with so much history that even the ghosts wait in line to get in.
questions.fun_fact: Lecumberri stopped being a prison in 1976, and since 1982 it has kept millions of documents from Mexico's history.

questions.question: At a lucha libre show, the crowd yells “¡Patada voladora!” What did the wrestler just do?
questions.answer: Jumped and kicked the rival in midair
wrong_answers: Kicked the rival lying on the mat
Sat down on the rival's back
Threw the rival into the ropes
hints: Look at the second word of the move's name.
For a moment, the wrestler isn't touching the mat.
The wrestler hits with the feet while up in the air.
questions.description: A shout in the arena that's even louder than your mom calling you to dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican lucha libre is famous around the world for its high-flying wrestlers, who leap off the ropes and even out of the ring.

questions.question: Rey Mysterio swings between the ropes and kicks a rival who is leaning on them. What is this signature move called?
hints: Its name is a three-digit number.
It comes from the part of California where Rey was born, right by the border with Tijuana.
It's the telephone area code of San Diego.
questions.description: A move named like a phone number… and nobody picks up.
questions.fun_fact: Rey Mysterio was born in Chula Vista, near San Diego, and 619 is the area code for that part of California.

questions.question: You're hitting a wrestler piñata and everyone sings “Dale, dale, dale…”. How many hits does the song count before your time is up?
hints: The song counts your hits one by one.
It's fewer than the fingers on one hand.
“…ya le diste ___ y tu tiempo se acabó” (“…you've hit it ___ and your time is up”).
questions.description: This cardboard wrestler is about to lose by knockout… and drop its candy.
questions.fun_fact: Masked wrestler piñatas are among the favorites at children's parties in Mexico.

questions.question: I wear a suit, hold a microphone, stand in the middle of the ring and shout each wrestler's name and weight as they come in. Who am I?
hints: I don't wrestle, and I don't judge the match.
My job starts before the first fall.
My famous line is “In this corner…!”
questions.description: Has the best seat in the arena, and didn't even have to buy a ticket.
questions.fun_fact: In lucha libre, the announcer also reads the result at the end and announces if someone lost their mask or their hair.

questions.question: I walk alone and people start whispering when I pass by; Rubén Fuentes wrote me and Luis Miguel sang me. Who am I?
hints: I'm a very beautiful woman carrying a great sorrow.
I became famous on mariachi trumpets in the 1960s.
My name sounds a lot like a two-piece swimsuit.
questions.description: A song so mysterious that even the town gossips can't agree on her story.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Miguel made “La Bikina” popular again in 2004 with his mariachi album “México en la piel.”

questions.question: You're at a wedding and “Adiós amor”, Christian Nodal's big hit, comes on. In which decade did the song come out?
hints: It was the song that made Nodal famous.
Nodal was born in the late 1990s.
He recorded it while he was still a teenager.
questions.description: A song everyone belts out between the cake and the waltz.
questions.fun_fact: Christian Nodal mixed mariachi with norteño, and his style was nicknamed “mariacheño”.

questions.question: In the fandango, dancers stomp on a wooden platform called a tarima while jaranas and the requinto play. Which state is this tradition from?
hints: It's a state with a long coastline on the Gulf of Mexico.
Mexico's highest volcano stands on its border with Puebla.
Its most famous port has the same name as the state.
questions.description: Here the wooden floor is part of the band too.
questions.fun_fact: At a fandango jarocho anyone can step up onto the tarima to dance, and the party can go on until sunrise.

questions.question: I was born in Sinaloa, they call me “La Luna de América”, and I sing “Quién como tú” and “Evidencias”. Who am I?
hints: I sing ballads and also rancheras with mariachi.
My voice is deep and raspy, very easy to recognize.
My stage name includes the name of an angel.
questions.description: A woman from Sinaloa who filled stadiums across the continent without ever changing her boots.
questions.fun_fact: Ana Gabriel was born in Guamúchil, Sinaloa, and her real name is María Guadalupe Araujo.

questions.question: It's made of hundreds of pieces of jade, covered a Maya king's face in his tomb, and was stolen from the National Museum of Anthropology in 1985. What is it?
hints: It's green.
Archaeologist Alberto Ruz found it in 1952, inside a pyramid.
Its owner is the most famous Maya king in Mexico.
questions.description: A treasure with more adventures than a telenovela hero: a tomb, a robbery and a homecoming.
questions.fun_fact: It was recovered in 1989, and today you can see it in the museum again.

questions.question: The Maya counted using their fingers and their toes too. What is their number system called?
hints: It's not the one we use today, which goes in tens.
Count all your fingers, and don't forget your toes.
Its name comes from the Latin word for “twentieth.”
questions.description: Math so old it had no calculator, but it did have a symbol for zero.
questions.fun_fact: French still keeps traces of counting in twenties: 80 is “four twenties” (quatre-vingts).

questions.question: In Yucatán there are fiestas with jarana until dawn, like the one in the photo. Where did they start in colonial times?
hints: It has to do with farm work.
It was celebrated when they finished branding the animals.
The fiesta is called a vaquería.
questions.description: Spotless white clothes, dancing all night and not a single stain: now that's Yucatecan magic.
questions.fun_fact: In the jarana the music suddenly stops, someone shouts “¡Bomba!” and recites a cheeky verse.

questions.question: Complete it: a biologist is to living things as an archaeologist is to…
hints: They work with a shovel and a brush, digging in the ground.
What they find often ends up in museums, next to ancient pots and sculptures.
In Mexico, they study places like Teotihuacan or Tulum.
questions.description: Some people spend their whole lives digging in the dirt, and they're not your dog.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has tens of thousands of recorded archaeological sites, but only a few hundred are open to the public.

questions.question: The Cueva de la Olla (“Cave of the Pot”), in Chihuahua's Sierra Madre, is famous for what's inside. Where does its name come from?
questions.answer: A large adobe granary shaped like a pot
wrong_answers: A pot of offerings found in a tomb
A pot-shaped rock at the entrance
A well where people filled their pots
hints: It is a site of the Paquimé culture.
The thing that gave it its name was built by the people who lived there.
They stored corn there for lean times.
questions.description: A cave with a kitchen name, but nobody ever sat down here for a plate of frijoles.
questions.fun_fact: The cave kept the rain off the building, which is why the mud granary is still standing after centuries.

questions.question: Look at this detail of an ancient jar painted in black and red on a light background. Which culture made it?
hints: It was a culture of northern Mexico.
Its great city had adobe houses several stories high.
Its capital was Paquimé.
questions.description: A jar with more geometric style than your sketchbook.
questions.fun_fact: Potters in Mata Ortiz brought this style back to life in the 20th century, and today their pieces sell all over the world.

questions.question: The Sultanes play baseball in Monterrey, “la Sultana del Norte.” And in Aladdin, Jasmine's father is a sultan. What is a sultan?
hints: He lives in a palace.
It was an important title in the old Ottoman Empire.
In Aladdin, Jafar wanted to take his throne.
questions.description: A word you can hear shouted in a Monterrey ballpark or in a Disney movie.
questions.fun_fact: Estadio de Béisbol Monterrey, home of the Sultanes, is one of the biggest ballparks in Mexico, with room for about 22,000 people.

questions.question: In baseball, the Diablos Rojos play at Estadio Alfredo Harp Helú, opened in 2019. In which city?
hints: It is a very big city, and very high up.
Careful: the other Diablos Rojos, the soccer team, are from a different city.
It is the country's capital.
questions.description: Devils who would rather be on a diamond than in the underworld.
questions.fun_fact: The Diablos Rojos del México have won more championships than any other team in the history of the Mexican Baseball League.

questions.question: This diver from La Paz, Baja California Sur, won synchro bronze at Beijing 2008 and silver at London 2012. Who is she?
hints: She competed on the 10-meter platform.
At Beijing 2008 she was also Mexico's flag bearer.
Her first name is Paola.
questions.description: She throws herself off a 10-meter tower while you get nervous on the diving board ladder.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, in Rome, Paola Espinosa became world champion on the 10-meter platform.

questions.question: In what event has Mexico won all its Olympic gold medals in track and field?
hints: It's a long-distance event, many kilometers long.
The judges watch how you step.
You move very fast, but one foot must always be touching the ground.
questions.description: An event that has put Mexico on the top step of the podium more than once.
questions.fun_fact: Daniel Bautista won Mexico's first Olympic gold in track and field at Montreal 1976.

questions.question: Daniela Romo had a hit in 1984 with “Yo no te pido la luna”. The original was heard that year at a famous European festival. What country was the original song from?
hints: The original language is very close to Spanish.
It was sung by a woman whose stage name is the name of a flower.
The festival was Sanremo.
questions.description: A diva so modest she didn't even ask for a natural satellite.
questions.fun_fact: Fiordaliso's original song was called “Non voglio mica la luna”.

questions.question: Three of these human groups are named after the place where their fossils were found. Which one is NOT?
hints: Look for the name that describes a skill, not a spot on the map.
The others come from a cave in Siberia, a valley in Germany and an island in Indonesia.
Its Latin name means something like “the one who is skilled with his hands.”
questions.description: Naming your family after your home address: a very prehistoric habit.
questions.fun_fact: Very few Denisovan bones are known: almost everything we know about them came from the DNA in a single finger bone.

questions.question: She was the Mexica goddess of ripe corn and of food. She was shown holding ears of corn, and her name means “seven serpent.” What was her name?
hints: Her name is also a date in the Mexica calendar.
At harvest time, young women carried ears of corn to her in a procession.
Her name ends the same way as the name of the Feathered Serpent.
questions.description: A goddess who knew there's no paradise without tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: Many statues show her with a large rectangular headdress called amacalli, “paper house.”

questions.question: This Mexica goddess, mother of many gods, is called Citlalicue. Her name means “she of the skirt of…”
hints: The skirt of snakes belongs to Coatlicue, and the skirt of jade to Chalchiuhtlicue.
“Citlali” is a very common girl's name in Mexico.
You can see her skirt at night, stretching across the sky.
