questions.description: A goddess with a wardrobe any fashion designer would envy.
questions.fun_fact: For the Mexica, the Milky Way was this goddess's skirt.

questions.question: I was sweeping on top of a sacred hill when a small ball of feathers fell from the sky. I tucked it against my chest, and that is how I became pregnant. Who am I?
hints: I am the mother of the 400 Centzon Huitznáhuac.
My son was born armed, ready to defend me.
My skirt is made of snakes.
questions.description: Sweeping has always been risky: you never know what you'll find.
questions.fun_fact: The huge statue of Coatlicue was dug up in the Zócalo in 1790, then buried again so people wouldn't worship it.

questions.question: “El color de tus ojos” is one of Banda MS's biggest hits. In which decade was the band formed?
hints: It's much younger than the legendary Banda El Recodo.
It was founded in the same century YouTube was born.
It started early in the 21st century.
questions.description: A band so big you need a whole truck just to get it on stage.
questions.fun_fact: The letters “MS” in the band's name stand for Mazatlán, Sinaloa.

questions.question: Which of these songs is NOT by Junior H?
hints: The answer is by another regional Mexican singer.
It's by a singer from Hermosillo, Sonora, who recorded with Bad Bunny.
It's by Natanael Cano and came out in 2019.
questions.description: For people who put their headphones on the moment they wake up.
questions.fun_fact: Junior H was born in Guanajuato and moved to Utah, in the United States, at 15; that's where he started uploading his songs to the internet.

questions.question: Led by Ricky Muñoz on accordion, it sang “¿Y todo para qué?” and formed in the early ’90s in a town on the Rio Grande. Where is Intocable from?
hints: Its music mixes norteño with the sound of the border.
The group has won several Grammy Awards.
It’s in the United States, the largest state that borders Mexico.
questions.description: A band whose name means “untouchable,” yet it never stops getting its hands on instruments.
questions.fun_fact: Intocable was born in Zapata, Texas, a town right across the river from Tamaulipas.

questions.question: A son jarocho group from Jáltipan is named after this dark bird with a crest and a red throat flap, living high in Veracruz's rainforests. Which bird?
hints: It is related to a very noisy bird that also lives in Mexico.
Its name comes from Nahuatl, and the group uses it in the plural.
Its name ends in “-lite.”
questions.description: A band that picked its name by looking up at the treetops.
questions.fun_fact: The cojolite and the chachalaca are relatives: both belong to the guan family, the cracids.

questions.question: It puffed black smoke, had a very loud whistle and carried Villa's troops across the north. What was the “iron horse”?
hints: It ran on coal or wood and water.
It pulled many cars full of people.
It ran on rails.
questions.description: Before buses, the Revolution traveled with lots of smoke and no air conditioning.
questions.fun_fact: Pancho Villa used trains to move thousands of soldiers, horses and even whole families.

review.feedback: The translation itself is fine, but in English it asks the same fact as approved q-8899: that the "iron horse" is the steam locomotive. Anyone who has seen one question already knows the answer to the other. Either keep only one of them in the English pool, or rework this one around a Mexico-specific fact about Villa's trains, which would make it a different question.

previous.feedback: This asks the same fact as approved q-8899: that the "iron horse" is the steam locomotive. Anyone who has seen one question knows the answer to the other, and the Villa setting doesn't change the fact being asked. The translation itself is faithful and natural ("camiones" correctly became "buses"), so the only problem is the duplicate; drop this English version or have the Mexican question ask something other than the nickname.

questions.question: In Mexico, people say I have seven lives. What kind of animal am I?
hints: I have whiskers and claws I can hide.
I purr when I'm happy.
Lions and tigers are my big cousins.
questions.description: An animal that spends lives like extra lives in a video game.
questions.fun_fact: In English-speaking countries, cats are said to have nine lives, not seven.

questions.question: The Stone Age is to stone as the first stage of the Metal Age is to…
hints: It is a reddish metal.
Today it is inside almost every electric cable.
The Statue of Liberty is covered in it, which is why it turned green.
questions.description: A caveman swapped his stone tools for something shinier and never looked back.
questions.fun_fact: Ötzi the Iceman, who lived about 5,300 years ago, carried an axe made of copper.

questions.question: In Mexico, what does “¡Échale ganas!” mean?
hints: People say it to you before a test or a game.
It's used when something takes a lot of work.
It's the opposite of giving up or doing things halfway.
questions.description: The favorite line of teachers, coaches and grandmas all over Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: The verb “echar” shows up in lots of Mexican phrases, like “echar aguas” (to keep watch), “echar relajo” (to goof around) or “echarse un taco” (to grab a taco).

questions.question: Someone criticizes another person for a flaw they have themselves. Finish the saying: «El burro hablando de…»
hints: It's a part of the donkey's body.
The saying makes fun of someone who can't see their own flaw.
They're for hearing.
questions.description: A saying for someone standing right in front of the mirror who still can't see themselves.
questions.fun_fact: A donkey's long ears help it hear from far away and let off heat in dry places.

questions.question: In Mexico, what does “echar porras” mean?
hints: It's a nice thing for whoever gets it.
Fans do it at a game.
It often comes with a shout of “¡sí se puede!”.
questions.description: A phrase that sounds like something you'd pick up at the hardware store.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, a group of fans who cheer together is also called a “porra”.

questions.question: What does the saying «perro que ladra no muerde» mean?
questions.answer: Those who threaten a lot do little
wrong_answers: Small dogs are the fiercest ones
Stay away from people who yell
Whoever yells the loudest is right
hints: People say it so someone won't get so scared.
It compares what someone says with what they really do.
It's said about someone who yells a lot but, when it counts, does nothing.
questions.description: A saying for the neighbors of the noisiest dog on the block.
questions.fun_fact: English has almost the same saying: “Barking dogs seldom bite.”

questions.question: What does the saying “el que se fue a la villa perdió su silla” mean?
questions.answer: If you leave your spot, someone else takes it
wrong_answers: You have to travel to find a job
Small-town chairs are the best ones
People who travel a lot always get tired
hints: You hear it at parties, on the bus and at the movies.
It's a rhyming joke said with a laugh to someone who has just come back.
If you get up, someone else jumps at the chance to sit down.
questions.description: The strictest law at any family party.
questions.fun_fact: Spain has an almost identical saying: “quien fue a Sevilla perdió su silla.”

questions.question: Which of these will you NOT find in Yucatán?
hints: It is a land of Mayan heritage and lots of heat.
Its ground is limestone, full of caves with water.
Yucatán is almost completely flat: its Mayan pyramids are some of the tallest things around.
questions.description: A trip where a hat is a must, and so is the heat.
questions.fun_fact: Yucatán has almost no rivers on the surface: the water flows through underground rivers that peek out in the cenotes.

questions.question: It lasts all night, almost nobody just watches, and in Tlacotalpan it happens at the Candelaria. What is a fandango from Veracruz?
questions.answer: A party with son jarocho and a tarima
hints: There's music, verses and lots of stomping dance steps.
It's played on jaranas and requintos.
People take turns dancing zapateado on a wooden platform.
questions.description: A word that can't sit still for a single minute in Veracruz.
questions.fun_fact: At a fandango the tarima is an instrument too: the dancers' feet on it keep the beat.

questions.question: Before they dance, the concheros raise the sahumador (incense burner) and greet “los cuatro rumbos”, one after another. What are these rumbos?
wrong_answers: The four corners of the churchyard
The four seasons of the year
hints: It has to do with the Sun.
The first one is usually where the sun comes up.
North, south, east and west.
questions.description: A dance that makes sure nobody gets left without a hello before it starts.
questions.fun_fact: For the Mexica (Aztecs), each direction of the world had its own color and its own gods.

questions.question: “Where the Air Is Clear” is Carlos Fuentes’s great novel about Mexico City. What is Juan Villoro’s great book of chronicles about it?
hints: It came out in 2018.
Its author is also famous for his writing about soccer.
Its title describes a city that grows more outward than upward.
questions.description: A city nobody ever finishes exploring, on foot or on the page.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Villoro is the son of the philosopher Luis Villoro.

questions.question: A newspaper called Alfred Nobel “the merchant of death.” Which of his inventions earned him that name?
hints: It was widely used to dig tunnels and mines.
It comes in sticks and has a fuse.
It goes BOOM in lots of Road Runner cartoons.
questions.description: A man who tried to clean up his name with the most famous prize on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: The newspaper ran the story by mistake: the one who had died was his brother Ludvig, not Alfred.

questions.question: I was written into Article 27 of the 1917 Constitution, I turned land from big haciendas into ejidos, and Lázaro Cárdenas pushed me like nobody else. What am I?
hints: Zapata would have been proud of me.
I have to do with the countryside, not with oil or factories.
My job was to hand out land to the people who worked it.
questions.description: A constitution with over a hundred candles on its cake that people still talk about.
questions.fun_fact: While Lázaro Cárdenas was president, about 18 million hectares (44 million acres) of land were handed out.

questions.question: The fight that began with the Plan de San Luis forced Porfirio Díaz to resign in 1911. To which country did he go into exile?
hints: He had to cross the Atlantic Ocean.
He sailed from Veracruz on the ship Ypiranga.
He spent his last years near the Eiffel Tower.
questions.description: Some farewells come with a handkerchief waving at the port, and others start with a revolutionary plan.
questions.fun_fact: The Plan de San Luis is dated in San Luis Potosí, but Madero wrote it while in exile in San Antonio, Texas.

questions.question: Complete it: Zapata is to the Plan de Ayala as Venustiano Carranza is to the…
hints: He signed it in 1913 at a hacienda in Coahuila.
It refused to accept Victoriano Huerta as president.
Its name is the same as Mexico’s most famous Virgin.
questions.description: Every revolutionary leader had a plan, just like every aunt has her own mole recipe.
questions.fun_fact: The Plan de Guadalupe gave birth to the Constitutionalist Army, and Carranza named himself its “First Chief”.

questions.question: I'm a mining city with the Cerro de la Bufa, and in June 1914 Pancho Villa took me by beating Huerta's army. Who am I?
hints: My historic center is a World Heritage Site.
I have a cable car that goes up my hill.
A very famous parade march carries my name.
questions.description: A city with a hill, with history, and with a whole lot of stairs to climb.
questions.fun_fact: Every June 23, Mexico remembers the 1914 capture of Zacatecas, one of the biggest victories of the División del Norte.

questions.question: What was the name of Francisco I. Madero's wife, who traveled with him on his 1910 anti-reelection campaign tour?
hints: She wasn't a soldadera; she went on to become first lady.
She had been married to Madero since 1903.
Her first name is the name of Abraham's wife in the Bible.
questions.description: Behind every anti-reelection tour there was someone else putting up with all those train rides.
questions.fun_fact: Sara Pérez and Francisco I. Madero were married for about ten years and had no children.

questions.question: In which year was the minimum wage written into Mexico's Constitution, in Article 123?
hints: It came after the Revolution broke out.
Venustiano Carranza was the “Primer Jefe” (First Chief).
It's the same year as the Constitution Mexico has today.
questions.description: A number everyone at home wants to see go up.
questions.fun_fact: The same Article 123 also set the maximum workday at 8 hours.

questions.question: Complete the first line of the Mexican National Anthem: “Mexicanos, al grito de…”
hints: It's sung during the flag ceremony.
Next comes “el acero aprestad y el bridón.”
It's the opposite of peace.
questions.description: The line sung every Monday at school with a hand over the heart.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem's lyrics were written by Francisco González Bocanegra and the music by Catalan composer Jaime Nunó; it premiered in 1854.

questions.question: Your ice cream falls on the ground and there's nothing you can do. What Mexican expression do you say to accept it?
hints: It's for when something went wrong and can't be fixed.
You say it with a sigh.
It has just two words, and the first one means “not even”.
questions.description: For those moments when the universe snatches dessert right out of your hands.
questions.fun_fact: «Ni modo» is so Mexican that it shows up on many lists of phrases for learning Spanish in Mexico.

questions.question: Colombia's peace deal with which guerrilla group earned Juan Manuel Santos the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: It was Colombia's largest and oldest guerrilla group.
The peace talks took place in Havana, Cuba.
Its name begins with “Revolutionary Armed Forces”.
questions.description: A signature with a very special pen that made headlines around the world.
questions.fun_fact: The deal was signed with a pen made from a bullet.

questions.question: This smiling old-man mask is from the famous Danza de los Viejitos. Who danced it first?
hints: It began in villages around a large lake, Lake Pátzcuaro.
The Purépecha people live there.
It's the state whose capital is Morelia.
questions.description: Some grandpas who look worn out… until the music starts.
questions.fun_fact: The dancers are often young people who walk hunched over with canes, then suddenly stomp their feet with tons of energy.

questions.question: This heroine of Mexican Independence was married to the man Quintana Roo is named after. Who is she?
hints: She came from a rich family in Mexico City.
She used her fortune to help the insurgents and passed them secret information.
She was declared “Well-Deserving and Sweetest Mother of the Homeland.”
questions.description: Behind every great state there was a great rebel marriage.
questions.fun_fact: Her husband, Andrés Quintana Roo, was born in Mérida, Yucatán, in 1787.

questions.question: Under this huge dome in Mexico City rest the remains of national heroes. Which heroes?
hints: The dome stands in the Plaza de la República.
That movement began in 1910.
Francisco I. Madero and Pancho Villa rest there.
questions.description: A dome so big it even has its own glass elevator for the view.
questions.fun_fact: This building was meant to be Porfirio Díaz's Legislative Palace, but work stopped halfway when the Revolution began.

questions.question: You're in Puebla helping grind the ingredients for mole poblano. Which of these does it NOT contain?
hints: Mole has loads of ingredients, almost all ground together.
One of them is also sprinkled on top when it's served.
The odd one out is a dairy product.
questions.description: A dish with more ingredients than your backpack on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says mole poblano was invented by nuns at the Santa Rosa convent in Puebla.

questions.question: Which of these states does NOT have a coast on the Gulf of Mexico?
hints: Think about which side of the country each state is on.
The Gulf is in the east, on the Atlantic side.
Acapulco is in this state.
questions.description: A geography test to find out which side of the country your vacation is on.
questions.fun_fact: Buried under the Gulf of Mexico coast in Yucatán lies the Chicxulub crater, left by the meteorite that wiped out the dinosaurs.

questions.question: These stone columns with waterfalls are in Huasca, Hidalgo. How did they form?
hints: Nobody carved them: nature made them.
They formed millions of years ago from something very hot.
The rock is called basalt.
questions.description: Columns so perfect they look like someone made them with a ruler and a square.
questions.fun_fact: The explorer Alexander von Humboldt visited and sketched these columns in 1803.

questions.question: Look at the map: every July, the capital of the highlighted state hosts the Guelaguetza. Which state is it?
hints: The festival is also called “Lunes del Cerro”.
The word “Guelaguetza” comes from Zapotec and means offering or gift.
This state is famous for tlayudas and chapulines.
questions.description: A party where the audience goes home with presents at the end.
questions.fun_fact: At the Guelaguetza, groups from the state's regions dance and then give the audience products from their land.

questions.question: Valentín Pimstein produced “Los ricos también lloran”, “Rosa salvaje” and “Quinceañera” for Televisa. In what country was he born?
hints: He wasn't born in Mexico, though he made his career in Mexican TV.
His home country is in South America.
It's a long, narrow country with the Andes on one side and the Pacific on the other.
questions.description: The man who made half a continent cry without chopping a single onion.
questions.fun_fact: Pimstein is seen as one of the fathers of the classic romantic telenovela: the poor girl who falls in love with the rich young man.

questions.question: Same story, new actors, sometimes decades later: “Corazón salvaje” has been filmed several times in Mexico. What is each new version called?
hints: It doesn't tell what happened afterwards or what happened before.
It is the same story, told again from the beginning.
The word starts with the prefix that means “again”.
questions.description: Tears, super-evil villainesses and a grandma who never misses an episode.
questions.fun_fact: “Corazón salvaje” had versions in 1966, 1977, 1993 and 2009.

questions.question: Arturo Peniche, the leading man of “María Mercedes”, comes from a family of actors. In which Mexican state was he born?
hints: His brother Flavio Peniche is also an actor.
He was born in the southeast of the country.
His hometown is Mérida.
questions.description: A telenovela heartthrob who brings the warm weather from home.
questions.fun_fact: In “María Mercedes” (1992), Arturo Peniche played Jorge Luis del Olmo, the rich man who marries Thalía's title character.

questions.question: I was an actor and then a producer. I made “Clase 406” and “Rebelde”, and the band RBD was born from it. Who am I?
hints: I specialized in teen telenovelas for Televisa.
I also produced “Primer amor… a mil por hora”.
My first name is the Spanish form of the apostle who, by tradition, was the first pope.
questions.description: He gave a whole generation a school uniform, a red tie and a playlist.
questions.fun_fact: RBD went from a band in a telenovela to filling stadiums in several countries.

questions.question: Which comedian starred in the telenovela “Una familia con suerte” (2011) as Pancho López?
hints: He first became famous on Televisa comedy shows.
He was part of “La hora pico”.
His last name ends with the Spanish word for a castle's tower.
questions.description: A telenovela so lucky that it even comes with a family included in the title.
questions.fun_fact: “Una familia con suerte” is a remake of the Argentine telenovela “Los Roldán”.

questions.question: You go to the Encuentro Internacional del Mariachi and also explore the same state. Which of these places is NOT in that state?
hints: The festival is held in the state's capital.
That capital is Guadalajara.
The place you're looking for is next to a lake in Michoacán.
questions.description: A whole week when nobody is surprised by a serenade anymore.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Look at the photo: according to legend, why did these dancers dance for the very first time?
questions.answer: To cheer up a sick boy
wrong_answers: To ask for rain for the harvest
hints: Look closely at the name of these dancers.
The legend tells of a rich lady who came looking for a cure.
They danced “para el chico”, Spanish for “for the boy”.
questions.description: A January fiesta where the masks smile more than the guests.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the lady was Doña María de Angulo, who arrived in the 18th century with her sick son.

questions.question: The Xochipitzahuatl is a son in Nahuatl danced at weddings in the Huasteca and the Sierra de Puebla. What is hidden in its name?
hints: Look at the beginning of the word.
The same thing appears in the name Xochimilco.
It's what the bride is given in a bouquet.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a tongue twister, yet at weddings everyone sings it without tripping up.
questions.fun_fact: Xochipitzahuatl means “tiny little flower,” and it is danced to honor the newlyweds and also the Virgin Mary.

questions.question: “Muerte sin fin” (1939), by José Gorostiza of the Contemporáneos group, reflects on God and form through water inside an object. Which one?
hints: Water has no shape of its own: it takes the shape of its container.
It's see-through, so you can watch the water inside.
You drink water from it at the table, and it has no handle or lid.
questions.description: A very deep poem... and filled right to the brim.
questions.fun_fact: Gorostiza was also a diplomat and became Mexico's Secretary of Foreign Affairs.

questions.question: In Laura Esquivel’s “Like Water for Chocolate,” Tita loves Pedro and every chapter brings a recipe. When does the story take place?
hints: Tita lives on a ranch near the border with the United States.
Because of a family tradition, Mamá Elena forbids her to marry, since she is the youngest daughter.
It is the time of Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata.
questions.description: A novel where feelings are cooked over a low flame.
questions.fun_fact: The 1992 film was directed by Alfonso Arau, who was Laura Esquivel’s husband at the time.

questions.question: This Mexican writer formed the core of the Latin American Boom with García Márquez, Vargas Llosa and Cortázar. Who is he?
hints: He was the son of a diplomat and grew up in several countries.
He wrote the short novel “Aura”.
He wrote “The Death of Artemio Cruz”.
questions.description: Four writers got half the world reading in Spanish, and here is one of them.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Fuentes was born in Panama City, where his father, a Mexican diplomat, was working.

questions.question: Which poet of the Contemporáneos group wrote “Nostalgia for Death” (1938), famous for its “Nocturnes”?
hints: He also wrote plays, such as “Invitation to Death”.
He was born in Mexico City in 1903 and died young, in 1950.
A major Mexican literary prize bears his name.
questions.description: A poet who did his best work on the night shift.
questions.fun_fact: Villaurrutia and Salvador Novo founded the magazine “Ulises” together in 1927.

questions.question: The Curies discovered it, it glows faintly in the dark, and its name starts like a device for listening to music. Which element is it?
hints: It is a chemical element.
It was once used on watches that glowed at night.
The device is used to listen to stations.
questions.description: A family where prizes were handed down like grandma's recipes.
questions.fun_fact: The Curie family won five Nobel Prizes in total, shared between Marie, Pierre, their daughter Irène and their son-in-law Frédéric.

questions.question: Which writer, who lived most of his life in Mexico, wrote “When he woke up, the dinosaur was still there”?
hints: He is a master of very short texts and humorous fables.
He was born in Honduras and grew up in Guatemala.
He wrote “The Black Sheep and Other Fables”.
questions.description: Seven words, zero filler, and a reptile that won’t leave.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, “The Dinosaur” has only seven words, and it is one of the shortest and most famous stories in the language.

questions.question: Which Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on famines and well-being?
hints: He was born in Bengal, India, in 1933.
As a child, he lived through the great Bengal famine of 1943.
His first name was chosen by the poet Rabindranath Tagore, also a Nobel Prize winner.
questions.description: An economist who counted not just dollars, but also plates of food.
questions.fun_fact: Sen argued that no major famine has ever happened in a democracy with a free press.

questions.question: Guess: I'm a giant black hole, and Andrea Ghez won the Nobel Prize for proving I exist. Where do I live?
questions.answer: At the center of the Milky Way
hints: I live very, very far from Earth.
Stars spin around me.
I sit at the heart of our own galaxy.
questions.description: An astronomer who spent years keeping an eye on a neighbor nobody can see.
questions.fun_fact: That black hole, called Sagittarius A*, has about four million times the mass of the Sun.

questions.question: It was founded in 1950, helps refugees and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981. In which city is its headquarters?
hints: It is a UN agency called UNHCR.
It is in a country famous for staying neutral.
It is the same city as the International Red Cross, on a big Swiss lake.
questions.description: An organization that won the same prize twice and still has no time to celebrate.
questions.fun_fact: When UNHCR was created in 1950, it was meant to last only three years; today it works in more than 100 countries.

questions.question: Which of these books was NOT written by Albert Camus, winner of the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature?
hints: The odd book out was written by an author from Prague.
In that book, a man wakes up to find he has turned into an insect.
Its author was Franz Kafka.
questions.description: A writer who wondered about the meaning of life, and played goalkeeper on the side.
questions.fun_fact: As a young man in Algiers, Camus played goalkeeper, and he said soccer taught him what he knew about morals.

questions.question: In 2010, Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Oscar for Best Director. How many Oscar ceremonies came before?
hints: The Oscars are given out once a year.
The first awards were handed out in 1929.
Subtract 1929 from 2010.
questions.description: Hollywood took longer on this than your brother takes in the bathroom.
questions.fun_fact: Bigelow won for “The Hurt Locker”, beating her ex-husband James Cameron, who was nominated for “Avatar”.

questions.question: At 73, actor Jack Palance did one-armed push-ups when he accepted his Oscar. In which decade did this happen?
hints: He won for a modern Western comedy, “City Slickers.”
It was a few years before “Toy Story” came out.
It was in 1992.
questions.description: The most muscular thank-you speech in history.
questions.fun_fact: Billy Crystal, the host, spent the rest of the night making jokes about Palance's push-ups.

questions.question: I hosted the first Oscars shown on TV, in 1953, and I have hosted the show more times than anyone else. Who am I?
hints: I was a very famous comedian from Hollywood's golden age.
I hosted the show 19 times.
My last name is the word for wishing that good things will happen.
questions.description: A host who felt as at home at the Oscars as on the living-room couch.
questions.fun_fact: Bob Hope never won an Oscar for acting, but the Academy gave him several honorary awards.

questions.question: The Oscars were first handed out in 1929. In which city was that first ceremony held?
hints: It was in the United States.
It's in California, on the Pacific Ocean.
It's home to the Hollywood neighborhood.
questions.description: A little golden man who never works out but is always standing up.
questions.fun_fact: The first ceremony, at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel, lasted only about 15 minutes.

questions.question: Who was the first Mexican-born actor to win an Oscar?
hints: He won in the 1950s.
He won twice for Best Supporting Actor.
He is famous for “Zorba the Greek.”
questions.description: An actor who had more roles than a bakery has rolls.
questions.fun_fact: Anthony Quinn was born in Chihuahua and won his first Oscar for “Viva Zapata!”.

questions.question: In what year did the slogan “Yes we can” become famous in a US presidential campaign?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
That year, the first African American president of the United States won the election.
It was the year of Barack Obama's campaign, four years before he was reelected.
questions.description: Three little words that fit on a cap, on a T-shirt and on the lips of millions.
questions.fun_fact: Obama had already used “Yes we can” in 2004, when he ran for senator in Illinois.

questions.question: When the US Civil War broke out in 1861, about how many people were enslaved in the country?
hints: It was more than one in every ten people in the country.
Nearly all of them lived in the Southern states, on cotton and tobacco plantations.
It is a number in the millions, but with just one digit.
questions.description: A number so big it changed a whole country forever.
questions.fun_fact: Slavery was abolished across the whole US by the 13th Amendment, ratified in December 1865.

questions.question: In 1962, in a stadium in Texas, I said: “We choose to go to the Moon in this decade.” Who am I?
hints: I am a US president of the 1960s.
My wife was named Jacqueline and was famous for her elegance.
My initials are JFK, like an airport in New York.
questions.description: A speech so ambitious that someone had to build a rocket to keep its promise.
questions.fun_fact: The speech was given at Rice University in Houston, and the Moon landing came in 1969, right on schedule.

questions.question: Which of these did NOT happen while Andrew Johnson was US president?
hints: Johnson became president in April 1865.
The one you're looking for happened before Johnson took office, while the war was still going on.
It was an order signed by the president before him, Abraham Lincoln.
questions.description: The man who inherited the hardest job at the worst possible moment.
questions.fun_fact: Johnson escaped removal from office in the Senate by just one vote.

questions.question: The first impeachment of a US president was in 1868. In which decade did the second one come?
hints: More than a hundred years passed between the first and the second.
Nixon resigned in 1974 before his could be voted on, so it doesn't count.
It was against Bill Clinton.
questions.description: When the boss of the whole country gets sent to the principal's office.
questions.fun_fact: No US president has ever been removed from office by impeachment: every one was acquitted by the Senate.

questions.question: In Spain, the defeat by the US that cost the country Cuba and Puerto Rico is called “the Disaster of ’…”. Which number completes the name?
hints: It happened at the end of the 19th century.
The US president at the time was William McKinley.
It's the year of the war, without the 18 in front.
questions.description: The day Spain looked at the map and found a few islands missing.
questions.fun_fact: After that war, the US also took the Philippines and Guam.

questions.question: You're at an IMSS clinic. Which of these can you NOT do there?
hints: The IMSS takes care of the health of workers and their families.
Each government office has its own job, and they don't all do the same things.
For this, you go to a Foreign Affairs office, because it's for traveling.
questions.description: An institution so big it has more lines than a taquería on a Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: The IMSS was founded in 1943 and today serves tens of millions of people in Mexico.

questions.question: I was born in Mexico after the great earthquake of 1985. I run the drills and check that schools and buildings are safe. Who am I?
hints: My job is to prevent problems before a disaster happens.
You see me in orange vests at the September 19 drills.
My name says I protect civilians, which means everyone.
questions.description: The people who make you leave the classroom calmly, even with the alarm at full blast.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's National Civil Protection System was created in 1986, one year after the 1985 earthquake.

questions.question: This party ruled Mexico from 1929 to 2000 and uses the colors of the flag. What do its initials, PRI, stand for?
hints: It was first called the PNR, then the PRM.
Its name recalls the Mexican Revolution.
The last word refers to institutions.
questions.description: Three letters that stayed at Los Pinos longer than many grandmas have lived in their own homes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2000, Vicente Fox of the PAN won the presidency, ending 71 years of governments from the same party.

questions.question: Look at this classic car that used to be a taxi in Mexico City. Which car is it?
hints: It was one of the most popular cars in Mexico for decades.
It was built in Puebla.
It's shaped like a beetle.
questions.description: A classic of the Mexico City streets that carried millions of passengers in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The world's last classic vocho rolled out of the Puebla factory in 2003.

questions.question: Pemex is Mexico's government-owned oil company. Which of these does Pemex NOT sell?
hints: Pemex works with oil and what is made from it.
Pemex turns crude oil into products at its refineries, like the one in Salina Cruz.
The CFE, with its poles and cables, is in charge of this one.
questions.description: A company that lives off a smelly black liquid and is still a source of national pride.
questions.fun_fact: Pemex was founded in 1938, after Lázaro Cárdenas nationalized the oil industry.

questions.question: I was born in 1990 and ran federal elections, and many people still call their voter ID card by my name. Who am I?
hints: My job was counting votes with ordinary citizens at the polling stations.
My photo card is used as official ID.
In 2014 they changed one of my letters and I became the INE.
questions.description: Acronyms, long lines and an office with the air conditioning on full blast.
questions.fun_fact: The IFE became the INE in 2014, but the phrase “get out your IFE card” is still alive.

questions.question: The slogan “2 de octubre no se olvida” recalls what happened in 1968 in this Mexico City square. Where is it?
hints: Students gathered there ten days before the Olympics.
It has pre-Hispanic ruins, a colonial church and modern buildings.
It's the Plaza de las Tres Culturas.
questions.description: Some dates get chanted at marches so nobody forgets the calendar.
questions.fun_fact: The 1967 treaty banning nuclear weapons in Latin America was also signed in Tlatelolco.

questions.question: Its cheer is “¡Huélum!”, its mascot is a white donkey and its colors are maroon and white. Which school is it?
hints: It is famous for training engineers.
Lázaro Cárdenas founded it in 1936.
Its students are known as “politécnicos.”
questions.description: A school where the donkey is the smartest one in class.
questions.fun_fact: The IPN was founded in 1936 so the children of workers and farmers could study for technical careers.

questions.question: In Mexico, when the PE teacher tells you to do “lagartijas”, what do you have to do?
hints: You do it on the floor, face down.
It takes a lot of arm strength.
You push your body up and down on your hands, like a lizard sunning itself.
questions.description: The sportiest reptile in the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: Real lizards do something similar: they push their bodies up and down on their front legs to tell other lizards that this spot is theirs.

questions.question: You're out in the countryside and a zorrillo turns its back and lifts its tail toward you. Why does it do that?
questions.answer: To spray you with a stinky jet
wrong_answers: To greet you as a friend
To ask you for some food
hints: It's defending itself because you scared it.
Your nose is going to notice.
Afterward you'd need lots of baths to get rid of the smell.
questions.description: The neighbor from the hills that nobody wants to pick a fight with.
questions.fun_fact: A zorrillo can hit a target about 3 m (10 ft) away, and its smell carries for more than a kilometer (over half a mile).

questions.question: In what year did Donald Trump win his first presidential election?
hints: It came after Barack Obama's two terms.
His opponent was Hillary Clinton.
The Olympic Games were held in Rio de Janeiro that same year.
questions.description: He used to fire people on TV; then he moved into a very white house.
questions.fun_fact: Trump is the second president to serve two terms that were not back to back; the first was Grover Cleveland in the 19th century.

questions.question: You're in Durango, shaking out your shoes before putting them on in case of scorpions. When do scorpions come out to look for food?
hints: During the day they hide in dark corners.
They like it when it's cooler and there's no sun.
It's when owls and bats come out too.
questions.description: A Durango tenant who pays no rent and lives in your shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Under ultraviolet light, scorpions glow a blue-green color.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this anteater lives in Mexico. In which part of the country can you find it?
hints: It likes heat and humidity.
It climbs trees and holds on with its tail.
It lives in places like Chiapas, Tabasco and the Yucatán Peninsula.
questions.description: An animal that never invites ants to its party, because the ants are the party.
questions.fun_fact: Its sticky tongue is about 40 cm (16 in) long, perfect for catching ants and termites.

questions.question: It has pyramids, colonial cities and nature reserves on UNESCO's list, and no country in the Americas has more World Heritage Sites. Which country is it?
hints: It's a country with a lot of pre-Hispanic history.
Its list includes several colonial cities that grew rich from silver.
Its list includes Chichén Itzá and Teotihuacan.
questions.description: A list of places so precious that the whole world promised to look after them.
questions.fun_fact: Even a university campus is on the list: UNAM's Ciudad Universitaria, since 2007.

questions.question: Legend says a bishop dreamed that beings came down from the sky and marked out Puebla's streets with cords. Who were they?
hints: In churches they're painted with wings.
People say everyone has a guardian one.
The city's old name was Puebla de los…
questions.description: A city that, so the story goes, was designed by no architect of this world.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this legend, Puebla is also nicknamed “la Angelópolis.”

questions.question: I was the priest of a town in Guanajuato and taught people to grow grapes and keep bees and silkworms. In September 1810, I rang the bell. Who am I?
hints: My statue, with white hair, stands in many town squares.
The cry I gave is remembered every September 15 at night.
Today the town where I was priest carries my last name.
questions.description: One September night, in a little town in Guanajuato, someone woke everybody up with a lot of noise.
questions.fun_fact: Dolores Hidalgo is also famous for its nieves (ice treats) in odd flavors like avocado, shrimp, and mole.

questions.question: In New Spain, people were sorted into castes by their parents' origins. Which of these names was NOT a caste?
hints: Three of these words appeared in colonial baptism records.
The odd word out was already in use before the Spaniards arrived.
It was the title of the Mexica ruler, like Moctezuma.
questions.description: In New Spain, the label you got depended less on you and more on your parents.
questions.fun_fact: In the 18th century, whole series of “casta paintings” were made, showing up to 16 combinations of parents and children.

questions.question: I'm a yellow, sweet, long fruit. I came from Asia on the galleon that crossed the Pacific, and today I'm grown a lot in Veracruz. What am I?
hints: My journey ended at the port of Acapulco.
I come from the same islands that sent silk and spices to New Spain.
I'm named after the capital of the Philippines.
questions.description: It sailed halfway around the planet just so you could eat it with chili and lime today.
questions.fun_fact: The Ataulfo mango, on the other hand, is as Mexican as it gets: it began in Chiapas in the 20th century.

questions.question: Moctezuma's headdress is huge. About how wide is it?
hints: It's much bigger than a baseball cap.
It's wider than a normal door.
It's more than a meter and a half, but less than 3 meters.
questions.description: The most stylish hat in Tenochtitlan, and not a single fashion store nearby.
questions.fun_fact: The headdress has hundreds of quetzal feathers and is so fragile that experts say travel could damage it.

questions.question: According to legend, the china poblana was a woman from Asia who reached Puebla on the Manila Galleon. In which century did she arrive?
hints: It was right in the middle of the colonial era.
New Spain had already existed for almost a hundred years.
It was in the 1600s.
questions.description: A legend that arrived by ship and ended up as a party dress.
questions.fun_fact: The woman of the legend, Catarina de San Juan, is buried in the Templo de la Compañía in Puebla.

questions.question: You're drinking a champurrado. Which of these ingredients came to Mexico from another continent after the Conquest?
hints: Three of them were already used by the peoples of Mesoamerica.
It comes from the bark of a tree.
It's the little brown stick many people put in café de olla.
questions.description: A hot cup with ingredients from both sides of the ocean.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is today one of the world's biggest importers of cinnamon, nearly all of it from Sri Lanka.

questions.question: In which century did Chinese porcelain start arriving in Acapulco on the Manila Galleon?
hints: It was just a few decades after the fall of Tenochtitlan.
King Philip II ruled Spain at the time.
It was in the 1500s.
questions.description: Plates so fancy you'd be scared to serve frijoles on them.
questions.fun_fact: Talavera pottery from Puebla copied the blue designs of the Chinese porcelain that came on the galleon.

questions.question: On my coast, Cortés founded his first town in 1519 and had his ships sunk so no one could go back to Cuba. Today I'm a state with a famous port. Who am I?
hints: I'm on the Gulf of Mexico.
My port is famous for its coffee, its danzón and its son jarocho.
My first town was called Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz.
questions.description: Here someone decided a return ticket wasn't needed.
questions.fun_fact: People say he “burned his ships,” but Cortés actually had holes made in them to sink them.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican actor. In “Güeros” I crossed Mexico City looking for a musician, and for Marvel I played Namor, king of Talokan. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Ecatepec, in the State of Mexico.
My Marvel character has little wings on his ankles and lives under the sea.
My first name echoes the name of the great capital of the Mexica.
questions.description: A king who never needs a swimsuit… well, almost never.
questions.fun_fact: In “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever”, Talokan is inspired by Maya culture, and Namor speaks Yucatec Maya in several scenes.

questions.question: Look at the photo: at the start of Alfonso Cuarón's “Gravity”, the astronauts repair this device in orbit. What is it?
hints: It has been circling the Earth for more than 30 years.
It has taken super famous photos of galaxies and nebulas.
It's called Hubble, after an American astronomer.
questions.description: A movie where nobody can run to the corner store for tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: “Gravity” won 7 Oscars, and Alfonso Cuarón became the first Latin American to win Best Director.

questions.question: It has canals, colorful trajineras and chinampas, and Leo San Juan searches there for lost children in “La Leyenda de la Llorona.” What place is it?
hints: It's in the south of Mexico City.
On weekends, families ride boats there with mariachis playing.
Its name in Nahuatl has to do with flowers.
questions.description: A story to make kids behave at bedtime.
questions.fun_fact: The canals and chinampas of Xochimilco have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

questions.question: “¡Ay, Jalisco, no te rajes!”, sang Jorge Negrete. If someone tells you “no te rajes”, what are they asking you?
hints: People say it a lot right before a challenge or a contest.
Someone who “se raja” doesn't do what they promised.
It's the opposite of chickening out and giving up.
questions.description: Jorge Negrete wasn't singing it to one person, but to a whole state.
questions.fun_fact: The film “¡Ay, Jalisco, no te rajes!” is from 1941, and the song was composed by Manuel Esperón with lyrics by Ernesto Cortázar.

questions.question: You're looking at an Oscar statuette. According to the most popular story, which Mexican posed as the model for it?
hints: He worked in Hollywood in the 1920s, before the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.
He was known for his fiery temper and strong, athletic build.
Besides acting he was a great director, and his nickname referred to his Indigenous roots.
questions.description: A golden Hollywood award with a very Mexican secret.
questions.fun_fact: “María Candelaria,” by El Indio Fernández, won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival in 1946.

questions.question: In Mexican ranchera movies, surprised characters shout “¡Ay, …!” with the name of a northern state that is also a dog breed. Which one?
hints: It is the largest state in Mexico.
Its capital has the same name as the state.
A dog of this breed fits in a handbag.
questions.description: What your grandpa says when he sees the price of tortillas.
questions.fun_fact: Chihuahua is Mexico's largest state: it is even bigger than the whole United Kingdom.

questions.question: Singer Lila Downs was born in Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca, and sings in Spanish, English and her mother's Indigenous language. Which language is it?
hints: Her father was American; her mother was from Oaxaca.
Tlaxiaco lies in a region named after that people.
Its speakers call themselves ñuu savi.
questions.description: A voice with two passports and roots planted deep in the Oaxacan mountains.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2003 Oscars, Lila Downs sang “Burn It Blue” from the movie Frida.

questions.question: According to the catalog of Mexico's National Institute of Indigenous Languages (INALI), how many Indigenous languages, or language groups, does Mexico have?
hints: Far more than the fingers on your hands.
The same catalog counts 364 variants, but there are fewer groups.
It's between 60 and 70.
questions.description: A catalog where every word comes with its own people.
questions.fun_fact: Those 68 languages belong to 11 different language families, as different from each other as Spanish and Chinese.

questions.question: The Kickapoo came from the Great Lakes and live in El Nacimiento, Coahuila. Why did Mexico give them land in the 19th century?
questions.answer: To defend the border from Apache raids
wrong_answers: To grow cotton for the army
To work in the silver mines
hints: It happened in the mid-19th century, in the north of the country.
They got land at the same time as the Mascogos, who also came from the United States.
The north suffered raids by nomadic peoples on horseback.
questions.description: A people who have traveled more miles than a truck on the highway to Laredo.
questions.fun_fact: The Kickapoo are a people of two nations: many spend part of the year in the United States and return to Coahuila.

questions.question: Arnulfo Quimare is an ultrarunner who lives in the canyons and is one of the heroes of Christopher McDougall's book “Born to Run”. Which state does he live in?
hints: It's a state in northern Mexico.
The Copper Canyon is there.
It's the largest state in the country.
questions.description: A man who turns any hill into a warm-up track.
questions.fun_fact: “Born to Run” became a worldwide hit and made running in minimalist sandals trendy.

questions.question: A famous fountain on Paseo de la Reforma shows a woman aiming a bow at the sky. Complete her name: Diana the…
hints: Her name tells you what she does.
She is named after the Roman goddess of the woods and the moon.
It's what you call someone who goes out hunting.
questions.description: A lady on Reforma who has been aiming at the sky for decades and her arm never gets tired.
questions.fun_fact: Her sculptor first called her “The Archer of the North Star.”

questions.question: Look at these balloons floating over Teotihuacán at sunrise. Why do people ride in them?

wrong_answers: To go fishing on a lake

From up high, everything looks tiny.
Down below there are huge ancient buildings.

questions.fun_fact: The flights leave very early because the wind is usually calmer at sunrise.

questions.question: This house in Chapultepec Park is called Los Pinos, and today it's a cultural center open to everyone. Who used to live here?

Whoever lived here changed every six years.
It was the person who governs the whole country.
questions.description: A house with a huge garden and very important neighbors in the woods.
questions.fun_fact: Lázaro Cárdenas was the first president to live there, in 1934; before that, the place was called Rancho La Hormiga.

questions.question: Look at this vessel from the Templo Mayor with the face of Tláloc. Why did the Mexica make offerings to him?
hints: It was very important for the milpas.
Farmers waited for it in planting season.
Without it, no water fell on the fields and the corn didn't grow.

questions.fun_fact: At the top of the Templo Mayor stood two shrines: one for Tláloc and one for Huitzilopochtli.

questions.question: Iztaccíhuatl, the “Sleeping Woman,” is the third-highest mountain in Mexico. About how tall is it?

It is just a little shorter than its neighbor, Popocatépetl.
questions.description: She has been napping for thousands of years, and nobody has managed to wake her up.
questions.fun_fact: The parts of Iztaccíhuatl are named after body parts: the head, the chest, the knees and the feet.

questions.question: Which of these places is NOT in Chapultepec Park (Bosque de Chapultepec)?
hints: One of them is in the Historic Center.

It's a white marble palace with orange domes.
questions.description: Ducks, rowboats and tamales: the classic Sunday outing for generations.
questions.fun_fact: Chapultepec Park is roughly twice the size of New York's Central Park.

questions.question: Necaxa was founded by workers of the power company and is named after a hydroelectric plant. Complete its nickname: los…
hints: Think about electricity.
They show up in the sky during a storm.
They flash down from the sky, and then the thunder rolls.
questions.description: A team with so much energy you could plug your fridge into it.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1930s, Necaxa was also called “the team of the Eleven Brothers” because they played so well together.

questions.question: I was US president and later Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, something no one else has done. I got a giant bathtub. Who am I?
hints: I was president from 1909 to 1913.
I was the first president to throw out the first pitch of a baseball season.
My last name has only four letters.
questions.description: A president who found the White House, quite literally, a bit of a tight fit.

questions.question: The stadium of Toluca's Diablos Rojos is one of the highest in Mexico. Roughly how high above sea level is it?
hints: Toluca is known as a very cold city.
It sits higher than Mexico City.

questions.description: The Red Devils play where even devils need a jacket.

questions.question: You go to the stadium dressed in the colors of the Rebaño Sagrado's uniform. Which of these colors are you NOT wearing?
hints: Rebaño Sagrado is another name for Chivas.
Their jersey has vertical stripes.
The jersey is red and white, and the shorts are navy blue.
questions.description: Check your closet before the game: the wrong outfit could start a feud in Guadalajara.
questions.fun_fact: Chivas are famous for fielding only Mexican players, a tradition that goes back almost their whole history.

questions.question: I'm a giant costume, usually an animal. I dance on the field before the game and get the porra cheering. What am I called in Mexico?
hints: There's a person inside me.
You also see me at kids' parties and outside stores.
I'm often the team's mascot.
questions.description: It has the hottest job in the stadium, and it never even kicks the ball.
questions.fun_fact: It can get extremely hot inside a botarga, so the people who wear them take breaks and drink lots of water.

questions.question: This women's soccer league started in 2017. Its first champion was Chivas, and América and Tigres play in it too. Which country is it in?
hints: Chivas is from Guadalajara.
Tigres is from Nuevo León.
It's the country of the Estadio Azteca.
questions.description: Here the players don't ask for permission: they ask for the ball.
questions.fun_fact: In the Liga MX Femenil, every team carries the name and colors of a club from the men's league.

questions.question: I'm short and reach just to the waist, I have sleeves and silver buttons, and mariachis wear me over the shirt. What am I?
hints: I'm part of the charro suit.

My name means “little jacket” in Spanish.

questions.fun_fact: The charro chaquetilla is usually short so the rider can move freely on horseback.

questions.question: Cocula, Jalisco, proudly calls itself the birthplace of some famous musicians. Which ones?
hints: They play as a group at parties and celebrations.

questions.description: A town in Jalisco that shows off its musicians the way other people show off their grandmas.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: The ranchera song is sung with mariachi and tells about life in the countryside. What place does its name come from?
hints: It's a place out in the countryside.
Cows, horses and chickens live there.
Cowboys work on one.

questions.fun_fact: Ranchera songs became famous around the world thanks to Mexican movies of the 1940s and 1950s.

questions.question: Jorge Negrete sang it in a 1941 film, and its title tells a Mexican state “¡no te rajes!”. Which state?

Its capital is Guadalajara.

questions.question: It's held in Aguascalientes, lasts almost a month between April and May, and is named after a saint who wrote a Gospel. Which fiesta is it?
hints: It claims to be the most famous fair in Mexico.

The saint is one of the four evangelists, along with Matthew, Luke and John.

questions.question: I wear a white terno embroidered with flowers, a rebozo and flowers in my hair, and I stomp the jarana facing my partner in a white filipina. Who am I?
hints: My clothes are cool and light, made for the heat and for big fiestas.

questions.question: Which of these things did the Maya goddess Ixchel NOT look after?

questions.question: The Bonampak murals in Chiapas show warriors, musicians and nobles. How long ago were they painted?

questions.question: I was made king of Palenque at age 12 and ruled for almost 70 years. In 1952 my tomb was found hidden inside a pyramid. Who am I?
hints: I was buried with my face covered by a green mask.

My Maya name means “shield.”

questions.fun_fact: Archaeologist Alberto Ruz spent four years clearing rubble from a secret staircase until he reached the tomb.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this round building at Chichén Itzá was used to watch the sky. What is it called?
hints: Its name comes from something it has inside.
Inside, it has a spiral staircase.
Its Spanish name is an animal that carries its house on its back.

questions.fun_fact: Some of El Caracol's windows point to where Venus sets on certain dates of the year.

questions.question: In 1519 he reached the coast of Veracruz with 16 animals like this one, the first the Mexica had ever seen. Who was he?
hints: He was a Spanish conquistador.

La Malinche was his interpreter.

questions.question: This stone of the goddess Coyolxauhqui turned up in 1978 in downtown Mexico City. In which museum can you see it today?
hints: The museum is a short walk from the Cathedral and the Zócalo.

questions.question: You're in the Zócalo, where the heart of Tenochtitlan once stood. About how long ago did the Spanish conquer it?

questions.question: It's only done for trusted customers, written down in a notebook, and typical of the corner shop. What is it?
questions.answer: Selling now so you pay later

Keeping a product aside for tomorrow

questions.question: Take a close look at this photo. What is it?

questions.question: If Mexico City counted its birthdays from when the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan, about how many candles would its cake have?

questions.question: Which of these rulers was NOT Aztec?
hints: Three of them ruled Tenochtitlan.

questions.question: The Mexica called it “itztli,” a black volcanic glass found in plenty near Teotihuacan. What did they mainly use it for?

questions.question: You're standing in front of the Pyramid of the Niches in El Tajín, Veracruz, and it's full of niches. What is a niche?

questions.question: Hellmann's is to mayonnaise as Tabasco is to…

questions.question: The adobe houses of Cuarenta Casas were built inside a cave in the mountains of Chihuahua. How long ago were they made?

It's the shortest month of the year.

questions.question: This woman is on the 100-peso bill and in this famous portrait from colonial times. What was she?
hints: Look at her clothes: no crown and no party dress.

questions.question: At a '90s party, the DJ plays nothing but Fey songs. Which of these can NOT come on?

questions.question: Los Teen Tops recorded “La plaga” and Enrique Guzmán “Popotitos”; in the 1960s these were called “refritos”. What was a refrito?

A bolero played at double speed
A Mexican movie theme turned into rock

The melody came from the United States; only the language changed.

questions.question: Maite Perroni played Lupita in “Rebelde” and sang in RBD. What was the group's lineup?
hints: There were six of them in total.
Anahí and Dulce María also sang in the group, alongside Maite.
There were as many boys as girls.

questions.question: Tijuana No! was born on the border in the late 1980s and shouted “Pobre de ti”. What did its music mix?
hints: It was fast music, with guitars and horns.
Its lyrics were protest songs.
One of its roots was born in Jamaica.

questions.fun_fact: Julieta Venegas played in Tijuana No! before going solo.

questions.question: In a Mazatec legend, the tlacuache (opossum) stole it from the gods by rolling it up in its tail, which is why its tail is bald. What did it steal?
hints: You need it to cook.
It gives heat and light.
The hair on the tlacuache's tail got burned off.

questions.question: It's a soft white powder that goes on a baby's skin after a bath, and Johnson's has sold it for over 100 years. What is it?
hints: It comes in a bottle with tiny holes in the lid.
It keeps skin dry so it doesn't get sore.
Its name comes from a very soft mineral.

questions.question: Ce Acatl Topiltzin, the priest-king of Tula, got drunk on pulque and fled his city in shame. Which rival god tricked him?
hints: He was a god of the night.

questions.question: We were the Popol Vuh gods' first try at making people. We talked nonsense, couldn't turn our heads, and water melted us away. Who are we?
hints: The gods wanted beings who would remember them and pray to them.

questions.question: She was the Tlaxcaltec water goddess, her name means “the one with the blue skirt,” and it's the old name of a volcano in Tlaxcala. Who is she?

She was thought of as Tláloc's partner.
Her name starts with “matlal,” which means dark blue in Nahuatl.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Matlalcueye ("owner of the blue skirt"), the Tlaxcalan water goddess and old name of La Malinche, checks out. But sources say she is a Tlaxcalan form of, or closely related to, Chalchiuhtlicue ("jade skirt"), which is one of the wrong answers. That makes the distractor arguable. Chalchiuhtlicue is also the deity usually called Tláloc's consort, so the hint "Tláloc's partner" fits both. I didn't check the volcano's height or the Puebla/Tlaxcala visibility; the Wikipedia figure I recall is about 4,461 m, which would fit "more than 4,400 m".

questions.question: In Mictlán, the dead crossed the Chiconahuapan River with the help of a dog. Which number is hidden in the river's Nahuatl name?

questions.question: It's the biggest ring road in Mexico City, has a “second deck,” and one stretch is called Boulevard Manuel Ávila Camacho. What is it?

questions.question: He started out as a child, sang “La incondicional,” and has a TV series about his life. What nickname is he known by?

questions.question: It was created for the 1968 Mexico City Olympics and runs about 17 km (11 miles) across the south of the capital. What is the Ruta de la Amistad?

A highway from the capital to Acapulco
A train linking the Olympic venues
hints: You can still see it from the car today.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Answer (sculpture corridor, ~17 km, Goeritz, 1968, south Periférico) is right and the wrong answers are wrong. But the fun fact says '19 sculptures by artists from five continents'. Sources say 19 stations on the route, plus 3 guest sculptures at Olympic venues (22 total), by 22 sculptors from 17 countries. So '19' is defensible for the route itself, but the 'five continents' claim and the artist count are loosely sourced. The hint 'over 10 m tall' is unverified, and some works are smaller.

Fact check: uncertain. Answer, 17 km, and Goeritz are right, and the wrong answers are wrong. The fun fact is shaky. Wikipedia says 22 sculptures (19 route stations plus 3 guest pieces at Olympic venues) from 17 countries. 'Five continents' appears only in Time Out. '19 sculptures' is accurate only for the route stations. I could not confirm the hint about works over 10 m.

questions.question: In the Churrigueresque baroque of New Spain, like the Sagrario Metropolitano, what job does the estípite do on a facade?
questions.answer: It acts as a column or pilaster
wrong_answers: It is the niche for a statue
It is the window of the choir
It is the arch over the door
hints: It repeats several times along the facade, standing upright.
Its shape looks like an upside-down pyramid.
It takes the place that a classical column would have in other styles.
questions.description: In the baroque, nobody settled for plain and simple, not even the facades.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish architect Jerónimo de Balbás made the estípite popular in Mexico with the Altar of the Kings in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

questions.question: It was born in Brazil, it scrubs burnt pots, and people once hung it on TV antennas. What is Bombril made of?
hints: If you leave it wet for a long time, it rusts.
The antenna trick worked because it carries electricity.
It's a metal made into very thin threads, like hairs.
questions.description: The only thing in the kitchen that can beat a pot burnt during Sunday lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Bombril became so famous in Brazil that “bombril” now means any metal scrubbing pad.

questions.question: The Chichimeca War lasted about 40 years and broke out over the roads to newly found mines in Zacatecas. What was dug out of them?
hints: The most famous coins of that time were made from this metal.
Taxco is famous for it too.
It's the metal of the second-place medal.
questions.description: A very, very long war over what the northern land was hiding.
questions.fun_fact: To settle the north, the Spanish sent Tlaxcalan families to live next to the Chichimecas.

questions.question: The Court of the Inquisition was set up in New Spain in 1571. About how many years did it last?
hints: It lasted almost the whole colonial era.
It ended just as Independence was about to be won.
It was abolished in 1820.
questions.description: A court so strict that even its building has a crooked corner.
questions.fun_fact: The Palace of the Inquisition has its entrance on a corner cut off at an angle, something very rare in Mexico City.

questions.question: At what point in a conversation do you say “ahí nos vidrios”?
hints: It's a funny, very Mexican way of saying something everyday.
It's a pun on a verb that has nothing to do with glass.
You say it right before you leave.
questions.description: A phrase that sounds like it came from a glass shop, but has nothing to do with windows.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has more puns like this one, such as saying “al ratón” (“to the mouse”) instead of “al rato” (“in a while”).

questions.question: Mexican actress Dolores del Río was a star of Hollywood silent movies. In which decade?
hints: It was long before color TV existed.
At the end of that same decade, movies with sound arrived.
It was the decade of the Charleston, which ended with the great crash of 1929.
questions.description: Before it could sing with mariachis, cinema had to learn to talk.
questions.fun_fact: Back in Mexico, Dolores del Río starred in “María Candelaria” (1943) alongside Pedro Armendáriz.

questions.question: My name was Adalberto Martínez, and I was a comedian and dancer of the Golden Age of Mexican cinema. What was my nickname?
hints: My nickname is a single word.
My nickname describes how I moved on the dance floor.
My nickname means the metal springs you find inside a mattress.
questions.description: A dancer who left every partner out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Clavillazo and Palillo, two of the other nicknames in the options, were also famous comedians in Mexican films of that era.

questions.question: I write poetry in Isthmus Zapotec, I was born in Juchitán, and from 2020 to 2022 I sat on the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Oaxaca, on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.
My poems have been translated into several languages.
My first name starts with the letter I.
questions.description: A poet who writes in two languages and took one of them all the way to New York.
questions.fun_fact: The UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues meets every year at UN headquarters in New York.

questions.question: I come from Nahuatl, and a country, its capital and a state next to that capital all carry me. What name am I?
hints: That neighboring state almost completely surrounds the capital.
It comes from the name of the Mexica, the people who founded Tenochtitlan.
Fans shout it at every match of the national team.
questions.description: A name more than 500 years old that is still just as famous.
questions.fun_fact: The country's official name is “Estados Unidos Mexicanos” (United Mexican States).

questions.question: Chapultepec combines “chapulín” (grasshopper) with “-tepec.” What kind of place is “-tepec” in Nahuatl?
hints: Popocatépetl has almost the same word in its name.
To reach Chapultepec Castle, you have to go up.
It's smaller than a mountain, but still tiring to climb.
questions.description: A grasshopper with a fancy address in the middle of Mexico City.
questions.fun_fact: The ancient glyph for Chapultepec shows a grasshopper standing on top of a hill.

questions.question: Volunteers around the world write me in hundreds of languages, and I even have a version in Nahuatl. What am I?
hints: Lots of people use me for homework.
Anyone can edit my articles, which cover almost any topic.
My logo is a globe made of jigsaw puzzle pieces.
questions.description: A project so huge that nobody has read all of it, not even the people who wrote it.
questions.fun_fact: Wikipedia in Nahuatl is called “Huiquipedia.”

questions.question: This museum in Guanajuato sits next to a cemetery, appears in luchador movies and is packed on Día de Muertos. What does it display?
hints: What's in its glass cases came out of the cemetery next door.
They are people from long ago who were preserved.
Egypt has them too, wrapped in bandages.
questions.description: A museum in Guanajuato that never goes out of style when November comes around.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody prepared them on purpose: they were preserved on their own by the dry, mineral-rich soil of the Santa Paula cemetery.

questions.question: It's a powder you mix with water, and it tastes like orange. In the 1960s, who made the drink Tang famous?
hints: They drank it in a place with no refrigerators and no fresh fruit.
They drank it far, far away from Earth.
It flew on the spacecraft of the Gemini program.
questions.description: A drink that has traveled more miles than your aunt.
questions.fun_fact: NASA didn't invent Tang: it was created in 1957 by William Mitchell, the same chemist who invented Pop Rocks popping candy.

questions.question: By the traditional count, how many niches does the Pyramid of the Niches at El Tajín, in Veracruz, have?
hints: Its number is thought to be linked to a calendar.
There are more than 300.
It's the number of days in a year that isn't a leap year.
questions.description: A pyramid from Veracruz with more little holes than a Swiss cheese.
questions.fun_fact: Next to El Tajín, the Voladores de Papantla perform, spinning upside down while hanging from a very tall pole.

questions.question: Xcaret is a park with underground rivers you can swim in, sea turtles and a big nighttime show. Which state is it in?
hints: Its coast faces the Caribbean Sea.
Cancún is in the same state.
Its capital is Chetumal.
questions.description: A park where even the rivers would rather travel underground.
questions.fun_fact: Where Xcaret stands today, there was once an ancient Maya port called Polé.

questions.question: It has canals, chinampas and trajineras. What does its Nahuatl name, Xochimilco, mean?
hints: It has a huge plant market.
Its name contains the word “xóchitl,” which is also a girl's name in Mexico.
The cempasúchil flower has the same word in its name.
questions.description: A Nahuatl tongue twister that chilangos say without blinking.
questions.fun_fact: Xochimilco has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, together with the Historic Center of Mexico City.

questions.question: A woman from Córdoba, Veracruz, locked up by the Inquisition, drew me in charcoal on her cell wall. She climbed onto me and vanished. What am I?
hints: The guard said the drawing was so good that all it needed was to move.
The guard saw her wave goodbye as the drawing began to drift away.
I have sails, and I need the wind to get anywhere.
questions.description: The most artistic escape in history: no file, no spoon, just a piece of charcoal.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican composer José Pablo Moncayo turned this legend into an opera: “La mulata de Córdoba.”

questions.question: I ride the roads at night and carry my hat in my hand, because I have nowhere to put it. Who am I?
hints: I travel on horseback, so I don't walk like other ghosts.
If you look at me from the front, you won't see my face.
I'm missing exactly the body part where a hat goes.
questions.description: A ghost who goes out for a stroll right when you want to sleep.
questions.fun_fact: The world's most famous headless horseman appears in an American story from 1820: “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” by Washington Irving.

questions.question: Which of these things did Mexican goalkeeper Jorge Campos NOT do?
questions.answer: Play for a club in Europe
hints: He was famous for his loud, brightly colored uniforms.
He sometimes went out to play as a striker for Pumas.
Outside Mexico, he only played for clubs like LA Galaxy and Chicago Fire.
questions.description: A goalkeeper so colorful that the balls got distracted before they reached the goal.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Campos was only about 1.68 m (5 ft 6 in) tall, very short for a goalkeeper, and he was still one of the best of his time.

questions.question: In an animated film, a boy and a skeleton sing “Un Poco Loco” at a talent show. Which film is it?
hints: It's a Pixar film that came out in 2017.
It takes place during the Day of the Dead.
The film is named after the boy's great-grandmother.
questions.description: A song so catchy that even skeletons dance to it.
questions.fun_fact: Coco won two Oscars: Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song, for “Remember Me.”

questions.question: I'm corn dough mixed into water, sometimes with cacao. In Tabasco and Chiapas, people take me to the fields and drink me cold from a jícara. What am I?
hints: It is very old: the Maya already drank it.
It is typical of the southeast, where the heat is fierce.
Its name is almost the same as the hominy stew served with radish and oregano, just one letter shorter.
questions.description: Long before soda existed, the Maya already had their go-to drink.
questions.fun_fact: Farmworkers carried pozol dough wrapped in banana leaves and mixed it with water at mealtime.

questions.question: If you walk across the Pons Fabricius in Rome, you step on stones laid there about… how many years ago?
hints: It crosses the Tiber River to reach an island in the middle of the river.
It was already standing when Julius Caesar lived in Rome.
It was finished in 62 BC.
questions.description: These stones have seen more feet go by than the front door of a shopping mall.
questions.fun_fact: The Pons Fabricius is the oldest bridge in Rome still in use almost exactly as it was built.

questions.question: Which of these tournaments is NOT run by Concacaf, Mexico's confederation?
hints: Mexico has played in this tournament, but as a guest.
El Tri reached the final of this tournament in 1993 and in 2001.
It's South America's tournament for national teams, won by Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay.
questions.description: A soccer geography test to see if you know which side of the map each trophy lives on.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico played the Copa América as a guest starting in 1993 (and again in 2024); in 1993 it finished runner-up, losing the final to Argentina.

questions.question: I paint my face green, white and red, put on a sombrero and shout “¡Sí se puede!” from the stands when El Tri is losing. Who am I?
hints: I'm not on the field.
I bought a ticket to get into the stadium.
I cheer for my team from the stands.
questions.description: Someone who has never kicked a ball at a World Cup, but ends up as tired as if they'd played all 90 minutes.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Sí se puede!” became famous in the 1970s with farm workers in the United States, long before it was heard in stadiums.

questions.question: He's nicknamed “Chucky” and played for PSV in the Netherlands and Napoli in Italy. What position does he play?
hints: He doesn't wear gloves.
He almost always plays near the other team's box.
His main job is scoring goals.
questions.description: A horror-movie nickname for a player who is nothing like a creepy doll.
questions.fun_fact: Hirving Lozano won the Italian league with Napoli in 2023, the club's first league title since the days of Maradona.

questions.question: It's Concacaf's tournament for national teams, played every two years, and its 2025 final was in Houston. Which country has won it the most times?
hints: It's one of the host countries of the 2026 World Cup.
It won the 2025 final 2-1.
Its players almost always wear a green jersey.
questions.description: A golden trophy that Concacaf teams fight over like the last tamal at the party.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico won the 2025 Gold Cup by beating the United States 2-1 in the final, bringing its Gold Cup titles to ten.

questions.question: El Tri lost to this team at the 2014 World Cup after a very controversial penalty, and “No era penal” was born. Which team was it?
hints: It was in the round of 16 at Brazil 2014.
It's a European team that has played three World Cup finals without winning one.
Arjen Robben went down in the box near the end of the match.
questions.description: The line millions of Mexicans still repeat, even though the referee never heard it.
questions.fun_fact: After the game, Robben admitted he had dived earlier in that match, though not for the penalty, and “No era penal” became a never-ending meme in Mexico.

questions.question: El Tri's big stadium in the south of Mexico City goes by several names. Which of these is NOT one of them?
hints: One of these names belongs to another stadium in the same city.
That other stadium is the home of the Pumas.
That other stadium hosted the 1968 Olympic Games.
questions.description: A stadium with more names than a kid whose grandma keeps making up nicknames.
questions.fun_fact: The Estadio Olímpico Universitario has a huge relief mural by Diego Rivera on its front.

questions.question: The Codex Nuttall is painted on deerskin, folds like a screen and dates from before the Spanish arrived. What does it mainly tell?
questions.answer: The family trees of the Mixtec lords
wrong_answers: The tributes paid by towns to Tenochtitlan
The routes of the Maya traders
hints: Its main characters have date names, like 8 Deer.
It shows weddings, births, journeys and conquests.
It traces who descended from whom among the ruling families of Oaxaca.
questions.description: A book with no loose pages that opens like an accordion, so you never lose your bookmark.
questions.fun_fact: Its star character is 8 Deer Jaguar Claw, a lord who united much of the Mixtec region around the year 1100.

questions.question: It was played with the hips on a long court with sloping walls, and a stone ring sat high on each wall. What happened if the ball went through the ring?
hints: It was incredibly hard to do.
The rings were very high and the ball barely fit through.
It was like a goal that ended the game on the spot.
questions.description: A sport where hands and feet had to sit on the bench.
questions.fun_fact: According to Spanish chroniclers, whoever did it could claim the cloaks and jewels of the spectators, who ran off so they wouldn't get caught!

questions.question: Founded in 1940, it is the winningest team in the Mexican Baseball League, and its great historic rival is the Tigres. Which team is it?
hints: It has won more than a dozen league championships.
Its games against the Tigres were called the “Guerra Civil” (Civil War).
Its name has a color and a character with horns.
questions.description: A team with more trophies than a grandpa has photos in the living room.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, the Diablos Rojos opened their new home in Mexico City: Estadio Alfredo Harp Helú.

questions.question: You're watching the Mexican Open tennis tournament, and between points the TV shows a famous bay. In which city is it played?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
In the mid-20th century it was the favorite beach getaway of Hollywood stars.
It's in the state of Guerrero.
questions.description: Rackets, sunscreen and a little sand in your sneakers.
