questions.question: If someone is called “a real Samson,” like the hero from the Bible, what do they have plenty of?
hints: It helps you carry all the grocery bags in without help.
The Samson of the Bible beat a lion with his bare hands.
It's what you train at the gym.
questions.description: A compliment that comes with a hairstyle attached.
questions.fun_fact: According to the story, Samson's secret was never cutting his hair; when Delilah had it cut, he lost his power.

questions.question: Joseph explained Pharaoh's dream: years of plenty would come, then years of hunger. How many years of hunger?
hints: In the dream there were fat cows and skinny cows, the same number of each.
It's the same number as the years of plenty.
It's the number of days in a week.
questions.description: The first harvest forecast in history came with skinny cows.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to that dream, Joseph stored up grain during the good years, and Egypt could even feed other peoples.

questions.question: I'm named after the first emperor of Rome. Which month am I?
hints: I'm a month with 31 days.
In many countries in the Northern Hemisphere, I'm a summer vacation month.
The emperor was Julius Caesar's adopted heir, and I'm the eighth month of the year.
questions.description: An emperor so important he still shows up on every calendar in the world.
questions.fun_fact: Before it was called August, the month was named “Sextilis,” because it was the sixth month of the old Roman calendar.

questions.question: What shape is a round arch, the typical arch of the Romans?
hints: Look closely at the name.
It's the shape of a rainbow.
Put two of them together and you get a whole wheel.
questions.description: The Romans put it everywhere, the way Grandma puts salt on everything.
questions.fun_fact: Round arches let the Romans build bridges and aqueducts that are still standing after 2,000 years.

questions.question: I'm from Carthage, and thanks to me the Romans saw elephants coming down the Alps. Who am I?
hints: I was Rome's worst enemy in the Punic Wars.
Carthage was in North Africa, in what is now Tunisia.
My name starts with H and ends in “-bal”.
questions.description: The first general who thought the best way to cross snowy mountains was by elephant.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the elephants survived the Alps, but nearly all died in the cold winter that followed; ancient historians say only one was left.

questions.question: I'm a metal eagle on top of a pole, and I go everywhere with Roman soldiers. What am I for?
wrong_answers: To announce the emperor is coming
hints: It was made of silver or gold and looked after very carefully.
Each group of soldiers had its own, and losing it was a disgrace.
Soldiers followed it into battle, like a flag.
questions.description: A bird that never flew, yet still conquered half the world.
questions.fun_fact: When Germanic warriors captured three eagles in the year 9 AD, Rome spent decades hunting for them until it got them back.

questions.question: Roughly how many kilometers of paved stone roads did the Roman Empire build?
hints: They ran all the way from Britain to Egypt and Syria.
It's more than the distance once around the Earth.
It would be enough to circle the planet about two times.
questions.description: No wonder all roads lead to Rome: the Romans paved them themselves.
questions.fun_fact: The Appian Way, built more than 2,300 years ago, can still be walked on near Rome.

questions.question: Legend says I searched for the Fountain of Youth and found a peninsula that I named Florida. Who am I?
hints: I was a Spanish conquistador and governor of Puerto Rico.
My legendary Fountain of Youth is the goal in the film “Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides”.
The last word of my name is the Spanish word for the king of the jungle.
questions.description: The first explorer to travel thousands of kilometers just to stop having birthdays.
questions.fun_fact: No document from his own time links his voyage to the fountain: the chronicler Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo tied the legend to him in 1535, after his death.

questions.question: In which country do most saigas, the antelopes with huge, droopy noses, live?
hints: It is a Central Asian country with huge steppes.
It was part of the Soviet Union.
It is the largest landlocked country in the world.
questions.description: An antelope that seems to be wearing a borrowed elephant trunk.
questions.fun_fact: Saigas were already grazing next to mammoths during the last Ice Age.

questions.question: It is related to the raccoon, has a long, very flexible nose, and walks with its ringed tail held high. What animal is it?
hints: It lives in the forests and jungles of the Americas, from Mexico to Argentina.
It travels in big groups and digs for insects with its snout.
In Colombia it is called a “cusumbo”.
questions.description: A raccoon that decided its nose deserved more of the spotlight.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, someone who goes around alone is called a “cusumbo solo” (lone coati), like the male coatis that live apart from the group.

questions.question: Germany, 1923: a loaf of bread costs billions of marks and prices rise every hour. What did many people use banknotes for?
hints: The banknotes were worth almost nothing.
Using them was cheaper than buying the thing they replaced.
They kept homes cozy and warm in winter.
questions.description: A time when going out for bread cost more in the afternoon than in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: In 1923, some German children made kites and toys out of bundles of worthless banknotes.

questions.question: This is the symbol of the ruble, the currency of Russia. In Russian, what sound does that letter make?
hints: Russia doesn't use the same alphabet as English.
In Russian, the currency's name starts with this letter.
It sounds like the first letter of “ruble”.
questions.description: A tiny symbol for the money of a huge country.
questions.fun_fact: Russia only officially picked the ₽ symbol in 2013.

questions.question: I make every US dollar bill, in Washington and in Fort Worth, Texas, but not a single coin. What am I?
hints: I work with paper, not metal.
A different office makes the coins.
My name lists two old ways of putting ink on paper.
questions.description: A factory where machines do what we all dream of: make real money.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, the Mint makes the coins, but a different office prints the paper money.

questions.question: Peso is to Colombia as baht is to…
hints: It is a country in Southeast Asia.
It is famous for its golden Buddhist temples, and the elephant is its national symbol.
It used to be called Siam.
questions.description: A currency with a name so short you've paid before you finish saying it.
questions.fun_fact: Thai banknotes always show the face of the king.

questions.question: I held a post of total trust: anyone who wanted to poison the king's drink had to get past me first. Who am I?
hints: I worked mostly at banquets.
My job had to do with wine.
My title comes from the vessel the king drank from.
questions.description: The castle worker with the tastiest job and the riskiest one, both at once.
questions.fun_fact: In the Bible, Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes.

questions.question: An old legend says the material in this photo was born when sailors lit a fire on the sand of a beach. Who were they?
hints: They were great sailors of the Mediterranean Sea in ancient times.
They lived where Lebanon is today and traded all around the Mediterranean.
Their name starts with “Ph”, and they are credited with the first alphabet.
questions.description: A beach bonfire that ended much better than with sand in your shoes.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder told the legend: the sailors rested their pots on blocks of natron, and the heat melted the sand into glass.

questions.question: Cellophane, used to wrap flowers and gift baskets, was invented by accident in 1908. What was its inventor trying to make?
wrong_answers: A bag to keep bread fresh
hints: Its inventor was a Swiss chemist in the early 20th century.
He wanted to make something waterproof by coating it with viscose, a material made from wood pulp.
The story goes that he saw wine spilled in a restaurant and wanted a cloth that wouldn't get dirty.
questions.description: Clear, crinkly and born from a plan that went completely backwards.
questions.fun_fact: Swiss chemist Jacques Brandenberger tried to give cloth a waterproof coating, but the coating kept peeling off as a clear sheet, and that is how cellophane was born.

questions.question: In which decade did clear sticky tape on a roll, the kind used to wrap presents, first go on sale?
hints: An engineer at the US company 3M created it.
It became popular during an economic crisis, when people fixed things instead of buying new ones.
It came out during the years of the Great Depression.
questions.description: The invention that rescues badly wrapped presents and torn books and never asks for anything in return.
questions.fun_fact: Before this, its inventor Richard Drew had created masking tape so car painters could paint neat two-color stripes.

questions.question: Complete: in “Austin Powers,” Dr. Evil's tiny clone is called Mini-…
hints: He was played by Verne Troyer, an actor who was 81 cm (2 ft 8 in) tall.
He is identical to his creator, but pocket-sized.
Dr. Evil sees him as a tiny version of himself.
questions.description: A villain so evil he had a pocket-sized copy made of himself.
questions.fun_fact: Dr. Evil is a parody of Blofeld, the 007 villain who is always stroking a white cat.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: GPS stands for “Global ___ System”.
hints: It works with satellites that circle the Earth.
It needs signals from at least four satellites to work properly.
The word comes from “position”.
questions.description: A gadget that makes getting lost almost impossible, even for a distracted spy.
questions.fun_fact: GPS was created by the US military, and today almost every phone in the world uses it.

questions.question: At the start of “GoldenEye”, 007 bungee jumps off a huge dam. In which country is that dam in real life?
hints: The dam is called Verzasca.
It is in the Alps, in a country with no coastline.
It is in the canton of Ticino, where people speak Italian.
questions.description: A jump so long that your stomach stays at the top and waits for you.
questions.fun_fact: The jump from the Verzasca Dam, about 220 m (720 ft) high, was voted the best movie stunt of all time in a poll.

questions.question: What is the Walther PPK that James Bond carries?
hints: It is made by a German company founded in 1886.
It appears in his hand on many of the movie posters.
It is his usual weapon.
questions.description: A name with more secret-code letters than an airport's Wi-Fi password.
questions.fun_fact: In “Dr. No”, M makes Bond swap his old Beretta for the Walther PPK.

questions.question: When are the Winter Paralympics held, compared with the Winter Olympics?
questions.answer: Shortly after, in the same host city
wrong_answers: A year before, in another city
At the same time, on the same slopes
Two years later, in another country
hints: Paralympic and Olympic athletes don't share the slopes at the same time.
They are never held before the Olympic Games.
The same venues are used twice in the same winter.
questions.description: Athletes who get down a mountain faster than you get down the stairs.
questions.fun_fact: The first Winter Paralympics were held in 1976 in Örnsköldsvik, Sweden.

questions.question: I sit on two blades with a short stick in each hand: I push with its spikes and hit with its blade. Which Paralympic sport am I?
hints: It is played on an ice rink, in teams.
There are goalkeepers, and players score goals.
It is the Paralympic version of a sport that is hugely popular in Canada.
questions.description: A sport where sitting down doesn't mean sitting still.
questions.fun_fact: Sled hockey was born in Sweden in the early 1960s.

questions.question: Which of these sports had still NOT made its Winter Olympics debut by 1994?
hints: It became popular with young people in the 1980s and 1990s.
It made its debut at the Games in Nagano, Japan.
You ride down the mountain with both feet on a single board.
questions.description: A trip back in time to 1994, when ski clothes came in neon colors.
questions.fun_fact: Curling also came back as an official Olympic sport at Nagano 1998.

questions.question: You're in Sapporo, Japan, famous for its snow sculpture festival. In which year did it host the Winter Olympics?
hints: They were the first Winter Games ever held in Asia.
It was more than 20 years before Nagano hosted its own Games.
It was early in the 1970s.
questions.description: A city where the statues are made of snow and the beer is named after it.
questions.fun_fact: The Sapporo Snow Festival began in 1950, when a group of students built six snow statues.

questions.question: Guess who: I founded a film studio in 1915, and for decades my last name sat in a logo with searchlights and a fanfare. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Hungary and came to the United States as a baby.
My studio merged with Twentieth Century Pictures in 1935.
My last name is also a clever animal with a bushy tail.
questions.description: A last name that spent decades on the big screen, until someone took it off the sign.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, after Disney bought it, the studio was renamed 20th Century Studios and dropped the word “Fox”.

questions.question: Before the bitten apple, Apple's first logo, from 1976, showed a scientist sitting under a tree. Who was he?
hints: He was English and lived in the 17th century.
He came up with the famous laws of motion.
Legend says a piece of fruit falling near him got him thinking about gravity.
questions.description: An apple that nobody dared to finish.
questions.fun_fact: Rob Janoff, who designed the bitten apple logo, said he added the bite so nobody would mistake the apple for a cherry.

questions.question: The Black Stone, set in silver, is one of the most revered relics of Islam. Which building is it set into?
hints: It is in Saudi Arabia.
Pilgrims try to touch or kiss it as they walk in circles around a building.
It sits in one corner of a large cube covered in black cloth.
questions.description: A stone in a silver frame, like grandma's photo but with millions of visitors a year.
questions.fun_fact: The Black Stone is broken into several pieces, which the silver frame holds together.

questions.question: On the umrah in Mecca, you walk around the Kaaba. How many times do you have to go around it?
hints: It's an odd number.
It's a prime number.
It's as many laps as there are days in a week.
questions.description: A walk in circles where nobody gets lost, even with thousands of people around.
questions.fun_fact: Unlike the Hajj, the umrah can be done at any time of year, which is why it's called the “lesser pilgrimage”.

questions.question: The Holy Door of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican only opens in Jubilee years. What is it made of?
hints: It's a metal.
It's not a pure metal but a mix of metals.
It's the metal of the third-place medal.
questions.description: A door that stays shut for years, and nobody ever asks the doorman for the key.
questions.fun_fact: Today's Holy Door, with 16 panels, was made by the sculptor Vico Consorti and put in place for the 1950 Jubilee.

questions.question: I'm a round building with a blue roof in Beijing, where emperors prayed for good harvests. What am I?
hints: I'm in China and I'm more than 500 years old.
Only the emperor could lead the most important ceremonies of the year here.
My name refers to what is above the clouds.
questions.description: Chinese emperors also had a favorite place to ask for favors.
questions.fun_fact: Its main building, the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, is said to have been built without a single nail.

questions.question: The top level of the Pont du Gard, a giant Roman bridge in France, didn't carry people but…
hints: The Romans finished it almost 2,000 years ago.
The Romans built it to supply the city of Nîmes.
It is part of an aqueduct.
questions.description: A bridge so fancy it wasn't even built for people.
questions.fun_fact: The aqueduct the Pont du Gard belongs to was about 50 km (31 miles) long, with a slope so gentle the water flowed down almost unnoticed.

questions.question: Who meets in the National Capitol in Bogotá?
hints: The United States also has a Capitol that does the same job.
Laws are debated and passed there.
It is the seat of the Congress of the Republic.
questions.description: A building where people talk so much they should be charged by the word.
questions.fun_fact: Work on the National Capitol began in 1848 and wasn't finished until 1926, almost 80 years later!

questions.question: The Greek writer Philo of Byzantium is credited with one of the first versions of a famous list. Which list?
questions.answer: The Seven Wonders of the World
wrong_answers: The Nine Muses of the Arts
hints: Philo lived more than 2,000 years ago.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were on it.
The only one still standing is the Great Pyramid of Giza.
questions.description: Long before internet rankings, the ancient Greeks were already making their own “top” lists.
questions.fun_fact: The original list didn't call them “wonders” but “theamata”, something like “things you must see”.

questions.question: The degu is a rodent that more and more people keep as a pet. In which country does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in South America.
It lives in dry scrubland west of the Andes mountains.
Its name comes from Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche people.
questions.description: A rodent with a tail like a paintbrush, as if it escaped from a box of watercolors.
questions.fun_fact: Degus can't eat sugar: they get diabetes very easily.

questions.question: I'm Hanno, a white elephant. In 1514, I traveled from Lisbon to Rome as a gift. Who kept me as a pet?
hints: By 1514, Rome hadn't had an emperor for about a thousand years.
My owner lived in the middle of Rome and was very important to Catholics.
My owner's name was Leo X.
questions.description: Once upon a time, there was a pet so big it couldn't fit through any door.
questions.fun_fact: Hanno is said to have knelt before his owner and sprayed the crowd with water from his trunk.

questions.question: The caduceus is to Mercury as what object is to Abundantia, the Roman goddess of prosperity?
hints: It is always drawn overflowing.
Fruit, flowers and grain pour out of it without end.
It is shaped like a horn.
questions.description: Being the goddess of prosperity also means carrying the right accessory.
questions.fun_fact: According to myth, the cornucopia was the horn of the goat Amalthea, who fed baby Jupiter with her milk.

questions.question: Named after the Roman god of the underworld, it was the ninth planet until it was reclassified in 2006. What is Pluto now?
hints: It still circles the Sun, not another planet.
It is round, but it hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects.
It's a new category, created in 2006, for worlds that are round but small.
questions.description: Kicked out of the planet club, and nobody even called to tell it.
questions.fun_fact: Pluto got its name in 1930 from Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old English girl.

questions.question: After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, what type of government did England become?
hints: There was still a king and a queen.
But the king could no longer do whatever he wanted.
Parliament and a 1689 Bill of Rights put limits on the monarch.
questions.description: A revolution so polite that people even call it “glorious.”
questions.fun_fact: After the revolution, William III and Mary II ruled together, though William was the one who ran the government.

questions.question: Corgis, Queen Elizabeth II's favorite dogs, are famous for having legs that are…
hints: The breed comes from Wales.
Long ago they herded cows by nipping at their heels, and that is how they dodged the kicks.
They look like a furry sausage with big ears.
questions.description: A dog that has visited more palaces than many presidents.
questions.fun_fact: Elizabeth II owned more than 30 corgis during her life.

questions.question: What is the name of the money used in Japan?
hints: It is an Asian currency with a very short name.
Its symbol looks like a letter with two little lines across it.
Its name has three letters and starts with Y.
questions.description: A letter that put on two belts to go to work in Tokyo.
questions.fun_fact: China uses almost the same ¥ symbol for its yuan, so you have to check which country you're in.

questions.question: It is the currency of South Africa, and its name comes from a ridge rich in gold. What is it called?
hints: Its name comes from Afrikaans, a language that grew out of Dutch.
Nelson Mandela appears on its banknotes.
It has four letters and starts with R.
questions.description: A currency born in a mountain full of gold, just as it should be.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2012, every rand banknote has shown the face of Nelson Mandela.

questions.question: I'm the castle of the very first Disneyland park, in California. Which princess am I named after?
hints: Her movie came out four years after the park opened.
Her story has three good fairies and one wicked one.
She pricked her finger on a spinning wheel and slept for a very long time.
questions.description: A castle where dreams come true… and so does the long wait.
questions.fun_fact: The Disneyland castle is only about 23 m (77 ft) tall, but it looks taller because the bricks get smaller toward the top.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: It has bellows that open and close.
It is the star instrument of Argentine tango.
It looks like an accordion, but it is square and has buttons on both sides.
questions.description: An instrument that takes a deep breath before getting dramatic.
questions.fun_fact: The bandoneon was invented in Germany to play church music, and ended up as the star of tango.

questions.question: The muiñeira, a dance from Galicia whose name means “miller's wife”, is traditionally played on what?
hints: It's music for playing outdoors, while walking through the village.
One of the instruments has a bag that the player fills by blowing.
Galicia shares its star instrument with Scotland.
questions.description: A dance named after a job, with the heart of a village party.
questions.fun_fact: The muiñeira is usually in 6/8 time, the same bouncy rhythm as many Celtic dances.

questions.question: Which sauce gave its name to the group of Spanish sisters who sang “Aserejé” in 2002?
hints: It's a sauce people often put on burgers and hot dogs.
It isn't green or yellow.
It's made from tomatoes.
questions.description: A pop group named after something you squirt on your fries.
questions.fun_fact: They got the name because their dad, a flamenco guitarist, was known as “El Tomate” (“The Tomato”).

questions.question: In what year were the MTV Video Music Awards first handed out?
hints: The MTV channel already existed.
It was in the same decade that the album “Thriller” came out.
At that first show, Madonna sang “Like a Virgin”.
questions.description: An award whose trophy is an astronaut, in case the stars didn't already think they were from another planet.
questions.fun_fact: In 2017 the trophy's name changed from “Moonman” to “Moon Person”.

questions.question: In which decade did “MTV Unplugged”, the famous acoustic concert show, begin?
hints: The MTV channel already existed.
Nirvana recorded one of its most famous concerts there in 1993.
It started when the MTV channel was only eight years old.
questions.description: Unplug that electric guitar: today we're playing it the old-fashioned way.
questions.fun_fact: Shakira recorded her own “MTV Unplugged” in 1999 and won a Grammy for it.

questions.question: When Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPod in 2001, he promised “1,000 songs in your…” what?
hints: Jobs wanted to show off how small the device was.
It's also a place where you keep coins.
Your jeans usually have a few of them.
questions.description: The gadget that squeezed your whole music collection into something about the size of a deck of cards.
questions.fun_fact: Apple stopped selling its last iPod model in 2022.

questions.question: The Jackson 5 became the first group whose first four Motown singles all reached No. 1 in the US. In what year?
hints: One of those four hits was “ABC.”
Michael Jackson was still a child.
It was the same year the Beatles broke up.
questions.description: Five brothers who never fought over the microphone, or so we were told.
questions.fun_fact: Those four hits were “I Want You Back,” “ABC,” “The Love You Save” and “I'll Be There.”

questions.question: I'm from Jalisco, Mexico, I sing corridos tumbados, and in 2023 “Ella baila sola” made me famous worldwide. Who am I?
hints: I have a thin mustache and a hairstyle you can't miss.
I sang “Ella baila sola” with the group Eslabon Armado.
Half of my stage name is the Spanish word for “feather.”
questions.description: Big hats, guitars and millions of streams: the corrido became the sound in headphones across half the planet.
questions.fun_fact: “Peso pluma” is Spanish for featherweight, a boxing weight class; his real name is Hassan Emilio Kabande Laija.

questions.question: This avenue in Madrid was begun in 1910 and is called “Madrid's Broadway” because of its theaters. What is it?
hints: Musicals like “The Lion King” have played there.
At one end stands the Metropolis Building, with its dome and a winged statue.
In Spanish, its two-word name means “great way” or “big road.”
questions.description: A street where people on the sidewalk sing more than the drivers honk.
questions.fun_fact: “The Lion King” in Madrid is one of the longest-running musicals ever staged in Spain.

questions.question: The title of the musical “Chitty Chitty Bang Bang” copies the sound of… what?
hints: It's a 1968 musical film with a flying invention.
The hero is an odd inventor with two children.
That “bang bang” comes from under the hood.
questions.description: A title that sounds more like a noise than a word.
questions.fun_fact: The story was written by Ian Fleming, the same author who wrote the James Bond novels.

questions.question: Which country was Stieg Larsson from, the author of the “Millennium” series with hacker Lisbeth Salander?
hints: It's a country in northern Europe, with very long winters.
Its capital is spread across many islands.
It's the home country of ABBA and of the Nobel Prizes.
questions.description: A country where winters are so long you have time to read a whole book series.
questions.fun_fact: Stieg Larsson died in 2004 before his series came out, and it went on to sell tens of millions of books around the world.

questions.question: Conan Doyle is to “A Study in Scarlet” as Wilkie Collins is to…
hints: It's an English novel from 1868.
Its plot centers on the theft of a diamond brought from India.
Its title names something that shines in the night sky.
questions.description: Elementary, dear player: here even the answer has an alibi.
questions.fun_fact: T. S. Eliot called “The Moonstone” the first, the longest and the best of modern English detective novels.

questions.question: I'm a luxury pen brand born in Hamburg; I engrave 4810 on my nibs and my logo is a snowy peak. Which mountain gave me my name?
hints: The number is its height in meters.
It's in the Alps.
Its name means “white mountain.”
questions.description: A luxury pen that writes with its head in the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: Although it is named after a mountain between France and Italy, the brand was born in Germany in 1906.

questions.question: You're setting up a fish tank. Which of these does NOT help put more oxygen in the water?
hints: Think about what each thing is for.
Plants do for water what trees do for the air.
Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
questions.description: Fish don't ask for much: water, food, and someone who remembers the air.
questions.fun_fact: The bubbles from an air pump help mostly because they stir the water's surface, which is where oxygen gets in.

questions.question: The guppy is a famous aquarium fish with a colorful tail. Where does it originally come from?
hints: Today it lives in rivers all over the world, because people brought it there to eat mosquito larvae.
One of its natural homes is the island of Trinidad.
It is native to rivers in Venezuela and Guyana.
questions.description: A tiny fish that has seen more of the world than most tourists.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Robert Guppy, a naturalist who sent specimens from Trinidad to the British Museum in the 19th century.

questions.question: A famous legend says a hidden “Hall of Records” lies beneath this statue. Who supposedly left it there?
hints: It's a modern legend, not something archaeologists have found.
According to the legend, they came to Egypt fleeing a great disaster.
Plato wrote that their island sank into the sea.
questions.description: A library so secret it doesn't even have opening hours.
questions.fun_fact: American psychic Edgar Cayce made this idea famous in the 1930s, but no such hall has ever been found.

questions.question: Monks Mound, near St. Louis (USA), is a huge earthen pyramid from ancient Cahokia. Who built it?
hints: It was built almost a thousand years ago, before Europeans arrived.
Its builders lived beside the Mississippi River.
They were Indigenous people from that very region.
questions.description: A pyramid made of nothing but dirt and a lot of patience.
questions.fun_fact: Around the year 1100, Cahokia may have had as many people as London did at the same time.

questions.question: I'm a 1989 movie: an English teacher has his students stand on their desks and call him “O Captain! My Captain!” What am I?
hints: Robin Williams plays the teacher.
It's set at a very strict boarding school, where the students meet in a cave to read poetry in secret.
The title names a secret club of poets who are no longer alive.
questions.description: A literature class where the desks double as ladders.
questions.fun_fact: “O Captain! My Captain!” is a poem by Walt Whitman written in honor of Abraham Lincoln.

questions.question: Kipling, author of “The Jungle Book,” wrote a poem of advice that ends “…you'll be a Man, my son!” What is it called?
hints: It is written as a father's advice to his son.
It is a list of hard situations and how to face them.
Its title is the two-letter word that begins many of its lines.
questions.description: A poem that sounds like one of Dad's lectures, only in its fancy clothes.
questions.fun_fact: Two lines of this poem are written above the players' entrance to Centre Court at Wimbledon.

questions.question: The Italian sonnet ends with two of these stanzas, and Dante wrote the “Divine Comedy” in them. What are they called?
hints: A sonnet has 14 lines.
Before them, this sonnet has two stanzas of four lines each.
Its name comes from the number of lines it has.
questions.description: A stanza that shows up late to the sonnet, but just in time for the big finish.
questions.fun_fact: In the “Divine Comedy” the tercets are linked: the rhyme of each middle line comes back in the next tercet.

questions.question: How many syllables does a hendecasyllable line of poetry have?
hints: It is the classic line of the Italian and Spanish sonnet.
Dante wrote the whole Divine Comedy in lines of this length.
Its Greek prefix is the same as in “hendecagon.”
questions.description: A line of poetry that takes counting on its fingers very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Dante’s Divine Comedy has more than 14,000 lines, almost all of them hendecasyllables.

questions.question: In ancient Greek, “practice” is to “doing” as “theory” is to…
hints: Think of someone sitting in the stands at a stadium.
It shares a root with the word “theater”.
It’s what a spectator does.
questions.description: Something that works perfectly every time, until you actually try it.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Greece, “theoroi” were envoys who traveled to festivals and oracles to watch, then came home to report what they had seen.

questions.question: Albert Camus championed it, used the myth of Sisyphus, and said we look for meaning in a universe that doesn't answer. What school of thought is it?
hints: Its great champion won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
For Camus, we must imagine Sisyphus happy.
Its name comes from a word for something that makes no sense at all.
questions.description: A philosophy made for Monday mornings.
questions.fun_fact: Camus played goalkeeper as a young man in Algeria and said that what he knew about morality he owed to the sport.

questions.question: Complete the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “All human beings are born free and ___ in dignity and rights.”
hints: The declaration was adopted in 1948.
Nobody is worth more than anyone else.
In math, it is written with the sign “=”.
questions.description: A text everyone quotes and almost nobody has read all the way through.
questions.fun_fact: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is one of the most translated documents in the world, available in more than 500 languages.

questions.question: Diprotodon, as big as a hippo, lived in Australia until about 40,000 years ago. What group of animals did it belong to?
hints: Its group is common in Australia today.
Its closest living relatives are wombats and koalas.
Its babies grew up in a pouch, like baby kangaroos.
questions.description: Australia has always had strange animals, but this one was huge too.
questions.fun_fact: It weighed about 2.5 tonnes (5,500 lb), more than many pickup trucks.

questions.question: In which period did the first looms for weaving cloth appear?
hints: It was the same period in which farming began.
The first fabrics were made from plant fibers, like oak bark or flax.
Its name means “new stone.”
questions.description: Before the loom, fashion was all fur and no seams.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the oldest surviving woven fabrics are about 8,600 years old and were found at Çatalhöyük, Turkey; they were made from oak bark fibers.

questions.question: On what day of the year does the King of Sweden hand out the Nobel Prizes in Stockholm?
hints: It's a cold, dark month in Sweden.
The date honors Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes.
Alfred Nobel died on this day in 1896, in the last month of the year.
questions.description: A king, a fancy hall and scientists who, for one night, dress better than they did at their own wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The Nobel Peace Prize is the exception: it isn't handed out in Stockholm but in Oslo, Norway.

questions.question: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to the blue LED, which made white LED light bulbs possible. In which country were its three winners born?
hints: It's a country in Asia.
It's a chain of islands with many volcanoes and earthquakes.
Its flag is a red circle on a white background.
questions.description: A color that kept everyone waiting for thirty years and finally lit up the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: Red and green LEDs had existed for decades; blue was the missing color needed to mix white light.

questions.question: Which king of Spain, a grandson of the Catholic Monarchs, was also Holy Roman Emperor?
hints: He was born in Ghent in 1500.
He spent his last years in retirement at the Monastery of Yuste.
In Spain he was the first king of his name, but as emperor he was the fifth.
questions.description: A king with so much land that, people said, the sun never set on it.
questions.fun_fact: In his retirement at Yuste, Charles V brought along a collection of clocks that he loved to adjust.

questions.question: I'm the giant spaceship where humans float around in chairs while a robot cleans up Earth. What's my name?
hints: I appear in a Pixar movie.
My captain is human, but my autopilot is a villain shaped like a ship's wheel.
EVE brings a small plant on board me in the movie about the robot WALL·E.
questions.description: A luxury cruise where the buffet lasts 700 years and nobody ever gets up from their seat.
questions.fun_fact: In WALL·E, the Axiom's passengers have gone so long without walking that their bones have grown weak.

questions.question: In time travel stories, what is the idea called that a tiny change in the past causes huge consequences?
hints: A scientist who studied the weather made the idea famous.
It's said that a flap of wings in one place could cause a tornado somewhere else.
The animal has colorful wings and used to be a caterpillar.
questions.description: For anyone who ever wanted to go back in time to fix something and made it worse.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from meteorologist Edward Lorenz, who studied why the weather is so hard to predict.

questions.question: I studied at Cambridge, married Jane, and an actor won an Oscar for playing me in a movie. Who am I?
hints: I was a British physicist of the 20th century.
I studied black holes and the origin of the universe.
I spoke with an electronic voice and used a wheelchair.
questions.description: A love story with more physics than kissing.
questions.fun_fact: Stephen Hawking was born on January 8, 1942, exactly 300 years after Galileo died.

questions.question: Who directed “Halloween” (1978), the Michael Myers movie, and also composed its music?
hints: He is American and, besides directing, makes music with synthesizers.
He also directed “The Thing” (1982).
He directed “Escape from New York,” starring Kurt Russell.
questions.description: A man who turned October 31 into more than just trick-or-treating.
questions.fun_fact: Carpenter composed the music for “Halloween” in just a few days because there was no money to hire a composer.

questions.question: How many times has Clint Eastwood won the Oscar for Best Director?
hints: One of those awards came with a western.
He won more than once, but fewer times than John Ford, who holds the record with four.
He won for “Unforgiven” and “Million Dollar Baby”.
questions.description: A Wild West cowboy who swapped his revolver for a director's chair.
questions.fun_fact: Clint Eastwood also composed some of the music for several of his films, such as “Million Dollar Baby”.

questions.question: I'm a Batman villain. Heath Ledger won an Oscar in 2009 for playing me in “The Dark Knight”. Who am I?
hints: My face is very pale.
I have green hair and a huge painted-on smile.
I always ask: “Why so serious?”
questions.description: Gotham City has plenty of villains, but only one keeps a golden statuette in the trophy case.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, Joaquin Phoenix also won an Oscar for playing this same villain.

questions.question: You've just won an Oscar and you walk up on stage. How long are you asked to keep your speech to before the music starts playing?
hints: The ceremony already runs for more than three hours.
It's less than one minute.
It's three quarters of a minute.
questions.description: Thanking your mom, your dog and your first-grade teacher comes with a time limit.
questions.fun_fact: The longest Oscar speech was given by Greer Garson in 1943, and it went on for more than five minutes.

questions.question: I was born in Jerusalem, studied at Harvard, and won the Oscar for Best Actress in 2011 playing a ballerina. Who am I?
hints: I won for “Black Swan.”
I also played Jane Foster in the Thor movies.
I played Padmé Amidala in “Star Wars.”
questions.description: An actress who took ballet so seriously she nearly wore out her pointe shoes.
questions.fun_fact: For “Black Swan,” she trained in ballet for about a year.

questions.question: George W. Bush was president of the US, and so was George H. W. Bush, who served before him. What was George H. W. Bush to him?
hints: Notice that they share almost the same name.
George H. W. Bush served from 1989 to 1993, just eight years before him.
John Quincy Adams was related in the same way to President John Adams.
questions.description: Some families hand down the farm; this one handed down the White House.
questions.fun_fact: His brother Jeb Bush also tried to become president in 2016, but he didn't win his party's nomination.

questions.question: A bridge of about 55 km (34 miles) in China reaches an artificial island out at sea. How does the road continue after the island?
hints: Huge ships pass through this area.
The island was built to switch from one kind of route to another.
Vehicles keep going, but below the water.
questions.description: A bridge so long it changed its plans halfway across.
questions.fun_fact: The undersea section is about 6.7 km (4 miles) long and lets big ships pass without hitting the bridge.

questions.question: The piers of the Confederation Bridge in Canada are cone-shaped at the waterline. Why?
questions.answer: To break up the sea ice
wrong_answers: To make power from the waves
To give seals a place to rest
hints: Winters there are extremely cold.
The cones protect the piers from a force of nature that pushes against them.
They work like the front of an icebreaker ship.
questions.description: A Canadian bridge with the pointiest feet in the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: At almost 13 km (8 miles), it is the longest bridge in the world over water that freezes.

questions.question: Complete: “Temples” are to ears as the “bridge” of a pair of glasses is to…
hints: Think about where glasses rest on your face.
After a whole day wearing glasses, two small red marks are left there.
It's what you pinch shut when something smells bad.
questions.description: A bridge nobody walks across, but everyone looks through.
questions.fun_fact: The first glasses, made in Italy around the year 1300, had no temples: they sat on the nose alone.

questions.question: A lack of vitamin B12, found in cheese, causes a disease that 100 years ago was treated by eating lots of liver. Which one?
hints: It affects the blood.
The body lacks healthy red blood cells.
Its name includes a word that means “harmful.”
questions.description: A vitamin that sounds like a move in Battleship: “B12!” “Hit! You sank my battleship!”
questions.fun_fact: The doctors who discovered the liver treatment won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1934.

questions.question: The original kumis, made by the nomadic peoples of Central Asia, comes from fermenting the milk of…
hints: It's an animal at the heart of nomadic life on the steppes.
Nomads also ride it to travel long distances.
It's the female of the horse.
questions.description: A drink that comes from cows in Colombia but changes owners out on the steppes.
questions.fun_fact: Steppe kumis has a tiny bit of alcohol from fermenting, while the Colombian version is made with cow's milk.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: in cheesemaking, to “coagulate” milk means…
questions.answer: To turn it into a solid mass
wrong_answers: To boil it until it foams
To remove all of its fat
To mix it with lots of salt
hints: It's the first big step in making cheese.
Something similar happens to blood when a cut stops bleeding.
The result is called curd.
questions.description: Before it becomes cheese, milk goes through a transformation worthy of a superhero.
questions.fun_fact: When milk coagulates, proteins called caseins clump together and trap the fat like a net.

questions.question: The bacteria that give Limburger cheese its strong smell also cause the bad smell of…
hints: It's a part of the body that stays shut in all day.
It smells worse after you run around and play sports.
It goes inside socks and shoes.
questions.description: A question with a smell your nose would rather forget.
questions.fun_fact: Mosquitoes that spread malaria are drawn to the smell of feet and to Limburger cheese alike.

questions.question: It's sold in tanks, used for cooking and turns liquid under pressure. Which two elements is propane made of?
hints: It's a fuel that comes from oil and natural gas.
One of the two is also part of water.
One of them is the element that coal is mostly made of.
questions.description: The gas that gets the grill sizzling, and sends someone running to the store when it runs out halfway through the barbecue.
questions.fun_fact: Propane has no smell at all: the nasty smell of cooking gas is added on purpose so leaks can be noticed.

questions.question: I’m a mixture, and you can see my parts with your bare eyes. Which of these am I?
hints: This is called a heterogeneous mixture.
You can pick my parts apart with a fork.
I have little pieces of apple, papaya and strawberry.
questions.description: A mixture that keeps no secrets from anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Blood looks smooth and even, but under a microscope you can see its cells: it’s a heterogeneous mixture too.

questions.question: Silica aerogel is one of the lightest solids there is. About what percentage of it is air?
hints: It's almost see-through and looks like a solid cloud.
A piece the size of a brick weighs less than an apple.
Almost all of its volume is empty space, full of tiny pores.
questions.description: People call it “frozen smoke”, and no, it's not a dessert at a fancy restaurant.
questions.fun_fact: NASA used aerogel on its Stardust mission to catch dust from a comet without destroying it.

questions.question: On television, what is “prime time”?
questions.answer: The time slot with the most viewers
wrong_answers: The first show of the morning
The premiere of a new season
hints: It’s a term from the world of TV and advertising.
It’s when the family is home and turns on the TV.
That’s why ads at that time are the most expensive.
questions.description: It sounds like a math lesson, but it’s really about the couch.
questions.fun_fact: “Prime” means “main” or “best”, which is why it’s the most valuable time on television.

questions.question: I was a supermodel, and I created and hosted a US reality show for years to discover new models. Who am I?
hints: My show first aired in 2003.
The show is called “America's Next Top Model.”
My first name starts with T.
questions.description: A reality show where walking in a straight line is an extreme sport.
questions.fun_fact: Tyra Banks made the word “smize” popular: smiling with only your eyes.

questions.question: Riddle: I show up under someone's name in a chat and vanish as soon as their message arrives. What am I telling you?
questions.answer: That the other person is typing
wrong_answers: That the other person read your message
That the other person is calling you
That the other person turned off their phone
hints: I show up right before something new arrives.
Sometimes I appear, disappear… and nothing ever arrives.
The other person is moving their fingers over the keyboard.
questions.description: The biggest suspense of modern life: waiting for a reply.
questions.fun_fact: Those little dancing dots have an official name: the “typing indicator.”

questions.question: Which expression do you use when problems or debts weigh on you so much that you can barely cope?
questions.answer: Be up to your neck in it
wrong_answers: Have your head in the clouds
Wear your heart on your sleeve
hints: The expression is about someone in big trouble.
It describes something that keeps rising until it gets dangerously close to your head.
The water already reaches just below your chin.
questions.description: A question for anyone who goes pale when they open the electric bill.
questions.fun_fact: A close cousin, “keeping your head above water,” means you are only just managing to cope.

questions.question: A saying in Spanish goes: when your belly is full, which part of your body is happy?
hints: Grandmas in Spain and Latin America love to say it at the lunch table.
It's an organ that works all day and never takes a break.
In emojis it's usually red and means love.
questions.description: The official motto of every grandma at lunchtime.
questions.fun_fact: Your stomach takes about 20 minutes to tell your brain that it's full.

review.feedback: no viaja

questions.question: Which of these customs is NOT part of Purim, the Jewish holiday?
questions.answer: Lighting a candle each night for eight nights
wrong_answers: Dressing up in costumes and having a big party
Reading the Book of Esther out loud
Making noise whenever the villain Haman is named
hints: Purim remembers the story of a queen who saved her people in ancient Persia.
Three of these customs recall the story of Queen Esther.
The odd custom belongs to Hanukkah, the festival of lights.
questions.description: A Jewish holiday so cheerful that even its cookies are named after ears.
questions.fun_fact: On Purim people eat triangular cookies called “Haman's ears,” known in English as hamantaschen.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an orisha, a deity of Santería?
hints: Santería was born in Cuba, with roots in the Yoruba people of Africa.
The orishas come from West Africa.
The odd one out is a feathered serpent of the Aztecs.
questions.description: A family of gods so big that a guest from another continent snuck into the party.
questions.fun_fact: Many orishas became linked with Catholic saints: Shango, god of thunder, is linked with Saint Barbara.

questions.question: This temple in Yazd, Iran, belongs to the religion of Zoroaster. What has been kept safe inside it for centuries?
hints: For Zoroastrians, it is a symbol of purity and of God's light.
Priests watch over it day and night so it never runs out.
It burns in a large metal bowl and is fed with wood.
questions.description: A religion so old it was already ancient when the pyramids of Teotihuacan were built.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the fire in the Yazd temple has been burning without going out for about 1,500 years.

questions.question: I'm the “décade” of the French Revolutionary calendar, and I last ten days. What did I replace?
hints: Months in the Revolutionary calendar had 30 days.
Each month had three of me.
What I replaced had seven days.
questions.description: Revolutionaries who wanted to count even time on their fingers.
questions.fun_fact: In that calendar, every day was named after a plant, an animal, a mineral or a tool instead of a saint.

questions.question: I'm a king of France before 1789, and people call me an “absolute monarch.” What does that mean?
questions.answer: That I rule with no one limiting my power
wrong_answers: That the people elected me in a vote
That I only rule in times of war
That my role is only for show
hints: It was typical of the Old Regime, the “Ancien Régime.”
People said my power came straight from God.
I make the laws, collect the taxes and judge cases all by myself.
questions.description: A boss who never had to ask anyone's permission, not even for dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Louis XIV is credited with saying “I am the State,” though he probably never said it.

questions.question: What was the Napoleonic Code, published in France in 1804?
wrong_answers: A system of weights and measures
hints: It is still used in France today, with changes.
It replaced hundreds of different local rules with a single text for all of France.
Lawyers study it.
questions.description: In 1804 Napoleon tried on a brand-new emperor's crown and, while he was at it, launched this other novelty.
questions.fun_fact: The Napoleonic Code inspired the civil codes of many countries in Europe and Latin America.

questions.question: In rugby, why does a player who has already crossed the line run around to a spot under the posts before grounding the ball?
wrong_answers: So the referee sees it better
hints: A try is worth the same wherever the ball is grounded.
It has to do with the kick that comes right after the try.
That kick is taken in line with the spot where the ball was grounded.
questions.description: A few extra steps that look like showing off but hide a carefully worked-out plan.
questions.fun_fact: If the try is scored in the corner, the conversion has to be kicked from far out to the side, which makes it much harder to get over.

questions.question: The film “Invictus”, about Mandela and the 1995 Rugby World Cup, is named after a work that inspired Mandela in prison. What is “Invictus”?
hints: It is an English work from the 19th century.
It is short: it fits on a single page.
It is written in verse and ends with “I am the captain of my soul.”
questions.description: A rugby film whose title wasn't won on the field, but in a prison cell.
questions.fun_fact: “Invictus” is Latin for “unconquered,” and the poem was written by William Ernest Henley.

questions.question: In rugby, they wear numbers 1 to 8, form the scrum and include the props and the hooker. What is this group called?
hints: They are usually the heaviest players on the team.
Players 9 to 15 make up the other group.
Their name tells you where they play: up front.
questions.description: They push like tractors and almost never look clean in the photos.
questions.fun_fact: In every scrum, all eight players of one team push at the same time against the eight of the other team.

questions.question: “Society of the Snow” tells the story of Uruguay's Old Christians rugby team, stranded in the Andes. Who directed it?
hints: He is a Spanish director.
He also directed “The Impossible” and “A Monster Calls”.
He directed one of the “Jurassic World” films.
questions.description: A question for the people who stay in their seats until the very last credit rolls.
questions.fun_fact: The film was nominated for the Oscar for Best International Feature, and part of it was shot in the Sierra Nevada mountains in Spain.

questions.question: It was born in Argentina on October 17, 1945, with a huge rally in the Plaza de Mayo. Which political movement is it?
hints: Its founder was president of Argentina three times.
Its anthem begins “Los muchachos…” (“The boys…”).
Its great female symbol is Evita.
questions.description: In Argentina, two topics are best left off the dinner table: soccer and this one.
questions.fun_fact: Its followers celebrate every October 17 as “Loyalty Day”.

questions.question: This drawing of a big-nosed man peeking over a wall appeared all over the world in the 1940s. Who drew it everywhere?
hints: In the 1940s, half the world was at war.
It showed up wherever Allied troops arrived.
It's even hidden on the war memorial in Washington.
questions.description: The king of graffiti: it reached more countries than any backpacker.
questions.fun_fact: Kilroy is secretly carved into the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C.

questions.question: During World War II, what was the Wehrmacht?
hints: It existed from 1935 to 1945.
Its name means “defense force.”
It was the one that invaded Poland in 1939.
questions.description: A German word that sounds like a sneeze, and still nobody said “bless you.”
questions.fun_fact: The Luftwaffe, the German air force, was part of the Wehrmacht.

questions.question: In Hamlet's most famous scene, set in a graveyard, what does the prince hold in his hand while he speaks?
hints: It's something the gravediggers dug up.
It belonged to Yorick, the king's old jester.
It's the part of the skeleton that sits on top of the shoulders.
questions.description: A Danish prince with too much free time and a huge urge to philosophize.
questions.fun_fact: Polish pianist André Tchaikowsky left his own skull to the Royal Shakespeare Company, and in 2008 an actor used it on stage while playing Hamlet.

questions.question: Rosalind calls herself Ganymede, Portia dresses as a lawyer and Imogen becomes a page. Who played these roles in Shakespeare's time?
hints: In the public theaters of England back then, the rules were very different from today's.
That made the disguise as a man a double joke for the audience.
They were young actors whose voices hadn't broken yet.
questions.description: A fake mustache and a deep voice: the survival kit of Shakespeare's heroines.
questions.fun_fact: Women could not legally act in England's public theaters until 1660, more than 40 years after Shakespeare died.

questions.question: It's white and pleated, circles the neck like a wheel, and was in fashion in Shakespeare's time. What is it called?
hints: It was starched so it stayed nice and stiff.
It appears in many portraits of Queen Elizabeth I.
The same name is used for a ring of fluffy feathers around a bird's neck.
questions.description: Elizabethan fashion: if you couldn't turn your head, you were well dressed.
questions.fun_fact: A large one could take several meters of linen, pleated and starched by hand.

questions.question: She marries your dad, isn't your mom, and in “Cinderella” she's the villain. What word is it, also the title of a telenovela?
hints: There's one in “Snow White” too.
Cinderella's two mean sisters are her daughters.
She's a kind of mother, but not the one who gave birth to you.
questions.description: The fairy tale character with the worst reputation of all, and she doesn't even have a broomstick.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's “La madrastra” (“The Stepmother”, 2005), starring Victoria Ruffo, is a new version of a Chilean telenovela from 1981.

questions.question: “Senda prohibida” first aired in 1958, was written by Fernanda Villeli and was its country's first telenovela. Which country?
hints: Its capital is one of the largest cities in the Americas.
The giant TV company Televisa was born there.
“La usurpadora” (“The Usurper”) and “María la del barrio” were made there.
questions.description: Before the thousand episodes and the evil twins, someone had to take the first step.
questions.fun_fact: “Senda prohibida” had 60 episodes of about 30 minutes each, shown Monday to Friday in 1958.

questions.question: In a telenovela, the heroine hits the villain on the cheek with an open hand. What is that called?
hints: It's loud and leaves the face red.
In telenovelas it goes “smack!” and the villain is left with her mouth open.
A high five is a friendly version of it, on the hand instead of the face.
questions.description: Every viewer's favorite sound, when the villain finally gets what's coming to her.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish it's called a “cachetada”, from “cachete”, a word for the cheek.

questions.question: At the Temple of Heaven in Beijing, the great Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests stands without a single nail. What is it made of?
hints: It is a material that comes from nature and can be carved.
Its pieces fit into each other like a puzzle.
Its huge columns were once tree trunks.

questions.question: What is the smallest number of seismic stations needed to locate an earthquake's epicenter?

questions.question: If a house is “earthquake-resistant,” what does that mean?

It doesn't move at all in a quake

questions.question: I'm a loose, colorful shirt from West Africa with V-shaped embroidery around the neck. What am I?

questions.question: The finest, most prized fabric for this Filipino shirt is woven from the leaf fibers of a fruit plant. Which one?
hints: It's a plant that grows fruit.

questions.description: A shirt so fine you can almost see through it, and it's not made of plastic.

questions.question: I twist long, skinny balloons into dogs, swords and flowers. Who am I?
hints: I often show up at birthday parties.

questions.description: An artist who lives in fear of just one sound: “POP!”
questions.fun_fact: You can make a balloon dog from just one long balloon and only a few twists.

questions.question: Trapeze artists, gymnasts and climbers rub this white powder on their hands. What compound is it?
hints: It soaks up sweat so hands don't slip.
Its metal burns with a very bright white light.

questions.description: The circus's least magical white powder: its only trick is keeping you from falling.
questions.fun_fact: Gym chalk isn't blackboard chalk: classroom chalk is almost always gypsum or calcium carbonate.

questions.question: In 1768, former cavalry sergeant Philip Astley set up the first modern circus, with a round ring. In which city?

questions.question: For more than a hundred years, I carried the big circuses of the United States from city to city, with elephants on board. What am I?
hints: It traveled mostly at night, between shows.

It ran on rails and went “choo-choo.”
questions.description: A ride where elephants are the passengers and clowns sit in first class.
questions.fun_fact: The Ringling Bros. circus train was more than 1.5 km (almost a mile) long.

questions.question: It sits under the liver, it's shaped like a small pear, and you can live without it. Which organ is it?
hints: It helps digest food, especially fat.
It stores a greenish-yellow liquid made by the liver.
Its name joins an old word for that liquid with a word for a bag.
questions.description: An organ that lives in the liver's basement, and almost nobody knows what it does down there.

questions.question: Dutchman Wim Hof, who bathes in ice, created a famous method that combines cold with exercises of… what?
hints: His method aims to help the body handle cold and calm the mind.

questions.question: You glide in a gondola under the Bridge of Sighs in Venice. According to the story, who sighed as they crossed it?

questions.question: In 1990, thieves dressed as police officers stole Vermeer's “The Concert” from a Boston museum. How many works did they take in total?

questions.question: I paid old investors with new investors' money, and Bernie Madoff made me the biggest in history. What am I?

questions.question: In 1788, Britain's First Fleet reached Australia to found a colony. Who were most of its passengers?

questions.question: In 2015, thieves drilled into a jewelry vault in Hatton Garden, London. The strangest part: who were they?
hints: They were anything but beginners.

questions.description: A drill, a long weekend and a vault full of jewels: the recipe for a very British heist.

questions.question: In cricket, it's made of wood, stuck in the ground behind the batter, and if the ball knocks it down, the batter is out. What is it?

questions.question: In cricket, what are the last batters in the order called, who are usually bowlers and often bat quite badly?
hints: They usually come in to bat when the innings is nearly over.
The name compares them to a part of an animal's body.
Think of the part a dog wags.
questions.description: Last in line, like when the birthday cake is handed out.
questions.fun_fact: Every now and then a tail-ender surprises everyone and saves the match with the bat.

questions.question: They call me a “golden duck”, and no cricket batter wants me. What am I?

Tripping and falling while running between the wickets
Getting hit on the helmet by the ball

After this, the batter has to walk back to the pavilion very early.

questions.description: A very fancy duck that nobody wants in their collection.
questions.fun_fact: It's called a “duck” because the zero on the scoreboard looks like a duck's egg.

questions.question: About how fast does a professional fast bowler in cricket bowl the ball?
hints: It's faster than a car driving in the city.

It's like a car on the highway, but a bit faster.
questions.description: If you have to bat against one of these, put on a helmet and say a little prayer.
questions.fun_fact: The fastest ball ever recorded in cricket went over 160 km/h (about 100 mph).

questions.question: The Marylebone Cricket Club has written the rules of cricket since 1788. Which city do you travel to if you want to visit it?
hints: It's in the country where cricket was born.
Its ground is called Lord's.
It's the city of Big Ben.
questions.description: A club so old its first rulebook was probably read by people in powdered wigs.
questions.fun_fact: The club's ground, Lord's, is known as “the home of cricket.”

questions.question: My name means “fears nothing,” I weighed as much as several trucks, and I was announced in 2014. In which country were my bones found?
hints: It was in the Americas.

questions.description: A dinosaur with a battleship's name and the size of a building.
questions.fun_fact: The skeleton of Dreadnoughtus is one of the most complete ever found for a giant long-necked dinosaur.

questions.question: It lived 60 million years ago, was about 13 m (43 ft) long, and its fossils came from the Cerrejón coal mine. What is it called?
hints: It is the largest snake known to science.

questions.question: In a Brothers Grimm fairy tale, I killed seven flies with one blow and set off to see the world. What is my job?
hints: The flies landed on my bread and jam while I was working.
I stitched “Seven at one blow” onto a belt I made myself.
My work is taking measurements and sewing suits.
questions.description: A fairy-tale hero with more confidence in himself than strength in his arms.
questions.fun_fact: In 1938, Mickey Mouse starred in a cartoon version of this tale called “Brave Little Tailor.”

questions.question: The classic Chanel jacket is made of it, it was born in Scotland, and it feels a little scratchy. What is tweed?
hints: People wore it for hunting and walking in the cold countryside.
It comes from an animal that says “baa.”
It's a warm woven cloth made with threads of several colors.

questions.question: A keyboard split into two tilted halves is sold as “ergonomic.” What does that word mean?
questions.answer: Designed to fit the human body
hints: The word comes from the Greek “ergon,” which means work.

questions.fun_fact: Split keyboards are designed so your wrists don't bend outward when you type for hours.

questions.question: Organic design prefers soft curves to sharp corners. What is it inspired by?
hints: Think of shells, leaves and bones.

The Tulip chair looks like a flower.
questions.description: Furniture that had a fight with the ruler and never made up.
questions.fun_fact: Eero Saarinen gave his Tulip chair a single leg because he said the tangle of legs under chairs and tables was a confusing, restless “slum of legs.”

questions.question: When the factory owner saw a new Italian scooter in 1946, he said it looked like an insect and gave it that insect's name. Which insect?
hints: I have a thin waist and a wide tail.

This insect has a stinger and yellow and black stripes.

questions.question: This frozen treat of ice, sugar and lemon is eaten for breakfast with a brioche bun. Which island is it typical of?
hints: The island belongs to Italy.

It is the largest island in the Mediterranean, at the “toe of the boot.”
questions.description: Crushed ice with sugar that went to school in Europe and came back with a fancy accent.
questions.fun_fact: In Sicily, granita with brioche is as normal a summer breakfast as coffee and toast is in other places.

questions.question: What is the name of the famous, now disproven, diagram showing the tip of the tongue tastes sweet and the back tastes bitter?
hints: It appeared in lots of school science books.

questions.question: Among the Aztecs, what could you use to pay at the market?
hints: It was a seed that grew in hot lands.

questions.question: You burned your tongue on hot chocolate. Roughly how long does it take for your taste cells to renew?

questions.question: This chocolate is named after a very expensive delicacy that dogs or pigs sniff out underground. What kind of living thing is that delicacy?
hints: It grows attached to the roots of trees like the oak.
It reproduces with spores.
It's a relative of mushrooms.

questions.fun_fact: Chocolate truffles were invented in France and got their name because they look like black truffles covered in soil.

questions.question: It's very sharp, fits into a small handle and gets thrown away when it goes dull. What is this disposable blade for?

questions.question: The Latin word “volvo” (I roll) is to the brand Volvo as the Latin word “sonus” (sound) is to…

Dresses in red and can help choose the pope.

hints: He was a young general, famous for his victories.

questions.question: Which of these songs is NOT by Juanes?

questions.question: In what year did AC/DC release their famous album “Back in Black”?

It was the first year of the eighties.
questions.description: An album dressed for a funeral that sounds like a party.

questions.question: Drop a coin in me, pick a number, and I'll play any song you want. What am I?

questions.question: Angus Young was born in Scotland, plays dressed as a schoolboy and grew up in the country where AC/DC was formed. Which one?

questions.description: A guitarist who never graduated out of his school uniform.

questions.question: Nazi Germany built it, it was the first human-made object to reach space, and its engineer later helped the US get to the Moon. What was it?

questions.fun_fact: Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945, less than a week after the city fell.

questions.question: In a Shakespeare tragedy, the hero says as he dies: “The rest is silence.” Which character is it?
hints: He is the hero of one of Shakespeare's most often performed plays.
A ghost asks him to avenge his father.
His story takes place in Denmark.
questions.description: The shortest, classiest goodbye in all of theater: not even a “see you later.”
questions.fun_fact: “Hamlet” is Shakespeare's longest play: performed in full, it can last about four hours.

questions.question: “Hamlet” is to Denmark as “Titus Andronicus” is to…
hints: Titus is a general who comes home victorious from the war against the Goths.
It is a revenge tragedy, one of the first Shakespeare ever wrote.
It is the same city where “Julius Caesar” takes place.
questions.description: Even before he was famous, Shakespeare knew that nothing sells like a good revenge.
questions.fun_fact: “Titus Andronicus” was probably Shakespeare's first tragedy, and in its day it was one of his biggest box-office hits.

questions.question: “The Winter's Tale” begins in Sicily. To which kingdom does the action move next, one Shakespeare gave a coast it doesn't have?
hints: Shakespeare took the story from a novel by Robert Greene, where the two kingdoms were the other way around.
It has no access to the sea.
Today it is part of the Czech Republic, and its historic capital was Prague.
questions.description: Shakespeare didn't have Google Maps, and it shows.
questions.fun_fact: This play has Shakespeare's most famous stage direction: “Exit, pursued by a bear.”

questions.question: Which Shakespeare character says “Out, damned spot!” while sleepwalking?
hints: She is one of the most famous villains in theater.
She helped her husband take the throne of Scotland.
Her husband's name is the title of the play.
questions.description: The toughest cleaning job in history: no stain remover can get this one out.
questions.fun_fact: Many actors believe saying “Macbeth” inside a theater brings bad luck, so they call it “the Scottish play”.

questions.question: I am a king of England. I lost my horse at the Battle of Bosworth and cried, “My kingdom for a horse!” Who am I?
hints: I was the last king from the House of York.
Shakespeare painted me as a hunchbacked villain.
In 2012, my remains were found under a parking lot in Leicester.
questions.description: The worst deal in history: a whole kingdom for just one horse.
questions.fun_fact: Richard III's remains turned up in 2012 under a parking lot in Leicester, and he was buried again in the city's cathedral in 2015.

questions.question: In “Romeo and Juliet”, which friar was meant to take Friar Laurence's letter to Romeo but couldn't?
hints: He was a Franciscan friar, like Friar Laurence.
He was locked inside a house for fear of a plague.
He shares his first name with the Beatle who wrote “Imagine”.
questions.description: A perfect plan, ruined by the postal service.
questions.fun_fact: Because the letter never arrived, Romeo didn't know that Juliet was only asleep from Friar Laurence's potion.

questions.question: Paola Bracho is rich and spoiled. She has a poor twin sister and pays her to pretend to be Paola at home. What is the telenovela called?
hints: It is a Mexican telenovela made by Televisa in 1998.
Gabriela Spanic played both sisters.
The title describes someone who takes a place or a throne that belongs to someone else.
questions.description: Being a millionaire wasn't enough: she also wanted a backup copy of herself.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriela Spanic played both twins, so in many scenes she had to act opposite herself.

questions.question: Just as the secret is about to come out, the episode ends. “The End” is to a movie as what is to that episode?
hints: It's a promise that the story isn't over.
You also see it at the end of many cartoons.
It starts with “To be…”.
questions.description: The writers' favorite torture: leaving your jaw on the floor until tomorrow.
questions.fun_fact: In English, this kind of ending is called a “cliffhanger,” after an 1873 novel in which a character is left hanging from a cliff at the end of an installment.

questions.question: In classic telenovelas, when do the two main characters finally get married?
hints: Before that, they have to get past a huge number of problems.
It's what the whole family is waiting to see.
Right after that scene, the words “The End” appear.
questions.description: After a thousand tears, a hundred misunderstandings and one evil twin, someone finally brings out the white dress.
questions.fun_fact: The final episodes of the most popular telenovelas could bring whole countries to a stop: even the streets were empty.

questions.question: I arrive after a blow to the head and make the handsome hero forget even his own name. What am I?
hints: It has to do with memory.
The hero doesn't even recognize his girlfriend.
It rhymes with “Indonesia”.
questions.description: The perfect trick when the writer wants to restart the story without changing the actors.
questions.fun_fact: In soap operas, memory often comes back with a second blow to the head, but that's not how it works in real life.

questions.question: “Topacio,” with Grecia Colmenares as a young blind woman, was a remake of “Esmeralda” (1970). In which decade did it premiere?
hints: It is a Venezuelan telenovela made by the network RCTV.
It premiered more than ten years after “Esmeralda.”
It came out in the same decade as the first Super Mario Bros. game.
questions.description: A precious stone that turned into another precious stone, and then back into the first one.
questions.fun_fact: The story came back in Mexico in 1997, called “Esmeralda” again, with Leticia Calderón in the lead role.

questions.question: Mexico City's cathedral on the Zócalo stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Which conquistador took that city?
hints: He was a Spaniard born in Extremadura.
He reached the coast of Mexico in 1519.
He met the Aztec emperor Montezuma.
questions.description: This cathedral took about two and a half centuries to finish, and you complain about your homework.
questions.fun_fact: The cathedral is slowly sinking because Mexico City is built on an old lake.

questions.question: They have their own small altar, open off the sides of a cathedral, and are often dedicated to a saint. What are they called?
hints: Rich families often paid for one so they had their own corner for prayer.
The same word is used for the prayer room in a school or a hospital.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the most famous one in the world, in the Vatican.
questions.description: Cathedrals have more rooms than Grandma's house.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chapel” comes from the cape of Saint Martin, which was kept in a small shrine guarded by priests called chaplains.

questions.question: It's in Saint Petersburg, has colorful swirled domes, and inside it's covered with over 7,000 m² (75,000 sq ft) of… what?
hints: It isn't paint on the wall.
It's made of thousands of tiny pieces.
Small colored stones and bits of glass set side by side.
questions.description: A church that looks like it's made of rainbow ice cream, but there isn't a drop of cream inside.
questions.fun_fact: The church took 24 years to build, from 1883 to 1907.

questions.question: They are holy images painted on wood with a gold background, typical of the Orthodox Church. Which empire does this tradition come from?
hints: It was the eastern half of the Roman Empire.
It lasted more than a thousand years, until 1453.
Its capital was Constantinople, today's Istanbul.
questions.description: Long before phones, there were little golden screens that everyone stood and stared at.
questions.fun_fact: The icons on your phone are named after these images: “eikōn” is Greek for “image.”

questions.question: I was once the minaret of a mosque, and today I'm the bell tower of Seville Cathedral. My name comes from my weather vane. What am I called?
hints: My lower part was built by the Almohads in the 12th century.
I'm a little over 100 m (330 ft) tall, weather vane included.
My name comes from the Spanish word for “to turn”, which is what a weather vane does in the wind.
questions.description: A tower that changed religions without moving an inch.
questions.fun_fact: Instead of stairs, it has 35 ramps inside, built so people could ride to the top on horseback.

questions.question: In 1880, Englishman John Milne founded the world's first seismological society. In which country did he found it?
hints: Milne went there to teach mining and geology at a university.
It is an island country in the Pacific Ocean, famous for its frequent earthquakes.
Its capital is Tokyo.
questions.description: An Englishman moved to a country where the ground won't sit still, and instead of leaving, he started measuring it.
questions.fun_fact: Milne felt so many earthquakes in his new home that he helped build one of the first modern horizontal-pendulum seismographs.

questions.question: Inside the Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a huge steel ball that steadies it in earthquakes and typhoons. About how much does it weigh?
hints: It has to be heavy enough to stop a giant tower from swaying.
But it still fits inside the building, hanging between the top floors.
It weighs about 660 metric tons (about 730 US tons).
questions.description: A skyscraper that swallowed a giant marble so it wouldn't get seasick.
questions.fun_fact: Visitors can go and see the Taipei 101 ball, and it even has its own cartoon mascots, the “Damper Babies”.

questions.question: The first worldwide network of identical seismic stations was set up partly to detect nuclear tests. In which decade?
hints: Nuclear tests were a major worry during the Cold War.
It was set up while the United States and the Soviet Union were negotiating a treaty to limit nuclear tests.
It started in 1961.
questions.description: Machines that listened to the Earth, and to what governments were up to while they were at it.
questions.fun_fact: Data from this network helped confirm plate tectonics, because it showed that earthquakes cluster along the edges of the plates.

questions.question: The earthquake alarm goes off in your city. Which of these things can that system NOT do?
questions.answer: Warn people days before the earthquake
wrong_answers: Warn people seconds before the strong shaking
hints: The alarm works because electrical signals travel faster than the earthquake's waves.
Mexico City has had one of these systems since the 1990s.
Nobody in the world can predict earthquakes ahead of time.
questions.description: An alarm that runs faster than the shaking ground.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico City, the alarm can give almost a minute's warning when the earthquake starts on the Pacific coast.

questions.question: The Marquis of Pombal rebuilt Lisbon after the great earthquake that destroyed it. In what year was that earthquake?
hints: The shaking was felt in other countries of Europe and even in North Africa.
