It struck on November 1, All Saints' Day.
It happened about 20 years before the United States declared independence.
questions.description: A minister who turned a city of ruins into a city built to take a shaking.
questions.fun_fact: To test his new wood-framed buildings, Pombal is said to have had troops march around scale models to imitate an earthquake.

questions.question: This skirt is worn to dance the hula. Where does that dance come from?
hints: It's a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
Visitors there are welcomed with flower necklaces.
It's where Lilo lives with her blue friend, Stitch.
questions.description: A skirt you never iron: at most, you water it.
questions.fun_fact: The hula tells stories: every hand movement has a meaning.

questions.question: Which plant dye is used to make these designs on the skin?
hints: It comes from the dried leaves of a shrub, ground into powder.
It is used a lot at weddings in India and in Arab countries.
Its name has two syllables, with a double “n” in the middle.
questions.description: A tattoo that comes with an expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: In India these designs are called “mehndi”, and many brides wear them on their hands and feet on their wedding day.

questions.question: Which of these words does NOT name something you wear on your head?
hints: The answer is very far from your head.
It's a word you hear a lot in Mexico.
They are sandals made of woven leather strips.
questions.description: A question to think about from head to toe.
questions.fun_fact: Many huaraches today have soles made from recycled car tires.

questions.question: I'm woven by hand in Ecuador from toquilla straw, but the world knows me by a name that isn't from Ecuador. What am I called?
hints: I'm light, cool and pale in color, made for hot weather.
The best ones can be rolled up and still spring back into shape.
My name is that of a country famous for a canal joining two oceans.
questions.description: A hat with a serious identity crisis.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012, UNESCO added the traditional weaving of Ecuador's toquilla straw hat to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

questions.question: I wear a skirt with lots of ruffles and polka dots, and I dance with castanets and clapping. Which country am I from?
hints: It is a country in Europe.
People there speak Spanish.
Its capital is Madrid.
questions.description: A dress that twirls more than a spinning top.
questions.fun_fact: The flamenco dress follows fashion: new designs come out every year for the April Fair in Seville.

questions.question: It looks like a light kimono, shows up at summer festivals in anime and is called a yukata. What fabric is it traditionally made of?
hints: It's a cool fabric, perfect for hot weather.
It comes from a plant.
Almost every T-shirt is made of it.
questions.description: Clothes for watching fireworks without melting in the heat.
questions.fun_fact: “Yukata” means something like “bath clothes”: at first, people wore it after taking a bath.

questions.question: Which African cloth, woven in narrow strips of bright colors, do you see in this photo?
hints: It comes from West Africa.
The Ashanti kings of Ghana wore it at their ceremonies.
Its name has five letters and starts with “K”.
questions.description: A cloth so elegant that once only kings were allowed to wear it.
questions.fun_fact: Every color in kente has a meaning: gold, for example, stands for wealth and royalty.

questions.question: At the eye doctor, you get a prescription for bifocal glasses. What is special about them?
questions.answer: One part is for seeing far away, the other for up close
wrong_answers: They turn dark by themselves in the sun
They have two layers so they don't get scratched
They make things look twice as big as other glasses
hints: The prefix “bi” means two.
Many grandparents use them to read the newspaper and also to drive.
The lower part of the lens is for reading up close.
questions.description: The only test where reading the tiny bottom row of letters makes you feel like a champion.
questions.fun_fact: The American Benjamin Franklin is credited with inventing bifocal glasses in the 18th century.

questions.question: Fred from Scooby-Doo wears a neck scarf like this one, called an “ascot.” Where does its name come from?
hints: The name was famous for something else long before it was something to wear.
The British royal family goes there every year, along with lots of very fancy hats.
It's a racecourse near London.
questions.description: A tie that thinks it's far too fancy for an ordinary knot.
questions.fun_fact: Royal Ascot is so fancy that it has official rules about the size of hats.

questions.question: “Scepter” is to “king” as “crosier” is to…
hints: A crosier is a tall staff used in ceremonies.
Its top usually ends in a hook, like a shepherd's crook.
It is carried by a church leader during ceremonies.
questions.description: A walking stick so important that nobody ever really walks with it.
questions.fun_fact: A bishop's crosier copies the shape of a shepherd's crook, which is used to guide sheep.

questions.question: I used to be made of leather or wood, now I'm made of rubber. I touch the ground all day, and the shoemaker replaces me when I wear out. What am I?
hints: I'm on the bottom of the shoe.
When I wear thin, water from puddles can get in.
I share my name with a flat fish.
questions.description: The most stepped-on part of the whole fashion world.
questions.fun_fact: Rubber soles caught on after Charles Goodyear invented vulcanized rubber in the 19th century.

questions.question: Which of these characters does NOT wear glasses?
hints: Three of them have very famous frames, round or square.
The character we're looking for has magic powers.
She's a queen of Arendelle who sings “Let It Go”.
questions.description: A question to find out who sees clearly and who needs a little help.
questions.fun_fact: A running joke in Scooby-Doo: Velma loses her glasses and crawls around saying she can't see a thing without them.

questions.question: The inventor of this boot with elastic sides made shoes for a queen and said she wore them every day. Which queen?
hints: Thanks to the elastic, you can pull them on with no laces or buckles.
This queen ruled for more than 60 years and gave her name to a whole era.
She was called “the grandmother of Europe” because her grandchildren sat on thrones all over the continent.
questions.description: Boots so comfy that even a queen could put them on without bending down.
questions.fun_fact: Decades later, The Beatles made a version of these boots so popular that it became known as “Beatle boots.”

questions.question: On the Magdalena River, people traveled in champanes, large boats pushed by bogas (boatmen) with poles. What replaced them in the 19th century?
hints: It was much faster than rowing or pushing with poles.
It burned wood to heat water.
It had a big paddle wheel and a smokestack.
questions.description: Going down the Magdalena once took nothing but muscle, until progress came around the bend.
questions.fun_fact: Magdalena steamboats burned so much wood that the riverbanks had stops just for loading it.

questions.question: Which of these words do Colombians NOT use to talk about money (plata)?
hints: Three of them are used to say how many pesos something costs in Colombia.
“Un palo” and “una barra” both mean a million pesos.
The answer is what people in Mexico call money.
questions.description: There are a thousand ways to ask for money, and almost none of them work on your parents.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign used for the Colombian peso is the same one used for the dollar.

questions.question: The country of Bolivia is named after a hero of independence. Which one?
hints: Say it out loud: it sounds almost the same.
He is known as “the Liberator.”
Bogotá's main square is named after him too.
questions.description: Some people get a street named after them; this one got a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: At first, in 1825, the new country was going to be called the “Republic of Bolívar.”

questions.question: It's 1840, and strongmen like José María Obando rebel against the government and declare themselves rulers of their provinces. What is this group known as?
hints: The war began in 1839 over the closing of some convents in Pasto.
The war is named after the group.
Each of them called himself the “supreme chief” of his province.
questions.description: When every province wanted its own boss, nobody sat still.
questions.fun_fact: During that war, Obando was accused of the murder of Sucre, which took place in Berruecos in 1830.

questions.question: What is the Bogotá soup made with chicken, three kinds of potato, corn on the cob and guascas called?
hints: It's a classic for cold days in the capital.
It's served with capers and heavy cream.
It has papa criolla, which makes it thick and yellow.
questions.description: A soup with so many potatoes that the potatoes can't tell which one they are anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Guascas, a little herb that grows like a weed, are what give ajiaco its special flavor.

questions.question: It's 1900, in the middle of the Thousand Days' War. The president, over 80, governs from Villeta until his vice president Marroquín overthrows him. Who is he?
hints: He was a Conservative, like his vice president.
He was born in Buga, in Valle del Cauca.
His surname contains the name of a saint.
questions.description: A president who preferred a little warmth to the chill of Bogotá.
questions.fun_fact: The coup of July 31, 1900, left José Manuel Marroquín in power, and he was also a writer.

questions.question: On what day is Colombia's Grito de Independencia celebrated?
hints: It falls in the middle of the year.
It happened in 1810, in Bogotá.
It's in the seventh month.
questions.description: The day everyone hangs out the flag and Mom gets out the big pot for ajiaco.
questions.fun_fact: August 7 marks the 1819 Battle of Boyacá, which secured independence.

questions.question: Antonio José de Sucre was born in Venezuela, became president of Bolivia and is called the “Grand Marshal of Ayacucho.” What is Ayacucho in that title?
questions.answer: A battle he won in Peru
wrong_answers: The Venezuelan town where he was born
hints: The title comes from something Sucre did in 1824, during Bolívar's campaign.
It sealed the independence of Peru and of all South America.
Ayacucho lies in the Peruvian Andes.
questions.description: A title so long it won't fit on a business card.
questions.fun_fact: After the Battle of Ayacucho, on December 9, 1824, Spain lost its last big army in South America.

questions.question: This man from Boyacá, in ruana and hat, is considered the father of carranga. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Ráquira, Boyacá.
He founded the group Los Carrangueros de Ráquira.
He sings “La cucharita” and is a veterinarian.
questions.description: A ruana, a tiple and a little spoon: that's all it took to start a whole country-folk revolution.
questions.fun_fact: Before devoting himself to carranga, Jorge Velosa studied veterinary medicine at the Universidad Nacional.

questions.question: It's December and the novena de aguinaldos at home has just ended. What is traditionally handed out afterward?
hints: One is sweet and one is fried.
One of the two is a little ball of cheese and flour.
One is cut into small squares and the other is round and golden.
questions.description: Praying makes you hungry, especially when the smell from the paila starts drifting out of the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional natilla is made with milk, panela and cornstarch, stirred for a good long while in a paila.

questions.question: This singer from Santa Marta mixed vallenato with rock and pop in the 1990s. Who is he?
hints: Before singing, he was a telenovela actor.
His album “Clásicos de la Provincia” was a huge hit.
He sang “La bicicleta” with Shakira.
questions.description: The man from Santa Marta who got half the planet dancing vallenato to an electric guitar.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Vives starred in the 1991 telenovela “Escalona,” about the vallenato songwriter Rafael Escalona.

questions.question: Teatro La Candelaria, founded in Bogotá in 1966, was the great laboratory of collective creation. Who founded and directed it?
hints: He was an architect before he turned to theater.
He led the group for decades alongside Patricia Ariza.
His last name is the same as that of the author of “One Hundred Years of Solitude.”
questions.description: Here plays aren't written by just one person: the whole group writes them, and sometimes even the cat.
questions.fun_fact: La Candelaria created plays collectively, such as “Guadalupe años sin cuenta” (1975).

questions.question: This stage cycling race was first held in 1951 and won by Efraín Forero, “el Indomable Zipa.” Which race is it?
hints: It travels through several regions of the country.
Its name says it goes all the way around something.
Its name means a lap around the whole country.
questions.description: A race where climbing the Alto de Letras counts as fun.
questions.fun_fact: In the first Vueltas, riders covered much of the route on unpaved roads.

questions.question: In the March 1990 elections, students pushed an extra, unofficial vote: the “séptima papeleta” (seventh ballot). What did it call for?
wrong_answers: The end of the Frente Nacional
hints: It wanted a very deep change in the country's rules.
Its result was signed the following year.
It led to the Constitution of 1991.
questions.description: Six ballots weren't enough, so some students invented one more.
questions.fun_fact: The 1991 Constitution replaced the one from 1886, which had lasted more than a century.

questions.question: This Colombian TV comedy show, on the air since 1972, is famous for its joke-tellers and sketches. What is it called?
hints: It's broadcast on Caracol TV.
You watch it on the weekend, in the afternoon.
In Spanish, its name tells you the day it airs and how it leaves you feeling.
questions.description: The only place where a bad joke can make it onto national TV and still get applause.
questions.fun_fact: Sábados Felices has been on Colombian TV for more than 50 years.

questions.question: This radio drama and comic book hero, heard on Colombian radio, dressed in white with a turban and told Solín: “Serenidad y paciencia” (“Serenity and patience”). Who is he?
hints: He had mental powers and traveled the world.
He was called “the incredible man.”
His name starts with K.
questions.description: A superhero with no cape and no cell phone: a turban and a lot of calm were all he needed.
questions.fun_fact: Kalimán was born in Mexico in 1963 as a radio drama, before becoming a comic book.

questions.question: It's in the news at the end of every year, it goes up every year, and many fines are based on it. What does SMMLV stand for?
wrong_answers: Sistema municipal de movilidad y licencias viales
hints: It has to do with what a worker earns.
The government, employers and unions negotiate it.
It's the least someone can be paid for a month of work.
questions.description: Five letters that get the whole country doing math every December.
questions.fun_fact: When the government, employers and workers can't agree, the minimum wage is set by decree.

questions.question: A T-shirt costs 40,000 pesos, and the seller gives you half off. How much do you pay?
hints: A discount means you pay less.
Half means splitting something into two equal parts.
Two 20,000 bills make 40,000.
questions.description: The most-used line at any plaza de mercado: “¿Me hace una rebajita?”
questions.fun_fact: At Colombia's market squares, asking for “la ñapa” (a little extra for free) or a small discount is almost a tradition.

questions.question: At the corner store they ask “¿no tiene ___?” because they're out of change. Which word, which also means “easy” in Spanish, fills the gap?
hints: You need it when you pay for something cheap with a big bill.
It's for paying for small things or getting exact change back.
It means having your money in coins or small bills.
questions.description: The money that jingles when you walk.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the change you get back is called “las vueltas”.

questions.question: It was founded in 1955, built Hidroituango, and every December turns on some of Colombia's most famous Christmas lights. Which company is it?
hints: It's a public company that brings water, electricity and gas to people's homes.
Its Christmas lights decorate the river of a big city in Antioquia.
Its acronym ends with the first letter of Medellín.
questions.description: The company that spends a whole year's worth of electricity on one river every December.
questions.fun_fact: National Geographic once listed Medellín's Christmas lights among the most famous in the world.

questions.question: I directed “La gente de La Universal” in 1993 and, years later, the dark comedy “El Colombian Dream”. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Bogotá and have made only a few films, but they are well remembered.
My 2006 film is famous for its wild style, full of effects and odd narrators.
My last name starts with A.
questions.description: A dream so Colombian that it was even christened in English.
questions.fun_fact: “La gente de La Universal” tells the story of a rather bungling detective agency in Bogotá.

questions.question: In “Golpe de estadio”, guerrillas and police take a break to watch the famous Colombia 5, Argentina 0 together. What year was that game played?
hints: It was played in the 1990s.
El Pibe Valderrama and Faustino Asprilla were on the field.
It was a qualifier for the World Cup in the United States.
questions.description: A truce even harder than agreeing on who gets the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: The 5–0 was played at the Monumental stadium in Buenos Aires, and the Argentine crowd ended up applauding Colombia.

questions.question: I founded the studio that made “Encanto”, the film about the Madrigal family, and my name appears at the start with a castle. Who am I?
hints: I was born in the United States in the early 1900s and started out drawing cartoons.
My theme parks have a princess castle.
My last name is the name of the studio.
questions.description: Behind every animated film is someone who first had to fill notebooks with doodles.
questions.fun_fact: “Encanto” is the 60th animated feature from Disney's studios.

questions.question: My group of filmmaker friends got my city nicknamed “Caliwood”, and my horror films started “tropical gothic”. I directed “Carne de tu carne”. Who am I?
hints: I was part of the Grupo de Cali in the 1970s and 1980s.
I also directed “La mansión de Araucaima”, based on a story by Álvaro Mutis.
With Luis Ospina, I made the short film “Agarrando pueblo”.
questions.description: A vampire who sweats in the tropical heat and talks with a Cali accent.
questions.fun_fact: “Agarrando pueblo” (1977) made fun of filmmakers who filmed poverty to sell it to Europe, something its makers called “pornomiseria”.

questions.question: I'm a journalist and documentary maker. I spent years filming the Havana peace talks between the government and the FARC for “El silencio de los fusiles.” Who am I?
hints: I was a foreign correspondent before I turned to film.
My documentary premiered in 2017.
My first name starts with N.
questions.description: A documentary where the loudest thing is the silence.
questions.fun_fact: The documentary got access to both sides of the negotiating table, something very rare in a peace process.

questions.question: “María”, based on Jorge Isaacs's novel, is considered the first Colombian feature-length fiction film. In which decade was it released?
hints: Films with sound didn't exist yet.
It's older than television in Colombia.
It came out a few years after World War I.
questions.description: A romantic tearjerker to watch with a handkerchief in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Almost nothing is left of the film “María”: only a few seconds of the original reel survive.

questions.question: Before the 2003 Film Law created the FDC, which state agency funded Colombian cinema from 1978 to 1993?
hints: Its name is an acronym.
It was shut down in the early 1990s.
Its name starts with “Fo” and ends with “cine”.
questions.description: Long before there was a film law, somebody was already picking up the tab for the cameras.
questions.fun_fact: Focine helped fund movies such as “Cóndores no entierran todos los días” and “Carne de tu carne”.

questions.question: The Colombian film “Embrace of the Serpent” was shot in a jungle region with pink dolphins, anacondas and the city of Leticia. Which region?
hints: It's in the south of Colombia.
There, Colombia borders Brazil and Peru.
The river that carries the most water in the world flows through it.
questions.description: A film set where the extras are anacondas and pink dolphins.
questions.fun_fact: “Embrace of the Serpent” was the first Colombian film ever nominated for an Oscar, in 2016.

questions.question: You're watching “Encanto” and Casita falls apart. Who helps the Madrigal family rebuild it?
hints: They have known the Madrigals all their lives.
Before, the family always helped them with their gifts.
They live in the same town.
questions.description: A house that dances, opens doors and even pulls a grumpy face.
questions.fun_fact: At the end, Mirabel puts the doorknob on the door and Casita's magic comes back.

questions.question: It has a long handle and is used to stir sancocho or arequipe without scratching the pot. What utensil is it?
hints: It's used while the food is on the fire.
It's the classic utensil that grandma stirs with for hours.
It's like the one you use for soup, but carved from wood.
questions.description: Grandma's secret weapon for keeping the arequipe from sticking.
questions.fun_fact: Wood conducts heat poorly, so a wooden spoon won't burn your hand even when the pot is boiling.

questions.question: The sombrero suaceño is woven from iraca palm and named after the town where it's made. Which department is that town in?
hints: It's a landlocked department in the southern Andes.
The Magdalena River flows through it near its source.
Its capital is Neiva.
questions.description: A hat with a hometown for a last name, like saying “nice to meet you, I'm from out that way.”
questions.fun_fact: The sombrero suaceño is the hat worn by couples dancing the sanjuanero at the San Pedro festivals.

questions.question: Anaco, chumbe, ruana and poporo: which of these is NOT a traditional piece of clothing?
hints: Three are worn on the body; one is held in the hand.
It's tied to the rituals of the peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
It's a container, and the Gold Museum has a famous Quimbaya one.
questions.description: Three you wear and one you carry: the Indigenous closet has a gate-crasher.
questions.fun_fact: The anaco of Misak women in Cauca is a dark skirt wrapped around the waist and held in place with a chumbe.

questions.question: Carved wooden masks of little bulls (toritos) and tigers are typical of a famous Colombian carnival. In which city?
hints: Its carnival is one of the biggest in the world.
Its carnival opens with the Batalla de Flores.
It sits where the Magdalena River meets the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: A wooden face that only leaves the house when there's a party.
questions.fun_fact: Many wooden masks for the Barranquilla Carnival are carved in Galapa, a neighboring town in the department of Atlántico.

questions.question: The carnival marimonda, with its long trunk, big ears and necktie, was created with a purpose. What was it?
questions.answer: To make fun of the rich and politicians
hints: It's a costume of ordinary people, made from old clothes.
It's a classic figure of the Barranquilla Carnival that people wear to dance in the street.
It's a caricature of the powerful.
questions.description: A long trunk, huge ears and dance moves you won't see at any zoo.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the marimonda was born when someone with no money for a costume put their clothes on inside out.

questions.question: I wear a bright dress, carry a basin of fruit on my head and walk through Cartagena. My town was the first free town in the Americas. Who am I?
hints: I sell cocadas, alegrías and fruit.
My dress often has the yellow, blue and red of the flag.
I come from San Basilio, about 50 km (30 miles) from Cartagena.
questions.description: A vendor with one rainbow on her head and another on her skirt.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque has its own language, palenquero, a mix of Spanish and African languages.

questions.question: You add water and ground coffee, put it on the stove or plug it in, and the morning tinto comes out of it. What is it?
hints: It's in almost every kitchen in Colombia.
What comes out of it is black and smells delicious.
Its name comes from the drink it makes.
questions.description: The machine that wakes up the house before the rooster does.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “tinto” means black coffee, not red wine like in other countries!

questions.question: I'm a little green leaf that smells fresh, like mint gum. In Colombia they make me into an aromática for tummy aches. What am I?
hints: I don't have yellow or white flowers in the cup.
My taste is fresh, not lemony.
My name means “good herb.”
questions.description: Grandma's remedy for when your tummy starts a rebellion.
questions.fun_fact: Yerbabuena is a kind of mint, and it's actually one of the two parent plants of peppermint.

questions.question: On the beaches of Cartagena, a white, creamy lemonade is famous. Besides lime, what fruit goes in it?
hints: It's a tropical fruit that's very common on the Caribbean coast.
On the coast, it's used to make the rice that comes with fried fish.
Inside, it has water and white flesh.
questions.description: A lemonade that went on a beach vacation and came back all white.
questions.fun_fact: Coconut lemonade is blended with ice, lime, sugar and coconut milk or cream, so it ends up almost like a slushie.

questions.question: The classic pocillo de peltre on Colombian farms is light, colorful, doesn't break when dropped and heats up fast in your hand. What is it made of?
hints: If it falls, it goes “clang” instead of breaking.
When it gets hit, the paint chips off and you see dark underneath.
It's a hard, shiny material covered with a glass-like coating.
questions.description: Grandma's cup: it has survived a thousand falls and still serves the tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Pocillos de peltre are usually white with a blue or red rim, and on many farms they pass from grandparents to grandchildren.

questions.question: Which Colombian YouTuber started very young with DIY, fashion and makeup videos, and is one of the most-followed women in the country?
hints: She started on YouTube as a teenager.
Besides tutorials, she posts vlogs about her daily life.
Her stage name is a short four-letter nickname plus her last name.
questions.description: With scissors, glue and a camera, you can go a very long way.
questions.fun_fact: Kika Nieto started her channel as a teenager, and her stage name became known all over Latin America.

questions.question: I come in a little blue jar, I smell strongly of mint, and Grandma rubs me on your chest when you have a cold. What am I?
hints: You don't drink it, you rub it on.
It leaves your nose clear and cool.
It's a menthol ointment Grandma rubs on you at bedtime to help you breathe.
questions.description: The official perfume of every Colombian grandma during cold season.
questions.fun_fact: Many Latin American grandmas use it for almost everything: bug bites, aches and even to “cure” a bad mood.

questions.question: In the Colombian countryside they call it “tigre”. It has rosette-shaped spots and is the largest cat in the Americas. What animal is it?
hints: It isn't a real tiger: tigers live in Asia.
It is a very good swimmer and lives in the jungle.
Its name starts with “ja”.
questions.description: The cat with more nicknames in the Colombian countryside than a soccer star.
questions.fun_fact: Many Indigenous peoples of the Colombian Amazon believed that shamans could turn into jaguars.

questions.question: Someone rubs an egg all over your body, cracks it into a glass of water and looks at it. According to the belief, what is it for?
wrong_answers: To tell if it will rain
hints: It is done mostly on babies and children.
People say the egg white shows the bad energy it took away.
It has to do with an envious stare.
questions.description: An egg that doesn't end up as breakfast but works as a detective instead.
questions.fun_fact: This cleansing ritual is practiced in many Latin American countries, from Mexico to Colombia.

questions.question: Finish the Colombian superstition: “If the palm of your hand itches…”
hints: It's about something you receive with your hand.
Many people rub their hand or close their fist so the luck doesn't slip away.
You keep it in your wallet.
questions.description: The only itch everyone wants to have.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions the hand matters: one hand means money coming in, the other means money going out.

questions.question: According to Colombian folk belief, what makes a baby “descuajado”?
questions.answer: A fall or a hard shake
hints: The “cuajo” is supposed to be a part of the belly.
They say it has moved out of its place.
That's why people ask you not to bounce a baby or toss it in the air.
questions.description: A diagnosis you won't find in any medical book, but you will in every kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: To “fix” a descuajado baby, tradition takes it to a sobandera, who rubs it and sometimes turns it upside down.

questions.question: I bathed in the river during Holy Week even though I was told not to, and I was turned into a water creature. I sing on the rocks and comb my long hair. Who am I?
hints: I trick fishermen with my singing.
I no longer have legs.
I'm half girl.
questions.description: She didn't listen to her mom and ended up with a radical new look.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this legend, many Colombian grandmothers said that bathing in the river on Good Friday would bring punishment.

questions.question: I came into Spanish with enslaved Africans, and in Colombia I mean thick, full lips. What word am I?
hints: People use me to talk about a part of the face.
When someone is angry and pouts, people say they're sticking it out.
It starts with B and has two syllables.
questions.description: A word that crossed the ocean and settled down right on your face.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish Royal Academy dictionary marks “bemba” as a word of Afro-American origin, like many words that came with the African diaspora.

questions.question: Brasier, carné and chofer are words Colombian Spanish borrowed from the same language. What are these borrowings called?
hints: Many of these words came with the fashion, cars and city life of the 19th and 20th centuries.
That language is a Romance language spoken in Europe, parts of Africa and Canada.
The name comes from Gaul, the old name of that land.
questions.description: Words that arrived without a passport but with plenty of style.
questions.fun_fact: “Brasier” comes from the French “brassière”, which once meant a little undershirt for babies.

questions.question: What do you call the accent of Medellín and Antioquia, famous for its “pues” and “¡ave María!”?
hints: It's the accent of the City of Eternal Spring.
It's the accent of the platter with beans, chicharrón and arepa.
It's a short word that comes from “paisano.”
questions.description: An accent that comes with an arepa on the side, pues.
questions.fun_fact: The word “paisa” comes from “paisano,” meaning someone from the same land.

questions.question: If someone says “¡achichay!” when it's cold, with a pastuso accent, they come from the highlighted department. Which one is it?
hints: It's on the border with Ecuador.
The Carnaval de Negros y Blancos is celebrated there.
Its capital is Pasto.
questions.description: Achichay, this question is freezing.
questions.fun_fact: Pastuso words like “achichay” (brr, it's cold) and “atatay” (yuck) come from Quechua.

questions.question: He's your child's godfather, your dad calls his best friend this, and vallenato songs say it all the time. What's the word?
hints: It starts at a baptism.
It doesn't come from a marriage, but from a church ceremony.
Think of a “father” shared with someone else.
questions.description: A relative you won't find on the family tree, but you'll find at every party.
questions.fun_fact: “Compadre” comes from the Latin “compater”, meaning “father together with another”.

questions.question: Over a century ago they came from Lebanon, Syria and Palestine with Ottoman papers and settled on Colombia's Caribbean coast. What were they nicknamed?
hints: The nickname came from the empire that ruled their lands.
That empire's capital was Istanbul.
It's what you call people from a country between Europe and Asia.
questions.description: A nickname that pointed at the wrong country on the map.
questions.fun_fact: Although almost none of them came from Turkey, the nickname “turcos” stuck because of the Ottoman passports they arrived with.

questions.question: If you visit the Salón Nacional de Artistas, you're at an event created in 1940 by an education minister who later became a Liberal leader. Who was he?
hints: He was a very popular political leader of the mid-20th century.
His death in 1948 set off the Bogotazo.
His face is on the 1,000-peso bill.
questions.description: The country's most senior art show, with more years behind it than many grandmothers.
questions.fun_fact: The Salón Nacional de Artistas is Colombia's oldest art exhibition, and it is still held today.

questions.question: It's a painting of the Virgin Mary on cotton cloth, kept in a basilica in Boyacá, and she is the patron saint of Colombia. Which one is it?
hints: It was painted in the 16th century, in colonial times.
The story goes that it was badly faded and one day suddenly got its colors back.
It is named after a town in Boyacá that starts with “Chi”.
questions.description: A painting so famous it gave its name to a whole town… or was it the other way around?
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the painting was miraculously “renewed” on December 26, 1586, getting back the colors it had lost.

questions.question: Many churches in Pasto and Popayán hold colonial sculptures with glass eyes and shiny skin, by masters like Caspicara and Legarda. Which school do they come from?
hints: It comes from a colonial city south of Colombia.
Its workshops were in an Andean capital, close to the equator.
Today that city is the capital of Ecuador.
questions.description: Saints imported from the south, with no passport and with glass eyes.
questions.fun_fact: Caspicara, one of the great sculptors of that school, was an Indigenous man whose name in Quechua is said to mean “wooden face”.

questions.question: In Tierradentro (Cauca), there are tombs dug into the rock underground, with spiral stairs and walls painted red, black and white. What are they called?
hints: You can't see them from far away: you have to go down to find them.
The name comes from Greek and means something like “under the earth”.
It starts with the same four letters as “hypothermia”.
questions.description: Basements with spiral staircases, and not a single piece of old junk stored in them.
questions.fun_fact: Tierradentro National Archaeological Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

questions.question: Which Colombian artist created “Musa paradisiaca”, a 1996 video installation with hanging bunches of plantains and small screens?
hints: He is a pioneer of video art in Colombia.
He was born in Bogotá in 1959, and his work deals with the country's history.
His surname is one of the best-known in Antioquia, shared with a famous historian of Colombia's independence.
questions.description: A work of art you could leave to ripen in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: “Musa paradisiaca” is the scientific name that Linnaeus gave to the plantain.

questions.question: I was an illustrator and engraver, I founded the “Papel Periódico Ilustrado” and in 1886 I created Bogotá's School of Fine Arts. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 19th century and died just one year after founding the school.
My newspaper was famous for its wood engravings of people and landscapes.
My last name is the same as that of a Venezuelan general who fought alongside Bolívar.
questions.description: The man who put inspiration on a class schedule.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá's School of Fine Arts is now part of the National University of Colombia.

questions.question: Which businessman from Antioquia founded the textile company Coltejer in 1907?
hints: He was a Medellín merchant in the early 20th century.
His surname became a byword for the paisa textile industry.
His surname starts with “Echa…”.
questions.description: Long before fast fashion, Antioquia was already serious about weaving.
questions.fun_fact: The Coltejer building, with its top shaped like a knitting needle, is one of the most famous sights on Medellín's skyline.

questions.question: I was born in Palenquito, Bolívar, I've sung bullerengue since I was a girl, and I'm called “the queen of bullerengue.” Who am I?
hints: My music has been heard on stages in Europe and on other continents.
I've been nominated for the Latin Grammy several times.
My first name starts with “Petr…”.
questions.description: A Caribbean voice that needs no microphone, just a drum and some clapping hands.
questions.fun_fact: Bullerengue is sung mostly by women, backed by drums and hand clapping.

questions.question: In “Encanto,” Luisa is the sister of Mirabel and one other Madrigal girl. Who?
hints: She is the oldest of the three sisters.
Everyone thinks she is perfect.
Her gift is making flowers grow wherever she wants.
questions.description: A family so big you need a family tree and a magic house just to keep track of it.
questions.fun_fact: The landscapes in “Encanto” were inspired by the Eje Cafetero and by towns like Salento and Barichara.

questions.question: Which TV host presented the kids' show “Animalandia” and later, for years, the morning show “Muy buenos días”?
hints: He was known for his humor and his dancing in the mornings.
His first name is how you say the letter J in Spanish.
His last name is also the name of a city in Spain.
questions.description: Get up early, have a tinto, switch on the TV: breakfast for half of Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: “Muy buenos días” was one of the longest-running morning shows on Colombian TV.

questions.question: I see the future, I live hidden inside the walls of the Casita, and my family would rather not talk about me. Who am I?
hints: I'm from the movie “Encanto”.
Rats are my friends and I wear a green ruana (poncho).
There's a very famous song with my name in it.
questions.description: The uncle everyone talks about at the very moment they say they don't talk about him.
questions.fun_fact: The song about Bruno was such a hit that it beat many songs by real singers on the charts.

questions.question: Who was the first Colombian to win the Giro d'Italia, in 2014?
hints: He was a fearsome climber whenever the road got steep.
As a boy he rode his bike to school on steep mountain roads.
He grew up in Cómbita, Boyacá.
questions.description: For a Colombian climber, the mountains of Italy are just a little hill on the way home.
questions.fun_fact: At the Giro d'Italia the leader doesn't wear yellow: he wears the pink jersey, the “maglia rosa”.

questions.question: TransMilenio is to bus as Metrocable is to…
hints: It doesn't travel on the street but through the air.
It climbs the mountains around Medellín.
Its cabins hang from a steel wire high above the houses.
questions.description: A bus so packed at 6 p.m. that even the air has to wait in line.
questions.fun_fact: TransMilenio started running in December 2000, and its long articulated buses have their own lanes down the middle of the avenues.

questions.question: The department highlighted on the map has a sanctuary built on a bridge over a canyon. Which one is it?
wrong_answers: Basilica of the Lord of Miracles of Buga
hints: It's very close to the border with Ecuador.
It's in the municipality of Ipiales.
Its name comes from the flat stones found there.
questions.description: A church that took the idea of building bridges between people very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: The neo-Gothic church of Las Lajas was built between 1916 and 1949, over the canyon of the Guáitara River.

questions.question: How many sculptures by Fernando Botero are there in Plaza Botero in Medellín?
hints: There are enough to keep you busy walking around the plaza for a good while.
There are more than a dozen.
It's a little less than two dozen.
questions.description: A plaza where nobody is on a diet, not even the horses.
questions.fun_fact: Botero gave these bronze sculptures to Medellín, his hometown, and they stand in front of the Museo de Antioquia.

questions.question: This national park lies in the highlighted department, on the Amazon River near Leticia. What is it called?
hints: Pink dolphins swim nearby.
Tikuna communities live inside it.
Its name has to do with hammocks.
questions.description: A river so wide that mosquitoes need a layover to cross it.
questions.fun_fact: Amacayacu means “river of hammocks,” and communities of the Tikuna people live on its land.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT typical of Santa Cruz de Mompox?
hints: You'll find three of them as you walk around the town, beside the Magdalena River.
The odd one out is a national symbol of Colombia.
It's woven from caña flecha in Córdoba.
questions.description: A town so calm that even the clocks take a siesta.
questions.fun_fact: Simón Bolívar said: “If to Caracas I owe my life, to Mompox I owe my glory.”

questions.question: This wooden lookout, in a town in Quindío, is famous for its view of the Coffee Cultural Landscape. Which town is it in?
hints: It's a neighbor of Salento, in northern Quindío.
It's famous for its handwoven baskets.
Its name sounds a lot like the name of a Nordic country.
questions.description: A wooden tower for looking at coffee fields without having to pick anything.
questions.fun_fact: On clear days, from the Filandia lookout you can see land in Quindío, Risaralda and Valle del Cauca.

questions.question: Zócalos, colorful reliefs on the lower part of houses, are the trademark of a town in Antioquia next to a big reservoir. Which town?
hints: It's in eastern Antioquia, about two hours from Medellín.
Next to it is a giant rock you climb by stairs.
People call it “the town of zócalos.”
questions.description: A town that decorated its houses as if they were birthday cakes.
questions.fun_fact: Guatapé's zócalos show pictures of animals, trades and scenes from town life.

questions.question: Barichara has stone streets, rammed-earth houses and a Camino Real that goes down to Guane. Which department is it in?
hints: It's the land of hormigas culonas (roasted big-bottomed ants).
It's near the Chicamocha Canyon.
San Gil, famous for adventure sports, is very close by.
questions.description: A town so pretty that even the street stones pose for photos.
questions.fun_fact: The stone Camino Real between Barichara and Guane takes about two hours to walk.

questions.question: You're at the foot of Monserrate in Bogotá and want to go up. Which of these will NOT get you to the top?
hints: Three of these options do go up the mountain.
One of them travels through the air, and another runs on sloping rails.
The odd one out is a train that moves around the city, not up the hills.
questions.description: A mountain that gets more visitors than Grandma does in December.
questions.fun_fact: The Monserrate funicular has been running since 1929, and the cable car came later, in 1955.

questions.question: It's the capital of Huila, lies on the Magdalena River, and its San Pedro festival crowns the National Bambuco Queen. Which city is it?
hints: It's in the south of the country, and it's very hot.
The Tatacoa Desert is nearby.
Its name starts with N.
questions.description: A city where the heat goes up and so does the bambuco.
questions.fun_fact: Neiva was founded three times: in 1539, in 1550 and, for good, in 1612.

questions.question: I'm an active volcano in Cauca, very close to Popayán. Sulfur was mined on my slopes for years, and condors fly in my park. Who am I?
hints: I'm in southern Colombia, in the Colombian Massif.
My national park has the same name as me.
My name starts with P.
questions.description: A neighbor of Popayán who lets out smoke now and then without asking anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Andean condors have been released in Puracé National Park so they can fly over the region again.

questions.question: This gold piece is one of the most famous in Bogotá's Museo del Oro. What is it called?
hints: It's shaped like a little bottle.
It was used to hold lime in Indigenous rituals.
The second word of its name is an Indigenous people of the Eje Cafetero.
questions.description: A little treasure so important that a whole museum started with it.
questions.fun_fact: The Banco de la República bought the Poporo Quimbaya in 1939, and the Museo del Oro collection was born with it.

questions.question: San Andrés is famous for its “sea of seven colors” in the Caribbean. Which of these Colombian islands is NOT in the Caribbean Sea?
hints: Colombia is the only country in South America with coasts on two oceans.
The odd one out is in Colombia's other ocean.
It lies in the Pacific Ocean, far off the coast of Valle del Cauca.
questions.description: A sea that couldn't pick just one color, so it picked seven.
questions.fun_fact: San Andrés is much closer to Nicaragua than to mainland Colombia.

questions.question: Say it fast: “Erre con erre cigarro, erre con erre barril, rápido ruedan los carros cargados de…” What are the carts loaded with?
hints: It's something you could load onto a train.
It comes from cane.
It's what you add to a tinto so it isn't bitter.
questions.description: A tongue workout you do at recess, not at the gym.
questions.fun_fact: Speech therapists use this tongue twister to help kids practice the tricky rolled double R.

questions.question: Many Colombian children learn to read with the sentence “Mi mamá me mima”. What does the mom do when she “mima”?
hints: It's something nice, not a punishment.
It has to do with hugs and kisses.
A “niño mimado” is a spoiled, much-loved child.
questions.description: The sweetest sentence ever to come out of a school reading book.
questions.fun_fact: Sentences like “Mi mamá me mima” repeat the letter m so children can learn to put syllables together easily.

questions.question: In the Tío Conejo stories, his great rival is strong, fierce and greedy, but always gets tricked. What animal is it?
hints: It’s a big cat.
In the Llanos, people also use this name for the jaguar.
It’s the biggest cat in Colombia’s jungles and has a mighty roar.
questions.description: The hungriest and least clever villain in Grandma’s bedtime stories.
questions.fun_fact: The Tío Conejo stories have roots in African tales that came to the Americas and mixed with Indigenous and Spanish stories.

questions.question: In the song, Pin Pon is a very handsome doll who washes his little face with soap and water. What is he made of?
hints: It’s a material that gets soggy easily.
Boxes are made of it.
In the Spanish song, the word rhymes with “jabón.”
questions.description: A doll so well-behaved he washes his face without anyone asking.
questions.fun_fact: Pin Pon also combs his hair with an ivory comb, and even when it pulls, he doesn’t cry or make a fuss.

questions.question: In which century did Rafael Pombo publish “El convite de Mirringa Mirronga,” about a fussy cat's party?
hints: Colombia was already independent.
It came out around the same time as “El renacuajo paseador.”
It was sometime in the 1800s.
questions.description: A cat party so fancy it still hasn't ended after centuries.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo published his children's stories in New York, where he lived for almost twenty years.

questions.question: It starts raining and you sing “Que llueva, que llueva, la Virgen de la cueva…”. Who is singing in the next line?
hints: They have wings.
They build nests in trees.
They chirp and tweet.
questions.description: The favorite song of anyone with a brand-new umbrella.
questions.fun_fact: The rhyme ends with “que sí, que no, que caiga un chaparrón”, and a chaparrón is a short, heavy downpour.

questions.question: In Colombia, it’s the angry heartache left by a love that ended; it’s cured with rancheras and even has its own music. What is it called?
hints: It happens to someone who just got dumped.
At parties people sing about it with an aguardiente in hand.
Darío Gómez was its king, and Paola Jara sings it today.
questions.description: When your heart ends up like a phone with a cracked screen.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia there are radio stations and bars that play nothing but despecho music.

questions.question: This band from Colombia’s Pacific coast won a Latin Grammy in 2010 with “De dónde vengo yo.” What is its name?
hints: Their name plays on the department where they were born.
They mix hip hop with Pacific coast rhythms.
Chocó and Quibdó are hidden in the name.
questions.description: A little piece of the Pacific with flow, marimba and lots of pride.
questions.fun_fact: “De dónde vengo yo” is a song about Chocó, one of the rainiest regions on the planet.

questions.question: Who was the first Colombian artist to reach number 1 on the US Billboard Hot 100?
hints: It happened in 2006.
It was with a song about hips.
She's from Barranquilla.
questions.description: The American chart where everyone wants to be first, like in the lunch line.
questions.fun_fact: “Hips Don't Lie” hit number 1 in 2006 and was one of the most-played songs in the world that year.

questions.question: I'm from Montería, I started out with “Una lady como tú” and in 2022 I got the world dancing to “La Bachata”. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Córdoba, on the Caribbean coast.
My brother Julián was part of my first hits.
People call me MTZ.
questions.description: A guy from the Caribbean coast who got the whole world swaying their hips side to side.
questions.fun_fact: “La Bachata” is a song by a Colombian and became a worldwide hit, even though the rhythm was born in the Dominican Republic.

questions.question: This singer from Santa Marta is the voice of Bomba Estéreo, the band behind “Fuego” and “Soy yo”. Who is she?
hints: Her hometown sits on the Caribbean coast, below the Sierra Nevada.
She mixes champeta, cumbia and electronic music.
Her stage name is short: two letters and a surname.
questions.description: Pure Caribbean fire with an electronic twist.
questions.fun_fact: The video for “Soy yo”, with a girl who dances without a care, became an anthem of self-confidence around the world.

questions.question: I'm from Medellín, they call me “Pretty Boy,” and in 2020 I sang about an ex showing off her trip to “Hawái.” Who am I?
hints: I made a remix of that song with The Weeknd.
I also sang “Felices los 4.”
My stage name is made from syllables of my family members' names.
questions.description: An island vacation someone posted only to make others jealous.
questions.fun_fact: The name Maluma comes from Marlli, Luis and Manuela: his mom, his dad and his sister.

questions.question: We're two Colombian brothers: we had hits with “Yo te esperaré” and then “Por fin te encontré” with Juan Magán. Who are we?
hints: Our names are Alejandro and Mauricio Rengifo.
One of us is also a producer who writes songs for other artists.
One of us has the world capital of salsa in his stage name.
questions.description: Two brothers who waited for each other and finally found each other.
questions.fun_fact: A young Sebastián Yatra also sings on “Por fin te encontré” alongside Juan Magán.

questions.question: If you strum a Colombian tiple once, across all its strings, how many strings do you hear?
hints: It has more strings than a guitar.
Some of its strings are tuned an octave higher, like a high echo.
There are four groups of three strings each.
questions.description: One sweep of the hand and you hear more string than in a hardware store.
questions.fun_fact: The tiple is considered Colombia's national instrument and stars in carranga and bambuco.

questions.question: They wear charro suits with silver buttons and huge sombreros, play trumpets, violins and guitars, and in Colombia people hire them for serenades. What is this group called?
hints: They come from a Mexican tradition.
They sing rancheras like “El rey” or “Volver, volver”.
Its name starts with “Ma”.
questions.description: The fanciest way to wake up the whole neighborhood at midnight.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: I'm from Antioquia, I sing música popular and heartbreak songs, and I married Jessi Uribe, another singer of the same genre. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Medellín.
We're one of the most famous couples in Colombian música popular.
My last name sounds almost like the Spanish word for a juice pitcher.
questions.description: A queen of heartbreak songs who, ironically, ended up very much married.
questions.fun_fact: Paola Jara started singing as a child at contests and parties in Antioquia before becoming a national star.

questions.question: In 1514, Martín Fernández de Enciso read the Requerimiento to two Zenú chiefs on the Sinú coast. What did they reply?
questions.answer: That the pope was giving away land that wasn’t his
wrong_answers: That they accepted the king and would give him gold
That they would rather hear it read in Latin
That they would first ask the sun about it
hints: Enciso himself wrote down their answer in a geography book.
The chiefs weren’t impressed by the papers.
The document said the pope had given those lands to the kings of Spain, and the chiefs didn’t think that was fair.
questions.description: A contract read in a language nobody understood: the great-grandfather of fine print.
questions.fun_fact: According to Enciso, the chiefs said the pope must have been “drunk” to give away what wasn’t his, and the king must be crazy to ask for it.

questions.question: Molas like this one are the textile art of the Gunadule people. In which region of Colombia do they live?
questions.answer: The Darién and the Gulf of Urabá
hints: They live near the Caribbean Sea.
Their people also live across a border, on some famous islands.
It's the corner of Colombia that touches Panama.
questions.description: Art made in layers of cloth: like lasagna, but you wear it.
questions.fun_fact: Most Gunadule live in Panama, on the Guna Yala islands, once called the San Blas Islands.

questions.question: If someone in Colombia says a person is “un guache”, what kind of person are they?
hints: It's not a compliment.
It has to do with manners.
It's the opposite of someone gentlemanly and polite.
questions.description: Colombian grandmas have words that even the translator on your phone won't dare to touch.
questions.fun_fact: “Guache” is thought to come from “guecha”, the Muisca word for their frontier warriors.

questions.question: Santa Marta, the oldest city in Colombia, was founded in 1525. Which conquistador founded it?
hints: He was a seafarer from Seville who explored the Caribbean coast.
Before he set off exploring, he worked as a scribe, something like a notary.
His surname ends in “-idas”.
questions.description: A city so old it had a beach before sunscreen was even invented.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Marta is one of the oldest cities founded by the Spanish in South America that is still standing.

questions.question: Women of an Indigenous people in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta weave it from sheep’s wool, and men wear it across the chest. What is it?
hints: It’s used to carry things.
Its patterns show nature and the thinking of its people.
Its name comes from the Indigenous people who weave it.
questions.description: Some people keep a diary; others weave one, one stitch at a time.
questions.fun_fact: Weaving a single Arhuaco mochila can take weeks, and it is said the woman weaves her thoughts into it as she goes.

questions.question: It grows underground, comes in criolla and pastusa, and is eaten fried or mashed. What is it?
hints: The Muisca already grew it in the cold highlands.
It has eyes, but it can't see.
The criolla kind is small and yellow.
questions.description: The star of ajiaco, even though it lives hidden underground.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia grows hundreds of native potato varieties, in yellow, red and even purple.

questions.question: You travel from Bogotá to Tunja across a high, cold plateau, about 2,600 m (8,500 ft) up, where the Muisca lived. What is it called?
hints: It's a plain, but high up in the Eastern Cordillera.
It's split between two departments.
Its name joins Cundinamarca and Boyacá.
questions.description: A land so high and so cold that even the cows wear a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago, much of this plateau was a huge lake, which is why the Sabana de Bogotá is so flat.

questions.question: Look at this statue from San Agustín. Which German ethnologist carried out the first scientific excavations there, in 1913 and 1914?
hints: He worked for the Ethnological Museum in Berlin.
He took several statues back to Germany, which caused controversy.
His last name sounds like Prussia.
questions.description: A visitor who came from Europe and started digging up stone giants.
questions.fun_fact: In 1929 Preuss published “Monumental Prehistoric Art”, the first major book on the San Agustín statues.

questions.question: Which Colombian poet wrote the line “One night, a night all full of perfumes, of murmurs and of the music of wings”?
hints: It comes from the poem known as “Nocturno.”
He was a poet from Bogotá in the late 19th century, a forerunner of modernismo.
His face is on the 5,000-peso bill.
questions.description: A line of poetry so fragrant it should be sold in a bottle.
questions.fun_fact: José Asunción Silva appears on both the old and the new Colombian 5,000-peso bill.

questions.question: Who wrote the 1848 program seen as the birth certificate of Colombia’s Liberal Party?
hints: He was a lawyer and professor from Boyacá.
He published it in the newspaper El Aviso.
His surname means “reds” in Spanish, very fitting for a Liberal.
questions.description: A document from 1848 that fueled almost two centuries of arguments at family dinners.
questions.fun_fact: A year later, in 1849, Mariano Ospina Rodríguez and José Eusebio Caro answered with the Conservative Party’s program.

questions.question: Someone came to borrow me to decorate a dinner honoring Villavicencio; my owner said no, and the quarrel turned into a revolt. What am I?
hints: It happened in Bogotá in 1810.
My owner was a Spanish merchant.
Today I'm kept in a museum on Plaza de Bolívar that is named after me.
questions.description: Never has a simple loan ended up changing the history of a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: The vase is kept at the Museo de la Independencia, known as the Casa del Florero, in Bogotá.

questions.question: I was US president in the early 20th century. I backed Panama's separation in 1903 and later boasted, “I took the Isthmus.” Who am I?
hints: I wanted to build a canal between two oceans.
I won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906.
Teddy bears are named after my nickname.
questions.description: A man who took home an isthmus the way other people take home a souvenir.
questions.fun_fact: The teddy bear got its name from this president's nickname, “Teddy,” after a 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a captured bear.

questions.question: This US company ruled the banana plantations of Magdalena, was the target of the 1928 strike and inspired a scene in “One Hundred Years of Solitude.” Which company was it?
hints: It had plantations in several countries in Central America and the Caribbean.
Its main product was yellow and you peel it.
In Central America it was nicknamed “el pulpo” (the octopus) because of its huge power.
questions.description: A foreign company with more power than some government ministers and more bunches than anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Over the years the company changed its name, and today it is known as Chiquita.

questions.question: Fans of Diomedes Díaz, writer of “Tres canciones,” called him by a nickname. What was it?
hints: The nickname includes the name of his hometown.
That town is in La Guajira.
The nickname compares him to the chief of a tribe.
questions.description: A vallenato idol whose fans almost never called him by his real name.
questions.fun_fact: “El Jilguero de América” was the nickname of another vallenato great: Jorge Oñate.

questions.question: It's made of crispy puff pastry, filled with shredded chicken, and sold in Colombian bakeries with a soda. What is it called?
hints: It leaves crumbs all over your shirt.
Its dough has lots of thin layers.
In Spanish, its name sounds like a dessert, but it's savory.
questions.description: The express lunch for anyone with five minutes and a soda.
questions.fun_fact: Puff pastry is made by folding the dough with butter many times, which is why it comes out in layers.

questions.question: Colombian asaderos (chicken grills) offer “pollo broaster.” What is it?
hints: It comes out crispy on the outside.
Its name comes from a brand of kitchen machines invented in the United States.
The machine that makes it works like a pressure cooker.
questions.description: A chicken with an English name and the heart of a Colombian asadero.
questions.fun_fact: “Broaster” was the brand of a pressure fryer invented in the United States, and in Colombia it stuck as the name of the dish.

questions.question: Which department of Colombia is highlighted on this map?
hints: It's in the northwest of the country.
Its capital is the city of eternal spring.
The paisas live there, and it's the birthplace of the bandeja paisa.
questions.description: A department so mountainous that even the cars huff and puff on the way up.
questions.fun_fact: Bandeja paisa comes with beans, rice, ground beef, chicharrón, chorizo, a fried egg, ripe plantain, arepa and avocado.

questions.question: It's the signature garment of Boyacá, woven on looms in Nobsa to keep out the highland cold. What is the traditional ruana made of?
hints: It comes from an animal.
You get it by giving the animal a haircut, without hurting it.
That animal says “baa.”
questions.description: The blanket that became clothing you can wear out on the street.
questions.fun_fact: Nobsa, in Boyacá, is famous for its wool ruanas woven on handmade looms.

questions.question: The telenovela “La Pola” told the life of Policarpa Salavarrieta. In everyday Colombian speech, what is a “pola”?
hints: It's a drink.
Adults order it cold at the corner store or at the stadium.
The word comes from a Bavaria company product that carried the heroine's nickname.
questions.description: A heroine so beloved that her name ended up on what people order at the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: Policarpa Salavarrieta appeared on Colombia's old 10,000-peso bill.

questions.question: In what year did Caracol and RCN start broadcasting as private TV channels in Colombia?
hints: It was at the end of the 20th century.
It happened a little over a year before “Yo soy Betty, la fea” premiered.
It was the same year as the World Cup in France.
questions.description: Before this, there was a lot less to fight over the remote about at home.
questions.fun_fact: Before 1998, Caracol and RCN were production companies that rented airtime on state channels.

questions.question: “Pasión de gavilanes” premiered in 2003. In which year did its second season arrive with the original cast?
hints: Fans had to wait a very long time.
It premiered after the COVID-19 pandemic.
It was the same year as the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: Some loves come back… even if they keep you waiting longer than a doctor's appointment.
questions.fun_fact: “Pasión de gavilanes” is a remake of “Las aguas mansas” (1994), and Julio Jiménez wrote both.

questions.question: Amparo Grisales is famous for three of these things. Which one has NOTHING to do with her?
wrong_answers: Being a judge on “Yo me llamo”
hints: She has been on Colombian television for more than five decades.
You can see her as a judge on a show for impersonators.
Betty was played by Ana María Orozco.
questions.description: Three truths and a fib walk into a TV studio, and only one of them gets sent home.
questions.fun_fact: Amparo Grisales started acting on television at a very young age, in the 1970s.

questions.question: In the biographical telenovela “Rigo,” young Rigoberto Urán sells chance on the streets of Urrao to help his family. What is “chance”?
hints: It is sold on almost any street corner in Colombia.
It comes on small printed slips of paper.
It is similar to the lottery.
questions.description: Before he climbed mountains on a bicycle, this champion was pedaling to help out at home.
questions.fun_fact: Rigoberto Urán won the silver medal in the road race at the 2012 London Olympics.

questions.question: In parqués, you roll dice like this one to move your pieces. How many dice do you roll each turn?
hints: It's fewer than the fingers on one hand.
To get out of jail, all the dice have to show the same number.
It's the same number as the eyes you have.
questions.description: A little dotted cube that decides whether you get out of jail or stay there crying.
questions.fun_fact: In parqués, rolling doubles lets you roll again, so a lucky turn can last quite a while.

questions.question: It's a school or parish party with food stands, games like rana and raffles to raise money. What is it called?
hints: It's usually held on a weekend, and families go.
The money raised goes to the school or the church.
It has the same name as Istanbul's famous covered market.
questions.description: Empanadas, raffles and the math teacher selling salpicón: something strange is going on at school.
questions.fun_fact: The word “bazar” comes from Persian and means “market.”

questions.question: In Colombia, when the “vientos de agosto” (August winds) arrive, what does it mean for many kids and families?
hints: It has to do with an outdoor game.
You need a long string and plenty of space.
The toy has a tail, but it isn't an animal.
questions.description: August shows up with messy hair and wants to go out and play.
questions.fun_fact: Kite festivals are held in many parts of Colombia in August, like the famous one in Villa de Leyva.

questions.question: I was born in Barranquilla, hosted Caracol's morning show “Día a día” for years and have hosted the Cartagena beauty pageant on TV. Who am I?
hints: My hometown is famous for its Carnival.
I was the male face of Caracol's mornings.
My last name starts with “Cal”.
questions.description: His smile gets up even earlier than the morning tinto.
questions.fun_fact: The broadcasts of the National Beauty Pageant are among the most-watched events on Colombian TV every November.

questions.question: I host “Séptimo día,” Caracol's Sunday night investigative show. Who am I?
hints: My accent shows that I wasn't born in Colombia.
I've led the show for many years.
My last name starts with “Teo.”
questions.description: God rested on the seventh day; this man starts digging instead.
questions.fun_fact: “Séptimo día” (“Seventh Day”) is named that way because it airs on Sunday, the seventh day of the week.

questions.question: Every November I'm crowned in Cartagena in front of millions of TV viewers. Who am I?
hints: My pageant is one of the most-watched events on Colombian TV.
Afterwards I can go on to international beauty pageants.
I represent the whole country, not just one festival.
questions.description: Her favorite accessory shines brighter than a brand-new light bulb.
questions.fun_fact: The National Beauty Pageant is held in Cartagena during the city's independence celebrations, around November 11.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Franky,” the Nickelodeon teen series filmed in Colombia, what is Franky really?
hints: A scientist created her in her lab.
Her name recalls a monster built by a doctor.
She has circuits instead of organs.
questions.description: A new girl at school with a secret her classmates never see coming.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Franky” was filmed in Bogotá and aired all across Latin America.

questions.question: Guillermina and Candelario, the young siblings from the Señal Colombia cartoon, live with their grandparents by the beach. In which region?
hints: It rains a huge amount there, and the jungle reaches all the way to the sea.
It is a region with a strong Afro-Colombian culture.
Humpback whales arrive there every year.
questions.description: Two little siblings whose playground is the sea.
questions.fun_fact: The series shows the music, food and customs of Colombia's Pacific region to kids all over the country.

questions.question: Every April in Valledupar, the best accordion players fight for my crown playing paseo, merengue, son and puya. Who am I?
hints: I'm a title you win in a music contest.
The winner is crowned on a stage in the Parque de la Leyenda.
My name includes the name of Valledupar's music.
questions.description: A crown you don't inherit: you win it with bellows and fast fingers.
questions.fun_fact: Alejo Durán was the first Vallenato King, at the first festival in 1968.

questions.question: I'm a small village of Valledupar at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, called the land of songwriters because Rafael Escalona was born here. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the municipality of Valledupar, in Cesar.
Freddy Molina, who wrote “Mi Pobre Valle”, is also from here.
My name sounds like the Colombian word for a big fruit that's green outside and red inside.
questions.description: A village so tiny it seems impossible it could hold so many songs.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Escalona, born in Patillal in 1927, inspired the telenovela “Escalona”, starring Carlos Vives.

questions.question: Consuelo Araújo Noguera, co-founder of the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata, was known as “La ___”. Complete the nickname.
hints: It was a nickname about command and power.
The nickname comes from the title of Indigenous chiefs in the Americas.
It's the feminine form of “cacique”.
questions.description: A woman so much in charge that she got a whole province dancing.
questions.fun_fact: The festival was born in 1968 thanks to Consuelo Araújo, Rafael Escalona and Alfonso López Michelsen.

questions.question: Rafael Pombo wrote his own Spanish version of the English nursery rhyme “Little Bo-Peep.” What is his poem called?
hints: Its main character is a country girl.
The girl loses her animals and doesn't know where they've gone.
She's the one who looks after the sheep in the fields.
questions.description: The first missing-animals case in Colombian children's literature.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo wrote many of his children's stories while living in New York, commissioned by a publishing house.

questions.question: In 1950, I signed the column “La Jirafa” in El Heraldo of Barranquilla as Septimus. Who am I?
hints: I was part of the Barranquilla Group.
My first novel was “La hojarasca.”
I was born in Aracataca.
questions.description: A long-necked columnist who looked at the news from way up high.
questions.fun_fact: The pen name Septimus came from a character by Virginia Woolf, one of his favorite writers.

questions.question: In Colombia, when you finally want to spend your savings, people say you have to “romper el…” (break the…)
hints: It's a kind of money box.
It's almost always made of clay or ceramic and shaped like an animal.
That animal goes “oink.”
questions.description: Saving is easy; the hard part is not breaking it before December.
questions.fun_fact: Many marrano money boxes have no lid: the only way to get the money out is to break them.

questions.question: This landscape with frailejones is on the 5,000-peso bill. Why is it so important for cities like Bogotá?
questions.answer: It stores and supplies their drinking water
wrong_answers: Almost all the coffee is grown there
The country's oil is found there
hints: It's cold there and almost always in the clouds.
Frailejones trap the moisture from the fog.
Many rivers are born there.
questions.description: A cold, fuzzy landscape full of plants that look like gentlemen in overcoats.
questions.fun_fact: A frailejón may grow just one centimeter (less than half an inch) a year, so a tall one can be older than your grandparents.

questions.question: Its name has just two letters, and it was born in Cali. What kind of products does the MK brand sell?
hints: They're sold in small boxes.
Lots of homes keep it in the medicine cabinet.
Acetaminophen, vitamin C… you buy them at the drugstore.
questions.description: Two letters that sound more like a license plate than a famous brand.
questions.fun_fact: Tecnoquímicas, the company that owns MK, is one of Colombia's biggest drug makers and has its headquarters in Cali.

questions.question: The logo of the Colombian bank Davivienda is a little house. What color is it?
hints: It's the same color as the signs on its branches.
It's a strong color, the color of warning signs.
It's the color of a ripe tomato.
questions.description: A bank that's always thinking about a roof and four walls.
questions.fun_fact: Davivienda started as a savings and housing corporation before becoming one of the biggest banks in the country.

questions.question: Two Swiss immigrants founded it in Sopó, Cundinamarca, in 1945, and it's famous for Bon Yurt. Which brand is it?
hints: It makes yogurt, cheese and kumis.
Its name brings to mind the mountains of Switzerland.
The most famous Swiss mountains are the Alps.
questions.description: Milk with a foreign accent, but raised on the Bogotá savanna.
questions.fun_fact: At first, its founders made cheese by hand from just a few liters of milk a day.

questions.question: In 2007 it became the first product from outside Europe with its name protected as a geographical indication in the European Union. Which Colombian product is it?
hints: It's grown on the slopes of the Andes.
Its symbol is a farmer in a hat with a mule.
In Colombia, a small cup of it is called a “tinto”.
questions.description: A Colombian product that arrived in Europe with all its papers in order.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to that protection, only coffee grown in Colombia can be sold in Europe as “Café de Colombia”.

questions.question: It was founded in 1953 by the Char family, and it also has radio stations called Olímpica Stereo. In which city was Olímpica born?
hints: It's a city on the Caribbean coast.
It's where the Magdalena River meets the sea.
Colombia's most famous carnival is held there.
questions.description: A supermarket named like a medal, with a radio station that has its own beat.
questions.fun_fact: Olímpica started out as a small drugstore before it filled up with supermarkets.

questions.question: Juan Valdez is to Conchita as Shrek is to…
hints: Conchita is not Juan Valdez’s wife.
Conchita carries the coffee sacks.
Conchita is a mule, and Shrek’s friend belongs to the same animal family.
questions.description: From the coffee mountains to the swamp, every long road has its own kind of hero.
questions.fun_fact: The Juan Valdez logo with Conchita and the mountains dates from 1981 and became one of the best-known coffee seals in the world.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian director. My first film was “La sociedad del semáforo,” and later I made the documentary “Señorita María, la falda de la montaña.” Who am I?
hints: My first fiction film came out in 2010.
My documentary follows María, a trans woman from a farming village in Boyacá.
I share my surname with the famous Colombian writer Plinio Apuleyo.
questions.description: A filmmaker who turns a red light into an entire feature film.
questions.fun_fact: “La sociedad del semáforo” tells the story of a waste picker who wants to make Bogotá's traffic lights stay red longer.

questions.question: I directed “El paseo,” the 2010 comedy about a chaotic family trip, and also “Mi gente linda, mi gente bella.” Who am I?
hints: I started with more serious films, like “Diástole y sístole.”
“El paseo” had so many sequels that it became a whole series.
In Spanish, my last name sounds like a wind instrument.
questions.description: A director who turned family vacations into pure chaos, aunts and uncles included.
questions.fun_fact: The “El paseo” series went past five films, something very rare in Colombian cinema.

questions.question: In “Romancing the Stone” (1984), Michael Douglas hunts for treasure in the Colombian jungle. Which country was it actually filmed in?
hints: Hollywood filmed the movie's “Colombia” in another country.
Many scenes were shot in the state of Veracruz.
It's the Latin American country closest to Hollywood.
questions.description: A Colombian treasure that traveled more than Michael Douglas's suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, Michael Douglas shares the adventure with Kathleen Turner and Danny DeVito.

questions.question: Take a close look: artisans in Ráquira, Boyacá, make pots and figures from this material. What is it?
hints: It comes from the ground.
When it's wet, it sticks to your shoes; baked in a kiln, it turns hard.
It's wet earth you can shape with your hands.
questions.description: A material that goes from the ground to the dinner table.
questions.fun_fact: Ráquira is called Colombia's handicraft capital, and many of its house fronts are decorated with clay figures.

questions.question: You're on a finca and a rider shouts that he lost an “espuela.” What fell off?
questions.answer: A metal piece worn on the heel of the boot
wrong_answers: A strap that holds the horse's saddle on
A leather ornament worn on the hat
A long rope for tying up the horse
hints: The rider wears it, not the horse.
It's used to nudge the horse forward.
It goes on the feet, at the back, and many have a small spiked wheel.
questions.description: A cry for help in the middle of the finca: something has gone missing in the pasture!
questions.fun_fact: The little toothed wheel of an espuela is called a rodaja.

questions.question: At the Barranquilla Carnival, many comparsas parade down the Vía 40. What is a comparsa?
questions.answer: A group of people in costume dancing together
wrong_answers: A giant float decorated with figures
A costume worn by just one person
hints: It isn't an object, it's people.
Neighborhoods, schools and companies spend months getting theirs ready for carnival.
It's like a dance team in costume.
questions.description: In Barranquilla at carnival time, nobody wants to stand still.
questions.fun_fact: In the Batalla de Flores, the parade that opens the Barranquilla Carnival, comparsas, floats and all kinds of costumes go by.

questions.question: I'm a wide-skirted dress with flowers and lace, and the queens wear me at the Festival del Bambuco in Neiva. Which dress am I?
hints: I'm danced at the San Pedro festivities in the southern Andes.
My dance partner wears an iraca hat and a red scarf.
My name recalls the saint whose festivities come in June, just before San Pedro.
questions.description: An outfit so elegant that the skirt could dance on its own.
