questions.fun_fact: The sanjuanero from Huila is a song, a dance and a dress all at once, and the song was composed by Anselmo Durán Plazas.

questions.question: It's woven from fibers like wicker, has a handle on top and you carry it on your arm to bring fruit home from the market. What is it?
hints: It's used to carry things.
It's stiff and shaped like an open container.
Little Red Riding Hood takes one to her grandmother's house.
questions.description: The shopping cart of the old days: no wheels, lots of style.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian towns, baskets are woven from fique, chusque (a mountain bamboo) or bejuco vines, depending on what grows nearby.

questions.question: In “Hannah Montana”, Rico is the kid who runs the beach snack stand. Which actor played him?
hints: He joined the show when he was only about 11 years old.
Later he acted in movies like “Ender's Game”.
His first name is the Spanish form of the prophet who parted the sea.
questions.description: Being the shortest in the group never stopped him from running the beach.
questions.fun_fact: Moisés Arias was born in New York, but his family is Colombian.

questions.question: I was born in Argentina to a Colombian dad, and I voiced the giftless girl with glasses from a magical house in Colombia. Who am I?
hints: I also played Detective Rosa Diaz in an American police comedy.
My character lives with her whole family in an enchanted house.
I voiced Mirabel in “Encanto”.
questions.description: The only Madrigal who didn't need magic to save the house.
questions.fun_fact: Stephanie Beatriz recorded the song “Waiting on a Miracle” on the same day she went into labor with her daughter, months before the film came out.

questions.question: He is a spook from Antioquia who roams abandoned mines and leaves a trail that dries up plants. What does his name, Patetarro, mean?
questions.answer: He has a can for a leg
wrong_answers: He kicks cans along the road
He has feet as wide as cans
He wears a can on his head
hints: The name is made of two words stuck together.
His name recalls what happened to him in a fight.
He lost a leg in a fight and replaced it with a container made of guadua (giant bamboo).
questions.description: A spook who left the mine but not his bad habit of messing everything up.
questions.fun_fact: The Patetarro's can is said to be full of filth, and nothing ever grows again where it spills.

questions.question: According to legend, who does the Hojarasquín del Monte punish?
questions.answer: Those who harm the forest and its animals
wrong_answers: Those who go out partying at night
Those who skip Mass on Sunday
Those who make fun of ghosts
hints: He's covered in leaves, moss and branches.
He looks like a walking tree.
He protects nature from hunters and loggers.
questions.description: A neighbor from the woods who dresses in whatever the wind knocks to the ground.
questions.fun_fact: Farmers describe him as a tree-shaped man and see him as the conscience of nature.

questions.question: In a legend from the Llanos, Florentino faces the Devil one night with harp, cuatro and maracas in a “contrapunteo.” What is that?
wrong_answers: A serenade for a young woman
hints: Playing well isn't enough: you need a quick tongue.
Whoever runs out of words loses.
Florentino is a folk singer who sings against the Devil.
questions.description: A duel before dawn where nobody pulls out a machete.
questions.fun_fact: The most famous version is a poem by Alberto Arvelo Torrealba, and Florentino beats the Devil at sunrise by praying the Creed.

questions.question: You hear it in the southern Magdalena valley, among bambucos and sanjuaneros, with a very sing-song lilt. Which accent is it?
hints: It comes from the south of the country, on the banks of the Magdalena River.
It is the land of the Tatacoa Desert.
The capital of that land is Neiva.
questions.description: Some accents are spoken, and others are almost danced.
questions.fun_fact: Every June, Neiva holds the Festival Folclórico y Reinado Nacional del Bambuco, with parades and sanjuanero.

questions.question: Complete Colombia's 1991 Constitution: “The languages and dialects of ethnic groups are also official in…”
hints: The 1991 Constitution recognizes Colombia as a multiethnic and multicultural country.
The article begins by saying Spanish is the official language of Colombia, then makes an exception for the languages of ethnic groups.
Not in the whole country, but on each people's own land.
questions.description: Even the Constitution has its own dictionary of who speaks what.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has about 65 Indigenous languages, plus Palenquero, San Andrés Creole and Romani.

questions.question: On the islands of the Raizal people, rondón is made in a big pot with coconut milk and eaten as a family. What is it?
hints: It is the most typical dish of San Andrés and Providencia.
It has seafood plus flour dumplings, plantain and cassava.
Besides fish, it has an animal with a spiral shell.
questions.description: A dish so tasty the whole sea wants to be an ingredient.
questions.fun_fact: The name “rondón” comes from the English “run down”, because it cooks until everything cooks down and blends together.

questions.question: In Colombia, peoples of Putumayo speak it in its Inga variety. What is the most widely spoken Indigenous language of the Americas?
hints: It is an official language in Peru and Bolivia.
English words like “llama”, “condor” and “puma” come from it.
It was the language of the Inca Empire.
questions.description: A language that came down from the Andes and never got tired of walking.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia’s Inga language is the northernmost variety of Quechua.

questions.question: You're in Bogotá's Plaza de Bolívar, facing the bronze statue of the Liberator by Italian sculptor Pietro Tenerani. In what year was it put up?
hints: Bolívar had already died, but not that long before.
At the time, the country was called the Republic of New Granada.
It was put up about 16 years after Bolívar's death, which was in 1830.
questions.description: It has stood in the square so long it has seen more pigeons than anyone.
questions.fun_fact: It is considered Colombia's first public statue and was a gift from José Ignacio París, a friend of Bolívar.

questions.question: What's the name of this reggaeton singer from Medellín?
hints: He's one of the artists who took Colombian reggaeton around the world.
He released an album called “Colores” with songs like “Rojo” and “Amarillo.”
His real first name is José, and his stage name starts with J.
questions.description: A paisa who made reggaeton an export product, just like coffee.
questions.fun_fact: On J Balvin's album “Colores,” almost every song is named after a color.

questions.question: Óscar Figueroa won Olympic gold in weightlifting and, as a farewell, left his shoes on the platform. In which city did it happen?
hints: At those Games, a refugee Olympic team competed for the first time.
It was in 2016.
It's the city of Christ the Redeemer and the Brazilian Carnival.
questions.description: Lifting more than twice your own weight: the workout your parents keep promising to start.
questions.fun_fact: Four years earlier, Óscar Figueroa had already won a silver medal at the London 2012 Olympics.

questions.question: Andrés Cepeda sings ballads, was the lead singer of Poligamia and has been a coach on “La Voz.” In which city was he born?
hints: It's a city in the Andes.
It sits more than 2,500 m (8,200 ft) above sea level.
It's the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: A balladeer so romantic that even the rainstorms sing backup for him.
questions.fun_fact: Andrés Cepeda has won several Latin Grammy Awards as a solo artist.

questions.question: “Tigre” is to Falcao as “…” is to Luis Díaz. Which nickname completes the phrase?
hints: It’s shorter than his name and sounds very affectionate.
Lots of people with the same first name get called this too.
It rhymes with “mucho.”
questions.description: In Colombia, nobody goes by their full name if they’ve got a good nickname.
questions.fun_fact: Luis Díaz was born in Barrancas, La Guajira, and has Wayuu roots.

questions.question: In “Pasión de gavilanes,” who is the eldest of the Reyes brothers, the one who falls in love with Norma Elizondo?
hints: He leads his brothers in their revenge.
His brothers fall in love with Jimena and Sara.
He is played by the actor Mario Cimarro.
questions.description: Three brothers, three sisters and more drama than a Sunday family lunch.
questions.fun_fact: “Pasión de gavilanes” is a remake of “Las aguas mansas,” another Colombian telenovela written by Julio Jiménez.

questions.question: “Pablito clavó un clavito: ¿qué clavito clavó Pablito?” What kind of phrase is this?
hints: There’s no answer to guess.
The fun is saying it very fast without slipping up.
Say it five times quickly and your mouth starts tripping over itself.
questions.description: Pablito has been hammering away at this one since your grandparents were in school.
questions.fun_fact: Tongue twisters exist in almost every language and are used to practice pronunciation.

questions.question: Tío Conejo tricks bigger, fiercer animals, and Pedro Rimales makes fun of the king, though neither is strong. What quality makes them win?
hints: It has to do with the head, not the body.
A fox is the classic symbol of this quality.
It means being sharp and quick-witted, always one step ahead.
questions.description: The superpower of those with no muscles but plenty of brains.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Rimales is a cousin of the rogues in Spanish folk tales, who also won with tricks rather than strength.

questions.question: I grew up in Puerto Rico, relaunched my career in Medellín, and in 2015 had a hit with “El perdón” alongside Enrique Iglesias. Who am I?
hints: There's a TV series about my life called “El Ganador”.
I had a hit with “Travesuras” on my own, and years later with “X” alongside J Balvin.
My stage name includes an English word for a fruit spread you put on toast.
questions.description: A Puerto Rican who became more paisa than a bandeja paisa.
questions.fun_fact: “El perdón” reached number one on Billboard's Latin charts and was played all over the world.

questions.question: What does paisa singer Camilo always wear on his face as his personal trademark?
hints: His fans copy it at concerts.
It's made of hair, and it needs care to keep its shape.
It sits between his nose and his mouth, with the tips curled upward.
questions.description: A trademark so famous it has more fans than many singers.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo is married to singer Evaluna Montaner, daughter of singer Ricardo Montaner.

questions.question: On the night of December 7, Colombian families light little lights on sidewalks, windows and balconies to kick off Christmas. What is that night called?
hints: It's the night before the Feast of the Immaculate Conception.
The lights go on the ground or inside paper lanterns.
People use tiny candles in many colors.
questions.description: The one night of the year when the sidewalk shines brighter than the Christmas tree.
questions.fun_fact: In Quimbaya, Quindío, there's a lantern contest that night where each neighborhood decorates its street.

questions.question: In the Muisca ceremony at Guatavita, the new chief covered his body with something and then washed it off in the lake. With what?
hints: It shone like the sun.
From the raft, very valuable offerings were also thrown into the water.
It's the precious metal that fills Bogotá's most famous museum today, but ground very fine.
questions.description: Ceremonial makeup that came off with a dip in a lake.
questions.fun_fact: Several treasure hunters tried to drain Lake Guatavita, and they only pulled out a few gold pieces.

questions.question: It's spicy, Indigenous peoples of the Americas grew it thousands of years ago, and in Colombia it goes on empanadas. What is it?
hints: You only eat it in tiny amounts.
Overdo it and you'll urgently ask for water.
In restaurants it comes as a little sauce with chopped onion and cilantro.
questions.description: The ingredient that makes the bravest people cry at lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Indigenous peoples of the Americas grew ají thousands of years before it reached Asia, where it is now a staple of Thai and Indian food.

questions.question: Look at this rock carved with channels and figures in the San Agustín Archaeological Park. What is it called?
hints: Water runs through channels carved in the stone.
It has carved snakes, lizards and people.
In Spanish, its name sounds like a place where you'd wash your feet.
questions.description: A water park more than a thousand years old: no slides, but plenty of snakes.
questions.fun_fact: The Fuente de Lavapatas is thought to have been a place for water rituals, and it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

questions.question: It's black and shiny, polished by hand with stones, and ajiaco and sancocho are served in it. Which department is this pottery from?
hints: It's made in a rural village on the banks of the Magdalena River.
It's a department in the center of the country, with no coastline.
The village is called La Chamba, in the municipality of Guamo.
questions.description: The pots that make sancocho taste like a Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: The black color isn't paint: it comes from the smoke that stains the pieces during firing.

questions.question: According to “El Carnero”, Juan Rodríguez Freyle's chronicle, what was the raft made of that carried the Muisca heir onto Lake Guatavita?
hints: It was a light material that grows on the shores of lakes.
The same material is woven into mats and baskets.
It's a long, thin water plant, much like totora.
questions.description: A boat ride so fancy that it ended up as a legend.
questions.fun_fact: “El Carnero” was written around 1636, but it only came out as a book more than 200 years later, in 1859.

questions.question: When Grandma says “lo que no mata engorda,” what kind of food is she usually talking about?
questions.answer: Food that fell on the floor
hints: Grandma says it so you won’t make a face.
It’s food that some people find a little gross.
Think of the pandebono that slipped out of your hand.
questions.description: A grandma’s saying with superpowers for the stomach.
questions.fun_fact: A German philosopher, Nietzsche, said something similar: “What does not kill me makes me stronger.”

questions.question: How does the saying “ojos que no ven…” (eyes that don't see…) end?
hints: It's about not suffering over what you don't know.
Like the first half, it names a body part, but not one on your face.
It's the organ that beats.
questions.description: The perfect saying for the last arepa that mysteriously vanished.
questions.fun_fact: English has a very similar one: “What the eye doesn't see, the heart doesn't grieve over.”

questions.question: According to a well-known saying in Spanish, God helps one kind of person in particular. Who?
hints: It's advice for lazybones.
It's about an everyday habit, not a virtue like generosity or patience.
When the rooster crows, this person is already awake.
questions.description: Grandparents have a saying for every occasion, and this is one of their favorites.
questions.fun_fact: Another saying talks back to it: “No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano” (getting up early won't make the sun rise sooner).

questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call the soccer goal, the one with three posts and a net?
hints: It's what the goalkeeper won't let the ball get past.
René Higuita guarded it for Colombia's national team.
It's the same word Colombians use for an archer's bow.
questions.description: Three posts, one net and a whole lot of people shouting “¡gol!”.
questions.fun_fact: René Higuita became famous around the world for the “scorpion kick”, a save he made with his heels at Wembley in 1995.

questions.question: The Humboldt Institute in Bogotá is named after a German explorer. What does it study?
hints: Colombia is one of the countries with the most species in the world.
Its explorer traveled through South America more than 200 years ago and tried to climb the Chimborazo volcano.
Its scientists count frogs, orchids and birds.
questions.description: An institute in Bogotá with a German surname and lots of fieldwork.
questions.fun_fact: Alexander von Humboldt visited New Granada in 1801, met Mutis in Bogotá, and later worked with Caldas in Quito.

questions.question: It's a fluffy sponge cake soaked in a sweet, cold liquid, topped with meringue and sold in little cups at bakeries. What is it called?
hints: You eat it with a spoon because it drips.
It's kept in the fridge and served very cold.
It's made with condensed milk, evaporated milk and cream.
questions.description: A sponge cake that jumped into the pool and refused to get out.
questions.fun_fact: Several Latin American countries, such as Nicaragua and Mexico, claim to be the birthplace of tres leches.

questions.question: In Cali, Popayán and other Colombian cities, what is “la galería”?
hints: People show up with a bag or a basket.
Vendors shout “¡a la orden!” from their stalls.
It's where people do the week's grocery shopping.
questions.description: A place with a fancy name and an atmosphere that is anything but quiet.
questions.fun_fact: At many market squares in Colombia, you can also have a cheap lunch at the food stalls.

questions.question: Someone makes you so angry that you lose your patience. In Colombia, they say that person “te sacó la…” what?
hints: It's something hard.
You find it in rivers or along the road.
If someone throws one at you, you could end up with a bump.
questions.description: A saying for when your patience runs out faster than your prepaid phone credit.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “piedra” also means anger: “¡qué piedra!” means “how annoying!”.

questions.question: I’m a green jungle bird that talks nonstop. In Colombia, someone who pesters you and won’t stop is “dando” my name. What am I?
hints: All the options are birds found in Colombia.
A kid who keeps bothering people hears “¡Deje de dar…!”
Its name rhymes with “Dora.”
questions.description: A bird that doesn’t need a cell phone to talk all day long.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has one of the largest numbers of parrot and macaw species in the world.

questions.question: A mechanic with a broken-down car, a barber with messy hair, a shoemaker with torn shoes. Who does «en casa de herrero, cuchillo de palo» make fun of?
questions.answer: People who don't use their trade at home
wrong_answers: People who spend more than they earn
People who talk a lot and work little
People who copy other people's work
hints: Look at what the three examples have in common.
Think about where each one has the problem.
The blacksmith makes iron knives, but at home he uses a wooden one.
questions.description: A saying for the mechanic who shows up on foot.
questions.fun_fact: A blacksmith worked iron at the forge, which is why the joke is that his own knife at home is made of wood.

questions.question: At a party, a couple wants to dance close together, cheek to cheek. Which of these rhythms is NOT danced that way?
hints: One of these is danced apart, with lots of energy.
It’s a rhythm from Colombia’s Caribbean coast with African roots.
It’s danced to drums, with jumps and super-fast moves.
questions.description: Some dances need lots of room; others only need a cheek.
questions.fun_fact: The name mapalé is said to come from a fish found off Colombia’s Caribbean coast.

questions.question: In Colombian telenovelas, moms are always telling their sons “venga, mijo”. Where does the word “mijo” come from?
hints: It's an affectionate word parents use.
It comes from joining two words together.
A daughter gets called “mija”.
questions.description: The sweetest way a mom has of saying “get over here right now”.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, people also say “mija”, and with extra love, “mijito” or “mijita”.

questions.question: You arrive at the neighborhood soccer field and hear your friends. Who is NOT saying hello?
wrong_answers: The one who says “¿qué más pues?”
The one who says “¿bien o qué?”
hints: One of them is already leaving.
Three ask how you are or what's new; the fourth doesn't.
It's like saying “see you.”
questions.description: Some phrases are for joining the parche, and some are for taking off.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “te pillé” means “I saw you” or “I caught you.”

questions.question: We go with you to school, to the park and to parties. According to the saying “Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres”, who are we?
hints: You choose who you hang out with.
You share secrets and jokes with them that nobody else gets.
They play with you at recess.
questions.description: A saying that judges you by your group photo.
questions.fun_fact: This saying appears in Don Quixote, spoken by Sancho Panza: “Dime con quién andas, decirte he quién eres.”

questions.question: I was born in Popayán, I measured the height of mountains with boiling water, and Bogotá's Universidad Distrital is named after me. Who am I?
hints: People called me “el Sabio” (the Wise One).
I took part in the Botanical Expedition and was a hero of Independence.
A department in the Coffee Region also carries my last name.
questions.description: A wise man who measured mountains with a pot, just like any grandma in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Caldas found that the higher up you are, the lower the temperature at which water boils, and he used this to work out how high a place was.

questions.question: In what year did the Papel Periódico de Santafé de Bogotá, considered Colombia's first newspaper, come out?
hints: It was founded by a librarian who had come from Cuba.
It came out around the time of the French Revolution.
It was at the end of the 18th century.
questions.description: Before news popped up on your phone, it arrived on paper, at the speed of patience.
questions.fun_fact: It came out weekly and ran for about six years, until 1797.

questions.question: In the kangaroo mother care method, created in Bogotá: the pouch is to a baby kangaroo as what is to a premature baby?
hints: The method was invented partly because there weren't enough machines.
What matters is warmth and skin-to-skin contact.
The baby stays pressed against its mom, day and night.
questions.description: A Bogotá idea that took its inspiration from Australia without needing a passport.
questions.fun_fact: Pediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria created it in 1978 at the Instituto Materno Infantil in Bogotá, and today it is used in hospitals around the world.

questions.question: Libertad 1, a satellite just 10 cm (4 in) across built in Bogotá, was the first Colombian one in orbit. In which decade was it launched?
hints: Cell phones with cameras already existed.
It was in the 21st century.
It was launched in 2007.
questions.description: A little cube that left Bogotá and didn't stop until it reached space.
questions.fun_fact: Libertad 1 was built by students at Universidad Sergio Arboleda and launched from Kazakhstan.

questions.question: In what year did the Zika epidemic that put all of Colombia on alert reach the country?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
It was shortly before the Rio de Janeiro Olympic Games.
It was a few years before the COVID-19 pandemic.
questions.description: A virus named after a forest, with a mosquito's bad reputation.
questions.fun_fact: Zika is named after the Zika Forest in Uganda, where the virus was discovered in 1947.

questions.question: Colombian scientist Manuel Elkin Patarroyo created the first synthetic vaccine against which disease?
hints: It is spread by a mosquito.
It is caused by a parasite called Plasmodium.
Its name comes from old Italian words for “bad air”.
questions.description: A Colombian who declared war on a mosquito, armed with chemistry.
questions.fun_fact: Patarroyo donated the patent for his SPf66 vaccine to the World Health Organization.

questions.question: This map from 1500 is the oldest surviving one to show the Americas. Which navigator made it and later explored Colombia's coast?
hints: He sailed with Christopher Columbus on his first voyages.
He owned the ship Santa María.
His last name contains the Spanish word for “thing.”
questions.description: The first selfie of the Americas, except it was drawn on leather more than 500 years ago.
questions.fun_fact: The original map is kept at the Museo Naval in Madrid and is drawn on animal skin.

questions.question: In which century was the Universidad Nacional de Colombia founded?
hints: It was founded when Colombia was already independent.
It was during the United States of Colombia.
It was in 1867.
questions.description: The country's biggest university has a few years behind it, though you can't spot the gray hairs.
questions.fun_fact: Its Bogotá campus is nicknamed “la Ciudad Blanca” (the White City) for the color of its buildings.

questions.question: In Colombia, people from Antioquia are “antioqueños”. What are people from Caldas called?
hints: It's the word for people from Manizales and the area around it.
It's also used for the coffee and the landscapes of that department.
It ends the same way as “costarricense” (Costa Rican).
questions.description: A riddle about where people come from, to win friends in the Eje Cafetero.
questions.fun_fact: The department of Caldas is named after the scholar Francisco José de Caldas.

questions.question: It's round, it has a stick, and when you finish the candy on the outside you find gum inside. What is it?
hints: It's a very famous Colombian candy sold in every neighborhood store.
It's made by Colombina.
It's a lollipop.
questions.description: A candy with a hidden surprise, like a chocolate egg but on a stick.
questions.fun_fact: Bon Bon Bum hit the market in 1970 and today is sold in dozens of countries.

questions.question: I was born in Cali, came to the United States with $300 and narrated the Perseverance rover's Mars landing in Spanish. Who am I?
hints: I'm an aerospace engineer.
I work at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
My last name is also the name of a city in Peru.
questions.description: From Cali to Mars, with a layover at NASA.
questions.fun_fact: It was NASA's first Spanish-language broadcast of a landing on another planet, in February 2021.

previous.feedback: Overlap in the pool: approved q-7947 ("Diana Trujillo, from Cali, led the team behind this Mars rover's robotic arm…") and q-8478 ("The Perseverance rover, which Colombian Diana Trujillo worked on…") both name the answer with the same clues (Cali, Mars rover, Perseverance), so seeing either one gives this question away. The translation itself is accurate and reads naturally. To fix this, take Trujillo's name out of q-7947 and q-8478 (e.g. "a Colombian engineer from Cali"), or retire this question. The same applies to the source pool.

questions.question: Many Colombian kitchens use leaves like this one. What are they almost always used for?
hints: The food cooks inside it.
It gets tied up with string before it goes in to boil.
Think of a Sunday breakfast in Tolima, with hot chocolate.
questions.description: Grandma's favorite wrapping, long before aluminum foil came along.
questions.fun_fact: You don't eat the plantain leaf, but it gives tamales a special aroma while they cook.

questions.question: These are patacones, like the ones eaten all over Colombia. What are they made of?
hints: It's a fruit, but it isn't eaten raw.
It's related to the banana.
It isn't ripe yet.
questions.description: It got squashed, fried all over again, and came out happier than ever.
questions.fun_fact: To make patacones, the plantain is fried twice: first in chunks, then again after it's flattened.

questions.question: Pan tajado comes in a bag, already cut into slices and ready for a sandwich. What flour is it almost always made from?
hints: It's not the same flour you use for arepas.
It comes from a cereal that grows in golden ears.
Almost all pan francés is made with this same flour.
questions.description: Bread that shows up at home with its hair combed, standing in a neat line.
questions.fun_fact: The first machine for slicing bread went on sale in the United States in 1928.

questions.question: On the beaches of Cartagena, street vendors carry a white Styrofoam box. What is it for?
hints: In the coastal heat, people are very grateful for it.
It's the vendor's most important tool when the sun is at its strongest.
Whatever they pull out of it is nice and icy.
questions.description: It walks the whole beach under the midday sun and still never stops smiling.
questions.fun_fact: Styrofoam is almost all air, which is why it's so light and keeps heat out so well.

questions.question: In Colombia, people say someone who eats a lot “come como lima nueva” (eats like a new lima). What is that lima?
questions.answer: A metal tool for wearing things down
wrong_answers: A fruit similar to a lemon
hints: It's not something you eat.
The saying is about how something works when it's brand new, before it wears out.
When it's new, it “eats” through wood or metal very fast.
questions.description: A saying for people who go back for seconds, and then for seconds of their seconds.
questions.fun_fact: A new file has very sharp teeth, so it wears everything down as if it had an endless appetite.

questions.question: It's a torpedo-shaped fried snack from Colombia's Caribbean coast, filled with ground beef or cheese. What is its dough made of?
hints: It's not the same dough as an arepa.
It's boiled and then mashed while still hot to make the dough.
The same root is eaten boiled in sancocho.
questions.description: A golden torpedo that explodes with flavor, not gunpowder.
questions.fun_fact: The carimañola is a faithful partner of the coastal breakfast, alongside the arepa de huevo and coffee.

questions.question: A ripe plantain is yellow with black spots and very sweet. In Colombia it's fried in long slices for lunch. What are they called?
hints: They come with a bandeja paisa.
They turn golden and a little sticky.
Their name comes from the Spanish verb “tajar”, which means to cut.
questions.description: The only plantain that gets better once it gets spots.
questions.fun_fact: The blacker the ripe plantain's peel, the sweeter the tajadas turn out.

questions.question: Colombian bakeries sell a soft yellow cake in little squares that crumbles easily. It's made with cornstarch, eggs and sugar. What is it called?
hints: You can find it in almost any neighborhood bakery.
It's usually sold in portions wrapped in paper or plastic.
Its name sounds like “manteca”.
questions.description: A ponqué so delicate it falls apart before you've even thought about it.
questions.fun_fact: Mantecada is usually eaten with tinto or hot chocolate at onces, the afternoon snack.

questions.question: Lots of Colombians drop little pieces of something into their hot breakfast aguapanela, and the pieces melt inside. What is it?
hints: It's white.
It's made from milk.
It gets stretchy and melted when you scoop it out with your spoon.
questions.description: A grandma's remedy that cures a cold and a craving at the same time.
questions.fun_fact: Aguapanela is also drunk cold with lime, like a panela lemonade!

questions.question: In Colombia, chócolo is grilled on the street with butter and salt, used for sweet arepas and always found in ajiaco. What is it?
hints: It's yellow.
It has lots of little kernels in rows.
The dried kernels of this plant are used to make crispetas (popcorn).
questions.description: It comes with hair, gets peeled and goes on the grill without complaining.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chócolo” comes from Quechua, like “choclo,” which is what tender corn is called in Peru and other Andean countries.

questions.question: It's a sweet, fermented drink from Bogotá, Boyacá and Santander, served cold with almojábana. What is Colombian masato made from?
hints: It's a thick, whitish drink.
It's cooked before being left to ferment.
It's the same white grain that comes with almost every Colombian lunch.
questions.description: A drink that took its sweet time to get good.
questions.fun_fact: Masato is left to ferment for several days, which gives it a slightly sour taste.

questions.question: This is the sacred lake of the Muisca, the one from the El Dorado legend. What do you call someone born in its department?
hints: The lake is Guatavita.
It's the department that surrounds the country's capital.
Its administrative capital is Bogotá.
questions.description: People hunted for gold here for centuries, and the only sure thing that came out was a name for the locals.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Muisca chief covered himself in gold dust and bathed in Lake Guatavita as an offering.

questions.question: Colombia’s “White City” is the capital of the department highlighted on the map. Which department is it?
hints: Its Holy Week processions are World Heritage.
The White City is Popayán.
It shares its name with the river that also flows near Cali.
questions.description: A city that has been painting itself one single color for centuries and never gets bored.
questions.fun_fact: Popayán’s Holy Week processions are on UNESCO’s list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

questions.question: This bird has a long reddish bill, lives only in the wetlands of the Cundiboyacense highlands and is endangered. Which bird is it?
hints: It hides among the reeds and is hardly ever seen.
It's a relative of moorhens and other rails.
In English it's known as the Bogotá rail.
questions.description: A Bogotá local who'd rather sit in a wetland than in traffic.
questions.fun_fact: The tingua bogotana is endemic to Colombia: it lives in no other country in the world.

questions.question: It's cooked in a big pot, served with rice and avocado on the side, and it's the king of river outings. What is a sancocho de gallina?
hints: You eat it with a spoon.
It has yuca, plantain and corn on the cob.
It's served hot in a deep bowl, with plenty of broth.
questions.description: The only dish that needs a pot the size of a washing machine.
questions.fun_fact: On many Colombian “paseos de olla”, sancocho is cooked over a wood fire on the riverbank.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this bread made of cheese and yuca starch is typical of one region. Whose tradition is it?
hints: It's eaten nice and warm with hot chocolate or tinto.
It comes from a warm region in the country's southwest.
Their department has a valley in its name.
questions.description: A bread so good that even its name says it's good.
questions.fun_fact: Pandebono is made without wheat flour: it has yuca starch, cheese and egg.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian actor married to TV host Mónica Fonseca, and in Marvel's “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.” I played an Inhuman who melted metal. Who am I?
hints: I built a career in telenovelas before reaching Hollywood.
In the Marvel series, my character was called Joey Gutierrez.
My initials are J. P. R.
questions.description: An actor who went from telenovelas to rubbing shoulders with superheroes.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Pablo Raba has also worked on productions in Venezuela, Mexico and the United States.

questions.question: Pedro Coral Tavera was nicknamed “el escamoso.” In Colombia, being escamoso means…
questions.answer: Showing off and acting like more than you are
hints: It has nothing to do with fish.
Pedro always wanted to look important and elegant.
It's similar to being “pantallero” or “creído.”
questions.description: A neighborhood heartthrob with more moves than a fish out of water.
questions.fun_fact: “Pedro el escamoso” (2001) made one of Pedro's dances so famous that people copied it at parties.

questions.question: In Colombia's most famous telenovela I was an over-the-top, mocking designer who was always criticizing the president's secretary. Who am I?
hints: The telenovela was set at a fashion company.
My character's name was Hugo Lombardi.
My first name is Julián.
questions.description: A fashion genius with a tongue sharper than his scissors.
questions.fun_fact: Hugo Lombardi was so popular that many foreign adaptations of Betty copied his style.

questions.question: I'm Mexican. In 2006, I put on glasses and braces to play Lety in “La fea más bella,” the Mexican version of Betty. Who am I?
hints: I'm an actress and a comedian.
My leading man in that telenovela was Jaime Camil.
My mother is the actress Angélica María.
questions.description: Betty went on a student exchange and came back with a mariachi band.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” has versions in more than 20 countries, from Mexico to India.

questions.question: In bowling, you knock down all ten pins with the first ball of your turn. What do people in Colombia shout?
hints: It's a short word people shout to celebrate.
It's the Colombian word for a strike.
The same word is used for a jab or prick with something sharp, like a needle.
questions.description: Ten pins standing, one heavy ball, and a shout they can hear across the street.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia people also say “hacer moñona” when everything goes perfectly for someone, as if they knocked down every pin.

questions.question: I'm made of paper or plastic and little sticks, I have a long tail, I dance in the sky, and a string ties me to your hand. What am I?
hints: I need lots of wind to go up.
People fly me in open fields and parks, especially on vacation.
In Mexico they call me “papalote.”
questions.description: A toy that goes out for a walk in the sky, but always on a leash.
questions.fun_fact: The same toy has many names in Latin America: “cometa” in Colombia, “papalote” in Mexico, “barrilete” in Argentina and “volantín” in Chile.

questions.question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, kids play a street version of a sport with a broomstick and caps like these. Which sport?
hints: It's very popular in Barranquilla and Cartagena.
One player throws the cap and another tries to hit it with the stick.
Édgar Rentería is a star of this sport.
questions.description: What your mom calls trash, kids on the Coast call a whole stadium.
questions.fun_fact: “Tapita” is so hard to hit because bottle caps curve in strange ways through the air.

questions.question: In the circle game “el gato y el ratón” (the cat and the mouse), kids hold hands in a ring. What do they do when the cat tries to get in?
questions.answer: Lower their arms to block the way
wrong_answers: Sit on the ground and sing
hints: The ring is like the mouse's house.
The kids in the ring are on the mouse's side.
They use their joined hands like a fence.
questions.description: A cartoon chase, but in school socks and uniforms.
questions.fun_fact: Before the chase, the cat and the mouse talk: “Ratón, ratón.” “¿Qué quieres, gato ladrón?” (“Mouse, mouse.” “What do you want, you thieving cat?”)

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The game mechanic is supported: one source says the children in the ring are the mouse's allies and lower their arms to keep the cat out. I could not find the exact rhyme "Ratón, ratón / ¿Qué quieres, gato ladrón?" in any source. The Colombian version may differ. The difficulty rating of 4 also looks high for such a simple question.

questions.question: In “tingo, tingo, tango”, kids pass an object around a circle. What does the one holding it get when “tango!” is called?
hints: The rest of the group decides it.
It could be singing, dancing or acting like an animal.
It's a funny punishment the group comes up with.
questions.description: Hot potato with a beat, where nobody wants to be left holding anything.
questions.fun_fact: Whoever says “tingo, tingo” has their back turned or eyes covered, so nobody knows when they'll shout “tango!”.

questions.question: A container ship leaves China and arrives at the port of Buenaventura. Which ocean did it cross?
hints: Buenaventura is in Valle del Cauca, not on the Caribbean coast.
It's the same ocean that washes the beaches of Nuquí and Bahía Solano.
It's the largest ocean in the world.
questions.description: A port so humid that even the containers arrive asking for a towel.
questions.fun_fact: Buenaventura is Colombia's most important port on the Pacific, and much of what arrives from Asia comes in through it.

questions.question: I'm a big nature park in the Santa Elena mountains near Medellín, and many people reach me by Metrocable from Santo Domingo Savio. What am I?
hints: I'm full of forests, trails and farmers' markets.
I have my own Metrocable line, built with tourists in mind.
My name is short: just four letters.
questions.description: To visit me, paisas ride in a car hanging from a cable and don't even mess up their hair.
questions.fun_fact: The Metrocable line to Parque Arví glides over forest for several minutes with no stops in between.

questions.question: I show up when a nail gets into a tire and lets the air out, and then it's off to the montallantas. What am I?
hints: It has nothing to do with other cars.
It's fixed with a patch or by changing the tire.
In Colombia people say the tire “se pinchó”.
questions.description: A teeny tiny hole that can ruin a whole road trip.
questions.fun_fact: That's why every car in Colombia must carry a spare tire and a jack to change it on the road.

questions.question: You ride the cable car to the top of Monserrate in Bogotá. Roughly how high above sea level are you?
hints: Bogotá itself sits at about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft).
From the top you see the whole city, so you're higher than it.
But not as high as the snowcapped peaks with year-round snow.
questions.description: Bogotá is already high up, but this outing takes you even closer to the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: You can go up Monserrate by cable car, by funicular or on foot along a stepped trail that many people from Bogotá climb on Sundays.

questions.question: Today there's pico y placa in your city. Which part of the car's license plate do you check to see if it can go out?
hints: Car license plates in Colombia have three letters and three numbers.
The rule changes depending on the day and splits cars into groups.
It's the one farthest to the right.
questions.description: A yellow rectangle that decides whether you take the car or the bus today.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, plates on private cars are yellow, while plates on public service vehicles like taxis and buses are white.

questions.question: You leave your car there for a while, the attendant gives you a ticket, and you pay by the hour when you leave. What is that place called in Colombia?
hints: It's not where they fix your car.
It's not where you wait for the bus either.
It comes from the word “parquear”.
questions.description: Where cars take a nap while you run your errands.
questions.fun_fact: Other countries say “estacionamiento” or “aparcamiento”, but in Colombia almost everyone says “parqueadero”.

questions.question: In Colombia, someone goes up to the finca on a muddy trocha (dirt track) in a campero. What is a campero?
hints: It has an engine and four wheels.
In the Eje Cafetero, people load it with sacks of coffee.
The famous Willys is one of them.
questions.description: It got its name because it loves mud more than pavement.
questions.fun_fact: In Armenia, the Yipao parade shows off Willys camperos loaded with coffee, furniture and even a whole family's move.

questions.question: You're on the bus and press the bell before your corner. Who has to respond?
hints: They work on the bus all day.
When they hear the bell, they stop at the next bus stop.
They sit up front, behind the steering wheel.
questions.description: A tiny button with huge power: stopping a giant machine.
questions.fun_fact: The red TransMilenio buses in Bogotá stop only at fixed stations, so nobody there needs to press the bell.

questions.question: It's smaller than a bus, carries passengers around the city, and you wave it down at the corner. What is it called in Colombia?
hints: It carries people, not dirt or broken-down cars.
You pay a fare to get on.
Its name sounds like a little bus.
questions.description: The bus's little sister, always in a rush.
questions.fun_fact: In countries like Mexico or Peru, a similar vehicle is called a “microbús” or a “combi”.

questions.question: I'm a journalist, and I created “Contravía,” an investigative show about the armed conflict and human rights in Colombia. Who am I?
hints: The show aired on Canal Uno in the early 2000s.
Years later, I ran a public TV channel in Bogotá.
My first name starts with “Holl.”
questions.description: A TV show that never paid attention to the one-way signs.
questions.fun_fact: “Contravía” won international journalism awards for its reports on victims of the conflict.

questions.question: In what year did Caracol's physical-competition reality show “Desafío” first air?
hints: It started in the 21st century.
It was in the first decade of the 2000s.
In 2024 it celebrated its 20th anniversary.
questions.description: A reality show where sand, sweat and victory screams all come in the same package.
questions.fun_fact: Over the years, “Desafío” has pitted teams from different regions, celebrities and even whole families against each other.

questions.question: I'm an actress, singer and writer from Cali, and in the early 2000s I hosted “Expedición Robinson” on Caracol. Who am I?
hints: I was also a beauty queen before I became an actress.
I starred in a very famous telenovela set in coffee country.
In that telenovela they called me “la Gaviota”.
questions.description: Surviving on an island without a cell phone: the real challenge of the 2000s.
questions.fun_fact: “Expedición Robinson” comes from a Swedish format where contestants survive on an island and vote each other off.

questions.question: Who hosts “MasterChef Celebrity Colombia” on Canal RCN?
hints: She started her career as a model before moving into TV.
She earlier hosted “MasterChef Colombia” with contestants who weren't famous.
Her last name starts with “Baha.”
questions.description: In this kitchen, the stars cry more over the judges than over the onions.
questions.fun_fact: The show's judges are chefs Jorge Rausch, Christopher Carpentier and Nicolás de Zubiría.

questions.question: What year did “Casados con hijos”, the Colombian version of an American sitcom, premiere on Caracol?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
It was in the first decade of the 2000s.
It was in the middle of the 2000s, a few years before 2008.
questions.description: A family so dysfunctional it makes yours look like a TV commercial.
questions.fun_fact: The original American series, “Married... with Children”, had versions in several countries, including Argentina and Chile.

questions.question: When you hear traditional vallenato, you're hearing world heritage. In what year did UNESCO declare it so?
hints: It happened in the 21st century.
It came long after the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata was born.
It was in the second decade of the 2000s.
questions.description: The day the caja, the guacharaca and the accordion got their world heritage papers.
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO put it on its list of heritage in need of urgent protection, so the tradition wouldn't be lost.

questions.question: I'm a 2012 telenovela about the life of the singer of El Binomio de Oro, starring Alejandro Palacio. What am I?
wrong_answers: Diomedes, el Cacique de La Junta
hints: I aired on Caracol TV.
My main character was from Becerril, in Cesar.
I'm named after the singer of “Momentos de amor”.
questions.description: A telenovela where even the villains sang along to an accordion.
questions.fun_fact: Alejandro Palacio, the lead actor, is also a vallenato singer in real life.

questions.question: You open “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” and in the first sentence Aureliano remembers discovering ice. Who brought it to Macondo?
hints: They came to the village every year with amazing inventions.
They put up tents and showed off magnets, magnifying glasses and other wonders.
The wise Melquíades traveled with them.
questions.description: Before the refrigerator came along, chilling a tinto took real magic.
questions.fun_fact: The idea of the ice came from a real memory: as a boy, García Márquez saw ice with his grandfather at a banana company in Aracataca.

questions.question: Which Rafael Pombo poem tells of a boy who called the pie man over to try his pies but had nothing to pay with?
hints: The main character is a very absent-minded boy.
In the poem, he makes one silly mistake after another.
His nickname says he isn’t very clever.
questions.description: History’s first customer who tried to pay with nothing but a cute face.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo was inspired by “Simple Simon,” an English nursery rhyme where a boy also goes to a pie man.

questions.question: In “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” which character was always surrounded by butterflies like these?
hints: He was a mechanic at the banana company.
He fell in love with Meme, the daughter of Fernanda del Carpio.
The family's last Aureliano carries his last name.
questions.description: Some people arrive wearing perfume; this one arrived with a flying escort.
questions.fun_fact: At the tributes to García Márquez after his death in 2014, people tossed yellow paper butterflies.

questions.question: I have a twin brother. I married Fernanda del Carpio, but my animals multiplied thanks to my lover, Petra Cotes. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the fourth generation of the Buendías.
My parties and feasts were famous all over Macondo.
My twin was named José Arcadio Segundo.
questions.description: A Buendía who mistook the economy for one endless parranda.
questions.fun_fact: At the height of his good fortune, Aureliano Segundo went so far as to paper his house with banknotes.

questions.question: A character in “One Hundred Years of Solitude” is named after this flower. She turned down Pietro Crespi and wore a black bandage on her hand. Who is she?
hints: She is the daughter of José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula.
She spent her life weaving and never married.
The flower in the photo is called amaranth.
questions.description: A flower that never wilts and a heart that never softens.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Greek and means “unfading.”

questions.question: You open a novel that begins: “It was inevitable: the scent of bitter almonds…”. How long did its hero wait for his beloved?
hints: The novel is “Love in the Time of Cholera.”
Florentino Ariza waited for Fermina Daza until she was widowed.
It was more than half a century.
questions.description: A love story with more patience than a bank line on payday.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez drew on his own parents' courtship, which had to overcome her family's opposition.

questions.question: You read “Teresa en cuya frente el cielo empieza” by Eduardo Carranza, leader of the Piedra y Cielo group. In which decade was that group born?
hints: It came before Nadaísmo.
It took its name from a book by Juan Ramón Jiménez.
It published its booklets just as World War II was starting.
questions.description: Poets so lofty they named themselves after something hard and something endless.
questions.fun_fact: The “piedracielistas” published their poems in small booklets meant to shake up Colombian poetry.

questions.question: I was born in Bucaramanga and served as a government minister. My most famous novel tells the life of a German who built trails in Santander in the 19th century. Who am I?
hints: The novel came out in the 1970s.
The German's name was Geo von Lengerke.
The novel is called “La otra raya del tigre.”
questions.description: Some writers look for inspiration in a café; this one found it on a stone trail in the mountains of Santander.
questions.fun_fact: Geo von Lengerke was a real person, and Santander still has hiking trails called the “caminos de Lengerke.”

questions.question: The morpho butterfly flies in Colombia's rainforests. Its wings are brown underneath and have no blue pigment. Where does its bright blue come from?
questions.answer: From tiny scales that reflect light
wrong_answers: From a pigment in the flowers it eats
From the sky reflecting off its wings
From a shiny oil that coats its wings
hints: It's not ink or paint.
It has to do with the way light bounces.
Soap bubbles also shine in colors without any ink.
questions.description: A flying jewel you won't find in any jewelry store downtown.
questions.fun_fact: Because its blue comes from the shape of its scales and not from a pigment, the morpho butterfly changes shade depending on where you look at it from.

questions.question: Look at these teeth. Which fish from the Amazon and Orinoco rivers do they belong to?
hints: It's a freshwater fish, not a sea fish.
In movies, it's famous for being a very hungry eater.
The best-known kind has a red belly and swims in big groups.
questions.description: A smile no dentist would dare to check.
questions.fun_fact: Piranhas replace their teeth in batches throughout their lives, so they never run out of bite.

questions.question: In “Encanto,” Isabela is to flowers as Antonio is to…
hints: His gift arrives on the day of his ceremony.
His room looks like a jungle full of life.
A toucan, a jaguar and a chigüiro are his friends.
questions.description: The littlest one in the casita got his own magic door too.
questions.fun_fact: “Encanto” features Colombian animals such as the chigüiro (capybara), the toucan and the jaguar.

questions.question: In Rafael Pombo's poem, Rin Rin Renacuajo “salió esta mañana muy tieso y muy majo”. What does “majo” mean here?
hints: Think about how the little tadpole was dressed.
He left home to pay a visit to Mrs. Mouse.
It's like saying he went out all “pinchado”.
questions.description: A poem Colombian grandparents can recite without blinking.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the poem, Rin Rin Renacuajo gets swallowed by a duck.

questions.question: Butterfly houses in Colombia have lots of capsules like this one hanging up. What are they for?
questions.answer: For a caterpillar to turn into a butterfly
wrong_answers: For keeping the butterfly's eggs safe
For the butterfly to sleep in at night
For catching mosquitoes like a trap
hints: Inside, there's an animal that is changing.
Before it went in, that animal crawled around eating leaves.
When it opens, something with colorful wings comes out.
questions.description: Hanging from a leaf, as still as a kid in time-out.
questions.fun_fact: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body breaks down almost completely and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.

questions.question: Dog is to “woof” as rooster is to…
hints: You hear it very early in the morning on a farm.
It's a long sound with lots of “o”s.
It starts with “cock” and ends with “doo”.
questions.description: The farm alarm clock, and it has no snooze button.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombian Spanish, the rooster doesn't say “cock-a-doodle-doo”, it says “quiquiriquí”.

questions.question: Hormigas arrieras (leafcutter ants) carry bits of leaf back to their nest. Why?
questions.answer: To grow a fungus that they eat
wrong_answers: To build the roof of the nest
To give shade to their eggs
hints: They can't digest leaves well.
They are farmers, just like people in the countryside.
What they eat grows on the leaves they bring, like mushrooms.
questions.description: The hardest workers in the forest, and they never ask for a Christmas bonus.
questions.fun_fact: The hormigas culonas eaten toasted in Santander are the queens of a kind of leafcutter ant.

questions.question: In which region of Colombia does this snake live in the wild?
hints: It loves fresh water and heat.
It lives in rivers, creeks and marshes that flood.
It's the land of joropo and chigüiros.
questions.description: Nobody would recommend a hug from this lady.
questions.fun_fact: Anacondas don't lay eggs: their babies are born alive.

questions.question: Listen: this buzzing isn't an insect, it's the wings of a bird. Which one?
hints: It's a very tiny bird.
It hovers still in the air in front of flowers.
It drinks nectar with its long, thin beak.
questions.description: A little feathered motor that never needs gas.
questions.fun_fact: Some hummingbirds beat their wings more than 50 times per second.

questions.question: Look at this wasp. How many legs does it have?
hints: It's an insect, not a spider.
All its legs come out of the middle part of its body.
It has the same number as an ant.
questions.description: It showed up uninvited to the paseo de olla and went straight for the soda.
questions.fun_fact: Only female wasps have a stinger, because it started out as a body part for laying eggs.

questions.question: It's underwear, it's the color of the sun, and you wear it new on the night of December 31. What is this Colombian agüero for?
wrong_answers: To travel a lot during the year
hints: It's a superstition for the year that's starting.
Some people swap yellow for red, but that's for something else: love.
It's about the new year going well for you.
questions.description: A piece of clothing nobody sees, but that works hard all year.
questions.fun_fact: For travel, Colombians have a different agüero: walking around the block with a suitcase at midnight.

questions.question: Asado huilense is the star of the San Pedro festivities in Huila. What meat is it made from?
hints: It's a very common farm animal.
It's marinated overnight and roasted in a clay oven.
It's the same animal used for lechona.
questions.description: A dish that takes its time in the oven, just like the good saints.
questions.fun_fact: Asado huilense is marinated with herbs and spices and baked in clay ovens, sometimes for hours.

questions.question: It has a wooden ring with little metal discs that jingle, and you hit it with your hand while singing Christmas carols. What is it called?
hints: It's a percussion instrument.
You can hit it or shake it.
It's round and goes “jingle-jingle” with every hit.
questions.description: The instrument that gets even the most serious aunt singing along.
questions.fun_fact: At many Colombian novenas, kids make their own tambourines from flattened soda bottle caps.

questions.question: You see carved pumpkins with faces and kids in costumes shouting “¡Triqui triqui!” to ask for candy. What date is it?
hints: It's before December.
In Colombia it's also called Children's Day.
It's the last day of October.
questions.description: The day vegetables start making scary faces.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian kids ask for candy by singing “¡Triqui triqui Halloween, quiero dulces para mí!” (“Trick or treat Halloween, I want candy for me!”).

questions.question: On that day at church, they put this cross of ash on your forehead. Where does the ash come from?
questions.answer: From burning last year's Palm Sunday fronds
wrong_answers: From burning the Año Viejo effigy
From the candles of Noche de Velitas
hints: It comes from something that was blessed in church.
It's from something used a year earlier.
They're leaves that people wave at church at the start of Holy Week.
questions.description: A little smudge on the forehead that nobody wants to wipe off.
questions.fun_fact: Ash Wednesday starts Lent, about 40 days before Holy Week.

questions.question: In which town in Cundinamarca is this cathedral, built inside a salt mine?
hints: It's a little over an hour north of Bogotá.
The Tren Turístico de la Sabana runs all the way there.
Its name recalls the zipa, the Muisca ruler.
questions.description: A church where, if you lick the walls, nobody will tell you they need more salt.
questions.fun_fact: The current cathedral opened in 1995 and sits about 180 m (590 ft) underground.

questions.question: You head down from Bogotá to Melgar, the rolos’ favorite “tierra caliente” getaway. Roughly what is the average temperature there?
hints: Bogotá averages around 14 °C (57 °F), and Melgar is much hotter.
Melgar is in Tolima, about 320 m (1,050 ft) above sea level.
Perfect for a day by the pool, but not hot enough to roast you.
questions.description: The long-weekend plan where the sunscreen runs out before the bag of chips does.
questions.fun_fact: Melgar is called “the City of Swimming Pools” because of the huge number of pools in its homes, hotels and condos.

questions.question: In which month are the famous corralejas of Sincelejo, in Sucre, traditionally held?
hints: They coincide with the feast of the Holy Name of Jesus (Dulce Nombre de Jesús).
They take place in the middle of the savanna's dry season.
Their most famous date is the 20th of that month.
questions.description: A party on the savanna where the bravest move isn't asking your mother-in-law to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The porro “Fiesta en corraleja” by Rubén Darío Salcedo became almost an anthem of these festivities.

questions.question: It's Sunday and you're out on your bike on Bogotá's Ciclovía. Roughly how many kilometers of road are closed to cars?
hints: It crosses the city from north to south and from east to west.
It's one of the longest Sunday car-free routes in the world.
Riding all of it would take you several hours, but not days.
questions.description: The one day when cars have to ask permission to get through.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá's Ciclovía began in 1974 and has been copied by cities around the world.

questions.question: Visit the “World Capital of Vallenato” in late April and you'll find the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata. In which decade was the first one held?
hints: The songwriter Rafael Escalona was one of its founders.
Alfonso López Michelsen also backed it, years before he became president.
It began right after the department of Cesar was created in 1967.
questions.description: A contest won by whoever opens and closes their instrument best without losing the beat.
questions.fun_fact: The first Vallenato King, in 1968, was the great Alejo Durán.

questions.question: You ride the Medellín metro from one end of the Aburrá Valley to the other. Which of these towns is NOT in that valley?
hints: Three of them have a metro station.
The odd one out is in eastern Antioquia, on the other side of the mountain.
International flights to Medellín land there.
questions.description: A valley so crowded that its towns no longer know where one ends and the next begins.
questions.fun_fact: The Aburrá Valley has 10 municipalities, and the Medellín River runs through it from south to north.

questions.question: In which decade was the Cristo Rey that watches over Cali from the Los Cristales hill finished?
hints: It's younger than the Eiffel Tower.
It was built in the 20th century, when Cali was already growing fast.
It was planned to mark 50 years since the end of the Thousand Days' War (1902).
questions.description: A caleño neighbor with open arms who never gets tired of saying hello.
questions.fun_fact: It stands about 26 meters (85 ft) tall with its base and can be seen from almost all of Cali.

questions.question: If you traveled back in time to see “the Blond Arrow” Alfredo Di Stéfano playing for Millonarios in Bogotá, which year could you go to?
hints: It was the El Dorado era, when many foreign stars came to the Colombian league.
After Bogotá he moved to Real Madrid, where he won five European Cups in a row starting in 1956.
Colombia's professional league had kicked off only one year earlier, in 1948.
questions.description: A time machine with a ticket for the main stand at El Campín.
questions.fun_fact: That Millonarios team played so beautifully that it was nicknamed “the Blue Ballet” (el Ballet Azul).

questions.question: You’re born in Cartagena in 1790 to parents who came from Spain. What did colonial society call you?
hints: Your parents were Spanish, but you weren’t born in Spain.
Many heroes of Independence belonged to this group.
Antonio Nariño and Camilo Torres belonged to this group.
questions.description: Being born in Cartagena with a surname from Seville had its perks… and its limits.
questions.fun_fact: Criollos called Spaniards born in Spain, without much affection, “chapetones”.

questions.question: In 1781, royal inspector Gutiérrez de Piñeres raised the alcabala in New Granada from 2% to… what?
hints: The alcabala was charged on every sale in markets and shops.
That increase helped spark the Comuneros revolt.
The tax doubled.
questions.description: A tax that went up so much it brought the people down to the town square.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, Manuela Beltrán tore down the edict announcing the new taxes in Socorro, and that’s how the Comuneros revolt began.

questions.question: About how many pre-Columbian gold pieces does the Gold Museum (Museo del Oro) in Bogotá hold?
hints: It's one of the largest collections of pre-Columbian gold in the world.
There are so many that they can't all be on display at the same time.
It's in the tens of thousands.
questions.description: A museum where everything really is worth its weight in gold.
questions.fun_fact: The museum's most famous piece, the Muisca raft, shows the ceremony that gave rise to the legend of El Dorado.

questions.question: You look at a map and read “Colombia.” Which famous figure is the country named after?
hints: He was a navigator.
He sailed from Spain with three ships.
He reached the Americas in 1492.
questions.description: A country that wears someone's name, like a fan wears a player's jersey.
questions.fun_fact: Columbus never set foot in what is now Colombia, but on his fourth voyage he sailed very close, along the coast of Panama.

questions.question: I was a lawyer from Seville. Sailing to Urabá, I found a stowaway hiding in a barrel on my ship: Vasco Núñez de Balboa. Together we founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién. Who am I?
hints: People called me “the bachiller” (the graduate).
I wrote the “Suma de geografía,” one of the first books to describe the New World.
My first name is shared with a saint famous for cutting his cloak in half for a beggar.
questions.description: History's first barrel ride didn't happen at Niagara Falls.
questions.fun_fact: Santa María la Antigua del Darién, founded in 1510, was one of the first Spanish towns on the American mainland.

questions.question: I was brought to Cartagena in chains, but one day I escaped into the hills. With others like me, I built a free palenque. Who am I?
hints: I was enslaved.
Benkos Biohó was one of us.
My name was also used for farm animals that went wild.
questions.description: A figure from colonial Cartagena who never showed up in the viceroys' portraits.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque, founded by cimarrones, is considered the first free town in the Americas.

questions.question: In colonial times, a Spaniard marries a Muisca Indigenous woman. What were the children of such a couple called?
hints: The children mixed two origins.
Today a large share of Colombians descend from this mix.
The word comes from the Spanish for “mixed.”
questions.description: Colombia's most famous mix, and no, we don't mean ajiaco.
questions.fun_fact: In colonial times there were paintings called “casta paintings” that tried to sort every possible mix into a category.

questions.question: In which century did Cartagena's market for enslaved people reach its peak, while Saint Peter Claver cared for the new arrivals?
hints: Cartagena had already been founded for decades.
It was the time when the Portuguese held the Crown's license for that trade.
Saint Peter Claver died in 1654.
questions.description: A hard page in Cartagena's history that never shows up on the postcards.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Claver called himself “the slave of the slaves forever.”

questions.question: Founded in 1653 by the Dominican archbishop Fray Cristóbal de Torres, it taught many independence heroes and is now a university in downtown Bogotá. Which one?
hints: It is one of Colombia's oldest universities and began as a “colegio mayor” in the 17th century.
Its colonial cloister is a few blocks from the Plaza de Bolívar.
Its name is that of a string of beads used for praying.
questions.description: A school so old that its former students end up on the banknotes.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo Torres and Francisco José de Caldas are among the independence heroes who studied there.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is right: Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, founded in 1653 by Fray Cristóbal de Torres, with Camilo Torres and Caldas among its alumni. The hints hold up. The only unverified part is the description's claim that former students appear on banknotes. A search found no Rosario alumnus on a Colombian banknote, and most notable banknote figures (Santander, García Márquez, Lleras Restrepo) studied elsewhere.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which military engineer expanded this Cartagena fortress in the 18th century and built the Bocagrande underwater wall?
hints: He was neither an admiral nor the city's founder.
He worked in Cartagena for more than fifty years and died there in 1800.
His last name is also the name of a town in Ávila, Spain.
questions.description: Pirates hated him without ever seeing him hold a sword.
questions.fun_fact: The Bocagrande wall is an underwater barrier that kept enemy ships from entering the bay through that opening.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Lucho Herrera and Nairo Quintana won this red polka-dot jersey at the Tour de France. Who wears it?
hints: You don't win it on the flat finishes.
Riders earn points by getting to certain spots first.
Those points are handed out at the top of mountain passes.
questions.description: A jersey that looks like it came from one of grandma's dresses, but every escarabajo dreams of wearing it.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Herrera won the Tour's mountains jersey twice, in 1985 and 1987.

questions.question: In 1984, on the climb to Alpe d'Huez, a Colombian won his country's first Tour de France stage. Who was it?
hints: Years later he also won the Vuelta a España.
He was born in Fusagasugá.
His nickname was “el Jardinerito” (the Little Gardener).
questions.description: A road with more twists than a telenovela, and a happy ending for Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: Alpe d'Huez has 21 hairpin bends, and each one has a sign with the names of stage winners there.

questions.question: Look closely at these little flowers: for centuries they have been dried to make an aromática (herbal tea) for stomachaches. What plant is it?
hints: People drink it hot, often before bed.
Its flowers look like tiny daisies.
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “earth apple.”
questions.description: Grandma has a remedy for everything, and it almost always comes in a pocillo.
questions.fun_fact: The name “chamomile” comes from the Greek for “earth apple,” because its flowers smell a little like apples.

questions.question: It has a big jar with a lid and spinning blades at the bottom, and in Colombia it's always there for making blackberry juice. What is it?
hints: You plug it into the wall.
It goes “brrrrr” really loud.
It turns fruit into juice in seconds.
questions.description: The noisiest machine in the kitchen on a Sunday morning.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia the blender works almost every day: juices of mora, lulo, guanábana or maracuyá.

questions.question: Look closely: what do Colombians call this sweet, bubbly drink?
hints: It comes in a bottle or a can.
It's best served ice-cold.
Its name comes from the gas in its bubbles.
questions.description: Bubbles that tickle you all the way up your nose.
questions.fun_fact: The bubbles in a gaseosa are carbon dioxide, the same gas we breathe out.

questions.question: “Popote” is to Mexico as which word is to Colombia?
hints: It lets you drink without lifting the glass to your mouth.
It's a thin little tube.
In Colombia the corner store hands you one with your juice.
questions.description: A little tube that travels all over Latin America and changes its name in every country.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain it's “pajita”, in Argentina “sorbete” and in the Dominican Republic “calimete”.

questions.question: Look at the photo: hot chocolate with melted cheese inside. Which Colombian city is this custom famous in?
hints: People usually have it at onces, the afternoon snack, with bread or almojábana.
It sits on a high plateau, up in the Andes.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: A piece of cheese that decided to take a nice warm bath.
questions.fun_fact: In Bogotá, the cheese goes into the chocolate and comes out melted on the spoon.

questions.question: Take a close look: this fruit from the banks of the Amazon has dozens of times more vitamin C than an orange. What is it called?
hints: It grows on shrubs that spend months with their feet underwater in the rivers.
It's small and round, with reddish or purple skin, and very sour.
Its name is one word said twice in a row.
questions.description: If fruits had an immune-system superhero, this one would arrive by canoe from Leticia.
questions.fun_fact: Camu camu is so sour that it's hardly ever eaten raw: in the Amazon it goes into juices, ice cream and raspados (shaved ice).

questions.question: Look closely at this fruit: it has about four times as much vitamin C as an orange. What is it?
hints: Inside, it's full of hard little seeds.
Its flesh can be pink or white, and it smells very strong when ripe.
Cooked into a sweet paste and served with cheese, it becomes a classic dessert.
questions.description: A fruit that bullies the orange on its own turf.
questions.fun_fact: 100 grams (3.5 oz) of guava has more vitamin C than an adult needs in a whole day.

questions.question: It comes in a brown pod, its sticky pulp is sweet and sour, and on the Coast people knead it with sugar. Which traditional candy is made this way?
hints: It has no coconut and no milk.
The fruit has hard, shiny seeds inside its brown pulp.
The same fruit makes a very popular juice on the Coast.
questions.description: A street vendor's treat where eating just one is never enough.
questions.fun_fact: Tamarind came to the Americas from Africa and Asia, and today the Colombian coast can't do without it in its sweets.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this palm fruit is eaten boiled, with salt and honey. Which region of Colombia is it typical of?
hints: It grows where it's hot and it rains a lot.
Its region is covered in rainforest and in rivers that run down to the sea.
In Cali it's sold on every street corner, brought in from the country's rainiest coast.
questions.description: Eaten with salt, with honey or with both, because nobody here is afraid of anything.
questions.fun_fact: Chontaduro grows on a palm whose trunk is covered in spines, so harvesting it is a real challenge.

questions.question: Take a close look: Urabá has huge plantations of this fruit, which Colombia sells to half the world. Which fruit is it?
hints: It grows in big bunches hanging from the plant.
It's picked green and ripens on the way.
When ripe it's yellow and you peel it by hand.
questions.description: The fruit that comes in its own packaging, and it's even easy to open.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is among the world's biggest banana exporters, and much of it comes from Urabá, in Antioquia.

questions.question: The mansion on the edge of the Salto del Tequendama, famous for its ghost stories, was a hotel for years. What is there today?
hints: It was restored after being abandoned for a long time.
It reopened its doors in the 2010s, after the restoration.
It displays the biodiversity and culture of the region.
questions.description: A hotel where, they say, some guests never checked out.
questions.fun_fact: The mansion was built in the 1920s in French style, right in front of the falls of the Bogotá River.

questions.question: A Colombian agüero (superstition) says that if you stand a broom upside down behind the door without saying a word, who will leave the house?
hints: It's a trick for when you want your home to yourself again.
It works without traps or bug spray.
They are people who came over to the house.
questions.description: A broom doesn't just sweep away dust: according to grandmothers, it sweeps away other things too.
questions.fun_fact: Another broom agüero says that if someone sweeps over your feet, you'll never get married.

questions.question: In many Colombian towns, an old Catholic tradition is to pray and light a candle on Mondays. Who does it help get out of purgatory?
hints: They aren't of this world, but they haven't reached heaven either.
They are souls waiting for someone to pray for them.
They also get their own day on November 2.
questions.description: Some people light candles to see, and some light them for the afterlife.
questions.fun_fact: Some Colombian towns still hold the “alumbrado de ánimas”, a night walk with candles and prayers.

questions.question: At a Colombian colegio, you go from sexto to once (grades 6 to 11) until you get your diploma. What is that stage called?
hints: It isn't the stage for the youngest kids at school.
When you finish it, you graduate from school.
When you graduate, you're called a “bachiller.”
questions.description: Six years of homework, flag-raising ceremonies and gym uniforms until mortarboard day.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, school ends in grade 11, while in many countries there is one more year: grade 12.

questions.question: You unwrap a bocadillo veleño at recess. Which of these does it NOT contain?
hints: It's a fruit sweet.
It's red inside and comes wrapped in a leaf.
The missing ingredient is white and comes from a cow.
questions.description: In Santander, a school break without this sweet is like a game without goals.
questions.fun_fact: The traditional bocadillo veleño comes wrapped in a bijao leaf, a big leaf that protects it.

questions.question: Colombia has six estratos, and 1 is the lowest. What happens with the utility bills of an estrato 1 home?
questions.answer: They pay less thanks to a subsidy
wrong_answers: They pay more due to a surcharge
They pay the full standard rate
They only pay for the water
hints: The estrato is used to share out the cost of utilities.
The estrato is printed on every utility bill.
The government helps cover part of the bill for the lowest estratos.
questions.description: A number from 1 to 6 that decides how much it hurts to open the electric bill.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the estrato is based on the home and its surroundings, not on the income of the people who live there.

questions.question: To graduate from high school in Colombia, students must do servicio social (community service). What is the minimum number of hours?
hints: It's done in the last grades of school.
It's more than a weekend, but less than a month of work without a break.
It's a number between 50 and 100.
questions.description: Graduating isn't just about passing classes: you also have to lend the community a hand.
questions.fun_fact: Mandatory community service was set by Resolution 4210 of 1996, and students usually do it in décimo and once, the last two grades.

questions.question: In Colombia, how many grades does primary school have?
hints: It starts with first grade.
Kids start at about age 6, right after transición.
As many as the fingers on one hand.
questions.description: The years of reading primers, copying lines and a teacher who knew your mom's name.
questions.fun_fact: Before first grade, Colombian kids go through preschool: prejardín, jardín and transición.

questions.question: A trapero has a long handle, gets dipped in the bucket and wrung out before you use it. What is it for?
hints: You use it standing up, without bending down.
Afterwards, the house smells of soap.
