You run it over the place where you walk.
questions.description: It has long hair, lives on the patio and dances with anyone who takes its hand.
questions.fun_fact: What Colombians call a “trapero” is a “trapeador” in Mexico and a “fregona” in Spain.

questions.question: Juanpis González is a gomelo who calls his dad “mi papi” and has his own show, “Juanpis Live Show.” What city is he from?
hints: He's played by comedian Alejandro Riaño.
He makes fun of the rich young people from the north of his city.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: A character who has never waited in line in his life, because his papi always calls somebody.
questions.fun_fact: On the “Juanpis Live Show,” Alejandro Riaño has interviewed real politicians and celebrities while staying in character.

questions.question: Catalina Sandino Moreno was nominated for the Best Actress Oscar for “Maria Full of Grace”. In what year was the ceremony?
hints: It was in the middle of the 2000s.
The film had come out the year before.
It was the 77th edition of the awards.
questions.description: A red carpet that still makes a whole country sigh.
questions.fun_fact: She was the first Colombian actress nominated for an Oscar, and the same role won her the Silver Bear at the Berlin Film Festival.

questions.question: They backed the King of Spain, were the majority in Santa Marta and Pasto, and fought the patriots. What were they called?
hints: Their name speaks of their loyalty, not of a place.
They wanted New Granada to stay a Spanish colony.
Their name comes from the word for what belongs to the king.
questions.description: While some shouted for independence, others kept sending love letters to Madrid.
questions.fun_fact: Simón Bolívar died in 1830 at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino in Santa Marta, the city that stayed loyal to the king for so long.

questions.question: Pablo Morillo came in 1815 to reconquer New Granada in the name of this king. Who is he?
hints: Napoleon held him prisoner in France.
In 1810 the criollos said they governed “in his name”.
He was the son of Charles IV.
questions.description: A gentleman who gave orders from very, very far away and never set foot in New Granada.
questions.fun_fact: While he was Napoleon's prisoner, Ferdinand VII was known as “el Deseado” (the Desired One).

questions.question: You are in the Plaza de Bolívar, celebrating 200 years since the Grito of July 20. What year is it?
hints: It is a year in this century.
Add 200 to the year of the Grito de Independencia.
It was the same year as the World Cup in South Africa.
questions.description: Two hundred candles: not even the biggest birthday cake in Bogotá can handle that.
questions.fun_fact: For the Centennial in 1910, Bogotá opened the Parque de la Independencia.

questions.question: Which of these independence leaders signed the Act of Independence of July 20, 1810, in Santafé?
hints: He was in Santafé that day, unlike some others.
He was a lawyer from Popayán.
He wrote the “Memorial de Agravios” in 1809.
questions.description: Signing a piece of paper had never been so dangerous or so famous.
questions.fun_fact: Antonio Nariño could not sign in 1810: he was a prisoner in Cartagena.

questions.question: During the Patria Boba, the Congress of the United Provinces, based in Tunja, went to war with Nariño’s Cundinamarca. Which side was the Congress?
hints: It was a fight among patriots, not against Spain.
One of Nariño’s great rivals in the Congress was Camilo Torres.
They wanted each province to govern itself almost on its own.
questions.description: Back when the homeland was so young it picked fights with itself.
questions.fun_fact: This period is called the “Patria Boba” (Foolish Fatherland) because the patriots fought each other while Spain prepared to retake the land.

questions.question: This Irishman was Simón Bolívar's aide-de-camp and wrote huge memoirs about him. Who is he?
hints: He arrived in South America as a teenager.
His son was named Simón Bolívar, after his dad's boss.
His last name starts with an O and an apostrophe.
questions.description: He came from very far away to write the longest diary ever kept about a famous friend.
questions.fun_fact: O'Leary's memoirs, published by his son, fill more than thirty volumes.

questions.question: At Pantano de Vargas (1819), Colonel James Rooke led European volunteers fighting alongside Bolívar. Where did nearly all of them come from?
hints: Many were veterans of the wars against Napoleon.
They came by sea from a kingdom made of islands.
Rooke himself was born in Dublin.
questions.description: They crossed an entire ocean just to wade into a swamp in Boyacá.
questions.fun_fact: The Pantano de Vargas monument, by Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, is one of the largest in Colombia.

questions.question: On July 20, 1810, a criollo urged the crowd in Santafé to demand a cabildo abierto (open town council). Who was he?
hints: He was a member of the Santafé town council.
His nickname came from an ancient Roman office that defended the common people.
He was called “the Tribune of the People.”
questions.description: Before megaphones, independence had to be demanded at the top of your lungs.
questions.fun_fact: Acevedo y Gómez shouted to the people that if they lost “these moments of fervor and heat,” they would be treated as rebels.

questions.question: This admiral, born in Riohacha, led the naval victory of Lake Maracaibo in 1823. Who is he?
hints: He is Colombia's great naval hero.
The Naval Academy in Cartagena is named after him.
The airport in Riohacha is named after him too.
questions.description: A sailor who won his most famous battle on a lake, not at sea.
questions.fun_fact: Every July 24, the anniversary of that battle, Colombia celebrates Navy Day.

questions.question: To see the Guatapé reservoir from above, people climb the Piedra del Peñol. Roughly how many steps does its staircase have?
hints: The climb takes a good while, not one minute and not a whole day.
The rock is about 200 m (650 ft) tall.
It’s hundreds of steps, but fewer than a thousand.
questions.description: A rock so big you need two breakfasts to climb it.
questions.fun_fact: The Guatapé reservoir was filled in the 1970s and flooded the old town of El Peñol, which had to be rebuilt somewhere else.

questions.question: In Colombia's Andean region, how many dry seasons are there in a normal year?
hints: Colombia doesn't have the four seasons of countries far from the equator.
Dry seasons and rainy seasons take turns throughout the year.
One comes around the end and start of the year, the other in the middle of the year.
questions.description: The Colombian sun also keeps visiting hours.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it's just a dry season, many Colombians call it “verano” (summer) and call the rainy season “invierno” (winter).

questions.question: You're walking among frailejones in a Colombian páramo. Roughly how high above sea level are you?
hints: It's cold and misty almost all day.
You're higher than Bogotá, which sits at about 2,600 m (8,500 ft).
You're above the forest, but below the snow of the snowy peaks.
questions.description: Up here, even the frailejones go around wrapped in a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Páramos work like giant sponges: they store the water that later reaches many Colombian cities.

questions.question: “I'm imaginary, I split the Earth into north and south, I cross southern Colombia and I gave my name to a neighboring country.” What am I?
hints: I go all the way around the middle of the Earth.
Because I pass nearby, Colombia's low-lying cities never get snowy winters.
The neighboring country named after me lies just south of Nariño.
questions.description: Nobody has ever seen it, but everyone has crossed it on a map.
questions.fun_fact: Because Colombia is so close to the equator, day and night last almost the same length all year round.

questions.question: In Colombia, which of these problems is NOT typical of the rainy season people call “invierno” (winter)?
hints: Think about what happens when a lot of water falls.
Three of these problems are caused by too much water.
The odd one out needs dry grass and heat.
questions.description: When the Colombian sky gets dramatic, grab your umbrella and your list of problems.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Colombia, April–May and October–November are usually the rainiest months.

questions.question: Complete it: because of its cold climate, many people from tierra caliente (the hot lowlands) call Bogotá “la…”
hints: The nickname comes from a kitchen appliance.
Inside this appliance, everything stays cold.
It's where you keep the milk and the ice.
questions.description: A city that comes with a ruana included.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá sits at about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft), and its average temperature is around 14 °C (57 °F).

questions.question: Look at the map: which department is home to the Combeima Canyon, which climbs toward a snow-capped peak?
hints: It's in central Colombia, between mountain ranges.
The canyon climbs up from the department's capital.
That capital is Ibagué, the “Musical City.”
questions.description: A canyon so green it's almost embarrassing to call it a canyon.
questions.fun_fact: The Combeima River, which carves the canyon, starts on the Nevado del Tolima and supplies water to Ibagué.

questions.question: Finish the chorus of Colombia’s national anthem: “¡Oh gloria inmarcesible! ¡Oh júbilo…!”
hints: It’s a word that has to do with life.
It describes something that lasts forever.
It’s the opposite of “mortal”.
questions.description: The part of the anthem that even people who don’t know a single verse sing at the top of their lungs.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem’s music was written by Oreste Síndici, an Italian who lived in Bogotá, and the words are by Rafael Núñez.

questions.question: Día de la Raza remembers three ships reaching America in 1492. From which country had they set sail?
hints: Columbus was born in Genoa, but that country didn't pay for the trip.
The monarchs who backed him were Isabella and Ferdinand.
They left from the port of Palos, in Andalusia.
questions.description: A trip on three ships with no GPS, no Waze and no asking for directions on the corner.
questions.fun_fact: The three ships were called the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María.

questions.question: Colombia's anthem starts with a glory that is “inmarcesible”. If a flower were inmarcesible, what would happen to it?
wrong_answers: It would glow in the dark
It would never lose its scent
hints: It has to do with the passing of time.
It's something that happens to flowers after a few days in a vase.
The word comes from Latin and is related to the Spanish verb “marchitar”.
questions.description: The strangest word in the anthem: everyone sings it, almost nobody dares to explain it.
questions.fun_fact: “Inmarcesible” comes from the Latin “marcescere”, which means to wither.

questions.question: In the Serranía de La Lindosa, in Guaviare, tens of thousands of figures are painted in red on the rocks. What is this kind of art called?
hints: It is rock art, made thousands of years ago.
The figures aren't carved into rock or drawn on the ground: they are painted on the stone.
The word comes from the Latin “pictus”, which means “painted”.
questions.description: These artists painted with no canvas, no gallery and no entrance fee.
questions.fun_fact: The figures at La Lindosa include animals, people and hands, and some are thought to be more than 12,000 years old.

questions.question: In the Sumapaz páramo, signs warn about hypothermia. Finish this: “hypo” means “under” and “thermia” means…
hints: It comes from Greek.
It's in “thermometer” and “thermos”.
Its opposite is cold.
questions.description: A long word for something that happens to you very fast in the páramo.
questions.fun_fact: The Sumapaz páramo, south of Bogotá, is considered the largest páramo in the world.

questions.question: You climb too fast to a place like this and get a headache, dizziness and shortness of breath. What is this illness called?
hints: It happens because the air up high has less oxygen.
In the Andes people also call it soroche.
You avoid it by climbing slowly and drinking lots of water.
questions.description: Going up fast is fine in an elevator, not in the Andes.
questions.fun_fact: The entrance to Nevado del Ruiz is above 4,000 m (13,100 ft), higher than any city in Colombia.

questions.question: How many medals did Colombia win at the Athens 2004 Olympics?
hints: None of them was gold.
One was won by weightlifter Mabel Mosquera.
The other went to track cyclist María Luisa Calle.
questions.description: The Greeks invented the Games, and in 2004 they welcomed them back home.
questions.fun_fact: Both of Colombia's medals at Athens 2004 were bronze, and both were won by women.

questions.question: In 2020, Mauricio Ortega from Antioquia threw over 70 m (230 ft) and broke the South American record. In which event?
hints: It's a track and field event that was already part of the ancient Greek Olympic Games.
The athlete spins inside a circle protected by a cage.
The object is flat, round and weighs 2 kg (4.4 lb), like a heavy plate.
questions.description: A man from Antioquia who made a living throwing things far away… and people cheer him for it.
questions.fun_fact: The men's discus weighs 2 kg (4.4 lb), while the women's weighs just 1 kg (2.2 lb).

questions.question: Surfers travel to Nuquí, in Chocó, for the Pacific waves. Which of these surf spots is NOT on the Pacific coast?
hints: Three of them face the same ocean as Nuquí.
The odd one out is near the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
It is in La Guajira, beside the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: Pack your board, your sunscreen and a map, because if you pick the wrong sea, you get no waves.
questions.fun_fact: Between July and October, humpback whales come to the waters off Nuquí to have their calves.

questions.question: Which of these Colombian athletes is NOT a golfer?
hints: Three of them have played in the big golf tournaments in the United States.
The odd one out was born in Cúcuta.
He was the top scorer of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil with Colombia's national team.
questions.description: Someone showed up at the golf club in the wrong uniform, and nobody dared to tell him.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo Villegas is nicknamed “Spider-Man” because he crouches almost flat on the ground to read the green, like the superhero.

questions.question: This tennis player was born in Cúcuta, won the junior US Open in 2019 and won the WTA tournament in Bogotá in 2021. Who is she?
hints: She is one of Colombia's highest-ranked tennis players in recent years.
She was born in 2001, so she is the youngest of the four options.
Her first name starts with C and her last name with O.
questions.description: From the heat of the border to clay courts around the world, racket in hand.
questions.fun_fact: The Bogotá tournament is played on clay at about 2,600 m (8,500 ft) above sea level, where the ball flies faster.

questions.question: Out in the countryside, you brush against a pringamosa, the nettle of Colombian farms, and your skin burns. What causes the burning?
hints: You see them better with a magnifying glass.
They cover the leaves and stems, and they're super thin.
They're like tiny needles that snap when you touch them and release substances into your skin.
questions.description: A plant that doesn't need fingernails to keep you scratching all afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: The tips of nettle hairs are made of silica, almost like glass, and break like tiny needles when you brush against them.

questions.question: On the flower farms of the Sabana de Bogotá, this flower is called “pompón.” Look at the close-up: which flower is it?
hints: It comes from Asia.
It's the symbol of the emperor of Japan.
Its name means “golden flower” in Greek.
questions.description: A flower so round it looks like it got its hair done for export.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the world's biggest exporters of chrysanthemums, and almost all of them come from the Sabana de Bogotá and Antioquia.

questions.question: Every February, Colombia ships flowers abroad for Valentine's Day. About how many stems does it send?
hints: Full cargo planes take off for weeks.
It's far more than the number of people living in Colombia.
It's hundreds of millions.
questions.description: Cupid works abroad, but his arrows come with Colombian flowers.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the big day for sweethearts isn't in February: it's Día del Amor y la Amistad, in September.

previous.feedback: Source: the 600 million figure is out of date. Recent seasons were about 700 million stems in 2024 and more than 900 million in 2025, nearing 1 billion, so the answer should become about 900 million or 1 billion, with wrong answers rebuilt around it. The English translation itself is faithful and natural ("6 billion" is the correct US rendering of 6000 millones), so it only needs updating once the source changes. Fact check: wrong. The 600 million figure is outdated. A 2023-era Portafolio piece cited a 600 million stem target. Reports for 2024 cite about 700 million stems, and Forbes and Portafolio coverage of 2025 cites more than 900 million (over 60,000 tonnes). La República's 2026 projection converts to about 980 million.

questions.question: Look at this white puff from a plant grown in Córdoba and Tolima. What is it?
hints: It's used to make T-shirts and socks.
It's white, soft and fluffy.
It's also made into little balls for cleaning cuts.
questions.description: A cloud that turns into a T-shirt instead of rain.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1970s, cotton was called “white gold” in Córdoba and Cesar because of all the money it brought in.

questions.question: Which of these will you NOT find at the Medellín Botanical Garden?
hints: Three of them have to do with plants and animals.
The odd one out is full of pieces made by Indigenous peoples.
That one is in Bogotá.
questions.description: A paisa stroll where the flowers play host.
questions.fun_fact: The Medellín Botanical Garden is named after Joaquín Antonio Uribe, a naturalist from Antioquia, and it's free to get in.

questions.question: In Medellín, whole bars and festivals are devoted to this dance. Which dance is in the photo?
hints: It reached Medellín on records from the south of the continent.
It is danced in a close embrace, with long, unhurried steps.
Its most famous singer, Carlos Gardel, is an idol in Medellín.
questions.description: For this question, knowing isn't enough: you also need rhythm in your feet.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, Medellín holds an international tango festival that draws dancers from many countries.

questions.question: In which town in Caldas is the Festival Nacional del Pasillo Colombiano held every year?
hints: It's in northern Caldas.
Its town center has steep streets with colonial architecture.
It's famous for hats handwoven from iraca palm.
questions.description: A town where even the steep streets move in 3/4 time.
questions.fun_fact: Aguadas is also the home of the aguadeño hat, handwoven from iraca palm fiber.

questions.question: In Barranquilla and Cartagena you hear it all the time: “¿Qué más, vale?”, “¡Ajá, vale!” What does “vale” mean there?
hints: It has nothing to do with saying “OK.”
You say it to someone you go everywhere with.
It comes from “valedor,” the one who keeps you company and stands up for you.
questions.description: In Spain it's how you say “OK”; on the Coast it's a different story.
questions.fun_fact: “Vale” comes from “valedor,” an old word for a person who protects and supports you.

questions.question: You're crossing the Sabana de Bogotá and you pass Chía, Zipaquirá and Facatativá. Which Indigenous people gave them those names?
hints: They lived on the high plateau of Cundinamarca and Boyacá.
Their language belonged to the Chibchan family.
They worshipped Bachué, the mother of humanity, and Sué, the Sun.
questions.description: Long before the traffic jams, the sabana already had names of its own.
questions.fun_fact: Chía was the Muisca goddess of the Moon, and the town of Chía is named after her.

questions.question: On the street you hear “vos sabés que sí, ¿cierto?”. Which of these groups does NOT usually speak with “vos”?
hints: The other three say “sabés” and “querés” all day long.
The group that doesn't use it prefers “usted” or “tú”.
They live in the country's capital.
questions.description: A verb form that divides the country almost as much as soccer does.
questions.fun_fact: Paisas mix “vos” with “pues” so often that it's almost their signature: “¿Y vos qué, pues?”.

questions.question: In the department highlighted on this map, people say “usted” (the formal “you”) even to their kids and partners, in a strong, direct tone. Which one is it?
hints: It is famous for its hormigas culonas (big-bottomed ants).
The Chicamocha Canyon is there.
Its capital is Bucaramanga, the “Ciudad Bonita.”
questions.description: A department where even “good morning” sounds like it means business.
questions.fun_fact: “Usted” comes so naturally to people from Santander that many even use it with their pets.

questions.question: I'm a custom from Colombia's Pacific coast: when a baby's umbilical cord falls off, I add powder from an animal, plant or mineral to pass on its strengths. What am I?
hints: It's done in the baby's first weeks of life.
The idea is that the child inherits the strength, cleverness or skill of what's applied.
My name comes from the Spanish word for the body part where the cord was.
questions.description: On the Pacific coast, babies get superpowers straight from the factory.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, what's used in the ombligada shapes the child's character: some families do it so the child becomes a good swimmer or a hard worker.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which Indigenous people of Colombia's Pacific coast coated their blowgun darts with this frog's poison?
hints: They live in the rainforest, not in the desert or the mountains.
Many of their communities live along the rivers of Chocó.
Their name starts with “E.”
questions.description: Tiny, shiny and more dangerous than a scalding-hot tinto in your hand.
questions.fun_fact: Just rubbing a dart's tip on the frog's back was enough to load it with poison.

questions.question: It's Colombia's rainiest region, its jungles lie next to an ocean, and humpback whales visit its beaches. Which region is it?
hints: It's not the region of the mountains.
Buenaventura and Tumaco are there.
It shares its name with the ocean on its shore.
questions.description: Here an umbrella isn't an accessory, it's part of your body.
questions.fun_fact: Lloró, in Chocó, is among the rainiest places on the planet.

questions.question: In a parade of traditional dress, the ruana is to the Andean region as… which item is to the Caribbean region?
hints: It goes on your head.
It is woven from caña flecha and has black and white stripes.
It is a symbol of Córdoba and of all Colombia.
questions.description: A fashion show where the runway is the whole map of Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: In 2004 the sombrero vueltiao was declared a cultural symbol of the Colombian nation.

questions.question: It's Colombia's largest coastal lagoon, between the Magdalena River and the Caribbean Sea, and home to Nueva Venecia, a village on stilts. What is it called?
hints: It's in the department of Magdalena.
Salamanca Island separates it from the sea.
It's named after Colombia's oldest city.
questions.description: A village with houses on the water: here, if you can't paddle, you can't get to the store.
questions.fun_fact: The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta is a Ramsar wetland and a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

questions.question: You're at a gathering of nothing but vallunos. Which guest sneaked in because they are NOT from Valle del Cauca?
hints: Three of them come from cities in Valle del Cauca.
The gatecrasher comes from the south, near Ecuador.
The gatecrasher's city is the capital of Nariño.
questions.description: A party where the salsa is playing and someone doesn't know the steps.
questions.fun_fact: Buga is famous for the Basilica of the Lord of Miracles, which draws pilgrims from all over the country.

questions.question: You travel the department of Cauca from end to end. Which of these places will you NOT find there?
hints: An island, a volcano and an archaeological park really are in Cauca.
The odd one out is farther north in the Cordillera Central, far from Popayán.
On clear days you can see it from Manizales, and it sits between Caldas and Tolima.
questions.description: A trip around Cauca with a map in your hand and no asking Google.
questions.fun_fact: Gorgona Island used to be a prison, and today it is a national park where you can see humpback whales.

questions.question: It's a small rodent, many homes in Nariño raise it, and in Pasto it is eaten roasted at festivals. Which animal is it?
hints: In other countries it is kept as a pet.
It is also eaten a lot in Ecuador and Peru.
Its name has only three letters.
questions.description: In other countries they buy it an exercise wheel; in Pasto they buy charcoal.
questions.fun_fact: The cuy has been raised in the Andes for thousands of years, since long before the Spanish arrived.

questions.question: Look at the map: what is the capital of the highlighted department?
hints: The department borders Ecuador and Peru.
It's the capital of Putumayo.
Its name starts with “M.”
questions.description: A capital surrounded by so much green that the GPS gets nervous.
questions.fun_fact: Mocoa sits where the Andes start to drop down toward the Amazon rainforest.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the Farallones de Cali are part of one of Colombia's mountain ranges. Which one?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: It's the range closest to the Pacific Ocean.
It's the lowest of the three cordilleras.
Its name tells you it lies to the west.
questions.description: Peaks that look down on Cali like a mother-in-law who came to visit.
questions.fun_fact: The Western Cordillera separates the Cauca River valley from the Pacific rainforest.

questions.question: It's a department of the Llanos, its capital is Yopal, and it's famous for the Cusiana oil field. Which department is it?
hints: It borders Boyacá.
Its name comes from a river.
It starts with “C”.
questions.description: Land of joropo, herons and horses that work harder than you do.
questions.fun_fact: Casanare has more head of cattle than people.

questions.question: In which century did the Spanish found Santa María la Antigua del Darién, near the Gulf of Urabá?
hints: It was a few years after Columbus's first voyage.
It was one of the first Spanish towns on the American mainland.
It was in the year 1510.
questions.description: A town so old that not even Grandma remembers when it was founded.
questions.fun_fact: Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas, set out from the Darién area.

questions.question: It's the highest and coldest piso térmico (climate zone), almost nothing grows there, and in Colombia only a few mountains have it, like Nevado del Ruiz. Which is it?
hints: It lies higher up than the frailejones.
It is also known as the zone of “nieves perpetuas” (perpetual snow).
Its name comes from the slow rivers of ice found on high peaks.
questions.description: Up here, not even a tinto stays hot for more than a minute.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's glaciers have shrunk enormously in recent decades.

questions.question: This animal is a Christmas dish in many Colombian homes. Which continent does it originally come from?
hints: Although it's eaten in Colombia today, it doesn't originally come from Colombia.
Wild turkeys still live in the forests of the continent it comes from.
It comes from the same continent as corn and potatoes.
questions.description: The star of Christmas dinner, who never asked to be invited.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient peoples of Mexico tamed the turkey about 2,000 years ago.

questions.question: In the novena de aguinaldos, right after the prayer to the Virgin Mary, who is the next prayer to?
hints: He's a saint who is in the pesebre (nativity scene).
He is part of the Holy Family.
He was a carpenter and Mary's husband.
questions.description: The moment in the novena when even the most restless cousins have to lower their voices.
questions.fun_fact: After the prayer to Saint Joseph come the gozos, the most sung and noisiest part of the novena.

questions.question: We live on very long wires, we blink on and off in colors, and in December we're hung on balconies and in Medellín's alumbrado. What are we?
hints: We run on electricity.
We go on the tree, in windows and in parks.
Each of us is a tiny bulb, and together we form long strands.
questions.description: December in Colombia: the season when even the balconies get dressed up.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín's Christmas alumbrado uses millions of bulbs, and people come from all over the country to see it.

questions.question: In May, Colombian schools celebrate their teachers with cards and flowers. What day in May is Teacher's Day?
hints: It's the day the Church named the patron saint of teachers.
It's closer to 10 than to 25.
It's half of 30.
questions.description: The one day teachers get more nice homework than they hand out.
questions.fun_fact: On May 15, 1950, Pope Pius XII named Saint John Baptist de La Salle the patron saint of teachers.

questions.question: In Circasia, Quindío, a cemetery from the 1930s buries anyone, whatever their religion or beliefs. What is it called?
hints: It was pushed for by Braulio Botero Londoño, a radical Liberal leader.
It was created because other cemeteries turned away people who weren't Catholic.
Its Spanish name is the opposite of “prisoner”.
questions.description: A Quindío graveyard where the flowers share the hills with the coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this cemetery, Circasia is nicknamed “the free town of Colombia”.

questions.question: Barón Rojo Sur sings in the south stand and is named after a famous German pilot. What is it?
hints: It's a group of fans with bass drums, flags and lots of red.
Its team is also called “los Diablos Rojos”.
Its fans call their team “la Mechita”.
questions.description: A war pilot who swapped his plane for drums and flags.
questions.fun_fact: The original Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, was the most famous pilot of World War I.

questions.question: Look at this trophy. With its 2016 title, how many times in total had Atlético Nacional won it?
hints: No other Colombian club has won it as many times.
Its first title came in 1989, with Francisco Maturana as coach.
It didn't win it again between 1989 and 2016.
questions.description: A cup that has its own shrine of memories in Medellín.
questions.fun_fact: In 1989, Atlético Nacional became the first Colombian club to win the Copa Libertadores.

questions.question: The mita was forced labor in shifts that sent people to the silver mines of Mariquita. Who had to serve it?
hints: They were not the ones in charge in colonial times.
The Spanish copied the idea from an Inca custom.
Those who served it were called “mitayos”, and many came from the resguardos (Indigenous reserves).
questions.description: The toughest work shift in history, and you couldn’t swap it with anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The word “mita” comes from Quechua and means something like “turn” or “shift”.

questions.question: It sticks out from the second floor of colonial houses. In Cartagena it's often wooden and full of flowers, and people watched processions from it. What is it?
hints: It's on the outside of the house, up high.
You reach it through a door from a second-floor room.
Romeo climbed up to one to see Juliet.
questions.description: In the Walled City, the houses have more flowers than a flower shop on Mother's Day.
questions.fun_fact: Cartagena's historic center, full of colonial houses with balconies, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

questions.question: He was the first Colombian to win a stage of the Giro d'Italia, in 1973, and earlier he had broken the amateur hour record. Which city was he from?
hints: He broke that hour record in Mexico City, in 1970.
His nickname was “Cochise”.
It's the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: Pasta, pedals, and a Colombian who showed the Italians how to climb.
questions.fun_fact: Martín Emilio “Cochise” Rodríguez got his nickname from an Apache chief in Western movies.

questions.question: It's Cali's most typical drink: served with ice and made with a mashed sour fruit, lime and sugar. What is it?
hints: It's cold and very refreshing.
It has little pieces of fruit in it, because it isn't fully blended.
Its name comes from the sour, orange-colored fruit it's made with.
questions.description: When a caleño gets hot from dancing salsa, they already know what to order.
questions.fun_fact: In some places, lulo is called “naranjilla” (“little orange”) because on the outside it looks like a small orange.

questions.question: Take a close look at this long, woody fruit: it's cañandonga, whose dark pulp is drunk with milk on the Caribbean coast. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Inside, it has many flat seeds in separate compartments.
It grows on a big tree with pink flowers, not on a palm.
It's the same family as beans, peas and tamarind.
questions.description: A fruit that looks like a club and smells like dirty socks, yet people still blend it with love.
questions.fun_fact: Cañandonga pulp smells so strong that many people hold their nose to drink it, but on the coast it's a traditional drink with milk.

questions.question: The palenqueras of Cartagena sing it, and sometimes it rhymes: it's the pregón. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To signal the stall has closed
hints: It's said before the customer shows up, not after.
It usually names fruits, sweets or fish.
It's like a commercial, but shouted in the street.
questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the neighborhood already had its own sound system: a good pair of lungs.
questions.fun_fact: Street vendors' pregones have inspired many salsa and Caribbean songs.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Colombia, these seeds go into tamales and rice. What are they used for?
hints: They barely change the taste of the food.
If you touch them, your fingers get stained.
They're why many dishes come out reddish or orange.
questions.description: Tiny little seeds with a permanent spot in the Colombian kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: The same achiote that colors rice also gives many cheddar-style cheeses around the world their orange color.

questions.question: Take a close look: this fruit makes breakfast jam and juice blended with milk. Which fruit is it?
hints: It's small and grows on thorny bushes.
It's made of lots of little balls stuck together.
When ripe it's almost black, and its name says so.
questions.description: The fruit that's always in grandma's fridge for the lunchtime juice.
questions.fun_fact: The Andean blackberry (mora de Castilla), the most grown in Colombia, is native to the Andes mountains.

questions.question: Complete the saying: “Yo no creo en brujas, pero…” (I don't believe in witches, but…)
questions.answer: de que las hay, las hay
hints: People say it when they have doubts, but just in case…
The ending sounds almost like a tongue twister.
It ends by saying that they really do exist.
questions.description: The favorite saying of people who swear they aren't superstitious, but knock on wood anyway.
questions.fun_fact: Galicia, in Spain, has its own version with “meigas”, the local witches: “Eu non creo nas meigas, mais habelas, hainas.”

questions.question: It's built right into the showerhead, heats the water just as it comes out, and is common in tierra fría. What is it called?
hints: It needs no gas cylinder and no sun.
It runs on electricity from the wall.
Touch it with wet hands and you might get a small shock.
questions.description: In tierra fría, the morning shower is an act of bravery… or of technology.
questions.fun_fact: Many electric showers have a knob for cold, warm or hot water, which really just changes how much power it uses.

questions.question: Before school, you have to iron your uniform. Why do people iron clothes?
hints: You do it on a long, narrow board.
You have to be careful not to burn yourself.
Afterward, the shirt is nice and smooth.
questions.description: On Sunday night, the school uniform goes to the spa.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric irons, people used heavy metal irons that were heated on the stove.

questions.question: In which city of the Viceroyalty of New Granada was the first government junta formed, in 1809?
hints: Its junta was formed on an August 10.
It was the seat of a royal audiencia in the south of the viceroyalty.
Today this city is the capital of Ecuador.
questions.description: In the race to set up government juntas, someone took off before the whistle.
questions.fun_fact: The Quito junta of August 10, 1809, is known as the “Primer Grito de Independencia” of Spanish America.

questions.question: At the Battle of Pantano de Vargas in 1819, a charge by horsemen from the llanos saved the day. What are those riders known as?
hints: Today a giant monument near Paipa, Boyacá, honors them.
Colonel Juan José Rondón charged with fourteen of them.
Their weapon was a very long pole with an iron tip.
questions.description: A sculpture so huge the horses look ready to gallop right out of Boyacá.
questions.fun_fact: The monument, by sculptor Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, is one of the largest sculptures in Colombia.

questions.question: Every July 20 I move through the streets with bands and flags, and the president watches me from a stand. What am I?
hints: I am shown on TV across the whole country.
The participants rehearse for weeks to stay perfectly in step.
The Army, Navy, Air Force and Police all march.
questions.description: A July 20 plan that half of Colombia prefers to enjoy from the couch.
questions.fun_fact: July 20 is also the day each year when Colombia's Congress opens its new session.

questions.question: On July 20, 1810, in Santafé, a Spanish merchant refused to lend a flower vase and a fight broke out. Who was he?
hints: He had his shop on the main square.
The criollos asked him for the vase to decorate a dinner honoring the commissioner Antonio Villavicencio.
People remember him in the phrase “el florero de…”.
questions.description: Never has a refused loan turned out so expensive.
questions.fun_fact: The original vase is on display today at the Museo de la Independencia - Casa del Florero in Bogotá.

questions.question: The cardón grows in La Guajira and the Tatacoa, stands several meters tall, and the Wayuu use its wood to build their homes. What is it?
hints: It lives in very dry areas.
It stores water inside and is shaped like a column.
It has spines instead of leaves.
questions.description: A neighbor of the goats in La Guajira, and quite a bit taller than them.
questions.fun_fact: The Wayuu use the dried core of the cardón, called yotojoro, to build the walls and roofs of their rancherías.

questions.question: It comes from mines like Muzo and Chivor in Boyacá, and Colombia's are famous worldwide. What precious stone is it?
hints: The Muisca were using it long before the Spanish arrived.
The ones from Muzo are famous for their intense color.
Its color is the same as the mountains of Boyacá.
questions.description: The stone that makes even movie dragons jealous of Boyacá.
questions.fun_fact: Many experts consider the stones from Muzo the best in the world for their deep color.

questions.question: The first verse of Colombia's anthem says: “The horrible night has ended! Sublime liberty pours out the auroras of its invincible light.” What time of day does it describe?
hints: Look at who wins the fight: darkness or light.
“Has ended” tells you the night has just finished.
An “aurora” here is the glow in the sky before the sun comes up.
questions.description: A song every Colombian knows by heart, even if they've never stopped to think about what it means.
questions.fun_fact: The “horrible night” in the anthem stands for the time of Spanish rule before independence.

questions.question: Which Colombian national symbol has the motto “Libertad y Orden” written on it?
hints: You can see it on official documents and government buildings.
A condor holds a ribbon with the motto on it.
It has three sections and some flags on each side.
questions.description: Two words every teacher would love to see written on the classroom board.
questions.fun_fact: The coat of arms shows the Isthmus of Panama because when it was designed in 1834, Panama was part of Colombia.

questions.question: It poisons rivers with mercury, leaves dredge holes in Chocó and the Amazon, and led to the Atrato River being declared a subject of rights. What is it?
hints: Park rangers and the security forces go after it.
It's looking for something at the bottom of rivers.
Its main goal is to get gold.
questions.description: A problem that leaves the rivers of the Pacific coast looking like they never want to get out of bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, Colombia's Constitutional Court declared the Atrato River a subject of rights, something almost no river in the world had.

questions.question: Which of these colors does NOT appear in the Olympic rings?
hints: There are five rings of different colors on a white background.
All three colors of Colombia's flag are in the rings.
It's the color of grapes and eggplants.
questions.description: Five rings and not a single wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The ring colors, together with the white background, were chosen because they could be used to draw the flag of every country in the world at the time.
