questions.question: Ingrit Valencia won bronze at Rio 2016, the first Colombian female boxer with an Olympic medal, fighting in the lightest women's class of those Games. Which was it?
hints: At those Games, her class had a limit of 51 kg (112 lb).
It's named after an animal.
It's an insect that buzzes.
questions.description: A weight class where every gram counts and the scale is the most feared opponent.
questions.fun_fact: At Rio 2016, women had only three boxing classes: 51, 60 and 75 kg (112, 132 and 165 lb).

questions.question: Its champions race on tracks and streets, and Colombia has topped the country table at its World Championships again and again. What sport is it?
hints: Many Colombian children join clubs for it at a very young age.
The athletes wear helmets and special boots.
Under each boot is a row of small wheels.
questions.description: In this sport, Colombia is like Brazil in soccer, just without the samba.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has skating clubs in almost every city, and many champions started skating before the age of 6.

questions.question: Elite runners from around the world say the Bogotá Half Marathon is one of the toughest on the planet. Why?
questions.answer: It's run at about 2,600 meters of altitude
wrong_answers: It goes up and down the eastern hills
It's always run in the rain
It has more than a hundred sharp turns
hints: The problem isn't the course, it's the air.
Runners who come from the coast feel it from the very first kilometer.
Bogotá is much closer to the clouds than to the sea.
questions.description: 21 kilometers (13 miles) that leave even the world's best distance runners begging for mercy.
questions.fun_fact: At Bogotá's height of about 2,600 m (8,500 ft), every breath brings in quite a bit less oxygen than at sea level, which is why many athletes train in the mountains.

questions.question: Its flowers look like a monkey's face, it grows in cloud forests, and it is most diverse in Colombia and Ecuador. Which orchid genus is it?
hints: Its name comes from Latin.
Its sepals end in long, pointed tails.
It shares its name with the most famous vampire in the movies.
questions.description: An orchid that poses for photos with the face of a cheeky monkey.
questions.fun_fact: “Dracula” means “little dragon” in Latin, after the long tails of its sepals, not after any vampire.

questions.question: In Medellín's Desfile de Silleteros, how much can a giant silleta weigh?
hints: One single person carries it on their back.
It can be more than 2 meters (6.5 ft) wide.
It can weigh more than the person carrying it.
questions.description: The prettiest and heaviest backpack ever carried in Antioquia.
questions.fun_fact: The silleteros of Santa Elena learn the craft from their families, and some children parade with kid-size silletas from a very young age.

questions.question: Colombia is one of the world's biggest exporters of this flower. Look at the close-up: which flower is it?
hints: Its petals have jagged edges.
It smells a little spicy.
Its Spanish name comes from the same word as the clove spice that goes into natilla.
questions.description: It flies more often than most business travelers, and always in refrigerated class.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish the carnation is called “clavel” after the “clavo de olor” (clove), because its scent is a reminder of it.

questions.question: In the Desfile de Silleteros, which category of silleta carries only bunches of flowers, with no figures or signs?
hints: It has no brands or ads.
It doesn't spell out messages or make pictures with flowers either.
It's put together the way the old silleteros of Santa Elena used to do it.
questions.description: A whole garden walking through Medellín on somebody's back.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Feria existed, the farmers of Santa Elena used the silleta to carry flowers down to sell in Medellín.

questions.question: There's a tiple requinto, a requinto guitar and a requinto clarinet. What does “requinto” tell you about an instrument?
wrong_answers: It's an old version from colonial times
It only keeps the rhythm, never the melody
hints: The word comes from old Spanish, not from an Indigenous language.
In carranga, the requinto plays the picked melody above the tiple.
Think of a “child” instrument that sounds higher than its “parent.”
questions.description: A word that shows up in three families of instruments, and nobody ever asks what it's doing there.
questions.fun_fact: In carranga, the tiple keeps the rhythm while the requinto decorates it with picked melodies.

questions.question: Paisa is to “vos” as costeño is to…
hints: It's the word for talking to a friend, in a relaxed and familiar way.
It's the same one used in most songs.
It's the one Carlos Vives and Shakira use when they sing to someone.
questions.description: A question that tastes of sea breeze and arepa de huevo.
questions.fun_fact: On the Caribbean coast “tú” is so common that many costeños use it even with people they've just met.

questions.question: In Pasto, in Boyacá and in Mexico, when someone calls your name, you answer “¿Mande?”. What does it mean?
hints: You say it to Mom, to the teacher and to your elders.
It comes from the Spanish verb “mandar,” to give orders.
It's like saying “I'm at your service.”
questions.description: In Pasto, answering when someone calls you comes with its own etiquette.
questions.fun_fact: “Mande” comes from “mandar”: it's like saying “give me your orders, I'm here to serve you.”

questions.question: Which of these Colombian expressions does NOT mean that something is good or fun?
hints: You'd say three of them at a great party.
You'd say the other one in a class that never ends.
In Colombia you say it when something is really boring or annoying.
questions.description: Colombian words have more moods than a Monday holiday.
questions.fun_fact: “Jartera” comes from “jartarse”, the popular form of “hartarse”: to be full of something or fed up with it.

questions.question: In Bogotá, this is the word for someone no longer a child but not yet an adult: in high school and always falling in love. What is it?
hints: This person is roughly between 12 and 17 years old.
Adults say it half fondly, half teasing, about kids starting to go to parties and have a boyfriend or girlfriend.
Its feminine form comes in a can.
questions.description: Too big for the piñata, too small for a tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Rolos also say “chino” or “china” for a child or a young person.

questions.question: Most Colombians live in this region, three mountain ranges cross it, and Bogotá is there. Which region is it?
hints: It's the region of the mountains.
Medellín and Cali are there too.
It's named after the longest mountain range in South America.
questions.description: So many people live here that even the tinto has to wait in line.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the Andes split into three ranges: the Western, Central and Eastern Cordilleras.

questions.question: At the Festival del Bambuco in Neiva, every candidate for queen must perform a sanjuanero. What is the sanjuanero?
hints: The candidates practice it for months.
It comes with band music and a handkerchief.
It's the signature tradition of Huila, and you need a partner for it.
questions.description: In Neiva in June, even the heat puts on a hat.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival del Bambuco falls during the feasts of Saint John and Saint Peter, the most joyful celebrations of the year in Huila.

questions.question: At the Festival Nacional del Porro in San Pelayo, Córdoba, bandas sabaneras compete. Which instruments make up these bands?
questions.answer: Clarinets, trumpets, bass drum and cymbals
wrong_answers: Gaitas, maracas, tambor alegre and llamador
hints: They're the same bands that liven up corralejas and town fiestas.
Elsewhere they're called bandas papayeras.
They mix brass and woodwind instruments with band percussion.
questions.description: In Córdoba, when they say a band is about to play, they don't mean a rock band.
questions.fun_fact: The bands of San Pelayo have played porro for generations, and the festival has been held every year since the late 1970s.

questions.question: A very famous cumbia tells the story of a boat like this one: the one belonging to Guillermo Cubillos. Who composed it?
hints: He was from El Banco, Magdalena.
He also composed “El gallo tuerto”.
The Festival Nacional de la Cumbia in El Banco is named after him.
questions.description: A song that has spent more than half a century sailing down the river without sinking.
questions.fun_fact: In “La piragua”, the boat travels between El Banco and Chimichagua, driven by twelve bogas (boatmen).

questions.question: I'm oval and sour, with red or orange skin. I'm blended into juice and ground with ají for empanadas. What am I?
hints: I grow in the Andes mountains, hanging from a small tree.
Inside I have little dark seeds and orange pulp.
My name puts together a salad vegetable and the place where I grow.
questions.description: The fruit that would rather end up in hot sauce than in dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Tomate de árbol is also called tamarillo, and it's a relative of the tomato and the potato.

questions.question: In Colombia, if people say someone “es como el arroz blanco” (is like white rice), what do they mean?
hints: The saying compares a person to the place rice has on the Colombian table.
It’s said jokingly and fondly about someone people know.
Just like rice at a Colombian meal, this person is never missing from anything.
questions.description: A saying that came straight out of the lunch pot.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia grows its own rice, mostly in the Llanos Orientales and in Tolima.

questions.question: Which freshwater fish, the most famous of the Magdalena River's subienda, is the star of a coastal sancocho?
hints: It's very bony, and on the coast people eat it fried or in sancocho.
It lives in the swamps and feeds on the mud and algae at the bottom.
Its mouth is very small.
questions.description: A fish that ends up in the pot after swimming upstream with the whole family.
questions.fun_fact: The “subienda” is the season when thousands of bocachicos swim up the Magdalena River and fishermen get a huge catch.

questions.question: I'm skinny and long, made of wheat dough rolled in a spiral around cheese, and I get fried for parties. What am I?
hints: I'm served on trays of party snacks at birthdays.
I'm crunchy on the outside, and the cheese melts inside.
I'm shaped like a part of your hand.
questions.description: The skinniest guest at the party, and the first one to vanish from the tray.
questions.fun_fact: In Venezuela, a very similar snack is called a tequeño.

questions.question: Emiliano Zuleta wrote it to mock Lorenzo Morales, and Carlos Vives made it famous in 1993. What did “La gota fría” grow out of?
hints: The song dates from the late 1930s and comes from the La Guajira and Cesar region.
Lorenzo Morales had sung something at Zuleta first, and this song was the reply.
Two juglares answer each other in verse to see who is better.
questions.description: A story from La Guajira that crossed borders with an accordion in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Emiliano Zuleta and Lorenzo Morales ended up as friends, and their rivalry became one of the most famous stories in vallenato.

questions.question: What is the head of the caja vallenata (vallenato drum) traditionally made of?
hints: It comes from a farm animal.
It's a small animal, very common in La Guajira and Cesar.
It says “baa” and its baby is called a kid.
questions.description: A drum small enough to fit between your knees, but it sounds like a giant.
questions.fun_fact: People often say vallenato's three instruments mix three heritages: the accordion is European, the caja African and the guacharaca Indigenous.

questions.question: Vallenato accordion players take great care of their instrument's bellows. What are the bellows of an accordion?
questions.answer: The folding part that moves the air
wrong_answers: The strap that holds up the accordion
The wooden box of the treble buttons
hints: Without them, the accordion wouldn't make a sound.
They stretch and squeeze while you play.
They work like the tool people use to blow air on a cooking fire.
questions.description: Some accordion players care for their instrument more than for their sombrero vueltiao.
questions.fun_fact: On a vallenato accordion, the same button plays one note when the bellows open and a different one when they close.

questions.question: On a bus, you hear someone say: “¡Ala, qué pena con usted!” Which region is that “ala” most typical of?
hints: It's a cold, high region of Colombia.
People there also love to say “sumercé.”
It's the area around Bogotá and Boyacá.
questions.description: A tiny word that means “wing” in Spanish, yet never takes flight.
questions.fun_fact: In Bogotá and Boyacá people often say “sumercé,” a warm, respectful way of saying “usted” (formal “you”).

questions.question: A Colombian teen says: “El domingo me toca almorzar con los cuchos.” Who is he having lunch with?
hints: In Colombia, Sunday lunch is usually a family plan.
“Cucho” is said of someone older.
He calls his mom “la cucha.”
questions.description: Teenagers have their own dictionary, and adults almost never understand it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “cucho” or “cucha” can also mean any older person.

questions.question: They talk to their plants, go grocery shopping in pajamas and sing at the top of their lungs on the bus. In Colombia, what do people say about them?
hints: It has nothing to do with money or with flirting.
It's said of someone who seems to have lost their mind.
The phrase is about something slipping out of place on a roof.
questions.description: For when someone's head is overdue for urgent maintenance.
questions.fun_fact: To say the same thing, Colombians also say someone «le falta un tornillo»: they're missing a screw.

questions.question: In Colombia, what is a “tajalápiz”?
hints: You use it with pencils and colored pencils.
When you use it, little wood shavings come out.
It makes a pencil pointy again.
questions.description: A tiny object that lives in every school pencil case.
questions.fun_fact: “Tajar” means to cut, so a tajalápiz is literally a “pencil cutter.”

questions.question: In Colombia, if a student “perdió el año,” what happened?
questions.answer: They have to repeat the same grade
wrong_answers: Their grades for the year got lost
They missed almost the whole school year
They had to switch to another school
hints: It has nothing to do with actually losing something.
It happens when the grades aren't good enough.
Next year they'll take the very same subjects again.
questions.description: Final report cards arrive, and the house feels as tense as a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Other Spanish-speaking countries say “repetir el año,” “repetir curso” or “reprobar el grado.”

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone “le tocó bailar con la más fea” (had to dance with the ugliest one), what happened to them?
questions.answer: They got stuck with the worst part
wrong_answers: They fell in love by accident
They arrived late to the party
hints: The saying isn't about real dancing.
It's said to whoever ends up washing all the dishes after the party.
It's the opposite of being lucky when things are handed out.
questions.description: A party saying that, oddly enough, almost never gets used at a party.
questions.fun_fact: The saying is used for any thankless task: the worst part of the job, the hardest shift or the chore nobody wants.

questions.question: In Antioquia you often hear “¡Ome, no me diga!”. Which Spanish word does that “ome” come from?
hints: It's a word that got shortened from people talking fast.
The original word starts with a letter that is silent.
It's the opposite of “mujer”.
questions.description: Three very paisa letters that get used for everything except staying quiet.
questions.fun_fact: Paisas also shorten “para” to “pa'”, as in “¿pa' dónde va, ome?”.

questions.question: In Colombia, which verb means going out with friends to dance and party until late?
hints: It has nothing to do with working or getting up early.
You do it at clubs, parties and casetas.
It comes from a word for a party with music and dancing.
questions.description: A word so Colombian it isn’t in Grandpa’s dictionary… or maybe it is.
questions.fun_fact: Rumba is also a Cuban rhythm, but in Colombia the word came to mean any party with dancing.

questions.question: How often, and in which month, is the Carnaval de Riosucio in Caldas held?
hints: It isn't held every year.
During the festival, the matachines recite teasing verses.
It takes place in odd-numbered years, in the first days of the year.
questions.description: A party so good that even the devil asks permission to show up.
questions.fun_fact: The star of the Carnaval de Riosucio is the Devil, a cheerful, teasing character, not an evil one.

questions.question: The gaitas at the Ovejas gaita festival have a beeswax head and a duck-feather mouthpiece. What plant is their body made from?
hints: It's a plant of dry lands.
The craftsman scoops out its soft inner pulp.
It's a tall cactus that gets hollowed out to make the flute.
questions.description: In Ovejas (Spanish for “sheep”), Sucre, the sheep don't bleat: they blow.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival Nacional de Gaitas Francisco Llirene has been held in Ovejas, Sucre, since 1985.

questions.question: It's a piece of guadua (giant bamboo) with a strip of its bark lifted up as a string, struck with a small stick to play the bass. What is it called?
hints: It belongs to the traditional folk music of the Colombian countryside.
It isn't scraped: the strip is struck and vibrates.
Its name sounds a bit like “caramba”.
questions.description: A rural folk band that lost its bass player and built a new one from whatever grew in the hills.
questions.fun_fact: Instruments like this one, where the string comes from the tube itself, also exist in Africa and Asia, such as the valiha of Madagascar.

questions.question: A chirimía band with clarinet, euphonium, snare drum, bass drum and cymbals is typical of one Pacific department. Which one?
hints: It is one of the rainiest places in the world.
It gets the Fiestas de San Pacho going.
Its capital is Quibdó.
questions.description: A band so loud that even the neighbors three blocks away end up dancing.
questions.fun_fact: The Fiestas de San Pacho in Quibdó, chirimía and all, are Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Finish what Colombians say about a song that gets everyone happily dancing: “Esa canción tiene…”
hints: It’s something good, not something that makes you feel bad.
It has to do with flavor and grace when you move.
It comes from the same word used for really tasty food.
questions.description: A word you pronounce with your hips.
questions.fun_fact: On Colombia’s Pacific coast, “vivir sabroso” means living in peace, as a community, and enjoying life.

questions.question: At a party where everyone dances, sings and has a great time, Colombians say: “¡Esto es una…!”
hints: It's something very cheerful.
It's said of a party nobody wants to leave.
It's also the title of a famous song by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony.
questions.description: The exact opposite of an afternoon spent doing homework.
questions.fun_fact: “La Gozadera,” by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony, names several Latin American countries, Colombia among them.

questions.question: Look at this island in Colombia's Pacific. Which conqueror named it Gorgona because it was full of snakes?
hints: He passed by on one of his trips south, looking for a very rich empire.
The snakes reminded him of Medusa, the Gorgon from Greek myth with snakes instead of hair.
He later conquered the Inca Empire in Peru.
questions.description: A christening with salt water, no godparents and plenty of snakes.
questions.fun_fact: Gorgona still has lots of snakes, so visitors to the national park must wear tall boots.

questions.question: You climb the Azufral volcano in Nariño and reach the Laguna Verde inside its crater. About how high up are you?
hints: It feels as cold as the páramo, and breathing is a little hard.
You are higher than Bogotá, which sits at about 2,600 m (8,500 ft).
You are almost at the top of the volcano, but there is no snow like on the highest snow-capped peaks.
questions.description: A lake so green it looks like someone went overboard with the food coloring.
questions.fun_fact: The lake's green color comes from sulfur and other minerals from the volcano, which is why you can't swim in it.

questions.question: Riddle: “I come from the Indian and Pacific Oceans and slipped into the Colombian Caribbean. I have stripes and venomous spines, and in San Andrés people eat me.” What am I?
hints: I eat the little reef fish, and almost nobody hunts me.
My long fins look like a mane.
I'm named after the king of the African savanna.
questions.description: A Caribbean reef where every neighbor dresses up like it's carnival.
questions.fun_fact: In San Andrés and on other Caribbean coasts, people hold lionfish fishing contests and cooking contests to keep this invasive species under control.

questions.question: A prisoner escaping the old prison on Gorgona Island had to swim to the mainland. About how far away is the coast?
hints: You couldn't swim it from the island in one calm afternoon.
Malpelo, the other famous island in Colombia's Pacific, is much, much farther away.
By speedboat from Guapi, you get there in a couple of hours.
questions.description: The prison with the best sea view and the worst reasons to stay.
questions.fun_fact: The Gorgona prison was open from 1960 to 1984; today the island is a national park, and the jungle covers the ruins.

questions.question: Look at the map of Colombia. Which sea washes its northern coast, the one at the top?
hints: Cartagena, Santa Marta and Barranquilla are there.
Its waters are warm and turquoise blue.
It's the sea you cross to reach the islands of San Andrés and Providencia.
questions.description: The warm water where half of Colombia goes on vacation to lie in the sun.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is the only country in South America with coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean.

questions.question: Englishman Quantic and Mario Galeano formed Ondatrópica in 2012 and recorded their first album at the legendary Discos Fuentes studios. In which city?
hints: It's not a coastal city, although the label recorded lots of coastal music there.
Discos Fuentes was born in Cartagena, but moved to another city in the 1950s.
It's the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: An Englishman and a guy from Bogotá walked into an old studio and came out with the most tropical record on the block.
questions.fun_fact: Ondatrópica brought together veterans of Colombian tropical music and young musicians, in the same studio where Fruko y sus Tesos recorded their classics.

previous.feedback: source: the fact check says Ondatrópica began in late 2011, and only the album was recorded in early 2012 at Discos Fuentes in Medellín. The source repeats "created Ondatrópica in 2012", so the error comes from the source and not from the translation. The source should be reworded first, for example "Quantic and Mario Galeano recorded Ondatrópica's first album in 2012 at the legendary Discos Fuentes studios. In which city?", and then translated again. Fact check: wrong. The question says Ondatrópica was formed in 2012. Sources say the project began at the end of 2011, and the album was recorded in January 2012 at Discos Fuentes in Medellín. The answer, Medellín, is right.

questions.question: La Sonora Dinamita, with hits like “Mi cucu” and “Escándalo,” took a Colombian rhythm all over Latin America. Which one?
hints: It doesn't need a star accordion or a llanero harp.
It's so loved in Mexico that many people there feel it's their own.
On the coast, it's danced holding lit candles.
questions.description: A band named after an explosive that has been blowing up dance floors for decades.
questions.fun_fact: La Sonora Dinamita was founded in Cartagena in 1960 by Antonio Fuentes, the founder of Discos Fuentes.

questions.question: In the Gran Cabalgata, thousands of riders parade on Paso Fino horses at a fair that starts in late December. In which city?
hints: The fair runs from December 25 to 30 and closes the year.
At the same fair, people dance in the Salsódromo.
It is the city of salsa.
questions.description: A parade where the ones walking with the most style have four legs.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Cali has been held since 1957, and every year it closes Colombia's calendar with horses, parades and salsa.

questions.question: You're at a street stand buying mango biche. Which of these do they NOT usually put on it?
hints: Mango biche is green and sour.
It's sold in little cups or bags on street corners and outside schools.
What doesn't go on it is something sweet you drink hot at breakfast.
questions.description: A fruit that isn't ripe yet but already has fans on every street corner.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “biche” means a fruit that isn't ripe yet.

questions.question: Sancocho trifásico has yuca, potato and plantain, and is cooked in a big pot on river outings. What does “trifásico” tell you?
wrong_answers: It is served in three bowls
hints: “Tri” means three.
The “three” is about what goes into the pot, not how it is cooked or served.
It has beef, pork and chicken in the same pot.
questions.description: A soup with so much energy, its name sounds like it came off a fuse box.
questions.fun_fact: “Trifásico” comes from electricity: three-phase power has three phases, just as the sancocho has three meats.

questions.question: You go to the market to buy plantain for sopa de plátano. Which of these is NOT a kind of plantain or banana in Colombia?
hints: Three of them grow in bunches.
The odd one out grows underground.
The odd one out is a root that goes into sancocho and looks like a white carrot.
questions.description: A shopping list with something sneaked in that doesn’t wear a yellow peel.
questions.fun_fact: For sopa de plátano, many grandmothers grate the green plantain instead of chopping it.

questions.question: You buy maíz peto at the market. Which of these dishes is NOT made with corn?
hints: The odd one out is typical of the Caribbean coast, especially Córdoba and Sucre.
It's eaten hot and served with white rice.
It's thickened with ñame, a root vegetable.
questions.description: A market where corn is the boss, but someone sneaked onto the list.
questions.fun_fact: In Antioquia, mazamorra made with maíz peto is drunk with milk and a piece of panela or bocadillo.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a pasta you add to soup?
hints: Pasta is made from wheat flour.
The odd one out grows on a plant, inside pods.
The odd one out is a small brown seed.
questions.description: The soup Mom serves before the main course, and you have to finish it before the good stuff arrives.
questions.fun_fact: With alphabet soup, lots of kids play at spelling their names on the spoon.

questions.question: I'm big and round, with a hard rind and orange flesh. In Colombia I'm made into a cream soup for lunch. What am I called in Colombia?
hints: I grow on a vine that creeps along the ground.
I'm a relative of the Halloween pumpkin.
In other countries I'm called zapallo.
questions.description: At lunchtime, Grandma's pot hides a secret from the vegetable garden.
questions.fun_fact: Ahuyama seeds can be eaten too: toasted with salt, they make a tasty snack.

questions.question: This freshwater fish is raised in ponds and served whole and fried with patacón; the red kind is the most famous. What is it called?
hints: It's the favorite on day trips to warm towns near rivers and reservoirs, like Melgar or Girardot.
It's flat and round, about the size of a plate.
Its name starts with “mo”.
questions.description: A fish that arrives at the table in one piece, looking like it has no idea what just happened.
questions.fun_fact: The red mojarra eaten in Colombia is actually a tilapia, a fish that came from Africa.

questions.question: This village in the Sierra Nevada belongs to Valledupar and is the main town of the Kankuamo people. What is it called?
hints: It sits on the slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, on the Cesar side.
The chicote, a traditional dance, is danced there.
Its name starts with A.
questions.description: A town so high up in the Sierra that vallenato arrives there a little out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Several vallenato songwriters come from Atánquez, where Indigenous music and the accordion met.

questions.question: You're in class and the teacher comes back shouting “¡Se acabó la recocha!” What does the teacher want stopped?
hints: It isn't homework or anything the teacher assigned.
It's about jokes, laughing and paper balls flying.
It's the opposite of sitting quietly and behaving.
questions.description: The teacher's patience has an expiration date, and today is the day.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, someone who is always joking and goofing around is called a “recochero.”

questions.question: You're making a poster for school: “scissors” is to cutting as “colbón” is to…
hints: Colbón comes in a bottle and it's white.
If it gets on your fingers, it dries and peels off like skin.
It keeps the paper shapes from falling off the poster board.
questions.description: The school poster at 10 p.m.: the real test for parents.
questions.fun_fact: “Colbón” started out as a brand name and ended up as every Colombian's word for white glue.

questions.question: I hide under your jeans, you change me every day, and Superman wore me in red over his suit. What do Colombians call me?
hints: Superman wore me over his blue tights.
You put me on before your jeans.
In other countries they call me “calzoncillos”.
questions.description: Nobody sees it, but everybody changes it every day (hopefully).
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the country, underwear is called “calzoncillos”, “chones”, “bombachas” or “bragas”.

questions.question: Rapunzel let me grow longer and longer, Elsa wears me in a braid, and in Colombia anyone who has me is called «mono». What am I?
hints: Rapunzel and Elsa have the same hair color.
My color looks like the sun or gold.
I'm light hair, almost yellow.
questions.description: In Colombia, this nickname has nothing to do with climbing trees or eating bananas.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, babies with very light hair are lovingly called «monitos».

questions.question: Faking being sick, heading to the park with friends and never showing up in the classroom. What do Colombians call that?
hints: It has to do with school.
If the parents find out, a scolding is guaranteed.
It means skipping class in secret.
questions.description: Math first thing in the morning against a sunny day in the park: a very unfair fight.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's “irse de pinta,” in Argentina “hacerse la rata” and in Spain “hacer novillos.”

questions.question: You ask someone, “¿Vamos por un tinto?”, and they answer, “¡Hágale!”. What are they telling you?
hints: It's a very Colombian word you hear all day long.
The same word is used to cheer someone on or tell them to go ahead.
It's like saying “¡de una!”.
questions.description: In Colombia, every important conversation starts with a tinto as the excuse.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “hágale” works for everything: saying yes to a plan, cheering someone on or saying “go ahead”.

questions.question: On a trip, which of these plans are chanclas NOT good for?
hints: They're light shoes, almost always made of rubber.
Chanclas leave your toes out in the air.
Look for the plan with snow and lots of cold.
questions.description: The secret weapon of Colombian moms, which you can also wear on your feet.
questions.fun_fact: Nevado del Ruiz rises over 5,000 m (16,400 ft) and has snow all year round.

questions.question: Costumbrismo portrayed ordinary people and their customs in stories and paintings. In which century did it peak in Colombia?
hints: It came after Independence.
In that era, Eugenio Díaz wrote the novel “Manuela.”
It was the century of the civil wars and the Rionegro Constitution.
questions.description: Literature for classy busybodies: what the neighbors eat, how they dress and what they get up to.
questions.fun_fact: The painters of the Comisión Corográfica made watercolors of farmers, miners and street sellers from all over the country.

questions.question: What do you call a man who, like this one, carries loads on mules along mountain trails?
hints: He's a classic figure of Antioquia and the Coffee Region.
He usually wears a sombrero, a carriel (leather shoulder bag) and a poncho over his shoulder.
His name comes from the shout “¡arre!” used to get the animals moving.
questions.description: Before tractor-trailers, freight transport had long ears and a bad temper.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century, arrieros carried much of Colombia's coffee out along the mountain trails.

questions.question: In the 19th century, Colombia exported tagua, “vegetable ivory,” to Europe and the United States. What was it mainly used for?
hints: It ended up sewn onto clothes.
It was cut into small slices and holes were drilled in them.
Shirts and coats had lots of them.
questions.description: A seed so hard that elephants should thank it.
questions.fun_fact: Plastic killed off the big tagua business, but today it's used again for jewelry and crafts.

questions.question: Why do farmers in Boyacá and Cundinamarca wear this piece of clothing?
hints: It's worn mostly up in the high country.
On the farm, it goes with a hat and alpargatas (rope-soled sandals).
It's nice and warm, and you put your head through a hole in the middle.
questions.description: The piece of clothing that turns any grandpa from Boyacá into a superhero with a square cape.
questions.fun_fact: Nobsa, in Boyacá, is famous for weaving ruanas from sheep's wool.

questions.question: Which of these places was NOT the site of a battle in the Thousand Days' War?
hints: That battle belonged to a different civil war.
It was fought in Valle del Cauca, in 1876.
It happened during the so-called “War of the Schools.”
questions.description: A thousand days of war is enough time to fight almost everywhere… but not quite everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: The Battle of Palonegro, near Bucaramanga, lasted about fifteen days in May 1900.

questions.question: Under President Mariano Ospina Rodríguez, a constitution turned the country into the Granadine Confederation, made of sovereign states. In what year?
hints: It was in the same decade that slavery was abolished in the country.
It replaced the Constitution of 1853 with an even more federal one.
It was three years before Mosquera took Bogotá in 1861.
questions.description: Constitutions in Colombia were like cell phones: every so often a new model came out.
questions.fun_fact: The Granadine Confederation had eight states, including Panama, which was then part of the country.

questions.question: On what day does Colombia remember the Battle of Boyacá?
hints: It's a holiday right in the month of wind and kites.
It's also the day Colombian presidents take office.
It's the seventh day of the eighth month.
questions.description: A teeny little bridge where something huge was won.
questions.fun_fact: The Puente de Boyacá is so small you can cross it in just a few steps.

questions.question: The Panama Railroad, opened in 1855 when Panama was part of Colombia, ran from ocean to ocean. What did its first passengers mostly use it for?
questions.answer: To go looking for gold in California
hints: Many passengers came from the east coast of the United States.
Their final stop was on the west coast of North America.
It was the time of the gold rush.
questions.description: From one ocean to the other in a day, no canal needed.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first railroad to cross the Americas from ocean to ocean, fourteen years before the one in the United States.

questions.question: I was a general of the Independence, of Pijao origin. In 1854, backed by the artisans, I led a coup against Obando. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Tolima.
My government lasted about eight months.
My first two names are the same as José María Córdova's.
questions.description: A general who got tired of waiting his turn to govern.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Colombia, Melo fought in Mexico on Benito Juárez's side.

questions.question: Its followers are called “godos,” its color is blue, and Mariano Ospina Rodríguez and José Eusebio Caro founded it in 1849. Which party is it?
hints: It's one of Colombia's two traditional parties.
Its historic rival is the red party.
Its name comes from wanting to conserve traditions.
questions.description: In Colombia, politics was all about colors, and not because of fashion.
questions.fun_fact: Conservatives and Liberals took turns in power in Colombia for more than a century.

questions.question: To play “cara o sello”, you toss a coin in the air. If it lands flat, how many possible results are there?
hints: Look at both sides of a coin.
One side is called “cara” and the other…
One is cara and the other is sello.
questions.description: The oldest and fairest way to decide who gets the last empanada.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico the same game is called “águila o sol”, and in Argentina “cara o ceca”.

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone says their motorcycle cost “dos barras,” how much money did they pay?
hints: It's much more than a few lucas.
A “barra” is the same amount as a “palo.”
Each barra has six zeros.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a candy bar, but it's worth way more.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombian slang, “un palo” and “una barra” mean the same thing: one million pesos.

questions.question: The Colombian bill with Gabriel García Márquez on it is worth 50,000 pesos. How many lucas is that?
hints: On the street, “luca” is a casual way to talk about money.
One luca is 1,000 pesos.
Just drop the last three zeros and you're done.
questions.description: The bill everyone dreams of finding forgotten in a jacket pocket.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriel García Márquez, the only Colombian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, is on the 50,000-peso bill.

questions.question: At an ATM you take out 100,000 pesos in 20,000-peso bills. How many bills come out?
hints: Count up by 20,000 until you reach 100,000.
Two bills make 40,000.
As many bills as fingers on one hand.
questions.description: The machine that never says “sorry, no change”… well, almost never.
questions.fun_fact: The world's first ATM was installed in London in 1967.

questions.question: You see a price with the “$” sign in a shop window. In which of these countries is that sign NOT used for its currency?
hints: Three of these countries have a currency called the peso.
The country you're looking for has a currency named after the Sun.
There, prices are written with “S/”.
questions.description: An S with a line through it that shows up in every shop window in the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before it was used for the US dollar.

questions.question: What does the Banco de la República do that no other bank in Colombia can do?
wrong_answers: Lend money to buy a house
hints: It's the country's central bank.
Its headquarters are in downtown Bogotá.
Every Colombian bill comes from there.
questions.description: The only bank that doesn't offer you a credit card the moment you walk in.
questions.fun_fact: The Banco de la República was founded in 1923 and also runs the Gold Museum in Bogotá.

questions.question: In Colombia, which of these phrases does NOT mean that someone is out of money?
hints: Three of these phrases are said when you can't even pay for the bus.
The phrase you want is said when you feel comfortable somewhere.
It's used when someone has settled in and is happy in their new city.
questions.description: End of the month in Colombia: a dictionary of empty wallets.
questions.fun_fact: “Varado” comes from ships stuck on the sand that can't move, just like someone without plata.

questions.question: Crepes & Waffles was born in Bogotá in 1980, is famous for its ice cream and has a special hiring policy. Who does it mainly hire?
wrong_answers: Young people in their first job
hints: It's a social policy the brand has had almost from the start.
It's a group that often struggles to find a steady job in Colombia.
Many of them raise their children on their own.
questions.description: A restaurant where even the ice cream has a social conscience.
questions.fun_fact: Its ice cream became so famous that the brand runs its own ice cream shops apart from the restaurants.

questions.question: In Colombia, Pequeñín is a famous brand of this product. Which company from Antioquia makes it?
hints: Its headquarters are in Medellín.
It also makes toilet paper and napkins.
Its name is the Spanish word for mom, dad and kids all together.
questions.description: A product that works all night long and never gets a thank-you.
questions.fun_fact: The same company sells toilet paper and baby wipes under its own name.

questions.question: Ego is a Colombian shampoo and hair gel brand from the company behind Savital and Bon Ice. Who was it made for?
hints: Its gel is famous for hairstyles with a really strong hold.
Its name is about self-confidence.
On the bottle, “Ego” is followed by two English words saying who it's for.
questions.description: A shampoo with so much self-esteem that it named itself after it.
questions.fun_fact: Quala, the company behind Ego, also makes Doña Gallina bouillon cubes.

questions.question: It comes in a cup with two compartments, and you mix it before eating. Besides yogurt, what does Bon Yurt have?
hints: It’s crunchy.
Many people eat it for breakfast with milk.
It can be Zucaritas or Choco Krispis.
questions.description: The little cup with more fans in the lunchbox than the sandwich.
questions.fun_fact: Because it comes separated, it doesn’t get soggy until you mix it, so it stays crunchy.

questions.question: The famous restaurant Andrés Carne de Res, full of wild decorations and partying, started in a town near Bogotá. Which one?
hints: It's in Cundinamarca, on the savanna north of Bogotá.
It's also known for its universities and shopping malls.
It's named after the Muisca goddess of the moon.
questions.description: A restaurant where dinner lasts until sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: Andrés Jaramillo founded it in 1982, and today it also has locations in cities like Bogotá and Medellín.

questions.question: It was born on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, is sung mostly by older women called cantadoras, and has its national festival in Necoclí. What accompanies the singing in bullerengue?
hints: It has no wind instruments at all.
It’s sung in a circle: the cantadora calls out a verse and the chorus answers.
It’s all percussion: beaten drumheads and clapping hands.
questions.description: A party where the grandmas sing louder than any speaker.
questions.fun_fact: Petrona Martínez, the great queen of bullerengue, was nominated for the Latin Grammy several times.

questions.question: You climb the Cerro de la Popa in Cartagena for the feast of the Virgen de la Candelaria. What is the date?
hints: Christmas and Three Kings’ Day are already over.
It falls early in the second month of the year.
It’s exactly 40 days after Christmas.
questions.description: A festival that climbs a hill carrying more candles than grandma’s birthday cake.
questions.fun_fact: The Virgen de la Candelaria is the patron saint of Cartagena, and her convent crowns the highest hill in the city.

questions.question: At the Feria de Cali, everyone goes out to dance salsa. Which of these is NOT a dance?
hints: Three of them are played at parties all over Colombia.
You can't listen to one of them on a speaker.
It's round, made of corn, and often comes with cheese.
questions.description: In Cali, even the traffic lights move to the beat of the clave.
questions.fun_fact: Cali is called the world capital of salsa, and its fair has a parade called the Salsódromo.

questions.question: On January 5 in Pasto, your face gets painted black. According to tradition, who asked for that day off in colonial times?
hints: It was in the 17th century.
They had no day of rest at all.
They were brought by force from Africa.
questions.description: A day when nobody in Pasto goes out with a clean face.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the Spanish Crown granted that day off after a revolt in 1607.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The core is right: Jan 5 is Día de los Negros, and enslaved people are said to have been given a day off. But the 1607 revolt and the Spanish Crown granting it appear in only some popular sources (Radio Nacional, Sitio Andino). Academic and local sources don't back it up, and El Tiempo gives 1854. The hint 'It was in the 17th century' and the fun fact depend on that shaky date. Some accounts also place the origin in Popayán.

Fact check: uncertain. The answer (enslaved Africans) is consistent across sources. The fun fact is shaky: sources disagree on the origin. One says a 1607 uprising in Remedios, Antioquia, led to the day off. Others say the enslaved people asked for it in Popayán. Others date it to 1854. The question says 'colonial times', but 1854 is after independence. 'Spanish Crown granted it after an uprising in 1607 (in Pasto)' is not well supported. The hint 'It happened in the 17th century' is also not firmly established.

Fact check: uncertain. Answer (enslaved Africans) and the Jan 5 'Día de los Negros' tradition are correct. The 1607 date is documented only in Wikipedia, which says the revolt was in Remedios, Antioquia, not Pasto, and flags the history as needing citations. Other sources call the carnival's origins '17th century' without a specific revolt. The hint 'They didn't have a single day of rest' is awkward but acceptable.

questions.question: Zorro wears one, and the Torito of the Barranquilla Carnival wears one with horns. It covers your face. What is it?
hints: In Barranquilla, many are carved by hand from wood.
There are animal ones too, like the tiger, the donkey or the Marimonda.
In Colombia it's often called a careta.
questions.description: At the Barranquilla parade, the Torito chases people and everyone runs off laughing their heads off.
questions.fun_fact: The animal masks of the Barranquilla Carnival are carved by hand in towns like Galapa.

questions.question: At the Carnaval de Barranquilla, people throw things at each other for fun. Which of these do they NOT throw?
hints: Three of them don’t leave your clothes sticky.
The odd one out goes on your toast.
It’s sweet and made from fruit.
questions.description: A battle where everyone loses and everyone leaves happy.
questions.fun_fact: At the carnival, lots of people wear goggles to protect their eyes from foam and cornstarch.

questions.question: I directed “Rodrigo D. No futuro” and “La vendedora de rosas”, both in competition at Cannes, with non-professional actors from Medellín. Who am I?
hints: I’m from Antioquia, and I’m also a poet.
My films show the lives of young people in Medellín’s comunas.
In 2004 I released “Sumas y restas”, also shot in Medellín.
questions.description: A filmmaker who would rather cast the kids from the neighborhood than Hollywood stars.
questions.fun_fact: For “La vendedora de rosas” (1998), Gaviria worked with children and teenagers who lived on the streets of Medellín instead of professional actors.

questions.question: We came from Italy, opened the Salón Olympia in Bogotá, and in 1915 filmed “El drama del 15 de octubre.” Who are we?
hints: We were film pioneers in Colombia in the early 20th century.
Our movie theater in Bogotá opened its doors in 1912.
Our surname sounds like the Italian word for “Sunday.”
questions.description: Immigrants who brought something from Italy even more useful than a pasta recipe.
questions.fun_fact: “El drama del 15 de octubre” told the story of a real political event in Bogotá and caused so much controversy that the film was almost completely lost.

questions.question: In which decade was Proimágenes Colombia created, the public-private fund that now runs the Film Development Fund?
hints: It was born shortly after Focine was shut down.
It came out of Colombia's General Law of Culture.
It was created at the end of the 20th century, a few years before the 2003 Film Law.
questions.description: The official piggy bank of Colombian filmmakers.
questions.fun_fact: Proimágenes was born in 1998, and since the 2003 Film Law it has managed the money collected from box office sales to make new films.

questions.question: In which decade did “Visa USA” come out, Lisandro Duque's film about a young man who dreams of moving to the United States?
hints: It was made in the era of Focine, the state film company.
Around those years, “Romancing the Stone” with Michael Douglas also came out.
It came out the same year as the World Cup in Mexico, Maradona's World Cup.
questions.description: An American dream that starts with standing in line at an embassy.
questions.fun_fact: “Visa USA” (1986) is one of the best-remembered Colombian films of the Focine era.

questions.question: In which decade was “Lila's Book,” Marcela Rincón's animated film made in Cali, released?
hints: It's a fairly recent film.
It tells the story of a girl who falls out of her book into a world made of paper.
It came out a few years after the World Cup in Brazil, where James Rodríguez shone.
questions.description: A girl who climbed out of her book without asking the author first.
questions.fun_fact: “Lila's Book” (2017) was one of the first animated feature films made in Colombia to reach movie theaters.

questions.question: In which decade did Víctor Nieto found the Cartagena de Indias International Film Festival?
hints: It is considered the oldest film festival in Latin America.
Its awards are called India Catalina.
It began shortly after the Cuban Revolution.
questions.description: A man from Cartagena decided the walled city also needed some movie screens.
questions.fun_fact: The festival began in 1960, and Víctor Nieto ran it for more than 40 years.

questions.question: To win the 2004 Copa Libertadores, Once Caldas knocked out three of these giants. Which one did it NOT face?
hints: Look at the Brazilian teams: Once Caldas met two of them in that tournament.
The final was against an Argentine team and was decided on penalties.
The missing team lost that year's semifinal to its eternal Buenos Aires rival.
questions.description: A team from Manizales went on a trip around South America and came home with the cup in its suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2004 final, goalkeeper Juan Carlos Henao was the star of the penalty shootout that won Once Caldas the Copa against Boca Juniors.

questions.question: “I’m in Neiva, on the banks of the Magdalena River, and Atlético Huila plays its home games on my grass.” What’s my name?
hints: All four are names of Colombian stadiums that honor a person.
My name honors a politician from Huila itself.
My name has a double surname: Plazas…
questions.description: A field where the heat of the San Pedro festival reaches all the way into the locker rooms.
questions.fun_fact: Atlético Huila’s women’s team won the Copa Libertadores Femenina in 2018, the first continental title for a Colombian women’s club.

questions.question: Up to 2025, in which of these cities had no club ever been tricampeón, with three Colombian league titles in a row?
hints: Think of the stars clubs wear above their crests and of their great winning streaks.
One club won five titles in a row in the 1980s.
It's the home city of Junior, a club with many stars that, up to 2025, had never won three straight.
questions.description: Winning once is luck, twice is a habit, and three in a row means it's time to print the T-shirts.
questions.fun_fact: América de Cali won five straight titles from 1982 to 1986, and Millonarios won four straight from 1961 to 1964.

questions.question: If a team is relegated from Colombia's Primera A, which tournament does it play in the next season?
hints: It's a lower-level tournament.
The teams there are all trying to move up to the top division.
Its name uses the letter that comes after A.
questions.description: An elevator nobody wants to ride going down.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, relegation is decided by a table that averages points over several seasons, not just one year.

questions.question: The club nicknamed “la Naranja Mecánica” wears orange, trained James Rodríguez in its youth system and comes from a town next to Medellín. Which one?
hints: It’s in the Aburrá Valley, south of Medellín.
Its stadium is called the Polideportivo Sur.
The club has the same name as the town, followed by “Fútbol Club”.
questions.description: A club so orange it looks like orange juice wearing cleats.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname, Spanish for “the Clockwork Orange”, comes from the Netherlands team of the 1970s, famous for its orange shirts and its “Total Football”.

questions.question: On TV you see the soccer score “Junior 0–1 Nacional”. By custom, the team listed first is…
hints: It has nothing to do with the goals.
It has to do with the stadium where the game is played.
Its fans usually fill most of the stadium.
questions.description: In math, the order doesn’t change the answer; on a scoreboard, it says quite a lot.
questions.fun_fact: Playing at home is a real advantage: in almost every league in the world, teams win more games in their own stadium.

questions.question: If a referee in the Colombian league shows a player this card, what happens to him?
hints: It's not good news for the player.
It's the same color as a traffic light telling you to stop.
He has to leave the field and can't come back.
questions.description: A little colored card that weighs more than a ball.
questions.fun_fact: A team left with fewer than seven players because of red cards or injuries loses the match.

questions.question: Colombian fan groups (barras) hang flags like these in the stands, called “trapos”. Which country did this fan-group culture come from in the 1990s?
hints: It's a South American country.
People there have talked about “barras bravas” for decades.
It's the home of Boca Juniors and River Plate.
questions.description: Banners so long that one of them could cover half the stands.
questions.fun_fact: Fan groups guard their trapos so closely that losing one to a rival group is seen as a huge disgrace.

questions.question: Your bike tire went flat and someone offers you “la bomba.” What are they offering you?
hints: What they're lending you will fix the tire problem.
You use it by pushing and pulling a handle.
It puts air into the tire so it's firm again.
questions.description: Without it, your bike stays home looking like a rainy Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “bomba” can also mean a birthday balloon or a gas station: it all depends on the situation.

questions.question: How many times has a Colombian cyclist finished the Tour de France wearing the white jersey with red polka dots?
hints: More than once, but Colombians don't win it every year.
Lucho Herrera won it twice in the 1980s.
Later, Santiago Botero, Mauricio Soler and Nairo Quintana took it home.
questions.description: A jersey that looks like it caught chickenpox, yet every climber dreams of wearing it.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Herrera won the mountains classification in all three Grand Tours: the Tour, the Giro and the Vuelta a España.

questions.question: It has three wheels, little kids pedal it, and in parks ice cream sellers sell ice pops from one. What is it called?
hints: It's a vehicle you move with pedals.
Many kids learn to pedal on it before moving up to a bike.
Its name starts with a word part that tells how many wheels it has.
questions.description: The first car a kid “drives” in the park, no license and no fuel needed.
questions.fun_fact: Many street vendors in Colombia use cargo tricycles to carry raspados, fruit or tinto through the streets.

questions.question: In 1988 I won the Dauphiné Libéré in the French Alps, and I won it again in 1991. Before that, I was the first Colombian to win a Grand Tour. Who am I?
hints: I raced in the golden age of the “escarabajos”, the Colombian climbers of the 1980s.
I was a small, shy climber who also won the mountains jersey at the Tour de France.
My nickname was “el Jardinerito” (the Little Gardener).
questions.description: An escarabajo who cruised through the French Alps as if they were the mountains back home.
questions.fun_fact: The first Colombian to win the Dauphiné was Martín Ramírez in 1984, with Bernard Hinault in the same race.

questions.question: I'm from La Ceja, Antioquia, and I'm a sprinter, not a climber. At the 2017 Giro d'Italia I won four stages and the points jersey. Who am I?
hints: I win in the last few meters, when everyone speeds up at once.
In 2018 I won the first stage of the Tour de France and put on the yellow jersey.
My first name is the same as a Spanish king's from the time of independence.
questions.description: An antioqueño who isn't scared of mountains, but would rather the race ended on flat ground.
questions.fun_fact: Gaviria made his name in 2015 by beating Britain's Mark Cavendish twice at the Tour de San Luis in Argentina.

questions.question: In what year did the first Colombian team in history ride the Tour de France?
hints: The team was named after a battery brand.
That year the Tour was opened to amateur riders for the first time.
It was one year before Lucho Herrera won on Alpe d'Huez.
questions.description: The escarabajos got on the plane, and France had no idea what was coming.
questions.fun_fact: Because of the time difference with France, many Colombians listened to Tour stages on the radio very early in the morning.

questions.question: This town in Boyacá is famous for its hot springs, Lake Sochagota and a cheese named after it. What is it called?
hints: It is near Tunja, on the Boyacá high plateau.
The Pantano de Vargas is very close, with its huge monument to the lancers.
Its name has only five letters.
questions.description: A town where even the water comes out nice and warm to welcome visitors.
questions.fun_fact: Paipa cheese has a protected designation of origin: only cheese made in that part of Boyacá can carry the name.

questions.question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, a red, sour juice made from corozo is typical. What is corozo?
hints: It grows in bunches, a bit like grapes.
The plant it comes from has long leaves and spines, and it loves the heat.
It's a distant relative of the coconut, which also grows on a tree with long leaves.
questions.description: A drink so costeño it starts sweating when you look at it.
questions.fun_fact: On the coast, people also make bolis (frozen treats) and sweets from corozo, not just juice.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer 'witches' fits folk belief (holy water repels witches, evil spirits, the devil), and the wrong answers (thieves, neighbors, debt collectors) are clearly wrong. But I found no source that documents this specific belief for Colombia, only the general practice of sprinkling holy water in corners, doors and windows for protection. Another answer such as 'evil spirits' or 'the devil' is at least as common in the tradition. The hint 'they get around on a broom' is generic witch lore. The fun fact is generally true.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. I found no source for the specific Colombian tradition that sprinkling holy water in house corners makes witches flee. Sources only show the Catholic and esoteric practice of sprinkling holy water in corners for protection against evil. Witches as the answer is plausible. The wrong answers (thieves, neighbors, debt collectors) are clearly not the folk-belief answer. The hints (flying at night, broomsticks) are generic folklore. The fun fact about fonts at church entrances and people taking holy water home is generally true. The first hint ('haven't come to borrow money') is odd and unhelpful.

Fact check: uncertain. I found no source for the Colombia-specific belief that holy water in the house corners makes witches run away. The common folk and Catholic accounts say it drives off the devil, evil spirits or bad energy. Witches are plausible, since the question's hints (broomstick, flying at night) point to them. The hints themselves are fine, and the wrong answers (thieves, neighbors, debt collectors) are clearly wrong. The fun fact is plausible but I didn't verify it. Hint 1 is vague. 'Evil spirits' or 'the devil' would be the better-documented answer.

Fact check: uncertain. In Colombian and Latin American tradition, holy water in the corners of a house usually drives away evil spirits, the devil or bad energies. Witches are not the standard answer. I did not verify this by search, so the claim that witches flee is shaky. The hints about broomsticks and night flight are generic witch lore, not Colombian tradition.

hints: Each station shows a moment of Jesus's path to the cross.

hints: It's what happens when someone jumps out behind you and yells “boo!”.

hints: It's a singing contest, not a cooking one.
