questions.description: A country house in Santa Marta with more history than any vacation farm.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar came to the Quinta as a guest of its owner, the Spanish merchant Joaquín de Mier.

questions.question: I was president of Colombia several times, pushed for the 1886 Constitution and wrote the lyrics of all eleven verses of the national anthem. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Cartagena.
I was also a poet and a journalist.
My first name is Rafael.
questions.description: He wrote eleven verses, and at school they almost always sing just the chorus and one of them.
questions.fun_fact: The music of the anthem was composed by Oreste Sindici, an Italian who lived in Bogotá.

questions.question: Villa del Rosario, near Cúcuta, hosted the Congress of 1821 and is where an independence hero was born in 1792. Who?
hints: He was vice president while Bolívar was president.
He is called “the Man of the Laws”.
Two Colombian departments carry his surname.
questions.description: A small town near the border with a résumé longer than many capitals'.
questions.fun_fact: Villa del Rosario still has the ruins of the church where the Congress of 1821 met.

questions.question: When the government declares national mourning, the flag is raised like this, not all the way to the top. What is this called?
hints: It has to do with the pole the flag goes up.
The flag ends up about halfway.
It rhymes with “half-past”.
questions.description: Sometimes even the flag knows how to keep quiet.
questions.fun_fact: By protocol, the flag is first raised all the way to the top and then lowered to the middle.

questions.question: For years, Falcao was “the 9” of Colombia's national team. Complete the sentence: in soccer, “the 9” is the…
hints: Think about where Falcao played on the field.
His job is to stay as close as possible to the other team's goal.
He's the player expected to put the most balls in the net.
questions.description: A number that weighs more in soccer than it does in the multiplication table.
questions.fun_fact: The custom of fixed numbers for each position comes from the days when the starting players wore 1 to 11.

questions.question: In January 2024, England's Chelsea signed a Colombian striker for the biggest transfer fee in women's soccer up to then. Who was it?
hints: She came to London from a Spanish club.
She played for Levante and is famous for her physical strength.
Her first name starts with M.
questions.description: When the English pull out their wallets, it means they spotted something very good in Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia reached the quarterfinals of a Women's World Cup for the first time in 2023, and Mayra Ramírez was on that team.

questions.question: In what year was the World Cup hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada played, with Colombia back on the field?
hints: It was the first World Cup with three host countries.
Colombia hadn't made it to the World Cup in Qatar.
It happened very recently.
questions.description: Three host countries, and only one yellow jersey in your heart.
questions.fun_fact: The 2026 World Cup was the first in history with 48 teams.

questions.question: I was born in Necoclí, Antioquia. I raced down the right wing, played many years for Juventus in Italy and celebrated my goals by dancing. Who am I?
hints: I was part of the team that played the 2014 and 2018 World Cups.
Before Juventus, I also played for Fiorentina and Chelsea.
My last name is the Spanish word for a geometric shape with four equal sides.
questions.description: Speed down the wing and dance moves after every goal: the full combo.
questions.fun_fact: Cuadrado played more than 100 matches for Colombia.

questions.question: Colombian coach Luis Fernando Suárez took Ecuador to the 2006 World Cup and Honduras to the 2014 one. Which national team did he coach at Qatar 2022?
hints: It's a Central American team.
It qualified for Qatar in a playoff against New Zealand.
Its nickname is “la Sele”, and its country is famous for “pura vida”.
questions.description: A paisa coach with more World Cup passports than many players.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian coach, Hernán Darío “el Bolillo” Gómez, also took three different national teams to World Cups: Colombia, Ecuador and Panama.

questions.question: In the group stage of the Paris 2024 Olympics, which team did NOT play Colombia's women's national team?
hints: Colombia was in the same group as the host nation.
Colombia beat New Zealand 2–0.
The team you're looking for went on to win the gold.
questions.description: Eiffel Tower, croissants and Colombian women going in hard for every ball at the Olympics.
questions.fun_fact: In the quarterfinals, Colombia was beating world champions Spain 2–0, but Spain tied the game and knocked Colombia out on penalties.

questions.question: This is the flag of Venezuela. How many stars does it have?
hints: The stars form an arc on the blue stripe.
There are more than seven.
It is the same number as a spider's legs.
questions.description: A neighbor dressed in the same yellow, blue and red, but with some extra sparkle.

questions.question: In what year were the London Olympics where Mariana Pajón, Rigoberto Urán and Caterine Ibargüen won medals?
hints: It came after the Beijing Games.
Four years later came the Games in Rio de Janeiro.
It was the same year many people thought the world would end.
questions.description: A Games with a queen, Big Ben and plenty of Colombian joy.
questions.fun_fact: In London, Colombia won 8 medals, its best Olympic haul up to that time.

questions.question: In what year did Ángel Barajas win silver on the horizontal bar, Colombia's first Olympic medal in gymnastics?
hints: It's a very recent medal.
He won it as a 17-year-old.
It was at the Paris Games.
questions.description: A kid who grabbed a bar and came down holding a piece of history.
questions.fun_fact: Ángel Barajas is from Cúcuta and became one of Colombia's youngest Olympic medalists.

questions.question: It's housed in the Casa Sámano in La Candelaria, used to be called the Museum of Urban Development, and tells how the capital grew. Which museum is it?
hints: It isn't about gold, independence or colonial art.

questions.description: Dusty display cases, creaky colonial floors and a guide who knows the gossip from two centuries ago.
questions.fun_fact: The museum keeps thousands of old photos showing what the capital looked like when streetcars still ran through its streets.

questions.question: Botero painted “The Presidential Family” in 1967: a president, his wife, a soldier, a priest and even himself painting. In which city is it today?
hints: It is not in Colombia.
A famous museum of modern art keeps it.
It is at MoMA, in the city of the Statue of Liberty.
questions.description: A family portrait where nobody went on a diet before posing.
questions.fun_fact: Botero painted himself behind an easel, just like Goya and Velázquez did in their portraits of the royal family.

questions.question: The British diplomat Edward Walhouse Mark painted watercolors of Colombia's landscapes and people while living there. When did he arrive?
hints: Colombia was already independent from Spain when he arrived.
At that time the country was called the Republic of New Granada.
He arrived a few years after the deaths of Bolívar and Santander.
questions.description: A diplomat who, instead of signing papers, sat down to paint landscapes.
questions.fun_fact: His watercolors are now one of the best windows into daily life in Colombia in the mid-19th century.

questions.question: The Bachué Group formed in Colombia in the 1930s, with artists like Luis Alberto Acuña and Rómulo Rozo. What did they want from their art?
questions.answer: Art of their own, with Indigenous and Latin American roots
wrong_answers: Abstract art made only of geometric shapes
A return to the religious themes of colonial times
hints: The group didn't just bring together painters and sculptors: it had poets too.
They took their name from a sculpture by Rómulo Rozo.
In Muisca myths, Bachué is the mother of humankind.
questions.description: A single sculpture gave its name to a whole group of artists, something even the best ad agency can't pull off.
questions.fun_fact: Rómulo Rozo carved “Bachué” in Paris in the 1920s, and it was shown at the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville.

questions.question: At an exhibition, you see the word “Colombia” written in the same curvy letters as the Coca-Cola logo. Which artist made it?
hints: He was a conceptual artist who worked from the 1970s on.
He is also famous for writing “Achiote” and “Maíz” as if they were brand names.
He is a man, and his surname is the Spanish word for “expensive.”
questions.description: A soda and a country that decided to wear the same jersey.
questions.fun_fact: The 1976 work became so famous that today it is sold on T-shirts and posters all over Colombia.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this monument in Cartagena is a giant pair of old shoes. Which poet does it honor?
hints: He was a poet from Cartagena known for his humor.
He wrote that his city inspired the fondness you feel for your old shoes.
He was nicknamed “el Tuerto.”
questions.description: A pair of shoes so big that nobody has ever managed to try them on.
questions.fun_fact: The monument is near the Castillo de San Felipe, and many tourists take photos standing inside the shoes.

questions.question: You’re at a party where people only want songs by Feid. Which of these is NOT his?
hints: Feid goes by “el Ferxxo” and loves dressing in green.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian singer?
hints: She sings reggaeton.

questions.description: She has more hits than the Medellín metro has riders at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: Karol G’s real name is Carolina Giraldo Navarro, and the G comes from her last name.

questions.question: You're at a concert: a banjo starts up and four guys from Bogotá sing “Cómo te atreves.” Which band is it?
hints: They're from Bogotá and have known each other since they were kids.

questions.question: Which of these Colombian singers is NOT a reggaeton artist?
hints: His music is played with accordion, caja and guacharaca.

His first name is the Spanish form of the name of the cat who chases Tweety.
questions.description: Three of these show up ready for perreo, and one brings his own parranda.

hints: It happened long before Mirabel was born.
Alma had to leave her village with her family.
Julieta, Pepa and Bruno had already been born, but they were very little.

questions.question: In Colombia it's chopped fresh over sancocho, goes into homemade ají and is sold by the bunch at the market. What is cilantro?

It's an aromatic plant, a relative of parsley.

questions.question: It smells very strong, grows wild in gardens, and Colombian grandmothers gave it on an empty stomach. What was paico used for?

questions.question: Look at this silleta. Before it was filled with flowers, what did farmers in Antioquia use it for?

questions.question: Which Colombian poet wrote poems posing as a woman, under the pen name “Edda la bogotana”?

questions.question: Shakira is to “Waka Waka” as J Balvin is to…

questions.question: You’re at Rock al Parque in Bogotá and four bands are announced. Which one is NOT Colombian?

questions.question: Karol G made feeling “bichota” trendy. Complete it: being a bichota means feeling…
hints: The word comes from Puerto Rican street slang.

questions.question: I was born in Cuba in the 19th century, I'm slow and romantic, Trío Los Panchos took me all over the Americas, and in Colombia I'm sung with heartbreak. What am I?

I share my name with a short jacket that bullfighters wear.

questions.question: It's Colombia's national instrument. It looks like a small guitar, and its strings are grouped in threes. What is it called?
hints: You hear it in bambucos, torbellinos and carranga.

questions.question: I was born in Socorro, Santander, wrote “Pueblito viejo” and “Ayer me echaron del pueblo”, and sang to a “Campesina santandereana”. Who am I?

questions.question: Rancheras are hugely popular in Colombia. Which of these artists is NOT famous for singing rancheras?

questions.question: Emberá Chamí women in Risaralda weave wide, colorful patterned necklaces called okama. What are they made of?

questions.question: Look at this gold piece from the Calima culture. In which Colombian department did this people live?

questions.question: The old town of Guatavita ended up under the Tominé Reservoir, and a new one was built. In which decade did this happen?

questions.question: Which of these foods is NOT a fruit?

questions.question: Which of these places is NOT in Bogotá?

questions.question: Of these ingredients in a bandeja paisa, which one does NOT come from an animal?
hints: It comes from a plant.
They're seeds cooked in a pot of water.
They're red or cargamanto and served with a little hogao.
questions.description: The heaviest platter in Colombia, and not because of the dishes.
questions.fun_fact: The Indigenous peoples of the Americas have grown beans alongside corn for thousands of years.

questions.question: In 1995, at Wembley Stadium, René Higuita pulled off his famous “scorpion.” What was that move?
questions.answer: A clearance with his heels, diving forward
wrong_answers: A backheeled penalty taken from his own goal
A one-handed save, hanging from the crossbar
A bicycle-kick goal after crossing the whole field
hints: It happened in a friendly match against England.
Higuita ended up almost lying flat in the air, face down.
His legs bent upward, like the tail of the animal it is named after.
questions.description: A goalkeeper who never read the instruction manual for his position.
questions.fun_fact: Higuita was also famous for dribbling the ball out of his goal, and as a goalkeeper he scored dozens of goals from free kicks and penalties.

questions.question: In Colombia, to make a trompo (spinning top) spin, you need the cabuya. What is the cabuya?
hints: It's often made of fique, a plant fiber.
It gets wrapped around the top before you throw it.
Think of a shoelace or a piece of twine.
questions.description: Without it, the top is just an ornament that refuses to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Fique, the plant used to make cabuya, is also used in Colombia to weave sacks and mochilas (shoulder bags).

questions.question: Which of these does NOT happen in Macondo in “One Hundred Years of Solitude”?
questions.answer: A volcano rises in the middle of the square
wrong_answers: An insomnia plague makes people forget names
It rains for almost five years straight
Yellow flowers fall from the sky
hints: Three of these are famous scenes from the novel.
The forgetting plague arrives in town with Rebeca.
The rain of flowers falls when José Arcadio Buendía dies.
questions.description: A town where the strange thing is when nothing strange happens.
questions.fun_fact: In the novel it rains for “four years, eleven months, and two days.”

questions.question: At the December novenas in Colombia, “Los peces en el río” is never missing. What is it?
hints: It comes up when the family gathers around the pesebre.
Many Colombian families know it by heart from childhood and repeat it every night of the novena.
You sing it, often with maracas and tambourines.
questions.description: Some fish that, it seems, get extremely thirsty in December.
questions.fun_fact: “Los peces en el río” is a traditional villancico that came from Spain, and its chorus says the fish “drink and drink and drink again”.

questions.question: Lent runs from Ash Wednesday to Holy Week. How many days does it last, according to tradition?
hints: It lasts more than a month.
It's a number that shows up a lot in the Bible.
Its Spanish name, Cuaresma, comes from the Latin “quadragesima”.
questions.description: The season when fish gets more popular than chicharrón.
questions.fun_fact: The 40 days recall the days Jesus spent in the desert, according to the Bible.

questions.question: In which decade was “Ojo al cine,” the film review magazine of the Grupo de Cali, born?
hints: It was the time when salsa was taking over Cali's neighborhoods.
Andrés Caicedo, Luis Ospina and Carlos Mayolo were behind it.
It came out a few years after the group's film club, founded in 1971.
questions.description: A magazine that told you to keep your eyes wide open before the lights went down.
questions.fun_fact: The name plays on “¡ojo!” (literally “eye!”), which Colombians say to mean “pay attention!”

questions.question: This market square in central Bogotá has a flower market that opens before dawn, and tourists go there to try exotic fruits. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the Los Mártires district.
It's on Avenida Calle 19 at Carrera 25.
In Spanish, “palo” (stick) + “quemado” (burnt), run together as one word.
questions.description: A place where, at 4 in the morning, it already smells of roses and lulo.
questions.fun_fact: At the Paloquemao flower market, huge bunches of flowers are sold at wholesale prices from before sunrise.

questions.question: In 2019, Maluma sang “Medellín,” about his hometown, with an American pop star. Who was she?
hints: She has been making music for more than 40 years.
The song opened her album “Madame X.”
She has been famous since the 1980s for “Like a Virgin.”
questions.description: From the Aburrá Valley to the Billboard charts, no layovers.
questions.fun_fact: Maluma and Madonna performed “Medellín” at the 2019 Billboard Music Awards in a show full of holograms.

questions.question: Every Holy Week in San Antero, Córdoba, I get dressed up as a queen, a soccer player or a politician and parade in my own festival. Who am I?
hints: I live in the countryside and carry heavy loads.
Cross me with a mare and you get a mule.
I have long ears and I bray.
questions.description: Endless patience, zero pay, and now a runway career too.
questions.fun_fact: San Antero lies on the Gulf of Morrosquillo, on the shore of the Caribbean Sea.

questions.question: Atlético Bucaramanga wears yellow and green and won its first league title in 2024. Which animal is its nickname?
hints: Its fans shout it every weekend at the Alfonso López stadium.
It's a wild hunter that lives neither in Colombia's jungles nor in its seas.
It lives in Africa and Asia and has a coat full of spots.
questions.description: A team from Santander that took decades to hunt down its first star.
questions.fun_fact: Bucaramanga won its first star in June 2024 in the final against Independiente Santa Fe, with Venezuelan Rafael Dudamel as coach.

questions.question: The Navarrese conquistador Pedro de Ursúa founded the city of Pamplona, in today's Norte de Santander. In what year?
hints: It was in the middle of the 16th century, when the conquest of the interior was already underway.
It was just over ten years after Jiménez de Quesada founded Santafé.
It was in the mid-16th century, less than a decade before 1550.
questions.description: A man from Navarre who went so far from home that he packed the name of his homeland in his suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, Ursúa set off down the Amazon River in search of El Dorado, on one of the most famous expeditions of the Conquest.

questions.question: In mazamorreo, in the rivers of Antioquia and Chocó, people wash sand in a wooden batea (pan). What are they looking for?
hints: The pan is swirled in circles with water and river sand.
What they're looking for is heavy and stays at the bottom.
It's the metal the Muisca and Quimbaya shaped into famous jewelry and figures long before the Spanish came.
questions.description: It has nothing to do with grandma's mazamorra, though it also takes a lot of patience.
questions.fun_fact: Mazamorreo was practiced before the Spanish arrived, and it still supports many families in Chocó today.

questions.question: Charles V signed them in 1542, and the encomenderos of the New Kingdom protested against them. What were the New Laws meant to do?
questions.answer: Limit the encomiendas and protect Indigenous people
wrong_answers: Close the Caribbean ports to pirates
Hand out more mines to the conquistadors
hints: Behind them were friars who spoke out about what was happening in the Americas.
The encomenderos disliked them because they lost privileges.
Friar Bartolomé de las Casas, the great defender of the native peoples, pushed for them.
questions.description: Laws so new the encomenderos found them about as comfy as shoes two sizes too small.
questions.fun_fact: The protests were so strong that the Crown had to soften part of those laws just a few years later.

questions.question: In 1793, Antonio Nariño secretly printed his translation of the Rights of Man in Santafé. What did he himself do with almost all the copies?
wrong_answers: He handed them out at Mass
hints: He knew the colonial government was watching him.
He wanted no evidence left behind.
He used fire.
questions.description: A translator who found out that in colonial times some ideas could cost you your freedom.
questions.fun_fact: He was caught anyway: Nariño was convicted and sent to Spain as a prisoner, but he escaped.

questions.question: They had a big house with a chapel, belonged to powerful families from Popayán or Santafé, and employed many workers. What were colonial haciendas for?
hints: They were in the countryside, far from the sea.
Much of the cities' food came from them.
Think of cows, sugarcane and corn.
questions.description: The country estates of colonial times: no Wi-Fi, but a chapel of their own.
questions.fun_fact: Hacienda El Paraíso, in Valle del Cauca, became famous as the setting of Jorge Isaacs's novel “María.”

questions.question: Muisca and Zenú potters made their pots without this machine. From which country did it reach what is now Colombia?
hints: It arrived about 500 years ago.
It came by ship, across the Atlantic Ocean.
It's the country Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada and the conquistadors came from.
questions.description: A machine that spends all day spinning and never gets dizzy.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Spanish arrived, nobody in the Americas used the potter's wheel: pots were built by hand from coils of clay, and they came out perfect!

questions.question: El Carmen de Viboral, in Antioquia, is famous for its hand-painted ceramics with flowers. What is mostly made there?
wrong_answers: Roof tiles, bricks and floor tiles
hints: You use them every day, three times a day.
They belong on the dining table.
They are for drinking your tinto or eating your fríjoles.
questions.description: An Antioquian town where the clay puts on its best flowered dress.
questions.fun_fact: In El Carmen de Viboral, even the house fronts and sidewalks are decorated with the same flower designs as its ceramics.

questions.question: You're at the Feria de las Flores and see an arriero with a carriel over his shoulder. What was the carriel used for in the old days?
wrong_answers: To carry water for the road
To bring food for the mules
hints: The arriero wore it hanging at his side, always within reach.
It has many pockets, some of them secret.
It held the arriero's most valuable things.
questions.description: The paisa accessory that was in style before shopping malls even existed.
questions.fun_fact: The traditional carriel has many compartments, and some are said to be secret ones for hiding money.

questions.question: Many call the formal dance of grado once students the “prom,” as in the US. What full word does “prom” come from?
hints: The word comes from French, and English borrowed it.
It has nothing to do with graduating or being promoted.
It means a stroll, like when couples paraded in to enter the dance.
questions.description: A tie, a gown, a salon hairdo and a dad crying at the door: the big night of grado once has arrived.
questions.fun_fact: “Prom” comes from “promenade,” the stroll guests made as they entered the dance in a line.

questions.question: It's small and soft, you rub it over what you wrote in pencil, and it leaves crumbs on your notebook. What is it?
hints: You need it when you make a mistake.
It works on pencil, but almost never on pen.
You rub it over the mistake and the mistake disappears.
questions.description: Small, soft and always lost at the bottom of your pencil case.
questions.fun_fact: Before rubber erasers existed, people rubbed out pencil marks with bits of bread.

questions.question: At a Colombian school assembly, several anthems are sung. Which one comes first?
hints: There's an official order; nobody picks it.
The same order is used at other official ceremonies.
It goes from the biggest to the smallest.
questions.description: Straight lines, spotless uniforms and that one kid who always laughs at the worst possible moment.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's national anthem has eleven verses, but usually only the chorus and the first verse are sung.

questions.question: In Colombia, when someone at school asks “¿qué llevas de lonchera?”, what do they want to know?
questions.answer: What food you brought for recess
wrong_answers: What homework you have to hand in
hints: It's not something you study with.
It goes in a little box or bag, separate from your notebooks.
It might have juice, fruit or cookies inside.
questions.description: Your mom packed it with love the night before while you were fast asleep.
questions.fun_fact: The word “lonchera” comes from the English word “lunch.”

questions.question: Édgar Perea, “el Negro Grande de Colombia”, was the voice of Junior de Barranquilla. In which department was he born?
hints: He wasn't born in the city that made him famous.
It's a department on the Pacific coast, one of the rainiest places in the world.
Its capital is Quibdó.
questions.description: A voice so big the radio could barely hold it.
questions.fun_fact: Besides calling Colombia's famous 5–0 win over Argentina in 1993, Édgar Perea went on to become a senator.

questions.question: “La Liendra” is the nickname of a very famous Colombian influencer. But what is a liendra, really?
hints: It's so small you can barely see it.
It stays stuck tight to a single hair.
The little critter that makes your head itch hatches from it.
questions.description: A nickname so sticky nobody can shake it off.
questions.fun_fact: In the dictionary the word is “liendre”, but in Colombia many people say “liendra”.

questions.question: The language of the Kogui, in the Sierra Nevada, belongs to the Chibchan family. Which people gave that family its name?
hints: This people worked gold and traded salt and cotton blankets.
Their rulers were the zipa and the zaque.
The Spanish also called them “Chibchas”.
questions.description: Language relatives who live far apart but recognize each other by the way they talk.
questions.fun_fact: The Chibchan family reaches into Central America: languages of Costa Rica and Panama are relatives of Kogui.

questions.question: In Colombia, what short, affectionate word do you call the man who runs the corner store?
hints: You hear it in the barrio.
It is a small piece of a longer word.
It comes from the Spanish word for someone who lives next door.
questions.description: The magic word that gets you bread on credit until Friday.
questions.fun_fact: “Veci” is short for “vecino” (neighbor), and in Colombia it is used both for the neighbors on your block and for the corner storekeeper.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. 'Veci' as a Colombian term for the corner-store owner is plausible, but I found no source for it. 'Tendero' or 'don' are the standard terms.

questions.question: In Colombia, a banana is also called a «guineo». On which continent is the region that gave it that name?
hints: Portuguese sailors called a coast they sailed along “Guinea”.
It has nothing to do with New Guinea, even though the name sounds alike.
That coast faces the Atlantic Ocean, south of the Sahara Desert.
questions.description: A fruit that has traveled more than most of us.
questions.fun_fact: The guinea fowl is also named after that African coast.

questions.question: It falls from the clouds on stormy afternoons, sounds very loud on tin roofs and can turn streets white. What falls in a hailstorm?
hints: You can pick them up in your hand, but they melt fast.
They are hard and can bounce on the ground.
It's frozen water in small, round lumps.
questions.description: When the Bogotá sky starts playing the drums without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: On November 3, 2007, a hailstorm in Bogotá was so strong that the ice piled up to almost 1 m (3 ft) on some streets.

review.feedback: source: the fun fact's claim that ice piled up to almost 1 m on some Bogotá streets is unconfirmed. The fact check verifies the November 3, 2007 hailstorm but found no source for the depth, and I can't confirm it from my own knowledge. The translation renders the source faithfully, so the source's fun fact needs correcting first, for example: "On November 3, 2007, a hailstorm in Bogotá, the strongest in almost 40 years, covered streets in ice and interrupted the Rock al Parque festival." Fact check: uncertain. The answer (balls of ice), the wrong answers and the hints are fine. The fun fact is only partly verified. A major Bogotá hailstorm on 3 Nov 2007 is well documented. It is described as the strongest in almost 40 years, and it interrupted Rock al Parque. I found no source saying the ice piled up to almost 1 m in some streets. Sources mention only streets covered in ice and flooded.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact's depth claim, repeated faithfully from the Spanish, is unconfirmed. The fact check found no source for "almost 1 meter" of ice in the November 3, 2007 Bogotá hailstorm, and I can't confirm it either. The source needs correcting, for example by dropping the depth: "On November 3, 2007, the strongest hailstorm in almost 40 years hit Bogotá, flooding streets and burying cars under ice." Fact check: uncertain. The answer (little balls of ice) is right, and the wrong answers (snow, ash, sand) are wrong. The hints are fine. The storm date is real: a record hailstorm hit Bogotá on Nov 3, 2007. I found no source for the 'almost 1 meter (3 ft) deep' figure. The only depth I found was 24 inches (~60 cm), and that was for a March 2015 storm in southern Bogotá, not 2007. The fun fact's depth is probably exaggerated or invented.

source: the fun fact's claim that ice piled up nearly 1 meter deep in Bogotá on November 3, 2007 is unconfirmed. The fact check found no source for it and one summary suggested about 20 cm, and I can't confirm it either. Correct the Spanish source first, for example to "strongest hailstorm in almost 40 years; it covered streets in ice and buried dozens of cars", then carry the change over to the translation. Fact check: uncertain. The answer (balls of ice) is correct and the wrong answers (snow, ash, sand) are wrong. The hints are fine. The fun fact's date (Nov 3, 2007) and its status as Bogotá's strongest hailstorm in about 40 years are confirmed. I found no source for 'nearly 1 meter (3 ft) deep'. Reports only say streets turned white and dozens of cars were buried. One search summary gave about 20 cm, but I couldn't tell whether that figure belongs to the 2007 storm. The question's stem also says it 'falls from the clouds ... pounds on zinc roofs', which is a loose description and not a factual error.

source: the fun fact's claim that ice piled up to "almost a meter" in the November 3, 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is unconfirmed. The fact check found the storm but no source for the depth, and I can't confirm it either. The translation renders the source faithfully, so the source needs softening first, for example: "a hailstorm hit Bogotá so hard that ice buried streets and dozens of cars." Fact check: uncertain. The Nov 3, 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is real, but I found no source for 'almost a meter (3 ft)' of ice. Sources only say streets were buried and dozens of cars were covered. The answer and wrong answers are fine.

Fact check: uncertain. The Nov 3, 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is real (strongest in ~40 years). I found no source for the "almost 1 meter (3 ft) high" depth. Sources say only that cars were buried and streets flooded.

Fact check: uncertain. The answer and wrong answers are fine, since hail is balls of ice. The Nov 3, 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is well documented, but I found no source for the "almost 1 m (3 ft) deep" figure. One Blu Radio piece mentions up to 1 m, but it seems to be about a different storm. Pulzo gives no depth.

Fact check: uncertain. The fun fact says hail piled up almost 1 m high on some streets on Nov 3, 2007. The storm and date are real, and it was the strongest in about 40 years. I found no source for the 1 m depth. A 50 cm figure I saw was for a different storm.

Fact check: uncertain. The answer (balls of ice) is correct and the 3 Nov 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is real. But the 'almost 1 m of ice on some streets' figure is only loosely supported. A BBC report cited 1.5 m of water and ice at one intersection, and I found no primary source for ice piled up on streets in general.

Source: the fun fact says the ice piled up "almost a meter" deep on some Bogotá streets on November 3, 2007. The fact check could not confirm that figure (the only source found says 1.5 m of water and ice at one intersection), and I can't confirm it either. Fix the source's fun fact first, for example: "On November 3, 2007, Bogotá's heaviest hailstorm in decades left ice piled up on some streets and trapped dozens of cars." Then carry the change into this translation. The translation itself is faithful and reads naturally. Fact check: uncertain. The 3 Nov 2007 Bogotá hailstorm is real. But the ice depth in the fun fact (almost 1 m on some streets) isn't confirmed. The only figure I found is 1.5 m (59 in) of water and ice at one intersection, from a forum quoting the BBC. Reports of how many cars were trapped also differ (30 vs 70).

questions.question: A country born in 1819 had a coat of arms with two horns of plenty and a bundle of spears. Which of today's countries made it up?
hints: Its first president was Simón Bolívar.
It broke up around 1830.
One of those countries has a very famous canal today.
questions.description: The coat of arms of a family that split up almost two centuries ago and still gets together for soccer games.
questions.fun_fact: “Gran Colombia” is the name historians gave it: back then it was simply called the Republic of Colombia.

questions.question: In the South American qualifiers for the 2026 World Cup, which place in the table sent a team to the intercontinental playoff?
hints: South America got more spots for that World Cup.
The 2026 World Cup is the first with 48 teams.
Six teams qualified directly.
questions.description: The second chance everyone wants to avoid and nobody wants to miss.
questions.fun_fact: For the 2022 World Cup, the team that finished fifth in South America went to the playoff.

questions.question: Which national team has won the most World Cups in history?
hints: It is one of Colombia's rivals in World Cup qualifying.
It won its first World Cup in 1958, in Sweden.
Pelé was born there.
questions.description: The most crowded trophy cabinet on the whole planet's soccer block.
questions.fun_fact: Brazil is the only national team that has played in every World Cup in history.

questions.question: At the 2014 World Cup, how did Colombia's national team players celebrate their goals?
wrong_answers: With a war cry from the fans
With a military salute to the crowd
With a group hug with the coach
hints: The players did it, not the fans.
They gathered near the corner flag.
They moved their hips and feet to the beat of the music.
questions.description: At Brazil 2014, scoring the goal was only the first part of the show.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's dance celebrations in 2014 got so famous that fans all over the world copied them.

questions.question: In July 2024, Colombia played a final against Argentina at Hard Rock Stadium. The stadium is in the metro area of which US city?
hints: The city has hot weather almost all year.
It has a huge Latino community, especially Cuban.
It's famous for the beaches of South Beach.
questions.description: Colombia reached the final with all its hopes high… and plenty of sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: Argentina won that final 1-0 with a goal by Lautaro Martínez in extra time.

questions.question: In the BMX final at Tokyo 2020, Mariana Pajón was going for her third Olympic gold. Where did she finish?
hints: It was a very close final.
She made the podium, but not the top step.
She came in behind a British rider.
questions.description: A tiny bike, a track full of jumps and a Colombian who isn't afraid of anything.
questions.fun_fact: At those same Tokyo Games, Colombian Carlos Ramírez won bronze in the men's BMX.

questions.question: How many Olympic medals did Colombian shooter Helmut Bellingrodt win in running target?
hints: All his medals were the same color.
He won in Munich and won again years later.
His first silver came at Munich 1972 and his last at Los Angeles 1984.
questions.description: A cardboard boar that runs faster than most people at the Sunday ciclovía.
questions.fun_fact: Bellingrodt's silver at Munich 1972 was one of the first Olympic medals in Colombia's history.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this bronze cat guards a riverbank in Cali. Which artist made it?
hints: Look closely: this cat is thin and elegant, nothing like a puffed-up figure.
The artist lived and worked in Cali for many years and gave the cat to the city as a gift.
His surname sounds almost like «tejado», the Spanish word for a tiled roof.
questions.description: A cat that settled down by the water and never moved again.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2006, the cat's «novias» (girlfriends), painted cat statues by different artists, have been set up around him.

questions.question: This painter from Cartagena moved to Paris and painted women resting among rocking chairs with almost photographic realism. Who is he?
hints: He died in Paris in 1988, before turning 45.
Besides painting, he made bronze sculptures of human figures.
He is the youngest of the four: he was born in 1944.
questions.description: A painter so detailed you could almost fold his bedsheets.
questions.fun_fact: His paintings are so detailed that many visitors first think they are photographs.

questions.question: Jorge Celedón, the voice of “Qué bonita es esta vida”, was born in Villanueva, a land of accordion players. Which department is it in?
hints: It's in the Caribbean region, right in vallenato country.
It's the northernmost department of mainland Colombia.
The Wayuu people live there, and so does the Cabo de la Vela.
questions.description: A town where kids learn to play the accordion before they learn to ride a bike.
questions.fun_fact: Every year Villanueva holds the Festival Cuna de Acordeones (Cradle of Accordions Festival).

questions.question: In what place did Rigoberto Urán, the cyclist from Urrao, finish in the road race at the London 2012 Olympics?
hints: He made it onto the podium.
He got a medal, but not the gold one.
He was given the silver medal.
questions.description: A paisa who pedaled even faster than he told jokes.
questions.fun_fact: Rigoberto Urán also finished second in the 2017 Tour de France, behind Chris Froome.

questions.question: You see the flower greenhouses of the Sabana de Bogotá everywhere from the highway. What are their roofs usually made of?
hints: It's a light, cheap material that lets light through.
It comes in rolls and can be folded like a bedsheet.
It's the same material as many bags and bottles.
questions.description: The Sabana's flowers live in a house of their own and never get wet when it rains.
questions.fun_fact: In the Netherlands many greenhouses are made of glass, but in the Sabana de Bogotá almost all are plastic stretched over wood or metal frames.

questions.question: Look at this ajiaco santafereño. Which yellow ingredient gives it its golden color and makes it creamy?
hints: It grows underground.
Fried and salted, it makes a tasty snack.
It's a potato, but not the pastusa kind.
questions.description: A Bogotá soup so thick the spoon can almost stand up on its own.
questions.fun_fact: Ajiaco uses three different potatoes (criolla, sabanera and pastusa), plus guascas, an herb that gives it its unique flavor.

questions.question: What do you use the rhyme “Tin marín de do pingüé” for?
wrong_answers: To lull a baby to sleep
hints: It's used before a game starts.
You point at each player in turn, one syllable per person.
Whoever lands on the last word is the one picked.
questions.description: A nonsense rhyme every Colombian kid knows by heart.
questions.fun_fact: Kids in Mexico and other countries chant it too, with small changes to the words.

questions.question: This Colombian singer is the voice of the pop star in Zootopia. What animal is that character?
hints: She's not the police officer or the mayor: she sings on a giant stage.
She eats only plants and has long, thin legs.
She lives on the African savanna, has horns and runs very fast.
questions.description: In this city of animals, even the pop star has a fan club and fancy backup dancers.
questions.fun_fact: Shakira recorded “Try Everything” for Zootopia, and in Latin America her Spanish version, “Lo intentaré”, was heard too.

questions.question: Which Karol G album became, in 2023, the first all-Spanish album by a woman to reach number 1 on the Billboard 200?
hints: The album includes songs like “TQG” with Shakira and “Provenza.”
That same year she released a second part nicknamed “Bichota Season.”
Its title promises that tomorrow will be better.
questions.description: La Bichota breaking records like a kid breaking a piñata at a birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: That album also won Karol G a Grammy for Best Música Urbana Album.

questions.question: In “Robarte un Beso,” Carlos Vives sings a duet with a younger Colombian singer. Who is it?
hints: He's a paisa, and at the time he was already all over the radio.
He was coming off the success of “Traicionera.”
Years later he sang “Dos Oruguitas” for Encanto.
questions.description: A song that can get you in trouble if you sing it while looking at the wrong person.
questions.fun_fact: “Robarte un Beso” came out in 2017 and reached number 1 on the Billboard Latin Airplay chart.

questions.question: A luthier shapes wood with gouges and varnish, and Chiquinquirá, Boyacá, is full of their workshops. What does a luthier make?
hints: What they make has to sound nice.
What they make has strings.
Without them there would be no bambucos and no carranga.
questions.description: A job that takes endless patience, leaves wood shavings in your hair and the smell of varnish all day.
questions.fun_fact: The word “luthier” comes from the French “luth”, which means lute.

questions.question: Look at this colorful mochila bag. Who traditionally weaves it?
hints: They live where it hardly ever rains and it's very hot.
Their land is a peninsula at the far northern tip of Colombia, on the Caribbean Sea.
They are the largest Indigenous people of La Guajira.
questions.description: It fits everything: your phone, your keys, your lunch and even the neighborhood gossip.
questions.fun_fact: According to Wayuu legend, a spider named Wale'kerü taught the women how to weave.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an instrument of traditional Colombian music?
hints: It's made of clay.
Women on the coast used to carry it on their heads.
It's a jar for fetching and storing water.
questions.description: A list with an intruder who sneaked into the parranda without knowing how to play a single note.
questions.fun_fact: The múcura is so loved on the coast that it has its own famous song: “La múcura está en el suelo…”.

questions.question: Lucho Bermúdez, the most famous son of El Carmen de Bolívar, composed great porros and cumbias. Which of these songs is NOT his?
hints: Three of them were played by a big orchestra with clarinets and brass.
The odd one out is from another genre: it's played on accordion, caja and guacharaca.
It's a vallenato by Emiliano Zuleta that Carlos Vives made famous around the world.
questions.description: An orchestra so elegant that even grandparents got out their Sunday best to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Bermúdez played the clarinet and took porro and cumbia from the coast to the elegant clubs of Bogotá and Medellín.

questions.question: I was born in Los Palmitos, Sucre, played accordion with Los Corraleros de Majagual and I'm called “el Macho de América.” Who am I?
hints: My music mixes cumbia, porro and paseo, and it was a hit in Mexico and Central America.
I'm also called “el rey sabanero del acordeón.”
My last name sounds just like the Spanish word for “table.”
questions.description: An accordion that traveled from the savanna to half the continent without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Los Corraleros de Majagual were a kind of all-star team of Caribbean coast music: several of Colombia's best accordion players passed through it.

questions.question: I'm a trombonist from Barranquilla, and in the 1980s I founded a salsa band named after giants, so they call me “el Titán de la Salsa”. Who am I?
hints: I'm not a singer: brass is my thing.
My band is named after the giants of Greek mythology.
I share a surname with the writer of “La piragua”.
questions.description: A giant nickname for an instrument that stretches and shrinks.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Barros also created “Tributo a la salsa colombiana”, a series of albums bringing together many of the country's salsa voices.

questions.question: You walk into the corner store and the shopkeeper says “¿cómo me le va?”. What is he asking you?
hints: People can say it to you on the street too, not just in a store.
The “me le” just adds warmth to the phrase.
You would answer “bien, ¿y usted?”
questions.description: At the corner store, this phrase comes with a free “me” and a free “le.”
questions.fun_fact: The “me” in “¿cómo me le va?” doesn't change the meaning: it just shows the person asking truly cares about the answer.

questions.question: It's very informal and comes from joining “qué” and “hubo”. What does “¿quiubo?” mean?
hints: You say it when you arrive, not when you leave.
It often comes with a handshake or a fist bump.
It's a quick way to say hello and ask how you're doing.
questions.description: Two syllables, zero formality, and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: “Q'hubo” is so Colombian that a popular newspaper in the country is named after it.

questions.question: In Colombia, what does the expression “estar pelado” mean?
hints: It has to do with your pockets.
There isn't even enough for a tinto.
You'll have to wait for the quincena (the mid-month payday).
questions.description: An expression nobody in Colombia wants to use, but everyone has used at least once.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia “pelado” also means kid or young guy, so a pelado can be pelado.

questions.question: In Colombia you hear it all the time at the store, at the bank and at home. What does “con mucho gusto” mean there?
hints: It's a polite reply.
They say it at the store or the bank after serving you.
It's like saying “don't mention it.”
questions.description: The most polite reply in the country, smile included.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian politeness is so famous that many foreigners are surprised to hear “con mucho gusto” even at the supermarket checkout.

questions.question: You hear it at school, at home and at work. In Colombia, what does “embarrarla” mean?
hints: It's nothing to be proud of.
Afterwards, you have to say sorry.
It's like “meter la pata” (putting your foot in it).
questions.description: A word with mud inside it, even though nobody ends up dirty.
questions.fun_fact: “Embarrarla” comes from “barro” (mud), and in Colombia people also say “regarla” for the same thing.

questions.question: In soccer, what is a “hincha”?
hints: They don’t play on the field.
They’re up in the stands.
In English you might call this person a “fan.”
questions.description: A word that, in Spanish, sounds like a balloon being blown up, and spends its Sundays at the stadium.
questions.fun_fact: The word is said to come from Uruguay, from a man who pumped up (“hinchaba”) Club Nacional’s balls and cheered nonstop for his team.

questions.question: Rodolfo Llinás says the larva of the sea squirt, a marine animal, “eats” its own brain. What does it do just before that?
questions.answer: It attaches to a rock and stops moving
wrong_answers: It lays its eggs in the sand
It changes color to hide itself
It swims up to the surface to breathe
hints: Llinás asks what a brain is really for.
When young, the larva swims like a tiny tadpole.
After that moment, it no longer needs to decide where to go.
questions.description: A sea creature with a habit that would make any neurologist faint.
questions.fun_fact: Llinás uses this example to back his idea that thinking is, at heart, movement that turned inward.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what do people in Colombia call this?
hints: The cars barely move.
It happens a lot at rush hour, when everyone leaves work.
It's the Colombian word for a traffic jam.
questions.description: A Colombian classic nobody invites, yet it shows up on time every day at six.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá has shown up several times on international lists of the cities where people lose the most hours stuck in traffic.

questions.question: In Colombia, a highway is to asphalt as a trocha is to…
hints: It's usually out in the countryside, on the way to a finca or a vereda.
When it rains, it fills with mud.
Nothing covers it: the surface is simply the ground itself.
questions.description: A long holiday weekend in Colombia: curves, mountains and someone asking “are we there yet?”.
questions.fun_fact: On railroads, “trocha” also means the distance between the rails, and Colombia's old railroads were narrow gauge.

previous.feedback: The English version of related q-5243 says "a muddy trocha (dirt track)". That gloss gives away this question's answer, "packed dirt". The fix belongs in q-5243: drop the "(dirt track)" gloss there or reword it so it doesn't define trocha. This translation itself is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: The Tren Turístico de la Sabana, famous for its steam locomotives, leaves from Bogotá. To which place, voted Colombia's first wonder, does it go?
hints: It's a religious place that also draws lots of tourists.
It's underground, inside a mine.
It's in Zipaquirá.
questions.description: A train ride where the most exciting part isn't the train.
questions.fun_fact: The Salt Cathedral was built inside a salt mine, about 180 m (590 ft) underground.

questions.question: Bogotá's TransMiCable opened in 2018, leaving Portal Tunal and climbing to hillside neighborhoods in the south. Into which locality?
hints: It's one of Bogotá's largest and most mountainous localities.
It lies west of Usme, next to the Tunjuelo River.
It carries the surname of the Liberator.
questions.description: A bus that got tired of the hills and decided to fly.
questions.fun_fact: The TransMiCable cut a trip of about an hour down to roughly a quarter of an hour.

questions.question: Which Colombian expression with a farmyard animal means joking around or teasing someone?
hints: It's used all over Colombia, but it's very typical of the Caribbean coast.
Gabriel García Márquez was famous for doing it with his friends.
The verb is the same one used for what a baby does with its bottle.
questions.description: A feathered expression you hear more often at the office than in the barnyard.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Spanish Academy's dictionary lists “mamar gallo” as an expression from Colombia and Venezuela.

questions.question: At a salsoteca in Cali, a salsa buff says the band “crossed the clave.” In salsa, what is the clave?
questions.answer: A five-stroke pattern that guides the rhythm
wrong_answers: The highest note the sonero sings
The basic step the dancers mark
The piano solo that ends the song
hints: It's something you play, not something you dance or sing.
It's marked with two wooden sticks struck against each other.
It's written “3-2” or “2-3,” depending on how the strokes are split.
questions.description: In Cali, salsa is taken so seriously that even the fans talk like music professors.
questions.fun_fact: The clave comes from Afro-Cuban music, and the two sticks used to play it are also called claves.

questions.question: A Cali salsoteca plays the same beloved classics night after night. Which of these genres is NOT part of its classic lineup?
hints: Three of them come from the Caribbean or from the Latino neighborhoods of New York.
The odd one out is played with harp, cuatro and maracas.
It's the typical dance of the Llanos Orientales.
questions.description: A place where the dance floor suffers more than the DJ.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali's salsotecas, collectors show off super-rare vinyl records they brought back from New York or Puerto Rico.

questions.question: Grupo Niche called Cali “pachanguero”, but pachanga is a rhythm from the late 1950s. What country does it come from?
hints: It comes from an island in the Caribbean.
Its creator was the composer Eduardo Davidson, around 1959.
It's the island where you'll find Havana.
questions.description: A word that in Colombia now means a party with no set time to go home.
questions.fun_fact: Pachanga was all the rage in New York around 1960, shortly before salsa was born.

questions.question: How does the saying «El que con niños se acuesta…» (“Whoever goes to bed with kids…”) end?
hints: The ending has to do with what happens in bed at night.
It's something unpleasant you discover as soon as you wake up.
Time to change the sheets.
questions.description: A saying grandma pulls out when someone trusted the wrong person.
questions.fun_fact: The saying warns that if you trust immature people with something serious, you have to live with the consequences.

questions.question: Which saying is used about an older person who still has a lot to give?
wrong_answers: Loro viejo no aprende a hablar
Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
hints: It praises experience.
It has to do with grandma's cooking.
It talks about a very tasty soup.
questions.description: A saying that aunts repeat proudly at every birthday.
questions.fun_fact: Cooking proves it right: older birds have more collagen and flavor, so they make a richer broth.

questions.question: Complete this Colombian greeting: “Hola, ¿bien o…?”
hints: The answer is a tiny word.
Friends say it fast, almost without waiting for an answer.
It's the same word hiding at the start of “¿quiubo?”, which comes from “¿… hubo?”
questions.description: A greeting that offers you two choices, but only one ever gets used.
questions.fun_fact: People almost always answer “¿bien o qué?” with “bien, ¿o qué?”, without really answering at all.

questions.question: In Colombia, someone very strong, healthy and full of energy is said to be “como un…” (like a…) what?
hints: It's a big farm animal.
There are lots of them on the cattle ranches of the Llanos.
It's the star of the corralejas.
questions.description: For when grandpa goes jogging at five in the morning.
questions.fun_fact: Someone who bounces back quickly from a cold is also said to have ended up “como un toro.”

questions.question: Complete the saying: “El que tiene rabo de paja…” (whoever has a straw tail…)
questions.answer: no se arrima a la candela
wrong_answers: no se sienta en la hamaca
hints: Think about what can happen to straw.
It has to do with the danger of getting burned.
“Candela” means fire.
questions.description: A saying for someone who suddenly doesn’t want to talk about the subject anymore.
questions.fun_fact: People say it about someone who has something to hide, so they avoid any topic that might give them away.

questions.question: You walk through a market in Bogotá and the sellers shout “¡a la orden!” at you. What do they mean?
hints: It's an invitation, not a scolding.
They want you to buy from them.
It's like saying “How can I help you?”
questions.description: The official catchphrase of every market seller with a megaphone.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “a la orden” is also a reply to “thank you,” a bit like saying “my pleasure.”

questions.question: In 1978, a hospital in Bogotá didn't have enough machines like this one, and that's how kangaroo mother care was born. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To lull babies to sleep with music
hints: Babies born very small lose something very fast.
In kangaroo care, the mother's body does the same job.
It has to do with cold and heat.
questions.description: A glass apartment for the hospital's tiniest tenants.
questions.fun_fact: Kangaroo mother care was created by Bogotá pediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria, and today it's used in hospitals all over the world.

questions.question: What was Medellín's Metrocable built for?
questions.answer: To take people to the hillside neighborhoods
wrong_answers: To bring coffee down from the farms to town
So tourists can see the snowy peaks
To cross from one side of the Magdalena River to the other
hints: People use it every day, not just on vacation.
You pay with the same card as the metro.
Its cabins climb the slopes of the Aburrá Valley, where lots of people live.
questions.description: Paisas brag about their metro even more than about grandma's arepas.
questions.fun_fact: The first Metrocable line opened in 2004 and was one of the first cable cars in the world used as mass public transport.

questions.question: In the late 1700s, Antonio Nariño secretly translated and printed a banned text in Santafé. What was it?
questions.answer: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
hints: The original was written in French.
It's a short text split into numbered articles, not a long book.
It came out of a revolution that began with the storming of the Bastille.
questions.description: A text so dangerous that printing it cost far more than a traffic ticket.
questions.fun_fact: For that translation, Nariño was sentenced to ten years in a prison in Africa, but he escaped when his ship reached Cádiz.

questions.question: I was born in Barranquilla to Lebanese immigrants, and I invented a valve that drains extra fluid from the brain. Who am I?
hints: I was a neurosurgeon.
I described a type of hydrocephalus that also bears my name.
My surname comes from Arabic.
questions.description: A first-class plumber, except the pipes he fixed were inside people's heads.
questions.fun_fact: The Hakim valve has been implanted in patients all over the world, and some versions can be adjusted from outside the body with a magnet.

questions.question: The 20,000-peso bill shows Julio Garavito's face and a drawing of the Moon, and a lunar crater bears his name. Why?
questions.answer: Because he studied the Moon's motion
wrong_answers: Because he was the first Colombian in space
Because he invented the Muisca calendar
Because he discovered water on the Moon
hints: He was a Bogotá scholar of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
He directed the National Astronomical Observatory.
He worked out astronomy calculations with pencil and paper.
questions.description: A banknote with its head in the clouds… and a little bit higher.
questions.fun_fact: The Garavito crater is on the far side of the Moon, the side we never see from Earth.

review.feedback: source: the question says the 20,000-peso bill shows Julio Garavito in the present tense (“lleva”), but the current series, issued since 2016, has Alfonso López Michelsen on the 20,000. Garavito was on the earlier design, so both the source and this faithful translation are out of date and need rewording, e.g. “The old 20,000-peso bill showed…”.

previous.feedback: source: the present tense “shows” is out of date. Since the 2016 series, the 20,000-peso note has shown Alfonso López Michelsen, and Garavito was on the previous series. The Spanish source (“lleva”) has the same error and should be corrected there, for example “The old 20,000-peso banknote showed…”. The translation is otherwise faithful.

source: "shows" (Spanish "lleva") is out of date. Since the 2016 series, the 20,000-peso note has shown Alfonso López Michelsen, and Garavito and the Moon appear only on the earlier series. The fact check missed this, and the rater flagged it. The source should change to the past tense ("showed" / "llevaba", or "the old 20,000-peso banknote"), and the translation should then follow it.

source: the present tense is out of date in the source as well as the translation. The current 20,000-peso bill (2016 family) shows Alfonso López Michelsen, and Garavito was on the earlier design. The source should say "the old 20,000-peso bill showed" or similar, and the translation should then follow. The translation is otherwise faithful.

questions.question: It has an outboard motor, works as a river bus in Chocó, and takes tourists from Cartagena to the Islas del Rosario. What is it?
hints: It travels on top of the water, not under it.
It's small and fast, and it splashes quite a bit.
A motor at the back drives it, and its driver is called a lanchero.
questions.description: In some towns on the Pacific coast, the bus stop is at the dock.
questions.fun_fact: In Chocó, the Atrato River is the main road for many towns: there, the motorboat is like a city bus.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Colombia, when this happens to a car on the road, what word describes it?
hints: Something broke on the car and it won't start.
Time to call a tow truck or a mechanic.
The word comes from ships that get stuck on the sand.
questions.description: The car said “this is as far as I go,” and nobody asked for its opinion.
questions.fun_fact: “Varar” comes from the world of ships: a “barco varado” is one that got stuck on the beach.

questions.question: You want to leave Bogotá's main bus terminal for the Caribbean coast without the crowds. Which time of year should you avoid?
hints: It's when lots of families go on vacation.
Most schools have finished the school year and the roads to the coast fill up.
It's the last month of the year.
questions.description: Where the buses barely sleep and even the suitcases wait in line.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá's Salitre bus terminal opened in 1984, and millions of travelers pass through it every year.

questions.question: In Santa Marta Bay, a traffic light is to cars as a lighthouse is to…
hints: It stands on the seashore.
Its light warns where there are rocks or where the port is.
They sail on the water.
questions.description: A tower that spends all night winking.
questions.fun_fact: Facing Santa Marta Bay is El Morro, a rocky island with a lighthouse on top.

questions.question: The Muisca, who lived on the Sabana de Bogotá, had never seen a horse. Who brought horses there?
hints: They came by sea about 500 years ago.
They arrived with the Conquest.
They spoke the same language people speak in Colombia today.
questions.description: The first four-legged car arrived by ship, with no license plate.
questions.fun_fact: Horses lived in the Americas millions of years ago but died out there, until the Spanish brought them back.

questions.question: Vallenato blends three heritages. Which people gave it the caja, the small drum played by hand?
hints: This same heritage gave the Caribbean coast many other drums, like those of cumbia and mapalé.
This heritage reached the Caribbean coast through the port of Cartagena in colonial times.
Think of the heritage that brought drums to San Basilio de Palenque.
questions.description: Small but loud, like the cousin who’s first to show up at the parranda.
questions.fun_fact: The cajero plays sitting down, holding the caja between the knees.

questions.question: The Accordion Museum in Valledupar keeps instruments more than 100 years old. From which country did the first accordions reach Colombia's Caribbean coast?
hints: It's a European country.
They arrived on trading ships at ports like Riohacha in the late 19th century.
Hohner, the favorite brand of vallenato accordion players, comes from there.
questions.description: A museum where the most valuable pieces have bellows and are ready to party.
questions.fun_fact: The museum was founded by accordion player Beto Murgas in his own home.

questions.question: In 1982 García Márquez took vallenato musicians to Stockholm and accepted the Nobel wearing a white outfit. What is it called?
hints: It wasn't the tailcoat that protocol called for.
It's a suit with a high, closed collar, typical of the Llanos.
Its name repeats the same word twice.
questions.description: Stockholm had never heard so much accordion on such a cold night.
questions.fun_fact: Gabo was one of the few winners that night who didn't accept the Nobel in a tailcoat.

questions.question: I'm green, with a crest of spines on my back and a flap of skin under my chin, and I sunbathe in park trees in Cartagena and Santa Marta. Who am I?
hints: I am a reptile with a long tail.
I don't eat meat: I love leaves, flowers and fruit.
My name starts with the letter I.
questions.description: A retired dinosaur who spends all day sunbathing in the park.
questions.fun_fact: Iguanas are good swimmers and can hold their breath underwater for about half an hour.

questions.question: You're in the Cocora Valley, standing before the wax palm, Colombia's national tree. How tall can it grow?
hints: It's considered the tallest palm in the world.
It's taller than a 15-story building.
It grows to more than 50 m (164 ft).
questions.description: A tree that doesn't need high heels to stand out in every photo.
questions.fun_fact: The wax palm can live more than 100 years and is home to the yellow-eared parrot, which nearly disappeared.

questions.question: In Colombia, if fixing the car “costó un platal”, what happened to the owner?
questions.answer: They spent a ton of money
hints: It has nothing to do with the metal.
Nobody wants to hear it at the repair shop.
It's like saying it cost an arm and a leg.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a silver mine and gets heard a lot at the repair shop.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, as in much of Latin America, “plata” (silver) means money, because centuries ago coins were made of that metal.

questions.question: You're at the Batalla de Flores of the Barranquilla Carnival and the biggest, most decorated float goes by. Who rides on top, waving?
hints: It's a person chosen especially for the carnival.
She wears a sparkly dress and often a crown.
Every year she is chosen and crowned before the parades.
questions.description: It's like a car, but it dressed up way too much for the party.
questions.fun_fact: The Batalla de Flores was first held in 1903 and is the oldest parade of the Barranquilla Carnival.

questions.question: Complete: at the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos, a “carioca” is a can of…
hints: It's used mostly on the Día de Blancos (Day of the Whites).
It comes out white and goes well with the talcum powder.
You press a button and it shoots out like shaving cream.
questions.description: In Pasto on January 6, nobody goes out without their secret weapon.
questions.fun_fact: The Carnaval de Negros y Blancos has been on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2009.

questions.question: The Colombian gaita is a tube of cardón cactus with a beeswax head and a duck-feather quill; there are male and female gaitas. What kind of instrument is it?
hints: It has no strings and you don’t hit it.
Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto made it famous.
To make it sound, you need your lungs.
questions.description: An instrument with a duck’s beak and a bee’s head: the carnival has its own monsters.
questions.fun_fact: Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto won a Latin Grammy in 2007.

questions.question: Papier-mâché is made from newspaper and a paste of flour and water, then dried and painted. What is it used for at carnivals?
hints: When it dries, it's hard but light.
In Pasto, craftspeople spend months working with it in their workshops before the big parade on January 6.
You can cover your face with it or make a giant puppet.
questions.description: Yesterday's newspaper gets a second life that's way more fun.
questions.fun_fact: The giant floats of Pasto's Carnaval de Negros y Blancos are built mostly from papier-mâché, and some are taller than a house.

questions.question: At the Feria de las Flores, people set up fondas paisas. For whom were fondas first made, as roadside inns?
hints: They were travelers who crossed the mountains of Antioquia.
They carried loads from town to town for days.
They traveled with mules and wore a carriel and a poncho.
questions.description: Cantina music, wooden tables and not a single traffic jam in sight.
questions.fun_fact: The carriel, the arriero's leather bag, became one of the symbols of paisa culture.

questions.question: It's the top prize for the dance groups and comparsas of the Carnaval de Barranquilla, named after a dance with turbans and mirrors. What is it called?
hints: It's given to the best groups in the parades.
The dance it's named after uses very tall, decorated turbans.
Its name combines an African-rooted dance and a golden metal.
questions.description: The trophy that makes a dance group rehearse all year long.
questions.fun_fact: The India Catalina, by contrast, is the award of the Cartagena International Film Festival.

questions.question: In Colombia a bike is called a “cicla”. If a park has 4 ciclas and 2 tricycles, how many wheels are there in total?
hints: First count the wheels on the ciclas, then the ones on the tricycles.
Each cicla has 2 wheels and each tricycle has 3.
8 wheels from the ciclas plus 6 from the tricycles.
questions.description: A math problem dressed up as a Sunday at the ciclovía.
questions.fun_fact: “Cicla” is short for “bicicleta,” and Bogotá's Ciclovía closes many streets to cars on Sundays and holidays so people can ride.

In Colombian Spanish "llanta" mainly means the tire. It can mean the whole wheel only loosely in everyday speech, and the standard word for wheel is "rueda". I did not search to check this, so I could not confirm the claim.

questions.question: You're learning to ride a bike with training wheels, and today they come off. How many wheels does your bike have left?
hints: There were two training wheels.
Now you have to keep your balance all by yourself.
One in front and one in back.
questions.description: The bravest day of childhood, scraped knees included.
questions.fun_fact: Many kids today first learn on a balance bike with no pedals and never use training wheels at all.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this is how the prologue that opens many cycling tours is raced. What kind of race is a prologue?
hints: It's short, just a few kilometers.
It's usually held the day before the first road stage.
Whoever covers the course in the least time wins, racing against the clock.
questions.description: The race's appetizer, served while everyone's legs are still fresh.
questions.fun_fact: A prologue is usually shorter than 10 km (6 miles), but it decides who wears the first leader's jersey.

questions.question: There are two of us, one for each foot. Push us down and the bike moves forward. What are we?
hints: We're down low, close to the ground.
We spin around when you ride a bike.
Your shoes rest on us while you ride.
questions.description: If a bike wore shoes, these would be them.
questions.fun_fact: The first bicycles had no pedals: riders pushed themselves along with their feet on the ground.

questions.question: In what year did Egan Bernal win the Tour de France?
hints: It was in the late 2010s.
Egan was only 22 years old.
The pandemic arrived the following year.
questions.description: The year half of Colombia got up early to cry happy tears in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: Egan Bernal was the youngest Tour de France winner in more than 100 years.

questions.question: Nairo Quintana and Egan Bernal both won the Giro d'Italia. Roughly how many stages does that race have?
hints: It is one of cycling's three Grand Tours, along with the Tour de France and the Vuelta a España.
It has a couple of rest days.
It lasts three weeks of seven days, nearly all with a stage.
questions.description: Pasta, mountains and a whole lot of days on the pedals.
questions.fun_fact: The trophy for the Giro winner is called the “Trofeo Senza Fine,” which means “endless,” and it is shaped like a spiral.

questions.question: It's made of metal, it needs grease, and if it slips off in the middle of the ciclovía, you have to put it back by hand. What part of the bike is it?
hints: It makes the wheels turn when you pedal.
It's made of lots of links.
It connects the pedals to the back wheel.
questions.description: Sunday at the ciclovía is pure joy… until something breaks.
questions.fun_fact: The bicycle chain became common around 1885 and made it possible for both wheels to be the same size.

questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Carlos Oquendo win the bronze medal in BMX?
hints: It was in Europe.
That same day, Mariana Pajón won her first gold.
The city of Big Ben.
questions.description: Jumps, curves and a medal that wasn't the only Colombian one that night.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Oquendo was born in Medellín, and his bronze was the first Olympic medal won by a Colombian man in BMX.

questions.question: I'm from Antioquia, I race on the track, and at Athens 2004 I won bronze in the points race: Colombian cycling's first Olympic medal. Who am I?
hints: I'm not a BMX rider.
I won in Greece, eight years before Mariana Pajón's first gold.
My last name is also the Spanish word for the street where cars drive.
questions.description: A woman from Antioquia who went around and around until she opened the way.
questions.fun_fact: The points race is held in a velodrome, and riders score points in sprints every few laps.

questions.question: It's a kola-flavored Postobón soda, and its slogan is “La nuestra”. Which one is it?
hints: It's golden, almost orange.
It often comes with lunch in Colombian restaurants.
Its name is the Spanish word for a woman born in Colombia.
questions.description: The soda that's always the home team at a corrientazo lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Postobón, the company that makes it, was founded in Medellín in 1904.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these sticks go into aguapanela and arroz con leche. What part of the plant do they come from?
hints: Centuries ago it was so valuable that Europeans sailed all the way to Asia to get it.
It is cut in thin strips that curl up by themselves as they dry in the sun.
It's like the “skin” of the trunk.
questions.description: The spice that makes grandma's kitchen smell like December.
questions.fun_fact: The most prized cinnamon, called Ceylon cinnamon, comes from Sri Lanka.

questions.question: In many Colombian towns, it sits by the front door in December and is burned at midnight on the 31st. What is “el año viejo”?
hints: It is put together from the family's old clothes.
It is stuffed with sawdust, paper or rags.
It has a shirt, pants and even a face, like a person.
questions.description: A December guest who never gets to see January 1.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian New Year's Eve agüero (superstition) is walking around the block with a suitcase so you'll travel in the new year.

questions.question: You're invited to “tomar onces” at 4 p.m., with hot chocolate, cheese and almojábanas. Which region of Colombia is this custom most typical of?
hints: It's a custom from the cold highlands.
There, people drink hot chocolate even in the afternoon.
It's the mountain region where the country's capital is.
questions.description: A little something between lunch and dinner, so your stomach doesn't complain.
questions.fun_fact: In Chile people also “toman onces”, and there it's almost a full afternoon meal.

questions.question: The Colombian molinillo is made of wood, has been used since colonial times and is spun by rubbing it between your palms. What is it for?
hints: It's used in a hot drink while it's still on the stove.
A Bogotá breakfast (desayuno santafereño) isn't complete without it.
Thanks to it, the drink turns out nice and foamy.
questions.description: A little wooden stick with more style than many musical instruments.
questions.fun_fact: The molinillo is used in Mexico too, and a children's song there goes “bate, bate, chocolate” (“whisk, whisk, chocolate”).

questions.question: A dessert from Colombian ice cream shops has cream, grated cheese and ice cream on top. What goes underneath, in small pieces?
hints: It's a fresh and very colorful dessert.
It all grows on trees and plants.
Mango, papaya, banana and strawberry, all cut up.
questions.description: A dish that takes putting cheese on everything very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Putting grated cheese on fruit salad is normal in Colombia, and it surprises many foreign visitors.

questions.question: It's nicknamed “La Minorista”, its official name is Plaza José María Villa, and it's one of Colombia's biggest markets. Which city is it in?
hints: It sits in a valley surrounded by mountains.
Its metro was the first in Colombia.
It's the city of the Feria de las Flores.
questions.description: Here you can find anything, from a lulo to a good haggle over prices.
questions.fun_fact: José María Villa was the engineer who built the Puente de Occidente over the Cauca River in Santa Fe de Antioquia.

questions.question: On the Caribbean coast they sell ciruela costeña: small, red or yellow, and many people eat it with salt. What's in the middle?
hints: You eat it in bites, without peeling or cutting it.
You have to eat around it.
It's hard, and you don't eat it.
questions.description: Small, tasty and the perfect snack for a day at the beach.
questions.fun_fact: The ciruela costeña is a relative of the mango and the cashew.

questions.question: You're on the street and buy chopped mango biche (green mango) in a cup. What do people in Colombia usually put on it?
hints: Both are things you'll find in every kitchen.
One is white and comes in tiny grains.
The other is green and sour, and you squeeze it.
questions.description: The official snack for when school lets out.
questions.fun_fact: Some people also sprinkle pepper or chili powder on their mango biche.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these are green plantains. What kind of plant do they grow on?
wrong_answers: A tree with a wooden trunk
hints: It can be taller than a person.
Its “trunk” is made of leaves rolled tightly around each other.
Its leaves are used to wrap tamales.
questions.description: The star of sancocho has a greener origin than you might think.
questions.fun_fact: A plantain plant isn't a tree: it's a giant herb, and each plant produces just one bunch.

questions.question: Which of these fruits do you NOT need to peel before eating it?
hints: Its skin is thin, green or yellow.
Inside it's pink or white, with lots of tiny seeds.
It's used to make bocadillo veleño.
questions.description: A question for people who eat everything without looking.
questions.fun_fact: Guava skin is edible and packed with vitamin C.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Guava is correct (edible skin, bocadillo veleño is guava paste). But granadilla is a weak wrong answer: you don't peel it either. You crack the hard shell open and eat the pulp, so a player could argue it also needs no peeling.

questions.question: In “Embrace of the Serpent”, Nilbio Torres plays the shaman Karamakate as a young man. Who plays him as an old man?
