hints: He wasn't a professional actor: he was an Indigenous man from the Colombian Amazon.
He was one of the last speakers of the language of his people, the Ocaina.
He shares a last name with “the Liberator” Simón.
questions.description: Two actors, one shaman, and a whole lot of jungle years between them.
questions.fun_fact: Ciro Guerra's “Embrace of the Serpent” was the first Colombian film nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

questions.question: Pedro Romero, a Cuban-born blacksmith, armed the artisans of his neighborhood. Under his pressure, in 1811 his city declared full independence from Spain. Which city?
hints: It is on the Caribbean coast.
Romero's artisans, armed as lancers, surrounded the government junta to demand independence.
It celebrates its independence every November 11, with festivities and a beauty pageant.
questions.description: A blacksmith who, instead of horseshoes, forged a date on the calendar.
questions.fun_fact: November 11, this city's independence day, is a national holiday in Colombia, though it moves to the Monday.

questions.question: In 1815, in exile on the island in this photo, Simón Bolívar wrote a famous letter imagining the future of the Americas. Which island is it?
hints: It is in the Caribbean Sea, south of Cuba.
Its capital is Kingston.
It is the land of Usain Bolt and reggae.
questions.description: Some people get gloomy in exile; others write the future of a continent.
questions.fun_fact: The letter was addressed to Henry Cullen, an English merchant living on the island.

questions.question: Which of these cities is NOT in the department of Bolívar?
hints: The odd one out is the capital of another department.
It lies near where the Magdalena River meets the sea.
It's the city of Colombia's most famous carnival.
questions.description: Three cities posing in the family photo, and one that snuck in from another family.
questions.fun_fact: The historic center of Mompox was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

questions.question: In February 1811 the “Ciudades Confederadas del Valle” were born: Cali, Buga, Cartago, Toro, Anserma and Caloto. What were they?
questions.answer: A patriot alliance against the government in Popayán
wrong_answers: A pact of cities loyal to the King of Spain
A yearly fair for cattle and sugarcane
The cities founded by Sebastián de Belalcázar
hints: They came together after Cali set up its own governing junta in 1810.
Popayán was ruled by Miguel Tacón, who was loyal to the king.
They joined forces to defend themselves and avoid being ruled by royalists.
questions.description: Long before group chats, the cities of the Valle were already starting their own group.
questions.fun_fact: With help from troops sent from Santafé, the confederated cities defeated Tacón at the Battle of Bajo Palacé in March 1811.

questions.question: In the war between Gran Colombia and Peru (1828–1829), which of these men was NOT on Gran Colombia's side?
hints: The odd one out led the opposing army.
He was the president of Peru.
Oddly enough, he was born in Cuenca, in today's Ecuador.
questions.description: A fight between neighbors where one of them was born in the other's house.
questions.fun_fact: The deciding battle was Tarqui, on February 27, 1829, won by Sucre.

questions.question: At New Year's in Colombia, many people walk around the block with a suitcase. What is this ritual supposed to bring?
questions.answer: Lots of travel in the new year
wrong_answers: A move to a new house
hints: It is done right at midnight on December 31.
The suitcase is the main clue.
It's a wish for airports, beaches and trips.
questions.description: Midnight on December 31: the only time it's normal to see your neighbor jogging with luggage.
questions.fun_fact: Some people pack the suitcase full to make the ritual work better, and some even put their passport inside.

questions.question: In Colombia, many people put a banknote inside their shoe to welcome the New Year. What is this superstition for?
hints: It has nothing to do with your feet.
What matters is what's hidden.
It's a superstition so your pockets are never empty.
questions.description: Walking around uncomfortable all night pays off, or so they say.
questions.fun_fact: Other Colombian New Year's superstitions include eating twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock, and carrying lentils in your pocket.

questions.question: For the Wayuu, it is a figure in the sky that shows up at night, and its name is also used to count months. What is it called?
hints: It shines at night, but it has no light of its own.
It changes shape over the course of the month.
It is the Moon in the Wayuunaiki language.
questions.description: In the La Guajira desert, people keep the calendar by looking at the night sky.
questions.fun_fact: In Wayuu mythology, Juyá is the rain, Pulowi is his wife, and Ka'i is the Sun.

questions.question: Many Colombian babies wear a little bracelet with an azabache to protect them from the evil eye. What is an azabache?
hints: It's hard and shines when polished.
It forms from fossilized wood, like coal.
Its English name, jet, is also the name of a very dark color.
questions.description: The smallest, shiniest bodyguard a baby can have.
questions.fun_fact: The belief goes that if the azabache cracks or breaks, it took the evil eye in the baby's place.

questions.question: In the novel “María,” Efraín's father sends him far from the hacienda and from María to study medicine. Which city does he go to?
hints: He has to cross the Atlantic Ocean.
It is a European city where people don't speak Spanish.
It is the capital of England.
questions.description: The saddest long-distance relationship in Colombian literature.
questions.fun_fact: El Paraíso, the hacienda where the novel takes place, really exists in Valle del Cauca and is now a museum.

questions.question: You're on a coffee farm and open a ripe coffee cherry. How many beans are almost always inside?
hints: Very few: you can count them on one hand.
Each bean has a flat side facing its neighbor inside the cherry.
It's a pair.
questions.description: Before it reached your cup, your tinto lived in a little red berry hanging from a bush.
questions.fun_fact: When a cherry holds just one small round bean, Colombians call it “caracol” coffee.

questions.question: Look at this cuatro, the instrument of llanero joropo music. Which family of instruments does it belong to?
hints: You don’t blow into it.
It is made of wood and has a round hole in its body where the sound comes out.
The sound comes from tight threads stretched along it.
questions.description: The llanero’s best friend, after his horse and his coffee.
questions.fun_fact: The cuatro is named for its four strings, and together with the harp and maracas it makes up the llanero band.

questions.question: “I am flat, hot land between the Central and Eastern ranges. Neiva, Girardot and Honda lie on me.” What am I?
hints: I am not in the east of the country, but in the middle of the Andes.
Steamboats once sailed my river from the coast to the interior.
I share my name with the river that meets the sea at Barranquilla.
questions.description: A giant mountain-range sandwich with a hot-land filling.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, the Magdalena Valley was Colombia’s “highway”: people and goods traveled along its river between the Caribbean and Bogotá.

questions.question: Bogotá is about 2,600 m (8,500 ft) up, Cartagena almost at zero and the top of the Ruiz over 5,000 m (16,400 ft). What is that measurement called?
hints: It is measured from sea level.
The higher you climb a mountain, the bigger it gets.
It comes from the Latin word for “high”.
questions.description: The measurement that explains why you wear a jacket in Bogotá and flip-flops in Cartagena.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá is one of the highest capitals in the world: there, water boils at about 91 °C (196 °F) instead of 100 °C (212 °F).

questions.question: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, which brings Colombia its rainy seasons, forms where what meets?
questions.answer: The trade winds of both hemispheres
hints: It happens in the air, not in the sea or on land.
Some blow from the northeast and others from the southeast.
Sailors once used them to cross the Atlantic by sailing ship.
questions.description: The reason an umbrella becomes Colombia's most popular accessory twice a year.
questions.fun_fact: From space, the Intertropical Convergence Zone looks like a band of clouds circling the Earth near the equator.

questions.question: Roughly how high is the tallest peak of the Farallones de Cali?
hints: They are much higher than the city of Cali.
At the top there is páramo, but no permanent snow.
It's almost four times the height of Cali, which sits at about 1,000 m (3,300 ft).
questions.description: The mountains people in Cali gaze at every afternoon over a glass of champús.
questions.fun_fact: The rivers that give Cali its water, like the Pance and the Cali, start in the Farallones.

questions.question: Look at the trees in this photo. In which of these places in Colombia do you find them growing in abundance?
hints: Look at where their roots are: that's not dry land.
They like heat and salt water mixed with fresh water.
They grow where rivers meet the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: Trees that put on stilts to keep their pants dry.
questions.fun_fact: Mangroves protect coasts from waves and storms, and they are a nursery for huge numbers of fish and crabs.

questions.question: This little bug can bite you when you visit the Amazon jungle or the Chocó. What do you put on your skin to keep it away?
hints: It's not for the sun or for your hair.
Its smell keeps the insect from coming close.
Its name comes from the verb “repel”, which means to push away.
questions.description: The only jungle guest who always shows up hungry and buzzing.
questions.fun_fact: Only female mosquitoes bite: they need the blood to lay their eggs.

questions.question: Parks in Colombia have signs that ban feeding animals like this monkey. Why?
questions.answer: They get sick and stop finding their own food
wrong_answers: They can only eat at night
They grow until they become giants
hints: Think about what we eat: chips, cookies, candy.
Their bodies are made for fruit, leaves and insects from the forest.
They also get used to begging from tourists.
questions.description: It gives you sweet puppy eyes, but your bag of chips is bad news for it.
questions.fun_fact: Animals that get used to tourist food can turn aggressive and wander near roads, where they're in danger.

questions.question: On the Nevado del Cocuy and the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, huge masses of ice slowly slide down the mountain and are melting. What are they called?
hints: They don't float in the sea or fall all at once.
They form from snow that piles up and gets pressed down over centuries.
Their name sounds like “glacial”, the coldest of Colombia's climate zones.
questions.description: A giant ice cream that has been sitting in the mountain's freezer for thousands of years.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has lost most of its glaciers in the last century, and today only a few of its mountains still have ice.

questions.question: In which sport has Colombia won the most Olympic medals in its history?
hints: It's a sport of pure strength, not speed.
It gave Colombia its first Olympic gold, at Sydney 2000.
Óscar Figueroa and María Isabel Urrutia are its big stars.
questions.description: Colombia has a favorite Olympic sport and makes no secret of it.
questions.fun_fact: Óscar Figueroa won silver at London 2012 and gold at Rio 2016 in the 62 kg (137 lb) class.

questions.question: Óscar Figueroa lifts a 20 kg bar with a red 25 kg plate on each side. How many kilos is he lifting in total?
hints: Don't forget to count the bar.
The two plates together weigh 50 kg.
Add the bar's 20 kg to the plates.
questions.description: Gym math: the only kind of sum that makes you sweat.
questions.fun_fact: In weightlifting, each plate color has its own weight: red is 25 kg, blue 20, yellow 15 and green 10.

questions.question: Colombian boxer Ingrit Valencia and her opponent step into the ring, each wearing her gloves. How many gloves are in the ring?
hints: Each boxer has two hands.
There are two boxers.
Two gloves plus two gloves.
questions.description: A question you can count on your fingers, even if they're well padded.
questions.fun_fact: In Olympic boxing, gloves are red or blue, depending on each boxer's corner.

questions.question: When Mariana Pajón wins a medal, she steps onto the Olympic podium. How many steps of different heights does that podium have?
hints: Only athletes who win a medal get to stand on it.
The steps rise from both sides toward the middle.
There is one step for each medal color.
questions.description: The shortest and hardest staircase in the world to climb.
questions.fun_fact: Gold, silver and bronze medals were first handed out at the 1904 Games in St. Louis.

questions.question: Which of these things does Mariana Pajón NOT wear when she races?
hints: Mariana races a BMX bike on a dirt track with jumps.
Three of these things protect her in a crash or help her grip the bike.
It helps you see underwater.
questions.description: Bag check before heading to the track: something here doesn't belong.
questions.fun_fact: A full-face helmet also protects the face and chin, because crashes are common in BMX racing.

questions.question: In which months of the year is the Barranquilla Carnival held?
hints: Its date changes every year.
Its date depends on the Christian calendar, just like Holy Week.
It ends right before Lent begins.
questions.description: The party where even grandparents grab the cornstarch and the costume.
questions.fun_fact: In 2003, UNESCO declared it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: It's known as “la Perla del Norte”, and its metro area has Colombia's busiest border crossing, the Simón Bolívar Bridge. Which city is it?
hints: It's on the border with Venezuela.
Very close by is Villa del Rosario, where Francisco de Paula Santander was born.
It's the capital of Norte de Santander.
questions.description: A bridge with more traffic than the line at the bank on payday.
questions.fun_fact: In neighboring Villa del Rosario, the first constitution of Gran Colombia was written in 1821.

questions.question: In Cali, the Bulevar del Río is a walkway along the Cali River. What is right underneath it?
hints: A very busy avenue used to run through this same spot.
The work was finished for the 2013 World Games.
Avenida Colombia was “buried” so people on foot could have more space.
questions.description: A place where the top is for strolling and the bottom is a different story.
questions.fun_fact: Because it was built for the 2013 World Games, people call it the Túnel Mundialista (World Games Tunnel).

questions.question: Look at the photo: this 1846 statue of Bolívar is Bogotá's oldest public monument. What material is it made of?
hints: Its dark, slightly greenish color is a clue.
It's a metal, not a stone.
It's the same material as third-place medals.
questions.description: Almost two centuries standing in the square, and still not a single day off.
questions.fun_fact: It was made by the Italian sculptor Pietro Tenerani.

questions.question: The Botero Museum in Bogotá's La Candelaria opened in 2000 from the artist's donation and is free. Besides his own works, what does it hold?
questions.answer: Works by Picasso, Dalí and other masters
hints: Botero was also a great collector.
Many of those pieces come from Europe.
There are paintings by very famous 20th-century painters.
questions.description: A museum where nobody is on a diet, not even the fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Botero donated more than 200 works, some his own and some by other artists.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this palace in Medellín, with a black-and-white checkered front, was designed by the Belgian Agustín Goovaerts. What style is it?
hints: It's a style that copies a much older era, like many buildings from the early 1900s.
It has pointed arches and little towers.
It looks like a medieval cathedral, but in a “new” version.
questions.description: A building that dressed up as a chessboard and never wanted to change clothes.
questions.fun_fact: It used to be the seat of the government of the department of Antioquia and is now a cultural center.

questions.question: It grows trampled in the pastures, and grandmas use it in a poultice. What is llantén used for?
questions.answer: To reduce swelling and heal wounds
hints: It's used mostly on the outside of the body, on the skin.
Grandmas put it on scrapes, bites and pimples.
It helps the skin heal and brings down the puffiness.
questions.description: A pasture leaf more famous than the family first-aid kit.
questions.fun_fact: Llantén came from Europe and spread so fast across the Americas that some Indigenous peoples of North America called it “white man's footprint.”

questions.question: Your tinto comes from Castillo, Cenicafé's coffee bred to resist leaf rust. It's a cross of Caturra with which other coffee?
hints: It appeared on its own on a plantation in the 20th century and is behind many rust-resistant coffees around the world.
It came from a natural cross between arabica and robusta coffee.
Its island is split between Indonesia and a country that became independent in 2002.
questions.description: A coffee in armor, raised in a lab to fight off fungi.
questions.fun_fact: The Castillo variety, released by Cenicafé in 2005, is named after Colombian researcher Jaime Castillo Zapata.

questions.question: For years, many Palm Sunday palms in Colombia were made from the leaves of a palm that nearly died out because of it; cutting it is now banned. Which one?
hints: It grows in the mountains, not on the beach.
It's the tallest palm in the world.
Its most famous forest is in the Cocora Valley.
questions.description: One Sunday when everyone leaves Mass holding a piece of tree.
questions.fun_fact: The Quindío wax palm can grow taller than 60 m (200 ft) and has been Colombia's national tree since 1985.

questions.question: This orchid, Cattleya trianae, is Colombia's national flower. Where does it grow in the wild?
hints: It doesn't need to be planted in the ground.
It lives in humid mountain forests.
It holds on to a branch with its roots.
questions.description: A flower so classy it was chosen to represent the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “trianae” in honor of Colombian botanist José Jerónimo Triana, who studied thousands of the country's plants in the 19th century.

questions.question: It's green and soft, grows on rocks and tree trunks in the hills, and every December people are asked not to pull it up. Why do so many take it home?
hints: It has to do with Christmas.
It goes in the living room, near the tree.
Baby Jesus, the Virgin Mary and Saint Joseph go on top of it.
questions.description: The softest carpet in the forest, and no store sells it.
questions.fun_fact: In the páramo, moss works like a sponge: it holds a huge amount of water that later flows slowly into the rivers.

questions.question: “Mesmo” instead of “mismo” (same) shows up in centuries-old books and is still heard in rural Boyacá. What is a word like that, surviving from old Spanish, called?
hints: It's the opposite of a brand-new word.
It comes from Greek and means something like “ancient.”
It shares a root with “archaic.”
questions.description: Words that skipped 400 years of updates.
questions.fun_fact: In rural Boyacá, words from Cervantes' time still survive that almost nobody in Madrid uses anymore.

questions.question: Leticia, on the border with Brazil and Peru, lies in one of Colombia's natural regions. Which one?
hints: It covers the south and southeast of the country.
It is almost all rainforest, crossed by huge rivers.
Pink dolphins swim there.
questions.description: A map without names is like a sticker album without stickers: you just have to guess.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon region covers more than a third of Colombia's territory, but very few people live there.

questions.question: I'm flat as far as the eye can see, my cowboys sing as they herd cattle, and harp, cuatro and maracas play at my parties. Which region am I?
hints: People dance joropo at my parties.
My lands are also called the Llanos Orientales (Eastern Plains).
My name comes from a big river I share with Venezuela.
questions.description: The horizon here is so flat you can see Saturday's rainstorm coming on Tuesday.
questions.fun_fact: In the Llanos, the canto de vaquería is a tune llaneros sing to calm the cattle while they herd them.

questions.question: The Victoria regia, the plant with giant leaves from the Amazon lakes, was named in honor of whom?
hints: A European scientist named it in the 19th century without ever seeing it grow in the Amazon.
“Regia” means “royal.”
This person gave her name to a whole era of English history.
questions.description: Leaves so big a small child could use one as a raft.
questions.fun_fact: The Victoria regia flower opens white on its first night and turns pink on the second.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It lies in the Cordillera Oriental, in the northeast of the country.
The Simón Bolívar International Bridge is there.
Its capital is Cúcuta.
questions.description: Finding a department on a map with no names is like looking for your keys without your glasses.
questions.fun_fact: In 1821 the Congress of Cúcuta met in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, and drafted the Constitution of Gran Colombia.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department of the Eje Cafetero is highlighted?
hints: It's the northernmost of the three Eje Cafetero departments.
It borders Antioquia.
Its capital is Manizales.
questions.description: Tiny on the map, but with more tinto per square kilometer than a coffee shop.
questions.fun_fact: Risaralda and Quindío were part of Caldas until they split off in 1966.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT typical of the Meta department?
hints: Meta is in the Llanos Orientales, the eastern plains.
The odd one out is a musical instrument.
It's typical of the Pacific coast and is played with currulao.
questions.description: An intruder sneaked into the Llano, and nobody invited it to the joropo.
questions.fun_fact: Caño Cristales, in the Sierra de La Macarena, turns red because of a water plant that grows on its riverbed.

questions.question: Before the Spanish arrived, which Indigenous people of Santander already ate hormigas culonas?
hints: These people lived near the Chicamocha Canyon.
A little stone village that belongs to Barichara still carries almost the same name.
The old stone-paved Camino Real from Barichara ends in that little village.
questions.description: Six-legged popcorn that people in Santander sell in little bags.
questions.fun_fact: Only the queens are collected, when they leave the anthills in the rainy season, mostly between March and May.

questions.question: Which animal is on the Colombian 1,000-peso coin?
hints: It's a threatened species protected in Colombia.
It can live for decades, longer than many pets.
It carries its house on its back.
questions.description: The coin that jingles loudest in your pocket carries a passenger who never pays the fare.
questions.fun_fact: Many sea turtles travel thousands of kilometers and come back to lay eggs on the same beach where they hatched.

questions.question: It has a slot on top, slowly fills up with coins, and sometimes you have to break it to get them out. What is it called?
hints: It's used at home, not in a store.
It's for saving money little by little.
Many are shaped like a little animal and rattle when you shake them.
questions.description: Saving is easy; the hard part is not spending it all the next day.
questions.fun_fact: People have been making clay coin banks shaped like little pigs for centuries.

questions.question: Restaurants in Colombia ask if you want to add an extra 10% for the waiters. What is that payment called?
hints: It isn't a tax.
Paying it is optional.
It goes to the person who served you, as a thank-you.
questions.description: That little number at the bottom of the bill that makes everyone at the table look at each other.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian law says the propina is optional, and the restaurant must ask you before adding it to the bill.

questions.question: You want to pay 300,000 pesos using only the bills with Carlos Lleras Restrepo on them. How many bills do you need?
hints: Carlos Lleras Restrepo was a president of Colombia.
He governed Colombia from 1966 to 1970.
Ten of those bills add up to one million pesos.
questions.description: When your wallet feels light but is worth a ton.
questions.fun_fact: The 100,000-peso bill with Carlos Lleras Restrepo went into circulation in 2016.

questions.question: It’s sold in neighborhood shops, comes in a small cup and has two colors. What is a Nucita?
hints: You don’t chew it.
You eat it by the spoonful.
One half is dark and the other white, with cocoa and milk flavors.
questions.description: The thing eaten first from the lunchbox, even when Mom says it’s for after lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Nucita is made by Colombina, a Colombian candy company.

questions.question: Carulla supermarkets are named after José Carulla, a Spanish immigrant who opened a store in Bogotá in 1905. Which region was he from?
hints: His region speaks another language besides Spanish.
His region is in northeastern Spain, on the Mediterranean, next to France.
It's the region of Barcelona.
questions.description: A last name that's been in Bogotá so long it's more rolo than ajiaco.
questions.fun_fact: Carulla is one of the oldest supermarket chains in Colombia and now belongs to Grupo Éxito.

questions.question: At what time of day does La Guacherna, one of the parades of the Carnaval de Barranquilla, take place?
hints: It's held on the Friday before the carnival.
Groups in costume parade to the sound of drums and the millo flute.
The marchers carry lanterns and candles to light the way.
questions.description: Barranquilla has a parade for every hour that someone might feel like dancing.
questions.fun_fact: Esthercita Forero, known as “la Novia de Barranquilla,” helped bring La Guacherna back in the 1970s and wrote a famous song about it.

questions.question: In a cycling stage race, which classification gives points to the first rider over the top of the climbs?
hints: Commentators call it by a three-letter abbreviation.
Colombia's escarabajos have won it many times in Europe.
At the Tour de France, its jersey is white with red polka dots.
questions.description: Here you don't earn points with luck, but with legs of steel and lungs to spare.
questions.fun_fact: Climbs are ranked by category, and the toughest are so hard they're called “hors catégorie”, French for “beyond category”.

questions.question: In a cycling stage race, what do you call the hardest stage of all, the one with the toughest climbs?
hints: It's almost always raced in the high mountains.
It's often the stage that decides who wins the overall classification.
If there were a king of stages, she would be his wife.
questions.description: The stage that makes even the team's massage therapist nervous.
questions.fun_fact: In the Giro d'Italia, the highest climb of the race is called the “Cima Coppi”, in honor of the champion Fausto Coppi.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this little gadget sits on a bike's handlebars. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To light the way at night
hints: You use it with your thumb.
It makes a sound.
People walking hear it and step aside.
questions.description: Small, shiny and always sitting in the front row of the handlebars.
questions.fun_fact: The first bicycle bells were invented more than 100 years ago, when bikes started filling the streets.

questions.question: Commentators say a cyclist “came in with the grupeta.” What is the grupeta?
questions.answer: The group of stragglers at the back
wrong_answers: The breakaway group out in front
The convoy of team support cars
hints: The word comes from the Italian “gruppetto.”
It's usually where the riders who aren't climbers end up.
If they reach the finish too late, they're out of the race.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a weekend bike ride with your friends.
questions.fun_fact: In the grupeta, riders from different teams work together so they don't get eliminated for finishing outside the time limit.

questions.question: Nairo Quintana won the Giro d'Italia in 2014. Two years later he won another of cycling's three Grand Tours. In which country is it raced?
hints: That race is held at the end of the European summer.
Lucho Herrera also won there in 1987.
It's the country of Madrid and Barcelona.
questions.description: Nairo collecting Grand Tours like stickers for a World Cup album.
questions.fun_fact: In that 2016 race, Nairo finished ahead of Britain's Chris Froome.

questions.question: Look at the photo: it's limoncillo, used for the herbal tea that smells like lemon. What kind of plant is it really?
questions.answer: A grass in the wheat family
wrong_answers: A shrub in the lemon tree family
A plant in the mint family
A vine in the vanilla family
hints: It has nothing to do with citrus fruits.
Its long, thin leaves all grow straight from the ground, with no trunk or branches.
It's in the same family as sugarcane.
questions.description: Grandma swears this cures everything, from a cold to a bad mood.
questions.fun_fact: Limoncillo's lemon smell comes from citral, the same scented substance found in lemon peel.

questions.question: Look closely: when fruit looks like this, not green but not fully ripe, what do Colombians call it?
hints: The word has to do with the colors showing up on the peel.
It's not “biche”, which is when it's still very green.
It sounds like “pintar” (to paint): the fruit is starting to paint itself yellow.
questions.description: An endless kitchen debate: can you eat it yet or not?
questions.fun_fact: Many people buy their bananas pintón so they can finish ripening at home without going overripe.

questions.question: Much of it is exported to Europe. Which department of Colombia has the most hectares planted with Hass avocado?
hints: It's an Andean department, with the mild mountain climate that Hass avocados love.
Many of its Hass farms are in the east and southwest of the department.
Its capital is known as the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: The green fruit that flies to Europe in a better class than a lot of tourists.
questions.fun_fact: The Hass variety is named after Rudolph Hass, a California mailman who planted the first tree.

questions.question: It's a long pod hanging from trees that give shade in coffee farms. When you open a guamo, what part do you eat?
wrong_answers: The juice stored in the pod
The flowers growing at the tip
hints: It's sweet and soft.
You eat it raw, with your hands, straight from the pod.
It's white and fluffy like cotton candy, and you spit out the seed.
questions.description: A snack that comes in its own factory-made case.
questions.fun_fact: Guamo trees fix nitrogen in the soil, which makes them good neighbors for coffee plants.

questions.question: I'm an honorary title first proposed by Mérida and confirmed for Simón Bolívar by the Caracas town council in 1813. What title am I?
hints: I was given after the Admirable Campaign of 1813.
I speak of what that man achieved in five countries.
I come from the word “liberty”.
questions.description: Some nicknames you earn at school, others you earn by crossing the Andes.
questions.fun_fact: Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar, the man who received this title.

questions.question: The 1819 Liberation Campaign began in the Llanos, crossed the páramo de Pisba and won at the Boyacá Bridge. Which city did Bolívar enter three days later?
hints: It lies south of the Boyacá Bridge.
Viceroy Juan Sámano fled from there when he heard of the defeat.
Today it is the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: A months-long walk across plains and páramos that ended in a victory parade.
questions.fun_fact: At the time the city was called Santafé, and Bolívar entered it on August 10, 1819.

questions.question: The Curupira, a spirit of the Amazon rainforest, has red hair and backward feet. Who does he lead astray with those footprints?
hints: He protects the animals of the jungle.
His footprints seem to go the opposite way.
Whoever chases him with a shotgun ends up lost.
questions.description: A redhead from the jungle with a serious shoe problem.
questions.fun_fact: The Curupira is one of the most famous figures in Brazilian folklore, and his story is told in the Colombian Amazon too.

questions.question: In the yonna, a woman in a long dress dances forward and the man steps back so he won't fall. Which Indigenous people dance it?
hints: It is danced to the beat of a drum called the kasha.
They are a desert people in the north of Colombia.
They live in La Guajira and are famous for their mochila bags.
questions.description: A dance where the man learns fast how to walk backwards.
questions.fun_fact: The yonna is also called chichamaya, and it is danced at the community's big celebrations.

questions.question: The Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, with the largest glacier area in Colombia, is in the highlighted department. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the Cordillera Oriental.
The colonial town of Villa de Leyva is there.
Its capital is Tunja.
questions.description: Here the ice drinks a nice hot tinto before the sun can melt it.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's glaciers are melting so fast that several snowy peaks lost all their ice in the last century.

questions.question: It's Colombia's highest volcano, the top of the Cordillera Central, and in 2007 it had its first recorded eruption. Which one is it?
hints: It's over 5,300 meters (17,400 ft) high.
It sits where three departments meet, including Cauca and Tolima.
It shares its name with the department whose capital is Neiva.
questions.description: A giant that slept so long that nobody had ever seen it wake up.
questions.fun_fact: The Indigenous Nasa people, who live on its slopes, consider this snowy peak a sacred mountain.

questions.question: Look at this crop covering the floor of the Cauca River valley. What is it mainly used to make?
hints: The ingenios of the Valle work day and night on this harvest.
Its tall stalks are cut and squeezed to get the juice out.
You add a spoonful to your juice to sweeten it.
questions.description: A landscape so green and so even that it looks like an endless carpet.
questions.fun_fact: In the Cauca River valley, cane is harvested all year round, because there are no seasons to stop it.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: El Totumo, near Cartagena, is famous for being a volcano of…
hints: Tourists climb inside and come out without getting burned.
Afterward, you have to wash off in the lagoon next door.
You come out brown and sticky from head to toe.
questions.description: A tiny volcano with a giant reputation among tourists.
questions.fun_fact: People say nobody sinks in El Totumo's crater: the mud is so thick that you float.

questions.question: Next to many Wayuu rancherías in La Guajira, a big hole is dug in the ground: the jagüey. What is kept in it?
hints: The whole community shares it.
In the long dry season it can end up almost empty.
It fills up when a downpour finally comes.
questions.description: In La Guajira, a hole in the ground can be the ranchería's most precious treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Many Wayuu homes are built with yotojoro, the dried core of the cardón cactus.

questions.question: Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and Indonesia are among about 17 countries called “megadiverse.” What does that mean?
questions.answer: They have a large share of the planet's species
wrong_answers: They have the most populated cities
They speak a huge number of languages
hints: It has to do with nature, not people.
Think of what you find in a rainforest like the Amazon or the Chocó.
“Diverse” here refers to living things.
questions.description: A club so exclusive that Colombia got in without waiting in line.
questions.fun_fact: Together, the megadiverse countries hold about 70% of the planet's known species.

questions.question: Some national parks in Colombia have camping areas. What do you do when you go camping?
wrong_answers: Ride a horse along the beach
Take a boat ride on a lake
hints: It's something families do on vacation, far from the city.
People often light a campfire and look at the stars.
You bring a little cloth house that you set up with poles.
questions.description: On this adventure, your backpack weighs more than your vacation suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia people often use the English word “camping”, even though Spanish has its own verb for it: «acampar».

questions.question: British rider Bethany Shriever beat Mariana Pajón in the Tokyo Olympic final. In what year was that final?
hints: It was a very unusual edition of the Olympics.
With that silver, Pajón completed three Olympic medals in a row.
It was one year after the year in the name of those Games.
questions.description: Jumps, tight turns and a paisa whose trophy cabinet is already full of medals.
questions.fun_fact: Bethany Shriever had to raise money online to pay for part of her Olympic training.

questions.question: In what year did Cali host the Pan American Games?
hints: It was more than 50 years ago.
It was early in the decade of disco music and bell-bottoms.
It was two years after the Moon landing.
questions.description: The “Sucursal del Cielo” has also been a branch office of sport.
questions.fun_fact: Ever since those Games, Cali has proudly been called the “sports capital of the Americas.”

questions.question: Medellín's Coltejer Building, with its sharp tip, was the tallest in Colombia in the 1970s. Roughly how tall is it?
hints: It has about 36 or 37 floors.
Each floor is about 4 or 5 meters high.
It's a little shorter than Bogotá's Torre Colpatria, which is 196 meters tall.
questions.description: A building that dresses up with a needle, but no thread.
questions.fun_fact: Its tip imitates a knitting needle, in honor of the textile company Coltejer.

questions.question: I’m a plant of the countryside and the pastures; brush against me and your skin burns and itches like crazy. What do they call me in Colombia?
hints: You’ll find me on farms and pastures in almost all of Colombia.
Touching me is worse than a mosquito bite.
I’m a distant relative of the nettle.
questions.description: A plant that doesn’t need thorns to earn respect.
questions.fun_fact: Its tiny hairs work like miniature needles that release irritating substances when they touch the skin.

questions.question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, people say a child is very “pechichón.” What is the child like?
hints: It has to do with how the child is treated at home.
Grandparents are usually to blame.
It comes from “pechiche,” a word for a little pampering.
questions.description: A word people on the Coast say with love… or as a scolding.
questions.fun_fact: On the Coast, “pechichar” means to pamper someone, and a “pechiche” is a little treat or indulgence.

questions.question: In Barranquilla, about someone who makes big threats but never does anything, they say: “Eso es puro…”
hints: It's a word from the Caribbean coast.
It's a lot of noise and very little action.
It looks a lot like the word “agua”.
questions.description: Lots of noise, lots of jumping around, and in the end nothing at all.
questions.fun_fact: Someone who does aguaje is called an “aguajero”: all noise and no action.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, it's used in Nariño and in Ecuador, and it names the little hollow in the belly where a baby's cord was. What's the word?
hints: It's a very short word.
Everyone has had one since the day they were born.
Elsewhere in Colombia it's called the “ombligo”.
questions.description: A word every one of us carries right in the middle of the tummy.
questions.fun_fact: In Nariño people also say “guagua” for a baby and “chuspa” for a bag, both from Quechua, and “taita” for dad, a word used across the Andes.

questions.question: In Boyacá and Cundinamarca, people often order “cuchuco de trigo”. What is cuchuco?
hints: You order it at lunchtime.
It's made with cracked grain.
It's eaten hot, with a spoon.
questions.description: What people in the cold highlands order with their ruana pulled on tight.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the wheat kind, there's also cuchuco made with corn or barley.

questions.question: What do you call someone born in the department of Cabo de la Vela, Punta Gallinas and the Manaure salt flats?
hints: It is the northernmost department of mainland Colombia.
A large part of the Wayuu people live there.
It is the shortest word of the four.
questions.description: Demonyms: the fancy way of asking “So where are you from?”
questions.fun_fact: Punta Gallinas, in La Guajira, is the northernmost point of all mainland South America.

questions.question: Encocado, fish or shrimp cooked in coconut milk, is typical of which region of Colombia?
hints: It rains a lot there almost all year.
That's where the marimba de chonta and currulao are played.
Tumaco and Buenaventura are famous for this dish.
questions.description: When a coconut decides to jump into the pot and get all dressed up.
questions.fun_fact: On the Pacific coast, coconut is grated and squeezed by hand to get the fresh milk used to cook encocado.

questions.question: I am a capital on the Atrato River, I celebrate the Fiestas de San Pacho in September, and it rains on me almost every day. Which city am I?
hints: I am a department capital in the Pacific region.
UNESCO lists my Fiestas de San Pacho as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
I am the capital of Chocó.
questions.description: A city where Saint Francis gets a bigger party than most rock stars.
questions.fun_fact: The Fiestas de San Francisco de Asís, or San Pacho, were added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity list in 2012.

questions.question: This huge river flows past Puerto Carreño and empties into the Atlantic through a large delta in Venezuela. Which river is it?
hints: It is one of the longest rivers in South America.
The Meta and the Guaviare end up pouring their water into it.
The Llanos region's official name is almost the same as this river's.
questions.description: A river so wide you'd better pack a lunch before heading for the other bank.
questions.fun_fact: The Orinoco starts in the Venezuelan rainforest and gives Colombia a river border in Vichada.

questions.question: They come out of the kitchen drawer, are played in pairs, back to back, and sound in the country music of Boyacá. What are they?
hints: They fit easily in one hand.
You hold them between your fingers and they go “clack-clack” against your knee.
You eat your ajiaco with them.
questions.description: An instrument your mom doesn't want to see outside the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Spoons are also played in the folk music of Ireland and the United States.

questions.question: In linear salsa, unlike Cali style, the dancer steps on 1, 2 and 3, then pauses. On which count do they step again?
hints: The full count goes up to 8.
The pauses fall on two numbers of the count.
You rest on 4 and on 8.
questions.description: A question for everyone who counts under their breath while dancing and thinks nobody can hear.
questions.fun_fact: Linear salsa gets its name because the couple dances back and forth along an imaginary line.

questions.question: Which Colombian scientist became a world authority on paracoccidioidomycosis, an infection caused by a fungus?
hints: She worked in Medellín for almost her whole life.
She is one of the most famous mycologists, or fungus experts, in Latin America.
She founded the Corporación para Investigaciones Biológicas (CIB) and shares a last name with a Colombian president of the 1910s.
questions.description: Some people fear the mold in the fridge, and some gave it their whole lives.
questions.fun_fact: Ángela Restrepo said she fell in love with microbes as a child, looking through her grandfather's microscope.

questions.question: Luis Soriano carries books to the rural villages of Magdalena on his donkeys, Alfa and Beto. Where do their names come from?
hints: It has to do with learning to read.
Think of the first thing you learn at school so you can read.
It's the list of all the letters, from A to Z.
questions.description: The most stubborn library in the world, and not because of the books.
questions.fun_fact: The Biblioburro of La Gloria, Magdalena, became so famous that it inspired documentaries and children's books in other countries.

questions.question: Chocoramo is rectangular, comes individually wrapped and is covered in chocolate. What kind of mecato (snack) is it?
hints: Inside, it's soft and spongy.
It's made by a company that has been making this snack for decades.
It's like a slice of what you'd eat at a birthday party.
questions.description: The king of the lunch box, wearing a chocolate crown.
questions.fun_fact: Chocoramo has been around since the 1970s and became one of the most famous snacks in Colombia.

questions.question: For a trip to which of these places in Colombia are you NOT advised to get a yellow fever vaccine?
hints: Think about where the mosquito that spreads it lives.
That mosquito doesn't like the cold of the mountains.
It is a city more than 2,600 m (8,500 ft) above sea level.
questions.description: A trip where the first outing is to the vaccination center.
questions.fun_fact: A single dose of the yellow fever vaccine protects most people for life.

questions.question: On the outside it's fried, golden mashed potato; inside it has meat, rice and egg. What fried snack is it?
hints: It's sold in the glass cases of fried snacks on street corners.
It has a round or oval shape.
In Spanish, its name tells you what it's made of and that it's stuffed.
questions.description: The glass case at the corner shop holds treasures worth more than a bank vault.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian cities, papa rellena is eaten with ají, just like empanadas.

questions.question: The recipe for cocadas calls for “coco rallado.” What does “rallado” mean here?
wrong_answers: Toasted in a pan until golden
Split in half with a machete
hints: It's something you do to the coconut before you cook it.
You use a kitchen tool covered in small sharp holes.
It's the same thing you do to cheese for pasta.
questions.description: A sweet from the coast so sticky that even the beach sand wants a bite.
questions.fun_fact: In Cartagena, the palenqueras sell cocadas from big bowls balanced on their heads, and their trade is a symbol of the city.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this boiled side is a must in sancocho. What is it?
hints: It's a long root with a thick brown skin.
Inside it's very white, with a stringy fiber down the middle.
In other countries it's called cassava or mandioca, and it's also eaten as fried sticks.
questions.description: The sidekick that always shows up when there's a big pot and a day trip to the river.
questions.fun_fact: Yuca is native to South America and today feeds hundreds of millions of people around the world.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this tall drum, played with the hands, joined the modern vallenato band. What is it?
hints: It came from Cuba, like many Caribbean rhythms.
It's long and narrow, and often two or three are played together.
It's big in salsa too, and its name is shared with a dance done in a line.
questions.description: A drum that came to visit from the Caribbean and moved into the parranda for good.
questions.fun_fact: The traditional vallenato band had just three instruments; congas, bass and guitar came later with the modern groups.

questions.question: The 2024 Netflix series “One Hundred Years of Solitude” was filmed entirely in Colombia. In which department was its Macondo built?
hints: Many people would bet on Aracataca, Gabo's hometown, but it wasn't there.
It's an inland department in the Magdalena River valley.
Its capital is Ibagué, Colombia's musical city.
questions.description: Netflix finally found Macondo's address, and it wasn't on Waze.
questions.fun_fact: The Macondo set was built near Alvarado and was one of Netflix's biggest productions in Latin America.

questions.question: Melquíades is to the parchments as Colonel Gerineldo Márquez is to the…
hints: The colonel used it during the civil wars.
During the war, the colonel was left in charge of Macondo while Aureliano fought far away.
Through it he told him: “Aureliano, it’s raining in Macondo.”
questions.description: Strange inventions arrived in Macondo every year, and some of them stayed for good.
questions.fun_fact: Gerineldo Márquez courted Amaranta for years, and she turned him down even though they played Chinese checkers together every afternoon.

questions.question: Picture book by Jairo Buitrago and Rafael Yockteng: a girl crosses the city with a lion and misses her dad. What is it called?
hints: It won the A la Orilla del Viento prize in Mexico.
The girl and the lion cross streets full of people, buses and noise.
The title describes what the girl does after school: head back home.
questions.description: A picture book where the companion has a mane and never pays the bus fare.
questions.fun_fact: The lion in the book has been read as a symbol of the absent father, a delicate subject told with great tenderness.

questions.question: This Colombian writer is the big name of a literary style. Which one?
hints: In his novels, a woman rises up to the sky and nobody finds it strange.
This style became famous around the world through Latin American novels of the 1960s.
In this style, fantastic things happen as if they were the most normal thing in the world.
questions.description: A famous mustache, a typewriter and plenty of Caribbean heat.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez said his style came from the way his grandmother told incredible things with a completely straight face.

questions.question: You walk into a viejoteca on a Saturday night. What music are you NOT likely to hear there?
hints: Think of the music your parents or grandparents danced to when they were young.
At a viejoteca, the old-school music of “back in the day” rules.
The odd one out got famous fairly recently and plays in every young people's nightclub.
questions.description: The place where parents prove that hips never retire.
questions.fun_fact: The name “viejoteca” blends “viejo” (old) and “discoteca” (nightclub): a party made for people over 40.

questions.question: In the Danza de las Farotas, men dance dressed as women. According to legend, why did the farotos dress up like that?
wrong_answers: To ask the gods for rain
To honor the Virgin of Candelaria
hints: The story takes place in the time of the Spanish Conquest.
The dance was born in a riverside town on Colombia's Caribbean side, near the Magdalena River.
The costume was a trap for some invaders who arrived by boat.
questions.description: Come Carnival, more than one guy ended up borrowing his sister's skirt.
questions.fun_fact: The dance comes from Talaigua Nueva, a town on the island of Mompox, surrounded by the Magdalena River.

questions.question: Paseo is one of the “aires” (styles) of vallenato. How many traditional aires are played in the contest at the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata?
hints: Not many: you can count them on one hand.
Besides paseo, there are son and merengue.
One more is missing: puya, the fastest of them all.
questions.description: An accordion with more personalities than a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Puya is the fastest vallenato style and tests the fingers of any accordion player.

questions.question: In the bandas papayeras (brass bands) of Colombia's Caribbean coast, this giant instrument booms out. Who plays it?
hints: It's the biggest brass instrument in the band.
It makes the lowest sounds, like a deep “oom-pah.”
The instrument's name starts with “tu.”
questions.description: The one instrument that takes all your air and still wants a hug.
questions.fun_fact: If you unrolled the tube of a tuba, it could measure more than 5 m (16 ft).

questions.question: Which group from the Montes de María won the 2007 Latin Grammy with the album “Un fuego de sangre pura”?
hints: They come from the department of Bolívar.
Their music mixes Indigenous and African roots.
Their name tells you the instrument they play and the town they come from.
questions.description: Grandpas who blow harder than an electric fan.
questions.fun_fact: The Colombian gaita has nothing to do with Scottish bagpipes: it is an Indigenous flute.

questions.question: In the traditional cumbia costume, which item does the man NOT wear?
hints: It's the item that moves the most when people dance cumbia.
It's long and full of ruffles.
It's the wide skirt the woman dancer sways from side to side.
questions.description: A fashion show where the models sweat to the beat of the drum.
questions.fun_fact: The famous song “La pollera colorá” is about this very skirt.

questions.question: In a salsa band, which musician usually picks up this instrument and plays it in the montuno, the hottest part of the song?
hints: This musician often switches instruments during the song.
His main instrument is smaller than the congas and is played with the fingers.
His other instrument is held between the knees.
questions.description: They hit it all night long without mercy, and it still sounds happy.
questions.fun_fact: In salsa, the cowbell played by the bongo player is also called the “campana de mano” (hand bell).

questions.question: I'm the daughter of a Colombian rhythm, but I was born in the working-class neighborhoods of Buenos Aires around 2000, with keyboards and street lyrics. What am I?
hints: I'm Argentine, not Mexican or Peruvian.
My name comes from what Argentines call poor neighborhoods.
In Buenos Aires, those neighborhoods are called “villas.”
questions.description: Cumbia packed its bags, headed south and came back with a whole new accent.
questions.fun_fact: Argentina is one of the countries where people dance the most cumbia, even though the rhythm was born on Colombia's Caribbean coast.

questions.question: In 2020, at halftime of the most-watched game in the United States, I danced champeta before millions of people in Miami. Who am I?
hints: I started recording albums very young, in Colombia.
I was born on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
I sang “Hips Don't Lie” and “Waka Waka”.
questions.description: Champeta got on a plane and landed on the most-watched show on American television.
questions.fun_fact: That Super Bowl show took champeta to screens all over the world.

questions.question: A woman from Antioquia carried the Christchurch mutation and, despite her family history, was spared for almost 30 years from which disease?
hints: It is a disease of the brain.
Her family is part of the group studied by neurologist Francisco Lopera.
It makes people lose their memory.
questions.description: A spelling mistake in DNA that turned out to be a stroke of luck.
questions.fun_fact: The Antioquia family studied by Francisco Lopera is the largest in the world with inherited Alzheimer's: thousands of people.

questions.question: Who performed the first keratomileusis in Bogotá, the cornea surgery that paved the way for laser correction of nearsightedness?
hints: He was an ophthalmologist, an eye doctor.
He was born in Barcelona and settled in Bogotá in the 1950s.
A famous eye clinic in Bogotá bears his last name.
questions.description: Thanks to him, many Colombians threw away their glasses without a fight.
questions.fun_fact: Keratomileusis is the grandmother of LASIK, the laser surgery that millions of people use today to give up their glasses.

questions.question: I was born in Bogotá, studied engineering in Cambridge, and in 1958 built a pacemaker so big it ran on a car battery. Who am I?
hints: My invention was one of the first of its kind in the world.
My device was worn outside the body and weighed tens of kilograms.
My last name sounds English, though I'm a true Bogotá local.
questions.description: Bogotá doesn't only export tinto and rainstorms: it also sends out inventions that go around the world.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Reynolds's first pacemaker kept an Ecuadorian priest alive, and he lived 18 more years.

questions.question: In Nariño it's eaten roasted, in many homes it's a pet, and its other name also means “test subject.” What else is the cuy called?
hints: It's a South American rodent, even though its other name sounds like it comes from another continent.
In the Andes it was tamed long before the Europeans arrived.
Its English name points to a country in West Africa.
questions.description: A rodent that is a pet in one part of the world and a party dish in another.
questions.fun_fact: The cuy is neither a pig nor from Guinea: it's an Andean rodent that people have kept for thousands of years.

questions.question: At the Vallenato Festival, some dancers act out pounding corn in an object like this one. What are these dancers called?
hints: The dance grew out of women's kitchen work in Cesar.
Their name comes from the object in the photo.
The object is a wooden mortar called a pilón.
questions.description: A dance that works your arms like a kitchen gym.
questions.fun_fact: The piloneras open the Vallenato Legend Festival in Valledupar with a colorful parade through the streets.

questions.question: In many Colombian kitchens, chicharrones are fried in a white fat. What is it?
hints: Grandmas kept it in tins and used it for almost everything.
It's also what makes tamales soft and tender.
It comes from the marrano.
questions.description: A cooking fat that has spent more years in the kitchen than most grandmas.
questions.fun_fact: Before vegetable oil became common, lard was the main frying fat in Colombian kitchens.

questions.question: It's peeled, cooked white corn, served with milk and a bit of panela or bocadillo. Where is this mazamorra typical?
hints: It's a region of mountains and arrieros (mule drivers).
It's a coffee-growing department in the Andes, in the northwest of the country.
It's paisa country.
questions.description: A drink you chew and a meal you sip, all in the same glass.
questions.fun_fact: Mazamorra antioqueña is sold from street carts, and in some towns it's even delivered door to door.

questions.question: They're big, flat, dark cookies made with wheat flour, panela and spices like cinnamon and cloves. What are they called?
hints: They're sold in neighborhood bakeries, often in packs.
They go great with a glass of milk.
Their name has just two syllables and starts with “cu”.
questions.description: Cookies so big they beat the hand that holds them.
questions.fun_fact: Cucas get their dark color from panela, the cane sugar used in almost all traditional Colombian baking.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: it's black, in Colombia it's stuffed with rice, and no picada is complete without it. What is it?
hints: It's a pork sausage.
Its dark color comes from blood.
In some regions it's also called rellena.
questions.description: A sausage that always has a line at the fritanga stand.
questions.fun_fact: In parts of Colombia, morcilla is called “rellena”, and in Bogotá people often eat it with papa criolla.

questions.question: Bocadillo veleño (guava paste) comes from Vélez, Santander, and each slice is wrapped in a leaf that gives it its aroma. What is that leaf called?
hints: It's a big green leaf from a tropical plant.
In some regions it's also used to wrap tamales and fiambres.
Its name starts with “Bi”.
questions.description: It comes gift-wrapped all the way from Santander, no bow needed.
questions.fun_fact: The bijao leaf doesn't just add scent to the bocadillo: it also protects it and helps it last longer without spoiling.

questions.question: Sugarcane is crushed, the juice is boiled in big pailas and then beaten until it turns into panela, in blocks or as powder. Where does all this happen?
hints: It's a place in the countryside, with ovens and pailas.
A machine there squeezes the juice out of the sugarcane.
Its name starts with the same three letters as “travel”.
questions.description: Before it reached the jar in the kitchen, this little powder had a really rough week.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the biggest panela producers in the world, second only to India.

questions.question: It comes in a small dark bottle, a few drops add flavor to a cake or arequipe, and it comes from an orchid first grown by the ancient peoples of Mexico. What is it?
hints: It's one of the most famous ice cream flavors in the world.
The orchid grows long black pods.
The Aztecs mixed it with chocolate.
questions.description: A few drops of this and the whole kitchen smells like someone is making something yummy.
questions.fun_fact: Vanilla is one of the most expensive spices in the world, because on most farms every orchid flower is pollinated by hand.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this famous combination called in Colombia?
hints: One part is white and salty.
The other part is red, sweet and firm, and it's cut into slices.
The sweet part comes wrapped in leaves from Vélez, Santander.
questions.description: A couple so perfect together that nobody dares to split them up in the lunchbox.
questions.fun_fact: In Brazil, this same combination is called “Romeo and Juliet.”

questions.question: You eat a Gansito at recess. Who is the Ramo brand named after?
hints: He founded the company in Bogotá.
The name joins the start of his first name and the start of his last name.
RA from his first name and MO from his last name.
questions.description: A goose that has traveled in lunchboxes for decades and never once flown.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Molano started out selling homemade cakes before creating one of Colombia's best-loved brands.

questions.question: It's thick, very sweet milk, drizzled over raspao and cholado, and invented over 150 years ago so milk would keep without a fridge. What is it?
hints: It comes in a can or a little pouch.
If you boil it in the can for a long time, it turns into something like arequipe.
Almost all the water is taken out of the milk and sugar is added.
questions.description: An ingredient that turns anything into dessert with just a little drizzle.
questions.fun_fact: American Gail Borden patented condensed milk in 1856, and it became famous because it didn't spoil on long trips.

questions.question: It's a ring-shaped sweet bread with sugar on top, filled with arequipe or bocadillo. What is it called in Colombian bakeries?
hints: It has a hole in the middle.
It's usually big and cut into slices to share at onces (afternoon snack).
Its name means a big “rosca”, a ring shape.
questions.description: A bread shaped like a swim ring, so it won't drown in your tinto.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, the most famous one is the roscón de Reyes, eaten on January 6 with a surprise hidden inside.

questions.question: Villavicencio is called “the Gateway to the Llanos.” It is the capital of which department, highlighted on the map?
hints: The department is named after a river that flows into the Orinoco.
It borders Cundinamarca, down the mountains from Bogotá.
Its name has only four letters.
questions.description: They say that behind this city begins a sea of grass, with cows instead of fish.
questions.fun_fact: Villavicencio is just a few hours’ drive from Bogotá, but more than 2,000 meters (6,600 ft) lower.

questions.question: Jesús María Ocampo, who founded Armenia in 1889, was known to everyone as “el…”. How does his nickname end?
hints: The nickname comes from a reputation he had in the wilderness, before he founded the city.
He earned it for his bravery in a very risky trade in the region's forests.
Country people back then called the jaguar “tigre.”
questions.description: Founding a city is easy; earning a nickname like that in Quindío is the hard part.
questions.fun_fact: Armenia is called “la Ciudad Milagro” (the Miracle City) because it grew so fast after it was founded.

questions.question: I'm made of leather, I hang from the shoulder of the Antioquian arriero, and I hold everything, even in hidden pockets. What am I?
hints: I'm part of the traditional paisa outfit.
The arrieros who crossed the mountains with their mules carried me.
I often have hairy hide on the outside and several compartments.
questions.description: When the arriero and his mule crossed the Andes, not even GPS dared to follow them.
questions.fun_fact: The carriel is also called a “guarniel,” and some have secret pockets for hiding money.

questions.question: You're in Pasto. If people from Bogotá are called “rolos”, what are people from here called?
hints: Pasto is the capital of Nariño.
The word sounds a lot like the city's name.
It ends in “-uso”.
questions.description: A city so cold that even its nickname for locals comes wearing a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Pasto sits at the foot of the Galeras volcano, one of the most active in Colombia.

questions.question: This statue of a naked Bolívar on horseback is the great symbol of the “Perla del Otún.” Who made it?
hints: The artist was from Antioquia.
He was born in Fredonia and became famous for his giant monuments.
He also made the huge monument to the lancers of the Pantano de Vargas, in Boyacá.
questions.description: A national hero showed up in the town square without clothes, and nobody said a word.
questions.fun_fact: The statue was unveiled in 1963, when Pereira turned 100.

questions.question: Rondón, the signature dish of San Andrés, is a stew of fish, conch, cassava and plantain. What is it cooked in?
hints: It's a very common ingredient in Caribbean cooking.
It comes from the fruit of a palm tree.
It's white, made by grating that fruit's flesh with water.
questions.description: An island stew that takes its sweet time while the sea plays the music.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the English “run down”, as the Raizal people of San Andrés call it.

questions.question: The Colombian series “Los caballeros las prefieren brutas” was based on a book. Who wrote it?
hints: She's a Colombian humor writer and columnist.
The book is a tongue-in-cheek guide to relationships.
She shares her last name with one of Colombia's best-known business families.
questions.description: A series with a cheeky title and an author who laughs at stereotypes before anyone else does.
questions.fun_fact: The book was sold as a funny handbook about love before jumping to TV as a series.

questions.question: If you laugh at Andrés López's “La pelota de letras,” whose childhood are you remembering?
questions.answer: People who grew up in the '70s and '80s
wrong_answers: People who grew up in the '50s and '60s
People who grew up in the '90s and 2000s
People who grew up in the '30s and '40s
hints: Andrés López looks back at the toys, TV shows and scoldings from Mom of his own childhood.
TV had only a few channels, and kids played games out in the street.
There was already color TV and the first video game consoles were arriving, but no internet.
questions.description: A comedy show that makes parents feel old in under two hours.
questions.fun_fact: “La pelota de letras” became one of the most-watched comedy shows in Colombia and was released on DVD.

questions.question: It's sold from street carts, topped with sauces and crushed potato chips. What is a “perro caliente”?
wrong_answers: A dog lying in the sun
hints: It's food, not a pet.
You eat it with your hands, wrapped in a napkin, and the sauce drips easily.
There's a sausage inside.
questions.description: Relax: no puppies were harmed in the making of this question.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, hot dogs get pink sauce, pineapple sauce and even quail eggs.

questions.question: Huevos pericos are scrambled eggs eaten for breakfast with arepa. What gets chopped into them to make them pericos?
hints: Two ingredients found in almost every Colombian kitchen, and they add color to the eggs.
One is red, and the other is long and green.
One of them makes you cry when you chop it.
questions.description: A breakfast named after a chatty bird that doesn't make a peep.
questions.fun_fact: They're said to be called “pericos” (parakeets) because their green, red and yellow colors look like a parakeet's feathers.

questions.question: It goes on the bandeja paisa: cooked, dried and ground until it's like a powder. What meat is carne en polvo made from?
hints: It's not the same meat as the chicharrón.
At the butcher's, you ask for cuts like posta or bola.
It comes from a cow.
questions.description: The only meat that could fly off the plate if someone sneezes at the table.
questions.fun_fact: Carne en polvo was born in Antioquia as a way to make meat last and use every bit of it.

questions.question: In the Colombian Amazon it's toasted on big budares (griddles), it's grainy and yellowish, and it goes into fish broth. What is fariña?
hints: Its name comes from Portuguese, because Brazil is right next door.
It's sold by the sack at the Leticia market and eaten daily there, like rice.
It comes from a root that is poisonous if it isn't processed.
questions.description: Golden jungle sand that, luckily, you can actually eat.
questions.fun_fact: Yuca brava has a toxic juice that Amazon peoples learned to squeeze out before toasting it.

questions.question: It goes on top of the round arepa, you buy it at the corner store, and it’s the everyday paisa breakfast. What is “quesito”?
hints: It doesn’t melt like pizza cheese.
It’s white and crumbles a little.
It’s a fresh cheese that isn’t aged.
questions.description: A paisa breakfast favorite whose name comes in a cute little size so it sounds even tastier.
questions.fun_fact: Quesito antioqueño is made from curdled milk and sold fresh, without aging.

questions.question: You open the fridge in the morning to make calentado paisa. Which two leftovers from yesterday are a must?
hints: They're heated together in the pan with a little hogao.
Both come from yesterday's lunch, the everyday meal in paisa homes.
One is a white grain, the other a red bean cooked in a pressure cooker.
questions.description: The breakfast that proves yesterday's leftovers can be today's stars.
questions.fun_fact: Calentado is usually served with a fried egg, an arepa and hot chocolate or tinto (black coffee).

questions.question: Omar Geles and Miguel Morales founded the group Los Diablitos in Valledupar. In which decade?
hints: It was a time when vallenato was reaching radio stations all over the country.
By the early 1990s they were already famous for “Los caminos de la vida”.
It was the same decade as the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: Little devils so nice they got half of Colombia singing.
questions.fun_fact: Omar Geles, the accordion player of Los Diablitos, wrote hundreds of songs, including “Los caminos de la vida”.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: You play it by opening and closing one part, as if it were breathing.
It has buttons or keys on both sides.
It's the main instrument of vallenato.
questions.description: An instrument that never misses a party and always shows up ready to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The accordion came to Colombia from Europe by ship and ended up as the king of vallenato.

questions.question: You hear someone say “¡ajá!” all the time, coastal style. In which of these cities would that be LEAST typical?
hints: The coastal “ajá” is heard mostly near the Caribbean Sea.
Three of these cities are on the coast or in the Caribbean region.
The answer is an Andean city in the south, near Ecuador.
questions.description: Ajá, so what? Ajá, well… this question.
questions.fun_fact: On the coast, “ajá” works for everything: saying hello, asking, doubting, and even starting a juicy bit of gossip.

questions.question: You reach the last pages of “One Hundred Years of Solitude.” Which of these characters is NOT a parent or grandparent of Aureliano Babilonia?
hints: One of his parents is always surrounded by yellow butterflies.
The character you're looking for is actually his aunt.
With her he has a son with a pig's tail.
questions.description: The Buendía family tree needs its own GPS.
questions.fun_fact: Aureliano Babilonia is the one who finally deciphers Melquíades' parchments, just as Macondo disappears.

questions.question: José Asunción Silva wrote his famous “Nocturno” after the death of his sister Elvira. In which decade?
hints: It was in the 19th century.
Silva was one of the forerunners of modernismo.
It was in the last decade of that century.
questions.description: A poem so sad that even the shadows cry together.
questions.fun_fact: Silva's portrait appeared on the Colombian 5,000-peso bill.

questions.question: In a fishing village, the sea brings in a huge man; the people name him Esteban and paint their houses bright colors for him. Which Gabo story is it?
questions.answer: “The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World”
wrong_answers: “A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings”
“Monologue of Isabel Watching It Rain in Macondo”
hints: It is a short story by García Márquez from the late 1960s.
The main character arrives floating in from the sea.
The village women say he is the best-looking man they have ever seen.
questions.description: A story where a whole village falls in love with someone who never says a word.
questions.fun_fact: The story is part of the 1972 collection “The Incredible and Sad Tale of Innocent Eréndira and Her Heartless Grandmother”.

questions.question: Liberals and Conservatives agreed on the Frente Nacional, which began in 1958. What was it created for?
questions.answer: To take turns holding the presidency
wrong_answers: To give power back to Rojas Pinilla
To replace both parties with a new one
hints: It came after years of violence between the two traditional parties.
Liberal Alberto Lleras Camargo and Conservative Laureano Gómez agreed on it in Spain.
Every four years, the presidency passed to the other party.
questions.description: A political deal with more fine print than a cell phone contract.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Lleras Camargo was also the first secretary general of the OAS, founded in Bogotá in 1948.

questions.question: In the early 1950s, Colombia's league played outside FIFA and signed stars like Alfredo Di Stéfano. What is that era called?
hints: Clubs paid salaries no other country could match.
Millonarios, with Di Stéfano, was nicknamed “Ballet Azul.”
It was named after the legend of the city of gold the conquistadors searched for.
questions.description: An era when Colombian clubs signed players as if money grew on the stadium goalposts.
questions.fun_fact: Di Stéfano joined Millonarios in 1949 and left Bogotá for Real Madrid in 1953.

questions.question: In 1992, an El Niño drought emptied the reservoirs, the power went out for hours, and the “hora Gaviria” appeared. What was it?
questions.answer: Setting all clocks forward one hour
wrong_answers: Cutting the power for one hour every night
A daily radio speech by the president
The hour when all businesses closed
hints: It had to do with making better use of daylight.
Several countries do something similar in summer.
Overnight, when it was 6 in the morning, the clock already said 7.
questions.description: A time when Colombians learned to do their homework by candlelight.
questions.fun_fact: The hora Gaviria started in May 1992 and ended in February 1993, so many people had to get up while it was still dark.

questions.question: Before it reached your cup as a tinto, the coffee was a red cherry. Where did it grow?
hints: It grows on a plant, up in the mountains.
In Colombia there are lots of them in the Eje Cafetero.
It's a field full of coffee bushes.
questions.description: The official fuel of every Colombian office.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia a tinto is a black coffee, but in Spain it's a glass of red wine.

questions.question: I'm a green insect that lives in the grass of cattle pastures. My back legs are super long, and I use them to make huge jumps. What am I?
hints: I have antennae and wings, but I'd rather jump
People sometimes mix me up with the cricket
My name says I hop around in the grass
questions.description: Green, skinny and always rushing across the pasture.
questions.fun_fact: A grasshopper can jump about 20 times the length of its own body.

questions.question: In the Colombian countryside they call it “cocuyo”: it's tiny, comes out at night, and kids chase it. What is it?
hints: It's a small animal that flies.
You see it best when everything is dark.
It switches its little light on and off like a light bulb.
questions.description: A word you hear on the farm more at night than during the day.
questions.fun_fact: Fireflies make light that gives off almost no heat; it's called bioluminescence.

questions.question: Look at this moray eel from the reefs of San Andrés. Why does it keep opening and closing its mouth?
wrong_answers: To lure fish with its tongue
To swallow sand from the bottom
hints: It has nothing to do with food.
It does it even while resting quietly in its cave.
It's about its gills: this pushes water through them to take out the oxygen.
questions.description: It looks like it's giving you a long lecture, but don't take it personally.
questions.fun_fact: Moray eels have a second jaw in their throat that shoots forward to pull in their prey.

questions.question: Look at this round hole in a tree trunk on the farm. Which animal made it?
hints: It was a bird.
It made it by hitting the wood many, many times.
Knock, knock, knock against the trunk all day long.
questions.description: Someone remodeled this tree without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: A woodpecker can peck about 20 times per second.

questions.question: Look at this pelican from the beaches of Santa Marta. What does it use the pouch under its beak for?
wrong_answers: To store food for several days
hints: It dives headfirst into the water
It works like a net
It lets the water drain out and swallows its catch
questions.description: A bird with more pockets than a pair of cargo pants.
questions.fun_fact: A pelican's pouch can hold about 10 liters (2.5 gallons) of water.

questions.question: Look at this toad. How many legs does it have?
hints: It has legs in the front and in the back
The back ones are longer for jumping
It has the same number as a dog
questions.description: In Colombia a «sapo» is someone who tells on everybody; this one only tells you how far it jumped.
questions.fun_fact: Most toads have 4 toes on their front feet and 5 on their back feet.

questions.question: At the corner store you buy a candy for 1,000 pesos and pay with a 2,000-peso bill. How much change should you get?
hints: You paid more than the candy cost.
Subtract the candy's price from what you paid.
It's exactly half of your bill.
questions.description: The tensest moment at the corner store: when the shopkeeper opens the coin drawer.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia change is called “las vueltas”, but in other Latin American countries it's “el vuelto” or “el cambio”.

questions.question: A heroine of the fight for independence who was a seamstress and a spy was on the old 10,000-peso bill. Who is she?
hints: She is said to have been born in Guaduas, Cundinamarca.
