She carried messages to the patriots in Santafé de Bogotá.
People called her “La Pola.”
questions.description: The old money in the drawer can keep secrets from the fight for independence too.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia celebrates the Day of the Colombian Woman on November 14 in her honor.

questions.question: Which of these store chains did NOT start in Colombia?
hints: One of them arrived in the country just over ten years ago.
It began by opening stores in the Eje Cafetero.
Its owner is a Portuguese company.
questions.description: Four supermarkets walk into a party, and one of them shows up with a foreign accent.
questions.fun_fact: Tiendas Ara belongs to Jerónimo Martins, the Portuguese group that owns the Pingo Doce supermarkets in Portugal.

questions.question: You're at the tienda picking out candy. Which of these is NOT made by Colombina?
hints: Three of them come from a company in Valle del Cauca.
The odd one out is made by the same company that makes Corona chocolate.
The odd one out comes with stickers to collect in an album.
questions.description: A family of candies with one cousin who sneaked into the photo.
questions.fun_fact: Colombina was born in La Paila, in Valle del Cauca, and its Bon Bon Bum is sold in many countries around the world.

questions.question: Conchita appears with Juan Valdez in the ads and the famous logo. What is her job?
hints: She's a pack animal.
She walks the coffee mountains with something on her back.
She brings the harvest down from the farm.
questions.description: The most patient coworker in all of Colombian advertising.
questions.fun_fact: Conchita is a mule, the offspring of a donkey and a horse, an animal widely used to climb Colombia's steep coffee farms.

questions.question: In which decade did Víctor Gaviria’s “Sumas y restas” come out? It follows a Medellín engineer who gets into the cocaine business.
hints: The story is set in the 1980s, but it was filmed many years later.
Gaviria made it after “La vendedora de rosas”, which is from 1998.
It came out in the 21st century.
questions.description: A film where the numbers never add up, however big your calculator is.
questions.fun_fact: As in his other films, Gaviria worked mostly with non-professional actors, people from the street with no acting training.

questions.question: I’m from Medellín. My short film “Leidi” won the Short Film Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2014, and later I directed the feature “Amparo”. Who am I?
hints: I studied film in London before coming back to shoot in my home city.
“Amparo” tells the story of a mother trying to get her son out of military service.
My second surname is Soto.
questions.description: A paisa who flew home from France with a little golden palm tucked in his suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: “Leidi” was the first Colombian short film ever to win the Palme d’Or at Cannes.

questions.question: “Soñar no cuesta nada” tells the true story of soldiers who find millions of dollars hidden by guerrillas in the jungle. What year did they find it?
hints: The soldiers were in a counter-guerrilla battalion, and many were poor young men from the countryside.
It happened in Caquetá, shortly before the movie was made.
It was in the first years of the 21st century.
questions.description: Dig a hole in the jungle and find something no backyard garden has ever grown.
questions.fun_fact: It was one of the most-watched Colombian movies of its year.

questions.question: What is the sequel to “Romancing the Stone” (1984), Michael Douglas's adventure in the Colombian jungle, called?
hints: It came out in 1985 with the same stars.
The adventure moves from Colombia to Africa.
It takes place near Africa's longest river.
questions.description: Michael Douglas left the Colombian jungle still hungry for more adventure.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, Kathleen Turner plays a romance novelist who ends up living an adventure of her own.

questions.question: Franco Lolli made his debut in 2014 with “Gente de bien.” What was his next feature, about a Bogotá lawyer caring for her sick mother?
hints: It premiered in 2019 at Critics' Week in Cannes.
The lead is played by Colombian writer Carolina Sanín.
Its title is the Spanish word for someone fighting a case in court.
questions.description: A director from Bogotá who likes family dramas without the soap-opera shouting.

questions.question: You're on a farm in the Eje Cafetero and “Mi cafetal” comes on the radio. Who wrote this song?
hints: Surprise: he wasn't from the coffee region but from the Caribbean coast.
He played the flauta de millo and always went barefoot.
He also wrote the song that goes “Yo no olvido al año viejo”.
questions.description: A song that smells like freshly brewed tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Crescencio Salcedo is remembered as “the barefoot composer” because he refused to wear shoes.

questions.question: If you go out with a couple and you're the extra person, Colombians say you are “tocando…”. Which instrument completes the phrase?
hints: It's a string instrument.
It's a classic instrument of symphony orchestras.
It rests between the shoulder and the chin.
questions.description: When the couple holds hands and you hold your juice, all alone.
questions.fun_fact: “Tocar violín” is a very Colombian expression: in other Spanish-speaking countries they say “hacer mal tercio” or “ser el chaperón”.

previous.feedback: The fun fact doesn't say what the source says. The source calls «tocar violín» very Colombian and says other countries use «hacer mal tercio» or «ser el chaperón». The translation instead says the phrase is also used in Chile and Peru, and that Spain uses «hacer de carabina» or «hacer mal tercio». The Chile and Peru claim is plausible, so the source's "very Colombian" may be overstated (source: worth checking). But the claim that Spain says «hacer mal tercio» can't be confirmed, since Spain typically says «hacer de carabina» or «sujetar la vela». Bring the fun fact back in line with the source, or keep only claims that can be confirmed (for example the Colombian saying plus the English "third wheel").

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone says “me toca camellar todo el sábado,” what do they have to do all Saturday?
hints: It has nothing to do with riding an animal.
Colombians say it a lot on Monday mornings.
At the end of the month, you get paid for it.
questions.description: A word that came from the desert without a passport and settled down in Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, a job itself is also a “camello”: “¡por fin conseguí camello!” means “I finally got a job!”

questions.question: In the Llanos, what do they call the guide who knows every stream, every trail and every crossing of the savanna?
hints: The word is also used in Venezuela and Argentina.
Without one, you'd get lost among the swollen rivers of the rainy season on the plains.
It sounds a bit like «vaquero» (cowboy), but starts with a B.
questions.description: The GPS of the plains: it wears a hat and its battery never dies.
questions.fun_fact: In Argentina and Uruguay they spell it «baqueano», and it means the same guide who knows the land by heart.

questions.question: In Colombia, this word describes a shirt in loud colors, a living room full of gold ornaments and someone showing off huge chains. What is it?
hints: It's a criticism, not a compliment.
It's the opposite of elegant.
It's also an animal that howls at the moon.
questions.description: In Bogotá fashion, this is worse than going out in your pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Something in really bad taste is also called “una lobería.”

questions.question: In Colombia, who is most likely to say “¡qué calor, oís!” or “oís, ¿me vas a ayudar?”?
hints: In their city, people dance incredibly fast.
People there eat chontaduro and drink lulada.
They live in the “World Capital of Salsa”.
questions.description: A question that expects no answer, just your full attention.
questions.fun_fact: Cali calls itself the “World Capital of Salsa” and holds its Feria every December.

questions.question: It's noon and you haven't had lunch. Three of these phrases mean you're hungry. Which one does NOT?
hints: One of the four sounds like it's about food, but it's a trick.
That phrase isn't about the stomach but about the heart.
A paisa says it when they like someone very, very much.
questions.description: Your stomach starts its concert right in the middle of class.
questions.fun_fact: In Antioquia, being “tragado” with someone means being head over heels in love.

questions.question: The plebiscite of December 1, 1957, the first in which Colombian women voted, approved the Frente Nacional. What share voted Yes?
hints: Both big parties asked people to vote Yes.
The country was tired of La Violencia and the dictatorship, and wanted a deal.
For every No vote there were about twenty Yes votes.
questions.description: An election where millions of Colombian women stood in line to vote for the very first time.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian women won the right to vote in 1954, under Rojas Pinilla's government, but first used it in this plebiscite.

questions.question: It's sold from carts on the street and comes in lots of colors. What is a Bon Ice?
questions.answer: A flavored ice in a little tube
wrong_answers: A shaved ice with syrup in a little cup
A frozen fruit pop on a little stick
An ice cream sandwich in a little wrapper
hints: It's sweet, and mostly kids eat it.
It comes in blackberry, lime and mango, and you find it in parks and outside schools.
You bite off one end and squeeze it up as you eat.
questions.description: A street-cart classic that every Colombian kid has asked for at least once.
questions.fun_fact: To eat one, you bite or cut off the tip of the tube and suck it before it melts.

questions.question: Many people call the Amazon rainforest “the lungs of the planet.” Why did it get that nickname?
wrong_answers: Because it looks like a lung on the map
Because all the winds start there
Because its rivers clean the seawater
hints: It has to do with the air we breathe.
Trees do something with sunlight.
The leaves release the gas we need to live.
questions.description: The biggest backyard Colombia has.
questions.fun_fact: In fact, the rainforest uses up almost all the oxygen it makes; its big contribution is storing huge amounts of carbon in its trees.

questions.question: Hardly anyone sees them now, but the Colombian peso is divided into centavos. How many centavos make one peso?
hints: It's a round number.
The dollar and the euro are split into cents the same way.
It's a 1 followed by two zeros.
questions.description: So tiny that in Colombia not even the piggy bank wants them anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Because of inflation, centavo coins stopped being used in Colombia decades ago, and today the smallest coin in use is the 50-peso coin.

questions.question: You're having Corona hot chocolate for breakfast. How long ago was its maker, the Compañía Nacional de Chocolates, founded in Medellín?
hints: Your grandparents were already drinking this company's chocolate as kids.
It was founded early in the 20th century.
It was founded in 1920.
questions.description: A company that has been sneaking into your breakfast for decades without asking.
questions.fun_fact: The Compañía Nacional de Chocolates is now part of Grupo Nutresa, one of Colombia's largest food companies.

questions.question: You’re at the laundry sink with a bottle of Límpido. Which of these should you NOT wash with it?
hints: Límpido is a chlorine bleach.
Chlorine removes stains… and other things too.
It can leave pale spots where there used to be dye.
questions.description: The laundry bottle your mom keeps on the highest shelf for a reason.
questions.fun_fact: Bleach should never be mixed with other cleaners like ammonia, because together they release dangerous gases.

questions.question: Savital, famous in Colombia for its sábila (aloe vera), is sold even in little packets at the corner store. What product is it?
hints: You use it in the bathroom.
You put it on with water and it makes foam.
It's for your head.
questions.description: A desert plant that became the star of the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: Sábila, also called aloe vera, keeps a gel inside its leaves that people have used to care for their skin for thousands of years.

questions.question: I directed “Pura sangre” (1982), about a tycoon who needs young blood, and the documentary “Todo comenzó por el fin.” Who am I?
hints: With my friends, I invented what came to be called “tropical gothic.”
For many years, I ran the Cali International Film Festival.
My last name is the same as that of a former president of Colombia.
questions.description: A millionaire whose diet needs a lot more than vitamins.
questions.fun_fact: “Todo comenzó por el fin” is a documentary about his own illness and his friends of the so-called Grupo de Cali.

questions.question: In which decade was the Cinemateca Distrital de Bogotá, now called Cinemateca de Bogotá, founded?
hints: It was born around the same time as the Grupo de Cali in Cali.
It came before Focine was created.
It was founded early in the decade when “Star Wars” came out.
questions.description: A place in Bogotá where old movies never retire.
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, the Cinemateca de Bogotá opened a new, modern building in the city center.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says the new Cinemateca de Bogotá building opened in 2019, but I recall it opening in December 2018, and the rater had the same doubt. Please verify. If December 2018 is right, the source should say 2018 or drop the year.

questions.question: On a Holy Thursday, an earthquake destroyed much of Popayán’s historic center. In which year?
hints: It was in the 1980s.
That year's Holy Week processions couldn't take place.
It happened two years before the Armero tragedy.
questions.description: A Holy Week when the city had to swap its processions for scaffolding.
questions.fun_fact: After the earthquake, Popayán restored its colonial churches and mansions one by one, and its historic center looks as it did before.

questions.question: The Carnaval del Diablo in Riosucio, Caldas, isn't held every year. How often does it take place?
hints: It's held in January.
You wait less for it than for a FIFA World Cup.
It falls on odd-numbered years.
questions.description: A devil who loves a party so much that the whole town keeps count on the calendar.
questions.fun_fact: The Riosucio devil isn't evil: he is a cheerful symbol of the town's Indigenous, Black and white people coming together.

questions.question: Tourists come to Minca, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, to look for the animal group in which Colombia has more species than any other country. Which group is it?
hints: Sometimes all you have to do to see them is look up.
Visitors get up very early to see and hear them.
Hummingbirds and toucans belong to this group.
questions.description: In this Sierra village, your tinto comes with a jungle view and a blanket of fog.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has more than 1,900 recorded bird species, more than any other country in the world.

questions.question: The name Chapinero, in Bogotá, comes from the nickname of a Spanish craftsman who lived there in colonial times. What did he make?
hints: It was something people used every day to go out on the street.
What he made was very fashionable among the ladies of the time.
A “chapín” was a kind of footwear with a cork sole.
questions.description: A Bogotá neighborhood with a name from a craftsman's workshop and nightlife to spare.
questions.fun_fact: The craftsman, Antón Hero Cepeda, made chapines, footwear with thick cork soles, which is why people called him “el chapinero.”

questions.question: This statue in front of the San Felipe Castle in Cartagena honors the admiral who defended the city from the English in 1741. Who is he?
hints: He was a Spanish sailor born in the Basque Country.
His nickname was “Mediohombre” (“Half-Man”).
He was missing a leg, an eye and the use of one arm.
questions.description: An admiral who rained on a whole fleet's parade before it even started.
questions.fun_fact: In 1741 the English admiral Vernon arrived at Cartagena with a huge fleet and even had medals made to celebrate a victory that never came.

questions.question: It's the classic juice of a Colombian breakfast, and there its fruit is often sold green on the outside even when ripe. Which juice is it?
hints: It's also a breakfast classic in many countries outside Colombia.
Its tree's white, sweet-smelling flowers are a traditional wedding flower, called azahar in Spanish.
You squeeze it after cutting it in half, like a big, sweet lemon.
questions.description: The liquid alarm clock that gets to the table before the school bus does.
questions.fun_fact: In the tropics, oranges often stay green on the outside because there are no cold nights to take the green color out of the peel.

questions.question: In an old house, doors open by themselves, footsteps are heard at night and light bulbs flicker for no reason. In Colombia, people say the house is…
hints: It's a word that turns up a lot in scary stories and horror films.
It's what people say when they believe a place has ghosts.
The word has to do with witches.
questions.description: Not even the best electrician in the neighborhood can fix this house.
questions.fun_fact: Old houses creak at night because the wood shrinks as it cools, and that's why many of them seem haunted.

questions.question: In the Colombian countryside, people say the basilisk hatches from a very strange egg, hides near houses and kills with a single look. What is it?
questions.answer: A creature half rooster, half snake
wrong_answers: A creature half toad, half fish
A creature half bat, half dog
A creature half lizard, half owl
hints: It's a creature that also appears in very old European legends.
They say its egg is laid by an animal that doesn't normally lay eggs.
It has a bit of farmyard bird and a bit of reptile.
questions.description: Better not meet this creature's eyes, not even for a photo.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the basilisk's egg is laid by an old rooster, which is why country folk are wary of very old roosters.

questions.question: Riddle: “I already died, but I come back at night to the house where I lived and scare the people there.” Who am I?
hints: It isn't someone from this world.
Before it scared anyone, it was a person just like you.
In Spanish, its name comes from what it does: it suddenly shows itself.
questions.description: A tenant who moved out years ago but refuses to hand back the house.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Colombia, the soul of a dead person who returns to earth is called an “aparecido” or an “ánima en pena”.

questions.question: In Colombia, many people “se echan la bendición” before a trip or a penalty kick. What gesture do they make?
questions.answer: Making the sign of the cross
hints: It's done with just one hand.
It's a religious gesture.
You touch your forehead, your chest and both shoulders.
questions.description: Travel insurance that doesn't cost a single peso.
questions.fun_fact: Many Latin American soccer players make this gesture as they step onto the field, and some finish by kissing their thumb.

questions.question: María Elvira Arango hosts “Los Informantes,” Caracol Televisión's feature-story show. In what year did it premiere?
hints: When it started, almost everyone was already watching videos on their phone.
It premiered one year before a soccer World Cup.
It was the same year Colombia's national team qualified for the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.
questions.description: For people who always ask “And then what happened?” after every news story.
questions.fun_fact: Before “Los Informantes,” María Elvira Arango already had a long career as a journalist on Colombian newscasts and magazines.

questions.question: In Spanish, “Carta Magna” is to the Constitution as “pabellón nacional” is to…
hints: It's another, more formal name for a national symbol.
The word “pabellón” also means a tent or a big exhibition hall.
In Colombia it's yellow, blue and red.
questions.description: On July 20, even the national symbols dress up in their fanciest names.
questions.fun_fact: The word “pabellón” comes from the Latin “papilio”, meaning butterfly, because tents looked like its open wings.

questions.question: In Colombia, when the national anthem plays at an event, who must stand up?
hints: It's the same at soccer games, school events and official ceremonies.
It's a sign of respect for a national symbol.
Nobody is left out.
questions.description: Those first notes that interrupt even the most interesting conversation in the stadium.
questions.fun_fact: By law, Colombian radio stations and TV channels must broadcast the national anthem at 6 in the morning and 6 in the evening.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this paisa golfer is nicknamed “Spider-Man” for crouching almost flat on the ground to read the green. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Medellín and played college golf in the United States.
He was one of the first Colombians to win PGA Tour events.
His first name is the same as that of the singer of “Vida de Rico”.
questions.description: A superhero who traded his webs for a golf club.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo Villegas won five PGA Tour events, including two FedEx Cup playoff events in 2008.

questions.question: Hip hop has four elements: rap, DJing, breakdancing and one more that turned Medellín's Comuna 13 into an open-air museum. Which one?
hints: The fourth element isn't something you hear: you look at it.
Tourists walk around Comuna 13 taking photos of its walls.
It's made with cans of paint on walls.
questions.description: Some bring the beat, some bring the rhymes, some bring the moves; somebody had to handle the decorating.
questions.fun_fact: Comuna 13 has outdoor escalators that help residents climb the neighborhood's steep hills.

questions.question: Which Colombian painter made “Mona Lisa, Age Twelve” in 1959, his own version of Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa?
hints: He lived in Europe for many years.
He was born in Medellín and also made sculptures famous around the world.
His style is named after his surname.
questions.description: A very famous Italian lady who crossed the ocean and came back with a different face.
questions.fun_fact: A New York museum bought that painting in 1961, which helped make Botero famous around the world.

questions.question: In Encanto, Mirabel's red-haired aunt, married to Félix and mother of Camilo, has a gift. What does she control with her emotions?
hints: Her gift really shows when she's in a bad mood.
Félix tells her to take a deep breath and calm down.
When she's sad, a little cloud appears over her head.
questions.description: An aunt whose moods change so fast the whole family keeps one eye on her face.
questions.fun_fact: In “We Don't Talk About Bruno,” Pepa says that on her wedding day Bruno predicted rain… and a hurricane broke loose!

questions.question: I have a raspy voice and many Latin Grammys, and in 2005 I sang a duet with Shakira on her album “Fijación Oral, Vol. 1”. Who am I?
hints: I'm famous above all for my romantic ballads.
I was born in Madrid and I love flamenco.
Our song together is called “La tortura”.
questions.description: Two stars, one microphone and a heartbreak sung as a duet.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, Shakira released the English-language half of the project: “Oral Fixation, Vol. 2”.

questions.question: My name is Gloria Martínez, I was born in Condoto, Chocó, and I sing in ChocQuibTown with my brother and my husband. What's my nickname?
hints: My nickname is short and sweet, like something your family would call you.
My brother goes by Slow and my husband by Tostao.
It's a four-letter nickname that starts with G.
questions.description: A nickname so short it fits in any post, and it still filled stadiums.
questions.fun_fact: The name ChocQuibTown combines Chocó, Quibdó and the English word “town.”

questions.question: Shakira sang it with Wyclef Jean in 2006, the video became a classic, and its title says one body part doesn't lie. Which one?
hints: It's a body part that moves a lot when you dance.
It's where you put your hands when you stand with your elbows out, like a teapot.
It's between your waist and your legs.
questions.description: A body part more honest than most politicians.
questions.fun_fact: As a girl, Shakira learned belly dancing because of her Lebanese roots.

questions.question: It's in the Manrique neighborhood of Medellín, a house museum of tango honoring the genre's most famous singer. What is it called?
hints: Manrique is one of the most tango-loving neighborhoods in Colombia.
The museum keeps photos, records and keepsakes of a singer who died in Medellín in 1935.
Its name comes from the surname of the “Zorzal Criollo”.
questions.description: A place where the bandoneon has more fans than reggaeton.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín holds an international tango festival every year, and many say it is the most tango-mad city outside the Río de la Plata.

questions.question: “Ay, mi llanura”, the song about landscapes like this one, is now the official anthem of Meta. Who wrote it?
hints: He was from Norte de Santander and wrote both llanera and Andean music.
He also wrote “A quién engañas, abuelo”.
His last name starts with B.
questions.description: Herons, sunsets and a sky so big it doesn't fit in the song.
questions.fun_fact: Besides being a songwriter, Arnulfo Briceño was a lawyer by profession.

questions.question: It’s a fragrant pasture plant that horses trample as they pass, and many folk verses say the land “smells of mastranto.” Which region is it from?
hints: There’s never a shortage of harp, cuatro and maracas there.
It’s a land of cowboys, egrets and endless sunsets.
Villavicencio and Yopal are there.
questions.description: A perfume you won’t find at the mall.
questions.fun_fact: The word “mastranto” comes from the Latin “mentastrum,” meaning wild mint.

questions.question: People shout it at the San Juan and San Pedro festivals, along with bambucos, tamales and lechona. Which region does “¡Juepa jé!” come from?
hints: The Magdalena River runs through it between two mountain ranges.
The sanjuanero is danced there.
Its capitals are Ibagué and Neiva.
questions.description: A shout you can hear for miles whenever there's a party and a tamal involved.
questions.fun_fact: Ibagué is known as the “Musical Capital of Colombia.”

questions.question: They dress in white, speak Ikʉ and weave mochila bags in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. Which Indigenous people are they?
hints: They have lived on that mountain range for many centuries.
The men wear a white cap that recalls the snowy peaks.
Their neighbors are the Kogi and the Wiwa.
questions.description: They've carried mochila bags since long before school backpacks existed.
questions.fun_fact: For the peoples of the Sierra Nevada, the mountain range is the “heart of the world.”

questions.question: At festivals in Tolima and Huila, what is an “insulso”?
questions.answer: A sweet corn and panela dough
hints: Families share it at festival time.
It's sweet, even though in the Spanish dictionary its name means “tasteless.”
It often comes with lechona tolimense.
questions.description: Its name sounds boring, but grandmothers from Tolima would disagree.
questions.fun_fact: In the Spanish dictionary, “insulso” means bland and dull: the exact opposite of this sweet!

questions.question: It lives on Gorgona Island, is brown with triangle-shaped markings and hides among fallen leaves. What is the mapaná?
hints: It's an animal that stays still for hours, waiting for its prey.
The Spanish conquerors said Gorgona was crawling with these animals.
Because of it, rural hospitals keep antivenom on hand.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a tropical dessert, but better not invite it to dinner.
questions.fun_fact: The mapaná causes most of the snakebites recorded in Colombia.

questions.question: Look at the map: this department is named after the great river that forms its northern border. Which is it?
hints: It lies between the Orinoquía and the Amazon region.
To the north it borders Meta.
Its river joins the Orinoco on the border with Venezuela.
questions.description: A department that inherited its name from its wettest neighbor.
questions.fun_fact: The Guaviare River is one of the largest tributaries of the Orinoco, and it separates Guaviare from Meta and Vichada.

questions.question: It was born in Puerto Rico and Panama in the 1990s, and artists from Medellín took it around the world. What genre is it?
hints: Today it plays at parties almost everywhere on the planet.
Its basic rhythm is called dembow.
J Balvin, Maluma and Karol G sing it.
questions.description: The genre that gets even the aunt who swore it was just noise out on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín became so important to this genre that many people call it the world capital of reggaeton.

questions.question: This old Argentine milonga, sung by Tita Merello, opened every episode of “Yo soy Betty, la fea” in Yolanda Rayo's voice. Which is it?
hints: It was written by the Argentine Francisco Canaro.
She sings that people call her ugly, but they still come after her.
The title sounds like gossip: what people are saying about someone.
questions.description: A song older than your parents, and still it played in prime time.
questions.fun_fact: The song was already more than 40 years old when Betty reached TV screens in 1999.

questions.question: In Colombia, a paradero usually has a little roof, a bench and a sign with route numbers. What is it for?
hints: People stand there for a while.
When you see your route coming, you stick out your hand.
Passengers get on and off there.
questions.description: A place where patience is measured in minutes and hope at every corner.
questions.fun_fact: In systems like TransMilenio, the paradero is called an “estación”, and you can only get in by paying with a card.

questions.question: Work on the dirt road between Mocoa and San Francisco, nicknamed the Trampolín de la Muerte, began in the 1930s. Why was it built?
questions.answer: To move troops to the war with Peru
wrong_answers: To get oil out of Putumayo
To take coffee to the port of Tumaco
hints: Think about what was happening on the country's southern border around 1932.
The government urgently needed a faster route from the Andes to the far-off Amazon.
Soldiers had to be moved quickly to the Amazon.
questions.description: A road where the GPS doesn't say “turn right” but “hold on tight.”
questions.fun_fact: The road is full of curves and cliffs, and on many stretches only one car fits at a time.

questions.question: In Colombia, cars over a certain age must pass the yearly revisión técnico-mecánica: brakes, lights and emissions. Where is it done?
questions.answer: At a Centro de Diagnóstico Automotor
hints: It's a place with machines that test brakes and measure smoke.
People know it by a three-letter acronym.
Its acronym starts with C and ends with A.
questions.description: A checkup at the doctor's for your car, minus the waiting room with old magazines.
questions.fun_fact: For the emissions test, they put a probe into the exhaust pipe to measure what comes out of the engine.

questions.question: “Chichipatos” is a Colombian comedy series on Netflix. In Colombia, what is a “chichipato” person like?
hints: The word is used more as an insult than as praise.
It has to do with money, and with how little someone is willing to let go of it.
It's the person who never puts in their share for the “vaca”.
questions.description: Netflix gave its own series to a word you hear on any Colombian street corner.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “chichipato” is also used for a small-time crook, the kind who steals little things.

questions.question: What was Colombia's first regional TV channel, founded in 1985?
hints: It's a public channel, like all of the country's regional channels.
It was born in a mountain region, not on the coast or in the capital.
Its headquarters are in Medellín.
questions.description: Every region has its own channel, just like every grandma has her own recipe for ajiaco or bandeja.
questions.fun_fact: Telecaribe, the channel of the Caribbean coast, went on the air just one year later, in 1986.

questions.question: In December, many Colombian families make “hojaldras” for the novena. What are they?
hints: Despite the name (“hoja” means leaf), no leaves of any plant are involved.
People nibble them during the novena, often with hot chocolate or tinto (black coffee).
They go into hot oil and come out thin and puffy, dusted with powdered sugar.
questions.description: A Christmas snack that vanishes from the table before the novena is even over.
questions.fun_fact: The word “hojaldra” comes from “hojaldre,” Spanish for puff pastry, a dough that separates into thin layers like leaves.

questions.question: In Tolima and Huila, a “pastel de arroz” (rice cake) is not a dessert and has no cream. What is it?
questions.answer: A bundle of rice and meats in plantain leaves
wrong_answers: A puff pastry filled with rice and chicken
A baked savory rice and cheese cake
A big arepa stuffed with rice and cheese
hints: It's savory and cooks for hours in a big pot.
It has chicken, pork and peas mixed in with the rice.
It's a lot like a tamal, but without the corn dough.
questions.description: The sneakiest cake in the country: no candles, no frosting, no “Happy Birthday”.
questions.fun_fact: In Huila, pastel de arroz is a must at the San Pedro festivities, along with asado huilense.

questions.question: There’s a rice dish with chicharrón, chorizo, maduro and fried egg all mixed together. It’s the rice version of which famous dish?
hints: It’s such a big dish that very few people finish it.
It’s usually served with everything separate on a huge platter.
It’s the typical dish of Antioquia, with beans, arepa and avocado.
questions.description: A rice dish that ate a whole meal and is very happy about it.
questions.fun_fact: A full bandeja paisa can bring together more than ten different ingredients on one platter.

questions.question: In a vallenato group, one item is called a “trinche.” What is it?
hints: It's made of metal and has several thin prongs.
In many Colombian homes, “trinche” is another word for a fork.
The musician who plays the grooved cane instrument uses it.
questions.description: A word that means one thing in the kitchen and something very different on the vallenato stage.
questions.fun_fact: A traditional guacharaca is made of cane or palm, with grooves carved into it so it can be scraped.

questions.question: In the piquería at the Vallenato Festival, singers challenge each other by improvising décimas. How many syllables does each line of a décima have?
hints: It's an even number.
It's the typical line of Spanish ballads (romances) and many folk coplas.
It's the same as the number of legs on a spider.
questions.description: A duel where the weapons are rhymes and the only thing that gets hurt is pride.
questions.fun_fact: The piquería is one of the contests at the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata, along with the accordion contest and the new-song contest.

questions.question: You're listening to sabanero-style vallenato, from the savannas of Colombia's Caribbean region. Which of these cities is NOT home to that style?
hints: The sabanero style is different from the one played at the foot of the Sierra Nevada.
The savannas of that style are in Sucre, Córdoba and Bolívar.
The answer is the city of the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata.
questions.description: Not everything that sounds like an accordion comes from the same backyard.
questions.fun_fact: In the savannas of Sucre, Córdoba and Bolívar, vallenato lives side by side with porro and fandango, other rhythms of the region.

questions.question: In Colombia, when someone says “andén,” what are they talking about?
wrong_answers: The stop for the city bus
hints: It's on almost every street in the city.
It runs right next to houses and shops, a little higher than the street.
It's where people go on foot.
questions.description: A word that changed jobs in Colombia without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain and Mexico, an “andén” is the platform where you wait for the train; in Colombia, it's where you walk along the street.

questions.question: I'm made of wool, I have two sleeves, and you wear me over your shirt when it's cold in Bogotá. What do Colombians call me?
hints: You pack me in your suitcase when you go up to the cold highlands.
In other countries they call me a suéter.
My name has four letters and starts with S.
questions.description: Bogotá at 6 in the morning: the best ad this piece of clothing could ask for.
questions.fun_fact: In many countries “saco” means a suit jacket, but in Colombia it's the good old wool sweater.

questions.question: In a Colombian corner store, what does “regáleme un pan” mean?
hints: It's a polite way of asking for something.
At the corner store, “regalar” doesn't mean what it means at a birthday party.
Right after you say it, you take out your wallet.
questions.description: A shop phrase that has puzzled more than one tourist.
questions.fun_fact: Many visitors are surprised the first time: in Colombia, “regáleme” is just good manners, and you still pay.

questions.question: In Colombia I arrive twice a month, and everyone at the office can't wait for me. What am I?
hints: It has to do with your salary.
It covers half a month of work.
My name comes from the number fifteen.
questions.description: The reason the shopping malls suddenly fill up.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombians get their salary every two weeks, which is why the malls are packed on those days.

questions.question: I'm soft and warm, and I cover you in bed on cold nights. What do people in Colombia call me?
hints: I live on the bed.
You pull me over you when you lie down.
I'm often made of wool or fleece.
questions.description: The best friend of cold mornings when nobody wants to get up.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia a “cobija” is the blanket on the bed, and in the cold highlands almost nobody sleeps without one.

questions.question: It goes in the pencil case, and almost every student has one. In Colombia, what is an esfero?
hints: You use it to write.
You can't erase it like a pencil.
It has a tiny ball at its tip.
questions.description: The thing everyone borrows in class and almost never gives back.
questions.fun_fact: “Esfero” comes from “esferográfico”, after the tiny ball (esfera) at its tip.

questions.question: In Colombia, when someone says “ojo al dato,” what do they mean?
wrong_answers: You have something in your eye
hints: It's said right before something important.
Teachers use it before something that will be on the test.
It's like saying “look closely.”
questions.description: In Colombia some phrases are heard more often than the national anthem.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “ojo al dato” is heard on the news, in soccer broadcasts and in classrooms.

questions.question: In “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” Fernanda del Carpio came to Macondo from a cold, gloomy city. What was she raised from childhood to be?
hints: Her family was noble but had come down in the world.
She learned to discuss affairs of state with foreign rulers.
She was taught that one day she would have a crown and a throne.
questions.description: A lady so prim that nobody in Macondo dared serve her tinto in an ordinary pocillo.
questions.fun_fact: Fernanda married Aureliano Segundo, who searched the whole country for her after meeting her at the carnival.

questions.question: The Cali River is one of the seven rivers that flow through Cali. Which of these rivers does NOT flow through the city?
hints: Three of them are in Valle del Cauca.
The odd one out is in the Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero).
It is the river that supplies Pereira with water.
questions.description: A city with so much water that even the cat sat down to watch the river.
questions.fun_fact: On the banks of the Cali River stands “El Gato del Río”, Hernando Tejada's sculpture, which now has several painted cat “girlfriends” by other artists beside it.

questions.question: Look at this swamp, also called the Ciénaga de Tesca: the airport sits between it and the sea. Which city is it next to?
hints: It's a city on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
Its airport is called Rafael Núñez.
It's the walled city.
questions.description: A puddle with a holy name and a front-row view of the planes.
questions.fun_fact: The Ciénaga de la Virgen connects to the sea through a man-made channel, built to refresh its water.

questions.question: If you are born in Cartagena de Indias, what are you called?
hints: The word comes from the name of the city.
It's a city on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
It ends in “-ero”, like “ganadero”.
questions.description: A city's last name, worn with heat and with pride.
questions.fun_fact: People from Cartago in Valle del Cauca are called cartagüeños, and people from Cartago in Costa Rica are called cartagineses.

questions.question: A santandereano offers you “culonas”: they're gathered in the April and May rains and eaten toasted with salt. What are they?
hints: Before they reached the bag, they were alive.
In Bucaramanga and Barichara they're sold in paper cones.
They're the queens of their colony and fly out of their nest underground.
questions.description: A Santander snack: crunchy, salty and full of history.
questions.fun_fact: Culonas are the queens of the anthill and are packed with protein.

questions.question: In which decade did the first stage of the Gran Malecón del Río open, beside the Magdalena in Barranquilla?
hints: It's a fairly recent project.
It turned a riverbank once full of warehouses and factories into a promenade.
It opened a few years before the pandemic.
questions.description: The day Barranquilla finally turned around and looked at its river.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, Barranquilla turned its back on the river: that bank was full of warehouses and factories.

questions.question: The map highlights the region the costeños come from. What is it called?
hints: Barranquilla and Santa Marta are there.
Its beaches face a sea famous for pirates.
It has the same name as the sea to the north of Colombia.
questions.description: The heat here is so friendly it hugs you all day long.
questions.fun_fact: The Caribbean Region is home to the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the highest coastal mountain range in the world.

questions.question: Thanks to the Zenú tradition of weaving on upright looms, this town in the Montes de María, in Bolívar, is famous for its hammocks. Which town is it?
hints: It is near El Carmen de Bolívar.
Its crafts are sold along the Troncal de Occidente highway.
It is named after a saint.
questions.description: The favorite bed for a Caribbean-coast siesta, no mattress needed.
questions.fun_fact: San Jacinto’s hammocks are woven by hand on upright looms, and finishing just one can take several weeks.

questions.question: Francisco Herrera Campuzano founded San Lorenzo de Aburrá, in what is now El Poblado park in Medellín. In what year?
hints: It was in the 17th century.
It was decades before Medellín was granted the title of “villa” (town).
Cervantes and Shakespeare both died that same year.
questions.description: No metro, no silletas: back then there wasn't even a village.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín was granted the title of villa in 1675, almost 60 years after that founding.

questions.question: It's lunchtime at Ecomoda and Bertha Muñoz sits with the “cuartel de las feas.” Which of these was NOT part of the group?
hints: One of them looks down on the others.
She's Marcela Valencia's best friend.
Her nickname is “la peliteñida” (the bottle-dyed one).
questions.description: A company's most important meetings don't happen in the boardroom, but in the restroom.
questions.fun_fact: The “cuartel de las feas” got so famous that almost every version of Betty around the world copied its gang of gossiping secretaries.

questions.question: In what year did RCN premiere “El capo”, with Marlon Moreno as Pedro Pablo León Jaramillo?
hints: It was around the same time as “El cartel” and “Sin tetas no hay paraíso”.
It came before “Escobar, el patrón del mal”, from 2012.
It was the year of the H1N1 swine flu.
questions.description: A boss so tough that not even the remote dared to change his channel.
questions.fun_fact: “El capo” was such a hit that several more seasons were made.

questions.question: Which actor played Pedro Coral Tavera in “Pedro el escamoso”?
hints: He is married to actress Catherine Siachoque.
He is not Armando Mendoza from Betty, nor the star of “El capo”.
His last name starts with V.
questions.description: Open shirt, a little mustache and a dance move that became a national treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Coral's dance became so famous that people copied it at parties and schools all over the country.

questions.question: You wave me down on the street, tell me the address, and when we arrive I charge you for the ride. My car is almost always yellow. Who am I?
hints: I spend the whole day driving around the city.
Sometimes I ask you: “Which way should we go?”
My car has a sign on the roof.
questions.description: Knows more shortcuts around the city than any app on your phone.
questions.fun_fact: In Bogotá, the taxi meter traditionally shows “units” instead of pesos, and a chart turns them into the fare.

questions.question: In Colombia, about how many seated passengers does a microbús carry?
hints: It carries more people than a taxi.
It's smaller than a buseta.
More than ten fit, but fewer than twenty.
questions.description: Not so big it won't fit down the street, not so tiny you have to stand… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian towns, the microbuses that work as a “colectivo” don't leave at a set time: they go when they're full.

questions.question: You're on a street corner in Bogotá, about to use the crosswalk, the “cebra”. What should you NOT do?
questions.answer: Run across looking at your phone
wrong_answers: Wait for the little green man
hints: Three of these things keep you safe.
Cars should stop, but you still have to pay attention.
Your phone can wait until you reach the other side.
questions.description: It has stripes, never neighs, and lives on almost every street corner.
questions.fun_fact: Colombians call it a “cebra” (zebra) because its white stripes look like the African savanna animal.

questions.question: Look at the photo: on many rivers in Colombia, people ride rafts like this one. What do they use them for?
questions.answer: To cross or travel down the river
wrong_answers: To plant rice in the water
hints: It floats on the water.
It moves with a long pole or with the current.
It takes you from one bank to the other.
questions.description: Where the river is boss, the guadua bamboo obeys and nobody's in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The balsa tree, which grows in Colombia, has wood so light that it's used to build model airplanes.

questions.question: The Ciudad Bolívar district of Bogotá honors the Liberator. Which of these places is NOT named after Simón Bolívar?
hints: One honors another hero of independence.
That hero was called the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho.
Its capital is Sincelejo.
questions.description: A last name so famous it was enough to name countries, plazas and half the map.
questions.fun_fact: Ciudad Bolívar, in Venezuela, used to be called Angostura; Bolívar gave his famous Angostura Address there in 1819.

questions.question: Look at the photo: on Colombian highways, what do you call this place where you pay to keep going?
hints: It has booths with barriers that lift up.
Trucks pay more than cars.
On long holiday weekends, lines form before you reach it.
questions.description: A barrier that won't lift even for your nicest smile.
questions.fun_fact: Today many cars drive through without stopping, thanks to an electronic sticker on the windshield that pays automatically.

questions.question: San Andrés airport is named Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, after a former president. Which of these airports is NOT named after a president?
hints: The one you want was a military hero of independence.
He is remembered for shouting “¡Armas a discreción, paso de vencedores!”
It is the airport that serves Medellín.
questions.description: Landing in Colombia is basically a history class with your seatbelt on.
questions.fun_fact: Gustavo Rojas Pinilla ruled from 1953 to 1957, and television arrived in Colombia under his government, in 1954.

questions.question: Which of these workers does NOT need a helmet to do their job?
hints: Think about who isn't at risk of hitting their head.
They work indoors, away from traffic, heights and fire.
Their job is all about heads… other people's.
questions.description: You only get one head, so you'd better look after it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, when two people ride a motorcycle, the passenger, the “parrillero”, must wear a helmet too.

questions.question: Someone gets on the bus, says “Buenos días, señores pasajeros, disculpen la molestia…” and offers candy. Who is it?
hints: This person doesn't work for the bus company.
This person carries a bag or a box full of things.
This person offers things “dos por mil” (two for a thousand pesos) to the passengers.
questions.description: The only place where you can buy a candy, a pen and a speech all in one stop.
questions.fun_fact: Many of them drop a candy in each passenger's hand, then come back to collect either the money or the candy.

questions.question: “Metástasis” was the Colombian version of “Breaking Bad.” Which of these actors was NOT in its cast?
hints: Three of them played the chemistry teacher, his wife and his partner.
The odd one out is better known as a leading man in telenovelas and films.
He's an actor from Cali who was also in Netflix's “Narcos.”
questions.description: A chemistry class that ended very, very badly.
questions.fun_fact: In “Metástasis,” Walter White became Walter Blanco and the story moved to Bogotá.

questions.question: The letters in “Noticias RCN” come from a network that started on the radio. Fill in the blank: Radio Cadena…
hints: It was founded by businessmen from Antioquia.
It was born in Medellín, back when the radio ruled Colombian homes.
It means the opposite of “regional.”
questions.description: Three letters that bring you the news every night, and almost nobody knows what they stand for.
questions.fun_fact: RCN started as a radio network in the late 1940s and only became a private TV channel decades later.

questions.question: What year did “Protagonistas de novela” start on RCN, the reality show where young people lived in a house to win a lead role?
hints: It was at the start of a new millennium.
Back then, reality shows were only just arriving on Colombian TV.
It was the same year as the World Cup in Korea and Japan.
questions.description: A casting call that lasted for months, with cameras even in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: The “Protagonistas de novela” format was exported, with versions in other countries such as the United States and Venezuela.

questions.question: My name comes from George Orwell's novel “1984,” where someone watched everyone. In Colombia, Caracol aired me. Which reality show am I?
hints: In the novel, posters everywhere warned that someone was watching you.
The format started in the Netherlands in 1999 and spread to dozens of countries.
My name is about a family member who keeps an eye on you.
questions.description: Smile, you're on camera… 24 hours a day.
questions.fun_fact: The Colombian version aired on Caracol in 2003.

questions.question: It's a thick yellow soup. Its star ingredient is grilled on the street with butter and salt, and in cold regions it's served piping hot. What is it called?
hints: Its base isn't milk or egg, and it has no beef tripe either.
To make it thick, part of the kernels are blended.
Its main ingredient is sold at the market still wrapped in its husks.
questions.description: A soup so yellow you want to give the bowl a pair of sunglasses.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “mazorca” means the whole ear of corn, and when the kernels are young and tender they're called “chócolo.”

questions.question: On frijoles antioqueños, what is the tomato and onion sauce served on top called?
hints: It's slowly fried in a pan with just a little oil.
It's the base of tons of Colombian dishes, from arepas to sudado.
Its name sounds like “ahogado” (drowned), because the tomato cooks until it falls apart.
questions.description: A pot that's been on the stove for hours and still needs its hat.
questions.fun_fact: In many paisa homes, the beans are cooked with pig's feet and bits of green plantain to make the broth thick.

questions.question: It’s yellow, thick and a little sweet, made from ground young corn and eaten with melted quesito on top. What is it called?
hints: It’s sold a lot along highways and on paseos de olla (riverside cookout trips).
Its dough is made from fresh kernels, not packaged flour.
Its name uses the Colombian word for young corn.
questions.description: The breakfast that makes your stomach growl before it even reaches the table.
questions.fun_fact: Arepa de chócolo is often folded like a sandwich around a piece of quesito or cuajada.

questions.question: You're having a corrientazo for lunch, and next to the rice comes a shredded cabbage salad. What orange vegetable is usually mixed in with the cabbage?
hints: It's eaten raw, grated into thin strips.
People say it's good for your eyesight.
It's the favorite food of cartoon rabbits.
questions.description: The salad everyone leaves for last and then fights over.
questions.fun_fact: The “corrientazo” is the set lunch of the day at Colombia's everyday restaurants, with soup, a main plate and juice.

questions.question: The tamal tolimense, eaten for breakfast with hot chocolate, is tied up with cabuya string. What leaves is it wrapped in?
hints: They are big, green and shiny.
They are passed over a flame to soften them so they don't tear.
They come from the same plant that gives you maduro and patacón.
questions.description: The Sunday breakfast that calls for pajamas and a steaming cup of hot chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: The tamal tolimense is filled with rice, peas, egg, carrot, chicken and pork, and it cooks for several hours in a pot.

questions.question: It's chopped fruit floating in watermelon juice, eaten with a spoon from a cup, sometimes topped with ice cream. What is it called?
hints: It's cold and sells a lot in hot weather.
It has papaya, banana, mango and other fruits in little pieces.
Its name comes from the Spanish word for “to splash”.
questions.description: A fruit salad that jumped into the swimming pool.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Colombia, salpicón is made with Colombiana soda instead of watermelon juice.

questions.question: Riohacha, the capital of La Guajira, is one of the oldest cities in Colombia. In which century was it founded?
hints: It was the time of the first Spanish conquistadors.
Santa Marta and Cartagena were founded in that same century.
Only a few decades had passed since Columbus reached America.
questions.description: A city so senior it had a sea breeze before your great-grandparents’ great-grandparents were around.
questions.fun_fact: Riohacha is the home of Admiral José Prudencio Padilla, a hero of Colombia’s independence.

questions.question: Of the four vallenato rhythms, or “aires”, which is the fastest and liveliest?
hints: Accordion players use it to show off how fast their fingers are.
Its name is also the word for a pointed stick used to drive cattle.
In Spanish it rhymes with “suya” and “cuya”.
questions.description: A rhythm for people who dance as if the floor were on fire.
questions.fun_fact: At the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata, accordion players must play all four aires: paseo, merengue, son and puya.

questions.question: In which region of Colombia is it typical to greet any friend with “¿Qué más, primo?”
hints: It's hot there almost all year.
It's the land of vallenato and carnival.
Barranquilla and Cartagena are there.
questions.description: Over there everyone is family, even without sharing a single last name.
questions.fun_fact: On the coast, a friend is also called “mi vale.”

questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call the appliance in the kitchen that keeps milk, eggs and cheese nice and cold?
hints: It's in the kitchen.
Inside, it's very cold.
Its name comes from the Spanish word for snow.
questions.description: The cereal is already in the bowl… and that's when you find out someone finished the milk.
questions.fun_fact: The word “nevera” comes from “nieve” (snow): long ago, food was kept cold with ice and snow.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do you call a group of friends who go out together to have a good time?
hints: The same word is also used to say that something is a good plan.
This word can also mean a small piece of cloth, or a sticker.
It’s what gets sewn onto torn pants, and young people ask “¿cuál es el ___ hoy?”.
questions.description: What comes together on a Friday when nobody has a plan but everybody’s in the mood.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia a good plan is “un parche”, and a really great one is “un parchesazo”.

questions.question: I'm a writer from Bogotá. My novel “Satanás” (Satan) won the Biblioteca Breve Prize in 2002 and became a film in 2007. Who am I?
hints: My novels often wander through the dark streets of Bogotá.
I also wrote “Scorpio City” and “La ciudad de los umbrales”.
I share a surname with Plinio Apuleyo, Gabo's friend.
questions.description: A writer who gave his book a title that could scare grandma right out of the bookstore.
questions.fun_fact: The film “Satanás” was directed by Andrés Baiz and starred Mexican actor Damián Alcázar.

questions.question: This García Márquez book came out in 1992, with stories of Latin Americans in Europe like “I Only Came to Use the Phone.” Which is it?
hints: Its stories take place in cities like Barcelona, Rome, Geneva and Paris.
Another of its stories is “I Sell My Dreams.”
Its title calls its characters unusual travelers far from home.
questions.description: Stories that traveled more than a Colombian with a brand-new visa.
questions.fun_fact: Gabo said he wrote these stories over almost 18 years, and that he lost some drafts along the way.

questions.question: I'm a poet and essayist from Tolima. My novel “Ursúa” (2005) began a trilogy about the Spanish Conquest, and the second book won me the Rómulo Gallegos Prize. Who am I?
hints: Ursúa was a conquistador from Navarre who searched for El Dorado.
The second novel in the trilogy is “El país de la canela” (The Land of Cinnamon).
I also wrote the essay “¿Dónde está la franja amarilla?”.
questions.description: A poet who went deep into the Amazon jungle without ever leaving his desk.
questions.fun_fact: The trilogy ends with “La serpiente sin ojos” (The Eyeless Serpent), published in 2012.

questions.question: In “One Hundred Years of Solitude”, Pilar Ternera was mother to two Buendías, lived past 100 and read the future with this. What was it?
hints: She used this on a table and could mix it up.
José Arcadio and Aureliano went to her to learn what lay ahead.
It's also what you use to play poker.
questions.description: The fortune-teller of Macondo, who never needed wifi to see the future.
questions.fun_fact: Pilar Ternera came to Macondo with the families who founded the town and lived almost to the end of the novel.

questions.question: Around 1850, the Liberal Party split into young free traders and military men allied with the artisans. What were the two factions called?
hints: Both factions belonged to the same party; this was not Liberals against Conservatives.
One name comes from a speech about the hill where Jesus was crucified.
The other name comes from Draco, a Greek lawmaker famous for his very harsh laws.
questions.description: A family feud so serious that each side ended up with its own nickname.
questions.fun_fact: In 1854, the draconianos and the artisans backed General José María Melo's coup.

questions.question: In the chicherías of 19th-century Bogotá, people drank chicha. What is this traditional drink made from?
hints: The Muisca were already drinking it before the Spanish arrived.
Its main ingredient is a grain that was grown in the Americas before Columbus.
It's the grain on a mazorca.
questions.description: The trendiest bar in 19th-century Bogotá: no neon lights, but plenty of totumas.
questions.fun_fact: In the mid-20th century, campaigns warned that “chicha makes you dumb,” and in 1948 a law banned homemade chicha to push people toward beer.

questions.question: Camilo Torres wrote the “Memorial de agravios” to complain to Spain that criollos had fewer rights. In what year?
hints: It was before the Grito de Independencia.
It was around the time Napoleon invaded Spain.
It was just one year before the incident of the florero de Llorente (Llorente’s flower vase).
questions.description: The most famous complaint in Colombian history, and it never even reached its address.
questions.fun_fact: The “Memorial de agravios” was never sent to Spain: the Santafé town council thought it was too harsh.

questions.question: Finish the line from Rafael Pombo's poem: the poor little old woman left only “gold coins, jewels, lands, houses, … cats and a turpial.” How many?
hints: The poem exaggerates everything the old woman owned.
She had more cats than fingers on one hand.
It's the number that looks like two wheels stacked on top of each other.
questions.description: Colombia's “poorest” lady, with houses, jewels and pets to spare.
questions.fun_fact: The joke of the poem is that the old woman is called “poor,” but she had everything.

questions.question: This is the Astronomical Observatory of Bogotá, one of the first in the Americas. Which scholar was its first director?
hints: He was a criollo, born in New Granada.
He worked on the Royal Botanical Expedition.
He was called “el Sabio” (the Wise One), and a department bears his surname.
questions.description: A building for stargazing back when Bogotá didn't even have light bulbs.
questions.fun_fact: The Bogotá observatory was finished in 1803 and is said to be the first of its kind in the Americas.

questions.question: Rafael Pombo wrote “Simón el bobito,” “Michín” and “El gato bandido.” In what city was he born?
hints: It’s a city with a cold climate.
A foundation named after him is based there.
It’s the country’s capital.
questions.description: The grandfather of every rhyming children’s story in Colombia had to be born somewhere too.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo lived for several years in New York, where he translated and adapted children’s stories into Spanish.

questions.question: The Convention of Ocaña met to reform the Constitution of Cúcuta, but it failed and Bolívar took dictatorial power. In what year?
hints: It came after the Constitution of Cúcuta.
It was before Gran Colombia broke apart.
That same year, in September, there was an attempt on Bolívar’s life in Bogotá.
questions.description: A meeting so successful it ended with no agreement and a dictatorship.
questions.fun_fact: At Ocaña, Bolívar’s supporters clashed with Santander’s, and the Bolívar camp walked out so the convention would lack a quorum.

questions.question: Today's Colombian bills have raised marks you can feel with your finger. Who are they mainly meant for?
questions.answer: People who are blind or have low vision
hints: They help some people handle their money on their own.
You use touch instead of your eyes.
They work a bit like braille.
questions.description: Paper with national heroes, flowers and animals that everyone wants in their pocket.
questions.fun_fact: On today's Colombian bills, each value has a different size: the more a bill is worth, the longer it is.

questions.question: This milk brand was born in Antioquia in 1964 and has no single owner: it's a cooperative of thousands of dairy farmers. Which is it?
hints: Its slogan says it «sabe más» (“tastes better” and also “knows more”).
Its headquarters are in Medellín.
Its name blends the words «cooperativa», «lechera» and «Antioquia».
questions.description: Thousands of cows, thousands of farmers and one tanker truck in a big hurry.
questions.fun_fact: The name Colanta is a mash-up of «Cooperativa Lechera de Antioquia» (Antioquia Dairy Cooperative).

questions.question: Which of these sections will you NOT find in a Homecenter store?
hints: Homecenter is a store for fixing up and decorating your home.
That's where you buy drills, tiles and light bulbs.
For flu pills, you have to go somewhere else.
questions.description: The place where dads go in for one screw and come out with a new kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: Homecenter is the Colombian name of Sodimac, a chain that started in Chile.

questions.question: It’s a hot drink from Nariño made with fruit juice like lulo, blackberry or passion fruit, and its name says how it’s made. What is it?
hints: People drink a lot of it on the cold nights of the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos.
It’s sold steaming on the street, from big pots.
Its name comes from what happens to water at 100 °C (212 °F).
questions.description: In chilly Pasto, no jacket will do the job: you need a cup.
questions.fun_fact: In Pasto, adults order it “con” (with) or “sin” (without), meaning with or without a splash of aguardiente.

questions.question: Two rivals sing me with guitars, making up verses on the spot to answer each other, and my national festival is part of the Feria de las Flores. What am I?
hints: I’m very typical of Antioquia and the Coffee Region.
Whoever has the cleverest verse and the quickest comeback wins.
My name shares its roots with the troubadours of the Middle Ages.
questions.description: Two paisas, one guitar and zero fear of running out of words.
questions.fun_fact: In trova paisa the singers improvise without a script, and they often trade playful jabs in verse that make the whole crowd laugh.

questions.question: It's July 16 and you see parades of cars, buses and boats decorated with flowers for the Virgen del Carmen. Whose patron saint is she NOT?
hints: The celebration really shows on the highways and in the ports.
Many buses and trucks have a little picture of her next to the steering wheel.
The people who celebrate her work on wheels or on the water.
questions.description: Today the buses are better dressed than you are for a night out.
questions.fun_fact: The Virgen del Carmen is also the patron saint of the Colombian Navy, and on the coast she is carried in procession out to sea.

questions.question: At town fiestas, people light buscapiés. Going by the name, what does a buscapiés do once it's lit?
questions.answer: It runs along the ground among people
wrong_answers: It shoots up and bursts into colors
It gives off colored smoke, standing still
It booms like thunder in the air
hints: It's a type of small firework.
It doesn't fly high.
Its name says which part of your body it “chases.”
questions.description: At town fiestas, the fireworks have more nicknames than the mayor.
questions.fun_fact: The buscapiés is an old firework: it was part of fiestas in Spain centuries ago.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Answer, wrong answers and hints fit the name (buscapiés = ground-running firework that 'chases feet'). But I found no source saying the buscapiés was used at Spanish fiestas centuries ago. Sources only show similar ground-running devices (ratas de tierra) in older Spanish pyrotechnics.

questions.question: Medellín’s Desfile de Mitos y Leyendas brings out characters from Colombian folklore. Which of these is NOT a Colombian myth?
hints: Three of them haunt Colombia’s hills and rivers.
The odd one out comes from Guaraní tradition.
It’s famous in Paraguay and northern Argentina.
questions.description: A parade where the spooks come out in broad daylight and people clap.
questions.fun_fact: The Desfile de Mitos y Leyendas is part of the Feria de las Flores and has giant floats with spooks from paisa folklore.

questions.question: I was a songwriter from Colombia’s Caribbean coast, wrote “Mi vieja Barranquilla” and in 1974 revived a traditional parade of the Barranquilla Carnival. Who am I?
hints: I also wrote a song called “La Guacherna.”
I was born in Barranquilla in 1919.
People called me “la novia de Barranquilla” (Barranquilla’s sweetheart).
questions.description: A lady who wrote serenades to an entire city.
questions.fun_fact: The Guacherna parade that Esther Forero championed became one of the best-loved parades of the Barranquilla Carnival.

questions.question: At school, everyone is playing amigo secreto (secret friend) for the Día del Amor y la Amistad. What month is it?
hints: In Colombia, it's not celebrated on the same date as in many other countries.
It comes after the midyear school vacation.
It's the month right before October.
questions.description: The month when Colombia fills up with chocolates and people pretending they don't know who their secret friend is.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia it's celebrated on the third Saturday of September, so the date changes every year.

questions.question: It hangs from the ceiling at birthday parties, is shaped like a character, and kids hit it with a stick until it breaks. What is it almost always made of?
hints: It has to be light enough to hang up.
It has to break without anyone getting cut.
It's the same stuff boxes and notebooks are made of.
questions.description: The only party guest everyone wants to whack, and she's happy about it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, a whole kids' birthday party is often just called “la piñata.”

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer (paper and cardboard) is right. Glass, metal and stone are clearly wrong, and the hints are fine. The fun fact, that in Colombia a whole children's birthday party is also called "la piñata", could not be verified. The sources I found only say piñatas are common at Colombian birthdays. I found nothing on the party itself being called "la piñata". The "hang from the ceiling" detail is also loose, since piñatas are usually hung from a tree or a rope. The image query "children birthday party balloons" doesn't show a piñata.

questions.question: Born in Santa Marta, a star at Atlético Madrid, he joined Millonarios in 2024. Which animal is Radamel Falcao's nickname?
hints: It's a wild animal that roars.
It's a big cat.
It has black and orange stripes.
questions.description: A striker so dangerous in the box that even the jungle respects him.
questions.fun_fact: His dad, Radamel García, was also a soccer player and named him “Falcao” after the Brazilian star Paulo Roberto Falcão.

questions.question: In the Colombian league, what Spanish word is used for a team that has gone the whole tournament without losing a single match?
hints: It may have drawn, but it has never lost.
The word comes from Latin and means “not conquered”.
It looks a lot like the word “invincible”.
questions.description: A team that treats defeat like broccoli: it won't even try a bite.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin “invictus”, meaning “not conquered”, a motto of many Roman emperors.

questions.question: It wears a red-and-white vertically striped shirt with blue shorts, and its mascot is a shark. Which Colombian club is it?
hints: It's a club from the Caribbean coast.
It plays its home games at the Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Meléndez.
Its fans chant “¡… tu papá!”
questions.description: A team that bites on the field, and not because it's hungry.
questions.fun_fact: Junior's stadium is named after Roberto Meléndez, a striker from Barranquilla who was the club's idol in the 1940s.

questions.question: In 2017, Atlético Nacional, the Copa Libertadores champion, also won the Recopa Sudamericana. Who was its coach?
hints: He's a coach born in Cali.
Later he coached the national teams of Chile and Colombia.
Before that he took Honduras and Ecuador to World Cups.
questions.description: A trophy for teams that already won trophies: the encore of the encore.
questions.fun_fact: The Recopa pits the Copa Libertadores champion against the Copa Sudamericana champion.

questions.question: Independiente Santa Fe was the first champion of Colombian professional soccer. In which year?
hints: It was in the middle of the 20th century.
It was shortly after World War II.
It was the same year as the Bogotazo.
questions.description: The early bird catches the worm… and sometimes the very first star.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Fe was also the first Colombian club to win the Copa Sudamericana, in 2015.

questions.question: Look at the photo: it's the flower of the maracuyá, which many Colombians call “flor de la pasión” (passionflower). Who gave it that name?
hints: It happened in colonial times, more than 400 years ago.
The first drawings and accounts of this flower traveled from the Americas to Rome in the early 1600s.
They were religious men who came from Europe to spread their faith.
questions.description: A flower so eye-catching that someone wrote a whole story on top of it.
questions.fun_fact: The “passion” in the name has nothing to do with love: it refers to the Passion of Christ, which the missionaries believed they saw drawn in the flower.

questions.question: I'm made of fique or plastic fiber. Coteros carry me on their shoulders at the market, filled with about 50 kg (110 lb) of potatoes. What am I called in Colombia?
hints: At the plaza de mercado, people buy wholesale this way.
That's why someone who never moves is said to look like one.
It's a big, tightly stuffed sack.
questions.description: It weighs more than your school backpack on a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, when someone plays badly in a match, people say they were “como un bulto”: all weight and no movement.

questions.question: The palenqueras come from San Basilio de Palenque. In colonial times, what was a “palenque”?
questions.answer: A village behind a stake fence where people who escaped slavery lived
wrong_answers: An open-air market where Caribbean fruits were sold
A stone fort where the Spanish kept watch over the port
A large hacienda where sugarcane was grown
hints: They were hidden in the wild, far from the cities.
The people who lived there were called cimarrones.
The word comes from the posts, or stakes, that surrounded the place.
questions.description: Long before it rang out on Cartagena's beaches next to the cocadas, this word meant something else.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque, whose history is tied to the rebel leader Benkos Biohó, was recognized by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: The word “mousse”, as in passion fruit mousse, means “foam”. Which people gave it that name?
hints: Their language has given cooking lots and lots of words.
It comes from a country famous for its pastries and desserts.
Their language is spoken in Paris.
questions.description: A dessert with a name so fancy it sounds like it studied abroad.
questions.fun_fact: Mousse turns out fluffy because air gets whipped into the cream or egg whites.

questions.question: In the Eje Cafetero, the season comes when pickers fill their baskets with ripe red coffee cherries. What is it called?
hints: It happens when the fruit is finally ready.
It comes after planting and waiting.
It's when you gather what was planted.
questions.description: In the Eje Cafetero, even the mountains wake up smelling of tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has two coffee harvests a year: the main one and a smaller one called the “traviesa” or “mitaca.”

questions.question: At the school snack shop, you buy a 1,500-peso empanada and a 2,000-peso juice and pay with a 5,000-peso bill. How much change do you get?
hints: First, add up what you bought.
The empanada and the juice cost 3,500 pesos together.
Now subtract 3,500 from 5,000.
questions.description: The only store where the line is longer than recess.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian school snack shops, the empanada with ají is the undisputed queen of recess.

questions.question: It's December 31, minutes before midnight, and in many Colombian homes people sweep from inside toward the door. Why?
questions.answer: To get rid of the year's bad luck
wrong_answers: To make it rain in January
hints: It's one of the New Year's agüeros, like the grapes or the yellow underwear.
It's about what you don't want to carry into the new year.
The bad stuff from the old year goes out the door with the dust.
questions.description: When the year runs out, even a broom gets superpowers.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian New Year's agüero is carrying lentils in your pocket or wallet so you never run short of money.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in Colombia, on sports day you don't wear your everyday uniform to school, but your…
hints: It's the PE uniform.
It's comfy for running and jumping in class.
It has long pants made of soft fabric and a sports jacket.
questions.description: A student's closet has two personalities.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian schools, seniors in grade 11 show off a “prom jacket” with their names embroidered on it.

questions.question: It stays at the bottom of the rice pot, comes out toasted and crunchy, and families fight over it. What do Colombians call it?
hints: In Spanish, its name tells you where it stays.
You can't serve it with a ladle: you have to scrape it off.
It stays stuck to the pot.
questions.description: The kitchen's hidden treasure isn't in a chest, but in a pot.
