review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The crispy rice at the bottom of the pot is usually called 'pega' (Andean region) or 'cucayo/cucallo' (Caribbean coast); 'pegao' is used informally and is the common name in the Caribbean/Puerto Rico, but it is not clearly THE Colombian term. 'Chicharras' is also a regional name. 'Cuncho' (which in Colombia often means dregs or sediment) was not confirmed as a name for this rice, but I can't fully rule it out as a regional variant. The hint 'stays stuck to the pot' gives it away. The fun fact about rice cookers is unverified.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. "Pegao" (pega/pegao) is a real Colombian name for the crispy rice crust, so the answer is plausible. However, the Caribbean coast's most common name is "cucayo", and "pegao" is mainly Andean/Antillean, so "Colombia" is somewhat ambiguous. I found no source showing "cuncho" means this in Colombia. Some dictionaries list "cuncho" as a Colombian word for dregs or residue, and I couldn't rule out regional use for rice. Hint 1 ("its Spanish name says where it stays") is vague. The rice-cooker fun fact is plausible but I couldn't verify it.

Source: the translation is faithful, but the fact check is uncertain on points I can't confirm either. "Cuncho" is Colombian for residue or dregs at the bottom of a pot, so it may be a defensible name for the same thing, and the claim that rice cookers leave almost no pegao, "which is why" people prefer pots, is unverified. The source needs a clearly wrong replacement for "Cuncho" and a softer or sourced fun fact; "pegao" itself is fine as a Colombian word, though "pega" and "cucayo" are also regional names. Fact check: uncertain. "Pegao" is used in Colombia, but sources mostly give cucayo/cucallo (Caribbean coast) and pega (Andean region) as the Colombian names. Pegao is the usual name in Puerto Rico. The wrong answer "Cuncho" could not be ruled out: the Spanish dictionary may list it in Colombia for the rice stuck to the pot, but I found no source for that. The fun fact about rice cookers was not verified. One source mentions a rice cooker designed to make pegao.

source: the fun fact is unverified. Neither the fact check nor I can confirm that electric rice cookers leave almost no pegao, or that this is why many people still cook rice in a regular pot. The source should soften or replace it, for example with a fact about the regional names pega and cucayo. The answer itself is fine: pegao is a widely used Colombian word, and the regional variants pega and cucayo are not among the options. Fact check: wrong. The main weakness is that Colombia has several regional names for this, so the question has more than one defensible answer. Cucayo (Caribbean coast) and pega (Andean region) are the most common; pegao is also used on the coast. The wrong answers are fine: chicharrón and calentado are different foods, and I found no source that lists 'cuncho' in Colombia (it looks like a variant of the Panamanian 'concho' or of 'concón'). Hint 1 ('Its name tells you where it stays') is inaccurate, because 'pegao' means 'stuck', not 'at the bottom'. Hint 3 ('stuck to the pot') gives the answer away. I couldn't verify the fun fact about electric rice cookers.

Fact check: uncertain. 'Pegao' (or 'pega') is a valid Colombian name for the rice crust, mainly in Antioquia, Bogotá and the Andean region. The Caribbean coast says 'cucayo', so the answer is region-dependent. 'Cuncho' is listed as a wrong answer, but it is a documented Latin American word for dregs or residue at the bottom of a pot. My searches did not confirm or rule out its use for rice crust in Colombia, so it may be a valid alternative. The question also says 'What do Colombians call it?', which implies a single name. The 'Cuncho' distractor is risky, and 'Calentado' (reheated leftovers) is fine.

Fact check: uncertain. Pegao is the standard Colombian term. But "cuncho" is also reported as a regional word for the rice crust or dregs in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, so it may not be clearly wrong. My search did not confirm or rule this out. Other regional names are cucayo (Caribbean coast) and pega.

questions.question: A delivery arrives at the portería (front gate) of your conjunto. What device rings in your apartment to let you know?
hints: It hangs on the wall, near the door or the kitchen.

questions.question: At a Colombian school, you're sent to talk to the person in charge of the whole school. Which office do you go to?
hints: The person in charge of the school has an office of their own.

questions.question: It's a Colombian government survey that sorts households into groups with letters and is used for subsidies and subsidized health care. What is it?
hints: A surveyor visits homes and asks how the family lives.

questions.description: A survey that comes to your house and doesn't ask your favorite color.
questions.fun_fact: In Sisbén IV, group A covers households in extreme poverty and group D those that are not poor.

questions.question: It's always on the preschool supply list: it comes in colored sticks, you knead it with your hands and make little figures with it. What is it?
hints: It's a cheap supply that kids love to use in art class.
It doesn't dry out, so you can use it again and again.
You roll it into little snakes and balls.

questions.question: You go to the Registraduría to get your cédula. The Registraduría is to the cédula as the Cancillería is to the…
hints: The Cancillería handles relations with other countries.
You need it to travel outside Colombia.
It gets stamped at the airport.
questions.description: Every document has its own window, and every window has its own line.
questions.fun_fact: The Registraduría also runs the elections in Colombia.

questions.question: In the name of the YouTube channel “Calle y Poché,” what is “Calle”?
questions.answer: The last name of one of them

The name of their first pet

Each of them put something of her own into the channel's name.
The other member is named Daniela, and on her ID card “Calle” comes right after her first name.

questions.question: This man governed New Granada from Santafé on July 20, 1810, and a few days later was arrested and banished. Who is he?
hints: He held the post of viceroy.
He was the last viceroy before the Grito de Independencia.
His second surname is the name of the Spanish royal family.
questions.description: On July 20, 1810, he got up as the boss and went to bed with his job up in the air.
questions.fun_fact: The viceroy's wife, Francisca Villanova, was also arrested, and the crowd insulted her on the way to jail.

questions.question: Pablo Morillo created me during the Reconquista to take the patriots' houses, estates and goods and hand them to the Crown. What was my name?
hints: I was one of the three courts of the Reign of Terror.
My job was to seize property.
My name uses a Spanish word that today makes people think of kidnapping.
questions.description: A lost-and-found office, except nothing had been lost.
questions.fun_fact: The Consejo de Purificación tried suspect officials and the Consejo de Guerra tried patriot leaders: Morillo had a court for everything.

questions.question: July 20, 1810, was a Friday and market day, and the criollos took advantage of a crowded spot in Santafé. Which one?
hints: It was the city's main square.
Back then it was called the Plaza Mayor.
Today the Capitol and the Primatial Cathedral stand around it.
questions.description: If you want half the town to see you, pick your day and your spot carefully.
questions.fun_fact: The house that held Llorente's shop, on a corner of that square, is now the Museo de la Independencia – Casa del Florero.

questions.question: This town on the banks of the Magdalena River declared full independence from Spain on August 6, 1810. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the department of Bolívar.
Bolívar said he owed it his glory.
It's famous for its gold filigree and its Holy Week.
questions.description: A town so peaceful today that it's hard to believe it once shouted so loud.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar said, “If to Caracas I owe my life, to Mompox I owe my glory,” because he recruited many of his first soldiers there.

questions.question: Which popular leader from Pasto kept fighting for the King of Spain until 1824, when independence had already been won?
hints: He came from a humble background and rose to colonel in the king's army.
In 1824 he attacked the town of Barbacoas, on the Pacific coast.
His surname begins with the Spanish word for water.
questions.description: While half the continent shouted “Long live independence!”, someone in the south was shouting something else.
questions.fun_fact: Today many people in Pasto remember him as a local hero, and he even has a monument in the city.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: in the Patria Boba, in New Granada, the “carracos” and the “pateadores” were…
wrong_answers: Two battalions of the patriot army
hints: They fought over how to organize the new country.
One of them followed Antonio Nariño.

questions.fun_fact: The rivalry between centralists and federalists led to civil war, which is why the period earned the name “Patria Boba” (Foolish Fatherland).

questions.question: In February 1816, the Battle of Cachirí, in Santander, left the road to Santafé wide open. Which side won it?
hints: It was fought on a cold páramo, on the road from the country's northeast to the capital.
The beaten army had been retreating from the north and broke apart after the battle.
The winners served Ferdinand VII.
questions.description: A cold páramo where they settled who would reach the capital first.
questions.fun_fact: After Cachirí, the king's troops marched into Santafé in May 1816 with almost no resistance.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what do people in Colombia call this plant that grandma uses for burns and for hair?
hints: Its leaves are thick, with little spines along the edges.
Inside, it has a clear, cool gel.
In other countries it's called aloe vera.
questions.description: Grandma has more plants on the patio than the corner drugstore has remedies.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, a sábila leaf tied with a red ribbon hangs behind the door to bring good luck and keep bad energy away.

questions.question: The peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta call themselves “older brothers” because, by their tradition, their task is to…

For them, the Sierra is the heart of the world and must be protected.
questions.description: Being the older sibling was never just about age… or about keeping the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: For the peoples of the Sierra Nevada, whatever happens in those mountains affects the whole planet, which is why they call it “the heart of the world.”

questions.question: “Se va el caimán” tells of a man who turned half caiman, and his town holds a Caiman Man Festival every year. Which town?
hints: It's in the department of Magdalena.

questions.description: A song that gets everyone dancing, even though it tells the story of a man with very bad life choices.
questions.fun_fact: “Se va el caimán” was written by José María Peñaranda and became so famous that bands all over Latin America have recorded it.

questions.question: In Colombian villages, if you twist your ankle, who do they take you to so it gets put back in place?
hints: You find one in almost every village, and many people trust them more than the hospital.

questions.question: They speak Damana, were once called “Arsarios” or “Malayos,” and live in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. Which people are they?
hints: They are one of the four peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.

questions.question: You're in the main square of San Basilio de Palenque, facing a statue of a man breaking his chains. Who founded the palenque?
hints: He was an enslaved African who escaped near Cartagena more than 400 years ago.

His name starts with “Ben…”.

questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque is seen as the first free town in the Americas, and UNESCO has listed it as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Many communities in Colombia are bilingual, speaking Spanish and their own language. Which of these languages is NOT one of them?
hints: Three of these languages are heard in La Guajira, near Cartagena and on the Caribbean islands.

questions.description: Speaking two languages is like having two keys to the same house.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has about 65 Indigenous languages, plus Palenquero, Creole and Romani.

questions.question: Colombia’s Ministry of Culture coordinates the law that protects the country’s native languages. In which decade was that ministry created?

questions.description: Even culture needs someone to do its paperwork.

questions.question: In Colombia you can call a friend «socio». Which of these words is NOT used in Colombia to mean the same?

questions.question: You're celebrating a goal by the national team and get sprayed with espuma carioca (party foam). What does the word “carioca” mean?
hints: It's a word that comes from Portuguese.
It's what people call the residents of a Brazilian city famous for its carnival.
That city is home to Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana beach.
questions.description: Carnival's most dangerous weapon: it leaves everyone white, sticky and happy.
questions.fun_fact: People from Rio de Janeiro are called cariocas, while people from the city of São Paulo are called paulistanos.

questions.question: Jorge Carrascal played for CSKA and Dynamo, two big clubs from the same capital city. In which country are they?
hints: It's a European country with very cold winters.
It's the largest country in the world by area.
Both clubs are from Moscow.
questions.description: A midfielder who has traveled the world more than a suitcase lost at the airport.
questions.fun_fact: Before joining River Plate, Carrascal had already played in Ukraine for Karpaty Lviv as a teenager.

questions.question: The 2021 Copa América was supposed to be played in Colombia and Argentina, but it moved in the end. Which country hosted it?
hints: That country had also hosted the previous Copa América, in 2019
Colombia finished third there
The final was played at the Maracanã stadium
questions.description: A tournament that packed its bags at the last minute, like someone leaving on a trip without telling anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia beat Peru 3–2 for third place, with a stunning last-minute goal by Luis Díaz from outside the box.

questions.question: At this stadium in La Paz, about 3,600 m (11,800 ft) up, Colombia's national team runs short of air. Who was Hernando Siles, the man it's named after?
hints: He wasn't an athlete
He lived in the early 20th century
He governed from the Palacio Quemado in La Paz
questions.description: A stadium where even running to the bathroom counts as high-performance training.
questions.fun_fact: Hernando Siles was president of Bolivia from 1926 to 1930, and his son Hernán Siles Zuazo also became president.

questions.question: At the 2014 World Cup, goalkeeper Faryd Mondragón became the oldest player ever to play at a World Cup. How old was he?
hints: He had already played at the 1998 World Cup in France
He was over forty
He had had his birthday just three days before the match
questions.description: A goalkeeper who proved that gloves don't come with an expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: His record lasted until 2018, when Egypt's Essam El-Hadary played at a World Cup at age 45.

questions.question: I'm a stretch of rapids and rocks on the Orinoco River in Vichada, next to El Tuparro park. Alexander von Humboldt called me “the eighth wonder of the world.” What am I?
hints: I'm on the border between Colombia and Venezuela.
My name comes from an Indigenous people who lived in that part of the Orinoco.
My name starts with “Mai…”.
questions.description: A stretch of river so wild that even a German scientist was left speechless.
questions.fun_fact: Humboldt passed through these rapids in 1800, during his famous journey along the Orinoco.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this fog covers the páramo almost every day. What does it give plants like the frailejones?
hints: Páramos are high, cold places where it's almost never hot.
The fuzzy leaves of the frailejones catch something the fog brings.
It's the same thing that later flows down the rivers to the cities.
questions.description: A cloud that got tired of flying and lay down for a nap on the páramo.
questions.fun_fact: Frailejones catch water from the fog and release it little by little, which is why páramos are like water factories.

questions.question: Tayrona Park closes several times a year so nature can rest. About how many days a year is it closed in total?
hints: For most of the year, the park does welcome tourists.
It usually closes three times: in February, in June, and between October and November.
Each closure lasts about two weeks.
questions.description: Even paradise needs to take a vacation now and then.
questions.fun_fact: The closures are agreed with the Indigenous peoples of the Sierra Nevada, who use them for rituals to spiritually cleanse the land.

questions.question: About how many protected areas are in Colombia's National Natural Parks System?
hints: There are more than you can count on one hand.
It includes parks, flora and fauna sanctuaries, and reserves.
More than 50 but fewer than 100.
questions.description: A sticker album that collects jungles, páramos and reefs instead of soccer players.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park was Cueva de los Guácharos, in Huila, created in 1960.

questions.question: You're on the páramo in a thick jacket. The jacket is to you as what is to the frailejón?
hints: Think about why you put on the jacket.
It's what protects it from the cold and the frost.
If you touch its leaves, they feel as soft as a blanket.
questions.description: On the páramo, even the plants got dressed before going out.
questions.fun_fact: Some frailejones grow only about 1 centimeter (less than half an inch) a year, so a tall one can be more than 100 years old.

questions.question: In the triple jump, Caterine Ibargüen landed in a place like this one. What is it called?
hints: Long jumpers and triple jumpers land here.
After each jump, a judge measures the mark you left.
It ends up full of footprints, like a beach.
questions.description: This is where Olympic dreams land… and sometimes faces too.
questions.fun_fact: Before each jump, officials smooth the sand with a rake so the new mark shows up clearly.

questions.question: In an Olympic BMX final, like the ones Mariana Pajón races, how many riders start together from the ramp?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than six.
It's the same number as a spider's legs.
questions.description: A race where rolling down a ramp is only the start of the scare.
questions.fun_fact: The start ramp on Olympic BMX tracks is about 8 m (26 ft) high, almost as tall as a three-story building.

questions.question: At the Olympics held in this stadium, which Colombian woman won a bronze medal in wrestling?
hints: The stadium is the famous “Bird's Nest” of Beijing 2008.
Four years later, at London 2012, she won bronze again.
Her first name starts with J.
questions.description: A stadium that looks like it was built by a bird with a huge budget.
questions.fun_fact: At those same Beijing Games, weightlifter Diego Salazar gave Colombia a silver medal.

questions.question: In this sport, which Colombian won the silver medal in the light flyweight class at Rio 2016?
hints: It was at the same Games where Ingrit Valencia won bronze.
In the final he lost to a boxer from Uzbekistan.
His first name is very rare and starts with “Yuber”.
questions.description: A weight class named after an insect, but with very real punches.
questions.fun_fact: At Rio 2016, light flyweight was the lightest class in men's Olympic boxing, with a limit of 49 kg (108 lb).

questions.question: In which of these sports did Colombia NOT win a medal at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics?
hints: Colombia won five medals at those Games.
Anthony Zambrano in the 400 meters and Sandra Arenas in race walking both won silver.
Colombia's men's national team in this sport didn't even qualify.
questions.description: Japan, 2021: a Games that showed up a year late, like the bus at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: The Tokyo 2020 medals were made from metal recycled from old cell phones and other electronics.

questions.question: I have four wheels and an engine, I ride close to the ground, and I have no roof or doors. Juan Pablo Montoya started racing me as a kid in Bogotá. What am I?
hints: There are tracks for me in several Colombian cities, even in some shopping malls.
Many Formula 1 drivers start out with me as kids.
Mario and Luigi race me too in a very famous video game.
questions.description: A real car that shrank in the wash but still goes super fast.
questions.fun_fact: Montoya started karting at age 6 and went on to win Formula 1 races in Monaco and Monza.

questions.question: You're watching Sebastián Muñoz from Bogotá win his first PGA Tour event in Mississippi, in a playoff. What year is it?
hints: Before turning pro, Muñoz played college golf at the University of North Texas.
It was in the 2010s.
It was one year before the COVID-19 pandemic began.
questions.description: Golf: the only sport where whoever hits the ball the least wins.
questions.fun_fact: With that win, Muñoz became the second Colombian to win a PGA Tour event, after Camilo Villegas.

questions.question: Alongside the National Games, Colombia holds another competition between departments, with sports like boccia and goalball. Who is it for?
hints: It is usually held in the same year and region as the National Games.
Its best athletes can go on to other games held after the Olympics.
Goalball is played blindfolded, with a ball that has bells inside.
questions.description: A competition where the medals weigh the same, but the stories weigh double.
questions.fun_fact: In goalball the crowd must stay silent, because the players find the ball by the sound of its bells.

questions.question: Which of these figures from Cartagena's history was NOT a sailor?
hints: Three of them are linked to sea battles or attacks on Cartagena.
The one you want became famous for something he wrote, not for a ship.
He translated the Rights of Man into Spanish.
questions.description: A question that smells of salt, cannon smoke and tales from the high seas.
questions.fun_fact: The Colombian Navy has a training ship called “Gloria” that has sailed around the world several times.

questions.question: Which art critic, born in Argentina, founded the Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá and championed Obregón and Botero?
hints: She was no painter: words were her weapon.
She also hosted art programs on Colombian television.
She was born in Buenos Aires and also wrote novels.
questions.description: This lady told painters what nobody else dared to tell them.
questions.fun_fact: Marta Traba was also a novelist: her book “Las ceremonias del verano” won the Casa de las Américas Prize in 1966.

questions.question: You're at the Casa del Florero in Bogotá, which remembers July 20, 1810. Which of these did NOT happen that day?
hints: Look for something that happened years later.
One of these was a fight between armies, far from Bogotá.
It happened in 1819, near a bridge.
questions.description: It all started because someone wouldn't lend out a table decoration.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Llorente vase can still be seen in the museum, even though it's broken.

questions.question: I'm an artist from Córdoba, Colombia: I fill whole rooms with soil mixed with cinnamon and cloves, as I did at the 2022 Venice Biennale. Who am I?
hints: You smell my works as well as look at them.
I was born in Tierralta, Córdoba.
My installation in Venice was called “Earthly Paradise.”
questions.description: An artist who filled an entire museum without hanging a single painting on the wall.
questions.fun_fact: Her mountains of soil mix mud, spices and even cassava flour, and the smell fills the whole room.

questions.question: Look at the department highlighted on the map. Its capital is famous as “the City of Parks.” Which city is it?
hints: It's a department in the eastern Andes, famous for its hormigas culonas (big-bottomed ants).
Its people are called santandereanos.
The city sits on a plateau, not far from the Chicamocha Canyon.
questions.description: A city with so many parks that even the squirrels have to wait in line for a bench.
questions.fun_fact: Bucaramanga is also called “the Pretty City of Colombia.”

questions.question: Look at this pedestrian street in downtown Bogotá. When people stroll along it with no rush, watching artists and street vendors, what do they call that outing?
hints: It's a very long street that crosses Bogotá from south to north.
It runs past the Plaza de Bolívar.
The name of the outing comes from the street's number.
questions.description: Strolling with no rush, buying mango biche and watching a mime: the perfect Sunday plan.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, the Carrera Séptima was the old road that led out of Bogotá toward Tunja.

questions.question: Johnny Cay is a small cay a few minutes by boat from San Andrés, full of palm trees and white sand. What is it made of?
hints: It formed little by little in the sea.
Tiny living things built it.
Its sand comes from the reefs around it.
questions.description: An island so tiny you can walk around it before your raspado melts.
questions.fun_fact: The San Andrés islands are part of the Seaflower Biosphere Reserve, declared by UNESCO in 2000.

questions.question: The Torre Colpatria in downtown Bogotá has 50 floors, stands 196 m (643 ft) tall and glows with colored lights at night. What is it mainly used for?
hints: It was built by a financial group that gave it its name.
Thousands of people go there from Monday to Friday.
Inside you'll find desks, computers and meeting rooms.
questions.description: Bogotá's tallest Christmas tree, switched on all year round.
questions.fun_fact: Every year there is a race to run up its nearly 1,000 steps.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The fun fact is off. The Torre Colpatria stair race is usually quoted as 980 steps over 48 floors, so 'nearly 1,000' is about right for that source. The race is also not clearly 'every year', and one source gives 943 steps for 50 floors. The step count is inconsistent across sources. Height (196 m), 50 floors and office use are right.

source: the description calls Colpatria "Bogotá's tallest" (Christmas tree), but Torre BD Bacatá (about 216 m, finished 2016) is now taller than Colpatria (196 m), so the claim is out of date. Fix the source description first (e.g. "One of Bogotá's tallest Christmas trees, lit up all year round") and then translate it again. The rest of the translation is faithful and reads naturally. Fact check: wrong. The fun fact says 'almost one thousand steps'. That is fine, since sources give about 980 steps and an annual climb race. But the description calls it 'Bogotá's tallest' tower. Torre BD Bacatá (216 m, completed 2016) is taller than Colpatria (196 m), so that claim is outdated.

questions.question: Look at the photo: it's the India Catalina monument in Cartagena. A small replica of this figure is the trophy for some awards. Awards for what?
hints: They have been handed out in Cartagena for decades.
They honor telenovelas, newscasts and hosts.
What they honor, you watch on the screen in your living room.
questions.description: A bronze lady from Cartagena who moves into celebrities' display cases every year.
questions.fun_fact: The statue, by Spanish sculptor Eladio Gil, was installed in Cartagena in 1974.

questions.question: Near Villa de Leyva there's a field of stone columns once used to track the sun, called El Infiernito. Which people built it?
hints: They lived on the high plateau of Cundinamarca and Boyacá.
They kept track of time by watching the stones' shadows.
They are the same people behind the legend of El Dorado.
questions.description: A place named after eternal heat, right in Boyacá's chilly highlands.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish named it “El Infiernito” (“Little Hell”) because they saw it as a place of non-Christian worship.

questions.question: The photo shows a silletero from the Feria de las Flores parade. Which corregimiento (rural district) of Medellín do the silleteros come from?
hints: It's in the mountains east of Medellín, on the way to Rionegro.
Parque Arví is there.
Its name is the Spanish name of the island where Napoleon died.
questions.description: More than sixty years of carrying flowers down the mountain on their backs.
questions.fun_fact: The first Desfile de Silleteros took place in 1957 with about 40 silletas.

questions.question: You climb the stone steps of Ciudad Perdida in the Sierra Nevada. Roughly when did the Tairona start building it?
hints: It was long before the Spanish arrived.
It's older than Machu Picchu.
It happened about 1,200 years ago.
questions.description: A city so lost it took centuries to show up again.
questions.fun_fact: Ciudad Perdida is about 650 years older than Machu Picchu, and it was rediscovered in the 1970s.

questions.question: Look at this hat that farmers on the Caribbean coast wear to work in the fields. What does it mainly protect them from?
hints: It's very hot on the Caribbean coast.
It has a wide brim that gives shade.
It's what burns the most in the fields at noon.
questions.description: A hat with so many twists and turns it would make anyone dizzy.
questions.fun_fact: The sombrero vueltiao is woven from caña flecha and has been a cultural symbol of Colombia by law since 2004.

questions.question: A feudal lord is to his serfs as a colonial encomendero is to…
hints: They paid him tribute and worked for him.
The Crown “entrusted” them to him so he would convert them to Christianity.
They were the first inhabitants of these lands.
questions.description: A look back at colonial times, when titles were long and rights were very short.
questions.fun_fact: The Crown created the resguardos, protected Indigenous lands, partly to shield them from abuse by the encomenderos.

questions.question: It's called Colombia's “river star”: the Magdalena and Cauca rivers start there, near San Agustín. What place is it?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: It's in the south of the country, between Cauca and Huila.
Two of the mountain ranges split apart there.
Its name includes the country's name.
questions.description: The shower faucet for all of Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: The Magdalena River starts at the Laguna de la Magdalena, in the Massif, more than 3,000 m (9,800 ft) up.

questions.question: I'm round and flat, people made me from corn before the Spanish arrived, and you eat me for breakfast with butter and cheese. What am I?
hints: I'm cooked on a grill or on a clay griddle called a tiesto.
There are chócolo, egg and cheese versions of me.
My name starts with “a”.
questions.description: A recipe older than your grandparents' grandparents' grandparents.
questions.fun_fact: Indigenous peoples were already grinding corn on stones to make arepas centuries before Spanish rule.

questions.question: Look at this flag: which country is it from?
hints: It's a South American country with coasts on two oceans.
Its flag has the same colors as a neighbor's, but with no coat of arms in the middle.
It's the country of Encanto, coffee and Shakira.
questions.description: A question so easy that even the family parrot knows the answer.
questions.fun_fact: The yellow stripe takes up half of the Colombian flag: it's twice as wide as the blue and the red ones.

questions.question: According to tradition, how long has tejo been played in Colombia?
hints: It's one of the oldest games in the country.
It's linked above all to the highlands of Boyacá and Cundinamarca.
People say the first tejos were gold discs made by the Muisca.
questions.description: A sport where winning literally sounds like an explosion.
questions.fun_fact: Tejo is also called “turmequé”, after a town in Boyacá.

questions.question: Which Colombian landscape is on the back of the 100,000-peso bill, the one with Carlos Lleras Restrepo?
hints: It's a green, cold place in the mountains.
It's in Quindío, near Salento.
The wax palm, the national tree, grows there.
questions.description: The bill that brings the most joy when you find it in a forgotten pocket.
questions.fun_fact: The Quindío wax palm can grow over 50 meters (160 ft) tall, higher than a 15-story building.

questions.question: Your December prima (the bonus every employer must pay) arrives, but it's only half of the year's prima. In which month do you get the other half?
hints: It's in the first half of the year.
It arrives just before the mid-year vacation.
By law it must be paid by the 30th of that month.
questions.description: The extra cash that shows up just in time for natilla and buñuelos.
questions.fun_fact: By law, the December prima must be paid by December 20 at the latest.

questions.question: In which decade was Leonisa, the underwear and swimwear brand from Medellín, founded?
hints: It's older than most of the parents who buy it.
It was born shortly after television arrived in Colombia.
It was born in the middle of the 20th century.
questions.description: Paisa fashion that has seen a whole lot of beach seasons come and go.
questions.fun_fact: Leonisa started in Medellín and today sells its clothes in many countries across the Americas and Europe.

questions.question: Besides the big Carnival, Barranquilla has another one with its own queen, dance groups and parade. Who dances in it?
hints: It's been a tradition of the Carnaval de Barranquilla for decades.
The queen of this carnival can't vote or drive a car.
They're the shortest people at the whole party.
questions.description: Barranquilla has so much carnival that there's enough left over for a second one.
questions.fun_fact: Barranquilla's Carnaval de los Niños also crowns a child queen, who joins the queen of the grown-ups' carnival.

questions.question: At the Feria de Manizales, a queen is crowned in the International Pageant of… what?
hints: Manizales sits high in the Andes mountains.
It's one of the products Colombia sells most to other countries.
Juan Valdez carries it on his mule.
questions.description: Manizales picks a queen, and half the planet sends a contestant.
questions.fun_fact: Contestants from coffee-growing countries on several continents come to the International Coffee Pageant.

questions.question: It's “Faltan cinco pa' las doce” (five to midnight) on December 31 and, as the song says, you run home. Why?
hints: The song is about getting there on time, before the year ends.
It's the first thing many families do when the clock strikes twelve.
You do it with your arms, and with the person who gave you life.
questions.description: On December 31, everyone turns into an Olympic sprinter for the last five minutes of the year.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, as soon as the clock strikes twelve, the family lines up so everyone can hug everyone.

questions.question: They're made of colored paper, set out on sidewalks and windows in December, with a small candle inside. Besides decorating, what are these lanterns for?
questions.answer: So the wind doesn't blow out the candle
wrong_answers: To store the sweets for the novena
To wrap the presents from Niño Dios
To mark the homes that pray the novena
hints: They're used on the Noche de las Velitas.
Think about what happens to a candle outdoors.
The paper works as walls around the flame.
questions.description: A colorful little house that lights up only one night a year.
questions.fun_fact: Every December, Quimbaya, in Quindío, holds a festival famous for its giant paper lanterns lit with candles.

questions.question: Its Holy Week processions date back to the 16th century and are on UNESCO's heritage list. Which Colombian city holds them?
hints: It's the capital of Cauca, in the country's southwest.
It's known as “the White City.”
Its name starts with P.
questions.description: One week when the whole city walks very slowly, candle in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Popayán's processions were added to UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.

questions.question: It has the child's name and the date, sometimes a drawing of a chalice, and guests get one at a first communion. What is it called?
hints: Guests take it home with them.
It's small and almost always made of paper or card stock.
Its name comes from the Spanish verb for “to remember”.
questions.description: The official souvenir of a day when everyone behaves like a little angel.
questions.fun_fact: Many families keep the recordatorios from their children's and nephews' first communions for decades.

questions.question: They call me the “West Indian cherry,” and I have far more vitamin C than an orange. What fruit am I?
hints: I grow on a shrub in hot climates.
My juice is red and a bit sour.
Health food stores sell me as a powder, as a vitamin C supplement.
questions.description: Small, red and with more energy than a double tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Acerola loses its vitamin C very quickly after it's picked, which is why it's almost always sold as frozen pulp.

questions.question: You're eating guanábana and picking out the black seeds. What does the plant need those seeds for?
hints: If you plant them in soil, something happens.
They're like little packages of life.
Trees, flowers and vegetables all start from one of these.
questions.description: What you spit out of your juice has bigger plans than you think.
questions.fun_fact: A guanábana can weigh up to about 7 kg (15 lb) and have more than a hundred seeds.

questions.question: In Colombia, about how old are students when they graduate from once, the last grade of school?
hints: They've already finished primaria and bachillerato.
Their quinceañera party is long behind them.
They're almost old enough to get their cédula.
questions.description: The last year of school: more photos than classes.
questions.fun_fact: Grade once used to be called “sexto de bachillerato” in Colombia.

questions.question: In Colombia, what is a “morral”?
questions.answer: A bag you carry on your back
wrong_answers: A box for carrying your lunch
A case for pencils and crayons
hints: You use it to go to school.
It almost always has a zipper and comes in lots of colors.
It has two shoulder straps.
questions.description: A word that sometimes weighs more than the kid carrying it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, a “mochila” is usually the hand-woven kind, like the Wayuu or Arhuaco bags, while the school bag is the morral.

questions.question: Panama became independent from Spain on November 28, 1821. Which country did it join soon after, of its own free will?
wrong_answers: The United Provinces of Central America
hints: It is a country that no longer exists under that name.
Its name came from a dream of uniting several South American nations.
It included present-day Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador.
questions.description: An isthmus that decided in 1821 it would rather not live alone.
questions.fun_fact: Panama broke from Spain almost without fighting: it is said that many Spanish troops were paid not to fight.

questions.question: When Gran Colombia broke up, around 1830, how many countries did it split into?
hints: Panama had not separated yet.
One of them was called the Republic of New Granada.
Venezuela was one of them.
questions.description: A country so big it ended up not fitting inside itself.
questions.fun_fact: The flags of Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador all share yellow, blue and red as a memory of Gran Colombia.

questions.question: As Colombian history tells it, at San Mateo in 1814 Antonio Ricaurte destroyed Bolívar's “parque” rather than surrender it. What was it?
wrong_answers: The chest with the troops' pay
hints: In the military language of the time, “parque” didn't mean what it means today.
Ricaurte guarded it in the upper house of the hacienda while Bolívar fought below.
Today you might also call it a magazine, and not the kind you read.
questions.description: A park where nobody ever went on the swings.
questions.fun_fact: Ricaurte was born in Villa de Leyva, and today a town in Cundinamarca and another in Nariño bear his name.

questions.question: On July 4, 1810, in Pamplona, a woman stood up to the Spanish magistrate and took away his staff of command. Who was she?
hints: She was a Creole woman from a well-off Pamplona family.
She did it before July 20.
Her married name was Villamizar.
questions.description: When the staff of command changes hands, history changes too.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar called Pamplona the “Patriotic City” for being one of the first to rise up for independence.

questions.question: In 1813, Bolívar set out from New Granada, crossed the Venezuelan Andes and about three months later rode into Caracas in triumph. What is this campaign called?
hints: It’s not the 1819 one that ended at Boyacá.
It began near Cúcuta.
Its name expresses wonder and praise.
questions.description: Three months of hiking through the mountains, in boots and without GPS.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar began this campaign with fewer than a thousand soldiers and still crossed all of western Venezuela to Caracas.

questions.question: I appear in the wild as a pretty woman to trick hunters and woodcutters, but I move in huge leaps because I'm missing something. Who am I?
hints: I protect the jungle from those who harm it.
What I'm missing is below the waist.
I have only one leg.
questions.description: A lady of the forest you'd better not go walking with.
questions.fun_fact: They say La Patasola can leap so far that she catches anyone running through the jungle, even with just one leg!

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Medellín is to paisa as Bucaramanga is to…
hints: It's the capital of a department in northeastern Colombia.
People there are known for talking loudly and for saying “usted” even to their own children.
It's the land of the Chicamocha Canyon and the hormigas culonas.
questions.description: A name game to see who really knows the map by heart.
questions.fun_fact: Many santandereanos get called “bravos” (angry) because of the way they talk, even when they're just chatting calmly.

questions.question: In Colombian Sign Language, I spell out names that have no sign: each letter is a hand shape. What am I?
hints: Interpreters use it when a proper name without a sign comes up.
All you need is one hand and someone watching you.
My name comes from the Greek “dáktylos”, which means “finger”.
questions.description: An ABC you don't read: you watch it and then applaud.
questions.fun_fact: Almost every sign language has its own hand alphabet, and they differ from country to country.

previous.feedback: The answer "the dactylological alphabet" copies the Spanish "alfabeto dactilológico" word for word. English speakers call it the "manual alphabet" or the "fingerspelling alphabet", so the correct option reads as translationese, and the question becomes a test of Greek roots. A natural version would use "The manual (fingerspelling) alphabet" as the answer. The options and hint 3 would then need new wording, because "manual" comes from the Latin for "hand" and the question already mentions hand shapes.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, in southwestern Colombia the store hands you one for your groceries, and it's usually plastic. What is a «chuspa»?
