questions.description: A city where even the spooks line up to see the lights.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín's Christmas lights are put on by EPM, the city's public utility company.

questions.question: Which of these roles has Colombian actress Natalia Reyes NOT played?
wrong_answers: Lady in “Lady, la vendedora de rosas”
hints: Natalia Reyes shared the screen with Arnold Schwarzenegger.
She also worked with director Ciro Guerra in La Guajira.
The odd one out is a hired killer from Medellín, taken from a novel by Jorge Franco.
questions.description: Her résumé has more twists than a 200-episode telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: In “Terminator: Dark Fate” (2019), Natalia Reyes plays Dani Ramos, the young woman a robot from the future comes to hunt.

questions.question: Grandma gives you this hot drink when you have a cold: a brown block made from sugarcane, boiled in water, with lime squeezed in. What is it called?
hints: It is sweet and a little sour.
The brown block is sold at the corner store.
In the hot lowlands people also drink it cold with ice.
questions.description: The official syrup of every Colombian grandma, no prescription needed.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the world's biggest producers and consumers of panela.

questions.question: In the legend from Antioquia, the Sombrerón rides out at night on a black horse with two chained dogs. Who does he chase?
hints: He appears at night in the streets of Antioquia's towns.
His victims are people who've gone down the wrong path.
He throws his hat at those leaving the bar or betting money.
questions.description: A man whose hat is so big it needs its own parking spot.
questions.fun_fact: They say the Sombrerón's hat grows as it lands on its victim until it covers them completely.

questions.question: In the Llanos, they say El Silbón roams the plains at night, whistling. If you hear his whistle very close, what does it mean, according to the legend?
wrong_answers: That he's looking for someone else
hints: The legend plays with the opposite of what you'd expect.
His whistle tricks your ears.
The dangerous thing is hearing it soft and distant.
questions.description: The only ghost who knows the whole musical scale and uses it to scare people.
questions.fun_fact: They say El Silbón's whistle climbs up the notes do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti.

questions.question: You go out with binoculars. In which of these places in Colombia would you NOT see a condor flying free?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: The condor needs high mountains and strong winds.
Its full name, “Andean condor,” tells you where it lives.
One of these places is low, hot jungle.
questions.description: A bird so big that if it landed on your balcony, you'd have to ask it to scoot over.
questions.fun_fact: The Andean condor's wings can measure more than 3 meters (10 ft) from tip to tip.

questions.question: A Colombian saying warns that on Tuesday the 13th you should neither get married nor… what?
hints: In Colombia this is the unlucky day, like Friday the 13th in other countries.
It has to do with a trip.
Long journeys used to be made by ship.
questions.description: A day so unlucky that even the black cats stay home.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia and much of Latin America, the unlucky day is Tuesday the 13th, not Friday the 13th.

questions.question: In which century was Colombia's national anthem first sung in public?
hints: It happened after Colombia's independence.
When it premiered, radio didn't exist yet.
It was in the 1800s.
questions.description: A song so old your great-great-grandparents already knew it, and still nobody skips the chorus.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem was first sung in public on November 11, 1887, in Bogotá.

questions.question: Look at the photo: when the anthem plays at school, many people put their hand like this. What are they showing with it?
hints: People also do it when the flag is raised.
It's a way to honor your country.
It's the same thing you show when you listen carefully to your teacher.
questions.description: A gesture that doesn't say a single word, and still everyone understands it.
questions.fun_fact: The right hand goes over the left side of the chest, where the heart is.

questions.question: The red stripe on Colombia's flag honors certain people from history. Who are they?
hints: They are celebrated on July 20 and August 7.
They fought so that Colombia could be free.
Simón Bolívar is one of them.
questions.description: The bottom stripe of the flag belongs to someone, and it's not the kids in the back row.
questions.fun_fact: The red of the flag is also explained as a symbol of the courage and honor of the Colombian people.

questions.question: You're watching TV as the presidential sash is placed on the new president in Bogotá. What date is it?
hints: It's a national holiday.
The day commemorates a battle.
It was the Battle of Boyacá, in 1819.
questions.description: A three-colored outfit that only gets a new wearer every four years.
questions.fun_fact: The presidential sash has the colors of the flag and Colombia's coat of arms embroidered on it.

questions.question: They come in July and August, flags hang from houses and there are independence parades. What are these celebrations called?
hints: Schools hold flag-raising ceremonies for these dates.
One is on July 20 and the other on August 7.
They celebrate the Grito de Independencia and the Battle of Boyacá: the birth of the nation.
questions.description: The time of year when the flag goes out for a stroll through every window.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, July 20 and August 7 are public holidays that are never moved to a Monday.

questions.question: In November 2023 in Barranquilla, Colombia beat Brazil in World Cup qualifying for the first time, with two goals by Luis Díaz. How did he score both?
hints: Brazil took the lead, and Colombia came back to win.
Both goals came late in the match.
Two crosses came in from the wing, and he jumped higher than the Brazilian defenders.
questions.description: Four minutes that people in Barranquilla still talk about as if they lasted four years.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won 2-1, and Luis Díaz scored both goals in just four minutes after Brazil had taken the lead.

questions.question: In what year did Colombia play its first final of a FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup, in India, against Spain?
hints: It was after the pandemic.
Linda Caicedo was already playing for the senior national team that year.
It was the year Argentina won the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: A bunch of teenage girls who went further than plenty of grown-ups.
questions.fun_fact: Spain won that final 1–0 and Colombia finished runner-up, with Linda Caicedo just 17 years old.

questions.question: I was born in Quibdó in 1999, came up through Atlético Nacional and played several years for Genk in Belgium. I'm a center back for Colombia. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four.
After Belgium I played for Galatasaray in Turkey.
My last name is the Spanish word for a steep slope.
questions.description: A wall that came from the Pacific coast and learned to defend in Belgium.
questions.fun_fact: Quibdó, the capital of Chocó, is one of the rainiest cities in the world.

questions.question: From 1968 I managed Colombia's natural resources and created many national parks; in 1993 the Ministry of the Environment replaced me. What was my name?
hints: I was a government institute.
My name was an acronym that started with “In”.
My acronym included “recursos naturales renovables” (renewable natural resources).
questions.description: An acronym that sounds like a tongue twister and looked after half the country.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park, Cueva de los Guácharos, was created in 1960, before this institute even existed.

questions.question: A Ramsar wetland in Guainía is named after the Inírida, Guaviare and Atabapo rivers, which meet there. Which great river do its waters flow into?
hints: It's one of the longest rivers in South America.
Alexander von Humboldt traveled along it and studied it in 1800.
It gives its name to one of Colombia's great natural regions, the Llanos.
questions.description: A star that doesn't shine in the sky but flows through the jungle.
questions.fun_fact: Nearby rise the Mavecure hills, giant rocks that are among the oldest on the planet.

questions.question: In Colombia's national parks, like Tayrona, who pays the highest entrance fee?
hints: Not everyone pays the same.
It depends on where the visitor comes from.
They come from other countries.
questions.description: Nature is free, but taking care of it costs a bit of plata.
questions.fun_fact: The money from entrance fees helps pay for trails, park rangers and conservation programs.

questions.question: It's a red flower that lasts a very long time without wilting, grows on sandy savannas and is named after a jungle capital. Which department is it from?
hints: It's a department in eastern Colombia, on the border.
It borders Venezuela and Brazil.
Its capital is Inírida.
questions.description: A flower that flat-out refuses to wilt.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the “eternal flower” because even after it's cut, it keeps its color for a long time.

questions.question: In 2018, Caterine Ibargüen became the first Colombian to receive a major international award. Which one?
hints: In 2018 she won almost every competition she entered.
Usain Bolt received it several times.
It goes to whoever had the best track and field season on the planet.
questions.description: A trophy you don't win by jumping for joy… although in this case, it helped quite a bit.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, the men's award went to Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge, who had just broken the marathon world record.

questions.question: Weightlifter María Isabel Urrutia is one of the great stars of Colombian sport. Which department is she from?
hints: It's a department with a coast on the Pacific Ocean.
She was born in Candelaria, a town very close to the department's capital.
Its capital is the city of salsa, the “Sucursal del Cielo”.
questions.description: Some people lift weights, and some people lift a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, María Isabel Urrutia became Colombia's Minister of Sport.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian weightlifter. At Rio 2016 I got bronze after a rival was disqualified, and at Tokyo 2020 I won silver. Who am I?
hints: I compete in one of the lightest weight classes.
In Tokyo I competed in the 67 kg class.
My last name is also the name of a town in Cundinamarca.
questions.description: A man who can lift more than a whole stadium's spirits.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won no gold at Tokyo 2020: it came home with four silvers and one bronze.

questions.question: Which Colombian tennis player won the 2017 Australian Open mixed doubles with American Abigail Spears?
hints: He is a doubles specialist.
He was born in Cali in 1986.
He shares his first names with the navigator Elcano.
questions.description: In January, Melbourne burns, and not just from the sun: the rackets are on fire too.
questions.fun_fact: That mixed doubles title in Melbourne was the first Grand Slam of his career.

questions.question: At town festivals, people put up a very tall pole covered in grease, with prizes at the top, and try to climb it. What is it called?
hints: Almost everyone slips before reaching the top.
Contestants stand on each other's shoulders to make it.
In Spanish, “sebo” is another word for grease.
questions.description: A game where butter is your worst enemy.
questions.fun_fact: Games like the palo encebado exist in many countries, from the Philippines to Italy.

questions.question: Its creator was a painter born in Medellín, and in this style everything looks huge and round: people, fruit and even horses. What is it called?
hints: Its sculptures stand in squares of cities all over the world.
Its creator gave many sculptures to a square in downtown Medellín.
The painter's first name was Fernando.
questions.description: A paisa paintbrush that has been to more museums than most tourists.
questions.fun_fact: Botero said he didn't paint fat people: he painted volume, because he loved how big shapes fill a canvas.

questions.question: In what year did Justin Bieber spray-paint graffiti on a wall on Bogotá's Calle 26 during a concert tour?
hints: It was during a world tour that took him through several Latin American countries.
It happened in the 2010s.
It was the same year Pope Francis was elected.
questions.description: A pop idol, a can of spray paint and a national scandal: the perfect recipe for the evening news.
questions.fun_fact: It caused an uproar because Bieber painted with a police escort, while many Bogotá graffiti artists complained that police chased them for doing the same.

questions.question: I'm an artist from Bogotá. In 2007 I opened a 167 m (548 ft) crack in the floor of London's Tate Modern and called it “Shibboleth.” Who am I?
hints: My works deal with memory and the victims of violence.
In 2018 I made a floor from melted-down FARC weapons, called “Fragmentos.”
My first name starts with D.
questions.description: A work of art that literally hit the floor.
questions.fun_fact: The crack of “Shibboleth” was filled in after the exhibition ended, but the scar is still visible in the Tate's floor.

questions.question: During Holy Week in Popayán, what are the men called who carry floats like the one in this photo on their shoulders?
hints: Popayán's processions have gone out at night since colonial times and are UNESCO heritage.
They walk under the float's poles, with a cushion on the shoulder.
Their name comes from the Spanish verb “cargar”, meaning “to carry”.
questions.description: A job for strong shoulders, slow steps and a lot of devotion.
questions.fun_fact: In Popayán, being a carguero often passes from father to son, and some families carry the same float for generations.

questions.question: El Pibe Valderrama played in three World Cups in a row for Colombia's national team. In which decade were they?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
One of those World Cups was played in the United States.
They were Italy, the United States and France, one every four years.
questions.description: A head of hair that deserves its own sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: In 1987, El Pibe became the first Colombian named South American Footballer of the Year.

questions.question: I was a philanthropist from Antioquia, lived in a Medellín castle that is now a museum, and gave Itagüí its first library. Who am I?
hints: My family was behind some of Antioquia's big textile companies.
I bought the castle in the 1940s and filled it with European art and furniture.
The library in Itagüí carries my full name.
questions.description: A man who lived in a castle without being a king or a fairy-tale character.
questions.fun_fact: Museo El Castillo, in El Poblado, copies the medieval castles of France and has gardens open to the public.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. Answer is right (Diego Echavarría Misas, Coltejer family, Itagüí library bears his name). But hint 2 is false: he did not buy the castle in the 1940s. He had it built (c. 1930–1932) as a home with his wife Benedikta Zur Nieden, and filled it with European art.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the carbonero flower looks like a red pom-pom. What are those red “hairs” really?
hints: They have to do with how the plant reproduces.
At the tip of each “hair” there's a tiny bit of pollen.
They are the male part of the flower.
questions.description: A flower that got its hair done for the party, and now every strand is standing on end.
questions.fun_fact: The carbonero's petals are so tiny and greenish that hardly anyone notices them.

questions.question: Colombia is one of the countries with the most orchid species in the world. About how many does it have?
hints: Colombia is one of the most biodiverse countries on the planet.
A single cloud forest reserve can have hundreds of orchid species.
It's thousands, but not tens of thousands.
questions.description: A flower so elegant it has more cousins than a paisa family in December.
questions.fun_fact: More than 1,500 of Colombia's orchids grow in no other country.

questions.question: I’m a woman from Colombia’s Pacific coast: in the arrullos I sing the lead and the others answer me in chorus, to the cununo drum. What am I?
hints: You find me at wakes and saints’ festivals in Guapi, Timbiquí or Tumaco.
The women who answer me in the chorus are called “respondedoras.”
My name comes from the Spanish verb for what I do with my throat.
questions.description: In Guapi, the marimba, the cununo and the downpour never take a day off.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, UNESCO declared the marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia’s South Pacific region an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: In Pombo's poem, Mirringa Mirronga, la gata candonga, is throwing a party. What does she ask all the cats not to eat for lunch?
hints: It's something a cat hunts on its own.
She also doesn't want them eating the mice's bigger cousins for dinner.
They love cheese and are scared of cats.
questions.description: A cat party you have to show up to on an empty stomach.
questions.fun_fact: «Candonga» is an old word for someone sweet-talking and crafty, perfect for a flirty cat.

questions.question: It came out in 2018, J Balvin and Nicky Jam sing it, and its title is a single letter of the alphabet. Which letter?
hints: It's one of the least used letters in both Spanish and English.
In math, it stands for the unknown.
On pirate maps, it marks where the treasure is.
questions.description: A song with a title so short it fits on a soda bottle cap.
questions.fun_fact: The song is also listed as “X (Equis)”, and a remix with Maluma and Ozuna came out the same year.

questions.question: In what year did Karol G and Shakira release their song together, “TQG”?
hints: It was in the 2020s.
It came out on the album “Mañana Será Bonito.”
It was the same year as Shakira's session with Bizarrap.
questions.description: Two Colombian women, one microphone and a message for someone who just wasn't up to it.
questions.fun_fact: “TQG” stands for “Te Quedó Grande.”

questions.question: Karol G and Nicki Minaj sang about this in 2019. Complete it: in Colombia, having “tusa” means being…
wrong_answers: Sick with a cold and fever
hints: It has to do with the heart.
Time heals it… and so does despecho music.
It happens when your boyfriend or girlfriend leaves you.
questions.description: A word you hear at every reggaeton party in Colombia, even though nobody wants to have it.
questions.fun_fact: “Tusa,” by Karol G and Nicki Minaj, came out in 2019, and its video passed 1 billion views on YouTube.

questions.question: You're in Cali, the marimba de chonta is playing and everyone is at the Petronio Álvarez Festival. What month is it?
hints: It's not during the end-of-year holidays.
It's in the second half of the year.
It's the month for flying kites in Colombia.
questions.description: When Cali swaps salsa for marimba for a few days… and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: The festival celebrates the music of the Pacific coast and is named after Petronio Álvarez, who wrote the famous currulao “Mi Buenaventura.”

questions.question: In what year did Andrea Echeverri and Aterciopelados release the album “El Dorado,” with the song “Bolero falaz”?
hints: It was in the golden age of Spanish-language rock in the nineties.
It was their second album: the first had come out two years earlier.
It was right in the middle of the decade.
questions.description: A bolero called “deceitful” that turned out to be faithful to Bogotá forever.
questions.fun_fact: Besides being a singer, Andrea Echeverri is a ceramic artist: she studied art and makes clay pieces.

questions.question: Jorge Villamil, the doctor from Huila who wrote “Los guaduales” and “Espumas”, died in 2010. In which decade was he born?
hints: He was from Neiva, on the banks of the Magdalena River.
His most famous songs were on the radio in the 1960s and 1970s.
He was born the same year as the great New York stock market crash.
questions.description: A doctor who prescribed bambucos and pasillos for a broken heart.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Villamil was an orthopedic surgeon who wrote songs in his spare time; many of them sing about the landscapes of Huila.

questions.question: I'm the paisa word for when you feel so at home in a new place that you don't want to leave. What word am I?
hints: It's a good thing: it describes someone happy where they are.
It's often used when someone moves to a new city and things go well.
It comes from “maña”, as when you get used to something.
questions.description: You came for a weekend and you're already asking how much the rent is.
questions.fun_fact: When a paisa says someone “se amañó” in another city, it almost always means they don't plan to come back.

questions.question: On the Pacific coast of Chocó, a “potrillo” is carved from a single tree trunk, carries plantains and children steer it from a young age. What is it?
hints: It's not an animal, even if the name sounds like one.
It's made of wood and used for carrying things.
It moves along rivers with a paddle.
questions.description: In Chocó it rains so much that even the bunches of plantains ask for an umbrella.
questions.fun_fact: Many towns in Chocó have no roads: the rivers are the highways, and almost everything travels by canoe.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, you hear it in Pasto and in Ecuador, and it means a baby still carried in arms. What's the word?
hints: Grandmothers in southern Colombia use this word all the time.
In Cuba, this same word means a bus.

questions.description: Sleeps all day, eats every three hours and runs the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: In Cuba and the Canary Islands a “guagua” is a bus, so if you ask for one in Havana, nobody will hand you a baby.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this traditional Colombian dish called?
hints: It's cooked in a really big pot, sometimes over a wood fire.
It's a thick soup with yuca, plantain and corn on the cob.
There's a chicken one, a fish one and even a “trifásico” one.
questions.description: Sunday at Grandma's: the whole family shows up hungry, and nobody wants to leave.
questions.fun_fact: Sancocho “trifásico” gets its name because it has three meats: beef, pork and chicken.

questions.question: It's part of the Eje Cafetero, its capital is Pereira, and it's named after a river. Which department is it?
hints: It's in the Andean region, between Caldas and Valle del Cauca.
Its capital has a soccer team nicknamed “Matecaña”.
Its name starts with “Risa”.
questions.description: A department so into coffee that its mountains wake up already wide awake.
questions.fun_fact: The Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, which includes part of Risaralda, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.

questions.question: You're touring the capitals of the Caribbean departments. Which of these cities is NOT on your route?
hints: Three of them have coastal heat; the other has jungle heat.
The odd one out sits at the gateway to the Amazon.
It's the capital of Caquetá, and its name is Spanish for a famous Italian city.
questions.description: A road trip with a sea breeze that someone crashed wearing rubber boots.
questions.fun_fact: Florencia, the capital of Caquetá, is known as “the golden gateway to the Colombian Amazon.”

questions.question: It lies south of Cartagena, it has the famous Playa Blanca, and the Canal del Dique separates it from the mainland. Which island is it?
hints: It belongs to the department of Bolívar.
The Islas del Rosario lie just off its coast.
Its name has only two syllables and ends in “ú.”
questions.description: An island that cheated: it didn't used to be one.
questions.fun_fact: Barú was once a peninsula: it became an island when the Canal del Dique was opened, linking the Magdalena River with Cartagena Bay.

questions.question: Which of these natural wonders is NOT in the department of Guainía?
hints: Three of them are near Puerto Inírida.
The odd one out lies between Caquetá and Guaviare.
Its tepuis hide thousands of very old rock paintings.
questions.description: A list of Amazon wonders with one lost tourist in it.
questions.fun_fact: The Cerros de Mavecure are rocks more than a billion years old that rise like towers out of the jungle.

questions.question: It is the widest of Colombia's three mountain ranges, and both Bogotá and the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy are in it. Which is it?
hints: It is the one closest to the Llanos.
It splits in two, and one branch runs into Venezuela.
It's on the side where the sun rises over Colombia.
questions.description: Three mountain sisters, and one of them had a much bigger lunch than the others.
questions.fun_fact: The Cordillera Oriental splits in two near Cúcuta: one branch goes on into Venezuela and the other, the Serranía del Perijá, heads toward La Guajira.

questions.question: Bolívar won the Battle of Carabobo on June 24, 1821. In which present-day country was it fought?
hints: June 24 is a national holiday there.
It's the country where Bolívar was born.
Its capital is Caracas.
questions.description: A battle dated right at the start of summer vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Today Carabobo is also the name of a Venezuelan state, and its capital is Valencia, near where the battle was fought.

questions.question: Long before the peso, the Muisca traded salt for cotton blankets without using coins. What is this kind of exchange called?
hints: It's one of the oldest ways of trading in the world.
Some fairs in Colombia still do it today.
It's like swapping album stickers with a classmate.
questions.description: The oldest business deal in the world: no card reader, no cash, no Nequi.
questions.fun_fact: Salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón was one of the most valuable goods the Muisca traded with other peoples.

questions.question: You're watching the Baloto draw on TV. Where do the winning numbers come from?
hints: They get mixed well before every draw.
They roll around inside a see-through machine.
The game's name comes from the Spanish word «balota».
questions.description: Dreaming is free; the ticket, not so much.
questions.fun_fact: In many lotteries around the world, the balls are weighed and checked before use so that none has an advantage.

questions.question: In which decade did Colombia's two-color 500-peso coin with the Samán de Guacarí start circulating?
hints: It was before the year 2000.
Your parents probably used it when they were young.
It came out shortly after the 1991 Constitution.
questions.description: A coin so leafy you'd want to plant it in the backyard.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012 a new 500-peso coin arrived, swapping the Samán de Guacarí for a glass frog.

questions.question: Fruko y sus Tesos plays the salsa you dance to. Fruco makes a sauce, or “salsa” in Spanish. What kind?
hints: Fruco is a brand you find in the kitchen, not at the dance club.
It goes great with French fries and hot dogs.
It's red and comes from a fruit many people think is a vegetable.
questions.description: One with a “K” plays at the party, the other with a “C” waits in the fridge: don't mix them up.
questions.fun_fact: Today Fruco belongs to Unilever, the same multinational that sells soap and ice cream in many countries.

questions.question: Deportivo Pasto's nickname comes from the landscape around the city. Complete it: “los…”
hints: Pasto sits at the foot of a very special mountain.
It's the most famous mountain in Nariño, and it sometimes makes the news.
It's called Galeras, and now and then it puffs out smoke and ash.
questions.description: A team from the south that plays with a giant neighbor watching from above.
questions.fun_fact: Deportivo Pasto won its only league title in 2006, the first time the trophy went to the south of the country.

questions.question: Deportivo Pereira, in yellow and red, won the Colombian league for the first time in 2022. Roughly how many years had it waited since its founding?
hints: The club already existed when professional soccer began in Colombia.
Its fans call it “el Grande Matecaña”.
It was founded in the 1940s.
questions.description: The patience of its fans belongs in a museum.
questions.fun_fact: Pereira won that 2022 final on penalties against Independiente Medellín.

questions.question: Coach Santiago “Sachi”, who managed Atlético Nacional, is the brother of a famous Colombia defender from the 1990s. Who?
hints: That defender spent almost his whole career at Atlético Nacional.
He was nicknamed “el Caballero del fútbol” (the Gentleman of Soccer).
He won the 1989 Copa Libertadores with Nacional.
questions.description: Two brothers, one shade of green, and a jersey worn close to the heart.
questions.fun_fact: Atlético Nacional won the Copa Libertadores in 1989, the first ever for a Colombian club.

questions.question: Wool comes from sheep the way fique comes from…
hints: It comes from a plant, not an animal.
That plant has long, thick, pointed leaves.
That plant looks a lot like the agave used to make tequila.
questions.description: The toughest “wool” in Colombia, and not a single sheep got sheared.
questions.fun_fact: Cauca, Nariño and Santander are among Colombia's biggest fique producers.

questions.question: It's part of the paisa arriero's outfit and its name comes from “escápula.” What is the escapulario?
questions.answer: A religious cloth worn around the neck
wrong_answers: A leather strap for carrying the machete
A rosary of beads used for praying
A small pouch for keeping tobacco
hints: The escápula is the shoulder blade, and this thing rests on the shoulders.

questions.description: The paisa arriero never leaves home without this, not even when he forgets his lunch.
questions.fun_fact: The escapulario has two small pieces of cloth joined by cords: one falls on the chest and the other on the back.

questions.question: The loom is to the ruana as what is to the Wayuu mochila?
hints: It's a small tool that fits in your hand.
You use just one, not two as in knitting.
Its curved tip catches the yarn.
questions.description: With this, Wayuu weavers make mochilas that outlast your phone.
questions.fun_fact: Wayuu weavers learn as girls and, according to tradition, weaving was taught by a mythical figure called Walekerü.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what covers the skin of this fruit?
hints: Touch it with your fingertips.
Its cousin, the nectarine, doesn't have it: its skin is smooth.
It's made of very fine little hairs.
questions.description: The fruit everyone loves to draw in their notebook, right after the apple.
questions.fun_fact: The peach comes from China, even though its scientific name, Prunus persica, points to Persia.

questions.question: You're in the kitchen and take a bag of frozen maracuyá pulp out of the freezer. What are you going to make with it?
hints: It's for drinking, not chewing.
Many Colombian families serve it with lunch every day.
It's served in a glass, sometimes with ice.
questions.description: In a Colombian freezer, there's always a little bag waiting for its big moment.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia you can buy frozen pulp of loads of fruits, from mora and lulo to guanábana and corozo.

questions.question: Many Colombians carry the prayer of the Justo Juez (Just Judge) in their wallet to protect them from enemies and spirits. Who is the Justo Juez?
hints: He is the central figure of the prayer.
In Christian tradition, he is the one who will judge everyone at the end of time.
He was born in Bethlehem.
questions.description: A pocket lawyer who never charges a fee.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombian drivers hang holy cards or rosaries from the rearview mirror to protect them on the road.

questions.question: I was Señorita Colombia in 1991 and Miss Universe runner-up the next year. Later I hosted TV shows and acted in US series. Who am I?
hints: My family has Lebanese roots.
I went back to the national beauty pageant in Cartagena, but as a host of several editions.
I share my last name with a 20th-century Colombian president.
questions.description: Before she held a microphone, she had to hold a smile in front of the judges.
questions.fun_fact: The 1992 Miss Universe pageant, where Paola Turbay came second, was held in Bangkok, Thailand.

questions.question: I came to Bogotá as a singer with an opera company and set to music the verses that begin “¡Cesó la horrible noche!”. Who am I?
hints: I didn’t write the anthem’s words: a president took care of that.
I stayed in Bogotá and taught music for many years.
My name sounds very Italian and starts with O.
questions.description: Some verses were wandering around without a tune until someone with an ear for opera showed up.
questions.fun_fact: Síndici stayed in Colombia for the rest of his life and died in Bogotá in 1904.

questions.question: What does the gallinazo have on its head?
hints: In this way, it looks like its big cousin, the condor.
It helps the bird stay clean when it eats dead animals.
If you look closely, it seems to be bald.
questions.description: A bird that's always dressed for a funeral, yet goes through life completely relaxed.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the gallinazo is also called “chulo” or “golero,” depending on the region.

questions.question: According to the best-known explanation, what does the name “Cundinamarca” mean?
hints: The name is said to come from Quechua, the language of the Incas.
It has to do with an animal of the Andes.
That animal is now Colombia's national bird.
questions.description: A department with a tongue-twister of a name that sounds like a poem once you translate it.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá is the capital of Cundinamarca, although as a Capital District it is run separately from the department.

questions.question: They are private protected areas: a landowner chooses to conserve the land, registers it with Parques Nacionales, and Law 99 of 1993 recognizes it. What are they called?
questions.answer: Reserva Natural de la Sociedad Civil
wrong_answers: Santuario Campesino de Fauna y Flora
hints: It is not created by the government, but by private individuals.
Its name refers to ordinary people, not the government.
Its name contains the word “civil”.
questions.description: Owning a farm and planting nothing can also be very serious work.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has hundreds of these private reserves, and some are farms of only a few hectares.

questions.question: Bogotá wetlands like La Conejera and Juan Amarillo are rest stops on long journeys. For which animals?
hints: They come from very far away, sometimes from North America.
They travel through the air.
They have feathers and move to a different place depending on the time of year.
questions.description: Right in the middle of the city, there are free hotels for travelers who never book ahead.
questions.fun_fact: The tingua bogotana (Bogotá rail) is a bird that lives only in the wetlands of the Bogotá high plateau and the area around it.

questions.question: How many gold medals did Colombia win at the Rio 2016 Olympics?
hints: It was Colombia's best gold haul in its whole Olympic history.
One of those gold medals came in weightlifting.
They were won by a weightlifter, a female BMX rider and a female triple jumper.
questions.description: A trip to Brazil with samba, beaches and plenty to celebrate.
questions.fun_fact: In total, Colombia brought home 8 medals from Rio: 3 gold, 2 silver and 3 bronze.

questions.question: In 2013, Cali hosted a big event with roller skating, lifesaving and tug of war. What was it called?
hints: They are held every four years by an association backed by the International Olympic Committee.
Some sports that went through them, like karate, later made it to the Olympics.
The name sounds like the whole planet is playing, not just one continent.
questions.description: A sports party in the Sucursal del Cielo, with sports you don't see every day.
questions.fun_fact: Cali was the first city in Latin America to host the World Games.

questions.question: For years, Catalina Peláez has been one of Colombia's top athletes in a racket sport. Which one?
hints: It is played indoors.
Catalina Peláez has represented Colombia at the Pan American and Bolivarian Games.
The ball is hit against the front wall of an enclosed court.
questions.description: A racket sport where you're guaranteed to sweat from the very first point.
questions.fun_fact: Squash was born in England, at Harrow School, around 1830.

questions.question: You shake me before using me, I let out colored paint, and graffiti artists use me on the walls of Bogotá. What am I?
hints: I'm made of metal.
Inside me there's a little ball that rattles when you shake me.
Press the little button on top and the paint comes out as a fine mist.
questions.description: A street artist without this is like a goalkeeper without gloves.
questions.fun_fact: Spray paint cans have a little ball inside that mixes the paint when you shake them: that's why they go “clack, clack”.

questions.question: The yipao is a Willys jeep loaded to the roof with coffee, plantains or a family’s furniture, and it has its own parade. In which department did that parade begin?
hints: It’s one of Colombia’s smallest departments.
The Cocora Valley, with its wax palms, is there.
Its capital is Armenia.
questions.description: A car that carries more than a mule and never asks for a break.
questions.fun_fact: In the Coffee Axis, “un yipao” is also a unit of measure: whatever fits in a fully loaded Willys.

questions.question: In many versions of the tale, a doll is placed on Tío Conejo’s path to catch him. What is it made of?
hints: The rabbit hits the doll because it doesn’t answer his greeting.
With every blow he gets more stuck: his paws won’t come loose.
It’s the sticky black stuff once used to seal wooden ships.
questions.description: Tío Conejo learned the hard way that not everyone who stays quiet is a friend.
questions.fun_fact: The same tale exists in the southern United States, where the doll is called the “Tar-Baby” and the one who falls for the trap is Br’er Rabbit.

questions.question: Paisa trovadores got their name from Europe’s singing poets, the troubadours. When did those first troubadours appear?
hints: It was long before Columbus reached the Americas.
Around the same time, the first Gothic cathedrals were going up.
We’re talking about the 11th to 13th centuries, in southern France.
questions.description: Long before rap battles there were rhyme duels, only with a ruana and a carriel.
questions.fun_fact: The first troubadours didn’t sing in French but in Occitan, a language of southern France.

questions.question: It’s said softly and repeated again and again in a well-known Colombian song. What is “arrurrú” used for?
questions.answer: To put a baby to sleep
hints: It’s sung at night.
It goes with gentle rocking in someone’s arms.
It’s the word that fills lullabies.
questions.description: A word so soft it sounds like a cat purring.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries the same lullaby is sung with “arrorró” instead of “arrurrú”.

questions.question: I'm a paisa, and in 2022 I released a song named after a famous nightlife area of El Poblado, in Medellín. Who am I?
hints: As a teenager, I took part in a talent show on Colombian TV.
In 2023 I released a worldwide hit with Shakira.
My album “Mañana Será Bonito” reached number 1 in the United States.
questions.description: A song named after a neighborhood, so that half of Colombia would learn the address.
questions.fun_fact: Provenza is an area of bars and restaurants in the El Poblado neighborhood of Medellín, and it became even more famous after the song.

questions.question: It's the name of Carlos Vives's band, it's in the title of his 1993 album “Clásicos de la…” and it names vallenato country. What word is it?
hints: It's a single word that refers to a place, not a rhythm.
On the Caribbean coast, people use it to talk about Valledupar and the area around it.
In Spanish, it's what Argentina and Ecuador call their main divisions.
questions.description: A word that came by donkey from Valledupar and ended up being heard all over the world.
questions.fun_fact: With “Clásicos de la Provincia,” Carlos Vives recorded old vallenatos with a rock and pop sound and took them around the world.

questions.question: Camilo released “Vida de rico” (“A Rich Man's Life”) in 2020. What does the song's title mean?
questions.answer: That love makes him feel rich
wrong_answers: That he misses simple life in his hometown
hints: Camilo is known for his cheerful, simple style.
It became one of his catchiest songs of those years.
What makes him rich is being with the person he loves.
questions.description: A song you sing with a ukulele and an ear-to-ear grin.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo sings many of his love songs with Evaluna, his wife, in mind, and she also appears in his videos.

questions.question: In Jorge Velosa's carranga, “merengue” isn't the egg-white dessert. What is it?
hints: Velosa's music grew out of the rural traditions of Boyacá.
On carranga records, this word appears next to the titles of many songs.
It's a musical style people dance to at town fiestas, just like the rumba carranguera.
questions.description: In Boyacá, even something that sounds like dessert gets played with a ruana on.
questions.fun_fact: Although it shares its name with the famous Dominican merengue, carranga merengue sounds like the Boyacá countryside, not the Caribbean.

questions.question: This charro in the photo is a must at every Colombian party. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Jalisco and sang for more than 50 years.
He is known as “the King of ranchera music.”
His version of “El rey” by José Alfredo Jiménez is the most famous one.
questions.description: At Colombian parties, around midnight, this Mexican guest always shows up.
questions.fun_fact: His most famous line was that as long as the audience kept clapping, he would keep singing.

questions.question: I'm a paisa pasillo heard at every wedding, graduation and birthday, and I make parents cry. What song am I?
hints: I am sung above all as a tribute to parents.
I was written by Héctor Ochoa.
My lyrics travel through childhood, youth, love, having children and old age.
questions.description: A song that sends parents reaching for a handkerchief before anyone has cut the cake.
questions.fun_fact: “El camino de la vida” was chosen as the Colombian song of the 20th century.

questions.question: In Spain, people address a group of friends as “vosotros”. What word is used in Colombia instead?
hints: It's for speaking to several people at once.
In Colombia it works the same with friends and with strangers.
It's the plural of the word you use to address a teacher.
questions.description: Cross the Atlantic and even the way you address your friends gets a new passport.
questions.fun_fact: In Latin America almost nobody says “vosotros”: you mostly hear it in the Bible, in prayers and in some old dubbed films.

questions.question: Colombian law protects a language spoken in Bogotá and Girón as a native language, even though it came from Europe. Which one?
questions.answer: The language of the Roma people
hints: Its roots go back much farther than Europe.
Its speakers are a people famous for centuries for moving from place to place.
Their communities are organized in kumpañy.
questions.description: A language that reached Colombia with more miles on it than a long-haul truck driver.
questions.fun_fact: Romani was born in India more than a thousand years ago and traveled across Asia and Europe before reaching the Americas.

questions.question: In Cali, wandering around with no plan, on foot or by car, and ending up with a champús (a cold corn drink) is called “dar un…” what?
hints: It's a plan for relaxing, not for working.
You also hear it in the Coffee Region (Eje Cafetero).
It rhymes with the Spanish word for “round”: “redondo.”
questions.description: The favorite plan of anyone who leaves home saying “be right back” and returns three hours later.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, a good afternoon borondo often ends with a champús or a lulada, a drink made from the lulo fruit.

questions.question: You hear it a lot in Boyacá, usually with a “sumercé” attached. What does “mi Dios le pague” mean?
hints: You say it after you receive something, not before.
Whoever says it feels they owe a favor they can't repay on their own.
It's what you're taught to say when someone gives you a present.
questions.description: A phrase so polite it even brings heaven into the conversation.
questions.fun_fact: The idea behind the phrase is that since you can't repay the favor yourself, you ask God to repay it for you.

questions.question: A sock without its partner is called a “media chulla,” from a Quechua word. In which Colombian department do people say it?
hints: It's in the south of the country.
It borders Ecuador.
It's home to the Carnival of Blacks and Whites (Carnaval de Negros y Blancos).
questions.description: The washing machine ate a sock, and one part of Colombia even has a word for the survivor.
questions.fun_fact: In Ecuador, people say “chulla vida” to remind you that you only live once.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It's in the north of the country.
Its capital is Montería, on the banks of the Sinú River.
It shares its name with a city in Spain and another in Argentina.
questions.description: A department that, seen from above, thinks it's one of a kind… just like all its neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The sombrero vueltiao, a cultural symbol of Colombia, is woven mainly in Tuchín, Córdoba.

questions.question: Juanchito, in Candelaria, lies just across the bridge over the Cauca River, and caleños have gone there on weekends for decades. What is it famous for?
hints: What people do there has a lot to do with Cali's fame.
People who go there usually come back at dawn with tired feet.
You go there to dance to timbales, trumpets and congas.
questions.description: A place where caleños lose all track of time every weekend.
questions.fun_fact: Juanchito is sometimes called “the cradle of Cali's rumba”, and although it belongs to another municipality, it's only minutes from downtown Cali.

questions.question: In the brass bands of the Córdoba savannas, one rhythm has the bombero (bass drummer) hit the drum's wooden rim, not the skin. Which one?
hints: It's played by brass bands with clarinets, trumpets and euphoniums.
You hear it at town festivals in the Sinú River valley.
Its name comes from «palito» (little stick), said the coastal way.
questions.description: A rhythm that makes the town band pull even the tuba out of the closet.
questions.fun_fact: Porro has two main styles: palitiao and tapao, where the bombero mutes the drum skin with his hand.

questions.question: In the Caribbean I mean “ruckus” or “a huge mess,” and in northern Cali I'm a famous salsoteca (salsa bar). What word am I?
hints: It's a word you hear in salsa songs from Cuba and Puerto Rico.
It's a cousin of “bochinche” and “zafarrancho.”
It rhymes with “loco.”
questions.description: A word with so much flavor it should be served with ice and lime.
questions.fun_fact: Cali's salsotecas have no live band: the star is the DJ with his old salsa records.

questions.question: My son Viviano Torres founded Anne Swing and sang champeta in my own Creole language, mixed with Spanish. What town am I?
hints: I'm in Bolívar, near Cartagena.
I was founded by enslaved people who escaped and made themselves free.
UNESCO declared me a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
questions.description: A town where the music pours out of the picó and the pride is heard at full volume.
questions.fun_fact: Champeta mixes rhythms of the Colombian Caribbean with African music, such as soukous from the Congo.

questions.question: Gustavo Quintero, nicknamed “el Loco” for his moves and shouts on stage, sang chucu-chucu in Medellín. With which band?
hints: Its records play every December at paisa parties.
Its name is a single plural word after “Los.”
Its name sounds like finishing high school or college.
questions.description: A singer who moved so much on stage that the microphone asked for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Around the same time, Rodolfo Aicardi was a hit in Medellín with Los Hispanos, another chucu-chucu star.

questions.question: It's held in Cali, salsa schools from around the world compete, and one of its categories is called “cabaret.” What does that category feature?
questions.answer: Lifts and acrobatics in the air
wrong_answers: A single dancer with no partner
hints: It's the most spectacular category of the Festival Mundial de Salsa.
This category takes a lot of strength and a lot of trust between the two dancers.
The couples do circus-like stunts.
questions.description: In Cali, salsa is taken so seriously that it even has its own world championship.
questions.fun_fact: Cali's salsa schools have won many world championships thanks to their lightning-fast footwork and their acrobatics.

questions.question: In 1804 a Spanish expedition reached Cartagena with a vaccine passed from arm to arm among children. Which disease was it against?
hints: It left marks on the skin of those who survived.
No mosquito spreads it.
It was the first human disease wiped off the planet, in 1980.
questions.description: A trip across the Atlantic where the smallest passengers were the most important ones.
questions.fun_fact: The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow, because the first one was made from cowpox.

questions.question: “Tarde lo conocí” told the life of Patricia Teherán. After singing with Las Musas del Vallenato, which group did she found?
hints: It was an all-female group, like the one before.
The new name also came from Greek mythology.
Like Athena or Aphrodite, who lived on Mount Olympus.
questions.description: An accordion, a caja and a guacharaca walk into a telenovela… and come out crying.
questions.fun_fact: Patricia Teherán was one of the first women to succeed in vallenato, a genre sung almost only by men for decades.

questions.question: In Bogotá, the word “ñero” came from clipping “compañero.” What does it mean today?
questions.answer: A rough, street-smart person with crude manners
wrong_answers: An elegant person from a good family
A person who is stingy with money
hints: It's not exactly a compliment.
You hear it in everyday Bogotá slang, never in a formal speech.
It's pretty close to what a gamín is.
questions.description: A word that went on a diet and lost two syllables along the way.
questions.fun_fact: “Ñero” started as a friendly short form of “compañero” and over the years came to mean someone rough and street-wise with bad manners.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea”, what is the name of Beatriz Pinzón Solano's strict, very protective father?
hints: He's an old-fashioned man who lives with his family in a Bogotá neighborhood.
He was played by actor Jorge Herrera.
He shares his name with the messenger of the Greek gods, the one with winged sandals.
questions.description: The most protective dad on Colombian TV: not even the clock in his house dared to go past ten.
questions.fun_fact: His role as the grumpy dad, always watching what time Betty got home, became one of the show's best-loved memories.

questions.question: I'm made of wood and shaped like a pear, my four strings are played with a pick, and in joropo I carry the melody next to the harp. What am I?
hints: I come from the plains that Colombia shares with Venezuela.
They don't strum me like the cuatro: they pluck me note by note.
In Colombia's Andean region there's an instrument with the same name as me, but with many more strings.
questions.description: The lead singer of the group, even though it never opens its mouth.
questions.fun_fact: The bandola llanera sometimes replaces the harp in a llanero group and carries the whole joropo melody on its own.

questions.question: What sets apart paso caleño, Cali's style of dancing salsa?
wrong_answers: Slow turns in a close hold
hints: Watch the dancers' legs in Cali's salsa shows.
It's said to have been born when people in Cali played records faster than normal.
The feet move so fast you can barely see them.
questions.description: A dance you have to warm up for, just like a soccer game.
questions.fun_fact: As the story goes, people in Cali played 33 rpm records at 45, and dancing to that sped-up music gave birth to paso caleño.

questions.question: Marimba is to the currulao of the Pacific as which instrument is to the cumbia of the Montes de María?
hints: It's a wind instrument.
There is a “female” one and a “male” one, and they are played as a pair.
It's made from cactus, with a beeswax head and a duck feather mouthpiece.
questions.description: A love match between an instrument and a rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: The female gaita carries the melody, while the player of the male gaita often shakes a maraca with his other hand.

questions.question: You arrive at a fandango in the savannas of Córdoba or Sucre. What will you NOT find there?
hints: The fandango is a party of the Caribbean coast.
There you hear porros played on trumpets, euphoniums and snare drum.
One of these belongs to another region: the land of joropo.
questions.description: A party where the musicians sweat more than the dancers.
questions.fun_fact: Every year San Pelayo, Córdoba, holds the Festival Nacional del Porro, where wind bands get the whole town dancing.

questions.question: At the Vallenato Festival, the accordion player announces an aire with the same name as the Dominican Republic's famous dance rhythm. Which one?
hints: It's one of the aires played in the competition in Valledupar.
It's cheerful and lively, but not the fastest of them all.
In the Dominican Republic it's played with güira and tambora.
questions.description: A rhythm with dual citizenship, or at least a double name.
questions.fun_fact: The Vallenato Legend Festival has been held in Valledupar since 1968, and the best accordion player is crowned the Vallenato King.

questions.question: I was born in Barranquilla, grew up in Argentina and worked at NASA. I helped find the ring of cenotes that reveals the Chicxulub crater in Mexico. Who am I?
hints: I'm a planetary geologist.
The crater I studied was left by the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
My last name is very common in Antioquia and Valle, and it starts with O.
questions.description: A costeña who went looking for rocks… and ended up looking at other planets.
questions.fun_fact: As a girl, Adriana Ocampo turned her dolls into astronauts and pretended to build spaceships on her rooftop.

questions.question: Fernando Gómez Agudelo organized Colombia's first television broadcast. In what year was it?
hints: It was in the 1950s.
General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla was in power.
It was on June 13, exactly one year after Rojas Pinilla took power in 1953.
questions.description: Before this, Colombians could only hear their telenovelas, not watch them.
questions.fun_fact: Almost nobody in Colombia owned a TV for that first broadcast, so the government put sets in shop windows for people to watch from the street.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian actor. In the country's most famous telenovela I was the president of Ecomoda, Marcela Valencia's fiancé, and I fell in love with my assistant. Who am I?
hints: My character's first name was Armando.
I worked alongside Ana María Orozco.
My character's last name was Mendoza.
questions.description: A boss who spent the whole telenovela with his tie too tight and his heart in a knot.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Enrique Abello played Armando Mendoza again in 2024, more than 20 years later, in the new season of Betty.

questions.question: It's the most typical shout of vallenato singers, heard right before a verse: “¡Ay, …!” What completes it?
hints: You hear it in almost every vallenato song, old or new.
On the coast people shorten their words, and this one lost a letter along the way.
It's “hombre,” said the coastal way, without the r.
questions.description: The official sigh of every heartbroken singer with an accordion by his side.

questions.question: Which singer and actor played Diomedes Díaz in the 2015 TV series “Diomedes, el Cacique de La Junta”?
