Architects and carpenters love it.
questions.description: A grass that grew so tall it forgot it was grass.
questions.fun_fact: Guadua can grow more than 10 centimeters (4 inches) in a single day.

questions.question: Colombian Éider Arévalo became world champion in 2017 in the track and field event shown in the photo. Which one is it?
hints: The judges watch very closely how the athletes move their legs.
Its classic Olympic distances were 20 km and 50 km.
Both feet must never leave the ground at the same time.
questions.description: A sport for people in a big hurry with even bigger patience.
questions.fun_fact: In race walking, the supporting leg must stay straight from the moment it touches the ground until it passes under the body.

questions.question: Which of these things does a track bike, like the ones Colombian track cyclists ride in the velodrome, NOT have?
hints: It's missing something almost every street bike has.
On the track everyone rides in the same direction and nobody has to stop suddenly.
To slow down, the rider pushes backward on the pedals.
questions.description: A bike that went to the velodrome and left something behind at home.
questions.fun_fact: A track bike has a fixed gear: if the wheel turns, the pedals turn too, so the rider can never stop pedaling.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian singer?
hints: He's from Antioquia and almost always sings with an electric guitar.
He sang “La camisa negra” and “A Dios le pido”.
His stage name joins his two first names: Juan and Esteban.
questions.description: A singer so famous that even your grandma has belted out his songs on the bus.
questions.fun_fact: Before going solo, Juanes played in Ekhymosis, a heavy metal band from Medellín.

questions.question: Bogotá's main square faces the Capitol and the Cathedral. Who is it named after?
hints: He is a hero of Independence.
He is called “the Liberator.”
A department on the Caribbean coast carries his surname.
questions.description: The living room of every Colombian's home, pigeons included.
questions.fun_fact: The Bolívar statue in the middle of the square dates from 1846 and is Bogotá's oldest public monument.

questions.question: The Rosario Islands are coral islands inside a national park. From which city do almost all the boats leave to visit them?
hints: It's a city on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
A famous international film festival is held there every year.
It's known as “the Walled City”.
questions.description: Water so clear the fish have nowhere to hide.
questions.fun_fact: The Rosario Islands are part of the Corales del Rosario y San Bernardo National Natural Park, created in 1977.

questions.question: I have colorful wings, and at the Quindío Botanical Garden I live with hundreds of others in a huge house. What am I?
hints: I love drinking nectar from flowers.
Before I could fly, I spent some time sitting still inside a chrysalis.
Before I had wings, I was a caterpillar.
questions.description: A glass house where the tenants pay no rent and fly in through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Seen from above, the butterfly house at the Quindío Botanical Garden in Calarcá is shaped like a butterfly.

questions.question: Arelys Henao is one of the queens of Colombian música popular. In which department was she born?
hints: It's a mountain department with many singers of música popular and heartbreak songs.
Its capital is a city famous for the Feria de las Flores.
People from there are called paisas.
questions.description: A voice you hear in every cantina, from the corner store to your uncle's finca.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian música popular mixes Mexican ranchera, tango and the country music of the mountains.

questions.question: I have four thick strings, I'm almost as tall as a person, I'm played standing up, and I have the lowest sound in the string orchestra. What am I?
hints: You'll also find me in lots of jazz bands.
I can be played with a bow or by plucking the strings.
My name starts with a word that means “twice.”
questions.description: In the orchestra everyone follows the conductor, though some pretend they can't see him.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian estudiantinas, the double bass joins tiples, bandolas and guitars to add the low notes.

questions.question: If a person is “ibaguereño” or “ibaguereña,” which Colombian department are they from?
hints: It's a department in central Colombia, in the Magdalena River valley.
The Colombian Folk Festival is held there, and lechona is queen.
Its name starts with T, and it shares it with a snow-capped volcano.
questions.description: The demonym: the fancy way of asking “so where are you from, then?”
questions.fun_fact: Ibagué, the capital of Tolima, is called the “Musical Capital of Colombia.”

questions.question: In Colombia, many moms call their baby “usted.” What does that “usted” almost always show?
hints: “Usted” isn't always about keeping your distance.
It often comes out while the mom is cuddling the baby and singing to it.
It's the same feeling the mom has when she kisses her baby.
questions.description: In Colombia, one little word works for the teacher, the boss and even the cat.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Colombia, some couples call each other “usted” their whole lives, out of pure affection rather than respect.

questions.question: In Cali, if people say a child is running around “viringo,” what is the child like?
hints: Something very important is missing.
The kid just got out of the bath and is running all over the house, laughing.
The kid looks just like the day they were born.
questions.description: A word from Cali that sends any mom running right as the guests arrive.
questions.fun_fact: Peru has a hairless dog breed that is also called the “perro viringo.”

questions.question: It comes from Quechua and you hear it a lot in Pasto and in Ecuador. What is a “guambra”?
hints: People often say it with affection.
It works for boys and girls alike: “el guambra” or “la guambra”.
In Bogotá they would say “sardino”.
questions.description: A word that crossed the Andes from the Inca Empire and settled down in Pasto.
questions.fun_fact: “Guambra” comes from the Quechua “wampra”, which means boy or girl.

questions.question: In the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago there is a place called Quitasueño. What is it?
hints: It lies far from the inhabited islands, north of Providencia.
Almost all of it is underwater.
Ships fear it because they can run aground there.
questions.description: A name that sounds like the herbal tea grandma makes you before bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012, the International Court of Justice confirmed that Quitasueño belongs to Colombia, in its dispute with Nicaragua.

questions.question: Colombian Crescencio Salcedo wrote “El año viejo.” Who recorded it in 1953 and made it a hit across the Americas?
hints: He was a singer, not a bandleader.
He recorded it in Mexico with Rafael de Paz's orchestra.
His last name is also the name of a city in Chihuahua.
questions.description: The unofficial anthem of the twelve midnight chimes, party hat and all.
questions.fun_fact: Many people in Colombia believe the singer of “El año viejo” was Colombian, but Tony Camargo was Mexican.

questions.question: At the party, someone crosses the room, holds out a hand and leads you to the dance floor. What do Colombians call that?
hints: It happens at weddings and quinceañeras.
It almost always starts with a one-word question.
It’s the opposite of staying in your seat the whole party.
questions.description: A moment of courage that begins on the far side of the room.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, the capital of salsa, there are schools where children learn to dance from a very young age.

questions.question: In soccer, what do Colombian commentators call a spectacular goal?
hints: The whole stadium jumps up to celebrate.
Commentators shout it, stretching out the last letter.
It’s the word “gol” with an ending that makes it bigger.
questions.description: The commentators’ favorite word, shouted until they run out of air.
questions.fun_fact: James Rodríguez’s goal against Uruguay at the 2014 World Cup won the Puskás Award for the most beautiful goal of the year.

questions.question: As you leave the corner store, the shopkeeper says “¡Que le vaya bien!”. What do people usually reply?
hints: It's a single word.
You give the shopkeeper the same wish back.
It means “same to you.”
questions.description: Words that in Colombia come out all by themselves as you walk out the door.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombians stretch out the goodbye: “que le vaya bien, que esté bien, saludes en la casa.”

questions.question: CIAT, in Palmira, keeps the world's largest collections of two staple foods in its seed bank. Which two?
hints: Both are staple foods in the tropics, from Latin America to Africa.
One grows in pods and the other is a thick root underground.
One goes in bandeja paisa and the other in sancocho.
questions.description: A pantry so big it could replant half the planet after a disaster.
questions.fun_fact: CIAT's seed bank holds tens of thousands of bean varieties brought from a great many countries.

questions.question: It records brain activity millisecond by millisecond with superconducting sensors near absolute zero, and Rodolfo Llinás used it. What is it called?
hints: It doesn't measure electricity directly with electrodes on the scalp.
It doesn't take pictures of tissue with radio waves either, like another famous scan.
Its name joins “magnet” with “brain recording.”
questions.description: The brain thinks so fast that it takes a very expensive machine to catch it in the act.
questions.fun_fact: The brain's magnetic fields are hundreds of millions of times weaker than Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: Bogotá-born Ana María Rey, a MacArthur “genius grant” winner, studies laser-cooled atoms in the world's most precise devices. What are they for?
hints: She works at JILA in Colorado, an institute famous for these devices.
The GPS on your phone depends on them.
They're the most precise version of what you wear on your wrist.
questions.description: A rola who makes atoms shiver with cold so they'll behave.
questions.fun_fact: The best atomic clocks would lose less than one second over the entire age of the universe.

questions.question: The Perseverance rover, which Colombian Diana Trujillo worked on, landed in Jezero Crater. Why did NASA choose it? Because long ago there was…
hints: NASA was looking for a place where tiny life might have existed long ago.
From orbit you can see a delta, like the one a river makes where it ends.
Still water sat there billions of years ago.
questions.description: To pick a landing spot on Mars, NASA had to look very, very far back in time.
questions.fun_fact: Perseverance stores rock samples in sealed tubes so a future mission can bring them back to Earth.

questions.question: In Bogotá and Medellín, depending on the day of the week, some cars can't be driven at the busiest hours. What is this rule called?
hints: It changes with the day of the week.
It depends on the numbers on the front and back of the car.
Its name joins the Spanish for “rush hour” with the Spanish for what shows a car's number.
questions.description: The rule that makes your dad check the calendar before taking the car out.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá started pico y placa in 1998, and many other Colombian cities later copied the idea.

questions.question: Carlos Vives was born in Santa Marta. What do you call someone from that city?
hints: The word doesn't look much like the city's full name.
Carlos “el Pibe” Valderrama is one too, and says so proudly.
It joins a little piece of “Santa” with a little piece of “Marta”.
questions.description: Born looking at the Sierra Nevada and the sea at the same time, like someone who can't make up their mind.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Marta, founded in 1525, is the oldest Colombian city still standing.

questions.question: I'm an actress from Cali and also a dancer. I played Rosario in “La hija del mariachi” and Policarpa Salavarrieta in “La Pola.” Who am I?
hints: I trained in dance before I became an actress.
Years later, I starred in a reggaeton series that was a big hit on Netflix.
I starred in “La reina del flow.”
questions.description: An actress who switches characters like switching steps on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: Before acting, Carolina Ramírez studied ballet at Incolballet, the Colombian Ballet Institute in Cali.

questions.question: Listen: this instrument joined the accordion, the caja and the guacharaca in modern vallenato. Which one is it?
hints: It sounds low, like a rumble underneath the melody.
You play it by plucking thick strings.
It looks like a guitar, but longer and with a much deeper sound.
questions.description: The musician almost nobody watches on stage, until the band tries to play without one.
questions.fun_fact: The electric bass took off in 1951, when Leo Fender launched his famous Precision Bass.

questions.question: Which style of vallenato did Rafael Orozco and El Binomio de Oro make famous from the late 1970s?
hints: It doesn't tell town chronicles or cowboy stories.
It's what plays most when someone is in love... or heartbroken.
Its name comes from the same word as “romance”.
questions.description: A group so good that even its name sounds like a jewelry store.
questions.fun_fact: El Binomio de Oro was founded in 1976, and its name comes from the duo of singer Rafael Orozco and accordion player Israel Romero.

questions.question: Look at this sea turtle. It nests on beaches of Colombia's Caribbean coast, and the plates of its shell overlap like roof tiles. What is it called?
hints: It is critically endangered.
It is usually seen around coral reefs.
Its shell was once used to make combs and eyeglass frames.
questions.description: An elegant swimmer wearing a suit of luxury armor.
questions.fun_fact: The hawksbill eats mostly sea sponges, even some that are poisonous to other animals.

questions.question: You're at the Feria de Cali, held every year from December 25 to 30. In which decade was the first one held?
hints: It's older than the Salsódromo.
Your grandparents could have gone to the first one when they were young.
Television had just arrived in Colombia a few years earlier, in 1954.
questions.description: A party so good it has been repeating itself every December for decades.
questions.fun_fact: The first Feria de Cali, in December 1957, had bullfights, a horse parade and a beauty pageant.

questions.question: Porro was born in the village brass bands of Córdoba and Sucre. Which bandleader took it to Bogotá's elegant clubs in the 1940s?
hints: He played the clarinet.
His wife, Matilde Díaz, sang with his orchestra.
He wrote “Carmen de Bolívar” and “Colombia tierra querida.”
questions.description: From the cattle pens of the savanna to a ballroom with crystal chandeliers: quite a musical move.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Bermúdez played the clarinet and wrote hundreds of songs, including porros, cumbias and gaitas.

questions.question: I was born in Chocó, played trombone and wrote arrangements for Grupo Niche in its early days, then founded Guayacán Orquesta. Who am I?
hints: I was not the founder or the leader of Grupo Niche.
I was born in Quibdó, just like Jairo Varela.
My first name is Alexis.
questions.description: A trombone that left one famous band to start another just as famous.
questions.fun_fact: Guayacán Orquesta is the band behind “Oiga, mire, vea,” which became almost an anthem of Cali.

questions.question: I live on the farm, lay eggs and look after my chicks. If someone is scared of everything, people say they're like me. What am I?
hints: I have feathers and can't fly very high.
My soup is what they give you when you have the flu.
I'm the rooster's wife.
questions.description: A saying that left the farm and moved into the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: Hens are not cowards at all: a mother hen will peck at anyone who threatens her chicks.

questions.question: At a party, if someone shouts “¡A mover el esqueleto!” (move your skeleton!), they want you to…
hints: There’s music playing.
You do it on the dance floor.
Salsa, cumbia or vallenato are perfect for it.
questions.description: An order you hear at every Colombian wedding right after the cake.
questions.fun_fact: An adult has 206 bones, and dancing puts a good number of them to work.

questions.question: Grandma says it when she makes you take an umbrella, a jacket and a helmet: “más vale prevenir que lamentar.” What does it mean?
questions.answer: Better to take care before something happens
wrong_answers: Crying helps when everything goes wrong
You never need to worry about anything
Scolding someone never does any good
hints: It’s about thinking ahead, before the problem arrives.
It’s like carrying an umbrella in case it rains.
Better to be careful beforehand than to regret it afterward.
questions.description: Grandmothers say this even more often than “¿ya comió?”
questions.fun_fact: Many languages have a similar saying; in English it’s “better safe than sorry.”

questions.question: I work on the street with a rag in my hand. When you go to park, I wave and shout “¡siga, siga, siga!” Who am I?
hints: You find me outside shops and restaurants.
At the end, you give me a few coins.
I tell you when to stop before you crash.
questions.description: A character of the Colombian streets who never needed GPS.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “siga” is also the polite way to say “come in” when someone arrives at your home.

questions.question: It rains on the day of the family outing and your mom says “al mal tiempo, buena cara.” Why does she say it?
questions.answer: To cheer you up even if things go wrong
wrong_answers: To get you to put on your raincoat
To tell you the outing is canceled
To scold you for getting wet
hints: It has nothing to do with clothes.
It’s about attitude.
It’s like saying: smile even if things don’t go the way you wanted.
questions.description: A saying that comes with its own weather forecast.
questions.fun_fact: This saying came from Spain and is used all over Latin America, not only when it rains.

questions.question: A mutation in the PSEN1 gene causes Alzheimer's before age 50 in thousands of relatives studied by Francisco Lopera. Where do they live?
hints: It's the Colombian region with the most families in the world affected by this mutation.
Neurologist Francisco Lopera worked at that region's public university.
The mutation was nicknamed after what people from Medellín are called.
questions.description: A family inheritance nobody wants, and scientists have been chasing it for over 30 years.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists see these families as a unique chance to test treatments that could slow Alzheimer's before any symptoms appear.

questions.question: Born in Bayamo, Cuba, he ran the Royal Library of Santafé and founded the Papel Periódico de Santafé de Bogotá. Who was he?
hints: He came to Santafé as a librarian, not as a politician or soldier.
He is considered the father of Colombian journalism.
His middle name is also a title of the Virgin Mary.
questions.description: Before social media, the news in Santafé arrived on paper with the ink still fresh.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Library he ran is the forerunner of the Biblioteca Nacional de Colombia.

questions.question: When you pay with a new 10,000-peso bill, you see the face of the anthropologist who studied the families of Colombia's regions. Who is she?
hints: She was one of the country's first anthropologists.
She wrote “Familia y cultura en Colombia.”
She was born in El Socorro, Santander.
questions.description: A scientist who studied Colombian families and now lives in all of their wallets.
questions.fun_fact: Her 1968 book “Familia y cultura en Colombia” showed that the family changes enormously from one region of the country to another.

questions.question: I was born in the capital of Norte de Santander, by the bridge that crosses into Venezuela, and I love pasteles de garbanzo. What am I?
hints: My city is one of the hottest in the Santanders.
Right next to my city, the congress that created Gran Colombia met in 1821.
The name of my city starts with “Cú”.
questions.description: A character who, the moment they say hello, is already telling you where they're from and why their land is the best.
questions.fun_fact: In Villa del Rosario, right next to Cúcuta, the Constitution of Gran Colombia was written in 1821.

questions.question: In 1848, settlers from Neira and Salamina made the “Expedición de los Veinte” to pick the site for a new city. Which city was founded there in 1849?
hints: It's part of the Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero).
Today it's the capital of a department created in 1905.
Its January fair has a famous international coffee beauty pageant.
questions.description: Twenty Antioquians, machetes and mules: the most ambitious weekend plan in history.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century, the Antioquian colonization founded dozens of towns in the mountains of west-central Colombia.

questions.question: Who donated the land on which the city of Cúcuta was founded in 1733?
hints: The donated land lay in the valley of the Pamplonita River.
She gave it so the neighbors could build a church dedicated to Saint Joseph.
That's why people say Cúcuta was founded by a woman.
questions.description: A city that exists because someone gave away a plot of land, and not for a parking lot.
questions.fun_fact: The donation was signed on June 17, 1733, the date taken as Cúcuta's founding.

questions.question: Which Colombian telenovela has the opening song “¿Quién es ese hombre?”?
hints: It premiered in 2003 and became famous in many countries.
It tells the story of three brothers who come to a hacienda for revenge.
The Reyes brothers fall in love with the Elizondo sisters.
questions.description: A song that made half the country sigh in front of the TV at dinnertime.
questions.fun_fact: There were three Reyes brothers in the telenovela: Juan, Óscar and Franco.

questions.question: Julio Jiménez wrote “Las aguas mansas,” the telenovela later remade as “Pasión de gavilanes.” In which decade did it first air?
hints: It came out before Caracol and RCN became private channels.
Its remake, “Pasión de gavilanes,” came out about nine years later.
It went on the air in the middle of that decade, in 1994.
questions.description: A writer who knew revenge is a dish best served over many episodes.
questions.fun_fact: Julio Jiménez also wrote “En cuerpo ajeno,” which was remade in the United States as “El cuerpo del deseo.”

questions.question: The 1988 series “Los pecados de Inés de Hinojosa” was based on a real woman from Tunja. In which century did she live?
hints: It was during the Spanish colonial era.
Tunja was a newly founded city back then.
Her story took place a few decades after Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded Tunja in 1539.
questions.description: A scandal so old the gossips of the day wrote with goose quills.
questions.fun_fact: Her story already appeared in “El carnero”, the chronicle Juan Rodríguez Freyle wrote in the 17th century.

questions.question: It's measured in points every night, and if it's too low, a telenovela can be taken off the air. What is it?
hints: It shows up in the entertainment news the next day.
Caracol and RCN fight over it every night.
It's how many people are tuned in to a TV show.
questions.description: Telenovela producers bite their nails the morning after every premiere because of this.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” reached some of the highest ratings in the history of Colombian television.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea,” what is the name of Ecomoda's vice president of sales, Armando Mendoza's best friend?
hints: He sits on Ecomoda's board and almost always takes Armando's side.
He was played by the actor Ricardo Vélez.
His first name is the same as Nintendo's mustached plumber.
questions.description: An executive who can sell anything at Ecomoda, except loyalty to the secretaries.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” has been remade in dozens of countries, from Mexico to India, and made Guinness World Records as the most successful telenovela.

questions.question: I show up in the middle of the song: over the accordion, the singer names friends, family and even whoever paid for the parranda. What am I?
hints: I’m not part of the song’s original lyrics.
Some people pay to be mentioned in me.
I’m named after what you do when you say “¡quiubo!” to someone.
questions.description: A parranda where the accordion never rests, the sancocho never runs out and nobody remembers to check the time.
questions.fun_fact: Some vallenato saludos became so famous that people know them by heart, just like the lyrics of the song.

questions.question: It's in Disney's “Encanto”, Carlos Vives sings it, and it mixes vallenato with cumbia. What song is it?
hints: It plays while the townspeople dance through the streets.
It has an accordion, like vallenato songs.
Its title includes the name of the country where the film takes place.
questions.description: A family with magic powers, and still the most magical thing was the soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: The song was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who also wrote the rest of the songs in “Encanto”.

questions.question: It's sung by candlelight on Christmas Eve, features a “holder Knabe im lockigen Haar” (lovely boy with curly hair), and exists in over 300 languages. Which song?
hints: It's a very calm, slow song.
In the song it's late, and everyone is asleep.
The title describes a night when not a sound can be heard.
questions.description: The one song where even the uncle who sings off-key is allowed to join in.
questions.fun_fact: The song was first sung in 1818, accompanied by a guitar instead of an organ.

questions.question: What trickles onto the floor when the Christmas tree slowly dries out in January?
hints: It's green and very small.
If you step on it, it can prickle a little.
A sewing kit has some too, but these come from the tree.
questions.description: The vacuum cleaner is putting in overtime again this January.
questions.fun_fact: The Nordmann fir is Germany's favorite Christmas tree, partly because it stays green for a very long time.

questions.question: It often has golden curls and wings, nobody sees it, and then a little bell rings. Why does the Christkind come on Christmas Eve?
hints: Children write it wish lists beforehand.
Afterward, there's more under the tree than before.
Think of packages tied with a bow.
questions.description: The only delivery service that always arrives on time but is never seen.
questions.fun_fact: Martin Luther made the Christkind popular so that children would get presents at Christmas instead of on St. Nicholas Day.

questions.question: Complete: Heiligabend is the evening before …
hints: The next day, almost everyone has the day off.
On this day, the whole family often gets together.
In Germany, it's the first of two holidays in a row.
questions.description: The longest evening of the year, at least for anyone under ten.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, Christmas Eve is not a public holiday, so many shops are still open in the morning.

questions.question: In early January, this chalk writing appears on many front doors. Why is “C+M+B” written there?
questions.answer: As a blessing for the house
wrong_answers: As a sign for the chimney sweep
As a receipt for the rent
As a note for the mail carrier
hints: Children dressed in royal robes write it on the door.
The letters stand for three Latin words.
“Christus mansionem benedicat” means: May Christ bless this house.
questions.description: Graffiti that even the building manager is happy to see.
questions.fun_fact: C, M and B also match the names of the Three Kings: Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

questions.question: These little cones smolder inside a Räuchermännchen (wooden smoking figure). What are they mostly made of?
hints: They have no wick and burn without a flame.
You light only the tip, and then they slowly smolder.
They glow a bit like the stuff in a barbecue grill.
questions.description: The little cone that turns any living room into a cozy smokehouse.
questions.fun_fact: With a Räuchermännchen, the smoke usually puffs out of the figure's mouth, as if it were smoking a pipe.

questions.question: You're at the Christmas table: roast goose, red cabbage and round Klöße (dumplings). What are the Klöße usually made from?
hints: It grows underground.
French fries are made from it too.
You dig them up in the field, often brown and lumpy.
questions.description: Round, soft and the secret stars of every gravy battle.
questions.fun_fact: Klöße are so popular in Thuringia that there's even a dumpling museum there.

questions.question: The Christmas duck is roasted crisp in the oven, served with red cabbage and stuffed first. With what, classically?
hints: It's something fruity.
It grows in German gardens too.
In the fall it hangs on trees, and it also ends up in strudel.
questions.description: A bird that comes to the Christmas table with a very full belly.
questions.fun_fact: Mugwort often goes into the stuffing too, an herb said to make fatty poultry easier to digest.

questions.question: In Germany, what is December 26 called, the day many people visit relatives once more?
hints: Almost everyone has the day off.
It's the day after December 25.
It's already the second Christmas day off in a row.
questions.description: The day when the leftovers from the big feast get their moment in the spotlight.
questions.fun_fact: In church, December 26 is also called St. Stephen's Day, after Saint Stephen.

questions.question: Nikolaus comes on December 6. How many little doors on the Advent calendar are open by then?
hints: You open the first door on December 1.
Exactly one more door opens each day.
Just count along: 1, 2, 3 …
questions.description: The day boots suddenly matter more than homework.
questions.fun_fact: Nikolaus goes back to Bishop Nicholas of Myra, a town in what is now Turkey.

questions.question: When someone keeps bugging you, Germans say “Du gehst mir auf den …”. How does the saying end?
hints: The missing word is something baked.
It is small, round and crunchy.
People like to dunk it in milk.
questions.description: A saying so annoying that it's starting to crumble.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody knows for sure where the saying comes from, but it has only been around since the 20th century.

questions.question: A Quarktasche from the bakery is filled with sweet quark. What is quark made from?
hints: It comes from the farm.
It comes from an animal.
Yogurt and cheese are made from it too.
questions.description: A pocket you don't put your keys in, you sink your teeth into it.
questions.fun_fact: Quark forms when milk turns sour and thickens; the liquid left over is called whey.

questions.question: It's a butter cake, often baked in a Gugelhupf pan, with light and dark swirls inside. Why is part of the batter dark?
hints: The cake is named after a kind of stone.
The ingredient comes from beans that grow in the tropics.
The dark part tastes of chocolate.
questions.description: A cake that looks like a stone floor, but luckily doesn't taste like one.
questions.fun_fact: To make the pattern, you drag a fork in a spiral through the two batters, and that's how the marble swirl appears.

questions.question: In German kitchens, this flour is Type 405. Which grain is it milled from?
hints: It's the most common grain for cakes and bread rolls.
It grows golden yellow in the fields, with short ears.
Most pasta is made from it too.
questions.description: A number that sounds more like a house number than a baking ingredient.
questions.fun_fact: The number 405 means that 100 grams (3.5 oz) of the flour contain about 405 milligrams of minerals.

questions.question: You cut into a thick Stollen full of raisins and powdered sugar. When in the year is it mainly eaten?
hints: It is usually cold outside then.
Many houses are decorated with string lights then.
Santa Claus is busy then.
questions.description: A bread that dusts itself with so much powdered sugar, you'd think it was off to a big party.
questions.fun_fact: The Dresdner Christstollen is famous: Dresden even holds a Stollen festival every year with a giant Stollen.

questions.question: Coconut macaroons are often baked on a thin white wafer (Oblate). What is it for?
questions.answer: So they don't stick to the baking sheet
hints: You simply eat the wafer along with the macaroon.
Macaroon dough is very sticky.
Without it, the macaroons are hard to get off the baking sheet.
questions.description: A Christmas treat that likes to sit on a thin white carpet.
questions.fun_fact: Oblaten are made of nothing but flour and water, baked wafer-thin.

questions.question: What topping is on this sheet cake?
hints: It is made from flour, sugar and butter.
You rub it between your fingers into little crumbs.
You also find this topping on a sweet pastry swirl at the bakery.
questions.description: The sheet-pan classic without which Grandma's coffee table would be only half as nice.
questions.fun_fact: Streuselkuchen is considered a specialty from Silesia and was often baked for family celebrations.

questions.question: What tiny seeds are on this bread roll?
hints: The seeds are blue-gray to black.
They ripen in the seed heads of a well-known flower.
A popular pastry swirl at the bakery is filled with them too.
questions.description: After this roll, take a quick look in the mirror before you smile at anyone.
questions.fun_fact: A single poppy seed head can hold more than a thousand tiny seeds.

questions.question: It's pink or white, gets wound around a wooden stick at the fair and melts in your mouth. What is it called?
hints: It is very light and fluffy.
It is made in a spinning machine.
Its name sounds like the soft fluffy stuff people use to take off makeup.
questions.description: At the fair the air smells so sweet that just breathing makes your fingers sticky.
questions.fun_fact: The cotton candy machine was co-invented in 1897 by a dentist.

questions.question: What do you bake in this appliance?
hints: The batter is runny and gets poured in.
What comes out has a grid pattern.
At fairs you often get them heart-shaped with powdered sugar.
questions.description: An appliance that promises love the moment you open it.
questions.fun_fact: Heart-shaped waffles are especially popular in Germany and Scandinavia.

questions.question: Yellow is to lemon drop as black is to …?
hints: It's a kind of candy.
It comes as wheels or sticks.
Some people love it, others find it gross, especially the salty kind.
questions.description: Color theory for kids with a sweet tooth.
questions.fun_fact: Licorice is made from the root of the licorice plant.

questions.question: Esspapier sits under macaroons and Lebkuchen, is paper-thin and tastes of almost nothing. What is it mainly made of?
hints: It's a lot like the wafer handed out in church.
This ingredient is also found in potatoes.
It's also used to thicken sauces.
questions.description: The only paper you're allowed to eat without getting in trouble.
questions.fun_fact: Nuremberg's Elisenlebkuchen are traditionally baked on Oblaten (thin wafers) so the dough doesn't stick to the baking sheet.

questions.question: You cook pudding mix in a pot, and the pudding sets as it cools. What do you stir into it?
hints: It is white.
It comes from a farm animal.
You also pour it over cereal.
questions.description: It wobbles and it shines, but it never clowns around.
questions.fun_fact: The company Dr. Oetker from Bielefeld has been selling pudding mix for more than 100 years.

questions.question: In Franconia, the big village fair is called “Kerwa”. It's dialect for a German word that starts with “Kirch…”. Which one?
hints: The fair celebrates an anniversary.
In other regions, the same fair is called “Kirmes”.
It celebrates the day the church was first consecrated.
questions.description: A Franconian party where even the name speaks dialect.
questions.fun_fact: In some Franconian villages, the Kerwa is solemnly “buried” at the end, with a funeral procession and lots of laughter.

questions.question: A poster says “Tanz in den Mai – April 30”. What happens that evening?
wrong_answers: You dance every evening all of May
You dance in a meadow of lilies of the valley
You dance only on the evening of May 31
hints: Look at the date on the poster.
The next day is a public holiday in Germany.
At midnight, the month changes.
questions.description: An evening when even Grandpa gets his dancing shoes out of the closet.
questions.fun_fact: Many villages put up a decorated maypole for May 1, often with a big party around it.

questions.question: In the chorus of “Viva Colonia”, the Höhner sing about what people in Cologne love. Which word is NOT in it?
hints: The song is about what makes partying fun.
The next line says they believe in God and are still thirsty.
Three of the four German words start with the same letter.
questions.description: A song that even people from Düsseldorf secretly sing along to.
questions.fun_fact: “Viva Colonia” came out in 2003, and since then no Cologne carnival party has been complete without it.

questions.question: On which day does “Helau!” ring out loudest through the streets of Mainz and Düsseldorf?
hints: It's a Monday.
Ash Wednesday comes soon after.
On this day, the big parades roll through town throwing Kamelle (candy).
questions.description: A word you can only shout for a few weeks a year without getting funny looks.
questions.fun_fact: In Cologne, people shout “Alaaf” instead of “Helau”, and mixing them up there earns you some funny looks.

questions.question: You're celebrating carnival in the Rhineland. Which call are you least likely to hear there?
hints: This call comes from another corner of Germany.
It belongs to the Fasnet in the southwest, with its wooden masks.
You'd hear it in Rottweil or Villingen rather than in Cologne.
questions.description: Shout the wrong thing here and you won't catch a single piece of candy.
questions.fun_fact: People along the parade route shout “Kamelle!” to ask for the candy thrown from the floats.

questions.question: At the Kirmes, you suddenly see yourself like this. Where are you?
hints: Nothing moves here except you.
Glass plays the lead role here.
The walls are curved so you look tall or wide.
questions.description: At the Kirmes there are booths where you can barely walk straight for laughing.
questions.fun_fact: Funhouse mirrors are curved: depending on the curve, you look taller, shorter, wider or thinner.

questions.question: Red nose, colorful wig and giant shoes: where does someone who always looks like this work?
hints: Acrobats work there too.
Jugglers and tightrope walkers perform there.
The show happens in a big round tent with a ring in the middle.
questions.description: The favorite costume for anyone who loves goofing around at Fasching.
questions.fun_fact: Many clowns invent their very own face and paint it exactly the same way every time.

questions.question: This tight zigzag track belongs to a ride at the Kirmes. Which one?
hints: It's a small roller coaster.
The tiny cars turn very suddenly.
Its name contains a small rodent.
questions.description: A ride for everyone who loves to squeal loudly.
questions.fun_fact: Wild Mouse cars turn into the curves very late, so it feels as if you're about to fly straight off the track.

questions.question: What are these colorful streamers made of?
hints: You can tear them very easily.
It's also what your sketchbook is made of.
You write and draw on it.
questions.description: In German they're called “air snakes”, and nobody has ever run away from one.
questions.fun_fact: Streamers are narrow strips of paper rolled up tightly; when you throw or blow them, they unroll.

questions.question: This red nose goes with lots of Fasching costumes. What do Germans call it?
hints: Clowns wear it too.
Germans also use the word for a silly joker.
It used to be made of stiff cardboard.
questions.description: The world's smallest costume fits in any pocket.
questions.fun_fact: Today most clown noses are made of foam, but Germans still call them “Pappnase”, a cardboard nose.

questions.question: In Cologne, the Dreigestirn rules over carnival. Who leads the carnival fools in Düsseldorf?
hints: They wear splendid costumes and ride in the Rosenmontag parade.
One of them goes by the name “Venetia”.
Two people, a man and a woman, both with royal titles.
questions.description: A government that only stays in office until Ash Wednesday, and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: Düsseldorf's carnival princess is always called “Venetia”, a name that recalls the carnival city of Venice.

questions.question: I'm still small, but I already wear a Häs (costume) and a mask and jump along in the parade. I'm the future of the Zunft (guild). What am I called?
hints: You hear the word mostly at the Swabian-Alemannic Fasnet.
In many guilds, we march as our own group in the parade.
My name compares me to something you plant so it can grow.
questions.description: Start early in the southwest, and you'll never get stage fright at Fasnet.
questions.fun_fact: Many fools' guilds in the southwest have their own kids' groups, who march in the parade in little Häs costumes.

questions.question: In this building, the members of parliament elect the German chancellor. Which building is it?
hints: The building is in Berlin.
The Bundestag meets here.
On its roof sits a glass dome that visitors can walk through.
questions.description: Here people vote, count, and then clap a whole lot.
questions.fun_fact: The vote for chancellor is secret: members fill in their ballots in voting booths set up in the plenary hall.

questions.question: I used to compete in trampolining, was the Greens' candidate for Chancellor in 2021, and then became Germany's first female Foreign Minister. Who am I?
hints: I come from Lower Saxony and lived in Potsdam for a long time.
In Olaf Scholz's cabinet, I was in charge of foreign policy.
My first name begins with “Anna”.
questions.description: From bouncing up high to aiming high in politics.
questions.fun_fact: As a teenager, Baerbock won several medals at German trampolining championships.

questions.question: Angela Merkel said “Wir schaffen das” (“We can do this”) at her summer press conference on August 31, 2015. What was the topic?
hints: That summer, the topic kept all of Europe busy.
The news back then was often about the Balkan route and Munich's main train station.
Hundreds of thousands sought safety in Germany in 2015.
questions.description: Three words that started more arguments than any family get-together.
questions.fun_fact: The phrase became so famous that it is still used as shorthand for Merkel's whole time as Chancellor.

questions.question: In old satire magazines, “Mutti” is to Angela Merkel as which fruit is to Helmut Kohl?
hints: The nickname poked fun at the shape of Kohl's head.
The satire magazine “Titanic” made it famous.
The fruit is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.
questions.description: Satire is when the fruit aisle suddenly goes into politics.
questions.fun_fact: “Titanic” mocked Kohl as “Birne” (pear) so often that the nickname became known across Germany.

questions.question: I'm elected by a special assembly: all members of the Bundestag and just as many delegates from the states, often celebrities too. Who am I?
hints: This assembly usually meets only once every five years.
Whoever is elected doesn't govern, but signs the laws.
The official residence is Schloss Bellevue in Berlin.
questions.description: An assembly that gets together for one single person, and no one else.
questions.fun_fact: Soccer coaches, actors and drag queens have all sat in the Federal Convention as delegates of the states.

questions.question: In Germany, convicted people can be pardoned. Who does NOT have this right?
hints: Who may grant a pardon depends on whether a federal or a state court gave the verdict.
In the states, the right lies with the state's leadership.
The one you're looking for leads the federal government.
questions.description: Mercy over justice, but only from the right office, please.
questions.fun_fact: Most requests for a pardon end up with the states, because most criminal verdicts are handed down there.

questions.question: The federal cabinet usually meets on Wednesdays at the Chancellery. What for?
questions.answer: To make decisions as the government
wrong_answers: To pass laws in their final form
hints: The chancellor and all the federal ministers sit at the table.
This is where draft laws get started, for example.
“Cabinet” is another word for the federal government.
questions.description: Not a piece of furniture, even though everyone takes a seat in it.
questions.fun_fact: A “cabinet” was originally a small side room where princes met in secret with their advisers.

questions.question: In which year did Olaf Scholz speak of a “Zeitenwende” (a turning point in history) in the Bundestag?
hints: Scholz had only been chancellor for a few months at the time.
Shortly before, Russia had attacked Ukraine.
The speech came in February, three days after the war began.
questions.description: One word, as heavy as a history book.
questions.fun_fact: “Zeitenwende” was chosen as Germany’s Word of the Year in 2022.

questions.question: The federal president is Germany's “head of state”. What does that mean?
questions.answer: He represents the country but doesn't govern
wrong_answers: He alone decides on the laws
hints: He welcomes state guests from all over the world.
He signs laws, but doesn't write them.
Someone else does the work of governing: the chancellor.
questions.description: Sounds like it comes with a crown, but gets by fine without one.
questions.fun_fact: In kingdoms like the United Kingdom, the king takes on the role of head of state.

questions.question: I loved cigars, and as SPD chancellor I was so close to company bosses that people called me “Genosse der Bosse” (comrade of the bosses). Who am I?
hints: Before becoming chancellor, I was Minister-President of Lower Saxony.
My vice chancellor was Joschka Fischer of the Greens.
I came directly after Helmut Kohl.
questions.description: Red party, fat cigar, pricey suit: something here doesn't quite add up.
questions.fun_fact: A photo of Schröder in a Brioni suit with a cigar became the symbol of the nickname.

questions.question: The Mercedes 300 from the 1950s carries the nickname of a chancellor who used it as his official car. Which chancellor?
hints: He was already over 70 when he became chancellor.
He was the very first chancellor of the Federal Republic.
His nickname was “der Alte” (the Old Man).
questions.description: A car with so much dignity that it got a chancellor's name.
questions.fun_fact: Adenauer's official Mercedes is on display today at the Haus der Geschichte museum in Bonn.

questions.question: Many German towns have “Bad” in their name, like on this sign. What does it mean?
wrong_answers: A town with a big outdoor pool
A town right by the sea
A town with its own swimming lake
hints: Some towns have carried this word in their name for over a hundred years.
They have things like healing springs, healing mud or especially clean air.
You can go there for a “Kur.”
questions.description: A town name that makes you want to dry your feet before you drive in.
questions.fun_fact: A town may only use “Bad” in its name if it meets strict standards, for example for healing springs and air and water quality.

questions.question: Garmisch-Partenkirchen, at the foot of the Zugspitze, holds a ski jumping event every New Year's Day. Which series is it part of?
hints: The series runs around New Year's Eve and New Year's Day.
The series has existed since the 1950s.
The jumping takes place on four ski jumps in total.
questions.description: For some people, the new year starts with a leap into thin air.
questions.fun_fact: Garmisch and Partenkirchen were two separate towns until they were merged in 1935 for the Winter Olympics.

questions.question: In fall 1989, thousands set out from this church every Monday, chanting “Wir sind das Volk” (“We are the people”). Which city is it in?
hints: The city is in Saxony.
It is known for its trade fair and the Thomanerchor, the St. Thomas Boys Choir.
The church is the Nikolaikirche, in the largest city in Saxony.
questions.description: A day of the week when nobody here wanted to stay home in 1989.
questions.fun_fact: On October 9, 1989, about 70,000 people marched peacefully in Leipzig, and exactly one month later the Berlin Wall fell.

questions.question: This composer was born in Halle (Saale) in 1685, and here is his statue on the market square. Who is he?
hints: He spent most of his life in London.
He wrote the “Water Music” for an English king.
His most famous work is “Messiah,” with the “Hallelujah” chorus.
questions.description: A gentleman in a wig who has been standing guard on the market square for over 150 years.
questions.fun_fact: Bach and Handel were born in the same year, only about 130 km (80 miles) apart, but they never met.

questions.question: I smell of cinnamon and cloves, Nuremberg has been famous for me for centuries, and I'm everywhere at the Christkindlesmarkt. What am I?
hints: I'm brown and usually round.
I'm often baked on a thin wafer.
At fairs, I hang on a string as a heart with sugar writing.
questions.description: This is someone who's in pretty high demand every December.
questions.fun_fact: “Nürnberger Lebkuchen” is a protected name: it really has to be baked in Nuremberg.

questions.question: When did people start building Cologne Cathedral?
wrong_answers: In the age of cell phones
hints: Back then there were no cranes with engines.
It was many hundreds of years ago, but people could already build huge stone churches.
Back then kings and noble ladies lived in castles, and men fought in armor.
questions.description: A construction project that makes even the most delayed airport look right on schedule.
questions.fun_fact: Building started in 1248 and was only finished in 1880, more than 600 years later.

questions.question: What is NOT found at Munich's Viktualienmarkt?
hints: The market has been in the middle of Munich's old town since the early 19th century.
The thing you're looking for draws crowds of tourists at set times every day.
There, mechanical figures dance every day while bells play.
questions.description: A market where you can buy Weißwürste, along with a few surprises.
questions.fun_fact: Several fountains at the Viktualienmarkt honor Munich folk singers and comedians, such as Karl Valentin and Liesl Karlstadt.

questions.question: In the German Donald Duck comics, you go shopping in Entenhausen. What money do you pay with there?
hints: Uncle Scrooge, or Onkel Dagobert, has a whole Money Bin full of it.
Long before the Mark, real money in Germany had this name too.
The English word “dollar” comes from this old name.
questions.description: In this town, a billionaire would rather swim in his money than in a pool.
questions.fun_fact: German readers owe the Taler of Entenhausen to the translator Erika Fuchs. In the American original, people pay in dollars.

questions.question: This port city on the Jade was given the name Wilhelmshaven in 1869. Who was it named after?
hints: The person behind the name was a ruler, not an artist.
At the time, he was King of Prussia.
In 1871, he became the first German Emperor.
questions.description: A harbor that wears its name like a sailor wears a tattoo: forever.
questions.fun_fact: Wilhelmshaven was founded as a navy port and today, with the JadeWeserPort, has Germany's only deep-water container port.

questions.question: This clock in Rothenburg ob der Tauber shows the “Meistertrunk”: a mayor drains a giant tankard. Which general does this win over?
hints: The story takes place in 1631, during the Thirty Years' War.
This general led the troops of the Catholic League.
His short name ends in “y”.
questions.description: A town saved by one single, very big gulp.
questions.fun_fact: The tankard is said to have held more than 3 liters (over 6 pints), and every year at Pentecost Rothenburg puts on the legend as a festival play.

questions.question: This huge monument in Leipzig commemorates the Battle of the Nations in 1813. Who was defeated there?
hints: He wanted to rule all of Europe.
He was Emperor of the French.
Two years later he also lost at Waterloo.
questions.description: A block of stone that makes every high-rise feel a little small.
questions.fun_fact: The Völkerschlachtdenkmal is 91 m (299 ft) tall and was opened in 1913, exactly 100 years after the battle.

questions.question: In December you send a wish list to the Christmas post office in Himmelpforten. Who writes back?
hints: The village is in Lower Saxony, in northern Germany.
This figure usually wears a red coat and has a white beard.
In the north he brings the presents on Christmas Eve, not on December 6, and he isn't the Christkind.
questions.description: A village whose name means “Heaven's Gates”, a fine address for big wishes.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, helpers in Himmelpforten answer tens of thousands of wish lists, and some come from all over the world.

questions.question: For decades, the Krombacher brewery has advertised its beer with which kind of water?
hints: The brewery is in the Siegerland region, not in the Alps.
The word names the place where the spring comes out of the ground.
It contains the German word for rock.
questions.description: An ad that aired so often it practically became part of the living-room furniture.
questions.fun_fact: Krombacher's ads use the slogan “Eine Perle der Natur” (“A pearl of nature”) and show an island in a lake.

questions.question: This German juice brand is named after a very high note in singing, and the name also hints at a vitamin. Which brand is it?
hints: The name is made of two words.
Oranges are full of this vitamin.
The note sits at the very top of the scale.
questions.description: A drink that goes down as well at a singing lesson as at breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: “High C” is a note that only trained sopranos and tenors can hit cleanly.

questions.question: This tea is made from small flowers that look like mini daisies, and people drink it for a tummy ache. What is it called?
hints: It isn't made from leaves.
The flowers have white petals and a yellow center.
Peter Rabbit's mother gives him a cup of it after his adventure.
questions.description: The tea grandmas brew before you've even said “ouch”.
questions.fun_fact: You can tell real chamomile by its yellow flower center, which is hollow inside.

questions.question: Sparkling water tingles on your tongue, is full of bubbles and hisses when you open it. What is in it?
hints: It doesn't taste sweet.
If the bottle stays open for a long time, it slowly disappears.
Without it, the water would be “still”.
questions.description: Water with way too much energy that just can't sit still.
questions.fun_fact: Some springs have water that bubbles up out of the ground already fizzy, all by itself.

questions.question: What are beer coasters (Bierdeckel) usually made of?
hints: The material comes from trees.
It is so cheap that the pub can simply throw them away at the end of the night.
Shoeboxes are made of a similar material.
questions.description: The little mat where the bartender often keeps your tab in pencil strokes.
questions.fun_fact: Some people collect beer coasters; the hobby is called “tegestology”.

questions.question: Erlangen's Bergkirchweih is one of the oldest beer festivals in Germany. Which holiday is it held around?
hints: People celebrate at old beer cellars on a hill at the edge of the old town.
It lasts twelve days and starts on a Thursday.
The holiday comes seven weeks after Easter.
questions.description: A festival where you have to walk uphill before you're allowed to sit down.
questions.fun_fact: The Bergkirchweih has been held since 1755, at the old beer cellars in the Burgberg hill.

questions.question: Cinnamon sticks often float in Kinderpunsch, smell like Christmas and are rolled up. What are they made of?
hints: They don't grow underground.
They roll up by themselves as they dry.
It is peeled off the trunk of the cinnamon tree.
questions.description: It smells like Christmas but looks like a tiny roll of paper.
questions.fun_fact: True Ceylon cinnamon originally comes from Sri Lanka.

questions.question: What do people in Germany call out when they clink glasses like this?
hints: You say it before the first sip.
Kids say it too, with Apfelschorle.
The word starts with “P”.
questions.description: A sound made when glasses briefly shake hands.
questions.fun_fact: “Prost” comes from the Latin “prosit”, meaning “may it be of benefit”.

questions.question: Hagebuttentee is red and a bit sour, and kids once made itching powder from the hairy seeds. Which plant do Hagebutten grow on?
hints: The plant has thorns.
Its flowers are very popular as a gift.
It is the fruit of a famous flower.
questions.description: A tea that used to double as a prank tool in the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: Hagebutten, known in English as rose hips, are packed with vitamin C.

questions.question: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa set out with a large army on a crusade to the Holy Land. In which century was that?
hints: It was in the High Middle Ages, the time of knights and castles.
The First Crusade began shortly before the year 1100.
Barbarossa set out in the year 1189.
questions.description: An emperor with a red beard packs his bags for the longest business trip of his life.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Barbarossa sleeps inside the Kyffhäuser mountain, and his beard grows through a stone table.

questions.question: You get black tea with a Kluntje (rock sugar) and a cloud of cream, and stirring is not allowed. In which region is this a tradition?
hints: People there drink more tea than coffee.
A people the Romans already knew lives here.
The region is in Lower Saxony on the North Sea, near the Netherlands.
questions.description: Here nobody stirs; here everybody waits patiently.
questions.fun_fact: People in Ostfriesland drink about 300 liters (80 gallons) of tea per person each year, more than almost anyone else in the world.

questions.question: Who lived in the forests of what is now Germany about 2,000 years ago, when the Romans came?
hints: These peoples lived in tribes and villages.
The Romans built a long border against them, the Limes.
The Romans named the land after them: Germania.
questions.description: Long before schnitzel, the Autobahn and the Bundesliga, things were already happening here.
questions.fun_fact: The Germanic peoples didn't call themselves that at all: the Romans gave them the name.

questions.question: “Nie sollst du mich befragen” (never shall you ask me): because Elsa asks his name anyway, the swan knight must leave her. Who is he?
hints: He arrives in a boat pulled by a swan.
Richard Wagner turned his story into an opera.
His father is the Grail king Parzival.
questions.description: A marriage with just one single rule, and of course that's exactly the one that gets broken.
questions.fun_fact: The famous bridal chorus “Treulich geführt”, known in English as “Here Comes the Bride,” comes from Wagner's opera about this knight.

questions.question: Legend says this jester was born near Braunschweig around 1300 and took every order literally. Who is he?
hints: He played tricks on farmers, craftsmen and princes.
He often wears a jester's cap with little bells.
His German name is made of the words for “owl” and “mirror”.
questions.description: Anyone who tells him to go jump in a lake had better be ready for a splash.
questions.fun_fact: His supposed grave is in Mölln in Schleswig-Holstein, and people say rubbing the thumb of his statue brings good luck.

questions.question: You're walking with your lantern in the St. Martin's Day parade. According to legend, why did St. Martin cut his cloak in two?
questions.answer: A beggar was freezing in the cold
wrong_answers: The cloak was too long for him
hints: It was a cold winter day.
Martin wanted to help someone.
A poor man without warm clothes sat at the city gate.
questions.description: A man on a horse, a sword, and a piece of clothing that ended up half its size.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says honking geese gave away Martin's hiding place when he didn't want to become a bishop, which is where the St. Martin's goose (Martinsgans) comes from.

questions.question: This monument honors the Germanic tribes' victory over the Roman general Varus. In which hills does it stand?
hints: The statue shows Arminius, chief of the Cherusci tribe.
These hills are in the north of Germany.
The monument stands near Detmold.
questions.description: A man holding up his sword who hasn't put it down since 1875.
questions.fun_fact: With its base, the Hermannsdenkmal is about 53 m (174 ft) tall, and until the Statue of Liberty came along in 1886, it was the tallest statue in the Western world.

questions.question: This Old Saxon epic was written around 830 in alliterative verse and tells of Jesus as a Germanic warlord. What is it called?
hints: It is one of the oldest major works in an early form of German.
It was written in the time of Louis the Pious, to convert the Saxons.
Its title is an old word for “Savior” (in modern German, “Heiland”).
questions.description: A Bible story with chain mail and a band of loyal followers.
questions.fun_fact: The epic has almost 6,000 lines, and the disciples in it appear like loyal warriors of a prince.

questions.question: In a medieval workshop, someone hammers glowing horseshoes on an anvil. What is this job called?
hints: He works with iron and fire.
Horses need him regularly.
A German saying calls everyone the … of their own luck.
questions.description: Back before machines, every workshop was a small gym.
questions.fun_fact: This job gave Germany “Schmidt,” one of its most common last names, just as it gave English “Smith.”

questions.question: Germanic tribes drank from the horns of a wild cattle species that died out in 1627. Which animal was it?
hints: It was a huge wild ox that lived in Europe's forests.
Today's farm cattle descend from it.
Its old German name is “Ur”.
questions.description: A cup you can't put down without spilling everything.
questions.fun_fact: Julius Caesar wrote that the Germanic peoples trimmed these horns with silver and drank from them at feasts.

questions.question: Emperor Tiberius ended the Roman campaigns in Germania and left the Rhine as the border. In which century did he rule?
hints: It was shortly after the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest.
He was the direct successor of Emperor Augustus.
He ruled during the lifetime of Jesus.
questions.description: An emperor who decided Germania just wasn't worth the trouble anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Tiberius spent his last years almost entirely on the island of Capri and ruled the empire from there.

questions.question: In 1924, a plan reorganized Germany's reparations and helped make the mark stable. Which American is it named after?
hints: He was a banker and later became Vice President of the United States.
He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1925 for the plan.
Five years later, the Young Plan replaced his plan.
questions.description: When the bill is far too high, only a payment plan with a fancy name can help.
questions.fun_fact: In 1911 he wrote a piece of music that became the pop song “It's All in the Game,” a No. 1 hit in the US in 1958.

questions.question: Anne Frank wrote her diary as letters to an imaginary friend. How did the greeting go on: “Dear …”?
hints: Anne got the diary for her 13th birthday in 1942.
At first Anne wrote to several imaginary friends before sticking to this one name.
It's also a cute English word for a cat.
questions.description: A pen pal friendship where no reply ever came back.
questions.fun_fact: Anne Frank was born in Frankfurt am Main in 1929, before her family moved to Amsterdam.

questions.question: Since 1996, January 27 has been Germany's day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism. Which camp was liberated on that day in 1945?
hints: The camp was in what is now Poland.
It was liberated by the Soviet Red Army.
Since 2005, this day has also been the United Nations' International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
questions.description: A day when candles burn all over Germany in remembrance.
questions.fun_fact: The memorial site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.

questions.question: Until the end of 2015, the holder of the rights to “Mein Kampf” blocked every reprint in Germany. Who was it?
hints: After the war, the Americans handed the rights to a German authority in their occupation zone.
The rights holder is based in a state capital.
It's the largest German state by area.
questions.description: A book that kept more lawyers busy than readers for decades.
questions.fun_fact: The annotated 2016 edition has more than 3,000 notes by historians and still became a bestseller.

questions.question: In March 1920, the German government fled Berlin to escape the Kapp Putsch. How did unions and workers bring the coup down?
hints: The answer came not from the army, but from factories and offices.
Even the SPD ministers of the government that had fled called for it.
Trains stopped, power and gas went out, and millions stopped working.
questions.description: A coup with the shelf life of an open carton of milk.
questions.fun_fact: The coup fell apart after only about 100 hours.

questions.question: Which painter was NOT part of the New Objectivity movement of the 1920s?
hints: New Objectivity painted everyday life in the Weimar Republic in a cool, precise way.
One of the four had already died in World War I, in 1916.
He painted blue horses and belonged to “The Blue Rider”.
questions.description: No more sentimental mush: they paint here as if the tax office held the brush.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from a 1925 exhibition at the Kunsthalle in Mannheim.

questions.question: Hoffmann von Fallersleben wrote it on Heligoland in 1841, to a tune by Joseph Haydn. In 1922 it became the national anthem. Which song?
hints: Haydn first wrote the tune for the Austrian emperor.
Today only the third verse is sung.
That verse begins “Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit” (Unity and justice and freedom).
questions.description: A song that makes players look suddenly very serious right before kickoff.
questions.fun_fact: In 1841 Heligoland belonged to Britain, so the words of the German anthem were written on British soil.

questions.question: On May 10, students in Berlin threw books by Erich Kästner, Heinrich Heine and many others into a fire. In which year?
hints: Beneath Berlin's Bebelplatz, a memorial with empty bookshelves recalls it.
The Nazis had been in power for only a few months.
It was the year Hitler became chancellor.
questions.description: If you can't argue with books, you grab a match – not a good idea.
questions.fun_fact: Erich Kästner stood in the crowd himself and watched his own books burn.

questions.question: You're watching “Babylon Berlin”, set in 1929. Which object really shouldn't show up in it yet?
hints: Today it lies in almost every drawer.
It wasn't patented until the late 1930s.
It was invented by a Hungarian named László Bíró.
questions.description: Time travel to 1920s Berlin – don't forget your flat cap.
questions.fun_fact: “Babylon Berlin” is one of the most expensive TV series ever filmed in Germany.

previous.feedback: Source: hint 2 says the ballpoint pen "wasn't patented until the late 1930s," which is false. John J. Loud patented a ballpoint pen in 1888; what came in 1938 was Bíró's practical pen. Reword the source hint, e.g. "The first one that wrote well was patented in 1938," then re-translate. The rest of the translation is faithful and natural.

questions.question: In July 1945, at Cecilienhof Palace, I negotiated with Stalin over Germany, having been US president only since April. Who am I?
hints: I took over from a president who had died shortly before.
I came from the state of Missouri.
My first name is Harry.
questions.description: A summit meeting in a palace: no cake, but plenty of maps.
questions.fun_fact: Churchill had to leave in the middle of the conference: he had lost the election, and Clement Attlee took his place.

questions.question: Who was the Lastenausgleich (burden-sharing law), passed by the Bundestag in 1952, meant to help?
hints: The money came from a levy on wealth that had come through the war intact.
The law was seen as one of the great social tasks of the young Federal Republic under Adenauer.
About 12 million people had come from the East to the West.
questions.description: A law from Bonn whose payments ran longer than many a marriage.
questions.fun_fact: Those who had kept their wealth had to give up half its value, spread over 30 years.

questions.question: Around New Year 1918/19, a new party grew out of the Spartacus League. Which one?
hints: Its founders included Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.
It looked to the revolution in Russia as its model.
In the Soviet zone, it merged into the SED in 1946.
questions.description: A group named after a gladiator: trouble was bound to follow.
questions.fun_fact: The name recalls Spartacus, a gladiator who led a slave revolt in ancient Rome.

questions.question: Which German World War I fighter pilot was called the “Red Baron” because of his red-painted plane?
hints: His favorite plane was a Fokker triplane.
In the “Peanuts” comics, Snoopy fights air battles against him.
He was a Freiherr, and his last name starts with “von R…”.
questions.description: With him in the sky, things over France were never boring.
questions.fun_fact: Strictly speaking his title was Freiherr, not baron, but English made him the “Red Baron” anyway.

questions.question: I'm made of many colorful pieces of glass, rods of a heavy, soft metal hold me together, and in churches I make saints glow. What am I?
hints: I'm see-through, but anything but colorless.
The metal in my name was once used in old water pipes.
People say “heavy as …”, and that very metal is in my name.
questions.description: A question for anyone who has ever started pondering life while cleaning windows.
questions.fun_fact: Gerhard Richter's window in Cologne Cathedral from 2007 is made of more than 11,000 small glass squares in 72 colors.

questions.question: When do people in Germany say “Guten Appetit”?
hints: It has to do with a meal.
It's a wish that the food tastes good.
Everyone is at the table and the plates are full, but nobody has started yet.
questions.description: Two words that make your stomach burst into applause.
questions.fun_fact: In some parts of Germany, people just say “Mahlzeit!” instead, even in the office hallway at lunchtime.

questions.question: In Germany, Sunday is a day of rest: no mowing the lawn, no loud drilling, and most stores stay closed. Where can you almost always still shop?
hints: It's not a big store for tools or sofas.
It sells drinks, snacks and magazines, and something for your car too.
This is where you fill up your tank.
questions.description: The one day of the week when the lawn mower is grounded.
questions.fun_fact: Sunday as a day of rest is even protected by Germany's Basic Law, which took it over from the Weimar Constitution of 1919.

questions.question: Carpenters on the Walz wear black outfits and big hats and travel for at least three years and a day. Which place is off-limits to them?
hints: They are actually allowed to go abroad.
They are meant to get to know new places and new master craftsmen.
They usually have to stay at least 50 km (31 miles) away from where they come from.
questions.description: Three years on the road, with work, a hat and no unlimited data plan.
questions.fun_fact: Traveling journeymen traditionally carry their belongings in a tied-up cloth bundle called a “Charlottenburger”.

questions.question: Meister Eder is planing wood in his Munich workshop when Pumuckl gets stuck to the glue pot. What does “Meister” in his name mean?
questions.answer: He passed the master craftsman exam
wrong_answers: He is the mayor of Munich
hints: It has to do with his job as a carpenter.
In a skilled trade, you first train as an apprentice, then become a journeyman.
After that comes a tough exam that allows you to run your own workshop.
questions.description: A man who understands wood, but would rather not deal with invisible kobolds.
questions.fun_fact: Pumuckl began in 1962 as a radio play on Bavarian Broadcasting (Bayerischer Rundfunk), created by Ellis Kaut.

questions.question: A black cat crosses your path. According to old superstition, what does that bring?
hints: Superstitious people don't like it at all.
Black cats were once thought to be companions of witches.
It's the opposite of what a four-leaf clover brings.
questions.description: An animal that can't help how strangely people think.
questions.fun_fact: In Great Britain and Japan, on the other hand, a black cat is often seen as a lucky charm.

questions.question: It's made of iron, horses wear it on their hooves, and many people hang it over the front door. Why?
hints: It isn't supposed to do anything practical.
It belongs to the same family as the four-leaf clover and the chimney sweep.
Many hang it with the open end up so nothing “falls out”.
questions.description: A shoe that starts a second career on the door once the horse is done with it.
questions.fun_fact: Superstitious people have argued for centuries over whether the open end should point up or down.

questions.question: At which later celebration is the baptismal candle traditionally lit again?
wrong_answers: First day of school or graduation
hints: Many people remember this day for the fancy clothes.
Most people celebrate it as a child or young teen.
At this celebration, you often confirm what began at your baptism.
questions.description: A candle with patience: it waits years for its next big moment.
questions.fun_fact: Many families also light the baptismal candle again every year on the anniversary of the baptism.

questions.question: How many Formula 1 world titles did Michael Schumacher win?
hints: More than Sebastian Vettel's four titles.
Lewis Hamilton later matched him.
This number is thought of as lucky.
questions.description: He drove in circles so fast he never got dizzy.
questions.fun_fact: Schumacher learned to race at the go-kart track in Kerpen, where his father worked.

questions.question: West Germans had paid with the D-Mark since 1948. Where else did it become official money on July 1, 1990?
hints: It was a direct neighbor.
In 1989, many people there had taken to the streets demanding change.
A few months later, this country no longer existed.
questions.description: A wallet that swaps out everything inside it overnight.
questions.fun_fact: At the time, wages and pensions were converted into D-Marks at a rate of 1:1.

questions.question: What is this medal awarded for in Germany?
wrong_answers: Many years as a civil servant
hints: The Federal President awards it.
Many volunteers have received it too.
Its German name contains the word “Verdienst” (merit).
questions.description: Jewelry you can't buy, not even at the clearance sale.
questions.fun_fact: Theodor Heuss established the Bundesverdienstkreuz (Federal Cross of Merit) in 1951.

questions.question: Which little black goblin from East German children's TV loves to shout “Ach du meine Güte!” (Oh my goodness!)?
hints: He appeared on the Sandmännchen show.
His best friend is a duck.
The end of his name is the German sound of a splash into water.
questions.description: A little rascal who has made whole generations giggle in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: Pittiplatsch is a hand puppet; his friends Schnatterinchen and Moppi are a duck and a dog.

questions.question: Which word is missing from the subtitle of “Die Sendung mit der Maus”: “Lach- und …geschichten”?
hints: This subtitle has been around since the show started in 1971.
This part of the show is more for wonder and learning than for laughs.
It rhymes with “Lach”.
questions.description: An orange mouse and a blue elephant: the perfect team for Sunday morning.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Sendung mit der Maus” has been on TV since 1971.

questions.question: In what year did Lothar Matthäus captain Germany to the World Cup title?
hints: The final was played in Rome.
The opponent was Argentina.
It was the year of German reunification.
questions.description: A captain who lifted the biggest trophy in the sport high above his head.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, Matthäus also won the Ballon d'Or.

questions.question: This mural shows Erich Honecker sharing a fraternal kiss with Leonid Brezhnev. Where in Berlin can you see it?
hints: It is painted on a real piece of the Wall.
It runs right along the Spree River.
The longest surviving stretch of the Wall was turned into an outdoor art show.
questions.description: A kiss that got more famous than any love scene in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: The artist Dmitri Vrubel painted it in 1990, copying a real photo taken in 1979.

questions.question: This man hosted “Wetten, dass..?” for decades. Who is he?
hints: He comes from Kulmbach in Upper Franconia.
He is famous for his wild outfits.
He made the “Supernasen” films with Mike Krüger.
questions.description: Blond curls, loud suits and a sofa full of world stars.
questions.fun_fact: His last “Wetten, dass..?” show aired in November 2023.

questions.question: It needs a majority in the Bundestag, and a successor must be elected at the same time. Who is removed by a constructive vote of no confidence?
hints: So far it has worked only once, in 1982.
It is set out in Article 67 of the Basic Law.
It hits the head of the government.
questions.description: A way to vote someone out that only works if you already have a replacement in your pocket.
questions.fun_fact: In 1972, an attempt like this against Willy Brandt failed by just two votes.

questions.question: In which era was the radio company Telefunken founded?
hints: At first it was about wireless telegraphy, long before everyone had a radio.
The big companies AEG and Siemens teamed up to create it.
The monarch himself is said to have pushed for its founding.
questions.description: A company name that sounds like it's about to beam itself across the airwaves.
questions.fun_fact: Telefunken developed the PAL color TV system, which West Germany used to launch color television in 1967.

questions.question: Lidl has a yellow, blue and red logo, the slogan “Lidl lohnt sich” and stores in almost every town. What kind of store is Lidl?
hints: Many families go there every week.
You can buy fruit, bread and milk there.
Similar stores are called Aldi, Netto or Penny.
questions.description: A name with just one vowel, but plenty inside.
questions.fun_fact: The name Lidl comes from a retired teacher called Ludwig Lidl, from whom the founder bought the rights to the name.

questions.question: Founded in 1999 by the Samwer brothers and sold after about 100 days, it was called “Alando”. Which US company made it its German branch?
hints: On the site, you could offer used things for sale.
You bid against others until the time runs out.
“3, 2, 1 … meins!” (“3, 2, 1 … mine!”) later became a famous ad slogan.
questions.description: Three brothers, one computer and a business that got resold faster than a used bike.
