questions.fun_fact: In Friedrichshafen you can still take sightseeing flights in a modern Zeppelin NT today.

questions.question: The name Haribo stands for Hans Riegel and his hometown. In which city were gummy bears invented?
hints: The city is in North Rhine-Westphalia.
Ludwig van Beethoven was born there.
It used to be the capital of West Germany.
questions.description: Bears you can put in your mouth without any fear.
questions.fun_fact: In 1922, Hans Riegel invented the “Tanzbären” (dancing bears), the ancestors of today's Goldbären.

questions.question: Legend says glassblowers in Lauscha blew the first glass Christmas tree ornaments. What were the glass balls meant to replace?
hints: It was something to eat.
It is harvested in the fall.
It grows on trees and is often red.
questions.description: Christmas made of glass: please don't drop it!
questions.fun_fact: Legend says a poor glassblower in Lauscha around 1847 couldn't afford real apples and nuts for his tree.

questions.question: Clocks in space run slightly differently than on Earth. Which technology would soon be off by miles without Einstein's theory of relativity?
hints: This technology is in almost every smartphone.
It needs signals from several satellites at once.
It tells you: “In 200 meters, turn right.”
questions.description: Time is relative, especially when you're waiting for the bus.
questions.fun_fact: Einstein published his special theory of relativity in 1905, when he was only 26.

questions.question: Every time the Sams grants a wish, something disappears from its face. What?
hints: Mr. Taschenbier met the Sams on a Saturday.
They are perfectly round and easy to spot.
They are the same color as the sky.
questions.description: Make a wish, but not too many, or it will show on your face.
questions.fun_fact: Paul Maar's first Sams book, “Eine Woche voller Samstage” (A Week Full of Saturdays), came out in 1973.

questions.question: What are the people called in the comic tale who built a town hall without windows and tried to carry light inside in sacks?
hints: Their stories were first printed more than 400 years ago.
In German, a really silly plan is still named after them: a “…streich”.
Their name starts with the German word for the shield a knight carries on his arm.
questions.description: A town full of clever ideas, just in the wrong order.
questions.fun_fact: The stories first appeared in 1597 in the “Lalebuch”; a year later came the version set in Schilda.

questions.question: A steam train puffs its way up to this summit. Which national park is it in?
hints: The park spans two German states in the north of central Germany.
In East German times, the summit was a closed military zone on the inner-German border.
On Walpurgis Night, witches are said to meet here on the Brocken.
questions.description: Up here you need hiking boots, a thick jacket and lots of patience with the weather.
questions.fun_fact: On average, the Brocken has a climate like Iceland's, with more than 300 foggy days a year.

questions.question: Until 2005, the Dreiborn Plateau in Eifel National Park was almost completely closed to hikers. Why?
questions.answer: It was a military training area
wrong_answers: It was an open-pit lignite mine
It was a princely hunting ground
It was a disease quarantine zone
hints: Back then, signs warned visitors of mortal danger.
The closure began shortly after the Second World War and lasted almost 60 years.
Instead of hikers, tanks and soldiers moved around there.
questions.description: Where wildcats prowl today, it was definitely no picnic spot back then.
questions.fun_fact: The plateau is home to the ghost village of Wollseifen, whose residents had to leave in 1946. Its church still stands today.

questions.question: Which winter sports town in the Sauerland is known for its bobsled track?
hints: The town is in North Rhine-Westphalia.
The Kahler Asten is very close by.
Its name combines a season with a German word for mountain.
questions.description: Here you race down the ice channel faster than any sled on a sledding hill.
questions.fun_fact: The Winterberg track has already hosted several world championships in bobsled, luge and skeleton.

questions.question: The Bruchhauser Steine are four huge rock towers in the Sauerland where peregrine falcons nest. Why do they stick out of the mountain?
questions.answer: Hard rock wore away more slowly
wrong_answers: People piled them up as a holy site
hints: The rock is about 380 million years old.
It formed in volcanic eruptions under a prehistoric sea.
The softer rock around them was worn away, but they weren't.
questions.description: Four stone giants who have been standing guard over the Sauerland forever.
questions.fun_fact: In prehistoric times there was a hill fort on the rocks, and you can still see its remains today.

questions.question: In a fairy tale, a hedgehog beats a hare in a race. Who put this tale into a famous collection?
hints: The collectors were language scholars from Hesse.
They worked as a pair and also started a huge dictionary.
They also gave us “Little Red Riding Hood” and “Hansel and Gretel”.
questions.description: A race full of cheating that still makes everyone laugh.
questions.fun_fact: The hedgehog wins because his wife, who looks just like him, waits at the other end of the field.

questions.question: Lars lives at the North Pole, has white fur and is the hero of books and a movie. What kind of animal is he?
hints: He swims well and likes to eat fish.
His parents are among the largest predators on land.
His movie is called “The Little …”.
questions.description: A children's book hero who will never, ever need a winter hat.
questions.fun_fact: Lars was created by the Dutch author Hans de Beer; the first book came out in 1987.

questions.question: Which small garden bird with an orange-red breast likes to hop next to the spade looking for worms while you dig?
hints: It sometimes even sings at night under streetlights.
It's small and round, with a brown back.
An old nickname for it is “redbreast”.
questions.description: A tiny singer who starts the concert before sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, the robin became the first Bird of the Year in Germany to be chosen by a public vote.

questions.question: Gardeners say to wait until after mid-May before planting delicate plants outdoors. What are May 11–15 called, when frost is still a risk?
hints: The farmers' saying behind them is many hundreds of years old.
They end with “Kalte Sophie” on May 15.
The first part of the name means frozen water.
questions.description: The calendar says spring, but your balcony plants are still shivering.
questions.fun_fact: Because of the calendar reform of 1582, the old cold-weather rule originally fell about ten days later in the year.

questions.question: Biosphere reserves like the Rhön or the Spreewald are divided into zones. What is the rule in the core zone?
wrong_answers: The visitor center and parking are here
Farming is done here on purpose
New villages may be built here
hints: The core zone is usually the smallest part of the area.
From the outside in, the rules in each zone get stricter.
People call it wilderness: here “nature can be nature”.
questions.description: Biosphere reserves: built like an onion, just with more trees and fewer tears.
questions.fun_fact: Around the core zone lies a buffer zone for gentle use and landscape care, and only in the outer transition zone do most people live and work.

questions.question: In German, lots of small, white, fluffy clouds are named after a baby animal: “…wolken”. Which animal?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It has white, curly fur.
Its wool is knitted into sweaters.
questions.description: A sky that sometimes looks like a petting zoo.
questions.fun_fact: Experts call these clouds altocumulus or cirrocumulus, and they can be a sign that the weather is about to change.

questions.question: These leaves smell fresh and cool. What do people in Germany often make from them for a stomachache?
hints: Grandma swears by it when your tummy hurts.
It's served nice and warm.
You pour hot water over it and let it steep in a cup.
questions.description: It smells like chewing gum, but it grows quietly in the garden like a good plant.
questions.fun_fact: Peppermint is a cross between water mint and spearmint.

questions.question: What is the tree in the song “O Tannenbaum” praised for most?
wrong_answers: It grows up to the sky
hints: The praise comes right at the start of the song.
The season plays a part.
“You're green not only in the summertime…”
questions.description: A Christmas carol that pays a tree more compliments than Grandma pays her favorite grandchild.
questions.fun_fact: The well-known Christmas version of the song was written by Leipzig teacher Ernst Anschütz in 1824.

questions.question: In October 1806, Napoleon beat the Prussians in Thuringia at Auerstedt – and on the same day near which city?
hints: Afterwards, Stein and Hardenberg reformed the Prussian state.
The city lies on the Saale River.
Schiller was a history professor there.
questions.description: A day when the Prussian army would have been better off staying in bed.
questions.fun_fact: At Auerstedt, the main Prussian army lost to a single French corps only about half its size.

questions.question: In 1530, a reformer had this seal designed, with a cross, a heart and a white rose. Whose emblem is it?
hints: The white rose was meant to stand for joy and peace in faith.
Its owner had once been a monk in the Augustinian order.
His theses of 1517 set off the Reformation.
questions.description: A coat of arms that looks like it came from a flower shop, yet hangs in churches.
questions.fun_fact: The Luther rose is still the emblem of many Lutheran churches all over the world.

questions.question: In Baden, people like to eat “Brägele” with their Schäufele: crispy, golden brown, fried in a pan. What are they made of?
hints: The name comes from the Baden dialect word for frying.
This ingredient grows underground.
Elsewhere in Germany they're called Bratkartoffeln.
questions.description: A word from Baden that sounds like a noise coming out of the frying pan.
questions.fun_fact: In Baden, potatoes are also called “Grumbiere,” from “Grundbirne,” meaning a pear from the ground.

questions.question: Saure Kutteln were a cheap meal in Swabia for a long time. What are Kutteln?
hints: It's one of an animal's insides.
Cows have several compartments of it.
Elsewhere in Germany it's called Pansen or Kaldaunen.
questions.description: A Swabian dish where it's better to ask what's in it after you've eaten.
questions.fun_fact: For saure Kutteln, the strips are cooked in a sauce with vinegar or wine and often served with fried potatoes.

questions.question: What kind of body of water is this deep-blue pool in Blaubeuren in the Swabian Jura?
hints: The limestone of the Swabian Jura plays the main role in how it formed.
Behind the pool lies a huge cave system that divers explore.
The water that becomes the river Blau bubbles up out of this pool.
questions.description: A pond so blue you'd think someone put a photo filter on it.
questions.fun_fact: Behind the Blautopf, cave divers have found miles of passages, some with huge halls, under the Swabian Jura.

questions.question: What kind of lake forms when gravel and sand are dug out of the ground and the pit fills with groundwater?
hints: This lake didn't form on its own.
There's often a gravel works right next to it.
In German, it's named after a big digging machine.
questions.description: Swimsuit on, towel off, but where does all that water actually come from?
questions.fun_fact: The water in quarry lakes is often very clear because it comes from groundwater.

questions.question: Which famous work did Theodor Storm write?
hints: Storm came from Husum on the North Sea.
The novella is set on a dike in North Frisia.
Its hero is a dike reeve who builds a bold new dike.
questions.description: A poet from the North Sea coast, where the weather is often gloomier than his characters' moods.
questions.fun_fact: Storm called his hometown Husum “the gray town by the sea.”

questions.question: On the Baltic Sea beach, people often rent a big seat with a roof that keeps off wind and sun. What is it called?
hints: On the North Sea and Baltic coasts, hundreds of them often stand in rows.
Most of them fit two people.
It is woven like a basket.
questions.description: A sofa that would rather live by the sea than in the living room.
questions.fun_fact: The first Strandkorb was built in Rostock in 1882 for a lady who wanted to sit on the beach in spite of the wind.

questions.question: What is the largest lake that lies entirely in Bavaria?
hints: It is also called the “Bavarian Sea.”
One of its islands has a palace built by King Ludwig II.
Its islands are called Herreninsel and Fraueninsel.
questions.description: Where Bavaria goes swimming when the Alps are too steep.
questions.fun_fact: Herrenchiemsee Palace was meant to be a copy of Versailles, but it was never finished.

questions.question: A German word for a topped slice of bread moved into Russian, where it means any open sandwich. Which word?
hints: The word is known all over Germany, not just in one region.
In Russia, people like it with sausage, cheese or caviar for breakfast or as a snack.
In Russian, it sounds like “buterbrod”.
questions.description: A German word that moved abroad and made a career there.
questions.fun_fact: In Russia, a slice of bread with sausage or cheese is also a “buterbrod”, whether or not there's any butter on it.

questions.question: For Abendbrot, many German families have just bread, cold cuts and cheese. When did the hot meal traditionally come?
hints: Children often just got home from school then.
School and work cafeterias still serve their main hot meal at this time.
This meal falls between breakfast and Kaffee und Kuchen.
questions.description: The meal where the stove finally gets to clock off.
questions.fun_fact: Many German families eat a cold supper because the hot meal traditionally came at midday.

questions.question: In Germany, almost every fridge has a tub of Quark in it. Which group of cheeses does it belong to?
hints: It doesn't need to age in a cellar for months.
You eat it very young, right after it's made.
The group's name sounds like “just made”.
questions.description: The secret reason Grandma's cheesecake tastes the way it does.
questions.fun_fact: English borrowed the word “quark” from German.

questions.question: Whole grain flour is dark, white flour is light. Which part of the grain kernel is missing from white flour?
hints: This part is full of fiber.
It protects the kernel like a shell.
Once ground, it's called bran.
questions.description: The bread that makes Grandma nod and the kid sigh.
questions.fun_fact: Germany has more than 3,000 different kinds of bread.

questions.question: At German parties, people snake through the room in a Polonaise. The name means “the Polish one”. Which language does it come from?
hints: Not from the language of the country the dance comes from.
This language was once spoken at many European royal courts.
“Mayonnaise” and “Marseillaise” end the same way.
questions.description: Hands on the shoulders in front of you, and the party turns into a train with no timetable.
questions.fun_fact: In 1981 Gottlieb Wendehals made the Polonaise a German party classic with “Polonäse Blankenese”.

questions.question: Which national park is this lake with the famous lakeside church in?
hints: You can reach the pilgrimage church only by boat or on long mountain trails.
The lake in the photo is the Königssee.
The Watzmann towers above the lake.
questions.description: The water here is so clear that even the mountains take a second look.
questions.fun_fact: For more than 100 years, almost only quiet electric boats have run on the Königssee, and at the Echo Wall a boatman plays the trumpet.

questions.question: It dams a river in the Sauerland, is called the “Westphalian Sea,” and its wall was breached by bouncing bombs in May 1943. Which dam is it?
hints: It is in North Rhine-Westphalia, not far from Soest.
In Britain, the attack on it became known as “Operation Chastise.”
The river it dams sounds almost like the German word for carrot.
questions.description: A sea in the middle of the land, with no salt and no guaranteed seagulls.
questions.fun_fact: The wall was quickly rebuilt after 1943, and today the reservoir is a popular place for sailing.

questions.question: Complete: “A Lahnung on the North Sea coast is …”
questions.answer: … a fence of posts and brushwood to reclaim land
wrong_answers: … a channel that winds through the mudflats
… a raised mound for a house to stand on
… a gate in the dike for ships to pass
hints: They stand in rows on the mudflats in front of the dike.
They slow down the waves so that mud can settle.
They are built from wooden posts and bundles of twigs.
questions.description: A word every dike reeve on the North Sea knows, but hardly anyone inland does.
questions.fun_fact: So much mud settles behind Lahnungen that, over time, new salt marshes grow in front of the dike.

questions.question: The Inn starts in Switzerland, flows through Tyrol and then forms the border between Bavaria and Austria. Which river does it flow into?
hints: It joins it in a city known as the “City of Three Rivers”.
That city is Passau.
The river it joins ends up in the Black Sea.
questions.description: A river with only three letters, but plenty of glacier water.
questions.fun_fact: In Passau, the Inn often carries more water than the river it flows into.

questions.question: Which German island is nicknamed the “Flower Island”?
hints: It lies in Lake Constance.
It belongs to the city of Konstanz.
Its name starts with the German word for a spring month.
questions.description: An island that wears more colors in spring than a paint box.
questions.fun_fact: The neighboring island of Reichenau, on the other hand, is known as the “Vegetable Island.”

questions.question: When did Count Wilhelm of Schaumburg-Lippe have the fortress island of Wilhelmstein built up in the Steinhuder Meer lake?
hints: The count was a well-known military expert of his time.
The island was slowly piled up from stones brought in by boat.
Frederick the Great was King of Prussia at the time.
questions.description: A count who dumped a fortress into the water, probably because there was no room left on land.
questions.fun_fact: One of Germany's first submarines, the “Hecht” (pike), is said to have been built on Wilhelmstein in the 18th century.

questions.question: In different parts of Germany, the butcher (Metzger) goes by different names. Which of these names does NOT mean butcher?
hints: The job you're looking for has to do with animals, but not with sausage.
This worker deals with animal hides.
His work turns hides into leather.
questions.description: In Germany, the people who make sausage have more names than a noble.
questions.fun_fact: The town of Hildesheim has the Knochenhauer-Amtshaus, a grand timber-framed building that used to be the butchers' guild hall.

questions.question: What is the “Frischetheke” in a German supermarket for?
questions.answer: Having sausage and cheese sliced to order
wrong_answers: Baking rolls yourself in a machine
hints: Staff stand there behind a glass screen.
You say how many grams you want.
You often hear “Darf’s ein bisschen mehr sein?” (“Is a little more okay?”) there.
questions.description: Here the scale is stricter than any gym teacher.
questions.fun_fact: The line “Darf’s ein bisschen mehr sein?” (“Is a little more okay?”) is so typical of German meat counters that it has become a common saying.

questions.question: This herb is green, hollow like a straw and tastes of onion. Chopped into tiny rings, it goes on Quark bread. Which herb is it?
hints: It's related to onions and garlic.
It's best cut with scissors.
Its German name, “Schnittlauch”, means “cutting leek”.
questions.description: The green hair gel for every slice of Quark bread.
questions.fun_fact: You can eat the purple flowers of chives too.

questions.question: I'm a cooked German sausage. In eastern Germany, I'm cut in thick slices, breaded, fried and served with pasta and tomato sauce. What am I?
hints: In the East, the dish is still called a “schnitzel”.
It was a classic in East German school cafeterias.
The dish is named after a man with a rifle and a hat in the forest.
questions.description: A schnitzel that has never been a schnitzel in its whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Order a “Jägerschnitzel” in the East and you often get breaded sausage; in the West, it's a schnitzel with mushroom sauce.

questions.question: You stop at an inn in the Black Forest for a “Vesper”. What usually ends up on the table?
questions.answer: Bread, cured ham, sausage and cheese
hints: It's a cold meal.
People like to eat it off a wooden board.
In Bavaria, the same thing is called “Brotzeit”.
questions.description: The reward at the end of the hike that makes every uphill step worth it.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Vesper” comes from the Latin “vespera”, which means “evening”.

questions.question: The “Historische Wurstkuchl” by the Stone Bridge in Regensburg is said to be one of the world's oldest cookshops. How far back does its history go?
hints: “One of the oldest in the world” is meant seriously.
It started as a kitchen for the workers on a building site.
The Stone Bridge was built in the High Middle Ages.
questions.description: Sausages have been sizzling here for longer than some castles have been standing.
questions.fun_fact: Regensburg's Stone Bridge is one of the oldest stone bridges still standing in Germany.

questions.question: Fleischwurst cut into strips, pickles and lots of mayonnaise: what is this salad from the deli counter called?
hints: It's a classic on a Brötchen.
It's more white than green.
Its name leaves out the sausage and uses a broader word instead.
questions.description: A salad where the vegetables only get a supporting role.
questions.fun_fact: Germany's official food guidelines, the Deutsches Lebensmittelbuch, set how much meat has to be in a Fleischsalat.

questions.question: In the folk song “Am Brunnen vor dem Tore”, a tree like the one in the photo stands by the well. What kind of tree is it?
hints: People like to make tea from its blossoms for colds.
Its leaves are heart-shaped.
A famous grand boulevard in Berlin is called “Unter den …”.
questions.description: A traveler, a well and a tree: that's all a catchy tune has needed for almost 200 years.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by the Dessau poet Wilhelm Müller; Franz Schubert set them to music in 1827 in his song cycle “Winterreise”.

questions.question: The song goes “Auf der Mauer, auf der Lauer sitzt 'ne kleine Wanze.” What do you do when you sit “auf der Lauer”?
hints: Cats love doing it in front of a mouse hole.
You stay very quiet while doing it.
You watch closely without being seen yourself.
questions.description: A song starring a little bedbug, and yet nothing itches.
questions.fun_fact: With every verse you leave one more letter off “Wanze” and “tanzen”, until in the end almost only humming is left.

questions.question: In the children's song “Grün, grün, grün sind alle meine Kleider” (green are all my clothes), you wear green because of your sweetheart's job. What is the sweetheart?
hints: He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He often wears a hat with a feather.
He sits up in a raised wooden stand, watching for deer.
questions.description: A song where your closet gives away who you're in love with.
questions.fun_fact: In other verses you wear black, for example, because your sweetheart is a chimney sweep.

questions.question: In the song, Bruder Jakob sleeps while these are ringing. Who is Bruder Jakob?
hints: He lives together with lots of “brothers.”
He wears a long robe with a hood.
He lives in a monastery and prays a lot.
questions.description: A song for anyone who hits the snooze button three times every morning.
questions.fun_fact: The song comes from France, where it is called “Frère Jacques.”

questions.question: At bedtime, children hear the song “Weißt du, wie viel Sternlein stehen” (do you know how many little stars there are). Who, the song says, counted all the stars?
hints: The song says not a single star is missing from his great count.
The song says he also knows every child.
You talk to him in your evening prayers.
questions.description: A lullaby for kids who want to squeeze in some math before falling asleep.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by the pastor Wilhelm Hey and first printed in 1837.

questions.question: As a child she won the Grand Prix der Volksmusik with her father, comes from the Vogtland and was married to Stefan Mross. Who?
hints: She grew up in Saxony.
Her father Eberhard is a folk music singer too.
Her first name is very close to her ex-husband's.
questions.description: Dirndl, yodeling, a never-ending smile: the must-see show for every Saturday night in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: Her winning song from 1992 was called “Über jedes Bacherl geht a Brückerl”.

questions.question: In the song “Summ, summ, summ,” the little bee should build “manche volle Wabe.” What is a Wabe?
hints: It is made of lots of tiny chambers.
Each chamber has six corners.
Bees build it themselves and fill it with their sweet supplies.
questions.description: A children's song where you don't need to be scared, even though there's a stinger.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by Hoffmann von Fallersleben, the poet who wrote the Deutschlandlied, Germany's national anthem.

questions.question: In the song “Hänschen klein”, little Hans goes out into the wide world alone. Who cries very hard about it?
hints: She raised little Hans.
She is the only one who knows him at once when he comes back.
She gets flowers on her own special day in May.
questions.description: A song about the very first time leaving home, with a walking stick and a hat.
questions.fun_fact: After seven years, Hans comes back all grown up: his sister doesn't recognize him, but his mother does right away.

questions.question: Where does the “Ballermann” on Mallorca get its name from?
hints: The name is really a Spanish word that Germans said their own way.
There are lots of them along the Playa de Palma, all numbered.
It means “Balneario 6”, a small beach stand.
questions.description: Germany's loudest party spot isn't actually in Germany at all.
questions.fun_fact: “Balneario” means something like “bathing place” in Spanish, and German vacationers turned it into “Ballermann”.

questions.question: In which year was the great Luther Monument in Worms unveiled?
hints: By then, Luther himself had been dead for more than 300 years.
The monument was paid for with donations from all over Germany.
The year is in the 19th century.
questions.description: A reformer in bronze who has stood on the same spot forever and still refuses to take anything back.
questions.fun_fact: Besides Luther, the Worms monument shows other figures such as Jan Hus, and it is one of the largest Reformation monuments in the world.

questions.question: This Ampelmännchen (little traffic light man) with a hat is a cult icon in Berlin today. Which state did he first come from?
hints: He was designed in 1961.
After reunification he was actually supposed to be replaced.
He comes from the socialist half of divided Germany.
questions.description: He wears a hat, never walks on red, and is still a star.
questions.fun_fact: The Ampelmännchen was invented by traffic psychologist Karl Peglau; after the Wall fell, protests by citizens saved him from being scrapped.

questions.question: In which century did Schwerin Castle get its fairy-tale look of today?
hints: It looks older than it is.
One of its models was the French Loire castle of Chambord.
It was built around the same time as Neuschwanstein, just a little earlier.
questions.description: A castle on an island: handy protection against uninvited in-laws.
questions.fun_fact: Today the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania meets in Schwerin Castle, and legend says a little ghost, the Petermännchen, haunts it.

questions.question: This giant figure stands high above the Rhine near Rüdesheim. Who does she represent?
hints: The monument honors the founding of the German Empire in 1871.
The figure stands for the whole of Germany.
Her name sounds like the Latin word for Germany.
questions.description: A lady with a sword and a crown who has been keeping an eye on the Rhine for over 100 years.
questions.fun_fact: The Germania of the Niederwald Monument is about 10.5 m (34 ft) tall and was unveiled in 1883.

questions.question: The world's largest model railway sits in an old warehouse, has a mini airport and millions of visitors. In which city?
hints: Its miniature worlds show landscapes from many countries, such as Scandinavia, Switzerland and Italy.
The city has Germany's largest port.
The Elbphilharmonie is not far away.
questions.description: A world where the trains are always on time, because they're only the size of a thumb.
questions.fun_fact: At the model airport in Miniatur Wunderland, tiny planes take off and land all the time, controlled by computers.

questions.question: In what year did artists from around the world paint the East Side Gallery in Berlin?
hints: Before that, painting on this spot was strictly forbidden.
It happened shortly after the Berlin Wall fell.
Germany was reunified in the same year.
questions.description: Probably the most famous wall where scribbling was officially allowed.
questions.fun_fact: At more than 1.3 km (0.8 mi), the East Side Gallery is the longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall.

questions.question: Which river flows right through the middle of Berlin?
hints: Tour boats on it cruise past the Reichstag.
It flows into the Havel in Berlin's Spandau district.
It also flows through a forest region famous for its pickles.
questions.description: The capital has wet feet, and not just when it rains.
questions.fun_fact: The Spree is actually longer than the Havel, the river it flows into at Spandau.

questions.question: I show surprise with “Ei verbibbsch!”, say “nu” when I mean yes, and turn Kaffee into “Gaffee”. Which dialect am I?
hints: In polls about favorite dialects, I often end up near the bottom.
My home is in eastern Germany.
You can hear me in Leipzig and Dresden.
questions.description: A dialect is speaking up for itself here, so please don't laugh.
questions.fun_fact: For his Bible translation, Martin Luther drew on the Saxon chancery language, which back then was considered especially refined.

questions.question: Which German state does this map show? The hole in the middle is not a printing mistake.
hints: It lies in eastern Germany.
The hole is a state of its own.
Its capital is Potsdam, home of Sanssouci Palace.
questions.description: Pine trees, lakes and sand: more nature here than headlines.
questions.fun_fact: The Brandenburg Gate isn't in Brandenburg at all but in Berlin; it's named after the road to the town of Brandenburg an der Havel.

questions.question: It’s named after a French city, it’s a classic in Saarland and it’s often eaten in slices. What is a “Lyoner”?
hints: You buy it at the butcher’s counter.
In Saarland, people also fry it in a pan with potatoes.
Elsewhere it’s often called Fleischwurst.
questions.description: France is right next door, and some things just stuck around in Saarland.
questions.fun_fact: In Lyon itself, the sausage is hardly known by this name, and where it really comes from is still unclear.

questions.question: You’re standing in front of Dresden’s Frauenkirche. What was on this spot for about 50 years before it was rebuilt?
hints: Nothing new was built on this spot in East German times.
The church was destroyed in February 1945.
Many of the old stones were used again when it was rebuilt.
questions.description: Dresden, the Elbe, Baroque style and a church with quite an eventful life story.
questions.fun_fact: The dark stones in the light-colored walls come from the old church, which makes it look like a jigsaw puzzle.

questions.question: The bear on Berlin's coat of arms: how many legs is it standing on?
hints: It is black and sticks out its red tongue.
It looks ready for a fight, with its claws stretched forward.
It stands upright, like a person.
questions.description: A furry resident of the capital who never had to go apartment hunting.
questions.fun_fact: The top prize of the Berlin Film Festival is a bear too: the Golden Bear.

questions.question: How many other German states does Mecklenburg-Vorpommern border?
hints: To the north lies the Baltic Sea, to the east Poland.
To the west it borders Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
To the south, only Brandenburg is left.
questions.description: There's so much Baltic Sea air here, they should really start exporting it.
questions.fun_fact: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has about 2,000 lakes, including the Müritz, the largest lake that lies entirely within Germany.

questions.question: The Rheinturm is about 240 m (787 ft) tall, stands next to the state parliament and shows the time with lights. In which city is it?
hints: People here prefer Altbier to Kölsch.
The Königsallee is a famous shopping street here.
This city is the state capital of North Rhine-Westphalia.
questions.description: A tower that tells you the time, if you can just count the lights fast enough.
questions.fun_fact: The lights on the tower's shaft are said to form the world's largest decimal clock.

questions.question: Who would typically call this pastry a “Brezn”?
hints: People there often call a bread roll a “Semmel”.
The region is in the south of Germany and reaches the Alps.
It’s the state whose capital is Munich.
questions.description: A pastry with its arms crossed and a different name depending on where you are.
questions.fun_fact: You can spot a Swabian pretzel by its thin little arms and its fat “belly”.

questions.question: Bats were once seen as witches’ animals that get tangled in your hair at night. Bats are mammals. What are their wings made of?
hints: Birds and bats fly in very different ways.
The wings are soft and stretchy and fold up like an umbrella.
The wing is a rebuilt hand, and you have its material all over your body too.
questions.description: It hangs out all day and still has a bad reputation.
questions.fun_fact: Bats don’t get caught in hair: thanks to echolocation, they can even dodge thin threads.

questions.question: What do Germans mean when they say “Das ist wie verhext!”?
wrong_answers: Someone is acting like a witch
Something has gone suddenly, eerily quiet
hints: People usually say it when they’re annoyed.
It feels as if someone had put a curse on things.
The key won’t fit, the printer won’t print, the puzzle piece is missing.
questions.description: A broom, a cauldron and a grumpy witch’s cat cooked up this saying together.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, people really did blame witches when the milk went sour or the butter wouldn’t set.

questions.question: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale, the big bad wolf eats Little Red Riding Hood and her grandmother. Who gets them both out of his belly?
hints: He hears the wolf snoring loudly.
He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He carries a rifle and wears a green hat.
questions.description: A wolf who clearly bit off more than he could chew at dinner.
questions.fun_fact: Afterwards they fill the wolf's belly with heavy stones.

questions.question: Sometimes mushrooms grow in a perfect circle on a meadow. According to legend, when did elves dance there?
hints: Elves don't like being watched by humans.
Elves love soft, silvery light.
The stars are shining in the sky then.
questions.description: A dance floor the lawn laid out all by itself.
questions.fun_fact: The mushroom ring forms because the fungus's web of threads underground grows a bit further outward every year.

questions.question: Superstition says that if you spill salt, you should quickly throw a pinch of it. Where?
hints: The salt is meant to hit someone lurking behind you.
That someone is the devil.
He sits on the side where your heart beats.
questions.description: A pinch of panic for the kitchen table.
questions.fun_fact: In Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper,” Judas has knocked over a salt cellar.

questions.question: In Germany, someone sneezes and you wish them not to get sick. Which word do you call out?
hints: You say it right after the sneeze.
Lots of Americans say it too.
It's the German word for “health.”
questions.description: The magic word after a big “Achoo!”
questions.fun_fact: People once believed that a sneeze could let illness or evil spirits slip into the body.

questions.question: It's white and fluffy, and you blow it away and make a wish. What hangs from each of its tiny parachutes?
hints: The wind carries the tiny parachutes far away.
Where they land, something happens later.
A new dandelion grows from it.
questions.description: A wish machine standing in every meadow.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny parachutes of a dandelion puff, the “Pusteblume”, can be carried many kilometers by the wind.

questions.question: In old German curses like “Zum Kuckuck!” or “Weiß der Kuckuck!”, the cuckoo stands for someone people didn't want to name. Who?
hints: People feared that saying his name would summon him.
He is said to have horns and a horse's hoof.
He supposedly lives in hell.
questions.description: A bird that has to fill in for somebody else entirely.
questions.fun_fact: German folk belief says you should jingle the coins in your purse when you hear the first cuckoo call in spring, so your money won't run out all year.

questions.question: Folk belief says witches mixed an ointment in their cauldron and rubbed it on their brooms. What was it for?
hints: They really needed it on Walpurgis Night.
They wanted to travel to the Blocksberg with it.
After that, things went sky-high.
questions.description: A beauty product made for one very special job.
questions.fun_fact: On Walpurgis Night, witches were said to fly to the Brocken in the Harz Mountains, also known as the Blocksberg.

questions.question: What does the old German farmers' saying „Grüne Weihnachten, weiße Ostern“ (“green Christmas, white Easter”) predict?
questions.answer: No snow at Christmas, but snow at Easter
wrong_answers: Snow at Christmas, but lots of sun at Easter
Lots of rain in December, lots of sun at Easter
Green fir trees at Christmas, white Easter eggs
hints: It's about the weather on two holidays.
The two holidays sort of swap their looks.
White is what drifts down from the sky in winter.
questions.description: The farmers' weather report always had a good eye for color.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Germany there's usually no snow at Christmas, so a “green Christmas” is more the rule than the exception.

questions.question: According to superstition, you should never give anyone shoes. What will the person do with them otherwise?
hints: Shoes are made for walking, after all.
The shoes carry them in one particular direction.
In the end, the giver is left alone.
questions.description: Under the Christmas tree, a shoebox looks more harmless than it really is.
questions.fun_fact: As a remedy, the person getting the shoes often hands over a small coin, so the shoes count as bought.

questions.question: Felipe González became Spain’s prime minister in 1982. Which party governed Spain right before him?
hints: It was a centrist party
It was founded by the first prime minister of the democracy
Its best-known leader was Adolfo Suárez
questions.description: Before the corduroy jacket moved in, someone else held the keys to La Moncloa.
questions.fun_fact: Felipe González governed for almost 14 years in a row, from 1982 to 1996: no one has held the office longer since democracy returned.

questions.question: In 1998, Real Madrid fans went wild celebrating “la Séptima” (the Seventh). What were they counting?
hints: As usual, the party ended at the Cibeles fountain.
The club had gone more than 30 years without winning this title.
Today it's called the Champions League.
questions.description: At the Bernabéu they count on their fingers, but they need both hands and a foot too.
questions.fun_fact: Real Madrid had waited 32 years: the previous one was in 1966, and the 1998 win came with a Mijatović goal in Amsterdam.

questions.question: In what year did Adolfo Suárez win the first democratic elections after Franco's death?
hints: It was shortly after Franco died in 1975.
It was before the Constitution was approved.
The Constitution dates from 1978.
questions.description: The ballot boxes had been in storage so long that someone had to dust them off.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2014, Madrid-Barajas Airport has been named after Adolfo Suárez.

questions.question: In October 1934, the CEDA party joining the government set off a workers’ revolution led by armed miners. Where did it succeed?
hints: It’s in the north of Spain
Its coast faces the Cantabrian Sea
The rebels even took the city of Oviedo
questions.description: An October that turned out far more eventful than the Republic had planned.
questions.fun_fact: To crush it, the government brought troops over from Africa, including Legionnaires and Moroccan regular units.

questions.question: At the opening ceremony of the Barcelona '92 Olympics, an archer shot a flaming arrow. What for?
hints: It had to do with fire
That fire travels from Greece
It burns for the whole Games
questions.description: A shot watched live by half the planet, with no pressure at all.
questions.fun_fact: The archer, Antonio Rebollo, was a Paralympic athlete, and his arrow actually flew over the cauldron.

questions.question: In November 1975, about 350,000 Moroccans walked across the border of Spanish Sahara, unarmed and carrying flags. What was it called?
hints: It was organized by King Hassan II of Morocco
The marchers carried Moroccan flags and copies of the Quran
Its name is the color linked with Islam
questions.description: A stroll through the desert with more people than a packed stadium… several times over.
questions.fun_fact: A few months later, in February 1976, Spain left Western Sahara for good.

questions.question: In 1968, the chosen singer wanted to sing in Catalan, Massiel replaced him at the last minute, and she won in London. What did she win?
hints: It's an international song contest
Each country votes for the others
TV channels all over Europe broadcast it every year
questions.description: A song with lyrics so easy that even the family parrot knows them.
questions.fun_fact: The next year Spain won again with Salomé, but in a tie with three other countries.

questions.question: After Franco died in 1975, who became Spain’s head of state?
hints: Franco had chosen him as his successor
He wasn’t elected at the ballot box
He was the grandson of the last king before the Republic
questions.description: November 1975: Spain gets a new boss and a whole new set of things to talk about.
questions.fun_fact: Franco had named Juan Carlos his successor, with the title of king, back in 1969.

questions.question: Spain's Second Republic was proclaimed in 1931. What form of government did Spain have just before?
hints: Two days earlier there were local elections
The head of state went into exile
Alfonso XIII was on the throne
questions.description: For something to be the “second,” something… or someone… had to come first.
questions.fun_fact: The Republic was proclaimed on April 14, 1931, just two days after local elections.

questions.question: When did Federico García Lorca write “Blood Wedding” and “Yerma”?
hints: He was friends with Dalí and Buñuel
He belonged to the Generation of '27
It was during the Second Republic
questions.description: Poet, playwright, pianist and artist: the Swiss Army knife of literature.
questions.fun_fact: Lorca ran La Barraca, a university theater group that toured Spain's villages performing classic plays.

questions.question: ONCE was founded in 1938; its lottery coupon is sold at street kiosks and drawn almost daily. Who does it mainly employ?
hints: Its sellers are spread across towns and cities all over Spain
ONCE pushed for many products and banknotes to have raised marks so they can be recognized by touch
Its full Spanish name includes the word «Ciegos»
questions.description: A little slip of paper that has promised happy days from the corner kiosk for decades.
questions.fun_fact: Today ONCE also employs people with other disabilities, not just visual ones.

questions.question: They were Muslims living in lands conquered by the Christian kingdoms, and they could keep their religion. What were they called?
hints: They lived mostly between the 11th and 15th centuries.
They were neither Christians nor converts.
Their name is also given to an art style of brick towers in Teruel.
questions.description: Lifelong neighbors who suddenly woke up with a new king.
questions.fun_fact: The Mozarabs were just the opposite: Christians living in al-Andalus under Muslim rule.

questions.question: Look at this close-up. Its Arabic name meant “Mount of Tariq”, after the general who landed here in 711. What is it?
hints: It stands by the sea, in the south.
From there you can see Africa.
It sits next to the strait that shares its name.
questions.description: A rock with more history than many countries.
questions.fun_fact: “Gibraltar” is the Spanish form of the Arabic “Jabal Tariq”, which means “Mount of Tariq”.

questions.question: Who carried the famous sword Tizona into battle?
hints: He was a Castilian knight of the 11th century.
He conquered Valencia.
His name was Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar.
questions.description: A sword with its own name, like the ones in the movies, but real.
questions.fun_fact: The sword kept as Tizona is in the Museum of Burgos, and El Cid had another famous sword too: Colada.

questions.question: The Umayyads ruled a huge empire until they were overthrown in 750, and one of them fled to al-Andalus. From which city did they rule?
hints: It's in the Middle East.
Today it's the capital of an Asian country.
It's the capital of Syria.
questions.description: A family move of more than 4,000 km (2,500 miles), with no moving van.
questions.fun_fact: The survivor, Abd al-Rahman I, founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756 and began building its great mosque.

questions.question: Ferdinand III the Saint conquered Córdoba and Seville. His son and heir, Alfonso, backed the Cantigas de Santa María. What was his number?
hints: He was king of Castile in the 13th century.
He got a nickname for his great learning.
He is known as “the Wise.”
questions.description: Taking the throne after a saint: talk about a high bar to clear.
questions.fun_fact: Ferdinand III inherited León in 1230 and joined it to Castile for good, even though his father, Alfonso IX, wanted to leave it to his daughters.

questions.question: In 1266, after a Mudéjar revolt, James I of Aragon conquered Murcia. Which kingdom did he then hand it over to?
hints: He did it because of a treaty signed years earlier.
He gave it to his son-in-law, Alfonso X.
It's the kingdom that Toledo and Seville also belonged to.
questions.description: Conquer a city just to give it away: medieval generosity knew no limits.
questions.fun_fact: With the Treaty of Almizra in 1244, Aragon and Castile had already split up the lands they still had to conquer.

questions.question: This room in Moorish Granada has star-shaped skylights in its ceiling. What was it?
hints: People went there often, and not to pray or to shop.
It had rooms of cold, warm and hot water.
The Romans had similar places called thermae.
questions.description: A place in Moorish Granada that nobody was in a hurry to leave.
questions.fun_fact: El Bañuelo in Granada, from the 11th century, is one of the best-preserved Arab baths in Spain.

questions.question: These ruins are at Empúries (Girona), a colony founded around 575 BC by a people who came by sea. Which people?
hints: Its ancient name, Emporion, means “market” in their language.
The same people also founded Massalia, today’s Marseille.
They are the people of Zeus, Athena and the first Olympic Games.
questions.description: A port on the Costa Brava that had tourists long before it had hotels.
questions.fun_fact: A large statue of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine, was found at Empúries.

questions.question: Spain has giant stones set upright in the ground, like this one. Who raised them?
hints: They're older than any castle or city.
Their builders didn't know how to write yet.
It was the age when people used stone tools.
questions.description: A stone that has been standing for thousands of years and has never once sat down.
questions.fun_fact: The word “menhir” comes from Breton and means “long stone”.

questions.question: Which Germanic people made Toledo the capital of their kingdom in Hispania?
hints: They ruled Hispania after the fall of Rome.
Their kingdom ended when the Muslims arrived in 711.
Their name means something like “western Goths”.
questions.description: They came from the north, stayed a few centuries and left gold crowns along the way.
questions.fun_fact: The Treasure of Guarrazar, found near Toledo, includes gold crowns that kings gave to churches.

questions.question: The Antequera Dolmens Site is a World Heritage Site. Which of these places is NOT part of it?
hints: The site includes three dolmens and two natural mountains.
One of the dolmens faces a mountain shaped like a face.
The odd one out is on the Málaga coast.
questions.description: A spot in Málaga where the stones weigh more than their builders' patience.
questions.fun_fact: The Dolmen of Menga faces the Peña de los Enamorados, which is very unusual for a dolmen.

questions.question: The Visigothic king Leovigild minted coins with his name, fought his son Hermenegild and in 585 conquered a kingdom in the northwest. Which one?
hints: That kingdom lay in the old region of Gallaecia.
Its capital was Braga, in today's Portugal.
It was a Germanic people that reached Hispania in 409, together with the Vandals and Alans.
questions.description: A king more eager to join maps together than to make peace at home.
questions.fun_fact: Leovigild was the first Visigothic king to sit on a throne and wear a crown, copying the emperors.

questions.question: Apulia, Italy, 216 BC: Hannibal’s Balearic slingers and Iberians surround a much bigger Roman army. Which battle is it?
hints: It was in the Second Punic War.
It was Hannibal’s great victory in Italy.
Its name sounds a lot like a French city famous for its film festival.
questions.description: A move so good that generals still copy it two thousand years later.
questions.fun_fact: The encircling move used at Cannae is still studied at military academies.

questions.question: This sculpture, the Lady of Elche, is one of the great treasures of ancient Hispania. Which people made it?
hints: It is older than the arrival of Rome.
This people lived in the east and south of the peninsula.
Their name sounds like the name of the peninsula itself.
questions.description: A lady with ensaimada-shaped hair who has been posing for 2,500 years.
questions.fun_fact: It has a hollow in its back, which may have been used to hold ashes.

questions.question: You're walking through the city the Romans called Caesaraugusta. What is it called today?
hints: It stands on the banks of the Ebro.
Today it's the capital of Aragon.
The Basilica of the Pilar is there.
questions.description: A name so long that the centuries had to keep chipping letters off it.
questions.fun_fact: Over the centuries, Arabs and Christians said “Caesaraugusta” until it turned into “Saraqusta” and then Zaragoza.

questions.question: Who painted these bison in the Altamira cave?
hints: They were painted thousands of years ago.
Back then, Europe was much colder than it is today.
They lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, using stone tools.
questions.description: Graffiti that no town hall has ever dared to scrub off.
questions.fun_fact: The paintings were discovered in 1879 by a girl, María Sanz de Sautuola, who looked up at the ceiling.

questions.question: These little brick columns stood under the floor of Roman baths and let hot air flow through. What is this space called?
hints: It was heated by a furnace burning at one side.
Its Greek name means “burned from below”.
Its name starts like “hypothermia”.
questions.description: Underfloor heating is more than two thousand years old, and this is how we know.
questions.fun_fact: At the Roman villa of La Olmeda (Palencia), a hypocaust survives beneath its mosaics.

questions.question: It stands on Madrid's Plaza de Oriente, Isabella II opened it in 1850 and it is Spain's great opera house. Which is it?
hints: It opened its doors in the mid-19th century.
It faces a huge palace.
Its name shares a word with the palace across from it.
questions.description: A place where people pay to listen to very well-tuned shouting for three hours.
questions.fun_fact: It was closed from 1925 because of damage to the building and didn't become an opera house again until 1997.

questions.question: This painting shows the surrender at Bailén in 1808. Which ruler saw his army lose its first big open-field battle there?
hints: He was French.
He crowned himself emperor in 1804.
He wore a bicorne hat and ended his days in exile on the island of Saint Helena.
questions.description: A painting where someone is having a much worse day than you.
questions.fun_fact: The general who won the battle, Francisco Javier Castaños, was later made Duke of Bailén.

questions.question: You're in Zaragoza's Plaza de los Sitios, which honors its stand against the French. How many sieges did the city go through in that war?
hints: They all took place between 1808 and 1809.
Agustina de Aragón became famous during the first one.
The second ended with the city's surrender in February 1809, and there were no more.
questions.description: A city that took “don't open the door to strangers” very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Benito Pérez Galdós devoted one of his “Episodios Nacionales” novels to these sieges, simply titled “Zaragoza”.

questions.question: Godoy signed the Treaty of Fontainebleau with Napoleon to split Portugal and let French troops cross Spain. In what year?
hints: Charles IV was still King of Spain.
The Mutiny of Aranjuez came soon after.
It was a few months before May 2, 1808.
questions.description: A “come on in, make yourself at home” kind of deal… and then nobody could get the guest to leave.
questions.fun_fact: Napoleon abdicated in that same Palace of Fontainebleau in 1814.

questions.question: The Spanish army took it in 1860, O'Donnell was made its duke, and a Madrid district bears its name “de las Victorias”. What city is it?
hints: It's in northern Morocco.
It later became the capital of the Spanish Protectorate.
It's also a station on Line 1 of the Madrid Metro.
questions.description: A war that left more names on Madrid's street map than in school textbooks.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Antonio de Alarcón went to that war as a reporter and told its story in his “Diario de un testigo de la guerra de África”.

questions.question: In which century did Rosalía de Castro, the great poet of “Cantares gallegos”, live?
hints: She lived at the same time as Bécquer.
She lived during the reign of Queen Isabella II.
She died in 1885.
questions.description: No, this Rosalía has never released an album or won a Grammy.
questions.fun_fact: Galician Literature Day is celebrated on May 17 because “Cantares gallegos” came out on that day in 1863.

questions.question: I helped draft the Bases de Manresa in 1892, cofounded the Lliga Regionalista and led the Mancomunitat of Catalonia. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Castellterçol in 1870.
I wrote the book “La nacionalitat catalana”.
I was the first president of the Mancomunitat, in 1914, and died in office in 1917.
questions.description: Bases that have nothing to do with baseball or pizza.
questions.fun_fact: As president of the Barcelona Provincial Council, he pushed for the founding of the Institut d'Estudis Catalans in 1907.

questions.question: Archduke Charles held his court in this city and married there in 1708, and the city held out under a long siege until 1714. Which city is it?
hints: It's by the sea.
Its fall in 1714 ended the War of the Spanish Succession on the Peninsula.
It's the capital of Catalonia.
questions.description: A would-be king left empty-handed, like someone who misses the last slice of tortilla.
questions.fun_fact: The archduke never got to reign in Spain, but in 1711 he became Holy Roman Emperor as Charles VI.

questions.question: Espartero and the Carlist general Maroto sealed the peace with the “Embrace of Vergara” in 1839. Which Carlist War ended this way?
hints: It had begun in 1833.
It broke out when Ferdinand VII died.
No Carlist War started before it.
questions.description: A hug so famous that streets are still named after it.
questions.fun_fact: Baldomero Espartero went on to become regent of Spain from 1840 to 1843.

questions.question: The building in the Puerta del Sol whose clock rings in the New Year was built under Charles III. What was it built for?
hints: It was designed by the French architect Jacques Marquet.
In front of it is the plaque marking Kilometer Zero.
Letters were received and sent from there.
questions.description: The most watched building in Spain, even if only for one night a year.
questions.fun_fact: The famous clock was put up in 1866, a gift from the clockmaker José Rodríguez de Losada.

questions.question: Spain lost Puerto Rico in 1898, along with Cuba and the Philippines. What is Puerto Rico today?
questions.answer: A territory of the United States
hints: People pay with dollars there.
It has its own flag and governor, but no army of its own.
It isn't a state, but it answers to Washington.
questions.description: An island that got passed from hand to hand like the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: More than a century later, Spanish is still the most widely spoken language in Puerto Rico.

questions.question: Which president of the First Spanish Republic resigned in 1873 so he wouldn't have to sign death sentences?
hints: He was a professor of philosophy.
He was the third of the four presidents of 1873.
He was born in Alhama la Seca, in Almería.
questions.description: A president who lasted in office less time than a yogurt in the fridge.
questions.fun_fact: His tomb in Madrid says he gave up power rather than sign a death sentence.

questions.question: You see on the news that someone has won three “Goyas.” What have they won?
hints: They're handed out every year at a big gala.
They're given by an academy based in Madrid, and the winners go up on stage to collect them.
They're like the Oscars, but in Spain.
questions.description: A big bronze head that lots of famous people dream of taking home.
questions.fun_fact: The statuette for these awards is a bronze bust of the painter Francisco de Goya himself.

questions.question: Which king approved the founding of the Real Academia Española (Royal Spanish Academy) in 1714?
hints: A war over the throne ended that same year.
He came to the throne in 1700 and reigned for more than 40 years.
He was the grandson of Louis XIV of France.
questions.description: The referee of the Spanish language: no whistle, just a very big dictionary.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Spanish Academy's motto is “Limpia, fija y da esplendor”: “It cleans, sets and gives splendor.”

questions.question: The red and yellow flag was born in 1785 under Charles III, because the old white flag was mixed up with those of other kingdoms. Who used it first?
hints: Charles III wanted it to be recognized from very far away.
It was raised at the top of masts.
It sailed the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.
questions.description: Two colors that have been waving from balconies across half of Spain for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: It only became the flag of the whole army in 1843, under Isabella II.

questions.question: Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar ride through town on floats, throw candy and collect children's letters. What is this parade called?
hints: It takes place on the evening just before the presents arrive.
The stars of the show come from the East.
It's a parade with camels, pages and three men wearing crowns.
questions.description: The only traffic jam of the year where everyone fights for the front row.
questions.fun_fact: Alcoy, in Alicante, claims to have the oldest Cabalgata de Reyes in Spain, dating from the late 19th century.

questions.question: This shiny ornament with a tail goes on top of the stable in the belén (nativity scene). What is it?
hints: Many people also put one on top of the Christmas tree.
The Three Wise Men followed it.
It has points and it shines.
questions.description: In every home there's a fight over who gets to climb up and place the last ornament on the belén.
questions.fun_fact: The painter Giotto painted the Star of Bethlehem as a comet, perhaps inspired by Halley's Comet.

questions.question: On New Year's Eve, TV shows the midnight chimes from Spain's most famous clock. Which Madrid square is it in?
hints: It's right in the center of Madrid.
Kilometer Zero of Spain's roads is set in its pavement.
Its name brings to mind the star that gives us light and warmth.
questions.description: The only moment of the year when eating fast is good manners.
questions.fun_fact: The famous clock was a gift from the clockmaker José Rodríguez de Losada and started running in 1866.

questions.question: In the Christmas lottery draw, a San Ildefonso schoolchild sings out the number drawn. What does their partner sing right after?
hints: There are two drums: one with the numbers and another one.
The second drum holds far fewer balls than the number drum.
Something like “¡mil euros!”.
questions.description: The only singing duo whose biggest hit is a list of numbers.
questions.fun_fact: The children of the San Ildefonso school have been singing out the lottery since the 18th century.

questions.question: In Spain, what does it mean when someone says «le ha tocado el Gordo»?
questions.answer: They won the lottery's top prize
wrong_answers: They gained weight over the holidays
They have to dress up as Santa
hints: It has to do with a draw in December.
Lots of people show up on TV popping open bottles of cava.
It's the biggest prize in the Christmas Lottery.
questions.description: Being called “gordo” in December has never been such good news.
questions.fun_fact: The first Christmas Lottery draw was held in Cádiz in 1812.

questions.question: A whole ticket for Spain's Christmas Lottery is cut into equal parts. What is each part called?
hints: It's what people share with family and coworkers.
Its name tells you how many parts the ticket is split into.
One ticket has ten of them.
questions.description: One ticket cut into pieces, and every piece comes with its own hope.
questions.fun_fact: Each décimo of the Christmas Lottery costs 20 euros.

questions.question: Which night is the Noche de Reyes?
hints: It comes after New Year's Eve.
In the evening there's usually a cabalgata (parade).
The next morning is a holiday, and there's roscón.
questions.description: The night kids go to bed earlier than ever and sleep less than ever.
questions.fun_fact: Many children leave water or bread for the camels next to their shoes.

questions.question: It's a tall cardboard cone, covered in cloth that hides the face, worn by nazarenos in Holy Week processions. What is it called?
hints: It goes on the head.
It's pointed, like a wizard's hat.
Its name starts with “capi”.
questions.description: A party hat, but for the most serious celebration of the year.
questions.fun_fact: The cloth over the face is there so nobody can recognize the penitent.

questions.question: You're making pulpo a la gallega: the octopus is boiled and sliced. What spice is sprinkled on top, with coarse salt and olive oil?
hints: It's made by grinding a dried vegetable.
It also gives chorizo its color.
It's a red powder made from peppers.
questions.description: Eight arms, zero complaints and a wooden plate waiting for it.
questions.fun_fact: Every August, the Festa do Pulpo in O Carballiño, Ourense, brings together thousands of people to eat octopus.

questions.question: Look at this aqueduct in Segovia. Which people built it?
hints: It was built almost 2,000 years ago.
The same people built roads, theaters and amphitheaters all over Hispania.
Their capital was in Italy and they spoke Latin.
questions.description: A bridge built for water to cross, not cars.
questions.fun_fact: Its stones are stacked without any mortar, and a legend says the devil built it in a single night.

questions.question: Every May, courtyards like this one fill with flowers and compete in a famous contest. In which city?
hints: It's a city in Andalusia.
The Guadalquivir River runs through it.
It's home to the famous Mosque-Cathedral.
questions.description: Here flowerpots climb up the walls and nobody calls the fire department.
questions.fun_fact: Córdoba's Courtyards Festival has been on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2012.

questions.question: In which decade did “Verano azul” (Blue Summer), the TV series filmed in Nerja, first air?
hints: Your parents or grandparents probably watched it as kids.
It aired soon after democracy came to Spain.
It premiered in 1981.
questions.description: Bikes, a gang of friends and a boat on dry land: vacations from another time.
questions.fun_fact: Nerja has a Verano Azul park with a replica of “La Dorada,” Chanquete's boat.

questions.question: Look at this map of Spain. Which sea washes the east coast, around Barcelona, Valencia and the Balearic Islands?
hints: Its waters are calm and fairly warm in summer.
It also washes the coasts of Italy, Greece and Turkey.
Its name means “in the middle of the lands.”
questions.description: A sea so famous that half of Europe spends the summer dipping its toes in it.
questions.fun_fact: The Mediterranean barely has tides: the water rises and falls very little compared with the Atlantic.

questions.question: I'm a cold, wavy sea in northern Spain. I wash the shores of Gijón, Santander and Bilbao. Who am I?
hints: I lie north of the Picos de Europa.
My name recalls an ancient people who fought against Rome.
My name is very close to that of the region whose capital is Santander.
questions.description: Cold water, big waves and surfers in wetsuits even in August.
questions.fun_fact: This sea is home to the galerna, a sudden storm that can turn a sunny day into a gale in just a few minutes.

questions.question: Of these animals that live in the sea off the coast of Spain, which one is NOT a fish?
hints: Three of them have fins and breathe through gills.
It has no fins and moves very slowly over the rocks.
It's a little spiky ball that hurts if you step on it.
questions.description: The Spanish coast is a neighborhood full of residents who never pay rent.
questions.fun_fact: The sea urchin is a relative of the starfish, and its mouth, on its underside, has five teeth.

questions.question: San Lorenzo beach, with its big staircase called “La Escalerona”, is in a city in Asturias. Which one?
hints: It's the most populous city in its region.
Next to the beach is the old fishermen's quarter of Cimadevilla.
It's the city of cider and of Sporting.
questions.description: A city beach where the tide plays hide-and-seek with the towels.
questions.fun_fact: At high tide, the sea covers almost all of San Lorenzo's sand and reaches the promenade wall.

questions.question: How many kilometers of sea separate Spain from Morocco at the narrowest point of the Strait of Gibraltar?
hints: On clear days you can see Africa from the coast of Cádiz.
A fast boat crosses it in less than an hour.
It's a bit more than the length of a 10 km fun run.
questions.description: The place where Europe and Africa almost shake hands, but don't quite make it.
questions.fun_fact: The Strait is one of the few places in Europe where you can spot dolphins, pilot whales and, in summer, orcas from a boat.

questions.question: Which of these Spanish islands was NOT formed from volcanic lava?
hints: Think about the type of rock: not all of them are made of dark volcanic stone.
Three of them belong to the same archipelago.
It's in the Mediterranean, not the Atlantic.
questions.description: Some islands were born from fire, and one rose from the seabed without making such a fuss.
questions.fun_fact: The 2021 eruption on La Palma lasted 85 days, and the lava reached all the way to the sea.

questions.question: In November 2002, Galician beaches like this one turned black with fuel oil after a tanker sank. What was the ship called?
hints: The disaster hit the Costa da Morte hardest.
Thousands of volunteers in white suits cleaned up the “chapapote” (thick oil sludge).
It gave rise to the slogan “Nunca máis.”
questions.description: A ship whose name nobody in Galicia ever wants to hear again.
questions.fun_fact: Hundreds of thousands of volunteers from all over Spain went to Galicia to clean the beaches by hand.

questions.question: Under the Treaty of Utrecht, Spain gave Great Britain Gibraltar and also an island. Which one?
hints: The British wanted it for its huge natural harbor.
It went back to Spain in 1802.
Its capital is Mahón.
questions.description: A treaty signed in the Netherlands that still gets people talking in the south of Andalusia.
questions.fun_fact: Under British rule, Menorca's capital moved from Ciutadella to Mahón because of its great harbor.

questions.question: The Guanches of Tenerife called her “mother of the sun”, and later she was linked to the Virgin of Candelaria. What was this goddess's name?
hints: She's a female figure from the Guanche religion.
She was a mother goddess who protected the island and its shepherds.
Her name starts with “Cha”.
questions.description: A goddess with a very responsible job: making sure the sky doesn't fall on our heads.
questions.fun_fact: In the square at Candelaria, next to the basilica, stand nine bronze statues of the menceyes, the Guanche kings of Tenerife.

questions.question: According to what grown-ups in Spain say, which children does the Hombre del Saco take away?
wrong_answers: The ones who get good grades
The ones who brush their teeth
hints: He was used to scare children.
They say he walks the streets with a big sack on his back.
If you do as you're told and behave, you have nothing to fear.
questions.description: A man who hasn't put his luggage down in centuries.
questions.fun_fact: He has cousins in other countries: in Italy people talk about the “uomo nero” and in Portugal about the “homem do saco”.

questions.question: The trasno is a mischievous goblin who hides things, moves the furniture and keeps you awake. Which region of Spain does its legend come from?
hints: It's a land in the north of Spain.
People there also tell stories of meigas and the Santa Compaña.
In the local language, a prank is called a “trasnada”.
questions.description: If you can't find your keys tonight, maybe it isn't your fault.
questions.fun_fact: Asturias has a very similar relative, the trasgu, and Cantabria has the trasgo.

questions.question: At what point in a story do you say “colorín colorado”?
questions.answer: At the end of the story
wrong_answers: At the start of the story
In the middle of the story
hints: It's not when the wolf shows up.
It often comes with “fueron felices y comieron perdices”.
Next comes “este cuento se ha…”.
questions.description: Stories that kids ask for again and again, even though they know them by heart.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish stories begin with “Érase una vez”, the Spanish version of “Once upon a time”.

questions.question: In Cantabrian mythology, if you get lost in the forest, which kindly being appears to help you?
hints: It's a female being, and a good one.
It carries a staff and helps travelers and the poor.
Its name starts with “an” and it's the good fairy of Cantabria.
questions.description: Better than GPS: its battery never dies, and it's a lovely person too.
questions.fun_fact: Its great enemy is the ojáncano, a one-eyed Cantabrian giant.

questions.question: In Spain, someone who is furious “se pone hecho un…” what?
hints: It's a very dangerous legendary creature.
Legend says it could kill with just a look.
It was half rooster, half serpent.
questions.description: When Dad sees your math grade and turns into a legendary creature.
questions.fun_fact: The basilisk had a surprising enemy: according to medieval bestiaries, a weasel could defeat it.

questions.question: According to tradition in Spain, what do the Reyes Magos (Three Kings) leave for children who have been naughty?
hints: It's black.
People used to burn it to heat stoves and power trains.
These days it's usually made of sugar, and you can eat it.
questions.description: Three gentlemen with camels who know exactly what you did in October.
questions.fun_fact: The Kings' coal sold in Spanish bakeries is actually a sugar candy dyed black.

questions.question: In the legend of Redondela, in Galicia, where did the Coca come from, the she-dragon that carried off young maidens?
hints: The townspeople had to join forces to defeat her.
The town still remembers her defeat at the Corpus Christi festival.
She came from the salt water that reaches the town.
questions.description: A dragon with very bad manners, and oddly enough, a festival in her honor.
questions.fun_fact: Every Corpus Christi the Coca parades through the streets of Redondela, along with girls carried on people's shoulders, the “penlas”.

questions.question: In the tale “La Ratita Presumida”, the little mouse finds a coin and buys a ribbon. What does “presumida” mean?
questions.answer: She loves dressing up and showing off
hints: It has to do with how she looks.
She leans out of the window with her new ribbon.
She wants everyone to admire her ribbon.
questions.description: A little mouse who, while sweeping the stairs, found the perfect excuse to go shopping.
questions.fun_fact: In the tale, the little mouse picks a husband by the sound each animal makes at night, and the donkey's bray doesn't win her over.

questions.question: Medio Pollito (Half-Chick), with one leg and one wing, went to see the king and ended up stuck forever on top of a bell tower. What did he become?
hints: On the way, he refused to help those who asked him for a favor.
His new job is very useful to the farmers and sailors who look up at the tower.
He shows which way the wind is blowing.
questions.description: Half a chicken, a whole journey and a fairy-tale ending nobody sees coming.
questions.fun_fact: The writer Fernán Caballero collected this Spanish folk tale in the 19th century.

questions.question: You stick them in an album, swap them on the playground, and the doubles are called “repes”. What are they?
hints: You buy them in packets at the newsstand.
They often show soccer players or cartoon characters.
You gather them to fill a collection made of paper.
questions.description: The only money the school playground takes without going through a bank.
questions.fun_fact: The Italian company Panini started selling soccer sticker albums in Modena in 1961.

questions.question: You're playing tute and hold the king and the knight of a suit that isn't trumps. How many points do you call?
hints: If they were trumps, you'd call a very famous number.
That famous number is in the saying “cantar las cuarenta”.
It's exactly half of forty.
questions.description: A game where the king and the knight sing together and nobody tells them to be quiet.
questions.fun_fact: The saying “cantarle a alguien las cuarenta”, telling someone a few home truths to their face, comes from this card game.

questions.question: In the Juego de la Oca, what do you say when you land on a goose? “De oca a oca y…”
hints: Landing on a goose is good luck.
After you jump ahead, your turn isn't over yet.
You pick up the die again.
questions.description: The only game where a bird moves you forward faster than a car.
questions.fun_fact: The Oca board has 63 squares in a spiral, and the last one is the goose's garden.

questions.question: I have tight threads, a shuttle goes back and forth through me, and in the Alpujarra people weave jarapas on me. What am I?
hints: I'm used to make cloth, not to spin yarn.
Blankets and rugs come out of me.
My name rhymes with “room”.
questions.description: Grandma's handiwork that keeps the whole village cozy in winter.
questions.fun_fact: The jarapas of the Alpujarra used to be woven from strips of old clothes, so nothing went to waste.

questions.question: You order it at the bar, it comes from the tap and it's served in a small glass. If someone in Spain goes out for “cañas”, what will they drink?
hints: It's a drink with foam on top.
It's made from barley.
In summer it's ordered ice-cold, with two fingers of foam.
questions.description: Half of Spain's favorite after-work plan, with free olives on the side.
questions.fun_fact: A caña has no fixed size: it's usually around 200 milliliters (about 7 fl oz), but it changes from city to city and bar to bar.

questions.question: I'm poured from very high up, I'm just a finger of cider at the bottom of the glass, and you drink me in one go. What am I called in Asturias?
hints: It's a very Asturian word.
It's a Spanish diminutive.
It refers to the bottom of the glass.
questions.description: In Asturias, pouring a drink well is all about good aim.
questions.fun_fact: The last drop of a culín is tossed on the floor to clean the rim of the glass, because traditionally the whole group shares it.

questions.question: In Spain it became trendy to serve it in a balloon glass with lots of ice and tonic. It’s flavored with juniper. Which spirit is it?
hints: It’s a clear spirit.
Its flavor comes from the berries of a shrub.
Its Dutch ancestor is called genever.
questions.description: A mixed drink that Spain serves in glasses so big they almost look like fishbowls.
questions.fun_fact: Tonic water contains quinine, a bitter substance that people once took to fight malaria.

questions.question: This climbing plant has flowers like little green pine cones that give beer its bitterness and aroma. In Spain, almost all of it grows in León. What is it?
hints: It's not a cereal.
It belongs to the same plant family as hemp.
IPA beers use huge amounts of this plant.
questions.description: The green part of beer, and we don't mean the bottle.
questions.fun_fact: León grows more than 90% of Spain's hops, mostly along the banks of the Órbigo River.

questions.question: It's very thick, served hot in a cup, and in Spain it's a tradition in the early hours of January 1. What is this chocolate for?
hints: It goes with something fried and sweet.
It's a long, ridged strip of dough.
Its chubbier cousin is called a “porra”.
questions.description: The official breakfast of anyone heading home from the New Year's Eve party.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolatería San Ginés in Madrid has been serving chocolate with churros since 1894.

questions.question: This town on the Alicante coast, with colorful houses by the sea, is famous for its chocolate factories. Which town is it?
hints: It's on the Costa Blanca.
Its name sounds like it means “joyful town” in Spanish.
The Chocolates Valor brand was born there.
questions.description: A coast so sweet that even the sea should come with milk.
