questions.fun_fact: Chocolates Valor was founded in Villajoyosa in 1881, and the town even has a chocolate museum.

questions.question: On Gallo Island, Francisco Pizarro drew a line in the sand with his sword, and only thirteen men crossed it. What was the line for?
questions.answer: To see who would go on with him to Peru
wrong_answers: To mark the border with Portugal
To draw a map of the coast
To share out the gold among his men
hints: His men were starving, and many wanted to go back to Panama.
Ships had arrived from Panama with orders to take the men back.
Those who crossed went down in history as “the Famous Thirteen,” headed for the Inca Empire.
questions.description: A day at the beach when a sword was used for something very different from fighting.
questions.fun_fact: Pizarro came from Trujillo, in Cáceres, where a large statue of him on horseback now stands over the main square.

questions.question: It was the motto of Charles I, it appears on Spain's coat of arms between the Pillars of Hercules, and a seaplane named after it crossed the Atlantic in 1926. What is it?
hints: It's in Latin.
It urged people to go beyond the Strait of Gibraltar, which the ancients believed was the end of the world.
It means “further beyond.”
questions.description: A motto with more miles on it than any passport.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Pillars of Hercules bore the words “Non plus ultra” (“nothing further beyond”), and Charles I dropped the “non” because his empire already reached America.

questions.question: October 12, Spain's National Day, is also the feast of Zaragoza's patron saint. Which Virgin is she?
hints: She is also the patron saint of the Guardia Civil.
Her basilica stands on the banks of the Ebro River.
Her name refers to a column.
questions.description: An October 12 with a parade in Madrid and jota dancing in another city.
questions.fun_fact: At Zaragoza's Ofrenda de Flores, millions of flowers are used to cover a huge cloak for the Virgin.

questions.question: Don Quixote sees some windmills in a field, charges at them with his lance and ends up on the ground. What did he think they were?
hints: He thought they were huge enemies.
Sancho Panza warned him they were just windmills.
He believed the sails were their extremely long arms.
questions.description: A classic case of seeing what you want to see.
questions.fun_fact: This scene gave us the phrase “tilting at windmills”, meaning fighting imaginary enemies.

questions.question: Philip V, the first Bourbon king of Spain, had the palace of La Granja built to remind him of Versailles. Which French king was he a grandson of?
hints: He was one of the most powerful kings in Europe in his time.
He ruled France for more than seventy years.
He was called the Sun King.
questions.description: He went to rule abroad and missed home so much that he built himself a copy of it.
questions.fun_fact: Philip V reigned twice: he gave up the throne to his son Louis I in 1724 and took it back a few months later, when Louis died.

questions.question: Which of these places is NOT in Madrid's Retiro Park?
hints: Three of them are a few minutes' walk from each other.
The one you're looking for is in another park, west of central Madrid.
It's a gift from Egypt, next to Plaza de España.
questions.description: A park so big it's hard to say what's inside it and what isn't.
questions.fun_fact: The Retiro began as the garden of Philip IV's Buen Retiro Palace and opened to everyone in 1868.

questions.question: When Charles I gave up the throne, his son Philip kept Spain. Who got the title of Holy Roman Emperor?
hints: He was family and already ruled the lands of Austria.
He was born in Alcalá de Henares.
He was also a grandson of the Catholic Monarchs.
questions.description: Splitting an inheritance is hard enough; imagine when it includes half the world.
questions.fun_fact: Ferdinand I was born and raised in Spain, yet he founded the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs, which ruled from Vienna until 1918.

questions.question: I'm a soldier of the Spanish tercios, and my firearm is so heavy I rest it on a forked stand to shoot. Who am I?
hints: My weapon has no blade: it makes noise and smoke.
It fired lead balls and took quite a while to reload.
Dumas made three French comrades in my line of work famous.
questions.description: In the 16th century, carrying a piece of furniture to work was perfectly normal.
questions.fun_fact: A musket of the time could weigh about 8 kg (18 lb), almost like carrying a big watermelon on your shoulder.

questions.question: It's a big sailing ship with several masts and cannons. It crossed the ocean loaded with silver for Spain, and pirates chased it. What is it called?
hints: It was bigger and heavier than Columbus's ships.
It sailed in fleets to defend itself from attacks.
Its name sounds like “galley” with a bit added.
questions.description: Silver's favorite moving truck… and the pirates' favorite too.
questions.fun_fact: The Manila galleon linked the Philippines with Mexico for about 250 years, one of the longest trade routes in history.

questions.question: You're watching Alberto Chicote rescue a restaurant on “Pesadilla en la cocina”. In what year did the show premiere in Spain?
hints: It airs on laSexta, a channel launched in 2006.
It's the Spanish version of a British Gordon Ramsay show that premiered in 2004.
It premiered the same year Spain won its second European Championship in a row.
questions.description: A fridge scarier than any horror movie.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Chicote is as famous for his shouting as for his bright, colorful glasses.

questions.question: It's the biggest-selling supermarket chain in Spain, it was born in Valencia and its own brand is Hacendado. Which is it?
hints: It opened its first store in 1977.
Its president is the Valencian businessman Juan Roig.
Its name starts with “Merca”, as in mercado (market).
questions.description: The place where Spanish families make their pilgrimage every Saturday.
questions.fun_fact: Mercadona has more than 1,600 supermarkets across Spain and Portugal.

questions.question: Which Spanish YouTuber is half Norwegian and stars in the comic and anime series “Virtual Hero”?
hints: He is one of the Spanish YouTubers with the most subscribers ever.
He became famous with Minecraft and Skyrim videos.
His real name is Rubén Doblas.
questions.description: Half Viking, half Andalusian, and one hundred percent glued to his microphone.
questions.fun_fact: He was born in Mijas (Málaga), but spent part of his childhood in Norway, his mother's country.

questions.question: I'm a journalist who hosted Spain's first “Gran Hermano” on Telecinco in 2000, and many more seasons over about 15 years. Who am I?
hints: Before the reality show, I was already famous for my TV interviews.
I'm from Barcelona and have a very energetic personality.
My first name is the same as a famous German car brand.
questions.description: A hundred days locked in a house, and someone had to keep order from outside.
questions.fun_fact: The house for the first seasons of “Gran Hermano” was in Guadalix de la Sierra, a village near Madrid.

questions.question: Who is this TV host, famous for her dresses during Antena 3's New Year's Eve Campanadas?
hints: She started out as a reporter on laSexta's show «Sé lo que hicisteis».
She hosts the Campanadas with chef Alberto Chicote.
Her surname starts with “Pedro”.
questions.description: Half of Spain watches the Puerta del Sol clock; the other half watches the dress.
questions.fun_fact: Every New Year's Eve, her dress is kept secret until the last moment, and it's one of the most searched things online that night.

questions.question: On Antena 3, Pablo Motos hosts a show with experiments and two puppets, Trancas and Barrancas. What is it called?
hints: Trancas and Barrancas are two insects.
The bugs in the title are easy to spot in any park or garden.
It's the name for the home of little bugs that carry off the crumbs from your picnic.
questions.description: The only TV studio where some of the co-hosts fit in your pocket.
questions.fun_fact: El Hormiguero started on Cuatro in 2006 and moved to Antena 3 in 2011.

questions.question: Aida Domènech, known as Dulceida, was one of Spain's first fashion influencers and married Alba Paul in 2016. In which city was she born?
hints: Her surname is Catalan.
It's a city with a beach and a port.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: Long before everyone posted photos of their breakfast, she was already posing with hers.
questions.fun_fact: Dulceida started with a fashion blog long before “influencer” was a job.

questions.question: Codorníu was founded in 1551, is one of Spain's oldest companies and made the first Spanish cava in 1872. Which region is it in?
hints: Its cellars are a Modernista building listed as a monument.
It's in the Penedès, a district full of vineyards.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.description: A company so old it was already raising a toast when Cervantes was still a little boy.
questions.fun_fact: Its Modernista cellars were designed by the architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch.

questions.question: Stradivarius is a clothing brand owned by the Inditex group. Which of these brands does NOT belong to Inditex?
hints: Inditex has its headquarters in Galicia.
The odd one out has its own founder and has never been part of Inditex.
Its name is also a tropical fruit.
questions.description: A brand named after a violin: it sounds nice, but who's really part of the family?
questions.fun_fact: Stradivarius is named after the famous Italian violin maker Antonio Stradivari.

questions.question: I started as a shop assistant in a shirt store in A Coruña, and in 1975 I opened the first Zara store there. Who am I?
hints: My company, Inditex, has its headquarters in Arteixo.
I'm one of the richest men in the world and almost never give interviews.
My daughter Marta is now the chair of Inditex.
questions.description: He started out folding shirts and ended up folding stacks of cash.
questions.fun_fact: Zara was going to be called “Zorba”, but a nearby bar already used that name, so they rearranged the letters they had.

questions.question: At a churrería, which of these is NOT usually dipped in thick hot chocolate?
hints: Three of them are sweet or made of fried dough.
Think about which one tastes salty, not sweet.
It's eaten as an appetizer, not as a sweet afternoon snack.
questions.description: A cup so thick the spoon stands up on its own and calls for help.
questions.fun_fact: Cacao came from the Americas, and Spain was one of the first countries in Europe to drink it, back in the 16th century.

questions.question: You're dressed in white, and when the chupinazo goes off at noon on July 6, you tie a red scarf around your neck. Where are you?
hints: It's a midsummer festival that lasts several days.
The festival honors San Fermín.
It's the capital of Navarre.
questions.description: A party where getting your white clothes dirty is almost required.
questions.fun_fact: Ernest Hemingway's 1926 novel “The Sun Also Rises” made the San Fermín festival famous around the world.

questions.question: On April 23, Saint George's Day, the streets fill with stalls and people give each other roses and books. Where is this custom typical?
hints: Its coast is on the Mediterranean Sea.
There, the saint goes by another name in the local language.
The Ramblas of its capital fill with roses that day.
questions.description: A saint who slew a dragon and ended up selling books.
questions.fun_fact: April 23 is also World Book Day, in memory of Cervantes and Shakespeare.

questions.question: Seville's Feria de Abril began in 1847, with casetas but much less dancing. What was it created for?
wrong_answers: To celebrate the end of a war
To send off ships to America
hints: It had to do with the countryside.
Cows, sheep and horses passed through it.
It was an animal market.
questions.description: Before the paper lanterns and the sevillanas, the feria smelled a lot less of rebujito.
questions.fun_fact: It was proposed by two city councilors who weren't from Seville: a Basque, José María Ybarra, and a Catalan, Narciso Bonaplata.

questions.question: In the feria's horse parade, the woman riding sideways behind the rider is going «a la…». How does it end?
hints: It's a part of the horse's body.
It's at the back, above the hind legs.
It's the horse's rump, just before the tail.
questions.description: Two people, one horse, and no arguing about who drives.
questions.fun_fact: At Seville's Feria de Abril, horses and horse-drawn carriages may only ride through the Real at set hours, roughly from noon to 8 p.m.

questions.question: About how long does a San Fermín encierro last, from when the bulls leave until they enter the bullring?
hints: It's shown live on TV at 8 in the morning and it's over in no time.
It's shorter than a long song.
It's less than five minutes.
questions.description: The world's most famous race where nobody wants to beat the ones with horns.
questions.fun_fact: The route of the Pamplona encierro is a little over 800 m (about half a mile) long.

questions.question: The Virgen del Carmen is to sailors as San Isidro is to…
hints: He is the patron saint of Madrid.
According to legend, angels helped him do his work.
He worked the land with a plow and oxen.
questions.description: Every trade has its saint, just as every village has its fiesta.
questions.fun_fact: On July 16, in many Spanish ports, the procession of the Virgen del Carmen goes out to sea in boats.

questions.question: You wear it at Carnival, it turns you into a superhero or a dinosaur, and then it sits in the closet until next year. What is it?
hints: It's not everyday clothing.
It makes you look like someone else or a character.
It often comes with a mask or face paint.
questions.description: A party where the confetti ends up even inside your socks.
questions.fun_fact: At the Cádiz Carnival, groups in costume called chirigotas sing funny songs through the streets.

questions.question: What was the large horse-drawn carriage called that carried passengers and mail from town to town on fixed routes?
hints: It shows up in lots of Western movies.
It stopped at coaching inns to swap its tired horses for fresh ones.
In Spanish it is called «diligencia», a word that also means care and speed.
questions.description: The fanciest traffic jam at the fair smells of hay.
questions.fun_fact: In 1939 John Ford directed “Stagecoach,” the Western that made John Wayne a star.

questions.question: Which guitarist took over from Paco de Lucía as Camarón de la Isla's guitarist in the late 1970s?
hints: He is from Almería.
He has recorded albums with the Dominican pianist Michel Camilo.
His stage name means “little tomato” in Spanish.
questions.description: Camarón needed six strings worthy of his voice, and not just any from the corner store.
questions.fun_fact: His nickname comes from his father, also a guitarist, who was known as “Tomate”.

questions.question: Look at this close-up photo: it's a classic dish in Spain's bars. Which one is it?
hints: It's made from something that lives in the sea.
Its sauce isn't made from tomato or paprika.
The animal makes the sauce's color itself, to escape from its enemies.
questions.description: A dish that comes out in black and white, but full of flavor.
questions.fun_fact: Squid ink was once used for writing and drawing, and its cousin the cuttlefish (sepia in Latin) gave its name to the color sepia.

previous.feedback: Source: hint 2 (“Su salsa no es de tomate ni de pimentón”) can't be relied on. Many classic recipes for calamares en su tinta (and chipirones en su tinta) start from a sofrito with tomato, and some add paprika. The fact check is "uncertain" and I can't confirm the hint either. The source's hint should be replaced with something safe, such as "The sauce gets its dark color from an ink, not from a spice." After that, re-translate it. Fact check: uncertain. The answer and the wrong answers hold up. Pulpo a la gallega, calamares a la romana and callos a la madrileña are all clearly different dishes. Hint 3 and the sepia fun fact are true. Hint 2 is shaky: many classic recipes for calamares en su tinta use a sofrito with tomato, and some add paprika, so 'isn't made with tomato or paprika' is not reliably true. This check was done from general knowledge, without web searches.

questions.question: This red powder is made by grinding dried peppers, and it gives chorizo its color. Where did peppers come to Spain from?
hints: They arrived about 500 years ago.
They came by ship, across an ocean.
They were brought back on Christopher Columbus's voyages.
questions.description: The red powder that turns any old sausage into a chorizo with attitude.
questions.fun_fact: Monks at the monastery of Yuste, in Extremadura, were among the first to grow peppers to make pimentón.

questions.question: I'm a big, fast fish, but at the supermarket I come in little pieces, in round cans with oil. I go in salads. What am I?
hints: I live in the sea.
I'm not small: in the sea I can weigh more than a person.
I'm the canned fish people use most in a Spanish ensalada mixta.
questions.description: A little can that turns a sad salad into a full meal.
questions.fun_fact: An adult bluefin tuna can weigh more than 400 kg (880 lb), as much as five grown-ups put together!

questions.question: They're ring-shaped, fried or baked, and in Madrid people eat them at the San Isidro festival. What are they called?
hints: They're sold on little paper trays at the stalls of a city festival.
They have a hole in the middle.
In Madrid there are “tontas” (silly) and “listas” (smart) ones.
questions.description: May in Madrid: chulapos, carnations and a meadow where nobody lets go of their snack.
questions.fun_fact: “Tontas” rosquillas have nothing on top, while “listas” ones have a glossy sugar icing.

questions.question: This head of garlic splits into little pieces. What is each little piece called?
hints: It shares its name with a spice.
That spice is a small brown dried flower bud, often used in gingerbread.
It rhymes with “stove”.
questions.description: The one thing no vampire wants to find in the kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain a garlic clove is called a “diente”, a tooth, and each one you plant grows a whole new bulb.

questions.question: This olive oil has the word “arbequina” on its label. What is arbequina?
hints: There are many like it: picual, hojiblanca, cornicabra…
It comes from Catalonia, though today it's grown all over the world.
It's small and round and picked in the olive groves.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a fairy-tale character, but gets served with bread.
questions.fun_fact: Arbequina is named after Arbeca, a village in the province of Lleida.

questions.question: I show up one morning a week with awnings and vans, sell clothes, fruit and cheap socks, and I'm gone by afternoon. What am I?
hints: I'm outdoors.
I set up in a street or in the town square.
The sellers shout their deals from their stalls.
questions.description: Here socks come in packs of three and haggling is an Olympic sport.
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's El Rastro, the most famous mercadillo in Spain, has been set up every Sunday for centuries.

questions.question: I'm small and silver, and I travel squeezed in with my sisters in a flat can. When a train is packed, people say they're packed like me. What am I?
hints: I'm a fish.
In summer they grill me on espetos (skewers) on the beaches of Málaga.
“Packed like … in a can.”
questions.description: From the sea to the can, and from the can to your breakfast toast.
questions.fun_fact: In Madrid, the Burial of the Sardine ends Carnival with a parade that finishes by burning a giant cardboard sardine.

questions.question: This is mojama, a salt-cured specialty of Cádiz and Huelva. What fish is it made from?
hints: It's an oily fish.
It's a huge fish caught with almadrabas, ancient maze-like net traps.
It's the same fish that comes in cans for salads and sandwiches.
questions.description: A fish that decided to retire in the sun and become a thin slice.
questions.fun_fact: The word mojama comes from Arabic and means something like “dry thing”.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact's etymology is wrong. The RAE traces mojama to Hispano-Arabic mušámma‘, from Classical Arabic mušamma‘, meaning “waxed”, not “dried thing”. The Spanish source needs this fix first, and then the translation should follow it (e.g. “The word mojama comes from Arabic and means something like “waxed,” for its shiny look.”).

questions.question: My crates hold apples, bananas, oranges and strawberries, and you buy them by weight. What shop am I?
hints: Everything I sell comes from trees and plants.
What I sell is sweet and full of vitamins.
I make sure you get your apple a day.
questions.description: A neighborhood shop where everything gets weighed and your change comes with a smile.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is one of the countries that sells the most fruit to the rest of Europe, especially oranges and strawberries.

questions.question: “The Catholic Monarchs created me, I tried the witches of Zugarramurdi in Logroño, and I was abolished for good in 1834.” Who am I?
hints: It was a religious court.
It went after heretics and anyone who strayed from the Catholic faith.
Its full name was “Tribunal of the Holy Office of the…”.
questions.description: A court that was a very sore loser, with an even worse sense of humor.
questions.fun_fact: At the Logroño auto-da-fé of 1610, dozens of people from Zugarramurdi, in Navarre, were tried on charges of witchcraft.

questions.question: It's the most famous urban legend of Spain's roads: a young hitchhiker warns of a danger and vanishes. Spaniards call her “the girl of the…” what?
hints: It's a place on the road.
Drivers slow down when they reach it.
A road sign warns of it with a bent arrow.
questions.description: A hitchhiker who never reaches where she's going, but always makes it into the after-dinner chat.
questions.fun_fact: Versions of this legend exist all over the world: in the United States it's called “the vanishing hitchhiker”.

questions.question: Tradition says the Virgin Mary appeared on a pillar in Zaragoza to encourage an apostle preaching in Hispania. Which one?
hints: He was one of the twelve apostles and, before that, a fisherman in Galilee.
He is the patron saint of Spain.
The famous pilgrim route, the Camino, is named after him.
questions.description: When you're feeling down, nothing beats a pillar to lean on.
questions.fun_fact: The feast of the Virgen del Pilar is on October 12, the same day as Spain's National Day.

questions.question: A Spanish saying claims sardines get so juicy they already “soak the bread”. From when?
hints: It's when the good weather is in full swing.
It's when sardines are fattest, as the heat begins.
It's at the end of June.
questions.description: A fish that gets so juicy it even asks people for bread.
questions.fun_fact: At the start of summer, sardines store more fat, so they drip juice when grilled and soak the bread.

questions.question: On Galician beaches on Saint John's Eve, some people jump over exactly nine waves. According to tradition, why?
questions.answer: To wash away bad luck and evil
wrong_answers: To bring a good fishing catch
To ask for rain for the fields
hints: It's about yourself, not about work.
The water on that night is believed to be magical and cleansing.
It's similar to what people hope for when jumping over the bonfire.
questions.description: A water-jumping workout that no gym will ever charge you for.
questions.fun_fact: At A Lanzada beach in Pontevedra, the nine-waves tradition was linked above all to the wish to have children.

questions.question: It's night and you're in front of a huge fountain that dances with water, lights and music, built for the 1929 International Exposition. Which city are you in?
hints: The city lies on the Mediterranean.
Behind the fountain, at the top of a grand staircase, stands a big palace that is now an art museum.
It's the city of the Sagrada Família.
questions.description: A fountain that just can't sit still once the music starts.
questions.fun_fact: Seville also held an exposition in 1929, the Ibero-American one, and its Plaza de España comes from it.

questions.question: The famous painted horses in the Ekain cave, in Gipuzkoa, are about 14,000 years old. Which Upper Paleolithic culture made them?
hints: It's the same culture as many of the paintings at Altamira.
It's the last great culture of the Upper Paleolithic in Europe.
Its name comes from the La Madeleine rock shelter in France.
questions.description: Some horses that have posed for thousands of years without moving a hair.
questions.fun_fact: To protect the original paintings, an exact replica was built for visitors: Ekainberri.

questions.question: Look at this bench of painted tiles, one of many, each dedicated to a Spanish province. Where is it?
hints: It was built for an exhibition in 1929.
It has a canal where you can go out in a rowboat.
It's in the city of the Giralda.
questions.description: A bench so pretty it feels wrong to sit on it.
questions.fun_fact: Seville's Plaza de España appeared in “Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones” as a palace on the planet Naboo.

questions.question: The Metrópolis building in Madrid, where Gran Vía meets Alcalá, once had a phoenix on its dome. What figure stands on top today?
wrong_answers: A bear with a strawberry tree
hints: The insurance company that built the building took the phoenix with it.
The figure has wings, like the bird before it.
It shows a goddess who celebrates triumphs.
questions.description: A building in a black-and-gold hat, dressed up to watch the traffic go by.
questions.fun_fact: The original phoenix was moved to another building of the same insurance company on the Paseo de la Castellana.

questions.question: Gaudí's La Pedrera, on Barcelona's Passeig de Gràcia, has a wavy stone front and chimneys that look like warriors. What was it built as?
hints: It was ordered by a wealthy Barcelona couple, the Milàs.
It has two large inner courtyards so light reaches every room.
People still live in some of its apartments today.
questions.description: A building so wavy it looks like it was left out to dry in the sun.
questions.fun_fact: It was nicknamed “La Pedrera,” Catalan for “the quarry,” because people thought it looked like a pile of stones.

questions.question: At Monte do Gozo, where pilgrims finally see Santiago Cathedral, a monument marks a pope's visit in 1989. Which pope?
hints: World Youth Day was held there that year.
He had already been to Santiago once before, in 1982.
He was pope for almost 27 years, until 2005.
questions.description: A hill where pilgrims get so happy they even forget about their blisters.
questions.fun_fact: “Gozo” means joy: the joy pilgrims felt when they finally saw the cathedral's towers.

questions.question: This large mosaic from the Roman villa of La Olmeda, in Palencia, shows a hero hiding among a king's daughters to avoid going to Troy. Who is he?
hints: His mother hid him dressed as a girl.
Odysseus found him out with a trick: he put weapons among the gifts.
His only weak spot was his heel.
questions.description: A Roman floor with more action than a Sunday afternoon movie.
questions.fun_fact: The villa of La Olmeda was discovered in 1968 when a farmer was plowing his land.

questions.question: Look at the Lady of Elche, an Iberian bust from about 2,400 years ago. What is it made of?
hints: It was found buried in 1897 and has held up very well.
At first it was painted in bright colors.
It was carved with a chisel out of rock.
questions.description: A lady whose hairdo would need three hours at the salon every morning.
questions.fun_fact: The Lady of Elche spent more than 40 years in the Louvre in Paris before returning to Spain in 1941.

questions.question: A Spanish saying claims that rain in May is worth gold for one crop. Which crop?
hints: It's a cereal.
Its flour makes something you eat every day.
The saying goes: «Agua de mayo, pan para todo el año» (“May rain, bread for the whole year”).
questions.description: A weather forecast that farmers have been repeating for centuries, but only in spring.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, to arrive «como agua de mayo» (“like May rain”) means to show up just when you were needed most.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this forest in the mountains north of Madrid is a World Heritage Site. What trees grow in it?
hints: It's one of the southernmost forests of its kind in Europe.
Its bark is smooth and gray, and in fall its leaves turn copper.
It's the famous Hayedo de Montejo.
questions.description: A Madrid forest that went looking for the north, got lost and decided to stay.
questions.fun_fact: The Hayedo de Montejo survives this far south thanks to the cool, damp air of the Jarama River valley.

questions.question: In Jaén it forms a true “sea”, and Spain grows more of its fruit than any other country. Which tree is the most grown in Spain?
hints: It's a tree with a twisted trunk that lives for hundreds of years.
Its fruit is eaten seasoned or pressed.
Its fruit gives us “liquid gold”.
questions.description: The Spanish countryside has a favorite, and it isn't Grandpa's tractor.
questions.fun_fact: Spain is thought to have more than 300 million olive trees.

questions.question: It runs across Andalusia to Alicante, pops up again in the Balearic Islands and holds the Iberian Peninsula's highest peak, Mulhacén. Which mountain range is it?
hints: It's in the south and southeast of Spain.
It includes the Sierra Nevada.
Its name comes from the Roman province whose main river was the Baetis, now called the Guadalquivir.
questions.description: Mountains so long that the Vuelta would need several stages to get across them.
questions.fun_fact: Mulhacén is 3,479 m (11,414 ft) high and is named after a Nasrid king of Granada.

questions.question: I'm a wild shrub with needle-thin leaves, bluish flowers and a very strong smell. People put me on roasts and chicken. What am I?
hints: I stay green all year, even in winter.
Bees love my flowers.
My Latin name means “dew of the sea.”
questions.description: A plant that smells like Sunday roast at your grandparents' house.
questions.fun_fact: Rosemary flowers make a much-loved honey, especially in eastern Spain.

questions.question: The stoppers in cava bottles are made from the bark of a tree that is very common in Extremadura and Andalusia. Which tree?
hints: Portugal and Spain produce most of this tree's bark in the whole world.
Its bark is thick, soft and spongy.
That bark is what we call cork.
questions.description: A tree that gets undressed every nine years and never complains.
questions.fun_fact: A cork oak can live 200 years or more and have its bark stripped many times during its life.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this tree blooms in the middle of winter, in January and February. Which nut does it give?
hints: It's very typical of Murcia, Andalusia and Majorca.
It's the main ingredient of turrón.
It's used to make marzipan.
questions.description: A tree so impatient it doesn't wait for spring.
questions.fun_fact: If there's a frost when the tree is already in bloom, almost the whole harvest can be lost.

questions.question: On a January morning on Spain's meseta, the grass and cars wake up covered in frost. Where does that ice come from?
questions.answer: From water vapor in the air
wrong_answers: From water rising from the ground
hints: It didn't rain or snow that night.
It usually shows up after very clear, cold, windless nights, on the coldest surfaces.
It's the same thing that fogs up the bathroom mirror, only frozen.
questions.description: Powdered sugar that covers the fields without anyone sprinkling it.
questions.fun_fact: Frost forms just like dew, but when it's so cold that the water turns straight into ice.

questions.question: Look at the photo: fields like this cover Andalusia and Castile in summer. What do people eat from these flowers?
hints: They come from the big center of the flower.
People snack on them in the park and at soccer games.
You crack the shells open with your teeth.
questions.description: Flowers with a stiff neck that end up in half the country's pockets.
questions.fun_fact: Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west; grown ones stay facing east.

questions.question: Spain has 16 national parks, such as Doñana and the Teide. What are they mainly for?
hints: Plants and animals live there that you can't find just anywhere.
Visitors must follow rules, like staying on the paths.
It's all about caring for the forest, the mountains and their critters.
questions.description: A Sunday plan with hiking boots, a sandwich and postcard views.
questions.fun_fact: Spain's first national park was the Montaña de Covadonga, created in 1918.

questions.question: Almanzor Peak is the highest summit of the Sierra de Gredos and of the whole Sistema Central. About how high is it?
hints: It is lower than Mulhacén, the highest peak on the Iberian Peninsula.
Mulhacén is about 3,480 m (11,400 ft) high.
Almanzor is about 900 m (3,000 ft) short of Mulhacén.
questions.description: The roof of central Spain, and you don't need a ladder to see it.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the peak is named after Almanzor, the Al-Andalus military leader, who is said to have camped at its foot.

questions.question: You're in northern Mallorca, by the Bay of Alcúdia, watching birds among reeds and canals. Which natural park are you in?
hints: It is the largest wetland in the Balearic Islands.
Its name has the same origin as a famous lake near Valencia.
It comes from Arabic and means “the lagoon”.
questions.description: A place where herons get sea views and nobody charges them for a beach umbrella.
questions.fun_fact: In 1988, S'Albufera became the first natural park in the Balearic Islands.

questions.question: This dark-water lake, surrounded by pine forests and rock walls, lies at the foot of the Picos de Urbión. Which province is it in?
hints: A glacier formed it thousands of years ago.
Antonio Machado tells its story in his poem «La tierra de Alvargonzález».
It's in the same province as Numancia.
questions.description: A lake so dark that even the legends take a flashlight when they go for a swim.
questions.fun_fact: The Duero River rises very close to the Picos de Urbión.

questions.question: In the fall, the brown bear of the Cantabrian Mountains eats tons of acorns and chestnuts, gets fat and looks for a cave. Why?
questions.answer: To sleep through much of the winter
hints: After fall comes the coldest season.
In winter there’s hardly any food in the mountains.
The fat helps it go without eating while it rests.
questions.description: A furry neighbor from Asturias who treats the fall like an all-you-can-eat buffet.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1990s there were fewer than 100 bears left in the Cantabrian Mountains; today there are several hundred.

questions.question: The Sil Canyon separates Lugo and Ourense, and its slopes have terraced vineyards. The area is called Ribeira Sacra. Why “Sacra” (sacred)?
hints: Think of the Middle Ages.
The area has one of the largest concentrations of Romanesque churches in Europe.
Santo Estevo de Ribas de Sil and Santa Cristina de Ribas de Sil are two famous examples.
questions.description: A canyon so steep that the grape harvest is almost a rock-climbing trip.
questions.fun_fact: Growing grapes on such steep slopes is called “heroic viticulture.”

questions.question: It’s a protected area of hills or coast, each Spanish region looks after it, and it can have villages and flocks inside. What is it?
hints: The animals roam free, not in cages.
You go there to walk on mountain trails.
Its name has the word “nature” almost whole inside it.
questions.description: A park with no swings or slides, but with real wild boars.
questions.fun_fact: The Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas natural park in Jaén is the largest protected area in Spain.

questions.question: You walk into the visitor center of a national park. What will you NOT find there?
hints: It's where they explain the park before you explore it.
It's like a small museum that shows you what the park is like.
To see animals locked up, you'd have to go to a zoo.
questions.description: The first stop before you get lost in the hills, with a map and no phone signal.
questions.fun_fact: Many visitor centers in Spain's national parks are free to enter.

questions.question: This is the largest palm grove in Europe, a World Heritage Site since 2000. Which city is it in?
hints: Its palm trees and irrigation channels date back to the days of al-Andalus.
It's in the province of Alicante.
It's the city where a famous Iberian stone bust of a lady was found.
questions.description: A forest with so many palm trees it looks like someone brought the desert home from vacation.
questions.fun_fact: In the Huerto del Cura lives the Imperial Palm, which has seven arms growing out of a single trunk.

questions.question: This noodle soup is made with the broth from a cocido. Which city gives its name to Spain's most famous cocido?
hints: It is served in three “vuelcos”: first the soup, then the chickpeas and vegetables, and finally the meats.
It is a city in the center of the peninsula.
It is the capital of Spain.
questions.description: The first round of a meal that lasts longer than a movie.
questions.fun_fact: With cocido madrileño, the courses are called “vuelcos” (tip-overs), because the pot gets tipped out three times.

questions.question: For patatas a la riojana, the potatoes are “cracked” instead of cut, with pimentón and a sausage that turns the broth red. Which sausage?
hints: It is a pork sausage that can be cooked, not just eaten as it is.
The pimentón in its own meat is what releases the color.
It is the same one that goes into lentil stew.
questions.description: A stew that turns red without saying a single word.
questions.fun_fact: Snapping the potatoes apart with the tip of a knife, instead of slicing them, makes them release starch that thickens the broth.

questions.question: Morcilla de Burgos is black and made with onion, spices and blood. Which animal does the blood come from?
hints: It's the animal behind most cured sausages in Spain.
It's pink and loves rolling in the mud.
It goes “oink”.
questions.description: A Castilian sausage with the darkest personality on the platter.
questions.fun_fact: Morcilla de Burgos has Protected Geographical Indication status and is made with a special onion called horcal.

questions.question: In Galicia, percebes sell for very high prices. What is a percebe?
wrong_answers: A mollusk with a double shell
hints: They are usually eaten boiled, especially at Christmas.
It lives on rocks battered by the waves.
It has a claw-like tip and a stalk you peel to eat it, and it is a distant relative of crabs.
questions.description: It looks like a dragon's finger and costs as if it were one.
questions.fun_fact: The percebeiros of the Costa da Morte pull them off the rocks while the waves crash over them, a very dangerous job.

questions.question: Look at this cold, creamy soup topped with egg and ham. Which region of Spain is it typical of?
hints: It's a very hot part of Spain in summer.
Gazpacho is typical there too.
Its most famous city for this dish is Córdoba.
questions.description: A soup so refreshing it's practically begging for summer.
questions.fun_fact: Salmorejo is made with tomato, bread, olive oil, garlic and salt, and it's much thicker than gazpacho.

questions.question: They're small, round legumes, stewed with chorizo, and the saying goes: “si quieres las comes, y si no, las dejas”. What are they?
hints: They're brown.
People say they're full of iron.
They start with the letter L.
questions.description: The only dish on the menu that comes with its own ultimatum.
questions.fun_fact: Lentils have been grown for more than 9,000 years: they were one of the first plants humans ever domesticated.

questions.question: You're having bread rubbed with tomato, olive oil and salt for breakfast. Which Spanish region is this recipe typical of?
hints: There it has another name, in the region's own language.
It goes perfectly with butifarra.
Its capital is Barcelona.
questions.description: A breakfast so simple it almost makes itself.
questions.fun_fact: In Catalan it's called «pa amb tomàquet», and it even has its own tomato variety just for rubbing: the “tomate de colgar” (hanging tomato).

questions.question: A restaurant menu lists clams “a la marinera”. How are they served?
questions.answer: Stewed in a white wine sauce
hints: It's a classic dish in bars and restaurants on the Spanish coast.
The clams cook in a clay pot until they open.
The sauce has a splash of wine in it.
questions.description: A recipe with a fisherman's soul and a taste of the harbor.
questions.fun_fact: Marinera sauce is often thickened with a little flour or breadcrumbs and topped with chopped parsley.
